text: 01 May 1951 - GALLUP POLL Goulburn Evening Post (NSW : 1940 - 1954), Tuesday 1 May 1951, page 5 GALLUP POLL A Gallup poll prepared in Vic-toria predicted that the Menzies-Fadden Government would be retained in office with a good chance of gaining a Senate majority in Queensland. The poll showed that in 1951 the Liberal-Country Parties would gain 52 per cent. of the votes compared with 50 per cent in 1949 ; Labour 47 (48) ; Indepen-dent 1 per cent (2 per cent).

11 Apr 1954 - PORTRAIT OF A POLLSTER Sunday Mail (Brisbane, Qld. : 1926 - 1954), Sunday 11 April 1954, page 25 PORTRAIT OF A POLLSTER by FRED HVBBARD DOY Morgan, a 45-year-old Australian who's always sticking his neck out, prepared to do so again last week. In Melbourne he and his staff of six sifted and tabulated \ reports from 200 part-time employees of Australian Public Opinion Polls. Then, as he does several times a year, Director Morgan* got ready to tell the nation, through its leading newspapers, how Australians currently feel about their political parties. Most readers would , treat his report — and successive ones in the next, few weeks — as reliable political barometers, and especially interesting at this time. . So, too, would most of the country's politicians. For there's an elec- . tion on May 29, and Roy Morgan has sucr cessfuUy tipped the *ot- *-. comes of the last -four Federal elections, *nd , . three of the last four national referendums. Moreover, he has also achieved a remarkable degree of accuracy in forecasting the actual voting percentages. Better system Morgan tipped the 1943 election experimentally, and just came out on the right side. He then developed a better system, which is still in use. Before the 1946 Federal ejection he announced that the Labour Party would win 54 per cent of the vote. It won 53.1 per cent. Tipping - a Liberal-CP victory in 1949, he came within 3. per cent of hitting the nail right on the head. In a 1051 forecast on that year's forced elections he was only 1.5 per cent out on the actual voting outcome. ', Last year many a voter and politipal pundit thought Morgan had gone haywire wnaHhe predic- . ted a naiTow'Oovernment victory in the Senate election. , ???,?? There was, you remem-' ber, a big nationwide swing to the Labour Party. But the Government won— by a narrow margin — and Australian Public Opinion Polls' prestige went a notch higher. What's the secret of his success? Well, Morgan is understandably anxious to guard a trade secret, so he won't go into detail about his system. 'I follow American Dr. George Gallup's system in general,' he says, 'but have added several refinements.' The only variation Morgan will talk about — and then only briefly —is that he has developed a new method of calculating economic cross-sections, based on . political affiliation. One of the most remarkable features of Roy Morgan's- ''Gallupwithvariations' system is the small opinion sample it takes. Although there are more than SWOjOOO Australian voters, /te interviews 'between only lwo and 2000 of theni. ?? . /,, Voting switch Most .errors, anyway,' says Morgan, are caused by 'changes in voting intention in the week between our final survey and voting day.' It was one of these last-minute vote* switches that lef-i him out' on a Umb in tne 1951 referendum on the question of banning the Communist Party. But the outcome was' so close (the votes of 50,000 people ? decided It) that nobody really held the erroneous forecast against the pollster. Roy Morgan himself is a dapper man who sports a moustache, wears thick-rimmed glasses, -and -is partial to bowties. Until 1940 he was a ? chartered accountant and -newspaper finance writers Then. : six Australian newspapers financed his, trip to the United States to study' the American Gallup Poll system. Every- lour ; years, at the invitation of Dr. Gauupr^h.6 also ? provides the dollars^Morean goes to the United States to assist Gallup in predicting, the Presidential elections.

29 Aug 1954 - PRE-ELECTION POLL Sunday Mail (Brisbane, Qld. : 1926 - 1954), Sunday 29 August 1954, page 4 PRE-ELECTION POLL Democrat swing in America From Our Own Staff NEW YORK, Sat — A Gallup poll shows that the United States election campaign has opened with the Democrats ahead.Only Only 20 per cent of the voters in the soutnern States favour the Republicans in the forthcoming poll for Congress. Outside the South, the parties are running neck and neck with 51 per cent favouring the Republicans and 49 the Democrats. This is interpreted by Dr. Gallup as giving the Democrats a lead, for they have only to win about one-third of the seats outside the South to gain control of the I House.

31 Oct 1954 - REPUBLICANS LOSE GROUND IN U.S. DESPITE IKE Sunday Mail (Brisbane, Qld. : 1926 - 1954), Sunday 31 October 1954, page 4 REPUBLICANS LOSE GROUND IN U.S. DESPITE IKE —Poll Tuesday FROM OUR OWN STAFF AND A.A.P. NEW YORK, Sat.— As President Eisenhower made a whirlwind 1400-mile tour to win votes this week, the latest Gallup Poll found the Republican's had lost further ground in the United State's Congressional election campaign. The President ended his four-State tour yesterday and said Republicans were confident of victory next Tuesday. But the same day the poll revealed there ha,d been a shift away from his party in nearly all the major voting groups.Only Only one final poll remains to be published. Fieures issued yesterday show that- only 46 per cent, of the men favour the Republicans, compared with 53 per cent, in 1952. Fifty-one per cent, of the women are on their side as compared with 58 p.c, two years ago. Workers The Republicans have lost heavily with the manual workers, only 36 per cent, of whom support them compared with 45 in 1952. In bis campaign, Mr. Eisenhower stood on his Administration's record and promised ' 'growing prosperity.' He said unemployment was still a major problem, but his administration was solving it without providing jobs 'through spilling the blood of our sons in the battlefields.' Meanwhile, the Democrat leader (Mr. Adlai Stevenson) is denouncing the VicePresident (Mr. Nixon) for leading what he called 'a frenzied outburst of smut, smear, and slander.' 'Close ranks'! Senator Joseph McCarthy, who has frequently been at loggerheads with President Eisenhower and his fellow Republican Senators, yesterday called on all Republicans to 'close ranks' behind the drive to return a Republican-controlled Congress.Apart Apart from this lastminute endorsement of the Republican ticket — which it is difficult for any prominent Senator to avoid — McCarthy has been remarkably silent throughout the campaign. But in terms of long-term strategy, said a Reuter correspondent in Washington, the recent 'silences of Senator McCarthy' have been more eloquent than those former outbursts against 'Communism in the Govern- 1 ment.'~

14 Jan 1972 - Men, women differ on recognition Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 14 January 1972, page 4 Men, women differ on recognition Six out of 10 men interviewed in a Gallup ? Poll said Australia should recognise the Peking Government soon, but women interviewed were uncertain about it. The question put to 1,236 men and J ,072 women in six States was: "In your opinion, when should Australia recognise the Peking Government as the Government of China? Soon? Not for some time? Never?". Usually, the Gallup Poll finds most men and women agree, but on China they disagree. Of the men, 61 per cent said Australia should recognise Peking soon, and 11 per cent said later. Only 11 per cent of the men opposed recognition, and 17 per cent were unde cided. Of the wo men, however, only 33 per cent said Australia should recognise Peking soon. Another 13 per cent said later, while 12 per cent opposed it and 42 per cent were undecided. Those for prompt recognition usually said, 'The sooner the better", "We trade with them" or "We can't ignore so many millions of people". Those against recognising Peking usually said they were against com munism. Of men and women who were ALP voters, 52 per cent would recognise Peking soon and another 10 per cent later. Of Liberal-Country Parly voters 46 per cent would recognise soon and 17 per cent later. DLP voters answered similarly. The same 2.308 people were asked: "If Australia docs recognise the Peking Government as (he Government of China, should the prcsenl Government of Taiwan still be recognised or not?" Continued recognition was favoured by 55 per ccnt. comprising 69 per ccnt of DLP voters, 65 per cent of L-CP voters and 52 per cent of ALP voters. They said, "It's a separate country", "We must not desert them". Only 13 per cent said we should cease to recognise the present Government of Taiwan. The other 32 per ccnt were undecided. (e) Boy Morgan and Australian Public Opinion Potts

17 Jan 1972 - Moderate 'yes' for Sunday drinks Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 17 January 1972, page 6 Moderate 'yes' for Sunday drinks In most States the public is inclined to approve Canberra's new law for liquor on Sundays but no State has a substantial majority for it the Gallup Poll says. Each of the 2,300 men and women interviewed throughout Australia was told that in Canberra an Sundays hotels could now open from 11.30am to 6.30pm; also that restaurants could serve liquor with meals on Sunday I'roni midday until llpm. Asked whether they would favour or oppose that. 49 per cent said they favoured it, while 41 per cent opposed it. The other 10 per cent were undecided. This small vote of 5 to 4 for having Canberra's law for liquor on Sunday was found in four States: NSW. WA, Queensland and Tasmania. In no State, however, did the favourable vote exceed 52 per cent. Majority favour law In both Victoria and SA, people were almost evenly divided about it. Analysis of Australiawide answers shows that 51 per ccnt of ALP voters favour the Canberra law. Liberal-CP voters answered: favour it 49 per cent, oppose it 41 per ccnt, undecided 10 per ccnt. Of younger people aged 16-29, 58 per cent favouv Canberra's law, compared with 50 per cent of those aged 30-49, 40 per ccnt of those 50-69, and only 28 per cent of those over 70. Usual reasons for favouring liquor on. Sundays were "People should be able to drink at any time" or "Same as the clubs". Those opposed usually said, "Si.v days a week is enough" or "I oppose drinking". (C) by Roy Morgan and Australian Public Opinion Polls.

21 Jan 1972 - 80pc for parties' Cabinet choice Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 21 January 1972, page 6 80pc for parties' Cabinet choice Cabinet Ministers should be selected by a ballot of all members of the ruling party in Parliament, eight out of 10 people said in the latest Gallup Poll. In this Australia-wide survey, 2,300 people were told that some political parties, when they were the Government,. let their leader, the Prime Minister, select the Cabinet Ministers. Other parties, however, decided by ballots who would be Cabinet Ministers. Asked which they favoured, 80 per cent said Cabinet Ministers should be selected by all members of the major party in Parliament. Only 13 per ccnt said the Cabinet should be selected by the Prime Minister alone. The other 7 per cent were undecided. This vote of 80 per cent for selection of Ministers by the party came from 87 per cent of ALP voters, 76 per ccnt of Liberal-CP voters and 75 per cent of DLP voters. Many of those who favour it said "no one should have all the say" or "cuts out favouritism". On the other hand, those who think the Prime Minister should select his Cabinet said "he knows his men" or "he's the captain and should pick his team".
