29 Feb 1972 - Mr McMahon and the delayed detente Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 29 February 1972, page 2 Mr McMahon and the delayed detente POLITICS by DAVID SOLOMON A BAD Gallup Poll result, a confronta-tion with the DLP over the amalgamation of four metal trades unions, a possible cen-sure motion on the Pea-cock invitation to visit China, continuing criti-cism over its refusal to consider taking any ac-tion on prices: it is not likely to be much of a week for the Govern- ment. For Mr McMahon, probably the worst aspect of each of these current problems is that his own supporters and Minis-ters are divided. He cannot go confidently into the House with only the Opposition to worry about; he must take ac-count of the dissension within the Government's ranks. The dramatic fall-off in support for the Government in the past lew months has given weight to those in the Liberal Party who have been complaining that Mr Mc-Mahon will not be able to lead the coalition to victory. MPs in marginal seats before could complain that no one should rock the boat: now they are beginning to believe that the worst thing for their own per-sonal prospects is inaction. Tonight, Mr McMahon has to face a specially called Government parties' meeting to deal with a group of Lib-eral and Country Party MPs who want the Government to act to stop the metal trades unions amalgamation. There is no doubt that Mr McMahon has the numbers on this, and the best of the argument too. The unions involved have been scrupulous in their en-deavours to keep to the law, and to prevent the amalgama-tion the Government would now have to introduce a retrospective law. At the same time the DLP's campaign against the amalgamations has come to a point where there is a real threat to the Govern-ment's proposed legislation on changes to the arbitration sys-tem. And of course, there are many MPs in marginal seats who do not want to upset the DLP, for fear of losing their preferences and consequently their seats. THE question of price con- trol presents problems both to Mr McMahon and his opposite number, Mr Whitlam. In the Government ranks only Mr Wentworth, the Minister for Social Services, has come out publicly in favour of some form of price control, while the former Minister for Labour and National Service, and now Treasurer, Mr Sned-den, has promoted the idea of a prices justification tribunal. Alter a week of resistance to the idea that there should be any interference in the "commercial" decisions of BHP, the Prime Minister last week tried to claim credit for some kind of attempt, by him-self, to persuade BHP not to increase its prices. His failure to produce the whole of the letter he wrote to BHP has not helped his cause, nor the rev-elation that at the time he wrote it he did not know any details of BHP's proposed price rises. The defence of BHP's decis-ion by the Country Party lead-ers, Mr Anthony and Mr Sinclair, also has come to appear a little misplaced in view of the results of an official survey of opinion of Country Party branches throughout Australia. An overwhelming major-ity in every State favoured the combined control of wages and prices as the Government's best prospect of curing infla-tion. It has taken Government members a long time to realise that there is a widespread public belief that both prices and wages need to be con-trolled, and that actions merely to control wages are not looked on entirely sympatheti-cally. (Meanwhile the Labor Party Leader, Mr Whit-lam, while taking a fairly conservative attitude on the practicability of price control, and its political dangers, has been left behind his party's drive for prices legislation. He will have to face attempts by the Caucus to bring him into line this week. Mr Whitlam has been disinclined to take advantage of the High Court's decision in the concrete pipes case, which appeared to give the Commonwealth an open-ing to bring in some form of price control. He has not wanted the court to have any opportunity of disturbing any action a Labor Government might take, but the result has been a program for price con-trol less ambitious than the Minister for Social Services suggested before he was sil-enced by the Prime Minister.) Yet the main focus of atten-tion when Parliament resumes will be on China, and it is here that the Government is most exposed to attack. The trouble arose out of an answer given by Mr McMahon to the House of Representa-tives on Thursday. It was an ill-judged answer, unnecessar-ily long, and in places mislead-ing. When it was first exposed to criticism, Mr McMahon would have been better advised to get up in the House on Thursday night and correct his answer, a perfectly proper procedure. But instead his defence of his original off-the-cuff reply has brought his Foreign Minister into the con-troversy, and compromised his former Army Minister, now Minister for External Territories, Mr Peacock. MR Peacock simply would not accept a proposal by the Prime Minister that he (Mr Peacock) put out a state-ment supporting the Prime Minister's stand on the issue, mainly because Mr Peacock had never been in a position to know for himself whether what the Prime Minister said was correct. Mr McMahon's statement to the House has come under a series of attacks. He said, "... initially they thought it would be wise, providing the Minister (Mr Peacock) gave up his portfolio, that he should be invited to go on what shall be called not so much a goodwill mission but a mission on which he could enjoy himself and enjoy the comforts and delights of Peking". On Thursday night the men who had acted as intermedi-aries between the Australian and Chinese Governments, Melbourne businessmen James and Brian Kibel, both denied that they had put to the Aus-tralian Government any sug-gestion that Mr Peacock would have to resign as Min-ister for the Army. Mr McMahon finally said, "When it was pointed out that it would require a ministerial resignation from the portfolio and that we had troops in Vietnam this non-official source promptly dropped the idea and never raised it again". This too has now been denied by Mr Brian Kibel. He said yesterday that his brother had never been given a reason for the Government's decision not to approve the visit by Mr Peacock and indeed, he thought it quite proper that Mr McMahon should have not told his intermediaries. One of the difficulties in understanding Mr McMahon's answer has been to work out who he meant the various times he used the word "they". Mr Bowen, on This Day To-night, asserted that in the last sentence of Mr McMahon's quoted above, "What the PM clearly indicated in his answer . . . is that he told Mr Kibel that it involved resignation". If Mr Bowen's interpretation is correct, then according to Mr Brian Kibel. the Prime Minister's statement is incorrect. It has become apparent from what the Kibel brothers have said that Mr Peacock's pro-posed "private" visit would have been semi-official. Appar-ently the Government was aware that Mr Peacock, as well as taking his wife, would probably be allowed to take a press group, and official advis- ers. It would have been less "private" than Mr Whitlam's visit to China. He, after all, was not invited by the Gov-ernment of China but by a semi-official foreign affairs institute. And Mr Whitlam asked for his invitation; the Chinese were proposing that Mr Peacock should visit them. WHILE much attention has focused on whether a Minister for the Army could visit China while we had troops in Vietnam (no one seemed to worry that President Nixon was in fact in a some what more powerful position vis-a-vis US troops in Vietnam when he went to Peking) it is probable that one of the more important concerns of those senior Ministers who decided to reject the China visit (not the whole Cabinet) was not that no Minister should go, but that some other Minister should go. It would be natural that both Mr Bowen, as Foreign Affairs Minister, and Mr Anthony, as Minister for Trade, would prefer that they, rather than Mr Peacock, should make the first ministerial contact with China. Mr Peacock's only qualification was that he was well known to, and trusted by, the Kibels. Following the success of Mr Nixon's visit to China, the Government seems almost obliged to make some effort to send a Minister and/or a trade mission to China to try to prove that it is not out of touch with world trends, and to try to prove to farmers that it is making real efforts to renew the wheat trade with China. If it does so, it now seems highly unlikely that Mr Peacock will be chosen (even though he is no longer Min-ister for the Army), and the nod will go to one of those who stopped him.

10 Jan 1988 - Vultures and abandoned animals and John Pilger Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 10 January 1988, page 2 I Vultures and abandoned animals and John Pilger S-UA/D-AV REFLECTIONS The week in review Vultures and abandoned animals and John Pilger THOSE Canberrans who leave their pets to starve while they go on holiday were set a won-derful moral example by a Mr Lind-bergh, 67, of some God-forsaken village west of Johannesburg who fed himself to his vultures. Mr Lindbergh, having decided to leave this mortal coil, was considerate enough to think of what would be- come of his vultures and so treated them to a farewell banquet, strip-ping himself naked and shooting himself dead under their tree. His clean bones were found some days later. • A MORGAN Gallup Poll showed that 32 per cent of people would like Mr Andrew Peacock, the Barry Manilow of Australian politics, to be the Leader of the Liberal Party and that only 22 per cent wanted the hapless and accident-prone Mr Howard to retain that position. The same poll showed that among Lib-eral voters Mr Howard's popularity had fallen, since the last poll, from 41 per cent to 24 per cent. Other polls, done by universities, showed that people think that Mr Howard is more sincere than Mr Hawke but that they do not think that his rela-tive sincerity makes him worth ac-tually voting for. In a speech to a conference of Young Liberals, in-sinuated, live, into 3250 hotels and clubs by Sky Channel to curdle the beer of the working classes, Mr Howard laughed through the pain of his mediocre ratings to champion "excellence" and to praise the quali-ties of Mrs Margaret Thatcher, none of which, alas, he shares. • IT MAY have consoled Mr Howard to learn that he was not the most accident-prone man in the world, a title which seems to belong to Mr Bob Renphrey of Wales. Al-ways accident-prone (he has been in sundry car crashes, has been knock-ed down by sundry vehicles, fallen in rivers, walked through glass doors, etc) Mr Renphrey has al-ready broken his wrist this year while trying (unsuccessfully) to stop his car from rolling down a hill and into a stone wall. He was treated, one imagines, at the same hospital at which his wife Betty received the stitches to a wound to her face sus-tained when Mr Renphrey threw a stick for their dog. The dog may or may not have picked the stick up (the report did not say) but could only have done so after it struck Betty a glancing blow. • THE aforementioned Gallup Poll showed that even the Prime Minis- ter's popularity had fallen from 63 per cent to 55 per cent among the masses at large and from 80 percent to 75 per cent among ALP voters but help may be at hand for Mr Hawke in the inevitable and saga-cious public reaction to an anti-Hawke diatribe to be seen in Aus-tralia in May in a three-part televi-sion series made by the unspeakable but very, very caring and concerned John Pilger. Word came from Eng-land, where this series plump with Pilgerisms has already been shewn, that the emotional Pilger asks what Mr Hawke has done for the Aborigi-nals and rages that he has done nothing and is a nasty piece of work and not nearly as wonderful a hu-man being as Pilger himself. If shewn at prime time this should do Mr Hawke some of the good that would be done to the Archbishop of Canterbury by a serve from a raving Mullah. • MR PILGER'S opus has been specially prepared for the bicenten-nial year as has an Australia Day concert in Sydney which, it was learned, will now have to go ahead without the participation of Mr Max Gillies, the inspired imperson-ator. His withdrawal seems all the more tragic given that his perfor-mance would have been a useful antidote to the poisonous and dreadful contributions to the con-cert to be made by Rolf Harris and Olivia Newton-John and by Cliff Richard, the celibate crooner, but Mr Gillies withdrew when he found that the concert was to be a Royal Command performance at the royal command of Prince Charles and Princess Diana. Mr Gillies said that he did not see why the British royal family, fine people in their own bai-liwick, had to haunt Australia dur-ing a year in which Australia should be celebrating its multiculturalism rather than its waning associations with the Old Dart. • OUR Rolf Harris and our Oli-via will turn a few stomachs at that concert but in Shanghai as many as 20,000 celestial stomachs were said to be turning already after wide- spread consumption of the raw clams which are considered a deli-cacy at this time of year. Closer to home, in Sydney, fabulously wealthy Australian Chinese were said to be the major victims of a cultured bank robbery, Australia's most profitable, which may have taken place on or around New Year's Day but which was not dis-covered until days later. Eighty safe deposit boxes were rifled and the gendarmerie, while admitting that the true haul would never be known, thought that a sum of $20 million might be involved. • THE macho mountebank, Syl-vester Stallone, was foiled when he attempted to have a meaningless interface with a 16-year-old girl he had met on the set where he is mak-ing yet another of his tasteful, so-cially responsible, movies. Several of the girl's brothers, armed with knives and blunt instruments, in-timidated the bodyguard outside Rambo's room and then went in to the room to deliver their sister from a fate infinitely worse than death. • IN the stimulating Soviet Union the name of Leonid Brezh-nev, given to a city, to a suburb of Moscow suburb and to a public square in Leningrad after his widely mourned death was removed from all three of them as part of an appar-ent process of revising the outmod-ed idea that his leadership had been a boon to the Soviet Union. The current view seems to be that he did for the Soviet economy what a be-lief in a flat earth once did to retard exploration. In Canberra, officials would neither confirm nor deny plans to change the names of sub-urbs once named after brilliant sta-tesmen and wonderful human beings now known to have been fools and swine. • IN unique New Zealand a five-year-old boy, Jamie Morris, discov-ered a rare fly unique to New Zea-land. The giant species, Exsul singularis, had not been seen since 1941. On another island, Australia's Phillip Island, Mr Ed Butler had his driving licence renewed for six years and will be 104 by the time he needs to renew it again. His car, an FJ Holden, will be 41. — IAN WARDEN

30 Jan 1988 - Australian Democrats 'have not moved... the road is being hogged on the right-hand side' Things are different since Don's Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 January 1988, page 15 Australian Democrats 'have not moved ... the road is being hogged on the right-hand side' fllinas are different since Don' Bv ANDREW FRASER BACK in the days whenDonChipp ledthe Australian Democrats, negotiations between the-Australian Labor Party and "Don's party" took on a happy personal note. Mr Chipp claimed Mr Hawke as a close friend, and if there were problems in the Senate over legislation, then Bob would.ask Don around to the Lodge, they'd have a bit of chin-wag about the cricket,-and then a bit of.yrtieeKng and dealing to get the relevant legislation'passed. : There was a lot of back-slapping mateship, and for Chipp, doing the rijght thing by Hawkey was never too much of£ t&iiirria.' Even now, long after he has left Parliament, Mr Chipp stands by his description of Mr Hawke as "the'greatest living Australian".; \ • The Prime Minister has had somewhat different relations with Mr Chipp's successor. In the .18 months since shehasbeen Leader of the Australian. Democrats,Janine Haines has been to see the Prime Minister: bnbe, and then in the rather formalsurroundings bf his office. At the 'time, Mr Hawkc was keen to get the Australia Card legislation passed, as well as the amalgamation between thirABCand theSBS. ' "I told him to stop whinging," Senator Haines ,said. "Hp'd got everything else that he'd wanted because; the Liberals were caving in all around. Why should we give him the remaining two? He got. a bit of a shock —. I don't think anyone has eVer told hiniloslop\vhingirig before." The >' Australian ' Democrats have changed :since the departure of Senatof Chipp. They started off in .1976 asthe.middle-of-the-road party, drawing people who thought the Liberal Party was heartless and the/ALP tbo doctrinaire. But they are a long way from'the middle of the road now, and in a: way ,are- Austra|ia's version of a Green Party, with their emphasis on environmental :and welfare issues, and a party structure that allows for a generous individual responsibility for each spokesperson. Senator Haines said, "Because the Labor Party has abandoned so many of its policies and so much of its commitment to its traditional support group, they now have to be placed very much to the right on that, linear political spectrum. That jiist n\eans that they've leapfrogged us. We've not moved — it's just that the road is being hoggedontheright-habd side." . Probably as significant a departer as Senator Chipp was John Siddons,. the former managing director of Siddons Industries; a man who recognised the primacy of economic debate.in modem politics. He left; .frustrated, because he thought the party was pacing too much attention to the peripheral areas, and'not enough to the central areas of political' debate. He did not go quietly, and sakrthc" party was being taken over by greenies and extremists, arid since his departure the emphasis has beert on welfare and eravironment issuer rather thaneconomic ones. • It was indicative of the way the Democrats were headed that as Mr Siddons stormed out of a party-room meeting for the last time, Senator Norm Sanders, the Democrats' colourful spokesman on the environment and the representative of everything Mr Siddons regretted about the direction of the party, said, "Hey, don't bang your ass on that door." Now he says, "Wc never really got on." Other party members recall that Senator Sanders invariably slept through his former colleague's economic homilies. Senator Sanders is a cheerful anarchist who has no time for party structures, and sees politics solely as a means to an end. While he obviously does not regret the departure of Mr Siddons, he is a lot warmer towards Mr Chipp, but adds that in some respccts the Democrats arc better off without him. "I've always got on well with Chipp — wc went down the Franklin together — but there were certain disadvantages with having him around," he said. "Many of my friends used to say, 'He was Minister for Defence in a Liberal Government; he sent people off to Vietnam; why should we vote for him?' And I'd say, "Look, he's come a long way since those days, he's resigned from all those positions.' If we in the peace and environment movement are trying to convincc people to change their minds, why should we deny Chipp that opportunity? "So Chipp was a liability in that sense, but he was also a great asset — he was a tremendous media person, and a tremendous parliamentarian — and I say that in all senses of he word. He knew a lot about parliamentary tactics, he had excellent parliamentary radar, he knew what was going to happen. "[But] we're a different type of party now — we don't go in for that personal type of wheeling and dealing that Chipp used to do, where he used to go and rap with Hawke, that kind of stuff. But we're more issue-oriented now — what you see is what you get — and it's all there on the floor of the Parliament." The middle-class awareness of the 1960s and 70s — particularly in regard to the environment — was the making of the Democrats. They are the only major political party formed since then, and their argument is that in the past 20 years the Marxist analysis of society as being based on bossies and workers has broken down, and yet this is still what the Liberal Party and the ALP arc based on. Quality-of-Iife issues arc more important, and it is no accident that environmental policy is one of the cornerstones of the Democrats now. As Senator Sanders says, "We're not fighting what's now the rather spurious class-struggle ' wars of the Labor and Liberal Parties, whose 1 roots are there. 1 mean, there's no class struggle i any more — who are the blue-collar workers, '• those guys with the fibreglass runabout, the 1 four-bedroom house, and the three cars? They're 1 not part of the equation any more, and yet that's ] still the basis of the battle between the Labor Party and the Liberal Party." The support the Australian Democrats are 1 picking up now does not come from people who cannot decide between the Liberal and Labor parties, but rather from people disenchanted with the Labor Party. The new corporate image of the ALP, while obviously having a broad popular appeal, also loses it support around the fringes, and it is this support that the Democrats are picking up. This fact is reflected in the Democrats' par Don Chipp is in the background of Janine Haines's Australian Democrats. iamcntary representation, though not their parly structure or membership. The actual party membership of the Democrats is a well-kept secret, party officials saying they just don't keep those sorts of records. But it is not much more than 2000 across Australia, and it is one of the gripes of the major parties that the Democrats have so few members and yet have the balance of power. In Tasmania, Senator Sanders cheerfully admits that the party has about 60 members, and with this base are able to clect a senator. Having a small party means that the splits that bedevil the major parties arc kept to a minimum. But the nine months or so between the departure of Senator Chipp and the last election was one of the most unstable for the Democrats, the activities of the then Senators Vigor and Siddons in particular casting the Democrats as a divided party. Both these men contested the election as members of the Unite Australia Party, a grbup which began as a far-right outfit, and neither came within cooee ofgetting elected. So how arc party-room meetings now? "Oh, blissful," says Senator Haines. "Of course we're not all of the same mind on all things, and we agree to disagree where necessary. But mostly it's not a problem. It's a huge relief." For the first time in their history, the Democrats have a senator from each state, two from South Australia. It is the most stable they have been, and yet, for all this stability, they do not seem to be going anywhere, either. In some ways the last election seems to have put them further into no man's land as a ginger party that stands for a protest vote, and isn't really taken seriously. Senator Haines recognises this, and says that if the party is to have a viable future it needs to get a representative into the Lower House soon. Yet it is a measure of' Ihe Democrats' confidence (or lack of it) that they have just passed up what will probably be their'best chance for a few years of getting someone into the Lower House. The circumstances for running Senator Haines in the coming by-election for the seat of Adelaide were the most favourable possible — there is normally a swing against the Government in by-clcctions. neither the ALP nor the Liberal candidate is particularly prominent, and Senator Haines, who lives just outside the area, is very well known. A recent Morgan Gallup poll in Adelaide found that she was the most popular political leader in Australia, marginally tipping out Mr Hawkc. Among women her credentials were particularly strong, with a 64 per cent approval rating. If the Democrats are ever to gel anyone clcctcd to the Lower House it would be in South Australia, which has a history of favouring small-] liberal groups such as the Democrats. "Unfortunately, it's come too soon for us after the last election." Senator Haines said. "The ccntral issue of the Australia Card is no longer around, and the party just doesn't feel it's appropriate for me to have a go at this stage." So it's confinement to the Senate, where Senator Haines has quite enough on her plate anyway. Relations between the Australian Democrats and the Government and the Opposition are now on a much more formal and proper level than they were under the gregarious Senator Chipp. who was able to appear as something of an elder statesman. In the Senate now, when the Democrats vote with the ALP. the Liberal and National Parties see it as just another shabby deal, but if the Democrats vote with ihcm, it is a principled decision made for the good of Australia. "Oppositions are always less rational than Governments, and it doesn't matter which party is the Opposition and which is the Government," Senator Haines said. "But in the last session, some of their right-wing hoons were getting up and alleging that we were constantly making deals with the Government, which got a bit much. "We had one Opposition spokesman from the Reps who got absolutely hysterical on the phone the other day when he was talking to one of my senior staff. She held the phone out to me and 1 could hear it from the other side of the room. "Now this was all because 1 wouldn't tell him what we were doing on a' particular piece of legislation. If I said we were supporting these elements and not others, he would have got on his high horse about shabby deals between the Government and the Democrats. "This was what happened with the fringe-benefits tax and the capital-gains tax legislation. There were a number of people in the Opposition who agreed with what the Government was doing, but once they found out we were supporting it, they could make themselves out as the good guys trying to keep everyone straight, and oppose it full-blast." When the ALP was in Opposition, it adopted similar tactics. Senator Haines recalls the salestax legislation introduced by the Fraser Government in 1981, which the ALP opposed as being a t;n on the necessities of life. Hut she says it covered nol jusl loud and clothing, but luxury goods such as gold-plated cutlery and mining equipment. Instead of seeking any exemptions (as the Democrats did), the ALP opposed the lot. and said the Democrats were the villains. Outside Parliament, the impact of the Australian Democrats on the political agenda is questionable. The Australia Card issue is a good illustration of the weaknesses of the Democrats today. They consistently opposed it. and in last year's election this opposition was prominent in their advertising. Yet when their NSW senate candidate. Paul McLean, organised an anti-ID card rally at Hyde Park. Sydney, only about a do/en people showed up. Opposition to the card became more widespread after the. election, and the Democrats were in there pushing at the time it finally came to grief. But they failed to make it an issue throughout the election, or even put it firmly on the political agenda. "It's very hard for us to actually get the ball rolling, but if there is another group in the community — and it needn't be a political group — that seems to make the difference," Senator Haines said. "We really have to react to that, to put our point of view as much as we can. and try to drag in a few more areas." In the case of the Australia Card, it seemed to be the Liberal and National Parties' belated push into the area that created the community concern. Senator Haines says the Democrats arc consistently about six months ahead of the political agenda, and in this case she may be right. But the bottom line is that the Democrats really have little power to raise matters. Asked what the Democrats have done for the good of Australia. Senator Haines points to their amendments to the fringe-benefits tax, although they strongly supported the principle, and their opposition to the Australia Card. "We've also made people aware of the disparity between the social-welfare sector and the corporate-welfare sector," she says. "Through our policy speech, we made people aware that negative gearing costs $1.5 billion." Put like that, it doesn't add up to much, and it points to the Democrats biggest problem — that there is a feeling that a vote for them is nothing more than an-effective protest vote. What they have to do is convince the electorate that a vote for them is a constructive vote. One small event a few weeks ago may point the way. The Government announced that S5 million would be made available for the investigation of practical applications of solar research in Australia, a condition that the Australian Democrats made in return for their support for a resources-rent tax. In this case they have achieved more than the simple blocking of legis lation. If the Democrats can make more things like this happen, and, more to the point, portray themselves as the people who make things like this happen, then they may have a long-term future after ail.

10 Feb 1988 - Labor support down Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 10 February 1988, page 3 Labor support down SYDNEY: Support dropped sharply for the NSW Government in January, defying the expected pro-Labor surge at the height of the bicentenary, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The figures, published in today's Bulletin, show the Opposition led by Mr Greiner opening an eight-point lead over the Government - double the gap in the previous month's poll -while Mr Grciner retained a lead over the Premier, Mr Unsworth, in leadership ratings. The poll found Labor had a 40.5 per cent share of the vote against 48.5 per cent to the Liberal-National Coalition, while Mr Unsworth enjoyed 43 per cent approval (down two) against Mr Greiner's 45 (down four).

22 Feb 1988 - 'Back to basics' election set for March 19 in NSW Unsworth names day Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 22 February 1988, page 1 'Back to basics' election set for March 19 in NSW Unsworth names SYDNEY: The NSW Premier, Mr Unsworth. named March 19 as state election day yesterday, setting the scene for a four-week campaign expected to be dominated by the issues of health, education and law and order. The Labor Party enters the campaign trailing by 8 per cent in the latest Morgan Gallup opinion poll, but the Liberal-National coalition needs a swing of almost 6 per cent, or more than 52 per cent of the vote, to win 12 seats for outright victory in the enlarged 109member Legislative Assembly. The ALP will campaign under the slogan "On the Right Track" against the Opposition's "A Change for the Better". The Leader of the Opposition. Mr Greiner. welcomed the announcement of the date with "tremendous enthusiasm and a sensible amount of confidence", though he predicted a closc outcome. The opening exchanges of the campaign turned on economic matters, Mr Unsworth promising to increase spending in his "back to basics" target areas. "We will increase spending in accordance to our budgetary ability and we will continue to increase spending in respect of those issues," he said at a news conference. "What the Opposition is proposing for NSW is a freeze on government expenditure. We make no such commitment. We will continue to provide improvements to the public-hospital system, the education system, to the system of law enforcement." He rejected suggestions that this approach was out ofkilter with the Federal Government's light economic strategy. "I'm not beholden to my federal colleagues," he said. "My mandate is to the people of NSW... and I'm quite satisfied they want to see a continuation of my program of more police on the streets... of more expenditure on the hospital system and more expenditure in the system of education." Mr Greineraccused the Government of attempting to bribe the electorate with undisciplined spending promises which contradicted common sense, the Federal Government and the average citizen, who had learned to cope on lower real wages. "No government of 12 years' duration that sees the need to bribe its way back into the halls of power, as the Labor Party so obviously does, deserves another opportunity,"1 he said. "We won't be entering a Dutch auction which Mr Unsworth is already indulging in and which he quite clearly will continue to do over the four weeks ahead. We believe, and the people of NSW will overwhelmingly believe, ilia! better management means lower costs and better results for all the people in this state." Mr Unsworth, seeking to counter accusations of hardened government arteries, said he had taken office only 19 months ago and that his Cabinet -leaving aside the ministers who will retire on election day - would have an average age of 44, three years less than the "shadow cabinet". He pointed also to the contrast between himself and his predecessor, Mr Neville Wran. "Clearly the main difference is that the days of lifestyle politics are over," he said. "We have to recognise the reality of the economic circumstances we're now in." On the Government's commitment to tougher restrictions on gun ownership, which the coalition opposes, he said, "They don't have the same concern for human life as we do." He painted the Opposition as dilettante politicians - "They think that by just waiting in line, their turn comes" - and said Mr Greincr had lined up a job with a London merchant bank in case he lost the election. Neither leader would comment on their future in the event of losing, each insisting he would win. Precise figures required by the Government and the Opposition to win the election are difficult to judge, because it will be fought on new boundaries after last year's redistribution of electorates. But the parties and leading psephologists are agreed on the key seats, ranging from city and outer metropolitan to country electorates, and including seats held by four ministers - even Labor strategists concede that if the Government retains office it is nevertheless likely to lose at least one minister. Swings of 5 to 6 per cent would unseat two left-wing ministers. Mr Frank Walker (Housing) and Mr Ken Gabb (Mines and Energy) in the southern metropolitan seats of Georges River and Earlwood. Whatever the outcome, the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, and the Leader of Mr Unsworth announces the NSW election at the State Office Block in Sydney yesterday. the federal Opposition. Mr Howard, have hastened to absolve themselves of any blame. Asked on the Nine Network's Sun day program how much responsibility he would accept if the Liberals lost, Mr Howard said, "I won't accept any. Likewise. if we win the NSW election, the credit for that will be overwhelmingly due to Nick Cireiner." Asked on the same program last week how much responsibility he would accept if the ALP lost. Mr Hawke said, "The answer is simple - none." In Adelaide, the federal Leader of the Australian Democrats, Senator Haines, predicted victory for the coalition with her own party grabbing the balance of power in the Upper House. Mr Jack Mundey said after yesterday's announcement that he would lead a team of community-based independents. representing ordinary people. for the Upper House. He said there was evidence the ALP was lining up dummy independents who would direct their preferences to Labor. The Liberals were expected to do the same. Mr Greiner and his wife, Kathryn, at the Liberal Party offices in Woolloomooloo yesterday.

25 Feb 1988 - Unsworth says it will be close on election day Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 25 February 1988, page 3 Unsworth says it will be close on election day SYDNEY: The NSW Premier, Mr Unsworth, continued lo meet the people on the third day of the election campaign yesterday, while the Opposition unveiled yet another policy. The Premier took his grassroots approach to a Danell Lea factory in Sydney's south, two shopping centres and a senior citizen's cen tre. Meanwhile, the Opposition Leader, Mr Greiner, revealed the coalition's policy on education. Mr Unsworth, wearing a hard hat, chatted to workers at the chocolate factory. He brushed off the results of the latest Morgan Gallup opinion poll showing the Government trailing the coalition by lOpcrcent. Mr Unsworth said he was encouraged by pollster Mr Gary Morgan's comment yesterday that while there was a wide gap between the parties now. it would be neck and neck on election day. Meanwhile. Mr Greiner referred to a crisis in confidencc in education standards after 12 years of Labor experimentation and in decision in NSW. Main elements in his policy included testing basic skills in Years 3,6 and 10 to ensure students were equipped with the required skills in literacy and numeracy; introducing new technology high schools to give training in science, computing and technology; and creating new selective high schools to give additional opportunities to all gifted students, particularly those from disadvantaged fami lies. Meanwhile, former Australian Olympic swimming star Dawn Fraser announced yesterday she would stand as an independent candidate in the election. Ms Fraser told John Laws on Radio 2GB that it was "the year of the independents". She will contest the inner city seat of Balmain which has been held by Labor MP Peter Crawford for 10 years.

09 Mar 1988 - Libs poll well Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 9 March 1988, page 3 Libs poll well SYDNEY: The NSW Opposition would have won an election during the state's petrol strike late last month, according to a Morgan Gallup poll in this week's Bulletin magazine. It showed support for Labor down three points from early February to 36.5 per cent and the Liberal-National Party down two points to 47.5 per cent

16 Mar 1988 - COUNTDOWN TO MARCH 19 Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 16 March 1988, page 3 COUNTDOWN TO MARCH 19 Full election coverage on Sunday Poll says ALP is closing gap SYDNEY: The NSW Labor Party has gained ground but still trails the coalition by 6 per cent, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in today's Bulle tin magazine. The ALP has made up 4.5 per cent over the previous survey with most of the swing showing through a loss of support among the independents. The figures showed the coalition leading by 53 per cent to 47 per cent in two-party preferred terms, which would represent a swing of between 8 and 9 per cent since the 1984 election. A spokesman for the NSW Liberal leader, Mr Greiner, said this agreed with the Liberals' own polling conducted in Parramatta on Monday night. This indicated a 9 per cent anti-Labor swing in the marginal seat, enough to sweep the coalition to power in Saturday's state election. But a buoyant Premier, Mr Unsworth, said yesterday he was "satisfied and encouraged" by the latest ANOP polling for the Labor Party, which showed his Govern-' ment would be re-elected with a clear majority of seats. Mr Unsworth said ANOP had recorded a pro-Labor movement which was gathering pace since the launch of his "fair go" package last week. He said the Government's commitments on social justice, the environment and on gun laws also had attracted support. Mr Unsworth had promised on Monday that his Government would provide an extra 1,250 beds in NSW public hospitals and contract with the private sector for orthopaedic services at no cost to Medicare pa tients. However, he said the "rebel" orthopaedic surgeons who had refused to return to public hospitals since the 1984 Medicare dispute would return after the election, because their dispute was politically motivated. Meanwhile, Mr Greiner said that opening hospital beds but not providing the resources to service them was an election ploy. "To pretend you can simply order beds open but not provide the resources to enable those beds to have sick people in them is just a very sick, sick exercise in every sense of the word," Mr Greiner said. The Government rejected the claim and attacked the Opposition for favouring the development of the private health sector as the best method to tackle what Mr Unsworth admitted were problems in the public health system. The Premier has already promised a $63 million increase in recurrent health expenditure; a $600 million capital program to construct 23 hospital buildings and a $200 •• million program to cut waiting times., But the Opposition spokesman on health, Mr Peter Collins, said Labor's real health policy could be seen in the overcrowded public hospitals and waiting lists which they still denied even existed. , Mr Greincr claimed on Monday that Mr Unsworth had botched the figures in his "fair go" election package, miscalculating the cost of abolishing deferred stamp duties by $60 million. However, a spokesman for Mr Unsworth responded yesterday that Mr Greiner had revealed himself as an "economic illiterate" by making the claim.

17 Mar 1988 - COUNTDOWN TO MARCH 19 Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 17 March 1988, page 3 COUNTDOWN TO MARCH 19 Full election coverage on Sunday Premier jokes as he battles on in Sydney suburbs From ANDREW FRASER, in Sydney Neville Wran would never have spent the third-last day before an election campaigning around the inner city, but Barrie Unsworth, fighting to maintain Labor's grip on NSW after 12 years in power, thought it necessary yesterday. Mr Unsworth spent the morning around the beaches on the northern suburbs, launching the Government's program against dune erosion, and meeting the people while walking through the Dee Why shopping centre. Then it was into the ALP headquarters at Sussex Street in central Sydney to launch a book about a former Labor Premier, Billy McKell (later Sir William McKell, Governor-General), a chat with some senior citizens at Surry Hills, and visiting a school in Woolloomooloo before heading back to his office. There might be an election on, but business goes on. While the ALP has held a Tarzanesque grip on the inner city of Sydney in both state and federal elections, it is being challenged this time by a swag of Independents. The most prominent of these are Mr Frank Sartor, a former public servant who fell foul of the NSW Government through his activities on the now defunct Sydney City Council and who is now running for the seat of McKell, and swimming legend Dawn Fraser, who is standing in the seat of Balmain. But if Mr Unsworth was worried by any of this yesterday he didn't show it, and he was clearly buoyed by the release of the Morgan Gallup poll, which showed that his Government has at least a fighting chance of survival on Saturday. The poll, taken last weekend, shows support for the ALP at 41 per cent and support for the Liberal-National coalition at 49 per cent, with 10 per cent going to Independents or the Australian Democrats. While this superficially looks bad for the ALP, a good deal of the preferences of the undeclared group are expected to go to the ALP, meaning that the election will be very close indeed. But when Mr Unsworth arrived at ALP headquarters for the book launching in front of the party faithful, he said he wasn't too worried by what the polls forecast. Chatting with former Prime Minister Gough Whitlam, Mr Unsworth told a story of how Billy McMahon used to ring pollsters up to tell them what results to give. Comrades Whitlam and NSW party secretary Stephen Loosely — a backroom boy who has been in the news almost as much as Mr Unsworth lately — both laughed. It is on occasions like this — when he is in the bosom of the party — that Mr Unsworth looks his best. He is, apart from all else, a party man, and the traditions of the NSW Labor Party, which has an enviable record of electoral success, obviously weigh heavily upon him. "Is Peter Walsh here?", he said, after recalling that the Minister for Financc had said last weekend that every party had a finite electoral appeal. On Tuesday, Mr Unsworth dismissed Senator Walsh, the scourge of the Expenditure Review Committee and the man Canberra public servants regard as the cutter of their precious programs, as "some sort of a wheat farmer from Western Australia who didn't have much of a connection with the ALP", but yesterday he was a man who didn't know anything about ALP history. "I mean, he's ignored the whole tradition that we've built up here in NSW, that we're building up in South Australia with Dunstan and now Bannon, and of course in the Federal Government," he said. Mr Unsworth revealed himself as something of a Labor historian, and even a romantic who sees himself in the long tradition of NSW Labor Premiers. He made much of his union background, and when speaking about McKeN, dwelt heavily on his union background as well. "He unionised the apprentices at Cocka too Island in 1912," said Mr Unsworth in a tone of wistful admiration. "If wc studied his achievements when'in power, we would ensure that we remained in government for a very long time. Look-at what he did. He went to Amcrica and saw tilings there... and as a result, in consultation with Chifley, he recognised that wc had great potential in the Snowy Mountains Scheme, and that was one of his major achievements. "He established a tradition, which has always been good Labor, which is tliat while people are punished when they go to jail, they arc, at the same.timc, rehabilitated, so they can come back to society. [ "That was McKell's viewpoint, that was the vision that he had, and that's the tradition that we continue today, which is in stark contrast to the attitude of our oppo nents. "We will always be in government provided wc follow these sensible, rational policies espoused by Billy McKell." Both in front of the party faithful and later in front of the senior citizens, Mr Unsworth had a simple message — thirigs are pretty good under this Government (and if you don't know about it that's the fault of the Fairfax Press), and just look.at what the Opposition has to offer. t "Greincr's sole pitch is that it's time for a change in NSW, and all of you know thaj a change of government in NSW would be a change for the worse," he told the senior citizens. Mr Unsworth even related in front of his elderly audience to the extent of cracking mother-in-lawjokes. - "We've combined the rail areas of Nqwcastle and Sydney, so that all pensioners can travel on the one ticket, instead ;lof leaping off at Morrisett or Narara,' he said. "I must admit I have a vested intercst:in this," he said. "My mother-in-law lives/in Sydney, she has a daughter in Maitlaod, and if she's up there she's not on my back," he said to much applause.

19 Mar 1988 - Liberals' lead narrowing ins NSW: late poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 19 March 1988, page 1 Liberals' lead; narrowing ins NSW: late poll A last-minute telephone poll has; shown that the Liberal-National Party coalition's lead over Labor has narrowed, going into today's NSW elec tion. However, the coalition lead was still substantial and it appeared that it would win — perhaps with the help of; independents' preference — unless the swing back to the Unsworth Government increased in the last hours before the polling booths opened this morning. The survey, conducted on Thursday night by Roy Morgan Gallup Polls, found that 47 per cent of electors said they would vote Liberal-National Party, down two points from a similar poll conducted last weekend. Forty-two per cent said they would vote Labor, up one point on the previous Morgan poll conducted last weekend, narrowing the gap between the parties from eight points to five. The pollsters said that if the state election had been held on Thursday night, preferences would have decided the result. Distributing second preferences would have given a two-party preferred vote of 52.5 per cent for the coalition (down half a point) and 47.5 per cent for Labor (up half a point), narrowing that gap by one point Eleven per cent said they would vote for the Australian Democrats, or a minor party, or an independent. Only 3 per cent were undecided or did not give a preference. Mr Barrie Unsworth's approval rating as Premier was 42 per cent, down 2 points, while approval for the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Nick Greiner, was down one point to 48 per cent. The results come from a special Morgan Gallup telephone poll of 610 people, usually published weekly in The Bulletin magazine. Asked whether Mr Greiner woold do a better job than Mr Unsworth as Premier, 35 per cent said better, 29 per cent said the same, 27 per cent said worse, and 9 per cent were'undecided.

19 Mar 1988 - Liberals focus on seats in the country Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 19 March 1988, page 2 Liberals focus on seats in the country ALP's opponents looking good only by default Bv ANDREW FRASER IT IS tempting to say that the Australian Labor Party is at the crossroads today, that the future of its various Governments — it began the 1980s in control of one state Government, and at the moment has all but two state Governments, plus the Federal Government — rests on the result of the NSW election and a number of Federal by-elections being held throughout the country. Certainly the ALP is in dire straits at the moment. It may, at best, sneak home in NSW and only the most diehard of its members are not expecting to lose some scats. The Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has emerged from this week in Parliament as some sort of a heavy gambling, mate-style buddy who looks after his friends at the expense of others and, more importantly, is unrepentant about doing so. In Victoria, the Morgan Gallup Poll shows that, for the first time for several years, support for the Liberal-National coalition is higher than for the ALP. But the crunch for the Opposition parties in all this good news is that while they look good by default, it is more a case of the ALP making mistakes than astute politicking by them. Their credentials as an alternative Government have yet to be established, and in this light the NSW election takes on a greater importance for them than it does for the ALP. Not that the ALP would be unaffected by the loss ofNSW. It is very much the jewel in the Labor crown, and the NSW branch tends to regard itself as a model electoral machine. In Sydney at the moment, helping out in the last week of the campaign, are several ALP organisers from interstate, who were invited a few months ago to see a real electoral machine in operation. It is an electoral machine with an impressive record. Until Sir Robert Askin brought the Liberals into power in 1965, the ALP had enjoyed 24 years of unbroken power, and after Askin Neville Wran won in 1976, paving the way for the present Government. It is an electoral machine which places great emphasis on style. Candidates are all told to brush their hair and keep their shoes polished, and the headquarters of the ALP at Sussex Street in central Sydney is full of gleaming young men who look as though they have just stepped out of a stockbroker's office. Significantly, there are few women among them. Involvement in sport, especially rugby league, NSW rivals: the Premier, Mr Unsworth, left, and the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Greiner. and the Roman Catholic religion arc actively encouraged. Discipline is the key to the party's electoral success, and this discipline is imposed through the trade unions. NSW, one of the most industrialised of the states, has long had a huge blue-collar workforce which has been efficiently unionised, and therefore provides a very solid base for the right wing of the ALP to build on. A glance through the list of ALP candidates for this election shows that the unions are still very much at the base of the ALP. Whereas in other states solicitors and schoolteachers tend to make up the bulk of the candidates, in NSW they are generally up-market unionists. Take the candidate for Heathcote, Mr Peter Presdee. He is NSW secretary of the Commonwealth Bank Officers1 Association, has rcfereed rugby league for the Western Suburbs District and the Cronulla Sutherland Junior League, and is a foundation member of the Sutherland Shire Catholic Club. Or the candidate for Kiera, Mr Colin Markham. An electrical fitter, he has been an active member of the Electrical Trades Union for 27 years, and had held several positions in the party. The Premier, Mr Unsworth, a former electrician without any tertiary education, who first joined a union when he was 16, is the epitome of the machine. He is a practising Catholic, and attributes some of his 50-vote majority in the Rockdale by-election (shortly after he became Premier) to his conversion to the St George football club, which flashed a message of welcome to him on its scoreboard a week before the by-election. The strength of the ALP in Sydney is in the western and southern suburbs, but it also has a fair hold on some country areas. In Burrin juck, Mr Terry Sheahan (educated Christian Brothers High School, father of eight) is the second generation of his family to hold the scat; in Albury, Mr Harold Mair took his popularity as Mayor into the state arena to hold what should be a National Party seat for the ALP. At a seminar for ALP candidates last year, the secretary of the NSW branch of the party, Mr Stephen Loosley, said that if the ALP held its country seats it would be safe in Government for a decade. In the 1984 election, while there was a swing to the Liberal Party in Sydney, there was little swing to either the Liberals or the Nationals in the country. The bush seats have been targets of the Liberal Party in this campaign, and its Leader, Mr Greiner, has ventured out of Sydney every couple of days. On Wednesday afternoon, for example, he made a flying trip to Wagga and Albury. He says he would not be surprised if the only seat the ALP held in the country after the election was Broken Hill. "The reason for the general swing last time around was corruption," he said. "People in the country see corruption as something that happens at Kings Cross, and it takes a longer time to get through to them. But this time around the underlying issues are stronger in the country than in the city — health, education and the state of the roads are felt very heavily in country areas. "Things like the Darling Harbour are very strong issues in the country — all people in the country see it as is a diversion from money for the Princes Highway, or whatever, and they're right, to an extent. On top of that you've got the guns decision and the timber decision, which were all attempts to win votes in the city. I don't think that they've won any votes in the city with them and I'm 101 per ccnt ccrtain that they're worth a lot of points to us in any country scat." In the city, one of the more interesting aspects of the election will be the performance of the Independents. There are three in the present NSW Parliament — Ted Mack in North Sydney, Frank Arkill in Wollongong, and John Hatton on the South Coast — but several more are challenging. In McKell, Frank Sartor has run an energetic campaign, mainly concerned about the style of this NSW Government. He was a member of the Sydney City Council, a group which regularly challenged planning decisions of the State Government, and was dismissed for its troubles. That dismissal is a strong issue in central Sydney, especially given the gentrification process which has led to the area being populated largely by educated people who have a well-developed sense of how a government should run. What Mr Sartor is trying to capitalise on is a feeling that the ALP has become too arrogant in its approach to Govern ment. Over at Balmain, Dawn Frascr is trying, on a less intellectual level, to do much the same thing. A study by the Department of Government at Sydney University has put Ms Fraser as the probable winner of the seat of Balmain, but she is adopting the same lackadaisical approach to campaigning as she did to representing Australia, and this will cost her votes. The Gallup Poll this week shows support for the Independents dropping away as the election becomcs closer, most of it being dissipated to the ALP. So while there are three Independents now in the Lower House, there are unlikely to be any more after today, regardless of the fright they have given the major parties. For the ALP generally in NSW, that is the major element of today's election — getting a fright. Even if it wins, and all polls indicate that it will be close, it will at least have received a solid kick from the electorate about not being too arrogant. There are a lot of dire predictions about how, if NSW falls, all the other states will follow, and the election undoubtedly does have Federal implications, but mainly for the Liberal Party rather than the ALP. If the Liberals lose, Mr Greiner could not expect to remain Leader (nor would he probably want to), and John Howard would be in trouble as Federal Leader. But it is a state election only, and it is unlikely that its implications will be felt in Victoria, the next state to go the polls.

23 Mar 1988 - Right meets, Unsworth pulls out Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 23 March 1988, page 1 Right meets, Uns worth pulls out The fallout from Labor's disastrous showing in Saturday's NSW election continued yesterday, with the Premier, Mr Unswortn, announcing he would not seek re-election as Labor's leader. Mr Unsworth's withdrawal was a surprise after his statement that he was "not a quitter" and intended to lead the ALP into the 1992 election. Although Unsworth supporters claimed yesterday that it was a personal decision, the Premier is understood to have been persuaded not to re-contest the leadership after a meeting of NSW Labor Right-wing power brokers at NSW Parliament yesterday. Those attending the meeting included Senator Graham Richardson, the president of the Legislative Council, Mr John "Johnno" Johnson, and Mr John MacBean, who is president of the NSW ALP and secretary of the NSW Trades and Labour Council. Mr Unsworth's withdrawal left the ALP in NSW without any obvious successor to the leadership, although the one-time Minister for Public Works, Mr Laurie Brereton, and the outgoing Minister for Police, Mr George Paciullo, are the present front-runners for the position which will be decided at a meeting of Labor MPs next week. Mr Unsworth's announcement, in which he accepted major responsibility for Labor's defeat, came as the recriminations con tinued from the loss of what has been regarded as the jewel in La bor's crown. In the federal Labor parliamentary caucus meeting yesterday, the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, faced a barrage of questions and criticisms over the setbacks suffered on "Super Saturday" elections in NSW, Western Australia, Victoria and Queensland and agreed he had to take some of the responsibility. However caucus sources said the criticism was general rather than directed explicitly at the Prime Minister. (Report. — Page 17) The Victorian Premier, Mr Cain, said Mr Hawke was going through a rough patch but was still a better leader than Malcolm Fraser. "In these jobs we all make mistakes and I think Bob's the first to recognise that he's made them," Mr Cain said on ABC radio. Mr MacBean continued his onslaught on the newly elected Coalition state Government yesterday, calling the Premierelect, Mr Greiner, a "wimp" and his deputy, Mr Murray, a "red neck". Mr MacBean's attack came despite attempts by the secretary of the ACTU, Mr Simon Crean, to hose down the feud which had erupted over the Coalition's industrial policies. Mr Greiner denied yesterday that the Coalition was trying to provoke industrial turmoil through its proposed legislation and said Mr MacBean's claims were, not genuine because they had been made two days after the election — not during the campaign. The unions are particularly concerned about Mr Murray's promise to introduce a Freedom of Association Bill which would end compulsory unionism. Mr Crean attempted to defuse the dispute, saying a war between the trade-union movement and the Coalition would depend upon the attitude the Government chose to adopt. Against the background of the fallout from the NSW election, the Morgan Gallup Poll to be published in today's Bulletin magazine shows a slight increase in support for the Hawke Govern ment. It found ALP support increased 2 per cent, from 41 per cent to 43 per cent in February, and support for the Liberal-National Party coalition fell three percentage points — from 39 per cent to 36 per cent. Mr Brereton, the former highflier who fell out with Mr Unsworth and resigned from the Cabinet in November, was expected by his colleagues to run for leadership of the ALP — but declined to comment. Mr Paciullo said Mr Unsworth had telephoned him yesterday morning and had urged him to run.

30 Mar 1988 - Keating leads poll for next PM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 30 March 1988, page 3 Keating leads poll for next PM SYDNEY: The Federal Treasurer, Mr Keating, has been named in a Morgan Gallup poll as the most popular candidate to succeed the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke. It is the first time Mr Keating has been given the nod of approval by voters ahead of the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Mr Hayden, the man usurped from the ALP leadership shortly before Mr Hawke became Prime Minister. A total of 38 per cent of those polled nominated Mr Keating as the ideal replacement, compared with 35 per ccnt who opted for Mr Hayden, according to the Bulletin magazine. Since the last poll taken in December, Mr Keating's popularity has risen by 8 per cent, while Mr Hayden has dropped by 8 percent More than 900 voters were polled on March 12 and 13. Although Mr Peacock's popularity as a possible Opposition Leader has dropped by 3 per cent since December, at 29 per cent he still beats Mr Howard (24 per cent).

01 Jun 1988 - Near-tie in latest poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 1 June 1988, page 10 Near-tie in latest poll SYDNEY: Only one percentage point separates the Government and the Coalition in the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in today's Bulletin. Of the 2147 electors from all states interviewed between May 14 and May 21, 44 per cent said they would have voted for the present Government, up one point from the April survey, and 45 per cent, , down one point, gave their support to the Coalition. The Liberal Party scored 36 per cent and the Nationals secured 9 per cent. The Democrats' support dropped one point to 8 per cent. An election would have been decided by prefer- . ences had voters gone to the polls in that week. Approval of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, was 1 steady at 78 per cent of ALP voters, with 46 per ! cent of Liberal voters, up 4 points, giving the nod -to the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard.

18 Jun 1988 - Elliott calls in a backroom boy as minder Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 18 June 1988, page 2 Elliott calls in a backroom boy as minder By PETER COSTIGAN BEHIND the least-noticed significant political appointment for a long time lie some of the biggest Australian political questions of 1988. They include whether the next election will be contested by both major parties under the leadership of new faces and whether Australia, let alone the Liberal Party, is ready to be led by a businessman for only the second time since Federation. Alister Drysdale, the new Elders-IXL manager for corporate affairs and political minder for its boss John Elliott, has had one of the most fascinating careers of any of the political backroom boys of the past 20 years. That background inspired Mr Elliott to entice him back to the shadowy world of political minding after a threeyear break. With the exception only of the Liberals' federal director, Tony E^gleton, who has advised every Liberal leader since Harold Holt, no minder has seen more of the inner workings and personal rivalries of the Liberal Party than Mr Drysdale. Very few knew it at the time, especially not the then Liberal Leader, Billy Snedden, but it was Mr Drysdale who was probably the key adviser to Malcolm Fraser in late 1974 and early 1975 when he tried, and finally succeeded in wrenching the party leadership from Mr (later Sir Billy) Sned den. Then working for the littleknown but quite successful Melbourne public-relations consultancy Royce PR, Mr Drysdale was assigned to teach Mr Fraser the techniques of handling the media, especially radio ana television, and to keep his ear close to the Liberal Party as Mr Fraser prepared his challenge. After Mr Fraser became Prime Minister, he called Mr Drysdale back to the political minding game. Through most of Mr Fraser's three terms, nobody apart from his wife was more often and more consistently his sounding board. During his term as Liberal Leader, Andrew Peacock also turned to Mr Drysdale for help. It is noteworthy that Mr Drysdale was frequently the man between Mr Peacock and the then party president, John Valder, when Mr Peacock was convinced that Mr Valder was leading the Sydney push to replace him with Mr Howard. With that background, it would be ludicrous to accept that Mr Drysdale's job is simply to devise smart PR campaigns for Fosters, even Kix. Indeed, Mr Elliott himself describes the job as one where the corporate-affairs manager will be keeping him in touch with political goings-on in Australia "every second week when I'm somewhere overseas". There being no vacant House of Representatives seat at present, Mr Elliott is not about to challenge for Mr Howard's job. Nor is there an overt push to replace Mr Howard — only a dull mood of disappointment throughout the Liberal Party that he has been unable, at least in the public's perception, to transform his own political promise and the mistakes of the Hawke Government into dynamic leadership of the Coali tion. His critics in the party acknowledge the problems he has faced; National Party turmoil, Labor's ruthlessly sophisticated campaign which gave it victory last year with a minority of votes, and lack of depth on the Coalition front benches. But even his most loyal sup Alister Drysdale: fascinating career. porters cannot ignore the public perception of him as an ineffectual leader, a perception reflected in the latest Morgan Gallup poll which gave him an approval rating of only 33 per cent, 17 points behind Mr Iiawke and 18 behind Paul Keating. Worse, since voters more easily say "no" to approval questions than actively declare disapproval of a politician, a massive S3 per cent disapproved of him. Mr Howard's blunt rejection of the idea of some form of treaty with Aborigines and pledge to tear it up as Prime Minister illustrated his problems with leadership. His view is probably silently shared by most nonAboriginal Australians and by many Aborigines. But he was unable to stop several members of his own party publicly repudiating his views and it would be no surprise if polls show the public regards his statement as an over-reaction to a document not vet written. As with Bill Hayden over the last two years of his leadership of the Labor Party, a majority of MPs in Mr Howard's party believe he would make a very good Prime Minister. They admire his integrity and intelligence, his grasp of economics, his persistence. But they wonder if enough of the public will ever perceive him as Prime Minister to lead them into pow er. Feeling the same about the only possible parliamentary alternative, they are unlikely to turn again to Andrew Peacock. So they muse about John Dorman Elliott. Those with a sense of history remember the only businessman who was ever Prime Minister of Australia, the later Lord but always lordly Stanley Melbourne Bruce, who led the country from 1923 to 1929 and became the only sitting PM to lose his seat. To the traditional politicians, Mr Elliott is severely handicapped, apart from not even being in Parliament. They fear what Labor's bovver boys would do with his business dealings over the years, his threats to shift Fosters' production overseas, especially in Melbourne, having his name instead of that of one of the team's many playing heroes on the new stand at Carlton's home ground, even his business-world nickname, the Thug. But Mr Elliott now has a political minder, one of the shrewdest. And a list exists of others to recruit, if he decides to make his run. Should Mr Keating maintain his new popularity lead over Bob Hawke or the latter tire of the game, the next big contest could be between Mr Elliott and Mr Keating, the businessman versus Labor's amazing mate of business.

03 Jul 1972 - Polls give parties even chance Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 3 July 1972, page 3 Polls give parties even chance If the results of the latest Gallup Poll were reflected accurately in an election, there would be only one or two seats, either way, between the I.iberalCountrv coalition and the Labor Party. 17 Jul 1972 - Many 'would limit foreign investment' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 17 July 1972, page 7 Many Vould limit foreign investment' Almost nine out of 10 people interviewed by the Gallup Poll in June would place a limit on the number of shares which overseas investors could buy in Australian companies. About two out of three people would limit overseas shareholdings to less than 50% of the shares of an Australian company. This is similar to a result obtained by the Gallup Poll in Oclober, 1968. People interviewed now and in the 1968 poll were asked: "In your opinion, should British, American and other foreign investors be allowed to buy any number of shares in Australian companies, and gain control of them — or should there be a limit?" In the most recent Gallup Poll conducted in June, 2.299 people in all States of Australia were surveyed. Answers obtained in June and in 1968 were: June, Oct, 1972 1968 Limit .. .. 88% 88% No limit .. 6% 8% Undecided . 6% 4% Most people in favour of limiting foreign investors buying shares in Australian companies said, "Keep control in Australia", or, "Keep profits in Australia". Those for no limit said we need overseas money. The 88% for a limit also were asked: "Of the shares in an Australian company, what's the biggest pe-centage you'd allow non-Australians to own?" Seven per cent would allow less than 20%, 20% would allow 20-29%, 11% would allow 30-39%, 25% would allow 40-49%. Those figures give a total of 63% who would limit overseas shareholders to less than 50% of the shares of an Australian company. Only 8% would allow overseas shareholders to own 50% or more of the shares. The other 17% of those who favour a limit could not say what the percentage should be. (C) 1972, Roy Morgan and Australian Public Opinion Polls.

15 Sep 1972 - Daylight saving preferred Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 15 September 1972, page 7 Daylight saving T Daylight saving for at least the four months, November - February, is wanted by about eight out of 10 people in NSW, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania, and by six out of 10 in Western Australia. Indeed, extensions lo the six-month OctobcrMarch might be approved in NSW, Victoria and Tasmania. In Queensland, however, opinion is fairly evenly divided, with 51% opposed to daylight saving for even four months. These are findings of an Australia-wide Gallup Poll last month. People were asked whether they wanted daylight saving again next summer. Of the 2.245 people interviewed throughout the six States, 74% said they wanted daylight saving. They were then asked whether they wanted it for four months to the end of February or for the six months to the end of March. Australia-wide, only 44% said they wanted six months of daylight saving. However, there were favourable votes of 61 To in Tasmania, 50% in NSW and 49% in Victoria. Daylight saving is slightly move popular among men than among women. Younger people are the most favourable to daylight saving. Four months of it, October-February, is wanted by 88% of those aged 16-20 and by 84% of those 21-29, compared with 73% of those aged 30-49, 65% of those 5069, and only 48% of those 70 and over, Six months of daylight saving from October 1 to March 31 is wanted by 62% of those aged 16-20 and by 53% of those 2129, but by only a minority of older people. (c) Roy Morgan and Australian Public Opinion Polls.

30 Sep 1972 - THE WEEK Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 September 1972, page 2 THE IUEEK MBB1/S By DAVID SOLOMON and MICHAEL JACOBS Mr McMahon (Prime Minister). - / asreed as to the date on which (the Prime Miniver oj New Zealand) should hold his election. rT,HE only MPs who arc at all interested in what is happening in Parliament arc the senior Ministers who are using it to reveal and give credence to policy proposals for this year's elections. The Prime Minister, two weeks in a row, has unveiled new schemes, one on urban and regional development, the other on foreign takeovers. The latter is not expected to take legislative form before the elections; legislation to set up the authority which will look after planning of the development schemes was supposed to he introduced this week, but is not yet completed. Backbenchers on both sides and the Opposition leadership are going through the motions of debate, but that is all. There have been few concerted Opposition attacks on the Government, except over the AGLstecl pipe issue, and attacks on Mr McMahon for his handling of the Jetair aircraft purchase in 1971. Mr Whitlam (Opposition Leader), at the Playhouse, opening the election campaign of Mr Endcrby (Lab, ACT). - Nobody knows when the election will be. Three people, it is suggested, have been told. I don't know whether they're here or above. ^HE Government introduced a motion into the Senate on Thursday delaying until October 26 the deadline for Senate Estimates committees to report back to the Senate. This means that the Senate will not complete its consideration of the Budget until that day, or the following day, a Friday. The major Budget Bills will then go back to the House of Representatives before going to the Governor-General for assent. By a strange coincidence, the Government has been planning to bring the House of Representatives sittings to a conclusion on October 26, so the return of the Budget Bills may be the very last event that takes place in the House before the final adjournment is moved. On the notice paper at the moment is a contingent notice of motion from Mr Gorton to bring on the highly divisive Territorial Sea and Continental Shelf Bill, which would certainly involve at (cast two defections from the Government's ranks. This notice comes into effect at the conclusion of the consideration of the two Appropriation Bills. 13 Oct 1972 - Abortion reform Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 13 October 1972, page 2 Abortion reform Sir, - There is no doubt that the 1972 Gallup Poll on abortion was bad news for the pro-abortionist lobby. Dale Dowse (Letters. October 2) ?may have convinced herself of the propriety of omitting this information from her review article. Rut there can be no justification for her quotation from the poll of an isolated figure which gave precisely the opposite impres sion. I repeat that the "estimate'' of 100,000 illegal abortions a year in Australia is a piece of fabricated nonsense, and I invite Dale Dowse to present any evidence she may have to the contrary. It is spccial pleading on her part to allege that the low number reported for maternal deaths from abortion is due to falsification of medical records, especially in view, of the screening process to which those records are subjected. .Her further unsupported assertion that full-term births are "far more risky" than abortions conducted by qualified practitioners is contradicted by documentation of the English experience, which shows the risks to >be equivalent. There is ample evidence that since the first year of implementation of the UK Abortion Act the number of legal abortions a year have increased fourfold, with consequent overcrowding of hospital wards and disaffection among gynaecologists and nursing staff, but without any decrease in the number of illegal abortions (British Medical Journal, May 1970, July 1972). Is that what Dale Dowse wants for this country? A glance at the Gallup Poll in question would have informed D. J. Rose (Letters, October 5) that his examples of uncertainties in the present law have no relevance to my statement on the poll results. Mr Rose will doubtless be relieved to learn that virtually all deaths from "maternal causes" in Australia are medically unpredictable and thus independent of the religions beliefs of doctors. The rhetoric of his peroration presumably requires no comment. J. CLEARY Yarralumla.

26 Oct 1972 - MANY PEOPLE AGAINST PREFERENTIAL VOTING Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 October 1972, page 13 MANY PEOPLE AGAINST PREFERENTIAL VOTING More than half the people voting at the Federal election on December 2 would mark their preferences reluctantly. They would prefer to be voting "first past the post", the Gallup Poll says. In an Australia-wide survey, 2,173 people were handed two examples of ballot papers. One was marked for preferential voting (used in the Federal election) and the other for first past the post (used before 1919). Asked which they favoured, 54% said first past the post, 39% said preferential and 7% were undecided. Of the ALP voters interviewed, 66% favoured first past the post, but 51% of Liberal-Country Party voters favoured the preferential system. DLP voters were fairly evenly divided. The only State where most people favoured pre ferential voting was Tasmania, where proportional representation is used at State elections. Those who favoured first past the post usually said "the biggest group should win" or "preferential is not fair because a minority can get power". Those who favoured preferential voting said "it gives everyone a fair go". (c) Roy Morgan and Australian Public Opinion Polls.

05 Oct 1988 - 'Let Bob keep the job' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 5 October 1988, page 5 'Let Bob keep the job' SYDNEY: Support for the Government and the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has risen in the past month, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in the Bulletin magazine, shows that the Government has recovered the support it lost immediately after the September referendums to rise 2.5 points to 47.5 percent. During the same period support for the Coalition has fallen 2 per cent to 42 per cent. Mr Hawke's personal approval rating has risen 2 per cent to 59 percent. But only If per cent 01 voters approve of the way the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, is handling his job. More than two-thirds of voters — 68 per cent — believe that Mr Hawke makes a better Prime Minister than Mr Howard. Only 20 per cent of voters favoured Mr Howard — a 1 per cent fall since the last poll taken early in September. A little more than 2000 electors were interviewed for the poll, which was conducted on the weekends of September 17 and 24.
