12 Jun 1972 - Majority favour child grant for homes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 12 June 1972, page 7 Majority favour child grant for homes Two in three people favour the proposal of giving child endowment in advance for a deposit on a home or to add rooms, the Gallup Poll finds. In this Australia-wide survey taken in April, 2,316 people were told of a _ suggestion that people with children should be given up to S3.000 of their child endowment in advance, for a deposit on a home or to add rooms. People were then asked whether they favoured or opposed that suggestion. A majority of 65To said they favoured giving child endowment in advance, 25% opposed the sugges- : lion and 10To were undecided. Men and women as separate groups gave similar answers. In homes where there were children 6^^ of people favoured child endowment in advance and 61% of people living in homes without children also favoured the suggestion. 24 Jun 1972 - Military service favoured for all Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 June 1972, page 11 Military service favoured for all GALLUP POLL More than 6 out of 10 people interviewed in a recent Gallup Poll favour compulsory military training for all young men. Those for compulsory military training for all young men were 2 to 1 in favour of six months in preference to three months. In this Australia-wide Gallup Poll 2,391 men and women aged 16 and over were handed a card listing the following alternatives: No military training; only full-time volunteers; all young men to camp for about three months; all young men to camp for about six months; onc-in12 called up for 18 months. People were then asked which one alternative came closest to their ideas about compulsory military training. The following .shows how people ans wered. All young men for six months — 42%. All young men for three months — 21%. Total al! young men — 63%. One-in-12 for 18 months, as now — 11%. Only full-time volunteers — 19%, No military training — 4%. No opinion — 3%. The vote for compulsory training for all young men came from 71% of L-CP voters, 63% of DLP voters and 59% of ALP vot ers. Men and women as separate groups gave similar answers. Answers, however, varied by age groups. Of people 30 years and over 67% favour compulsory training for all young men, as do 59% of those aged 21-29 years. Minors aged 16-20 years answered: All young men for six months — 28%. All young men for three months — 15%. Total for all young men — 43%. One-in-12 for 18 months, as now — 16%. Onlv full-time volunteers — 31%. No military training — 8%. No opinion — 2%. People were also asked their second choice. Eighty-two per cent of all people surveyed mentioned compulsory military training of three or six months for all young men as either their first choice or second choice. Those in favour of compulsory military training for all young men usually said, "Essential for defence of Australia", "Beneficial training"' or "Teaches discipline''. Those in favour of only volunteers doing military training usually said, "Nobody should be forced". (C) R of Morgan and Australian Public Opinion 1'olls.

14 Jul 1988 - IN BRIEF Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 14 July 1988, page 3 IN BRIEF Legal aid for widower SYDNEY: The NSW Premier, Mr Greiner, confirmed last night that legal aid would be granted to the husband of a woman killed in a mudslide at Coledale on the NSW South Coast, but said local residents would not be funded to appear at the inquest. Mrs Jenny Hagan and her two-yearold son, James, were killed in the mudslide in April. A spokesman for Mr Greiner said the dead woman's husband would be given legal aid "without any doubt" and the residents' interests would be adequately canvassed by Mr Hagan's legal repre sentative. Aid to Timor Children and mothers in the Indonesian province of East Timor will benefit from an Australian grant of $654,000 to a UNICEF project, the acting Minister for Foreigri Affairs and Minister for Trade Negotiations, Mr Duffy, announced yesterday. The project emphasised nutrition, endemic-disease control, women's development and education, water supply and sanitation, and food production. Security guard dies MELBOURNE: A 35-year-old security guard died last night after being critically wounded during an armed hold-up outside a Melbourne supermarket on Monday. Police said Mr Dominik Hefti, of Melton South, who was shot twice in the chest as he struggled with a bandit, died in Royal Melbourne hospital at 6.59pm. Mr Hefti was one of two security officers escorting about $35,000 in cash from a Coles New World store in suburban Brunswick to an Armaguard van. The company has offered a $100,000 reward to try to help police track down the bandit who shot Mr Hefti. Setbacks for Ahem BRISBANE: The Queensland Premier, Mr Ahern, battling to win; the South Coast by-election, was hit yesterday by an U-point plunge in approval ratings and by criticism from former Cabinet colleague Mr Russ Hinze, who said he was. a failure as Premier and should stand down. The Morgan Gallup poll in yesterday's Bulletin said Mr Ahern's approval had fallen from 63 to 52 per cent while the National Party's approval had slipped by 5 points.

14 Jul 1988 - People 'insufficiently informed on casino issue' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 14 July 1988, page 9 People 'insufficiently informed on casino issue' Social-impact report on Civic 'ignores evidence' JULY 11-13 19IS THI AUSTRALIA *1 NATIONAL UNIVIRSITY 2JUP bitrnimniil ronfrrrm r on Amiralij n gambling Bv MARK UHLMANN Dr Hcctor Kin loch, Reader in History at the Australian National University and a member of the Committee for a CasinoFree Canberra, strongly attacked yesterday 'the social-impact report on the proposed Civic Square Redevelopment (Section 19). Addressing the Bicentennial Conference on Australian Gambling, at Burgmann College, ANU, organised by the National Association for Gambling Studies, Dr Kinloch said the report was "shockingly deficient in its ignoring of evidence from the field of city planning and urban research". He also said Australians were insufficiently informed that a casino was proposed for their national capital and no attempt was made to obtain opinions from overseas. It was glaringly obvious "that there are no references whatsoever to the history and nature of Canberra" in the report He found it "incomprehensible that a team asked to examine the image of the national capital, and perceptions of that image, ignored the historical actuality of the city . There, was also an absence",of "any adequate discussion of Canberra as the ccntre of national politics; and the implications for the nation of that status of the city [if a casino was established]". - The Roy Morgan public opinion poll, which surveyed the opinions of 500 people in the ACT and a lesser number in each of the state capitals on the casino issue, was "biased and unprofessional" and inadequate. This was because the preamble to the question which was asked involved several value judgments weighted toward acceptance of the redevelopment (The preamble read: "There is a proposal to develop a new cultural centre in Canberra which would include a small casino"). The social-impact study team should have included "specialists in history, political science, economics and a range of experts in the field of urban studies and city planning". Dr Kinloch said the team had done well considering these deficicncics and the lack of time they had been given to complete the report. He placed the blame "squarely on [the minister responsible for the ACT] Mr Punch and on his political and Public Service advisers (pushed by individuals, orga nisations and institutions with vested interests), who put their need for a quick report and snap decisions ahead of any genuine concern to give the team the necessary time and resources to do their work". The chairman of the social-impact study -team, Dr Geoff Caldwell, said that although the team would have liked more time to polish its report, it understood that time limits had to be imposed. . It was unlikely that its conclusions would have changed if more time had been avail able. He was surprised by Dr Kinloch's criticism on the lack of historical research. Dr Kinloch had had two chances at public hearings held by the study team to suggest that historical considerations be given more weight, but he had not done so. The team had seen the preamble to the Morgan poll question as being an accurate description 01 the proposal, but the people in other capital cities who were questioned about the redevelopment "almost didn't understand the question" because it was of "no moment" to them. Most regarded Canberra as a dead, boring city and that anything to improve its nightlife would be a good thing. The team could have advertised the proposed redevelopment more widely across Australia but, apart from letters initiated by Dr Kinloch, "I don't think we got any response outside the ACT" to the advertise ments.

14 Dec 1988 - PM beats Howard in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 14 December 1988, page 2 PM beats Howard in poll SYDNEY: The Federal Government had a solid lead in public support when the Opposition launched its Future Directions manifesto, according to the Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll, taken on December 3 and published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine, had Labor support at 48.5 per cent and the coalition at 43 percent. The Government improved 1.5 points on a fortnight earlier to build a lead that would translate into a comfortable election win. The leader of the Opposition, John Howard, who is counting on the manifesto to revive his fortunes, had an approval rate of 30 per cent (up one point) and a disapproval rating of60 percent. In contrast, approval of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, also rose one point to 59 per cent, with 31 percent disapproval. Some 69 per cent of voters (up one point) thought Mr Hawke would make the better Prime Minister, while just 18 per cent (down one point) preferred Mr Howard.

19 Dec 1988 - NSW could be bankrupted: Greiner Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 19 December 1988, page 5 NSW could be bankrupted: Greiner It is crunch time for State Rail SYDNEY: A consultancy group has been appointed to put in place the specifics for a complete overhaul of the NSW railways, following a report which said State Rail needed a cash injection of $16 billion ovpr 14 years. The NSW Premier, Nick Grcincr, warned it was crunch time for State Kail and that unless drastic measures were taken, the state would be bankrupted by its massive losses. A spokesman for the Minister for Transport, Bruce Baird, said the report by PA Consulting Services listed all options open to the Grciner Government, the worst scenario being to conduct "business as usual". In that case, State Rail's compounding capital debt would reach almost $31 billion in the year 2002, or in other words, $6000 owed by every person in NSW. "It has come to a crunch situation. Something must be done or the state will go broke," the spokesman said. "What we have had is a massive bureaucracy with 15 levels of management, a situation which has festered over many, many years. "This is a reform government now in power, and it intends to take on the task of cleaning up State Rail," he said. The report warned that State Rail Bruce Baird had to reduce its operating costs, at present mostly responsible for a $3 million a day cost to the state's tax payers. It said labour costs comprised 74 per cent and materials 26 per cent of State Rail's operating costs. The SRA's annual report showed a total staff of 36,700. The spokesman said the aim of the Government was to break down the bureaucracy and create two business areas for operations — com muter services, and freight and country passenger services. In addition, he said the Government would continue its policy of getting rid of surplus land (a St Leonards site was recently sold for $15 million and space above St Leonards station leased for 99 years for $67 million). A summary of the PA Consulting Services report was to be issued by Mr Baird this week, and transport consultants Booz, Allen and Hamilton would begin to formulate the ideas for restructuring. The spokesman said rail unions had already been briefed on the report and pointed out, "No-one will have a job if State Rail continues to lose these huge amounts of money." He insisted the task was not an impossible one, and that State Rail chief executive Ross Sayers was confident it could be achieved without having to break the bank simply in order to implement the changes. Meanwhile, Booz, Allen and Hamilton has commissioned pollsters Roy Morgan Research to conduct an extensive survey on Sydney's suburban and inter-city train services. "A new feature of this survey will be the determination of priorities of passengers' preferences and willingness to trade off service attributes such as fares, personal security, travel time, ease of fare collection," the spokesman said.

24 Dec 1988 - X-rated videos win in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 December 1988, page 2 X-rated videos win in poll The majority of ACT adults do not want the sale and hire of X-rated videos banned in the ACT, according to the results of a Morgan Gallup poll issued yesterday. The telephone poll of 248 men and 247 women aged 18 years and over was commissioned by the Adult Video Industry Association and conducted earlier this month. Last month the Government decided not to amend laws which allow the importation of X-rated videos into Australia, their sale and hire in the ACT to people aged over 18 and their distribution to the rest of Australia. The Opposition early this month introduced a private Mem ber's Bill to ban the videos. The poll showed that 35.4 per cent of people wanted the sale and hire ofX-rated videos banned, 59.5 wanted arrangements to stay as they were, and 5.1 could not say. The poll explained that the X-rated movies and videos were films of an erotic nature which showed explicit sex scenes but not violence. A further breakdown of the figures showed significant differences between the attitudes of men and women, and young and old. Of the men, 25.6 per cent wanted the videos banned compared,with 45.2 per cent of women; 68.2 per cent of men wanted the sale and hire allowed as now, 50.7 of women. In the 18-24, 25-34 and 35-49 age groups the majority of people did not Vant the videos banned (67.3, 66.1, 58.7) whereas in the 50-plus group this dropped to 47 per cent with 46.6 voting for the ban. Most of the respondents, 43.3 per cent, thought that a movie or video was given an X-rating if it had explicit sex, 13 per cent if it had extreme violence and 32.6 if it had both. It was more important for censors to control extreme violence than explicit sex scenes in movies according to 62.6 per cent of the respondents, 28.8 said both should be controlled, 6.1 explicit sex, 2.5 could not say. Comparing men to women, 70.2 per cent of men thought it more important to control extreme violence, 54.9 of women. Women thought it more important to control both, 35.6 per cent compared with 22.1 pc of men. More than half of the respondents, 70.7 per cent, said that the X-rated film censorship classifica tion was allowed on videos in the ACT, 85.4 per cent said the G-rating was allowed, 84.5 the PGR, 82.4 the M, 77.2 the R-rating and 1.6 percent could not say. The AVIA says the poll shows "popular support" for the Government's decision to set up a working party to look into violence on video, it says the results confirm that many people are ignorant about the contents of X-rated (non-violent erotic) films, 46 per cent "mistakenly believing that they contained violence in one form or another". Association lobbyist Robbie Swan said in a statement that the ACT Liberal Party's negative, stance on X-rated videos proved that the party was out of touch with local feelings. "Canberrans will not vote [in the ACT self-government election] for a party that endorses blanket censorship moves from minority groups," he said. Canberrans enjoyed their sex life and resented any one trying to fit them into straitjackets and stereotypes.

30 Dec 1988 - IN BRIEF Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 30 December 1988, page 3 IN BRIEF Older people targeted SYDNEY: The NSW Cancer Council said it might change its target group after a survey published yesterday showed few sunbathers aged over 55 used sunscreens. A Saulwick poll published in yesterday's Sydney Morning Herald showed that 80 per cent of under-25s used sunscreens always or often, but 60 per cent of people over 55 rarely or never used sunscreens. Christmas Appeal Australian Catholic Relief hopes to raise more than $70,000 in the CanbetTaGoulburn area for relief for flood victims in Bangladesh. This year's Christmas Appeal by the Archbishop of Canberra and Goulburn, the Most Reverend Francis Carroll, has already raised many thousands of dollars but donations can still be sent. The director of Australian Catholic Relief, Mick Sullivan, said yesterday that among the 65 parishes in the archdiocese, St Christopher's Cathedral in Manuka had raised $3447 and St John Vianney in Waramanga had raised $2700. Donations can be sent to the Archbishop's Christmas Appeal, GPO Box 42, Canberra ACT 2601. Rights for blind New legislation which came into effect yesterday will afford a deaf or blind person with a guide dog the same rights of access to public places in the ACT as other citi zens. 30 Dec 1988 - Canberrans prefer Hawke, Peacock Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 30 December 1988, page 3 Canberrans prefer Hawke, Peacock Almost twice as many Canberrans would prefer Andrew Peacock to Opposi-tion Leader John Howard as Liberal Par-ty Leader, according to an opinion poll published yesterday. Mr Peacock, the Opposition's Deputy Leader and treasury spokesman, was also the preferred choice among Liberal vot-ers, and Prime Minister Bob Hawke was streets ahead of Treasurer Paul Keating in the Labor Party's leadership stakes. The poll by ANOP Research Services was conducted for Capital Television and covered a telephone sample of 1,200 Canberra adults interviewed between December 15 and 18. Of those surveyed, 31 per cent thought Mr Peacock would make the best Liberal leader, followed by the Opposition's spokesman on industry, technology and commerce, Senator Fred Chaney (23 per cent), Mr Howard (17 per cent), and Lib-eral Party federal president and Elders-IXL chief John Elliott (8 per cent). About one in 10 either thought none of the four would make the best leader (12 per cent), or were undecided (9 per cent). The survey showed 51 per cent of the total sample thought Mr Hawke the bet-ter Labor Party leader, well ahead of Mr Keating (19 per cent), the Minister for Industry, Technology and Commerce, Senator John Button (12 per cent), and the Minister for Defence, Kim Beazley (8 percent). Ten per cent either thought none of the four made the best leader or were unde-cided. Among Labor voters, 68 per cent pre-ferred Mr Hawke as leader, leaving Mr Keating a very distant second at 17 per cent, followed by Senator Button (7 per cent) and Mr Beazley (5 per cent). Of Liberal voters, 24 per cent preferred Mr Howard as leader, slightly behind Mr Peacock with 28 per cent. Senator Cha-ney was preferred by 18 per cent and Mr Elliott by 11 percent. 31 Aug 1988 - MIDWEEK MAGAZINE Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 31 August 1988, page 27 BREAKING HOT AIR WITH THE D8VN AS AN ABC trainee, I was taught that, whether interviewing the President of the United States or a drunk in the gutter, the reporter should always take charge of the situation. Hence the journalist was to direct the interviewee where to sit, to cut out incoming telephone calls, close windows to block out noise, etc. And miraculously, as long as you pretended to know what you were doing, cooperation was always forthcoming. That is, until my first Canberra interview with William George Haydcn - an introduction to the fact that the city is full of professional interviewees who can be pretty tough operators when they want to be, notwithstanding any vice-regal aspirations. Having been ushered into the foreign Minister's office, I was seated in the chair opposite his desk. After a preliminary chat, 1 duly instructed Mr Haydcn to join me on my side of the desk so he would be within microphone range. He refused. I therefore invited myself to move around to his side of the desk. The answer was "No." He then explained his actions by saying he needed to refer to some confidential briefing notes during the interview. Not realising the extent of the Foreign Minister's famed paranoia, I volunteered to sit beside him without looking at his notes. You can guess the response. In the end I had to conduct the interview lying across the ministerial desk. Mr Hayden said this would blunt my "combative" interviewing style. 1 suspect it did. But it's not just politicians in Canberra who can demonstrate a difficult approach. A tiny minority of journalistic colleagues play rough too - a situation which was exacerbated by the appallingly cramped working conditions in the old Parliament House. For example, early in my time in Canberra I had to share a desk with Max Walsh, Pru Goward and another one-time big ABC name. In order to fully appreciate the resulting tale, it must be understood that trying to get daybreak interviews with politicians is useless without a large collection of MPs' home telephone numbers, holiday home numbers, mistresses' numbers, etc. Thus After four years of waking federal politicians for early-morning interrogations on the ABC's AM program, Michael Dodd has left the Parliamentary Press Gallery to head overseas to interview some "real people". He looks back with the view that working in the national capital is a tougher but zanier experience than most Australians might imagine. my contact book bccame not only the product of obsessive collecting, but a much-used resource for the whole office as well. Alas, one day it mysteriously disappeared. After a week of fruitless searching, I returned from an assignment to find that all that day's notes, as well as the Tasmanian telephone book I'd been using, were in the rubbish bin. After a full-scale investigation, the one-time ABC big name confessed sheepishly that he'd thrown them out because they had been on what he regarded as "his" desk. Under further cross-examination, he admitted that my beloved contact book had been treated in the same way. But he didn't apologise. Notwithstanding this, once I'd managed to build up a replacement contact book, he never had any qualms about asking me for politicians' numbers. Those politicians who do give out their numbers love to complain about journalists ringing them at ungodly hours. BuI AM is generally a little kinder to politicians than some of them like to make out. Writing after his ministerial career abruptly came to an end, Barry Cohen, former Environment Minister, said, "God, how I miss the Fourth Estate. Those early-morning wake-up calls. 'Is that you, Barry? It's Michael here... from AM. I'm sorry to disturb you...' And you knew how genuinely sorry they were from the tone of their voice - 'What time is it, Michael?1 '5.30am ..'Oh, how nice to hear from you so early. What is it you want to know?'" Without wishing to destroy Mr Cohen's yarnspinning credibility, a little more attention to detail would be in order. His anecdote comes unstuck by virtue of the fact that I was never on "Barry" terms with him. (Perhaps it was because of my beard that he regarded me as a closet environmentalist, and hence a natural enemy.) Besides, as a humanitarian gesture, I never phone politicians uninvited before 6.30am - unless they live in an unfortunate time zone like Western Australia or Queensland in summer, which Mr Cohen doesn't. Anyway, it's not always the journalists who pester politicians at irregular hours. Former "Mouth from the South" Michael Hodgman would frequently call me early with some supposedly earth-shattering crime committed by the Hawke Socialist Government which you just had to interview him about. And when you gave him the brush-off, he used to ring the producer and try to bust his way on to the program that way. But one morning I fixed him for good, when the following recorded exchange took place: M.H.: What Mr Howard has done, according to the most recent Morgan Gallup Polls, is to sack the six most popular members of the Liberal Party in the House of Representatives. We have a situation where he's sacked Mr Peacock, who was the most popular Liberal in Australia. He sacked Mr Macphee. He sacked Mr Everingham, who's now leaving federal politics. He sacked Mr MacKellar and he sacked me. M.D.: That's only five. M.H.: I beg your pardon. M.D.: That's only five. M.H.: I beg your pardon. M.D.: That's only five. M.H.:... (pause)... One, two, three, four, five .. .Are you there? M.D.: Yes. M.H.: Sorry, you threw me then. Just hang on a minute. One, two, three, four, five. Five of the six, you are right. Do you want to run that again? M.D.: No, no. That's all right - who's the other one? M.H.: Oh, hang on Mike. Just hang on a minute. This is stupid. One, two... Yeah, he sacked five. I beg your pardon. I should have said five of the six most popular. Do you want to run that again? Despite Mr Hodgman's pleas, I could not bring myself to edit the tape, and it went to air uncut. Consequently my popularity amongst politicians on both sides of the House soured. Better still, Mr Hodgman never offered himself again. But it's not only politicians who pursue journal ists for favours. One day I received a call from someone I hardly knew who kindly thought I ought to know that the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation was asking questions about me. After some investigation 1 obtained the home telephone number of a senior ASIO employee who was rather taken aback that I was able to track him down. He also appeared, to be quite stunned that his organisation's inquiries about me had been discovered. He .then stressed that I had not done anything "wrong", though he refused to divulge more over the telephone - leaving me to wonder whether the KGB was also monitoring my activities. He then requested a face-to-face meeting. So where did he want to meet - under a bridge? In a disused factory? No, in the bar of the National Press Club! My James Bond instincts having been quelled, this most unclandestine of meetings eventually took place after he apologised for being half an hour late. He also apologised for having questions asked about me behind my back, explaining that ASIO was concerned about adverse publicity when approaching journalists - wanting to find out about them before risking a direct approach. He then revealed that the organisation wanted me to give it some information about an acquaintence ofmine whom it suspected of being a spy. I explained that, despite being a patriotic Australian, I regarded it as a breach ofjournalistic ethics to become an ASIO informant - though I did volunteer not to publicly name their suspect At least there was no apparent retribution-with ASIO chief Alan Wrigley, unlike his predecessors, often prepared to give ABC radio interviews. This included a "live" telephone interview on the day of his appointment, which resulted in a crossed line with a pair oflovers. The result was as follows: M.D.: Mr Wrigley, what aims do you have for the future ofASIO? Man: Yeah, it's just dropped out. A.W.: I think broadly the objectives have been set out by the Prime Minister in a statement not long ago. Man: I think we have a crossed line. Woman: I think we have, Don... Oh Don, love you. Man: Love you. A.W.: But essentially they pick up from Justice Hope's recent findings and the principal objectives I think are to continue the work of restructuring and revitalising the organisation to be more responsive to the priorities that the Government sees for it today. Woman: I love you... Oh right, hahahahaha. M.D.: Do you believe that ASIO has big prob lems as it is now? Man: I don't know. A.W.: I don't think they can be said to be big. The inquiry has identified some management and administrative improvements that could be made and should be made. And that's probably a realistic thing in most organisations. I am in no position to say whether they are abnormally high. Woman: Yeah, love you darl. M.D.: Have y.ou ever worked with ASIO before?. A.W.: No. M.D.: Is that going to put you at a disadvantage? A.W.: I don't think so, no. Woman: Oh well, you know where it is. Man: I know where it is. A.W.: I have had a number of dealings with some aspects of intelligence, not entirely-the same sort of intelligence as ASIO's central interests are but in the sense that 1 have had a number of connections with the intelligence world of one sort or another over the years I am fairly familiar with the processes. Woman: I should have given you some this morning. Unfortunately, subsequent interviews with Mr Wrigley have never topped that one - which perhaps means it's the nght time for a break from Canberra, and time to interview some "real people". That is, people not heavily involved in the political process, who might be inclined to give less calculated answers, and who may even do what they're told to do by interviewers. If I meet enough of them I could - for a time at least - turn into a real person myself.

01 Sep 1988 - Referendum is 'on the skids' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 1 September 1988, page 10 Referendum is 'on the skids' BRISBANE: The Morgan Gallup poll in The Bulletin magazine showed Labor's referendum proposals were on the skids, the Queensland Premier, Mr Ahern, said yesterday. The poll indicated people were finally waking up and realising there was a hidden agenda. They were studying the fine print and deciding to vote "No" across Australia on all questions, he said. The poll, conducted 10 days ago, found only the question on fair and democratic elections could win the necessary support in four states. Meanwhile, two prominent Queensland political analysts have urged a "Yes" vote to the one vote, one value referendum question to ensure a return of "electoral democracy" in the state. In a joint statement, Dr Peter Coaldrake, of the Queensland Institute of Technology, and Dr Kenneth Wiltshire, of the University of Queensland, referred to a comment by former South Coast member Mr Russ Hinze that many seats had "rigged" boundaries. The present system allowed one party to go into elections with 20 to 22 seats "in the bag" and win 56 per cent of seats with only 39 per cent of the votes. "As the population grows, the Queensland zonal gerrymander becomes worse each day, skewed in favour of the Government," they said.

21 Sep 1988 - Poll shows Cain's support up Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 21 September 1988, page 3 Poll shows Cain's support up SYDNEY: The Victorian Labor Government would have been returned to power with an increased majority if an election had been held in mid-September, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. Voters were almost evenly divided on whether the Liberals would do a better or worse job than Labor, the poll found. Published in The Bulletin today, the poll also found that the Liberals were favoured by more than two to one as the best party for reducing state taxes and charges. The approval rating of the Premier, Mr Cain, rose by two points in a week to 56 per cent; 31 per cent disapproved of him and 13 per cent were undecided. The approval rating of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Kennett, also rose by two points to 31 per cent, with 55 per cent disapproving and 14 per cent unde cided. Held on September 17-18, the poll found that 50 per cent of electors would have voted for Labor and 44 per cent for the Liberals or Nationals. On a two-party-preferred basis, Labor would have received 53 per cent of the vote, and the Liberals and Nationals 47 per cent. Meanwhile, another poll published in The Bulletin showed that the Federal Government would have relied on preferences to remain in power if an election had been held early this month.

06 Mar 1972 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 6 March 1972, page 2 (Drakm Wmts Monday, March 6, 1972 LEADERSHIP NEEDED 1 USTRALIAN political leadership is not only at a low . ,**■ level it is seen to be so by most voters. The level of approval of both Mr McMahon and Mr Whitlam, ; as shown by the Gallup Poll findings published last week, is astonishingly low. It is a sign of an unhealthy democracy when Utile more than a quarter of a representative group of voters "approve of" the Prime Minister and barely a third "approve of" the Leader of the Opposition. It is true that evidence of this kind needs to be regarded with caution and that the results are not quite as bad as they may appear, particularly for Mr Whitlam. But thev arc bad enough to worry not only the two leaders but anyone who fears the results of a complete breakdown of trust between the electors and the possible heads of government. What can be said in mitigation of these dismal figures? First, electors' opinions about politicians tend to be extremely changeable: much more so than their opinions about parties. It is conceivable that one or both leaders could make a sudden recovery in popularity, though what might cause this is anything but clear at present. Second (though this will give comfort only to . Mr Whitlam and his supporters), polls show it is • common for an unpopular Prime Minister to drag his opponent down with him. in popularity, ft is as though . the voters extend their disapproval of the Prime Minister to politicians in general so that, contrary to what we might expect, a fall in the popularity of a Prime Minister is not usually accompanied by a rise in the popularity of the Leader of the Opposition. Third, Mr Whitlam can at least claim that since becoming Leader of the Opposition he has become unpopular at a slower rate than Mr Gorton and then Mr McMahon. Low as }iis present level of approval is, he can say that the Prime Minister is now more unpopular still!

13 Mar 1972 - GALLUP POLL 40-hour week favoured Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 13 March 1972, page 7 GALLUP POLL 40-hour week favoured Only a small minority of 13 per cent favours reducing the standard working week to 35 hours immediately, the Gallup Poll finds. In this Australia-wide survey, more than 2,000 people were asked whether the standard working week should be kept at 40 hours, or reduced gradually to 35 hours, or reduced immediately to 35 hours. In addition to the 13 per ccnt who favour having 35 hours now, another 22 per cent want it introduced gradually. That makes a total of 35 per cent for a 35-hour week in the foreseeable future. But against them, there arc 60 per cent who say "keep the 40-hour week". The other 5 per cent are undecided, This vote of almost twoto-one for keeping the 40 hour week came from 72 per ccnt of Liberal-CP voters, 58 per cent of DLP voters and 52 per cent of ALP voters. Usual arguments were: Too much spare time now, Economy could not stand 35 hours, 40 hours work is not too much. The 13 per cent who favour an immediate cut to 35 hours comprise 15 per cent of the men and 11 per cent of the women interviewed. They often said it would rcduce unemployment. Exactly the same question has been asked by the Gallup Poll 5 times since 1968. The following table shows that the 13 per cent for "35 hours now", although only a small minority, is double the 6 per cent vote 15 months ago: 1970 1971 1972 Nov. 29 Sep 1947 - MEET MR. AMERICA Goulburn Evening Post (NSW : 1940 - 1954), Monday 29 September 1947, page 4 MEET MR. AMERICA Gallup Poll Discovers the Kind of Man He is After ten years of malking the average American of his? opinions and then 1selling them back' to him, operators, of the Gallup poll plunged into their files to discover the sort of fellowwith whom they had been doing -business. Recently they published the resu!ts. 'The average U.S. man is 5 ft. 9 ýin.' tall and weighs 158 lb. Pace Anita Loos. six out of ten prefer' brunettes (a happy choice, since only 8 per cent. of U.S. women are natural blondes) and they think-although they are at least half responsible for it-that women get kissed and petted too much before marriage. The average U.S. woman is plumper than she would like to admit--she is 5 ft. 4 in. tall and weighs 132 lb. She is more interested in having a good-tempered husband than a faithful one, althougn she wishes he were more romantic. She believes three children constitute the ideal family, wants no babies until the second year of marriage. DOGS PREFERRED Most of the quarrels between Mr. and Mrs. America are prompted by" (1) money, (2) jealousy, and (3) children-in that order. Seven out of ten U.S. adults believe in spanking their offspring. Less . than a third of U.S. families say grace at meals. Seven out of ten prefer a dog to a cat as a family pet and only one in 20 keeps a canary. Almost no parents want their sons to go into politics; they are certain that a political career leads ot graft and crookedness. One out of three U.S. citizens complains that his feet hurt. Two out of three adults wear scectacles. One out of five is troubled by a degree of deafness. Two out of ten can't learn to whistle. One-tenth of the population is left-handed and less than a third can remember the numbers on their automobile licence plates. One in three has a terrible time getting up in the morning, but only one in five has any difficulty in dropping off to sleep. The average citizen goes to bed at 10 o'clock, gets up at 6.30 six days a week, stays up until 11. on Saturday and snoozes until 8 on Sunday morning. NO BLACK CATS Six out of ten U.S. adu'ts drink; the same number smoke. One-half of the population thinks Hitler is still alive. Two out of three believe Abraham Lincoln was greater than George Washington. The five living humans most admired by Americans are: General of the Army Douglas MacArthur, General of the Army Dwight D. Eisenhower, Winston Churchill, President Harry Truman and Secretary of State George C. MIrshall. Ninety-six per cent. of Americans believe in God and 76 per cent. in life after death. Only 4 per cent. are convinced that they are unhappy; 57 per cent. think they are fair!y happy; 38 per cent. consider themselves very happy, and 1 per cent. can't tell. Nevertheless, one in three knocks on wood for luck, one in ten'believes in throwing spilled salt over his shoulder and one in five shudders when a black cat crosses his path.

08 Apr 1910 - A VILLAGE POLLING DAY. Cobar Herald (NSW : 1899 - 1914), Friday 8 April 1910, page 7 A VILLAGE POLLING DAY. SOME INCIDENTS. Soon after seven on a dark January morning we alighted at the station nearest our destination — the typical Lancashire village of X. 'I think we had better walk it,' sug-gested the vrt!.'dlng officer, sifter a-.i impatient wait of five m'nutcs; 'we ought to manage the four miles in time for the opening of the poll.' Vh« we'cn-i\j rattle ot wbw'i, however, quickly i/iy.yed -ri' anxiety, jmd soon the itity of three was hudi'.lv.d together in the ricketty carrier's cart. 'Hoo's rare an' fr*«ly this mornin',' Fait' the driver fron his seat; ' it's ?wunnerful -what yon owd m.-.re can do when she's win up— hoo'l 'a yo' theer I1 hayve an hour — it's th' excitement as does it.' The horse certainly did move; but the strides were chiefly up and down, after the manner of Pecksniff's pony, and Ms'a^t'on caused the cait to jolt most uncomfortably. 'And ? they say as animals knows nowt,' continued the driver, calmly ignoring the fact that we were continually being flung to the 'jottom of the cart by the erratic movements of his horse. 'Ton horse knows as there's summat i' th' air; hoo's a seet moor sense till mony a woman, aye.an'mony a Christian, that hos 'as.' BILL YATES CASTS HIS VOTE. Having arrived at the polling station, the carrier adjourned to the publichouse opposite. 'I met as weel stop an' put ma cross to t' papper while I'm on t' spot,' was his parting greeting. As he did not enter the polling booth until close on noon, it was evident that voting was a serious matter to our friend the carrier. When, with the assistance of two village constables, tho boxes had been duly placed and unsealed, the poll was declared open. 'I'm Bill Yatcs.' he said genially, 'an1 eighty-three last wick.' 'For fifty year,' he continued, 'me an' owd Mo powd fost at every election i' this village. But th' owd lad is deawn wi' t' rheumatics badly, so he cannot turn eawt this time. Poor awd Mo, he'll be gradely frettin' abeaut it a' — I mun goo an' ha' a word wi' th* owd lad — he were always on t' reet side, an' would be now if he but cood.' And with a parting flourish of his stout cudgel Bill left the booth. Mine host from across the way was the next to vote, and with an eye to business he informed us that refreshments could be ordered at any hour. Soon after breakfast time some little commotion was heard at the entrance, the sound of a shrill voice being very persistent. 'You cannot come in with him,' said the constable firmly, as he blocked the door with his body. 'He'll goo an' vote for t' wrong felly it I dunnot,' replied a female voice. 'Ast do nowt o't kind,' growled a pro-, testing voice; 'dost think I'm a born foo'?' 'Tha were never owt else sin I wed thee — thee'at three parts drunk awready, and ? ' By this time the voter had managed to enter the room. 'Neaw what would to do wi' a wife like you ?' he began, turning to the policeman. 'Get on wi' thi' votln', lad, and move on,' replied the officer, sharply. 'It's bad enoo neaw,' grumbled the unlucky wight as he left the room a few minutes later, 'but what'll it be when they're getting f. vote?' NOT BROWN, BUT ANOTHER. For the greater part the workmen who came in during the day were quiet and businesslike in their manner of voting; very few needed any instructions, and. the general improvement in the education of the people is perhaps never so noticeable as on these occasions. ..?..-, ... There was one exception. A ???'?;b:B.': surly-looking man who , came to the table witih the demand, 'Gie us a'card!' 'Name, please?' requested the clerk. 'What's that to theu? I vote -by ballot,' he snapped out. - „? :'l-.. Even when it was pointed out to him that his name was necessary to prove his right to vote according to the regster he. refused to budge, and not until the officer came to escort him to the door did ho give the required Information. 'The The local gentry, including tfhe clergy and doctors, nearly all recorded their votes before lunch. In several ca^es they did not think It necessary to give their names until requested. 'Ha — yes,, of course, of course,' blustered one, 'you are strangers to the village, otherwise you would have had no need to ask for my name.' It afterwards transpired that this individual was a recent settler in the village, ?'.??'? 'Lives in a big new place on th' 'ill—, of no fambly whatever, tries to mix up with our best famblles, who don't want none of him,' remarked the constable scathingly. . During tflie afternoon very little pc'iing was done; but one old fellow created a mild diversion. 'Con yo tell me which o1 these chaps Is Brown?' he inquired. 'Certainly,' responded the presiding officer, indicating the name on the voter's paper; then, suspecting an illiterate voter, he asked the old man whether he could read and write. 'Aye, lad, I con write reet enoo for this job, but ml seet Is none so good as It were. Art. sure this is Brown?' he continued. . On belnc reassured that it was, the, old man retired to tine ballot-box to make his cross. 'That's aw reet, isn't It?' he remarked, showing his paper to the presiding officer.'But 'But you have not voted for Brown.' said the official, after examining the paper. 'I ne'er Intendit to,' chuckled the old fellow, winking- his eye slily, 't'other chap's my mon, an' I wanted to mak' no mistake about him.' THREE CHEERS FOR 'OWD MO.' The return of the out-workcrs to their homes brought the usual rush in the closing hours of the poll. The rival candidates roused local excitement to fever heat by their final vJslts to the neighboring comriittee rooms. With the last half hour came a constant succession of cheers and countercheers, as the remaining voters came up. 'Three cheers for t' Squire — he's coom all f way fra Scotland!' shouted someone outside as a motor car catne panting up. qg . 'Three cheers for Owd Mo!' called out the leader of the opposition party. The two came in together, the Sctulre helping the crippled old man, whose right leg was swathed in red flannel. The Squire waited untU the old maa ?had voted, In order that he might assist him out again. 'You must come in the motor— I'll see you safe home.' 'Nay, nay, Squire, I mun stick to ml colors. I'd a gone wi' th' owd Squire I reet willingly; he were always for fi poor people; he'd seed 'em starve for; bread an' knew what Protection meant! for such as us. I've had childer cryln'l for bread, and I've worked wick in, j wick -eawt, an' not been able to give i 'em one gradely meal i' th' day. Nay, ! nay, Squire, no Protection for the likes) o' me; we mun go our own ways; th' j lads browt me here i' th' donkey cart, an' I reckon th' owd donkey ''11 take mej back agen — mayhap ast ne-er vote agen, j Squire; but if it is last time I know! awm on t' right side. Good - neetj Squire!' . ? j And with blazing eyes the old fellow! drew himself up and hobbled painfully' to the door with th-. aid of his stick. J And a- the polling closed a mighty' cheering broke out, 'Three cheers for! Owd Mo!' — H.L.. ln the 'Daily News.'.

04 Mar 1948 - Gallup Poll AUSTRALIANS "DON'T KNOW" PALESTINE Goulburn Evening Post (NSW : 1940 - 1954), Thursday 4 March 1948, page 3 -Gallup: Poll, : AUSTRALANS "DON'T KNOW" PALESTINE U.N.'s indecision and vacillation about Palestine is reflected in Australian thought and opinion, as revealed .by a Galliup Poll this mqnth. On tivo questions about the partition of Palestine and the need for an armed force to con'rol Palestine, Australian opinion is confused. In this nation-wide survey. people interviewed by-the Gallup poll were first asked:Do you think the decision of the United Nations to divide Palestine between the Jews and Arabs is right or wrong? -. This is one of the few occasions in the six years' experience of the Australian Gallup Poll that neither side has attracted anything like a maJority. 37 per cent say. "It's right to divide Palestine." 23 per cent shy,': "It's - wrong," and 40 per cent are undecided. INTERNATIONAL ARMIY? The United Nations Palestine Commission has told the Security Council 'that it canniot carry out its assignments of enforcing partition unless it is backed by an international army.-: To find •out Australian opinion on the idea of an international armed force, the Gall1up Poll asked:Do you think the United Nations. should, or should not, enlist an armed force and send it to control Palestine?. Answers show that the indecision about partitioning Palestine is accompanied by a division of .opinion regarding an armed force: 41 per cent say, "'U.N. should send an armed foroc to control Palestine.?" 35 per cent oppose the idea, and 24 per cent are undecided.

28 Mar 1966 - Britain's opposition Conservative Party has cut the ruling Labour Party's 12 per cent lead by three-and-a-half per cent in the past week, according to the latest Gallup Poll. The poll result, published in the Sunday Telegraph, gives Labour 50½ per cent, Conservatives 42 per cent, Liberals seven per cent and others one half per cent of votes in next Thursday's general election. Wilson woos the middle class Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 28 March 1966, page 2 Britain's opposition Conservative Party has cut the ruling Labour Party's 12 per cent lead by three-and-a-half per cent in the past week, according to the latest Gallup Poll. The poll result, published in the Sunday Telegraph, gives Labour 50} per cent, Conservatives 42 per cent, Liberals seven per cent and others one half per cent of votes in next Thursday's general election. Wilson woos the middle class From JAMES JUPP JJAROLD Wilson has cautioned against overconfidence based on public opinion polls, fearful that it might bring a low vote, which always .penalises the Labour Party. There is plenty of evidence that the British public is not actively involved in politics in the sense that was true between 1945 and 1955. They have become passive television watchers, a medium on which Mr Wilson shines. The mass parties have lost much of their drive, and a lot of the noise and energy in British politics has been made by the racialists of the extreme Right and the CND - anarchist - "angrics" on the Left. This relative apathy towards mainstream politics while noises are made at the ex tremes has been typical of the the United States and, to a lesser extent, of Australia, Germany and Scandinavia. It seems to be related to affluence and the withdrawal from class politics which this brings. Particular grievances like racialism, and the attraction, of moralists, ideologues and psychological. , misfits into noisy- movements, .present poli tical features which were ab- ? 'sent from the earnest twoparty slogging of 10 years ago. Even the now waning Liberal revival in Britain was, in part, a reaction against convergence towards the centre. The new Liberal Party' of Mr Grimond was quite distinct .from, the dusty Gladstonian relic which his predecessors bequeathed to him. That Liberalism does seem to be declining may be due to the fact that, once in Parliament, Liberals have converged as rapidlv as anyone else towards the common ground shared by large sections of the two major parties. Part of Mr Wilson's strategy over the past year has been directed towards the twin goals of sustaining public interest in politics while, at the same time, presenting Labour as a rational and trustworthy Government. He has probably come close to the second objective without attaining the first. In contrast to the sustained hatred which Conservatives were able to work up in the 1940s, Mr Heath and his followers seem mild and ineffectual. Rather than this election being "dirty." there was less resort to racialism and personal sneering at Wilson than there was in 1963. The passions aroused by the Conservative victory at Smethwick after a racialist campaign have abated. The extreme British National Party has been so annoyed by Alderman Griffiths' mildness once he got into Parliament, that they are running against him. This will almost certainly return Smethwick to a strongly anti-racialist Labour candidate. The noisy extremists will get very few votes in this election. But the quieter approach of the established parties brings with it the problem of a low poll. The importance of this to Labour can best be understood by looking at the type of seat it hopes to win. In many cases Labour is now looking to areas which have never been Labour before, except perhaps in 1945. With a few exceptions like Smethwick, L e y t o n and Slough, lost on the immigration issue, there are now few clearly "working class" constituencies which arc not Labour hejd. The last pocket of working class Conservatism in Lancashire was cleaned out by , Harold, V'ilson, a local. MP, in the -1 election. Now Labour is looking to medium sized towns like Reading, Oxford, Cambridge, Exeter, Yarmouth and Colchester. While all of these have industrial plants they are primarily commercial ccntres with a large middle class. Similarly, the London suburbs likely to fall include Norwood, Chiswick, Chislehurst, South Croydon, Hornchurch, Hampstead, Lewisham and other essentially residential districts. For Labour to win these seats there must be a high turnout, maximising the working class vote, as well as the positive swing among the middle classes which opinion polls have noted over the past year. That Labour should be thinking in terms of winning Hampstead or Oxford is a mark of the progress made over the past two years. Even the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Heath, in the suburb of Bexley, could be defeated if he does not work very hard indeed. The very areas with a high standard of living, good education and pleasant housing which have always been thought of as Conservative, are those which Labour now seems likely to capture. In 1963 Labour won, by seven votes, its first seat ever in Sussex and its first seat ever in a major seaside resort. Now it can look on the whole hoominc South East as an asset. Of the 65 Conservative seats most likely to be lost, 2^ are in the south east. There is almost no scope left for further Labour gains in Scotland, Wales,, the north and Midlands. The Prime Minister, Mr Wilson The Economist has even argued that Labour should forget about its stronghold north of the Trent and fight a modern, television election directed towards the prosperous middle classcs and skilled workers within seventy miles of London. Mr Wilson is a bit too clever to do that, knowing the strong Conservative traditions of many Midlands and Lancashire workers. But he also knows that the "Coronation Streets" have been squeezed dry of potential converts. , r Bccausc the election is very much a.vole of confidence for a government which has struggled with a small majority, there are few genuine issues. Just as immigration provided an unofficial plank for some Conservatives, so an attack on trade unions is featured as a hastily constructed "issue" in the present contest. Mr Heath himself has prommised to make the union "closed shop" illegal if re turned and lo legalise union - employer contracts, presumably by using the cort o£ penalties which operate in Australia. British unions have been less widely accepted than Australian ones, and have less legal restriction. Reports of unofficial union persecution of "blacklegs" have been seized on. Most Conservative workers are either not in unions or are very inactive, despite party attempts lo organise them. Thus Mr Heath may appeal to middle class resentment without losing his remaining working class, essentially nonunionist, support. But it is a fairly empty issue with a negative appeal. It may simply antagonise the increasing number of technicians and while collar unionists to whom Mr Wilson appealed in 1963. As a way of closing the per cent popularity gap, attacks on the unions will probably be less effective than was the "immigration issue".

15 Sep 1966 - Advertising Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 September 1966, page 9 k 0 about margarine and butter The Australian Dairy Industry Council has attempted once more to confuse the public in an advertisement published in leading newspapers. Marrickville Holdings now reply to the statements made. What the Dairv Council said* 1. "This policy, which is the very basis ot Australian prosperity, is that we must build up in this country efficient local industries that create wide employment. "If we allowed free imports of every commodity that could be dumped here by foreign competitors we would have ample "freedom of choice." But it would be a freedom that you could not exercise." A - ' 2. "It should be clearly understood that there is no restriction on any kind of margarine other than table margarine." . ? <. . C' r-l ' : ./' V ?" y '? . ? ; .; ; - -:r . .: r; '' ' > ' : 3. "So far as table margarine is concerned, the quota system is part of a general Australian policy for ensuring the sec security of, 'X ient local industries." 4. "The Dairy Industry contributes $120-million a year to Australia's export income, thereby aiding full emblovment." . ' S. "The Dairy Industry Is' an efficient industry." Marrickville reveals the truth. The quota system threatens efficient local industries. Marrickville Holdings is an all-Australian company; one of the few left in the food industry in Australia today. It employs 3,000 Australians. This year it will buy almost $20-million of Australian primary products. Marrickville asks simply that table margarine made from all-Australian raw materials be free of quota control, and that the people should be free to choose between Australian butter and Australian margarine. The Dairy Industry wants to stop this from happening. Marrickville has bent all its efforts to encourage and promote the growth of Australian food manufacturing and of Australian primary industries. Unless the quotas are lifted- on table margarine, the livelihood of thousands of Australian workers will be in jeopardy and a major market will be lost to Australian oilseed growers, threatening the whole future of that industry. This is false. State Government' regulations control even the size, of printing type used on cooking margarine packet?;. State Government laws prevent cooking margarine from containing more than a small percentage of edible vegetable oils. These laws are specifically aimed at restricting cooking margarine sales and at closing out a big and growing market for Australian, edible oilseed growers in cooking margarine. The quota system protects the inefficient. The quota system is a dagger aimed straight at the hearts of two rapidly growing and efficient Australian industries: . The Australian Margarine Industry. . The Australian Edible Oilseeds Industry. No other Australian product is restricted by quota from selling without limit on the Australian market. But housewives foot the bill. Australia's export sales of butter are made at low. prices. The losses on these exports are made up by high home-prices for butter. The Australian housewife is subsidising these export losses. In'effect, the Dairy Industry is itself dumping butter on overseas markets and the Australian housewife foots the bill. The Australian housewife pays 53 cents a lb. for butter while her English counterpart pays only 40:41 cents. The Report of the 1960 Dairy Industry Inquiry Com mittee denies this. The Dairy Industry receives a $27-million subsidy each year from the taxpayers of Australia. In 1959, the Commonwealth Government set up a Committee to inquire into the state of the.Australian Dairy Industry. In 1960, the Parliament received the report, made by experts after a long and exhaustive inquiry. Certain sections of the report were devoted to a damning indictment of numbers of dairy farmers as being lazy, inefficient, having a couldn't-care-less attitude and being concerned only with extracting the maximum financial reward from their farms consistent with the minimum amount of work. The Committee described the attitude of the Dairy Industry as being one of rigidity of mind and thought regarding its problems. In summing up the issue of margarine and butter, the report stated: "Table margarine as at present manufactured and presented for sale is a wholesome nutritious food closely resembling butter in appearance and pack and is obtainable at about two-thirds the price of butter. Restrictions on the production of such a food are repugnant to freedom-loving Australians and as such could scarcely be justified, even on the grounds of 'the greatest good for the greatest number'." "Firstly, the Australian Dairy Industry does not advocate a complete embargo. "The Australian Dairy(Industry does not wish to see any other primary industry' - such as the vegetable oils industry - restricted through :unfair regula tion." . 9. 14 Nov 1966 - The Gallup poll and politics Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 14 November 1966, page 2 and politics By DAVID SOLOMON ,rTHE Australian Gal lup poll conducted :by Mr Roy Morgan, of Melbourne, has done much to influ: ence the course of the : present election campaign. | Earlier this year Mr Morgan Had found there had been a six per cent swing against the Labor Party from its position in 1963 — when it was heavily defeated by the Liberal-Country Party Government. That result has helped influence the announced policies of both parties. The Prime Minister, Mr Holt, judged that there was no need for him to make any spectacular promises for the election. He could afford to take on the air of a man showing great responsibility which in turn would assist him in • his denunciations of the financial impracticability of the schemes of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Calwell. The Gallup poll also showed that the Vietnam issue was unlikely to be an election winner for the Labor Party, so making it easier for Mr Holt to agree to an earlier demand from Mr Calwell that this should be the issue in the campaign. Politicians react strongly to Gallup poll results. They have no other accurate, independent way of assessing public opinion — except in elections, which give the final (for three years) verdict of the people. Public opinion polls give politicians an indication of whether they should change their policies, or change the emphasis given to particular policies, or even initiate new policies. They may even affect the way people vote. The announcement that a public opinion .poll shows there is a large majority in favour of one party may encourage people who might normally vote for it to give a vote foi the other party, in the knowledge that their protest vote will not deprive the.party thej really support of power. Or il might enaourage a "sympathy' vote for the underdog. It might, on the other hand, persuade people that they should vote for the winning side. The polls affect the way in which a parly approaches a campaign. There can be little doubt that Ihe confidence of the Government and the despondency of the Opposition have both been largely caused by published poll results. Mr Calwell has attempted to rally his forces with optimistic predictions of private polls, and has succcedcd to a minor extent. But Ihe most important polls lor the parties are those which are published. These aITcct not only the politicians, but also those who contribute funds. The effect in this regard is cumulative. A poor showing in a poll will tend to decrease the willingness of backers to put up money. This in turn will reduce the advertising campaign the party can muster, which in turn is likely to affect its popular standing. In Britain and the US, public opinion polls have become a competitive business, with several organisations striving to prove that their accuracy surpasses that of their opponents. Under such conditions the polls show results which generally are within one per cent or two of each other and (his seems to be about their maximum order of accuracy at the moment. In Australia there is only one organisation devoted primarily to sampling public opinion — Mr Roy Morgan's ' organisation — though some advertising agencies regularly sample public opinion for their market research activities, and can on request carry out the political-type surveys similar to Mr Morgan's Gallup poll. [The Labor Party has in ■ some previous years had public : opinion polls taken by its ad' vertising agency. This year it t felt, it could not afford to have ' a survey taken.] Mr Morgan's Gallup polls are published in seven metropolitan newspapers. He claims a high degree of accuracy for them, and says they have predicted the result df every Federal eleclion since 1943 (They began in 1941). It has made errors (e.g., it failed to see that the 1951 referendum on communism would be- defeated or that in 1954 NSW voters would decide on 10pm closing of hotels) but in these cases the margin of error has been "very small". It also has given a wrong emphasis in its predictions, as in 1963 when it thought the Labor Party would be only narrowly defeated in the Federal eleclion. Mr Morgan explains the 1963 result as having been caused by substantial changes in public opinion in the last week of the campaign (his last survey then, as it will be this year, was on the weekend before the election), rather than by many errors in his technique of sampling public opinion. The Kennedy assassination was the cause of an abrupt change in voting intentions, he believes, and in Australia this was magnified by the particularly violent television advertising which the DLP had been conducting against the ALP. One inherent problem the Gallup poll faces in trying to predict elections is the nature of the electoral system. The system used for electing Members of the House of Representatives means that the number of seats a party wins does not necessarily correspond with the percentage of the Australia wide vote that it receives — and it is the overall percentage vote which the Gallup poll is aimed at predicting. The electoral system has the effect of magnifying party majorities in the House of Representatives. If we had a straight two-party system and a party with a one per cent majority of votes had a oneseat majority in the House, then if the party had a four per cent majority its majority in the House would be far more than four seats (it would probably be from 12 to 20). But the system is not even as simple as this. The presence of the DLP and other parties and independents complicates the lask of predicting results, even at the best of times. But as Mr Morgan pointed out to me last week, this is not one of the "best of times" for his poll. The electoral system is not operating at its best at present because an electoral redistribution is long overdue. Electorates vary tremendously in size, some having double the populations of others. Large majorities for a party in several of these large seats would bring in distortions — votes for that party would have been wasted, so far as the task of winning seats, rather than percentages, is concerned. And in the future, things could be worse. As the Deputy-Leader of the Opposition, Mr Whitlam, told an election rally in Melbourne last week, one of the hidden issues in this election is control of the next redistribution of seats. Under legislation already put through Parliament, country seats will have fewer voters than city seals. This will mean, according to Mr Whitlam, that the city man's vote will have two-thirds the value of the vote of the man who lives in the country. The Gallup poll will be able to make adjustments for this sort of manipulation of the electoral system, but it is probably true that a straight percentage win for the Labor Party will no longer mean the winning of a majority of seats. (In the States gerrymandering by both sides has introduced the same complication. It means that instead of 50.1 per cent being the margin needed for victory, 52 or 53 per cent is needed by one side for victory while the other needs 48.1 or 47.1 per cent of the overall vote.) A further complication is that in some "swing" seats, personal factors may tend to be more important than genera] political considerations. Such cases however tend to even out, leaving the overall result unaffected. The greatest hazard for the pollster, however, is the occurrence in the last week of the campaign of a major unexpected crisis which changes people's voting intentions. In 1963 it was the Kennedy assassination. In 1966 some unexpected development could in the week before November 26, cause five per ccnt or more of the population to change their voles. All the Gallup poll interviewer can hope to find out is a man's voting intentions now. Mr Morgan uses a "probability sampling" method to select those who will be asked to state their opinions for the Gallup poll. A series of "starting addresses" is selected mathematically from all the electoral rolls in Australia. Each of the 200 interviewers then sees one person (the youngest available voter) from each of 10 consecutive houses moving clockwise round a block from the selected "starting address". As well as answering about 10 different topical questions people who are interviewed have to give their names, occupations, religions and voting behaviour at the previous election. A subsequent check of all these questions allows Mr Morgan to be sure that his sample does contain a statistical cross-section of the Australian community. His office also checks back with a percentage of those interviewed to ensure that ihe interviewers have accurately recorded the opinions they sought. Apart from the accuracy of the poll, Mr Morgan's proudest boast is its impartiality. He is a convinced Liberal, and has stood for public office as a Liberal. He says this is well known to Labor men who nevertheless acknowledge that his. poll attempts to present an unbiased, true picture of the current State of public opinion.
