21 Nov 1967 - TELEVISION Knowing your politicians Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 21 November 1967, page 14 TELEVISION Knowing your politicians by JOHN HAY "H°w many of the Viewers tonight watching this programme know their representatives in the Senate?" asked Mr Roy Morgan, the Gallup Poll man, a guest on Saturday night's Four Corners Senate feature. What The People Think. To ACT viewers, along with criminals and the insane, the question does not mean very much, but since TV political campaigning has become as the same guest put it "a battle of the giants", most of us have not been able to avoid either the PM or Mr Whitlam over the last week. Faced with the same prospect again this week, we could come to the conclusion as casual, unheatcd observers that there is still plenty to be learnt by the two giants, just as the commercial stations can learn from the ABC and vice versa. The Whitlam opening production was an ordinary film and the television make-up specialist had prepared him for the' harsh, blemish-revealing lights of the television studio. This gave the Leader of the Opposition a rather pallid look like the villain in an old movie comedy. A pity, because Mr Whitlam is on6 of the few TV politician naturals we have. Looking back at the politicians who have been prominent in Australia, electors are not noted for choosing good looks, they seem willing to accept their politicians au naturel. Anyway, television presentation is still very much an unknown factor in the final outcome of elections. The documentary approach of film clips on poverty, Vietnam and the Sno«V were used effectively and the PM the previous night could have used these to segment his sitin approach and to help the dry words. Mr Whitlam's stand up, 6it down technique on the other hand tends to break concentration on what he is sayin|, and if the public opinions man had taken a survey next day, he may have found that the viewers knew how many times he was up and down — but not what he said. However, as we complained about the dullness of presentation in the 1966 television election, here at least was one break-away attempt. It was a lively commer cial. The PM, on the other hand, gave a careful caretaker presentation, he was stern and it was quite possible with the fixed camera to be mesmerised by the neat suit, the folded hands and the visual tip of the white handkerchief showing from the breast pocket. Unlike the Leader of the Opposition, the words were verbal anaesthetic; "prosperity continues"; getting on with the country's business "at home and abroad" and "keystones of our security" all helped make at tention wander. In future presentations, if the PM gets a lively script writer and Mr Whitlam sits on his performance, we may get the best of both per formers. AS with last night's warm interviews by Mike Willesee with the PM and specially Mrs Holt, on Senate campaigning, TDT and Channel 3 did a great service on Sunday night with the special repori on the devaluation (lap. Rounding up expert economic opinion from Melbourne, Sydney and Canberra, Bill Peach and Gerald Stone received, apart from expressions of surprise, some clean - cut answers to the involved affair of how it would affect us. This on the spot discussion must have eased plenty of bank books back into desk drawers and the programmers deserve the public's grati tude. npWO late reports . . . Channel Seven will have Seven Days' producer John Moses round from about nine o'clock on Saturday night, to report at intervals on the progress of the Senate. Elections. The producer will also be covering from the local studio for ATTN Seven, Syd ney. Later tonight Channel Seven hopes to run the hour long debate between the Treasurer, Mr McMahon, and thd Leader of the Opposi^ tion, Mr Whitlam, which ' was shown in Sydney on Sunday night's Seven Days Special.

24 Oct 1967 - Little comfort from the poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 24 October 1967, page 2 e rom ;vT AST weekend's / Gallup Poll result was cold comfort for : the Government with • the Senate election now just four and a ; half weeks away. It showed that support for the Liberal-Country Party coalition . had slipped a depressing eight per cent since its peak of popularity last "February and a substantial four per cent compared with ■ Mr Holt's great victory at the i polls last November. Significantly, three-quarters !of the drop in the Govern'mcnt's support has taken place since the last GalJup Poll late in July. The Government then had 49 per cent of the vote, ] whereas now it is down to 46 . per cent. The poll also showed a recovery in the DLP vote back .to its regular showing of seven per cent. Altogether, these rej suits speli danger for the Gov ernment on Senate election date — November 25. On the other side of the fence, the poll results show no improvement on the 45 per cent recorded for the ALP in ; July, despite an uncharitable "Federal Budget and the auguries of the Corio and Capricornia by-elections. Of course, the poll was taken before the announcement of the increased commitment of Australians to the "Vietnam war, and the election campaign is still to come. Now that Mr Whitlam has brought ■Labor back to electoral taws, it may well be the campaign that will make the difference for one side or the other in this vital Senate election. - This time the national election campaign will be short but unfortunately not so sweet, with the shadow 6f the Viet-, nam war looming largest amongst the issues competing for the voter's attention. The DLP has taken a threeday start with its Leader, Senator Gair, beginning his campaign in Brisbane on Monday, November 6. But the main event will begin on Thursday, November 9 when the Prime Minister fires the gun on a 30-minute national television and radio hookup. Mr Whitlam starts in Sydney the following Monday and for a hcctic fortnight the two main political chiefs will cross campaign trails around the continent through the capital cities and some of the main provincial centres in the battle for control of the Upper House. The third man of politics, the Country Party Leader, Mr McEwen, will be out of the country doing battle against threatened American import restrictions at a "protest" meeting of GATT Ministers in Geneva, But he will be here in spirit, campaigning, thanks to prerecorded television and radio speeches. Officially, both the Government and the ALP give the Vietnam war second place amongst the list of election issues which will be competing for the attention of the sixmillion-odd electors on November 25. Privately, one wonders whether they think the former Labor Leader, Arthur Calwell, might have been right last week when he dubbed the Senate poll a referendum on the Vietnam war. The announcement of the new Vietnam commitment only five weeks before th< election, boosting the Vietnam force to a higher leve even than the peak of the Korean war must force the issues of Australian involvemenl in the war even more clearlj in front of the ordinary Australian. Certainly the Government': tactics in Federal Parliameni last week made it plain thai Mr Holt is not going to lose any opportunity during the POLITICS by JONATHAN GAUL campaign to remind the people that Mr Whitlam refused to debate Vietnam in the House of Representatives . on the motion to take cote of the Prime Minister's statement announcing the extra 1,700 men for the war. In the long run, it was probably sound tactics for Mr Whitlam to dodge the issue, with his party still committed to a policy of conditional withdrawal from the war. Unless, that is, Mr Holt can make enough out of the incident during the remaining fornight of Parliamentary sittings, and during the campaign, to produce the sort of electoral rejection of Labor's Vietnam policy that he aroused last November For his part, Mr Whitlam will be plugging away at his now familiar theme that Australia — as America's only "respectable" ally in Vietnam — should be using her influence with our great and powerful friend to pause the bombing of the North and stop the continuing escalation of the war. But according to the two leaders, this is only the secondary issue. Mr Holt says the prime issue is whether the Government should have a majority in not just one, but in both the Houses of Federal Parliament, so that it can govern effectively. Mr Whitlam will be concentrating on a range of domestic issues that have been raised during the present Parliamentary session. Government waste in defence spending, particularly the F-lll bomber price, will loom large. One of his main themes will concern the role of the Senate if the electors give him a Senate majority. Mr Whitlam wants to establish at least eight standing committees of the Senate on a range of domestic subjects from repatriation to poverty. The work of these committees would be in preparation for a Labor win in the House of Representatives election in 1969. If the Vietnam issue allows him, Mr Whitlam is expected to make a lot of use of this "preparing for Government" role of the Senate if he gets an ALP majority there. It is a bigger "if' for Mr Whitlam than for Mr Holt, as both need to win five of the six States by a three-two majority on November 25 to control the Upper House in their own right. Even taking into account the slip in Government popularity, Mr Holt on paper has a better chance of achieving this, although it is only a shade of the long odds on either of them winning five States. The Government, will be happy if it wins only four States, giving it 30 seats in the Senate against its present 28. This would be enough for it to control the Senate on most major matters although it would still have to count on the two DLP Senators in a pinch. The dangers for the Government are in Queensland, where the DLP could pick up the fifth seat and in Western Australia and Tasmania where the ALP is hopeful of winning three-two. One of the factors in all this , will not be decided until next Friday when the draw for po sitions on the Senate ballot 1 paper in each State is con- ' ducted after the close of nomi- 1 nations. 1 A favourable draw for ' either the Government, the ALP or the DLP could be ' enough to tip the scales under the evenly-balanced propor- ! tion representation system of Senate voting. 1 Since 1958, the Govern- ] ment has won the best ballot ( paper draw six times, the ALP i five, the DLP four, and the s Communist Party three times. This time the Communists are likely to run candidates in l only two States. On the law of j averages, it is the DLP's turn ] for a favourable draw. j With the Gallup Poll now 1 giving the Government and the ALP almost equal popu- 3 larity, it could be the sort of l thing that will tip the Senate < scales. • <

06 Mar 1968 - More than the Presidency at stake Comeback by the Grand Old Party? Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 6 March 1968, page 2 More than the Presidency at stake Comeback by the Grand Old Party? From JOEL BUSCH, in California A RECENT Gallup Poll revealed "that for the first time in the 32-year history of scientific sampling of public opinion the Re-publican Party has be-come, in effect, a third party in American poli- tics". Out of 100 American adults, this survey showed, only 27 considered them-selves Republicans, 31 said they were independents, and 42 claimed allegiance to the Democratic Party. Yet by all other accounts there is no indication of a moribund Grand Old Party. There is no tight party orga- nisation in America with card-carrying members, and dues are paid on an entirely volun-tary basis. To say "I am a Republican", therefore, may mean something and it may not. It may mean something one election year and not the next. In any case this is what the Republican Party wishes to emphasise right now. In this election year 1968 the long-time minority party senses its chance to come in out of the cold at last. Many observers, including the venerable Walter Lippmann, agree that an his-toric turning point in Ameri- || Barry Goldwater Nelson Rockefeller || can politics may, indeed, be at hand. American parties are coali-tions of more or less power-ful interests. The party that puts together and holds to-gether a solid coalition of interlocking and complemen-tary interests is likely to domi-nate American political life until it breaks up and impor-tant elements seek their satis-faction in the other party. This breaking up is now well under way in the so-called Democratic coalition, a combination including organ-ised labour, farmers, ethnic groups, minorities, most of the intellectual community and the young voters. They were all brought to-gether by Franklin D. Roose-velt in 1932 at the height of the Depression. Today labour has risen to middle-class status, the influ-ence of the farmers has been reduced sharply, important racial and ethnic minorities have become thoroughly alien-ated. Perhaps most crucial, however, is the fact that most of the intellectual community has deserted President John-son and seems ready to bolt party lines even to prevent his re-election. Finally, there is virtually no enthusiasm for the President among young American voters. How is the Republican Party prepared to meet this challenge? There are two things a party needs most to be effective: Money and power. In both respects the GOP appears to be on the right road, namely to a broad and spreading base. No longer is there a single man or even a "group of wilful men" with a monopoly on the funds and the finesse needed to nomi-nate a President. Gone are the days when GOP finances were dominated by Wall Street and a few eastern "kingmakers" met in smoke-filled rooms to pick the party's candidate. THE influence of Wall Street has been reduced by the growth of independent finan-cial centres in the Mid-West and Far-West of the country. Moreover, the bulk of GOP funds today comes from mil-lions of small contributors in amounts of $10 and less. Tele-vision appeals to that effect have more than supplemented the canvassing of large, cor- porate donors. This has given the top can-didates a freedom seldom en-joyed before. The "fat cats" across the country now seek out the candidate in hopes of gaining a share of party power, or merely a chance to put their ideas into practice. If there is no longer any one small group of men who can claim to control party finances the same is true as far as party power is con-cerned. A number of power centres can be determined. There is first the Republi-can Party in the Senate. It has some prestige simply be-cause the US Senate is held in high regard. But the Senate Republicans are led by Everett Dirksen, a man fond of TV appearances where the image he projects was once aptly Richard Nixon Everett Dirksen || described as that of an old ruined Shakespearean actor. This year Dirksen is further hampered by having to con-duct a campaign for his own re-election. THE picture looks entirely different in the House of Representatives where, after a number of internal "coups", a new generation of Republicans has appeared under the leadership of representatives Ford and Laird, who have moved into the key positions of minority leader and chair-man of the Republican Con-ference (caucus) respectively. Fired by the personal am-bitions of these two men, the House Republicans have spawned a rash of new propo-sals based on the work of a dozen task forces sifting and analysing the problems the nation is confronted with. This activity has restored an aura of positivism to the Republi-can minority and has all but erased the image of a trucu-lent opposition, ever ready to jump on the majority party and its President without being able to suggest viable alternatives. The House Republicans are looking forward to the Repub-lican National Convention to exert maximum influence in the selection of the party's standard bearer. A third, albeit a somewhat messy, centre of power is said to be the conference of the Republican Governors of the nation. Although this group has overcome the Goldwater disaster of 1964 and has, in fact, purged the party organi-sation of Goldwater left-overs such as national chairman Dean Birch, it does not pre-sent a united front. The Gov-ernors provided the first declared presidential candi-date, George Romney, but they remain divided by regional and ideological dif-ferences as well as personal ambitions. A rapidly shifting fourth power centre is that of the presidential candidates now campaigning against each other in that amazing circus of American politics, the pri-maries. All candidates now running appear to be exceed-ingly well financed, foremost among them the perennial Richard, Nixon. Yet the real question, as suggested earlier, is whether the Republican Party will be able to forge a winning coalition of interests capable of wresting political power from the crumbling Democratic coalition. The question for the Repub-licans, therefore, should be: Who will be most likely to bring together white moder- ates, Negroes, intellectuals, the vast middle class of the country as well as the young in search of an idol? THIS question bares the dilemma of the Grand Old Party, bccause the only pro-minent Republican with a strong appeal to all these groups is Governor Nelson Rockefeller. Till last week the Governor had been playing the most accomplished game of hide-and-seek in modern American politics. If Nixon makes any kind of a showing in the primaries it would be against all rules of fair play to deny him the nomination. The party would then pin its hopes on a candi-date who is widely considered a nice enough workhorse but for whom there is absolutely no enthusiasm whatsoever. He is, and this is crucial, not the candidate for whom many Democrats would be prepared to leave their party. Many Democrats may then vote for President Johnson more or less, out of despera-tion over the lack of a real choice. But many, perhaps more, may not vote at all. There is a real chance that there will be, as Walter Lipp-mann has pointed out re-cently, "a large exodus from the political arena into some form of political nihilism — despair, drugs, withdrawal, sporadic violence, refusal to play the game, including attempts to break up and interfere with the game". Such is the opportunity and the threat facing America's minority party. More is at stake than merely regaining the Presidency.

23 Sep 1969 - Britons cooler to EEC membership Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 23 September 1969, page 6 Britons cooler to EEC membership LONDON, Monday (AAP-Reuter). — A Gallup Poll reported today a substantial decline in the number of Britons favouring Britain's entry into the European Com mon Market. The poll, published by the Daily Telegraph, said that a little more than a quarter of those questioned were in favour of British entry. This is the lowest figure ever recorded by Gallup on this subject. People were asked between September 11 and 14 whether they thought that, if an opportunity occurred for Britain to enter the market, the nation should try to join or abandon the idea. Only 26 per cent were in favour of joining compared with 57 per cent in favour in March, 1965. The pro-market figure for a poll in January, 1964, was 36 per cent. In the latest poll, 57 per cent favoured abandoning the idea compared with 22 per cent who said this in March, 1965, and 24 per cent in January, 1964. Pollsters noted that as market membership became more and more identified with Labour Party policy, Conservative and Liberal voters moved away from it. Cold feet United Press International reported yesterday that Britain, a twice spurned contender for Common Market membership, was showing signs of cold feet. Just when European leaders have agreed to a summit meeting in November that may start tearing down the blocks against Britain put up by the former French President, General de Gaulle, opposition to joining the six-nation community is mounting. The six Common Market countries are France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. . Officially, Britain's three main political groups, the governing Labour Party, the Conservatives and the Liberals, continue to support its bid to join. But a grass-roots revolt in all three is causing concern among party leaders. The Liberal Party at its annual convention at Brighton on Friday voted overwhelmingly for early talks to get Britain into the mar ket. But it did so onlv after an often angry debate in which several delegates warned of rising hostility in Britain against joining. Instead of voting blanket endorsement for market membership as in the past, the Liberals this time tacked on a series of conditions. Among them were that a future united Europe including Britain should have its own foreign and non-nuclear defence policies, a democratically elected European parliament, full economic and monetary union and sharply slashed farm prices. Fierce battles on the market issue were predicted at the Labour Party and Conservative conference, also at Brighton, in the first half of October. Labourite left-wingers and several powerful labour unions planned an all-out attack against a bid to join by the British Prime Minister, Mr Wilson. The resolution for debate called on him to cancel it. At the Conservative Party conference only eight of 32 resolutions on the Common Market submitted for debate voiced wholehearted support for joining.

13 Oct 1969 - Election 'jitters' reason shown by survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 13 October 1969, page 1 Election 'jitters' reason shown by survey By JONATHAN GAUL, Political Correspondent The latest Gallup Poll has explained the unusually severe case of election "jitters" which was so evident within the Liberal Party backbench during the last few weeks of the parliamentary session; The individual soundings of Government backbenchers in their electorates had indicated a large drift in support from the Government, despite the concessions of the August 12 Federal Budget. But there was no ready explanation for these pessimistic forecasts in economic conditions of prosperity and full employ ment. The opinion poll published on Saturday, how ever, has backed the subjective judgment ot" backbench Government politicians. with a far more reliable, but not infallible; analysis. The poll showed that the Labor Party's support had improved by an astonishing 4 per cent since a similar poll taken in August, just after the Federal Budget. The overall improvement for Labor since June is 7 per cent. This means that Labor has improved in four months from the electoral position where nobody but its most optimistic supporters gave it a chance to the p o i n t where it has a strong prospect of victory on polling day, October 25. Translating the 7 • per -ent swing to Labor to individual electorates, Labor could win 18 seats from the Liberal and Country parties, assuming that the j swing applies evenly- on October 25. Another six Government scats could be very much in the balance. Another, Riverina, depends on unusual circumstances, and another two could go to Independent Liberals. Labor needs 21' seats to be the Government. On Saturday's opinion poll results, it would go very close-, to defeating the Liberal-Country • Party coalition after. 20 years in opposition. Electoral Irfiuble The poll was taken the weekend before last, after Mr Whitlam's policy speech, but before Mr Gorton's television opening last Wednesday. Mr Whitlam has-been campaigning hard around Australia and drawing large, responsive audiences, but Mr Gorton's main campaigning efforts are still to come. There will be another poll next weekend which will show whether Mr Gorton's campaign is arresting the drift against him and the Government. Unless it does, he is in trouble for October 25. On Saturday's poll figures, Mr Gorton will need not only the preferences of the DLP, which were in doubt until early last week, but some also from the large number of Independent candidates in. the October 25 contest. It seems likely that Mr Gorton will have to abandon his low-key "stand on the record" campaign for a far more aggressive effort in the last fortnight. The actual poll figures on Saturday were: L-CP 42 per cent, ALP 45, DLP 5, No State Aid 1, Independent 2, and "No ans wer" 5. Weight of opinion. .— Page 2. Gallup Poll which said (he j Government could win the Federal election only with DLP preferences. "It doesn't square with the reports we have been getting in from the elec- I torate", he said. ;

14 Oct 1969 - Ten more worrying days for Mr Gorton Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 14 October 1969, page 2 Ten more worrying days for Mr Gorton POLITICS . . .by JONATHAN GAUL ' CAN the fate of the Government depend on a television image? The Gallup poll results published at the weekend, with their astonishing improvement in Labor support, have left Mr Gorton in the unenviable position of depending on a TV performance he has already made. The performance was his televised policy speech, prerecorded last Sunday week and broadcast last Wednesday. The big Gallup Poll swing to Labor was sampled after Mr Whitlam's campaign opening, but before Mr Gorton's. There is one more poll to conic before the election on October 25. It will show whether Mr Gorton stopped the Labor bandwaggon with a low-key speech in a TV performance which has been uni versally judged to be less than his best. 'T'HE excuciating part of it all for Mr Gorton and the Government is that not much can be done in the way of salvage. The Prime Minister may transform his tactics for the remaining 10 campaigning days ) into an aggressive last-ditch ef fort, but he will not have another opportunity for a nationwide TV audiencc and a policy speech. The Prime Minister's big TV effort has already been made. If it were as disappointing as general comment suggests, and the trend to the ALP continues, then the Government could lose the election. Of course, the Gallup Poll could be wrong, but past experience shows that its results have been well within reasonable levels of accuracy. Between 1946 and 1954 its final election predictions were all within 1 per cent of the final result. In more recent years predictions near the end of campaigns have not been so accurate as those early in the campaigns, such as the one with which Saturday's figures compare. In the last Federal election, the Senate election of 1967, the poll over-estimated the Government vote by 3 per cent, and under-estimated the Labor vote by 1 per cent and the DLP vote by 2 per cent. However, there has been no doubt about the accuracy of the poll's prediction of trends, in this case a trend of 7 per cent away from the Government since June, and 4 per cent since the August Federal Budget. The trend shows the Government is in trouble. Just how much trouble will be clearer when the results of the final poll, to be taken during next weekend, are published a few days before election day. By then it will certainly be too late for corrective action. It is one thing to note the strong trend against the Government, but it is another to explain it. The great question of the election campaign and the months preceding it is why the Liberal-Country Party coalition should suffer such a drastic decline in its popularity in the prevailing conditions of full employment and prosperity. What has happened to the famous theory of the late Labor Prime Minister, J. B. Chifley, about the most sensitive part of the voter's anatomy being the hip pocket nerve? It was a theory that was apparently re-endorsed in the 1961 Federal elections when the credit squeeze brought the Government within a whisker of defeat. This time it is not working. Perhaps this has been Mr Gorton's big mistake in the election campaign. He opted for an early election, a short campaign, mostly on TV, and a policy of standing on the Government's record combined with selective promises aimed at electorally vulnerable points — railways in South Australia, a nava! base in the West, port works at Darwin, some reform of the health scheme and so on. ""PHE first two, the early poll and TV concentration, suited Mr Gorton's style and the attempts he has made to bring a fresh appearance to the policies of a 20-year-old Government. But the policy speech and the technique of its TV presentation was a retreat from Gortonism. It robbed the Prime Minister of one of his big electoral assets, his relaxed, informal TV.style which weighed so heavily in his victory in the Liberal leadership stakes in January, 1968. Mr Gorton probably made another mistake in electoral strategy by beginning his formal campaign too late. Mr Mr Gorton Whitlam had a long week's start during which he set the campaign off firmly on domestic issues. Mr Gorton has been trying unsuccessfully to steer the campaign back on to defence and foreign policy is sues ever since. Mr Gorton has himself to blame as much as anyone else. He had been warned of discontent in the electorate long before it began to show up in the opinion polls even to the extent where pressure was applied on him to hold the election in September. During the Budget session of Federal Parliament the Liberal backbench was riddled with election jitters as private members reported the results of their own assessments back in the electorates. Furthermore, all of Labor's election promises were well known publicly from the time of the ALP Federal Conference at the end of July, except for Mr Whitlam's promises on housing interest subsidies and land prices. The Government was not taken by surprise cither by the trend against it, or by Labor's list of new challenges in domestic policy. It merely misjudged the strength of both. The election campaign itself has served to emphasise and sharpen this same pattern, a pattern of the Government's consistent under-estimation of the Labor challenge. The events of the campaign give the examples. Mr Whit lam launched it on October I at the Sydney Town Hall with a spcech that was the result of several years of policy preparation. He offered a blueprint for social change and reform. Mr Whitlam was relaxed, confident, and occasionally humorous. His telecast came Mr Whitlam over live backcd by a large audicncc of enthusiastic Labor supporters. The next night it was Mr Gorton's turn to reply at a Liberal dinner at Ashfield, Sydney. He attended several functions during the day, managed to give the Press a quick off-the-cuff preview of his speech at 6pm, was delayed half-an-hour in reaching the dinner, and interrupted it in the middle to speak without a prepared text so that reporters could catch the morning paper deadlines. TUJE result was that Mr Gor ton was on the back foot from the beginning, from the negative position of attacking Labor's promises as costly and dangerous rather than the positive position of comparing them with his own proposals which he could not make for another six days. In those six days Mr Whitlam was off around the country. At Griffith he drew 800 to a meeting compared with 42 at an opposition meeting in the same small town by the Country Party Deputy Leader, Mr Anthony. But it was the next night at New Farm in Brisbane that Mr Whitlam's campaign settled down into the pattern that has since been repeated around the suburban areas of the capital cities. The Labor Leader had a relatively young, responsive, and large audience and he spoke about the problems of affluence, health, schools, welfare, housing, sewerage, roads and so on, all tinged with a large measure of Labor's traditional concern for the opportunities of ordinary people. Mr Whitlam was funny where previously he has been witty, earthy where previously his jokes have been erudite. The pattern has been repeated around the fringes of the great cities, at Dandenong in Melbourne, Blacktown in Sydney, Glenelg in Adelaide: the same sort of audiences re sponding to the same issues." At all these meetings, for instance, the most enthusiastic response has been for the abolition of university fees. Mr Whitlam has virtually ignored defence and foreign policy. He is concentrating on the problems of suburbia. He knows that if he can win the suburban vote, particularly in Sydney and Brisbane, he has a good chance of winning the election. While Mr Whitlam's humour has been effective, his homework also has been impressive. He is never at a loss for a quote from Hansard to illu strate a conflict between Mr Gorton and one of his Ministers on how much a Labor policy is going to cost, just what the dollars and cents impact of a Government promise would be, or what a Government in a "comparable" country is doing about health or education, or you name it. These have been the elements of what have already been dubbed everything from the politics of laughter to the Whitlam bandwaggon. Slogans aside, the Labor Leader has mounted an impressive campaign with a degree of success which would have been unthinkable a few months ago cxcept to dyed-in-the-wool Labor supporters. The Government's campaign is quite a different one in the sense that it is mainly negative. It warns of the great cost of Labor's promises and the inflationary or extra tax dangers involved, and it warns that Labor will endanger the nation's security. But it ,too makes promises. "BEGINNING with Mr Gor ton's first campaign speech at Ashfield, he and his Ministers have been attempting valiantly to drive home the "where is the money coming from?" attack on Labor while presenting the Government as a model of economic safety and responsibility. It took the Treasurer, Mr McMahon, 10 days to obtain from the Treasury a detailed costing of Labor's promises, despite the fact that almost all the Labor promises have been publicly known since the end of July. In the interim, Mr Gorton made his policy speech with its own promises on health, housing, tax relief, and development. Taken together with the measures of August's electionyear Budget, plus the promises between then and the policy speech (loans for the Queensland power station and for more wheat storage), they add up to a formidable list. By this week the stage had been reached where Mr Gor- ton had claimed that Labor promises would cost $893 million a year, Mr McMahon had claimed they would cost btcween $540 and $640 million a year plus $250 million capital outlay, and Mr Whitlam had said it was impossible to calculate how much Liberal promises would cost. Mr Gorton says his pledge will cost $419.5 million plus another $228 million a year in re curring expenses. Labor insists that the Liberal costing of $138 million a year for its health scheme comprises money which the Commonwealth already is spending on health. If one accepts this, the differences in costs are not great on cither side. The net result appears to have been that the cost issue does not seem to be working as well as the Government might have hoped. It was not helped by some discrepancies, either. For instance, Mr McMahon allowed $20 million for Labor's promise to end rationing in the War Service Homes scheme, when the Prime Minister had earlier directly denied that there was any such rationing. ANOTHER puzzling - aspect was the Prime Minister's health promises. His policy speech made no mention of increased health insurance fund contributions, and the following day Mr Gorton said there should have been a supplementary statement on this subject released with his speech. As it eventually became clear, Mr Gorton's health reform to greatly increase benefits will involve about 62 per cent of fund contributors in payments of 10c a week extra and ,15c in NSW. About 30 per cent will have to pay another 25c a week, and the remainder 35c a week more. The effect of this is that a contributor will now have to pay $91 a year for full medical and intermediate hospital cover, compared with Labor's maximum $100 limit for its scheme.

14 Oct 1969 - 'Loss of 27 seats' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 14 October 1969, page 14 'Loss of 27 seats' The Government would have its majority reduced from 38 to 11 if the latest Gallup Poll, indicating a 7 per cent swing to Labor since the 1966 election, were accurate, Mr Malcolm Mackerras said on the television programme 'This Day Tonight' last night. Mr Mackerras, author of 'The 1968 Federal Redistribution', said, however, that he usually allowed for a 2 per cent inaccuracy in Australian Gallup polls. Swings of 9 per cent — which Labor would need to win power — were "not uncommon". But a nation-wide swing of that size was not likely with the relative prosperity of the economy. He did not think the poll would cause a snowballing swing of uncommitted voters to Labor.

15 Oct 1969 - BETWEEN THE LINES Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 15 October 1969, page 2 By DON AITKIN v THE Gallup poll last weekend must be a great shot in the arm for the Labor Party. Only six. months ago Labor seemed to have as much chancc of winning power as of winning first prize in the Opera House lottery. Now they are beginning cautious discussions about who is to be the next Minister for Whatever. And all in the dazed and mildly apprehensive tones of the man who still can't quite believe it. Not, of course, that Labor partisans don't believe that their party ought to win — they've known that for years. But decades of defeat, and the consistently gloomy picture of the electorate that the polls have drawn over the past 18 months have made them prepared for yet another walloping. Indeed people even had discussions about whether there would be such losses that Jim Cairns would have the numbers in a new bid for the throne. So there is a good deal of uncertainty amid the euphoria, and the ALP is right to feel uncertain. On the one hand, the signs look promising. Their own policies were better presented and more coherent than at any time in the past 20 years, and their leader excels in campaigning. The Government decided . to stand on its record, but its record is so long (no pun intended) that it has begun to lose its partisan comparison: what's the point in comparing what the Gorton Government has done with what the last Labor Government did more than 20 years ago? Given the vast growth in Australia's population, resources, and wealth, the changing nature of its problems, the constant inflation, and the virtual absence of all the political actors of the 1940s, what comparisons with the 19461949 period really make any sense? In short, it was not the time for Mr Gorton to stand pat, especially as his own image has been that of a man of decision, a man ready to deal quickly with problems as they arise — the compleat pragmatist, armed with a six-gun. lyfOREOVER, the mood lrj- of public and Press comment about the Government over the past few years has been one of constant, though muted criticism. It is a long time, I think, since editorialists and other commentators have produced sustained applause for the Government. It may be that in the past applause was relatively infrequent also, but certainly criticism of the kind wc have been observing was rare. Perhaps it is the temper of the times. In any case, the point is that the Labor Party has had, for most of the past two years, a guardedly sympathetic Press, and in the past few weeks, an overtly sympathetic one. Mr Whitlam's policy speech was generally praised, Mr Gorton's generally panned. Since the Prime Minister has deflated the Red Bogey (and all credit to him for doing so) the electorate has been in the rare position of being able to compare the rival parties, leaders, and policies without the usual accompanying threats of doom and. destruction should Labor get in. At the moment the comparison should, I think, favour Labor. Another ingredient is prosperity, a factor which is supposed to work to the benefit of the Government. The theory is that the Government is responsible for the state of the economy: when things arc good you keep it in power, when things arc bad you turn it out. The theory is based on the assumption that people do see the Government as responsible, and the evidence- presented to justify it is impressive enough: ail but one of Australia's Governments which went to the polls between 1929 and 1932, the worst years of the Depression, were defeated, and since the Depression there has been remarkably little change in the governments. Should Mr Gorton's Government be defeated on October 25 it would be a striking exception to the rule. Yet it may well be that Australians generally -do not credit the Government with our present prosperity. They may see it as the consequences of the mining boom, or as an act of God, or even as just a natural thing consequent upon Australia being the Lucky Country. In all of these cases there would seem ho great need to keep voting for the Government, nor to worry about the Opposition securing power. JJUT it may be more sophisticated than that. We have had unparalleled prosperity lor the past 10 years, and acceptance of it as a fact of-life may have bccomc widespread. Because of this very prosperity, we might argue people's expectations have risen, and they have bccomc concerned about the quality of goods and services in the public sector, the state of public education, of health, of muni cipal services, and so on. • "If we're so well oil", they might be asking, "why are the schools in such a mess?" Instead of merely looking to the Government to keep things prosperous, they may be asking it do something with the prosperity. If this be the ease, then the Government has badly • missed the mark in its campaigning strategy, while t the Opposition has not. So/ : for one reason after - an-"' other, Labor's chances at the election might seem fair indeed, and its coijfi- " dencc well justified. But the only objective test of its chances is' the Gallup poll, and the poll has just shown that in the past month or so a quarter of a million voters have changed their minds and decided to vote Labor. Now that is, in Australian terms at least, a very large movement of opinion in such a short time, particularly when very little that was dramatic happened. It is hard to reconcile with the repeated survey findings that election campaigns are not times when large-scale conversions from one party to another take place. To explain it we would need a theory that the election campaign acted as a time of decision, that all those voters who six months ago said they were going lo vote Liberal were in fact in their heart of hearts inclined to vote Labor, and decided to do so once the campaign began. This is an appealing argument, but it is one for which there is very little evidence. The safest reaction is to doubt one of the poll findings: if support for the ALP really is high now, then it wasn't as low a month ago as the polls say. If the old polls were right, then the ' one last weekend probably overstates Labor's present position. It is a choice which each of the parties makes with case: Labor has no doubt that the new polls are right, the Government believes the old. There will be another poll released on Saturday, and yet another the day before polling day. It is safe to predict that they will provide as much argument as illumination.

17 Oct 1969 - Policy views continue Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 17 October 1969, page 11 Policy views continue A Gallup poll published yesterday showed that big majorities continue to favour the ALP policies of ending the means test for pensions, cancelling the F-lll contract and signing the Nuclear Non-proliferation Treaty. Similar big majorities, however, continue to oppose the policies of ending national service and withdrawing Australian troops from Malaysia. A small majority favours withdrawal from Vietnam. 21 Oct 1969 - Five more long days Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 21 October 1969, page 2 Mr Gorton Five long more days POLITICS . 7. By JONATHAN GAUL Mr Whitlam ALTHOUGH the re cent nation-wide Gallup poll figures showing the big trend to the Labor Party were astonishing enough to provide the turning point of the election campaign against the Government, reports of the State-by-State figures in the same poll were even more sur prising. The States breakdown of the poll figures were not published, but reports about them have circulated widely amongst party officials on both sides. They report that the poll showed a 10 per cent swing against the Government in Victoria and more than 20 per cent in South Australia. Those are swings by comparison with the results of the 1966 House of Representatives election. In Victoria, according to party officials, the poll breakdown showed that Labor had improved from 35 to 45 per cent. In South Australia the Government dropped from 58 to 36 per cent, they say. If these reports are correct, and in the case of Victoria they do seem to be incredible, then the poll results indicate an even more serious position for the Government than had been thought. For such a swing in Victoria would, if borne out on election day, allow Labor to win a number of seats in Victoria and remove the barrier to its electoral suc cess. It has been a truism of Federal politics since the Labor split and the formation of the DLP that Labor cannot win a Federal election unless it wins a number of seats in Victoria. It holds only nine of the 33 Victorian electorates at present. Given the strength of the DLP in Victoria — its home territory and the source of its largest vote — plus the continuance of the left-oriented Victorian Labor Executive, it is hard to believe that the Government should have lost so much ground in that State. But if it is so, there can be no other conclusion but that the Government is in serious danger. TTHE South Australian figure is larger than expected, but it fits with the feeling on both sides that there would be a large trend back in that State from the 1966 landslide percentage for the Government. Nevertheless, the poll figure indicates a loss of six Government seats in South Australia, where the previous maximum predicted number had been four. The reports of the State breakdown figures also showed a fall in Government support in NSW, Queensland and Western Australia and a slight improvement for the Government in Tasmania. However, since that poll, events have occurred and situations developed during the election campaign which may have altered its validity. The Liberal Party argument about it is this: The poll was taken after Mr Whitlam's policy opening, but before the Prime Minister's. The Prime Minister is now hitting his stride and getting the campaign back on to the issues of defence and foreign policy and the inflationary danger of Labor's election promises. During this last crucial week of the campaign Mr Gorton's campaign is going to "peak" with saturation television propaganda throughout the country and more public meetings than he has held till now. The Liberal Party is also confident that there will be student demonstrations at the Prime Minister's public meetings at Hurstville in Sydney tonight and at Moonee Ponds in Melbourne on Thursday night. They arc just as confident that these demonstrations will weigh heavily in the Government's favour on election day next Saturday. The Liberal Party knows also that it can count on the support of the majority of newspapers this week, although a feature of the campaign till now has been the lack of really strong Press support for the Govern ment. Even that dyed-in-the-wool bastion of uncritical Liberalism, the Sydney Daily Telegraph, has been giving some prominence to the Labor as well as the Liberal campaign speech reports. The Labor Party argument about the election campaign is this: Mr Whitlam got the cam paign initiative firmly on to domestic issues with his policy opening and he also had a valuable one week start on the Prime Minister. He has concentrated much more on public meetings throughout the country, and particularly in the suburban rcd-brick belts around the great citics where most of the votes arc. He is continuing to draw large and responsive audiences sympathetic to the issues of education, health, and the improvement of urban facilities on which he is campaigning. T'HE Labor Party claims that the opinion polls confirm the trend its way and that the Prime Minister missed his big opportunity with a poor TV policy speech performance which would have strengthened the trend against the Government. The Prime Minister's campaign began to get into gear in Adelaide last week when lie faced a hostile group of students in his audience at the Adelaide Town Hall. Had it not been for the large group of students the meeting would have been poorly attended, as the local Liberal organisation had not advertised the meeting in the morning newspaper, the Advertiser, and had cancelled plans to televise the meeting. But the students provided the spur and the Prime Minister turned in a more aggressive and better constructed speech than had been heard from him in the campaign. In Launceston at a lunch the next day the Prime Minister tended 1o become long-winded again before a Liberal audience, but in Hobart that night, once again under the spur of a large group of hostile students, Mr Gorton turned in another aggressive attack on Labor, concentrating mostly on defence and mixing it with his opponents in the audience. By Friday, at the National Press Club in Canberra, Mr Gorton had improved greatly by comparison with his first week of campaigning. The newest turn in the cam paign came on Saturday morning with the publication by two major newspapers of (i statement by the former Labor Leader, Mr Arthur Calwell, of a spccch he intended to make to a rally which raised the spectre of internal brawling in the Labor Party on the eve of the election. Mr Calwell told only two newspapers of his intended speech, which claimed that a Labor Government would immediately release gaoled conscripts, release conscripts from the Army immediately, and bring the troops home from Vietnam by Christmas. Mr Calwell also encouraged young people and demonstrators to go along to political meetings (o make their views felt and heard. On this last point Mr Calwcll was directly repudiating Mr Whitlam's appeal to demonslrators to let the Prime Minister be heard at his public meetings. On the point of Vietnam withdrawal, Mr Calwell was speeding up Labor's planned withdrawal time from June 1970, to Christmas, 1969. Mr Whitlam would withdraw one battalion in December and the other two by June. But in a surprise move on Saturday the secretary of the Victorian ALP, Mr Bill Hartley, came out with a statement supporting official policy and repudiating Mr Calwell's call for demonstrations. Mr Hartley said Mr Calwell had been asked not to make his spcech. Mr Calwell did not go to the rally at which he was to have made the speech. Has Mr Calwell done serious damage to Labor's campaign? The answer may depend on Mr Calwell's electoral image, whether or not he is regarded as a spent force politically, or whether the electorate will ignore him. His was certainly an unexpected blow to Labor's high hopes. Together with the p'ossibility of student demonstrations against the Government during this last week of the campaign, it can only have boosted the Government's chances.

11 May 1970 - Training favoured Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 11 May 1970, page 8 Training favoured MELBOURNE, Sunday. — A rcccnt Gallup poll showed that electors were three-to-two in favour of compulsory military training. The poll was conducted among 1,800 people, who were reminded that one in two of all young men of 20 in Australia were called up for national servicc. Asked if , that training should continue, 55 per cent said yes, 39 per cent said no and six per cent were undecidcd. This was the third Gallup poll held on the subject since 1966. The latest poll shows that support for compulsory military training has dropped by 10 per cent since 1968. In 1968 there was 65 per cent in favour of it and 29 per cent against with six per ( ccnt undecided.

22 Mar 1971 - GALLUP POLL Many want to pack bags, leave Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 22 March 1971, page 5 GALLUP POLL Many want to pack bags, leave LONDON, Sunday (AAP-Reuter). — Two in five people living in Britain would be quite happy to pack their bags and emigrate, according to a poll published in a British Sunday news paper. The Sunday Telegraph said a rccent Gallup poll revealed that this figure was higher than in six other countries polled last month by Gallup organisa tions. Most contented with their lot seemed to be the citizens of the United States. Only 12 per cent of those interviewed want to leave. Then, in order of discontent, came the Netherlands, with 16 per cent, Sweden 18 per cent, Finland 19 per cent, West Germany 27 per cent, Uruguay 32 per cent and Britain with 41 per cent. The British survey was carried out between February 8 and 14. A representative cross-section of 1,247 adults were interviewed throughout Britain. Compared with previous polls here, the "want-togo" people were well up on the figures for July 1966 and equalled those at the time of devaluation in I November 1967. But the Sunday Express said in a front page article that fewer Britons were seeking a new life in the sun, because people were j waiting to see how thing* worked out under a Conservative Government. Inquiries about emigration to Australia dropped by 25 per cent after the | Conservatives came to power last June and wer« still on the decline. The article added that figures on emigration to the United States and Canada were also down. A big_ surprise, the article said, was the determination among redundant Rolls-Royce workers to stick to Britain.

30 Nov 1970 - The appeal of poker machines Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 30 November 1970, page 2 The appeal of poker machines By G. T. CALDWELL* JUST as West Berlin is an island city sur-rounded by hostile ter-ritory, so is Canberra an island city sur-rounded by poker machine country. How-ever there are moves afoot to change this situation in Canberra and some ACT clubs are seeking to have poker machines intro- duced. Surprisingly enough, for a period there were fruit mac-hines in the Federal Territory, but in August 1939, a police ordinance was invoked forbid-ding the ownership or use of poker machines in the ACT. ======== The real history of poker machines in Australia lies squarely within the boundaries of NSW, for it is only within this State that these gambling machines have made dramatic impact. Their significance dates from 1945, when the NSW Labor Government ini- tiated long-awaited liquor re-forms. One important clause led to the expansion of the number of the clubs from 85 to 414. From the early 1900s till 1945, there were only 85 re-gistered or licensed clubs in NSW. Fruit and poker mac-hines, although illegal, were usually tolerated by the police and government officials, apart from the occasional police raids and periodic destruction of machines. Presumably it was felt that because poker machines were being used privately in clubs away from the general public, little harm was being done. Furthermore, the clubs had come to depend on the poker machines as key sources of funds. This official tolerance of poker machines was continued from 1945 to 1954, when the number of clubs expanded five-fold. Poker machine profits were used by the clubs to build large, attractive, comfortable premises and club members, perhaps for the first time, were experiencing prompt, courteous service in their leisure drink-ing hours. MR Justice Maxwell, who is- sued the Royal Commis-sion report on liquor in 1954, recommended an increase in the number of club licences. The hotel trade was, of course, feeling the pinch. The hotelkeepers, some of whom had acquired an unfortunate reputation during the war not only for indifferences to, but exploitation of the drinking public, became alarmed by the growing expansion and afflu-ence of clubs. In 1956, the United Licen-sed Victuallers Association, now the Australian Hotels As-sociation objected successfully to the renewal of the licences of 47 clubs on the grounds that these gaming devices, the poker machines, were being used illegally. The State Government was now forced to decide whether to legalise the poker machines upon which most clubs depen-ded for the major source of their finances, or to banish the machines from the clubs. In deciding to legalise the poker machines, the State Gov-ernment gave enormous stimu-lus to the club movement, for, to borrow Lord Thomsons words from another context, the clubs had been given "a licence to print money". It is doubtful whether the clubs could have dreamed up any better way of raising fin-ances. Last year, for instance, 1457 NSW clubs made a net profit of approximately $130 million, and the State Govern-ment extracted $30 million in poker machine licence fees and supplementary poker machine taxes. It is no wonder that some ACT clubs would like to have poker machines. At the mom-ent, only punchboards are per-mitted in ACT clubs and many of them rely on them for a major part of their finances. But punchboards run a poor second to poker machines in terms of appeal to the club members. WHY is it that people like to play poker machines? In the first place there is a great deal of visual and auditory ap-peal about poker machines. Machines produced in re-cent years have been designed with dazzling neonlit facades protecting their internal elec-tronic gadgetry, and rows of them have a certain garish ap-peal. The names on the machines are suggestive of gold and gold-rush days — for instance they bear titles like Gold Award, Wild Aces, Ace of Clubs, Gold A Go-Go, Inca Gold and Show Poker. At the large NSW clubs, some of the casino atmosphere is generated in those rooms or lounges crowded with players and machines. An air of ex-citement exists, largely because of the admixture of sounds, the endless thump of poker mac-hine handles being pulled; the constant crash of coins thud-ding into the metal payout trays indicating wins to the players; the buzz of bells which on some machines accompany jackpots, and the announce-ments of "Three aces in the main bar", "Gold awards in the mixed lounge" or "Four stars in the auditorium", which blare forth over the club's public address indicating jack- pot wins. All these factors contribute to a general air of excitement although individually most players may be stoical in their reactions to wins and losses on the machines. The American sociologist, Irving Goffman, who has worked as a croupier at the Las Vegas gambling casinos has argued in his book "Where the Action Is" that people need to participate in fateful or "consequential" activity — that is to say, people need to be involved "in the action". To Goffman, gambling is the epitome, the prototype of action. For many people, the dull, routine nature of their jobs or home situation may not allow for much excitement or stimu-lation. For such people, gamb-ling on the poker machines may be an easily accessible and usually harmless way of finding excitement or a "piece of the action". One characteristic of the poker machine that may un-consciously appeal to the player is the rapidity with which a bet is made and deter-mined. In any gambling situa-tion there are four phases — firstly, one decides to place a bet and the means of distrib-uting the prize is agreed upon. Secondly, the contest or event takes place; thirdly the winner or the result of the event is announced; and finally the bets are settled. In buying a lottery ticket, one cannot expect a result for a few days. Even with betting on a horse race there may be a lapse of an hour or more be-tween the placing of the bet and settling. But poker machines have a special significance, for the four phases of a betting situa-tion can be completed within five seconds. Few other gamb-ling machines or situations offer such an incredibly rapid result. In fact, the poker machine player can get up to 13 or 14 results every minute, whereas in a day's racing, one gets only six or seven results. Malcolm Muggeridge over a decade ago noted the appeal that poker machines had for Australians. He commented that those who bet on football pools and horses, even those who played chemin-de-fer and roulette believed that the skill and knowledge gained through experience helped them to gamble with greater chances of success. But with poker machines, no skill is required (apart from those few who have mastered the "rhythm" method or "jug- gling"). Playing the poker machines is a purely mechan-ical task, and the lawyer, doc-tor or company manager has absolutely no advantage over the labourer or housewife in playing the "pokies". Within the sphere of gambling the poker machine is a great equaliser. WHEN one asks people why they play machines, a mul-titude of reasons are given, but probably the main reasons are as follows: to play for amuse-ment or relaxation, to win jackpots, or to win some money, but not necessarily jackpots. There are indications that approximately 25 per cent of club members in a large club never play or rarely play the machines. A majority would appear to play for amusement or relaxation. Those who set out to win jackpots are in many cases confirmed poker machine players, but nobody has apparently yet carried out an investigation to determine the percentage of club mem-bers who are poker machine addicts. There are some empirical results about poker machine playing, but unfortunately, none of these give accurate information about the extent of compulsive playing. In March, 1966 the Regis-tered Clubs Association com-missioned Roy Morgan's Gallup Poll organisation to conduct a survey into the poker machine playing habits of men and women in NSW metropolitan and country areas. Fifty-six per cent of males and forty-five per cent of fe-males said that they played poker machines. In answer to the question, "Have you, personally, ever lost more than you felt you can afford?", 6 per cent of men and 3 per cent of females answered in the affirmative. In the same year, the association quoted statistics from the Commonwealth Statistician indicating that the rate of gambling per head in NSW was $100 compared to Vic-toria's per capita rate of $99 where there were no poker machines. Dr Lyn Barrow, a Sydney psychologist, estimates that there may be as many as 30,000 compulsive gamblers in Sydney, but only a percentage of these would be addicted to poker machines. Tony Vinson (formerly of the University of NSW and now at the University of Syd-ney) and Arthur Robinson (design consultant, Canberra) conducted a survey of club life in Sydney commencing in 1965. Of an area probability sample of 755 Sydney adults, 182 were club members. The club members were asked how their time was mainly expen-ded at their favourite club. Twenty-three per cent said they mainly concentrated on playing poker machines, 26 per cent on drinking, 29 per cent on meeting and talking with friends, 8 per cent watch- ing entertainment, 5 per cent on dining with family and friends and 9 per cent on at-tending meetings or participat-ing in hobbies or sports. These results suggest that NSW clubs serve a range of leisure functions and are much more than gambling dens. WHILE the extent of com- pulsive poker machine gambling remains unknown, there is no doubt that some addicts do cause financial and social hardship to themselves and their families. Some poli-ticians and churchmen argue that for this reason poker machines are a social evil and should be illegal. In that event, it is likely that many of the compulsive poker machine players would turn to other legalised forms of gamb-ling. Who is it that suffers from the poker machines? Certainly the addicts and their families. . Certainly hotels, restaurants, cinemas and some retailers are not making the profits that they might if there were no poker machines in clubs. But those in building trades, furniture manufacture and en-tertainment are benefiting sub-stantially from the NSW club boom. Money lost on poker mach-ines, or on any other form of gambling, is not burnt up in thin air, it is merely redistrib- uted. In NSW poker machine profits are distributed, not to individuals (for the clubs are non-proprietary), but are spent to develop and sustain leisure activity within the clubs and club activity in that State has, and is, bringing about a leisure revolution. * The author is a research scholar In the School of Social Sciences of the Australian Na-tional University. He is making a three-year study of regis-tered clubs in NSW as leisure institutions.

12 Oct 1970 - Poll result disputed Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 12 October 1970, page 3 Poll result disputed MELBOURNE, Sunday. — The result of a Gallup poll on whether marihuana should be legalised was due to the public having been mis-informed about the drug, a Labour MHR said today. Dr Moss Cass (Lab, Vic) said this was the only explanation for the poll's result, in which 84 per cent of the Aus-tralians questioned said they thought the drug should not be legalised. The Gallup poll also showed 9 per cent thought it should be made legal and 7 per cent were undecided. Dr Pass said the main reasons given for opposing legalisation had been, "It's harmful to health", "It's a drug", and, "Leads to stronger drugs". Dr Cass, who gave evidence to the Senate Committee inquiring into drugs in Australia, said none of these beliefs was true. Every official inquiry into marihuana had found that its long-term use had had no harmful effects. The problem was that in most Western countries the use of marihuana brought people into contact with the underworld which wanted to push hard drugs. 'There is no other basis for progres-sion from marihuana to other drugs", he said. People in the 21-29 age group were the keenest on legalisation, but of those only 14 per cent were in favour of legalisation. Those who wanted legalisa-tion usually argued it was less dangerous than alcohol or tobacco. The proportion favouring legalisation was up by 2 per cent and this could br a slight shift in opinion, or merely a chance difference, inherent in "sampling referendums", the poll said.
