26 Apr 1980 - Games boycott opposed: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 26 April 1980, page 3 SYDNEY: Fifty-three per cent of Australians oppose a boycott of the Olympic Games in Moscow, according to the latest Gallup Poll published in The Sun, Sydney, yesterday. Forty-one per cent were in favour of a boycott and 6 per cent are undecided. The number of people opposing a boycott has risen 7 per cent since a similar poll in February. KATOOMBA: The NSW Young Liberals backed the Federal Government's move to boycott the Olympic Games at their State convention in Katoomba yesterday. PORT MORESBY, Friday (AAZP). — The Papua New Guinea Government has endorsed the decision by the previous Somare Government to boycott the 1980 Moscow Games. MELBOURNE: The Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, said on Thursday that there was now an effective boycott of the Games. The West German Government's decision to call on that country's athletes to stay away from the Games affected this.

24 Oct 1979 - Fresh points on cycle paths Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 24 October 1979, page 25 Fresh points on cycle CjALLUP polls may be all very well for those interested in predicting election results but, to my mind, the best way of finding out what people are really thinking is to invite readers of The Canberra Times to express their opinions. Your replies to my request for suggestions re cyclc paths has brought forth not only what might be called "the usual pros and cons", but some of you have raised points that I was totally unaware of, in spite of the fact that I thought I was conversant with most aspects of the matter. A. C. of Holder, for instance, while acknowledging that recreational cyclc paths that meander through the bush are fine for families that want to spend some part of the weekend away from traffic, points out that if an elderly person riding along them were to suffer a heart attack, it might be some time before he was discovered, and even then, it might be difficult, if not impossible to get an ambulance to him. A.C. also raises another point, and a very disturbing one it is, too. Cycle paths or, more accurately, the bush surrounding them, can be the haunt of perverts and molesters, and although 1 do not want to be in any way alarmist, I hope that parents of young children who arc reading this think twice before allowing their youngsters to ride unaccompanied along any paths that wander through the bush. On the other hand, G.P. of Mawson, far from finding cycle paths too isolated, is annoyed at the number of cars that he finds on them. These, he says, are usually service vehicles but, as he points out, they rarely seem to be servicing the cycle paths themselves. ' Which reminds me that almost every letter complains about the broken glass, empty cans etc, that litter the paths. Most people think that the paths ought to be serviced more often (with more service vehicles to get in the way?), but only D.T. of Fisher gets to the heart of the problem — that it would not be necessary to clear away litter and rubbish if the people of Canberra did not put it there in the first place. However,! feel S.R. of Turner has a point when she suggests that rubbish bins should be placed where cyclists have to slow down or stop, i.e. where cycle paths meet roads — so that "breakfast-on-the-bike cyclists don't have to carry soggy apple cores for miles and miles". Are you making notes, NCDC? The suggestion that cycle lanes be marked on present through-roads evoked mixed reactions. Most people were hesitant about expressing an opinion and seemed to feel that they might be all right, providing the idea worked — which really meant "provided the motorist kept out of them". On the topic of motorists, there was universal condemnation of the attitude of the Canberra driver. P.M. of Curtin writes, "Our motorists are not sufficiently educated and/or disciplined", while D.H. of Fisher has this to say, "My fundamental complaint relates to the attitude and behaviour of Canberra drivers who appear to have little understanding of the needs and rights of cyclists". M. and C.H. of Giralang go further, "Motorists take no notice of me, and in fact deliberately drive close to me to push me off into the gravel or gutter". P.M. of Curtin refers to what he calls "the Public Service Grand Prix", but it is one thing to isolate a problem, and quite another to suggest a solution to it. 1 have a shrewd suspicion that this attitude on the part of Canberra motorists has only come about since the introduction of freeways, which lead the driver to cxpect that every road has been built for his sole use, but even if I am right, the authorities arc unlikely to plough up all their lovely new roads. 1 am fairly sure, however, that this attitude will change only when the motorist has become accustomed to sharing the road with cyclists, and this time, according to most readers, is not too far off, since "an increasing number of friends (all in the late 20s or early 30s) have taken up cycling as a positive gesture towards better health and energy conserva tion". In America, by the way, sales of bikes have outnumbered sales of cars for the past two years, but unfortunately, as one writer comments regretfully, Americans are a race of bike owners, but not bike users. Quite a few readers feel that they would only use cycle lanes on roads if they were separated from the main traffic stream by a narrow median strip or kerb (as already exists near Parliament House), but the real problem is that as hardly anybody has any experience of such lanes, nobody really knows what the effect would be. Two readers suggest that our authorities should have a good look at Holland where unprotected lanes are universal. As R.F.P. of Yarralumla points out, our roads are much wider and much less congested than those in Europe, and it should therefore be a comparatively simple matter to mark off a cycle lane which will not restrict the motorist in any way. My own suggestion, for what it is worth, is that a scction of one of our wide through-roads be selected as a trial horse, and that a "cyclists only" lane be clearly marked on it. It docs not appear to be generally rccognised that even if a bush path could be constructed so that it was the same length as the main road, it would still be slower to use, as the road has priority over side roads, whereas the bush path user has to give way every lime he comes to a street. Of course, some may feel as J.H. of Griffith does — that "It is-; a good deal more pleasant to be separated from the inccssant rush of traffic and the inevitable fumes". J.H. also compares communing here with his experiences in Melbourne — to the lattcr's great disadvantage — while A.D. of Cam perdown, NSW, writes "Cycle paths " arc Great! 1 wish the Sydney people ' ■ would do something on these lines for the Sydney cyclists, as we have,, no other place to ride but on the roads". And just in case anybody thinks that the Canberra cyclist is an un- • grateful complaining whinger, let ; me finish with a few more quota tions. "1 have travelled a lot, and always thought that Newcastle was the City . of Cycles, but now think that New-, castle has lost its crown to Can- ■ bcrra". "Canberra leads the way for the cyclist in making cyclc paths". . "I extend our sincere thanks to all. those who have worked and planned for the development of cyclc paths throughout Canberra. We are in deed a fortunate community to have , any, let alone so many. May the good . work continue". NCDC: Take a bow!

02 Nov 1988 - Election a 'close call' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 2 November 1988, page 2 Election a 'close call' SYDNEY: Preference voles would have decided the outcome of a federal election if it had been held in the aftermath of the Oxley by-election, according to a poll published in today's Bulletin. Labor retained the Oxley seat vacated by the Governor-General designate, Mr Hayden — despite a 12 per cent swing against it. A Morgan Gallup poll found the Liberal-National Party Coalition 2 per cent ahead of the ALP. The survey was taken on the weekends between October 15 and 16 and October 22 and 23 and surveyed 2988 electors. It also found the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, continued to hold the lead in popularity stakes — up a point to 56 per cent — against the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, whose rating remained unchanged at 29 per cent.

24 Nov 1988 - Minister refuses permission for approval Suit threat over sex-shop delay Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 24 November 1988, page 5 Minister refuses permission for approval By GRAHAM DOWNIE Legal action is being consid-ered because of delays to plan approvals by the ACT Admin-istration for an adult shop at 37 Northbourne Avenue, Civ-ic. The directors of West Savoy Theatres Pty Ltd issued a statement yesterday saying that the company's efforts to establish a "mature book and video shop" were being slowed by the Administration and the min-ister responsible for the ACT, Clyde Holding. The delay in plan approval was causing the company to lose sub-stantial amounts of money and legal action was being considered to re-cover its losses from the appropriate authorities. Partitioning plans for the shop had been lodged with the Adminis-tration's building section but, de spite the payment of a special fee to expedite their approval, the com-pany had waited several weeks. Yes-terday the company had been advised that Mr Holding had re-fused permission for the approval. "The reasons for this decision are not known but it is understood that they do not relate to structural mat-ters," the directors said. The building controller in the ACT Administration, Leigh Palm-er, said plans had been lodged on October 5 but amended plans had been lodged on November 8. The plans had been referred to the Ad-ministration's leasing section for its approval. The director for lease policy and compliance, Stuart Sankey, said that legal advice had been sought on the company's original plans and this had caused some delay. Yesterday the company had been advised that the minister had de-clined to approve the proposal. Mr Sankey said this had been in accordance with Mr Holding's in-struction, issued this week, that planning and lease approvals for sex shops be deferred until he had re-ceived a report on the location of sex shops in Canberra and on pow-ers available to control them. Mr Sankey understood that yes-terday's decision did not necessarily mean a complete rejection of the company's application. In its statement, the company questioned whether it was appropri-ate for the minister to become in-volved in matters concerning perceived morality. Four Morgan Gallup polls, com-missioned by the industry, had "conclusively ascertained" that more than 60 per cent of people did not oppose the establishment of such shops. The Northbourne Avenue shop, when operational, would sell mat-ure publications and videos, all of which had been vetted by govern-ment officers and permitted for im-port and sale: The company believed that the proposed location would comply with zoning requirements in any other Australian capital city and would be preferred, being distant from residential areas. The area was largely used for night clubs and other adult venues and was not fre-quented by minors.

30 Nov 1988 - Poll shows Howard popularity still low Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 30 November 1988, page 2 Poll shows Howard popularity still low SYDNEY: The Federal Leader of the Opposition, John Howard, would have led his party to another defeat against Labor had an election been called in mid November, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The survey of 2740 voters published in The Bulletin yesterday put support for the ALP at 47 per cent, up three points in a fortnight, with the Liberals down three points at 43 per cent. Mr Howard was the preferred Prime Minister for just 18 per cent, down one point, while the preference rating for the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, was a steady 68 per cent. Mr Hawke also gained another two points in the approval ratings, with 58 per cent of the population now believing he is doing a good job. However, the survey showed that 59 per cent of voters disapprove of the way Mr Howard is handling his job as Opposition Leader.

06 Nov 1972 - GALLUP POLL Labor Party has narrow lead Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 6 November 1972, page 8 GALLUP POLL Labor Party has narrow lead If a Federal election had been held in the past fortnight, the Australian Labor Party would probably have won with a small majority, the Gallup Poll says. In the last two weekends, 1,830 electors were' interviewed throughout all of the 126 Federal electorates except the Northern Territory. All except 4% marked ballot papers for the party which would now receive their first preference. Of. the ballots, 47% were for the ALP, an increase of 1% on similar Gallup Polls in August and September, and the same as at the last Federal election for the House of Representatives in 1969. The Liberal - Country Party coalition received 42%, 3% less than the last Gallup Poll in September and 1 % less than at the election in 1969. The Democratic Labor Party, with 5%, .is unchanged since September, but 1% down on the 1969 election. Minor parties and independents at 6% are 2% up on, both the September Gallup Poll and the 1969 election. Because many ALP voters . are concentrated in "safe" seats, the ALP probably needs more than 50% of the votes to win. . However, of the 6% for "others", 4% are for the Australia Party and candidates from the Defence of Government Schools group, both of which have said their second preferences will go to the ALP. It seems, therefore, that if an election had been held in the last fortnight, the ,ALP would probably have received more than 50% of the first and second preferences for the first time since _ the DLP was established in 1955. 30 Nov 1972 - Most are against foreign control Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 30 November 1972, page 17 Most are against foreign control , At least seven out of 10 Australians would not allow overseas in vestors to buy control, of Australian com panies, the Gallup Poll finds. : For the third time since 1968, an Australia-wide cross-section of more than 2,000 people has been asked: ?; "In your opinion, should British, American and other foreign investors be allowed to buy any number of shares in Australian companies and gain control of them, or should there be a limit?" The following table shows that opinion has been steadfast and that nine out of 10 people now say "there should be a limit on foreign buying of shares": 1968 1972 Latest Oct % J une % % Limit 88 88 91 No limit 8 6 6 JJndecided 4 6 3 On this question there is exceptional uniformity of opinion in all major population groups. The 91% who said foreign buying of Australian shares should be limited were asked: "Of the shares in an Australian company, what is the biggest percentage you would allow non-Australians to own?" Twelve per cent would not allow more than 20%, 20% would allow 20-29%, 13% would allow 30-39%, 10% would allow 40-44%, 15% would allow 45-49%, 7% would allow 50% or more, and 14% could not give a limit. 10 Jul 1975 - 'Selling comrades down river' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 10 July 1975, page 3 "Selling comrades down river" The anti-Labor parties were alternately aghast and delighted by the switch. But only the Liberal Movement leader, Mr Robin Millhouse, was swift and decisive enough to take deadly advantage of it. Within hours, his voice was spitting its response on all the local air waves: "Mr Dunstan is now prepared to sell down the river his Federal political brothers — his comrades and brothers and fellow members of the Labor Party in Canberra, the same party to which he belongs himself. "He says it hurts him to be linked with the Canberra loans affair. Well, it hurts him because what's being said is true. And what he is now doing is running out on his mates. "It shows that when he is in trouble, he will sell any- one down the river — he'll let anyone down. What I want to know is how he will let all South Australians down next time he gets him- self into trouble". That is the backdrop to the now frantic last-minute struggle to save the Dunstan Government from extinction by the tidal waves of fear and confusion rolling across the State after the volcanic upheaval in Canberra and the stunning impact of the Labor disaster in Bass. No "expert" political opinions by "observers", "usually reliable sources", academics, journalists, or unnamed party spokesmen are now worth much as a guide to the final result. The situation is too fluid, too changing, too vulnerable to more fall-out from the battle now at its climax in Canberra and to the un- precedented avalanche of advertising, debate and talk- back swamping the media night and day. Advertising campaign The two principal daily newspapers in Adelaide are now carrying an estimated $10,000 to $15,000 worth of advertising a day on the subject. At least the same amount of money is being spent on radio and television. The general consensus is that Labor's paid publicity is beating that of its oppo- nents into a pulp. One of the best of the Labor advertisements is a three-minute television com-mercial in which the Pre-mier himself takes the view- er right into the Cabinet room in the State Admini- stration Building in Victoria Square. He seats himself comfortably at the head of the table around which sit his colleagues; introduces each in turn, explains what they are doing and praises their achievements. Every 15 of 20 seconds, a picture of a massive building, a school, a factory, a busy harvesting scene on a farm, or a peaceful rural setting is flashed on screen to illus-trate the work of the Cabi-net minister under dis-cussions. Dunstan's splendidly modulated voice annotates the whole smooth program. He concludes, with a mel- ting smile, "These men around me are Australia's best, most united team of Cabinet Ministers. They are doing great things for YOU, and I'm sure you want them to go on doing such work". Confrontation on TV All day and most of the night, the campaign ebbs and flows in a gigantic me- lange of talk and music and slogan and debate inter- mixed with commercials for paint, food, clothing, liquor, cars, washing machines, the Menzies Scholarship and — "for those who care abut their loved ones" — a uniquely equipped firm of funeral directors who will "discuss sensitively and sensibly the way they can help you in ber- eavement . . ." Last night, the Premier and his principal opponent, the Liberal leader Dr East- ick, came face to face on ABC television for one of their rare personal con- frontations. It was not a success, though not a disaster, for Dr Eastick. He was no match for his brilliant, smooth-talking rival, and was not helped when the ABC compere, Nigel Starck, asked him to-ward the end of the seg- ment, "Dr Eastick, do you sometimes yearn a little wistfully for the days when you were Mayor of Gawler and a leader of the Boy Scout movement . . .?" 'Incomplete' disaster "Was he a complete dis- aster?" asked one anxious Liberal worker who missed the program, "No", mourned her friend. "An in- complete one!" Mr Dunstan is getting the better of the radio cam- paign. Even Liberal Party monitors say that the callers on talk-back are pre- ponderantly Dunstan's way. A Scottish woman who rang to read a poem she had written emotionally lauding him in the style of Robbie Burns. Another woman said Dr Eastick had "sat on last night's TV program like a big sulky child with his lips puffed out and holding back the tears as the Pre- mier hit him". And then, herself on the brink of tears, she said she was a Catholic with six children and she wouldn't have a bar of the Labor Party if she thought all the smears about Labor and communism were true. "But I know what Labor has done for us", she cried. "I have seen the schools go up in this district and all the other things Mr Dun- stan has done for us and I pray to God he gets back". One of the full-page Labor advertisements in today's issue of The Ad- vertiser is signed by 500 prominent supporters in- cluding Johnny Farnham, Sir Robert Helpmann, Rob-ert Morley, Peter Scul- thorpe, Patrick White, David Williamson, Frank Thring and many other writers, art-ists, musicians and academ-ics. 'Cultural centre' "The Dunstan Govern- ment has wisely and directly funded the arts through individual, community, company and educational grants", it says. And Roy Dotrice adds: "In my opin- ion Don Dunstan has done more than any other politi- cian I have met anywhere in the world to promote the arts and has made Adelaide the cultural centre of the Southern Hemisphere". But a few pages further on, a Mr Keith Frost of the hills suburb of Belair has taken a page on behalf of unnamed friends to write an open letter to the people of South Australia: "Are we barmy?" he asks. "Or do a lot of you feel the same? If you look at the bloody mess we're in you can't say it's not poor old Donny's fault, it's all Whitlams. The fact is most of the strife we're in is the result of all this Socialism, and Donny D's Labor Party has exactly the same Socialist aims as Whit- lam's Labor Party. "I love South Australia and I and my friends are deeply and non-party con-cerned for what is happen- ing to it. Don't you want, as my kids say, to do your own thing any more? No more being a mechanic be- cause you love engines as well as the pay? No more building a house well be- cause it's just a bit more than laying bricks. . . . At all events, we're voting in this State election against Socialism. It'll be too late in 1978". But regardless of the last- minute publicity and emotions, the pre-election day polls are pointing in only one direction. From being an odds-on favourite a fortnight ago, Dunstan and his Government are clearly fighting for their lives. A Roy Morgan poll conducted on the Liberal Party says there was a swing of 11 per cent against Labor even before the Cairns affair blew up. It was a telephone poll of only 350 people. Dunstan says. "That sort of poll would be clearly biased against my party". But the Liberals say another poll of 800 people conducted by them independently in the past fortnight gives much the same results. Labour it- self admits to a possible swing of 5 to 6 per cent — not enough to put it out. An average 9 or 10 per cent would have to occur to do that. Finally, the independent ANOP research organi- sation revealed last night that a poll it conducted in four Adelaide subdivisions last weekend showed a large 15 per cent of voters unde-cided as to their voting in- tentions only a week before polling day. In last Weekend's survey, ANOP reinterviewed 320 to 400 voters whom it also interviewed last year in the metropolitan seats of Gilles East, Hanson East, Nor- wood and Semaphore. The ANOP survey in December last year gave Labor 58 per cent of the vote, the Liber- als 24 per cent, the Liberal Movement 13 per cent, others 3 per cent and unde- cided 2 per cent. 'Unprecedented indecision' But last weekend, Labor received only 44 per cent, the Liberals 24 per cent, LM 16 per cent, others 1 per cent and undecided 15 per cent. The managing director of ANOP, Mr R. Cameron, said, "In my experience as a political pollster the extent of indecision regarding vot-ing intention is quite un- precedented in elections, particularly State elections". It was the ANOP polls which decided members of the Dunstan Government and their campaign officials to switch tactics and launched Mr Dunstan's dra-matic statement to the elec- torate today: "I think the Federal Government has made a number of mistakes and I don't want to be sad- dled with them. I have been quite frank about that. The mistakes which have been made are serious and real. People have been worried about this". So there it all is. And just to emphasise the fact that it is no longer exclusively a South Australian election, the Premiers of Queensland, NSW and Western Australia are all campaigning here simultaneously with the local Liberals, Liberal Movement and Country Party to try to convince South Australians that their role on Saturday will be even more vital to Australia than that of the voters of Bass a fortnight ago. 29 Sep 1971 - The trouble with polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 29 September 1971, page 2 The trouble with polls By DON AITKIN* THE weekend's Gallup Poll set me wonder- ing again about what is going on out there in the mind of the Great Electorate (a distant rel-ative of the Great Pump-kin, he comes once every three years, in-stead of once a year). For the electorate seems to be behaving in a very mysterious fashion. Let us look first at the stand-ing of the parties. Labor col-lected 47 per cent of the vote in 1969, and according to the Gallup Poll it has been hover-ing around the low forties most of this year. But since a poll early in August it has picked up 5 per cent to rest for the moment at 46 per cent, which is a good position to challenge from, given that it needs 50 per cent to win. The Government, which won only 43 per cent in 1969 and needed many DLP and other preferences to hold on to office, has been hovering around the mid-forties, and is currently at 45 per cent. The DLP is at 7 per cent, and Independents and others at 2 per cent. If you are the Prime Minis-ter the poll might be a mildly pleasant surprise. The Liberal Party has had many more downs than ups this year, and the Country Party has the spectre of the rural collapse just over its shoulder. The reasonable man might have been looking for signs of electoral retribution; but they are hard to find. Mr McMahon need not worry unduly about Labor's small lead while his own coalition stays up in the mid-forties, for Labor will not get much change out of DLP preferences, and it never does very well out of Independent and minor party supporters either. You can award some 6 per cent extra at least to the coalition, and that is enough to keep it in power. ON the other hand, if the Prime Minister wants to be alarmed by the figures there is plenty to be anxious about. The DLP is probably closer to 6 per cent than 7 per cent. Then there is the pro-Labor trend. It is not, I agree, a very long trend; but it is there. The next Gallup Poll will tell us whether there is any force to it. And there are good specula-tive reasons for supposing that there might be a trend away from the Government that has only just developed. When Ted St John began his one-man campaign to bring down Mr Gorton in 1969 many of us looked at the polls to see what effect all these juicy non-revelations had had on the electorate. At the time the polls stayed rock-steady. Six months later, however, and for no obvious reason, the Government's posi-tion began to slip. Labor made two dramatic gains and went on to pile up a very creditable 47 per cent in the elections. One possible implication of those events was that a time lag of some six months operated between a political "crisis" and its effect on the electorate. It worked, we argued, something like this: When a crisis happens, nearly everybody hears about it. But not very many, know what it means; most people need to have it evaluated for them. According to the famous "two-step" theory of political influence, this evaluation is done by opinion leaders, people among one's circle of friends and acquaintances whose opinions are taken notice of. So far, so good. Now we know from other evidence that people are re-luctant to change their vote; it represents a set of basic, long-established loyalties as well as a particular decision to support a certain candidate at a ccrtain election. So it is un-likely that people will change their party loyalty immediately following a political crisis, or even after an opinion leader has pronounced his verdict on the whole affair. IN fact the most likely course of events is that those affected by the crisis will mull over it all for some time, during which they will be more than usually alert to casual conversations, scraps of comment, news broadcasts, television programs and the like. During this period their loyalty to their former party is slowly eroded, and there will come a point when they realise that they will no longer vote for it. Such a process will happen faster for some people than for others, but it is quite possible that a period of months could be involved. Mr McMahon This whole argument is a plausible one, especially now that television has given politics an ambience of high drama (like 'The Plane-makers', or 'Dynasty'). It is possible, then, that the second downfall of Jolly John has deeply disturbed many erstwhile Liberals, who are in process of becoming future Labor voters (at least for 1972). And that the polls have shown only the beginning of this movement. The next poll will see it in full force. This is perhaps the way that Mr Whitlam has interpreted the polls, and if so, good luck to him. But no doubt he and Mr McMahon will both have puzzled over two other regular poll soundings, their own re-spective standings in the eyes of the public. Mr McMahon got some of his support within the Liberal Party because of Mr Gorton's calamitous slide down the popularity charts. In April 1969 Mr Gorton was ap-proved of by nearly two voters Mr Gorton in three. By October in that year, just before the elections, this approval was felt by just over two in five, and it stayed at about that level thereafter. Mr McMahon's election as leader was followed by a jump in the public standing of the Liberal leader: from about 44 per cent (Mr Gorton) to 55 per cent (Mr McMahon). It was not the world's longest honey-moon. In June he had the sup-port of 53 per cent, on August 7 only 44 per cent, and a week later, just after the Budget, a risible 37 per cent. If Mr McMahon's election was intended to replace Mr Gorton by a man who would attract wider support among the electorate, it can only be said that so far the plan has not worked. Yet if you think that all this must have worked to Mr Whit- lam's advantage you will have to take account of the cor-responding decline in Mr Whitlam's own standing. More than two years ago, in April 1969, Mr Whitlam was ap-proved of by 54 per cent of all voters. Since then he has gone almost steadily downhill. At the last count he had the sup-port of only 38 per cent, just one per cent more than the Prime Minister. What does it all mean? The simplest explanation is that the electorate is not particularly enchanted with either leader. They are equally ineffective in winning voters to their parties' competing causes. This sug-gests that the performance of the Government over the next 12 months, rather than the appeal of the party leaders, is likely to be the critical factor in determining the outcome of the next election. If the Government looks on top of things, it is likely that Mr McMahon's standing will rise. If it does not, and the Opposition begins to belt it around the field, then Mr Whitlam's standing will rise. He who picks the winner must keep his eyes not just on the horse, but the horse plus the jockey plus the state of the track. At this distance it's any one's race. * This is Dr Aitkin's last Between the Lines. Dr Aitkin is leaving Canberra to take up an appointment as Professor of Politics at Mac- quarie University,

29 May 1973 - Pera Labor likely to change the Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 29 May 1973, page 2 ££lbor likely to change the voting system •POjJTICS By DAVID SOLOMON The latest Gallup poll probably puts the finishing touches to a new Labor electoral plank: as from the July Federal Conference the Labor Party is likely to have a policy of first-past-thepost voting, and optional preferential voting. The policy could not be implemented before the next Federal elections, partly because Mr Whitlam gave an undertaking before the last elections that it would not be, and partly because such a change in the voting, system could not get through t^e Senate. However, after a double dissolution later this year, Labor could try to change the system if it won a majority in both Houses of Parliament. The fear that this cotild indeed occur is one of the factors being pushed by Country Party and DLP leaders who want their parties to amalgamate so that it might be prevented. Labor policy on the voting system at present is in limbo. L'p until the last Federal Conference, the ALP favoured a first-past-the-post system whereby voters mark the ballot papers only in one place, for the person they wish to win, and the candidate with the largest number of votes, whether he has more than 50% of the votes or not, is elected. At the Launceston conference, however, the Labor Party decided to refer the whole question to the Federal Executive for a special report, and the executive in turn referred the matter to a special committee. Within the Labor Party the most significant development since has been Mr Whitlam's espousal of optional preferential voting. Under this system, voters could mark as many preferences as they liked — from just a simple' "x" against one name, (ie, first-past-thepost method of voting) to the numbering of as many preferences as the voter felt he wanted to give. This would almost certainly cut down on the number of informal votes by people who fail to put numbers in some squares (some feel that by putting a number against the person they do not want to win, they are somehow having to vole for him) and those who simply mark a first preference. In counting the ballots, preferences would be distributed for as long as there were preferences marked. The argument that informal voting would be reduced was ad vanced in February by the Minister for Services and Property, Mr Daly. When Mr Whitlam raised the first-past-the-post voting issue, in the week before the last elections, he attacked the idea that the ALP would automatically lose votes if it adopted the policy. "This is no longer an ogre", he said. "People no longer believe it is reasonable that you can vote for some people who cannot get in and then have a vote of undiminished value for somebody else". Mr Whitlam's ' remarks came a month after the publication of a Gallup poll which suggested he might, be right. According to the poll, 39% favoured the current system of preferential voting, but 54% favoured first-past-the-post, while the remaining 7% were undecided. The subject was raised again by the Gallup poll this month, but it altered its question to take in Mr Whitlam's and Mr Daly's proposal for optional preferential voting. This time the result was compulsory preferential 31%, optional preferential 27% and lirst-past-the-post 35%. There are several ways of interpreting the result. It can be said that 58% of people want some kind of preferential voting system, for example. However, the interpretation which will be favoured in ALP circics is that the number of people supporting the present system of preferential voting is only 31%, and this is a significant 8% less than was measured by the poll seven months ago. Now over 60% favour either first-past-thepost or optional preferential, and of course, first-past-thepost is a form of preferential voting. A 62% level of support for a change in the present system is a very high measure of dissatisfaction, and provides Mr Whitlam with solid backing for his argument that the people are unlikely to be terrified by a proposal to change the voting system. Within the ALP, the first moves will be taken soon by the electoral committee established by the Federal Executive. Chaired by the retiring Federal President, Mr Tom Burns, its members include the Minister responsible for electoral matters, Mr Daly, plus Mr Whitlani. The other members are Senator Murphy, the Attorney-General; Mr Cope, the Speaker; Mr Dunstan, the Premier of South Australia, and his Attorney-General. Mr King; and Senator O'Byrne, the Labor Senate Whip. It is expected to meet within the next few weeks, and the likelihood is that it will come out with a proposal for optional preferential voting (including first-past-the-post, for those who nominate just one preference). The proposal will not have an easy time getting through the Federal Conference, however, as it will come up against a completely different scheme, as well as having to face the disapproval of those who do not wish to rock the boat (or vote). There is expected to be considerable support at the Federal Conference for a system of proportional representation being adopted for the Lower House, adapted from the system now used in the Senate elections. The scheme has considerable support in Victorian ALP circles. It envisages that each State would be broken up into a number of electorates, each electing five or seven MPs by a proportional representation method. Its proponents say that the system helps reduce the possibility of gerrymanders, and gives the ALP better use of votes which are at present "locked" up in its safe seals. Under this scheme, Labor would have won the 1961 election as well as the 1972 election, presuming that people voted the same way for the PR system as they did for the preferential voting system actually used. The trouble is that the system would also help minor parties to be elected to Parliament, and hence help them to survive the rigours of electoral competition. The DLP would certainly gain some representation, and the Australia Party probably would also. And there is a strong prejudice in the ALP against any measure which helps the survival of small parties. There is also something of a prejudice against proportional representation. There are many in the ALP who remember that it was Arthur Cahvell who was responsible for the introduction of proportional representation into the Senate elections, and under that system the ALP has almost no hope of ever gainins a working majority in that Chamber. The ALP at that stage miscalculated the possible benefits of changing the system, and that could happen again. It is therefore not a valid argument that if the Labor Party adopts a new system of voting, such as optional preferential, it will necessarily benefit from it. However, the thinking of people like Mr Whitlam and Mr Daly is that the Labor Party would indeed benefit from a change, particularly when that change is taken in conjunction with measures which Mr Daly will be bringing forward shortly to change the Electoral Act, such as providing that names of parties should be included on ballot papers. The Labor Party almost ccrtainly loses more votes than the Liberals through its nominal supporters making simple mistakes with their ballot papers and having them lost as informal votes. The parties which would suffer most from the abolition of compulsory preferential voting would be the DLP, Australia Party and other small groups, which depend on the argument that a vote which gives them a first preference is not "wasted" because it is fully transferred on to other groups if necessary. However, DLP voters show such strong loyalty to their how-to-vote cards (over 90% generally) that the DLP would probably not suffer too greatly in an optional preferential system (though the way things are going, it cannot afford to lose any votes at all). Australia Party voters are presumed to be mainly middle class and reasonably intelligent and capable of operating within a new system such as optional preferential. What the new system would do is help reduce the number of three-cornered battles between Liberal, Labor and Country Party. Where the two major non-Labor parties were scared that they might lose seats contested in this way, it would be a matter of bluff as to which survived. Some of those in the Country Party who seek amalgamation with the DLP do so on the basis that the additional DLP sup port would help them win in such situations and persuade the Liberals not to take them on. J But no one can be sure £ actly what would happB ■ Once the rules of the gaBa are changed, the voters miyit look at the parties in a slightly different way. Besides, there will be no proof, one way or the other, unless the Federal Conference does adopt a new policy, and the Labor Party can manage to get enabling legislation through both Houses of Parliament. As to the latter, while Mr Whitlam has stated no change will be brought in before the next elections, there is no reason why legislation which authorises a new voting system to come into force, say, after 1975, could not be introduced into the present Parliament, and added to the list of Bills rejected by the Senate and made the subject of doubledissolution proceedings. After a double dissolution, if the Labor Party won its way back in the House, but still could not quite control the Senate, it would be able to have all the double-dissolution Bills passed by means of a joint silting of both Houses. To date no such sittings have been held, because double dissolutions have resolved the situation. But the ALP may have to consider such steps as it comes to accept that no matter what it does, getting a majority in the Senate could be next to impos sible. Guess what? I've just declared you a disaster area.

30 Jun 1973 - WRITERS WORLD Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 June 1973, page 10 By MAURICE DUNLEVY GETTING ENTOMBED IN FICTION ANTHOLOGIES IF you are a mediocre fic- tion writer and want your reputation buried de-cently, the best way to bury it is in a good short story anthology. Anthologies are the Forest Lawns of literature. In them the great lie down with the lowly. Visitors must stumble over the tombstones of non-entities to pay homage to the great. Take A. D. Maclean's "Win-ter's Tales 18" (Macmillan, 256 pp., $6.35) for example. On this its 18th birthday it displays the work of 10 short story writers, representing the best from Britain in the past year. Of the 10 only four might be regarded as well known: Brian Aldiss, Mervyn Bragg, Susan Hill and Frank Tuohy. And of these only Bragg and Tuohy have established sub-stantial reputations, although Miss Hill has won several im-portant prizes. The remainder — Freda Bromhead, Manoj Das, Andrew Graham, John Haylock, Roy, Holland, and Anne Marriott — are little known. Perhaps some of them will in time achieve greatness. If not, they may be consoled by the fact that no future his-torian of the British short story will be able to ignore the work of Mr Tuohy and Miss Hill, and will probably have to stumble over eight tombstones to reach theirs. Looking back over the 18 volumes of "Winter's Tales" one can't help but be struck by the transience of a short story writer's reputation. Of the 12 writers represented in "Winter's Tales 1" only Mr Tuohy has survived into 18, although the reputations of several others in Number 1 is fairly secure for the time being: Kingsley Amis, L. P. Hartley, Frank O'Connor, and V. S. Pritchett. But what his-torian today would even men-tion Storm Jameson, Brian McMahon, Osbert Sitwell, or Peter Lowry? And what critic preparing a literary pantheon would give a dime for the work of anyone but Mary Lavin in "Winter's Tales 5". P. B. Abercrombie, Elizabeth Berridge, Pauline Clark, Rumer Godden, Andrew Gra-ham, Elizabeth Holland, Storm Jameson, Mary Lavin and Tom Macdonald? There is plenty of other evi-dence to suggest that the repu-tations of few short story writers survive even the run of an annual anthology. Mr Mac-lean's best known predecessors were Edward J. O'Brien's "The Best Short Stories" annuals and Woodrow Wyatt's "English Story" series. My collection of the O'Brien annuals begins with Number 8, "The Best Short Stories of 1929". Of the 23 writers represented only Nugent Barker, H. E. Bates and Frank O'Connor survived in "The Best Short Stories of 1940", although Sean O'Faolain might well have done. Of the 30 writers repre-sented in Woodrow Wyatt's first volume (1941) none sur-vive in the ninth (1949). The reputations of American writers seem a little more secure, if one can judge by two surveys conducted by Whit Burnett who, with Hallie Burnett, was editor of Story magazine and of the annual anthology, "The Best American Short Stories". In 1942 Mr Burnett brought out "This Is My Best", a treasury of favourites by 93 "great living authors". The writers represented did not necessarily have to be short story writers. The important things were that they should be living and should be chosen by a large cross section of literary high priests and lay readers. Twenty-seven years and 25 anthologies later Mr Burnett compiled a new "This Is My Best" to cover the second third of the twentieth century. He received 1,010 responses to the 6,500 questionnaires be mailed to 11 categories of voters, including booksellers, librarians, publishers' salesmen and readers of literary magazines. Voters were limited to 75 choices from the 500 living authors on the ballot paper. Of the 27 authors in the 1942 anthology who were still living, 18 were selected again in 1969. This suggests that fame and longevity have at least some relationship in the United States. Six of the 18 were among the top 24 in 1969. Having listened to some gentle academic depreciation of the gentlemen recently, it is interesting to note that the top two in the survey were Ten-nessee Williams and John Steinbeck. Williams was among the first five nominees on 10 of the 11 lists and never ranked lower than third. The remainder of the top 10 were all creative writers, except for Walter Lippmann and John K. Galbraith, who tied for 10th place. The others were: W. H. Auden, J. D. Salinger, Edward Albee, Thornton Wilder, Art-hur Miller, Vladimir Nabo-kov, and Archibald MacLeish. It is notable that most of them worked in several different literary forms and that seven of them achieved some fame as playwrights. Only two were poets. In fact, the man generally consid-ered by critics to be America's leading contemporary poet, Robert Lowell, rated only 14th place and even then was behind a poet of somewhat lesser critical distinction, Ma- rianne Moore. Mr Burnett's survey was an interesting way of dealing with the living, but perhaps not the best way of assessing the repu-tations of the dead. Neverthe-less, the dead may also be assessed statistically. In 1968 Lawrence F. Macnamee com-piled "Dissertations in English and American Literature", a tome of more than 1,000 pages which lists all the liter-ary dissertations lodged in the archives of universities in Eng-land, Germany and the United States. Saturday afternoon barrack-ers for doctoral theses may be interested in the following league table of dissertations on great American novelists: Hawthorne (77), Melville (75), Faulkner (54), Poe (47), How-ells (44), Cooper (27), Hem-ingway (21), Willa Cather (20), Sinclair Lewis (12), and Scott Fitzgerald (10). So the conclusion must be that if you can't make the doctoral theses league table, try hard for the best antho-logies. Another interesting con-clusion which might be drawn is that if you want to drive the critics — those lice on the locks of literature —from the face of the earth, the way to do it might be to replace them by opinion polls. I'm sure most readers of these pages would be more interested if Roy Morgan's Gallup Poll were to ask whether you thought Patrick White and Thomas Keneally had been doing their jobs well recently than in answers to similar questions about Messrs Whitlam and Snedden. It would also make a literary columnist's job easier: "Patrick White's recent intervention in urban affairs has cost him a loss of support in the suburbs. On the other hand observers believe that Keneally has been overexposed on television. The party machines...."

27 Apr 1977 - It is nice to find people interested in what you think Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 27 April 1977, page 20 It is nice to find people interested in what you think By PETER GEORGE JL HANK you Roy Morgan and Friends! You have proved, to my satisfaction at least, that someone really does care about what I think. And that, despite what my friends, colleagues and boss may say. 1 know that you are the head of a largo organisation which conducts polls and research into all sorts of different things and thus it makes me all the more privileged (hat you have taken the time to write to me personally. You even managed to spell my name right — quite a feat, as few other people manage to do first time. I know how you found me. Someone in authority leaked my name to you. Your letter, you may remember, starts off with the heading 'About Your Car?' and goes on to say that "from registration statistics, we notice that you recently bought a new car". I am giad that you want : to know all about my reaction to my new car. Generally I abhor unsolicited mail. Or unsolicited anything for that matter. I wish Time-Life could forget I exist and thus stop sending me expensively tempting invitations to buy books about the world. I cannot even afford a monthly . subscription to Readers' Digest, let alone bound volumes on how to build a birdcage. Infuriated 1 am constantly, infuriated by insurance representatives, purporting ' to have been introduced by "friends", telephoning me before the sparrows are up. Encyclopedia salesmen pounding on the door with all the insistence of a policemen may tie their collected volumes around their necks and plunge into Lake Burley - (or Ginninderra if it's closer). But, Mr Morgan, I love my new metallic-grey station wagon. I heap more affection on it than I ; do on my long-suffering family. My bank manager was locked away after I told him that I was planning to spend vast sums on building a garage in which I would toil to keep it pampered. 1 So your letter came to mc as quite a surprise. In (act, a two-fold surprise. The first was that you, among all other people, should seek my views. Secondly, I was surprised to find that you really did exist and that you really do carry out surveys at all. No one I've ever known has been asked for their opinions by any of the firms that conduct opinion polls. None of my cats have ever been asked what food they prefer (mine prefers raw meat). I've always been rather under the impression that a poll firm whips around the office with a hat and all the workers write their preferences on a scrap of paper. Acutally, I find that a good indication of the way an election is going to go is to read graffiti. It's a simple matter of just adding up the nasty things said about each leader and you've got the score. Still, the point is that you are asking about what makes the consumer tick when it comes to cars. And you're asking me. You ask me to sum up my feelings and rate the car. But you only give me boxes marked "poor", "fair" and "good", t put two ticks beside "good" because there was no chance of ticking some statement such as "1 just love it". You have ommittcd a few relevant points, so I'll put them in now and hope you have a chance to take them into account. The location of the driver's ashtray was definitely designed by a non-smoker. There is no way I can use it without taking my eyes off the road and without getting ash on my right trouscr leg. I also find the ticking of the clock rather annoying, especially when I'm trying to sleep in the back. I'd have liked a revolutions counter because I think they tend to make it look as if the driver knows what he's doing. Still, 1 suppose they are minor points. I've ticked almost all the little boxes which give a "good" rating. Actually, I've suddenly noticed that I almost put a tick against statement 12 in section two. How could you have been so sneaky? I was beginning to have faith in you, Mr Morgan. You ask, "perhaps some of the following may have been reasons why you chose your present car rather than some other" and then proceed to give me 28 different options. And I find that No 12 states "Wanted a more prestige car". You don't know inc well, do you'? Or do you know me better than I know myself? Could I have chosen gun-metal grey because of some darkly hidden desire to have shouldered arms for my country? I just missed out on call-up (they chose dates either side of my birthday) and, frankly, I do recall feeling just a little piqued. What have I to tell my grandchildren when they ask "poppy, what did you do in the war?" Do the snazzy striped material inserts in the reclining bucket scats speak worlds for a need to be "sporty"? As I roll down East Row uo I peak from the windows, like colleague Ian Warden (who has no hidden desires), at the young schoolgirls, praying for one of them to ogle at me? Wished I wonder if the station waggon body reflects the fact that f've always wished I was a little more outdoorsy than I am. Does some part of my being I scream silently to be recognised, for people to say "what a man he is! What a rugged person! Only fools, heros and he dare visit the barren hinterland which is his domain". Perhaps what 1 need is a sort of cross between a Porsche and a Land Rover, complete with Rolls Royce grill. 1 am now on the fourth and final page of the questionnaire, Mr Morgan, and 1 have almost forgiven you. 1 have breezed through the part where you stress that I need not identify myself and then ask how much I earn. But I choke on the final part. You ask "which one/s of the following statements best describe your car?" and my hand races down the line ticking "a dependable and reliable car", "safe", "value for money", "easy to handle" And 1 almost find myself ticking "a car for people moving up in Hie world". What a hide. Of course, I realise I am moving up in the world. But would I buy a car because of that? I mean, a young, aspiring man like myself. Of course I'm moving up.... Although, conic to think of it, it's been ages since 1 had a rise in salary. My wife say? I'm on the way up, but I can't think of anyone else who's said that recently. Mum rang me recently to say she thought something I wrote was "simply magnificent". No one else even mentioned it — did they read it? I can feel a migraine coming on .. the warning symptoms of insomnia arc there.. Mr Morgan, I abhor unsolicited letters. Can'tyou leave me alone?

06 Jul 1973 - Court 'should fix doctors' fees' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 6 July 1973, page 6 Court 'should fix doctors' fees' At least six out of 10 people think the Arbitration Court should have power to fix doctors' fees, the Gallup Poll finds. To make the question realistic, 2,253 people aged 16 and over were asked; "If a referendum Is held to give the Government power to have doctors' fees fixed by the Arbitration Court would you probably vote to have doctors' fees fixed by the government or not?" Australia-wide, in this mini-referendum: 61% said they would vote "yes", so doctors' fees could he fixed by the Arbitration Court; 27% said they would vote "no" and 12% were undecided. "Yes" voters included: 64% of the men and 57% of the women, more than 60% in each of four States, NSW, Victoria, Queensland and SA; 70% of those aged 16-19; 67% of those 20-29, 63% of those 30-49, and 54% of those 50-69, but only 40% of those over 70. Chief arguments for fixed fees were: establish standards for everything; doctors earn enough money. Those against fixed fees said: doctors should be independent; they work long hours so their fees should not be fixed, (c) Roy Morgan and Australian Public Opinion Polls.

29 Sep 1976 - The powers of the Governor-General Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 29 September 1976, page 16 The powers of the Governor-General r. to the Editor* \ Sir, - Mr Glover {(Letters, July 7) would do .well to re-examine his ; original letter before Ijthrowing his own failings jback at me. Nowhere in {'that letter does he munition the Senate or the rejection of Supply. His contention was simply that jt h e Governor-General (should exercise his power >io sack the Government {whenever he judges that jlhe electorate is sick of e.that Government's in eptitude. Although he claims in his second letter that the Governor-General "should neither appoint a Government nor sustain it in office" he still adheres to his "pro-bonopublico" doctrine which permits the GovernorGeneral to sack any inept and discredited Government. If the viceroy is to sack then he must ob viously also employ his powers under Section 64 of the Constitution to appoint so that government may be carried on, and if he is to use these powers whenever he believes that the incumbent Government is inept and discredited then we have government by vice-regal caprice. The point ot my "fanr tasy" was to ask: By what criterion is the Governor-General, a single appointed official, to determine when an elected Government has become discredited and incapable of governing? Mr Glover's first letter claimed that, in sacking the Whitlam Government, Sir John "correctly assessed the wishes of the nation", and that the calling of a general election gave "proper expression" to those wishes. However, an ANOP poll early in November, iust prior to the sacking, found that 63 per cent thought deferral of the Budget unjustified and 58 per cent opposed an early election. Moreover, the same poll gave Labor a 2 per cent lead in the capital cities. What were the people's wishes? Should the GovernorGeneral's resolution of the deadlock have been determined on the basis of a personal assessment of the people's wishes, a personal decision as to which side was the most incompetent followed by a deliberate effort to disadvantage. that side as much as possible, or on the basis of what was right, according to the Constitution. to convention, and to the advice of the Prime Minister and the law officers of the Crown? I believe the answer is clear. I do not gloss over the problems of the deadlock situation, nor do 1 pretend that Sir John Kerr was in an easy position. However, I believe that the Governor-General was guilty not merely of atrocious misjudgement in going against convention, fairness, and his Prime Minister's advice, but also of bad faith in deliberately deceiving his constitutional advisers as to his true intentions. My answer to Mr Glover's original question was implicit in my earlier letter: an elected Govern mcnt that is guilty -only of ineptitude must be allowed to serve out its full term. If that Government should resign, call an early election, or lose its Lower House majority before that time, that is fair enough, but unless it is guilty of some illegal or unconstitutional action it cannot be forced out of office. To claim that the sacking of an elected Government by an appointed official was "an enormous service to the . .. democratic principle" is quite beyond the bounds of sense, but if Mr Glover wishes to advocate a system of recall and referendum, or to assert that the Whitlam Government was guilty of illegal or . unconstitutional conduct, then he should do so openly. D. E. MILLER, Watson.

11 Oct 1976 - Indonesia 'overseas threat No 3' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 11 October 1976, page 1 Indonesia 'overseas threat No 3' By a Staff Reporter The fear of external aggression has grown rapidly among Australians in the past few years with the Soviet Union, China and Indonesia, in that order, seen as the outstanding potential aggressors. Fifty-one per cent of Australians feared external threat in a survey conducted in March this year compared with. 36 per ccnt in February 1974 and 42 per cent in August 1971. The countries most often listed by this 51 per cent as potential threats were, in order: Russia, China, Indonesia, Vietnam, Japan, India, Germany, France, America and Britain. However, the emphasis placed on the first three countries was significant. Respondents seeing a threat were asked to rank Australia's five most likely external aggressors. The countries least frequently excluded from the ranking scorcd high est. Only 12 per cent excluded the Soviet Union, for example. Seventeen per cent excluded China and 28 per cent excluded Indonesia. The next highest threat, Vietnam, was excluded by a much larger 39 per cent of respondents. The results were an incidental product of a national poll of Australian attitudes to Japan, conducted for the Japanese Embassy in Australia by Australian National Opinion Polls in late March and early April, and earlier polls conducted by ANOP dealing with the external threat question. ANOP tends to believe that Australians' perception of an external threat is influenced by the Government in office at any particular time, declining with the accession of the Labor Government and rising with the accession of the LiberalNational Country Party Government. Of the actual ranking that emerged, ANOP's commentary said, "« . . It is the traditional nonWestern nations of China and Russia which are seen to pose the greatest threat to Australia by th; majority of the Australian population which perceives a threat at all. "Only 17 per cent and 12 per cent respectively of the sample placed neither China nor Russia in the five greatest threats to Australia. "Indeed, China to some 31 per cent of the Australian population and Russia to some 28 per cent were perceived as the greatest threats. "Indonesia (21 per cent) was perhaps surprisingly placed at a not too distant third as the next greatest potential threat among those Australians feeling threatened. These three countries predominated the analysis of perceived greatest threats. "Japan was perceived as the fourth greatest threat of the 10 countries presented. However, _ it was a fourth placing with some considerable sp'ace between the more highly threatening Indonesia". Continued on Page 7. Overseas 'threats' Continued from Page 1 The break-down of the 51 per cent sample which, feared an external threat led the ANOP to conclude: "This fear was significantly stronger among women, among Liberal voters, among residents in the smaller States -and particularly the mineral States - among middle-income earners and among (hose respondents who were categorised on ANOP's occupation scale as 'lower' white-collar work ers. "But it is particularly important to note that the fear of external threat lo Australia was felt more keenly among the younger segments of the population. It was as high as 56 per cent in the 35-44-year-old age group; it was at 55 per cent in the 25-34-year-old age group; and it stood at 51 per ccnt in the under-25vear-oid age segment; it stood at 47 per cent at both the 45-54 and over54-year-old age segments. "These differences are not very large that they are in a direction suggesting that it is by no means the older, World War II veterans or World War II infants that most fear a threat. Quite the reverse. "So it is the younger, smaller-State-residing, female office worker with no experience either directly or indirectly of the war who is most likely to fear a threat to Australia from outside its borders in the next 15 years. "Perhaps this is as good a shorthand pen picture of middle Australia as one is likely to get".

16 Feb 1977 - Mr Fraser's performance Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 16 February 1977, page 18 Mr Fraser's performance Sir, — It would seem from the latest Morgan poll that the Fraser Government is now manifestly unpopular with the electorate. One would hope that the Governor-General will once again invoke his seemingly limitless reserve powers and declare another election. After all, a democracy, if that is what we are supposed to be, should offer the ALP the same opportunity as was handed to the Liberals a year or so ago. But rather than go on about the GovernorGeneral, I have more serious matters to discuss. Now that the polls are out, and the cold light of reality is dawning over Australia, it is time to take stock of this Government's performance. Relative to the constraints and problems that bedevilled the Whitlam years, this present Government should have had a dream run in 1976. They came in with a massive mandate. They had no obstructive, hostile majority in the Senate to contend with. They had an extremely low rate of industrial strife (not, I hasten to add, that any credit for that is due to them). As an international backdrop to their efforts, they had a slow but steady recovery in most Western economics. They had no unexpected, massive increases in oil prices, no precipitate collapse of the beef market, no disasters of Darwin magnitude, no personal scandals on the part of senior ministers (at least none that we can talk about at the moment). They had no large election promises to deliver since, by my recollection, the only comprehensible statements made by Mr Fraser before the last election were about things he would not do. Unfortunately most of the things he said he would not ao he has done — the examples of his guarantees about Medibank, wage indexation, the ABC, Legal Aid and no - jobs -for - the - boys, come immediately to mind. Since Mr Fraser and his cohorts seem to prefer thinking in negative terms, let us examine what he has not done. He has not controlled inflation. We are still, to use his own fatuous analogy, like a family who has lost control of its household budget. Speaking of budgets, the deficit — which at one point appeared to be the only economic item Mr Fraser had ever heard of — is now as large as it ever was, and will no doubt grow larger as Mr Fraser takes more knee-jerk decisions to bolster the failing nerve of his backbenchers. Unemployment is, of course, well on the way to being Australia's largest industry. That is hardly surprising for a Government of Mr Fraser's colours, I suppose, but what is surprising is that business confidence at present seems to be about the level it must have been on Wall Street in late 1929. Leaving the economy (which I am sure most of us would like to do) we might take a look at foreign policy. It won't take long; after all, Mr Fraser has a whole Government to run single-handed so, apart from the odd overseas junket (remember "we don't want a tourist for a Prime Minister"?) he only has time to trample over the head of the unfortunate Mr Peacock very occasionally. Not that he has been ineffective on those occassions. No indeed — under Mr Fraser's baton, great Russian phantoms have been conjurcd up in the Indian Ocean, the communists are all about us, and the nastier little dictators in the South-East Asian area have been transformed into pillars of democracy. Suffice it to say that Australia is now well back on the road to being regarded as, to borrow Patrick White's phrase, "a nation of rustic clowns". We could move on to social welfare and education, but that would be far too depressing. The national consensus, which was dealt a vicious blow in November 1975, has been given the coup de grace as Mr Fraser endlessly seeks out more and more scapcgoats for his hopeless ineptitude in government. So far, we have had the "dole bludgers", (that was before too many voters joined the ranks of the unemployed — like the Budget deficit, we have heard less and less of dole bludgers lately), the unions, the public servants and now even Mr Fraser's beloved businessmen (who, if I interpret Mr Fraser correctly, stubbornly continue to refuse to fill up their yards with items they can't sell). God knows who will be next. To return to my original point; a majority of the voting population now regards Mr Fraser as an inadequate Prime Minister. To bring it a little closer to home — Mr Frascr's opprobrium could help the Member for Canberra make history at the next elections by being the first parliamentary incumbent ever to lose his deposit. Were I one to believe that Governors-General should be anything more than ribbon-cutters and airport-tarmac decorations, I would now be inclined to ask: Sir John, where are you now we really need you? JAMES DOUGLAS Deakin.

18 Feb 1977 - Whitlam 'more popular' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 18 February 1977, page 6 Whitlam 'more popular' SYDNEY, Thursday. — According to a new public opinion poll the Leader of the Federal Opposition, Mr Whitlam, is more popular than the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser.
