27 May 1977 - Abortion blamed for long wait to adopt Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 27 May 1977, page 1 Dr Overduin addresses the in quiry yesterday. Abortion blamed for long wait to adopt There was a six-year waiting list for adoptions in the ACT because abortion had become so common, Right to Life Association witnesses told the ACT Legislative Assembly abortion inquiry yesterday. The situation for those on adoption lists was "desperate" and a council member of the Association, Mrs Kath Wooir, rejected suggestions that the waiting period was due to more single mothers keeping their children. The Right to Life Association presented a 53-page submission to the Assembly's standing committee on health and education which is inquiring into abortion in general and into the possible operation of private abortion clinics in the ACT. Appearing on behalf of the association were its ACT president, Mr Frank Street, as well as Mrs Woolf and the executive director of the Right to Life Association in South Australia, the Reverend Dr Daniel Overduin. The submission said that "in the ACT we have reliable evidence that the Abortion Counselling Service actively dissuades women from regarding adoption as an alternative io abortion. One inquirer was told that adoption is "a most traumatic experience not recommended by psychiatrists". , 'Misleading' The association said "it is most disturbing that private counselling services are able to provide misleading information in such a vital area of human relationships". All abortion counselling services were accused by the association at today's hearing of being biased in favour of abortion. The submission said, "We would mention here the great possibility for privately operated counselling services to provide a positive impetus towards abortion by bias, general attitude and by misinformation". An Australian article on "Pregnancy and Neuroticism" was quoted as saying that several hundred women attending an ante-natal clinic in early pregnancy were significantly more neurotic and more anxious than women who had recently given birth. The submission said this "indicates that pregnant women are more suggestible than normal and may be easily led into taking actions which they may later judge, when in a calmer state of mind, to have been very ill-advised". Dr Overduin told the inquiry that women were "hoodwinked" into believing that abortion was a simple medical procedure, but any medical procedure which interfered with the body could cause medical complications. "The risks of abortions are simply swept under the carpet", he said. If abortions were to be done, they should be performed by skilled people, to lessen the risks to the mother from an unhygienic environment. This did not mean that abortion should be legalised and "clean killing" allowed. Dr Overduin said he saw a relationship between abortion and euthanasia. In every country where abortion was legalised a drive for active euthanasia had followed, Dr Overduin said. The association asked that the ACT Legislative Assembly recommend to Ministers that private abortion clinics should not be established in the ACT, that any approved abortions should take place in a prescribed public hospital, and that all applications for abortion should be considered only by an official terminations committee, whose role should be to determine whether the foetus constituted an "imminent" threat to the mother's life. Poll 'amusing' Dr Overduin said he was amused that the results of an ANOP survey stating that more Canberra people favoured easier abortion laws made Page 1 of The Canberra Times yesterday. However, he felt the poll was worthless and misleading because the people interviewed did not know the full implications of the questions they were beine asked. 'Few applications' to abortion committ tee. — Page 3.

16 Jun 1977 - The abortion issue LETTERS to the Editor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 16 June 1977, page 12 The abortion issue LETTERS to the Editor Contraceptive failures Sir, — Until now I have refrained from entering the abortion debate for fear of being accused of being a male chauvinist interfering in mat-ters which are not my concern. But I do have a rather vital in- terest: I was born when my mother was 38, and I know that my impend-ing arrival caused some concern and re-shaping of plans. I also know that my parents are now very glad I did happen to come along. Further, my two delightful chil-dren are adopted. To quote the pro-abortionists, we are all "contracep-tive failures". In the enlightened society they envisage I don't suppose we would have survived very long, so I have quite a direct interest in their arguments. Three points in particular bother me: (1) They say the arguments against abortion arc merely "re-ligious" or "philosophical". While I wouldn't reject arguments on these grounds, I think the prime objection to abortion is quite pragmatic. The aim of laws in society should be to protect innocent persons from attack, and certainly from being selected to be killed. (This is true even when the person is causing grave inconvenience to others, such as trying to walk across Barry Drive.) If the law does not attempt to fulfil this basic responsibility it can hardly expect respect in other areas. Some argue that an unborn child is not a "person" in this sense, but if the child is a person one minute after birth, what is it one minute before, and one month before, and seven months before? From the time of my conception I was fated, for better or worse, to be a male with blue eyes, brown hair, etc — in fact to be me. Then began a period of slow and gradual development that will not end till the day I'm planted six feet deep. If this is philosophy, then so be it; so is one plus one makes two. (2) They say it is better not to be born than to be disadvantaged. In one letter (The Canberra Times, May 2) it was even said that it was better not to be born than to miss out on breast feeding! Is there anyone who doesn't feel disadvantaged in some way? Should we all go and jump in the lake? We may feel like it occasionally, but fortunately few of us do. Most of the time I'm very glad I was born. I'm pretty sure my children feel the same. (3) They say that the law is not effective: that women will have abortions anyway and that im-prisonment is not an appropriate deterrent for a distraught woman facing an unwanted pregnancy. This may be true, but what is needed is a constructive social en-vironment that will help the woman and her unborn child. In times of stress we all seek the easy way out, and most of us will take it if it is offered, as they say abortion should be offered. Maybe my mother would have done the same. I'm immensely grateful that my children's mothers didn't. I know I've occasionally wished some people would disap-pear, but the knowledge that society takes a rather dim view of putting arsenic in their tea has greatly helped my keep a rein on such speculations! RODNEY BAXTER Reid. Survey procedures Sir, — You have published sever-al letters and comments (eg, The Canberra Times, April 27 and May 2) on a survey I conducted with the help of students in 1969 on 'At-titudes to taking human life'. Now that Mr Brewer has adequately de-fended our survey procedures (Let-ters, May 18) and an independent survey has found similar results af-ter a lapse of eight years, I need not further defend the research but I wish to express my regret at the way it has been used and misused. It has been suggested (by Frank V. Street, Letters, May 25) that poorly designed research was pro-moted to create a climate of opinion favourable to abortion-law reform by reporting (falsely) that public opinion already favoured the pro-posed changes. I was particularly saddened to learn that Professor Moran (Let-ters, May 2), one of Australia's most distinguished scholars, should have lent his name to such a shabby business. His statement was pure humbug. Let the public beware of authorities who would protect the naive! But, he only did what I was tempted to do myself. The strange thing about all this is that I have been cast in the role of supporter of abortion-on-demand. I published an article in a scientific journal which reported reasonably reliable survey results indicating (among other things of greater in-terest to me) that public opinion in Canberra appeared to favour a change in that direction. However, I did not agree with the majority then and still have serious reservations. I do not believe abor- tion is a private matter, and I fear that very serious social conse-quences could follow from the wide-spread practice of the kind of social and biological engineering of which abortion is one small part. I should confess that I was reluc-tant to publish the results at all and did so only after a year and then without drawing it to the attention of the daily Press, because I feared it might be used for undesirable purposes. When it appeared I re-ceived a number of inquiries from other research workers (most from overseas) and none of them was in any way critical of the survey meth-ods — which were in fact quite standard, like those employed by the ANOP, Gallup Poll, the Australian Bureau of Statistics and other repu-table organisations. Indeed, in another survey at the same time, using exactly the same methods, I predicted the results of the 1969 Federal election with an error of less than one per cent. It was only when the results were used in public debate for ends I would probably oppose, that critics were found to mislead the public into thinking I biased the survey in the opposite direction to the way I would have done had my scientific scruples been surrendered to my moral inclinations. (Professor) D. G. BESWICK Director, Centre for the Study of Higher Education, University of Melbourne Melbourne, Victoria. Objections to poll Sir, — I refer to the recent ANOP survey of attitudes to abortion in Canberra. As one of the 400 voters polled in that survey I wish to state my dissatisfaction with it. The key question was: "Do you approve or disapprove of easier abortion laws?", and like most peo-ple in Canberra I am confused about the present abortion law as it stands. No attempt was made to explain the present law to me before I answered the question, and so a lack of knowl-edge could easily have led me to give the wrong answer. Secondly, "easier abortion laws" could mean anything from a slight relaxation of the law to a total lack of control over abortion in the ACT. There was no scope whatever for me to explain what I understood "easier abortion laws" to mean — apparent-ly I had to choose between all or nothing. I also wish to comment on the "representative" character of the survey. In our household I was re-quested to answer the survey be- cause I was the member closest to 18 years of age. Surely this does not result in a random survey. As well as this, I was informed by my questioner that she had a sub-stantial number of interviews to make at random but in our im-mediate area. If only 400 people are to be questioned in a city the size of Canberra it does not seem terribly representative to chose more than one or two from any area of a few blocks. Lastly, in criticising what I con-sider to be a biased survey, I wish to object to being characterised by my religion. I answered the survey questions after having thought about them on their merits and I was disconcerted when asked my re-ligion at the end. Having seen the results of the survey I notice that religious groups were singled out for special attention. Why? If the Legislative Assembly is to take any notice of this sham, it must take at least equal notice of the objections I have raised above. RUTH HARRIS Dickson. A christian view Sir, — At a meeting of the Baptist Memorial Church held recently, it was decided to make the following expression of opinion on the ques-tion of abortion. It seems to us as Christians that in the abortion debate men and women are relying too much on their own wisdom and judgment, and los-ing sight of the basic principles of God, the Creator, Redeemer and final Arbiter of all mankind. While the abortion issue is cer-tainly complex, the solution seems to lie neither in the principle of whole sale abortion on demand, nor in the principle of birth in any circum-stances. We believe that the key to the problem lies in the Christian principles of compassion, mod-eration, understanding, tolerance, and mutual respect between all hu-man beings, and particularly be- tween men and women. The Bible shows us the extent of Christ's love and respect for men, women, and children, and teaches us that the key to a successful marriage — the only divinely sanctioned form of sexual relationship — is true affection and mutual respect be-tween husband and wife, with each partner having clearly defined re-sponsibilities towards the other. We believe that if these principles were more widely practised in socie-ty today, there would be fewer prob lems such' as "unwanted pregnan-cies", which are symptomatic of our disregard of the laws of God, and that many women (and some men for that matter), would then not feel the need to be "liberated". We be-lieve that true liberation comes only from following God's teaching. (Reverend) ROY B. HENSON, for The Baptist Memorial Church Dickson

12 Jul 1977 - Funds for women's groups Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 12 July 1977, page 2 Funds for women's groups Sir, - Mrs Crisp, the Deputy Commissioner of the Capital Territory Health Commission, is quite adamant that the Abortion Counselling Service does not receive any funds from the community health grants given by the commission. The recipient named in the grants under discussion is apparently the Canberra Women's Centre In formation and Health Counselling Service (The Canberra Times June 21). Is Mrs Crisp aware that this interesting amalgam was formed prior to application for a community-health grant in 1975 by co-operation of the Women's Movement, the Women' Electoral Lobby, and the Abortion Counselling Service; this information was supplied by an officer of the Health Commission upon inquiries at the time. Further, Senator Brian Harradine is taken to task for his statements recently in the Senate that such grants do nevertheless benefit the Abortion Counselling Service. Mrs Crisp admits that the grant to the Information and Health Counselling Service helps towards the salary of a person to answer the telephone and give advice about women's health, etc. How the Abortion Counselling Service does not benefit is difficult to see. It has the same telephone number as the Information and Health Counselling Service. The same (subsidised) answerer will pass a caller straight to the Abortion Counselling Service. The two services do not appear to be very clear themselves about their "separate" functions. The recent ANOP poll conducted in Canberra concerning attitudes towards abortion laws was commissioned by the Women's Information and Health Counselling Service. So it was reported by The Canberra Times and to the Legislative Assembly's Inquiry into Abortion. Yet the June 1 issue of the Australian National University's student newspaper Woroni made an appeal for funds to cover the cost of the poll for its sponsors. The appeal was inserted by the Abortion Counselling Service. Perhaps readers now share Senator Harradine's confusion. Possibly the Capital Territory Health Commission would be better advised to investigate the spending of its grants than to score points off an elected Member of the Federal Parliament whose duty it is, especially as a member of the Senate Estimates Committee, to see that public funds are not improperly used. KATHLEEN WOOLF Garran.

27 Sep 1977 - LIBERALS WEIGH THE ODDS FOR AN EARLY ELECTION Smokescreens to hide the crucial issue—the economy Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 27 September 1977, page 2 LIBERALS WEIGH THE ODDS FOR AN EARLY ELECTION Smokescreens to hide the crucial issue — the economy POLITICS By GAY DAVIDSON FOR the Prime Minister, the common sense of the Government going for an election — or at least ensuring that it is in the best possible position to do so — in December has not been in doubt for months. The leaked internal document from the Reserve Bank at the weekend added little to what was already known about the low state of the economy, and was used as basic information by pol- iticians and observers in their mounting expectations of a De- cember election. Even Mr Fraser yesterday, after confirming the authenticity of the document, commented only that "it is on the gloomy side"; he was not denying large chunks of it. So, with common sense telling Mr Fraser to go to the polls while he can probably win, before voters' percep-tions of the state of the economy and of the rates of unemployment and inflation sharpen against the Gov-ernment, it is illuminating to see how Mr Fraser has been setting the political climate in which the elec-tion campaign will be fought. It is essential for the Government not to let the economy — or, worse still, the Government's economic management — become the major issue. Last November, just before the devaluation, a Morgan Gallup Poll found that, after a year of coalition Government, there was a spirit of cautious optimism among voters. Some 48 per cent (compared with only 37 per cent a year earlier) expected the economic outlook to improve in 1977, and 28 per cent (down from 37 per cent a year earlier) expected it to get worse. Blame Twenty-one per cent (up from the previous year's 16 per cent) thought 1977 would be prosperous, and 54 per cent (down from 64 per cent) thought the year would be difficult. "Maybe if we wait a bit it'll swing back". Mr Fraser . . . kicking the can There have been no similar polls since then. However, with the polls on the popularity of the Government parties and their leaders consistently declining in recent months, it is reasonable to assume that the op-timism has gone, and some votes with it, and that the Government must focus attention elsewhere. "Elsewhere" currently is other in-stitutions supposedly to blame for high wages and consequent in-creased unemployment (the Arbi-tration Commission), insufficient help for industry and consequent unemployment (the Industries As-sistance Commission), creating an issue out of uranium (the ALP and militant unions), and ALP leaders who question what the Government intends doing about maintaining the value of the dollar. In each case the Government has acted only for political advantage, doing nothing to contain the prob-lem, effect improvement, or inform rather than propagandise the public. Advisers On uranium, its response to the ACTU referendum demand could have been very different if it had balanced the threats of union mili-tancy — and the uneasiness of many ordinary voters — against the free world's actual requirements of uranium. There are none in Europe or Japan up to 1985, according to the Government's own official advisers — the Department of National Re-sources (in respect of Japan), and the Ambassador to the EEC, Dr J. W. C. Cumes (Europe). That means there was no need for a decision this year to mine and export, and there is still time for debate aimed at achieving con- sensus. Authoritarianism But the Government has chosen differently. It has not released the official advice (or answered ques-tions about it as the advice has found its way into print). It has merely asserted that there are no problems over safeguards or waste disposal. And it is turning the issue against the unions as "who's run-ning the country?" A similar authoritarianism emerges over the currency question. With the large outflows of capital this month it was legitimate for the Opposition to ask what action the Government intended taking. It would have been equally legit-imate for the Government to lie if it was considering devaluation. But instead it did nothing for business or anyone else's confidence when for days it refused to give any informa-tion and simply condemned the Op-position for asking the question. Attacks The attacks on the two independ-ent statutory authorities are smokescreens, and also raise ques-tions about the Government's ap-proach. The IAC has not been guilty of reporting inadequately on the em-ployment effects of its advice and recommendations to the Govern- ment, and Mr Fraser has acknowl-edged privately that he has been kicking the can there, presumably to please the manufacturers. The Arbitration Commission has maintained throughout that it is not an instrument of the Government s economic policy. If it has been labouring under a misapprehension the Government has not sought to put it right, or even to make changes to its charter. Obvious Both institutions have produced public information and comment which the Government would have preferred to keep out of the public arena — particularly the IAC over the costs to the community (not the Government which decides the pro-tection) of continually helping high- ly protected and profitable in dustries. If the Government were con-cerned about the unemployment ef-fects of what the Arbitration Com-mission decides or the IAC recom-mends, the obvious answer would be to take complementary action. Instead, by insulating manufac-turing industry from the real world it is ensuring worse problems in the future as the various sectors get out of balance, and immediately adding to the costs of the other sectors, and of all of us as consumers. And on unemployment, it refused a submission from Mr Street that unions, employers, the Government and the public should be brought together in a comprehensive ex-amination of the problems, particu-larly the short-term unemployment problems in the manufacturing sec- tor. Paid off It chose not to have information, public debate and nation-wide in-terest centred on the issue during an election period. This seems to have paid off. According to a private survey for the Liberal Party the public has shown a mixed reaction on where the blame for unemployment lies. Predictably, Labor voters blamed the Fraser Government, Liberals blamed other factors including the Whitlam Gov-ernment, and un-committed voters blamed wage increases more than either Government. That result can only strengthen the ALP's instincts against a De-cember election, in its own interests of gaining more time to put its version to the public of the effects of Government policies. It can only strengthen Mr Fraser's instincts to go sooner rather than later. In the meantime, while the Gov-ernment is avoiding talking about the important issue and is making political capital out of asking "Who's running the country?", it would be more to the point if the rest of us asked. "Who is advising the Government?", and, "What else is being hidden from the country?"

06 Oct 1977 - BRITONS AFIRE WITH APATHY Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 6 October 1977, page 3 BRITONS AFIRE WITH APATHY .AUSTRALIA'S electors suffer from several of the corporate debilities of lemmings and of sheep, and yet, alas, have none of the redeeming features that characterise those two sweet and affable brutes. None the less, rcccnt opinion polls taken in Australia do tend to suggest that at least our sheep and lemmings are a lot more decisive than their British cousins. In a Morgan Gallup Poll published last month a cross-section of our masses was asked whether they thought Mr Frascr was doing a good job or. a bad job and whether they thought Mr Whitlam was doing a good job or a bad job. For all I know they may have been asked whether the Queen Mother and Kojak were doing good jobs or bad jobs too, but if so those results weren't published. Thirty-nine per cent of Australian sheep and lemmings approved the way Mr Frascr was doing his job, and 47 per cent disapproved. Forty-one per cent thought Mr Whitlam was doing a good job and 43 per cent were spiteful enough to say that no, they didn't think he was doing a very good job, so there. Aren't some people cruel? But the most important statistics for this story arc that only 14 per cent of sheep and lemmings had no opinion at all on Mr Fraser's performance, and only 16 per cent had no point of view about how Mr Whitlam was going. A British survey done at about the same time, asking the British to ex press a view about the quality of the job being done by Mr Callaghan, Mr Thatcher's wife Margaret and by young David Steel, the Liberal leader, revealed that 51 per cent had no opinion on the performance of their Father Christmassy Prime Minister, Mr Callaghan, 45 per cent didn't know how they felt about Mrs Thatcher's performance, and 50 per cent had no idea what kind of a job Mr Steel was doing. It might have been revealing to ask this same sample, "What is your name?" or "Is today Wednesday?", but that was not done and we do not know whether this indccisiveness was merely confined to matters of politics or to the whole world and to life itself. How are wc to explain the Australian voter's far, far greater readiness to pass judgment on the performances of his elected leaders? There may, of course, have been some differences in the ways the two samples were questioned, but this is not apparent from the literature accompanying the polls. It may be a temporary matter. It may be that the British find Mr Callaghan, Mrs Thatcher and Mr Steel just too boring and inconsequential for words, while Australians find that strong loyalties and loathings are kindled in their breasts when they contemplate the present brace of heavyweights who dominate our parliamentary politics. If this is the case such statistics could be reversed with changes of personnel at the top in both countries. Meanwhile, 'tis a mystery. Is there a political scientist in the house?

28 Oct 1977 - 'No big role' for Chipp Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 28 October 1977, page 1 'No big role' for Chipp The Australian Democrats would not play a significant role in the elections, the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, said in several interviews yesterday. He did not explain why the Australian Democrats leader, Mr Chipp, had not been allowed to speak after his election announcement in Parliament, but he volunteered, "They don't have very much in the way of policy. In mid-term you have people gathering . . However, major pollsters disagreed with Mr Fraser. Mr Irving Saulwick, of Australian Nationwide Opinion Polls, said that if the Australian Mr Chipp Democrats held to their present 7 or 8 per cent, their preferences would be critical to the outcome of the election, and he did not know how their prefer ences would be distributed on the day. Of the people now supporting the Australian Democrats and who had voted in previous elections, twice as many had voted Liberal. "The question is, will they return home?" Mr Saulwick said. "And that depends on whether you see their present adherence as a protest or a migration". Mr Gary Morgan, of Roy Morgan Gallup Polls, said that with the strength of the major parties being similar at 43 to 44 per cent, the Australian Democrats preferences were crucial. He also thought that Mr Chipp had a good chance of a Senate seat in Victoria and that a minor party could take one in NSW.

05 Nov 1977 - Street-march ban 'approved' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 November 1977, page 1 Street-march ban 'approved' BRISBANE: The latest political poll figures show that the stand by the Premier, Mr Bjelkc-Petersen, against street-protest marches had public approval, according to the National Party State executive director, Mr Mike Evans. He said that the latest Morgan Gallup Poll taken over the four weekends in October showed that support for the party rose from 23 per cent to 31 per ccnt. The increase of eight percent was unprecedented in any poll and had been based on a sample of about 600 Queenslanders. "The figure is absolutely incredible", he said. "We believe the huge increase in public support is due to the Premier's determination to ensure that our streets are not taken over by a militant minority". Queensland election reports. — Page 3.

07 Dec 1977 - State-by-State study suggests dead heat Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 7 December 1977, page 14 cwwtt.. ;«w»»hiiwmk. • • m&s&xw&wmm Dr Butler By BRUCE JUDDERY A 62-62 dead heat between Labor and the Government parties was suggested by a Stateby-State breakdown of the recent ANOP publicopinion poll, a leading British student of elections, Dr David Butler, said in Canberra yesterday. Nationally the poll suggested a 51-49 popular margin in favour of the coalition parties, or a Government majority of about 16. "But if you look at the State-by-Statc poll, you find the swing [to Labor] is very much greater in Queensland than it is in NSW — 8.7 per cent against 3.2 per cent — which is very much less favourable to the Govern ment. "If you pursue this, you get not a majority for the Government of 16 but a majority of nothing — 62 scats to 62", he told a packed Australian National University convocation luncheon. Confessing that "I don't think federally", Dr Butler, of Nuffield College, Oxford, declined to forecast what cffcct the present Queensland State coalition dispute would have on the poll, at least in that State — but did point out that a number of disparate events (including loss of the World Cup) had been credited with British Labour's loss in the June, 1970, elections there. "I see Australia from Canberra outwards", Dr Butler admitted. "I certainly find Queensland politics more totally baffling than the politics of any other Australian State". Dr Butler, founder of the "science" of psephology, or the study of elections, warned that "prediction is a very dangerous thing . . . There is nobody who knows how millions of their fellow-countrymen will hrhflvr. fnrlnv nr cr»vf>rnl rlovc In <1^ However, the results of the elections could be rcduccd to a manageable number of possiblitics. The most recent polls indicated a Government margin respectively of 3, 2 and 2 per cent. But the latest British election had recorded "massive" swings in the last days of each campaign, against the Government "or, as I believe, against the party which the polls showed as being ahead". In Britain, as Australia, there was a "deep suspicion" of office-holders. Like the British, the Australian electorate was increasingly volatile. "If Don Chipp actually records 10 per cent of the vote next Saturday, then there has been a greater net switch of votes than in any election since the war . . . There is a greater degree of volatility in the electorate than ever before". Indications were that the Australian Democrats' preferences would divide in the range 40-60 per cent to 60-40 per cent, accounting for 1 or 2 per cent of the entire electorate. The count of the vote would be slower, and the fate of more scats would be unknown on December 20, "than in any previous election". Dr Butler said that the performance of publicopinion polls in Britain, and probably in Australia, would get worse and worse, not because of any deterioration in the pollsters' expertise, but bccause of electoral volatility. For Mr Chipp "to have brought things up from nothing suggests there were people who wanted an 'out' from the existing parties". The Australian Democrats might not succeed in creating a long-term party, but in 'the future there was potential for a centre party as "a kind of escapist thing, but at escape to the centre and not to the extremes .... "The party system as we know it is not immutable. We are bound to go on with a party system, but not necessarily this party system".

09 Dec 1977 - POLITICS Playing to the TV gallery as the campaigns wind down Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 9 December 1977, page 2 Playing to the TV gallery as the campaigns wind down By GAY DAVIDSON "A foreign journalist who has been observing the campaign described it as 'US politics circa 1910 — materialistic, moralistic, appealing to greed, nothing for the heart or the head, an accountant's view of what the voters want' THE swearing-in of Sir Zelman Cowen as Governor-General yesterday was a model political event, well ordered, politicians dignified, television cameras unobtrusively recording. It was a far cry from the rallies of the past three weeks. They are not even meant for people. They are for the TV cameras, for the advertising agencies' perceptions of what the viewing public will tune to, or at least not switch off from. Mr Fraser's rally in Sydney at the Opera House on Tuesday was a shock for anyone who still believes that during an election campaign rational choices are offered for citizens to make rational judgments. Tumultuous After an hour of entertainment — a band, Ukrainian folk music, so-called Greek dancing (girls dancing sensually to Zorba music!) — the Prime Minister got a tumultuous welcome from a predominantly migrant audience. After his short speech, when the TV lights switched off, a commercial newscaster was hailed by a group from the Liberal advertising agency. "What did you think?" they asked. "Oh, about one minute thirty", he said. "Yeah, we thought one thirty to one forty", was the response. Mr Fraser: received a tumultuous welcome They were referring to the spot in the late TV news for which the event was staged. Mr Fraser had not said anything new for the morning newspapers or the radio, but the rally still had to be mentioned because it had been on TV. The audience were not there as thinking voters. They were TV film extras, responding to the music with a beat, to the dancing, the Young Liberal lady cheerleaders, and to the Leader depicted on all the posters. A foreign journalist who has been observing the campaign described it as "US politics circa 1910 — materialistic, moralistic, appealing to greed, nothing for the heart or the head, an accountant's view of what the voters want". Mr Fraser has had few interjections to deal with since his audiences are for ticket-holders. He has not been quick with a good riposte on the odd occasion when one was required. However, the next night at Moon-ee Ponds, in Melbourne, when an interjector (outside the hall making use of an air vent) screamed, "lies, lies", Mr Fraser rapped back, "That is the voice of Labor. When a totalitarian party can't stand the truth they shout 'lies!'". It went down well in a migrant0 communities audience whose posters read, "Croatia supports Lib-eral", "Fraser the Saviour", "Polish Australians welcome Fraser". There was another Mr Fraser liked and commented on. "One of those placards down there", he said, "sums up a lot about this election — 'Australia doesn't trust Mr Whitlam'". And Mr Fraser is almost certainly right. Mr Whitiam's audiences are not chosen, and they largely fall into two groups. They are the committed young and the committed old. Not frenzied His rally in Melbourne on Tuesday "White-collar workers for Labor", was like that, and it was warm rather than frenzied. But it was not enough. Some of his team looked at the lack of 30- to 50-year-olds and knew it then. The next day all knew it when they saw the three opinion polls — Irving Saulwick's in The Age, Melbourne, and The Sydney. Morning Herald saying 54 per cent to the Government and 46 per cent to Labor, the Gallup Poll in The Herald and Weekly Times saying 53 per cent and 47 per cent, and the Morgan Gallup Poll in The Bulletin taken a week earlier. That poll did not give a two-party preferred result, but on its first preferences it was in line with the others' polls of the same date, November 26-27, giving the Government 45 per cent, Labor 43, Australian Democrat 9, and others 3. When the polls message became Mr Whitlam: lacklustre press conference known Labor officials and staff were disheartened, and soon afterward Mr Whitlam and Mr Hayden gave a lacklustre press conference in Brisbane. Mr Whitlam's last TV appearances on Wednesday night were similarly dull. However, the polls have a few other messages too. More than usually they are offering warnings against being taken to the last percentage point. They recognise the high volatility of an electorate which has taken Mr Chipp to heart. They differ about the Australian Democrats second preferences, while pointing out that more than 40 per cent of Chipp voters think the election is unimportant anyway. And they show that more voters than usual, particularly among the Australian Democrats, could still change their mind about their vote.

10 Dec 1977 - It's all over, bar the shouting — if the pundits are right Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 10 December 1977, page 2 It's all over, bar the shouting — if the pundits are right POLITICS By GAY DAVIDSON JLoDAY Australia will return the coalition parties to Government with A smaller majority, and put Labor in a better position to train for and aim at government next time. Labor, with time, and a rtcw leader, will lose the "three dark years" image. Much of the interest in politics over the next three years will focus on the directions in which their policies and priorities change. But on both the Government drid Opposition sides of Parliament therfi will be another major interest —' how each deals with the Australian Democrats in the electorate and the one or more in the Senate. If the numbers in the Senate are very close, Mr Fraser will have to work very much harder to ensure that defections from his own team are fio more embarrassing than the threat over pensioner funeral bene fits. Hostility In addition, he may well have considerable problems with the Senate and Joint Committees. Vociferous Labor and Australian Democrat Senators could do a great doal for democracy — not to mention public information — in that Chamber, and thus for Parliament as a whole. All of which makes Mr Eraser's lightly-veiled hostility towards the "Chippoerats" unwise. Looking back over the' campaign, this ap pears to be the only political mistake he has made.. He has said Mr ChippVpolicies are aligrted with Labof'S aild he has not backed away from Mr Anthony's scofriful "lily-livered and irresponsible" Comment on Demo crat voters. Deals More recently he has accused the Democrats 6f Conriivance with La" bor. , Yesterday, at his press conference at Kirribilli House, he was asked if he thought there had been any deals. "That would be a fairly obvious assumption to make under the circumstances", he replied. "It's the assumption orie makes from what's happened". Was he awafe of any action by the Liberal Party in Sdutli Australia (o take court action to restrain Mrs Janine Haines (Australian Democrats) from taking the Senate seat vacated by Mr Steele Hall (formerly Liberal Movement Leader and now a Liberal Party member)? "1 haven't discussed it with anyone from South Australia. I'll talk about things sifter the election". In view of the South Australian decision to recommend the appoint* ment of a Democrat, did he wish he had drafted the referendum on the Filling of casual Senate vacancies differently? "I think that'we always tinderSto6d that there could be circumstances where, if there were a dis* puter it would have to be determined by a Court". , Was" not the intention of the referendum to replace a retiring 6r dead senator with an appointment from his own political party? "Isn't tfve argument then that the Libcfal Movement merged with the Liberal Party? If the major part of it joined with the Liberal Party, as it did, I would have thought you'd say the LM merged With the Liberal Party". In those answers Mr Fraser contiriuddtO allege deals which both the Labor and the Australian Demo-, crats parties have denied. Absorbed He continued td assert that the LM had gone to the Liberal Party — in spite Of the fact that the former LM leader irt South Australia Mf Robin Millhoase, claims that it has been absorbed by the Democrats, whom he now leads and represents. In spite also, of the fact that Mrs Haines was an LM Candidate and is now with the Denldcrats, and that the South Australian Crown Solicitor reportedly advised the Dunstan Government in favour of a Democrats nomination. Mr Fraser also left no room for doubt that the Liberal Party would pursue the Democrats nomination in court to have it set aside. If, as suggested by the most recent Morgan Gallup poll, Democrat voters' approval for Mr Fraser has dropped Six per cent, in the past week, while approval for Mr Whitlam has risen by nine per cent, Mr Fraser can blame only himself. If Democrat second preferences today look any higher than expected for The swinging voter Labor, he can also blame those remarks. If Mr Chipp's and Mr Fraser's antipathy for each Other clouds the Prime Minister's political judgment to the point where he will make no effort to assuage Mr Chipp and Chippocrat feelings, and no effort to conciliate on policy differences, the Liberal Party and parliamentarians will need to do some fast footwork in the next week or two. The first thing they will have to ensure — and it will be against Mr Fraser's wishes and manoeuvrings — is the election of a "small-l" Liberal Deputy Leader. Obvious Preferably, they will need to get the party-room numbers for one who has. remained personally friendly with Mr Chipp, and who has been publicly moderate enough to appear respectable to Democrat voters, and respectable enough to justify Mr Chipp's voting with the Government on all but the most contentious is sues. Mr Peacock is the obvious candidate. Mr Snedden could be another, except that recent history is not on his side as far as his colleagues are concerned, and in the past week he has also suggested that a Democrat vote is a wasted first-preference vote. If Mr Fraser does not learn to woo, or at least to negotiate and conciliate, the Australian Democrats may well be his undoing. ■ Observers of the political scene have been frequently surprised at the general acquiescence to Mr Fraser's "crash-through" tactics, and his penchant for arranging circumstances to provide the confrontations suited to such tactics. If he does not bend this time, or if moderation is not imposed on him, he too could crash.

22 Aug 1978 - Case against whaling Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 22 August 1978, page 2 Case against whaling Sir, - In reference, to Mr Athol Thomas's article on the closure of the Cheynes Beach Whaling Com pany (The Canberra Times, August 4), it is indeed unfortunate that the whalers and their "press" gang should, in criticising the emo tionalism of the anti-whaling lobby, themselves resort to emotional argu ments. It should be noted that the argu ments of the anti-whaling lobby are based on scientific, economic, politi cal and moral grounds, in that order of importance. Briefly, the following are but a few examples of the misin-formation contained in Mr Thomas's article. Firstly, as to the alleged loss of 102 jobs, no less an authority than the Commonwealth Government has stated that the present development of large-scale fishmeal processing plants in Albany will readily absorb those employed by the whaling com pany. Secondly, contrary to Mr Thom as's assertion that the IWC's quota system has blunted criticism, it has only served to sharpen it. The world's leading bio-statisticians and whale biologists have, at two sepa rate meetings, virtually heaped copious quantities of manure on the theory, its application and the in formation input. Thirdly, Mr Thomas claims that the catch level is only 1.18 per cent of the total southern-hemisphere population level. No population studies have been done, and the estimates of population vary so wide ly as to be ridiculous. The whalers' estimate the sperm whale population off our coast at anywhere from 15,000 to 60,000. They split the difference, working on a figure of 30,000 with a 10 per cent error margin. Thus the 1.18 percent figure is almost as frivolous as Mr Thomas's article. Fourthly, the closure of the com pany is not a hollow victory, hollow ness being restricted to the cranial capacities of those who discount the advance. Australia, a major power in the IWC, can now join a majority of member nations pressing for a 10 year moratorium on whale slaughter. Fifthly, contrary to Mr Thomas's assertion, Australia may, as Canada does, retain its quota, saving 1,000 whales per annum from perfume, soap, oil and dog-food factories. Sixthly, the anti-whaling group is not a vocal minority, but a vocal majority of Australians; 80 per cent, according to an ANOP poll. Finally, as both space and patience are running out, comments made by Mr Thomas, and those quoted by him with approval reflecting on the quality and stature of an independent inquiry headed by a knight and distinguished former Chief Justice of the PNG Supreme Court are totally unjustifiable and most reprehensible. Emotional, illogical and misleading comments tainted with bitterness and vindictiveness only cloud the scientific, economic and political is sues on which the future of whaling must be decided. On all points, we argue the industry is unjustifiable, and a positive threat to this most remarkable creature. PETER WATERS Weetangera.

27 Sep 1978 - NSW ELECTION The contest seems already over, bar the shouting Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 27 September 1978, page 2 NSW ELECTION The contest seems already over, bar the shouting A CERTAIN inevitabili- ty of a Labor victory ap-pears to hang over NSW's October 7 election and it is difficult to find a commen-tator who seriously doubts that the Premier, Mr Wran will win, probably well. A recent ANOP-National Times poll suggests that 64 per cent of New South Welshmen are satisfied with Mr Wran's Government. The Premier himself gets a satis-faction rating from 79 per cent of people, while the Opposition leader, Mr Coleman, is pleasing just 29 per cent of the potential voters. It is a state of affairs which is reflected in the campaigns. While Mr Wran has been able to eschew extravagant promises and point reassuringly to stable, respon-sible government over the past 28 months, Mr Coleman has been forced to delve into the world of near-melodrama and, some would have it, economic fantasy. Freeways Liberal advertisements showing youths preparing heroin and inject-ing it — an attempt to portray Labor as "soft" on the drug issue — were branded "immoral" by some drug educators and rejected by some tele-vision stations. Another advertisement, on La-bor's freeways policy, was with-drawn after complaints that it was inaccurate. And though few people would complain that Mr Coleman's policy speech, delivered on September 21 at Hurstville Civic Centre, was not attractive, surprisingly vigorous and inventive, the economic feasibility of cutting personal income tax by five per cent, the immediate abolition of death duties and cuts in payroll tax, have been called into question by even the most conservative elements. The Sydney Morning Herald greeted Mr Coleman's speech thus: "The question is whether a Liberal Country Party Government would find the fulfilment . .. within the State's financial capacity .... A big question mark hangs over Mr Col-eman's program. It is attractive, but is it financially possible?... He will have to convince voters that it is". Mr Wran is one who is clearly not convinced. "We've costed all these promises of income-tax cuts and the like and they add up to over $800 million in a year", he said. Impossible "They would mean all existing State taxes or charges would need to be increased by 50 per cent if these promises were to be carried out. "A tax-cut to wage-earners of this size is absolutely impossible", says the Premier. For all that, it is not an easy campaign for Mr Coleman, and many impartial observers might feel the Opposition leader has done well. Certainly there has been little sign that it is a token battle of rhetoric, little sign that basically October 7 has been conceded to Labor. Desperation For the coalition the omens are not good. Last time Mr Coleman faced Mr Wran was in the by election for the former Premier Sir Eric Willis's vacated seat of Earl wood on July 15. Labor took the seat Sir Eric had held for 28 years with a swing of almost 10 per cent. Electoral expert Mr Malcolm Mackerras is one who has predicted a 20-seat majority for Labor — it is a three-seat majority since Earlwood — with a general swing to Labor of about seven per cent. But Mr Coleman has given every indication of someone who has put the pollsters and the bleaker possi bilities behind him and come out fighting, albeit with a trace of des-peration. For example, he found Labor's policy speech so "uninspiring" and "dull" that it did not require much comment. Barring some strange upset, Mr Coleman and his Country Party counterpart, Mr Punch, will not oust Labor on October 7. But in an ironical way the good tidings for Labor, emanating for months now from surveys and parties research, could give Mr Coleman an oppor-tunity to do a deal better than some people expect, and enough to retain his job. Harbinger The coalition's stock has been so low at times during the past 2½ years that some feel all Mr Coleman has to do to achieve a kind of "suc-cess" is simply to stave off a disaster — a landslide to Labor — of which Earlwood could have been a harb-inger. This, of course, is assuming that Mr Coleman manages to retain his own seat of Fuller, vulnerable to Labor on a swing of just over four per cent. As mentioned already, it is not an easy campaign for Mr Coleman. Labor spokesmen freely concede that Mr Wran is its most marketable commodity, and Labor's campaign is centred firmly around its adept Pre- mier. The Premier leads an apparently unified party with its fair share of conservative, "Establishment" fig-ures at Cabinet level. Aside from two comparatively minor instances fea-turing the Mines and Energy Min-ister, Mr Hills, and the Attorney-General, Mr Walker, no public dis-agreement between Premier and Cabinet has surfaced in 28 months. There are those who may fear what a Wran Government with an unassailable majority might get up to, but they have little upon which to build their fears. Disunity For Mr Coleman it is a different story. He can hardly be promoted Wran-style. He has been in the job a meagre few months. There was disunity, and what one Liberal official called "organised chaos", when the then Premier, Mr Lewis, was supplanted by Sir Eric Willis. There was much of the same as Sir Eric battled to stem the tide of Mr Wran's rising popularity. Few Liberal MPs could honestly claim that Sir Eric had the sort of backing in some parliamentary quarters that he probably deserved. When he was replaced by Mr Col-eman, after the media had tossed name after name around for weeks, the Liberals in NSW had taken on the look of a party that only a masochist would want to lead into an election within about five years. Mr Coleman had been in charge a matter of weeks when reports of moderate versus right faction-fight- ing within the party (The Canberra Times, 19 May) gave Mr Wran a golden opportunity to talk patron-isingly of the need for governments to face an effective Opposition under the Westminster system. On the basic election quin-tessential issues Mr Wran has left Mr Coleman and Mr Punch precious few pickings. Public transport, an issue for Op-position in NSW since most people can remember, is being hailed by the Transport Minister, Mr Cox, as a Labor success. It is, says Mr Cox, being rejuvenated, improved and its fiscal deficit merely a matter of updating what 11 years of coalition rule allowed to degenerate. Unemployment, something NSW led Australia in, has been brought under control, says Mr Wran. Statistics are open to different in terpretations, but rccent figures sug-gest that the State has graduated from first to fifth in the jobless stakes. A senior Labor source commented this weekend, "I've got nothing against Peter (Coleman). I quite like the bloke. I think he's doing the best anybody could do. But if he wins this one he'll defy logic". Mr Wran: 79 per cent satisfaction rating Mr Hills Mr Walker Disagreements — but only minor ones.

27 Oct 1978 - UK GALLUP POLL Labour 5½pc ahead' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 27 October 1978, page 6 UK GALLUP POLL Labour *5Vipc ahead' LONDON, Thursday (AAP-PA). — Labour leads the Conservatives by 5'/j per cent according to the latest Gallup poll reported in the Daily Telegraph last night. The poll shows a massive turn-around in public opinion. Last month the Conservatives were said by the same poll to hold a 7 per cent lead. The percentage of people finding the performance of the leaders satisfactory compared with last month were: The Prime Minister, Mr Callaghan, 55 per cent (51), the Leader of the Opposition, Mrs Thatcher 40 per cent (39), the Liberal leader, Mr Steel, 44 per cent (34).

20 Mar 1979 - Top marks to poll from Gallup Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 20 March 1979, page 3 Top marks to poll from Gallup SYDNEY: Gallup polls were one of the really constructive developments of a democratic world, the man who founded the poll said yesterday. Dr George Gallup, 77, once described as "America's chief soothsayer and oracle", was speaking in Sydney after addressing the annual seminar of the Australian Association of National Advertisers. He said the concept of a world poll, which could report what the majority of the world's inhabitants thought within a few days, would be operating in the next decade or two. "With this kind of people-to-people communication, perhaps some of the frictions which cause misunderstandings and wars can be removed in the future", he said. In 1935 Dr Gallup began taking polls based on "scientific sampling" — a concept then unique in determining public opinion. The Gallup poll is now established in about 30 countries, reflecting public opinion on anything from politics to soap powder. "We could poll the whole US in about six hours now by telephone", Dr Gallup said yesterday. "Of course that is due mostly to the fact that 93 per cent of all Americans have telephones. "But if any great crisis occurred and you wanted to get the public reaction to it we could get it between six o'clock and midnight". The poll had progressed from where its margin of error was 5 per cent, up to the last Congressional elections in the US in November, when the margin had been reduced to half a percentage point. It was "sheer nonsense" to suggest polls influenced public opinion. They were an accurate reflection of public opinion, and "the public more often than not has come to a better conclusion or decision than their leaders".

12 Jun 1979 - Energy crisis imaginary to many in US Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 12 June 1979, page 15 Energy crisis imaginary to many in US 22 From JUREK MARTIN, in Washington SEVENTY-SEVEN per cent of the American public, according to the latest Gallup Poll, do not believe the energy crisis is real. They are convinced that the long lines at the petrol pumps in California and some eastern cities and the one-third increase in the price of petrol is a confection of the oil companies wanting higher profits, or of their own Federal Government, or even both working together. Occasionally, but much less so than in 1973-74, they blame the Arabs, It is true that Americans are buying more smaller, often foreign, cars, which use less fuel, even driving less without discomfort. But what is more true . is that they are craving for an explanation of what is going on. Lacking it, they are suspending belief that the problem is real and looking for scapegoats to point at in the meanwhile. It is against this background, for the existence of which he must be held at least partly responsible, that President Carter is trying to forge an energy policy which not only meets America's needs but also spares the rest of the world from the excess of US consumption. A major clement of that policy began to take effect recently when the first stage of his phased decontrol of domestic oil prices was instituted. But for every piece of the jigsaw that he has managed to put in place, matching elements are missing - indeed it is at least conceivable that even the decontrol plan could yet be reversed by the Congress. Last year's Energy Act typically gave Mr Carter half a loaf: he finally obtained the gradual removal of restrictions on natural-gas prices. But he was denied the well-head tax on crude oil. Congress cnactcd modest proposals to encourage the use of coal, but did not really deter Detroit from continuing to produce cars with heavy petrol consumption. Mr Carter never claimed the Act was more than a beginning but a beginning was the most he could seek. This year, his chances of a similar mix look better in the wake of the Iranian shortfall and OPEC's aggressive pricing policies, which have accentuated the need for greater domestic output (though how much extra would be generated by decontrol is a matter of dispute even inside the Administration). Assuming he can head off liberal opposition to decontrol, the President should obtain a windfall profits tax on the oil companies. From a political standpoint, the imposition of such a levy looks inevitable. The question is, who gets the proceeds - the Government, to dispose of as it wishes, or the companies, to plough back into exploration? The extremely powerful oil-industry lobby will be pitted in Congress against influential regional, environmental and consumer causes and it is Congress, not the President, who will determine the final outcome. The Administration does have - and has used - a variety of executive powers to deal with specific contingencies: these include the "gasoline tilt" - regulations to promote greater petrol production; subsidies for the importing of diesel and heating oil to build up depleted stocks in the summer; giving State governors limited extra powers to control petrolpurchasing habits; relaxing anti-pollution rules; controlling public-building thermostats and enforcing the 55mph speed limit. There are many others, though each is little more than a palliative. The President was also empowered by law to come up with a standby petrol-rationing plan, but the House of Representatives, at its most parochial and confused, denied him even this residual authority. And yet it may be this very multiplicity of tools - some in the President's hands, some in the lap of Congress, some relying on the price mechanism, some on tax - which contribute to the public bewilderment. This is a country which has always possessed the capacity to energise itself in pursuit of a perceived goal, but nobody has yet satisfactorily identified the target. Moreover, the US is currently in something of a mean-spirited mood: the President's Press Secretary, Mr Jody Powell, described it the other day as an attitude of "me first, last and always: give me mine and to hell with the rest of the country". This is overstated perhaps, but hardly a day goes by without some special interest group "demanding" this or that of the President or the Congress. Mr Carter has had to say no so often that he has got himself into deep political hot water. His perceived neglect of traditional democratic constituencies has made all,the more alluring the alternative candidacy of Senator Edward Kennedy, whose own constituency as a liberal and a north-easterner is much narrower than the Presi dent's. Mr Kennedy, at least, I has the virtue of being consistent to his beliefs, which is more than can be said for many of his colleagues who, lacking decisive guidance from either the Congressional hierarchy or from the White House, have found it simpler to take the side of pajrtial powerful interests and painless to deny less influential supplicants (witness the cuts in the Foreign Aid Bill, for example). But a President, America likes to think, is supposed sometimes to rise above the battle. Prisoner of circumstanccs though he may be (even to the extent of having to rely on the oil industry for energy data), Mr Carter has, by common agreement, not helped his own and the nation's cause by neglecting fully to use the educative powers of the presidency. Diagnosis has never been a problem for Mr Carter: conveying it to the public has proved much more difficult. He said recently he thought the public was beginning to get "aroused" about energy: according to Gallup only 23 per cent are sufficiently aroused to believe the problem is real, and the US Congress is nothing if not close to the public. Financial Times.

01 Sep 1941 - GALLUP MAJORITY AGAINST HITLER PEACE OFFER Northern Star (Lismore, NSW : 1876 - 1954), Monday 1 September 1941, page 1 GALLUP MAJORITY AGAINST HITLER PEACE OFFER NEW YORK, Saturday (AAP).— A Gallup poll reveals that 58 peri ct-nt. of Americans would reject a new Hitler peace offer "even if it included the restoration of every scrap of Nazi conquest excepting Russia." 16 May 1988 - I've no leadership worries: Ahern Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 16 May 1988, page 3 I've no leadership worries: Ahern Queensland Premier Mr Ahern dismissed yesterday allegations that he was having leadership problems and expressed strong confidence in the Queensland National Party's future. Speaking on the Nine network's Sunday program, Mr Ahern said he resented any interpretation of his refusal to sign the Loan Council Agreement as that of a Premier trying to shake off an indecisive, wimpish im age. He said he would resent any suggestion he acted at last week's Premiers' Conference in any way other than what he saw as the primary interest of the people and state of Queensland. Pointing to the last Morgan Gallup Poll's 63 per cent approval rating on his leadership, Mr Ahern said, "I don't think 1 need worry about it [my leadership] very much." Asked if he was worried about the criticism that he was friends with everybody — unlike his predecessor Sir Joh Bjelke-Petersen — Mr Ahern said he did not think that was a problem. "1 have not seen that turn up in our research," he said. Mr Ahern also said the Federal Government had misunderstood a requirement to segregate capital funding provided by the states into at least two parcels — economic and social. The Federal Government had lumped capital funding together and then said there was too much capitalborrowing going on, he said, whereas it should have looked at where the money was actually being spent. Meanwhile, Queensland Opposition Leader Mr Wayne Goss predicted yesterday that the Nationals would lose another safe seat should stooddown Cabinet Minister Mr Hinze retire. But it would be an open contest as to which other party would win the South Coast seat. He said it was unfair that Mr Hinze — despite being named at the Fitzgerald Inquiry — could retire with his superannuation payment [$750,000] while police and public servants could not. He said this indicated preferential treatment given to politicians by the Government. "At present, the situation is that Members of Parliament can just take the money and run," Mr Goss said.

19 Aug 1940 - Notes on the Cables "ON THE SPOT" Argus (Melbourne, Vic. : 1848 - 1957), Monday 19 August 1940, page 3 Notes on the Cables "ON THE SPOT" Wendell Willkie and the Dictators By A. L. BRUNT Isolationists-once very noisy and strid- ent are getting scarce In the United States. The most recent Gallup Polls have shown a decided decrease in their numbers; but it was not so certain that! their leaders variously and not always honourably actuated-had ceased their activities. Death cut one of these short not very long ago. When his widow, who had thought him a comparatively poor man, opened his safe deposit box, it? contained a quarter of a million do lars! There are some isolationists maris and encouraged to persist. A But the latest statement by Mr. Wen. dell Willkie, upon accepting nominated as the Republican candidate for the Fire sidency, will leave them little scope f86 I their perfidy. The world already 'knew what President Roosevelt, at the heart of the great Democratic party, thoughtia'DOUt Hitler and Mussolini. As the spokesman of decent opinion among his countrymen he has given some hard knock fo both the Nazi and Fascist leaders, probably never before in history have Ap& heads of States had to submit to such unrestrained criticism from the <^hy=f Executive of a "friendly" nation. TVnigh hides and cowardice can put up with in a lot! REPUBLICAN POJLVCY Now we know what Mr. y Wendell Willkie at the head of the great Republican party, thinks of the dicteA/jrs across the Atlantic. Little notice n s I be taken of his aspersions upon President Roosevelt's conduct of le feign affairs rather wide and vague a description considering that the g a later part of the eight most critical yt /rs In world history Is embraced. He would be a paragon, indeed, who could speak his mind and it happened to be the, mind of the people at large-about su 26, persons as Hitler and Mussolini upon s t> many provocative occasions, without offending against some of the niceties t>V diplomacy in the eyes of a man of President Roosevelt's calibres as they are in the eyes of all canal, upright, God-fearing people, Hitler and Mussolini merit only contempt, a day the utmost contempt at that. If of. willkie should ever reach White Hou to, and the hated dictators are still on ev! /'ocnt-which is not so likelyhe will, in the weird and wonderful language of. American journalism, be as anxious as anybody else to splash a bucket at lead in the faces of the bad men." 7, WORTH OF BRITISH NAVY The ,, main points in Mr. Wilkie's de-can Zion are those in which he expresses BBr smear with President Roosevelt And thy j are (ne essential points because they lc etc to the future, with which, as an 0 spiring occupant of the White House, T #r Willkie must prepare to deal Briefly stated, Mr. Willkie declares his agreement with the present Roosveltian policy of giving material aid to Great Britain, short of war. It is true that he I goes one step further than the President, when he says that he does not understand this to mean America's active participa-tion in the present hostilities." But the reservation loses a good deal of its scope when he admits in the next sentence that the British Navy is part of the defences of the United States, and that as such its destruction would leave the Atlantic dominated by Germany, a Power hostile to our way of life." NAZI TRADE METHODS And it is not only the military danger to the United States that Mr. Willkie envisages. His discerning business eye foresees an attempt by a successful Ger-many to dominate world trade by Nazi methods, thus reducing to naught 65 per cent, of the world's gold, now held by the United States. The prospect of having, perforce, to copy Germany's totalitarian methods of doing business among the nations is utterly abhorrent to American lovers of democracy. Mr. Wilkie's criticism of President Roosevelt's handling of the war position apart-and it is mostly electioneering material for the Presidential campaign to be held between now and the first Tuesday in November it will be seen that the Republican leader is at least as violently opposed to the dictators as is the Democratic leader. THE DAY MUST COME Hitler, and Mussolini know beyond doubt that whatever may be their successes in Europe to-day, or to-morrow, or the day afterwards, they must eventually face the United States, potentially the greatest military Power on earth. That will be their plight-whoever wins in November, Roosevelt or Willkie from this moment until January 1, 1945. A rather despairing prospect for the dictators, and in the case of Hitler especially galling because of the latest leader to put him on the spot is a first generation Ger- man-American.

21 Sep 1944 - FIRST FISSURES Argus (Melbourne, Vic. : 1848 - 1957), Thursday 21 September 1944, page 2 FIRST FISSURES An Impromptu "Gallup poll"! conducted among German prisoners by our staff correspondent, MR. GEOFFREY HUTTON, and recently set out in detail on this page, yielded interestling results. Out of some 300, I only 42-about one in seven thought that Germany would win the war. The few optimists were fanatical believers in the miracle-working FUHRER; their faith was compounded of divine right seriously challenged by the recent attempt on HITLER'S life-and secret weapons more than challenged by our advance along the Pas-de-Calais coast and our sudden irruption into Holland. These prisoners had, of course, had a gruelling experience; but not more gruelling than that of Germans captured some weeks earlier, and our correspondent noticed, even among officers, a sharp decline of cocksureness." Taken in conjunction with reports that have appeared on the internal situation in Germany, the results of this inquiry justify the supposition that those first fissures are at last beginning to appear in the structure of German morale which will eventually lead to catastrophic collapse. Such a collapse, as we have argued more than once in this column, could not come from internal causes only; it had to be brought about by defeat in the field; and of that there has been no lack since D-Day of more than three months ago. Portents There have been other portents besides direct military defeats, though these have been on a shattering scale and must come first in our estimate of the situation. Constant air-raids, for example, must surely have made some impression on the German man in the street, who has in one city after another been transformed, in numberless cases, into a man on the street. The plot against the FUHRER must have made it clear that some Germans, at any rate, had serious doubts about HITLER'S mission and infallibility; and such scepticism could hardly fail to produce a certain amount of contagion, however secret. The more secret it is, in fact, the more dangerous it must be, for secrecy in this case is a challenge to regimented fanaticism. The plot mis-carried and was followed by a drastic purge; but this purge was in turn fraught with perilous consequences. On the one hand it must have created quite a large amount of resentment in military circles, more especially as highranking German officers were executed in a manner that was as degrading as it was barbaric; and on the other hand, it could not fail to bring about some misgivings in the minds of the people as to the integrity or the infallibility of the German High Command. This infallibility has been further and more devastatingly shaken by military defeats that no censorship can hide. In Black and White For evidence of it is there, in black and white, on a map that cannot be faked by GOEBBELS and his henchmen, seeing that it takes in the Fatherland itself. Whatever the German faith or lack of faith in the FUHRER may be, the cold hard fact remains that a few weeks ago the German armies were fighting hundreds of miles away from their own frontiers, while today they are defending Germany on Germany's own "sacred" soil. Add to this the serious sapping that is taking place in the morale of German airmen owing to their in-sufficiency of aircraft and fuel, and the total does not amount to anything outstand-ingly cheerful from a German point of view. Defeat is inevitable, and foreknowledge of it is beyond the control even of a HIMMLER. The reasons for this inevitability are daily Continued in Next Column LEADER (Continued) becoming more patent; these reasons are more than fissures in the walls, they are gaping holes, and once they become fully apparent the whole inhuman structure of militant pan-Germans must come crashing to the ground, ending, as it began, in blood and tumult.
