16 Dec 1944 - Over 1,000 Employees Tell Housing Needs for Village Argus (Melbourne, Vic. : 1848 - 1957), Saturday 16 December 1944, page 8 Over 1,000 Employees Tell Housing Needs for Village While the majority of Dunlop employees want to live near their work, some have said they do not desire to do so because they might feel they are "right on the doorstep of the factory." This picture of a section of the residential area of Dunlop Garden Village 'to be built at Beaumaris has | been drawn by Stephenson and Turner, architects, to show that although close to the homes the new factory (in the background to the right) will be isolated from them. The shopping centre flanked by hostels for single employees is shown in the middle of the background. Questionnaires Act As "Gallup Poll" For Dunlop Company By a Special Correspondent ONE of the most pleasing features of Dunlop Rubber Australia Ltd's scheme for transferring its factory from Montague to Beaumaris and establishing there a garden vil- lage for the convenience of em-ployees, is the "Gallup Poll" which has, ascertained their wishes. Its most pleasing aspect lies in the company's attitude towards those men and women it employs, for it shows keenness to consider their wishes in every respect. They have been asked not only if they would like to live near their work, but the type of accommodation and facili-ties they would prefer. This is probably the first time a cross section of housing needs has beer obtained from a large body of workers, and the company's request for this information has met with already response. Of the 1,061 questionnaires sent to married men at the Montague and Abbotsford factories, 1,008 have been Live near work or away from it? Near Work, 53%; Near Beach, 26%; Inner Suburb, 4%; Outer Suburb, 17%. Rent or Ownership? Single Storey?. Brick or Timber? filled in and returned in recent weeks. The questionnaires, besides being valuable as a guide to the company in its planning of Dunlop Garden Village, will be found intensely in-teresting by many outsiders, showing as they do the reactions of so many workers to important features of housing. Another pleasing feature is the ob-vious thought given by employees to the questions before replying to them. There was not one facetious or abusive reply. Any comment that was made was either to praise the scheme or to offer some constructive suggestion. One man even sent along the plan of his home because he and his family, having found it a con-venient place to live In. thought it might be helpful to the company's architects, Stephenson and Turner, in drawing up plans for the houses. Married employees who are in the forces were not forgotten, and of 97 questionnaires sent to date, 52 re-plies have been received. ACCOMPANYING questionnaires sent to servicemen was a letter from Mr W. A. Bartlett, general manager of "the company. This contained the following remarks: "Here is a matter vital to you and very much in my mind in contem-plating your return to us. namely, the acute shortage of housing ac-commodation throughout Australia. This problem will become even more serious upon the return of service-men to home life. Therefore, it is essential that we complete the plans for Dunlop Garden Village at Beau-maris in readiness for building to commence as soon as circumstances permit. "I think it will be your wish as a Dunlop employee so to assist in planning the undertaking - the first of its kind in Australia - by indi-cating your thoughts as to the type of house in which a serviceman upon return to family life would like to live. "In answering the queries on the enclosed questionnaire, please'under-stand you will not be entering into any obligation nor. committing your-self in any way. You will, however, be providing information which will form the basis of the Garden Vil-lage scheme. "It may not be possible, of course, to incorporate all the features men-tioned in the questionnaire, but your reply, together with those of your colleagues at Montague, will assist the company to plan this project so that as far as possible homes of the kind which employees most desire will be available." Here are some of the replies Mr Bartlett received from men in the services. "I think it is a fine gesture on the part of the company to go to the trouble of seeking the opinion of their employees, and it should augur well for the success of the great move." "I wish to thank you for letting me, an employee, air my views on your wonderful scheme. I know it will be a major success. It will certainly solve a great problem for servicemen -housing." "The Beaumaris scheme sounds great for returned servicemen." "I consider the questionnaire a very good idea, and I sincerely hope the day is not far distant when we can take up residence at Beaumaris." "I think it is a wonderful scheme. I have sent the form to my wife, together with my views on the ques- tions." "It is my intention on returning to civilian life to purchase a house of my own. Therefore. I would like to know upon what terms X would be able to purchase the house through your scheme, which I think a splen-did idea." (An explanation regarding . this query will be contained in next week's article on this page.) Curious as to why some employees answered some questions in the way they did, THE ARGUS représentative interviewed them. Their remarks are given, along with the result of the "Gallup Poll." LIVING NEAR WORK: Would you prefer to live near your work? There are 533 who say they would prefer to live near their work; 463 say they would rather not. and 12 do not indicate one way or the other. Of the 463 who would sooner not live near their work. 257 want to live near the beach, 165 would prefer to live in outer suburbs, and 41 in inner suburbs. Of the 52 servicemen who replied, 39 would prefer to live near their work, 12 do not want to, and one is neutral. At present, 17% of the married em-ployees live along the beach from St Kilda to Frankston; 33% in the inner industrial suburbs-North. Mel-bourne, Carlton, Fitzroy, Collingwood, Richmond, Prahran, South Mel-bourne, Port Melbourne; 46% in the cuter or residential areas, and 4% in outlying places such as Greens-borough, Bayswater, Springvale, Mitcham, Croydon, Dandenong. "We don't want to feel we are right on the doorstep of the factory after working there all day." This was the reason some of the men gave for not wanting to live near their work. At the same time they said they had not realised when replying to the questionnaire that the new factory at Beaumaris, although only half a mile from the farthest house, would be quite apart from the residential area, and this has since made all the difference to their views in this regard. One contended that In such a com-munity everybody would know every-body else's business and this did not appeal to him. To avoid this he would sooner travel a long distance to work, despite the extra expense. Others who did not want to live near their work were Influenced by the fact that they were at present residing in a congested industrial area, and thought the atmosphere at Beaumaris might be the same. They admitted they might alter their minds after having seen the plans for the garden village. Other employees who are buying their homes in various suburbs and have put a lot of work into their gardens do not feel like leaving them. RENT OR OWNERSHIP ? : If a suitable house were available would you prefer to rent it or purchase it over a period on a rental-purchase basis? As was to be expected, home owner-ship appeals to the majority, 833 wishing to purchase their homes over a period on a rental-purchase basis and only 175 preferring to pay rent. Fifty of the 52 servicemen want Eating and Relaxing? to purchase their homes, the other two desiring more details before de-ciding. "The sooner the Beaumaris scheme goes ahead the better pleased my wife and I will be," said one young man, who would like one of the Beaumaris homes on a rental-pur-. chase basis. Since he was discharged from the Army Ave months ago, this ex-mem-ber of the AIF, his wife and child have been living in a shop, the only accommodation they could get. Only 24 now, he enlisted when he was 19. and had five years' service in the Middle East and up north. He was wounded in the Middle East. HOUSING: Would you prefer a single or two-storey house, flat, or maisonette? It is not surprising that 879 want single-storey nouses and that flats are unpopular* in view of the number wanting to buy their homes. Only 13 want flats, 59 prefer two-storey houses, and 57 maisonettes. Only one of the 52 sarvicemen does not want a single-storey house, and he would prefer a maisonette. BRICK OR TIMBER?: If you pre- fer a single-storey house, would you prefer brick or wood con-struction? There are 789 who want brick and 90 timber. There are 42 servicemen who prefer brick and nine timber. One employee suggests that homes be built of concrete so as to save maintenance costs. FOR LIVING: In planning living room accommodation would you prefer lounge, dining-room, kitchen; lounge - dining - room (combined), kitchen; lounge-din-ing-room-kitchen (combined) ? There are 681 who want separate rooms for lounge,' dining-room, and kitchen; 243 lounge-dining-room (combined) kitchen; and 84 loungeroom separate, dining-room-kitchen (combined). "Please give us roomy rooms," writes one man. "I feel it is as im-portant for the working man's family to have space for living as it is for anyone else. I would like to see lounge dining-rooms not. smaller than 18ft x 18ft and kitchens 14ft x 14ft. There is nothing so discour-aging to the woman who spends so much time there as a small kitchen. Plenty of light and hot water are also essentials." Other suggestions are that chim-neys be built on the outside walls so as to save space and avoid the cut-ting'of floor coverings. FOR THE INNER MAN: By what means would your wife prefer to cook? Dunlop workers' wives say: Gas, 491. Electricity. 277. Fuel. 20. . There are 200 who desire a fuel stove as well as a gas or electric one -a safeguard against breakdowns, no doubt. A small number do not mind whether they cook by gas or electricity. . AND SO TO BED: How many bed- rooms would you need? One.wants two single rooms only. Other figures, according to family needs, are: 282: 1 double room, 2 s ngle rooms; 200: 1 d.r, 1 s.r{ 176: 2 d.rs, 1 s.r; 170: 2 d.rs; 53: 3 d.rs; 40: 1 d.r; 3 s.rs; 45: 2 Gas? Electricity? Fuel? or Fuel Flus Electricity or Gas? ? d.rs, 2 s.rs; 24: 1 d.r; 10: 3 d.rs, 1 s.r; 5: 2 d.rs, 3 s.rs; 1: 3 d.rs, 2 s.rs; 1: 3 djrs. 3 s.rs. BATHROOM-TOILET: If you are hrv'ng a two-storey house v)ould you rather have the bathroom and lavatory on the ground or top floor? There are 40 who want the bath-room and lavatory upstairs and 17 downstairs, while two want a lavalory both upstairs and downstairs. HOT WATER: Do you consider a hot-water service essential? The desire for a hot-water service is almost unanimous-90%. Most of the 10% who do not regard a hot-water service as essential say they consider it a luxury, and as long as they have a gas bath heater they will be content. "I don't believe in a working man living above his means, and that is one reason my wife and I said 'no' to a hot-water service," said one man. "What we have never had we will not miss," said another. He added, however, that if the majority of the homes were to have hot-water ser-vices and this meant that the cost of installing them would be much cheaper than before the war he would also say "yes" to this ques- tion. IAUNDRY: Where would you like 1 your laundry done? Employees' wives apparently have no Monday morning complex, for 947 want to do their own washing. Only 46 want the full services of a laundry, while 15 who would like their linen washed at a laundry would r.refer to iron it themselves. One employee said: "My wife and I have been married 16 years, and our laundry has always been done at home. I think many husbands and wives like doing things for each other, even if it is only washing." Another said he thought his wife would be lost on a Monday if she did not go as usual to the wash-tub. Others contended that the laundry received more care and did not get shabby so quickly if done at home, and. of course, it was cheaper. WASHHOUSE: Ho you consider the washhouse should be separ-ate from the house or attached to it? There are 682 who want the wash-house attached to the house, and 265 ask for a separate building. Questioned regarding this, one man said the house he and his wife were living in at present had the laundry apart from the house, and he sup-posed that was why ihey said they preferred it that way. "It's just what We've been used to, but we would not object if it was under the same roof as the house," he added. WALLS: What finish to the walls would you suggest? The answers show a definite ten-dency towards painted or texture walls in preference to paper, par-ticularly in living rooms. GARAGE: Would you require a garage? While 817 want a garage, 191 do not feel one is necessary. FAííILY: How many childten have you? The 1,008 employees have 1,136 children. This includes one famlly. of 10 children, while there are sbc with six children. There are 380 families, or 40%, with no children at all. THE ARGUS representative took the opportunity while at the Montague factory of interviewing the proud father of 10 children, who is among those wanting to live at Beaumaris. -His eldest child is 15} years and the youngest l8 months, i For four years' the family hap been living in one of the Housing 'Commission homes at Fishermen's Bend. His wife and he prefer a singlestorey house because of the children, and they want It built oí brick. They have asked for two double bedrooms and a dormitory for the younger children. s This is the ao commodation they have at present, although they would welcome more and ' smaller bedrooms if possible. They would want their lounge, dinng-room, and kitchen separate. rhey want to cook with gas, and do not regard a hot-water service as es-sential, although if not too expen-sive they would welcome one. The mother of 10 has always done her own laundry, and does not ieel the need of outside help with it. The couple would like to buy their house if the terms are reasonable. With the imformation it has to hand, the Company feels well equipped to proceed with its plans for Dunlop Garden Village as soon as building and manpower regula-tions are lifted. Whether it will be economically sound to meet the requirements of all employees will depend on how much assistance is given by the Go-vernment in making loan money available at low interest reates and also on its policy regarding rental subsidies for workers. There are two Very good reasons why the Go-vernment should give its blessing to the undertaking. It shows initiative on the part of the Company which should be encouraged, and it plans to house 5,000 people, which would release a large number of houses in other suburbs. That the scheme will be a suc-cess there Is little doubt, and that being the case other big industrial organisations may want to follow suit, thus relieving the Government still further in the major housing problem .with which it is faced. 02 Apr 1975 - ALP 'would win election now' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 2 April 1975, page 3 ALP 'would win election now' The Australian Labor Government would retain office if an election was held now a Morgan Gallup poll issued in Canberra last night shows. The noli, commissioned by the Channel 9 network, showed that the ALP's approval rating has risen by 6 per cent 10 49 per cent. It sho,wed also that the popularity of the Prime Minister, Mr Whitlam, had risen strongly, up 7 per cent to 46 per cent. The Liberal and Country Parties1 popularity fell by 4 per cent to 44 per cent. The former Leader'of the Opposition, Mr Sncddcn, fell to .'an nil-time low of 21 per cent ? approval. His popularity before the latest poll was 25 per cent, then an all time, low for an Opposition Leader. The poll was taken between March 15 and March 22, eliding on the weekend after the Liberals elected their new leader, Mr Fraser. Mr Fraser's first approval rating as leader was 36 per cent, about the-same level as Mr Snedden's first approval rating.

02 Mar 1983 - Hawke cites figures Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 2 March 1983, page 1 Hawke cites figures lm joblesi predicted From TERESA MANNIX, in Sydney The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Hawke, produced independent research figures yesterday which predicted that Australia's unemployment could be more than a million by June under current Government policies. Mr Hawke held a news conference in Sydney to present the figures, compiled by the Parliamentary Research Service. The figures showed that it would not be unreasonable for the figure to go to above one million or 14.2 per cent of the workforce. If the participation rate remained static, there would be 885,000 Australians unemployed in June, or 12.8 per cent of the workforce. Unemployment is now just over 10 per cent. Mr Hawke said the country was facing "nothing less than a disastrous explosion in unemployment" under the Government's policies. There were already indications of the further decline in the levels of manufacturing in Australia. Twenty-four out of 28 industrial sectors were now showing significant declines in the three months to January, compared with the same period last year. "Now, in confirmation of what must be involved in a continuation of that trend under the 'no change of policy' position of Mr Fraser, we have a confirmation of what the unemployment position is likely to be, even by June of 1983," Mr Hawke said. "It is a totally disastrous picture. You can't overestimate the dimension of the tragedy confronting this country under a continuation of the economic policies of the Fraser Government. "The employment and unemployment projections have been done by economics and commerce group of the Legislative Research Service of the Parliament of Aus tralia and they made projections to June of this year on the basis of making assumptions about the existing participation rate and what they see is happening to the economy under existing policies. "They are projecting a June unemployment figure of just under 900,000 or 12.8 per cent. The actual figure they're projecting is 885,000 but they go on to say that if, in fact, you get some increase Politics debased, Pryor, Editorial. — Page 2. Letters. — Pages 2, 28. Additional campaign reports. — Pages 8, 9, 19. in the participation rate, the sort of thing which has happened in the past, they go on to say that on those assumptions you could be looking at 1.1 million unemployed by June of this year — an unemployment rate of 14.2 per cent. Mr Hawke emphasised that the figures had not been produced by the Labor Party. He quoted the document, saying that "projections of one million unemployed by June are not unrealistic". "1 want to make it clear that what this country is facing on the basis of the official statistics that have been released and the projection provided in the form that I've just indicated is nothing short of a disastrous explosion in unemployment," he said. He had concentrated during the campaign on putting forward policies to "turn around this disastrous explosion". "And it is absolutely essential for the people of this country to have hope instead of despair, growth instead of contraction, that they make the decision on March 5 to bring in a government which is committed to a change of policies," he said. "A continuation of these policies. on all the evidence, poses nothing short of an economic and social disaster for this country." The Speaker of the House of Representatives, Sir Billy Sned den, questioned last night the significance of the unemployment figures issued by Mr Hawkc. In a statement issued in Can berra, he said the papers had been prepared by the Legislative Research Service of the Federal Parliamentary Library and as such bore no official sanctions. "They are dependent upon the specifications set by the individual Member who requested it. The paper is then private and confidential to the Member. Any paper is not an official document and bears no more authority nor wisdom than the person who prepared it," he said. "The parameters set by the Member determine the guidelines for preparation and the answers are dependent on these guidelines. Mr Hawke has attributed to his paper a quality which it does not possess. "Mr Hawke does not add to the paper's authenticity by using his position to quote from it and Mr Hawke well knows that. I am surprised and disappointed that Mr Hawke should misuse a paper prepared by the research service in the way which he has. "This is not the first occasion on which an ALP Member has used such a tactic. Other ALP Members have since ceased to use that tactic. "Any person can find another to tell him what he or she wishes to be told." Poll shows Labor lead of llpc The Morgan Gallup poll to be published in today's Bulletin magazine is expectcd to show Labor has increased its lead over the Government to 11 per cent. The poll, taken last weekend, reportedly gives the ALP 52 per cent of support and the LiberalNational Party 41 per cent. This compares with the previous poll, taken over the weekend of February 19-20, which gave Labor 52 per cent against the coalition's 42 per cent. However, Mr Fraser said yesterday that he did not believe the gap was unbridgeable, even at this stage of the campaign. "There has been increasing attention to policies and issues and Australians are going to focus their minds more sharply than ever before," he predicted. "There is only one poll that counts .. . and my instincts in relation to that have not been wrong." Asked why his Government had lost popular support, Mr Fraser said, "Whenever it has been put to the test before the people of Aus tralia we have had the support that | is necessary for government." Rivals on TV The Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, and the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Hawke, will be interviewed on Melbourne's Channel 10 tonight. The two politicians will never actually face each other. They will answer the same questions while sitting in separate studios and being picked up by remote cameras. The two segments will be screened consecutively. Mr Fraser's program for today revealed that he was due at the Channel 10 studios for a live in terview at 7.30pm. Mr Hawke was due at 7pm. Television sources last night confirmed that the interviews would take place. Sydney radio personality John Laws will be the moderator, with the editor-in-chief of The Daily Telegraph, lta Buttrose, Melbourne newsreader David Johnston and political journalist Laurie Oakes asking the questions. The program will be pre-recorded and screened between 10 and Upm, just before the electronic-media blackout takes effect. Baume criticised The Minister for Education, Senator Baume, and the Opposition spokesman on education, Mr Hurford, are locked in a dispute over the propriety of Senator Baume's sending Liberal Party election-campaign material to school principals. A spokesman from Senator Baume's office said the Senator had sent more than 10,000 copies of the party's education policies to both government and non-government schools in Australia. Under the letterhead "Minister For Education", a letter attached to the brochures read, "I am sending the Liberal/National Party Government's policies on education direct to you. Education is an important issue for this Government and I hope you will see fit to pass the material on to your staff." Mr Hurford labelled the move "another coalition dirty tricks scandal". He said the Minister's use of taxpayers' money through the abuse of his postage allowance was scandalous.

12 Mar 1983 - MEDIA SURVEYS SHOW UP OUR TASTE IN NEWS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 12 March 1983, page 12 MEDIA SURVEYS SHOW UP OUR TASTE IN NEWS writers' world By MAURICE DUNLEVY I V WHEN I succeed Bob Hawke as emperor of Australia my first piece of legislation will be aimed at book editors. .Any editor who litters his or her text with acronyms and abbreviations will be hanged, drawn and quartered because I feel that's what's happened to me when I read a piece of prose such as this: "Until 1971, only one polling organisation, MGPO, met these criteria. In that year AGEP and ANOP also qualified and from 1973, so too did MCNA. MGPN replaced MGPO in July 1973." This swirl of fog drifted in from the foreshores of a valuable compendium of public opinion, 'The Media: Questions and Answers: Australian Surveys 1942-1980' by Henry Mayer, Pauline Garde and Sandra Gibbons (Allen and Unwin, 206 pp., $29.95). They might plead that the meanings of these abbreviations are given at the beginning of the book, but that won't save them when I am emperor. It will be straight to the gallows if I find 10 abbreviations on a halfpage, as I do on page 13 of this book. Apart from that I have very little to complain about. This book is a goldmine for people who teach courses in public opinion and mass communication and even contains nuggets for the general reader. It pulls together the questions pollsters and other survey researchers have asked their samples about the Aus tralian mass media over 40 years and records the answers they got. Dull? Not a bit. Let me toss you a few of the questions and see if you don't want to know the answers. How often does it happen that you can find nothing you want to watch on television? Would you favour an outspoken press, radio and pulpit campaign on -venereal disease? Would you find a program on birth control embarrassing or in poor taste? We live in the age of survey research and even if Bob Hawke, rather than Public Opinion, is emperor of the earth, it's nice to know your public opinions are valuable ftnnuoh tn hft Inrn^H .inln rim! impulses and stored in computerised data banks. I got a great kick but of being a respondent last year in a national survey on employment, even if all I had to tell the interviewer every month was that I still had the same job. She looked so disappointed at the last interview that she made me feel guilty for being unenterpris-, v ing. (And, yes, now" you know some- 1 one who really has been in a survey!) One of the most important media surveys in Australia was done in 1966 by J. S. Western and Colin A. Hughes who used a national sample to explore the political use and evaluations Australian electors made of the mass media. The questions and answers from this survey are incorporated in the Mayer book. But in 1979 they followed this up with another survey of about 1,000 electors and they have produced what they modestly call a second edition of their 'The Mass Media in Australia' (University of Queensland Press, 209 pp., $9.95). 1 would call it virtually a new book. * It's not the kind of book that will set your hormones aflutter; it suffers all the drawbacks of survey research and content analysis; but it contains a wealth of interesting findings and here are some of them. Between 1966 and 1979 there was a decline in the proportion of people who read newspapers and an increase in the proportion who attended to radio and television. In 1966, 84 per cent got a daily paper but in 1979 only 70 per cent got one. Moreover, the proportion of people relying on radio and television only, rose from 8 to 28 per cent while those relying on press only, declined from 8 to 1 per cent. These figures support those which show a decline since the mid-1950s in newspaper circulation relative to the population, although the findings suggest that newspaper readers are reading their papers more carefully than they used to. , Predictably, the higher the level of a person's occupation the more likely he is to read a paper. But education seems to have no relationship to newspaper reading, although the better educated tend to read more than one paper (and also tend to read Fairfax papers). About one in every four people listened mostly to ABC radio, two in three to commercial stations and 10 per cent divided their attention about equally between the two. The ABC is favoured by the better educated (or, as one of the surveys in the Mayer book has it, is aimed at "executive types"). More than half the sample watched television every night no matter what was on, 15 per/cent watched almost every night and the remainder were more selective.' (This no doubt accounts for the mass masochism evident in the durability of 'Prisoner'). One in every two people usually watched the commercial channels, one in four the ABC, and one in four divided their attention between the two. (Cognitive dissonance is no doubt widespread in the last group). Again the better educated favoured the ABC. The political' paradox is that coalition partisans outdo ALP partisans in their support for the state-run channel. (I've always suspected Doug Anthony was secretly a socialist.) Western and Hughes found that in 1979 partisans were less likely than in 1966 to sec any medium as fair to their own party and were more likely to see a medium as fair to their opponents but not to their own parly. Twice as many ,ALP partisans as coalition partisans saw the press and commercial television as unfair to their party. The press was the medium most suspected of bias but in general it was seen as'fairer to the coalition than to the ALP. Radio was seen as the least biased medium but ALP partisans Who listened to the ABC tended to do so because they thought the commercial stations were unfair to their party. Coalition partisans who listened to the ABC also thought the commercials were unfair to their party and commercial listeners among coalition voters thought the ABC was unfair. When they asked whether each medium gave "too much", "right amount" or "not enough" (or "don't know") news, they found a! striking difference between the two siirveys.More people said too much news in 1979. They also found an increased interest in national and state politics, and a decrease in the interest in international and local politics. On the question of which medium performed best, they found a massive shift away from the press to television while the evaluation of radio had not changed'during the period. Most of the respondents thought television' presented the. news most intelligently, gave the clearest understanding of the issues, did most for the public, and gave the best understanding of leaders. But perhaps the most striking evaluation was that television gave the most complete news. (You can fit the number of words in a bulletin of ABC National News into less than two-thirds of this page of The Canberra Times). Preference for the press increases with higher levels of education and those with post-secondary education gave it the best rating for "gives the most complete news". Fairfax, readers were much more likely to rate the press as the most satisfactory of the three media on each of the evaluations. They are some of the highlights of the survey findings. The remainder of the book is devoted to three studies: 1. the geographical sources of news in Australian papers; 2. a case study of how the press covered the deposing of John Gorton; and 3. another on how the press covered Murdoch's takeover bid for the Herald and Weekly Times.

17 Mar 1983 - S. Africa sport ban opposed Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 17 March 1983, page 1 I i S. Africa sport ban opposed SYDNEY: The majority of Australians are against the ban on sport with South Africa, according to the results of a Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday. Seventy-s£ven per cent of people interviewed agreed that Australian teams should be allowed to play against South Africa, and 81 per cent said they believed sporting authorities should allow individuals to compete there. Australian cricketers wishing to tour South Africa were supported by 66 per cent, and about 83 per cent believed the ban infringed the rights of the individual. Sixty-five per cent said they believed Australia should trade with South Africa. The poll was conducted last month, and about 1,100 males and females aged 14 and upward were interviewed. Under the code of conduct adopted' by Commonwealth countries at the Brisbane Games, individual Commonwealth sportsmen and women and sports administrators are barred from arranging or competing in sporting contests involving South Africans. A spokesman for the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Mr Hayden, said yesterday that there would be no government reaction to the findings of tjie poll.

28 Mar 1983 - Poll: Peacock preferred to Howard Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 28 March 1983, page 8 Poll: Peacock preferred to Howard MELBOURNE: Mr Andrew Peacock would make a better Leader of the Federal Opposition than Mr John Howard, according to a Gallup Poll. Seventy-one per cent of people asked by Australian Public Opinion Polls said Mr Peacock would be a better leader. Only 10 per cent said Mr Howard would be a better Leader of the Opposition and 3 per cent said someone else, including Mr Ian Macphee or Mr Doug Anthony, would be better leaders. The poll was conducted on the first two weekends after Mr Peacock was elected leader. The poll was conducted throughout Australia and replies were very similar between men and women and the young and old. Labor and Liberal-National Party voters also shared similar views. But 7 per cent of Labor voters preferred Mr Howard compared with 11 per cent of Liberal-National Party voters. Mr Peacock and Mr Howard polled best in their home States — and 77 per cent preferred Mr Peacock in Victoria and 12 per cent preferred Mr Howard in NSW. Mr Howard, left, with Mr Peacock outside Parliament House earlier this month.

07 Apr 1983 - IN BRIEF Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 7 April 1983, page 6 IN BRIEF Library acquires j author's papers The National Library .of Australia has announced the acquisition of a number of papers by a former Bulletin writer and author, the late Mr W. E. (Bill) Fitz Henry. The papers includc a uncompleted history of The Bulletin, 1800-1900, and four volumes of 'The Gentle Bohemian' and other essays. The manuscripts librarian, Mrs Pam Ray, said the acquisition of the papers was a story in itself. Following Mr Fitz Henry's death in 1957, the library moved to acquire the papers, but' was informed by his son that he was revising his father's manuscript and planned to complete it. However, in 1982, following the death of Mr Owen Fitz Henry, the papers were offered to the library by Mr and Mrs W. Crozier. Mrs Sylvia Crozier is William Fitz Henry's stepdaughter. 22 Jan 1984 - BRITAIN Labour Party closes gap Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 22 January 1984, page 5 BRITAIN Labour Party closes gap LONDON, Saturday (AAP). -Britain's Labour Party is closing the gap with the governing Conservatives, according to a Gallup Poll published in yesterday's Daily Telegraph. The poll shows Labour with 38 per cent support - just 3.5 per cent behind the Conservative Government, which was returned with 44 per cent of the vote in last June's general election. Labour captured only 28 per cent. Support for the Liberal-Social Democratic alliance, which received 26 per cent in the election, was down to 19.5 per cent, the poll showed. A Market and Opinion Research International poll published in The Standard on Tuesday gave the Conservatives 42 per cent - 5 per cent higher than Labour - and the alliance 19 per cent. The reports in the World News pages are contributed by the following agencies (abbreviations in brackets): Australian Associated Press (AAP), Associated Press (AP), Agence France-Press (AFP), The New York Times News Service (NYTNS), the Press Association (PA), Chicago Sun-Times (CST) and Reutcr.

26 Jan 1984 - Coalition supporters favour Hawke over Peacock: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 January 1984, page 1 Coalition supporters favour Hawke over Peacock: poll More Liberal and National Party supporters prefer Mr Hawkc as Prime Minister than Liberal leader Mr Peacock, a Morgan-Gallup Poll published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine says. The poll showed that, of LiberalNational Party voters, 43 per cent of those polled said Mr Hawke would make a better PM, against 38 per cent who preferred Mr Peacock. A principal of the polling firm, Mr Garry Morgan, said that he could not remember a poll which showed coalition supporters favouring a Labor leader over their own. The poll also shows that Mr Hawke's popularity rating has jumped to a massive 73 per cent with only 15 per cent of voters disapproving of him and a further 12 per cent undecided. The Morgan poll shows that, among Labor voters, Mr Hawke's rating has jumped to 91 per cent with only 3 per cent disapproving and 6 per cent un decided. Mr Peacock's approval rating has steadied at 41 per cent but only 16 per cent of those polled would prefer the Liberal leader as Prime Minister. 'l'he poll indicates that support for the Labor Party rose 2 per cent to 54 per cent with the coalition parties slipping back to 39 per cent. Had an election been held in the first two weeks of January, the ALP, on these figures, would have won easily. The Bulletin notes that the poll findings may reflect "a certain amiable post-Christmas holiday mood" among voters. "In recent years the Morgan-Gallup Poll has found support for the party in office has risen in January," it said.

20 Feb 1984 - RADIO "The m ystery of who takes part in radio surveys Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 20 February 1984, page 23 RADIO By SHELLEY DEMPSEY The m ystery of who takes part in radio surveys I^.ADIO-ratings sur veys, it seems, arc a bit like Gallup polls - no-one ever knows anyone who has ever taken part in one. Still, the vagaries of mass random sampling being what they arc, one assumes that some people do actually receive those all-important little books to fill out. What's more, some of these elusive people in Canberra even got theirs delivered one week early this year, courtesy of McNair Anderson, the market-research company which carrics out all national surveys but which got the dates wrong in this instance. The ratings were due to begin yesterday, not the previous Sunday. Added to all that is the ridiculous practice of the surveys dividing listening time into blocks of 15 minutes. Any person who tunes in to a radio station for this duration is counted. Anyone who tunes in to one station all day, however, is not. The nature of radio, one would think, would demand that surveys have a built-in acknowledgment that this medium, unlike television, is usually only a -backgound noise which' docs not command one's undivided attention, and an intermittent one at that. To add insult to injury, Canberra's ratings season this year might not be as tam.c as this radio writer blithely claimed last week. The Australian Broadcasting Tribunal licencerenewal hearings of 2CA and 2CC on Tuesday yielded the information that the former is highly dependent on local advertising, whereas the latter gleans most of its revenue from national advertisers. Top spot in the ratings attracts the more lucrative national market, at least one good reason for 2CA to continue its determined fight back against a seemingly in vulnerable 2CC. And on the"subject of the hearings which give the stations a licence to broad cast ior another three years, both station managers, Mr John McCormack, of 2CC, and Mr Ron Collins, of 2CA, seemed quite confident afterwards. Mr Collins said that a matter of "a couple of mistakes" by 2CA last year seemed to have been ironed out. They had involved the failure of the station to provide the required amount of religious and Australan music content over four weeks in September and October because of a changed format and the introduction of computer scheduling. The secretary-manager of the ACT Racing Club, Mr Don Anderson, appeared at the 2CA hearing to criticise the general lack of radio racing coverage in Canberra. The appearance was not directed at 2CA in particular, but was a lobbying tactic aimed at supporting Canberra and District Racing and Sporting Broadcasters in its application for the public broadcasting licence. One of the other three applicants for this licence, Canberra Stereo Public Radio, has appointed a chief engineer and acting manager - Mr Terry McGcc, formerly of 2XX. Mr McGec said a meeting held at the studios of CSPR last week had attracted 57 people, and that training programs had been organised for volunteers. The courses, which began on February 11, would be ideal for high school media students, he said. The Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, will address the National Press Club about his rcccnt Asian tour on Wednesday and can be heard in a live broadcast on 2CN at 1.10pm.

23 Feb 1984 - Record popularity Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 23 February 1984, page 1 Record popularity Record public-approval levels for the Government and the Prime Minister con tinued in the first part of this month, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll figures published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday. Mr Hawke's personal rating increased by 1 per cent to 73 per cent, equal to the peak reached in the first part of January. The Labor Party's rating remaining steady at 57 per cent, equalling the record level recorded in the second half of January. The proportion of respondents who considered that the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, would do a better job than Mr Hawke fell 2 per cent to 15 per cent.

10 Nov 1983 - Wran's approval rating drops Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 10 November 1983, page 8 Wran's approval rating drops SYDNEY: The popularity rating of the NSW Premier, Mr Wran, has fallen, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll, published in The Bulletin. After months of corruption allegations against his Govern mcnt, Mr Wran's rating fell by 8 per cent last month, to 46 per cent. His approval rating was exactly the same as that of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Greiner.

17 Nov 1983 - Peacock support wanes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 17 November 1983, page 12 Peacock support wanes Only 43 per cent of Liberal Party-National Party voters think the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, would make a better Prime Minister than Mr Hawkc, according to a poll published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday. The Morgan Gallup Poll showed that 37 per cent of coalition voters^ said Mr Hawkc would make the better Prime Minister. Mr Peacock's support by his own voters was down 3 per cent on the previous poll taken in mid-October while Mr Hawke's support among coalition voters was up 2 per cent. Political observers say the results, from a poll taken during the last weekend of October and the first weekend of Novem ber, are not encouraging for Mr Peacock. Mr Peacock was heavily involved in the Queensland State election campaign in which the Liberal Party lost many seats and in the Moreton by-election which, although retained by his party, resulted in a swing of only 1.5 per cent against the Federal Gov ernment

08 Dec 1983 - Poll shows Wran trailing Greiner Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 8 December 1983, page 3 Poll shows Wran trailing Greiner SYDNEY: For the first time sincc taking office in 1976, the approval rating of the NSW Premier, Mr Wran, has dropped behind that of the Leader of the Opposition, heightening pressure for a Cabinet reshuffle. Yesterday's Morgan Gallup Poll shows that Mr Wran, with a 41 per cent approval rating, his lowest, is 3 per cent behind the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Greiner. This represents a 13 per cent drop since September's poll. Mr Wran is expected to meet the Minister for Decentralisation, Mr Day, and the Minister for Lands, Mr Gordon, within the next week to pressure them to retire early so he can bring new faces into Cabinet well before the next election. Both men have already announced they will retire at the next election, due in September, and have made it plain they want to stick to their original plan. Mr Wran wants the two min isters to announce early retirements when the Deputy Premier, Mr Ferguson, decides to resign as deputy, which is expected next year. This would give Mr Wran three new faces in Cabinet. It is understood that no Cabinet reshuffle will occur before the next caucus meeting, scheduled for Febuary 1.

02 Oct 1983 - Influences on smoking Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 2 October 1983, page 2 Influences on smoking Sir, — Given the current coverage in the media about cigarette ad-vertising, one might think this is a major public concern. Independent opinion polls suggest it is not so. A major study conducted by independent researchers for the Australian Advertising Industry Council in October, 1982, showed that advertising of any sort was not a "top of the mind" concern. Only 8 per cent believed advertis-ing needed immediate attention and change, ranking well behind the cost of living, Government, trade unions and politicians. When asked about personal criticism of advertising, only 2 per cent nominated cigarette advertising. Even when pressed to say whether the Government should place further restrictions on cigarette advertising, only 10 per cent agreed. On the other hand, some 12 per cent wanted to see restrictions lifted! In May and again in August this year, the Roy Morgan Research Centre polled people in all States on the question of whether sponsorship of sports by tobacco companies should be allowed. A three-quarters majority replied: yes. NSW (79.3 per cent), Victoria (71.2 per cent), Queensland (80.2 per cent), Tasmania (76.1 per cent), South Australia (80.7 per cent) and Western Australia (76.6 per cent). The Morgan surveys also showed that four out of every five surveyed stated that friends and family were the main influences on smoking in itiation — a commonplace view that closely reflects research on this sub-ject. To conclude, cigarette advertising is not a subject that the average person gets excited about. Active anti-smokers succeed in having their voice heard, but they are in the minority. Those who still believe that we live in a free society in which individuals can make their own decisions about personal lifestyle must surely be con-cerned about the activities of people who wish to impose their prejudices upon others. It is to be hoped that politicians will not mistake the clamour of this unrepresentative pressure group for the views of the majority. PHIL SCANLAN Manager, Corporate Relations and Public Affairs, Amatil Limited Sydney, NSW.

05 Oct 1983 - QUEENSLAND STATE ELECTION THIS MONTH Rural seats the likely battleground Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 5 October 1983, page 25 QUEENSLAND STATE ELECTION THIS MONTH Rural seats the likely battleground fi H H THE Queensland State election on Octo ber 22 will probably be won or lost in the battle for the rural seats. # Both the Nationals and the ALP agree that if'cither is going to win government in its own right, it will have to win rural seats. Even if the Liberals collapsed totally, the splitup of the scats w<jiuld not take either the Nationals or Labor to tht 42 seats needed for government. liCity and urban scats tend to be volatile, with electors changing their preferences more frequently than country voters. The rural seats are the hardest to win, which is why the Nationals an<d Labor arc spending so much time in them. ||Thc Nationals say the country is their territory. "Country people arc our base of support and w(iile some were tempted to Mr Hawkc last M|iirch, I think his broken promises will bring thfcm back home to us," said National's Minister for Primary Industries, Mr Ahcrn. ;'"Most of the country is traditionally Labor, because we held those seats for 40 years, longer thltin the Nationals," ALP president Dr Murphy said. "Those rural scats voted Labor to government nearly 70 years ago and we need them just asj much to form government today." !? While the Nationals and Labor can argue over which party traditionally "owns" the seats, the facts arc that the Nationals now hold most of th'cm. iiThcre arc 80,000 Queenslandcrs in primary industries and another 500,000 mainly in country towns and provincial cities in support industries. Ttie Nationals hold six of the seven western and far-northern zone scats. Labor, which now holds only Cook in this zone, 30 years ago held every seat. J The Nationals hold 14 of the 15 country-zone seats. The ALP holds Mourilyan. but when last in" power held half these seats. Some of the other rural seats Labor held, especially in dairying and small crops, since taken over by the urban sprawl in south-east Queensland, have been held by Liberal and Nationals, and arc the target of Labor's urban push. Labor lost many of its rural seats in the 1940s and 1950s with changes in technology cutting the number of rural workers, the basis of Labor support. The splits in the ALP through the 1950s pushed most of the remaining rural scats to the then Country Party. Not even Labor Premier Ned Hanlon's zonal system could save the Labor rural seats. Another of Labor's problems in the bush was that its settler schemes and rural marketing schemes were politically counter-productive. The battler farmers from the turn of the century to World War II tended to vote Labor, the party which introduced producer boards and cooperatives, and cut down the big estates. After the war these people bccamc successful and began voting heavily for the Country Party. A typical example was a Kingaroy farmer whose peanut farming was helped by a Laborset-up producer board. His name was Joh Bjclkc Peterscn. Queensland's agricultural marketing system, which the Liberals like to call agrarian socialism, is little changed in 50 years. It is as much an article of faith as the free-hospital system. When Labor was largely controlled by a trade union coterie in the 1960s and 1970s, rural people and rural matters were largely ignored. Meanwhile the Nationals were doing just as Labor had done for the 40 years before; cultivating an image as the "farmers' friend" and the only party willing to stand up for country people. "Country people are very loyal. If you talk to them and listen to them they appreciate it, probably much more than urban people," Mr Ahern said. "If you promise something and keep your promise they'll stick with you through thick and thin. "We've kept our promises while over the years Labor has made all sorts of promises and not kept them, so they won't attract that loyalty." However, Mr Ahern concedes that support for the Nationals outside the major cities did drop last year and early this year. "I don't think the former federal coalition was too popular because they promised things and then didn't carry them out. "But Mr Hawke's honeymoon with rural Queenslanders is well over - the Federal Budget saw to that. "He promised fuel-price reductions and then after the election he's put it up - that's probably the biggest overall issue from farwestern graziers to fishermen and anyone who lives outside Brisbane. "Hawkc has also broken promises to the sugar farmers. "Labor puts these nice guys up front as their rural spokesmen and ministers, but they don't get the backing and aren't put in cabinet. "The ALP don't have a chance in the country because they don't understand it - they may have once, decades ago, but they don't now." Mr Bjelke-Petcrsen is making a major effort to persuade rural people that the Nationals still care for them foremost, although the party's name has been changed from the Country Party and most of the electoral thrust appears to be on the south-east corner. Labor says the Nationals now rate rural people second to tourist developers and urban entrepreneurs. "Gone arc the days of the old Country Party, designed to help and protect rural industries and people, because the Nationals are now just a protector of foreigners, the fast buck and the quick profit," said Labor leader Mr Keith Wright, announcing Labor's rural policy in the Canegrowers Association headquarters in Brisbane. Labor has been trying to rebuild its country support for three years, with many trips to rural areas to start new branches and show the flag, often for the first time in a decade. Dr Murphy claims country support for Labor is now growing, with Morgan Gallup Poll figures showing Labor up more than 3 per ccnt to 41.6 per cent, and Nationals down 4 per ccnt to 40.2 per cent in all Queensland outside the Brisbane statistical region. For the first time in a decade, Labor claims it is ahead of the Nationals in provincial Queensland. Of course, this region includes provincial cities where Labor holds nine of the 13 seats. The Liberals have about 14 per cent of this provincial vote, but most of it is concentrated in its three non-Brisbane seats of Townsvillc, Toowoomba and Ipswich. In most of Queensland the small Liberal vote flows to the Nationals, but not as much as it used to. In the 1980 election about 25 per cent of the Liberal provincial vote went to Labor. It will probably be higher this election, although the number of voters could be down. While the Liberal preferences could decide several of the country scats, the battle for the rural vote is largely between the Nationals and Labor. Needing 17 seats to form government. Labor thinks half these will have to be won in the country, mainly along the sugar belt. Labor's target country seats arc Warrego. Mount Isa. Barron River, Hinchinbrook. Burdekin, Flinders. Whitsunday. Mirani and Mulgrave, plus holding on to its own marginal seats of Bundaberg, Maryborough and Mourilyan. .Labor hopes to win Warrego, in western Queensland, and later more of the western seats on the basis of a demographic change with an influx of government workers and a decline in the number of graziers and their families. Labor's hopes in the far-northern seats rest largely on the smaller sugar farmers who, before 1957, were solid Labor voters. The biggest section of Labor's rural policy, which the party claims is the biggest and best-researched of any of its policies, is on sugar. It got in first with several promises to the sugar industry which the Nationals will now probably have to match at their policy launch. Labor is also making much of an improved quality of life for rural people. "Too many young people in the country have not reached their potential in education, technology or sport because of poor facilities," said Mr Wright, a former tcacher in country schools. Labor is promising better facilities for education, sport, government housing, government ser viccs. better health care and more, to overcome the disadvantages of isolation. The reason for these promises is that most of the country voters, while to a larger or smaller degree dependent on rural industries, arc not farmers and are more interested in quality-of-lil'c issues than farm-product policies. It is an area the Nationals admit they have fallen behind in, but promise to catch up before the election. Labor says its promises are firm, citing the SI 3 million for the Burdekin Dam, the first time a Federal Government has come good with a Burdekin Dam promise in more than 40 years. But the Nationals say the fuel-price rises alone will hold its marginal seats and win Mourilyan. Cairns, Cook, Callide. Maryborough and Caboolturc (which is now a predominantly urban scat). The Nationals say their other votcwinncr is their support of the present electoral system. Nationals' president. Sir Robert Sparkes. worried that Labor's one vote-one value proposal was gaining acceptance in the country, made a tour to defend "the weightage system". He said the response was good when it «a* pointed out to country people that the north and west would lose seven scats to Brisbane in a one vote-one value system. The Nationals will run a campaign in country areas to reinforce this message, saying Labor's one vote-one value electoral system will "rob" country people of seats. Both National and Labor parties mentioned the NSW Premier, Mr Wran. when talking of rural seats. Mr Wran won government by winning rural seats and Labor now holds more rural seat* than either the National or Liberal parties and sees them as the basis for future Labor government because they are so loyal. Labor in Queensland hopes to emulate Mr Wran. The Nationals arc even more determined to hold their rural stronghold.

20 Oct 1983 - Bjelke-Petersen still confident Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 20 October 1983, page 3 Bjelke-Petersen still confident BRISBANE: The Premier of Queensland, Mr Bjelke-Petersen, was still confident yesterday that his National Party would poll strongly at Saturday's State election. Voters would opt for performance, not promises, he said. The main campaign issues were taxes, jobs, promises and performance. The National Party would come out in front on all counts. The election was important for Queensland and the nation because of its implications for economic management. He reaffirmed his intention to retain the Treasury portfolio if the National Party won, a post traditionally awarded to the Liberal Party Deputy Premier, and ruled out any question of a challenge to his leadership, as suggested by the Leader of the ALP, Mr Wright. He also defended the State's four zone electoral system against ALP and Liberal proposals for an electoral redistribution to introduce a one-vote, onevalue system. He said he believed country people would recognise the value of the present arrange ment. The managing director of the Roy Morgan Research Centre, Mr Gary Morgan, said today that events in the past two weeks meant that anything could happen in Saturday's poll. Morgan Gallup poll figures published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday showed that the National Party would have been returned when the poll was taken two weeks ago. "But in this campaign there have been more upsets in the last two weeks than most national election campaigns have had put together," he said. Mr Morgan referred to backing from three former Liberal Premiers and Tasmania's current Liberal Premier, Mr Gray, for the Nationals and reports of a threat by former Minister for Health, Mr Austin, to Mr White's Liberal leadership. The Morgan poll showed National Party support at 35 per cent (27.6pc at the 1980 election), Liberal support at 16pc (26.9pc) and ALP support at 46pc (41.8pc).

03 Feb 1983 - Hayden slips in the ratings Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 3 February 1983, page 1 Hayden slips in the ratings The public-opinion rating of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Hayden, has slipped while the rating of the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, has risen, according to results of a poll published yesterday. The number of people who believed Mr Hayden would make the better Prime Minister had fallen five percentage points to 33 per cent from November to January, the Morgan Gallup Poll said in The Bulletin maga zine. Fifty per cent of the 1,687 people polled said they believed Mr Fraser to be the better Prime Minister, a rise of six percentage points. Mr Hayden was supported by 63 per cent of Labor voters, but 21 per cent said he would not be a better Prime Minister than Mr Fraser. Of Australian Democrat voters, who could decide the election outcome in several marginal scats, only 20 per cent believed Mr Hayden would be a better Prime Minister and 60 per cent opted for Mr Fraser. Mr Hayden is in Brisbane for a meeting of the Federal ALP executive today. His deputy, Mr Bowen, refused yesterday to be drawn on the question whether Mr Hayden would lead the party at the next general election. Asked in an interview whether he was a "strong supporter" of Mr Hayden, he said, "I don't answer these questions." Question: If you are a strong supporter, though, wouldn't you like to give your support now? Mr Bowen: It's not a question of that. He's the leader. Will he be the leader for the foreseeable future? Mr Bowen: Well, the party always meets and discusses matters. That's their privilege, not mine. Is it certain he'll lead the party at the next election? Mr Bowen: I'm not answering the matter. Mr Fraser said in an interview at Parliament House yesterday that he was trying to time the election for next year. Under the Constitution a general election can be held as late as three years and three months from the previous election. The House of Representatives first met after the 1980 election on November 25 that year, which means the next election need not be held until more than a year from now. The ABC agreed yesterday to give the Opposition equal time on national radio and television to reply to comments by Mr Fraser in his Australia Day address last Sunday.

11 Feb 1983 - New poll puts ALP 8pc ahead Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 11 February 1983, page 9 New poll puts ALP 8pc ahead SYDNEY: The first Gallup poll sincc the election was announced shows Labor is 8 per ccnt ahead of the Liberal-National Party coali tion. The poll, published yesterday in The Sun, Sydney, shows that if the election had been held last weekend, Labor's lead would have been enough for it to win. In the poll, Labor was favoured by 50 per cent of those questioned, the Liberal-National Party coalition by 42 per ccnt and the Australian Democrats by 8 per cent. The poll's organiser, Mr lan McNair, said the margin of error on the sample of 1,100 people was 3 per cent cither way. He said this was because the sample was only half the size of a usual Gallup poll. The 8 per cent difference between the two major parties is a slight improvement for the Fraser Government on the last Gallup poll, taken in November. At that time, the difference was 10 per cent, with Labor on 51 per cent and the Liberal-National Party coalition on 41 per cent. The Leader of the Australian Democrats, Senator Chipp, said his parly would win nine Senate seats and six House of Representatives seats on the Gallup poll results. He was delighted with the Democrats' 8 per cent showing and surprised that Labor had gone to such a big early lead. "But the Liberals arc always capable of pulling back — they've got millions of dollars at their disposal," he said. "1 would expect the Liberals to launch the dirtiest and filthiest campaign against Labor and the Democrats during the last week."

17 Feb 1983 - ALP 11pc in front: Gallup Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 17 February 1983, page 16 ALP llpc in front: Gallup SYDNEY: The ALP is jubilant and the Liberals "still confident" after publication yesterday in The Bulletin of the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll shows the Labor Party with 52 per cent — ahead by 11 per ccnt — in a survey taken on February 5 and 6, just after the Federal election was announced and Mr Hayden stood down as Leader of the Opposition. In 1977, the Morgan poll taken four weeks before the Federal election showed the ALP and the Liberals ncck-and-ncck on 43 per cent. One taken four weeks before the 1980 election showed the ALP with 47 per cent, 3 per cent ahead of the coalition. The latest Gallup poll also showed a drop of 9 per cent in Mr Hawke's personal popularity, to 53 per cent, from the January figures. Approval of the way Mr Fraser was handling the job of Prime Minister rose 1 per cent to 39 per cent.

21 Feb 1983 - Hawke wins approval Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 21 February 1983, page 1 Voting trends in marginal Queensland seats hard to predict. Hawke pledges a better deal for country people. Senator Ryan's record of service. Howard predicts dangerously high deficit under a Labor government. The Tasmanian dam issue to "help Labor gain power". Page 10. Survival common to both leaders. — Page 12 Hawke wins approval MELBOURNE: In the first Gallup poll taken since Mr Hawke became Leader of the Opposition, 46 per cent of people approved of the way he was handling his job, 22 per cent disapproved and 32 per cent were undecided. Mr Fraser rated 40 per cent approval, 52 per cent disapproval and 8 per cent were undecided. Most of those who said they were undecided about Mr Hawke in his new role said he had not been in the job long enough to assess him. Almost half the people in the poll (49 per cent) said Mr Hawke would make a better Prime Minister than Mr Fraser, while 38 per cent said the reverse. Mr Hawke had a higher rating among young people than Mr Fraser and "won" in all States except NSW and South Australia. The poll was taken over the two weekends up to February 13 among 2,095 people.

If they are short, they never pine to be tall, but adopt the engaging premise for themselves that "good things come in small papkages." Colouring plays an importent part in establishing type-- at least outwardly. Blondes, brunettes, and redheads sound more definite in their types than they often turn out to be. Complexion tones may be played up or toned down by the colours worn to set them off. Pale blondes appear more fragile when they dress consistently in pastel shades. Brunettes snap the imagination to attention when dressed in vivid rich colours, or in stark white. ·No one dares to intervene when a redhead makes up her mind to conquer In red, but she can arrange an exciting palette in greens, pinks, and browns, not to miention black, that will do even more for her. In the last analysis, character determines your type more definitely than anything else. Character develops your selection of clothes and decides on the way you will wear them. Are you inclined to be direct, or cautious, casual, excitable, gentle, bold or dainty? The answer to this ques-. tion-and the consideration of many other aspects not enumerated-gives you a broad hint as to your type. Decisive or Frothy ' Clothes selected are not always true to type. You may be by nature someone of easy pliability, but not being completely aware of thiS, may choose clothes for yourself whose appearance indicates that you belong to exactly the opposite type-clothes' that are trim, decisive, tailored with mannish details and giving the Impression that you belong to the adamant never-apt-to-change your mind group. On the other hand, your clothes may be frothy and feminine, never betraying for an instant that somewhere in your make-up you have a hidden vein of steel. Ideal, however, is the combination where clothes and character complement each other, and a sweet reasonableness is apparent to all concerned. Coiffure, Clue To Type Hair arrangement often offers a clue to type. A coiffure, too, provides one of the most satisfactory and simple ways of giving yourself a change. Those who go through life brushing their hair in a single repetitious arrangement-and mothers seem most often to fall Into this celfeffacing category because they seldom take time off to consider themselves-almost shake their univers'e if they make a change. Why not jump the gun and start making changes early In the game? Give yourself over to pleasant variety before you become stereotyped. Page-boy haircuts are sleek and consistently young and glamorous. These set a definite type to carry to completion in clothes and character. For sophistication, tile upsweep continues to set the stage. Windswept feather cuts and curls continue to be soft and feminine, and suit different types. Your type may find .expression in the casual and classic, in the dainty, devastating, or daring. Sportswear may offer, the best medium for accenting and setting off your type-or it may be sheer elegance. But whether you choose one type to follow forever, or prefer variations, it is more Intelligent and more Interesting to know what you are doing than to plan without ,purpose.

19 Feb 1944 - Men and Ideas: REALITY AND THEORETICAL DIMENSIONS Argus (Melbourne, Vic. : 1848 - 1957), Saturday 19 February 1944, page 5 I ai¡J_^u_lum_Mmám_mil_mttlmm Mentone Ideas: IIIIIIIIIIIIIIMIIIIIIIIIIlItlIlllllllllllllllllllllllllllll ___?__?__! aBiMh|MMBMBI0MMaaB|^MMM___i__r alarms REALITY AND THEORETICAL DIMENSIONS ' By AUSTER HAS your opinion ever been asked in connection with a Gallup poll? For my own part, I can honestly say that I have never been consulted in such inquiries; that no radio announcer has ever pounced on me in the foyer of a theatre to ask if I knew who wrote As You Like It, or whether Milton died earlier than Queen Victoria. I feel sure you have enjoyed the same immunity, being an ordinary inoffensive individual like, myself. We are then, you and I apparently not average citizens, cross-sections of the community. who are those mysterious and elusive individuals? They do exist, for we have all seen the result of Gallup polls- and heard answers to the questions asked in the foyer. Do they live in a different dimension, so that they remain invisible to us? Believe it or not, they do. For an average, of whatever kind, is only a mathematical concept, not a concrete and tangible reality. It's all very well to say at the end of a year that my average daily consump-tion of tea during that period was 4 cups. I know perfectly well that the theoretical being who each day methodically drank those 4 cups was not myself. Yet he exists, and his existence depends on me and my tea-drinking capacity. He is not a mere shadow of myself, because then he would have the same irregularities and lapses; but we know that he is regular to an exasperating (1866 Now a Gallup poll or an averageseeking inquiry of the sort undoubtedly addresses itself to real people, and its results, apparently are often fairly accurate gauges of what is going to happen - in an election, for instance. In some mysterious way it contrives to dip into that elusive dimensions where dwells the average citizen; and there it gets a rough idea of what most of us are thinking. The strangest thing about these average and theoretical people is that without them the world would be more or less empty. No human being has ever seen the 400 odd million people that live in India. They exist only as a mathematical or statistical concept, and yet they occupy real space and eat real food. J. HESE average dimensions, therefore, have definite points of contact with concrete and individual reality - facets which help us to conceive the whole, just as a man looking at a few trees knows that he has a forest in front of him. This is so obvious that we take it for granted; no one ever questions the census returns of a given country or the results of a cross-section inquiry. We are so used to catching these elusive dimensions by one of their visible corners that we can do such tricks almost unconsciously. Is it not possible that other dimensions lie close to us also, but that we are unaware of them because we have never caught one of those in-dispensable aspects whereby they im-purge on our workaday world? An artist, sometimes, by looking at an object in a certain light or from a certain angle, actually makes of it a contact leading to a new dimension. You can call it vision or inspiration or anything you please; but what he has really, done is to find a new world co-existing with the old one. Explorers have done the same sort of thing. Columbus first saw America as part of a theoretical dimension; otherwise he would never have discovered it at all. There are cases, of course, where these contractual aspects can be rather misleading. One of the most striking instances is the light coming from a dead star. At what point does that light cease to be a reality; at what point does it become a reality; or is it entirely an illusion? And similarly, when we think of the world's past, at what point does reality fade out of the picture altogether? Is Pitt more real than Caesar? Or Gladstone more real than Pitt? Or all three more real than King Solomon? Or do they all live in the same dimension, on the plane of history's human average? Or is the whole postulate of reality a mere illusion, so that this day in which we move and think is no more real than its predecessor, being nothing more than tomorrow's yesterday, and therefore, from the point of view of 2 days hence, a merely theoretical dimension? You may argue that today is today, a tangible, visible reality. But was an hour ago part of it, or is that lost hour already a mere memory? What then of a minute ago? Or a second? Is to-day's reality so wholly concentrated in the present that it is without dimension at all? But if it exists neither in space nor in time it is not a reality at all. PETER SIMPLE'S POSERS 1. Which of the following are known as the Lake Poets: Wordsworth, Keats, Tennyson, Coleridge, Southey, Shelley? 3. A landau is: Four-wheeled carriage with roof that folds down; fourseated motorcar with fixed hood; horse-drawn cab without a hood? 4. Ohm was never like this, muttered Professor Catswhisker, as,, he tried to fix the wireless. Actualizan ohm is: A unit of electrical resistance; an electrical circuit; the light-ing element in a globe? 5. A plant grade Is an animal. Right; but is it an animal that: sleeps standing up; walks on the sole of the foot; chews the end? 6. RAMC is an abbreviation mean-ing Royal Army Medical Corps. What does RAOC represent. 7 Mohair is a cloth made from the hair of: Camel; Angora goat; Thibetan yak? 8. Henry VIII married Anne of -Cleves, and 6 months later: Had her beheaded there and then; declared the marriage null and void; found that she had gone back to her mother? 9.
