02 Mar 1986 - Takover bids unsettling Black knight likely to succeed Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 2 March 1986, page 9 Takover bids unsettling Black knight likely to succeed Supply and Demand CCORDING to a rccent Morgan Gallup poll, the majority of Australians oppose the bid by the Western Australian high flyer, Mr Robert Holmes 5 Court, to take over the "Big Australian", BHP. In corporate language, he is seen as a "black knight", someone trying to gobble up a solid well-run company for no apparent reason other than to make money. To date no "white knight" has emerged to buy back BHP shares from Mr Holmes a Court's Bell group of companies and save the day. The entry of white knights into the stock market usually ensures that the black knights sell out at a nicc profit. However, it may be too late for a white, knight to save BHP. The oilprice slump has forced the price of BHP shares well below the $7.70 cash that Mr Holmes a Court will pay for half the shares held by every BHP shareholder. Some brokers arc now recommending that this offer is too good to refuse. Their clients should (log off half their shares and use the proceeds to buy even more BHP shares at the current low price. This seems to indicate two things. The first is that Mr Holmes a Court is likely to succecd in his takeover bid, barring intervention by some government agency or restraining court action. The second is that BHP remains a solid stock for long-term investment. There is little doubt that in the longer term oil prices will recover. The current bargain prices will surely increase consumption and cut surplus stocks of oil. In a world concerned about the safety of nuclear-power plants and the disposal of their waste products, oil is the safe alternative. Last year BHP invested heavily in the US oil industry and this could pay off inside the next decade or so. Apart from that, there is little else that can power motor vehicles and aircraft. In the meantime, we should remember that BHP does far more than extract oil from Bass Strait. Take steelmaking for example. Lower oil prices will reduce operating costs throughout the giant conglomerate called BHP. The Holmes a Court offer is due to close within a few weeks and it appeared until about the middle of last week that only a sudden hike in BHP shares beyond $7.70 would thwart him. But suddenly it all began to happen. The Big Australian, which has hufTed and puffed about how its army of loyal shareholders would remain faithful, suddenly got the wind up when confronted by the oil-market slump and its weakening shares. BHP commenccd two legal actions in the Victorian Supreme Court -the first against the National Companies and Securities Commission for modifying its takeover code in favour of Mr Holmes a Court, with the second action against the takeover bid itself. The Trade Practices Commission took court action that could temporarily block the takeover while its legality is determined while, early next week, federal Cabinet is tipped to establish a wide-ranging inquiry into the bid for BHP. The Hawke Government has come under pressure from both the NSW Government and the trade-union movement which are worried that a victorious Holmes & Court might shed part of the giant conglomerate and thereby reduce its employment levels. There is little doubt that while people are intrigued by the nerve of the takeover specialists, there is growing concern about the value of takeovers to the nation. Much tax revenue is lost as the cost of takeovers is written off as business expenses and if money is borrowed overseas to finance large share purchases, this can add to Australia's balance of payments problems. Takeover bids are unsettling and take the attention of boards and directors away from day-to-day management and toward the task of defending themselves against the raiders. Takeovers usually add nothing to national wealth or to job creation while lining the pockets of the smart operators. Here is a piece of news not to be sniffed at. The world grows more than two billion kilograms of garlic a year, about half a clove for every person, every day. Recently I was seated on an aircraft about 10 metres from an habitual garlic muncher. Every time he turned his face in my direction I tried to open the window. Luckily, for everyone on board it would not open. - TOM CONNORS

06 Mar 1986 - Death penalty favoured by 43pc, poll finds Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 6 March 1986, page 9 Death penalty favoured by 43pc, poll finds SYDNEY: Australians arc almost equally divided over whether or not to introduce the death penalty for serious crimes, according, to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll, published in this week's Bulletin magazine, shows 43 per cent favour the death penalty, 41 per cent are opposed, preferring imprisonment, and 16 per cent have no view. The figures are almost unchanged from the last poll on the death penalty, in 1980, despite the recent furore following the brutal murder of Sydney nurse Mrs Anita Cobby. The latest poll also showed that 73 per cent of respondents believed Australians found guilty of drug trafficking in Malaysia should be executed, in accordancc with the law there. The poll asked whether the penalty for murder should be death or imprisonment; whether imprisonment should be for life or a number of years set by the judge; and whether the death penalty should apply to drug traffickers in Malaysia. It showed that people living in NSW and South Australia favoured the death penalty, while Queensland residents favoured imprisonment and other States were evenly divided. People aged over 25 years were more in favour of the death penalty and more men favoured it than women.

04 Apr 1994 - Voters' faith in ALP, PM returns: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 4 April 1994, page 2 Voters' faith in ALP, PM returns: poll The federal Labor Government has continued to regain the support of voters, according to the latest Morgan poll. The poll, to be published in this week's Time Australia magazine, said support for the ALP picked up two percentage points to 41 per cent over the final two weeks of March. At the same time, support for the federal Coalition dipped three points to 43.5 per cent. The poll of 2249 voters across Australia was taken after Carmen Lawrence's win in the Fremantle by-election, and was completed after the resignation of former Health Minister Graham Richardson. Democrats' support was steady on 6.5 per cent, while that for the Greens was up half a point to 4 per cent. On a two-party basis, the Coalition slipped three points to 50.5 per cent, slightly ahead of Labor's 49.5 per cent. If an election had been held in March, the result would have hinged on minor party preferences. The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, remained preferred prime minister with 50 per cent support, up two points, compared with 33 per cent (down three points) for the Opposition Leader, John Hewson. Mr Keating's approval rating also rose three points to 38 per cent, while his disapproval rating dipped five points to 52 per cent. Dr Hewson's approval rating dropped one point to its lowest ever at 24 per cent, and his disapproval dropped one point to 62 percent

04 Apr 1994 - The facts are ignored by feminist myth-makers Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 4 April 1994, page 9 The facts are ignored by feminist myth-makers ANDREW McINTYRE argues that those who toe the politically correct line are out of touch with reality. MAYBE the times are changing, and the long-awaited swing of the pendulum is actually hap-pening. An increasing number of media commentators in Aus-tralia are beginning to question the untouchable politically cor-rect premises of the powerful feminist lobby groups. Over the last 20 years the gender ideologues have to a large extent captured Western leaders and creat-ed in them a "female vote depen-dency" like heroin to a junkie. Both the Liberal and Labor parties in Australia have been captured, as have much of the media. Women in this society, electoral-ly speaking, have a majority of the sort that Paul Keating or John Hewson could only dream of, but the gender ideologues claim for them the status of a powerless vic- tim class. To dispel the constant equal op-portunist contention that men have most of the real power in govern-ment, the judiciary, the military, in-dustry and the financial world, one has to be reminded that the power elite pyramid is very sharp and says little about the majority of men who are systematically and in-correctly associated with this power elite in the feminist cosmology. One simply cannot generalise about power from the sex of a single prime minister, or a whole Cabinet for that matter. Modern political elites do not as a rule represent, nor are they elected to represent, only men or only women. Femi-nists, in any case, are always con-founded by the likes of Margaret Thatcher, Bronwyn Bishop, Benazir Bhutto or the present reality of a female Prime Minister in Turkey. One really needs to look at some facts. Most social commentators use health and life-expectancy statistics as measures of oppression and vic-timisation. For instance, the life ex-pectancy of Aborigines is very much lower than that of white Australians and is immediately seen as a measure of powerlessness and dispossession, a lack of control over one's own life or, at the very least, an injustice. When applied to gender politics different inferences can be made, as American author Warren Farrell has done in a very timely book The Myth of Male Power: Why Men are the Disposable Sex (Simon and Schuster). Farrell points out that men die earlier than women from all 15 of the leading causes of death, and that these causes are largely due to industrialisation. In- dustrialisation has allowed women to increase the life-expectancy gap from one year to seven since 1920. If you divide Australia into two groups, Aborigines and whites, you discover a difference in life expect- ancy. The immediate conclusion is to pour money into health service access for Aborigines. If you divide Australia into males and females you discover a difference in life ex-pectancy (at retirement age women can expect to live twice as long as men). What does government do? It spends $17 billion of the Austra-lian national health budget on women, $5.4 billion more than on men, and the feminist lobby in Canberra is demanding more. Whilst it is true that obstetrics ac-counts for some of it, $2 billion of this differences comes from the simple fact that women live longer. Women die marginally more from breast cancer than men do from prostate cancer, but spending by the National Health and Medi-cal Research Council on breast-cancer research is around $1.4 mil-lion compared with $362,000 for prostate-cancer research. It is obvi-ous which of the two is uppermost in the public mind. If men were ed-ucated to go for routine rectal ex-ams for prostate cancer prevention ||Women given status of powerless victim class|| and to, do routine testicular self-exam-inations — the way women are educat-ed to do routine breast self-examin-ntinns — we would keep thousands of men alive just as we are now keeping thousands of women alive. Recently there has been criticism of AIDS research — aimed pre-dominantly at men — being dis-proportionately funded in compari- son with breast-cancer research. Apart from an erroneous compari-son — AIDS is a viral epidemic that has the potential to infect both sexes — the extent of funding is best interpreted as an example of yet another special-interest group, this time homosexual, getting more attention than it warrants. How many of the following areas of men's health are being ac-tively remedied by anyone in Aus-tralia: a men's birth-control pill; suicide; post-traumatic stress syn-drome; circumcision as a possible trauma-producing experience; the male mid-life crisis; dyslexia; the cause of male violence; recidivism; homelessness; steroid abuse; colour blindness; testicular cancer; prostate cancer; hearing loss over age 30; sexual impotence; non-specific ure-thritis; epididymitis; Klinefelter's disease; ALD, and other male-only inherited diseases? We should add paedophilia. Some claim it is cur- able. In relation to crime and violence even the Governor-General, Bill Hayden, felt the need to expose the recent scandalous Melbourne Age campaign on "Violence Against Women" as a demonstration of media bias. The Age (June 4, 1993) had a headline "War on Women — 321,000 are victims". When analysing figures from the very Saulwick Age Poll that created the headline, they showed that for every 12 female victims there were seven male victims. On the basis of 321,000 victims and their own sur-vey, where was the subheading "And at least 140,000 were men abused by violent women". This fact was not mentioned in any of the learned commentary provided by The Age writers, who continued the tired but politically correct at-tacks on male-dominated society. Men, and particularly young men between 18 and 24, are four times more likely to be exposed to vio- lent attack and murder than are women. According to the International Crime Victim Survey, rape in Aus-tralia constitutes only 7.8 per cent of all violent crime, or 1.1 per cent of the total female population. Men are the primary victims of all other violent crime. If one is not convinced of male dispossession and social alienation, how do we explain that of all Australians who sleep without a shelter of any kind, more than 80 per cent are men? In the justice system much atten-tion has been focused on judicial bias against women, but it is com-mon knowledge that men account for around 90 per cent of prison inmates in all countries. There is evidence that men are dealt with far more severely than women in sentencing, and that early-prison-re-lease schemes, property settlement, child access and almost all other aspects of court dealings are almost entirely unfavour- ably to men. How much research has been done in Aus-tralia to look into these matters? In education we see a glaring inconsistency in poli-cies set to overcome apparent pre-judice against girls at school and, as a consequence, inappropriate ex-penditure, especially on affirmative-action schemes. The Victorian Lib- eral Government set up a working party last year on Opportunity for Girls in Education, but recent fig-ures show that three times more boys drop out of secondary educa-tion than do girls. This fact was not even discussed in the guide-lines. Department of Employment Eduction and Training figures for 1992 show that Victorian school re-tention rates to Year 12 completion are 7.8 per cent for males and 92.8 per cent for females; 17,497 males and 22,357 females successfully commence post-secondary educa- tion. A recently published analysis of New South Wales Higher School Certificate results leads to a similar conclusion. The present Victorian Govern-ment still maintains an Equal Op-portunity Officer, set up by the previous Labor Government, in ev-ery single primary and secondary school in the state for a staffing cost of around $3.5 million. If this is necessary policy, how do we ex-plain that 28 per cent more females ||Women have increased the life-expectancy gap|| actually com-mence tertiary studies and well over 30 per cent more females graduate in Aus-tralia with pri- mary degrees than do males. One argument used to explain this educational injustice is that professional outcomes for women are still not as good as those for men. But what are the professional outcomes for the majority of men? Published figures from the Victo-rian Department of Occupational Health and Safety Authority show that of a total of the 370 work-place fatalities in Victoria since January 1985 more than 97 per cent were male. Men are overwhelmingly repre-sented in the dirty and dangerous jobs. By contrast, those occupa- tions having attractive work char-acteristics such as physical safety, being indoors, desirable or flexible hours, and contact with people, are largely occupied by women. Work-ing women value flexibility and part-time work. A recent Institute of Family Studies survey indicated that two out of five working moth-ers, if they had a choice, would stay at home. When it comes to women in the armed forces there are enough land mines to discourage the keenest equal opportunist. Apart from the need for adopting double standards and unequal treatment if women are to survive there, it should sim-ply be noted that the hasty and ideologically ill-prepared rush to in- clude women in the three armed forces of Australia is already tak-ing its toll with the current spate of media publicity on sexual ha- rassment. There is enough evidence to seri-ously question the myths surround-ing feminist advocacy. Those of us who somehow doggedly believe in reason and plain facts would love to see the Government and the Op-position, from the Prime Minister down, respond less like gender junkies even though we live in a climate of political correctness and the post-modern deconstructionist dreamtime. Andrew Mclntyre is a Victorian secondary teacher and freelance writer. This is a modified version of an article that first ap-peared in IPA Review.

First, you say there is always "a vein of discontent in the community about the level and composition of immigration". A major vein, may I suggest, or even an artery. There has been community disquiet about high levels of immigration reflected in opinion polls taken over the past 15 years which have shown that the majority of Australians consider immigration levels too high. Do we want further development? Mike Berwick, the mayor of Douglas Shire in far north Queensland, has just been re-elected with an increased majority after running on the plank that he will cap population growth and development in his shire. So who's afraid of a rational debate on immigration? Not us. Rational debate, however, requires weighing up all aspects: environmental, economic,' social and humanitarian. But is it too much to ask the Minister for Immigration to take a precautionary approach on immigra tion until such time as the •House of Representatives Standing Committee on Long-Term Strategics reports on the carrying capacity of this country? They may find we have exceeded it already. JENNIFER GOLDIE President, Australians for an Ecologically Sustainable Population enough police officers to' enable this serious issue to be constantly monitored. Time and again we see people facing the courts on their second, third or more DUI offence. Their licence is suspended — so what, they just go out and re-offend without a licence. Innocent families, often the victims of these irresponsible menaces, should be able to use the roads when they so wish, without having to worry about facing some idiot going like a bat out of hell on the wrong side of the road. Driving under the influence should entail a mandatory two years' jail, without appeal. Fines and licence suspension are not getting through the thick-headed Australian mentality that says it is acceptable to drive this way because that is the way of Australians — always to have a stubbie in one's hand. Until this nation rids itself of its beer and sport mentality, the problem of deaths on the roads due to alcohol will never go away. It comes down to human selfishness — not, to care about others with whom we share the roads. ROGER DESHON Rivett It is the words that count I WAS pleased to see a letter concerning the Government's Read My Lips campaign, developed by the Office of the Status of Women on the issue of consent in sexual relations (CT, April 2). Your correspondent, Elizabeth Brenan, was perplexed by what she saw as a contradiction in our bus advertisement between the attractive lips and the words "NO. Sex without consent is a crime". Ms Brenan has fallen for a myth that misinforms many people in our community by suggesting that confidence, beauty, cheek, lipstick, friendliness (or. that kind of image) constitutes consent to sex. Our message, designed to appeal to a young audience, is that no matter how a woman is dressed, where she goes or what she's said or done in the past, she is perfectly entitled to say "no" and for that response to be heard and respected. ANN SHERRY First Assistant Secretary Office of the Status of Women AIDS testing not the answer YOUR editorial "AIDS testing call divides doctors" (April 7) is correct in concluding that the (few) patients who refuse to advise their HIV status should be treated as HIV positive and universal precautions adopted. This is already the case. The NSW AMA's argument that compulsory HIV testing is the solution to the problem of needle-stick injuries in the healthcare setting is a leap of logic. Firstly because it ignores other diseases such as Hepatitis B, which is more infectious than HIV. Secondly, most cases of HIV infection from needle-stick injuries have occurred when the health-care workers knew a patient was HIV positive. Knowing a patient's HIV status is therefore no guarantee. The most appropriate solution is to improve the training of doctors to avoid injuries and to adhere to universal infection-control precautions. This provides adequate protection for both patient and doctor and provides no excuse to refuse treatment to a patient. MATTHEW GILLETT Acting Executive Officer AIDS Action Council of the ACT Inc. 24 Apr 1994 - In God we trust, everybody else cash Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 24 April 1994, page 30 PENELOPE LAYLANP In God we trust, everybody else cash NOT MANY surprises in last week's 77'me-Morgan poll which rated newspaper journalists second-last of 23 listed professions in terms of honesty and ethical behaviour. No surprises, but a few questions. How. is the list of professions selected? What makes one form of endeavour a profession and another not, in these days when one practically needs a degree in hospitality to get a job cleaning rooms at a highway motel? Why is something like newspaper journalism, which everyone engaged in the business knows is actually a trade (or worse, semi-skilled labour), pitted against medi cine and the law? The word "profession" comes from the verb "to profess" and it was originally used to describe the vows taken by someone upon entering a religious order. These days, ministers of religion do not even make it onto the list of 23. Even giving the word "profession" its most liberal interpretation, it is difficult to see how some of the job titles made it onto the 77me-Morgan list. . Most people, I am sure, would still regard a "profession" as a'career path involving some specialist training, some formal knowledge, perhaps even a paper qualification. So how do state and federal members of parliament make it onto the list? And another thing. Politics is not usually a life-long profession. Many MPs spend about the same length of time in the "profession" as single mums spend on the single parents' pension, but you do not see single mums on (he list of 23. A pity. Newspaper journalists might have managed number 21, instead of number 22. While I am on the subject of MPs, it seems curious that they rate so poorly (state MPs came in at 17, federal ones at 18), when medicine and the law — the real "professions" from which huge numbers of our politicians are briefly extracted — rate relatively highly in the honesty and ethics stakes (3 and 11 respectively). What happens to these honest, ethical doctors and lawyers once they are elected to parliament? Do they undergo a moral metamorphosis and become suddenly dishonest and unethical? And what happens when they return to the surgery or the court room once they have lost an election? Do they go back to being honest and ethical just because they go back to being doctors and lawyers? 1 think not. They are probably morally polluted for life. Minor mystery While the manner in which the list of "professions" was compiled is a minor mystery (who, for example, decided that used car salesmanship was a profession; viho decided that motor mechanics and cordon bleu cookery were not?), the biggest unsolved mystery is how people decided that nurses (number 1) were more honest and ethical than doctors (3), or insurance brokers (16) more honest and ethical than real estate agents (19). How many of the respondents have had enough contact with just one director of a public company, let alone a whole swag of them, to be able to judge how honest and ethical they are? How about engineers? Stockbrokers? Surely the respondents did not base their gut feelings on the stories about lawyers they read in the newspapers, because those stories were all written by newspaper journalists and so by definition must be full of lies. I have a theo ry. I think people base their opinions about the honesty and ethical capacity of various professions upon nothing more than hope. I hope the doctor who is about to cut me open is honest and ethical (not to mention steady of hand) because there is no-one else to whom I can go if I want this ingrown toe nail fixed. 1 hope my lawyer is ethical and honest because a lot of money is at stake. I hope my child's teacher is ethical and honest because I want my child to be exposed to such behaviour from her role models. 1 even hope, in a silly kind of way, that the guy reading the news on television is.honest and ethical because he has such a nice face, and I'd like to believe that pretty people are pretty inside too. I hope politicians are unethical and . dishonest because 1 have to blame someone for the "state of the nation" and I would hate to blame someone nice. An newspaper journalists? Well, we all need someone to hate without having to intellectualise our position. I wonder if people believe that the "honesty quotient" they assign to the professions carries beyond professional dealings and into the personal lives of the professionals involved? Do police (7th) have fewer extramarital affairs than insurance brokers (16th)? Do dentists (5th) park in handicapped parking zones less frequently than car salesmen (23rd)? So many unanswered questions. Just one .more:. Is there any creature more untrustworthy than a politician who used to be a newspaper reporter?

26 Feb 1987 - Coalition 'within days of collapse' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 February 1987, page 3 Coalition 'within days of collapse' BRISBANE: The Queensland Premier, Sir Joh Bjelke-Petersen, said yesterday that the federal coalition between the National Party and the Liberal Party was within days of collapsing. Sir Joh said he was confident of this as a result of the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin magazine. Talking to the media after a meeting of the National Party state parliamentary wing, Sir Joh said he believed the party's state management committee and central council meeting at Hervcy Bay this weekend would automatically endorse his call for an end to the coalition. He also confirmed he had thrown his support behind Brisbane restaurateur Ann Garmcs to replace Senator Stan Collard in the No 2 spot on the National Party Senate ticket to be chosen tomorrow night. Describing the poll figures as "good", Sir Joh said they were in line with his assessment of the political mood that he had made. "They indicate quite clearly that people arc interested, are prepared to support the attitudes and policies I have spoken of and intend to elaborate more on as we get towards the election period," he said. The Morgan Gallup Poll shows support for the coalition running at 48 per cent, up 2 points, compared with 42 per cent for the Government, a fall of two points. It showed a new party led by Sir Joh and Mr Peacock would receive 30 per cent of the vote, while Mr Howard's Liberals would attract 17 per cent and Mr Sinclair's Nationals just 3 per cent.

28 Feb 1987 - Howard clearly still has the numbers Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 28 February 1987, page 2 Howard clearly still has the numbers By PAUL MALONE, Political Correspondent Labor backbcnchcr and Left convener Mr Gerry Hand docs not usually get his numbers wrong. But when he announced on Tuesday night that Mr Andrew Peacock had the numbers in the Liberal Party leadership battle he was mistaken. According to Mr Hand an Opposition Member ' had shown him a hand-written piece of paper which contained the names of all Liberal Members and senators. Beside each was a letter — either H (for Howard), P (for Peacock) or F (for fence-sitter). The count was 31 for Howard, 35 for Peacock and eight undecided. Going over the list I can say that based on my own background talks with Members and senators (far from a complete ring-around) four people on the list have definitely been wrongly classified. There may be more. Howard supporters say that there were seven mistakes on the first page of the three-page document. If nothing else, this ability to quickly note errors suggests that some serious head-counting was going on early in the week in the Howard camp. The errors were all to the disadvantage of Mr Howard. The obvious conclusion to be drawn from this is that the list was prepared by a Peacock supporter doing a bit of wishful thinking. As 1 said last week, Mr Howard clearly has the numbers and is in no immediate danger. The Liberal Party numbers do not work out the way one would have expected three months ago because some strange new allegiances have formed. At the top of the list, precipitating a re-think of alliances, is the suggested joint ticket of Queensland Premier Sir Joh Bjelke-Pctersen and Liberal front-bencher Mr Andrew Peacock. On the surface it looks like a good ticket. Sir Joh would attract a new red-neck vote and Peacock some trendies who voted Labor in the last election. In between there would be the block of votes which the conservative parties always pick up. But this potential leadership partnership worries a number of parliamentary Liberals who in past years have supported Mr Peacock. Their support for Peacock was not simply because he was the most likely Liberal to win an election. They also happened to have believed that his views more closely corresponded to their own "small I" liberal views. But a Pcacock-Joh alliance — especially one with Joh emerging as the more senior partner — does not promise a "small 1" liberal Government. On social issues the opposite would be the case. The "small 1" liberals are sometimes labelled crudely as the "wets". But the categorisation of Mr Howard: Not a bad week. "wet" or "dry" is best restricted to economic issues. The "dries" advocate smaller government, cutting tariffs, deregulation, lower taxes, a freeing up of the market. The "wets" would prefer to sec the Government intervene to ameliorate the adverse operations of the market. But there arc other non-economic issues which politicians are concerned about — civil liberties, abortion, Aboriginal land rights, the environment, foreign policy, etc. A significant number of the "small 1" liberals in the Liberal Party are now willing to go along with the "dry" economic policies preached by John Howard. Some of these members have traditionally been Peacock supporters. They have shifted to reluctant support for Howard because they fear that a Peacock dog would be wagged by a Joh Bjclkc-Pctcrsen tail on all issues, including social matters. The "small T liberals would end up still sitting on the backbench with no meaningful say in government policy. As things stand, they reason, at least they know where Howard stands. He will stick to the "dry" economic position he has developed over the years and he will maintain a more tolerant posi tion on other matters. One recalled this week that it was the then deputy leader, Mr Howard, who, in a major speech to Parliament, hosed down the Peacock-led Opposition when it was in danger of developing an immigration policy reliant upon whipping up racist sentiment in the community. A prominent member of the "small I" liberal camp. Senator Robert Hill, president of the South Australian Liberal Party, who has previously been counted as a Peacock supporter, has also argued that if Sir Joh succeeded in his goal of destroying Howard he would not stop there. He would immediately turn his attention to Peacock. Mr Howard hit back at Sir Joh (and indirectly the Peacock push) in the Liberal Party room on Tuesday telling members that in the event that Sir Joh succeeded in breaking the coalition the Liberal Party would campaign with "all the forces at its disposal". His most telling point was that the Liberal Party is not going to be pushed around by any outside force. Party members, who have spent many years at long boring meetings working their way up the hierarchy before winning their prc-sclcction, like that sort of talk. They do not warm to the idea that Sir Joh, on a whim, can annoint an outsider to take their placc. In the end it turned out tp be not a bad week for Mr Howard. He got the support of the party room on Tuesday and on Wednesday the Minister for Education, Senator Ryan, handed him the confidential minute on interest rates which he was able to use to beat the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, about the head. It is the interest-rates issue or, more, broadly, the state of the economy, which most threatens the survival of the Government. It may well be that only the divisions within the conservative forces will save Labor. It is true that some uninformed commentators examining the Morgan Gallup Poll this week expressed surprise at the result which showed that Labor was the big loser from Sir Joh's intervention into Federal Politics. But there was nothing surprising. As 1 pointed out 10 days ago, for a short time mavericks on the political scenc attract a large following which quickly drops off. The Australian Democrats were said to have the support of 60 per cent of the population when they first emerged on the scene in 1977. Even a month before the election the pollsters would have us believe that 33 per ccnt supported the Democrats. But at the poll that counts they managed only three senators. How a quaint little backwater became an apt Queensland Nationals' gathering place From ANDREW FRASER, in Queensland The Mclanesian village, about 300km north of Brisbane at Hcrvcy Bay, is an apt place for the Queensland Nationals to confer. Until a few years ago, Hcrvey Bay was a quaint little backwater whose main claim to fame was that it was the mainland point from which the ferry to Fraser Island departed, and the mosquitoes bred well in what was mainly tea-tree swamp. But in the past few years, the swamps have been drained and the developers have moved in, leading to a small population explosion, mainly in people of retirement age. There seems to be a bowling club on every second corner, and the crowning glory of the new Hervey Bay is the Melanesian Village, which is based around a man-made lake and has been designed for rich tourists and conventions. While most of the new residents are elderly, there is still a demand for jobs, and the Melanesian Village has helped bring jobs and some prosperity to the area. This is the Queensland of Sir Joh Bjclke-Petersen —jobs (in the service industries) for those who want them, and conspicuous development. The drive up from Brisbane to Hervey Bay is Sir Joh country. The road goes past the Big Cow, the Big Pineapple, SuperBee, the Deer Park, the Christian Outreach Centre ("where the happiest people are") and the Rural Youth Club to Hervey Bay, with its new shopping development ("now leasing"). It is the good life, and don't you worry about it. At the Melanesian Village itself, the 300 or so delegates to the Central Committee of the Queensland National Party are in a mean mood. Buoyed up by last year's state election result, they say Mr Sinclair is a loser, and so is Mr Howard, for that matter. All of the Opposition in Canberra are losers. Sir Joh is a winner, and he's got to become Prime Minister if this country is to get moving again. It is a mistake to think of^Sir Joh's backers as being purely the "white shoe brigade" of Gold Coast millionaires. Certainly Mr Mike Gore and his ilk arc willing to bankroll Sir Joh in any bid for Canberra, but where his huge support base lies is in the petit bourgeoisie, the god-fearing shopkeepers and small-business owners who want to be come big-business owners. The National Party, especially in Queensland, has changed composition mainly as a result of this. Sir Joh himself is a dyed-in-the-wool old-time Country Party man, the sort of rugged man on the land who would go to town every couple of days. But what the National Party has become is not the visitors to town businesses, but rather the town businesses themselves. There are still farmers and graziers to spare, but there are an increasing number of businessmen, in both small and big business. The choice that the Nationals were agonising over last night and were due to finalise at about 2am this morning represents these two streams. Under threat of losing his Senate seat is Senator Stan Collard, who, as a member of the Opposition's front bench, would normally be entitled to the No 1 position, but this is occupied by Senator Florence Bjelke-Petersen. Senator Collard's main challenge to the safe No 2 spot is Mrs Ann Garms, and during this week Sir Joh made it quite clear who he wanted. Mrs Garms had always been a very good worker, he said, and she was needed in Canberra. Sir Joh was expected to swing his support strongly behind Mrs Garms in the hothouse atmosphere of the Central Committee. Senator Collard is a former engine-driver who is based in the central Queensland city of Rockhampton, and is the Opposition's spokesman on arts, heritage and environment. He has virtually no profile at all in Canberra, with the apparent zenith of his career being an announcement that the Opposition would not take environmental factors into account when granting export licences, a roundabout way of saying that sand mining would go ahead on Frascr Island. Even this went comparatively unnoticed. But it is a different story in North Queensland, where Senator Collard's beaming features arc a familiar sight on North Queensland television. An ABC reporter who had worked in Townsville for three years said that Senator Collard always called in to them and the commercial television station every time he was in Townsville. If Mrs Garms, who runs a restaurant in Brisbane, gets the nod ahead of Senator Collard, then all the Queensland National Party senators will be based in south-east Queensland. Senator Shicl comes from the Gold Coast, Senator Boswcll from Brisbane, and Senator Bjelkc-Petersen from Kingaroy, about 100km from Brisbane. National Party voters in the rest of the state arc currently represented by Senator Collard, and will have no representation at all if Mrs Garms is elected at Senator Collard's expense. This is not just an interesting geographical fact, but rather an indication of the way-the Queensland National Party is going, which in turn gives an indication of where Sir Joh's appeal lies. The conference delegates and the Queensland National Party generally arc Sir Joh's people. • There is a convenient myth that Qucenslandcrs are different, which is often used to explain away Sir Joh's success. But the sort of people who think that the Federal Government encourages homosexuality, single mothers and dole bludgers, that politics is a lot of rot anyway, and that Australia needs a return to good basic common sense (whatever that is) exist outside of Queensland as well. It is a ground fertile for revolt, and it is in this ground that Sir Joh's seed has been planted.

26 Jun 1986 - Good news for Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 June 1986, page 14 Good news for Labor SYDNEY: The Labor Governments of South Australia, Victoria and Western Australia were maintaining their popularity despite national economic problems, the Morgan Gallup Poll has shown. The poll, published in the Bulletin magazine, found Labor would have been returned with an increased majority in Western Australia if an election had been held in May. The ALP recorded 55 per ccnt support and although the approval rating of the Premier, Mr Burke, dropped 1 per cent it was still high at 72 per cent. The Opposition Leader, Mr Hassell, gained three percentage points to reach 37 per cent, but only 12 per cent of voters thought he would do a better job as Premier than Mr Burke. A survey at the same time in South Australia put the popularity of the Premier, Mr Bannon, at 80 per cent and that of the Liberal Leader, Mr Olsen, at 42 per ccnt. The Labor Party in South Australia was rating 55 per ccnt — 3 per cent more than in a poll taken two months earlier. The Liberal Party dropped 5 per cent to 34 per ccnt in the same period. In Victoria, support for the Government and Opposition remained unchanged in the May poll compared with the one taken in April. Labor rated 49 per cent and the Liberal-National Party coalition 43 per cent. The personal popularity of the Premier, Mr Cain, dropped two points to 59 per cent, while that of the Opposition Leader, Mr Kennctt, was static at 30 per cent.

03 Jul 1986 - Spreading its wings Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 3 July 1986, page 16 Spreading its wings Supervisor Mr Gordon Davidson with some of the furniture for sale at The Mancare Community, Mildura Street, Fyshwick. THE SALVATION Army has plans to spread its wings into the Gungahlin, Tuggcranong Valley and Weston Creek areas. The divisional commander for the ACT and Southern NSW, Major William Guy, said the Army looked to the future and the "sky is the limit". Major Guy has been a Salvationist for 35 years, and has served in Tasmania and Victoria before he came to Canberra. The ACT and Southern NSW division had 30 congregations, six of them in the ACT. The six covered five social needs -elderly, family welfare, youth accommodation, emergency accommodation, and alcohol and drug rehabilitation. The division had about 3000 officers and soldiers. The greatest need in Canberra was to re-establish the strength of the family unit. "The answer is a spiritual program with con version by people to the Christian faith and acknowledgment of the standards and principles of a love relationship between a husband and wife, extending out to the children," Major Guy said. The Salvation Army preached not only verbally, but by example. "Love and compassion, they arc the values which work in the lives of people," he said. The public had a high respect for and appreciation of the Army. A Morgan Gallup poll indicated that 98 per cent of those surveyed thought the Army was doing a good job. This "not only gladdens my heart, but frightens me". Salvationists had to perform to the highest levels, but he was fearful that sometimes the Army might not live up to people's expectations. The Army had been placed on a pedestal. The feeling that it could let people down held a degree of fear. "But 1 have such confidence in my officers and soldiers that I do not think they will," he said. One of the areas the Army would be addressing was the welfare and unemployment of teenagers. A task force was looking at the problems and what could be done. A program called Employment 2000 would begin in Canberra. The eight-week training scheme gave participants confidcnce to go out and look for employment. The program was in all other Australian capital cities. Major Guy said other areas of need were for long-term accommodation for teenagers, and resident-funded accommodation for the elderly. The Army was preparing for a "revolutionary" Sunday-school program. To begin in January, 1987, it was based on the "most modern educational methods for teaching and training in the scripture for young people."

10 Jul 1986 - Let very premature babies die, 22pc say in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 10 July 1986, page 8 Let very premature babies die, 22pc say in poll SYDNEY: A survey published yesterday showed that nearly a quarter of Australians -especially the elderly - believed very premature babies should not receive specialist care to keep them alive. The Morgan Gallup Poll, published in The Bulletin, showed that 22 per cent of people surveyed believed that babies born 12 weeks or more prematurely should be left to die. When told it cost about $50,000 to give each of these babies specialist care, another 4 per cent opted in favour of letting the babies die, and spending the money elsewhere. More young people were in favour of helping premature babies live, with 77 per cent of the respondents in the 14 to 24 age group approving, compared with 55 per cent of those aged 50 and over.

17 Jul 1986 - Support for Hawke up in latest poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 17 July 1986, page 13 Support for Hawke up in latest poll SYDNEY: The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, and his Government improved in the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published yesterday by The Bulletin. Support for the Labor Party was up 2 percentage points to 48, and support for the Liberal-National coalition dropped 3 points to 43 percent. Nine per cent supported other parties. The poll was taken on the weekends of June 28, 29 and July 5, 6 before the round of strikes over super annuation. If an election had been held, the ALP would have been returned. Mr Hawke's approval was up one point to 54 per cent overall, and the Opposition Leader, Mr Howard, moved up a point to 32 per cent. Mr Howard also increased support among coalition voters - 41 per cent approved of the way he was doing his job, an improvement of 3 percentage points. Of all voters asked who would make the better Prime Minister, 69 per cent answered Mr Hawke and 18 Mr Howard. This was an improvement of one point for the Mr Hawke and a loss of one for Mr Howard.

28 Jul 1986 - Setback for Qld Liberals Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 28 July 1986, page 11 Setback for Qld Liberals BRISBANE: Smallbusiness owners in Queensland have dumped the Liberal Party, according to the state secretary of the Labor Party, Mr Peter Bcattie. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll, conducted in Queensland during May and June, had found that only 21 per cent of small-business owners supported the Liberals, Mr Bcattic said at an ALP meeting in Charlcvillc on Saturday. The poll, covering 1S68 people, found 31 per cent support from the group for the Labor Party and 45 per cent for the National Party, he said.

30 Jul 1986 - Hawke's rating slumps Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 30 July 1986, page 13 Hawke's rating slumps MELBOURNE: The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has slipped 5 per ccnt since April, a Gallup Poll has found. The ALP's lead over the coalition panics has dropped 4 per ccnt to only 2 per ccnt. The poll, taken during the first fortnight of July and published in yesterday's Sun News-Pictorial, showed Mr Hawkc's approval rating was 56 per ccnt, down from 61 per cent in April. The rating of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, dropped from 37 per ccnt in April to 34 per ccnt in July. Approval of Mr Hawkc's performance was highest - 61 per cent - in Western Australia, followed by 57 per ccnt in NSW. Disapproval of his performance was highest in South Australia, 61 per ccnt, followed by 60 per ccnt in his home state of Victoria. Fifty-eight per ccnt of people aged 16 to 39 approved of Mr Hawke compared with 53 per cent of those 40 and over. Mr Howard won greater approval from those aged 40 and over.
