31 Jul 1986 - PM 'more unstable than the dollar' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 31 July 1986, page 11 PM 'more unstable than the dollar' The Treasurer, Mr Keating, might have banana republics on the brain, but the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, suffers from a more serious complaint, according to the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard. "I think the Prime Minister's gone bananas," he said yesterday, somewhat surprised at Mr Hawke's early morning outburst on the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. Mr Hawke, he said, appeared to be "more unstable than the Australian dollar". The Prime Minister, peeved by his Government's slump in popularity, had earlier dismissed the Liberal Party's federal council meeting in Adelaide as the stuff conjured up by magical wands out of thin air in airy-fairy land. A televised debate would sort the matter out, Mr Howard said. "If Mr Hawke feels so vehemently and is so worked up and so strong in his denunciation of what I stand for, well why won't he debate the issues with me?" Mr Howard asked. As for his own electoral standing, Mr Howard smiled, saying the poll had not given him indigestion at breakfast.

03 Sep 1994 - Saturday FORUM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 3 September 1994, page 17 Saturday FORUM Downer about to take next risky step POLITICS Ross Peake IT'S TEMPTING to write off Alex- ander Downer right now for his abysmal performance so far as Op-position Leader. That' might sound like a harsh judg-ment against a man who has been sit-ting in the leader's suite for a short time. But voters are already deserting him in droves as he compounds gaff upon gaff, backflip upon backflip, all done against an ambience of a policy vacuum. Voters are watching Downer's vital signs closely, trying to sense if his condition is becoming terminal. Yesterday's Saulwick poll confirms the slide, which has reached dangerous pro-portions and is rapidly approaching the point of no return. With the election up to 18 months away. Downer may have time to arrest the decline and make voters believe in him. The big question now is: does he have what it takes to lead this country? It seems just like yesterday that he and Peter Costello were being touted as the Dream Team, the generational change that the Liberals could use to make themselves relevant to the commu- nity. He is now seemingly intent on throwing away what looked like the Op-position's best chance in many years to dominate politics. He had a clean slate on which to work, and a Prime Minister to attack who is not liked in the com-munity. What went wrong? For a start, he shot himself in the foot, both feet, sever-al times. Left to his own devices. Down-er has rearranged his public image from a Fresh Young Leader to a Stumbler and Bumbler. He lacks judgment, particularly for crisis management: when to cut your losses and how to extricate yourself from a mess. It is surprising for some-one who has lived and breathed politics for most of his life. He is extremely pragmatic, and will not make the Hewson mistake of lock- ing himself into policy. But the other ex-treme — slipping and sliding around on issues as an excuse for no policy — leaves him open to criticism by the La-bor Party and an electorate which in-creasingly wants performance from its elected representatives. A backbench watches carefully when its leader cops flak. How he or she acts under fire is an important indicator of leadership ability. Downer has failed this test. His initial response to the League of Rights row is almost unfathomable. When he needed to give a clear explana-tion — maybe own up to being sucked in to speaking at the 1987 league meet-ing — he avoided the issue. It was only after Keating's vicious personal attack that he was stung into action. In the aftermath. Downer might pick up the sympathy vote, but the row again confronts the community with the spectre of a leader who tries to bluff his way through a crisis. As well, he does not do his homework. Liberal support ers who saw Downer go on the front foot on Thursday over the League row would have been. heartened by his style, but his attack on Keating was blunted by his lack of research. As well, he did not know the party's policy on Aborigi-nes before he blundered into Central Australia. Imagery is of primary importance in politics. Good policies should be backed by a leader who is compassionate, au-thoritative. charismatic, visionary, and responsive io the changing needs and moods of the community. So much for the ideal; where does Downer lie on this leadership spectrum? Badly, according to soundings with se-nior Liberals, who are'extremely worried about his standing in the polls. They are agitated that the pointer has swung so extraordinarily quickly to the down side. Some are despondent that the new lead-er has enjoyed such a short honeymoon and is now spiralling downwards, per- haps irretrievably, when he had an op-portunity to make a fresh start. Downer seems pathologically unable to avoid the stumbles, and their impact is cumulative in the public's mind. When the details of a row are long forgotten, voters still vaguely remember it. The television screen may be turned off, but the image persists. Mention Aboriginal land rights and people might conjure up the searing and damaging sight of Downer umming and ahhing, searching for an illusive answer. Liberal Party research has been show-ing for some time that the public is very unclear on what the party stands for. Against that worrying background. Downer is about to take the next risks step in his battle to maintain his credi-bility and, ultimately, to live at The Lodge: on Monday, he will unveil his own directions statement. The two-part document is long on "the vision thing" and short on policy detail. There is a lot of talk of Liberal Party philosophy and goals lor the Op-position. The directions statement is a huge gamble. Downer knows that and has de-liberately downplayed expectations. He is prepared to take the risks involved in presenting such a lightweight document to the electorate, because it gives him a chance to put his imprimatur on the party. He almost had to do it to differ-entiate between his leadership and the reign of John Hewson. With this launch on Monday, he steps across the line: he exposes himself to further scrutiny and judgment and possi-bly ridicule. In repackaging the party's guiding philosophy, he is essentially put-ting his views on trial. Expect the judgment from the Gov-ernment to be scathing if the directions statement reveals Downer has the same ultra-conservative stance held by former Opposition Leader John Howard. (How-ard's Future Directions came with a pic-ture of an "ideal family" in front of a house with a picket fence.) Downer has set himself firmly apart from the Hewson tradition by consulting widely on the statement. Last week MPs were able to peruse the document but only in the ante-room of Downer's of-fice, where a running tally was kept of who had seen it and their comments. One MP was so bored he left after reading just three pages of rhetoric. Downer will use the statement to spell out his vision of an independent Austra-lia. Me made the first attempt at a Na-tional Press Club address several months ago. when he tried to take the focus off the republican push and on to foreign debt. The statement is expected to confirm the Liberal Party's commitment to the constitutional monarchy and say the current system has worked well, thereby firmly marking out the battle lines against republicans — inside and outside the party. The inherent risk for Downer in the directions statement is that you can in-terpret it anyway you like. Liberal faith-ful will likely see it as a bold vision. La-bor will see it as meaningless and outdated, but voters may perceive it as so much fairy floss, worthy but of little practical value. If the worse-case scenario occurs, ex- pect Downer's slide to accelerate and desperate and troubled talk about his future to dominate an unhappy Liberal Party.

06 Sep 1994 - Lawrence finds survey 'disturbing' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 6 September 1994, page 2 Lawrence finds survey 'disturbing' MELBOURNE: A national sur-vey which revealed one-third of Australians did not believe injecting heroin would be bad for their health was "extraordinary" and "disturbing", federal Health Minis-ter Carmen Lawrence said yester-day. Dr Lawrence raised doubts about the accuracy of the findings, saying it was easy to get misleading survey results, depending on the types of questions asked of participants. The survey, sponsored by the Sal-vation Army, also found that 48 per cent of people believed smoking a cigarette each day would not harm their health. It also revealed 37 per cent thought smoking marijuana once a cday would not be damaging, and 77 per cent said daily alcohol con-sumption would not be harmful. "I found the findings extraordi nary," Dr Lawrence said. "I'd really want to go back and look at the re-search sample and the way the questions were asked. "It seems to me that it's unlikely that people would be so blase about heroin for example. "After a very long period of edu-cation about the damaging effects of tobacco smoking, that again seems to represent a level of uncon-cern, which I find disturbing." Dr Lawrence said as a former re-searcher herself, it was easy to get results that "are a bit misleading". Asked if the attitude to tobacco smoking revealed in the survey demonstrated a complacency among people because they had become hardened to anti-smoking messages, Dr Lawrence said that that could be the case. But she said the findings could also reflect an unusual sample of survey respondents. "In the area of public health, you have to have continual programs," Dr Lawrence said. "You can't drop them off and hope that a generation will pick it up [anti-smoking advice] from par- ents or friends." Dr Lawrence said the Govern-ment would launch a major anti-smoking campaign aimed at young people later this year, after research showed that more youth were tak-ing up smoking after years of de-cline among teenagers. The Roy Morgan poll of 1229 men and women over the age of 14, and issued yesterday, coincides with the start of Alcohol Awareness Week. It showed people aged be tween 14 to 24 were more tolerant about marijuana, heroin and tobac-co, while middle-aged people had a more accepting attitude to alcohol.

17 Sep 1994 - Saturday FORUM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 17 September 1994, page 14 Saturday FORUM Limping along in the bear pit of federalism The environment, too often, slips through the constitutional cracks, says PHILLIP TOYNE IN HIS 1989 environment statement. Our Country, Our Future, Prime Minister Bob Hawke announced the national goal of planting a billion trees by the year 2000. This was to help counteract the widespread land degradation problems arising from vegetation clearance and unsustainable land use. In 1991. George Quaid on his North Queensland property, Sou'thcdge, destroyed an estimated two million trees in clearing an area of about 50sq km on the banks of the Mitchell River. Many of the trees were bulldozed into the river, which was being dammed to construct Australia's biggest private water storage, which is to cover some 3000ha and apparently to become a part of a major real estate subdivision offering lake front blocks. ; There is no national native vegetation retention scheme in place in Australia, and the Queensland Government was uniible to prevent the widespread clearance on Quaid's property. It was eventually able to force the removal of the dead trees from the" river. Only South Australia has laws requiring approval to clear native vegetation. I could give many other examples of similar gaps in our coverage of problems which occur in each state and territory and which together threaten our national interest. Other forms of land degradation, loosely described as "landcare" problems. are some. The regulation of experimentation with genetically manipulated organisms and the control of their release is another. The protection of endangered species is a third. The problems are not limited to environment matters but occur across the range of governance and public administration. This need not be the case, as the native vegetation issue illustrates. The Commonwealth could legislate for a national native vegetation retention scheme if it chose to. If it based such a law on the "corporations" power in the Constitution, it would be at least applicable to private and government trading corporations. There are other mechanisms available to the Commonwealth to initiate national programs. Together they add up to a formidable capacity to act. The numerous challenges against them by the States and Territories have seen the High Court interpreting the Constitution in an expansionary way, and with subsequent challenges entrenching and reaffirming federal power, not reducing it. Perhaps the most significant development in this respect is the increasing number- of international measures by nations aware that many environment problems now require multi-national responses.- Australia is a parly to many, such as the World Heritage Convention, the Biodiversity Convention, trade in protected species, the control of whaling and those protecting migratory birds. This constitutional "sea change" is not reflected in the intergovernment arrangements now being pursued where States continue jealously to guard their rights and the Commonwealth only occasionally challenges them. Political factors have often inhibited or stopped timely and adequate action on environment problems. It is remarkable that we do not accept a single, national scheme to regulate protected species management. This is symptomatic of a bigger dilemma. The reluctance to accept Federation resulting in genuine nationhood, which characterised the attitude of many of the colonial politicians drafting the Constitution; still produces a hostile response from the states to the assertion of a national interest. The commonwealth now needs seriously to reexamine its approach. If the cooperative federalism approach is not' working adequately, what will work? We, as a nation, could boldly assert the need for our Constitution to reflect a new role for the Com monwealth to be centrally involved in environment management as a national issue. A new power could be provided under Section 51, giving the Commonwealth power over the discharge of substances .on to land, air and water affecting more than one state or territory, the prevention of land, air or water degradation affecting more than one state or territory, the use of nuclear fuels, energy or ionising radiation, the protection of areas of national or international significance, or of a species of flora or fauna from extinction, and the regulation of novel life forms and other genetically or biologically manipulated releases. This would create clarity and certainty but may not be necessary given that the Commonwealth already has its wide-ranging .capacity under its powers to act in most circumstances. The missing element in any attempt to establish a national approach to environment management is the will to do it, not the power to do it. In relation to World Heritage listing, there should be a firm assertion of the Commonwealth's international responsibilities. The states could be invited to suggest areas Tor nomination, and their expert agencies could be involved in preparing justification materials, but the Federal Government must preserve the capacity and the resolve to act alone on nominations. With the protection of the National Estate — components of our natural or cultural environment of aesthetic, historic, scientific or social significance'or other special value for future generations as well as the present community — there needs to be a fundamental reappraisal. The register of our national treasures seems even more important today than it was when Moss Cass and Gough Whitlam created it 20 years ago, and yet we are seeing the ongoing process of places inscribed being destroyed. Many of these are the consequences of decisions of the Fed eral Government. In relation to Aboriginal involvement in protected area management, there is a strong argument for the wide extension of the Uluru model to many other parks and conservation areas throughout Australia. Whether this comes about as a response to native title claims, as part of the broad process of "social justice" or as part of the general search for reconciliation with indigenous Australians, the arguments for it are compelling. Each of the ideas I have outlined would be politically difficult and controversial. Each would also attract a large measure of popular support in the community. A number of opinion polls point to a stronger concern for the protection of the environment and for a national response to them. Take for example, a Saulwick Poll conduct ed on March 29, 1994, and published in The Sydney Morning Herald. This showed that overall 57 per cent of respondents put environment protection as a higher priority, with only 33 per ccnt rating, economic growth as more important. Despite this community sentiment, our political leaders have always attempted to juggle the pursuit of the politically popular with the pragmatic realities of federalism. Paul Keating, so often seen as the arch' enemy of the states, at least when it came to sharing revenue and more recently over native title, accepts them as the backdrop to our po litical affairs. THERE are compelling rea sons to plan nationally and act locally. We readily understand the economic advantages of such a vision. 1 am, by personal predisposition, in favour of Australia becoming a republic, and yet I find myself increasingly frustrated at the inordinate attention we pay to this symbol of nationhood while we neglect the nation itself and the basic mechanisms needed to make it work. Our country's environment problems are huge and complex. They will not be adequately addressed if governments limp along in the bear pit of federalism. The problems will not go away: their solutions require much more attention and the community expects more. It is time for our leaders to deliver more. Phillip Toyne's series on Government decision-making and the environment, with case studies of issues such as Fraser Island, the Franklin Dam and Coronation Hill, begins on Radio National's Green and Practical program at 9.30 this morning. The book of the series, The Reluctant Nation, of which the above is an extract, will be launched by Graham Richardson on Monday. Phillip Toyne: if the cooperative federalism approach is not working adequately, what will work?

19 Sep 1994 - IN BRIEF Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 19 September 1994, page 2 IN BRIEF Police still looking for a lead SYDNEY: Police say they are still a long way off finding the killer of NSW MP John Newman. Mr Newman. Member for the western Sydney scat of Cabramat-ta, was shot dead outside his Ca-bramatta home on September 5. The Cabramatta Patrol Com-mander, Chief Inspector, Alan Leek, said detectives were still sift-ing through a mountain of infor-mation and had not yet found a definite lead. "We are sifting through a huge amount of information in an ef-fort to focus on a clear direction to achieve our objective, which is the pursuit, apprehension and bringing to justice of those respon-sible for Mr Newman's murder." he said. □ The Sun-Herald reported yes-terday that Mr Newman had not changed his will to include his fi-ancee, Lucy Wang. According to the report, he left his Cabramatta home to his moth-er and the rest of his estate, in-cluding a $187,000 pay-out from his parliamentary pension, to build a multicultural centre to help the youth in the constituency. Teenager dies SYDNEY: A 21-year-old man from Chipping Norton, in Syd-ney's west, has been charged after an accident at Chipping Norton in which a teenager was killed and four others were injured. A police spokesman said a 16-year-old boy died in Liverpool Hospital yesterday morning after the accident. Two other boys are in a serious condition in Liverpool Hospital. CB licence fees go Owners of individual CB radios and handphones will no longer have to pay an $18 licence fee un-der new arrangements to be intro-duced on October 3. Paul Elliott, parliamentary se-cretary to the Minister for Com-munications. Michael Lee, said CB radios and handphones would come under class licensing to be introduced by the Spectrum Man-agement Agency. But CB repeater stations, not covered by the class licence, still require individual licensing. Wetlands to benefit Almost half Australia's most significant wetlands regions will benefit from $500.000 in govern-ment funding announced yesterday by the Minister for the Environ-ment, John Faulkner. Senator Faulkner said the mon-ey would be used to improve man-agement at 17 of Australia's 42 wetlands of international import-ance, known as Ramsar sites. Govt under pressure MELBOURNE: The Victorian Opposition has vowed to keep pressuring the State Government on its appointment of Tabcorp chief Ross Wilson after a new controversy on his $8 million re-cruitment surfaced yesterday. According to a report in yester-day's Sunday Age, Mr Wilson was given the top job without being short-listed by an executive place-ment firm hired by the Govern-ment to find the right person. Call for unity SYDNEY: Voters in marginal federal Labor electorates believe Australian coal companies should combine for a better deal when selling coal to Japan. The Saulwick poll conducted on behalf of the Construction, Forest-ry. Mining and Energy Union found that 57 per cent of those polled supported collective, rather than individual bargaining to get the best price when selling coal to Japan. Murder charge ADELAIDE: A 34-year-old man will appear in the Adelaide Magis-trates Court this morning charged with the slabbing murder of a 73-year-old woman. A spokesman for the South Australian Police said the man had been arrested and charged on Saturday night in relation to the murder which is believed to have taken place at Nailsworth in Ade-laide's northern suburbs on Thurs-day. The spokesman said neigh-bours from the block of units in which the woman lived found her body lying in a pool ol blood al-ter they became concerned at not seeing her for more than a day.

08 Jul 1987 - Latest poll still tips Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 8 July 1987, page 19 Latest poll still tips Labor SYDNEY: The Hawke Government would have been returned with a slightly increased majority if the federal election had been held last weekend, according to the final 1987 election Morgan Gallup poll, to be published in The Bulletin today. The Opposition closed the gap on Labor in the survey of 4199 voters, a larger sample than usual, but there were still four percentage points between them. Forty-eight per cent said they would vote for the Labor Party, down half a point, while a similar increase for the National Party lifted support for the coalition to 44 per cent. Unlike the Herald Survey published in The Sydney Morning Herald yesterday, which showed 12 per cent support for the Australian Democrats, the Morgan poll showed the Democrats steady on 7 per cent. The personal approval rating of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, dropped two points to 56 per cent, while the Opposition Leader, Mr Howard, gained an extra one percentage point to 41 percent. Mr Howard also gained three extra points on the question of who would make the better Prime Minister, but at 28 per cent still lagged heavily behind Mr Hawke's 60 per cent, down four points. Meanwhile, the poll found decreasing support for the Liberal Party's tax package. Fifty-one per cent (up 515 points) said they preferred the existing tax structure, and 42 per cent (down 2.5 per cent) said they favoured the proposed tax cuts.

02 Jun 1991 - THE FIGHT FOR THE LODGE Howe rushes back Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 2 June 1991, page 5 THE FIGHT FOR THE LODGE Howe rushes back On hand to take over as Deputy PM CANBERRA: The Federal Government's most senior left-wing minister and a contender the Deputy Prime Ministership, Brian Howe, will return to Australia this morning in time for the crucial ALP caucus leadership vote. Mr Howe cut short an overseas trip after the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, called a caucus meeting for tomorrow morning to allow a leadership ballot after a challenge by his deputy, Treasurer Paul Keating, on Thursday evening. In a statement on Friday from Stockholm. Mr Howe said he would be prepared. to stand as Deputy Prime Minister at the meeting if the position were de clared vacant Two caucus meetings on Friday morning failed to resolve the issue, which exploded the night before when it was revealed Mr Hawke had reneged on a pact to stand down after the 1990 election to allow Mr Keating time to settle in as Prime Minister. Mr Howe missed the meetings, along with backbencher Barry Jones, who also was overseas, and the Minister for Industrial Relations, Peter Cook, who was airborne over Canberra and unable to land because of fog. Sources said Mr Howe would arrive in Melbourne this morning and would fly to Canberra later in the day. Most MPs appear to be returning to Canberra tonight to avoid the fog which often closes the airport in the early morning at this time of year. • Two-thirds of voters in Sydney and Melbourne prefer Bob Hawke to Paul Keating as Prime Minister, according to a special Saulwick poll taken for The Age on Friday night Only 18 per cent of voters chose Mr Keating, and 16 per cent could not choose between them. The poll of 665 voters from both cities was published in yesterday's Age and had 65 per cent supporting Mr Hawke as the person to lead Labor into the 1993 federal election, while Mr Keating scored 24 per cent. From the voters surveyed in Sydney, 20 per cent said Mr Keating would make the better Prime Minister, compared with 16 per cent in Melbourne. • When the Hawke-Keating contest first flared in August, 1988, 70 per cent of voters wanted Mr Hawke to lead the Federal Government into the next election (held in March, 1990), while Mr Keating attracted only 16 per cent, The Age said.

22 Jun 1991 - Labor draws more low opinions Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 22 June 1991, page 9 Labor draws more low opinions LABOR governments throughout the country con- tinue to fare badly. According to Morgan Gallup Poll results published in The Bulletin, South Austra-lia's Labor Government is lagging a long way behind the Opposition — although the cult of personality is alive and well and there is still strong support for the Premier, John Bannon. Support for the SA Government rose slightly, to 35 per cent, in April May on its March rating of 32 per cent. The Opposi-tion Coalition had dropped by three points to 49 per cent, but still had a healthy lead. Support for the Democrats was unchanged at 12 per cent and 4 per cent supported other parties. Despite the low opinion the electorate holds of his Government, Mr Bannon enjoyed a 53 per cent ap-proval rating, up nine points from a low of 44 per cent in March. Forty per cent disapproved of him and 7 per cent were undecided. Opposition Leader Dale Baker had a 36 per cent approval rating, but 33 per cent disapproved of the way he was handling his job and 31 per cent were undecided. Sixty per cent of South Australians (up six points) thought Mr Bannon made a better premier than Mr Baker would. Support for Mr Baker as leader dropped seven points to 27 per cent. In another forum, Mr Bannon will give up his posi-tion as national president of the Australian Labor Party at the ALP's biennial national conference in Hobart next week. Among those tipped to replace him are the party's current senior vice-president, Stephen Loosley, and the Minister for Immigration, Gerry Hand. A dark horse to watch in the race is ACT delegate Sue Robinson. Ms Robinson has been a member of the National Executive since 1987 and is best known as senior private secretary to the ACT Minister for Health, Wayne Berry. Ms Robinson is from the left wing of the party (which is not surprising in the almost completely left-dominated ACT ALP).

27 Jun 1991 - Most Olympians hazy on value of carbohydrates Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 27 June 1991, page 39 Most Olympians hazy on value of carbohydrates Less than 30 per cent of Australia's Olympians were aware of the importance of carbohydrates in their diets, a symposium on nutrition at the Australian Institute of Sport was told this week. Gary Morgan stressed this when presenting to the symposium the findings from a recent Morgan Gallup Poll of current dietary habits of our top athletes. The symposium was part of Olympic Awareness Week. Former Olympic swimming champion and vice-president of the Australian Olympic Committee (which hosted the symposium) John Devitt welcomed guests, who included a group of leading scientists, coaches and athletes. Keynote speaker Dr David Costill, world-renowned for his work in the field of sports nutrition, spoke on the value of carbohydrates and exercise perform ances. He was supported by Dr Mark Hargreaves and Dr Louise Bourke, the Australian Institute of Sports dietitian. Dr Dick Telford, from the Sports, Science and Medicine Centre, chaired the symposium on behalf of the Australian Olympic Committee. — PETER WADDELL |

29 Jun 1991 - Hawke considered safe bet for PM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 29 June 1991, page 9 Hawke considered safe bet for PM MOST electors still consider Bob Hawke to be a safe bet as Prime Minister, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll of 2484 people published in this week's Bulletin showed that 49 per cent of people prefered Mr Hawke as leader, compared with 38 per cent who favoured the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, for the top job. Thirteen per cent could not say who they would support, or nomi nated someone else. Mr Hawke's approval rating fell 5 percentage points (to 39 per cent from 44 per cent at the beginning of June) in mid-June after the much publicised leadership brawl with the former Treasurer and KirribilH coconspirator, Paul Keating. Support for Mr Hewson also fell by 2 percentage points since the beginning of June. But support for the ALP was unaffected by the infighting, standing firm on 38 per cent, and support for the Liberal/National coalition was also steady on 45 per cent. Seven per cent of electors supported the Australian Democrats and 10 per cent opted for minor parties. People who prefered Mr Hawke as prime minister made comments such as "he is a more experienced leader", "he has a better understanding of politics in general", "better the devil you know* and "don't know enough about Hewson". Those who opted for Mr Hewson thought that he "should be given a chance" had "a better command of economic policy" and "given time he will be more forceful". The ALP conference managed to avoid another potentially messy issue by leaving its three-mine uranium policy unchanged even though Mr Hawke has branded it "illogical". The conference merely noted the report of its internal uranium review committee—established in 1988 — and defeied making a decision on the issue. While sucn inaction could not have served to win over business community confidence, as the Min ister for Industry, Technology and Commerce, John Button, noted yesterday on ABC radio, the position seems to enjoy some popular support according to a Morgan poll of 1085 people. The poll shows that 56 per cent are against opening new mines but 61 per cent think Australia should continue to export uranium. Sixty two per cent of respondents thought Australia should develop and export uranium for peaceful purposes, 31 per cent said no and 7 per cent could not say. Only 36 per cent of respondents thought that new uranium mines should be allowed while 56 per cent said no to new mines. Eight per cent could not say what the policy should be. The no vote was 62 per cent among ALP voters, 63 per cent among Democrat voters, 46 per cent among coalition voters and 73 per cent among Independent and other voters. Those who voted no to new mines believed that there was too great a risk involved. Those who voted yes believed that uranium mining was of great potential benefit to the Australian economy.

06 Mar 1994 - Samuels drew a short straw when asked to inquire into ASIS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 6 March 1994, page 2 Samuels drew a (short straw when asked to inquire into ASIS MUNGO MacCALLUM on the likelihood of an effective spy investigation. SO GORDON SAMUELS has drawn the short straw. He becomes the latest in a scries of retired judges to conduct an inquiry into what are -laughingly known as our "security" services - particularly our overseas spooks, the Australian Secret Intelligence Service. Over recent weeks the usual allegations "have emerged: ASIS is power-mad, out of control, staffed largely by paranoics and loonies, and has become a domestic and international embarrassment, held in contcmpt by its fellow spy networks who nonetheless use its technicians to do work too dirty for them to touch them selves. There is no serious reason to cook or falsify any of this; after all, an organisation whose job description includes ex .. "j pcrtise in perjury, fraud, corruption, bribery, blackmail, coercion, theft, conspiracy, deception, extortion, betrayal and the general subversion of legally constituted authority is unlikely to work in a manner which would be considered totally orthodox in polite society. Mf Samuels' problem is that by its very nature it is unlikely to be receptive to a judicial inquiry charged with finding out just what the hell it has actually been up to, and whether it might not be better to try to achieve at least a modicum of accountability. It must be said that history is not on his side. In the past both ASIS and its. domestic counterpart, the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, have been quite remarkably successful in persuading judges that, despite all public evidence to the contrary, not only are they doing a truly great job in protecting the country from everything from Martian invasion to athlete's foot, but that they should be given even more licence, more secrecy and more funny toys than they already enjoy. To do this they generally employ what I call the Elephant Repellent Theory. 1 have used elephant repellent since birth, and have never been trampled by a rogue elephant. It follows as the night the day that elephant repellent is the only effective protection. Similarly, since the formation of our security services, Australia has never been taken over by foreign invaders, and has been free from internal terrorism - well, almost. Can we deny our spooks the credit for a job well done? It is true, of course, that this happy situation also obtained for the period before the formation of our security services, but this seems not to have carried much weight with previous inquiries, which have generally patted the spooks on the head, told them not to forget to pack clean handkerchiefs in future, and sent them out to wreak more havoc. What the inquiries should be doing, of course, is considering not how the spooks operate, but whether we need them at all. It is often forgotten that both ASIO and ASIS were set up, not because the Australian Government saw any threat to the nation, or bccause of some public demand for a national security blanket, but because of pressure from overseas. The argument was that first the Brits, and later the Yanks, couldn't really trust us, or even take us seriously, Unless we had spook forces with which their spook forces could liaise. Leaving aside the question of whether we ever really needed to know their secrets, even in the depths of the Cold War, there emerges the question of whether the somewhat unbalanced chaps in the trench coats and the false noses were the right people to receive them. Episodes like the simulated raid on the Sheraton Hotel in Melbourne, in which ASIS creat ed a near riot while pretending to extricate a colleague (or something - the full story of this bizarre cops and robbers exercise was, of course, never revealed) do not exactly engender confidence. Nor do the cases of .mistaken identity by ASIO, one of the most notorious being the confusion of Bob Hogg, then Bob Hawke's principal adviser, with ANOP pollster Rod Cameron during another inquiry into the organisation's behaviour. Everybody can make a mistake, but with most people - even, in theory, with the police forces which could easily take over the few aspects of the spooks activities which are actually worthwhile -such mistakes have to be acknowledged and corrected. With ASIS and ASIO they are simply covered up and repeated. Like everyone else, I have an ASIO story; the difference is that mine can actually be confirmed in print. When Tudor Harvey Barnctt, a man with a disarming manner, a genuine love o.ff ticket and eyes like a Spanish Inquisitor, retired as director-general of ASIO, he took the unusual step of writing his memoirs. The tone was largely self-justificatory and not enough beans were spilled to make five. One anecdote concerned a story I had written mentioning Barnett during the Hope Royal commission into ASIO, In reporting this trivial incident, Barnett managed 40 get the story completely wrong, and had it appearing in the wrong paper. He also misspelled my name. If the director-general of ASIO can make three mistakes in one paragraph in public, can we really trust his underlings in private? Mr Samuels, I rest my case.

07 Mar 1994 - Optimists to the fore on economic questions Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 7 March 1994, page 4 Optimists to the fore on economic questions There has been a surge in con sumer confidence, according to a new Seven News-Morgan poll. In February, the Roy Morgan consumer-confidence rating increased by seven points to 127.5, the highest level since - the organisation began such surveys in March 1973. Confidence increased on each of five key questions. 33 per cent of respondents said they were better off compared with a year ago - 6 per cent more. The number who felt they were worse off declined by 3 per cent to 31 per cent. There was an increase of 5 per cent, to 37 per cent, in the number of people who thought they would be better off in a year's time. Only 10 per cent, down 1 per cent, predicted that they would be worse off. Good times for the economy gen erally during the coming year were envisaged by 49 per cent of respondents, an increase of 7 per cent; 17 per cent were pessimistic, a decline of 6 per cent. 45 per cent of respondents fore shadowed good economic progress in the next five years, and there was a 2 per cent decline, to 15 per cent, in the number who expected the economic situation to be poor.

28 Mar 1994 - Bishop rules out Hewson challenge Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 28 March 1994, page 1 Bishop rules out Hewson challenge By JODIE BROUGH Bronwyn Bishop formally ruled out a challenge against the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, yesterday as her opponents within the Coalition gloated over her disappointing showing in the Mackellar by-election on Saturday. Leadership aspirant John Howard said he was "a bit surprised at the swing" of 5 per cent against the Liberals, and the Premier of Victoria, Jeff Kennett, a Hewson supporter, said the result "could have been better". Mr Kennett suggested the Mackellar result reflected voters' opinions of the candidates' personalities, not dissatisfaction with Dr Hewson and the Opposition, and slated party members with "individual ambition". "Invariably, those who pursue their goals publicly or privately are not those who can easily ever assume the real rrtantle of leadership," he said. "They can never demand or give the sort of leadership that they have been unable to display while trying to pursue their own ambitions." Mrs Bishop, who blamed a "poisonous campaign" by Independent Bob Ellis for the result, said she had "no plan to challenge" Dr Hewson. "I have a plan to go into the Parliament and represent the people of Mackellar," she said. "We fought a strong campaign, and we won. Sixty per cent of the two-party preferred is not a bad result. If we could repeat that across Australia, we would be in government not just once but for a genera tion." Dr Hewson refused to respond when asked if he was quietly pleased that Mrs Bishop was not as popular as she had thought, saying, "I don't make those judgments." He said both Mackellarand War ringah had been "good solid results in line with our expectations on our historical experience; that's about where we thought they'd come out". "And I think the key issue is that the Keating Government didn't have the guts to run a candidate," he said. Speaking at the Liberal Party's Victorian conference, Dr Hewson made it clear he intended to hold on to the leadership and made pointed references to Sir Robert Menzics, who had been "decisively written off by the media" but contradicted the pundits. The by-election results came as the Bulletin AGB McNair poll showed the ALP in front of the Coalition for the first time in nine months, up two points to 43 per cent; the Coalition remained steady on 42 per cent. But the Time Morgan poll showed the Coalition ahead - 46 per cent to 41 percent. However, only 36 per cent of voters believed the Coalition would win the next election, while 46 per cent expected Labor to win. The federal director of the Liberal Party, Andrew Robb, said it was difficult to make a judgment about the Mackellar results without Labor candidates. But they were "quite good within historical voting patterns" as the Liberal primary vote normally dropped up to three points at byelections. There had been a strong swing of 1 to 5 per cent to Mrs Bishop in ALP booths. Mr Ellis said he believed the Mackellar poll had "spiked Mrs Bishop forever as a potential leader of the Liberal Party, because she's achieved a swing against her which if duplicated across the country would more than halve their number of seats". 30 Mar 1994 - POLL-WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 30 March 1994, page 2 See-saw polls now put ALP in the lead The see-sawing nature of recent opinion polls was reflected yesterday in an AGB McNair-SM//ef//i opinion poll which has the Labor Government ahead of the Coalition. The poll said a survey in late February and early March had Government support up 2 per cent to 43 per cent, while backing for the Coalition was unchanged at 42 per cent. This contrasted with a Time Morgan poll issued on Sunday which had the Coalition, ahead of Labor 46 per cent to 41 per cent in terms of voting intentions. The AGB McNair poll found that Paul Keating had maintained his lead over Opposition Leader John Hewson as preferred prime minister by a margin of 39 per cent (down 2 per cent) to Dr Hewson's 25 per cent (up 1 per cent).

02 Jan 1992 - Rain dampens ACT festivities Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 2 January 1992, page 4 Rain dampens ACT festivities Thousands arrested across Aust By CHARLES MIRANDA and AAP ;Police said New Year's Eve was quieter than usual in the ACT as rain became the real show stopper to many people's celebrations. ;A spokesman for the Australian Federal Police said the force on du ty; were "quite content with the night's activities" in what was a "fairly quiet" entrance to the New Year. He said it seemed the rain had put a damper on many parties around Canberra, although there had been the usual trouble. Police were investigating yesterday the early morning assault and robbery of an 18-year-old man in City Walk, Civic. -About 3am the man was withdrawing money from an automatic teller machine when he was "seriously" assaulted and robbed of cash and personal belongings. Police are calling on any witnesses to the assault to come forward. police were also investigating a serious car crash that involved an aitibulance and left a woman in hospital with several broken bones. Night duty ambulance Superintendent John McLaren said that about 11.10pm on New Year's Eve an ambulance was attending what was believed to be a stabbing when it collided with a vehicle at the intersection of Northbourne and Wakefield Avenues. 'He said the ambulance went through a green light as it was heading down Northbourne and attempted to avoid the car coming from Wakefield Avenue, but failed. The elderly woman driver of the other car received a broken leg and seyeral broken ribs and is in a stable condition at Woden Valley Hospital. The ambulance driver received minor cuts and scratches and super intendent McLaren said the ambulance was unserviceable. Police also arrested 13 people for drunken and disorderly behaviour. Two people have been killed, a bashed grandfather has died and thousands of people have been arrested for drunkenness as the New Year got under way across Australia yesterday. But, in a ray of New-Year hope, Australians enjoyed one of their safest motoring years on record in 1991, with 210 fewer deaths than in 1990. In Sydney, in the first three hours of the New Year, a 32-yearold man was kicked to death after a New Year's Eve party. Two men have been chained with murder over the killing, in Bidwell, in Sydney's west. A crowd hurled rocks and bricks at a police car after it was called in to help a fire crew in southern suburban Minto overnight. They were called to a large blaze allegedly started by a group of between 20 and 40 people who used tyres, timber and accelerants to build a bonfire. In Brisbane, a 29-year-old woman was bashed to death with a brick and a broom handle in Wynnum. Police, called to the scene at 3am by a neighbour, found the woman lying in the backyard. In peak-hour traffic on a major Brisbane freeway yesterday, 19 New Year's revellers were caught by a police booze bus between 7am and 10am. In Surfers Paradise, four policemen were assaulted after they were called to a unit after gunfire was reported. One was knocked unconscious, another had a broken nose, and two others were assaulted. Two men have been charged with as sault. In Queensland, the arrest tally early yesterday morning was 250 and the number was expected to grow. In Victoria, police arrested 1067 offenders, mostly drunks. Heavy rain lashed Melbourne in the early evening, blacking out 120,000 households and flooding major roads. In South Australia, police arrested 54 people on Tuesday night, mainly for public drunkenness or behaviour offences. In Western Australian, police thanked the public for one of the quietist New Year celebrations in recent years. Only 210 arrests were made throughout the state. In the Northern Territory, police reported a reasonably quiet New Year's Eve, with 62 arrests for drunkenness in Darwin and Alice Springs. There was good news on Australia's roads: NSW and Victoria both posted their lowest road tolls since 1950 and the toll was down in South Australia arid the ACT. And as the New Year arrived, Australians were surprisingly optimistic about 1992. A Morgan Gallup poll in Time magazine's New Year edition shows 54 per cent believe it will be a better year than last year. This is the highest Australian confidence has reached since it peaked at 57 per cent in 1983 and 1984. Only 33 per cent of Australians, compared with 56 per cent, foresee economic difficulty.

02 Jan 1992 - New poll shows hint of optimism Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 2 January 1992, page 3 New poll shows hint of optimism SYDNEY: Despite the recession, Australians are surprising' ly optimistic about 1992. A Morgan Gallup poll in the new year edition of Time magazine shows 54 per cent believe 1992 will be a better year than 1991. This is the highest Australian confidence has reached since it peaked at 57 per cent in 1983 and 1984, a reflection of the country's emergence from the economic travails of 1981 and 1982. The poll shows the surge of confidence is reflected across the political spectrum, with some 60 per cent of Labor voters seeing a better 1992, 48 per cent of Coalition supporters and 57 per cent of Democrats. Only 33 per cent of Australians (compared with 56 per cent previously) foresee economic difficulty in the year ahead. Nevertheless, the magazine says, only 10 per cent are sufficiently confident to tip a return to economic prosperity and 57 per cent believe conditions will stay the same or are not prepared to guess. Australia comes fourth in a list of the 47 most optimistic nations for 1992, behind Argentina, where 61 per cent believe 1992 will be better than last year, the US (also 61) and Israel (57). The poll surveyed face-to-face 1265 people aged over 14 in Australia over the weekend November 16-17.

03 Jan 1992 - Grey to wait and see if NRMA will invest Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 3 January 1992, page 3 Grey to wait and see if NRMA will invest BRISBANE: Compass Airlines' chief executive, Bryan Grey, said yesterday he would "wait and see" if Australia's largest traveller organisation, the NRMA, would invest in the revival of his collapsed airline. Mr Grey said he had spoken to a member of the NRMA council, Richard Talbot, a number of times about a potential investment. Although it was a "wait and see" situation, Mr Talbot was "very very confident", Mr Grey said. An NRMA council faction headed by Mr Talbot, the Motorists Action Group, "is apparently very strong for an involvement with Compass". Mr Grey made the statement when he spoke yesterday to journalists outside Compass headquarters. He has been involved in talks with the provisional liquidator, Ian Ferrier, of Sydney-based accountancy and insolvency firm Ferrier Hodg son and Co. The pair were "almost working on the same package", Mr Grey said of a proposed financial rescue for the airline. "I think it's fair enough to say, without putting words into his mouth, that he's progressing on the basis that Compass will fly again," Mr Grey said of his talks with Mr Ferrier. They were now "checking the viability of that" and a "rationale" for investors. Information was still being provided to Mr Ferrier. Mr Grey said he was "very opti mistic" for a Compass relaunch, but said, "I just can't put a date on it or a time". He said it was "interesting" that his airline's five seized aircraft were, according to reports, staying in Australia. Tlie provisional liquidators would talk soon to the aircraft's owners, he said. Commenting on criticism of Compass from a former federal minister for tourism, and now Tourism Task Force leader, John Brown, Mr Grey said he was "a little bit intrigued". "He approached myself some eight months ago requesting a contribution of $20,000 from Compass to that task force, which we refused to do," Mr Grey said. The Tourism Task Force is funded by about 60 tourism-related organisations, including former Compass rivals Ansett, Eastwest and Australian Airlines. Of the criticisms, Mr Grey said, "That's his [Mr Brown's] business and I'm not going to waste my time worrying about it." Commenting on the possibility of the entrance of Sydney's AAA Airlines into the domestic market, Mr Grey said there would still be room for Compass. He said Compass's technical staff had signed a statement saying they would "stay around" until every effort to help the airline was explored. They had shunned approaches already made by others. Mr Grey said he believed flight attendants now working for other airlines would "come back to us, don't worry about that" if Compass flew again. . Eighty-five per cent of Australians want Compass Airlines to fly again, and SO per cent believe the Federal Government should help with financial backing, according to a new poll. A national Morgan Gallup Poll carried out this week also shows that 82 per cent of those surveyed expect air fares to rise if a rescue bid for Compass fails. The telephone poll, which surveyed 645 people around Australia, was commissioned by the Friends of Compass group, which has already raised $4.9 million through pledges and cash to help revive the airline. An overwhelming 89 per cent of those polled supported rescue attempts by the group, which comprises former Compass staff. Gary Morgan, of the Roy Morgan Research Centre, said his company's poll showed there was strong support for Federal Government aid to help Compass get back in the air. "The 50 per cent figure is high in relation to whether the Government should be giving Compass money in what are difficult times," Mr Morgan said. Forty per cent opposed Federal Government financial help for Compass, and 10 per cent could not say.

08 Jan 1992 - Govt ahead in Entrance Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 8 January 1992, page 5 Govt ahead in Entrance SYDNEY: The NSW Coalition Government has a narrow lead over the Labor Opposition in the run-up to the January 18 by-election in The Entrance, according to a Morgan Gallup poll published in Time magazine. Morgan Gallup's December survey found the Liberal-National Government's support to be up half a point from November at 42.5 per cent, while support for the ALP rose the same amount, to 40.5 per cent. Backing for Democrats and Independents was down 1 per cent at 17 per cent. The by-election was announced last week in the wake of a Court of Disputed Returns decision that the Liberal candidate's win in The Entrance at the NSW general election in May was invalid. The Coalition is expected to remain in government, even if Labor wins the by-election.

09 Jan 1992 - Democrats not running in Tas Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 9 January 1992, page 5 Democrats not running in Tas HOBART: The Australian Democrats have urged supporters to vote for Tasmania's Green Independents after the party decided not to contest next month's state election. Democrats state president Sarah Briggs said in Hobart that the party was not ready for an election campaign so early in the year. "Rather than risk splitting the Green vote we have decided not to stand," Ms Briggs said. "We believe this is an important step in the journey towards closer Democrat-Green relations." Ms Briggs said the Democrats were in complete agreement with the Greens on economic and environmental policy - key issues in the run up to the February 1 poll. She said members had been informed by letter of the state executive's decision and the response so far had been positive. Australian Democrats Senator Robert Bell said yesterday that his party was determined to ensure that Senator Robert Bell: rejects that Democrats will lose credibility. an alternative vision was presented to Tasmanian voters and the Greens could achieve this. "Exactly who does it is less important than the fact it has to be done," Senator Bell said. "We can see in a practical sense the Greens have a much greater chance of achieving our alternative vision for Tasmania." Senator Bell rejected statements that the Democrats would lose credibility by not contesting the election. He said the party would still endorse candidates for the next federal election and contest local council elections under the Democrat ban ner. The Democrats' decision gives a significant boost to the electoral chances of the Greens who are striving to win government in their own right. The five Greens, who held the balance of power in the last parliament, are confident of increasing their numbers in the 35-seat House of Assembly as a result of yesterday's pledge by the Democrats. Greens leader Bob Brown said the Democrats' decision showed there was solidarity between the two proenvironment parties. A recent Morgan Gallup poll put support for the Greens in Tasmania at 15.5 percent.

15 Jan 1992 - Round 1: Keating, not ALP, on ropes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 15 January 1992, page 1 Round 1: Keating, not ALP, on ropes SYDNEY: The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, has scored an approval rating of only 25 per cent in the first Morgan Gallup Poll since he deposed Bob Hawke as Labor Party leader. But voter support for the Government is up more than 3 percentage points. The results, to be published in Time magazine today, show that the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, has lifted his approval rating by three points to 62 per cent. The 25 per cent rating for Mr Keating is one point less than Mr Hawke received in his last poll in December. Support for the ALP was at 35 per cent, up 3.5 points since the leadership challenge. Coalition support fell by the same margin, to 49 per cent. Time noted Labor's improvement came in the wake of the visit of the US President, George Bush -and the party had still rated worse than in October and November. Head-to-head in the preferred Prime Minister poll, Dr Hewson was favoured by 48 per cent of voters (down from 51 per cent against Mr Hawke in December) and Mr Keating by 35 per cent. In a footnote to history, respondents were asked whether they preferred Mr Hawke or Mr Keating as Prime Minister. The result was 56 per cent for the old, 31 per cent for the new and 13 per cent could not say or named someone else.
