22 Jan 1992 - Confidence on the rise, according to Morgan poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 22 January 1992, page 5 Confidence on the rise, according to Morgan poll SYDNEY: People feel more confident about the economy this month than they have since October, according to the latest Roy Morgan consumer confidence rating, to be published in Time today. Time also will publish figures from a November Morgan Gallup Poll indicating why the rise in confidence has not helped the Labor Federal Government. The November poll indicated that 53 per cent of Australians blamed the Government for unemployment, the first time it had been placed alone at the top of a list including world pressures (47 per cent) and trade unions (26 per cent). These figures contrasted with those at the depths of the 1982-83 recession; the December 1982 survey found that 52 per cent blamed world pressure and only 37 per cent blamed the Government. A record 78 per cent also said in November that the Government was not doing enough to stem the rising number of jobless. The proportion who felt their jobs were safe dropped to 69 per cent. O Public opinion is a demonstrably fickle thing, as the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, could tell you. On Monday, 70 per cent of Australians questioned in a survey thought he was arrogant, 64 per cent thought he was evasive, and only 38 per cent believed him credible and sincere. But after just one television interview, on the Nine Network's A Current Affair with Jana Wendt on Monday night, Mr Keating's ratings have improved dramatically. The show commissioned special prcand post-interview polls to find whether a television interview can change voters' perceptions of a politician. It appears it can. One thousand and sixty-two people nationwide were asked for their voting intentions and their impressions of Mr Keating, then were asked again after the interview. Four hundred of the original group responded to the second survey. Those who found Mr Keating arrogant dropped from 70 to 33 per cent, those who thought him sincere rose from 38 to 5}, and evasive from 64 to 55, while those who perceived him as aggressive fell from 56 to 13; credible increased from 38 to 48 per cent.

13 Jun 1994 - Good times predicted Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 13 June 1994, page 2 Good times predicted Australians' confidence in the economy reached an all-time high this month, according to the latest poll published in this week's Time Australia magazine. The Roy Morgan Confidence Rating found 50 per cent expected good times in the year ahead, up three points on last month, while 13 per cent, down five points, expected bad times. Looking five years down the track, the number of people ex pecting good times remained unchanged on 46 per cent, while 13 per cent, down two points, thought things would be bad. Assessing their personal finances, 33 per cent of the people surveyed expected to be better off. The number of people who. felt they would be worse off fell by one point to 11 per cent. The number of people who said they were better off this year rose to 32 per cent, up three points.

19 Jun 1994 - Fahey moves to reclaim law initiative Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 19 June 1994, page 6 Fahey moves to reclaim law initiative COFFS HARBOUR: The Premier, John Fahey, moved to reclaim the political initiative on the key election area of law and order yesterday, after publicly conceding his minority coalition Government faced an uphill battle to remain in office beyond the next election. Mr Fahey promised a new round of government announcements on law and order issues — as well as increased spending on police — in response to recent attempts by the Labor Party to portray the Government as being "soft" on crime. Mr Fahey said at yesterday's conference that Labor was likely to run what he termed a "dishonest" election campaign at next year's election, focused on a clutch of 10 marginal seats. Mr Fahey said such a campaign, aimed at the Government's weak seats, would be at the expense of rural and regional NSW and pose a difficult task for the Govern ment in its bid to win the March 25, 1995, state election. "It will require enormous effort. We are in a traditional Labor state," Mr Fahey said. At the same time Mr Fahey nominated two of Labor's marginal seats — Coogee and Parramatta — to be targeted . by the Liberals. And he confirmed the Liberal Party would try to wrest Manly from Independent Peter Macdonald. Despite his public caution about the Government's electoral chances, Mr Fahey said recent public opinion polling suggested the Government was "in a dammed good position". The latest Saulwick opinion. poll, published in Friday's Sydney Morning Herald, put support for the Coalition at 57 per cent, giving it a commanding lead over the Opposition, which had 43 per cent support. Mr Fahey said the Gov ernment could not rest on such results, and moved to restate the Coalition's com mitment to tough law and order policies. • The NSW National Party backed away yesterday from a proposal that it reserve winnable positions in the Parliament for women. Instead, delegates said on ly that they would work to I support assisting National Party women into Parlia ment. A motion from the party's Albury electorate council suggested the Nationals "adopt a policy of assisting women to enter the legislative council or senate by reserving winnable positions on the ticket for women". But the 600 delegates defeated that motion, instead adopting a broad policy that commits the Nationals to helping women get into Parliament through seminars, and the development of a women's policy. The amended motion also said the Nationals should target prominent women with a view to encouraging them to enter the state and federal Parliaments.

06 Dec 1985 - In-fighting is nothing but self-destructive A lesson the Liberals would be wise to learn from Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 6 December 1985, page 2 In-fighting is nothing but self-destructive A lesson the Liberals would be wise to learn from Labor POLITICS | By PAUL MALONE | The Hawkc Government learnt its political survival lesson the hard way in the December 1984 poll. But the lesson has been learnt if 1985 is anything to judge by. Faction fights which at the start of the year seemed certain to ensure that this would be the last term for the Government, have been curbed. Federally, the party now looks more unified than it has for years and the Government is well prepared for the run to an election at the end of its three-year term. This was not an accident. After the 1984 election, there was a feeling within the Left and Centre-Left that if Labor was going to be kicked out at the end of this term then at least they were going to ensure that something was achieved. They were not going to accept the prescription for the first term — do nothing radical and Labor will win the middle ground and be assured of a further term. The second Hawkc Government was going to be a "Labor" Govern ment. This view made its impact • almost immediately with the MX missile decision. The Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, the Minister for Foreign Afiairs, Mr Haydcn, and the then Minister for Defence, Mr Scholcs, had quietly decided on November 16 last year to provide Australian support for the US missile tests. When the news leaked out it provoked an outcry from within the party. Left and CentreLeft spokesmen openly voiced their opposition. Finally, in the United States, Mr Hawkc bowed to the pressure and the ofTcr was withdrawn. But the political problems did not end there. A poorly worded communique agreed to by Mr Hawke on his US trip suggested that Australia approved of the US strategic modernisation program. Again, there was a public outcry from Labor Party leaders before the matter was clarified and any suggestion that Australia had endorsed the program was removed. All these problems were occurring at about the same time as New Zealand and the US were at odds over the nuclear-armed ship visits. As a result the issues were intertwined. Politically, one would think it was a bad start to the year. But the polls did not show this. According to the Irving Saulwick poll, the Labor vote in March measured 48 per cent compared with the actual election vote of 47.5 per cent in December, 1984. The Morgan polls had Labor at 48, 47, 48 and 48 in March and April. Nevertheless, il was clear to all in the Labor Party that things could not go on as they had. The public statements by factional leaders had to end. The constructive way to do this was to give those dissatisfied members of the Government a hearing. The Left had been ignored in the two previous years as the "pragmatists" had implemented their do-nothing program. But this had produced a poor election result. So there was a feeling that there was nothing to lose by trying the alternative — try to get Labor policies in placc. If the leadership was not going to go along with this, then those who wanted to get things done would publicly air their views. The damage this could cause was apparent to all. The Treasurer, Mr Keating, summed up the situation when he noted — at the peak of the factional speak-out early in the year — that "the trouble with a lot of people in the Labor Party is they've got long tongues and they want to keep advertising them selves". "One of the problems about factionalism in the Labor Party is that every faction thinks they've got to have their viewpoint in the marketplace and a few of them would do well just frankly to shut up," Mr Keating had said. He said also that the "fourth graders", who were trying to crash PUBLIC OPINION OF THE PARTY LEADERS OPINION HAWKE Nov June Aug Sept Oct 1984 19B5 HOWARD Sept Oct 1985 PEACOCK Nov June Aug 1984 1985 Very good 25 S 9 14 12 8 5 4 5 3 Good 39 30 35 34 34 29 27 17 22 21 Fair 26 41 39 35 38 37 42 40 43 46 Poor 5 11 10 10 9 9 11 21 17 17 Very Poor 4 8 5 6 5 7 7 15 10 10 Not ture 1 2 10 8 into the act, would be better to shut up. The number of caucus committees was doubled as a result of the MX decision and a factional deal was stitched together to allocate the positions of chairman and secretary of cach of the committees. A divisive ballot was thus avoided. But of greater importance was the real wilingncss demonstrated by the Government leaders to start taking into account all party views. The Right's views were no longer simply handed down from on high via Cabinet. Nowhere was this more clcarly demonstrated than in determining the final position on tax. In the short term, the tax debate was bad for the Government. The polls — the only guide we have — showed a crash in Government popularity in May, June and July. Preparing a tax-reform package was, politically, an extremely difficult task. No community consensus was ever going to be achieved. Self-interested sectional groups were going to scream. All the screaming was in the open in the months leading up to the tax summit. Mr Keating trooped the country trying to sell "Option C", which contained the broadly based consumption tax — a tax popular in Liberal Party and Treasury circles. In the fluid state before the policy was determined, other leading party representatives took the opportunity to speak out against it. The consumption tax was a politically absurd proposal for Labor. The inequity of the tax was to be overcome by other compensating measures. This proposition was rather like a doctor suggesting to a patient suffering cholera that to cure him he would fracture his skull, then apply the best medical techniques to overcome this damage and offer other treatment so that in the end the patient would be better olT. Better simply to forget the inequitable tax and apply only the constructive treatment. The consumption tax was opposed across the Labor movement throughout the country — the Left, the Centre-Left, the Victorian Labor Unity faction and Independents. The only real support for it was in Mr Kcating's home State, and even there key union members in his own faction opposed the tax. The decision to throw out the consumption-tax proposal was Mr Hawkc's clearest demonstration of his new rcccptivcness to party views. The decision may have upset Mr Keating and the business community, but the vast majority of the party was pleased. The tax package the Government eventually announced was one a unified Labor party — Left, Centre, Right and unions — could get behind and sell in the community. If Labor had been divided, as it would have been with the consumption tax, the political consequences would have been disastrous. It was not a victory for the Left . or for the unions. It was a recognition of Labor values, a policy truly in line with Labor tradition. Mr Keating was to get his way in other less obvious, but nevertheless inportant, areas. Deregulation and foreign bank entry were two. He also had a major victory in Budget strategy. On the Left, there was a push for a bigger Budget deficit. Mr Keating argued against this and favoured restraint. With LABOR'S POLLING •84 '85 gQ Dec Mar Apr May Jun Jul AugSepOct 1 1 <1> ,L 0(5) / s 1 y\ / V \ (3)/ V (1) — MX Issue. (2) — Tax debate gets under way. (3) — Tax summit (4) — Howard replaces Peacock. (5) — Tax package announced. the wisdom of hindsight, he was clearly right. The economy was starting to take off and, in classic Keyncsian terms, it was appropriate to cut back public-sector spending. The Left suffered other losses during the year, such as the Federal Executive's decision to allow four right-wing unions which left the ALP in the 1950s to reafTiliate. But for the majority of the Left, this did not provoke a bitter reaction. Partly, this was due to a more pragmatic leadership but it was also due to the fact that consideration was being given to Left views. The Left was not being frozen out. It could start to feel that the second Hawke Government was worth fighting for. It was certainly not worth damaging the Government over anything but a major issue. While the Labor Party was moderating its faction fights during the year, the Liberal Party was developing the art. This led to the "dry" or rightwing faction leader, Mr Howard, ousting the more middlc-ofcthe road Mr Peacock as leader on September 5. Mr Peacock was seen by many Liberals as too wishy-washy. Mr Howard, in contrast, had strong views. But just as a Labor has to compromise to bring its factions together, Mr Howard will have to learn to compromise or he will have little chance of success at the next election. Mr Peacock's political career looked to be finished in Setember. But the party will be watching Mr Howard's performance very carefully next year. Liberals do not have a history of loyalty to leaders who fare badly in the polls. Mr Bill Snedden got one chance in 1974. In NSW, before Mr Nick Greiner, there was a period when there was a change in leadership almost monthly. The federal parliamentary Liberal Party seems almost as ruthless. Members may recall that Mr Peacock did surprisingly well in the 1984 poll. They could come to regret the consequenccs which flowed from their initial decision to support Mr Howard in the ballot for the deputy leadership. Mr Howard, of course, invited a challenge at his first press conference when he said he would remain leader "so long as I deliver the goods". The polls with all their faults — a demonstrated ability to frequently be wide of the mark — will be a key measure used by members to determine whether Mr Howard is delivering the goods. The policies developed in industrial relations, taxation and privatisation will be another measure. Most Liberal Party members will have to feel satisfied with these if Mr Howard is to prove a success. If a significant block feels disaffected, the Liberal Party will continue to capture the headlines — but they will be the wrong sort of headlines.

31 Dec 1985 - Tobacco sponsorship Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 31 December 1985, page 6 Tobacco sponsorship Received December 23 Sir, — R. Thornton cnticiscd (letters, Dccembcr 12) my company's recent sponsorship of the Winfield Socceroos. While a vocal minority oppose commercial free spcech and freedom and responsibility for choice in this country, the majority of Australians continue to support tobacco-company sponsorship of sport and the arts and the maintenance of cigarette advertising. In the latest public-opinion poll conducted by the Morgan Research Centre, 77 per cent of those questioned said sponsorship should be allowed to continue. An overwhelming majority (96 per cent) of non-smokers said it was unlikely that tobacco-company sponsorship would make them take up smoking. Should my company, or more correctly the television channels, have consistently ignored the broadcasting ban on cigarette advertising, as alleged by your correspondent, he may be assured that the due processes of the law would have applied. Regarding the claimed kicking of "the company's proposed advertising package off the ground" in Glasgow, your correspondent may be interested to know that four signs were booked from Australia through the Hampden Park contractor, Arena Sports Advertising. The intended message was 'Winfield Socceroos' with the flag. This was refused by the Scottish football authorities. As the authorities permitted a veritable slather of liquor advertising around the pitch and in the program and even a cigarette advertisement, not my company's, in the program, we can only conclude that their real concern was to ensure that nothing was allowed which might help motivate or encourage our team, playing so far away from home in front of one of the world's most partisan crowds. In spite of the difficulties and a mere handful of spiteful criticisms, such as that of your correspondent, my company was proud to be of assistance to a courageous and skilful outfit of Australian ambassadors. A. A. WOOD Rothmans of Pall Mall Sydney.

16 Apr 1987 - Unsworth approval rating continues to increase Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 16 April 1987, page 9 Unsworth approval rating continues to increase SYDNEY: The popularity of the NSW Premier, Mr Unsworth, continues to increase, leaping 34 percentage points since August last year, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The March poll, published in this week's Bulletin magazine, also showed his Labor Government would have been returned to power if an election had been held last month. Mr Unsworth's approval rating of 60 per cent is his biggest ever, a jump of 6 points since a February poll, and a huge increase over his August record low of 26 per cent.

23 Apr 1987 - IN BRIEF Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 23 April 1987, page 8 IN BRIEF Death of doctor due at tribunal SYDNEY: Police are waiting for post-mortem examination reports before deciding whether to hold an inquest into the death of a doctor who was due to appear before the Medical Disciplinary Tribunal in Sydney yesterday. Dr Peter John Donnelly, 28, who practiced at Nimbin, northern NSW, was charged with professional misconduct after he was convicted of 26 drug offences. He appeared before.the tribunal on February 18 and the hearing had been adjourned to yesterday. Police said Dr Donnelly had been found dead at his surgery at the Nimbin Health Centre on March 6. Bannon most popular ADELAIDE: The Premier of South Australian, Mr Bannon, has retained the title of Australia's most popular political leader, according to a poll published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday. Nearly 1000 people were covered in the poll by Morgan Gallup and 71 per cent approved of the way Mr Bannon was handling his job. For Greek Catholics The Pope has established the diocese of St Michael of Sydney for the Greek Catholic Melkites in Australia, and has appointed the Reverend Georges Riashi, presently the parish priest of Our Lady of Redemption in the Archdiocese of Detroit, as the first bishop, the Apostolic Pro-Nuncio, Archbishop Franco Brambilla, said yesterday. Bad news for media SYDNEY: The majority of Australians think news organisations invade people's privacy, a poll in The Bulletin magazine said yesterday. The Morgan Gallup survey of 1217 men and women also found many people, six in 10, believed the media concentrated on bad news and seven in 10 believed the media invaded people's privacy. Rebate cut opposed MELBOURNE: Proposals to cut the Medicare rebate were opposed yesterday by the Combined Pensioners' Association, the Doctors' Reform Society and the Doctors for a Free Rebate Group.

29 Apr 1987 - COMMENT Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 29 April 1987, page 1 No real choice at all - Mr .Howard's decision to reject yesterday's coalition agreement proposed by the National Party was, if not made without some agony, one in which he really had little choice. For one of the side results of last week's reshuffle of the Opposition's front bench is that for Mr Howard, there can be little room for compromise. He is being pressured on one side by the "wets" in the party, and on the other by Sir Joh Bjelke-Petersen. While Mr Howard has had a good few weeks and the way in which he changed the Opposition front bench has been generally well received, his grip on the leadership is still not as firm as he would like. Today, yet another opinion poll will come out which shows that Mr Peacock, one of the men he consigned to the back bench, is still more popular than he is. The Morgan Gallup Poll, in today's Bulletin magazine, shows that 59 per cent of those surveyed think that Mr Peacock would be a good Prime Minister, while only 33 per cent thought similarly of Mr Howard. While Mr Peacock's supporters within the Liberal Party will point to the poll as evidence of the electoral appeal of their man, Mr Howard's action in refusing to be dictated to by • the National Party will counter-bal ance this. But there is more bad news for the Opposition generally in today's polls — they show that the Government has now slipped ahead of them in approval ratings, and now has an approval rating of 47 per cent, compared to 46 per cent for the Opposi tion. - ANDREW FRASER

06 Jul 1994 - COMMENT Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 6 July 1994, page 1 mmmammm Peter Cole-Adams . Dangerous issue for Downer From the moment he won the Liberal leadership, Alexander Downer has behaved like a man convinced that Paul Keating's passionate republicanism could be turned into a political plus for the Coalition. Now he is learning that the issue is as dangerous for him as for Keating, potentially more so. Continued on Page 2. The republic becomes a dangerous issue for Downer Continued from Page 1. The matter of the noisily monarchist Tony Abbott and the so-called secret republican cell within the party — surely, when /conservatives get conspiratorial, they form cabals — is not important in itself, but as a symptom of a division that goes much deeper and wider. And this probably explains why yesterday we saw a new Downer line — one borrowed from John Hewson. For a month now, the Liberal Leader has been explaining his op position to a republic largely in terms of the immensely complex rewriting of the Constitution that he insists such a change would in-, volve, and suggesting that the nation faces such pressing problems that it should not even be thinking about such a distraction now. An easy line, but unconvincing. Since when was running away from difficult challenges a political virtue? Yesterday Downer twice called on Keating to put up specific proposals. "He says we are fogeys for defending the existing Constitu tion, but he is completely gutless because he won't come forward and tell Australians what changes he wants to make." The intention seems clear enough: get the heat back on Keating. A Cabinet committee has been discussing the Turnbull report for months and apparently does not plan to come down with any recommendations till late this year. When the Government does eventually endorse a specific proposal, the Opposition will be able to oppose that proposal, rather than the principle. Broadly, Liberals are divided into three groups: committed monarchists, among whom older Australians are disproportionely represented; those who feel a republic is probably inevitable, but who don't want Keating to get the credit; and republicans, including some powerful figures in NSW (notably Premier John Fahey) and many Young Lib erals. Downer's problem is that while the first two groups almost certainly comprise a large majority of party members — and of his shadow cabinet;— they are a minority of the electorate. The latest Saulwick poll, in The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age, showed that support for some sort of republic was down four points from February, to 59 per cent, but that support for the monarchy was still only 35 per cent. Prince Charles's latest confessions seem unlikely to help. No wonder Downer wants Keating to give him a clear target to shoot at; no wonder Keating is in no hurry to oblige.

11 Jul 1994 - Economy on way up: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 11 July 1994, page 3 Economy on way up: poll Australians remain generally confident about their economic future, the latest Morgan poll to be published in this week's Time Australia magazine has found. The poll of 1206 people found the Morgan confidence rating down only 0.4 per cent in early July compared with the all-time high in June. The number of people predicting good times ahead dipped from 50 per cent in June to 47 per cent in July, while those expecting bad times increased four points to 17 per cent. Over the next five years, 41 per cent of respondents said they expected good times while only 14 per cent expected the economy to worsen. On personal finances, 34 per cent of respondents (up two points) believed they were better off now than a year ago while 27 per cent (down two points) believed they were worse off. Over the next year, 35 per cent said they expected to be better off and 10 per cent said they expected to be worse off. — AAP

11 Jul 1994 - 75pc for fresh air dining Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 11 July 1994, page 2 75pc for fresh air dining ! SYDNEY: Three out of four Australians want restaurants to be smoke-free but more than 60 per cent of people also believe tobacco companies should be allowed to sponsor sport. A Saulwick poll, published in Saturday's editions of The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, showed 75 per cent of those surveyed said smoking should not be allowed in restaurants, while 22 per cent said it should. Three per cent were undecided. But asked whether they believed smoking should be allowed in bars and clubs, 50 per cent replied "yes" with 46 per cent saying "no." Four per cent had no opin ion. On the question of whether cigarette companies should sponsor sport, 62 per cent said "yes," 34 per cent said "no," with 5 per cent unsure. Federal Health Minister Carmen Lawrence has signalled her intention to tighten the Tobacco Advertising Prohibition Act (1992) to ensure there are no exemptions for sporting events. Presently some international events are excluded, such as the Australian Formula One Grand Prix. But poll researchers said Dr Lawrence might need to reassess those intentions as six out of 10 Australians want to see tobacco companies continue to sponsor sport and give financial help to clubs. The survey interviewed 1027 people nation-wide on June 28. And of interest to Opposition Health spokeswoman Bronwyn Bishop will be the results that 70.9 per cent of Coalition voters backed continued sponsorship of sporting teams by cigarette companies, compared with 53.4 per cent among Labor. The finding suggests Mrs Bishop is reflecting the views of Conservative party voters when she said in late May that if a product was legal, then it should be able to be advertised. Figures were rounded to the nearest whole number.

02 Apr 1986 - Poll shows Australians pessimistic Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 2 April 1986, page 10 Poll shows Australians pessimistic MELBOURNE: Most people believe Australia's inflation and unemployment rates will rise, according to a Gallup Poll. Of 2,131 people surveyed across Australia, 70 per cent said they believed inflation would increase over the next few months. The forecast, published in yesterday's Melbourne Herald, showed 63 per ccnt of those surveyed expected the unemployment rate to increase, while 55 per cent thought interest rales would rise even further, at least in the short term. Women were more prone than men to forecast an increase in the inflation rate. Seventy-six per ccnt of people living in the country areas and 67 per ccnt of city dwellers thought the inflation rate would increase. More people living in Tasmania, Queensland, and the Northern Territory forecast an increase in unemployment. Canberra was the only place in which most of those interviewed predicted a cut in the unemployment rate. One in three people thought interest rates would begin to drop over the next few months. However,- more than half feared interest rates would rise even further.

08 Apr 1986 - Lindy poll finds nation 'divided' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 8 April 1986, page 11 Lindy poll finds nation 'divided' MELBOURNE: The latest Gallup poll has found that Australians are divided over Mrs Lindy Chamberlain's release from jail. Forty-six per cent of respondents said she had been in jail long enough, while 41 per cent disagreed and 13 per cent were uncertain or did not reply. Mrs Chamberlain was released by the Northern Territory Government after the discovery of a baby's matinee jacket and criticism of forensic evidence. More than 2,000 people in Australia were asked: "Even if a judicial inquiry confirmed the previous findings, do you think Lindy Chamberlain has spent enough time in prison?" Fifty-three per cent of women and 40 per cent of men felt that she had been in jail long enough. People in the Northern Territory and South Australia were more likely to think she had spent enough time in prison, the poll found.

10 Apr 1986 - Interest-rates question backfires Another leak hurts Howard Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 10 April 1986, page 1 Interest-rates question backfires Another leak hurts Howard By PAUL MALONE, Political Correspondent The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, had the rug pulled from under him yesterday when attempting to pin the Government down on the question of interest rates. Mr Howard asked the Prime Minister, Mr Hawkc, how long the Government's promise of a fall in interest rates would last before it was broken. Mr Hawke replied by quoting another leaked Opposition document circulated by Mr Howard to all his Coalition colleagues in which it was stated that the outlook for interest rates was for further falls. The leak came on top three bad polls for Mr Howard published yesterday morning. The Irving Saulwick poll published in The Sydney Morning Herald found that more Liberal voters approved of the way Mr Hawke was doing his job than approved of Mr Howard. The Newspoll published in The Australian found that more people would like to sec Mr Andrew Peacock as leader of the Liberal Party than Mr Howard. The Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin found that 53 per cent of voters disapproved of the way Mr Howard was doing his job, the worst figure he has recorded. The polls were conducted after Mr Howard received much adverse publicity from the leak of an internal Liberal Party hit list of businessmen who had to be neutralised to ensure that the Opposition's policy on industrial relations was favourably received. Mr Hawkc did not quote the latest internal, Liberal Party document in full on the question of interest rates. The paper, prepared in Mr Howard's office, says the Government has chosen to allow interest rates to drift down slightly, but not significantly. The stance reflected the stated intention of the Government to shift the burden of policy away from mon etary policy and more towards fiscal policy. The Government was now dearly concerncd as to whether the high interest rates it had crcatcd had overdone the slowing in domestic demand intended, the paper said. "The outlook for interest rates is therefore for further falls," it said. "However, how far they fall will depend on the resilience of the $A, the performance of the current account deficit and further evidence on the slowing of domestic demand'". It was recommended that the Opposition continue to highlight that, notwithstanding the recent falls, interest rates still remained high, interest rates in overseas countries had fallen considerably, the over reliance on monetary policy continued placing the recovery at risk and interest rates could be significantly lower if the Government adjusted both its wages and fiscal policies.

11 Apr 1986 - Drug-campaign director says it may not work Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 11 April 1986, page 1 Drug-campaign director says it may not work By DEBBIE CAMERON The Government's $100 million anti-drugs campaign launched last week by the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, may not work, according to a key campaign organiser. The director of the National Cam paign Against Drug Abuse, Mr Mike Delaney, yesterday said that he did not know whether the three-year campaign would succeed. But he did not know what else to try. "The best advice I've had from anybody involved with this whole drugs field is that there are no right ways or wrong ways, any way that works is OK," he said. He denies running a campaign to flatter Federal and State Govern ments. "For most Governments it would* be safer altogether not to have a campaign like this because it is actually politically risky.'... we can't be sure it's going to work. We can't be sure." He says that except for the launch, politicians will be nearly invisible. Within the next month, the AttorneyGeneral, Mr Bowen, and the Spccial Minister of State, Mr Young, arc expected to prepare the way for police phone-taps. And, apart from State health ministers, politicians will play no further role. Less than a week into the campaign, Mr Delaney already has his detractors. Hardened anti-drugs campaigners such as the Reverend Ted Noffs of the Kings Cross Wayside Chapel arc critical of the campaign and so are drug-dependence counsellors in State and regional health networks. "I didn't expcct everyone in Australia to stand up and clap," Mr Delaney said. There has even been criticism from visiting rock star Sting, who said that if the Prime Minister said something like taking drugs was not "hip" then it was. • Sting has Mr Delaney to answer to. Mr Delaney wants to meet him about, his comments... "The Prime Minister wasn't negative in the way Sting thought becausc [Mr Hawke] has had the same problem himself." "It is a real middle-Australia problem and people are just terrified." Mr Delancy says that he has still not finalised a way to measure the success of the campaign. "We arc going to market testings, researching and monitoring right throughout this campaign we cxpcct to buy one-ofT questions on the tail-end of Morgan Gallup Polls or ANOP's about drug abuse or drug use." He said that the campaign would commission its own services about once a year to see whether the campaign had changed perceptions about drugs, whether drug-use figures change. ".. .and if it doesn't w<jrk we'll have to go off and have another go some other way." It might take "ages" for the campaign to Work, Mr Pelaney said. Antismoking campaigns were only now beginning, to be effective after 12 years. .

13 Feb 1986 - Support for Government steady, poll shows Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 13 February 1986, page 10 Support for Government steady, poll shows The ALP would have won easily in a Federal election and in a Victorian State election if they had been held last month, but less easily in NSW, according to the latest Morgan Gallup polls. The polls, published in yesterday's Bulletin, showed support for the Labor Federal Government remained steady at its highest level since it won the December, 1984, election. Of almost 3,000 voters polled, 50 per cent supported the Government and 42 per cent preferred the coalition. The Labor result was un changed from the previous poll last month. Support for the Liberals went down one point and for the Australian Demo crats went up one point to 6 per cent. Personal support for the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, went down one point to 61 per cent, and for the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, rose one point to 34 per cent. But 66 per cent (down two points) said they preferred Mr Hawke as Prime Minister and only 19 per ccnt (down one point) preferred Mr Howard for the job. In the Victoria poll, 51 per ccnt said they would have voted Labor, 36 per ccnt Liberal and 5 per cent National Party. Support for the NSW Labor Party fell by two points to 46 per cent, but it would still have won a January election.

27 Feb 1986 - BHP takeover against wish of most Australians Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 27 February 1986, page 11 BHP takeover against wish of most Australians SYDNEY: Most Australians oppose the bid by Mr Robert Holmes a Court to take over BHP and want the Federal Government to intervene, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in the Bulletin magazine. Fifty-eight per cent of people sur' veyed said they would prefer BHP to stay in the hands of its present directors, U per cent .preferred a takeover by Mr Holmes a Court's Bell Resources group, and 31 per . cent could not say. Forty-three per cent of those sur veyed said the Government should legislate to stop partial takeovers, 32 per cent were against, and 25 per cent could not say. Mr Robert Holmes a Court Professional people and managers were most opposed to the takeover, with 73 per ccnt supporting the present BHP board — but 47 per cent opposed any Government action. The poll, which surveyed 1,520 people on the weekend of February 15, also showed that 16 per cent of those surveyed had not heard of tlje takeover bid. Asked if Mr Holmes h Court should be offered , a seat on the board of BHP, 45 per cent of people said yes, 27 per cent said no and 28 per cent were ^undecided. Other information from the latest poll was that support for the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, and his Government has fallen, while the Opposition has become more popular. But the poll showed that Mr Hawke and his party would still have won government if an election had been held at the time of the poll — the weekends of February 8 and 15. It showed that Mr Hawke's approval rating fell '4 per cent to 57 per ccnt, while support for his party had dropped two points to 48 per cent since the previous poll taken on the weekends of January 25 and February 1. The Opposition's popularity rose 4 per cent to 46 per cent, while that of its leader, Mr Howard, slipped by two points to 32 per ccnt. Last November Mr Howard's approval rating had been as high as 44 per ccnt. The poll showed that 60 per ccnt of men (down 3 per cent) approved of the way Mr Hawke was doing his job, compared with 54 per cent of women (down 5 per ccnt). The poll surveyed 2,864 electors. In Melbourne, Mr Howard welcomed yesterday the improved showing by his party in the poll. He said the result was encouraging, but stressed that it was only one poll and that not too much should be made of it.

02 May 1994 - Labor would have won April poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 2 May 1994, page 2 Labor would have won April poll Labor would have narrowly won an April federal election, according to a Morgan poll to be published in the next edition of Time Australia Magazine. The survey, based on interviews with 2269 electors on the weekends of April 16-17 and April 23-24, indicated that support for Labor had increased by two percentage points to 42.5 per cent. Support for the Coalition dropped 1.5 points to 43 per cent. For the first time since June last year, the two-party preferred vote put Labor (50.5 per cent, up 2.5 points) ahead of the Coalition (49.5 per cent, down 2.5 points). The personal approval rating of Prime Minister Paul Keating was unchanged from the previous survey at 42 per cent, however his disapproval rating dropped one point to 48 per cent. Approval for the way John Hewson was handling his job as Opposition Leader fell to 25 per cent and his disapproval rating rose two points to 61 per cent.

02 May 1994 - Letters to the Editor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 2 May 1994, page 12 Letters to the Editor ACF backs public transport YOUR correspondent Ms L. Jensen has raised valid concerns about the position(s) of the con servation movement on urban con solidation and public transport (Letters, April 25). I'cannot speak about the policies of the Conservation Council to which Ms Jensen refers, but I can summarise the position of the Australian Conservation Foundation, which is a different organisation. ACF is a national community-based organisation. Its policies are developed in a democratic manner by its 35 councillors who are elected by its 20,000 members. ACF is a strong supporter of public transport and those forms of urban consolidation which are environmentally sound, socially equitable and aesthetically pleasing. We see a valuable role for urban village development, especially in the town centres. With increased residential population densities in the town centres, a light rail system joining the centres could be economically viable. In the future, we could see local public transport services within individual suburbs and feeder services into the town centres provided by a combination of buses on fixed routes and minibuses on flexible routes (which could be booked by phone). It is possible that the whole system could provide a much more frequent and reliable service than the present one at the same or reduced cost. ACF is a catalyst for the National Public Transport Action ■Week, which is being held from May 1 to 7. In Canberra, there will be a public meeting on "The Future of Canberra's Public Transport" on Wednesday, May 4, at 7.30pm at the Bogong Theatre, Gorman House. (Dr) MARK DIESENDORF National Campaign Convener, Energy and Transport, Australian Conservation Foundation Problems with Moscow Circus I'D LIKE TO respond on Animal Liberation ACT's behalf, to an article (CT, April 24, p.4) on the Moscow Circus. We are delighted that, according to your article, Mr Edgley now appears to Abortion is a choice we deserve WHY DO ageing politicians and judges believe they can dictate to upcoming generations that abortion is wrong? I feel that they have no right to tell any woman what she can do with her unborn baby. At age 19, and halfway through completing a higher educational degree, a baby is the last thing I would want. Given my current circumstances, abortion would be my first and foremost option. Under present law, however, I would have to prove that continuing with the pregnancy would be damaging to my mental and/or physical health. Isn't it terribly sad that in today's society I am to be penalised for having a rational mind that sees securing a career and financial stability, perhaps even marriage, as a priority to bringing an unnecessary and unwanted baby into the world? Indeed into a society that already places enormous strains on its limited resources and hands out thousands of dollars each year in welfare to single mothers and "under-privileged" children? Alas, such foresight is only deterred under current laws! I don't believe that abortion clinics will be seen as a form of contraception and a means of encouraging unprotected sex. I doubt that there is little, if any, proof of such a correlation in a world where the risk of contracting a sexually transmitted disease is so high. Such clinics would be available for those of us who are unlucky enough to fall pregnant due to some contraceptive failure or even rape. I am not saying that abortion is right or wrong, but dependent on an individual's upbringing, beliefs, education and lifestyle. It is not fair for one group in society to impose their views upon all. We are not all opposed to abortion, nor are we all ardent Catholics, and for those of us who are not, abortion is another option we should be able to consider should pregnancy arise. The choice to abort should not be influenced by a dictatorial society with archaic values and laws. After all, isn't that what living in a democratic society is all about? JUSTINE WRIGHT Barton be taking a more enlightened stand on animal welfare — no doubt in response to the concerns raised by the animal-welfare movement —. as there have been animal-welfare problems associated with the Moscow Circus in the past, the most recent being on the 1992 tour of New Zealand when the Royal New Zealand SPCA laid 32 charges following a joint inspection with the Ministry of Agriculture, and numerous warnings regarding the inadequate housing of the monkeys, dogs and bears. Regrettably, a technicality concerning inspection warrants caused the case to be dismissed, prompting the authority of an'inspector's warrant to be more clearly defined in future law. . "It is interesting to note that an A. G. B. McNair poll commissioned by Edgley Ventures last May and taken in Townsville, Cairns, Mackay, Rockhampton and Toowoomba to assess community attitudes to circuses, showed that the majority of people do not attend circuses to see animal acts. Whereas 97 per cent of people polled expect to see animals in circuses (ie, they expected it to be the norm), 61 per cent said it would make no difference to their attendance if there were no exotic animals used. In fact a further 9 per cent said they would be more likely to attend if there were no animals. This figure would have undoubtedly been higher were the poll taken in areas where animal welfare has a higher profile. We would encourage Mr Edgley to respond to the changing attitudes in the community by focusing on the excellent human acts for which the Moscow Circus is renowned. SYLVIA COOPER President, Animal Liberation ACT Airport in a minefield THE DITCHING of a DC-3 aircraft into Botany Bay on Sunday, April 24, highlights not only the unsatisfactory single-engine climb performance of these aircraft but also the stupidity of expanding aircraft operations at Sydney Airport. - If the aircraft had crashed into an oil installation or storage facility the crash would no longer be described as an accident but a disaster of catastrophic proportions. Sydney Airport is located virtually in the centre of a chemical minefield and the sooner aircraft operations are scaled down and transferred to Badgerys Creek the sooner passengers will be protected by a relatively safe operating' environment. IAN CAMERON Former president, Airpilots Guild of Australia Sylvania, NSW Hard-working doctors I RECENTLY read Ian Warden's "Reflections" on doctors who work in emergency departments who face up to "hard, hands-on work". That sounds like good news for patients. On reflection, it seems to me there are some people in life who do the "hard, hands-on work" and some who pompously judge them from behind their security blankets. SHEELAGH SNEDDEN Hughes Insult to those who died WHILE I am relieved that everyone survived the DC-3 ditching in Botany Bay, and rather sad that a classic old aeroplane ended up like that, I'm quite amazed to learn that they were going to join in Anzac Day commemorations on Norfolk Island. In 1992 Norfolk Islanders opted out of being fair-dinkum Aussies and became citizens of convenience. They refuse their civic duties to vote or pay taxes but cling to all the advantages of being nominal Australians. In those circumstances any Anzac ceremony on the island must surely be an insult to the sacrifices of those who died for our ideals of democracy, duty and doing the right thing by your mates. DAVID H.
