11 May 1994 - Opposition reduces gap Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 11 May 1994, page 2 Opposition reduces gap The federal Coalition has narrowed 'the gap on the Government to just two points in the latest Bulletin-AGB McNair poll. The poll, to be published in this week's edition of The Bulletin, shows the Government with 43 per cent, down two points, and the Opposition 41 per cent, up one. Prime Minister Paul Keating's approval rating remained steady on 33 per cent. Dr Hewson's performance rating was up one point from 20 per cent to 21 per cent.

26 May 1994 - Downer told to drop all-male mates Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 May 1994, page 1 Downer told to drop all-male mates By JODIE BROUGH Prime Minister Paul Keating challenged Opposition Leader Alexander Downer yesterday to resign from the exclusive Adelaide Club, saying it was inappropriate for him to belong to a club which excludes women from membership. But the woman closest to Mr Downer, his wife, Nicky, rejected Mr Heating's comments as inappropriate, dismissing any suggestion of sexism. Mr Keating told ABC TV's 7.30 Report that the Melbourne and Adelaide Clabs were symbolic of "entrenched privilege and prejudice". He said Mr Downer should have resigned "between now and when he stands up to lead a major party in the Parliament next week" rather than be a member of a club which excluded "half the population". "He should resign ... on the basis that in 1994, not 1894, no leader of a party that wants to be Prime Minister of this country should be a member of a club that will not have women as members,'' he said. Mrs Downer said she was "not at all" offended by her husband's membership of the club, scoffing at the idea. "I wouldn't have thought it was appropriate for Mr Keating to be telling anybody what to do," she said. "I thought we lived in a free society ... I don't think Alexander would tell him what he could belong to." Mr Downer was not available for comment last night. Mr Keating launched a broadside at his social views, saying he had "a great question mark hanging over multiculturalism and immigration. This is a leader who would take his party back to the policies of Malcolm Fraser and that is basically back to the kind of society and the kind of attitudes which just about broke us." Mr Keating scoffed at a Saulwick Poll which gave the Coalition a 20-point lead over the Government: "If you believe in that you'll believe in anything."

26 May 1994 - Hewson's softer role Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 May 1994, page 1 Hewson's softer role By KEITH SCOTT Former Opposition Leader John Hewson has said he may want a non-economic portfolio in the Coalition's new shadow ministry rather than a finance job of lesser status than shadow treasurer, which will go to deputy leader Peter Costello. The new trimmed-down shadow ministry will be announced by Opposition Leader Alexander Downer today. Mr Downer and National Party Leader Tim Fischer agreed yesterday that the Nationals would lose only one front-bench position. Continued on Page 2 Hewson's softer role Continued from Page 1 The eliminated position would possibly be that of shadow special minister of state, Ian Sinclair, in the reshuffle. The shadow cabinet will be cut to about 30 from the present 37. Mr Downer and Dr Hewson spoke yesterday afternoon about a possible position for Dr Hewson, but it appears Dr Hewson might be unwilling to take on an economic portfolio. He said on Sydney radio that he did not know what "commitments" Mr Downer had made to others, but "something broadly based would be good". "I mean, I have spent a lot of time in economic areas, maybe , a non-economic portfolio — the arts and communications or tourism," he said. "I have not decided." "We have always had a tradition where the Deputy Leader picks their portfolio and I have no doubt that Peter Costello has picked Treasury." Mr Costello confirmed yesterday that he would be shadow treasurer, saying speculation that he would take over that position was "soundly based". Mr Downer refused to comment on a Saulwick poll published in The Sydney Morning Herald yesterday which put him 9 percentage points ahead of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating. The poll also put the Coalition 19 percentage points ahead of the Government. In contrast, an AGB McNair poll published in The Bulletin, taken in the lead-up to the Liberal leadership ballot, put the Government ahead by 4 percentage points. Also yesterday, Dr Hewson continued to express concern that the Liberal Party should not be dominated by Victoria — a reference to senior Victorian Liberals who backed Mr Downer in the leadership — and said he was disappointed by Opposition defence spokesman and his one-time deputy, Peter Reith who, in part, precipitated the lead- i ership spill. "This might be a failing in politics again, but I thought Peter Reith was a real friend of mine," he said. "I had put a lot of time into Peter and his career... essentially built him in the political game. That is not to say he was not well known, but we built his reputation in the economic area in particular ... I hope that we can re-establish a friendship."

30 May 1994 - Consumer confidence on a high Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 30 May 1994, page 1 Consumer confidence on a high Consumer confidence is at its highest point in the past 20 years, according to a poll to be published in this week's Time magazine. The Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence Rating for April was 127.7 points, two points higher than last month's rating and the highest since the survey began in March, 1973. The poll showed 49 per cent believed there would be good times for the economy over the next year, while only 17 per cent thought there would be bad times. Over the next five years, 46 per cent expected good times and 12 per cent expected the economic cli mate to worsen. But the survey showed people were less optimistic about their per sonal finances. When asked to consider their fi nancial situation now compared with a year ago, 31 per cent said they were better off, and 32 per cent, up 3 per cent, said they were worse ott. — AAP |

01 Aug 1994 - Party outdated: Hewson Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 1 August 1994, page 1 Party outdated: Hewson Former Opposition Leader John Hewson strongly attacked the Lib-eral organisation yesterday, declar-ing it outdated, and sounded a fur-ther warning about the need for the party to say "very clearly" what it stood for. Dr Hewson described the party's organisational structure as out of the 1940s and in need of a strong federal executive. Speaking out provocatively for the second time within days, Dr Hewson said the party had failed to beat Labor in a state or federal election in the 1970s and 1980s un-less the Labor government had been involved in some scandal. He told the Nine Network's Sunday program that the party structure was "a very loose confed-eration of independent state ad-ministrations that are focused prin-cipally on state politics". "We need an effective national campaigning force which obviously goes to everything from the ads, which were clearly wrong last time, through the election strategy, through our capacity to match the union movement on the ground." On Friday Dr Hewson said Lib-erals must have sufficiently detailed policies to be able, in office, to claim a mandate to convince the Senate to pass their program. Opposition Leader Alexander Downer repeated yesterday that he would issue "detailed" policies "at a time of our choosing". "We need a mandate to govern and policies will give us that man-date," he said. "No political party should go to an election without detailed policies and I have said since my election as leader, Aus-tralians would get them." However Dr Hewson's comments are likely to needle Mr Downer, who is concerned that Dr Hewson — still bitter at losing the leader-ship — should not undermine Op-position unity. Continued on Page 3 Liberal Party organisation outdated: Hewson Continued from Page 1 In a wide-ranging interview, Dr Hewson: Conceded that the republic could become an election issue and argued the party needed to participate con-structively in the debate without being tagged as "old fogies or young fogies". Repudiated monarchist MP Tony Abbott's suggestion that a NSW State Council resolution reaffirming support for the existing constitution was a gag on further debate. Favoured broad constitutional re-form to Commonwealth-state relations after "93 years of a federation that just plain doesn't work". Accused his colleagues of reacting like "headless chooks" to the 1993 election defeat and seeking to drop substantive policy in favour of looking "warm and fuzzy [to] try and get across the line". His comments came as the latest Bulletin AGB McNair poll showed the margin between the ALP and the Co-alition narrowing. The ALP's support rose one point to 41 per cent; the Co-alition fell three points to 45 per cent. Mr Downer's lead over the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, as preferred prime minister also slipped, down one point to 41 per cent. Mr Keating gained three points to 36 per cent. In mid-July, Mr Downer had a nine point lead over Mr Keating. But the Time Morgan poll showed Mr Downer consolidating his lead as preferred prime minister, up two points to 49 per cent, while Mr Keating was unchanged on 40 per cent. Coalition support rose one point to 47.5 per cent while the ALP dropped two points to 39 per cent. Dr Hewson said he was not sur- prised at the Bulletin result as a new leader was "going to get profile and it's going to be reflected in the polls". "But as time goes on, the question becomes can you sustain that? And of course you do less media, you are less the focus of attention, and the num-bers come back," he said. "I'm sure Alexander's not worried about that." Dr Hewson's comments will be monitored closely by the Downer camp, where there have been mutter-ings in recent weeks that Dr Hewson has come close to speaking out of turn on the republic and policy in general. Dr Hewson said the attempts to avoid serious policy formulation were doomed to failure because Fightback's legacy was that the level of political debate in Australia had been raised. "I think now, particularly in the af-termath of Fightback, we are going to have to be prepared to say what we stand for very clearly ... so that peo-ple say 'yes, we want those people to replace the Labor Party because they will do these things'," he said. Meanwhile, the NSW Liberal Party's state director, Barry O'Farrell, repudi-ated as "completely false" suggestions that a resolution of the NSW state council on Saturday had effectively gagged debate on the republic. He said while council had reaffirm-ed support for the existing constitu-tion, it had also stated Liberals would be "fully involved in the debate". The party's federal director, Andrew Robb, was not available for comment.

04 Aug 1994 - A few downers for Alexander Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 4 August 1994, page 11 A few downers for Alexander WO MONTHS ago the fledgling alternative prime minJL ister, Alexander Downer, didn't have the look of a man who' could come a cropper on a matter 'as arcane as citizen-initiated referendums. 1 The orthodoxy among the influ; ential members of the Parliamentary Press Gallery in the weeks af ter Downer was elected was that. ,at last the Libs had a leader with • political instincts. ' '1 . 1 Not a good track rfecord on substance and pretty week on policy; traits belatedly recognised as John Hewson positives. Nevertheless a hard political nose, perhaps even canny, and a coalition of backers who were showing signs of doing anything — anything — to end the run of losses. The honeymoon was, by normal political post-nuptial measures, an unusually languid one. The polls showed week after week that Downer was looking just the ticket for the embattled Opposition. But citizen-initiatcd referendums, Aboriginal land rights and the republican issue — and a dis'tinct lack of discipline among his new front bench — linvi* millprl the silk sheet from under Downer. "He should have sensed the sudden shift in sentiment, even before this week's revelation in The Can-; berra Times of his remarkable, backflip on the citizen-initiated referendum issue. Over recent weeks, each, of the political commentators of weight have begun the process of questioning the new leader's credentials. Ten days ago, Geoff Kitney in The Sydney Morning Herald was the first to become impatient at the apparent lack of progress on Downer's promised "direc tions" statement. Downer had undertaken to out line his major philosophical preoc"'" mipations in the manoeuvring around the time of the Liberal leadership fight in May. Ten • weeks later only the most vacuous of statements had emerged. More to come, promised Downer's office. Other commentators wrote variations on the theme. Tom Burton in Tlii' Australian Financial Review warned of Paul Keating's formidable political skills and won dered aloud whether Downer's camp was underestimating the potential danger from such a common street-fighter as the Prime Minister. The political new boy was starting to get a little of the niggling sort of media coverage that is stock-in-trade for leaders of major parties, the sort that saps confidence of even the most hardened politicians. Into the gathering scrum stepped the battle-scarred veteran columnist Alan Ramsay who writes a tart, sometimes vitriolic, always idiosyncratic weekly piece in The Sydney Morning Herald. Ramsey loosed an uppercut and connected right on the point of Downer's blue-shaven jaw. It was all very well, wrote Ramsay, for Downer to rail and thunder about a Government now in its 12th t year led by a Prime Minister people would willingly throttle if only they could be convinced of a bet ter alternative. "It's something else to come up with ideas both contemporary and creative that are seen to have substance and viability, however, arguable the specifics, which give people something to vote for, not merely against, as well as something to believe in. That's always the hard part," he wrote. RAMSAY'S piece appeared two days before polling undertak en by Irving Saulwick was published in The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. The polling confirmed that the sudden souring of attitude, among the Press Gallery was reflected in a significant weakening in public support for the new Coalition leader as the "fresh-look" began to wear off. The Saulwick poll showed Downer's popularity rating had dipped for the first time since becoming leader, from ? high of 54 per cent to 49 per cent as preferred Prime Minister. Keating, who has become used to some savaging at the hands of poll interviewees, received a minor reassurance with a lift from 31 to 36 per cent approval. As Mr Saulwick said yesterday, "The media were pretty prescient on this: they picked up [the mood change] over Downer's first fumbles. Now they'ie running at him... it's no longer kid gloves." The poll, published on Monday, is in fact available to the inner circles on the papers from about mid-morning on Friday. It is undertaken during the previous week. So the inevitable turning of the high popularity tide was drawn from the period of the Downer honeymoon, with none of the present problems relating to referendums, Mabo or the republic being reflected. Without Parliament sitting, the Prime Minister has not had available his usual forum for forensic dismemberment. Aside from acting prime-ministerial, Keating has been circling his new opponent looking for strategic weaknesses, trying an occasional goad ("flaky policies" and "policy free zone" have been favourites), and biding his time. Republicanism, while ostensibly a dangerous play by Keating, was always going to be an area of difficulty and confusion for the Coalition. It was thus remarkable that Downer's first serious foray into the republican spider-web was so heavy-handed. In the midst of all the static at the end of the day, it was virtually impossible to determine the position he actually adopted. He succeeded not only in dismaying his far-right flank of constitutional monarchists with some bizarre comments about the irrelevancy of the Queen to the constitutional debate. but also alienated the moderates in his party over his apparent anti-republican stance. Not bad for a day's work and offthe-cuff remarks to keep the Liberals within the mainstream of the unfolding debate about Austra lia's national identity. By last weekend, the strident ultra-monarchists such as newly elected NSW Liberal MP Tony Abbott had seized on the opportunity to regain lost ground on the republican issue. The Downer intervention, coming on top of a concerted push by influential sections of the NSW Liberal Party to stem the republican tide have only widened the deep divisions within conservative ranks. IT HAS flushed out the most se nior Liberal politician in the land, NSW Premier John Fahey, to distance himself again from the anti-republicans. At the same time, an obviously irritated Fahey has found himself being forced to go public in virtual open criticism of Downer on yet another front: Aboriginal land rights and the Government's Mabo legislation. Fahey is no Liberal "wet" but his instincts derive from the practical application of power and the daily encounters with the concerns of the middle-class suburban Liberal heartlands in Australia's largest city. He may argue that the Government's Mabo legislation needs amendment, but he is definitely not about to turn the clock back and campaign to have the legislation repealed. Yet on a visit to Western Australia on the weekend, that is precisely what Downer was suggesting he would consider if and when he became Prime Minister. His comments led to a predictable barrage of shock and horror from Aboriginal leaders throughout Australia. But just as noisy was the National Farmers' Federation which had laboured long and hard to shape the final outcome of the Mabo legislation and had, painfully, come to terms with the final compromise. Now here was their supposed political ally lining up with the rednecks and the Premiers of Western and South Australia. The NFF's Rick Farley joined Fahey in trying to kill off such nonsense, leaving Downer looking silly and remote from the direction of the debate. On top of his woes, Downer has been caught out in one of the oldest political traps: taking a strong stance on a matter about which he had conveniently forgotten he had previously taken a contrary position. The oddity here is that the issue — citizen-initiated referendums — was put on the agenda by his new-found mate and political ally in the leadership play earlier this year, Peter Reith. Reith went public in The Australian newspaper last week in an attempt to get some momentum into the issue, one which had no legs at all until his move. Downer's Coalition leadership partner Tim Fischer tried to knock the idea on the head at birth, but only stimulated interest in the matter. With the media intrigued, it was only a matter of time and some good honest journalism before Downer's volte face on the issue was unearthed. Downer is going to start needing all the friends he can muster if he keeps giving free kicks to the Prime Minister, but not friends like that. And there is one "friend" who must be very pleased that the Liberal leadership fray turned out the way it did: Downer's deputy, Peter Costello. Until late yesterday Costello was conspicuously silent all week on every one of the issues which has left dung on Downer's boots. As the damage bill rose, Costello was forced to step in to defend his leader, arguing that Downer hadn't said the things he had been reported as saying. It was a careful statement, supporting his leader, but also making it clear that the Coalition would not automatically ditch the Mabo legislation. Costello seems to be making sure he suffers the minimum collateral damage. Wonder why?

15 Aug 1994 - Opposition still on downer: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 15 August 1994, page 3 Opposition still on downer: poll A Morgan opinion poll has reinforced the findings "of a recent Newspoll that the personal popularity of the Leader of the Opposition, Alexander Downer, crashed in the wake of his mishandling of Aboriginal land issues. The Morgan poll, to be published in the next issue of Time Australia magazine, showed that between late July and early August Mr Downer's personal approval rating fell 19 points to 34 per cent. His disapproval rating rose 17 points to 40 per cent. In the same period, the approval rating of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, fell one point to 38 per cent. This meant that instead of being 14 points behind Mr Downer's approval rating, Mr Keating was four points in front. On the measure of preferred Prime Minister, Mr Keating scored 45 per cent compared with Mr Downer's rating of 41 per cent. Support for the coalition fell 3.5 points to 44 per cent, while backing for Labor increased by four points to make it neck and neck with the Opposition.

15 Aug 1994 - Waiting lists can be cut: AMA Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 15 August 1994, page 6 Waiting lists can be cut: AMA By BILL NORMAN, Health Writer The queue of patients waiting for elective surgery could be cleared within a year — without employing, more, surgeons —, according to the Australian Medical Association's director of hospital policy, John O'Dea. Mr O'Dea said hospital waiting lists were caused by under-funding of public hospitals, leading to in. sufficient surgical beds and the> atre time, not . by a shortage of ' specialist surgeons. He. issued the results of a survey of surgeons commissioned by Roy Morgan Research. About 90 per cent of the surgeons in the specialities of orthopedics, ophthalmology, ear-nose-and throat, urology and plastic surgery polled by Roy Morgan, said they had operating sessions cancelled in the past year, affecting an estimated 27,000 patients. At least another 13,000 patients were estimated to be "bumped" from their scheduled operations because surgeons' sessions were shortened. The problem of hospital waiting lists is the most serious concern of most Australians, ahead of crime and education, according to one recent survey. Writing yesterday in Australian Medicine, Mr O'Dea estimated that 40,000 of the 64,000 people now waiting for surgery in these specialties could be treated if governments provided more beds and theatre time. "Nearly half the surgeons surveyed indicted a willingness to undertake more sessions," Mr O'Dea said. "The extra sessions that surgeons have indicated they would be prepared to undertake would clear waiting lists.Within.a year." The surgeons also complained that their existing theatre time was used inefficiently, with poor organisation, fixed finishing times, staff shortages and patients not turning up. . The results of the survey; paid for by the AM A and the Australian Doctors' Fund, will be sent to Professor Peter Baume, who the Federal Government has asked to report on the surgical workforce. When announcing the Baume inquiry 10 weeks ago, Health Minister Carmen Lawrence strongly hinted that she believed a shortage of specialists was the root cause of hospital queues. Dr Lawrence said the Baume review was "a particular priority" in view of "widely held concerns about excessive waiting lists in public hospitals ... access to specialists ... has to be assured."

19 Oct 1986 - Victoria's finest, honest and 'ordinary' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 19 October 1986, page 12 Victoria's finest, honest and 'ordinary' THE PEOPLE'S FORCE: A History of ihe Victoria Police. By Robert Haldane. Melbourne University Press. 372pp. $27.50. Reviewer: JOHN GRAHAM. 6 A PARCEL of big ugly fatxTl neckcd wombat-headed big bellied magpic-Icggcd narrowhipped splay-footed sons of Irish bailiffs or English landlords which is better known as Officers of Justice or Victorian Police." So Ned Kelly described his adversaries the year before he was captured at Glenrowan. It is a tribute to the research of Robert Haldane that Kelly's outburst can be justified in at least one particular - the Victoria Police Force in 1870 was 82 per cent Irish. Haldane, an inspector with the force, has written its history with the blessing of its Chief Commissioner and earned a PhD from Latrobe University in the process. It is a remarkable account, not only for detail but for its theme that the police should be the servants of the community and not its masters. Haldane takes us from the very beginnings of the force in 1836, when the untrained constables supplemented their meagre and often unpaid salaries through pocketing half the fines imposed on those they arrested, through the Eureka Stockade, the hunt for Ned Kelly, John Wren's totalisator empire, the police strike of 1923, the Thomas Blarney and Bertram Wainer affairs, the Vietnam demonstrations of the '60s and early '70s to the present. What emerges is a body which is conservative, sometimes reactionary, and always lagging behind its community. It has been badly paid for more than a century, with constables still earning 21 per cent below the average weekly wage in 1970, and overworked by Australian standards. Promotion is traditionally by seniority rather than merit, and the number of university graduates is still 1.25 per cent of the force. Haldane sees this conservatism as, at least in one respect, a virtue. It means, he says, that the police do what they are told within the limits of public acceptability. When those limits are breached, as they were in 1923, the public quickly realises what life is like without the police. Goaded by low pay, a seven-day working week, barracks "unfit for human habitation" and an insensitive Chief Commissioner, more than one third of the force went on strike on the week of the 1923 Melbourne Cup. Two were killed and hundreds injured in the riots that followed, and order was only restored by a volunteer con stabulary force under Sir John Monash. Haldane shows, too, that police can be goaded by the equally damaging effects of their own ignorance and rigidity on public issues. They responded to the protests of the 1960s with their traditional legalism. It was not until 1971, when a senior officer who had studied police response to confrontation in Northern Ireland was given responsibility for the situation in Victoria, that the right to demonstrate was accepted and the avoidance of violence made a primary aim of police strategy. But they can react to social change. The officer who made those recommendations, S. I. Miller, is now the Chief Commissioner and the architect of a number of reforms aimed at increasing communication between the police and the community. Innovations by Chief Commissioners who have risen through the ranks have been the exception. Haldane makes clear his preference for the appointment of outsiders to the position on a regular basis. He characterises the historic pattern as "a recurring sequence of change in command leading to a spate of reforms followed by a period of relative stagnation and decline." Most of the reforms come, he says, from the outside. Despite its innate conservatism, or perhaps bccause of it, the Vic toria Police Force seems to have the support of the Victorian community. A Morgan Gallup poll recently rated it fourth out of 15 occupational groups for honesty and ethical standards. Haldane puts this down to its "ordinariness". Because policemen and women are largely drawn from the working classes into the lowest strata of the public service, he says, they understand the needs of ordinary people. Nor do they try to dictate what kind of police service there should be. This is a view of the police with which many would disagree. The cynics would ask what the doings of Squizzy Taylor and John Wren and the allegations of Bertram Wainer reveal about the integrity of the Victoria Police. Haldane does not avoid these questions, but does not really answer them except to imply that a little corruption is inevitable in any police forcc. Haldane's view of the police is not, and could not be, a moral one. It is the work of a talented professional who sometimes sees his colleagues as fallible human beings but basically as trustworthy tradesmen doing a difficult and unrewarding job with the mini mum of fuss. It is a pity that this history is confined to Victoria. An interstate comparison of policc-community relations could tell us a lot about regionalism in Australia. A Victorian mounted policeman in bush dress, 1861.

23 Oct 1986 - Differing results in Qld polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 23 October 1986, page 3 Differing results in Qld polls BRISBANE: National Party Queensland president Sir Robert Sparkes conceded yesterday the latest Morgan Gallup Poll showed the Australian Labor Party could win government at the November I state election. But Sir Robert issued the results of another poll taken by his party last week which showed equal support for the NP and the ALP statewide and far greater approval for the NP than the ALP in the country -both results contradictory to the Morgan Gallup Poll. He told a news conference the results indicated the NP would probably hold its seats in Brisbane and edge over into a majority. The Morgan Gallup Poll gave the NP a drop of 7 percentage points in Brisbane to 20 per cent, against a 9 points lift for the ALP to 42 per cent. The Liberals were down 4 points to 27 per cent. In the country the NP was down 10 points to 34, while the ALP was up 10 to 42. Liberal Party state director Mr Gary Neat said the Morgan Gallup Poll, compared with the results of the 1983 election, showed a 21 per cent turnaround in the fortunes of the Liberal Party in Brisbane. This put the party on the path to regain all the seats lost to the NP. Pryor's view. - Page 2

19 Oct 1994 - IN BRIEF Photographer safe and well Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 19 October 1994, page 2 IN BRIEF Photographer safe and well Government sources have con firmed, that Canberra freelance photographer Bill Errington es caped injury during a military skir mish on Bougainville last week. Mr Errington, an army photo grapher during the Vietnam War. entered Bougainville illegally through the Solomon Islands three weeks ago on a freelance assign ment for a New Zealand news paper. The alarm was raised when he did not arrive back in Canberra as scheduled late last week. It was revealed that a European man answering Mr Errington's de scription had been involved in a skirmish between the Bougainville Revolutionary Army and the Pa pua New Guinea Defence Force at 6am last Wednesday. Early reports suggested that Mr Errington could have been shot during the clash. A Department or Foreign Af fairs spokesman yesterday de scribed the Errington affair as a "storm in a tea cup". McDougal resigns The marketing director of the Canberra Tourism Commission. Ian McDougal, announced yester day he would resign on October 2S to take up another tourism indus try appointment. Mr McDougal said he was sad to leave Canberra, "having devel oped a deep affection for the capi tal, its tourism product and its tourism industry over the past two years". Bulletin poll Labor has outpolled the Coali tion in 11 of 12 key policy areas, according to an AGB McNair poll published in this week's Bulletin. magazine. The only area in which the Co alition scored best was economic management with 36 per cent of respondents supporting it com pared with 33 per cent for the Government. Toyota winner Iris Montero, of Charnwood, won the Canberra Times Direct Toyota Camry Draw and received a Toyota Camry CSI valued at $32,081. She was presented with the car by Lachlan Amifield, of The Canberra Times Cannons, and Keith Taske, of Canberra Toyota. Priest jailed SYDNEY: A 55-year-old Catholic priest was sentenced to day to two years in jail for inde cently assaulting two school-aged boys 10 years ago. Father Peter Lewis Comensoli pleaded guilty of two charges of indecently assault ing two boys between 1976 and 1983 while he was a parish priest in the Wollongong area, on the NSW south coast.

24 Oct 1994 - Lib leader given six months to perform Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 24 October 1994, page 3 Lib leader given six months to perform By PAUL CHAMBERLIN Alexander Downer received renewed . warnings yesterday about the tenuous nature of his hold on the leadership of the federal Liberal Party, with party president Tony Staley agreeing he might only have until early in the new year to showcase his skills. A respected former NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, said Mr Downer had only six months to reclaim the middle ground or the party would be left in a political wilderness, while a prominent business leader called into question its ability to explain where it stands. Mr Downer's rating in the polls also remains low, with the AGB McNair Bulletin poll showing his support level has risen only 1 point from the low of 23 per cent recorded earlier in the month. However, when voting intentions were polled, the ratings of the Prime Minister and his Government fell and the Coalition moved up to.be only three points ; behind the Government's 44 per 'cent.', Mr Greiner was reported in The Sunday Telegraph as saying Mr Downer had only six months to reposition the party effectively to attract swinging voters, or the party would face Labor being in power until the next century. Following closely his Menzies Foundation speech .last week which was critical of the party's outlook, he said it would lose the support of a generation of younger voters if it continued to take such a conservative line on Mabo and the republic. Mr Staley said Mr Greiner's view about Mr Downer was one commonly held, but only because the leader was still not well known. "I think what he said is only what the people say," Mr Staley said on Network Nine's Sunday program. "They say 'we don't really know him yet'. "We had high hopes and I think those early high hopes underlined the fact that people have had enough of Keating. "Then [there were] a couple of gaffs, which Alexander admitted, those early mistakes, and he's coming back from that. So, you know, fair enough, as he said, the jury is still out." The president of the Business Council of Australia, Ian Salmon, said there was a need for a better outline of policies and positions from the federal Liberal Party. "There's certainly a need for the Opposition party to regularly state its case and strongly state its case, stick to it, and be seen to be a true alternative government ... they must get their policies completely clear so that we can all understand them and stick to them and pursue them," he said on the Business Sunday program. Mr Staley also outlined the reasons why the party's federal executive should be given expanded powers to intervene in preselections. A motion supporting this will be debated at the 50th anniversary council meeting in Al* bury, beginning on Friday. The powers would only be used in emergencies, like "when you get a candidate who it is suddenly known is a fright, a real worry, in terms of the electorate, where there's some deep scandal, some criminal allegations, matters like that. "And these things, unfortunately, even in the best of families, happen from time to time." As well, "it's fair to sfiy that even without official powers we've done a lot in one or two states around the country in the last year or two, where there have been severe financial difficulties." Mr Staley stressed these powers would not be used to remove MPs causing disunity, such as former Leader John Hewson, who has said he has been approached to form a new party. Although reports circulating yesterday suggested Dr Hewson's preselection was under threat, sources said this was very unlikely. Mr Downer, his deputy Peter Costello, federal director Andrew Robb and other senior Liberals have backed the proposal. However, at least two state branches are opposed. Following the trouble the party had in finding a suitable candidate for the Victorian seat of Kooyong, Mr Staley said party members must ,be pcepared to sacrifice their profitable business careers for the sake of community service. It was "appalling" that greed should determine whether potential MPs became candidates for preselection in the first place, he s^id.

31 Oct 1994 - 45pc believe health services are deteriorating, says survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 31 October 1994, page 3 45pc believe health services are deteriorating, says survey By BILL NORMAN Health Writer Australians believe their health service is getting worse and the queue for elective surgery is their greatest fear, according to a national survey last weekend. The poll of 1020 people nationally found that three times as many people (45 per cent) thought the health system was getting 'worse as thought it was getting better (14 per cent.) Of those surveyed, 36 per cent were concerned about waiting lists, 10 per cent mentioned overworked hospitals and a further 9 per cent complained of lack of facilities or services. The Roy Morgan poll, conducted for the Medical Benefits Fund, found that people disagreed with government policy on health insurance in many areas. Four-fifths of those questioned said the Government should offer tax incentives to encourage people to take out health insurance.' The Government has repeatedly rejected this option. Sixty-nine per cent- thought that people who paid for health insurance should pay a lower Medicare levy, while 64 per cent thought it should be a straight choice. The former federal Health Minister, Graham Richardson, proposed a staged levy last year, but was over-ruled'by the Prime Minister, Paul Keating. About 37 per cent of Australians pay for private health insurance, but the survey revealed widespread ignorance about the recent health insurance reforms proposed by the Health Minister, Carmen Lawrence. Dr Lawrence announced the proposals as a way of slowing the exodus of people from health in-* surance - but the deputy chief of the federal Health Department, Dr John Loy, said yesterday that this was not the main aim of the policy. "The basis for making these changes was to provide a framework for the private health insurance industry ... to offer more Consumer-orientated packages of care," Dr Loy said. "It is not directly aimed at reducing premiums and therefore not directly aimed at increasing or slowing the decline of participation in that sense." The Lawrence reforms were widely attacked at an Australian Medical Association conference addressed by Dr Loy yesterday. AMA president Dr Brendan Nelson said insurance premiums were certain to rise, while the president of the Australian Association of Surgeons, Dr Philip Nash, said the Lawrence package amounted to a managed care pro ' gram and would produce a second, more expensive Medicare. "Most Australians have not had an occasion to test Medicare for anything other than GP consultations, laboratory tests and serious emergencies," he said. "If we as doctors who can clearly see the problems ahead tell the truth, we are quickly attacked by our politicians as greedy doctors consumed with self-interest." The Opposition's spokeswoman on health, Bronwyn Bishop, said the Government's real objective was total control of doctors. The Constitution prevented the Government from controlling doctors' fees, so it was using the health insurance funds to achieve the same result. Mrs Bishop said the Government's aim was to replace the present 80 private health insurance funds with a single insurer.

04 Jun 1987 - Morgan Poll has Labor well ahead Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 4 June 1987, page 8 i Morgan Poll has Labor well ahead SYDNEY: The Labor Government is well ahead of the Opposition in the lead-up to next month's election, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published yesterday. Labor's approval rating stood at 48 per cent - 3 per cent ahead of the. combined figure for the Opposition parties - when the poll was taken on the weekend of May 23 and 24. The Prime Minister, Mr Hawkc, was well out in front with a 60 per cent personal rating -his highest sincc May last year. Mr Hawke's standing among ALP voters was up 3 per cent to 86 per cent, among male voters up 4 per cent to 63 per cent and among women voters up 1 per cent to 56 percent. People asked to say whether they preferred Mr Hawkc to the Opposition Leader, Mr Howard, for Prime Minister placed Mr Hawke ahead by 68 per cent to 18 percent. Only 42 per cent of Liberal voters said they approved of how Mr Howard was handling his job. The poll, published in The Bulletin magazine, said that if an election had been held on May 23 the Hawke Government would have won with about the same majority as it has now.

14 Aug 1986 - ALP support down in WA, SA Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 14 August 1986, page 9 ALP support down in WA, SA SYDNEY: Labor Party support was being eroded in Western Australia and South Australia, but not enough for the party to have lost a June or July state election, according to two Morgan Gallup Polls. 06 Aug 1942 - SHIP SINKINGS DISTURB AMERICANS Argus (Melbourne, Vic. : 1848 - 1957), Thursday 6 August 1942, page 1 SHIP SINKINGS DISTURB AMERICANS From Our Own Correspondent NEW YORK, Wednesday A Gallup poll on what Americans Regard as the most important problem facing the USA in its war effort reveals that shipping is worrying the country more than anything else. 28 Sep 1942 - DAILY DIGEST Argus (Melbourne, Vic. : 1848 - 1957), Monday 28 September 1942, page 3 DAILY DIGEST Compiled by A.L.B. HOW TO TREAT~POST-WAR GERMANY A Gallup poll shows that 70% of Americans feel they, aro fighting against Hitler, and not against the German people. This is n false and dangerous belief, which will lead to the same deceptions as the last war. The German warrior people as an ?.. entity, guided by Us intelligentsia, -first followed the Kaiser, and now follows a proletarian In its desire to . conquer the world. Hitler is Ger- many. We can effectively protect curselves' against the war passion of the German people only by taking out of their hands for a certain time 3 things left to them in Hie Versailles Treaty-anns, education, and government. With pence every . weapon inside the German frontiers, every gun in the hands of a soldier or a policeman, should be carried . by a non-German. Education must fall into the hands of non-Germans who can speak German. Religion, history, philo-sophy all teach principles foreign to the German character, and can only be infused gradually-tolerance to-ward other races, and acknowledg-ment that the spirit is superior to force. As no one knows when the Germans will be ripe for self-government, the first years after a peace a protective aovernment like the one the English for 40 years exercised in Egypt should reign in Germany. What I propose 13 not a punishment, but a temporary declaration of political Immaturity.- (Emil Ludwig;, eminent German writer, now In exile, speak-ing at Los Angeles, 8/7/42.) CUSTOMS OF THE REGIMENTS Many of the customs cherished by individual regiments of the British Army are connected with dress. For instance, lhere aro G regiments that wear red roses in their hats on Minden Day because they plucked roses from a garden and stuck them in their hats as they went into action at Maiden in 17SD. Among the odd things that other regiments wear, perhaps the best known, because it is so conspicuous. Is the "flash" of 5 black ribbons that the Royal Welch Fusiliers wear at the back of the collar. When the régiment returned from overseas in 1B05 they were so proud to find that they alone of the British Army were wearing pigtails that they askod per-mission to wear the flash, rhich was meant to represent not the pigtall, but the black leather pouch in which the pigtail was housed so that it shouldn't, soil the uniform. Then, of course, there Is the badge that tile Gloucester Regiment wears at the back as well as at the front of their headgear because they beat off the invincible legion of French cavalry at Alexandria in 1801, fighting back to back. At Festubert in 1915, sur-rounded by the Germans, they re-peated the some feat, and were allowed to wear a rather larger badge at the back. There is a belief that Highland regiments took to wearing spats be-cause they retreated so far to Cor-unna that their shoes wore out, and tliey had to bind up their feet with strips toni from their shirt tails. The same sort of custom survives In the South Staffordshfres. Here they Incorporate a piece of brown canvns into their uniforms, indicating Eackcloth and ashes, because in 1707 the regiment became completely forgot-ten about in the West Indies, and remained there for 50 years, getting untidier and untidier and more and more out of date. For a long time the Wiltshire Regi-ment wore buttons with dents in them as they ran out of ammunition at Carrickfergus Castle, and sub-jected the enemy to a fierce button barrage, which they followed up by hurling bricks. The Oxford and Bucks cherish a privilege dating from Dettingen. when some of the regiment, instead of advancing, went to the assistance of George II. who had fallen off his horse. In return for this loyal act, and as the Sovereign had fallen off a white horse, the regiment has always been allowed to wear a white tie with its mess kit. Moreover, it was the action of this regiment In smearing mud over its white breeches which led to the introduc-tion of khaki. —(Lt. Dan Pettiward, in the BBC "Listener," 21/5/42.)

30 Nov 1944 - HONOUR TO WEIZMAN Hebrew Standard of Australasia (Sydney, NSW : 1895 - 1953), Thursday 30 November 1944, page 7 HONOUR TO WEIZMAN To Commemorate His 70th Birthday Contributed by the Jewish National Fund of N.S.W. If a Gallup Poll would be held to determine who is the best known and most representative contemporary figure in Jewish public life, Prof. Chajm Weizman would be sure, to win. Every non-Jew interested in Jewish affairs and certainly every Jew, whatever his political views or cultural level, knows tne name (jnaim Weizman. As president of the Jewish Agency for Palestine and of the World Zionist Organisation, Prof. Weizman bears the responsibility of a statesman. The fact that in his political and diplomatic work, he has not the backing of a State, adds to his burden, and only an outstanding ' personality like Weizman could master the enormous obligations of a prime minister without a state organisation. His political and diplomatic achievements are already history. The Balfour Declaration, which forms the legal foundation of trie establishment of the Jewish National Home in Palestine, was the outcome of Prof. Weizman's negotiations with the British Government. I During the term of his leadership of the | Zionist World ? Organisation, the Jewish ?I population of Palestine increased from | 18,000 to over 600,000, and become a political and economic factor. It was largely due to Prof. Weizman's personality that the 'Jewish State in the making' also gained recognition in the field of world diplomacy. Prof. Weizman never subscribed to extreme views. In his work he relies more on tactful persuasion than' forceful argument. His indomitable courage and his immaculate character jand last, hut not least, his unshakable belief in the future and destiny of the Jewish people, have won Dr. Weizman the respect even' of his adversaries. ? ~ His achievements as a scientist in the field of chemical research have been outstanding. In the service-of the British Admiralty he discovered during the last war the acetone-butyl ' fermentation, which greatly helped the Allied Nations at a crucial time of the last war. During the present war, Prof. Weizman's research work has once more proved of great value to the Allied war effort. When asked by David Lloyd George, the British Prime Minister- during the last war, what he wanted as compensation for his services to the British Empire, Prof. Weizman replied: 'Noth-ing for myself, but something for my people.' \ Those who have willingly followed the leadership of Prof. Weizman, admiring his never-failing promptness .and his striking utterances, almost forgot, that Chaim Weizman, too, gets older in years. It, therefore, struck many of us as unexpected news that he will be 70 on November 27th. World Jewry will make this indeed worthy date an occasion to honour this outstanding man in an extraordinary way. In response to suggestions made from many quarters of the Jewish public, the Head Office of the Jewish National Fund in Jerusalem has placed its organisation at the disposal of the Jewish public for a universal inscription of Dr. Weizman in the Golden Book in Jerusalem. This way of honouring Dr. Weizman appears appropriate in view of the democratic nature of the Golden Book and its tradition as an outstanding Roll of Honour. Great Britain has undertaken to inscribe Prof. Weizman 1,000 times and Canada 700 times. The Australian J.N.F. has pledged to inscribe Prof: Weizman 100 times, in the Golden Book. Donations for inscriptions of Dr. Weizman are being gathered from Hebrew Congregations, Jewish societies and individuals. It is proposed to incorporate the in- ' scriptions in a special volume of the Golden Book as a collective and impressive tribute of Jewry to Prof. Weizman. 'Funds Funds so subscribed will be devoted to the redemption of a tract of land in Eretz Israel, on which settlements will be established linked with the name pt Chaim Weizman. This will surely be a worthy project to honour this great man and will be expressive of the esteem and gratitude of the Jewish people for Chaim Weizman's life work for Jewry.

03 Sep 1989 - Libs poll badly all around Aust Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 3 September 1989, page 5 Libs poll badly all around Aust By IAN COLLIER A round of weekend opinion polls has spelt out bad news for the federal Liberal Party. By far the worst result for the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, was the Saulwick survey published in The Age newspaper. The poll clearly shows that the recent week-long mock election campaign, supported by a $1 million advertising blitz featuring Mr Peacock, was nothing short of a waste of money. The mid-term campaign apparently did not succeed even among Liberal Party supporters. The poll found that 71 per cent of Labor voters believed the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, was doing a good job or better. The bitter pill for the Liberals is that only 30 per cent of Liberals gave their leader a similar rating. Continuing with that rating, only 3 per cent of ALP voters think Mr Hawke is doing a poor or very poor job as leader. That has to be compared to 21 per cent of Liberals who said this about Mr Peacock. In other words, more than twothirds of his own party supporters think Mr Peacock is doing less than a good job as leader while just over one in five of Liberals believe he is not performing at all. Another worrying factor for the Liberals is Mr Peacock's apparent loss of support in Sydney and Melbourne, areas where senior Liberal officials have remained confident they will pick up big slices of the traditional Labor vote. The Melbourne vote, in particular, is very important to any chances the Coalition has of winning the next federal election. It is also very important for Mr Peacock, personally, as this is his home power - base and where he would be expected to have a very good rating. But the proportion of voters in the Victorian capital who believe the Opposition Leader is doing a good job has dropped from 23 per cent to 14 per cent over the past month, according to the poll. The news in Sydney is also bad, with 48 per cent of voters in the NSW capital saying Mr Peacock is doing a poor job. This is a jump of 10 per cent over the previous month, and clearly indicates that NSW Liberals are still taking time to forgive the Peacock forces over the dumping of the Sydncy-based John Howard for a Melbourne leader. While the results tend to bring into question any belief that Mr Peacock would lift the Coalition's image after Mr Howard, the survey could also indicate that the Opposition is being battered by its prob-, lems. over lack of clear policy' directions, particularly in the areas of the economy and taxation. Another major problem for the Coalition has surfaced in Queensland, another key state in any bid to winning back power from the Hawke Government. A survey taken by the CourierMail in Brisbane shows that the state ALP is on course for a win at the next Queensland election, with 40 per cent support. The Liberals were 5 percentage points ahead of the National Party and gaining momentum in country areas. Liberal-National combined support was one percentage point behind Labor at 39 per cent. For the federal Coalition this poll is yet another worry as the federal Liberals will be counting on the federal Nationals to win back rural Queensland seats currently held by the ALP, such as Leichhardt and Hinkler. The Coalition also needs to retain current National Party seats such as Kennedy and Dawson. If support for the state ALP is reflected by their federal counterparts, the conservatives at state and federal levels have, at the very least, reason for thought.

05 Sep 1989 - The return of Howard 'inevitable' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 5 September 1989, page 1 The return of Howard 'inevitable' By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent John Howard and the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, have been having "amicable discussions", and Mr i Howard's return to the Opposition front bench is inevitable, according to senior Liberal Party sources. But nothing will happen until late this year, at the earliest. "Cups of tea have been had," according to a senior Liberal Member, indicating that the relationship between the former and present leaders was mellowing. Mr Peacock had realised it was in his interests to have Mr Howard back in the fold, and there was a strong feeling among MPs that it should happen as soon as possible. Pressure had increased since the call al the weekend by the NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, to have Mr Howard elevated swiftly in the interests of party unity. Mr Greiner repeated his call yesterday, saying it was "painfully, blindingly obvious that the Federal Opposition would have its best chance if it had complete unity, and Mr Howard's obviously part of that". The comments followed another public-opinion poll that showed Mr Peacock losing favour — and Mr Howard gaining. The Australia-wide Roy Morgan poll found that while support for Mr Howard had increased by 16 percentage points to 43 per cent since May, Mr Peacock's popularity had fallen 16 points, to 44 per cent. However, senior Liberals discounted the poll, pointing out that similar polls conducted while Mr Howard was leader showed "mirror-image" results. They said Mr Howard would be reinstated to the front bench for the simple reason that he was needed. But there was little chance he would be elevated until towards the end of this year. And if the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, called an early election, Mr Howard's return from the wilderness would be postponed. There were simply no senior shadow cabinet vacancies at present, and Mr Peacock, anxious not to cause Further internal dissension while Parliament is sitting, would not reshuffle until Parliament went into recess. To move Mr Howard into a "suitable"shadow portfolio would require a reshuffle of several front-benchers. There was no indication yesterday on what shadow portfolios might be offered to Mr Howard. Mr Peacock and Mr Howard avoided being drawn into the debate yesterday. A •spokesman for Mr Peacock said he had "no response al all", and Mr Howard said he would not make any comment. Mr Howard's return to the front bench is complicated by the conditions he placed on the issue soon after he was deposed on May 9. When Mr Peacock offered him the education portfolio, Mr Howard turned it down as too junior and insulting. He wanted foreign affairs or defence. When the Opposition spokesman on housing and finance, Wilson Tuckey, and the Opposition spokesman for business, privatisation and consumer affairs, John Moore, revealed themselves on the ABC's Four Corners program as conspirators in Mr Howard's downfall, Mr Howard said he would not.sit on a front bench' with .them. Mr Howard has not repeated these conditions publicly for some time, and he would not be quoted along these lines yesterday. There is speculation among his colleagues that time is beginning to-heal Mr Howard's-wounds. In an interview published by the Melbourne Sun yesterday, he declared his period of self-imposed political low profile was over." He has emerged as a columnist with The Australian newspaper and has several publicspeaking engagements lined up. There is little likelihood of Mr Peacock dumping Mr Tuckey and Mr Moore. Mr Tuckey said yesterday, "I'm certainly not negotiating with Mr Howard. He's made the conditions — it's his problem." However, Mr Tuckey would have no problems serving alongside Mr Howard.

16 Sep 1989 - X-rated videos backed in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 16 September 1989, page 7 X-rated videos backed in poll A majority of Australian adults believed the sale and hire of X-rated videotapes should be allowed, a Morgan Gallup poll commissioned by the Adult Video Industry Association has found. A national survey by the Roy Morgan Research Centre issued yesterday found 53 per cent were in favour of X-rated videotapes; 41 per cent wanted their sale and hire banned. However, the association warned of misconceptions about non-violent erotic videos and called for more specific classifications. Fourteen per cent of those surveyed thought X-rated videotapes contained only violence while almost half said they contained both explicit sex and violence. Association lobbyist Robert Swan said the chief Commonwealth censor, John Dickie, should be extremely disappointed by the lack of understanding of Australia's videotape-ratings system. A cross-section of 1263 men and women aged 18 and over were interviewed in an Australia-wide poll from August 29 to 31. They were told X-ratcd videotapes showed explicit sex scenes and were non-violent, and were then asked if the sale and hire of X-rated videotapes should be allowed or banned in their states. Residents of the ACT — where the sale of X-rated videotapes is allowed — were most in favour (61 per cent), followed by 59 per cent in Western Australia, 57 per cent in NSW, 52 per cent in Victoria and 51 per cent in Queensland. In South Australia and Tasmania, a majority of people wanted them banned. Sixty-three per cent of men and 50 per cent of women wanted X-rated videotapes allowed. People under 25 were more in favour of X-rated videotapes — 70 per cent — while 54 per cent of those over 50 wanted them banned. ' The association said a large slicc of the community still reacted badly to the X label because they associated it with violence.

16 Sep 1989 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 16 September 1989, page 9 SUPPORT for the National Party in Queensland has dropped to a re cord low of 17 per cent, with support for the Liberal Party at 29 per cent and the ALP at 45 per cent, according to the Saulwick poll. Even given the electoral system in Queensland, it seems virtually impossible for the National Party to survive the coming election in its own right, and the main question now is whether Queensland will be governed by the ALP or a Liberal/National coalition. The poll, taken on September 6 and involving 1000 voters, also shows ALP leader Wayne Goss well ahead in the popularity stakes with 46 per cent saying he would make the best Premier. Next is the incumbent Premier, Mike Ahern, with 21 per cent, followed by the leader of the Liberal Party, Angus Innes, with 19 per cent. In NSW, the Morgan Gallup Poll shows that support for the Liberal Government of Nick Greiner has risen by 3 per cent over August to 45 per cent, while the ALP was able to command the support of 43 per cent of those polled. The poll of 1362 electors also showed support for the Australian Democrats at 6 per cent and others at 6 per cent The approval rating of Mr Greiner stood at 45 per cent, up from 41 per cent in Augast, while 39 per cent of those polled approved of the way his . ALP counterpart, Bob Carr, was doing his job. From the United States, a poll in the Washington Post shows that after a year in the job, Dan Quayle has yet to convince the country that he is quali fied to become President. A poll of 1022 people across the country found that 52 per cent thought Quayle not qualified to take over the presidency if something happened to George Bush, with 38 per cent saying he would be qualified. But Americans seem to like Quayle as vice-president — 43 per cent approve of the way he is doing the job he has now, 34 per cent don't know or ' have no opinion, while only 22 per cent of those polled oppose him outright. — ANDREW FRASER .

20 Sep 1989 - Science deserves more funding Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 20 September 1989, page 2 Science deserves more funding Australians believe more money should be spent on scientific research to improve the quality of life, according to a poll conducted in Victoria, NSW and Perth for New Scientist magazine. The poll, conducted during May by Roy Morgan Research Centre, also showed that Australians believed the Labor Party cares more about science and technology than the Liberal-National Party coalition, though 80 per cent of respondents felt politicians did not know enough about science and technology to judge its importance. Medical research was named as first priority for spending, with the control and reduction of pollu tion ranked second and third. The public was less interested in money being spent on computers, nuclear energy, biotechnology, space exploration and robotics. Women's priorities were different from men's, with more support for areas affecting quality of life and less concern for economics. Faith in research was high, with 65 per cent saying science could solve many of the world's problems. Sixty-three per cent felt national prosperity depended on technology. Medical research was also popular with 63 per cent saying it inspired a "great deal" of confidence. Only 10 per cent thought science and technology did more barm than good.

22 Sep 1989 - Desperation for the heartland Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 22 September 1989, page 1 Desperation for the heartland COMMENT By ANDREW FRASER The strategy of the Queensland National Party with an election coming up is clear — with virtually no chance of winning in its own right, it is going all-out to maintain its support in its heartland and be the majority partner in any coalition. At the moment, the National Party has 47 of the 89 seats in Queensland: 45 seats are needed for a majority, and 23 to be the majority partner in a coalition with the Liberal Party. Of the Nationals' 47 seats, 11 are in the south-east zone, the urban seats they picked up when they moved to Government in their own right in 1983, but the party has virtually written them off for this elec tion. Continued on Page 2 Desperation for the heartland Continued from Page 1 There are another seven seats in the provincial cities, which Nationals concede they are unlikely to win. This gives the National Party 29 seats in the northern and western zones, its traditional base. With so much of a swing against it, these are the seats the Nationals must keep if they are going to retain power as the senior coalition partner. This is where the change in leader and Sir Robert Sparkes comes in. Mike Ahem has always been the Nationals' symbol of the way they had broadened their ranks. He hada university degree and he used his time as Minister for Industry -and Development from 1983 to 1986 to build a wide range of contacts with industry. Unlike Sir Joh, he was relatively urbane. He Is not a back-slapper and his background is not in small country halls where Sir Joh's remarkable oratorical style had its roots. The Nationals are in trouble state-wide — the latest Morgan Gallup Poll shows support for them running at only 17 per cent across the state. The urbane Mr Ahern has struck out not only in the urban areas but in the bush as well. The one thing the Nationals have left to keep their hopes up is the gerrymander the country areas have most votes. So the strategy is to keep those heartlands, best done through a change of leadership. Russell Cooper, the man who would be premier, only entered Parliament in 1983, but he is one of the old school of the National Party—a grazier, former shire councillor, no tertiary education. His political stocks rose when as Prisons Minister he toughed out a disturbance at Boggo Road Jail. They like firm leadership in the bush. What the "keeping the heartlands" strategy also requires is for the Liberal Party to pick up the seats the Nationals drop and not let too many go to the ALP, which needs only 15 seats to win Government. Politics abounds in irony, but this one is supreme — the party the Nationals set out to destroy is the one they are now counting on to rescue them. With Sir Robert Sparkes as the main opponent to Mr Ahem, the Premier knows his days are numbered. But he had one left yesterday, and he gave a remarkable interview on Brisbane radio when he reminisced on the high points of his premiership.

23 Sep 1989 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 23 September 1989, page 9 Tie Liberal-National Coalition made slight gains at the ex pense of the ALP and would win government if an election were to be held now, according to a Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, taken between September 2 and 9 and involving 1861 voters Australia-wide, shows support for the ALP at 43 per cent and the coalition at 45 per cent, after the last poll taken between August 20 and 27 showed the two parties equal at 44.5 per cent. But the Coalition picked up only 0.5 per cent of the 1.5 per cent the ALP lost The Australian Democrats picked up the other 1 per cent to take their support to 9 per cent. The poll shows Prime Minister Bob Hawke's approval rating has dropped to 50 per cent from 54 per cent, and the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock's approval rating has dropped to 28 per cent from 34 per cent. An environment poll by Morgan Gallup, conducted for the NSW Electricity Commission across NSW, found that Australians are far less concerned than the rest of the world about the ozone layer and the greenhouse effect, but far more concerned about I water pollution. The poll, which was conducted among 1200 residents throughout July and asked people to name what they thought was the most pressing environmental problem, found that 24 per cent of those surveyed thought that cutting down forests was the major environmental problem, the same as for the rest of the world.. Of those polled, 14 per cent thought weakening the ozone layer was the biggest problem (23 per cent for rest of world) and 10 per cent thought the greenhouse effect was (16 per cent for rest of world). But while in the rest of the world 11 per cent thought water pollution was the biggest problem, 21 per ccnt of those polled in NSW agreed. — ANDREW FRASER

25 Sep 1989 - Survey shows Greiner's approval rate has dropped Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 25 September 1989, page 4 Survey shows Greiner's approval rate has dropped SYDNEY: A Newspoll survey showing NSW Premier Nick Greiner's approval rating was at its lowest since the LiberalNational Coalition won government in March 1988 proved it was a one-term government, the Leader of the Opposition, Bob Carr, said yesterday. "People will never forgive Mr Greiner for his 150 broken promises," Mr Carr said. He said the Labor Party had kept count of Mr Greiner's broken promises since he took office. The Newspoil survey, conducted for the Sunday Telegraph during July and August, found support for the Coalition parties had also dropped and was now neck and neck with the ALP. For the first time in a year, Mr Greiner and Mr Carr tied in approval rating. The survey showed 56 per cent of people polled were not satisfied with the way Mr Greiner was doing his job, compared with a 46 per cent disapproval rating in the previous May-June Newspoll survey. "People will never forgive Mr Greiner for his attacks on education and his increased charges causing ordinary families to pay an extra $1000 a year," Mr Cansaid. "This is an unfair government." July and August were marked by public demonstrations against the Greiner Government, including the "day of outrage" on July 25 when 100,000 NSW workers went on strike to protest against job cuts. On July 1 Mr Greiner announced increased charges for transport, electricity, third-party car insurance, water rates, daily public-nospital bed prices, a 3 per cent petrol tax and an $80 environmental levy for all ratepayers. The poll found 36 percent were satisfied with the way Mr Greiner was doing his job, compared with 44 per cent in the previous survey. Only 1 per cent more (Coalition 43 per cent, Labor 42 per cent) said they would vote for the Government if an election were held at the time. Mr Carr's popularity remained almost unchanged from the previous survey with 37 per cent of- those polled saying they were satisfied with the way he was_doing his job, comparedwith 35 per cent who " were dissatisfied.' \ " '* '

30 Sep 1989 - Govt handling of pilots' row wins support Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 September 1989, page 9 :Govt handling of pilots' row wins support THE GOVERNMENT'S handling of the pilots dispute is generally approved of, if the findings of a Saulwick poll taken among 600 people in Sydney and ^Melbourne 10 days ago can be extended to the rest of the population. Fifty-five per cent of those polled supported the Government's tough line against the pilots, but at the same time, 59 per cent thought the Government and airlines should negotiate while the pilots refused to work normal hours. Thirty-seven per cent of those polled disapproved of the Govern, jnent's handling of the dispute, while 6 per cent were undecided. . But the pilots are not at all popular — 75 per cent of those polled thought their wage claim of a 30 per cent rise was unreasonable, only 18 per cent thought it justified and 5 per cent were undecided. Another poll taken by AGB:Spectrum and published in Business Review Weekly shows the perception of big business of the main parties' wages policy is worrying for the Opposition. The poll, taken among 160 chief executives of Australia's 500 biggest companies, shows that 55 per cent thought the ALP best suited to run wages policy, as opposed to 21 per cent who thought the Coalition was. It also showed that 70 per cent of those polled did not understand the Opposition's economic policy, with the lowest support in Sydney, where only 19 per cent of those polled said they understood the Opposition's economic policy. At the same time, the poll also indicated that big business was reasonably comfortable with a Labor Government — in June 56 per cent of those polled thought the Government's performance was bad in relation to business, while in this survey, only 47 per cent thought so. The "average" or "good" rating rose from 44 per cent to 53 per cent. The poll was taken after Budget changes to business taxation but before the announcement of the $2.6 billion current-account deficit for Aueust. — ANDREW FRASER

04 Nov 1989 - Swimming against a tide of unfavourable opinion Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 4 November 1989, page 9 Swimming against a tide of unfavourable opinion THE ALP still has the capacity to claw its way back in opinion polls despite the Morgan Gallup Poll this week showing a big lead for the Liberal-National Coalition. The poll showed support for the Coalition at 46 per cent and support for the ALP at 41 per cent, with the Australian Democrats at 9 per cent and others at 4 per cent. In March last year the Coalition had a lead of 7 percentage points over the ALP, but by the start of this year the two parties were at level 'pegging again. However, the problem for the -ALP in this case is that an election must be held at some stage within -the next six months, and there are several institutional factors - mainly economic - which will work against them. The approval rating of the parties' leaders shpws support for Mr Hawke at 43 per cent, slightly up from the last poll but well down from the general level it has been, while Mr Peacock's approval rating rose to 31 per cent, well up from its general level. / The ALP could also take no com fort from' a poll in last Saturday's West Australian which showed they would lose four seats in Western Australia at the next election. But before a federal election can be held there are two state elections, one in Queensland and one in South Australia. In South Australia the ALP, led by John Bannon, is well ahead, but in Queensland, the situation is far closer, with a poll this week showing the ALP's support would have to be well targeted in specific seats for it to win. The poll showed support for the ALP at 46 per cent, support for the Liberal Party at 28 per cent, and support for the National Party at 20 percent. But there is little comfort for either the Liberal Party or the National Party in the poll, as they would require a very tight exchange of preferences to win, and in the past two elections 25 per cent of Liberal preferences and about 10 per cent of National preferences have gone to the ALP. Overseas, the approval rating of the British Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher, has plummeted to an all-time low, eclipsing even the 25 per cent approval rating she had just before she dispatched troops to the Falklands Islands in 1982. Just 24 per cent of voters polled by The Independent were satisfied with Mrs Thatcher's record, while 62 per cent expressed dissatisfaction. The lowest previous popularity ratings, recorded by Gallup and Mori, were 25 per cent in December 1981 after she had been in power some 30 months. Polls in several British newspapers last weekend pointed to a Labour victory, with the smallest margin that Labour was ahead of the Tories being 7 percentage points. Poll: Morgan Gallup. Date taken: Oct 14-15, Oct 21-22. No polled: 2614. Method: Face to face. Coverage: National. Lib-NP 46%, ALP 41%, AD 9%, Other 4%. Poll: Morgan Gallup. Date taken: Oct 21-22. No polled: 1337. Method: Face to face. Coverage: Queensland, state-wide. ALP 46%, Lib 28%, NP 20%, Others 6%. Poll: Independent. No polled: 935. Coverage: Britain. Question: Are you satisfied with the performance of Mrs Thatcher as Prime Minister? Yes, 24%, No 62%, undecided 14%. - ANDREW FRASER
