14 Nov 1989 - Hungry for science but fe Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 14 November 1989, page 9 Hungry for science but fe THE PUBLIC might be the great urW washed, but it seems the scientific; community is the great unloved')? Opinion polls have pui scientists on about level with journalists, that is slightly .abovjefc real estate agents, but! still trailing behinp| child molesters. Why do pe'ople believe the laboratory rats are the ones wearing the white coats? Before scientists start deserting the sinking ship, of popularity, it's worth taking a look at the way. this "evidence" against them has been compiled. The method most comrtionlyused for testing public opinion of scientists is the Draw-A-Scientlst-Test. This test supposedly overcomes problems that children (who have been the largest group surveyed) might have articulating their perceptions of a scientist. According to Renato Schibeci, from Murdoch University, the results show a stereotyped image of scientists, and in fact even scientists, when asked to draw a picture, will produce a stereotype, which can be summarised as follows: the scientist is a male and has facial hair. Often his work is of a secret or dangerous kind. His "discoveries" are generally the result of a brief period of intense thinking and his preoccupation with matters scientific is such that he has little time for mundane matters such as family, sport or entertainment. . This "negative" stereotype is said to pervade the .mass media. Presumably the negative aspects are the secretive, dangerous work and emotional coldness, rather than the fact that our scientist is male, as most arc, and hirsute. "Stereotype" has certainly become a dirty word, yet it is a useful form of communications shorthand, as cartoonists and advertisers constantly demonstrate. Take advertising for example. I'd hate to defend most of this medium bccausc there's no doubt it's sexist, racist and worst of all; tasteless, but try telling a story in 15 seconds without resorting to stereotypes. Common criticisms of science fiction are that we never see "normal" scientists, only the mad or sociopathically dedicated ones, and that we don't see scientists achieving results in a realistic way -as the result of painstaking, lengthy pursuit of scientific knowledge - but rather as the result of a sudden flash ofinspiration. On the first point, it's true that the characters in a lot of science fiction provide a rich hunting ground for political and social metaphors, a source wellused by academics in search of a thesis, but surely the same criticism could be applied to most works .<Sf fiction, especially those about soldiers or police, jMb are portrayed as either heroes or villains when '^theirioccupation is important for the plot. Some '^ljqw&nce has to be made for literary devices. ':-f As for the criticism that results come so'quickly to celluloid scientists, who has the time or inclination to sit through the boredom and banality of everyday working life on the screen? Before anyone criticises film and TV-program makers for speeding things up and cutting out the boring bits, they should sit through a few hours of day-time soap operas, where the storyline does follow real-time, then they'll be begging for celluloid characters who can brainstorm their way through a plot. Dr Roslyn Haynes, a former biochemist who now lectures in English, writes in the November issue of Media Information Australia that there are six basic literary stereotypes which have had a profound and continuing influence on the attitudes of our own society to science and scientists. She classes these as: the evil alchemist figure; the silly scientist; the emotionally deficient researcher; the heroic adventurer or Utopian world saviour; the !,reckless or evil destroyer; and the helpless scientist unable to control his discovery. Haynes says that if scientists want to improve their public, image, they should take notice of the way they've been portrayed over the centuries, because these stereotypes influence public images of the scientist. Richard Eckersley, Senior Media Liaison Officer at CSIRO, says the image of scientists has suffered, because of our.enthusiasm for global technology. "Until the'60s Australian scientists were portrayed as heroes, especially the CSIRO scientists, who were working on the development, of rainmaking techniques and myxomatosis," Eckersley said. Scientists were seen to be working in the national interest by developing the country's natural resources, but now, like miners and farmers, they are considered environmental rapists by some. "People don't realise that we need science more than ever now-it should be seen as part of the solution not the cause of our current problems. "As we've become more cosmopolitan and urbanised with global technology, Australian science has lost its national identity and scientists aren't held in the same regard by the public," he said. ?Debra Mayrhofer investigates the gap between- the' media 'image of scientists and the public's desire for more news about research. It's difficult to form much of an opinion about how the news media portrays scientists because they seem to be the invisible tribe. The reason can't have anything to do with whether people like'or , loathe them; look at the amount of time anctspace .given to murderers, cheats and other.miscrea'nts Could, it'be that thc'public'just-aren't interested in scientists1 or -the work they: do? Let's hppe. not; becausefas Federal Science Minister Barry Jo.nes1;. has often said, "those who can't understand ,'the^ ideas and practices of science and canTcbhimjini^i cate about them are cut off from a fundamental part: of today's culture. They are as efTectively .cut'ofl}; from the wider culture as those who have not yet'i learned to read or write." ? ' . Dr Peter Pockley, who for the. past 25 years has been a tireless campaigner for better public understanding of scientific issues, says he believes the situation in Australia is similar to that in the UK where the public is interested in science, and wants more of it, even though there is a very low level of understanding of the facts and principles involved. Pockley is currently trying to get the proposed Australian Science and Technology Information Service off the ground. This service will provide an Australian register of scientists in a wide variety of fields who are willing and able to speak to the media and will also link up with its American and Europe an counterparts, virtually offering journalists a world-wide information base. The scientific community has already contributed funds for'working plan for the service. All that v remains is for the Federal Government to distribute . some of the millions it promised generously in its May economic.statement. > . v In September this year the Age and the Sydney ;? Morning Herald ran the results of a Saulwick opiniion poll which showed that 60 per cent of readers :;'\v6uld read, stories about medical discoveries and'' ,:"54 per cent'would read about other scientific discoveries before they'd-rtad about politics and sport. ? New Scientist also published the results of its ^survey which , indicated that the Australian public has .favourable attitudes towards science.' It seems that 56 per cent of people believe that science does ;,more good than harm; 61 per cent believe the ' Government should spend more on research; and 63 per cent believe our national prosperity depends on science and technology. Given this evidence of public interest, why ? hasn't the media been giving better coverage to the work of scientists? A few major papers now have regular science coverage; the ABC and Channel Seven have Quantum and Beyond 2000, respectively, and the ABC Science Unit produces six different science pro grams each week. Perhaps we should be grateful that even though the electronic media coverage is scant, it is of such quality. Professor John Henningham ofthe University of Queensland has found an alarming disparity be-' tween what journalists think the public wants, and what the public really wants. More than 78 per cent of TV viewers say that they ha ve a very high interest in scientific and medical discoveries, yet only 3 per cent of news stories arc devoted to these subjects. In a survey of Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane viewers, Henningham found that from a list of 15 news categories, journalists.put science and medicine sixth on their own lists of interests, yet when asked to rank viewers' interests, they put science and medicine 13th. And the viewers' choice? Science and medicine was voted number one. The same disparity showed up in current affairs categories. The journalists placed science and medicine fourth and the environment third, in their list of interests, yet relegated science and medicine to . 7th and the environment to 13th in their estimates of the viewers' interests. Once again the viewers proved them wrong, voting science and medicine top of the list and the environment second. These results are alarming and make you wonder how the media can be so far off the beam in "giving the public what it wants". Is it because journalists really underestimate the intelligence of their audiences, or is it that the media really aren't capable of . dealing with scientific issues? A ^number of writers in the. November issue of Media Information Australia, which has science and'technology as its theme, analyse the troubled relationship between science and the media, and all . concur that both sides need to make more effort to communicate. , ? Ian Barnes blames the pressures of sales, readership or ratirigs for influencing the content and style of media presentations, making it hard to provide accurate, detailed reports of scientific research. Also, he says, the media, particularly TV, provides a fragmented view of issues, and perhaps most importantly, it is a promoter of the commodity culture, so news is largely entertainment framed within the important process of selling commodities. Professor Stephen Hill writes that the popularisation of science has been a confused field of media activity, with the promoters of the subject not sure whether they want to make science part of the general culture, promote the ideological strength that flows from science or promote the eponomic competitiveness of the society which is scientifically literate. Most scientists seem to have a positive attitude towards the media. According to Dr Jim Peacock, from CSIRO's Division of Plant Industry, we need to improve the communication-betwcen scientists and the community, and the press is one of the best ways to do this. "Certainly in the last few years scientists have realised the need to inform the public of their work and people generally seem a lot more interested in what we're doing and why we're doing it.' Professor Dick Frankham, from Macquarie University, also believes scientists arc more motivated now to seek publicity for their work. "We don't always make good copy, because we tend to qualify our findings and so be as objective as possible, which can be frustrating for a reporter. "Science, like most news, tends to be sensationalised, but no more than other issues. "Accuracy can suffer under the pressure of deadlines and sub-editing, you have to accept this to some extent," he said. Barry Jones, another contributor in the November issue of Media Information Australia, warns that scientists shouldn't overestimate the media's capabilities. "The media succeed best at what they da best, and that is raising issues. But there has. been little success in going beyond that, cither through making a concerted effort to help people understand :he principle... or, more importantly, to seriously consider the implications of new technology." Jones also points out one area where the media and scientists could work to their mutual advantage - in the promotion of celebrity scientists who could popularise their profession. "Despite tiie world-class work being performed by Australian scientists we don't have any who have become household names like David Suzuki, Carl Sagan or Stephen Jay Gould in North Ameri ca." Jones suggests one of the reasons for this could be.that scientists aren't willing to risk the scorn of their colleagues by popularising their profession. It's time for scientists to leave the shelter of their laboratories and start making the news. As the old saying goes, the only enemy of science is the igno rant.

15 Nov 1989 - Government approval up Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 15 November 1989, page 2 Government approval up SYDNEY: The Federal Government has bounced back in front of the Opposition in the election polls, according to a Morgan Gallup poll published in today's Bulletin magazine. 18 Nov 1989 - An election mode talk by Hawke Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 18 November 1989, page 5 An election mode talk by Hawke By TOM CONNORS The Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, went into "election mode" last night, delivering a speech designed to try and stir the Labor Party out of the doldrums and ready itself for an election which he said would be fought "within the next six months". In his address to the Evatt Foundation at the NSW Parliament House in Sydney, Mr Hawke said it was nonsense to claim that there were no differences between the Labor and Liberal parties and then set out in some detail where he believed they differed on social welfare, industrial relations, foreign affairs and in overall philosophy. The last page of the address reads like the end of an election campaign launch with short sharp sentences in which Mr Hawke promised to fight harder than ever before to win the election. The usual launch cliches were in abundance. He said the choice at the next election was stark, the stakes were huge and Australia could not afford "lost opportunities". He declared the next election the "most important since 1949" (when the Chifley Labor Government lost office) and it would determine the "nature and quality of the Australia we take into the 21st century". Other major points in the speech included an attack on the Coalition's plan to abolish the capital-gains tax, with reference to the personal benefits flowing to the Liberal Party president, John Elliott; a promise of improved community services for those living in the outer suburbs of big cities; the setting of social-justice priorities for the 1990s and a renewed commitment to a multicultural Australia. Mr Hawke reminded his audience that by the time of the next election he would be the longest-serving Labor Prime Minister. He also paid tribute to the former Labor Leader, Dr H. V. Evatt, after whom the foundation is named. Last night's speech follows the revelation. on Thursday that Mr Hawke had written to all his ministers seeking their thoughts on Labor's election strategy and proposals for a fourth term of office. He will call a full meeting of the ministry in early January to discuss the campaign. The burst of prime ministerial energy comes after a poor parliamentary per Bob Hawke ... Promise to fight harder than ever to win next election. formance by the Labor ministry over recent weeks, some squabbling between ministers and growing public disenchantment over the state of the economy. The only recent ray of hope for the Government was this week's Morgan Gallup poll showing the Government had regained a lead over the Coalition as its popularity rose two points and the Coalition's fell by four. However, many observers are sceptical of the poll outcome. The Prime Minister told his audience that the ideological gulf between Labor and Liberal, always a wide one, had never been wider than it was today. The parties were at odds on how employers and employees should relate to each other in the workplace, on the question of how economic prosperity should be distributed within the community and on Australia's role in the international community. He said the Liberals abhorred the central wage-fixing system and gave aid and comfort to the Australian Federation of Air Pilots in pursuit of a 30 per cent pay rise. Their obsession with labour market deregulation would destroy an industrial relations system that had created jobs at a rate twice as fast as the rest of the Western world.

19 Nov 1989 - Innes offers cash for home owners Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 19 November 1989, page 2 Innes offers cash for home owners BRISBANE: Queensland Liber al Leader Angus Innes launched his party's campaign for the December 2 election yesterday with an offer of cash grants for 80,000 Queensland families "struggling under Labor's burden" of high home-interest rates. The cash grant scheme would provide $25 per week for one year to homeowners hardest hit by the interest-rate squeeze. Mr Innes attacked the Nationals on corruption and Labor on its trade union links and history of corruption and finan cial mismanagement when in govern ment elsewhere in Australia. "In Queensland, only the Liberal Party is committed to both private enterprise and honest government because we re cognise that, hand in hand, they are the foundations on which our future progress depends," he said. Placard-waving Liberal supporters crowded into a function room at Bris bane's Parkroyal Hotel to hear the federal Liberal Leader, Andrew Peacock, the NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, and Bris bane's Lord Mayor, Sallyanne Atkinson, list the reasons why a Liberal government should be elected in Queensland. Mr Innes repeated his pledge not to serve as a junior partner in a coalition with the Nationals, saying "a vote for a Liberal candidate is a vote for a Liberal government". He promised to introduce freedom of information legislation and legislation for citizen-initiated referenda. Other initia tives included: 1 800 more police on the beat. Tougher action against the drug trade. BRISBANE: Support for the Queensland Labor Party has risen to 50 per cent and the approval rating for leader Wayne Goss to 66 per cent, according to the latest Newspoll published in the Weekend Australian newspaper. The National Party's state-wide support has fallen by 14 percentage points to 25 per cent since the 1986 election but the Government remains ahead of the Liberals, at 21 per cent. The Premier, Russell Cooper, has an approval rating of 33 per cent and Liberal Leader Angus Innes scored 44 per cent. If an election had been held last weekend, Labor would have won nar rowly on leaked Liberal preferences. The Nationals would have remained the dominant conservative party, the report said. The poll was held between Novem ber 9 and 12 and is based on a state wide sample of 1010 voters. The Newspoll survey comes after a Courier-Mail poll on Friday which showed the Nationals' only hope of holding power lay in a coalition with the Liberals. The poll, of more than 1000 voters in four electoral zones, showed Labor support up 2 percentage points to 44 per cent, Nationals on 18 per cent and the Liberals static at 17 per cent. $120 million more for education in the first two Liberal Budgets. Raising the payroll tax threshold to $1 million. Tripling Juvenile Aid Bureau's resources. Increasing the capital works subsidies to local government authorities from 10 to 15 percent. Expanding the port of Townsville. Declaring Iron Range and Mcllwraith Range on Cape York Peninsula nation al parks and doubling the area of the state's national parkland. A "world-class stadium" as part of the redevelopment of the Brisbane Exhibi tion Grounds. Investigating funding options for a major new road from the Darling Downs to Townsville. Mr Innes said he was promising what the Nationals would not deliver-imple mentation of the Fitzgerald-recommend ed reforms, honest and accountable government, a fair electoral redistribu tion and creation of the right conditions for economic growth and prosperity. And, unlike Labor, the Liberals could promise the aims of privaite enterprise, maintenance of essential services and the introduction of voluntary unionism. Meanwhile, a Gold Coast Liberal offi cial has attacked his party's decision to give second preferences to Labor in the seat of Albert at the electipn rather than to National Party Minister for Health Ivan Gibbs, who they claim is still under a cloud over ministerial expenses. Vince Camilleri, the vice-president of the Paradise Point-Runaway Bay Liber als, said in yesterday's Gold Coast Bulle tin that the decision was "crazy and futile" and could mean the seat would be lost to Labor. The Premier, Russell Cooper, was in Cooktown yesterday to support the Na tional Party candidate for the far north ern seat of Cook, Lester Rosendale, and officially open a new $9 million pipeline to augment the town's water supply.

23 Nov 1989 - Poll 'may help' Qld Liberals Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 23 November 1989, page 4 Poll 'may help' Qld Liberals BRISBANE: A Morgan Gallup Poll showing support for the Labor Party at 53 per cent could prove to be counterproductive for the ALP, Liberal state campaign director David Fraser said yesterday. Mr Fraser said the poll may have an "underdog effect" in the minds of the electorate which could benefit the Liberal Party. "The classic case was in the 1980 federal election where polls indicated that Bill Hayden would win the election," he said. "In the last seven days there was a swing back to the Fraser Government simply because the polls suggested that Labor was going to win." The Morgan poll, based on interviews with 475 electors and published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine, shows support for the ALP at 53 per cent with both the Nationals and Liberals at 19 per cent.

25 Nov 1989 - Bannon is battling to shake federal Labor association Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 25 November 1989, page 3 Bannon is battling to shake federal Labor association From TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent, in Adelaide John Olsen A last-minute poll in South Australia shows that Labor Premier John Bannon is likely to lose government today. The Morgan Gallup Poll showed the Liberal-National Opposition 8 percentage points ahead of the Bannon Government - an extraordinary swing of 3 per cent in a week towards John Olsen's Opposition, and a swing of 5 per cent against the Government. - The figures showed support for the Opposition at 48 per cent, while the Government could muster only 40 per cent. If the poll results translate uniformly across the marginal seats in the electiqn today, Mr Olsen will gain government narrowly. The reason, according to virtually all observers, has little to do with state issues. Indeed, Mr Bannon's Government is generally considered clean, responsible, pragmatic and moderate, if a little dull. The issue that has bitten deepest in the past fortnight is high interest rates, a national problem. The Opposition has successfully linked Mr Bannon - the national president of the Australian Labor Party - with the Hawke Government and its failure to reduce inter est rates. Full-page advertisements placed by the Opposition in yesterday's Adelaide newspapers showed pictures of Mr Bannon and the Treasurer, Paul Keating, side by side, with the caption, "If you want any chance of owning your own home, get rid of these two! Get rid of high interest rates. Get rid of Labor." Mr Bannon is one of Australia's most popular politicians, but yesterday's poll figures showed his personal popularity rating had slipped by 2 points to 56 per cent in a week. Mr Olsen's personal popularity rose 5 points to 37 per cent. The poll confirms that a swing against the Government detected last week has continued to grow as the election nears. Newspaper polls showed the swing growing day by day - the last poll, taken on Tuesday and published yesterday by the Adelaide Advertiser, showed the swing had grown to 5 per cent in the marginal seat of Fisher. But yesterday's poll, commissioned by the Nine Network and announced last night, contained the worst possible news for Mr Bannon. The outcome of the election rests on eight marginal seats in metropolitan Adelaide. The Opposition must win six of those to win government. Five would change hands with a swing of less than 3 per cent. But with the 8 per cent lead detected by yesterday's poll, the Government could also take Norwood, held by Education Minister Greg Crafter by 6.4 per cent, Unley, held by Sports Minister Kim Mayes by 5.1 per cent, or Todd, held by Emergency Services Minister John Klunder by 6 per cent. Mr Bannon, who has already conceded his Government is likely to lose several seats and who recognises publicly that he is in a very tight spot, called last night for every eligible South Australian to vote. "Every single vote counts," Mr Bannon said. Mr Olsen, perceived until recently as something of a carping whinger -to the point that his party has kept his voice off campaign advertisements - tried a little poetic levity yesterday when asked how many seats he expected to win. "Just enough, to get me over the line, will suit me fine," he said. Tony Wright's politics column. - Page 9 John Bannon

25 Nov 1989 - Labor steams ahead in Qld but a close call likely in SA Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 25 November 1989, page 9 Labor steams ahead in Qld but a close call likely in SA NOT SURPRISINGLY, opin ion polls focused on the South Australian and Queensland State elections this week where very different issues seemed to be at stake. The Morgan Gallup poll, released in the Bulletin magazine, indicated that a close finish was likely in South Australia, while the Labor Party moved steadily ahead in Queensland. The poll suggested that the ALP would have won a Queensland state election late last month, with dwindling support for the Liberal and National Parties. It said that, after Premier Cooper's election announcement, support for the ALP increased 7 per cent to 53 per cent and the Nationals' slipped 1 percent to 19 percent. Liberal support fell to 19 per cent - a 9 per cent decline. . It was conducted in the last weekend in October and the first two in November. The Australian's Newspoll backed up the Morgan Gallup poll's conclusions, showing that the ALP had established a firm lead for the December .2 election. It suggested that most Queensland voters were concerned with corruption, the economy, and education, followed by health and the environment, and that they saw the ALP as being able to deal with these issues most effectively. The ALP only fell short on the issue of economy in the state's provincial cities, western and far northern areas, and country zones, when competing with a combined conservative vote. The poll was based on 1010 telephone interviews conducted from November 9 to 12. The Morgan Gallup poll highlighted that the outcome of the South Australian election would rest with Australian Democrat and minor party preferences. Voting in the election is today. South Australian voter sentiment has undergone substantial changes since a Morgan Gallup poll earned out in October-November. Support j for the ALP slipped 4 per cent to 45 per cent, the Liberal-National parties .climbed to 45 per cent from 38 per cent, the Democrats were down 4 per cent to 7 per cent, and others were on 3 per cent. The result was reinforced by an ABC poll conducted in the South Australian seat of Haywood last j week. This showed a 4 per cent swing against the ALP since the last election in 1985, indicating that the j Liberals would win the seat but not office if the turnaround was applied on a state-wide basis. South Australian Premier John Bannon, regularly touted as Australia's most popular Premier, saw his personal popularity decline 10 per cent to" 58 per' cent. His Liberal counterpart, John Olsen, gained 9 per cent in a climb to 32 per cent. The poll was conducted with 607 voters on November 18 and 19. - HELEN SEIDEL

29 Nov 1989 - Moleskins and Nationals part of the uniform in Goombungee Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 29 November 1989, page 3 Moleskins and Nationals part of the uniform in Goombungee From ANDREW FRASER, in Queensland Goombungce, a town of some 200 people about 50km west of Toowoomba on the Darling Downs and boasting a wide main street containing hitching posts, a general store and a pub, may not be the epicentre of National Party territory in Queensland -but it can't be too far from it. It is in the electorate of Cunningham, the safest National Party seat in the state requiring a whopping 29.9 per cent swing to fall to the ALP, just up the road from Kingaroy, and still dependent on primary produce. The locals are under the impression that the Federal Government is a socialist Government but, being easy-going folk, they bear no ill-will toward the one ALP voter in town, whose particular voting habits seem a matter of public knowledge. And despite the safety of the National Party's margin, the Liberal Party is convinced it can win the scat and its candidate, Max Wilson, billed by his party organisation in Brisbane as a "mad bastard", has his picture up on a lot more trees in the electorate than the National Party man. Mr Wilson is an energetic vet - a handy profession for a prospective MP in a rural seat - from Oakey, the biggest town in the electorate, and he has been conspicuous in the electorate in recent weeks. So the local member, Tony Eiiiot, came to Goombungee yesterday with a portable PA he ran off his car's battery, determined that even if the party should lose Government on Saturday, at least Goombungee would remain safe for the National Party. Four school children and seven adults, only one of the latter under 70, sat in the main street listening to Mr Elliot's pitch, which was basically that the gerrymander delivered services to people in towns such as these, and the ALP team were really Bob Hawke and Paul Keating in disguise. "Most democracies in the western world under the Westminister [sic] system have some sort of electoral weighting, and in Queensland we actually have a lot less than many others," he said. "But you never hear them talking about that. Oh no, it's very fashionable to kick Queensland about down south you know. "But we are seeing the nation brought to its knees by the Hawke-Keating Government. You never even hear Goss talking about the fact that he is a Labor man, but if you get their manifesto and look at it, you'll see that it is exactly the same." Mr Elliot is only 45, a comparatively young man in the National Party, and he wore the countryman shirt, moleskins and elastic-sided boots that seem to be the uniform of the rural MP. He stressed to his audience that schools and roads in the electorate had improved markedly and, if the electoral system were changed, then the power would rest with Brisbane, the Gold Coast, the Sunshine Coast and Toowoomba, rather than with them. The result - dirt roads and further to go to schools. Meanwhile, back in Brisbane, the National Party has softened its hard line against a coalition with the Liberal Party, and yesterday Mr Cooper said only that he would predict a "conservative" victory on Saturday, rather than a National Party victory. However, the latest poll shows that the , ALP is still well ahead. The Morgan Gallup Poll to be published in today's Bulletin shows support in Queensland for the ALP at 53 per cent, the Liberal Party at 19 per cent, and the National Party at 29 percent.

01 Dec 1989 - Liberals' Innes wishes good riddance to Sparkes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 1 December 1989, page 3 Liberals' Innes wishes good riddance to Sparkes By ANDREW FRASER The Liberal Party is approaching tomorrow's election in Queensland as the party with clean hands, and at a time when politics are on the nose it is making a virtue out of not being in power at cither state or federal level. A vote for the Queensland Liberal Party is very much a protest vote - to tell the State Government you don't want corruption, and the Federal Government you don't want high interest rates. Yet according to a Morgan Gallup poll conducted on Wednesday night the Liberals command only 20 per cent support in Queensland. One reason is the performance of their leader, Angus Innes, whose popularity dropped dramatically. Mr Innes was the final speaker in the Brisbane Press Club's series of lunches at Dooley's Hotel, which ironically under a previous owner was one of the hotbeds of vice that came under the spotlight of the Fitzgerald Inquiry. He devoted half his speech to an attack on the ALP and a quarter to an attack on the National Party, including a savage attack on the National Party's president, Sir Robert Sparkes. "And as the chapter closes on the history of the National Party Government, one of the greatest benefits will be the end of the domination of Queensland public life by Sir Robert Sparkes, the party official, never elected by the people of Queensland, who has stood over his par ty, the Government and the state through influence and manipulation," he said. "He has been given unprecedented power, power that flies in the face of our democratic tradition, and the principles of good government. He has imposed a totally unacceptable personal rule on Queensland. "He. must take a lion's share of the responsibility for the perversion of public administration that has been created in Queensland in recent years.' "While he leads the National Party, the National Party has sunk farther and further into the quicksand of corruption and maladministration. "Every conservative voter who feels betrayed and let down by Sir Robert Sparkes and the Nationals must turn their vote to the Liberals - not just to end the National Party Government, but to drive Sir Robert Sparkes out of Queensland public affairs." As for the ALP, "in every case where the people have called the Labor Party to govern, they have failed", Mr Innes said. "The formula for Labor throughout the 1980s has been the same everywhere - ,they find a presentable bland frontman who won't upset anyone and who looks OK on TV, and they put him up as leader of the motley factionalised group of ex-union and party hacks who make up the rest of the Government, and who they keep well hidden and silent throughout the election." The question the Liberals are studiously avoiding is what they will do if the National Party needs their support for a coalition government. The Liberals have said that they will serve in a coalition only if they are the senior partner, which means they must win at least 23 seats if Angus Innes is to be the next Premier. This is a tall order for a party which currently has 11 seats, and senior party officials concede they could actually lose five seats - Mt Isa, Nundah, Ashgrove, Yeronga, and Stafford. The aim of the Liberals in this election is to get back the section of the conservative vote that they lost to the Nationals in first the 1983 then the 1986 election, and their best hope for doing that is on the Gold Coast south of Brisbane, the Sunshine Coast to the north, and around the Darling Downs area. Former premier Mike Ahem said yesterday that he did not believe the Liberals would gain more seats than the Nationals in Saturday's poll. Although previously strongly opposed to a National-Liberal coalition, he said any form of conservative coalition would be better than a Labor government. The State Electoral Office says voting will go ahead in the far and central west despite widespread flooding. Pryor'8 view. - Page 8. Liberals face a painful squeezing out - Page 9.

Losing a favourite son and gaining a politician Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 11 December 1989, page 9 ! % Bob Hawke talks about political life, foreign debt and personal pursuits to John Macgregor in his interview to mark the Prime Minister's 60th birthday last Saturday. i Eosing a favourite son and gaining a politician IN THE middle of our interview, an aide stuck' his head in the door and told the Prime Minister he was required in a division. What scenario did he see in terms of a new ALP leadership? "I simply refuse to address that. I just don't take lypothetical questions. I never have." He thought for a moment. "I profoundly believe that this next election is the most important elec tion for Australia since 1949 - for it will determine the nature and quality of the Australia that we take into the 21st century. This had added to the debt problem at the moment, but in the future it's going to be a very significant source of foreign income to us." Was Hawke happy that the debt (and the restructuring being proposed to deal with it) is shaping as a major election issue? "I'm more than content to face the issue, both intrinsically and in terms of the Opposition's posi tion." When the foreign debt arises, everyone seems to turn on the Government. One rarely hears the private sector criticising itself for lack of creativity or initiative. "The statistics are very interesting-62 per cent of the foreign debt is by the private sector. It is their decisions which have increased it. The Commonwealth Government has no net foreign debt. We are a net foreign creditor.". . . . , v, ^,v Could Hawke be more specifiocon 'what'" can be done to reduce the debt - in particular to lustimulate *v exports m and rfeplace imports^ orfi j "One doesn't have to be theoretical about this. These things are being done. What we've got now is the most massive microeconomic restructuring that has ever occurred. "There's the deregulation of the financial markets, the entry of foreign banks, the massive tariff cuts, and the ending of the two-airline system. "There's the deregulation of the monopoly in the wheat transport industry. There's the award restructuring. There's a massive change in education, training and re-training. "Now, for 31 of the last 34 years the conservatives have been in power. All the structures and practices of Australia were the product of 31 years of conservative Government. "In my seven years we have done more to change those structures than have ever been thought about in the past." The Hawke Government has considerable respect for Australia's newspapers and reacts to reportage with great agility. But is the "respect" for the newspapers' power or the journalists' skill and integrity? Paul Keating, for one, regards most senior members of the Canberra press gallery as hopelessly backward. How did Hawke judge the quality of . Australian political analysis? < "Quite frankly, I think the standard of political analysis and reporting is very, very mediocre. I don't say that just in terms of how they treat the Government. It's across the board. There's a bit of a herd instinct, and there's a lot of laziness. I could give you example after example where they've just been so fundamentally wrong. "And I'm not saying this in a bitchy way. It's rather from a sense of disappointment. There's a paradox, too. The electorate has become somewhat more sophisticated in the eighties - but that is to a large extent despite the Canberra press gallery. "Television is now more important. You have the opportunities to get directly to the people, with out the intervention of k $ppn thp ran?/ incompetent media." IS seen me mosi What did he mean, ralia chirp 1949 specifically, by "incomraua since uyj ?etent media"? is the focus too narrow, the economic understanding faulty? "Well it's a mixture. I mean, as a trained economist I find it a little bit amusing to see some of those people..." He laughed aloud for the first time. "I can't name names. I mean, I would off the record-one or two stick very much in my mind. But when I see some of those of people - who wouldn't know a propensity to consume from an alcoholic problem -writing about matters economic with apparent profundity, I get a little bit amused, and, I must say, disappointed. "Also," he added, "they are tremendously judgmental. But when they've been proved wrong, you spend your time in vain looking for any acknowledgement of error." The Head of Strategic and Defence Studies at the ANU, Dr Des Ball, states that Soviet missile and satellite launches are monitored from the United States' base at Nurrungar in South Australia, and that this information is used in "Star Wars" research. This contradicts an "unqualified assurance" given to Hawke by the US Administration that US bases on our soil play no part in the "Star Wars" program. "The assurances we have been given are accurate and well-founded... There is an unbelievable degree of misinformation, prejudice and paranoia about this issue. "The facts are very simple - they're not complicated. The joint facilities in this country have played an integrally important part in maintaining the absence of conflict. They enable us to do two things: a monitoring of existing agreements between the superpowers and they provide an early warning system." I RANG Dr Ball to get his view on this. "I go to the Pentagon every two months," he said. "I go into the Strategic Defence Initiative ["Star Wars"] program, and I see the information from Nurrungar. I mean, it's not a big issue: the SDI is dying anyway. "But the reason I bring it up - whenever I see Defence Minister Beazley for instance - is to try and force a bit of honesty onto these people. The facts are that Nurrungar's job is to monitor Soviet missile launches, and that this information does and up with the SDI program." I asked Hawke what cultural pursuits he had. Books, for instance? "I used to be an avid reader. But the volume of reading required for this job is just staggering. So that two or three weeks I take off over Christmas and New Year - that's the only time I get to, say, read a novel. "In the last brecfk I took great pleasure in reading Peter Carey's Booker Prize novel [Oscar and Luanda], I thought it was just brilliant. I loved that. Just a fantastic piece of writing." Films? "I don't go out to the cinemas. Occasionally I see a video, but it would be dishonest to say that I had any outstanding favourites. I find that a bit of a disappointment, because I've got great pride in the Australian film industry. "Every time I go overseas Australian films get talked about. It's across the range too: our quality feature films and, when I was in the United Kingdom in the middle of this year, I was just staggered by the number of people who talked about Neighbours. It was just about every second person -which is great." Was he a Neighbours fan himself? He laughed, looked at the ground, became uncharacteristically sheepish and - obviously keen to retain the Neighbours vote - muttered something semi-inaudible about "not having time". What were his musical tastes? "Very much classical. In my office I've got a large player. Most of the time I have classical music playing in the background." Which composers did he like? "The two discs I have there at the moment are the Beethoven Triple Concerto, which I'm enjoying very much. And also I've got two violin concertos - the Bruch and the Mendelssohn." The Prime Minister is going on leave around December 15. What did he intend to do. on his holidays? "It's pretty difficult to go to a holiday resort, and have an unintruded break. So I tend to go to Kirribilli and lay in the sun and read, or play a game of golf, or play with the grandchildren. It's the easiest - and, I must say, very salubrious." Blind Freddie could predict that Labor will, at the very least, get a rebuff at the next federal election. Perhaps the best trouble-predictor is the steady disappearance of what Bob Menzics described as "Australia's great middle class". While the poor shall always be with us - indeed their families are roughly static - middle-income earners are shrinking as a group. Higher-income earners ($50,000. plus in 1986 dollars) - who only accounted for 15 percent of the population in 1976' - now make up more than 30 per cent. These demographics are tricky for the Govern ment. While Rene Rivkin and his ilk flirted with Labor during its second and third terms, the better-off will now be increasingly tempted to vote Liberal. The Liberals' economic policies - replacement of capital gains tax; simpler and lower tax scales -will suit them nicely. (Though it must be added that the Liberals won't spell out details or costings of their tax scales till they attain Government.) For Labor this may leave the shrinking middle class, and the electorally unreliable poor, from whom to win a majority of the Lower House's 148 seats in 1990. Hawke's speech was powerful, concise, succinct and fact-laden Cliff-hangers in Victoria, Western Australia and South Australia also point to a very difficulty federal election. Saulwick polls confirm it. They gave Hawke approval ratings in the mid-60s in 1984. Now he's in the low 30s. This personal element in Labor's declining popularity is undoubtedly important. After seven years of Hawke as Prime Minister, many Australians feel they have lost a favourite son and gained another politician. Hazel Hawke (one of the warmest and most unpretentious women in Australian public life) is being given a higher profile, in an effort to "humanise" Hawke. But the Hawke we knew at the other end of the decade was consummately human. MANY people miss this Hawke of old, and want him to throw away the script occasionally. (A few of his answers to my questions were almost verbatim quotes from his Evatt Lecture.) His rare spontaneous comments - like the one to the "silly old bugger" - are gleefully picked up by the media, which runs with th$m for days, if not weeks. Ten years ago Hawke gloried in such frank, public conflict: today he issues letters of apology. Peacock refused to comment for this article. But Democrat Leader Janine Haines (who looks like taking one of Labor's Lower House seats herself) was happy to speak with her accustomed frankness. "Out in the community Hawke is perceived as a man who has lost his way. He is appearing on television, and even in the print media, to be inarticulate in a way he never appeared before. The arm movements, the body language, are all becoming uncoordinated," she said. "And people are reacting to that - perhaps subliminally - and assuming that he is uncoordinated in policy direction as well. Of course, the pressures on a Prime Minister are incomparable. While most of us can afford the luxury of permanent equivocation of most issues -or of never thinking them through at all - a Prime Minister is allowed no such indulgence. He is put on the spot on a huge range of matters, virtually daily. In these, he must not merely comprehend the detail, but balance the impact of his eveiy pronouncement on one interest group (or faction, or country) against another. Little wonder Prime Ministers lose their spontaneity. For all that, Hawke looks neither stooped nor tired - as some have alleged. Indeed that taut body, and those steely eyes, exude a vigour that will make him one of the best-preserved sexagenarians in the country. At the end of the interview when he was being photographed, a flash of the old Hawke crept through. "Trust me," said the photographer, who got him to pose in this way and that. He complied for a few moments and then said from the side of his mouth, in a thick European accent: "Trust me. I'm from the Government." And roared with laughter. John Macgregor is a freelance journalist living in Adelaide. The part one interview appeared last Saturday.

30 Dec 1989 - Writers' World Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 December 1989, page 17 By MAURICE DUNLEVY Politics and good news seen as box office poison WHEN THE Berlin Wall was breached recently commentators told us that it was one of the most historic events of the postwar world. But American television ratings told us the story was box-office poison. As thousands scaled the wall and hundreds of thousands poured into West Berlin, millions of Americans tuned out their TVs from what commentators said were wonderfully moving pictures of freedom sweeping all before it. Freedom can, of course, be interesting news. The freeing of a girl trapped in a well and of three whales trapped in pack icc greatly outrated the freeing of the oppressed in Europe. They were nice little melodramas of freedom with a beginning, a middle and an end. But the lack of interest in political freedom in the land of the free worried newspaper columnists such as Russell Baker and Art Buchwald. They said the trouble was that a breached wall, freedom and falling communist dominoes was good news. And in spite of what they tell pollsters, people don't like good news, particularly if they have to know history and geography to understand it. Buchwald had his network president telling his news executives, "When will you all learn that a little freedom on television can go a long way?" Asked whether they should cut back on Gorbachev too, the president replies, "No, his ratings are still okay. I wouldn't want to have him on every night, but the guy does have charisma." My theory is that good news is only half the problem. The other half is that it's political news - and people aren't keen on that either. Only one in three of 800 voters surveyed in a recent Saulwick Age Poll said they were very interested in news items about politics. One in two said they were moderately in terested. But given the fact that there's often a gap between what people say they like and what they really attend to, the proportions of political news consumers are probably considerably smaller. For most people most of the time political news is a bit of a bore. And yet a high proportion of news in serious broadsheets and in serious radio and television news programs is news of politics. Moreover, politicians, professional communicators, lobbyists, interest group advocates, the politically triumphant and the politically aggrieved arc climbing over the top of each other to become part of it. They realise that if you want to play the game of politics today, the news media provide the most public arena in which to play it. The media have improved the quality and speed of the information disseminated to citizens and changed its nature. They have allowed politicians to bypass some of the traditional power structures and talk directly to the people via TV and radio. They have helped make the reputations of politicians such as Hawke and Keating and ruin those of a Billy McMahon or an Arthur Calwell; They also help people choose between' parties, policies and politicians, and express divisions and choices in society. But they have also heightened political conflicts and stereotyped adversaries. They have created their own mass-mediated "reality" of politics - a reality that concentrates largely on stones of political actors rather than on analyses of issues and processes, on dramas and melodramas starring elite people rather than on issues an institu tions. Moreover, they have presented them in self-contained dramatic capsules, like the rescue of the girl from the well and the whales from the ice, so that they lack continuity and explanatory power. In other words, they have given us political news that is personalised, dramatised, fragmented, normalised and simplified - news full of "tax dodgers", "welfare bludgers", "special interests", "fat cats", "Iron Ladies" and "Great Communicators". Political news may be boring, but it's clearly important, as Rodney Tiffen demonstrates in News and Power (Allen and Unwin, 255pp, $19.95 paper). His investigations of the relationship between news and politics in Australia is based on open-ended interviews with 223 journalists and a comparative study of news stories, mainly about federal elections and 23 party leadership challenges between 1968 and 1965. It has chapters on the Australian mass media, newsgathcring, news values, public relations in politics, leaks and briefings, election campaigns, leadership challenges and agenda-setting. Its key propositions arc that political news is the product of the interaction of institutions; it is strongly influenced by political groups who have realised it is the central arena in which to play politics; and its most important impact is not on passive readers and viewers but on active political people and groups. News is certainly the product of the interaction between institutions, as Leon V. Sigal demonstrat Art Buchwald cd in his study of The New York Times and The Washington Post. News organisations arc themselves classic bureaucracies and their little bureaucrats gather most of their news from other bureaucracies because this reduces uncertainty about'what. isine\ys;,it can be done routinely, arid it legitimates what is news because it emanates from elites. Tiffen found; much the', same, iri' Australia although he expresses it; less elegantly. Political newsgathering is organised into rounds; reporters frequent official fountains of facts; they pick up and qualify official releases; they bounce them off opponents; they get tip-offs and trade-ofis by cultivating sources, and they treat them with restraint and responsibility if they know they will have to return to them regularly. They welcome leaks. They value cabinet members more than backbenchers, ministers more than shadow ministers. In some fields, such as business, they may get so close to their sources that they adopt their values. But most political news is not produced by journalists who arc deliberate propagandists. Journalists have to make their decisions under the pressure of deadlines. They must choose from an over-supply of news and from a wealth of exceptional cases. Consequently decision-making in news bureaucracies is preoccupied with immediate practical problems; it's concerned with concrete solutions rather than long-term strategies or general principles; and it's biased against coherence and reflection. Journalists are influenced by their news values - they need them as props to simplify their choices. They are influenced by the " need to appeal to large audiences, ? by competition between newsgath- . ering organisations and by compcti- . tion with other journalists, ? ,, including those in their own organi sation. Their image of their audience is ' more a product of gut feeling rather , than audience surveys. The pressure of competition encourages conformity and consensual news judgments by rival organisations but also encourages bcat-ups from individual journalists. It increases the power of sources who play one journalist off against another but it also keeps journalists on their toes. . Political news may not rate well against whales but it docs absorb " political players, who try to shape ?and manipulate it and use it for , their own ends. Tiffcn estimates . that the number of people em ployed in public relations grew ten- , fold between the mid-1960s and the mid-1980s, and if you add to this ' the exponential growth in pollsters,; political strategists, special consul-. tants and other shamans, you get a big industry. These people arc out to market . their programs, their protests, their parties or their bosses. They are .. professionals and most of them . know what reporters need, even if in supplying it they don't always get. what they want. Tiffen explores ?, some of their manoeuvres in the ; chapters on PR and election campaigns. In the chapters on leaks and briefings he concentrates more on, the manipulations of politicians . themselves. In his concluding chapter he ar-. gues that "politics as we know it is inconccivable without the news . media. They arc the central forum of political communication in modern democracies. Battles for favour able news coverage are a major, arena in political conflicts, and the news provides a common reference' point to which the different sides ; relate in their subsequent actions -... However, the media arc under-' equipped for this overwhelming re- ' sportsibility >- ip"." "" But for all their inadequacies/ -they do influence politics, mainly ' becd'ii'se'thby; aird'adydtVea'to'discJo-.'! sure' and -&mmcntary.fiTliey affect ; the timing!' marinbr and extent of ' revelations about powerful groups ? and make official secrecy;: machine politick and abuse of corporate power, more precarious. In other . words; they perform a useful watch dog function. One would think that a book about such colourful institutions could not be dull, but that undcres-' limatcs the power of academia to make anything dull. Covering much the same subjects, New York Times Pulitzer-prizewinning journalist Hedrick Smith produced a national bestseller in the United, states in 1988 with The Power. Game: How Washington Works. He personalised, dramatised, fragmented and simplified the processes of power and political communication - and made them something you could take in with your whales in the pack ice and ' your girls in wells. Politics, he, showed, need not be dull. But Rodney Tiffen demonstrates,' no such powers of dramatisation. He has produced mainly academic; sludge, ill-written, poorly organised, dreadfully dull and reverberat ing with badly paraphrased echoes; of many of the American classics in' this field. Still, it's the only book ofits kind on the Australian scene, so; beggars can't be choosers..

30 Dec 1989 - Preferences key to parties' prospects Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 December 1989, page 9 Preferences key to parties' prospects IN 1989, the plethora of polls about federal voting intentions showed that support for the Liberal-National Coalition varied little throughout the year, but support for the ALP was highly erratic. The Coalition's support rarely dropped below 40 per cent and rarely rose above 45 per cent, while the ALP's support reached a low of 33 per cent in the Saulwick poll in April and a high of 46 per cent in the Morgan Gallup poll in October. ' But this is not quite the good hews it initially seems for the Coalition, as when the ALP's support has shown these periodic drops the Coalition does not pick up all the dissatisfied vote, which instead is mostly going to the Australian Democrats or minor parties. Another omen for the Coalition is that even when the polls consistently were looking good for them, they still needed about 50 per cent of the preferences of the Australian Democrats and other minor parties to win. In the 1987 election the Australian Democrats' preferences ran about 2 to 1 in favour of the ALP, and given the Democrats' recent performences, most of their support would seem to be coming from disaffected ALP voters rather than disaffected coalition voters. The Coalition's best performance was in April, when the Saulwick poll showed ALP support at 33 percent and Coalition support at 45 per cent, while the Morgan Gallup poll showed the ALP at 42 per cent and the Coalition at 46 percent. One of the great ironies of the year's polls is that this was just before the then Leader of the Opposition, John Howard, was replaced in this role by Andrew Peacock. The Opposition's other high point came in early November, when the Morgan Gallup poll showed its support at 46 per cent and the ALP at 41 per cent, while the Saulwick poll showed the ALP at 36 per cent and the coalition at 43 percent. This came after the release of the Coalition's Economic Action Plan. The. year began with both parties at level pegging, and it finished with them close or inconclusive enough to be again on level pegging, with the Morgan Gallup poll showing the ALP at 43 per cent and the Coalition at 45 per cent, and the Newspoll showing the ALP at 44.5 per cent and the Coalition at 40 per cent. 01 Jan 1990 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 1 January 1990, page 8 CEhc Catikrra (Eimis Monday, January 1, 1990 Room for optimism about the 1990s TIE decade of the 90s, which the world enters today in the vernacular if not in fact, is already showing more positive signs than any other this century. There is less conflict between nations than at almost any time this century. In '.Eastern Europe over the past year, gigantic strides in liberalisation of totalitarian regimes have occurred — more amazingly, they have occurred with the blessing, and sometimes the assistance of the Soviet ,regime. There has been major progress in disarmament, and superpower tensions have probably not been lower for 40 years. Quite apart from the new freedoms in the Soviet bloc, a number of nations in Africa and South America have made substantial progress to democracy over the year. Even South Africa saw substantial reform, though it has far to go. Only in China could it be said that there was a turn for the worse, with the crushing of student protest at Tiananmen Square. Conflict, and 'famine, persisted in the Horn of Afri ca and Israel continued to fail to come to terms with the Palestinians; despite an international peacekeeping conference the problems of Cambodia were not resoived. There is still war and active violation of human rights and freedoms in a number of nations of Central South America. Yet if 1989 did not see a resolution of all these problems, it saw some progress with most of them and the situation did not get worse. All seemed more tractable this year or this decade. There is a lot of scope for optimism. This optimism is reflected in a recent Saulwick Poll, where Austra, lian respondents were asked about their opinion on the world's pro• spects and the likelihood of major ' war. A similar poll had been con^ ducted at the end of 1979. A decade ■ ago, 66 per cent of respondents , thought there would be an increase in international conflict and instability over the next decade, and 23 per cent thought the level would remain ; the same. Only 8 per cent thought the \,level, of tension and conflict would decline.: J.he, poll ,^X thQ^ndj of 1989 ■« • "sa w44> percent thinking-there would'' be reduced conflict over the next 10 • years; 29 per cent thinking it would "' MIMjW 'dbyii^the 'saifiifej' 'and 'only .23 :i>» , per cent thought it would get worse." _ A decadejago, 19 per cent thought a • major war was very likely in the next : decade; today only 3 per cent think •j so. 15 per cent now think a major " war quite likely, compared with 37 " per cent a decade ago. 79 per cent '.think such a major war is unlikely or - very unlikely, compared with 43 per cent a decade ago. If there are some positive signs ."that the world may become a more peaceful place, there are also grounds for taking an optirpistic view of human progress and of the-world in " general. Environmental conscious ness is now much stronger; there is developing international cooperation on the problems of pollution, the greenhouse effect, on the ozone layer and rather more being done about conservation of natural resources. To be sure, some of the galvanisation, both at a national and international level, has occurred only after .the damage done has become too evident and the repair jobs that will be necessary may be the more difficult for their belatedness. On the other hand, the resources a freer, more stable world may be able to throw at the problem may now be the greater. The increased awareness by politicians of environmental issues has followed rather than led popular opinion. Australia is p good example of this. In the past decade, politicians have assiduously wooed the "green vote", indeed, capturing this vote for the Labor Party is now one of its major political strategies, and perhaps the most obvious example of where the economic pragmatism of the Hawke Government takes second place to pure politics. The debate about development is still fierce, but the rules have changed profoundly and in many cases environmental consciousness has the inside running. In the next decade the rules of sustainable development will have to be worked out; if Australia, or other countries, are going to grow or even maintain their place, some value judgments will have to be made. This has always been so, but at least now a proper consciousness of the environment and the need to preserve it is well to the fore. THE area in which there has been least progress is in. ordinary community relations. For a country such as Australia — still, despite the economic storms it has weathered over the past decade, a prosperous community capable of providing well for all — the evidence is in areas such as drug abuse, suicide and the appalling problems of those who do not share in the community's well-being: Aborigines, homeless children and so on. At a world level; the north-south divide, is now starkly, more ' prominent'"than-< Hastiest,' and the economic conditions of the 1980s have, generally, worsened the, positions of most Third-World coun- • tries.' '' It is always simplistic to say that the opportunity cost of a battleship or a fighter aircraft is a hospital or an agricultural program. But the marked reduction of world tensions, and the evidence that military spending might now begin to fall, gives the world powers, even Australia, an opportunity to rededicate resources never previously available to programs and systems which improve the lot of all. It may still be too much to hope for. But in this last decade of the 20th century, the prospects have never seemed as bright.

03 Jan 1990 - Govt would win: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 3 January 1990, page 2 Govt would (win: poll • SYDNEY: Australians are gloomy about the year ahead but are likely to return the Hawke Gov ernment to power, according to two Morgan Gallup Polls conducted late.last year. Published in the latest issue of the Bulletin, one poll conducted in December showed support for the ALP was up one percentage point to 43 per cent and sup-port for the Coalition was down 1.5 to 43 per cent. With the Democrats polling 10 per cent and others 4 per cent, the Hawke Government would have been returned on preferences, the report said. Prime Minister Bob Hawke's approval rating was up three points to 46 per cent, the highest since mid-September. His dis-approval rating fell three points to 44 per cent. Opposition leader Andrew Peacock's approval rating was unchanged at 31 per cent. Fifty-nine per cent of respondents (up three percentage points) said Mr Hawke would make the better prime minister, with 26 per cent preferring Mr Peacock. Although Mr Hawke has always out-stripped Mr Peacock as the preferred prime minister, the December result was the highest margin since mid-September. Support for the Liberal Party was down half a percentage point to 37 per cent and support for the Nationals fell one point to 6 per cent. A separate poll conducted in Novem- Bob Hawke: Approval rating at 46 per cent. ber showed that only 8 per cent (down 4 per cent) of those surveyed expected 1990 to be a year of of economic prosperity while 44 per cent expected a year of diffi-culty. Around 48 per cent (down 8 per cent) thought the economy would remain the same or did not know. Thirty-six per cent (up 3 per cent) ex-pected more strikes and industrial dis-putes, with 17 per cent expecting a decrease in industrial disruption.

06 Jan 1990 - Low-key PM wins back some ground Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 6 January 1990, page 9 Low-key PM wins back some ground A STINT away from the national spotlight seems to be making the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, more popular with voters, according to a recent Morgan Gallup poll. Mr Hawke's approval rating rose 3 percentage points to 46 per cent, his highest since mid-September, when the pilots dispute really started to have an effect on the population. But his popularity is still well down from the heady days early in his administration, when he commanded an approval rating of 75 per cent in March 1984. Mr Hawke's approval rating last year was consistently below 50 per cent, reaching a low of 41 percent in early November, although in the most recent federal election, in 1987, his approval rating was 58 per cent. The consequence of this decline in popularity is that in the coming election campaign the ALP plans to focus attention on other senior ministers, in particular the Minister for Industry, Technology and Commerce, Senator John Button, and the Minister for Primary Industry, John Kerin. In regard to leadership, the ALP will focus on contrasting Mr Hawke directly with his Opposition counterpart, Andrew Peacock, whose approval rating, ^'whi'ch'-has-beeti fajr^'steady.since-he: resumed, leader*, ship of the Opposition, stands at 31 per cent. Overall, the two parties are still level-j>egging, with support for the ALP up one percentage point to 43 per cent and for the Coalition down 1.5 points to 43 per cent. The Australian Democrats' support seems to be firm jj^iftg'at somewhere between 9 and 10percent.nationally,i although in Adelaide,'the'home to\vri of the party's' leader, Janine Haines, the latest Morgan Gallup poll shows it running at 17 per cent. Other parties are generally polling around 5 per cent, and it is the preferences of this body plus the Australian Democrats — around 15 per cent of the electorate — which will decide the next federal election.
