10 Jan 1990 - NSW, Vic Govts faced dismissal, poll shows Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 10 January 1990, page 2 NSW, Vic Govts faced dismissal, poll shows SYDNEY: Voters would have changed the Governments in NSW and Victoria in December, according to Morgan Gallup polls published in today's Bulletin magazine. In NSW, the Coalition picked up half a percentage point since the November survey to poll one point behind the Australian Labor Party, which lifted half a point to 42.S per cent. Although the Democrats were down two points to 7 per cent, the report said their preferences would have ensured an ALP win. The Premier, Nick Greiner, remained the preferred leader by 48 per cent of respondents, up one point, compared to Opposition Leader Bob Carr, who remained steady on 32 per cent. Support for the ALP Government in Victoria rose one point to 41 per cent, while that for the Coalition fell two points to 44., The Democrats polled 10 per cent and others 5 per cent. Their prefer-' ences would have ensured an ALP defeat, the. report said. The Premier, John Cain, remained the preferred leader, with 50 per cent (down one point) over Opposition Leader Alan Brown, who was unchanged on 32 per cent. In Tasmania, support for the ALP ' fell three points to 40 per cent compared with July-August, while that for the Liberals remained steady on 44 per cent. Support for the Democrats rose one point to 3 per cent, and support for others rose two point to 13 per cent, enough to buoy up an ALPGreen Independent coalition. The Opposition's Robin Gray was the preferred leader, with his approval rating rising 10 points to 54 per cent, well ahead of Premier Michael Field, whose rating was up three points to 45 per cent. Forty-seven per cent (up seven) of those polled said Mr Gray would make the better Premier compared with the 41 per cent (down one) preferring Mr Field.

10 Jan 1990 - Losing the battle against drug use and crime Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 10 January 1990, page 9 Losing the battle against drug use and crime Yoiith suicide and drug use, as well as violence and crime, are increasing. Richard Eckersley suggests some reasons in the third of ci four-part series on the social impact of rapid economic and technological change. , THE PERSONAL and social costs of both the specific and more general consequences of rapid social, economic and technological changes are clearly apparent in the rising rates of depression and suicide among youth, and in the "wars" we are fighting, and losing, against drugs and crimc. There is now good evidence that in western societies depressive illness, once regarded as a malady of the. middle-aged and elderly, has become more common among teenagers and young'adults, with the increase particularly marked among those born after World War II. While depression has historically been two to three times more common in women than men, this difference may now be narrowing because of the increasing rate of depression among young men. In Australia, suicide among males aged 15-24 has-trebled over the past three decades. Suicide has also risen, but less dramatically, for men up to the age of 35. It fell among mefn over 40, most significantly among those in their 50s, until a few years ago, but has since increased in these' age groups as well. The overall,suicide rate for men in 1987 reached 22 per. 100,000, just two short of the highest level this century — 24, during the Great Depression, when the unemployment rate climbed.to 28 per cent. Suicide among females does not show the same pattern, and has fallen significantly sincc peaking in the mid-1960s (particularly among older women; it has fallen little, if at all, among young %vomen).. Many personal and social factors have been implicated in suicide. The pioneering French sociologist, Emile Durkheim, argued that suicide was related to the degree of social integration and cohesion in a society and thus the likelihood of individual isolation and alienation. Several of the pos siblc explanations for the difference between suicide trends for men and women relate to this factor. For example, men (and, in particular, young men) may feel more exposed 'to the pressures of a changing, more competitive and less structured world, with its greater financial and social uncertainties. On the other hand, social changes of the past two decades have, perhaps after an initial period of confusion and uncertainty (which may have contributed to the mid1960s peak in female suicide), improved the status of women and, with their greater participation in the'workforce, have led to greater freedom and independence. Women also still have the option of a fulfilling roje in the home, and so may be less affected by unemployment, while better welfare provisions have improved the situation of unmarried, divorced or widowed mothers. Some evidence suggests that young boys arc worse affected than girls by family breakdown, and that boys tend to have a bleaker, more hopeless view of the world and the future; if true, these factors might conceivably also ,play. a part in patterns of youth suicide. / '/ THERE is anpthcr,quite different, possi ble explanation'of the different trends in male and female suicide: more women today survive /suicide attempts because of advances' in intensive-care technologies. Women tend to prefer poisoning, often by "overdosing" on drugs, and so are more often saved through medical intervention than men, who tend to choose more certain methods such as shooting or hanging. The rate of attempted suicide is many times that'of successful suicide. The extent to whichj adolescent suicide has become part of our common experience is shown by a recent Saulwick poll, which found that 21 per cent of Australians (and 40 per cent of those aged 18-24) personally knew of teenagers who had attempted or committed suicide. • • At the beginning of the 1960s, the United States was the only country with a significant illegal drug problem, and international authorities believed they had the matter under control. Instead, the Parliamentary Joint Committee on the National Crime Authority notes in its report on Drugs, Crime and Society, that we have entered an era in which the consumption of illicit drugs "has increased beyond the most alarmist predictions". International trade in these drugs has become a $300 billion industry. Drug use has now become epidemic inmany parts of the world, especially among the young. In recent years, according to a World Health Organisation report, the average age of users has declined, and mul tiplc drug use has bccome more common. Around the world, authorities are admitting the war against drugs is being lost. In its report, the Parliamentary Joint Committee says that over the past two decades, Australia has devoted increased resources to drug-law enforcement, increased the penalties for drug trafficking and accepted increasing inroads on civil liberties as part of the battle to curb the drug trade. It concludes, "All the evidence shows, however, not only that our law enforcement agencies have not succeeded in preventing the supply of illegal drugs to Australian markets but that it is unrealistic to expect them to do so." Statistics indicate there has been at least a four-fold, and possibly eight-fold, increase in deaths due to heroin and other opiates in Australia since 1970. Heroin use may now have levelled, but we have probably yet to feel — because suppliers have yet to target us — the full impact of drugs such as cocaine and its potent derivative, crack, which has wreaked so much damage in the poorer districts of the US. On current trends, an American researcher told me, 70 per cent of marriageable-age black males will be dead in jail or addicted to drugs by the year 2000. US authorities now fear a new wave of heroin use because a boom in global opium production has pushed high-purity heroin on to the market. The purer heroin is easier to smoke, making it more attractive to those put off by syringes and the risk of AIDS. Hospital emergency admissions linked to heroin are already showing sharp rises in many parts of America. The illicit drugs arc not, of course, the only drug problem, or even the biggest in terms of their impact on health. The number of young people smoking cigarettes remains unacceptably high (and may still be rising), given what we know about its health effects. Today more young people are drinking' alcohol, they arc drinking at an earlier"age, ■ and they are drinking more: in the words of one study, "their frequent aim is to get drunk and get drunk quickly"; A recent survey of NSW students showed that almost a half of the boys and a third of the girls aged 16 drink on at least a weekly basis. Drug use is not a "pure" index of serious social malaise, and can be linked to factors such as supply — the more readily available, the greater the use — and cultural attitudes — the more fashionable or social-, ly acceptable, the more widespread the use. ' Availability and fashion would be major influences on the vast majority of users who take drugs only on an occasional or social basis. However, drug use, and particularly abuse, is also associated with'feelings of alienation and low self-esteem. Tougher penalties and education programs might dc-. ter those who use drugs because they are . available and trendy, but they are unlikely to put off those who turn to drugs out of emptiness, confusion and despair. r LIKE illicit drug use, violent crime is; mainly a resort of the young (especially males in their teens and twenties). It is also another indicator of our troubled timcs^ According to the Commission for the Future survey on change and the future, more than one out of 10 Australians believe crime and violence has become worse over the past 20 years, with 49 per cent saying it has become much worse; 75 per cent believe crime and violence will continue to worsen over the next 20 years. Crime statistics bear out the validity of this perception: in the past 15 years, for example, the rate of serious assault has risen four-fold, rape almost three-fold, and robbery two-and-a-half-fold. While these statistics have to be interpreted cautiously, and 'also reflect changes in reporting levels and ! legislation," there can be little doubt there has been a substantial rise in violent crime. This is borne out indirectly by changes in other factors that are "linked to criminal behaviour, including unemployment, poverty, family conflict, drug abuse and depres sion. Behind a problem like rising violence lies a complex interplay of factors, perhaps biological as well as social. As already noted, the incidence of depression is rising among young men. One study found that the wish to hurt other people was the second most common response to severe depression among teenage boys, after the desire to run away and ahead of thoughts of suicide. There is a I[nk between male hormone levels which rise at puberty, and aspects of aggression in boys in their mid-to-late teens, .but this relationship disappears within a few years as other more complex social influences comc into play. However, if these cultural constraints weaken or fail, either because of specific problems such as parental neglect, family conflict and unemployment, or a more general sense of alienation, then it seems likely that this tendency to violence could continue into later years, : and become more serious. Drugs, depres sion and exposure to violence in the media could reinforce this inclination. The explanations for the worsening problems of youth today are complex and incomplete. Many factors arc involved and they may interact in ways that create a vicious spiral of destruction from which individuals find it impossible to break free. Unless we understand and address the fundamental causes of the problems, it is unlikely we will ever resolve thctn. Tomorrow's conclusion: facing the problems and making decisions.

11 Jan 1990 - Brighter future requires a change of attitude Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 11 January 1990, page 9 Brighter future requires a change of attitude In the final of his four-part series, Richard Eckersley looks' at the costs of self-interest, and the alternatives for long-term, community benefits. WHILE the problems of youth suicide, drug abuse and violent crime are serious, it must be acknowledged that, for all the rising trends, they involve directly only a small proportion of the population. Their indirect impact can, however, be much wider. Hard drugs may claim only a few hundred lives each year, but they loom in the public consciousness as one of the greatest menaces to society, and are a major source of community anxiety. The social consequences of violent crime reach far beyond the perpetrators and victims to affect the entire community. As the National Committee on Violence has warned, Australians risk becoming more socially isolated because of exaggerated fears of ra ndom violence. These tears can intensify other tensions:"for example, parents become fearful of letting their children out of sight, thereby increasing the strain on family life. There is also the economic cost of rising crime. Despite the strong economic pressures on governments to reduce expenditure, NSW, for example, has almost doubled spending (in current dollars) on law and order since 1984-85 to $1.7 billion this financial year. The social deterioration that these problems signify is also apparent, in more subtle forms, in the population at large. Take the case of the alleged social conservatism and political apathy and cynicism of Australians today. The hardening of attitudes towards the disadvantaged is apparent from a longrunning survey conducted by Australian National University researchers, in which people have been asked what they thought the Government should do if faced with the choice of reducing taxes or spending more on social services. In 1967, 68 percent said more should be spent on social services; 26 per cent opted for tax cuts. Twenty years later, with poverty much greater, only 26 per cent said government should spend more on social welfare, while 72 per cent wanted lower taxes. Shifts in social and political mood tend to be most marked among youth, perhaps because of their energy, naivety and impetuosity, and so it is with this trend. Surveys suggest that the young take a tougher line on unemployment than older people, and that there has been a marked shift in this direc tion in the 1980s. A series of polls of people aged 15-24 by ANOP shows a swing in the perceived main causes of youth unemployment from social factors to personal. The proportion nominating "the apathetic attitude of young people", for example, climbed from 20 per cent in 1984 to 25 per cent in 1986 and 39 per cent in 1988, making it by far the most commonly cited cause. The conservatism does have a positive dimension. It suggests many young people are taking more responsibility for their own lives, buckling down, and working harder (and expecting the same of others). Today's youth seem less sullen and resentful than the youth of a decade ago — as if they are coming to terms with the harsher realities of life, and are determined to make the most of it. What is worrying, although understandable, is that this new self-reliance also appears to be associated with a new self-centredness and materialism. A tertiary teacher complained to me that, yes, kids were working harder these days, but they had no passion for learning. The overriding objective was to get good marks to get a good job that paid lots Of money. One consequence, he said, was that cheating had become much more common. Among youth today, there appears to be less interest in participating in the political processes of a democratic society, and a greater indifference to the plight of the disadvantaged and dispossessed. As a generation, they seem to have no more respect for "the system" than the youth of the 1960s and 1970s, but they have given up trying to change it — the problems, it seems, have become too big. Now they are intent on working the system to their own personal advantage. I have argued that the problems Australians face are resulting in a serious loss of confidence and purpose in ourselves as a nation and, in many cases, as individuals. I have also suggested that this failure of nerve has become so pervasive and serious that it will, unless overcome, effectively rule out any recovery from our predicament. Even without this explanation, the extent of our problems, across the entire economic, environmental and social spectrum, makes it clear that solutions will require much more than a fine-tuning of the status quo, and will have to embrace fundamental changes at the personal and social level. Australians seem to recognise this. When wc asked in the Commission for the Future survey what were the most important steps Australians needed to take, individually or as a nation, to manage change better and improve our future prospects, most responses (42 per cent) related to changes in personal values and behaviour: things such as working together, being more tolerant, working harder or taking more pride in our work, being less greedy, doing more for the country, and raising moral standards. The second largest group (29 per cent) concerned the need for better government, and reflected both a perceived need for more effective leadership and for people to take a more active part in politics. This was followed by more specific action such as strengthening the economy, improving education and protecting the environment. If we are to overcome our problems, and restore our sense of confidence and purpose, nationally and individually, then each : i one of us must look long and hard at our personal values and priorities. But the reassessment must also extend beyond the jsersonal, to reshape our social and political goals. At this level, we need to achieve a much better balance, integration, and reconciliation of economic, environmental and social objectives than currently exist. This is not a question of putting less effort into the generation of wealth, but more into its distribution and conservation. Furthermore, this balance must be expressed in an ideology or vision of who we are, what we believe, and where we want to go. One consequence of the recent shift in politics from ideology to management, especially economic management, has been that voters no longer have a wider, social context in which they can assess, and attempt to make sense of, a vast array of disparate policy issues. This, too, has contributed to our confusion. In a recent CSIRO occasional paper, I suggested that a national program of environmental restoration (involving, amongst other things, massive reforestation and revegetation) could provide one example of how economic, environmental and social objectives could be integrated in a major, highly visible, policy initiative. Benefits would include: Countering land degradation (costing us up to $2 billion a year), the greenhouse effect (growing trees is one of the most cost-effective approaches), and the threatened extinction of many of our unique plants and animals (clearing bush is the main threat). Maintaining the productivity of our agricul tural industries (by making them sustainable), increasing our timber resources (we have a $1 billion-plus annual trade imbalance in timber and related products), benefiting tourism (by enhancing the beauty of the Australian bush), and developing an export industry based on environmental management skills and technologies (an area where we have comparative advantages). ' Creating thousands of socially useful and. personally worthwhile jobs (thus reducing the high personal, social and economic cost of unemployment), as well as opportunities to provide training and affordable housing. In achieving all these things, the program could help to create a vision of an Australia that is vigorous and enterprising and, at the same time, far-sigh ted! and humane. It would help to engender among us the sense that we can tackle the problems confronting us and take charge of our national destiny. In doing this, it would help to overcome the growing disillusionment and cynicism with which Australians regard politics, and the dismay with which many view the future. In its report. The effectiveness of land degradation policies and programs, issued in November last year, the House of Repre scntatives Standing Committee on Environment, Rccrcation and the Arts recommended that the Federal Government convene a working group to evaluate the proposal and identify ways in which it could be implemented, noting that it "contains the breadth and depth of vision necessary to provide solutions to Australian's land-degradation problems". <\ This sort of program is not all that we need to resolve our difficulties. But it is a good example of an initiative that would , reflect the scale of endeavour and the values. •_ that we need, and in doing that, would help ' to bring about the change in social direction ) that we must make. There would be great value in linking ' environmental and social objectives. Envi-" ronmental protection and restoration is per- • haps the one thing Australians have;; indicated a ready willingness to pay for. The . environment is probably the one issue that J, can succeed in making us look beyond im mediate, personal self-interest towards the " long-term good of the whole community. J Circumstances will eventually force radi-,J cal changes upon modern society; economic -developments and environmental prob-" lems are already exerting this pressure. But .-) those societies that are the fastest, most positive and most visionary in their re sponse will be those that gain the greatest ^ advantage and suffer the least cost. ' ^ Australians face a choice between a na- ' tion in transition, or a nation in inexorable decline — a choice between making Austra-1 lia a more dynamic, independent, fair and far-sighted society, or allowing it to degen-.] erate into one that is strife-torn, impover- ' ished, fearful and subservient. , Despite taking some significant steps in ' the 1980s, we have yet to face up to our'' situation. The longer we delay in choosing,'rthe harder the right choice will become.' ' i

11 Jan 1990 - New direction for Victoria Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 11 January 1990, page 5 New direction for Victoria MELBOURNE: A major economic statement planned by the Victorian Government would make clear its policies and priorities for the 1990s, the Acting Premier, Joan Kirner, said yesterday. "The policies of the 1980s are not adequate for the 1990s and we will have to, over the next two months, make clear statements on our economic strategy and our social-justice programs," she said. Good government meant setting future directions, explaining them clearly, listening to people and getting them on side. The Victorian Certificate of Education was one of the most significant social-justice reforms undertaken by the Government, which was leading the nation and the world in a number of its environmental policies. "I think we've been through a rough and tough period, but this year will be the time to make a much clearer statement than we've been able to make over the last 12 months about where we're,.going,; and wc are the only party 4lr}at: can do that," she said. She made the comments-after be ing asked about the latest Morgan Gallup poll, which showed a onepoint popularity drop for.the Government and for Premier John Cain from November to December. She said'polls caused great interest in the media, but were not something she had ever been1 keen on using as a basis for government comment or action.

13 Jan 1990 - Quick death better than lingering deterioration Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 13 January 1990, page 9 Quick death better than lingering deterioration The figures seem to support the argument for the National Party to merge with the Liberal Party. By Andrew Fraser I HAVE a sister who is a die hard ALP voter but on her first.vote, back in 1972 as a yourig schoolteacher in Charleville in western Queensland, she cast'her vote for the then Country Party. As she explained, everyone else in the town voted for them and it was just like being in a social club and, for a young schoolteacher who knew no-one else in town, you needed all the society you could get. But this was nearly 20 years ago, and the handy division of the conservative parties whereby the Liberal Party picked up the urban conservative vote and the Country Party — now the National Party — picked up the large rural conservative vote, is a thing of the past. The truth, as always, is in the figures'-^- in 1969, the Country Party picked up 8.6 per cent of the primary vote. In 1972 the figure was 9.4 per cent;,in 1980 it was 8.9 per cent; and in 19&3 it was 9.2 percent. Now, according to the Morgan Gallup poll, it is closer to 6 per cent nationally, and if anything the Nationals are in a worse position than the figures indicate. The Morgan Gallup poll measures overall support, while the percentage of the primary vote should be lower because the Na tional Party does not contest all seats. In terms of seats held, the Country Party held 20 out of the 125 seats in the House of Representatives in 1969, and in 1980 it was in exactly the same position. But with an extra 23 seats in the House of Representatives throughout the 1980s, to 148 seats, the National Party has actually gone backwards in representation, and now holds only 19 seats. In the coming election there is a simple reality: the Coalition needs a swing of 2.3 percent to win the election, but if the ALP holds its rural seats — the seats the National Party have to pick up if the coalition is to win — then the swing required by the coalition is 4 per cent. A swing of this magnitude and nature is entirely possible but if it happens, the Liberals aren't going to be terribly chuffed about going into coalition with a party it would see as getting there on its coat-tails. In the states, the National Party is in the worst shape it has been for the past 20 years. In Victoria it has nine MPs; in South Australia there is one maverick from the Eyre Peninsula; while in Western Australia there are six MPs. In all three states the state of the coalition is pretty tender, and in the state elections m Victoria and Western Australia in-fighting between the Liberals and Nationals was one factor which cost the conservative coalition victory. In Western Australia in particular, the Leader of the National Party, Hendy Cowan, made .statements in the final week of the election campaign which the ALP jumped on and turned to their electoral advantage. In Tasmania, the party doesn't even exist. In the Northern Territory it half exists as the Country Liberal Party, while in the ACT it polled 1.3 per cent in the first self-government elections. Now to the hig two states — New South Wales and Queensland. In NSW the most recent Morgan Gallup poll shows its support at 6 per cent, and in the 1988 state election, while the party achieved a post-war high of 13.5 per cent of the primary vote, it was largely in seats where there was a two-way contest and the Liberals had withdrawn from the fray. Only in one seat, Monaro, did the National Party manage to knock off the Liberal Party to win a seat. And since the Coalition came to government in NSW, the main millstone around its neck has been the corruption allegations coming out of the Independent Commission Against Corruption, and these have been directed almost exclusively at the National Party. It is not as if it is only a few individuals with tentative links to the National Party who have become involved in the commission's proceedings. No less a party identity than the party's NSW president, Doug Moppett, while not being personally accused, has nonetheless taken the commission to task for its modus operandi, referring to its operations as "McCarthyist" and "one-sided". In days when politicians are not held in high regard for criticising cor Charles Blunt, John Stone, John Sharp and Peter McGauran ... not enamoured of hand-out mentality. ruption commissions, the appearance is given — and after all, politics is -about how things seem rather than how they actually are — that they are not all that keen on cleaning up the political process. The Nationals' approach in that state contrasts strongly with that of the Liberals in that state, where NSW Premier Nick Greiner has made it quite clear that he wants to see the commission run its course fully. Privately, some NSW Liberals concede that the performance of the National Party in that state is affecting the public's perception of them. Which brings us now to Queensland, where the party suffered a swing of 17 per cent in the recent state election to get 23 per cent of the primary vote and where, with an electoral redistribution imminent, the party faces further inroads into its representations. A further problem for the National Party is that the party machine has become dependent on being in government, as was well illustrated by the Fitzgerald Inquiry. And, without the backing of the public purse and promise of access to Ministers, the party machine will have to find a new, more orthodox way of operating. The Queensland result also showed that the National Party lost their new constituency in that state in the urban and provincial areas. The party lost all its seats in Brisbane, and on the Gold Coast their six scats — known as the six-pack — were reduced to two. Up on the Sunshine Coast, even the flow of conservative southerners into the Noosa area — which was a bastion of support in the Joh-for-PM campaign — couldn't stop the ALP getting elccted. But, out in the bush, the National Party were more successful in holding their support. In the country zone, for example, the National Party still hold 13 out of the 17 seats, although its vote dropped from 57.3 per cent to 44.6 per cent since the 1986 election. In the western and northern zone, the National Party's vote dropped from 48.3 per cent in 1986 to 42 per cent, and the party picked up six of the eight seats available. The National Party's loss and the ALP's victory in Queensland has im plications for the federal election as well, because four of the seats which the Coalition needs to pick up in order to win government are in Queensland. If they do not fall to the coalition, then that means an extra four seats need to be picked up else where. As well, the ALP are hopeful of picking up two north Queensland scats in Dawson and Kennedy, currently held by the National Party. It shows the relative strengths of the coalition partners that, at a time when when the ALP are looking to hold their seats against the Liberal challenge, they arc looking to actually take seats off the National Party. What all this indicates is that if the National Party has any future at all it is in the bush, and their grand dream of being the dominant conservative force of Australian politics is now only a passing wish, if that. Yet even here, the Nationals face problems in hanging on to what has been their traditional constituency. For years, the National Party's simple raison d' etre was to deliver services to the bush. It did not exist to provide a rational input into Australian politics, it existed solely to make sure that people outside the capital cities got the roads, hospitals and schools they thought they deserved. There was a very large element of the old country-versus-city mentality in this where country people, with their simple but hard-working ways and living close to the land rather than in those grubby secondary industries, thought that they were morally superior to those "city sharpies".. But the federal conference of the National Party is as good an indication as any of the priorities of the party, and that showed that the party is rapidly turning into a group of the sort of economic rationalists who dominate the Liberal Party organisation, if not their parliamentarians. In the National Party the senior ranks of parliamentarians are red-hot economic rationalists, with former secretary of the treasury John Stone foremost among their ranks. Significantly, Stone has spent almost his entire life in cities, and is certainly not enamoured .with the handout mentality of the old National Party. The party's leader, Charles Blunt, falls into the same category, as do the party's young up-and-comers such as John Sharp and Peter McGauran.. There are very few philosophic differences between them and the Liber al Party, and that is exactly thejioint — why are they, then, in two different parties, with two separate organisations and the potential for conflict? For coalition disunity is becoming almost as big a boon to the ALP as factional punch-ups with the party were to the conservatives for years, providing an opportunity for political opponents and no-one else. Having two separate parties advocating much the same thing only creates problems, and the parties have to hold meetings such as that on Wednesday in Melbourne, to make sure they speak with a united voice. What is likely to happen, then, is that over the next few years there will be vigorous competition between the two parties for the rural conservative vote. Precedent would show that the competition between the two parties, far from being healthy gung-ho, may be the "best man win" sort of style, and will probably be nasty and vitriol ic. . The added spice to this competition will be the entry into Parliament as a Liberal Party MP of former president of the National Farmers Federation lan McLachlan, still a revered figure in the bush, whose affiliation with the Liberal Party will again cause people in the bush to ask why they should have a National Party when their hero is in the Liberal Party. At the end of the day, the National Party's real problem is to find a reason for its existence. At the moment, it is becoming a pale imitation of the Liberal Party. If it persists in this course, the Liberal Party will eventually take it over completely. Under lan Sinclair's leadership the party hardly progressed, and under Charles Blunt it faces further problems. The National Party would do well to take note that Doug Anthony, the last really successful leader of the National Party, urges amalgamation with the Liberals. It may be the end of the party, but a quick death to help give another party more life is preferable to the lingering painful deterioration the party faces otherwise.

13 Jan 1990 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 13 January 1990, page 9 ADs look set for Senate balance The Australian Democrats are on target to win at least three Senate seats in the coming election, meaning that they will probably hold the balance of power in the Senate regardless of which major party wins the election. The quota for election to the Senate in a half-Senate election is 14.3 per cent, and the Morgan Gallup Poll shows support for the Australian Democrats in South Australia at 17 per cent. In NSW, the party's support is running at 13 per cent and in Victoria it is running at 12 per cent, and in both these cases the preferences of Independents alone would be enough to make the Democrats confident of another Senate place. In Queensland the party's support is at 9 per cent and in Western Australia it is at 8 per cent, and in both of these states the party should also be optimistic of picking up a place. In Tasmania the party's support is running at 5 per cent, which is well down from its general level of support, but the Democrats' loss of support has largely translated into support for the Green Independents who help hold power in that state. In Tasmania, "others" poll 13 per cent, and most of this could be assumed to be support for the Green Independents. Another informal poll taken by an academic at the University of New England, Grant Harman, among his peers in the profession, shows that only 22 per cent of those polled thought that the Federal Government was moving in the right direction in education. When the poll was split on an institutional basis, it showed that support for the Federal Government's moves, was strongest among academics in newer institutions such as the University of Western Sydney and the Charles Sturt University in the Riverina. — ANDREW FRASER

18 Jan 1990 - Button tips poll in May or April Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 18 January 1990, page 3 Button tips p oll in May or April By IAN COLLIER Speculation on federal election dates mounted yesterday with one of the Hawke Government's senior ministers tipping an April or May election date. The Government Leader in the Senate and the Minister for Industry, Technology and Commerce, Senator John Button, said that reports of a May or April polling date were "fairly sensible". Speaking on Melbourne radio, Senator Button's comments came as rumours of an early election swept the foreign-exchange market in Sydney, causing the dollar to dip slightly against the US currency oh late morning trading. One foreign-exchange official told The Can berra Times that the rumour centred on the'* Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, having visited Government House to seek an immediate election. In fact, Mr Hawke was at Liverpool, in Sydney's western suburbs, to visit a Youth Access Centre at the time the rumour had him paying a call on the Governor-General, Bill Hayden. Mr Hayden was in Canberra, but he was attending the funeral of Alan Woods, a former senior federal public servant. However, the market rumours were enough to have a spokesman for Mr Hawke forced to deny the speculation, with election fever threatening to become totally out of hand. The spokesman said it was "absolute nonsense" that an election was about to be immediately called. The speculation came as the latest Morgan Gallup poll showed that' Labor would win an election, to be returned fora fourth term. According to the polC Labor would lose in Western Australia and Victoria a total of between eight and 10 scats but this would be balanced by gaining three seats in Queensland, one in NSW and three in Tasmania from the Opposition. This would mean a net gain for the Coalition but not enough to change governmen t. The Opposition has to win at least 10 seats to tip out the Hawke Government. Labor officials told The Canberra Times last night that the poll confirmed party research which indicated the ALP was in trouble in Western Australia and Victoria. The ACTU also entered the election lead-up battle with reports again indicating that unions would be pushing for full consumer-price index pay rises and tax cuts of between $6 and $7 a week for average wage-earners. As reported in The Canberra Times last Saturday, this would mean that workers on average weekly wages of just over $500 could expect to be at least $40 a week better off, but if this is coupled with increases'in'employer contributions to superannuation payments it could well move the total package to nearer $50 a week. The new wage-tax trade-off package will be negotiated between the ACTU and the Government at the end of this month and will form the basis of the-new prices-and-incomes accord. Industry groups have already hit out at any wage-tax deal and the powerful National Farmers Federation called on the Government yesterday to honour a verbal undertaking to consult with employers before any agreement on a final out come. The NFF warned that unless there was consultation, employers would consider withdrawing from the next national wage case.

20 Jan 1990 - Polls v folk wisdom: which will be the winner in the federal election? Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 20 January 1990, page 9 Polls v folk wisdom: which will be the winner in the federal election? THE CONVENTIONAL wisdom that Australian voters differentiate between state and federal issues appears to be breaking down. This week's Morgan Gallup Poll shows that the ALP would win an election if it were held now, but it would lose seats in Western Australia and Victoria, the two states where the state governments are most unpopular. By contrast, support for the ALP is up in Queensland, following the election of a new ALP government there, and the ALP vote federally is holding in NSW, where the coalition State Government is less popular than the ALP Opposition. The poll, probably the most extensive undertaken since the 1987 election, was done on a state-by-state basis, and shows that the Hawke Government would be returned with a reduced majority. The poll shows that the ALP would drop between four and six seats in Victoria and four in Western Australia, but would pick up three seats in Queensland, three in Tasmania, and one in NSW. Contrasting the current standing with the vote obtained in the 1987 election, the poll shows that in NSW, the coalition has dropped 4.1 per cent to 41 per cent, while the ALP vote was down 2.2 per cent to 43 per cent. In Victoria, the coalition has remained fairly steady on 44 per cent, while the ALP has dropped nearly 5 percentage points to 42 per cent. In Queensland, support for the ALP has risen by 5 points to 50 per cent, while the coalition vote's has dropped 7.5 points to 42 per cent. In this state there has been a massive re-arrangement within the coalition, with the Liberal Party picking up 8 points and the National Party dropping 15.5 per cent, but this can be attributed mostly to conservative voters who left the Liberals for the Nationals in that state returning to the fold. In South Australia, the ALP is holding steady at around 44 per cent, while the coalition has dropped 7 percentage points to 39 per cent. In Western Australia, the ALP has dropped a massive 15.5 per cent, while the coalition has risen about 4 percentage points to 53 per cent. In Tasmania, the ALP has risen 2 percentage points to 47 per cent, while the Liberals (there is no National Party in Tasmania) have dropped 7 points to 42 per cent. The combined Democrat and other vote is highest in South Australia at 17 per cent, mainly because the Australian Democrats are running at 14 per cent there. In the 1987 election, these two forces only totalled about 9 per cent of the vote in South Australia. But it is NSW which is feeling the politics of disillusionment most keenly, with 16 per cent of the population intend voting outside the major parties, after only about 9.5 per cent did so in 1987. The combined Democrat and others vote is running at over 10 per cent in all states except Queensland, where state factors appear to have a heavy bearing on this poll at least. From Great Britain, the latest Mori survey shows Labour increasing its lead over the Conservatives to 8 percentage points during the last quarter of 1989. If the result of the poll, taken for 77;e Times newspaper, was transferred to a general election result it would give Labour an overall Commons majority of SO seats. The poll (with the previous quarter's figures in brackets) shows Labour at 48 per cent (45 per cent), the Tories at 40 per cent (38 per cent), Liberal Democrats 4 per cent (5 per cent), Greens 4 per cent (7 per cent), and the Social Democrats at 2 per cent (4 per cent). Poll: Morgan Gallup. Sample: 5365. Coverage: National. Method: Telephone, face-to-face. Poll: Mori. Sample: 8753. Coverage: all Great Britain. — ANDREW FRASER

But the ALP would have won an election only with the help of minor party preferences.

Given that we rate Malta highly enough to have . , a High Commissioner, then there must be an argument for setting up shop at least in Czechoslovakia if not Romania and Bulgaria. Why, I asked the production manager, could I open a Canberra Milk carton with ease? Why didn't they have the same problem? A different manufacturer. Not Tetra Pak but Pure-Pak. And then I discovered the best news of all. Dairy Farmers puts its cream into Pure-Paks, the system which works. So the solution to my problem is at hand. Within days of the reports of plastic being the major component of the waste found in the Australia-wide clean-up day, good, old-fashioned brown paper bags made their appearance at Deakin. The next step should be to give us a choice between large paper bags, boxes and those plastic carry bags at the checkout. ★THETang Dynasty ai Kingston isa restaurant I have rated highly on several occasions. I've recommended to Leo Schofield that the Tang Dynasty continue to. take part. ^A_THE campaign against us smokers has reached new heights. The very chummy employer and employee have set up house in Canberra, where their liaison passes virtually without comment in a city where divorce is a way or life. But back in the good senator's home state, where his former wife. and five children remain, his infrequent appearances have guaranteed that his new domestic arrangements are quite a talking-point. ★LABOR will not doubt take heart from events of the past week. The first tentative reduction in interest rates, yet another Morgan Gallup poll showing it could win and the Opposition's exposure on health costings were all good news. But the truth is that the real bcncficiarics of last week have been, yet again, the Democrats and Independents. The cynical swinging voter won't. have seen much to rejoicc in about bank bill Talcs . falling three quarters of a percentage point. Any reduction in mortgage rates if and when it comcs will, by the definition of the outer suburbs, be far too late. These people really are searching for another way for their country to be run. 07 Mar 1990 - Peacock at sea on tax figures Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 7 March 1990, page 1 Arms stretch out for the Leader of the Qpposition, Andrew Peacock, at a shopping centre in Hurstville yesterday. The Morgan Gallup poll in today's Bulletin shows support for the Opposition falling and Mr Peacock's personal approval rating unchanged. Peacock at sea on tax figures From TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent, in Sydney The Coalition's election campaign suffered what appeared to be a serious blow last night when the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, clung obsti■ nately to figures which have been proved conclusively wrong. Mr Peacock said his calculations showed that about 75 per cent of people paying the capital-gains tax earned less than $35,000. The extraordinary nature of this claim is that it has been known publicly for more than a week that the correct figure, issued by the Australian Taxation Office, is 69 percent Before the1 official figure was released, Mr Peacock claimed that it was 80 percent. Mr Peacock said last night that the figure of 75 per cent had come from his staff, but failed to explain how this could vary from the official figure. Questioned by Paul Lyneham on the ABC's 7.30 Report, Mr Peacock said, "Our records, our calculations are that it comes out at three-quarters." Lyneham: You have better records than the Tax Office? Mr Peacock: No Paul, I do not have better records than the Tax Office, but ELECTION 90 MARC H 24 the figures that I was working on I believe to be correct and I have had corroborated. Lyneham: By whom, Mr Peacock? Mr Peacock: My staff. The Hawke Government is certain to use last night's performance to portray Mr Peacock as a leader who does not know what he is talking about. The Government has been saying that the Opposition's plan to abolish the capital* gains tax will put millions of dollars in the pockets of the rich, while Mr Peacock has been saying that the vast majority of those paying the tax are relatively low-income earners. Mr Peacock stumbled from one apparent disaster to the next during last night's interview. He said it "did not particularly con cern him" whether the waiting list of patients trying to get hospital treatment was 100,000 (his figure) or 70,000 (the figure issued by his health spokesman, Peter Shack, last week). A spokesman for Mr Peacock tried last night to explain the Leader's poor performance on the 7.30 Report by saying that the ear-piece provided by the ABC kept falling out of Mr Peacock's ear, and he virtually had to "lip read" questions. Mr Peaqock's stumbles come on top of complaints by journalists travelling with him during the election campaign that he would not give a press conference to explain costings of his promises made at Monday's Liberal Party policy launch. There has been speculation among the travelling media party that Mr Peacock was deliberately avoiding a full press conference because he was uncertain about his figures. The shadow treasurer, John Hewson, was left to face the media yesterday while Mr Peacock opted for one-on-one interviews with Lyneham and Radio 2UE's John Laws. However, Mr Peacock has promised a full media conference in Melbourne this morning, and he is certain to be grilled on his comments on the ABC last night.

07 Mar 1990 - POLL WATCH Liberal drop after debate Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 7 March 1990, page 1 Liberal drop after debate SYDNEY: Support for the Federal Coalition dropped in the wake of the Great Debate, according to the Morgan Gallup, poll in today's Bulletin. The poll shows support for the Coalition down from 40 per cent to 39 per cent of a sample of 2490 voters. But with Labor steady at 42 per cent, the election could still be decided on preferences from the Democrats (steady at 14 per cent) and other smaller parties (up a point to S per cent). The poll was taken after the debate and the bad January balance-of payment figures. In personal approval ratings, the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, rose from 44 per cent to 47 per cent. His disapproval rating dropped four points to 42 per cent. The personal rating of the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, was unchanged at 28 per cent. His disapproval rating rose two points to 61 per cent. Asked who would make the better Prime Minister, 60 per cent said Mr Hawke and 26 per cent Mr Peacock.

09 Mar 1990 - Women voters are returning to Labor after Coalition fling Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 9 March 1990, page 5 ELECTION 90 MARCH 24 Women voters are returning to Labor after Coalition fling New Morgan Gallup Poll analysis indicates that women voters are edging toward Labor whereas in the 1987 election the Coalition picked up more of the women's vote. Morgan Gallup polls conducted on election days showed that in the 1975,1977 and 1980 elections, all won by the Coalition, the women's vote strongly favoured the Liberal and National parties. In the 1983 and 1984 elections, which the Coalition lost, the ALP picked up the most women's votes. In 1987 the Hawke Government sneaked home despite being 2 per cent behind the Coalition in female support. Analysis of the most recent poll, conducted on March 3 and 4, showed that 42 per cent of women surveyed supported Labor. Thirty-two per cent backed the Liberals and 7 per cent the National Party, giving a total for the Coalition of 39 per cent. The Democrats attracted 14 per cent female support and other parties 5 per cent. . According to other recent Morgan Gallup polling, the Coalition was attracting 2 per cent more of the women's vote in a February 17-18 survey. I 1

13 Mar 1990 - Keating on Lib hit list Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 13 March 1990, page 1 From TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent, in Melbourne Opposition strategists are work-ing on new ways to capitalise on what their research shows is a pub- lic perception that the Treasurer. Paul Keating, is simply waiting in the wings to become Prime Minis-ter after the election. The Liberals have not ruled out a last- minute advertising campaign based on the theme of "a vote for Bob Hawke is a vote for Paul Keating" even though both Mr Hawke and Mr Keating have stated that Mr Hawke will not step aside for Mr Keating during a fourth term of Labor Government. "Our research shows that there is still a deep-seated worry that Keating will take over," the Liberal campaign chief, Tony Eggleton, told The Canberra Times yesterday. "Keating still frightens the horses. We'll certainly be mentioning Keating during the next days. "I don't entirely rule out the possibili-ty of using paid advertising to use him as an issue, though I'm more inclined at this stage to put the emphasis in our paid advertising on the central issues." But it has recently become obvious that Mr Keating is being kept out of Labor's campaign spotlight, and the Op-position believes Labor is worried about the public perception of the Treasurer. The Liberals will use both the shadow treasurer, Dr John Hewson, and the in-dustry spokesman, John Howard, in new campaign advertising designed to claim the political agenda during the last two weeks of the campaign. ELECTION 90 MARCH 24 INSIDE: Page 8: Editorial. Page 2: Meta, strike averted. Page 3: Hawke plans US base takeover. Page 5:. Election reports, candidate profiles. "There's no doubt that Dr Hewson has been a great success during the cam-paign," Mr Eggleton said. ' "Our polling is showing that he is pre-ferred as treasurer over Paul Keating." Mr Eggleton's remarks came after a. day of curiously mixed poll results. The Opposition received a boost yes-terday when the latest Age-Saulwick poll showed that support for Labor had slipped 5 percentage points in the past two weeks, and that 39 per cent of voters now supported Labor while 39 per cent supported the Coalition. This would leave Labor in a narrow winning position after preferences were distributed, but it means that Labor's dependence on Democrat preferences is increasing, while the Coalition's position remains almost static. But the latest Roy Morgan Poll, re-leased last night, showed Labor as the overwhelming favourite to win. The poll, taken last weekend, found 71 per cent of voters believed the Govern-ment will 'be returned — up 3 per cent over a Week before, compared with 16 per cent who thought the Coalition would win, down 5 per cent. The poll, commissioned by the Nine Network, found 87 per cent of ALP sup-porters thought the Government would win, but only 33 per cent of Coalition supporters thought the Coalition would win. The Liberals' latest television adver-tisement, screened for the first time last night, features an animated John Howard declaring "get rid of the capital-gains tax — it's not a tax on the rich... in the end it will reduce the superannuation pay-outs of four million Australians". Mr Howard's statements are in direct conflict with the position of the Govern-ment, which maintains that the capital-gains tax has no effect in real terms on superannuation funds (see report below). The next advertisements to appear will have Dr Hewson addressing the question of "where the money's coming from" to pay for the Coalition's election promises, and Mr Peacock declaring that Australians have a simple, stark choice on March 24 — more of the same under the Hawke Government or "a change for the better" under the Coalition. The Liberal campaign for the last two weeks of the election is fuelled by re-search showing almost half Australia's voters still have made no final decision. Continued on Page 2 Keating on Lib hit list Continued from Page 1 The Liberals will try to focus the debate on just three or four key issues during the next two weeks. Using the new series of television advertisements, the party will high-light what it says is the unfairness of the capital-gains tax, argue that the Coalition offers economic credibility and try to convince voters that the choice between a Hawke Government and a Coalition government is stark. Central to the campaign is the spec-tre of continuing high interest rates under Labor, or "significant, sus-tained" falls in rates under a Coalition Government. "Our research shows that interest rates are still top of the pops — it has been exactly the same from the start of the campaign to now," Mr Eggleton said. The Opposition will hammer the message that the Hawke Government has pushed interest rates so high that ordinary families cannot afford to buy ordinary homes. Mr Peacock used this message sev- eral times yesterday during a visit to two provincial NSW marginal seats of Calare and Hunter, held by the Gov-ernment by margins of less than 3.5 per cent. Mr Peacock pointed to a survey on home affordability in marginal seats carried out by the Real Estate Institute of Australia. The survey showed that the average monthly mortgage repayment in Ca-lare and Hunter had risen by 90 per cent from June, 1986, to September, 1989. Median annual family incomes rose by 23.5 per cent at the same time, leaving the average family unable to afford an average family home. The main purpose of the renewed campaign will be to persuade un-decided voters to make up their minds. According to Mr Eggleton, private polling shows that about 20 per cent of voters have still made no decision about which party they will vote for, and another 25 per cent say they might switch their vote before polling day. "That's a big black hole that we want to fill," Mr Eggleton said. "It is the first time in the 13 federal campaign's that 1 have been associated with that we have got so far without the political pundits being prepared to call the outcome." Mr Eggleton said he expected that as the campaign entered its last week there would still be about 15 per cent of voters undecided. "Every day and every last hour will be important," he said. "We will be telling our people that they can't afford to slack oft in any way until 6 o'clock on Saturday evening, March 24, when the polling booths close." He predicted that Democrats, Greens and independents would ac-count for about 12 per cent of the total vote — up from 8 per cent at the last election. "We have a very anxious communi-ty, looking for solutions to this coun-try's problems, and what we have now is a real opportunity to give confi-dence that we offer the answers," he said.

15 Mar 1990 - Scrap gains tax, 'majority' say Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 March 1990, page 11 Scrap gains tax, 'majority' say MELBOURNE: More than half of people surveyed in a poll last week approved of the federal Coalition's plan to abolish the capital-gains tax, shadow treasurer John Hewson, said yesterday. The poll, by the Roy Morgan Research Centre, showed 84 per cent of people surveyed believed there should be no CGT on superannuation funds. Dr Hewson, who released details of the survey yesterday, said the results vindicated the Opposition's policy to abolish the CGT, which was introduced by the Hawke Government. The Opposition has argued that four million Australians would be affected by the impact of the CGT on their superannuation pay-outs. But the Government argues the tax has no impact at all on super benefits bccause of dividend imputation credits. The telephone poll questioned 1 i 78 electors in marginal electorates on March 6 and 7. It found that 52 per cent of those surveyed were not aware that superannuation schemes were subject to CGT. Additionally, 53 per cent of those surveyed approved of the Coalition's plan to abolish the tax, while 30 per cent believed it should stay. "Australians now realise that capitalgains tax hits up to four million Australians in super schemes, despite attempts by [the Prime Minister] Mr Hawkc and [the Treasurer] Mr Keating to say it doesn't," Dr Hewson said in a statement. Dr Hewson said the Coalition would abolish the CGT and tax short-term speculative gains at a declining rate over five years so that there would be no tax on capital gains. Meanwhile, The Australian Lifcwriters Association has criticised politicians on both sides for having "heaped confusion on confusing" in their war of words about superannuation policies for the coming election, economics writer Tom Connors says. The association called for a commitment from Labor and the Coalition to convene a superannuation summit after the election to achieve an agreed strategy on the future of superannuation. The association's executive director, John Davies, said that by throwing into the debate such elements as the capitalgains tax, industrial relations and social security, it was little wonder people were confused.

21 Mar 1990 - Steady as she goes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 21 March 1990, page 1 Steady as she goes The latest Morgan Gallup poll in to-day's Bulletin indicates little change in the fortunes of either Labor or Coali-tion. Asked who would make the better Prime Minister, 60 per cent of respon-dents chose Bob Hawke, the same fig-ure as in the last Morgan poll. Andrew Peacock's approval was down 2 points to 26 per cent. 22 Mar 1990 - Hogg slams Morgan poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 22 March 1990, page 1 Hogg slams Morgan poll Labor Party federal campaign director Bob Hogg described as a disgrace and palpable nonsense a Morgan Gallup poll broadcast last night showing a big swing against the ALP. "You don't get swings of 3.5 per cent in three days in the last days of a campaign," he said. He said the change was the "now well known Morgan swing" toward the Liberal Party in the last days of a campaign. The poll, commissioned by the Nine Network and carried out over the past three days, showed a 3.5 per cent swing away from Labor to give them 39.5 per cent support. The Coalition gained 1.5 per cent to 40.5 per cent to lead for the first time in the campaign. But Mr Hogg said his political experience and private Labor polling showed the Morgan poll was wrong. "This election is very tight, very close," he said. "For [MorI gan] to come out with a poil say Bob Hogg ing there is a 3.5 per cent swing in three days is disgraceful. "The poll... is palpable non sense." Mr Hogg said he was annoyed the election result could be affected, saying both he and Liberal campaign director Tony Eggleton agreed the election was close. 24 Mar 1990 - Gap between the major parties is narrowing Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 March 1990, page 9 Gap between the major parties is narrowing By HUGH LAMBERTON THE last polls before today's election found the gap between the major parties narrowing and some evidence that voters were drifting back from the Australian Democrats to Labor. The final Morgan Gallup poll found national support for Labor unchanged at 43 per cent with Coalition support up one point to 39 per cent. i The survey of 2492 voters conducted on March 17-18 indicated Democrat support was unchanged at 14 per cent. Of particular interest was the finding that Labor was slightly ahead in Victoria where th'e Liberals are expecting major gains. The national margin of 4 per cent puts the parties in the ;samc position as the final week in 1987. ) ! But the Democrat and Independent vote is likely fo be much larger and its direction ^vill be decisive. The Morgan poll was published in The Bulletin which said Democrat preferences appeared to be running at 65 per cent to Labor. The results of a separate Morgan poll indicated the Democrats would finish with nine senators after this election — two more than at present. Leadership approval ratings hardly varied. The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, dropped one point to 48 per cent, with a disapproval rating of 42 per cent and 10 percent undecided. Coalition leader Andrew Peacock's approval rating remained at 29 per cent, while his disapproval rating climbed one point to 60 per cent with 11 percent undecided. A Lower House breakdown of the Morgan results showed Labor ahead in Queensland, NSW and Tasmania, slightly ahead in Victoria and the Coalition leading in Western Australia. In the Senate, both major parties will return 12 senators with the ma jor parties fighting out the sixth senate position in Victoria, Queensland and South Australia. In Western Australia, the Liberals will fight it out with Independents as will Labor in Tasmania. A Newspoll published in The Australian yesterday gave the ALP a three percentage point lead over the Coalition. The poll of almost 2000 voters was taken on Tuesday and Wednesday nights and found ALP support had increased by three points to 42 per cent, with the Coalition unchanged on 39 per cent and the Australian Democrats at 14 per cent. Combined support for the Democrats and other parties had fallen from 21 per cent to 19 per cent, with the drop in Democrat support (from 17 to 14 per cent) apparently going to the ALP. Democrat and other voters were found more likely to change their votes in the last days of the campaign. The good news for Labor was that 60 per cent of Democrat and other voters planned to give their second preference to Labor, and 40 per cent to the Coalition. Sixty-eight per cent of all voters polled and 46 per cent of Coalition voters thought the ALP Government would be returned. An AGB:Spectrum poll taken on Wednesday night and published yesterday-found ALP support at 33 per cent, with Coalition support running' at 31 per cent, the Democrats rating 14 per cent and 15 per cent still undecided. And a sobering thought for politicians who believe the populace hangs on their words. With all the rage about the Multi-function Polis, an AGB:Spectrum poll of 1700 voters on Wednesday night found only 50 per cent were aware that there was a plan to establish an MFP in Australia. Of those in the know, 40 per cent agreed with the Coalition plan not to go ahead with the MFP, while 33 per cent were in favour of the MIT.

02 Jun 1990 - Little chance of Labor win now, says survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 2 June 1990, page 9 Little chance of Labor win now, says survey THE LABOR Party would seem to have little chance of repeating its March 24 election victory if another poll were held today, according to a poll published yesterday. A Saulwick poll published in The Sydney Morning Herald found that the Labor Party was trailing the Opposition in public support by 10 percentage points. The poll found that 45 per cent of those surveyed would vote for the Coalition and 35 per cent for Labor. The national poll of 1000 peo-ple was conducted over May 28-30. A Morgan Gallup poll pub-lished in The Bulletin showed that the popularity of the Leader of the Opposition was higher than that of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, for the first time since mid-1985. Mr Hawke's approval rating had dropped by four points on the last Morgan poll to 47 per cent while his disapproval rating in-creased by the same amount to 43 per cent. Dr Hewson's approval rating rose to 50 per cent while his dis-approval rating was 17 percent. However 33 per cent of respon-dents were undecided. On voting intention, the poll indicated another close contest. In contrast to the Sydney Morning Herald poll, the Mor-gan results showed Labor support up two points to 42 per cent with Coalition support down one point to 44 per cent. Australian Democrat support was 10 per cent with other candi-dates 6 per cent. The Morgan poll of 2102 people was conducted over the weekends of May 12-13 and 19-20. Despite Dr Hewson's populari-ty, Mr Hawke still was the pre-ferred Prime Minister to 50 per cent of respondents. However Dr Hewson also im-proved in this area with 35 per cent of people preferring him and 15 per cent being undecided. In another area, the medical profession has topped a poll of whom Australians believe are the most ethical and honest members of the community. ' Pharmacists and doctors were the top two careers with about 70 per cent of respondents rating them highly for their ethics and their honesty. Dentists ranked third (62 per cent) and school teachers (61 per cent). Engineers, police officers and university lecturers completed the callings that rated 50 per cent or more. Bank managers and accoun-tants came next with 49 and 47 per cent respectively. Lawyers were rated highly by 37 per cent of those interviewed with a big gap back to business executives on 19 per cent. Bottom-ranked jobs included journalists (10 per cent), union leaders (8 per cent), advertising people (7 per cent) and car sales-people (4 percent).

09 Jun 1990 - The power and passion of a PM in a pickle Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 June 1990, page 9 The power and passion of a PM in a pickle By Tony Wright PASSION and ego are the twin devil-angels that might comc to mind if you were searching lor the urges that drive Bob Hawke. Here on one hand is a man who can c|7 in public for a child, a father, and even, in the case of the Jews and the Chinese, for a whole people. Here on the other is a smallish man who wears built-up heels, who wears his virility like a pistol on a cop's belt, who hates to lose at anything. Passion and ego. They are a potent mix in a powerful man. It is a mix that got him into something of a pickle this week. First, the passion. A year ago, when the world was still feeling with disgust at the events that took place on June 4 in Tiananmen Square, Iteijing, Bob Hawke spoke at a scrvice in Canberra dedicated to the memory of those who died at the hands of the People's Army. y- As the Prime Minister spoke of bullets mowing down the Tiananmen Square demonstrators, of tanks running them over, he became overwhelmed by emotion, and it is hard to forget the television pictures of him, tjie light picking out the tears streaming from his face and dribbling from the end of his nose. No one could doubt the sincerity of Hawkc's anguish or the depth of his emotion. f A year on, he arrived back in Canberra this week after an absence from the Prime Ministerial throne enforced by an operation that, to a man like Hawke, must have been galling in the extreme. .7 And so, to the ego. There is an unmentioned symbolism to a prostate operation, a sort of psychic stripping of a man's virility, that pays no regard to the medical fact that such an operation has no negative efTect at all on a man's potency. There arc men who would rather say they were going to hospital for a bowel removal than admit they were going for a prostate operation. Thus, when Hawkc arrived back in Canberra this week, he was pretty keen to prove to the world that he was still, metaphorically speaking, virile as all get-out. He had another reason for wanting to prove he was still on top. While he was away, Paul Keating had been acting as ifhe was actually Prime Minister, not simply the Acting Prime Minister. Gearly, Hawke had to be seen to be reasserting his authority. Just as old stallions have to fight oft young pretenders until the day comes that they can no longer kick and bite with the viciousness required, so do Prime Ministers. Sincc Parliament was not sitting (and therefore there could be no grand gestures from the floor of the House), there was only one thing for it: a nationally-broadcast television interview. Publicity has always been central to the power game. Oncc upon a time, if a chap like Bob Menzies had wanted to make a big point, lie would phone up the editor of the biggest-selling newspaper in the land and grant an interview. Sadly for us newspaper hacks, those days are long gone. Television is now the power-junkies' medium. When Bob Hawkc decided to make his re-entry to public life, his ofTicc phoned Jana Wendt, presenter of the Nine Network's A Current Affair. Not only is Ms Wendt considered one of the premier interviewers in the country, with a show that reaches an extraordinary number of viewers, but one gets the distinct impression that Bob Hawke enjoys mightily the sensation of gazing into her splendid eyes. Thus, on Wednesday night, a fair slicc of Australia got to see Bob Hawke in his sitting room in Parliament House trying to present himself to Jana as a Prime Minister in total control and a man in the prime of his life. "No, I'm not tired," he declared. "I've never felt better really. I feel on top of things mentally in a way I haven't before really. I mean I've always felt good mentally but I feel better than I ever have before. And physically I'm great." Get the message? Are you listening, Paul? Are you listening, everybody? Well, the conversation went on for a bit — Hewson's remark about Hawke being too old for the job was stupid; nope, he wasn't handing over the reins to Paul, unless, of course, he got ran over by a bus; nope, Walsh's remark about "Old Jellyback" hadn't caused him to miss a wink of sleep and yep, when Hawkie says something's going to happen, well Jana, it's going to happen, you bet. Jana Wendt has this little habit of nudging the conversation on to a new subject and just plonking a comment that seems quite innoccnt right into the centre of things, and it is so... spot on... that you can just about hear it slap on the table. And so, right about the time Mr Hawke was getting wound up about how his word is law, Ms Wendt switched to the subject of the first anniversary of the events in Tiananmen Square. .. There is a point of view that there never was a massacre in Tiananmen Square," she said. And right there, Jana Wendt pulled together the two strands of Bob Hawkc's personality, fusing them into something quite electric. Hawke's passionate commitment to the martyrs of Tiananmen Square, portrayed so vividly at the memorial service a year ago, was being called into question. And neither his emotions nor his ego would allow that to happen. He flared. "That's a nonsense view." THOUGH it was cut from the interview that went to air, Mr Hawke went on to compare the doubters with those revisionists who claim that the Holocaust never happened to the Jews. He was clearly cut raw by the question. Deftly, Ms Wendt steered the conversation to the question of the status of Chinese students in Australia. And Hawke, with his passion and his ego firing in synch, stepped right in. First; "There'll be an announcement about that very soon." Soon was hardly the word for it Within scconds, Hawke was making the announce meht There would be a spccial catcgoiy crcatcd for Ihc more than 20,000 Chinese students who were in Australia before Tiananmen Square. If you wanted proof that Hawke was back in control, you could hardly go past this. The Cabinet hadn't even got around to discussing the matter. There were, and are, quite a mob of tricky, unanswered questions about what Mr Hawke proposed. But regardless, he had gone and announced what the policy would be, right there on Jana Wcndt's national TV program. Passion and ego. it's the only reasonable explanation. The Cabinet was left flat-footed and a little amazed. Hawke pre-empts Cabinet, said the headlines. One wit in the PM's office offered another line — Hawke didn't exactly pre-empt Cabinet, he just helped its members make up their minds. Hawke will get away witii this for two ve>7 good reasons. One: He's the Prime Minister. Two: His decision is right To order home China students who could face harsh punishment or death for being seen to support the pro-democracy demonstrators of Tiananmen Square would be monstrous. But Hawke didn't stop there. Ms Wendt prompted him to speak about his Government's decision to ask the Cambodian Government to take back boat people who had arrived in Australia. Hawke was still revved up. He could simply have said that the issue was the subject of extremely dclicatc negotiations and the status of the boat people was still under review. JL Indeed, he probably should have said,.-} this, for it is true. ■■ The Determination of Refugee Status -1 Committee (DORS) was still trying to'decidc whether the boat people could be judged political refugees or not.
