10 Jun 1990 - Carr applauds ALP recovery Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 10 June 1990, page 2 Carr ALP recovery SYDNEY: The NSW Opposition Leader, Bob Carr, confessed yesterday to the ALP state conference that he was surprised by the rapid resurgence of the NSW ALP after it was devastated by its loss to the Greiner Government two years ago. "I have to confess, delegates, that I did not then foresee how quick would be our recovery," he said. "1 just did not realise how inept and bad the Grcincr/Murray Gov ernment would be." in the keynote address to the three-day conference, Mr Carr said it could be the last annual conference before the next NSW election. He said the expected Cabinet reshuffles by the Greiner Government would be unable to save it from defeat. The most recent Morgan Gallup poll has put support for the Opposition one percentage point ahead of the Government at 42.5 per cent. Mr Carr committed the ALP to restoring North Coast, Armidale and Canberra rail services as part of a new deal for rural communities. He said the country communities had been ruthlessly betrayed by the NSW National Party. The five-point plan would restore 1000 teaching positions for country schools, restore the XPT to Canberra, sleepers and the Motor Rail to the North Coast and a passenger link to Armidale. The plan would also reallocate resources into country hospitals and phase out dangerous pesticides. Mr Carr also outlined details of a new-cities program for a dozen inland cities to be promoted for population and high-tcch industrial growth. He also attacked the Greiner Government for the increase in violent crime since 1988. "The Greiner Government has failed to contain crime primarily because of the doubling of police resignations," Mr Carr said. Street muggings and sex offenccs were up by 23 per cent and 32 per cent respectively, he said. Burglaries, car theft, armed hold-ups and drug offences were all on the rise, he said. He also attacked the Government for the 80,000 drop in TAFE enrolments and the declinc of confidence in the state school system. But the Greiner Government's economic record came in for the most scathing criticism. Mr Carr condemned Mr Greiner's financial management, citing a $3 billion blow-out in the state debt, which bought the total debt to $27 billion. "Delegates, on those figures he's the worst corporate cowboy in the country," he said. "The state's total liabilities had increased by more than $8 million a day with Mr Greiner as Treasurer," he said. While Labor had left office with a S315 million surplus, the Greiner Government had predicted a budget deficit of $375 million this financial year, he said. Shooting spurs call for inquiry SYDNEY: The NSW ALP annual conference has renewed calls for the State Government to launch a separate judicial inquiry into the activities of the Special Weapons and Operations Squad, after the fatal shooting of David Gundy last year. It unanimously passed a motion for an inquiry into the NSW Police squad, with special reference to the death of Mr Gundy, an Aboriginal, and the changes needed to ensure such an incident did not happen again. Mr Gundy died in April last year after being shot during a raid by SWOS officers on his Redfcrn home. The ALP motion also called for substantial compensation to be paid immediately to Mr Gundy's family. "We note the inherent limitations of any coronial inquiry in investigating the broader question of the activities of the SWOS of the NSW Police Force," the motion said. "We are appalled at the contrast between the [Premier Nick] Greiner Government's actions to hold a public and timely inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the laying of criminal charges against a white former policeman — the Blackburn inquiry — and its deafening silence about the killing of an innocent black citizen by members of the NSW Police Force." The conference also expressed its concern about continued efforts to hamper the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody. Labor to reject 'stars' SYDNEY: Calls for high-profile candidates to be installed unchallenged to Labor seats has been rcjcctcd by tilt ALP NSW president, Terry Sheahan, during the opening of the conference yesterday. The outgoing ALP state general secretary, Stephen Loosley, had made the call earlier, further fuelling existing rank-and-file anger at the prc-selcction of imported "stars" at the expense of local candidates. Two reccnt controversial cases involved the pre-selection of former dual rugby international Mi chacl Geary to the traditionally safe Labor seat of Coogce, and the installation of a former Minister for Police, Peter Anderson, as the candidate for Liverpool. But Mr Shcahan told members the issue would be discussed on the final day tomorrow, but there would be no changes to the preselection system in which election candidates were chosen solely by the local branches. The ALP hierarchy two weeks ago ignored calls by Coogce branch members for a pre-selection ballot and reinstalled Mr Cleary.

13 Jun 1990 - Approval rating: gap closes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 13 June 1990, page 3 Approval rating: gap closes The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, has again scored a higher approval rating than the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, but the gap is narrowing and more people still prefer Mr Hawke as Prime Minister. In the latest Morgan Gallup poll, published in today's Bulletin, Dr Hewson received a 50 per cent approval rating, compared with Mr Hawke's 49 per cent. But while Dr Hcwson's approval rating was unchanged over the previous poll, Mr Hawke's increased 2 per cent from 47 percent. Dr Hewson's disapproval rating was 17 per cent and Mr Hawke's 43 per cent. Dr Hewson, who took over from Andrew Peacock after the Coalition's federal election loss, is still an unknown quantity for much of the electorate. While 9 per cent of those polled could not decide whether they approved or disapproved of Mr Hawke, 33 per cent were undecided about Dr Hewson. And 48 per cent still preferred Mr Hawke as Prime Minister (50 per cent previously), while 35 per cent preferred Dr Hewson (35 per cent). The Coalition increased its lead over the ALP to four percentage points from two in the previous poll. The latest poll found support for the Coalition increased to 45 per cent, from 44 per cent, while support for Labor dropped to41 percent from 42 percent. At the March 24 federal election, Labor received 39.4 percent of the vote and the Coalition 43.2 per cent. The latest Morgan Gallup poll, of 3130 voters, was conducted on the weekends of May 26-27 and June 2-3.

16 Jun 1990 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 16 June 1990, page 9 Hewson still ahead in popularity THE LEADER of the Opposition, John Hcwson, again performed well in the popularity stakes this week when he scored a higher approval rating than the Prime Minister, Bob Hawkc, for the second time. In the latest Morgan Gallup poll, published in this week's Bulletin magazine, Dr Hcwson received a 50 per cent approval rating, compared with Mr Hawke's 49 per cent. However the gap is less than the three percentage points difference found in the last poll taken on the weekends of May 12 and May 19. Also in Mr Hawke's favour was the fact that more people still preferred him as Prime Minister. The poll of 3130 voters was conducted on the weekends of May 26-27 and June 2-3. Dr Hewson's approval rating remained static since the last poll while Mr Hawke's increased from 47 per cent last time. The Opposition leader also had a substantially smaller disapproval rating at 17 per cent to Mr Hawke's 43 per cent. But the percentage of undecided respondents indicated that many Australians arc still unfamiliar with DrHewson. Thirty-three per cent of interviewees could not decide whether they approved or disapproved of his leadership. Only nine per cent were undecided about the Prime Minister. On the question of who %vould make the better Prime Minister, 48 per cent nominated Mr Hawke (down from 50 per cent) and 35 per cent preferred Dr Hewson (unchanged). The voting intention of the sample showed the Coalition extending its lead from two to four points. Support for the Liberal-National parties was running at 45 per cent and support for Labor at 41 per cent. The Democrats received 11 per cent of the sample with other candidates gaining 3 per cent. At the March 24 federal election, Labor received 39.4 per cent of the primary vote and the Coalition 43.2 per cent. A second Morgan "poll indicated that the new Premier of Western Australia, Car.men Lawrence, had, gained 10 points in her popularity rating since March. Her approval rating was now running at 62 per cent compared to former Premier Peter Dowding's 33 per cent i'n January of this year. However the poll of 706 WA voters in April and May showed' support for the Labor Party had fallen four points to 38 per cent while the Liberal-National parties had moved up 3.-5 points ro 46.5 per cent.

23 Jun 1990 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 23 June 1990, page 9 Controversy damages PM's rating WITH the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, involved in controversy over the fate of Chinese nationals in Australia, the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, has managed to move further ahead in the popularity contcst between the two men. A Newspoll published in The Australian this week gives Dr Hewson an eight percentage point lead over Mr Hawke. The survey of 2268 people was carried out on the first and third weekends of June — about the time of Mr Hawke's statements on the Chinese students. This was the first time a Newspoll had recorded a higher rating for an Opposition leader over Mr Hawke. However, Dr Hewson has been ahead in recent Morgan Gallup polls. The poll found 46 per cent of voters were satisfied with Dr Hewson's performance as Coalition leader while only 33 per ccnt approved of Mr Hawke's performance as Prime Minister. In recent Newspolls, Dr Hewson's approval rating has improved from 33 per cent in April while Mr Hawke's has dropped from 42 per cent just before the March 24 federal election. However, 33 per cent of voters arc undecided in their view of Dr Hewson and only 9 per cent were undecided about Mr Hawke. On voting preference, support for the ALP had dropped to 37 per cent- while ■ support for the Coalition remained at 46 percent. The Australian Democrats received 12 per cent of the sample and other parties and candidates 5 percent. A Morgan Gallup poll has,indicated that the Premier of South Australia, John Bannon, would be easily re-clected despite the surprisingly close result of the last state election. The poll of 992 voters, conducted over April and May, showed support for the -Labor administration was up one point on the election to 46 per cent while support for the Coalition was running at 40 per ' cent (up three points). Meanwhile, Democrat support had fallen to 12 percent. Mr Bannon's personal support fell slightly to 66 per cent while Opposition leader Dale Baker's approval rating fell one point to 30 percent. Sixty per cent of the respondents pre- Sl ferred Mr Bannon as Premier compared to 18 percent who preferred Mr Baker. !

27 Jun 1990 - PM loses some appeal Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 27 June 1990, page 2 PM loses some appeal SYDNEY: The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has fallen four points behind the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in today's Bulletin magazine, shows that Mr Hcwson's approval rating remained steady on 50 per cent and his disapproval rating climbed two points to 19 per cent. Mr Hawke's approval rating fell three points to 46 per cent and his disapproval rose by the same figure to 45 per cent. In the "preferred Prime Minister" category Mr Hawke improved a.point to 49 per cent while Dr Hewson dropped by the same margin to 34 per cent. The Opposition continued to lead the most preferred government category, although support for it dropped 1.5 points to 43.5 percent. The ALP was up one point to 42 per cent and the Australian Democrats were up 0.5 to 11.5 percent.

30 Jun 1990 - Coalition stays ahead of Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 June 1990, page 9 Coalition stays ahead of Labor THE FEDERAL Coalition con tinued to lead the Labor Party in the primary vote, according to latest Morgan Gallup results, while the "third force" of voters shunning the two major parties remained at a high level. The poll was the sixth fortnightly survey since the March 24 federal election and found support for Labor running at 42 per cent against 43.5 per cent for the Liberal-National parties. Published in The Bulletin, the results showed that the alternative vote totalled 14.8 perccnt, which is down slightly from the 17.4 per cent election total. The large flow of preferences to Labor from this group has been credited for Labor's survival into a fourth term. This "third electoral force" had remained steady in the last decade of federal elections at around 7-8 per cent of the total primary vote. However, since the election high it has remained in the vicinity of 14-15 per cent. A large count for the Australian Democrats and minor parties, particularly Green parties, should continue to worry Coalition strategists. It has often been said that the people voting for these parties are more likely to be disaffected Labor voters than converts from the Liberal and National parties. As such, it is difficult to see a significant change in the flow of preferences occurring before the next election. The Prime Minister, Bob Hawkc, saw his personal approval rating drop a further three percentage points to 46 per cent while his disapproval rating rose by the same margin to 45 per cent. Nine per cent remained undecided. The Leader of the Opposition, John Hcwson, continued his good run in polls with his approval rating steady at 50 per cent and a disapproval rating up slightly to 19 per cent. Thirty-one per cent of the respondents were still undecided. In the head-to-head contest for preferred Prime Minister, Mr Hawke still led by 49 per cent to Dr Hewson's 34 percent. Seventeen per cent opted for other candidates.

04 Jan 1989 - Poll finds ACT rule opposed by 51 per cent Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 4 January 1989, page 3 Poll finds ACT rule opposed by 51 per cent By ANDREW FRASER Fifty-one per cent of Canberra citizens are not in favour of local government for the ACT, according to a poll conducted by ANOP for Capital Television.' The poll, conducted by telephone among 1200 ACT residents between December 15 and December 18, found that the major reason people did not want a change in the form of administration was that it might lead to a rise in rates, and the current system worked well enough as it was. Other minor reasons for rejecting self-government were a feeling that Canberra was over-governed and that there were quite enough politicians already; that a new government would quickly become too bureaucratic; that the standard of services would decline; and that a previous referendum (1978) had come out against self-government. Thirty-three per cent of those polled were in favour of self-government, largely because it gave locals a say, and because there would be more control over issues affecting Canberra. Other minor reasons in favour of self-government were that Canberra was big enough to warrant local government, Canberra should have the same status as the states, and that self-government would be a more accountable system. Sixteen percent were undecided about. whether they wanted self-government or not. Forty per cent of those polled said that they would not vote for a candidate who ran solely on a platform of abolishing self-government, while 15 per cent said they definitely would, and 27 per cent said they would consider such a move. While it is impossible to predict results under the modified d'Hondt system being used in the ACT, under proportional representation, if the above figures were accurate, it would be possible that three of the 17 members of the first ACT Assembly would be committed solely to wiping out the Assembly. Public servants were the ones who were most against the notion of self-government, with 56 per cent of public servants polled against self-government, while only 33 per cent were in favour. There was little difference between ALP and Liberal voters among those who were against self-government, but 40 per cent of Labor voters supported self-government, while only 31 per cent of Liberal voters favoured it.

06 Jan 1989 - Casino poll support up, pro-porn numbers down Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 6 January 1989, page 3 Casino poll support up, pro-porn numbers down By ANDREW FRASER A poll conducted by ANOP for Capital 7 has found that public opinion in the ACT is moving in favour of a casino, but against the sale of X-rated videos in the ACT. The survey, conducted among 1200 voters before Christmas, found that 52 per cent of those polled were in favour of a casino, while 38 per cent were against, and 10 per cent were unde cided. Men were more in favour of a casino than women, with 56 per cent in favour compared to : 48 per cent of women. Forty per cent of women polled were against the casino, as opposed to 36 per cent of men. . More ALP than Liberal voters were in favour of the casino - 57 per cent of ALP voters were , for a casino while 35 per cent were against, while 48 per cent of Liberal voters were in favour, and ; only 41 per cent against. ? Fifty-one per cent of those polled were against ,the sale or hire of X-rated videos in the ACT, 37 per cent were in favour, and 12 per cent were ; undecided. ; More women than men were against X-rated ; videos. Sixty-three per cent of women were ?against the sale or hire of X-rated videos, while only 39 per cent of men were against them. I Liberal rather than ALP voters were against 'X-rated videos. Sixty-two per cent of Liberal voters polled were against X-rated videos, as opposed to 41 per cent of ALP voters, while 47 per cent of ALP voters were in favour, compared ito only 28 per cent of Liberal voters. ' ! The findings of this survey are at odds with one conducted before Christmas by Morgan Gallup for the Adult Video Industry Association, which showed that 35.4 per cent of people wanted the sale or hire of X-rated videos banned, and nearly 60 per cent wanted the current arrangements to stay. One possible reason for the difference is that many ACT residents do not understand the current situation, which the Morgan Gallup survey referred to, while the ANOP survey asked people if they were in favour or against X-rated videos. Another is the size of the sample - 1200 people were polled in the ANOP survey; 495 for the Morgan Gallup poll. The Morgan Gallup poll asked, "Do you want X-rated videos banned, or are you in favour of the current situation?" The ANOP poll asked, "Are you in favour of X-rated videos being for sale or hire in Canberra? Or are you not in favour?" A spokesman for the Adult Video Industry Association, Robert Swan, said the ANOP survey was "totally flawed" because it did not explain what an X rating was. Mr Swann said the Morgan Gallup poll found that half of those surveyed thought there was explicit violence in an X video, but X-rated erotic videos contained no coercion or violence. The Liberal Party spokesman on police and justice, Gary Humphries, said last night the poll results showed the ACT Liberal Party was "totally in touch" with its policies of supporting the casino and banning the sale and distribution of X-rated videos.

07 Jan 1989 - Haines faces another year on cliff top Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 7 January 1989, page 9 Haines faces another year on cliff top [PO^CS^ By Andrew Fraser THESE days, when people say that the Australian Democrats arc at the crossroads, Janinc Haines just laughs. "We're always at the bloody crossroads," she says. The Democrats arc not always at the crossroads so much as always beside a steep cliff", and they live ever in peril of toppling over. There is a different twist to the situation in which the Democrats find themselves this year, in that it is very much in their interests to reject Government legislation and hence create the necessary pre-conditions for a double dissolution. This is simply because a double dissolution places them in a far better position than the half-Senate election which is due before the middle of next year. Four of the.'Dcmocrat senators - one each in Tasmania, Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia - are up for reelection, and changes made to the size of Parliament in 1984 will affect them tremendously in the event of a half-Senate election. In the event of a double dissolution, the-Democrats have a better than even chance of maintaining their current position, or at least getting close to that position. But the Senate has not actually rejected any piece of legislation twice, despite the Government's noises about an uncooperative Senate, and the excuse is just not there for a double dissolution. The Government can actually run until the middle of next year if need be, as there is a half-Senate election due then. Should the Senate maintain this attitude and a half-Senate election eventuates, the Democrats are as George Bush would say, in deep doo-doo, largely because at the same time that numbers in the. House of Representatives were increased, the number of senators each state elected was raised from 10 to 12. In the next half-Senate election, there , will be six senators elected from each state instead of five. Previously, to get three out of five senators, a party had to getabout 49 per cent of the primary vote, which was pretty well impossible, but now, to get three out of six senators,-they only need 42.6 per cent of the vote, a feat well within the reach of both the ALP and the coalition. It is quite possible that they could each get 43 per cent of the vote and three senators each, while the Democrats get the remaining 14 per cent of the vote and no senators. ? Likewise, it is quite possible for this to happen in every state in Australia except South Australia and Tasmania. In South Australia, Senator Haines has enough of a personal following and the Democrats have enough of a presence to get the required 14.2 per cent of the vote which constitutes a quota, while in Tasmania, long-time independent Brian Harradine would probably have enough also to get a quota. In the Northern Territory and the ACT, it is virtually impossible to get any result other than one senator from each party, and the net result would be a senate in which the numbers were equal and Senators Haines and Harradine held the balance of power. This is not a rccipc for stable government. The next problem for the Democrats, and Senator Haines in particular, is whether or not to stand for the House of Representatives. This is to be decided at a meeting of the South Australian state council in February, and Senator Haines said throughout the week that she would leave this decision entirely up to the meeting of the 40-odd members. But in an ideal world, she would like to make the change, largely because she sees the lower house as being where the action is. "Getting our message across is far better done in the lower house rather than in the Senate because that's generally where policy positions are put. There's a lot more press people in the house, whereas over in the Senate we get one scribbler from AAP. Nothing against them, but it's not quite enough. "But it's not just a matter of me deciding what to do, the party has most to do with it. We all have to answer to our parties. I mean, look at Gareth Evans and Fred Chancy, they've both had a go at trying to. change houses, but they couldn't because of what was happening in their parties." - "It would be a tremendous risk for me, not least financially. .My term doesn't finish until 1993, and I stand to lose a great deal if I give up my seat in the Senate. If 1 don't win any seat in the Reps... well, it's goodbye." THE time for change, however, is not ri{>e. If ever the Democrats, or Sena tor Haines in particular, had a chance at a scat in the lower house, it was early last year when the seat of Adelaide was vacated by Chris Hurford when he left to become Australia's Agent-General in New York. Senator Haines lives just out-, side the seat and is well-known within it, neither the ALP or the Liberal Party ran prominent candidates, and a Morgan Gallup Poll at the time found that she was the most popular political leader in Australia, marginally tipping out Bob Hawkc. But it was too soon after the 1987 Senator Janine Haines ... a different twist. election. "I was only six months into a six-year term and didn't feel it was right to let the people who'd voted for me down," she said. "You've got to give the voters credit for having some intelligence. I know we're not supposed to do that!" Senator Haines acknowledges that this Pessimism on poll for half Senate is not the best time, but says she will be guided by whatever the party thinks. But if she stands for a federal seat and loses, she can take some comfort from the fact that she will not be the only Democrat leaving at the next election. Her deputy, the popular (in Democrats' terms) and capable Michael Macklin, from Queensland, has said that he will not be standing, and Norm Sanders, from Tasmania, is also highly unlikely to stand. But unhappy scenarios (for the Democrats) of this nature have been written before, and the actual election has yet to be held. The main problem for major political parties is getting people out to vote for them, as th\e most noticeable political trend in Australia at the moment is a disillusionment with the major parties. There are large numbers of people trying to capitalise on this - look at Katharine West's "community movement" which will, she assures, us, sweep to power at the next election, while in the local ACT elections an as yet unknown number of independents are standing, all with the message that they are not tied to major political machines. WHILE Senator Haines would of course prefer that people voted for the Democrats because of their policies, she acknowledges the Democrats are well placed to tap into this vote. The Democrats have been picking up this sort of protest vote for years and my guess is that while there is more competition for this vote, it is bigger now than it was a few years ago. Where is Don Chipp when you need him? What a field day he would have assuring the electorate this this time around, the Democrats would surely "keep the bastards honest". In the current climate, it's the Democrats's best hope for survival.

12 Jan 1989 - Received January 11 Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 12 January 1989, page 6 Received January 11 I THOUGHT I was becoming ac customed to the sexist and disparag-ing similes The Canberra Times uses to entertain its readers (such as Craig McDermott bowls like a girl, or that Mr Border bats like a wom- ah), but an article appearing on Fri-day, January 6, 1989, took the pavlova. To suggest that Liberals vote like women, and to back this up with statistics from a recently conducted ANOP poll on ACT citi-zens' attitudes to X-rated videos and to a casino in Canberra, is hit-ting below the cummerbund. Please allow me to quote selec-tively: "Men were more in favour of a casino than women, with 56 per cent in favour compared with 48 per cent of women ... 48 per cent of Liberal voters were in favour, and only 41 per cent against. Sixty-three per cent of women were against the sale or hire of X-rated videos, while only 39 per cent of men were against them ... Sixty-two per cent of Lib-eral voters polled were against X-rated videos, as opposed to only 41 percent of ALP voters..." To suggest that Liberals think like women is sexist, but to imply that women think like Liberals is very disconcerting. What do Liberal women think like? Anyway, we all know how real men think! Baiting, baiting, baiting . . . M. BOROWIK Florey

12 Jan 1989 - Letters to the Editor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 12 January 1989, page 6 Opinions divided on opinion poll results Received January 11 CONTRARY to your report (CT, January 6), the recent ANOP poll does not show "that public opinion in the ACT is moving in favour of a casiho". Any claimed movement in public opinion requires an earlier point of reference. As your report provides no such reference, your assertion of increasing support for a casino has no basis. Barely half of ANOP's respondents favoured a casino. This is considerably less than the "overwhelming" level of support previously claimed by the Government and others. After 17 months of controversy, the result may merely reflect some effect of the constant bludgeoning by casino proponents, and their use of considerable resources to press spurious and irrelevant claims. The poll does not show any real desire or eager clamouring for such a facility. PETER HICKS Committee for a Casino-Free Canberra

17 Jan 1989 - IN BRIEF Libs 'could lead Govt' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 17 January 1989, page 4 IN BRIEF Libs 'could lead Govt' BRISBANE: It was possible to have a coalition in Queensland with the Liberal Party as the senior partner, state Liberal Party leader Angus Innes said yesterday. Mr Innes said Morgan Gallup polls showed the Liberal Party's popularity was improving and people were becoming dis-illusioncd with the Nationals. If the polls continued to go in the Liber-als' favour, it was possible the party could win enough seats to become the senior partner in a coalition after the next state election, he said. The Queensland National Party now governs in its own right, and has done so since it split with the Liberals before the 1983 state elections. Anti-drink campaign "Alcohol: It can turn you into a jerk." The message is on the move about Can-berra, courtesy of the National Campaign Against Drug Abuse and ACTION buses. NCADA has begun a national transport advertising campaign and some of Can-berra's buses are carrying the above mes-sage and two others: "Alcohol: Someone's always watching you" and "Alcohol: It can turn you into a joke". Swimming pool death MELBOURNE: A two-year-old boy drowned in a private swimming pool in bay-side Mt Eliza, in the outer southern suburbs, on Sunday, after he wandered out of his mother's sight into a next-door yard. Police have not released his name. Aboriginal jail guards SYDNEY: Aboriginal custodial officers are to be recruited by the NSW Corrective Services Department after recommenda-tions by the Muirhead Royal commission. The jobs were being advertised through Aboriginal publications and through con-tact with Aboriginal communities, the Corrective Services Minister, Michael Yabsley, said yesterday. Crushed to death DARWIN: A 25-year-old man died in an ore crusher on Sunday night at the Goodall gold mine, about 140km south of Darwin. Police said the man had been feeding a shute that led to a conveyor belt emptying the ore into the crusher. Privacy hotline SYDNEY: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunities Commission has set up a hotline to deal with a flood of calls about privacy safeguards when the Federal Government's new tax-file-number sys-tem comes into effect on February 1. The privacy hotline number is toll free 008- 02 3985.

18 Jan 1989 - IN BRIEF Police check diary found at dump Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 18 January 1989, page 2 IN BRIEF Police check diary found at dump Police have found at a Canberra garbage dump a diary that may be linked to the slaying of police chief Colin Winchester outside his suburban home last week. A police spokesman said last night that forensic tests were being carried out. The diary was found yesterday by police searching the tip for clues in the hunt for the killer of Mr Winchester, an Australian Federal Police assistant commissioner. The diary contains photographs of po-lice and was wrapped in a copy of last Thursday's Canberra Times, which car-ried a front-page picture of an emotional AFP Commissioner Peter McAulay at a press conference the day after the killing. Earlier WA poll might have differed SYDNEY: If the Western Australian election had been held a month earlier, it would have been decided on the prefer-ences of minor parties and Independents, according to a Morgan Gallup poll pub-lished in today's Bulletin magazine. The poll, which surveyed 392 electors throughout Western Australia in Decem-ber and early January, found that the La-bor Government had trailed the Opposi-tion by 1 per cent when the February 4 ballot had been announced. Support for the ALP had been down seven points compared with the 1986 elec-tion to 46 per cent. Combined Liberal-Na-tional party support had been up two points to 47 per cent. The Australian Dem- ocrats had had 5 per cent support.

18 Jan 1989 - MIDWEEK MAGAZINE Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 18 January 1989, page 29 MIDWEEK MAGAZINE,. Admiring snakes ) from afar f^l^CApmu. by 'INDIGOFERA' OPPORTUNISTIC ants were already at work on a dead but almost completely intact brown snake that we found beside Belconnen Way some days ago, galloping around its eyes and in and out of its nostrils and its mouth like commuting Londoners patronising that city's tube system. Snakes have no eyelids and cannot blink and the edible eye is only covered by an edible capsule or spectacle. With my two senior urchins I went back to look at the rather snake-like object we had passed about 50m before. My son strode to it with alacrity while his smaller sister sidled up with trepidation. Their mother's gait was a blend of these two because, while I do admire snakes and while I. can ogle them from a safe distance, I harbour a few irrational fears about them. The snake, well over a metre long, was in mint condition if one discounts the fact of its recent death, and rigor mortis (if dead snakes go through such a phase) had not set in and I toyed with the idea of shaking off the ants and putting the serpent in the letterbox of one of my more irritating neighbours or better still, just under the lid of my rubbish bin to startle the dustbin-lid frisbeeing garbos who throw my lids as far as they can. But I decided, reluctantly, that such a thing would outrage the dignity of the deceased serpent. The ants were at work on the snake's face and were using the aforementioned entrances because snakes are otherwise rather armour clad things and difficult and perhaps impossible for small ants to pene trate. Snakes are scaly, the larger scales constituting plates, because evolution has given them a covering designed to permit the maximum possible water retention. Snakes have to retain a water balance within their bodies but do very little drinking. The many species that live in phenomenally diy deserts cannot rely on the availability of drinking water and depend entirely upon the moisture they take from the things they eat. Most mammals (including ourselves) are about 85 per cent water so that a snake's prey is literally food and drink at the same time. The local species with which we have the most interfaces and the species which provided the one being fed on and cleaned up by nature's garbos beside Belconnen. Way, is Pseudonaja textilis whose range extends into some of the hot, dry, Gobi-like bailiwicks of far west crn NSW and Queensland and central Australia. Thanks to the tough scales, which are completely waterproof, snakes do not lose any of their precious intake of water by sweating and also, as a further part of this adaptation (and I hope that you have finished your Nutri-Grain) they shed very little water with their faeces. Once in a while a Canberra Pseudonaja textilis will appear in a suburban swimming pool having come down to drink on a hot day while suffering from heat stress but Richard Longmore tells me that snakes seem to do very little drinking in the wild and only a little more in captivity where, perhaps, thirst is sometimes artificially enhanced by the Dead brown in mint condition temperature of the house in which the creature is kept. A Saulwick opinion poll has shown that women are nearly twice as likely as men to believe in astrology and I wonder if there can be any connection between this disposition and the fact that women are nearly twice as likely as men to be afraid of snakes. In my experience the fears that women have of snakes are based upon a more imaginative contemplation of what snakes might do and where they might go just as a readiness to believe in astrology gives the stars more credit for being mysterious and capable of infinite permutations than is given them by boring old scientists. "But what if..." women will say as you attempt to put them at ease' about snakes, going on to wonder what if one was to slither into the fridge in search of frozen fish fingers or what if one was to climb into the back of the television and come out during The Addams Family? Assurances that snakes are not particularly fond of frozen fish fingers and that a television set is not a snake's chosen habitat are of little avail. And then, a lot of rational discussion of snake behaviour is undone by true stories like unto the one about the brown snake which some days ago was last seen slithering under a car at Lake Ginninderra and was accidentally driven to a driveway and a garden in Holt (where snake charmer and rescuer Richard Longmore captured it) after having wriggled up into some part of the car's undercarriage. I mention this because, having turned away from the aforementioned deceased serpent to return to the car my usually rather valiant daughter noticed that her brother had left his door wide open, surely enabling another serpent to slither out of the bush and into the haven of our modest family saloon. She called the dear boy several names (of which "Idiot!" was by far the most amiable) and I had to examine the car before we could press on to our destination. In her defence it must be said that she once, when she was six, found herself in an outdoor but enclosed swimming pool with a brown snake slithering about between her and the exit. THIS column shudders at the thought of turning the reporting of the lives of "my" goshawks on Bruce Ridge into a kind of ornithological version of Neighbours but, having reported last week that I had watched two goshawks, an adult and an adolescent, in the same place where goshawks nested last season I should now report that on Monday evening I watched two adolescents in the same bailiwick. No adult put in an appearance, this time, during the half hour I was there. I am a flawed amateur ornithologist but even I can, especially with my binoculars and my field guide, tell the difference between a grown up goshawk and a young one, so it is not that I mistook the other youngster for a grown up in last week's report. The grown ups have been more fecund than I thought. Both youngsters were greatly agitated, shrieking to one another from about 50m apart, but I could not tell whether they were agitated by me or by the occasional hopelessly disorientated orienteer who stumbled past in the gloaming. What I did get wrong, last week, was the characterisation of that shriek as a kind of "eck eck eck eck". Listening to the same hullabaloo on Monday and divining that it had more "ee"-like shriekings in it and wondering how on earth I could compare it to human phrasing I was reminded that Graham Pizzey in his A Field Guide to the Birds of Australia speaks of "the stupidity of trying to cramp bird calls into human phrases". Then he goes ahead and docs it anyway, albeit with more skill than I can muster, even insisting that the call of the Willie Wagtail is "Sweet pretty creature" when to my untutored ear it is "I am Clint Eastwood". Yesterday morning I saw yet another goshawk pursuing a flock of pigeons beside Baldwin Drive and above the paddocks just opposite ornithologically rich Kaleen. The pigeons maintained, in spite of their terror, a rather orderly formation as they reeled and weaved to try and shake off the monster who, while I was watching, was having a singular lack of success.

20 Jan 1989 - Video X-rating misunderstood Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 20 January 1989, page 6 Video X-rating misunderstood Received January 16 SENATOR Shirley Walters's claims (CT, January 9) that the ANOP/Capital Television poll on Xrated non-violent erotic videos "has clearly shown that the Federal Government is completely out of touch with the community are, as usual, based on false and misleading infor mation. Senator Walters and Senator Bri an Harradine, both elderly Tasmanian Christian politicians, nave continually tried to deceive middle-class Canberrans as to the existence of violence in X-rated NVE movies. For the record, the legislation says "no coercion of any kind". Senator Walters knows full well that when an opinion poll asks a question about "X-rated movies" without any clarification of that unfortunate generic term "X-rated", most respondents will immediately think of the worst movie they can imagine in formulating their re sponse. Things like The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, I Spit on Your Grave, and even Rambo, which are actually R and M rated. The ANOP/Capital Television poll which asked whether its respondents were for or against X-rated movies, really askea the question "Do you like excessively violent movies?" This mistake was highlighted in a Saul wick/Age/Sydney Morning Herald poll conducted last August. It went as far as to ask the question "Do you approve of X-rated violent movies?" The next day, both The Age and the SMH wrote extensive retractions. So in the Morgan Gallup Poll which the Adult Video Industry Association commissioned in December, the industry was very careful to ask Canberrans, first, what was their perception of an X-rated video and, after setting them straight with the legal definition, to ask them were they in favour or not. It was not surprising to find that half the population (49 per cent) were ignorant as to what an X-rating was given for. It was also not surprising to see that when they found out, the majority (60 per cent) said "no" to a ban on innocent adult video erotica. The Morgan Gallup Poll substantially'backed up The Canberra Times data poll on December 23,1988, which showed that X-rated NVE videos were not a voting issue with most Canberrans. The problem arises from the long-term labelling of explosive boxes, hard liquor and other "nasties" with the "x" mark. We have also traditionally regarded "x" as a negative statement opposite the true or good one, which is qualified with a tick (/). It is not surprising then that many people who have not followed the X-rated-video issue closely would regard an "X-rated movie" as obviously something that involved violence and other anti-social activities. Consenting sex has never been regarded as anti-social, and it should never be so in a civilised democracy. The Chief Commonwealth Censor should be relabelling all those excessively violent movies as X-rated, and adopt a new classification of NVE for adult erotica. Only then will the conservative political parties lose their platform of misinformation and deceit. ROBBIE SWAN Lobbyist for the Adult Video Industry Association

20 Jan 1989 - Sisters' belief begs explanation Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 20 January 1989, page 6 Sisters' belief begs explanation ASP ALUM ^?P^PLACE__ By lin W»iH»n FROM The Skeptic, the journal of the Australian Skeptics (who claim that almost all their members are highly educated but whose spelling, in their journal, makes this very hard to believe) I learn that two authoritative polls have shown that women are twice as likely as men to believe in astrology. This finding was made, independently, by the National Social Science Survey conducted by the Australian National University and by a Saulwick poll. Given that the ANU survey asks questions about beliefs in the paranormal one must assume that the survey is the work of the ANU's fabled School of Inconsequential Studies. I must say that the finding that women are more likely than men to be credulists does coincide with my own experience. In the days when I used to go to parties, before a phobic fear of these folkloric interactions turned me into a hermit, it was always women who strode up to me to interrogate me about my star sign. Men, by contrast, wanted to talk about car parts and superannuation. When I found out that none of them (the women) would believe that 1 really was a Sagittarius (we are all supposed to be tall, dark saxophonists, with barely controllable sexual impulses, ruthless ambitions and an allergic reaction to apricots and hedgehogs) I began lying that I was a Scorpio (shy, sentimental, gullible, red-haired, scholarly mesomorphs with no sexual impulses to speak of) just to avoid arguments. Given that astrology is nonsense and that professional astrologers are either charlatans or loonies (the Skeptics are always demonstrating this to the satisfaction of anyone who is the entire rouble) I find myself wondering why my sisters are so prone to a belief in astrology. As a good feminist I find myself looking for an explanation which will flatter women, perhaps one jwhich attributes this gullibility to the extra flexibility of the female imagination. Although I cannot think of an explanation myself I am sure that there is a feminist analysis of this phenomenon which shows it to be the fault of men. Perhaps a Ph.D has been written about it and is already published as a scholarly but bitter paperback published by Jezebel Press, arguing that men, by making women's real daily lives so unutterably hellish, have encouraged them to live rich fantasy lives in which the tedious and of course man-made and chauvinistic laws of natural science and of logic are shackles to be broken if women are to feel free. Perhaps women, horrified by the thought that their lives are controlled by men, prefer to believe that their lives are controlled, instead, by permutations of the firmament. Meanwhile, given that astrology is nonsense and that a belief in it tells us something of the quality of the minds of the believers I intend to haunt every meet-the-candidates meeting during the ACT election campaign to ask the female candidates about their beliefs in the paranormal. If Ms FoUett confesses to any of the New Age enthusiasms, to a belief in crystal healing, acupuncture, the mystical properties of muesli and alfalfa and in the superi or intelligence of dolphins she and her talented and charismatic team need not expect my vote, but then it is most unlikely that the grim, greedy pragmatists of the modern ALP are people who have any truck with anything mystical. Hard on the heels of the alarming discovery that women are vulnerable to astrology I have received a hamper of literature and some "subliminal persuasion self-hypnosis" cassette tapes from a company called Potentials Unlimited Inc. The literature contains photographs, above the caption "Meet Your Hypnotist", of Barrie Konicov, the founder and chairman of the American company. He has a lovely smile. Potentials Unlimited sells more than 160 of these tapes but Barrie has only sent me two of them of which one, designed to help me take exams without fear, is quite superfluous since the only course 1 am doing (I am studying, by correspondence, to be a professional dwarf throwing referee in anticipation of this being the growth sport of the 1990s) relies on continuous assess ment. The other tape seeks to help me with stress and anxiety, of which I have a superfluity, and I have already listened to it. It relies upon some soothing music commixed with the sound of waves beating upon a shore, but, listening to it while sitting and with my eyes closed as instructed I find myself stressed and made anxious by the thought that the tide is coming in and that any moment now a wave will break over me or that, since I am on a tropical beach, huge carnivorous crabs are bearing down on me to pluck lumps from my flesh. Looking at the list I think that some of the other tapes may have been of more use to me although "Natural Bust Enlargement", "Removal of Warts", "Freedom from Sexual Guilt", "Freedom From Acne", "Thumb Sucking", "Get More Out of Sex" and "How To Be Popular" all deal with problems and maladies that do not afflict me although I suppose that I would like to know how to be popular in-Queanbeyan where, unaccountably, I am not well liked. But it is not obvious how subliminal persuasion would help that problem, any more than it is obvious how a bust can be subliminally persuaded to enlarge itself. Women, as discussed, will be particularly interested in the tapes of "Hypno-Astrology". Mr Konicov explains that "Each sign of the Zodiac has its positive and negative aspects ... Each tape in this series makes you aware of your sign's strengths and weaknesses. Then you are guided into a technique that frees you from tHe negatives through the alchemy of your mind...." There are also tapes about past lives. There is "Past Life Regression" and, better still, "Past Life Regression With Mate Or Lover." "Have you lived a former life with your present mate or lover?" Mr Konicov asks, impertinently. "Sometimes you may get that feeling, and rightly so." Reading further one finds that he is not making the point that some relationships seem so tedious and drawn out that they seem to have lasted for more than one lifetime but that "We tend to return to life surrounded by those persons who will afford us the greatest opportunity for spiritual growth." Mr Konicov says, as do all apologists for the probing of past lives, that such investigations "will add meaning and understanding to your present life experience" but I am afraid that I find the concept rather worrying. What if one regressed and made the discovery that those lives were not ideologically sound? What if one found that one was a part of the mob that called for the release of Barabbas and for crucifixion of Our Redeemer? What if I had been a magistrate fond of sentencing witches to death by burning? What if I was Jack the Ripper? What if I was, in one or more of those lives, a socialist or a cannibal or a fan of country music or, worse still, a woman? ,

23 Jan 1989 - 'Softly, softly' a 'liability' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 23 January 1989, page 4 'Softly, softly' is a 'liability' From ANDREA DOWNES in Brisbane Sections of the National Party fear the "softly, softly" approach of the Queensland Premier, Mike Ahern, may be becoming an electoral liability, highlighted by the messy sack-ing of the Minister for Health, Leisha Harvey, last week. National Party fears of potential- ly damaging by-elections have seen both the Premier and the party ac- cused of taking the soft option against Mrs Harvey and disgraced former minister and self-confessed tax cheat Don Lane. The lack of decisive action may backfire against the Nationals in this year's state election, forcing it back into coalition with the Liber- als. Opinion polls show Queensland voters are abandoning the National Party in favour of the Liberal and Labor parties, with support for the Nationals at 24 per cent, the Liber-als at 27 per cent and Labor at 42 per cent. The Morgan Gallup poll showed conservative Coalition would have won government with a com- bined vote of 51 per cent had an election been held at the time of polling in November and December last year. The Liberal Party has launched petitions to tap public outrage that Mr Lane is still receiving his full parliamentary salary despite telling the Fitzgerald inquiry that he was one of 14 past and present ministers who rorted their ministerial ex-penses. Mr Lane has ignored tradition by refusing to resign from his inner Brisbane seat of Merthyr. The Na- Mike Ahern tional Party simply agreed to his suggestion that his party member-ship be suspended, allowing him to return to Parliament in March as an Independent, pending the outcome of the Fitzgerald inquiry. "I have repeatedly said and will say again that we are cleaning out the stable," Mr Ahem said at the time of Mr Lane's suspension last November. But one stable he did not clean out until too late was Mrs Harvey's. Her sacking gave her political ammunition to accuse Mr Ahern of lacking humanity over her appoint-ment of an ex-prisoner to her staff, when her demotion to the back bench in last week's reshuffle would have been seen as strong leadership. Mr Ahern's apparent acquies-cence following her thinly veiled threats that she would resign from Parliament to cause a by-election if dropped from Cabinet merely pro-longed the political damage. He relieved Mrs Harvey of the health portfolio in the reshuffle, leaving her with family services, and ordered her to take only six of her ten personal staff members with her to her new ministry. Mrs Harvey was plagued by con-troversy during her 13 months as Health Minister. Hospital doctors threatened to resign over their working conditions and her lack of consultation, and she appointed relatives, including her daughter, and sister-in-law, as personal staff. The final straw, according to Mr Ahern, was her failure to tell him she had appointed a 22-year-old typist, the daughter of family friends, who had been imprisoned for fraud totalling $29,000. Mrs Harvey retaliated by accus-ing the Premier of having "no heart for the average human being". Mrs Harvey's sacking less than two hours before she was due to be sworn in to the reshuffled Cabinet led to Opposition claims that Mr "Ahern was "wimpishly" using the ex-prisoner's appointment as an ex-cuse for a political sacking. "This young woman is the unfor-tunate scapegoat in the latest con-fused episode of National Party intrigues," Deputy Opposition Leader Tom Burns said. "The truth is Leisha Harvey was never Cabinet material and her poor performance should have guaranteed her dis- missal. — AAP

30 Jan 1989 - Poll shows WA Labor slipping Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 30 January 1989, page 1 Poll shows WA Labor slipping PERTH: Support for the Western Australian Labor Government has slumped only a week before the state election, according to a poll published yesterday. The Morgan Gallup poll, which appeared in the Sunday Times newspaper, indicates (he election next Saturday will be a cliffhanger. It showed support for Labor fell by 3.5 percentage points in the past week to 44.5 per cent. It also showed Premier Peter Dowding's popularity crashed by 6 percentage points. Liberal support was steady on 40 per cent, with support for the Nationals up one point to 4 per cent -giving the Liberal-National Coalition 44 per cent. The minor parties, which are expected to decide the election outcome, were on 10 per cent.

04 Feb 1989 - Few marginal seats to decide WA poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 4 February 1989, page 1 Few marginal seats to decide WA poll From ANDREW FRASER, in Perth PERTH: The home of an Independent candidate in the Western Australian election was firebombed and blasted with a shotgun early yesterday, police said. A police spokesman said Jack van Tongeren, who is standing for the seat of Helena on an anti-Asian platform, woke about lam when several bombs were thrown at his home in suburban Gosnells. A shotgun was also fired at the house, smashing windows, the spokesman said. Mr van Tongeren is leader of the Australian Nationalists Movement He is opposed to the "Asianisation of Australia and to Zionist control of Australia". Police were investigating the incident, but had no firm leads yesterday afternoon. The preferences of Independent candidates in a handful of marginal seats scattered around Perth suburbs are expected to be the decisive factor in the state election in Western Australia today. The latest Westpoll shows that support for the ALP state-wide is running at 48 per cent and support for the Liberal-National Coalition is 46 per cent. The Morgan Gallup poll showed support for the ALP at 45 per cent and for the Coalition at 44 per cent. A win by the Coalition would lift the morale of the Liberal Party in particular in much the same way that the win in NSW by Nick Greiner did last year, and put the party on an optimistic note heading into a year in which a federal election will probably beheld. For the ALP, it dearly needs to recovt'x its electoral momentum, after losing NSW last year and just holding on to Victoria towards the end of the year. The Coalition needs a swing of about 6 per cent, or eight seats. All polls indicate that the Coalition has not achieved a swing of this magnitude, but the ALP's performance is also well down from the 53.2 per cent of the vote it gained in the 1986 state election. The major Independent groups running in today's election are the Australian Democrats, whose support is estimated by the Morgan Gallup Poll at l.S per cent, and Greypower, a team of senior citizens whose support is estimated at about 3 per cent of the electorate. There are no high-profile Independent candidates, such as Dawn Fraser who won Balmain in the NSW election last year, and an independent analyst, Professor David Black of the Curtin University of Technology in Perth, said that it was unlikely that Independents would actually capture a seat today. "I would think minor parties will become more important in the future as people get used to voting for them," he said. "We'll probably follow South Australia and NSW and start having minor parties in the Upper House. We may do this time, but it's not as likely." The preferences of these minor parties are expected to gO' mainly to the Liberal Party, and certainly the ALP regards Greypower as a front for the Liberal Party and a means of siphoning off its support among elderly voters. The only small-party preferences which are expected to go the ALP are those of the Australian Democrats, who have traditionally never polled well in Western Australia, and the various environmental parties, who are expected to make an impact only in areas which are ALP strongholds already. For the Liberal Party, its hopes mainly rest on some of the odium of WA Inc sticking, and it has released a barrage of detailed policies. There has been some pressure on the Liberal Party this week to substantiate allegations that the massive Bond Corporation, which was named by the leader of the Liberal Party, Barry MacKinnon, as being in partnership with the Government in WA Inc, donated $3.5 million to the ALP campaign, and some of this pressure has come from its coalition partner, the National Party, led by Hendy Cowan. But mostly there has been a fairly amiable show of coalition unity, and should it lose, there will be a great deal of soul-searching. In the event of a Liberal loss the position of the current leader, Barry MacKinnon, would become untenable. Polls have been fairly static in the past two weeks, with no decisive trend showing up one way or the other. 07 Feb 1989 - Liberals plan joint ACT-NSW prison Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 7 February 1989, page 1 Liberals plan joint ACT-NSW prison By FIA CUMMING A Liberal Government in the ACT would set up a taskforce with NSW on options for a new, shared prison. The NSW Minister for Corrective Services, Michael Yabsley, and ACT Liberal spokesman on law and order, Gary Humphries, announced the proposal yesterday. Although ACT sites will be considered, it is likely the new prison will be built in NSW, not far from the Territory border. Mr Humphries singled out Yarrowlumla Shire Council as one border area which has sought a new prison project. Mr Yabsley said that the taskforce would comprise himself, as NSW Minister, the relevant ACT Minister, and senior officials from both NSW and the ACT. The plan would benefit NSW, which has a shortage of around 750 jail places, as well as the ACT. "It is inevitable that a prison facility in respect of the ACT be established, The Electoral Commission has warned of a serious delay in printing ballot papers for early voting, if parties and candidates for the election do not nominate quickly. The ACT Electoral Officer, Geoff Maries, urged all parties and Independents who wanted to stand to formally nominate early this week, although nominations do not close until noon on Friday. With up to 33 registered parties nominating candidates, and an un known number of Independents, the draws for ballot-paper positions could be badly delayed if all nominations were left to the last minute. Two draws will take place after close of nominations — one for parties, one for Independents. uWe need to complete these draws by early afternoon so that we can start printing ballot papers to allow eligible people to pre-poll vote from the following Monday," Mr Maries said. and that should be done in a spirit of cooperation between NSW and the ACT," he said. The taskforce would go ahead only if the Liberals won government in the ACT, but said this was only because of Labor Party policy. "I think the Labor Party has been stupid enough to dismiss the idea of a jail for the ACT," he said "I think that is the ultimate head-in-the-sand approach. "I think it really does boil down to this, that each society needs prisons to accommodate offenders within that society. "As the ACT approaches self-government, it really is an appropriate time for that need to be addressed." Until yesterday, the Liberal Party had promised to examine setting up a jail within the ACT, using existing buildings if necessary. But Mr Humphries said a shared facility made much better economic sense. A new prison would cost $25 million to $30 million, catering for fewer thanlOOprisonersatany time. "We probably couldn't fill a prison exclusively for ACT prisoners and make it economical," he said. "We wouldn't say no if it turned out it was better to have the prison over the border in Yarrowlumla Shire, as long as the ACT has significant control over prisoners in that system." Shared control would probably mean that the ACT would have to pay part of the capital and running costs. At present, the Federal Government pays NSW about $2.4 million to keep prisoners from the ACT. Mr Humphries said that the need for a prison for ACT offenders had become more marked in recent yean for legal and humanitarian reasons. Lack of effective control over what happened to prisoners was a disincen tive to ACT judges and magistrates to impose jail sentences. Also, it was unfair for families, who were often poor, to have to travel long distances to see relatives in NSW pris ons. "It is not our object to fill jails to overflowing with criminals to satisfy the retributive instinct, or to blitz crime by putting as many people behind bars as possible," Mr Humphries said. "But it is a fact that courts are discouraged from sentencing people who deserve custodial terms because of the present situation. "That is bad for the community, and it blunts efforts to deal with crime effectively." The joint taskforce proposal does . not commit a Liberal Government to spend any money on a prison in its first budget, and Mr Humphries stressed that the new prison was a long-term goal. Liberal prison plan Continued from Page 1 However, according to a Morgan Gallup poll conducted for the Liberal Party, most Canbcrrans support the plan for a new prison., , The poll of 252 people taken on January 14 and 15 found that 59 per cent of voters believed an ACT prison was a good idea, almost 22 per cent of them strongly. Only 33 per cent disagreed, 17 per cent strongly. Even among Labor voters there was a majority of 52.4 per cent in favour of a prison. If it does go ahead, Mr Yabsley said the new prison would cater mainly for maximum-sccurity prisoners, because this was the area of greatest shortage in NSW. But minimum arid medium-security facilities would also be available for ACT prisoners. The -special needs of juveniles and women w6u!d be looked after. The Liberal Party is committed to maintaining the Belconnen Remand Cen trc for the foreseeable future, and to administering it separately from the prison. While disturbed by the low rate of jail sentences in ACT courts at present, Mr Humphries said a Liberal Government would not put pressure on the courts to "get tough". In another move to improve law and order in Canberra, the Liberal Party has promised to reintroduce the offence of consorting with known criminals. This is an offence in all the states, but was removed from the ACT statutes in 1984 by the Hawke Government. Mr Humphries said the Federal Police were highly concerned that the absence of such a law had greatly hampered their efforts, especially in heading off crimes before they occurred. A Liberal Government would make it a crime to consume alcohol in a bus station or shopping centre, except on licensed premises.

18 Feb 1989 - Poll puts me ahead: Haines Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 18 February 1989, page 7 Poll puts me ahead: Haines BRISBANE: Australian Democrats Leader Senator Janine Haines believes she has a better than 50 per cent chance of winning the federal seat of Kingston in South Australia. She said yesterday that a Morgan Gallup Poll survey done for the Democrats over the past four weeks had put her support at around 32 per cent. "The indication is at the moment that I am running ahead of the Liberal Party candidate," she said. "All I need to win is 33 per cent of the vote and Liberal Party preferences." The Morgan figure was way ahead of the 11 per cent of the vote gained by the Democrat candidate for Kingston at the last election. "There's no doubt at the moment that it's better than 50 per cent that I'll win the seat from Labor's Gordon Bilney," she said. Senator Haines has announced she will relinquish her Upper House position to contest the House of Representatives seat. Kingston used to be fairly safe Liberal but was now marginal Labor following boundary changes. The Democrats' Leader was in Brisbane to launch the party's candidature for the by-election for the state seat of Merthyr, recently vacated by disgraced former minister Don Lane. She said that apart from the general feeling that people were tired of the established parties, she had a high profile in South Australia ana people knew what they were getting. This was why other women, like the Liberals' Kathy Sullivan, had turned Moncrieff on Queensland's Gold Coast into a fairly safe Liberal seat, and Elaine Darling had made her Brisbane seat of Lilley much safer for Labor. Paul Malone's column. — Page 9.

24 Feb 1989 - Libs want contracts for senior bureaucrats Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 24 February 1989, page 2 Libs want contracts for senior bureaucrats By FIA CUMMING All senior public servants in the ACT Administration would be placed on contracts and all Public Service positions would be open to outside applicants under a Liberal government. And a senior executive selection panel, including people from outside the ACT Administration, would be set up to advise the Chief Minister on selecting candidates for senior managerial positions. But, in a backdown from its earlier proposal, the Liberal Party has dropped a plan to use outside consultants to rate the performance of government departments each year. In a major concession to Public Service unions, it has also now promised full mobility between the new ACT Administration and the Commonwealth •Public Service. Releasing the final policy, Liberal leader, Trevor Kaine, dissociated himself from the draft policy and a draft policy speech, leaked to The Canberra Times. Mr Kaine said the alleged policy containing derogatory references to lazy and selfish public servants, had never been endorsed by the party executive. He said the Liberal Party recognised the importance of the Public Service, which would be entrusted with implementing all the policies of the incoming government, and wanted the highest quality bureaucracy possible. Key points in the Liberal policy include: The head of Administration will be appointed by the Chief Minister; deputy heads and agency "Trevor Kaine heads will be appointed by the Ghief Minister, in consultation with the relevant minister. A review of ACT statutory'au thorities to consider whether their functions would be better performed by thd Public Ser vice. Government businesses and de partments will have to operate on a commercial basis as far as possible. An agreed percentage of the funds for each department and agency to be allocated to staff training and development. Salary and leave provisions will be the same as the Common wealth Public Service initially, but may be reviewed and if possible improved in time. Complaints from the public "about bad management or de cisions will be heard by an [un specified] independent arbiter' and Freedom of Information legislation introduced. Liberal spokesman on public administration, Bill Stefaniak, said his party would create an open and accountable administration that would aim to be a m6del for other states and territories. "We will create an innovative and dynamic Public Service that will be one of the most effective in Australia and which will at tract the top performers in public administration Australia-wide," Mr Stefaniak said." "No-one will be dismissed as a result of the setting up of an ACT Public Service and conditions of service will not be adversely af fected." On the senior executive service, Mr Stefaniak denied that the new selection panel would open the way for political appointments and said only people well qualified to sit on the panel would be chosen. He said its members might include outsiders, such as former federal public servants, but no members of the ACT govern ment. But he did admit that contract appointments, as proposed by the Liberals, could be politicised, referring to the Federal Government's refusal to reappoint Mr Ian Temby as Director of Public Prosecutions. "I would hope that our senior executive selection panel, those experts, do ensure that the best person for the job is hired," he said. "The whole reason is to have a panel of people who are non-political, who are the. best people to make the best appoint ments." On outside appointments, Mr Stefaniak said even a departmental head could come from outside the service under the Liberals' open selection policy, if their qualifications were good enough. But he said this was most un likely "unless some whizz-kid" applied, because of the number of talented people within the Administration. Mr Stefaniak said a Liberal government would aim for as little disruption as possible of the Public Service because so much change had already been endured. He said no changes would be made to conditions, salaries or appeals without consultations, especially with Public Service unions. In a further change from the draft, the final Liberal policy does not threaten penalties for government departments or authorities which submit their annual reports late. But it does require them to hand in the reports within two months of the end of the financial year — a deadline which Mr Stefaniak said was quite achievable. To encourage efficiency, Mr Stefaniak said departments which did not spend annual budgets would not have their next year's allocation cut. The surplus would be used for other department functions. Alliance calls for a review of ACT taxes The Rainbow Alliance has called for a thorough review of the ACT system, in consultation with the public. It also wants the Federal Government to delay phasing in new Grants Commission funding arrangements till the new ACT government has had a full term in office. Alliance candidate Alan Runciman said the review would identify "regressive, inefficient and nuisance taxes". He would listen to the community's views.on what level of taxation it was willing to bear. , "We believe it is vital that the Grants Commission properly recognise the costs and lost revenue which decades of Commonwealth policies and the on-going Commonwealth presence place on ACT finances," Mr Runciman said. Mr Runciman said the RA would aim for better efficiency in the ACT administration, including the use of forward estimates and program budgeting. It also supported a betterment tax of 100 per cent to prevent windfall gains to landholders at the expense of the community. To create jobs, the RA wants more support for co-operatives and small business. It would create a Local Employment Agency to oversee all support for small business, and co-ordinate "home work", or people working from home. "Home work is the preferred mode of operation for many sections of the community," said RA candidate Sarah Kirschbaum. "But it also frequently leads to exploitation of workers through sub-standard pay and inadequate safety and other work conditions. It will be a duty of the agency to facilitate the extension of home work, as well as protect the rights and conditions for homeworkers." The RA would aim to generate environmentally sensitive employment initiatives, such as recycling and planting gum plantations. Opposition still uncommitted The Federal Opposition has not yet committed itself to maintaining the current financial arrangements for transition of the ACT to self-government, but it is unlikely to change them. The Opposition spokesman on the ACT, Senator Robert Hill, said yesterday that the coalition had not decided on transitional arrangements for the ACT,and it would have to be decided in a total budgetary context. Under current arrangements, the Federal Government would continue to fund the ACT Budget at the current rate for another two years, and for two years after that, phase it down to where the ACT was being funded by the Federal Government at a similar rate on a per capita basis to the other states. — ANDREW FRASER Unskilled turn Liberal By ANDREW FRASER An interesting thing happened in January to' that statistical group classed as "unskilled workers" — in the ACT they stopped supporting the ALP and gave allegiance to the Liberal Party. A Morgan Gallup poll commissioned by the ACT Liberal Party found that in January, 58 percent of unskilled workers supported the ALP and 26 per cent supported the Liberal Party, which is not a surprising figure. But in February, the Morgan Gallup poll showed that support for the Liberal Party among unskilled workers was 42 per cent, which was ahead of the ALP which commanded the support of only 38 per cent of this group. Another area where the Liberal Party polled comparatively well was among young people. In January, 55 per cent of people aged 18 to 24 supported the ALP, and only 18 per cent supported the Liberals. Again, this is about the usual situation. But in the February poll, 37 per cent in this age group supported the ALP, while support for the Liberal Party was 32 per cent. While the ALP is still ahead, the gap has been considerably narrowed. However it is clerical workers — or public servants — who will decide the outcome of the election. Support for the Liberal Party among this group is not high — about 15 per cent — but the ' Morgan Gallup poll shows that support for the ALP among this group has dropped from 44 per cent to 30 per cent. This still leaves a huge vote among the clerks that goes to neither Labor nor Liberal, and the survey shows that the remainder of support among this group is spread among the Residents Rally, Family Team, No Self Government Party, Canberra First Party. The survey also says that support for the ALP has dropped from 40 per cent to 30 per cent. But the Liberal Party worker who gave these figures to The Canberra Times was not all that helpful when it came to listing the current levels of support for his own party. The Canberra 77wiej/Datacol survey showed support for the ALP at around 20 per cent, and for the Liberal Party at about 10 per cent. Candidates warned ACT accounting bodies warned all ACT election candidates yesterday against increasing business taxes. The ACT division of the Australian Society of Accountants and the ACT branch of the Institute of Chartered Accountants said they did not wish to enter election politics but wanted business in the ACT to prosper. They said tax increases would encourage businesses to move out of the ACT. Berry's 'no' to debate on health Continued from Page 1 Mr Berry said he had considered the debate too narrow in its concept, and had advised the organisers of this when he had been invited to be involved. He had taken part, with Mr Cornwell, in a public debate on health issues, organised by the Public Health Association, only two nights ago, which had shown Labor was not scared to debate but wanted a broader debate, involving other candidates. Mr Berry had told Dr Newcombe he had serious reservations about the narrowness of a debate simply on the role of private enterprise, and had asked that other candidates be included, to broaden it to cover all aspects of health. Limiting the debate to some assets of Liberal health privatisation policies might suit some doctors but was not acceptable to the Labor Party. A Labor spokesman said late yesterday that Mr Berry had set some conditions on his participation, but the organisers had been unable to meet them, and so he had not accepted the invitation. "The whole thing had been organised before Wayne was contacted," the spokesman said.

08 Mar 1989 - Parliament and politics ALP 'popularity fall' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 8 March 1989, page 10 ALP 'popularity fall' SYDNEY: Australia's record January trade deficit appears to have reduced electoral support for the ALP, according to the most recent Morgan Gallup poll.
