27 Mar 1989 - Survey: ban all tobacco advertising Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 27 March 1989, page 1 Survey: ban all tobacco advertising By FIA CUMMING A large majority of NSW voters support tougher anti-smoking measures, including higher cigarette taxes and a ban on all cigarette advertising, according to a new sur vey. The Morgan Gallup poll of more than 800 people of voting age found that nine out of 10 favoured an increase in tobacco taxes, if the money raised went toward anti-smoking and health-promotion campaigns. Two-thirds of those surveyed wanted a ban on all forms of cigarette advertising, and almost three out of five wanted a tougher government anti-smoking campaign — including one in three smokers. The survey even showed strong support for a ban on sports sponsorship by tobacco companies. Forty-seven per cent of voters surveyed unconditionally approved of a sponsorship ban A farther 21 per cent said they would approve if the government used the money from higher tobacco taxes to fund sport, in place of the tobacco companies. Significantly, the survey found political preferences did not affect support for the anti-smoking measures, with almost equal support among Liberal-National, Labor, and Demo crat voters. Labor voters tended to be slightly less in favour of the measures applied unconditionally, but made up for this with stronger support for the measures if they were accompanied by redirection of tobacco taxes to positive causes. The NSW Cancer Council, which commissioned the poll, says the, results show widespread public con-, cera about the health effects of smoking. Although the survey was confined to city and country areas in NSW, a council spokesman, Stephen Woodward, said yesterday that he believed a survey in the ACT would find simi lar support for anti-smoking mea sures. "With a preponderance of better educated people, they tend to be a bit more aware, and I think the results in Canberra would be as strong if not stronger," he said. Mr Woodward said the council was not surprised by the results, although they contradict fears on both sides of politics that a further crackdown on the tobacco industry could create a public backlash. The Cancer Council has asked the NSW Government to ban tobacco advertising, but Cabinet decided in favour of a voluntary code instead. "We actually expected these results, we wanted to demonstrate to the NSW Government that action in this area does have a substantial amount of public support, and that that support is widespread across electors of all parties," Mr Woodward said. But he said the results also contained a message for the Federal Government and the incoming ACT Assembly. He said the Hawke Government had done only one significant thing to tobacco policy since it was elected in 1983 and that was banning smoking on domestic aircraft. That ban had proved "an outrageous success", with less congestion For passengers checking in, reduced cleaning bills for airlines, and virtually no complaints from passengers wanting to smoke. Mr Woodward said the aircraft ban was a good example of how the tobacco companies made an issue controversial before the decision was made, but the public supported it after the event. In the ACT, Mr Woodward said the new ACT Government should take heed of the survey and find the courage to take tougher anti-smoking measures. "First, they would find that there is likely to be very strong public opinion in favour of it, and secondly, it will be of considerable benefit to the health of thepeople of the ACT," he said. NSW now spends less per capita on . smoking-reduction programs ' than any other state. Its yearly bud get of $1.3 million represents only 22.5c a person, compared to $ 1.21 in Western Australia, 72c in Victoria and 71c in Queensland. The NSW Cancer Council is particularly concerned at children taking up smoking. The council's'executive director, Elaine Henry, said one-third of NSW school children were smokers. "A child who starts to smoke aged 14 years or younger is. five times more likely to die of lung cancer than a person who starts aged 24 or more years, and 15 times more likely to die of lung cancer than a person who never smokes," Mrs Henry said. "Similar effects have been noted with other diseases due to smoking."

04 Oct 1989 - Decision in the wind for December 2 election Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 4 October 1989, page 1 Decision in the wind for December 2 election By TONY WRIGHT The Government is likely to decide next week on whether to go to an early election on December 2 this year. The decision will be made after the Opposition releases its long-awaited tax policy. Government tacticians have already spent several weeks "testing the waters" among members in marginal seats around Australia to gauge support for a December election. According to Canberra sources, some campaign workers have been told to begin clearing their diaries in November and early December in the expectation of an election. The Opposition has been preparing for an early election for some time, and the Liberal Party is understood to have virtually completed its campaign plans. Its Sydney advertising firm, George Paterson, is in the final stages of preparing campaign advertising. In the Liberal Party room at Par Iiament House yesterday, Opposition leader Andrew Peacock called for his shadow ministers to begin "singing the same song" on whatever issue was current. Mr Pcacock is keen to play down any perception of disunity in the Opposition as the poll date nears. The Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has not yet given his approval for an election this year, but senior party officials say that if the Opposition's tax policy proves easy to attack, the Prime Minister could be convinced to run. Such a prospect will be given a boost today by a Morgan Gallup poll to be published in The Bulletin show ing the Government leading the Opposition in popularity, 43.5 per cent to 42.5 per cent. The Opposition plans to release its tax policy to the media in a "lock-up" in Parliament House at 2pm on Wednesday or Thursday next week, and Mr Peacock will give a news conference two hours later. The biggest question hanging over the policy is how the Opposition plans to slice more than $1.2 billion from public spending and still retain the faith with the voting public. A likely sector to suffer the knife is the long-term unemployed, with special attention being paid to reducing fraud in social security, education and Aboriginal affairs. However, the ex tent of fraud in these sectors has not yet been determined. The Opposition also plans phasing in a two-tiered taxation system, with reduced personal income tax. Labor analysts Hill go through the policy with a fine tooth-comb, looking for the sort of basic miscalculations that blew the 1984 Opposition tax policy out of the water. This time, the Opposition has hired consulting firm Access Economics to check all the calculations. Labor will also be looking at the policy as a possible "smoke-screen" — a plan that promises much but, in fact, does very little. In that case, it is highly likely that the December 2 election date will become a matter of fact. The plan among Labor tacticians is for Mr Hawke to call the election within a week of his return from the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Kuala Lumpur starting on October 18. Continued on Page 2. Election in wind for December 2 Continued from Page 1 He will return to Australia on October 25, so the announcement could be expected to be made on November 1 or 2. This would leave a four-week election campaign. Labor will want want a short, sharp campaign to prevent Andrew Peacock from making too much running on the precarious nature of the economy. A Labor win would be a fine birthday present for Mr Hawke, who turns 60 on December 9. The tacticians were considering a December 2 election more than a fortnight ago, but appeared to drop the idea because the pilots' dispute was going so badly. But the plan has been revived following the release of the record balance of payments deficit for August, the realisation that interest rates will not drop in the foreseeable future, and the reliance on "damage control" measures to keep up appearances that the Government is coping with the economy. The. one hope on Labor's horizon is that the pilots' dispute is close to resolution — the Industrial Relations Commission has agreed that the individual contracts being offered to pilots could become the basis of an award. Mr Hawke, who has staked his career on the issue, said yesterday he believed a resolution was in sight. Clearly, if the dispute was solved, Mr Hawke would go into an early election with an enhanced reputation. However, one of the Hawke Government's most serious problems in the near future could be greater pressure on the balance of payments. The value of two of Australia's most valuable export commodities, wool and wheat, has taken a sharp dive this year. The wool clip and wheat contributed $8.22 billion last year. But wool prices have plunged recently to the point that the Australian Wool Corporation has been forced to buy up to 50 per cent of wool offered at some recent sales, and there is a shortage of wheat for export. On present indications, wheat and wool might contribute only around $4.5 billion to export income this year. Combined with lost revenue through the long-running pilots' dispute, this could have a serious effect on the balance-of-payment figures for some time, reducing further the Government's chances of controlling the damage to its image in the electorate. This alone would be a powerful incentive for an early election. Two wild-cards remain in the timing of a federal election. Dates for the Queensland and South Australian elections have not been announced. Those in the Labor Party who want a federal poll on December 2 are counting on a South Australian election in November — with a Labor Government victory — and a Queensland election further down the track. Neither of these can be counted on at this stage.

07 Oct 1989 - Even struggle between parties Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 7 October 1989, page 9 Even struggle between parties S THERE is an error factor of 3 per cent in most polls JL JL the ALP's lead of 1 per cent over the Liberal-National Coalition in this week's Morgan Gallup Poll tends to indicate that the parties are still fairly evenly matched in the electoral struggle. The poll showed that support for the ALP is at 43.5 per cent while the Coalition is at 42.5 per cent. There has been very little between the two parties since March last year when the Coalition was well ahead, but more worrying for the Coalition is the gradual decline in the popularity of its leader, Andrew Peacock. Mr Peacock's approval rating has dropped steadily and is now at 27 per cent, and while the approval rating of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has also dropped, it is still considerably higher than Mr Peacock's at 48 per cent The level pegging of the two parties was emphasised by the Newspoll which shows that support,, for the parties is equal at 42.5 per cent. Another poll on attitudes towards homosexuality shows that nearly 58 per cent of Australians think that homosexuality should be legalised, while 34 per cent think not. But at the same time, less Australians are prepared to grant them the same level of social rights and benefits as heterosexual couples — only 37 per cent think they should while 54 per cent think not, and 10 per cent are undecided. The poll was also broken down into states and, in some cases, between capital cities and rural areas, and shows that intolerance of ho mosexuality is highest in rural Victoria, where 51.4 per cent believe male homosexuality should be illegal and 49.3 per cent thought female homosexuality should also be illegal. While homosexuality is legal in Victoria, a majority of people polled in states where it is. illegal — Queensland, Western Australia, and Tasmania — all thought homosexuality should be decriminalised, with 56 per cent in Queensland, 47 per cent in Tasmania (41.5 per cent thought it should remain illegal) and 74 per cent in Western Australia. But while support for homosexuality has risen 4 per cent overall since a previous poll was taken 15 years ago, those who believed such behaviour should be made illegal also had risen to 34 per cent — a rise of eight per cent since 1974. 14 Oct 1989 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 14 October 1989, page 9 The alp is hoping thata a big win in the South Australian election,due due before the end of the year, will set up a winning sequence with the (Queensland election following and then the federal election in the first half of,next year. The Morgan Gallup Poll shows that the ALP would win easily in South Australia, with support for the ALP at 46 per cent, the Coalition at 38 per cent, the Australian Democrats at 12 per cent, and others at 4 per cent. Compared with the last election in 1985, the ALP's vote is down by 4 per cent, and the Coalition vote down by 6 per cent. The Democrats appear to be the main beneficiary of the disillusionment with the major parties, their vote being up by 8 per cent. The ALP's main asset in South Australia appears to be Premier John Bannon, whose personal approval rating is 71 per cent, while Opposition Leader John Olsen only commands 44 per cent. Sixty-four per cent of South Australians polled think that Mr Bannon would make the best Premier, while 23 per cent chose Mr Olsen. In Queensland, the ALP needs a swing of about 5.5 per cent, but while they achieved'this, the swing must be closely targeted in specific seats because of the curious nature of the state's electoral system. Federally, the two parties remain neck and neck, with the Saulwick poll showing a slight lead for the Coalition and the election outcome being decided by the preferences of the minor parties. The poll found that 38 per cent of Australians would vote for the ALP and 41 per cent for the Opposition, with the Democrats at 10 per cent and minor parties and Independents at 11 per cent. It comes back to preferences, and recent elections show that 57 per cent of the preferences of the Australian Democrats go to the ALP. The Morgan Gallup Poll issued last week showed that the ALP was slightly ahead, but in all polls there is a variation factor of about 4 per cent, meaning that as an indication the federal election is still too close to call. 11 Apr 1990 - Cain 'would have won' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 11 April 1990, page 2 Cain 'would have won' SYDNEY: The Victorian Labor Government would have been returned to power had an election been staged in March, according to the latest Morgan gallup poll. The survey results published in this week's Bulletin magazine suggest the assumption that John Cain's Government was largely to blame for the Federal Government's loss of nine Victorian seats in the March federal election was wrong. It showed Mr Cain would have been returned to office, with ALP support up 1.5 per cent on the previous survey to 43 per cent. The Liberal and National Parties' vote was up 1 per cent to 41 per cent in the poll of 1616 electors. The Democrats lost ground (1 per cent to 12 per cent) as did "others" with 5 per cent (down 1.5 percent).

18 Apr 1990 - Hewson as leader boosts Libs' stocks Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 18 April 1990, page 2 Hewson as leader boosts Libs' stocks The Libera] Party's selection of John Hewson as leader appears to have paid off with a boost in the opinion polls. Dr Hewson's popularity in his first week was 34 per cent, compared with Andrew Peacock's 24 per cent in his last week in the job just after losing the March 24 federal election, according to a Morgan Gallup poll to be published in today's Bulletin magazine. Prime Minister Bob Hawke's popularity was 53 per cent, a 7 per cent increase since the election.

02 Oct 1987 - More seek to be seen as Aborigines Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 2 October 1987, page 6 More seek : to be seen as Aborigines More Australians than ever before want to be identified as Aborigines, the country's most underprivileged and. disadvantaged group, thf federal Minister for Aboriginal Affairs, Mr Hand," said yesterday. Mr Hand said new census figures showed that the number of people identifying themselves as Aborigines or Torres Strait Islanders had increased nationally by 42 per cent since 1981. In a statement on the 1986 Population and Housing Census carried out by the Australian Bureau of Statistics; Mr Hand said the rise showed racism and discriminatory attitudes were gradually declining. "In the past, people may have felt that such identification could have been detrimental to their employment opportunities or community acceptance," he said. Mr Hand said the most recent Morgan Gallup Poll showed that more than 70 per cent of Australians believed that recent initiatives for Ab original advancement should be maintained or that more should be done for Aborigines. But, he said, the census also depicted the reality that Aborigines remained Australia's most underprivileged and disadvantaged group, with many continuing to live in substandard housing. Life expectancy for Aborigines at birth was 20 years less than for other Australians, and Aboriginal child mortality three times higher than the national average. Mr Hand said that, on average, Aborigines earned only half the income of other Australians and their unemploy ment rate was six times the national average. A special effort had been made in the census to consult with Aboriginal communities and to use Aboriginal collectors and field officers. Bureau figures show the Aboriginal and Islander population nationwide in 1971 at 115,953, in 1976 at 160,915, in 1981 at 159,897 and in 1986 at 227,645.

06 Oct 1987 - Poll finds most oppose sell-off Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 6 October 1987, page 3 Poll finds most oppose sell-off MELBOURNE: Most voters oppose total or partial privatisation of Australia Post, the Commonwealth Bank and Qantas, according to a Saulwick Herald poll published in yesterday's Sydney Morning Herald and Melbourne Age newspapers. But a majority supported the total or partial privatisation of Australian Airlines and Telecom. The poll found 59 per cent of respondents opposed the sale of Australia Post, 64 per cent opposed privatisation of the Commonwealth Bank, and 52 per cent opposed the sale of Qantas Airlines. Thirty-one per cent of respondents said Telecom should be sold to private enterprise, 22 per cent said the Government should sell part of Telecom but keep control, and 44 per cent opposed any sale. The poll found 30 per cent wanted Australian Airlines sold, 28 per cent wanted the Government to sell part of the airline but maintain control and 40 per cent opposed any sale. The poll questioned 876 voters I last Tuesday and Wednesday nights.

07 Nov 1987 - Qld Liberal leadership 'talk' on tape Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 7 November 1987, page 8 Old Liberal leadership 'talk' on tape BRISBANE: A taped car-telephone conversation between two senior state Liberals revealed an intention to replace the Liberal Parliamentary leader, Sir William Knox, the Brisbane Courier-Mail reported yesterday. The report said the tape was of a conversation between former Liberal leader Mr Terry White and former Young Liberals president Mr Santo Santoro on Wednesday afternoon. The tape was given to Channel 9 in Brisbane which broadcast a report and passed the tape to the Courier-Mail. A Channel 9 spokesman said the tape came from an eavesdropper using an electronic scanner. On the tape, Mr Santoro and Mr White refer to poll results, in particular the Morgan Gallup poll on Wednesday morning, which showed the Liberals had gained 6 per cent since last year's state elections, the report said. The two men discussed a "changeover" which should be "bloodless and dignified', it said.

08 Nov 1987 - Howard on decline, poll shows Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 8 November 1987, page 1 Howard on decline, poll shows MELBOURNE: A public opinion poll last week showed that the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, trailed the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, by a big margin, the Age newspaper reported yesterday. The Saulwick Age Poll measured support for Labor in Sydney at 38 per cent, with the Liberals on 39 per cent, and well behind the combined conservative vote of 43 per cent. Outside Sydney the Liberal vote dropped sharply. Overall, the Labor and conservative parties in NSW were level on 40 per cent while the Democrats had 12 per cent support. The Age said the standing of the parties would be of considerable concern to the Unsworth Government which is drawing close to an election. (Report. — Page 3). A nation-wide telephone poll on Wednesday and Thursday evenings found that the number of people who thought that Mr Howard was doing a good or very good job had dropped by a third, while those who thought his performance poor or very poor had risen by a similar amount. The Age said that, for the first time since the July election, Mr Howard had returned to a position of net unpopularity. Mr Hawke remained on the posiitive side: more than twice as many people approved as disapproved.

10 Sep 1987 - 3m Australians 'have tried marijuana' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 10 September 1987, page 9 I ' 3m Australians 'have ' tried marijuana' SYDNEY: More than three million Australians ' have smoked marijuana at some time in their lives, according to a Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin yesterday. The figure was projected from a survey of 1203 i men and women across the country. Forty-eight per cent of the 25-34 age group admitted to having smoked the illegal drug, and 33 per cent of the 14-24 age group had tried it The figures had doubled since a similar survey in 1977, according to The Bulletin. i However, not all who had tried it supported its legalisation: only 28 per cent of men and 22 per cent of women favoured relaxed legislation. --- r--r rr--- r :

04 May 1990 - Libs sensitive to aged in post-poll strategy Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 4 May 1990, page 4 Libs sensitive to aged in post-poll strategy The Federal Opposition will consider ways to reduce the impact of controversial economic and health policies on elderly Australians to maintain its hold on the aged vote. Liberal Party strategist Graham Morris confirmed yesterday that party analysis of Morgan Gallup polls since 1985 had shown the Coalition's share of the primary aged vote slipped from 64 per cent to 60 per cent The Opposition spokesman on social security, Richard Alston, said any Coalition debate on a possible consumption tax must consider its impact on fixed-income social-security pensioners and beneficiaries, particularly the aged and the unemployed. "I certainly would want there to be a proper consideration of the impact on social-welfare recipients," Senator Alston said. Mr Morris issued the party an alysis results to Liberal parliamentarians at their two-day seminar this week on the March 24 election loss. The main pressure in the Coalition to reject the tax probably will come from the National Party reacting to concern among asset-rich, but income-poor, farmers. Welfare groups consistently have rejected any tax reform involving a consumption tax. The Australian Catholic Bishops' Welfare Committee said this week higher prices triggered by a consumption tax severely could affect people on low incomes and families with small children. Australian Taxpayers' Association national director Eric Risstrom said on Tuesday social security pensioners were not the only elderly Australians needing protection from a consumption tax.

05 May 1990 - Hewson gains but Labor still leads Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 May 1990, page 9 Hewson gains but Labor still leads THE HAWKE Government has maintained its slight lead over the Coalition since the election despite greater public approval for John Hewson as parliamentary leader, according to the latest Morgan Gallup polls. Voting intention polls conducted over the April 14-15 and 21-22 weekends showed support for Labor up half a percentage point to 43.5 per cent. The Coalition received 41.5 per cent of the sample of 1910 electors, up 1.5 points on the election result. The "third force" of Australian Democrats and Independents droppedslightly slightly from 17.4 to 15 per cent. In the personality stakes, the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, saw his approval rating remain high at 56 per cent (up three percentage points), his disapproval rating steady at 37 per cent and 7 per cent of respondents undecided. Dr Hewson has made a good start in leadership with an approval rating of 54 per cent, up 11 points since the last poll. However Mr Hawke was still preferred as Prime Minister by 51 per cent of interviewees, 31 per cent nominating Dr Hewson as the best man for the job. Dr Hewson also did well in a poll of preferred party leadership. Thirty-five per cent of the 946 electors interviewed on April 14-15 said he would be the best leader of the Liberal Party. Preference for election leader Andrew Peacock has dropped from 35 per cent in December 1988 to just 5 per cent. Fred Chaney, former Senator and now a Member, remained at around 8 per cent. The only "old" face to gain more approval was former leader John Howard, who came in second with 21 per cent, down from 28 per cent in January 1990 but up from 17 per cent in December 1988. He was favoured by 28 per cent of voters to succeed Dr Hewson as leader well ahead of Mr Chaney and the former chief of the National Farmers' Federation, Ian McLachlan. On the Labor side, Mr Hawke remained the clearly preferred leader with 49 per cent. The Treasurer, Paul Keating, rated only 9 per cent and the Minister for Industry, Technology and Commerce, Senator John Button, 7 per cent As to who should succeed Mr Hawke, 42 per cent nominated Mr Keating, 13 per cent new Member and the Minister for Science and Technology, Simon Crean, and 8 per cent Senator Button.

08 May 1990 - Harmonising helps with the old folks at home Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 8 May 1990, page 15 Harmonising helps with the old folks at home It used to be that people didn't age. They died. But, not any more. We now live longer. And with this phenomenon comes a cornucopia of changing social is-sues. Increased life expectancy means more frail, elderly people and more multi-generational families. Among older people with adult children, about 40 per cent are heads of four-generation families, 94 per cent have grandchildren and 46 per cent have great-grandchildren. And among adult children, more than 80 per cent of middle-aged cou-plcs have at least one living parent, compared to fewer than half at the turn of the century. So for many middle-aged couples, now freed of the responsibility of their own children, there is the new need to care for elderly parents. One of the great surprises of grow-ing up is to find that whether you are 18, 30 or 50, your relationship with your parents doesn't at any stage automatically become adult. Perfectly, sensible middle-aged women are often driven to a frenzy of dusting and cleaning at the thought of a visit from their mother. Rational men will put on a singlet and carry a clean handkerchief to go to their mother's for dinner. It is necessary to see that learning to cope with ageing parents, to be patient and loving, is going to be quite different from dealing with the problems of an elderly neighbour or casual acquaintance. For. a start, they didn't change your nappies when you were a baby, they didn't insist you ate those beans for dinner and they probably wouldn't have cared had you gone off and married the delinquent you thought you were in love with when you were 18. And knowing all this doesn't make it any easier when it gets to the stage when parents need looking af- ter. A Morgan Gallup poll commis-sioned by the Bulletin magazine in March, 1988, showed that by far the greatest fear of elderly people was the inability to care for themselves. This was followed by fears of losing their health or becoming senile, both factors which would lead to depen-dency. Almost one-quarter of those polled feared having to depend on their family. Interestingly, it seems that while many adult children worry about not coping with Mum or Dad, the truth is Mum and Dad probably don't want to be there either. As one woman said, how can I expect my father to accept our household. My teenagers have parties, their friends drop in all the time, one dresses like she's dropped in from outer space and the other thinks about football all the time. And while it might be true that some elderly parents develop debilitating ailments there are some who main-tain good health. Certainly not all the elderly re-quire care. Today, there arc a great many people in their 60s, 70s and beyond living healthy and happy lives, totally independent of nursing and extended care. These retirees are A Senior Citizens' Week look at longevity, by Despene Clarke. active, joining committees, travel-ling and even taking on part-time work as they continue to enjoy their later years. No longer tied to their children or the responsibility of jobs, many are now more active than ever. In fact, this new-found independence can be something that many adult children have trouble coming to terms with. One woman was hurt to find her mother, who was always free to ba-bysit for her older sister, was now too busy. And many of these parents arc also financially secure — by this stage of life, mortgages are often paid up, children have left home and there arc few large purchases such as appliances to worry about. Sadly, this is not the case for all pensioners. The hidden poor are of-ten widows caught in a vicious circle of poverty, unable to get out, yet unable to seek help. In 1976, the Federal Henderson inquiry into Poverty found elderly people are the second latest group of poor people in Australia, single parents being the first. For many, the only solution is giving up what is left of their inde-pendence and moving in with their children. And it isn't always a lack of financial security that might mean an elderly person needs family care. For someone who has led a healthy life, the demise of their phys-ical_ condition to the point of help-lessness can be devastating — mentally and physically. Disease, not age, is the villain. But many of the diseases that now afflict the ageing can be effectively treated. Senility is probably the most dreaded of all debilities, yet only about 15 per cent of those over 65 suffer serious mental impairment. Alzheimer's disease, now considered the scourge of old age, accounts for more than half that total. And one of the most frequently ignored disorders among the elderly is depression, often mistaken for se-nility or dementia. While some medications can be blamed for this, the old arc more vulnerable to depression bccausc they have suffered more life stresses, including the death of friends, spouses, retirement or simply just living alone. The classic symptoms of depres-sion - guilt, hopelessness, sleepless-ness, lack of appetite and suicidal thoughts - arc more likely to be noticed in younger people than older people because they arc so out of character. The trouble is most of these symptoms are often dismissed as being old folks'crankiness. Women caring for their husbands seem to suffer the most. They have to learn to cope with emotional, fi-nancial and physical burdens in ad-dition to the assault of ageing on their own body. And there is the growing number of families provid-ing long-term care to older relatives - a number that is expected to con-tinue to grow over the next decade. What this will mean is an increase in the number of women caught in the middle of two generations. This woman is -usually aged between 35 and 55 and is sandwiched between the demands of the older and youn-ger generations. For many of these women, the feeling of freedom from her children becoming independent is over-shadowed by the fact she is now caring for her parents. The emotional pull for many women is just too strong and many will drop a project at work for family needs while men seem to get away with insisting they are too busy. And.it seems that at work and at home women continue to remain the symbolic mothers, always avail-able and nurturing even when they arc supposed to be at work. These women find themselves caring for their parents, giving at-tention to their spouses, running the house, looking after their children — and ignoring their own needs. According to Sue Townsend, au-thor of Adult Children & Their El-derly Parents, (Bantam, $16.95) there arc ways to seek help. She sug-gests sharing responsibilities with other family members, hiring out-side help and learning to accept and relate better to parents. Townsend says it is important to realise that major issues like a par-ent's political beliefs will not create friction as much as less obvious issues, such as snoring in front of the television, dunking biscuits and in-sisting on telling you how to run things. Townsend also believes that gran-ny flats, if one is possible, can pro-vide the right mixture of privacy and intimacy. This arrangement can col-lapse if there is some discrepancy over the amount of involvement ex-pected of everyone, she says. And so it seems that living with your parents again requires a great deal of adjustment, understanding and patience, something that just does not come naturally to all.

12 May 1990 - Poll confirms Victoria's marks for Cain Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 12 May 1990, page 9 Poll confirms Victoria's marks for Cain THE LATEST Morgan Gallup poll has confirmed the message of the March 24 federal election that the Victorian Government of John Cain is in serious electoral trouble. The Hawke Government lost nine Victorian seats in the federal poll as a mixture of national and state issues combined to inflict heavy losses on the ALP. Published in this week's Bulletin magazine, the Morgan poll puts support for the Cain Government in April at 37 per cent, down six percentage points on the March figure. Support for Alan Brown's Opposition climbed seven points to 48 per cent in the same period. The poll of 1150 electors gave the Australian Democrats 11 per cent of the vote {down one point), while Others remained at 4 per cent. Much of the fall in popularity could be attributed to the internal shuffling that has occurred in the Cain Ministry since the election, including the resignation of the Trea. surer, Rob Jolly, and rumours of leadership challenges. In the personality stakes, John Cain has fallen to his lowest level so far with a 28 per cent approval rating (down 11 percentage points) and a disapproval rating of 63 percent (up nine points). However, the Leader of the Opposition, Alan Brown, saw his approval rating rise only one point to 35 per cent and his disapproval rating fall three points to 35 per cent. Almost one-third of respondents remained undecided. On the question of who would make the best Premier, 41 per cent nominated Mr Cain (down nine percentage points) and 39 per cent Mr Brown (up six points). . The number of interviewees deciding to nominate another candidate increased from 3 per cent to 20 per cent. CONTRARY to the prevailing wisdom it seems that the television generation of Australians reads more books than those over the age of 55. A Saulwick Age national telephone poll of 1000 people on April 30 and May 2 found that 11 per cent of people ; over 55 were found to be non-readers of books - more ' than any other age group. People aged 25 to 39 were the heaviest book-buyers, followed by the 40 to 54 years group. More than six out of 10 in the group surveyed had . more than 100 books. Only one person in 12 said he or she had fewer than 10 books. Respondents over 55 had the lowest percentage of | those with more than 100 books at home (49), and the » highest percentage of people who did not buy books (20). j Book borrowing was found to be most common among ' people aged 18 to 24. Thirty-four per cent of the younger ( group borrowed more than 30 books a year. I Females were found to have slightly more interest in j books than males, and tended to read more fiction. I Non-fiction books are generally more popular in the j population and Democrat supporters were found to be j the heaviest readers among political groups.

15 May 1990 - Button forecasts swift action on polis after feasibility study Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 15 May 1990, page 3 Button forecasts swift action on polis after feasibility study By HUGH LAMBERTON The Hawke Government will act quickly oncc the recommendations of a feasibility study into the Multi-Function Polis arc handed down in mid-July, according to the Minister for Industry, Science and Technology, Senator John Button. Senator Button told the ABC's Four Corners program last night that if all went well, the Government would move "very quickly" on the proposal. \ When asked whether this meant within the year, Senator Button replied, "Absolutely." Speaking earlier in Parliament, Senator Button tried to play down media reports that he had already made up his mind in favour of the Multi-Function Polis. "I have not reached any conclusion about the feasibility of the project," he said. "A range of studies arc presently under way to help determine the economic and social feasibility of the project and until these arc concluded, no-one is in an informed position to properly assess the feasibility of an MFP project in Australia." However, Senator Button said he had decided the concept was "worth pursuing" and that he had "some optimism" about the feasibility of the project. This was the general preliminary view among participants in the feasibility study. Answering a Question Without Notice from his own party, he said the project would not go ahead unless "full" economic and feasibility was proven. The Sydney Morning Herald reported yesterday that Senator Button was preparing a Cabinet submission to create a secretariat which would sec the concept through to implementation. A final decision on the viability of the projcct is scheduled to be handed down by the joint Australia-Japan steering committee on July 13. Senator Buiton's secretariat would replace the present two organisations which expire on June 30. While Cabinet, approval of such a secretariat does not make the committee's decision a foregone conclusion, the article suggested that Senator Button was moving to establish an irresistible momentum. The secretariat would canvass opinion on how the development should proceed; look for foreign investors beyond the current Australia-Japan base; and examine the cf fccts on nearby communities of the development. The Federal Opposition believes the Government is overdoing its support for the Multi-Function Polis. The Opposition spokesman for industry, Ian McLachlan, warned the Government against proceeding with the projcct before detailing the role of the polis or securing finance for it. The discussion of the Multi-Function Polis comcs on top of new cvidcnce that the majority of Australians arc against the current high levels of immigration. A Saulwick poll published yesterday showed that more than 60 per cent of Australians oppose the annual migrant intake of 140,000. Forty-six per cent of those interviewed said Australia should accept fewer immigrants while almost 20 per cent said there should be no immigration. When asked what kind of immigrants would be best, 62 per cent of respondents said more emphasis should be paid to skills and only 15 per cent preferred immigrants under the family reunion plan. 16 May 1990 - Poll: Hewson win in May Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 16 May 1990, page 1 Poll: Hewson win in May SYDNEY: The new Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, would have easily defeated the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, if the federal election had been held in May, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, in this week's Bulletin magazine, showed that in the wake of "further dire economic predictions and worsening debt figures" support for the Labor Party had dropped 3.5 percentage points to 40 per cent. Support for the Coalition had increased by the same margin to 45 per cent. The poll was conducted over the weekends of April 28-29 and May 5-6 when 2238 voters were interviewed face-to-face.

19 May 1990 - Consumption tax pressure grows Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 19 May 1990, page 3 Consumption tax pressure grows MELBOURNE: Australia would be under increasing pressure to introduce a value-added tax in the next few years, an International Monetary Fund official said in Melbourne yesterday. Alan Tait, of the IMFs fiscal affairs section, said a world trend towards VAT had seen 52 countries adopt it and if Australia did not do so it would eventually be the only Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development country relying on a wholesale tax. He was speaking at a conference of business leaders and taxation experts organised by the Business Council of Australia and the Victorian Employers' Federation. The tax on goods and services had provided about 20 per cent or tax revenue in countries where it had been introduced, he said. Speakers also said that although Federal Treasurer Paul Keating had ruled out a consumption tax, it had clear support from the business community and descrved'morc informed debate. Victorian' Employers' Federation executive director David Edwards said a Morgan Gallup poll conducted recently showed that 54 per cent of electors supported the option of a 12.5 per cent consumption tax. Mr Edwards said many Australians saw a switch to indirect tax as being fairer and recognised it would allow a corresponding cut in other taxes. .

19 May 1990 - Coalition would have scored in May election Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 19 May 1990, page 9 Coalition would have scored in May election THE LATEST public-opinion figures suggest Aus tralians would have elected a Coalition government if a federal election had been held earlier this month. Published in The Bulletin magazine, the Morgan Gallup poll showed Labor Party support had dropped 3.5 percentage points to 40 per cent. The Coalition had boosted its support by the same margin to 45 per cent support from the sample. At 11.5 per cent, the Australian Democrats had lost half a point on the last poll while "other candidates" had picked up by the same margin to 3.3 percent. The poll of 2238 electors was conducted over the April 28-29 and May 5-6 weekends. Responses showed the popularity of the leaders following a similar path to that of the parties. The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, dropped five points to 51 per cent - the lowest rating since the eve of the election. His disapproval rating increased two points to 39 per cent, with 10 per cent undecided. In contrast, the Leader of the Opposition; John Hewson, saw his approval rating rise 3 percentage points to 48 percent. His disapproval rating dropped by 1 point to 12 per cent, with 40 per cent still undecided. However Mr Hawke was still seen as the preferred Prime Minister by 49 per cent of respondents. Dr Hewson was nominated by 32 per cent, with 19 per cent choosing an "other candidate". A Saulwick poll published on Monday found that more than 60 per cent of Australians opposed the current annual migrant intake of 140,000. Of those interviewed 46 per cent said Australia should accept fewer immigrants, while almost 20 per cent said there should be no immigration. When asked what kind of immigrants would be best, 62 per cent of respondents said more emphasis should be paid to skills and only 15 per cent preferred immigrants under the family-reunion plan. Immigrants with money to invest were nominated by 11 per cent and refugees by 8 per cent.

24 May 1990 - Leadership threat to Murray fizzles Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 24 May 1990, page 12 Leadership threat to Murray fizzles SYDNEY: The Deputy Premier of NSW, Wal Murray, retained the leadership of the National Party yesterday when an expected challenge did not eventuate. Despite hectic numbers counting going on late on Tuesday night, the Minister for Administrative Services, Robert Webster, failed to mount a challenge, party sources said, and the leadership issue was not raised. "Amazingly, no-one said anything about it," the source said. On Tuesday night, there had been talk of a plan to get the seven National Party MLCs to move that they be allowed to vote in leadership ballots. This also was not raised in yesterday's meeting, the source said. The seven are excluded from joining their 20 Lower House colleagues in leadership votes. Mr Murray's leadership has been the subject of public speculation for months bccause of Opposition allegations of impropriety in his handling of his State Development portfolio and the investigation by the Independent Commission Against Corruption. Now his position looks secure at least until the next party meeting, not due until the next Parliament session in Sep tember. A special party meeting would have to be called before then to have a leadership spill. A spokesman for Mr Webster said he would not comment on the party meeting or any reports of a leadership challenge. Mr Webster, the member for Goulbum, is the most junior minister in the coalition. A spokeswoman for Mr Murray said there had been no challenge and he enjoyed the full support of his party colleagues. It would be a relief to him when the findings of the independent commission were released next month, he said. The poor performance of the Nationals in NSW in the March Federal election has been attributed to the public perception that Mr Murray was pro-North Coast development and was the subject of an corruption commission investiga tion. It was widely believed at a federal level that Mr Murray's public profile was responsible for the loss of the North Coast seat of Richmond, relinquished by former federal leader, Charles Blunt, in the Federal election. And the poor performance of the Nationals across NSW did effectively keep former Opposition leader Andrew Peacock from the Lodge. Things got even tougher for Mr Murray last month when The Land newspaper said he was a lame duck leader and called for his resignation. The traditionally conservative paper argued in an editorial headed, "Greiner Inc in trouble", that Mr Murray's political image had been seriously tarnished by the constant stream of allegations put before the independent commission, that he intervened improperly in North Coast land develop ment. While The Land said it was a "safe bet" the allegations had no real substance, the damage had been done and "Mr Murray has become the favoured target of sections of the city media". "The constant harping by the media about his alleged involvement in impropriety is taking its toll on the image of the National Party at a time when the party's popularity is sliding," the editori al said. The final indignity came last week when a Morgan Gallup poll showed National Party support in NSW slumped from almost 14 per cent in the March 1988 state election to 4 per cent.

27 May 1990 - Paul's performance might soothe nervous Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 27 May 1990, page 2 Paul's performance might soothe nervous FARMER'S FIELD PAUL KEATING'S performance as acting Prime Minister last week will have set al rest the minds of any waverers in the Labor Party who doubted that he was the right person to succeed Bob Hawkc when the master vote-winner decides to step down. The mantle of leadcr. ship sal easily on the Treasurer's shoulders and, what's more, he showed us that he has a wonderful grin to go with his previously proven ability to snarl. Prime Minister Keating displayed his smooth and smiling side, the side that will be most important when it comes to a . leader's primary task of winning elections, in television interviews with Jana Wcndt and Paul Lyneham. The questions might ,havc been hard, zeroing in as they did on . the country's economic troubles, but the , ?- answers were soft and friendly. Keating . , exuded confidence and, combined with the ? difficult decisions that he and his Cabinet colleagues had made in the previous few days, left me with the impression that Labor would have nothing to fear from his . , possession of the topjob. In the past 1 had pondered whether the hard man that a Treasurer must of necess ity be could adjust to the needs of a Prime Minister to present himself as the warm and compassionate leader who acts firmty more in sorrow than in anger. Keating crcatcd the prime ministerial impression for mc with the skill with which he handled questions about his former colleague. Senator Peter Walsh. There was just the right amount of a smile as he categoriscd people as pessimists, realists and optimists and put Walsh into the box of the naturally pessimistic and himself in the camp of the realists. It was a kind dismissal of the views of a friend and colleague who must actually be annoying the Treasurer quite a lot with his weekly episodes of doom and gloom. Even the attempts to bait Keating about his clash with his other colleague, John Button, were parried with the aplomb of a very experienced politician. Having shown that he has mastered the art of answering the questions without saying a thing, it seems to mc that Paul Keating is as ready as he will ever be to take over the Labor Leadership. Cynics might suggest that creating that impression while the boss was away was the vciy reason that the acting PM went on television. He denied just such a suggestion with a new-found humility and we should treat the rejection of his immediate leadership ambitions in just the same way as we treat the promise of Bob Hawkc to lead Labor to the next election. In brief, you can take your choice. What we can be surer of after the Keating performance as acting Prime Minister is that the real Prime Minister, when he chooses to step down, will be able to do so with confidence that he will be succeeded by a man capable of casting ofTin a very short space of time the grim-reaper image he has acquired as Treasurer. SHOPPING at Yarralumla has taken on a new peril for me after some remarks in this column last week about the correctness of the decision to close some of Canberra's schools. I really got an earful yesterday morning, having failed to scurry into the supermarket unnoticed by the Save Our School campaigners. As I understood the argument, I should accept that there should be no cuts in education spending and that all schools should remain open as they are now. The neighbourhood school concept, I gathered, is so sacred that it should be maintained at any pricc. I don't believe any such thing and the only effect on me of this quite amiable confrontation was to admire even more the courage of Education Minister Gary Humphries. He must have to put up with this kind of discussion every time he goes anywhere and to listen to the selfish views of people conccrncd about the closure of Royal Canberra Hospital as well as those determined to maintain the status quo at Canberra's badly under-used schools. What a difficult double Humphries has been given! I can understand the desire of our local government to make savings in education spending. It is a substantial part of the ACT Budget and, as I don't detect any community support for increased taxes, then cuts there will have to be. But even if the SOS campaigners persuade the Government that education spending should remain at its present levels, I would hope that they failed to persuade it to keep all the existing schools. Neighbourhood schools, with their captive enrolments combined with no risk of closure, do not have to be responsive to the educational wishes of parents. I'm sure that they have bred in teachers a complacency about the correctness of their views on such things as spelling and grammar and other aspects of the curriculum. There is no cost to them of parents voting with their feet and sending their kids off to Grammar or St Eddie's or wherever in the private-school system. The move from the government school system to the private system is continuing apace in Canberra and would be even faster if there were not restraints imposed by waiting lists at the better schools. The solution surely should be to make government schools compete for students in the same way as their private peers. Let government allocate payments to government schools on the basis of so much a head. When they cannot attract enough students to pay for the costs of running them, schools would be faced either with closing or changing the style of the school. My guess is that the schools that survived best would be those with an emphasis on discipline and spelling and grammar and reading and writing and arithmetic -all the things which make modern educational theorists tear their hair out and the lack of which makes parents send little Johnny and Sally off to private school. A system of choice like this might mean that those active parents and teachers at Yarralumla who are so obviously passionate about their school would have the op Paul Keating: Displayed his smooth and smiling side. portunity to keep it open. Without the introduction of competition between schools then the only way they can succeed is by spreading the effects of budget cuts through all schools. Instead of Hackett and Griffith being closed, every school would lose a teacher. Preservation of schools would result in the very decline in educational standards the SOS campaigners kid themselves they are fighting for. I CONFESS to some puzzlement about mutual insurance societies and the question of their reserves and can't help thinking that some of the plans for them are based more on the desires of management to be part of an expanding business than the interests of the policy-holders who, in theory, control them. Why should an existing National Mutual policy-holder, for example, be concerned about the fact that more capital is needed to allow the salesmen to sell more policies? Might not he or she be better off if the society stopped writing new business altogether and paid out all Gary Humphries: What a difficult double he has been given. the existing reserves eventually to existing policy-holders? I will investigate further the question of who reaily controls the mutual institutions which, in turn, control so much of Australian business. 1 THOUGHT Robyn Nolan was a little churlish when she callcd on her Alli ance Government colleague Craig Duby to follow her example and step down from ministerial office. Mrs Nolan resigned from her post as Executive Deputy assisting the Minister for Finance and Urban Services on Tourism, Business, Employment, Transport and Rural Matters after being found guilty of three tax-evasion charges, and wanted Mr Duby to stop being Minister for Finance and Urban Services because he had been convicted six weeks before on a charge of refusing a breath-analysis test. For my part the only reason for a politician to stop being a minister is when he or she has done something that the government thinks will impede its chances of being returned to office. Maybe Mrs Nolan reached the conclusion that her conviction was in that category and that the Liberal Party, to which she is loyal, would be hurt by her staying on. Mr Duby doesn't have a party to hurt and surely there is no chance of his being returned to office. In these circumstances, surely Mrs Nolan could have been gracious enough to just go quietly. 1DO concede, however, that there is some irony about Mr Duby's being our transport minister at a time when the Commonwealth Government is linking extra road funds to the introduction of a 0.05 breathalyser limit. He was hardly in the best position to argue against this imposition of the federal will in a way that further changes the balance of power between Canberra and the states even more in Canberra's favour. IT WAS with some delight that I noticed this week that Woodstock wines are now being distributed in Canberra. The McLaren Vale winery of the Collctt family is producing some great wines with the combination of the experience of Doug Collett and the flair of his son Scott. Doug is a veteran of the Australian industry and . transformed the Berri Cooperative into one of the world's best producers of inexpensive table wine before becoming a consultant to such companies as Tulloch, Coolawin, Krondorf and Hungerford Hill during the 1960s. He established Woodstock in 1974 and, a year or two back, handed over the wincmaking duties to Scott, who had served his apprenticeship at San Bernadino in Griffith and in California after graduating from Roseworthy. Father and son have made some great wines over the years and I still have very fond memories of an outstanding 1985 chardonnay and a noble dessert wine of the same vintage. Both, alas, are long gone but there is at least a worthy successor to the sweet wine in the 1987 Woodstock Botrytis Sweet White. Very full, soft flavours on the palate and enough crispncss to prevent it being cloying on the palate. For under $ 10 a 375ml bottle it is a wonderful medium sweet wine to drink with fresh fruit. My favourite of the Woodstocks I've seen on Canberra shelves is the 1987 cabernet sauvignon, which is now starting to develop some bottle complexity to bring together the full fruit tastes and excellent wood. There's enough acid to maintain freshness in this full-flavoured wine that will be even better in a year or two. Priced around $13 a bottle, it is a first-rate cabcrnct sauvignon. Woodstock is a name to remember and if you see it on a restaurant wine list, try it with confidence. Scott Collett is a one of this country's young wincmakcrs whose reputation is on the up and up. MY speculation about an early NSW election has proved fruitless quickly. In what was quite a surprise, the Premier, Nick Grcincr, obtained Democrat support in the state's Legislative Council to redraw electoral boundaries to accommodate a reduction in the number of MPs. As the existing state boundaries severely disadvantage the Liberal Party, Grcincr would need to be very confident indeed to go early now that next year he will be able to fight an election that new boundaries will make much easier to win. THE interest of the Governor-General, Bill Hayden, in pollsters continues. Irving Saulwick was a visitor to our vice-regal representative when he was in Melbourne last week and that followed an earlier lunch with Gar)' Morgan in Sydney. Perhaps of equal note was the visit of a gentleman publisher, which followed the earlier visit of that well-known literary agent, Harry M. Miller. What can it all mean? THE pressure to ban liquor advertising continues apacc, the Western Aust ralian Premier, Carmen Lawrencc, floating the idea and the Democrats planning legislation in the Senate to stop the use of television by beer, wine and spirit companies. The Democrats' move is easy to understand but Lawrence's conversion to the cause is harder to understand. The anti-alcohol movement docs not yet have many adherents among the blue-collar workers that arc still at the heart of Labor's support. Banning the beer ads would alienate a lot of Labor supporters who don't much fancy what they see as wimpishncss.

05 Apr 1989 - Libs up in March Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 5 April 1989, page 2 Libs up in March SYDNEY: The Federal Opposition would have won a general election in. mid-March with minor party preferences, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. And the popularity of Prime Minister Bob Hawke is continue ing to go down.

09 Apr 1989 - Approval for Hawke increases Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 9 April 1989, page 2 Approval for Hawke increases MELBOURNE: Approval of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has increased marginally, according to the latest Saulwick Age Poll. The poll, issued by the Age newspaper, said 35 per cent of voters surveyed believed Mr Hawke was doing a good or very good job as Prime Minis ter. Approval of the Opposition leader John Howard's performance fell slightly during the month. Another Saulwick Age opinion poll this week showed the Opposition would defeat the Government in an election. Mr Hawke's approval among women, which fell sharply two months ago, stayed at 30 per cent, one percentage point up on last month.

12 Apr 1989 - Labor slipping, say latest polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 12 April 1989, page 3 Labor slipping, say latest polls SYDNEY: Labor Party state governments in Victoria and Western Australia would have been put out of office had elections been held last month, according to the latest Morgan Gallup polls. The results of the surveys, published in this week's Bulletin, showed also that the South Australian Labor Government would have relied on Democrat preferences to be returned to power. And in NSW the ALP lost ground to the Greiner Government. Since being returned to power in the WA election in February, support for Premier Peter Dowding's Government slipped by almost 2 per cent. In Victoria, 42 per cent backed Labor (down six points) but the Liberal-National Party support jumped four points to 47 percent. The Democrats made big advances in SA, grabbing a 3 per cent increase for a 12 per cent total of the survey vote. The NSW government was holding its ground, but the Labor opposition was going backwards.

19 Apr 1989 - Hawke's rating rises Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 19 April 1989, page 4 Hawke's rating rises SYDNEY: The personal approval rating of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawkc, has risen by 2 percentage points to 49 per cent, the first rise in six months, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in today's edition of the Bulletin magazine, shows the Federal Government, at 42.5 per cent, still trailing the Coalition by 2 points despite a O.S point rise since the last survey in mid March. Conducted earlier this month, the poll showed the Coalition's approval rating dropped by 1.5 points to 44.5 percent. The personal approval rating of the Leader of the Opposition, John Howard, remained static at 35 percent.

11 May 1989 - On Page Three Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 11 May 1989, page 3 Mfltefou perm Three IT was a dramatic old bus ride for a group of innocent commuters yesterday morning as their ACTION bus driver broke their morning reverie by threatening to smack a cyclist fair in the mouth. The driver, apparently annoyed that a mere cyclist should make use of public roads, threatened to wipe him out after asking him if he wanted the aforementioned wallop. The stunned busload of passengers sal qui etly, as good Canberrans always do in' such an ugly fracas. The driver went, on to mumhle that thousands of dollars were spent on bicycle paths but inconsiderate cyclists continued to use the roads. It's probably not even worth mentioning that there was no cycle' path present. "DOOR old Ken didn't last long. In * yesterday's classics: "On 9.5.89 Ken M. had a schooncr at the Belconnen Soccer Club. So much for giving up the grog!" This followed a notice at the weekend which said Ken was giv- ] ing up drinking from Monday (On Page Three, Tuesday). C'mon Ken, do I the right thing. A H, A chauvinist in serviceman's ! clothing. A Narrabundah woman was not impressed with the man who came to fix her male friend's oil heater yesterday. She asked him to tell her what was wrong so she could report back to her friend. "Just tell him I serviced it," he said, with the "You wouldn't understand" left unsaid. "Try me," she countered. So he told her that there was a loose electrical connection which had interrupted the circuit and had thus prevented the heater from igniting. Wow, that's high-tech. She wonders how the serviceman's wife gets on. Or how he got one. SO HOW come you don't trust us? The latest Morgan Gallup Poll on ethics and honesty in the professions shows print journalists way down near • the bottom of the popularity stakes, gaining only a 9 per cent rating; Only' advertising people, union leaders and car salesmen scored worse in the sur vey, published in The Bulletin. 11 May 1989 - Professional popularity figures out Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 11 May 1989, page 7 Professional popularity figures out SYDNEY: Public confidence in the honesty and ethics of bank managers has fallen dramatically in the past 10 years, according to the i latest credibility poll of professional jobs. Of 21 professions surveyed in the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine, pharmacists held on to the top spot, gaining a 76 per cent approval rating, unchanged since last year. The credibility of bank managers took the biggest tumble over the decade, rating only 50 per cent (down 4 per cent from last year and 16 per cent since 1979) in the professional popularity stakes. Although holding eighth position on the latest survey, it was a fall of two places since last year and a massive seven places since holding top position in 1979. Although dentists and doctors came in sccond and third respectively, both professions had lost credibility in the past year, with doctors taking the biggest fail of the year, down from 67 per cent to 62 per cent. Other professions on the slide in the public's view were university lecturers, down one to 52 per cent, accountants down one to 46 per cent, business executives down one to 20 per cent, and print journalists, down two to nine per cent. Police popularity varied widely from state to state, but remained unchanged nationally since last year - 53 per cent - but up five percentage points since 1979. While print journalists languished near the bottom of the honesty pile with 9 per cent, television reporters debuted on the poll with 16 per cent, ahead of both state and federal MPs (15 per cent), insurance brokers (13 per cent) and real estate agents (11 per cent). Advertising people ran with the same popularity as print journalists, but marginally improved their rating by 1 per cent, as did union leaders up 2 to 9 per cent. The most maligned profession, car salesman, remained at the bottom of the list with 4 per cent, but did gain 1 percentage point for the decade.

14 May 1989 - POLITICS Howard addogged man, not a mongreled man, not a mongrel Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 14 May 1989, page 6 ^POLITICS Howard a dogged man, not a mongrel p By Peter Costigan JOHN Winston Howard, is fin ished as a political force for one reason. He lacks a bit of the mongrel in him. The big question now is whether Andrew Sharp Peacock, who oncc also lacked the quality so well summarised by the old bush phrase, has developed it during his four years in the Wilderness. It is a very Australian term which distinguishes from lesser mortals those men and women who emerge from the pack, is more sensed than dcscribabic and is well understood in sport. Champion footballers have it. Reserve players don't. Cricketers such as Border, Lillec, Thompson and all West Indian fast bowlers certainly possess it. In entertainment, most Oscar winners, Graham Kennedy, all prima donnas and Frank Sinatra have it. It's not hard to see in politics who unquestionably has it: Bob Hawkc docs and Paul Keating, in spades. Fraser and Whitlam, indeed all Australian Prime Ministers cxcept'Billy McMahon, had quite big bits of the mongrel in them. Bill Hayden did not have enough of it, Ian Sinclair always had too much. In John Howard's case, the lack was often overlooked by enemy and ally alike because both were inclined to concentrate too much on other aspects of his character, especially his Honest John straightforwardness and his lack of public charisma. Neither are or ever were ultimate aids or barriers to success and John Howard himself managed to get veiv close indeed to, becoming Prime Minister less than two years ago. But what finally got him was the conviction of powers in the Liberal Party that he lacked enough of the stuff of leadership to lead his party to power. John Howard is no simpering weakling, far from it, and is onc of the most tenacious people seen in Australian politics for many years. Yet he was never able to demonstrate that particular brand of toughness which lifts a handful of politicians on to a special level of leadership and power. " Though widely regarded inside and out of Cabinet as an excellent Treasurer for nearly six years, he was never able to push his own agenda through a Cabinet dominated by tough men such as Fraser, Doug Anthony, Peter Nixon and, yes, Ian Sinclair (all boys from the bush who ccrtainly understood and possessed that certain ingredient.) Voters ccrtainly understood the shortcoming in John Howard's political makeup. The recent Morgan Gallup Poll showing only 6 per cent of voters thought he was a strong leader (34 per cent saw strength in Bob Hawkc) was a catalyst,for the coup which handed Andrew Peacock and Fred Chancy the Liberal reins. AS THE powers in the Labor Par ty in early 1983 had ;dccided they could not be sure Bill Hayden could lead them to power when the party had everything else going for it, Liberals decided John Howard might save them from the jaws of victory. Thanks to the glamour surrounding Andrew Peacock, the decisiveness of his victory, the excitement engendered by the clean sweep of the Opposition front benches and the feeling that the conservatives have finally got their act together, a snap election now would tumble the Hawke Government out of power. For that reason, the Opposition has denied Bob Hawke one of his election options: an early poll to capitalise on the July tax cuts and John Howard's perceived weakness. On the other hand. Labor pollster Rod Cameron says the Liberals erred in timing and that they should have waited till closer to the election to reinstate Peacock. In fact, last week's events could force Labor to go to the polls much later when high interest rates and tough monetary policy have pushed Australia into a recession. What Labor is now counting on, and Cameron's views presumably reflect, is its assessment that the tough boys in Parliament will bash Peacock's feathers of popularity out of him. , f In his two years as Opposition Leader up to September, 1985, Andrew Peacock's performance was not brilliant. But, perhaps significantly, the Labor bovver boy who got under his skin moist effectively was Mick Young ("Show us your serious face, Andrew!"), who is no longer there. j It was the lack of fire tn Peacock's Parliamentary performance then, combined with the reputation he got as a minister in the Fraker government of contributing little outside his portfolio in Cabinet meetings which held the uncommitted Liberal caucus votes behind Howard for so long. Andrew Peacock says privately that he is a much tougher politician than his media reputation. It may prove to be significant that in his 3'/: years as John Howard's deputy there has been a greater perception of Peacock as a hardworking, loyal deputy. And during the ups and downs of his private life, there has been nothing but public approval of his grace and dignity. ' He is 50 now, and light years politically from the days of Sheridan sheets and flippant society. With Parliament in recess,, he tours the country next week to prove he has the look of prime minister about him. It will take longer to leam whether after all his years ip politics Andrew Peacock has developed a bit of the mongrel in him, that this week's brilliant coup, was more than a flash in the pan. To John Howard supporters at least, that certainly was a real mongrel of an act.

17 May 1989 - Liberal front-benchers were 'stupid and tasteless' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 17 May 1989, page 3 Liberal front-benchers were 'stupid and tasteless' . by PAUL MALONE Political Correspondent and AAP Liberal Party front-bcnchers Wilson Tuckcy and John Moore had been "stupid and tasteless" for giving detailed accounts of the leadership coup planning to the ABC program Four Corners, the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, said yesterday. The program, screened on Monday night included admissions of lying to journalists and manipulation of MPs to stop them being lobbied by Howard supporters. And it produced an on-the-record firsthand account of events that differed in an important way from that given by Mr Pea cock himself. Mr Moore said on Four Corners that he had shown Mr Peacock a draft plan of the coilp two weeks before the challenge. But while agreeing that Mr Moore had spoken to him at that time, Mr Peacock says he was never shown a document. Mr Peacock has sought to minimise his direct involvement in the coup and tried to create the impression that he was "drafted" to take over the leadership. The Four Corners program's on-the-record first-hand accounts tend to discredit his story. Yesterday one of Mr Howard's supporters, Senator Michacl Baume, bluntly put the question: "Who is lying — Moore and Tuckey or Andrew Peacock?" Mr Howard agreed yesterday that the program had shown "treachery" and said it had hot assisted Liberal Party unity. Another Howard supporter, Senator Tony Messner, said the public boasting, gross disloyalty, and admitted dishonesty of the former members of Mr Howard's shad ow cabinet was a sad event for the Liberal Party. "It is clear that the anti-Howard conspiracy has been running for several months during which time, without declaring their real intentions, those persons involved have been party to the most sensitive shadow cabinct and other political discussions with the former leader," he said. "In these circumstances it would have been the proper course for these persons to have removed themselves from the inner councils of the Liberal Party". ' "These revelations are insulting to all those Liberal Members of Parliament and the thousands of our supporters who, in good faith and commendable honour, have carried out their faithful duties in support of the Liberal Party". Mr Peacock says that, at his meeting with Mr Moore two weeks before the challenge, he told him he was not satisfied there was proof of sufficient discontent with Mr Howard to justify a challenge. It was not until the Friday before the challenge that he had seen any document. Mr Peacock said people had been coming to him for months to express dissatisfaction with Mr Howard. While he had tried to hose them down, he had not told Mr Howard about them. Mr Peacock said he did not believe the Four Corners revelations tainted his leadership. Mr Tuckey said he had not intended to gloat publicly over his role in helping to organise the challenge. He accepted the reprimand from Mr Peacock for giving the interview. Mr Peacock said he had told the two coup organisers that they had hardly done the party a service by doing the interviews. "I am angry that at a time when there should be a healing proccss, people are seemingly gloating in their roles," he said. The Tuckey-Moore account made it clear they were part of a small group who had been plotting for months to overthrow Mr Howard. "I'll take my punishment if Mr Peacock is concerned," MrTuckey told AAP. "If he believes we were doing it for the purpose of gloating, I will apologise to him." Asked if he had revealed deviousncss, Mr Tuckey said, "Because the thing was planned in great secrecy docs not mean that it was devious, I don't accept that." "We believed that it had to be kept within a small group to avoid the type of knockdown brawl carried out through the media in relation to past challenges. "We certainly were not intending to gloat. "We did it to explain the way things were done because there arc many people who did not think the Liberal Party was capable of carrying out such a change efficiently." He was also asked if the disclosures by himself and Mr Moore had damaged the Liberal Party's public image. "I'll be terribly disappointed if that is the case because the organisation was done by a group of people within the Liberal Party and not by the party itself," MrTuckcy said. As if Liberal Party's post-coup problems were not enough, a Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin today found that the Coalition was supported by 45 per cent of those polled compared with Labor's 42 percent. Surprisingly, this result is exactly the same as that obtained by a poll conducted on April 26 and May 6 when John Howard was Still Leader. Pryor's view. — Page 8.

24 May 1989 - Hawke's more popular than Peacock: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 24 May 1989, page 15 Hawke's more popular than Peacock: ooll SYDNEY: A Morgan Gallup poll conducted three days after Andrew Peacock overthrew John Howard as Federal Opposition leader found that only 35 per cent of voters would prefer him as Prime Minister. Bob Hawke was preferred by 51 per cent in the poll of 1016 electors surveyed on May 12, but Peacock's popularity was significantly higher than in most previous such polls. In March 1984, only 13 per cent of voters preferred Mr Peacock to 75 per cent for Mr Hawke, but in July 1985 the two leaders attracted support of 54 and 33 per cent respectively. In the May. 12 poll, published in today's edition of The Bulletin, 89 per cent of ALP voters supported Mr Hawke for Prime Minister, compared with 5 per cent for the Opposition leader. Mr Peacock's support was higher among National Party voters with 84 per cent, compared with 10 per cent for Mr Hawke. Six per cent could not say. Among male voters, 52 per cent supported Mr Hawke, 36 per cent Mr Peacock, with 12 per cent unable to say. Fifty-one per cent of women preferred Mr Hawke and 35 per cent Mr Peacock.

14 Jun 1989 - Govt falls behind in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 14 June 1989, page 5 Govt falls behind in poll SYDNEY: The popularity of the Hawke Government has.dropped to its lowest level in 12 months, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in today's Bulletin magazine.
