17 Jun 1989 - Labor may have lost the Hawke charisma factor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 17 June 1989, page 9 Labor may have lost the Hawke charisma factor By Paul Malone IN THE 1987 election Labor had two clear advantages over the conservative parties. Firstly, the conservative leaders were divided and spent more time attacking each other than attacking Labor. And secondly, Labor was led by Bob Hawke. Mr Hawke went into the last election with an approval rating of 58 per cent, a remarkably high figure for an Australian prime minister of more than four years. In over twenty years, no prime minister with an approval rating in the 50s has been defeated at an election. But Bob Hawke's rating has now slipped below 50 per cent. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in the Bulletin magazine has Mr Hawke at 47 per cent. This does not mean that all is lost for Labor. Malcolm Fraser won elections with approval ratings around the 40 mark. But it may well be that Labor has at long last lost the advantage of the "Hawke charisma factor". Mr Hawke has pulled himself up from approval ratings in the forties before. In June 1985 when the Government was toying with the introduction of a consumption tax, Mr Hawke's approval rating fell to 47 per cent. But the tax was dropped and Mr Hawke was able to pick up enough support to be rating at 58 per cent by the time of the July 1987 election. . Mr Hawke's popularity also plunged as low as 44 per cent in March 1988 at the time of the NSW election, the Harris Diashowa affair and the Paul Keating bid for party leadership. But after these matters faded into the background he again managed to pick up support. Anyone who has seen the extraordinary reception Mr Hawke receives when he meets pensioners or school children, shoppers or workers, would not write-off his chances of boosting his ratings yet again. . But the figures for 1988 do suggest that Labor can no longer count on Mr Hawke to draw the extra couple of percentage points that wins the marginal seats. Labor's advantage has also been eroded by the fact that Mr Hawke will not be standing against the hard-working but elcctorally colourless John Howard. He will be up against the marketable image of Andrew Peacock. Mr Peacock got off to a bad start on re-election to the leadership of the Liberal MAR 83 MAR 84 DEC 84 JUN B5 JUL 87 AUG 87 MAR 88 APR 88 JUL 88 AUG B8 SEP 88 OCT 8B NOV 88 DEC 89 JAN 09 FEB 88 MAR 89 APR 89 MAY 89* § Party. But the bad publicity the conspirators gave the party is now behind him. The Liberal and National parties learned a few lessons from the last election and there should be no more Joh for Canberra campaigns or serious public divisions in the conservative ranks in the run-up to the next election. In the present economic climate there is no chance of an election for the House of Representatives. The Government lives in hope that Australia's trading account will improve, enabling interest rates to fall. Government members also pray that this turn around will occur without an accompanying recession. The election for the House of Representatives does not have to be held until November next year. But a half-Senate election must be held before June next year. The half-Senate election can be called any time from now, although the newly elected senators would not take their places until July next year. Six senators from each state would have to face the people. In five of the six states Labor would have only two retiring senators. Only in Queensland would it have three. This mean that Labor's Senate num bers are not greatly threatened by the half Senate election. If the party can achieve a vote of 29 per cent in a state it will get two senators elected and if it gets 43 per cent of the vote it gets three senators. There is little chance that the Labor vote would drop below 29 per cent and so at worst Labor will be only be down one senator overall. There is, however, a risk that instead of seeing Australian Democrats and Nuclear Disarmament Independents elected, Labor would see the last Senate seats filled by Liberal and National Party members. The Liberals and Nationals could then conceivably have the numbers in their own right to block legislation in the Senate. If it won the next election, Labor would then face a frustrating three years in government. Labor strategists do not see this as a likely outcome, pointing out that at the moment the swing in the electorate is going to the Independents and Democrats and not to the two conservative parties. The Democrats have similar research and they believe they would benefit from a lone half-Senate election. They believe that a half-Senate election will give them a higher profile. The Government cannot fall on the result and therefore, they say, there will be more attention paid to the Democrats and the Independents. For the Government the advantage of a half-senate election would be that the election for the House could be put off until as late as November, next year, Government members pray for an improvement in the economy allowing more time for the economy to improve. Mr Peacock would dearly like an election - any election - a by-election, a half-Senate election or a full-blown election for the House. He needs something to get up some momentum. So far the fall in the Government's standing in the electorate has not flowed to the Opposition. It has gone to the Australian Democrats, the Greens and other Independents. A by-election would be the ideal way for Mr Peacock to lift his profile and achieve a positive result. If Labor backbencher, Mr Barry Cohen, resigns from his seat of Robertson he would provide Mr Peacock with the gift he is looking for. Mr Cohen has been a Labor member for nearly 20 years. He is threatening to resign because he doesn't like the man who is likely to be pre-selected to succeed him, the former left-wing NSW minister, Frank Walker. Having enjoyed the patronage of the right-wing faction for many years, Mr Cohen suddenly discovered earlier this year that he did not like the factions system. It was purely coincidental that Mr Cohen made this discovery shortly after being dumped by his own faction. Rather than show loyalty to the party that has given him a pretty good ride for twenty years, Mr Cohen is threatening to repay the party by giving the Opposition the gift of a by-election. Robertson requires a swing of only 4.6 percent to fall to the Opposition. In the current climate, Mr Peacock could be expected to achieve a swing of at least 10 per cent in a by-election. If Mr Hawke does lose his charisma, the Labor Party cannot turn to the Treasurer, Paul Keating. Mr Keating's image goes from bad to worse in the electorate. Cartoonists no longer depict him as the undertaker. He is now death itself. As long as the economy appeared to be well run, Mr Keating had a chance of being respected, if not liked. And with such respect he stood a chance of winning an election, just as others who were not well liked in the electorate, such as Malcolm Fraser, have done. But with the economy in trouble, Mr Keating cannot even command respect. Mr Keating says that in a new role he would only have to turn on the charisma tap to win over the electorate. But the reality is that when the electorate has formed a low opinion of a politician it is extremely difficult for him to shake the image. One has only to think of Biliy McMahon or John Howard to realise the truth of this. While respecting his talents, many in the Labor Party realise the electoral problem Mr Keating poses. This concern perhaps helped fuel wild rumours which swept the House earlier this week that there was to be a cabinet reshuffle and Mr Keating was to be moved from Treasury. But moving Mr Keating will not solve Labor's problems. Only an improvement in the economy will save the Govern ment.

28 Jun 1989 - Coalition 'would have won' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 28 June 1989, page 4 Coalition 'would have won' SYDNEY: Federal Opposition leader Andrew Peacock would have narrowly led a LiberalNational Coalition to victory if an election had been held in early or mid June, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. However, the poll, published in the Bulletin magazine, found Labor's standing rose a point to 41 per cent while the Coalition remained steady at 43 per cent. The survey showed support for the Democrats at a record 11 per cent for the second successive poll. Bob Hawke's standing as preferred Prime Minister rose a point to 53 per cent. Mr Peacock's dropped one to 29 per cent. The poll of 1842 electors was conducted over the weekends of June 10-11 and 17-18. .

05 Aug 1989 - Liberal tactics 'successful' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 August 1989, page 3 Liberal tactics 'successful' By TOM CONNORS The Liberal party has pronounced this week's trial election campaign by the Opposition Leader, Andrew Peacock, a success. The party's federal director, Tony Eggleton, said yesterday that a telephone poll conducted by the Roy Morgan Research Centre on Thursday night found that 77 per cent of the 513 people surveyed were aware of the campaign while 67 per cent were specifically aware of Liberal advertising on television. Only 30 per cent of those who watched the advertisements disagreed with their message. Mr Eggleton said 62 per cent of respondents had heard of Mr Peacock's proposal to remove the effect of inflation when taxing interest earnings and only 38 per cent disagreed with it. He said that even 50 per cent of Labor voters agreed with it. In answer to a question about the economy only 26 per cent believed it was heading in the right direction with 62 per cent talcing the opposite view. Mr Eggleton claimed that the survey results represented a serious erosion of confidence in the Hawke Government. He said that confidence in the Coalition's ability to run the economy had risen by 12 per since June. In terms of voting intention, Mr Eggleton saw the poll as recording a strengthening trend for the Coalition, reinforcing its average 6 per cent lead (outside of Sydney).

09 Aug 1989 - Labor improving its stand Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 9 August 1989, page 3 Labor improving its stand SYDNEY: The Labor Party has improved its electoral standing while support for new Opposition Leader Andrew Peacock continues to slide, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. Published in today's Bulletin magazine, the ■ poll showed that support for the ALP jumped 3 per cent to 44 per cent in late June, putting the Government back in front of the Coalition. „ The survey of 2643 electors was conducted over the weekends of July 22-23 and July 29-30 after the launch of the Government's environment strategy on July 20. . Had an election been held in late July, the ALP would have won with the aid of minor party preferences, the Bulletin said. "■ Support for the Liberal-National coalition slipped 0.5 per cent to 43.5 per cent, with the Democrats shedding 1 per cent to 9 per cent and t other groups losing 1.5 per cent to 4 per cent, t Mr Hawkc's personal-approval rating climbed J; 1 per cent to 46 per cent, with a 2 per cent rise among women voters to 44 per cent. However, Mr Peacock, whose mid-term election campaign tour was not covered in the poll, faced setbacks on all fronts. Asked who would make a better prime minister, 57 per cent nominated Mr Hawke (up 2 per cent), while 29 per cent named Mr Peacock (down 2 per cent). Mr Peacock's personal-approval rating slipped 1 per cent to 31 per cent and his disapproval rating rose 3 per cent to 49 per cent, its highest level since he took over from John Howard. The results support the latest Newspoll figures published in the Australian newspaper, which showed support for the Coalition had fallen from 44 per cent to 41 per cent in July, while ALP support had risen 2 per cent to 42 per cent. Satisfaction with Mr Peacock's leadership was down 2 per cent to 26 per cent in the Newspoll survey, compared to Mr Hawkc's rating of 40 per cent (up 6 per cent).

15 Aug 1989 - OPINION Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 15 August 1989, page 8 By Tom Connors Peacock potshots too personal Andrew peacock copped a hammering lasl week, and many people must have felt sorry for him. It was not just the fact that the latest Morgan Gallup poll showed that Labor had moved to a one per cent lead over the Opposition whereas, when Mr Peacock took over as leader. Labor was; three points behind. It was the personal abuse tlVe man had to endure, such as The Bulletin proclaiming him a "hollow jman" and its three full-page advertisements in the daily press that described Mr Pcacocic as "all feathers and no meat". In this country, probably more than most in the Western world, politicians are fair game. Tli^y are the butt of jokes; it is assumed that they are drongos and bludge'rs unless proved otherwise and how can they have the cheek ever to seek a pay rise when they are already overpaid? I have watched politicii'.ns!in action for many years and have come to the conclusion that it is a'tough job and hardly worth the wages paid despite the generous super and perks of office. The hours are very long in Parliament and when back in the electorate, the MP or senator is expected to open every cat show, attend every school speech night, and lead the fight to increase or maintain local facilities. Those in marginal seats have to work the electorate very hard indeed and keep the local me dia on side. The strain on health and personal relationships can be intense. Many marriages have failed because the member is rarely home. However, the hardest job in Parliament is Leader of the Opposition. Yes, it is even harder than that of Prime Minister. The Opposition Leader has^lo develop a full set of policies to match the Government without the resources of the Public Scrvicfc1. The handful of economists that .a'dvise Mr Peacock are lined up against the Treasury, the Taxation Oflicb. the Department of Finance and the economists of every other depart ment. Most members of the sHadow ministry have to scrounge advice and assistance from wherever they can as they have no more staff than the ordinary backbencher. Shadow ministers- in the minor portfolios have great1 difficulty getting a run in the media and impressing M_f Peacock that they are worthy of promotion and this can tempt th'6m to release a plethora of half-backed, poorly researched press statements that end up in the waste paper basket. ■; This does their or the Opposition's reputation no good at all. It is unfortunate for Mr Peacock that he has a number of shadow ministers who, on current indications, would make mediocre ministers. Maybe some would bloom under departmental guidance. The Opposition has put some heat on itself with the double, coup carried out earlier this year against John Howard and Ian Sinclair, the former respective leaders of the Liberal and National parties. The new boys, Mr Peacock and Charles Blunt, have been hard at work to prove to their own parties and the nation that they are betteruvalue than the men they dispatched to the backbench. .=> Mr Blunt has criss-crossed the nation addressing conferences of his party's faithful and pressing 'he flesh of rural folk to prove his leadership credentials but Mr Peacock set out recently to win over the nation with his so-called mock election campaign. The task was not only to demonstrate to those Liberals still \ipset about the way Mr Howard was dumped from office that Andrew Peacock was (like Bob Hawke for Labor in 1983 when Bill Hayden was dumped) the man to lead,them to victory but to remind the electorate that he was a first-rate performer on the hustings. The Liberals claimed that, their research and a poll show that the week-long campaign was a great success and if an election were held immediately the Coalition would win government by 16 seats. However, this began to look like bravado in the light of the Morgan Gallop poll that indicated that not only did Mr Pcacock have an image problem but most voters were in the dark about his policies. It appears that like some in his shadow ministry Mr Peacock is having trouble getting policies together, especially ones that will stand close scrutiny. His tax break for the inflation component of interest earnings was the "crown jewel" of the mock campaign, yet it disintegrated imo an unworkable, half-backed concept when economists gave it the'once over. There was even a dispute within the shadow cabinet over how far the tax break should extend. But the final nail in the coffin was driven home by the Treasurer, Paul Keating, last week, when armed with detailed research from his department, he put the Pcacock concept to rest, possibly once and for all. It would, the Treasurer said, increase tax on business, cause the dollar to slump, reduce investment in the Australian economy and lift the inflation rate. Mr Peacock's response was almost as pathetic as the tax break itself. At least he was trying.lo do something to stimulate savings, he said, while the Government had given up. Because he went cm the mock campaign without firm policies Mr Peacock deserves criticism, but not the personal type in the Bulletin advertisements. 7

16 Aug 1989 - Peacock popularity up Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 16 August 1989, page 3 Peacock popularity up SYDNEY: A stint on the campaign trail appeared to have paid dividends for the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in The Bulletin magazine, showed a six percentagepoint improvement in Mr Peacock's approval rating to 37 per cent, his highest rating since taking the leadership from John Howard. Mr Peacock's disapproval rating also fell twp percentage points to 47 per cent after the dry-run campaign through NSW, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania. The poll of 1144 electors interviewed on August 5 and 6, found support for the Liberal-National Party rose two points to 45 per cent, while ALP support slipped 1 per cent to 43 per cent. The Liberal Party Vote climbed 3 points to 38 per cent, while the National Party dropped one to 7 per cent. The poll found support for the Coalition was significantly higher than in the 1987 election in Victoria, South Australia, and Western Australia, while it was six points in NSW and Tasmania. The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, climbed one point to 47 per cent, while his disapproval fell a point to 43 per cent. Mr Peacock registered an improvement in a head-to-head contest as preferred Prime Minister, gaining two points to 31 per cent, while Mr Hawke fell one point to 56 per cent. Senior Coalition men reprimanded Federal Coalition backbenchers reprimanded senior party members yesterday for endangering the parties' electoral standing by intimating a Coalition government would slash welfare funding. Nine backbenchers told yesterday's meeting of the Liberal and National parties that comments on welfare spending by Liberal federal president John Elliott, Coalition finance spokesman John Stone and Coalition Treasury spokesman John Hewson had damaged the Opposition. At a media briefing after the meeting, the joint-parties' spokesman, Peter Shack, denied the nine backbenchers had "carpeted" the three senior Coalition men over their remarks on welfare cuts. The call to temper the remarks came as Opposition Leader Andrew Peacock told Coalition members they would have to lift their game if the Opposition was to win government He warned the Coalition was in for a tough parliamentary session and that the Government would not "roll over and play dead" and allow the Coalition to easily win the next election. Coalition members were also warned of a growing despondency within their ranks over their prospects of winning the next election. Liberal Party deputy director'Andrew Robb reportedly told the meeting that the despondency was not warranted, but that Coalition fears of another election loss could become a self-fulfilling prophecy if they continued. Mr Shack said there was no move by backbenchers to put a clamp on the public remarks of Mr Elliott, Senator Stone or Dr Hewson. Comments by them in the past few weeks resulted in widespread media reports that a Coalition government would slash welfare funding as part of an overall drive to cut government expenditure. The backbenchers told yesterday's meeting that such comments had caused concern within the community and allowed Government supporters in marginal and Opposition seats to bucket the Coalition's policies. The backbenchers had expressed concern about the publicity resulting from the remarks and had warned party members that if they did not exercise total care in their public comments "it could lead to headlines that we think as less than desirable", Mr Shack said. They had argued "very cogently" that the Coalition needed to be wary of saying things that would lead to the sort of uncoordinated publicity that created concern in the community. He said Mr Peacock had revealed his office was reviewing key Opposition policies with a view to updating them.

23 Aug 1989 - Peacock 'lacks support' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 23 August 1989, page 5 Peacock lacks support' By ANDREW FRASER The main electoral problem of the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, appears to be keeping the support of members of the Liberal Party, according to the Morgan Gallup poll in today's Bulletin magazine. The poll was taken the weekend before last, which was before the Budget but after the Liberals' minicampaign, and while it shows little change in the levels of support for the ALP and the Liberal-National Coalition, it shows a marked lack of support for Mr Peacock. Over the course of the week that the mini-campaign was under way, Mr Peacock's approval rating dropped six points to bnly 31 per cent, while the percentage of people who disapproved of him rose by 7 points to 54 per cent. Among Liberal voters, support for Mr Peacock dropped three points, and at the same time his disapproval rating rose by three points. Mr Hawke's approval rating con tinued to remain high at 50 percent, an increase of three points, while his disapproval rating dropped by three points to 40 percent. While only 10 per cent of the 1155 people polled had no opinion on Mr Hawkc, in Mr Peacock's case, 15 percent had no opinion, possibly reflecting the fact that although Mr Peacock is a familiar face, he is still a new leader to many people. On the broader front, the ALP commanded the support of 43 per cent of those polled and the Liberal-National coalition 44 per cent, while support for the Australian Democrats has remained relatively steady at around 9 per cent. While the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, and the Treasurer, Paul Keating, are travelling around Australia selling last week's Budget, Mr Peacock is also out on the hustings, and in Perth yesterday he said he could take anything the Government could throw at him. They arc behind and they'll do anything to try to cling to power. They're shovelling as much abuse on me as they can in the hope that it may destroy me. Well, you know they can turn the blowtorch on to me but I've got a fairly tough asbestos suit for a skin these days." Mr Peacock was also highly critical of the increase in stamp allowance the Government is granting to MPs, saying the rise had been granted "for political purposes", and that his party would reverse it. "It's quite clearly being used so those in safe seats can hand over their stamp allowance for MPs to keep in touch with their constituents, but to jump it without a tribunal finding on the eve of an election is clearly part of the Labor Parly's marginal scat strategy," he said. Mr Peacock said his members would be taking advantage of the rise in stamp allowance, and "it might sound a trifle hypocritical to you but the reality is I can't say to my blokes, 'Don't avail yourself of this while your opponents are'". Pryor's view. — Pago 8. Ian Sinclair Sinclair continues his Coalition criticism The former Leader of the National Party, Ian Sinclair, has continued his criticism of the Coalition, claiming on Monday that it was. not accepted as a viable alternative government. On Sunday, Mr Sinclair was strongly critical of the current Leader, Charles Blunt, but he denied on Monday that he was destabilising the party by continuing with his public comments. "I have a real concern that people out there, for reasons that I don't know, are not accepting us as they should, as a viable alternative government," Mr Sinclair said. "I think we have a major chal lenge to make sure that people understand that the policies we'd be implementing would solve Australia's problems and I think that's really going to be the challenge for the leadership of the Coalition and indeed for each of us in this next little while." Referring to the change in Coalition leadership which saw him and John Howard dumped as leaders of their respective parties, Mr Sinclair said, "What is, is", and "I don't think it is a matter of comparing leadership". He also denied that he had indicated that a challenge to the leadership of Mr Blunt was on.

29 Jul 1989 - Peacock needs to provide more than photo opportunities Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 29 July 1989, page 9 Peacock needs to provide more than photo opportunities By ANDREW FRASER LIVE in a marginal seat and you arc likely to find yourself at some stage in the next nine months on television as a Prime Ministerial hopeful trudges through the scat with a full media contingent in tow. Real estate agents really ought to pay attention to this sort of thing, as the politicians generally come bearing gifts. They could even make use of it in advertisements (3 bed, ver, marg elect.). The suburbs have been Andrew Peacock's background for the past few weeks as he tries to impart the sort of folksiness and warmth the Liberal Parjy thought John Howard incapable of. As a leader, Pcacock has benefited from the fact that his rival is Bob Hawke. For both of them, successful leadership has been defined simply as whether they are winners or not. This style of leadership has very little to do with leading or inspiring a political movement, but rather, how their individual leadership affects the popularity of the political party. Trooping this style of leader through the marginal seats — which Peacock has been doing for a few weeks now, and will doubtless do more of as the election gets nearer—is a fully understandable tactic from a party intent on winning. But the main problem is that while Peacock is out there with the aim of wooing the voters, the Opposition is losing direction politically. The leader's role as a setter of policy direction has taken a back seat to the other role of a popular figurehead. The implications of this are felt in many policy areas. Take defence, for example. Peacock says he put Jim Carlton, a former shadow Treasurer and a management expert, into the defence area because he would be able to identify savings through a leaner Andrew Peacock ... out wooing the voters. administration. Carlton didn't see his role at all that way — he saw it as managing the overall defence policy, and any savings made by trimming the fat would go back into the defence area. As he sees his task, "it is to ensure that resources are properly managed and any savings applied to more effective defence effort". Carlton has indignantly denied there is a "split", and he's quite right, but without a list of specific cuts, you can only guess what the coalition's priorities are . in this area. Is the money they hope to save through trimming the fat part of the $1 billion worth of cuts, or will it go back into the dcfencc area somewhere el$e? The trading bloc is another case in point. On the day of his ascension to the Opposition leadership, Peacock criticised the Government for not doir^ enough to promote regional trade, and said in Government he would form a regional trade bloc. But his shadow Minister in the area, Robert Hill said that he could see little value in such a bloc. Peacock's office told The Australian the reason for the confusion was that their boss didn't really understand what a trading bloc was. When pressed a bit further, it seems Peacock is not quite as strongly in favour of the idea as he was originally. It is a point of confusion that should have been cleared up before talking publicly about it. Then there is welfare. John Stone, as shadow Finance Minister and the man who in Government other ministers would have to justify their programs to, has strong views about the welfare state, and is not afraid to express them. Now John Elliott has weighed into the area as well. So what does the coali tion plan to cut in this area? Aged pensions? Certainly not, as Peacock was quick to assure this group, who he courted so enthusiastically in 1984. Are unemployed people in the firing line? What about single mums? No answer is the deafening reply. And this week, Peacock had to deny that he had two lists of proposed expenditure cuts, one to be made public after the Government brings down the budget in August and the other a backup list of further cuts if they find things far tougher than they first thought. Peacock passed this intelligence on to a group of executives from John Fairfax and Sons, not exactly the act of a professional politician, which is what Peacock prides himself on being. He was, after all, talking to a group of newspaper executives about the "two lists", and this is hardly a group of people who anyone would choose to confide in, let alone confide political secrets. Peacock's explanation is that he will make public his list of expenditure cuts after the budget, but if the election is not held until the end of next year they may have to produce another list, because the economic climate will have changed. Despite Peacock's high-profile ascenden cy and his television extravaganza, he does not seem to have captured the national imagination, according to polls. In the Newspoll conducted by The Australian this week, the ALP is actually one point ahead of the coalition. In March, the Morgan Gallup Poll put the coalition 7 points clear of the ALP, but in early July, the same poll showed support for the ALP at 41 per cent and support for the coalition at 43.5 per cent. To have gone from 7 points clear to only 2.5 points ahead is hardly good news for the coalition, especially after both parties in the coalition have changed leaders with the idea of getting a more saleable product in. On contests of leadership popularity, Hawke still enjoys an approval rating of 45 per cent, well ahead of Peacock's at 32 per cent. Hawke's rating is holding fairly steadily, Peacock's is actually going down. One reason is perceptions of Peacock. Party research reproduced in the Bulletin magazine shows typical phrases used to describe Peacock are "a puff of smoke", "glamour boy" and "a flower arrangement". "He's good at PR and that's about it". Peacock has been the subject of a torrent of abuse from the Government since he was elected — early on he was "our recycled friend", then he became "our empty-headed friend". This week, he became John Elliott's puppet, and Bob Hawke emerged from a day of cutting Government programs in the Expenditure Review Committee to run this line. "He's acting as Mr Elliott's puppet, and perhaps the puppeteer told the puppet. . Mr Peacock can continue to spend much of his time visiting marginal electorates, but if he docs the real policy drift that is occuring in the Liberal Party at the moment will also continue. The Liberal Party arc playing a dangerous game, as their tactics are based on the assumption that they will win the next election by default as voters, cheesed off with the economic management by the ALP, will turn to them in droves. The first part of the equation is definitely on, the second part not necessarily so. In all state elections except for NSW in the past 18 months the message has been clear — voters are turning away from the ALP, but they are generally turning to independents or small parties like the Australian Democrats. The next two weeks will see another advertising blitz as the coalition runs national television advertisements, the basis for a mini advertising campaign. It will cost about a million dollars and the aim is simply to get the election machinery running smoothly. It is still a long row to hoe for the Liberal Party in the policy area, and Andrew Peacock needs to spend the few weeks after the mini-campaign ensuring the policy line remains consistent rather than trotting around the marginal electorates exchanging pleasantries and providing photo opportunities. At a time when the country is walking up the f>ath of despair, seeking some sort of alternative to the ALP, where is Andrew Peacock? Right behind them, admiring the cut of their trousers.

12 Jul 1990 - Morgan does the sums on Hawke Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 12 July 1990, page 2 Gary Morgan at the National Press Club yesterday. Morgan does the sums on Hawke By TOM CONNORS There was more than a touch of irony evident at the National Press Club yesterday when the Liberal Party's pollster, Gary Morgan, declared the Labor Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, a "great leader" who could lift his approval rating. That day's issue of The Bulletin ran the results of a Morgan Gallup poll, conducted by Mr Morgan's company, the Roy Morgan Research Centre, showing that Mr Hawke's approval rating had fallen in the last week of June to 43 percent, down three points on two weeks earlier and nearly half his peak 75 per cent rating in March, 1984. The same poll has the Opposition Leader, John Hewson, holding on to a high 50 per cent approval rating but Mr Morgan had a word of warning for Dr Hewson — he had been dancing around the issues" and needed to be more forceful and positive. Either Mr Hawke or his Treasurer, Paul Keating, could turn the Australian economy around, Mr Morgan said, and he blamed the Labor Left for causing problems within the economy. Mr Morgan had a message for the major parties as they muse about strategies for the next federal election — the party most committed to micro-economic reform would win. Mr Morgan said the ALP had propagandised people to have them believe that it was the low popularity of the Victorian State Labor Party that nearly cost Mr Hawkc the last federal election, but his polling clearly showed that it was the way the Government had handled the Multi Function Polis which had almost brought Labor undone. The MFP had been seen as likely to result in a Japanese enclave. Attempts by the ALP to exploit the opposition of the then Liberal Party leader, Andrew Peacock, to the MFP had backfired, especially in Victoria. It had bccome obvious in his poll in the last days of the campaign that immigration, the issue stirred up by the MFP debate, had boosted the Coalition's chances. Mr Morgan was highly critical of politicians, journalists and others who "abused" public opinion polls. He said that the leaking of an Australian National Opinion Poll in December, 1982, had been the catalyst that caused Bill Hayden to be replaced by Mr Hawke as Labor leader. He said democracy required not only freedom of information, but the supply of accurate information and a political process that did not abuse the freedom of accurate information.

12 Jul 1990 - Libs want war-time cabinet to save Vic Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 12 July 1990, page 4 Libs want war-time cabinet to save Vic MELBOURNE: The Liberal Leader, Alan Brown, urged the Victorian Government yesterday to include him in a wartime-style Cabinet to save the State from economic ruin. Mr Brown said the Opposition should have a say in all major economic and financial policy decisions taken by the Government. He said the Government should begin preparing for an early election by appointing a caretaker Labor Premier to replace John Cain. Mr Brown's extraordinary suggestions were prompted by a new opinion poll putting Mr Cain's personal popularity at an all-time low of 18 per cent. The Morgan Gallup poll in The Bulletin magazine this week gives the Government only a 32 per cent chance of winning an election in the wake of the Pyramid building societies collapse. Mr Cain refused to discuss his future as leader in the wake of the poll, but said that "whoever" led the Government at the next election would beat Mr Brown. Key factional figures within the Government dismissed the poll results as alarmist and said there would present no challenge to Mr Cain who could remain leader "for as long as he wanted to". They also said the poll result was based on interviews with oniy 324 people and was therefore too small to be taken seriously. Mr Brown said it showed voters were deserting the Labor party in "droves" after a series of financial scandals which had placed Victoria in a disastrous economic position. But Mr Brown said he would not exercise his only means of forcing the Government to go to the polls early and block supply bkause the Government was elected for at least a three-year term. "John Cain must go now in the interests of Victoria," Mr Brown said. "We need an election sooner rather than later ... in the interim, no doubt, there should be a new leader for the Labor Party and that person, he or she, should act in a caretaker capacity involving the next government." A Government spokesman said Mr Brown's suggestion was "nothing more than a cheap media shot". Earlier, Mr Cain ruled out any change in his style of government in the wake of the latest poll. "I'm not going to respond to polls. I'll go on governing in what I believe to be the best interests of the people," Mr Cain said. "I said before that I was not going to make decisions about Pyramid that were calculated to shore up political support or do the popular thing - the whole issue is too important for that. "To be suggesting that the Government ought to be tailoring its responses and tailoring the things it does to shore up short-term political support is wrong and we wouldn't do it." Significantly, the poll showed that Mr Brown had for the first time outpolled Mr Cain as the voters' preferred Premier, scoring 48 per cent of support to the Premier's 28 percent. But Mr Cain appeared untroubled by this result, which came despite Mr Brown's absence overseas. "I don't care who is the leader of this party, they'll beat the Opposition, and I'll beat the Opposition when I am and the leader at the end of this time," Mr Cain said. "This Government I believe has done the right thing in its 8V2 years of office and I intend to go on ensuring it does the right thing and I am not going to discuss polls."

18 Jul 1990 - Question of interpretation Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 18 July 1990, page 8 Question of interpretation Received 17 Julv IN REPLY to Teresa Mannix's letter (CT, July 15). Ms Mannix has her facts wrong, as we so often see with people employed by Forest Industries. In fact, she even managed to get the Department's name wrong. DASETT is the Department of Arts, Sport, the Environment, Tourism and Territories, not the Department of Art, Sport, Environment, Territories and Tourism. The DASETT report, released by the Total Environment Centre in Sydney, under Freedom of Information does not criticise the actual terms of reference of the Biological Resources Study, being conducted by the Commonwealth-state Joint Scientific Committee. It states quite clearly that a problem exists with the committee's interpretation of the terms of reference. Five of the six so called "honest brokers" who are deciding on the future of the South-East Forests come from a background in forestry, not ecology, and will try to justify the destruction of our children's forest heritage regardless of the evidence. The only truly independent report on the South-East Forests was recently completed by the Australian Museum. The findings from the draft report must cast many doubts on the integrity of the BRS. I do find myself in agreement with Ms Mannix on one point, it is the public who own the forests, not the timber industry. The true owners of our state forests have shown by nearly 1000 arrests in a civil disobedience campaign in the South-East, as well as a number of well publicised polls in the past 12 months, that they have little faith in the ability of the industry to manage our forests and think saving the forests is more important than timber workers' jobs (Heraid/Saulwick poll, February 1990). A view far more radical than most conservation groups, who see a need for bal ance. This, yet another example of poor research and bad interpretation of evidence by pro forestry "experts" that led to the DASETT report in the first place, brings me to the inevitable conclusion that our forests are being managed by incompetents. The only warm, inner glow we will be left with, if current forest management practices continue, will be that created by the greenhouse ef fect. JIMEKINS O'Connor

21 Jul 1990 - POLL WATCH Popularity slump for Greiner Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 21 July 1990, page 9 Popularity slump for Greiner THE GREINER Government in NSW would have fallen if an election had been held last month, according to this week's Morgan Gallup poll. Published in The Bulletin magazine, the survey found support for the Coalition dropped three percentage points to 39 per cent while support for the ALP jumped 2.5 points to 45 percent. The Australian Democrats were steady on 9 per cent and support for other candidates rose marginally to 7 per cent. In the popularity stakes, the Leader of the Opposition, Bob Carr, received a higher approval rating than the Premier, Nick Greiner, but remained behind in the head-to-head contest for preferred Premier. Conducted in June, the poll of 1764 voters indicated Mr Carr's personal approval rating was running at 44 per cent (up from 38 per cent in May) compared with Mr Greiner's approval rating, which remained at 41 per cent. Mr Greiner's disapproval rating rose from 49 per cent in May to 52 per cent in June, with 7 per cent of those polled undecided compared to Mr Carr, whose disapproval rating dropped three percentage points to 33 per cent with 23 per cent undecided. However, Mr Greiner had a 43 per cent to 38 per cent edge in the preferred Premier contest. According to the latest Saulwick poll, Australians take a rather dim view of the service provided by public transport. The national poll, which rated public satisfaction with six services, found that only 22 per cent of the 1000 people surveyed thought public transport did a good or very good job. Twenty-one per cent used the words poor or very poor instead. Services which received a high rating were those provided by chemists, restaurants, cafes and supermarkets. A majority rated these services as good to very good and 49 per cent nominated banking services as providing the same standard. Public transport also rated as the service least used with 38 per cent of the sample stating they did not use it. This compared with 16 per cent for restaurants and cafes, 4 per cent for banks and chemists and 3 per cent for supermarkets.

04 Aug 1990 - Hewson seen as good alternative Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 4 August 1990, page 9 Hewson seen as good alternative WHILE the Hawke Government finds itself tangled up in debates over privatisation and the environment, polls show the Leader of the Opposition, John Hcwson, is increasingly regarded as a better alternative. An image poll conducted by Morgan Gallup found voters felt Dr Hewson was more capable, articulate and honest than the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke. Published in this week's Bulletin magazine, the survey conducted on July 7-8 found the images of both Mr Hawke and the Treasurer, Paul Keating, had suffered since last August. Of the sample of 1116 voters, 35 per cent rated Dr Hewson as capable compared with Mr Hawke (33 per cent) and Mr Keating (30 per cent). He was also seen as more articulatc by 21 per cent compared to 13 per cent for Mr Hawke and 10 per cent for Mr Keating. Slightly less than one-fifth of the sample viewed Dr Hewson as honest while only 10 per cent described Mr Hawke as such and 6 per cent Mr Keating. However Mr Hawke fared better on the questions of friendliness (21 per cent), strong leadership (28 per cent) and fairness (13 per cent). In these areas, Dr Hewson rated 16 per cent, U per cent and 9 per cent respectively. Mr Keating scored 18 per cent for strong leadership but only 3 per cent for friendliness and 6 per cent for fairness. But in another blow to Mr Hawke's credibility, 30 per cent of voters saw Mr Hawke as a Prime Minister who changes his mind and 30 per cent also said he broke his promises. The unproved Dr Hewson scored only 3 per cent and 1 per cent on these questions. Mr Hawke was seen as insincere by 17 per cent compared with 4 per cent for Dr Hewson and 19 per cent saw him as indecisive compared with 10 per cent for the Opposition leader. Dr Hewson also maintained his lead over Mr Hawke in voter satisfaction, according to the latest Newspoll published in The Australian. The poll of 3399 people found Dr Hewson's approval rating running at 43 per cent with a third of the sample undecided. By comparison, only 37 per cent of voters were satisfied with the way Mr Hawke was performing in his job. \ The Coalition continued to lead Labor in overall support with a 45 per cent to 38 per cent rating. Support for the Australian Democrats remained steady at 12 per cent.

08 Aug 1990 - Poll shows Hawke well behind Libs Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 8 August 1990, page 1 Poll shows Hawke well behind Libs The federal Opposition has opened up its biggest lead over the Government since the March election. In the latest Morgan Gallup Poll of 2211 voters, conducted between July 7 and July 14,47.5 percent of electors said they would vote for the Coalition federally, up from 44.5 percent in the previous poll. This equated to a 9 per cent lead over the Hawke Government, which dropped 2.5 points to 38.5 percent. The Australian Democrats were steady at 11 percent. .. However the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, retained the lead for the title of preferred leader, albeit a dwindling one, over the Opposition leader, John Hew son. " Mr Hawke dropped three points to 44 per cent, while Mr Hewson remained steady at 37 percent.' The number of people unable to give an answer when asked to pick their preferred Prime Minister increased from 15 per cent to 19 percent.

18 Aug 1990 - Australians tip a Coalition election victory Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 18 August 1990, page 9 Australians tip a Coalition election victory MORE Australians not only want a Coalition government but believe the Liberal and National parties under Dr John Hewson will be successful at the next election, according to a special Morgan Gallup poll. The survey found 49 per cent of voters wanted a Coalition government and 50.5 per cent felt the Coali tion would win. Only 35 per cent wanted a Labor victory with 30.5 per cent believing in a fifth term for the Hawkc Government. Published in The Bulletin magazine this week, the poll of 1795 electors was conducted over the weekends of July 28-29 and August 4-5 and provides a stark contrast to a similar poll conducted on the eve of the March 24 federal election. At that stage, 45 per cent of voters wanted a Coalition win compared to 49 per cent for Labor. There was a huge difference in the predicted outcome with 63 per cent forecasting a Labor victory. In a breakdown of the sample by voting intention, 72 percent of Coalition voters believed their parties would be successful, 15 per cent thought Labor would win again and 13 per cent were undecided. , In the Labor camp, belief in a fifth term was running at 52 per cent while 29 per cent thought the Coalition would win and 19 per cent were undecided. Separate polls found the Western Australian Labor Government likely to fall despite the popularity of the new Premier, Carmen Lawrence. Dr Lawrence's approval rating had increased two points to 64 per cent. Her party also increased its support by two points to 40 per cent but remained behind the Coalition's 47 per cent. In NSW, the Greiner Government improved its rating three points to 42 per cent -just behind Labor which was down one point to 44 per cent. And in South Australia, John Bannon's approval rating dropped six points to 60 per cent but Labor kept a 44-40 point lead over the Coalition.

25 Aug 1990 - 'Worst Budget' for several years Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 25 August 1990, page 9 'Worst Budget' for several years VOTERS expect the federal Budget will impact adversely on Australia and their personal situation, saying it is the worst Budget for several years. According to the latest Saulwick poll, published yesterday, voters (39 per cent) anticipate that detriment to Australia will be greater than the personal hardships they expect to endure. This is in marked contrast to public opinion on the Budgets and economic statements of the past two years, when Saulwick polls showed that people tended to believe a harsh Budget in personal terms would be good for the coun try. Four per cent of the 1000 people polled said they would be better off after \he announcement of the Budget on Tuesday night, compared with 15 per cent last year. There were no marked differences between age groups in attitude to the Budget's effect on the country but people aged more than 40 believed they would be worse off than did younger people. The poll was conducted nationally by telephone, the day after the Budget. The poll consolidated the Federal Government's woes, with a Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin earlier this week indicating that the popularity of the leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, had reached a high of 54 per cent (up from 50 per cent). Approval , for the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, increased three percentage points to 45 percent. Mr Hawke, however, was still rated as the preferred Prime Minister, with 47 per cent opting for him (up three points), compared with 39 per cent for Dr Hewson (up two points). But voters would have preferred to see the Opposition in power, with approval at 47.5 per cent. The figure was unchanged from when the last poll was taken in late July. ' Support for the Government (38.5 per cent) and Australian Democrats (11 per cent) was steady. The poll of 2387 electors was taken over the weekends of August 4 to 5 and 11 to 12, which, significantly, was after the beginning of the Gulf crisis but before the Opposition announced its plan to go to the next election with a consumption-tax proposal.

08 Sep 1990 - Kirner effect not publicised Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 8 September 1990, page 9 Kirner effect not publicised SOMETIMES the most important polls are the ones the public do not get to read about - or at least that is now what the managing director of the Roy Morgan Research Centre, Gary Morgan, says. Mr Morgan's organisation produces the Morgan Gallup poll published in the Bulletin magazine. This week the Bulletin did not publish what Mr Morgan believes was "one of the most important findings we've had since we started publishing in the Bulletin 18 years ago". * *"* ' -:yw ' ? V The unpublished poll showed that the new Premier of Victoria, Joan Kirner, has turned around the mood of the electorate despite the collapse of the Farrow group, the privatisation of the State Bank of Victoria, and fears that Labor would be rolled if it faced a state election. It showed that after a month in office Mrs Kirner's popularity stood at 42 per cent, with her Opposition counterpart, Alan Brown, at 34 per cent. Of those interviewed, 24 percent remained undecided. Mr Morgan told ABC Radio he appreciated the opportunity to publicise the result. "Not publishing the figure of course doesn't let the electorate realise that Mrs Kirner has in fact already changed the mood of the electorate in Victoria," he said. But the major political parties had access to the results because they subscribe to media releases produced by Morgan Gallup polls. Mr Morgan said it was incredible that the Bulletin had not published the figure. Instead, the magazine published polls on the NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, and the Leader of the federal Opposition, John Hewson. It also published a poll on Mrs Kirner - "Kirner boosts Labor"-but the figure was excluded. The poll on Dr Hewson showed that despite the improved popularity of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, his Opposition counterpart had maintained a substantiallead. A national poll of 2245 electors on August 18-19 and 25-26 showed Labor's support up 1.5 points to 39 per cent, approval for the Opposition down 1.5 points to 46 per cent, and support for the Australian Democrats steady at 11 per cent. Conducted on the weekends before and after the federal Budget, the poll suggested the Opposition under Dr Hewson's leadership would have won an election easily.

15 Sep 1990 - Strong support for Gulf action Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 15 September 1990, page 9 Strong support for Gulf action AUSTRALIANS strongly support the trade embar go and naval blockade against Iraq, according to the latest Saulwick poll. A large majority also agreed with the presence of United States and other military forces in Saudi Arabia. But opinion was divided on whether Australia should send forces to Saudi Arabia to remove the Iraqis from Kuwait. The national telephone poll of 1000 people showed that 89 per cent support ed the United Nations trade embargo and 85 per cent approved Australia's move to suspend trade with Iraq. However, opinion on Australia's nava! contribution to the blockade opinion was split, with support standing at 67 per cent and opposition at 27 per cent. The poll paralleled public opinion in the US on the matter of US and other military forces being stationed in Saudi Arabia. In the US, polls have consistently shown that more than 70 per cent approved the action of President Bush. Though 46 per cent of Australians said the Government should send military forces to Saudi Arabia, an equal number opposed such a plan. Sixty-one per cent favoured the use of military force to oust the Iraqis from Kuwait, but only 48 per cent believed that Australian forces should be used. About 65 per cent agreed with the Government's position that its stance on the crisis would not be affected by threats to Australian hostages. The poll showed men were more gung-ho on Australia's participation than women. Though 77 per cent of men backed Australia's role in the naval blockade, it was approved by only 56 percent of women. The Bulletin magazine published a poll on Victorian politics this week after the managing director of the Roy Morgan Research Centre, Gary Morgan, said the result was "one of the most important findings we've had since we started publishing in the Bulletin 18 years ago". It showed that after a month in office the new Premier of Victoria, Joan Kirner, was preferred as Premier (42 per cent) over her Opposition counterpart, Alan Brown, on 34 per cent. Mr Morgan criticised the magazine for not publishing the result last week.

22 Sep 1990 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 22 September 1990, page 9 TV stations get vote of confidence TELEVISION advertising should be controlled by the channels - not the Government, according to just over half the respondents in a Saulwick poll. Thirty-five per cent of the 1000 respondents said the number and length of advertisements should be controlled by the Government, with 12 per cent undecided. The poll was conducted shortly after the Australian Broadcasting Tribunal announced that it would let television networks continue self-regulation of the amount of advertising screened. The announcement followed a two-year trial of self-regulation. Fifty-nine per cent of women were will- > ing to leave control over the amount of . advertising in the hands of the networks, compared with 49 per cent of male respondents. A majority of all states except Victoria supported self-regulation. This stance was most widely held in South Australia and Western Australia (61 percent), NSW (55 percent), Queensland (52 per cent) and Victoria (47 per cent). However, almost as many Victorians (44 per cent) said advertising should be controlled by the Government. Younger adults were more likely to be satisfied with control by the networks than were people over 25. And support for government control ? over advertising was higher among white-collar workers (40 per cent) than blue-collar workers (30 per cent). Guidelines adopted by the networks -suggest a maximum of 13 minutes an hour for advertisements during deregulation. But the tribunal found that in some cases the average exceeded 16 minutes an hour. The national telephone poll was conducted on September 3 and 5. THE LEADER of the Federal Opposi tion, John Hewson, is close to replac ing the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, as the ' voters' preferred prime minister, accord-, ing to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in the Bulletin magazine, shows 44 per cent of voters would prefer Mr Hawke to be Prime Minister, , compared with 40 percent favouring Dr Hewson. However, it puts Dr Hewson's "person al approval" rating at 54 per cent, com- . pared with 43 per cent for Mr Hawke. The Opposition also moved to a ninepoint lead over the Hawke Government at 48 per cent, leaving the ALP unchanged at 39 percent.

03 Oct 1990 - Coalition ahead in new opinion poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 3 October 1990, page 2 Coalition ahead in new opinion poll The Federal Coalition was 10 percentage points ahead of the Labor Government in the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. However, the poll showed that Bob Hawke was still the preferred Prime Minister over Opposition leader John Hewson by 45 per cent to 39 per cent. On the broader front, the Morgan Gallup Poll, published in The Bulktin magazine today, indicated that the Federal Government's popularity, down 2 per cent to 37 per cent, was at an all time low compared with the Coalition's 47 per cent, which was down 1 per cent on the previous poll.
