06 Oct 1990 - Black armbands for beloved papers Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 6 October 1990, page 9 Black armbands for beloved papers By Tony Wright REPORTERS in the cavernous News Ltd office in the Parliamentary Press gallery were wearing black armbands yesterday. Whatever else you might think about journalists, wc are a sentimental lot, particularly about the monsters for which we work. The death of a masthead is a matter for grief. The mastheads of the Daily Mirror, The Telegraph, The Sun-News Pictorial and The Herald represent far more to journalists than mere titles. They represent decades — and in the case of The Herald, almost 150 years — of tradition, of ripping yarns, of legendary writers, photographers and drunks, of long-gone Linotype operators, of esoteric forms of printing that threw up a unique language: hot metal and cold metal, the stone, chases and ilongs, ems and picas, slugs and fonts... To journalists, who tend to be a pretty insecure bunch, a masthead is a bit like a home town: a place you can belong to that comes with its own history and its own ambience. And so, when Rupert Murdoch announced this week that he was ditching the old mastheads and blending the four papers into two, they broke out the black armbands in News Ltd. On the other side of the press gallery corridor, where the commercial TV stations occupy their offices and studios, there was not much grief to be found. Indeed, there was a certain amount of satisfaction among the TV folk who have suffered for months the jibes of newspaper smarty-pants as the networks have progressively spiralled into deeper and deeper trouble. Suddenly, no-one in the media can afford to be smug. A walk down the long press-gaJlery corridor is a salutary lesson in the dipping fortunes of the media. You can visit all the major media from all the major cities of Australia during that walk. Start at the northern end and you will find The West Australian. It is owned by the Bell Publishing Group. Bell — an Alan Bond outfit — is in lerrible shape. It has debts of around $825 million. Wc will come back to The West Australian later. Wander south past The Canberra Times (which, we blushingly declare, appears to be in good financial shape under the ownership of the canny Kerry Stokes) and you will come to Austra lian Associated Press (AAP), the country's biggest news agency. AAP has been losing contracts lately, is not replacing staff who leave and has put a freeze on staff movements between offices around the country and overseas. Not surprisingly, there is deep angst among staff. Around the corner you will find the networks 10 and 7. They arc both in receivership, and no-one can read their futures. The 7 Network, formerly owned by Christopher Skasc, has been in receivership for so long that staff have become accustomed to it, but the problems at Steve Cosser's 10 are still fresh and you can just about sec the folk there quiver every time a new rumour about staff retrenchments comes scudding in on the breeze. THE ABC is across the corridor and, apart from the perennial whinge about lack of funding, it is the one media giant that appears safe from real problems. Indeed, ABC radio is planning a newsagency service to provide news copy to commercial stations — causing further jitters at AAP, which stands to lose heavily from such competition. Down the track is a branch off the main corridor that is known affectionately as Radio Alley. Not so long ago, lots of commercial radio stations had studios there — and most of them were in some form of financial trouble. A few months ago, a solution of sorts was found — merge most of the little offices into one mega news supplier. And so, 2UW, 2CH, 2SM, 2WS and Austereo became Network Radio. Now there are just three operations in Radio Alley — Network Radio, SBS Radio (which feeds to ethnic and community radio stations) and Hoyts Media. Hoyts turned in a loss of more than $100 million last week. Trundle back along the main path and you will find Macquarie News, which appears in reasonable shape, and 2UE, another Bond outfit, which is also in receivership, future unknown. Next up is the Nine Network, recently purchased by Kerry Packer from Bond. Last week Nine posted an annual loss of $619 million. Cruising right along, you will find in three adjoining offices The Sydney Morning Herald, The Financial Review and The Age. No joy here, either. These three papers are owned by John Fairfax Group Pty Ltd. The group lost $60 million in the past year, bringing total accumulated losses to $532.97 million. Worse, Fairfax directors warned that a continuing depressed advertising market could cause the company to breach banking covenants by December this year, possibly leading to insolvency. The company has total borrowings of a staggering $1.9 billion, $1.67 billion of which is non-current. Down yet another branch from the main corridor you will find News Ltd, home of the black armbands. Here you will find the new Herald-Sun and The Telegraph Mirror, The Australian, the Brisbane Courier Mail and the Adelaide Advertiser. Out of these offices comes the political news for almost 70 per cent of Australia's newspapers, for that is the extraordinary hold that Rupert Murdoch holds on this country's print media. Yet the market does not have a great deal of faith in the Murdoch empire, either. Shares in News Ltd were selling for more than $12 last year. Now they are down to $6.80. And yesterday Moody's Investment Services announced that it was reviewing News Corporation Ltd for a possible credit-rating downgrade! The wander along the press-gallery corridor, then, is a severely depressing experience for anyone in the media industry. We do not need to go into detail about what caused all this mess — it has already been wellchronicled, and it boils down to a tale that involves bad decisions by inexperienced media players, changing viewing and reading habits, a general economic malaise in Australia and masses of debt that just cannot be serviced. What is — or should be — of greater interest is just where these problems will taKe the media. The greatest danger would appear to be a shrinking of the number of media outlets. Murdoch has started the ball rolling by cutting the number of his titles in Melbourne and Sydney by half. Perhaps we can get a sharper focus on the future by looking west. Perth's The Daily News faced crisis a few weeks ago. Either it would close, or the powers-that-be would allow it to be purchased by The West Australian. The problem was that if The West Australian bought the afternoon paper, a monopoly would be created. The Trade Practices Commission — which, of course, has allowed Murdoch to gain control of 70 per cent of the nation's newspapers — decided that there was no way The Daily News could be purchased by The West Australian. And so the paper closed, 200 pepple lost their jobs and another masthead bit the dust. Meanwhile, The West Australian, up to its eyeballs in debt, is still seeking a buyer for itself. Robert Maxwell, the British media tycoon, is very keen to buy the paper. The Treasurer, Paul Keating, has said that is simply not on. It is the principle of the thing. You cannot have a foreigner buying up an Australian paper (Rupert Murdoch is an American citizen, but that is beside the point, apparently). THE problem is that there is no Australian who appears to have the cash or the will to buy the paper. There seems no way out of this stalemate (a point recognised by Maxwell, who is retaining a very active lobbying effort in Canberra, obviously in the belief that he can change the Government's mind). The Opposition Leader, John Hcwson, has also recognised an opportunity in all this. Asked on the ABC's AM program this week about how he might handle the matter of foreign ownership — specifically if a foreign buyer might appear for the Fairfax papers — he said he would not rule out foreign ownership. "I think the foreign ownership rules have to be maintained on a case-by-case basis, but in saying that I wouldn't rule out foreign ownership," he said. "I think that as long as you have a fair coverage of print media sources, some domestic, some foreign, particularly in a world where people get their information from a number of media sources, you shouldn't be too concerned about foreign ownership." The choice for the print media that is in trouble, then, seems to be to hang out for a Liberal victory at the next election and then to seek foreign owners, or to simply muddle on through the existing mess, when more titles might possibly go down the same one-way street as the Perth Daily News. It is a bit like the choice between the devil and the deep blue sea. Support for Labor dips further SUPPORT for the Hawke La bor Government has hit its lowest ebb since it came to power in 1983, falling to 30 per cent, according to the latest Saulwick poll. The poll showed that if an election had been held at the beginning of the month, the Liberal and National coalition would have polled 47 per cent of the primary vote. And though the Liberal and National Parties are in a strong position, support for them has dropped five percentage points from a Saulwick poll last month when it won approval from 52 per cent of the electorate. Blue-collar support for the ALP remained stable at 33 per cent, though it declined four points to 45 per cent for the Coalition. But white-collar approval for the Government and the Opposition remained unchanged at 25 and 52 per cent respectively. Support for the Democrats moved up to 13 per cent, a two-point increase on last month. Approval for other parties rose to 10 per cent, compared with 7 percent in September. On a state basis, 40 per cent of voters polled in NSW said they backed the Coalition, 33 per cent supporting Labor. In Victoria — scarred by the collapse of banking institutions, instability in the state Government, and the loss of the 1996 Olympics bid — support for the ALP fell four points to 24 per cent. The national telephone poll of 1000 respondents was conducted on October 1 and 3. However, the Morgan Gallup poll showed support for the Government had slumped to a low of 37 per cent. Approval for the Coalition had dipped only one percentage point to 47 per cent, and support for the Democrats was up two points to 12 per cent. Significantly, combined Democrat and "other" party support was at 16 per cent — up three points on the last poll — indicating that voters disillusioned with the two major political parties are continuing to transfer their support to the minor players. Approval for the Prime Minister, Bob Hawkc, moved up one point to 44 per cent; his disapproval rate dipped one point to 46 percent, with 10 per cent undecided.

13 Oct 1990 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 13 October 1990, page 9 Carr crash in the latest NSW polls THE LEADER of the NSW Opposi tion, Bob Carr, is having a hard time gaining voters' support, with the Premier of NSW, Nick Greiner, remaining a strong favourite in the elector ate. The approval rating of Mr Carr has hit its lowest level since November 1988, but Mr Greiner's rating has jumped to its high est level since Octobcr 1988. A Morgan Gallup poll also showed that Mr Carr's disapproval rating slumped to a new low, while Mr Greiner again moved up to a new high in the preferred Premier stakes. Published in the latest Bulletin magazine, the poll showed that support for the Greiner Government stood unchanged at 46 per cent But the approval rating for the ALP slipped two percentage points to 38 per cent. Support for the Democrats remaining unchanged at 9 per cent, with 7 per cent (up two points) backing other parties. As a result, had an election been held in September the Greiner Government would have easily scored a victory. Half of the respondents believed Mr Greiner was handling his job well (up two points), with 41 per cent disapproving of his performance (down four points),and 9 per cent undecided (up two points). But only 35 per cent thought Mr Canwas doing a good job (down six points), with 41 per cent disapproving of his performance (up two points to a new high), and 24 per cent were undecided (up four points). On the preferred Premier count, 54 per cent backed Mr Greiner (up four points) and 28 per cent supported Mr Carr (down three points), with 18 percent nominating other candidates. Of Coalition voters, 84 per cent said Mr Greiner would be the better Premier, but only eight per cent backed Mr Carr. Mr Carr was supported by 52 per cent of Labor voters in the preferred Premier stakes, while a significant 27 per cent gave Mr Greiner their approval. The state-wide poll of 1971 respondents was conducted in September. In Victoria, a poll of 2166 electors in September showed support for the ALP steady at 31 per cent and approval for the Opposition stable at 52 per cent.

15 Oct 1990 - Richardson backs Kelly Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 15 October 1990, page 3 Richardson backs Kelly By HELEN SEIDEL and AAP The former federal Minister for the Environment, Graham Richardson, has dismissed criticism of his successor, Ros Kelly, saying greens could not have won the debate on logging in National Estate areas of the NSW south-east forests. Senator Richardson said yesterday that for Mrs Kelly "times had to be tough" after the last election because the first environmental battle she had faced was the controversial south-east forests issue. "The green movement were never going to have a big win on that and so, when [it] lost, blame might have gone to her," he said. "Any suggestion that I would have got a different result is ridiculous." Conservationists were angered by the Cabinet decision last week which allowed logging in about 40 per cent of the three most contentious areas in the National Estate of the south-east forests — Coolangubra, Tantawangalo and Yowaka. Senator Richardson, now the Minister for Social Security, said most criticism of Mrs Kelly was unfair and denied that attacks had come from inside party ranks and Cabinet colleagues. He told the Nine Network's Sunday program that if a poll had been conducted after the Cabinet debate late last week on introducing plans to cut grccnhousc-gas emissions by 20 per cent from 1988 levels by 2005, "1 think she would have come through with flying colours". Cabinet endorsed Mrs Kelly's plan to cut greenhouse-pas emissions within 15 years as an interim measure, while the cost to industry and the economy was assessed. Senator Richardson denied also that the Government had turned a paler shade of green and swung in favour of development. Senator Richardson said Professor Henry Nix, "one of the great green scientists of our time", and an author of the the Joint Scientific Committee report, had come out in favour of the document, which the federal Government had adopted as a foundation for deciding the future of the south-east forests. "If it was all that horrible, I'm sure Henry Nix would have had something to say about it, and he didn't," he said. "So I think that you are bound to accept the science just as those who criticised the Wesley Vale decision should just go back and try and re member there was evidence from CSIRO and scientists that caused us to take that decision too." Conservationists and Mrs Kelly attacked the JSC report for advocating scattered and small reserve areas and recommending the protection of regions already cleared. 'Senator Richardson admitted that Mrs Kelly, the only female Cabinet member, was a victim of sexism in the press gallery and Cabinet. "It's hard when you're the only woman in Cabinet," he said. " But she'll handle it and I thought on Wednesday [when the greenhousegas targets were debated] she did remarkably well." However, the executive director of the Australian Conservation Foundation, Phillip Toyne, attacked Mrs Kelly's performance, saying it was based on political rather than ecological considerations. "There's absolutely no doubt that she continues to reflect the conventional thinking that we will give something to the greens, we will give something to the industry. If they're both unhappy then we've probably got the balance right," he said. The Leader of the Australian Democrats, Janet Powell, added yesterday that Mrs Kelly and the Government "are seeing it all in terms of trade-offs and we're really at the point on this planet, and here in Australia as well ... of not being able to afford to do that," she told the radio program Sunday National. Recession 'not worst since WWII' The NSW Opposition Leader, Bob Carr, came under fire yesterday for saying Australia was facing its worst recession since World War II. "It is nothing like the worst recession since World War II," the federal Minister for Social Security, Senator Graham Richardson, told the Nine Network's Sunday program. He suggested Mr Carr might be distancing himself from the. Federal Government in an attempt to improve Labor's prospects in NSW. A recent Morgan Gallup poll showed Mr Carr's approval rating at its lowest since November, 1988. Mr Carr found an unusual ally yesterday in the federal Opposition Leader, John Hewson. "Senator Richardson should, for once, put politics aside and confront the fact that the economy is in severe recession," Dr Hewson said. He said Senator Richardson's comments (lew in the face of the facts and were an attempt to "put down" Mr Carr. Also yesterday, Senator Richardson replied to criticism of his proposal to extend pension benefits. Senator Richardson wants health, transport and other pension conces sions extended to all over-65s, with states bearing the brunt of costs. He described as an "extraordinary exaggeration" NSW Premier Nick Greiner's claim the proposal would cost NSW $200 million a year. But it was too early to put an exact value on the plan, Senator Richardson said. "For Nick Greiner, he would not want a lead-up to an election with any concentration on the fact that NSW provides Jess for those people who are getting on in years [than] in some other states," he said.

16 Oct 1990 - Labor to power eventually: Carr Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 16 October 1990, page 4 Labor to power eventually: Carr SYDNEY: The NSW Labor Party faced a massive battle to win back office at the next state election, the Opposition Leader, Bob Carr, admitted yesterday. "Certainly the task before us looks formidable," he said on ABC Radio. Mr Carr said he had been chosen to lead the party in the wake of one of the party's biggest defeats in its history, at the 1988 election when the Liberal Party swept into power, led by Nick Greiner. "That meant leading the Labor Party if necessary over a long stretch of time," he said. "That's the job before me and I've got to do it — through the tou^h times as well as the easy times." Mr Carr made his comments against the background of the ALP's continuing slide in the most recent Morgan Gallup opinion poll, which showed that support for the party had fallen to 38 per cent. In the same survey, the Government's support had increased to 46 per cent. Mr Carr's personal approval rating had declined to 35 per cent while that of Mr Greiner was solid at 56 per cent. Mr Greiner was a "formidable opponent" but Mr Carr blamed the Federal Government "partly" for his depressed personal popularity rating. He said last week that Australia was experiencing its most serious recession since World War II. The federal Minister for Social Security, Graham Richardson, accused Mr Canon Sunday of trying to shift blame for his popularity decline on to the Federal Government to save his own political career. Mr Carr denied that there had been increasing unrest within the party about his performance. There had been rumours of plans for a leadership chal lenge before the next election, which is expected before the end of next year. "The journalists who cover state parliament ... who know what's happening in the caucus, don't write those sorts of stories," he said. "The simple fact is I've got the overwhelming support of my parliamentary colleagues." While the substance of the Greiner Government's policies remained "very bad", it had put a lot of effort in recent months into public relations, he said. "Certainly they've been working hairier at public relations and that means we have to work more vigorously at selling our perspective," he said. "We are campaigning as a political party in the middle of what is a very serious recession at a time when there is a Labor Government in federally and Labor throughout Australia is copping responsibility for that recession." The collapse of the Victorian Labor Government had contributed also, although it had followed very different policies from those adopted by NSW Labor governments between 1976 and 1988.

18 Oct 1990 - Govt sinks to all-time low in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 18 October 1990, page 1 Govt sinks to all-time low in poll The Federal Government's popularity has dropped to an all-time low of 34 per cent and support for the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has sagged substantially, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in The Bulletin covering the end of September and the beginning of October, showed a 3 per cent Labor fall on the previous poll. Mr Hawke's approval rating fell from 44 per cent of those surveyed to 38 per cent. His previous lowest rating was 41 per cent in November, 1989. His six-point lead as the preferred Prime Minister has been cut to 2 per cent. He is on 43 per cent and the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, on 41 per cent. A small saving grace for the Government was that Dr Hewson's personal approval rating fell from 54 to SO per cent.

18 Oct 1990 - Keating in slanging match amid rowdy scene in House Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 18 October 1990, page 1 Keating in slanging match amid rowdy scene in House By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent The Treasurer, Paul Keating, launched a vicious attack yesterday on the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, portraying him as a country-property-owning yuppie lacking compassion for ordinary Australians. Dr Hewson later issued a statement saying that the attack was an overreaction which displayed an acute sensitivity to what was "the worst poll of all time for the Hawke Government". He was referring to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin (see report this page). , Mr Keating's attack on Dr Hewson in Parliament swung attention away from an earlier attempt by the Opposition to embarrass the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, over criticism by Anglican Archbishop Peter Hollingworth of the Government's economic policy. The attacks and counter-attacks in Question Time led to the rowdiest scenes in. the House of Representatives this year. The attack on Dr Hewson began when the Minister for Community Services and Health, Brian Howe, read from a newspaper article which quoted Dr Hewson as saying he believed there was no need for a federal Social Security Depart ment. The article said Dr Hewson favoured greater funding for community-based groups such as the Salvation Army and the brotherhood of St Laurence to support the needy "at the coal face". Mr Howe said such an attitude revealed that Dr Hewson "suffers not so much from prejudice as from sheer ignorance". The social security system was far more complex than could be understood by "throw-away lines about being at the coal face". . 'Vicious' politics Mr Keating picked up on the article quoted by Mr Howe, and used it to launch his extraordinary, personal attack on Dr Hewson. Mr Keating said that Dr Hewson's view showed a major change in Liberal Party thinking. It "was not the Liberal Party of Menzies, it was not the conservatives of Australia picking up the old British Liberal Party tradition of compassion". Mr Keating: This is just vicious, sectional, ideological politics — that is all this is — by somebody who would not know any better; someone from Bellevue Hill [Sydney) who spends the weekend on the farm at Moss Vale. How would we expect somebody like that to know about mainstream Australia ... Alexander Downer (Liberal frontbencher): Where do you go at weekends? Acting Speaker (Ron Edwards): Order, the Honourable Member for Mayo! Mr Downer: You are a social climber. Acting Speaker Order! Mr Keating: How would we expect anybody like that to have a morsel of compassion for ordinary Australians... Mr Downer: You are at the art galleries and the football. Acting Speaker Order! I warn the Honourable Member for Mayo. Mr Keating:.. .the aged, the children, the sick and the infirm, when he comes out with trash like this, with disgraceful rubbish like this, that one can take $40 billion and dump it on its head in some voluntary agency. Neil Brown (Liberal frontbencher): He has gone mad! Mr Keating: You have gone made with your vicious politics. Continued on Page 3 Keating in a slanging match Continued from Page 1 The House was in such uproar by then it was almost impossible to hear who was saying what. Earlier, the Opposition had seized on comments by Archbishop Hollingworth in an attempt to embarrass the Government. In Melbourne, Archbishop Hollingworth had said that families were being "savagely affected by the adverse economic conditions in which we find ourselves". Half a million children in poverty in Australia and low-income families were being dragged deeper into poverty because" of the percentage of their disposable earnings that went on housing, he said. Restraints had to be applied to the economy but keeping interest rates high was a "very blunt-edged instrument, very hurtful to a lot of families", the Bishop said. When asked in Parliament about the Archbishop's comments, Mr Hawke chose to attack Bishop Hollingworth's knowledge of economics. The churchman could enter a dissertation about the Holy Trinity — the Father, Son and Holy Ghost — but he knew nothing about the "unholy trinity" — wages policy, monetary policy and fiscal policy, Mr Hawke said. Mr Hawke said Bishop Hollingworth didn't know what he was talking about when he said the Government was using only interest rates to solve Australia's economic problems. It was also using "the tightest fiscal policy in history" and a tight wages policy, Mr Hawke said. Dr Hewson later issued a statement noting that despite the Bishop Hollingworth's assertion that high interest rates had increased the number of children living in poverty to more than 500,000, Mr Hawke had not once mentioned child poverty during his speech to Parliament.

20 Oct 1990 - Telecom-OTC merger plan disagreement Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 20 October 1990, page 9 Telecom-OTC merger plan disagreement DEEP divisions have emerged in the electorate over the sale of government assets, with scep-ticism about the potential benefits of the Tele-com-OTC merger. The latest Saulwick poll is the first measure to gauge reaction to the Federal Government's decision last month at the special national conference to sell all of Australian Airlines, 49 per cent of Qantas, and 30 per cent of the Com-monwealth Bank. Half of the re-spondents opposed the plan to sell the airlines and bank, but 40 per cent gave their support and 10 per cent were undecided. On the proposed Telecom-OTC merger, 59 percent of respondents believed they would be worse off or no better off than they were now. A total of 28 per cent thought the merger would be beneficial, but 26 per cent did not, and 33 per cent believed it would make no difference. About 13 per cent had no opinion on the issue. There was a clear split on the airline sales among men and women — 49 per cent of men supported the sales as opposed to only 32 per cent of women. The poll showed no major differences between Lib-eral and ALP supporters on aviation asset sales, but Coalition voters took a dimmer view than the Labour faithful on the Telecom-OTC merger. Only 27 per cent of Coalition supporters thought they would be better off as a result of the merger, compared to 32 per cent of ALP voters. And 29 per cent of Coalition voters and 19 per cent of Labour supporters believed they would be worse off under the merger. There were also clear differences between the states and the cities and rural areas on the aviation asset sales. The poll showed that 41 per cent of NSW voters backed the sales, with 51 per cent opposed. In Victoria, only 30 per cent of respondents gave their approval, but 61 per cent were against the plan. Australia-wide, 43 per cent of city voters approved the sales, with 48 per cent not giving their support. In rural regions, the sales were endorsed by 36 per cent and opposed by 54 per cent. The national telephone poll of 1000 voters was conducted on October 1 and 3.

26 Oct 1990 - PM says he's better than Paul and Kim Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 26 October 1990, page 2 PM says he's better than Paul and Kim By HUGH LAMBERTON The Prime Minister, Bob Hawkc, believes he must lead Labor to the next election because he has more chance of winning than either of his heirs apparent, Paul Keating or Kim Beazley. Last night, Mr Hawke said yet again he would stay on at least until the next election because he had been a "good Prime Minister". He also believed he could win that election more easily than any alternative leader within the party. Tm there. Fve had the opportunities, so people tend to identify with you a bit. But even when they don't agree with you on everything, they say, 'Well, we know Hawkie'." In an interview to mark the 10th anniversary of SBS, Mr Hawke dismissed the Government's poor per formance in recent polls. He said the Government had been written off many times before. Last week's Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin magazine showed the Government trailing the Coalition 48 per cent to 34 per cent "If I'd listened to all the panic merchants back there in 1987 and before the 1990 election, I would have gone and shot myself or something like that," Mr Hawke said. He admitted the Government had never been so far behind in the polls but attributed this to the troubled Victorian Government. Mr Hawke said he had a faith in the Australian people that they would respond to an honest message of "Look, we're not perfect". Although the Federal Government decided earlier this year to cut immigration from 140,000 to 126,000 each year, Mr Hawke backed a high level of immigration but said it was impossible to set a population target at pres ent "I think that it's in the interests of this generation and future generations of Australia that we build that population up as much as we can." Mr Hawke said the level of immigration needed to be integrated with our economic and employment growth but also had to be acccpted by the community.

08 Nov 1990 - Restructuring due for the Lib-Nat coalition Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 8 November 1990, page 16 Nick Grelner: result 'defensible'. Restructuring due for the Lib-Nat coalition SYDNEY: The NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, has confirmed that the LiberalNationaJ coalition arrangement is being restructured, four days after the Cons Harbour by-election, to allow three-cor nered contests. The National Party suffered a 30 per cent decline in primary votes in the North Coast scat but was expected to hold the seat comfortably for the Government once preferences were distributed, reducing the swing to about 12 per cent. Speaking for the first time since Saturday's poll, Mr Greiner said the result was "defensible" despite the latest Morgan Gallup poll, which showed the Greiner Government 14 per cent ahead of the Opposition. "I think it's perfectly obvious that the National Party would have liked to have got more votes than they did," he said. The result was "defensible". "It was not as good as those who want to say it was good and not as bad as those who want to say it was bad," he said. "It was a pretty predictable result." There had been "a lot of huffing and puffing" bccause the Coalition agreement not to compete with each other in seats was being renegotiated. "What will happen inevitably is that both parties will agree that where a seat is vacant, either party can run or in a seat held by a sitting member it will not be contested except by invitation," Mr Greiner said. In reality the agreement had been "a dead letter for ages", he said. "If we had wanted to run in Armidale or Coffs Harbour we would have run [and] the National Party wouldn't have tried to stop us by invoking the rule," he said.

10 Nov 1990 - Kirner Government loses ground in state-wide survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 10 November 1990, page 9 Kirner Government loses ground in state-wide survey HAD A state election been held in Victoria in October, the Liberal and National Opposition would have toppled the Premier, Joan Kirner, according to a Morgan Gallup poll in the Bulletin maga zine. The state-wide poll of 1532 electors shows support for Labor down five points to 26 per cent, support for the combined Liberal and National parties up four points to 56 per cent, support for the Democrats down two points to 10 percent and support for others up three points to 8 per cent. More voters opted for the Opposition Leader, Alan Brown, as preferred Premier. Mr Rrnum npv/»r to better John Cain as preferred leader during Mr Cain's premiership. Mrs Kirner's approval rating dropped five points to 38 per cent and her disapproval had risen seven points to 44 per cent, with 18 per cent undecided. Mr Brown's approval rating dropped four points to 36 per cent and his disapproval rating increased one point to 38 per cent, with 26 per cent undecided. SUPPORT for the NSW Labor Party is at its lowest since just after the March 1988 election loss, accord ing to a Morgan Gallup poll. The poll of 1342 electors state-wide in October found support for the Government at its highest since May 1988. The approval ratings of the Premier, Nick Greiner, and the Opposition Leader, Bob Can, improved, but Mr Greiner widened his lead as the preferred Premier. Support for the Liberal-National Coalition Government was up three points to 49 per cent, support for the Labor Opposition was down three points to 35 per cent and the Democrats were steady at 9 per cent. Mr Greiner's approval rating rose eight points to 58 per cent and his disapproval fell six points to 35 per cent, with 7 per cent undecided. Mr Carr's approval rose four points to 39 per cent, his disapproval fell two points to 39 per cent and 22 per cent of respondents were undecided.' As Premier, 58 per cent of electors (up four points) preferred Mr Greiner, 27 per cent (down one point) named Mr Carr and 15 per cent could not say. IN'LONDON, three opinion polls show that British Prime' Minister Margaret Thatcher's ruling Conserva tive Party, has lost significant ground in the past week. A Mori survey in The Sunday Times and a Harris poll in The Observer both showed the Conservatives 16 points behind the Opposition Labour Party. A poll in The Independent showed them trailing by 10 points.

22 Nov 1990 - PM's job still in reach: Keating Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 22 November 1990, page 3 PM's job still in reach: Keating Low opinion-poll ratings would "not necessarily" cost him the prime ministership, the Treasurer, Paul Keating, said yesterday. However, he conceded that his unpopular image would be "an issue" if he took over as Prime Minister. "Everyone would prefer to be more liked than less liked," Mr Keating said when asked by a radio commentator, John Laws, about a recent spate of poor opinion polls. The latest, a Morgan Gallup poll out on Sunday, showed that the Minister for Transport and Communications, Kim Beazley, was preferred to him as Mr Hawke's successor. Fifty-one per cent of 991 voters polled in mid-October said they preferred Mr Beazley, compared with 29 per cent for Mr Keating. Among Sydney ALP supporters, however, Mr Keating was the preferred prime minister — 48 per cent to Mr Beazley's 35. The erosion of Mr Keating's long-standing status as the man most likely to lead Labor next coincides with a major shake-up of the Treasurer's inner network of advisers. The changes, seen as significant by observers, include the addition to his staff in February of the Western Australian ALP branch secretary, Stephen Smith, and a Sydney Morning Herald journalist, John Edwards. They replace a senior adviser, Tom Mockridge, who is leaving after almost seven years, and Ian Ross, who has been on secondment from the ACTU. Mr Smith is a rising star in the ALP, credited with masterminding the dumping of Peter Dowding for Carmen Lawrence as the WA Premier. Dr Edwards is a long-standing personal friend of Mr Keating and has just completed an economics doctorate in the United States. Asked about Opposition Leader John Hewson's taunt that Mr Keating was "Mr Seven Per Cent" — his rating as preferred Prime Minister in an earlier poll — Mr Keating linked his popularity with the state of the economy. "If we had the economy booming again and we had employment strong and what have you, you'd find my popularity level comes up," he said. "When the economy is slowed up and we've had interest rates up, even though they're coming down, people take the bat on you and that's part of the job." Mr Keating said his succession to the prime ministership was a "different issue altogether" from his public popularity, and when Mr Laws interjected that one would ultimately lead to the other, the Treasurer said, "Not necessarily." Mr Keating said he had always sought the support of "earnest people" who understood what was happening and could see the value of changes. "That turns around the others," he said. "When you're in trouble in public life is when the earnest ones or the informed ones dump you. Now, I've never had that position, fortunately." He said preferred-prime-minister polls were "dud polls" because supporters of the major parties tended to support the existing leader. Popularity ratings were more important for Mr Hawke because he was leader. "If I was leading at some point, leading the Labor Party, then one's popularity becomes an issue in the public debate, much more an issue," he said. "But the job I'm in basically is about getting the mail through, getting the de cisions made." As Treasurer he often had to talk about interest rates, Australia's structural weakness, the current account, inflation and the foreign debt. "It is very hard to be giving the Ipana smile when you're answering a cold turkey question on something like that," Mr Keating said.

28 Nov 1990 - Govt popularity at record low: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 28 November 1990, page 3 Govt popularity at record low: poll SYDNEY: —Support for the Hawke govern-ment has slumped to a record low and most Australians would like to see the Coalition win power, according to the latest Morgan Gallup polls published in The Bulletin magazine. The first poll saw the gap between the ALP and Coalition widen by 3 per cent since the last poll to 18 per cent, Government support having reached a record-low 32 per cent and the Coali- tion's an equal high with August 1986 of 5O. Held 011 November 10-11 and 17-18, the polls showed that the Prime Minister's approval rat-ing at the first weekend increased by 2 per cent to 37 (since the October 27-November 3 poll) but fell to a record-low 33 at the second. Opposition leader John Hewson's approval peaked at 55 per cent on the first weekend (up 1 per cent) and was 48 per cent at the second.

01 Dec 1990 - Support for Labor at a record low Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 1 December 1990, page 9 Support for Labor at a record low THE FEDERAL Opposition has moved another three percentage points ahead of the Government in the latest Morgan Gallup poll, widening the margin between Labor and the Coalition to 18 percentage points. Published in The Bulletin magazine this week, the poll of 2188 voters found support for the Hawke Government at a record low of 32 per cent, 1 point less than thp incf noil Sunnnrt for the Coalition was up two points to an equal high of 50 per cent. Conducted over the weekends of November 10 and 17, the survey found support for the Australian fCIIIUbiaia naj running at 9 per cent. The poll would seem to indicate that the personal attacks on the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, by both the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, and the Treasurer, Paul Keating, have made little impact on the standing of the parties. However, when personalities were examined, it seemed that the bad publicity did contribute to a fall in Dr Hewson's popularity rating. While the ratings of both leaders rose slightly over the first weekend, Dr Hewson's fell by seven points to 48 per cent on the second weekend and his disapproval rating rose by nine points to 22 per cent. Mr Hawke also saw his approval rating fall on the second weekend to a low of 33 per cent and his disapproval rating up four points to 57 per cent. When asked who would make the better Prime Minister, respondents gave Mr Hewson a 43-40 per cent lead on the second weekend, which was a narrower contest than on the first weekend. IN BRITAIN, it seemed the departure of Margaret Thatcher from Number 10 has rejuvenated the elec toral prospects of the Conservative Party. Under the new Prime Minister, John Major, the Tories now hold an 11-point lead over the Labour Opposition, according to an opinion poll carried out for Independent Television News this week. On the premise of a general election "tomorrow", 49 percent of respondents said they would vote Conservative, 38 per cent Labour and 9 per cent Liberal Demo crat. Two-thirds of respondents said replacing Mrs Thatcher with Mr Major was a correct move and the same proportion said the new Prime Minister should not continue with Mrs Thatcher's policies. The poll was based on interviews with 1092 people.

06 Dec 1990 - 65pc approve VFT idea, more know its benefits Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 6 December 1990, page 4 65pc approve VFT idea, more know its benefits By PHILIP HOBBS The Very Fast Train is approved by 65 per cent of the residents in Victoria and NSW, according to a survey conducted by the Roy Morgan Research Centre. The survey found a high level of public awareness of the VFT. More than 80 percent of those interviewed were able to name at least one advantage arising from the project. The poll suggested that the VFTs ability to provide quick, time-saving travel between capitals was its greatest advantage, mentioned by 42 per cent of respondents. Twenty-one per cent said taking the train would be cheaper than flying. The survey, in which 1009 people were interviewed in Sydney, Melbourne and country areas of NSW and Victoria, found that 13 per cent of respondents were opposed to it and 22 per cent did not have a view. The ability of the VFT to take cars, trucks and coaches off the road was rated as an advantage by 9 per cent. On these figures the ratio of support to opposition for the VFT is 5:1 in favour. The chief executive of the VFT Joint Venture, Alan Castleman, said yesterday that the approval rating was an extraordinarily favourable result. The figures confirmed the results of a number of independent surveys and showed little variation from a similar Roy Morgan poll commissioned by the Joint Venture five months ago. "The results indicate that there is a continuing high level of support for the VFT," Mr Castleman said. "This follows the recent issuing of a cost-benefit analysis that has demonstrated the project is good for the nation and [supports] the decision by the Joint Venture to opt for the inland VFT route." Respondents were interviewed on the nights of November 15, 16, 17 and 18. They were asked two questions. "Do you favour the VFT project and what are the advantages, if any, of the VFT project?"

06 Dec 1990 - Vic ALP loses most of its support: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 6 December 1990, page 6 Vic ALP loses most of its support: poll MELBOURNE: Support for the Kirner Labor Government in Victoria has declined sharply again to 22 per cent, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The 4 per cent decline in support for Labor between October and November puts the Kirner Government 37 per cent behind the Liberal-National Party Opposition. Labor's support is also 7 per cent below the 29 per cent recorded just before John Cain handed over the leadership to Joan Kirner in July. In another blow to Mrs Kirner, the poll published in yesterday's Bulletin showed only 34 per cent nominating Mrs Kirner as preferred premier— down from 42 per cent in Sep tember — and her support among women voters falling, the approval rating down 2 per cent to 39 per cent in November, and her disapproval rating among women up seven points to 47 per cent. In the same period, the proportion preferring the Opposition Leader, Alan Brown, as premier increased from 38 per cent to 47 per cent. Approval of Mr Brown increased two points to 38 percent in November. His disapproval rating declined one point between October and November to 37 per cent. The poll was based on interviews last month with 1287 electors throughout the state.

06 Dec 1990 - But Greiner continues to get the thumbs-up Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 6 December 1990, page 6 But Greiner continues to get the thumbs-up SYDNEY: The NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, continues to get (he personal thumbs-up from the electorate, maintaining his 58 per cent approval rating, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The November poll, published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine, also showed 58 per cent of the 1511 people surveyed thought Mr Greiner made a better premier than would his Opposition rival, Bob Carr. Only 26 per cent thought Mr Carr would make a better premier, down one percentage point from the October poll. If an election had been held in November, the Government would have been easily returned to office, with 48 per cent saying they would vote for the LiberalNational coalition, down one point from October's survey. Thirty-seven per cent would have voted for the ALP, up two points from the last survey. Support for the Democrats fell one point to 8 per cent. Mr Carr gained slightly in approval as its leader, up one percentage point to 40 per cent, with his disapproval rate standing at 39 per cent. Thirty-four per cent of people disapproved of Mr Greiner, down from 35 per cent in October.

08 Dec 1990 - Coalition ahead in two major states Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 8 December 1990, page 9 Coalition ahead in two major states THE FORTUNES of the governments of Austra lia's two most populous states were in stark contrast this week, according to the latest Morgan Gallup polls. A poll of 1511 found that 58 per cent approved of the way the NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, handled his job and the same number believed that he was a belter Premier than Opposition Leader Bob Carr would be. Published in The Bulletin, the survey found that WATCH only 26 per cent thought Mr Canwould make a belter Premier, down one percentage point since Octo ber. If an election had been held in No vember, the Government would have been easily returned to office, 48 per cent saying they would vote for the Liberal-National Coalition, down one point. Thirty-seven per cent, up two points, would have voted for the ALP. Support for the Australian Democrats fell one point to 8 per cent. Mr Carr gained slightly in approval as Opposition Leader — up one point to 40 per cent with 39 per cent disapproving. Thirty-four per cent disapproved of Mr Grciner. In Victoria, support for the Labor Government of Premier Joan Kirner dived four points to 22 per cent. The drop puts the Kirner Government 37 points behind the Liberal-National Party Opposition. In a further disappointment for Labor strategists, the poll of 1287 voters shows only 34 per cent nominating Ms Kirner as preferred Premier, down eight points since September. Over the same period, the number preferring Opposition Leader Alan Brown as Premier rose from 38 to 47 per cent. Ms Kirner's approval rating fell three points to 35 per cent in November, and her disapproval rating rose eight points to 52 per cent. Approval of Mr Brown rose two points to 38 per cent, and disapproval fell one point to 37 per cent. In the United States, a Washington Post-ABC News poll found that 90 per cent of respondents approved President Bush's offer to send the Secretary of State, James Baker, to Baghdad for talks with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. However, 53 per cent did not think the talks would do any good. The poll, published this week, found that 69 per cent approved of the United Nations resolution authorising use of military force if Iraq did not withdraw from Kuwait by January 15. The poll also showed that support for Bush's handling of the Persian Gulf crisis was at 61 per cent, roughly the same as in October and November but well below September's 78 per cent.

12 Dec 1990 - Hawke is up while Govt stays low Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 12 December 1990, page 2 Hawke is up while Govt stays low SYDNEY: Support for the Hawke Labor Government remains at a record low although the personal popularity of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has increased, according to a Morgan Gallup poll published in this week's Bulletin magazine. The poll of 3669 voters, taken over the weekends of November 24-25 and December 1-2, found support for Labor steady on 32 per cent. The Opposition dropped one percentage point since the last poll taken mid-November, but still held a commanding lead over the Government with 49 per cent. Support for the Democrats and other parties was steady at 9 per cent and 10 per cent respectively. Mr Hawke's personal popularity increased three points to 36 per cent, with 55 per cent disapproving and 9 per cent undecided. Approval of the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, rose five points to 53 per cent, 22 per cent disapproved and 25 per cent I were undecided.

15 Dec 1990 - Voters like Hawke, ALP less and less Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 15 December 1990, page 9 Voters like Hawke, ALP less and less THE FORTUNES of the Federal Government and the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, hit record lows this week, according to a poll published in The Australian newspaper. The Newspoll of 2279 voters, taken over the weekends of December 1-2 and 8-9, found support for the ALP had fallen six percentage points since the March Federal election to 33 per cent. In contrast, the Opposition had gained 6.5 points to 50 per cent. Unly ji per rent of those surveyed said they were satisfied with Mr Hawke's performance; 62 per cent were dissatisfied. The Leader of the upposiuon, Lir John Hewson, scored 48 per cent satisfied, 25 per cent dissatisfied and 27 per cent uncommitted. A Saulwick Age Poll published in The Age found the Labor vote still below 30 per cent and particularly weak in Victoria. The national vote had improved from its disastrous 24 per cent a month ago, but only to 29 per cent. The Coalition maintained 51 per cent support. In Western Australia, a Morgan Gallup poll of 830 voters published in The Bulletin this week found support for the Labor Government of Premier Carmen Lawrence had fallen seven points to 28 per cent in October and November. The Opposition would have stormed to victory in an election, with 55 per cent support. However, Dr Lawrence was still more popular than the Leader of the Opposition, Bany MacKinnon, with 51 per cent support compared with Mr MacKinnon's 18 per cent. American support for military action in the Gulf waned, according to an ABC-Television poll of 518 people published this week. Only 58 per cent of those polled favoured war with Iraq if it did not withdraw from Kuwait by the UN deadline of January 15, compared with 63 per cent a week ago. Most people still believed UN economic sanctions would fail to push Iraq out of Kuwait, but the percentage had fallen from 66 per cent to 59 per cent.

17 Dec 1990 - Australians support SPC wage deal: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 17 December 1990, page 3 Australians support SPC wage deal: poll MELBOURNE: Australians overwhelmingly supported moves by Victorian SPC cannery to press ahead with a controversial wagecutting deal, a company leader said yesterday. Chairman of the Shcpparton-based fruit cannery, John Corboy, said a Morgan Gallup Poll showed 88 per cent of Australians approved of the deal, which will be heard in the Industrial Relations Commission today. Mr Corboy said the poll confirmed the actions of management and workers at the cash-strapped north Victorian plant. About 300 workers at SPC recently voted to sacrifice a range of award payments to save the cannery $2.5 million during 1991 and keep the plant viable. However, the Victorian Trades Hall Council and unions fear the agreement, if ratified, will set a dangerous precedent and effectively open the floodgates for employers to pursue similar award-cutting deals. VTHC secretary John Halfpenny warned last week that other unionists in the Shepparton area could block the distribution of products from the company if SPC moved ahead with the claim. But Mr Corboy said yesterday that his company understood what could happen and nad gone into the deal with its eyes open. He said the results of the poll showed Mr Halfpenny was out of touch with what the workforce wanted, whereas "we've used a good bit of common sense and country logic". The Australia-wide poll of 1023 men and women held last Thursday found 88 per cent approved of what the workers were doing, 7 per cent disapproved and 5 per cent could not say. When asked whether workers should be allowed to take voluntary wage cuts or whether the issue should be decided by the Government or unions, 77 per cent favoured a workers' decision, 12 per cent favoured the unions, 5 per cent the Government and the rest were undecided. Mr Corboy said today's hearing before Commissioner Malcolm Donaldson would determine through which avenue the claim was to be pursued. He said he was confident the deal agreed by workers and management would be ratified. "We believe it should be a speedy process and will be listed for a full hearing this week," he said. Mr Corboy said 93 per cent of his workforce had supported the 12 month deal, which included 11 trade-off conditions. He said the agreement was tied to a profit-sharing deal which was expected to come into force when the company was in the black again. The company chief anticipated the new deal would turn a $9 million loss in 1990 to a profit by the end of the 1991 calendar year. On Friday, the federal Minister for Industrial Relations, Peter Cook, indicated the deal had a good chance of gaining the backing of the commission. SPC said it was receiving increasing support including the donation of 360 Christmas food hampers for SPC workers from a Melbourne company and offers from several firms to send employees to SPC for a free day's labour.

17 Dec 1990 - SA Liberals beat Labor in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 17 December 1990, page 2 SA Liberals beat Labor in poll ADELAIDE: South Australia's Liberal Opposition is more popular than the reigning Labor Government led by John Bannon, a newspaper poll revealed yesterday. The Newspoll survey published in Adelaide's Sunday Mail found the Liberal-National coalition leading the ALP by 47 per cent to 41 percent. The October-December survey recorded that the Premier's approval rating was down slightly from 60 per cent at the November 1989 state election to 56 per cent, but it was still 20 points ahead of that of the Opposition Leader, Dale Baker, which stood at 34 per cent, an eight-point increase since that of the March quarter. The telephone survey of 1160 electors throughout the state found Mr Baker's dissatisfaction rating meanwhile had increased from 11 per cent to 32 per cent. Forty per cent of interviewees were dissatisfied with the way Mr Bannon was doing his job, 6 per cent more than in March. Support for the Australian Democrats had increased from 10.3 per cent at last year's election to 11 per cent.

22 Dec 1990 - Support for Labor in the Senate dwindles Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 22 December 1990, page 9 Support for Labor in the Senate dwindles THE COALITION would have won easily a full Senate election if one had been held in November, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in The Bulletin magazine, found the ALP would have lost up to three seats in a half-Senate and up to seven if it were a full Senate poll. ALP support in the Senate in November was 30 per cent, up one percentage point on October but down four on September. Liberal support increased by 3 per cent to 44 per cent, National Party support was unchanged at 5 per cent and Democrat support was down 2 per cent to 11 per cent. Support for other candidates was 10 per cent, while 4 per cent of those surveyed were either undecided or did not give a response. The poll showed the Liberal Party easily outpolling Labor throughout the na tion. It indicated the Coalition would have gained two senators in NSW and possibly one in each of Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and Western Australia while losing one in Queensland if a full Senate election had been held in November. A half-Senate election in November would have resulted in a Coalition gain of one senator in NSW and possibly one in each of Victoria and WA". The poll surveyed 9271 electors who were asked which party would receive their first preference votes "if a senate election was held today". Most Australians would prefer the Minister for Transport and Communications, Kim Beazley, to succeed the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, rather than the Treasurer, Paul Keating, according to a poll published in the Sunday Sun. The telephone poll was conducted by Newspoll after last week's leadership showdown between Mr Keating and Mr Hawke. When asked to select their preferred candidate, 25 per cent of respondents 1 POLL "'1 F chose Mr Beazley, 20 per cent Mr Keating, and 10 per cent the Minister for Education, John Dawkins. A breakdown of voters showed most who selected Mr Beazley were Liberal and National party supporters. Twenty-eight per cent of Liberal-National supporters thought Mr Beazley should succeed Mr Hawke, compared with 20 per cent of ALP supporters. Forty per cent of ALP supporters believed Mr Keating should follow Mr Hawke, while 20 per cent wanted Mr Beazley as successor. Only seven per cent of ALP voters chose Mr Dawkins. Mr Dawkins was preferred as successor to Mr Hawke by 13 per cent of Liberal-National supporters, while 9 per cent said they preferred Mr Keating. The poll showed that 47 per cent of voters surveyed wanted Mr Keating to remain as Treasurer at least until the next election, while 20 per cent wanted him to formally challenge Mr Hawke. Nearly three out of four people in Britain support military action against Iraq if sanctions fail, according to poll conducted for the British Broadcasting Corporation. Fifty seven per cent of those questioned expected sanctions would not work. The poll showed 71 per cent of the 1091 people interviewed nationwide on December 12 and 13 favoured military action if United Nations sanctions did not force Iraq to leave Kuwait. Britain has contributed ground troops, planes and ships to the US-dominated multinational force in the Gulf.

27 Dec 1990 - Green support still strong in spite of slump Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 27 December 1990, page 7 Gteen support still strong in spite of slump MELBOURNE: National support for conservation groups was still widespread despite the economic slump, according to the latest Saulwick poll conducted by the Melbourne Age news paper. Published in yesterday's Age, the poll found that 63 per cent of the 1000 people questioned nation-wide believed environmental groups made reasonable demands and 79 per cent believed the threat to the environment was real. According to the poll, support for the environment among Labor Party voters had declined by 12 per cent While 92 per cent of Labor Party voters polled 18 months ago thought the threat to the environment was real, only 80 per cent thought so in the latest poll. Asked to choose between economic growth or environment protection, 26 per cent favoured economic growth, 62 per cent opted for the environment and 12 per cent said "don't know".

03 Jan 1991 - Hawke support up slightly Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 3 January 1991, page 2 Hawke support up slightly Support for the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has risen slightly, but the Opposition still would have won an election easily last month, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll published yesterday. The poll, in The Bulletin magazine, showed support for the Government up one point to 33 per cent while the Liberal and National parties dropped half a point to 48.5 per cent. Support for the Democrats was unchanged at 9 per cent. The poll, conducted oyer the December 8-9 and December 15-16 weekends, was compiled from interviews with 3781 electors. Approval for the Prime Minister rose for the third consecutive poll by two points to 38 per cent, while the approval rating of the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, increased by a point to 54 per cent. Asked who would make a better Prime Minister, 45 per cent opted for Dr Hewson and 42 per cent for Mr Hawke. In another Morgan Gallup poll, a clear majority of Liberal and National voters indicated they thought the conservative parties should merge. The poll, conducted on the November 17-18 weekend, found 72 per cent of Liberal voters and 66 per cent of National voters favoured the idea.

05 Jan 1991 - Australians gloomy about the new year Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 January 1991, page 9 Australians gloomy about the new year Australians arc more pessimistic about the coming year than ever before, according to the latest special Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll, published in The Bulletin magazine, found 49 per cent of people, up 14 percentage points on 1989 — believe things will be worse in the next 12 months. Only 33 per cent believe they will be better — down 10 points on 1989 and one point higher than during the recession of 1982. The poll also found that most Australians — 56 per cent, up 12 points since 1989 — believe 1991 will be a year of economic difficulty. Some 54 per cent — up 31 .points — of Australians believe there is at least a 50 per cent chance of a world war in the next 10 years and 61 per cent (up 33 points) believe this year will see much international dispute. Some 44 per cent believe domestic industrial disputes will increase (eight points higher than 1989 but lower than results in 1981 and 1982). The special poll was conducted throughout Australia on the weekend of November 17-18, when 1218 people were interviewed. In another Morgan GalJup Poll, also published in The Bulletin, a majority of Liberal and National voters think the conservative parties should merge. A poll of 1063 electors conducted on November 17-18, 1990, found 72 percent of Liberal and 66 per cent of National voters in favour of the idea. The poll also found that a combined party under John Hewson's leadership would attract an extra one percentage point in support. A Morgan Gallup poll conducted on December 8-9 and 15-16 found the Hawke Govern ment slightly improved its popularity. The poll, published in The Bulletin, shows support for the Government up one point to 33 per cent while support for the Liberal and National Parties was down half a point to 48.5 per cent Support for the Democrats was unchanged on 9 per cent. Approval of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, rose for the third consecutive poll — up two points to 38 percent—while Dr Hewson's approval rating was up one point to 54 per cent. THE LATEST survey into the readership of newspapers has shown that one in three readers surveyed could recall reading over half of a number of selected editorial items and more than half could remember seeing them. The survey was conducted by Quadrant Research Services for the Newspaper Advertising Bureau of Australia. The study examined reader interest in editorial subject matter, and the highest score of 80 per cent went to material about the environment and pollution. It was followed by legal/court cases 78 per cent, accidents and disasters 71 per cent and crime/drugs 69 per cent Politics and government policy rated 67 per cent and major events 65 per cent. The study measured readership of250 editorial items selected at random which appeared in recent months in metropolitan and regional dailies and Sunday and national newspapers. It was shown that page one had the highest level of regular readership (93 per cent) while general news scored 82 per cent, world news 79 per cent, TV guides 77 per cent entertainment 62 percent, lifestyle 61 per cent, spon 60 per cent, comics 56 per cent, business and finance 44 per cent, travel 42 per cent and motoring 31 percent. The study measured readership of 250 items selected at random which appeared in recent months in metropolitan and regional dailies and Sunday and national newspapers.

09 Jan 1991 - Tobacco 'acceptable' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 9 January 1991, page 5 Tobacco 'acceptable' IN BRIEF SYDNEY: The vast majority of Australians find tobacco sponsorship of sporting events, art and concerts acceptable, despite increasing bans on cigarette advertising, according to a poll. About 72 per cent supported allowing tobacco sponsorship, barely less than the 75 per cent in 1988, the Roy Morgan , Research Centre poll for the Tobacco In stitute of Australia found. • The poll results, carried in The Bulletin magazine, show 83 per cent of smokers and 68 per cent of non-smokers accept the sponsorship and only 11 per cent feel it might encourage members of their fami lies to smoke. Only 2 per cent of non-smokers feel it might lead people to smoke. More than 1000 people, aged 18 and more, across Australia were surveyed.

12 Jan 1991 - A wanted war, but hardly the good fight Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 12 January 1991, page 9 A wanted war, but hardly the good fight Bob Hawke's nation-wide consensus will disintegrate when the body bags start to come home, predicts 'lottery' survivor Jeremy Thompson. TWENTY-FIVE years ago Aus- tralians were overwhelmingly in support of sending troops to Vietnam. We supported conscrip- tion, where one in seven Australian boys won the lottery and got to serve and, in many cases, to die in Viet- nam. I remember clearly the night in 1970 when my marble was in the barrel. The process was televised. A grey-suited man reached into a box and pulled out little balls on which was printed a date — a day and month. If that date was your birthday, you were in. Although I went on a couple of desultory anti-war marches through the university town of Armidale in those days, I was still young enough and dumb enough to accept my fate if my number came up. Fortunately, it did not, leaving my limbs and psyche intact. Others were not so for-tunate. Some 500 Australians died in Viet-nam, and thousands more were wounded. Many others believe they were affected by Agent Orange. Time has proved the error of John F. Kennedy's logic of the domino effect, and the paranoia which attributed to commu-nism levels of power, evil and influence it could never achieve. History, too, had its say when it became clear the Vietnamese were not fighting for communism but freedom — freedom taken from them when their land was handed back to the French as a colony after World War II. It was not a time in our history that Australians can be proud of. The name of the Prime Minister who first committed troops, Robert Menzies, will always be con-nected with the terrible error that was the Vietnam War. But at that time, public support for the war was unquestionable. The propaganda of the "red menace" and the "domino effect" went unchallenged by all but a few. It was only after the Tet offensive of February 1968 that most people started to realise that the Viet Cong and the North Vietnam Army 'were not the easybeats first thought. And it was only when the deaths started to mount that the ground swell of opposi- tion became a torrent that could no longer be ignored. Like the early stages of the Vietnam war, the Australian public is in favour of using military force in the Gulf, and supports Australian involvement in that force. A || GULF COUNTDOWN || Morgan Gallup Poll published this week found about 57 per cent agreed with force and about 54 per cent supported Australia joining the anti-Saddam forces. Those figures must give Bob Hawke heart. At this stage he has consensus, from the biggest caucus in the nation, for war. Back in the '60s, when people supported the Vietnam War, I rarely — if ever — heard a debate about the historic and moral rights and wrongs of the conflict. This time it is different. Historians such as the eminent Manning Clark point out that perhaps — just perhaps — Iraq has a genuine historic claim on Kuwait. He says the whole region wound up as a dog's break-fast after arbritrary divisions drawn by Brit-ain after the World War I. Iraq was left with limited access to the Gulf and a long-standing claim on Kuwait and its rich oil fields. THAT is not to say Saddam Hussein is a wonderful, warm, misunderstood hu- man being. He began his political life as an assassin, in fact, and spent years in exile as a result of his activities. He is a dictator's dictator. His frequent purges of the ruling Ba'ath party have stamped out any possibility of a challenge — which is why those who believe a loss of face would unseat Mr Saddam are wrong. Mr Saddam lost a million souls to win a few square kilometres from Iran, but when this latest crisis began, he handed the hard won territory back, along with prisoners of war. Loss of face? A coup? Never. His murder of tens of thousands of Kurds in northern Iraq is the most frequent ly used example of his good nature. The use of poison and nerve gases to ensure a good kill — too bad about the associated agony — underlines the message. But the fact he is a ruthless dictator is irrelevant in the context of war. After all, the United States has often unashamedly sup-ported dictators. Lyndon B. Johnson de-scribed the Nigaraguan dictator Somoza as, "a son-of-a-bitch, but our son-of-a-bitch". The US supported Mr Saddam against Iran during the eight years of war as, I suppose, the lesser of two evils. The US loathed Ayatollah Khomeini more than it loathed Mr Saddam. It was, after all, the followers of the Ayatollah who humiliated the US when they took US Embassy staff as hostages which, in turn, led to the debacle when US forces tried to free the captives. In a twist of logic, the US then used honey to trap the bee. The patriotic Colonel Oliver North secretly supplied arms to Iran to use against Iraq — which was also using American arms. One condition that the US put on its support of Mr Saddam during the war was that Iraq withdraw its support for interna tional terrorism. Iraq said it would — but did not. According to former US State De-partment officials, the US knew Iraq was still harbouring and funding terrorists but turned a blind eye. So if Iraq had good reason to believe it could get away with murder — literally — in the Middle East, it was about to be pres-ented with more evidence. As Iraqi forces massed around the Kuwaiti border early last year, the diplomatic feelers were out. What, Iraq asked, was the US position on the long-standing border dispute between Iraq and Kuwait? The answer came directly from the US State Department: we have no position on the border question, senior officials said. A nod is as good as a wink to a blind horse. On August 2 last year, the tanks rolled and the helicopters took off. It was all over in a few hours. The response by the US — and from almost everyone else — must have sur-prised Mr Saddam. Instead of the usual vocal but ineffectual condemnation in the United Nations, military action was threat-ened! America, Britain and France were quick to deploy forces. Tiny Australia, in another hemisphere on the other side of the world, convinced President Bush to ring the Prime Minister so it too could become in-volved. The United Nations condemned the in-vasion and set in place a blockade of Iraq. But this was not like the pitiful sanctions faced by South Africa, where most nations traded on regardless. This was a total block-ade, enforced by military might, and deny-ing Iraq not only imports to keep industry working but, more importantly, blocking the export of oil and the income Iraq so desperately needed. Estimates vary about how long such a blockade would take to bring Iraq to its knees, but does it really matter? Surely a long and vastly expensive blockade of Iraq must be far preferable to war and the tens of thousands of killed and maimed that would be the inevitable legacy of war. But the US was not prepared to wait — and Bob Hawke applauded its next move in the UN. It forced through the Security Council a deadline, January 15, after which military action could be used to liberate Kuwait. The theory, presumably, is to place Mr Saddam under the most intense pressure, to force a last-minute withdrawal from Ku-wait. But it is no carrot-and-stick approach. The US has refused to offer even a small concession — like negotiations on how to improve access to the Gulf — let alone a big one, like talks on the Palestinian question. The huge error of defining January 15 as a deadline is that it forces the US into military action if the deadline is ignored President Bush has painted himself into a corner and now has no option but the mili-tary one. The generals talk of "surgical strikes" and a blitzkrieg that would defeat Iraq in a few short weeks, perhaps even days. I guess if they say it often enough people start believing that sort of rubbish. The theory that Allied air power would crush Mr Saddam's air force before it could leave the ground is pure fantasy. Far more likely is that a massed Allied attack on air bases would find a reception from hundreds of accurate ground-to-air missiles. Above, Iraqi fighters would defend their territory, while Iraqi fighter-bombers massed at the Gulf, spraying Exocet missiles at everything within range — including Australian war-ships. Mr Saddam's long-range missiles would be deployed — but probably inflict little damage. They are not accurate. But the ones sent towards Tel Aviv would attract mas-sive retaliation from Israel. Israel has long been itching to wipe out Iraq as a threat to its security. Suddenly the equation changes: where the US enjoyed Arab support, the entry of Israel in the war would, to the Arab world, be intolerable. All at once it would no longer be Iraq versus the rest of the world, it would be Arab versus infidel. Israel has nuclear weap-ons; Iraq has chemical and nerve agents. And sitting in the middle, three Australian warships. MR HAWKE and his Government have the option, if they so wish, to tell the US that Australia will stand fast on the blockade for as long as it takes, but war? No thanks. We'll move our ships out of harm's way, if you don't mind. Sadly, that won't happen. As we always have, we'll toady along and do what we're told. During the Falklands War, Argentina showed what an Exocet could do to a mod-ern warship. Remember HMS Sheffield — or what was left of it after it virtually melted as the result of an Exocet attack? That is why our sailors have spent untold hours on fire drill. If an Australian ship is hit, it is then that Mr Hawke will find support for his war drying up. Two postscripts: A television reporter was interviewing a defence analyst from the ANU just before Mr Hawke announced Australia would be sending ships to the Gulf. "If they send Australians to the Gulf, then they must ensure an adequate supply of body bags," the analyst said And: the one piece of news I found par-ticularly chilling during the week was the approval of Australia's own awards for gal- lantry. Now Australian personnel can win 15 home-grown awards from a Meritorious Unit Citation to the Victoria Cross for Aus- tralia. The timing — a week before the war deadline — is disturbing. trust the medals can be awarded post-humously. In the Sunday Magazine tomorrow: A talent for terror . . . how Saddam Hussein graduated from boyhood violence to a showdown with the world.

24 Jan 1991 - Govt less liked Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 24 January 1991, page 11 Govt less liked Support for the Hawke Government had declined to its lowest point before hostilities broke out in the Gulf, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll published yesterday. The poll, in the Bulletin magazine, shows that support for the Government has sunk to equal its lowest point, 32 per cent, recorded in November last year. The poll of 2137 electors was conducted during the first two weekends of January, and showed that support for the Liberals had increased to 44.5 per cent, and to 4.5 per cent for the National Party, giving the Coalition 49 per cent support over all. Support for both leaders declined in the month, Mr Hawke's rating falling by three points to 35 per cent, and the Opposition Leader, John Hewson, losing five points to 49 per cent.

31 Jan 1991 - Super Bowl poor scorer in TV poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 31 January 1991, page 22 Super Bowl poor scorer in TV poll NEW YORK: Sunday's Super Bowl XXV was the second-lowest rated on television in 17 years and the eighthlowest overall, according to Nielsen poll figures. The New York Giants' 20-19 victory over the Buffalo Bills on ABC-TV rated 41.8, which represented the percentage of sets in the country which were tuneid to the match. A rating point represents 931,000 homes. The only lower-rated Super Bowl since 1974 was last year's on CBS (39.0) when the San Francisco 49ers beat the Denver Broncos 55-10. ABC officials said they were happy with their rating. "We figured it would do in the 42 to 43 range, Alan Grossinger, of the network's sports research department, said. "It pretty much came in where we expected." Grossinger and other TV analysts said ratings for the Super Bowl had declined with network ratings in general. Also, this year's match was lower because the two teams were from the same region. "Considering the game was very competitive, maybe it could have done a little better," Grossinger said. "It was very regional, and that had an effect." The Super Bowl started at 6.19pm local time and ended about 9.3S. Cable News Network's rating during that time was 3.1, six times higher than its rating during the 1990 Super Bowl. About 1.75 million homes were watching the all-news channel during this year's match. In addition, the Bills generally have a much lower national following than other American Football Conference teams, such as the Los Angeles Raiders or Miami Dolphins, if merchandise sales can be used as a guide. "The Buffalo market is the secondsmallest of the National Football League markets," Grossinger said. "That could have an effect. "This is a fairly new team to a lot of America, even though it showed its stuff in the play-offs." — AP
