30 Mar 1991 - Writers World Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 March 1991, page 17 By MAURICE DUNLEVY Reports of the book's demise are exaggerated IT'S official: the best-selling nov el of 1990 was Jean N. Auel's The Plains of Passage. Publishers Weekly has just released its sales figures for 1990 and they show that The Plains of Passage sold almost 1.7 million copies in the United States last year, or about 200,000 more than her The Mammoth Hunters sold in 1985. And while the book was No 1 on the US best-seller lists it was also topping the lists in Australia, Canada, Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Denmark and Sweden. In the US its nearest rival was Stephen King's collection of novellas, Four Past Midnight, which sold 1.2 million copies. King was, of course, the best-selling novelist of the 1980s, racking up million-copy sales throughout the decade, and last year he even scored another place in the top 10, coming in at No 7 with a reworking of an old book — The Stand: The Complete and Uncut Edition — which sold about 650,000 copies. The best-seller lists are not. the places to find first novelists. Not one of the books that sold more than 100,000 copies in the US last year was by a first novelist. Indeed, the top 20 novels were all by veterans of the best-seller lists. The five that sold more than a million cop-' ies, for example, were by Jean N. Auel, Stephen King, Scott Turow, Sidney Sheldon and Danielle Steel. The remainder included names such as Jackie Collins, Robert Ludlum, Judith Krantz, Barbara Taylor Bradford and Colleen McCullough — all best-sellers here in Australia as they were there. These megastars of the best-seller lists are all writers of "light fiction". You have to go down to No 28 before you find your first "serious" novel, The General in His Labyrinth by Gabriel Garcia Marquez (179,000 copies), then to No 36 to find the next, Rabbit at Rest by John Updike (150,000+). They were the only serious novels in the top 50. In another survey I was intrigued to see the tastes of the masses reflected in the tastes of their leaders. The Library of Congress, which holds the world's largest collection of books, surveyed the tastes of Congressmen last year. Their favourite author was Danielle Steel. Among their other favourites was Judith Krantz. True, they also read some serious, though popular, nonfiction. In Britain, at least one serious novel fared better than the two in the US by The Bookseller's rather different measure of success. A. S. Byatt's Booker Prize-winner, Possession, achieved fourth place for 1990 with 14 weeks on the magazine's weekly best-seller list. But it was outranked by such light fiction as Mary Wesley's A Sensible Life (20 weeks), Wilbur Smith's Golden Fox (19) and Rosamund Pilcher's September (18). Clearly being serious and being popular are not often the same thing, although in nonfiction you can be both. The top hardcover nonfiction title in Britain was Stephen Hawking's A Brief History of Time, which was on the list for 45 weeks, and the No 2 nonfiction. best-seller in the US was The Civil War by Geoffrey C. Ward with Ric Burns and Ken Burns — a phenomenal performance for a book that cost $US50. But that was about it in both countries. The top US hardcover nonfiction book was A Life on the Road by the television personality Charles Kuralt, and the others included self-help and cookbooks, animal books and collections of columns by widely syndicated newspaper funnymen, such as my own favourite, Dave Barry (Dave Barry Turns 40). You have to go to No 40 to get a substantial work of serious nonfiction: Robert A. Caro's second volume of his biography of Lyndon Johnson, Means of As cent. Meanwhile, crappy concoctions of folk wisdom such as Robert Fulghum's It Was on Fire When I Lay Down on It were enjoying their second year on the list. In fact, Fulghum's mindless musings were so popular that a special gift edition of the first chapter of his million-copy best-seller, All I Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten sold 233,000 copies in 1990. If "the book" dies in the age of the 30-second grab, it will no doubt be replaced by the chapter. But the best-seller lists from both sides of the Atlantic surely put paid to any notions that the book is dead. I had just read a number of such silly assertions and forecasts in the proceedings of the 23rd International Publishers Association Congress (Books in the 1990s) when I was confronted with the 1990 statistics. According to a number of speakers at the Congress, books were being killed by television and videotape. What rot! In fact, books were being made by television. The top hardcover publisher in Britain in 1990 was the BBC with 111 "book weeks" or appearances for 11 titles in The Bookseller's hardcover bestseller lists. They included such titles as Michael Pain's Around The World in 80 Days and The Trials of Life by David Attenborough. In the United States the three leading nonfiction sellers were all TV tie-ins and many of the authors of books on both the fiction and nonfiction lists are almost as well-known on radio and television talk shows as they are in the book world. The print medium feeds off the electronic media and vice versa. And certainly it is difficult to argue that the book is dying or is dead when you look at the sales of mass market paperbacks. In what golden age of the "living" book could you say that 123 mass market titles had in-print figures of at least a million copies, as we could of paperbacks published in the US in 1989 and 1990? Danielle Steel's Zoya had an in-print figure of 3.9 million copies, her Star had 3.75 million and she reprinted Daddy was on the best-seller list with 3.5 million. This doesn't look like the death of the book, although it may say something about the decay of the mass mind, as would the figures for Tom Clancy's Cardinal of the Kremlin (3.8 million), Rosamund Pilcher's The Shell Seekers (3.66 million) and Fulghum's All I Need to Know... (3.62 million). But even serious books put up good performances in paperback: Hawkmg's Brief History... sold 365,000 in its US paperback edition, Thomas Friedman's From Beirut to Jerusalem sold 210,000 and Shelby Foote's The Civil War: A Narrative sold 210,000 — an amazing feat for a three-volume work of history. If more evidence were needed that the book is still a centra! part of Western culture, we might look at the giving and receiving of it. An American Booksellers Association survey conducted on January 21 -23 showed that 47 per. cent of all adult Americans gave and/or received a book over the holiday season — an increase of 21.5 per cent over the figure from a similar poll in 1989. One or more books was received by 67 million Americans or 36 per cent of the population and 63 million gave one. And let me remind you that the book isn't dead in Australia either. A Philip Shrapnel survey showed that in mid-1989, 54 per cent of respondents to a household survey were currently reading a book, 11 per cent said they had bought a book during the preceding week and 17 per cent said they had borrowed one. Nor has television killed the book here. A Saulwick telephone poll of 1000 people done on April 30 and May 2 last year showed that Australians who grew up in the television era read more books than people over the age of 55 (the children of the supposed golden age of reading). Young adults are generally more literate than their parents, but Australians in general are, comparatively speaking, a nation of bookworms: 31 per cent of adults said they borrowed, and 16 per cent said they bought, more than 30 books'a year, and 54 per cent of houses held more than 100 books. Figures like that explain why two out of three readers of this newspaper look at the book pages and why we have such a large number of bookshops per capita compared to other nations. Our reading may not be serious but we do a lot of it.

27 Apr 1991 - Caucus mutterings first? Or media speculation? Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 27 April 1991, page 9 Caucus mutterings first? Or media speculation? POLITICS By Tony Wright THE Press Gallery scores much flak for its fascination with political leadership, or more specifically, its fascination with the subject of unstable leadership. Indeed, it is often said that journalists in the Press Gallery actually cause instability in the leadership of political parties and governments. There is right now a great deal of mutter-ing in the office of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, about this very subject. The only people getting in a lather about leadership, Mr Hawke's people will tell you, are the clowns in the Press Gallery. It's an old theme—as old, indeed, as the impossible question about the chicken and the egg. What comes first: loose talk among caucus members, or speculation in the me- dia? John Gorton, Billy Sncdden, Bill Hay-den, Andrew Peacock and John Howard all felt they had reason over the years to blame the media for their problems. All, at one time or another, would have cursed the Press for feeding the fires of discontent over their leadership. And yet, was it really the media avJio brought them down, or their own disloyal team members? Derek Parker, a former aide to both John Howard and Andrew Peacock, de-votes a fair slice of his new book, The Courtesans — The Press Gallery in the Hawke Era, to the proposition that jour-nalists at Parliament House are interested primarily in conflict and dissension. Mr Parker charges that the media were largely to blame for the image problems that finally brought Mr Howard down — a charge, it must .be said, that few in the Press Gallery would care to debate. He goes on to charge that the Press Gallery has been consistently biased in favour of Mr Hawke and his Government. If that were indeed so (and Mr Parker would get a debate over that assertion), the sands seem to have shifted. Now it's Mr Hawke's turn. The Prime Minister is growing increas-ingly exasperated by the continuing series of reports suggesting that the caucus is restive about his leadership. The speculation got a mighty kick along this week when the highly-influential jour- nalist Laurie Oakes, writing in Wednes-day's Bulletin, suggested that a move to replace Mr Hawke with his deputy, Paul Keating, might be only weeks away. In Darwin, on Thursday, Mr Hawke was asked by Helen Dally of the Nine Net-work's Sunday program, "As you travel around northern Australia do you think people up here care about issues like par-liamentary performance on, like, the lead-ership issue?" Mr Hawke: Well, not as much as you do, Helen, and the media. I mean, if I were to be influenced in my decision by the way in which you — I mean I'm saying generically not just you Helen, but the media generally — if I were to be believe that what you go on with reflected what the Australian peo-ple think about, you know I would say — you know, I'd give up. Not just in regard to present circumstances but generally be-cause I love you all, you know that. I love you all. But you really arc not representa-tive of the Australian people and let me say specifically as I've moved as I have now around northern Australia, I've been out for a couple of days; Bundaberg, in Maree-ba, Atherton, Darwin. You know, I hate to, you know, upset you but they ain't talking about it, kid. If Mr Hawke had hoped that would crush the journalists and would divert their attention from the leadership issue, he was to be mistaken. The very next question was this: Mr Hawke, reports through from Canberra [say] that there are noises at least in the party that the leadership issue hasn't been resolved. Do you hear these noises? Mr Hawke: No, I don't. I go back to what I said. Don't think that the Gallery or a few people in Canberra reflect the reali-ties out here. I'm very, very happy, exuber-ant one might say, about the feeling I get from Australian people as I move around amongst them. I love them and I still think they've got a bit of affection for me. The questioning continued along those lines for a while, with Mr Hawke growing constantly more annoyed. It was, he said "as boring as buggery". And then came the final question — why is the leadership speculation continu-ing? Here, Mr Hawke departed from the line that it was all a figment of the media's collective imagination. Instead, he de-clared it was the fault of two former ministers hoping to get their bums back on to ministerial seats by supporting a change of leadership. The comment was pretty clearly direct-ed at Stewart West and Peter Duncan, two members of the Left dumped from the Ministry last year. They are no friends of Mr Hawke, and it was widely known that they were involved in a discussion at a supposedly secret meeting of the Left at which the subject of leadership was freely canvassed. Mr Hawke, by pointing the finger at these two men, actually succeeded in re-ig-niting speculation about the leadership. Reporters naturally phoned Mr West and Mr Duncan for their responses to Mr Hawke's comments. Mr Duncan, in particular, didn't mince words. Sure he'd been talking about the leadership — why, everyone in the Caucus was talking about it, he said, making the most of the free kick provided by Mr Hawke. The result of all this was predictable. Front-page headlines across the land yes-terday. So what came first — the chicken or the egg? Mr Hawke says it is the media dreaming up the stories, and then admits that two of his former Ministers are at the bottom of the plot. It is all a very vicious cycle. It is also perfectly predictable that this is al-ways the way it will be. Politics is about power. In the end, that is why men and women are prepared to sacrifice a stable, normal life to enter the madhouse that is the parliamentary system. Power is a pyramid — and there is room at the top for only one. There is always someone who will covet the top spot, because there lies the power. Those of us who have chosen to watch and report the political system inevitably will find our eyes drawn to the goings on at the very peak simply because power is magnetic. When we hear and feel the beginnings — even the mere vibrations — of strife at the top, we report it and we watch even harder. The fact is, power plays are compulsive viewing. A few years ago, sitting by a log fire in a stockman's hut on the cold Bogong High Plains in Victoria's alps, an old fellow from over Omeo way told me a wonderful tale of the struggle for power. He was, he said, one of the few men alive who had seen a wild young stallion chal-lenge and fight for the right to lead a herd of mountain brumbies. The old stockman said he had tracked the mob, on and off, for weeks. He had seen the marks on the earth that showed several fights, and knew that the old stal-lion in charge of the herd had been under pressure from young horses, though he hadn't seen the fights first-hand. It was pretty clear that the old horse had put several young bucks to flight. Finally, the stockman had caught up with the horses, and the picture became too obvious. Here was the old stallion, his neck and chest torn from fighting, standing with the herd. And here was a tough looking young stallion, standing off a hun-dred yards. The stockman had sat in a clump of snowgums and watched as the younger horse whinnied and squealed and circled the old horse, who simply stood and pawed the ground. The fight, when it came, was brutish but short. It ended with the old horse clumping off into the trees alone, and the young stallion galloping off with the herd of mares. It was, the stockman said, as if the old stallion had finally lost the will to fight any more. None of the reporters in the Press Gal- lery can possibly predict with any certainty • the outcome of a challenge to Bob Hawke from Paul Keating, nor even how such a challenge might come about. But we are not so different from that old stockman, tracking the brumbies because he knew there would be a young stallion ready to fight for power. The chance of such a sight was irresistible. It seems beyond doubt now that either Paul Keating or Bob Hawke must move on, however it happens, simply because there is room for only one at the top Until that time, members of the Caucus will remain restive — and the Press Gal-lery will watch ever closer, drawing charges that the whole sorry business is the fault of ■ the reporters jumping at shadows. So who's at fault? Hell, let's just blame the magnetism of power, because we'll never find a scoundrel between the chicken and the egg. Committee style instead of Westminster tradition By LEANNE MASON "ABRAHAM Lincoln spoke of 'government of the people by the people for the people' — this does not describe the government of the ACT — this is government by the Public Service and four ministers." So begins an article in the Febru-ary edition of the Residents Rally Review. Its author, John Ballard, a former senior member of the Ad-ministrative Appeals Tribunal, is encouraging the RaHy to support a committee form of government — something like the Brisbane City Council style of government rather than the traditional Westminster system we have now. Mr Ballard points out that the Rally, before it went into govern-ment, did tend to support a commit-tee system where all members of the Assembly were able to participate in decision making. However, the idea is not yet Rally policy. It has the support of the party's policy com-mittee and is about to go to the executive and party for approval. But why a committee system? Mr Ballard believes the Westmin-ster system works well in a national arena where decisions are made con-cerning defence, foreign affairs, na-tional security and the national budget. In the article he describe the West-minster system as, "based on confi-dentiality — policy is formulated in the public service, approved by ministers and implemented through a parliamentary majority." However, he argues that every-where else m Australia, this system runs in conjunction with local gov- ernment "In the ACT there is no reason why all the functions devolved to the territory government should not be exercised through the procedures ap-propriate to local government," he said. "It is clear that people do want to be involved in policy formulation and are not prepared to accept min-isterial rubber stamping of public service decisions." Brisbane had the largest local au-thority in Australia controlling a budget of similar size to the ACT's. The city council was divided into seven committees, all members were involved, members of the majority party chaired each committee and a principal coordinating committee functioned as a cabinet. Mr Ballard argues that an ACT government would not need Federal Government approval to adopt such a system. "This will be implemented by the rewriting of Standing Orders and will not require concurrence of the Federal Government by amending the JACT Self- Government Act]," he said. "Under such a system ministers would become chairmen of commit-tees, Public Service submissions would go to the minister in commit-tee, a committee could sit in public if it wished." Different committees would be formed to cover the whole area of government, with the exception of certain basic matters reserved for the coordinating committee (Cabinet). "Cabinet would have direct re-sponsibility for the budget, dealing || All members take part in decision making || with the Commonwealth and inter-state matters," Mr Ballard said. "A separate standing committee would be retained to scrutinise public ac-counts and public works." Mr Ballard concedes that, ulti-mately, the majority party or a ma-jority coalition in the Assembly would have the final say on any is-sue. Committees covering educa-tion, health and other areas of government would also have to gain the coordinating committees ap-proval when making financial deci- sions. "The ultimate sanction remains refusal of appropriate funds," he said. Mr Ballard hopes the idea will go before the next annual meeting of the party for endorsement He real-ises that it will not be popular with the major parties or the public ser- vants and doubts also whether it will be accepted by the Press. Neverthe-less, he is confident the Rally will back the idea, particularly because he argues that under such a system the burden of government will be more evenly distributed amongst all members of the Assembly rather than the four members of Cabinet. He argues that this would then allow proposals and actions of the public service to be better scrutinised. UI would hope you are going to have positive scrutiny through the committee system rather than an op-position type of scrutiny [as current-ly operates]," he said. Public servants would have to get used to appearing before their re-spective committees to explain just what was happening in their agen-cies. Specific committees on issues such as the casino, HIV and fluoride would not have to exist. The health committee, for instance, would look at issues such as HIV and fluoride as part of its daily work. Mr Ballard's idea is not particular-ly new but it is going to be hard to sell. The Rally is not going to win government in its own right at the next election so, if this idea is to ever get off the ground, the Rally will have to sell it to at least one other major political grouping. As Mr Ballard realises, the ALP and the Liberal Party have evolved with the Westminster system and are unlikely to want to stray from something they believe is tried-and- true. A version of his committee idea was also canvassed in the lead-up to self-government It was not particu-larly supported at this time. It is also interesting to go back to ideas floated by the leader of the Rally, Bernard Collaery, and the leader of the Liberal Party, Trevor Kaine, soon after the 1989 election. When it became obvious that no party had won an outright majority, Mr Collaery suggested rotating the chief ministry, and the other three ministry positions amongst all the elected groups. He said a consensus-style govern-ment, with all groups taking part, was likely to ensure a stable form of government At the time, Mr Kaine disagreed. He instead suggested a cooperative power-sharing arrangement through a series of "executive committees" at ministerial level which would in-volve all parties.

29 Apr 1991 - By-elections major test for Goss Govt Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 29 April 1991, page 12 By-elections major test for Goss Govt By IAN DICK BRISBANE: New figures on bankruptcies and people's attitudes to high unemployment have given the opposition parties in Queensland a boost in by-election battles for Toowoomba South and Nundah. But the Fitzgerald report on Fraser Island could well provide the Goss Government with some by-election problems if it is issued before the May 18 polls. It is a "sleeper" issue that could influence government actions if released beforehand. Tony Fitzgerald, QC, was expected to hand his long-awaited report to the Government this week, but comments on Friday by the Premier, Wayne Goss, cast doubts on this. He said the report was due in early May, and he would be returning from a China trip on May 12. "Subject to what I hear next week, I would be expecting to get it the day I get back, and be looking to get it out fairly quickly, once ministers have had a look at it." What the Government does not want is another potentially long-running environmental sore breaking out before the two by elections. What Mr Fitzgerald recommends, and how the Government handles this, should be fascinating to watch if the report is made public before May 18. If, as some people suspect, Mr Fitzgerald recommends that logging on the island be phased out, does the Government bite the bullet, ban logging in quick time and announce compensation for the Maryborough area? Could encouragement be given for another industry, or industries, to be created in the area? The normal process would see the Government accept the report, study it, get submissions from all involved departments over time, listen to public reaction, and then make a decision. But the report could pose some tricky questions for a government facing two mid-term by elections. Regardless of the timing, however, it seems the Fitzgerald factor is again set to have a big influence on politics in this state. While logging, or lack of it, on the island does not directly affect voters in Toowoomba South and Nundah, the wider issue is that of Mr Goss's leadership and the Government's overall perform ance. And these seem certain to be by-election issues, given that Mr Goss stands unchallenged as Labor leader, while his counterparts in the National and Liberal parties, Russell Cooper and Denver Beanland, are less secure. The Fitzgerald report will set a scenario that could make life difficult for Labor's local Member Bob Dollin (Maryborough), who has spent a lifetime's work in the timber industry. In the longer term, Maiybor ough and coastal seats like it will be vital to Labor's re-election at the next state election. So there will be avid interest in how the Government handles the whole situation, including the reaction of more radical figures in the conservation movement. Bankruptcy figures and the Morgan Gallup poll survey of people's attitudes on unemployment show up deficiencies in the national economy, something the National and Liberal parties hope will nib off on Labor in the two by-elections. Mr Beanland has already commented that the bankruptcies, which rose 71.5 per cent in Queensland over the past year — more than in any other state — showed the state Government had lost control of the economy. The Morgan poll found unemployment to be the top voting issue, with 74 |)er cent of voters rating it as very important as how they would vote in a federal election. Unemployment in Queensland in March rocketed to 10.2 per cent, the second worst in the nation. Mr Beanland has set the reces sion, the economy, unemploy ment and general economic issues as his agenda, and in the last sitting of Parliament Mr Cooper also turned his attention this way. But the Premier's office sees unemployment and bankruptcies as federal issues. Mr Goss will not seek to ignore the fact that the state and national economies are causing people a lot of grief, and could make them feel bad about Labor. But people have also shown they can differentiate between state and federal issues — these were very strong at the last state election which Labor won in a landslide, and such issues had little impact in the recent local-gov ernment elections. Mr Goss will be pushing other issues, such as his leadership as compared to his opponents', whether Queensland is on the right trac£ cleaning up corruption and the overall question of honesty in government. However, the basic fact remains that mid-term by-elections are notoriously difficult for governments, and Labor admits that taking Toowoomba South from the Nationals will be difficult, as will retaining Nundah. Despite this, Mr Goss will be "pushing a good strong message" over the next few weeks that the state Government moved early to help tackle unemployment with its accelerated capital works program, and more training places announced by the Minister for Employment and Training, Nev Warburton. As well, the Treasurer, Keith DeLacy, maintains Queensland will lead the nation out of the recession. Recent housing figures show that Queensland is outstripping the rest of Australia in private housing. The housing sector is seen by Treasury as a major indicator of economic strength, given its multiplier effect. If the Liberals' stocks are as low as suggested by the dumping of Sallyanne Atkinson as Brisbane Lord Mayor, the Liberals will need the Nationals' preferences in Nundah if they are to take the seat from Labor. It will be a testing time for Mr Beanland's leadership. — AAP

04 Apr 1991 - Hawke Govt approval drops: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 4 April 1991, page 12 Hewson Hawke Govt approval drops: poll SYDNEY: Support for the Hawke Government dropped two percentage points to only 33 per cent after the Prime Minister's Industry Statement, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll in this week's Bulletin. Support for the LiberalNational Party Opposition rose a point to 49 per cent, giving John Hewson's team a 16-point lead over the ALP. The Democrats gained a point to 8 per cent The poll suggests the Government would have been swept from office had an election been held in mid-March. It was conducted in the wake of Mr Hawke's Industry Statement to Federal Parliament, and after remarks by the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, about sending troops on to the wharves in the event of strikes. Approval ratings for both Mr Hawke and Dr Hewson dropped for the third successive poll. Mr Hawke's standing was down marked ly, by seven points to 38 per cent, with 52 per cent disapproving of him and 10 per cent undecided. This rating is similar to the rating registered before the onset of the Gulf war. Dr Hewson's approval rating was down a point to 47 per cent, while disapproval was up two to 29 per cent and 24 per cent were undecided. When electors were asked to nominate their preferred prime minister, 44 per cent said Mr Hawke, 42 per cent wanted Dr Hewson and 14 per cent couldn't say or named someone else. Of ALP voters, 86 per cent said Mr Hawke made the better prime minister, 6 per cent said Dr Hewson would, and 8 per cent could not say. Of Coalition voters, 74 per cent said Dr Hewson would be a better PM, 14 per cent preferred Mr Hawke and 12 per cent could not say. The poll was taken during the weekends of March 16-17 and 23-24. 06 Apr 1991 - Hewson takes the cake then rolls in the muck Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 6 April 1991, page 9 Hewson takes the cake then rolls in the muck WEDNESDAY was a big day for John Hewson. Staff in his Sydney office, 11 floors above Phillip Street, presented him with a chocolate cake adorned with a single candle. A bottle of Yellowglen sparkling wine was uncorked and a toast was drunk to the first anniversary of Dr Hewson's leadership of the Opposition. Lying on a desk nearby was a copy of The Bulletin magazine. It contained the latest Morgan Gallup Poll findings on who was fashionable and who was not in the only game that anyone at the jolly little gathering cared about — federal politics. You can check the details elsewhere on this page, but suffice to say that the poll showed Bob Hawke to be decidedly unfashionable among those who were asked, and John Hewson to be very chic indeed. It was as if the Gulf War had never happened — the poll trend lines were right back to where they were before the war blew them all to hell. So John Hewson had every reason to feel contented with life as he sipped wine and munched chocolate cake on Wednesday morning. In just a year he had established himself as the unquestioned leader of an Opposition that had previously been riven with intrigue and self-doubt, and he had swept to popular acclaim among those who counted, the voters. However, Dr Hewson doesn't seem the sort of man who can bear contentment for more than a small slice at a time. Perhaps it is the hard Baptist upbringing, but he seems always a little too tightly wound to keep from twitching at the edges and occasionally springing out at the most unexpected angles. John Hewson: not exactly the gentle soul he might like to project. And so it was on Wednesday. Before the day was out he would do something that might in time come to be regarded as a profound turning point in his career. Here is what he did. He got down and rolled in the smelly stuff that most long-term politicians recognise with a mixture of loathing and loving as the muck of their trade. It is a heady mulch of deal-doing and point-scoring, and it is all the more potent when some of the points are scored below the belt. To express surprise that a senior politician would be prepared to grubby himself in the muck would be naive in the extreme, but Dr Hewson has led us to believe that he is no ordinary politician. He has always sought to give the impres sion that he would go to considerable effort to skirt around the muck rather than dirty his boot by so much as stepping in it. On Wednesday, however, he let us all know that, in fact, he is not much different from the rest of them. It may be remembered as the day he became a politician. He had received a letter a few days previously from the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, inviting him to discuss how they could reach bipartisan agreement on extending the term of the House of Representatives from three to four years. The benefits of such a move have been obvious for many years: a guaranteed fouryear term might allow a Government to govern, rather than simply administer, plans could be made and carried through, rather than the present system, where governments sec an election only three years away and fly towards it by the seat of their pants. Indeed, Dr Hewson agrees heartily with the idea. What's more, he said so—almost a year ago, when he had made it crystal clear that he would be happy to talk turkey with the Government over such a proposi tion. The thing was, the Government hadn't got back to him, and patience isn't Dr Hewson's strong point. Finally, just a week before this week's Constitutional Centenary Conference—at which it was obvious things like four-year terms would be discussed — Mr Hawke's letter arrived. It came, too, a few days after the Queensland Government had failed to convince electors to support a referendum on four-year terms in that state. Dr Hewson smelled a rat. Moreover, he was still steaming at the ears over the Government's decision to ban political advertising on television and radio.

17 Apr 1991 - ALP 'in deep trouble in WA, SA, federally' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 17 April 1991, page 2 ALP 'in deep trouble in WA, SA, federally' The ruling Australian Labor Party is in deep electoral trouble federally and in Western Aus-tralia and South Australia, ac-cording to an opinion poll published yesterday. The Morgan Gallup poll in the Bulletin magazine shows support for Labor premiers in Western and South Australia to be at all-time lows. It shows that the Prime Min-ister, Bob Hawke, would be de-feated, although the Federal Government has shaved the lead held by the Liberal-National co- alition. The polls in March and early April show that SA Premier John Bannon's government "is in real . . . trouble" and the Hawke government too would have been defeated easily. A poll in WA just before last week's Geraldton by-election, in which Labor lost a previously safe seat, showed "approval of Premier Carmen Lawrence dropped to her lowest-ever rat-ing". While the government had "enjoyed a slight fillip during the Gulf crisis, the improvement evaporated after the war". "Lawrence's approval dropped eight points in March to 47 per cent — 15 points lower than in December-January — while 38 per cent of voters approved the performance of opposition leader Barry MacKinnon," the Bulletin reported.

21 Apr 1991 - Sheer panic reigns among those who kneecapped Hayden Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 21 April 1991, page 2 Sheer panic reigns among those who kneecapped Hayden MANABOOTTOWN BY KEN BEGG WHO IS mixing the drinks on The Hill these days? I mean, are we supposed to take this latest round of leadership rumours seriously? True, the Prime Minister hasn't had the best two weeks of his career, but does he deserve the sack? (Please don't all answer that; not at once anyway). If he does have to go, arc the party's hard men going to replace him with Paul Keating? You may remember Labor's hard men; that was the group that persuaded the party to dump Bill Hayden back in February, 1983. They kneecapped Hayden and the party's long tradition of loyalty to the leadership. Why? Because they didn't believe Hayden could beat Malcolm Fraser in a general election. So Hayden had to go. Thirty-one days later Bob Hawke was • Prime Minister, Fraser was history and Hayden was headed for Yarralumla. Would these same hard-heads now have " -us believe seriously that Paul Keating could win the next general election? I doubt it. And I doubt that veiy many people on The Hill believe it, either. In fact, the last time any of us was consulted about our views on Labor's leadership was back in November last year, when a Morgan Gallup poll showed 34 per cent in support of Hawke as Prime Minister while Keating rated a miserable 7 per cent. What is it about the Labor Party that compels ccrtain factions to go on canvassing political suicide? Panic, probably. Sheer panic. The Labor Party is on the nose with the electorate and the party's nervous nellies know it. Sure, Paul Keating performs well in Parliament. He always does. So did Gough Whitlam during the constitutional crisis. He cut Fraser to pieces in Parliament. Did that matter to the electorate? No, it didn't. They tossed Whitlam out of office. Labor's leadership rumours won't go away. Not now. They have a life of their own. Rumours of leadership rivalry (real and imaginary) plagued John Howard and Andrew Peacock, and eventually destroyed them both. Bob Hawke and Paul Keating are seemingly set on the same fatal course. The Prime Minister still trails John Hewson in the opinion polls and probably will continue to do so until the economy shows some signs of recovery. Nevertheless, unless someone apart from Keating wants a crack at leadership, or the Prime Minister quits, Bob Hawke remains the Government's only chance — a poor chance at the moment — of surviving the next election. IN THE meantime, as our poor country reels under the growing weight of its jobless, maybe our elected representatives will spare a thought for our survival as well as their own. You don't need an economics degree to know things are crook. You may not know that they're not as bad here as they are elsewhere in the country. The reason for that is largely the Commonwealth's steadying influence on the local economy. This influence over the private sector means we have few booms or busts, but with the advent of self-government the Commonwealth is no longer guaranteeing the loan borrowings of the ACT, which means we now need a credit reference. Have you ever tried to borrow money without one? The ACT needs to borrow about $44 million next financial year. That's well below Loan Council limits but a lot of money nevertheless. The ACT Under-Treasurer, Richard Madden, agrees that it's a big task, but he's optimistic about a successful outcome. "If we can have a budget of the strength of last year... when we managed a major turnaround ... we'll go very, very well... but it will be a very big test." Part of that test will be persuading the credit-rating agencies that the ACT has the capacity to repay its debts in a timely manner. Dr Madden says the agencies "devastated" Victoria and Tasmania with their ratings. "We have to now stand up in that quite competitive field and see how we go." Keep your fingers crossed. LIBERAL party warhorse Sir Robert Cotton was in fine form at an informal farewell for Tony Eggleton at Parliament House last week. A one-time senator, minister and Ambassador to the United States, Sir Robert recalled the advice he had received when he arrived in Canberra as a young senator from NSW. Don't be rude, he was warned, because the opposite side is better at it; don't pretend, because someone will always catch you out; and don't eat fish in the dining room! Sir Robert is a driving force behind a bipartisan committee of the Parliament (a rare oasis in Parliament these days) called the Political Exchange Committee. The committee dispatches the country's brightest and best young political leaders overseas to further their experience and contacts. Tony Eggleton — "The Maltese Falcon" as he was known to the press gallery during his days as Liberal Party federal director — is now quitting the committee to begin a new job for an old boss. The new role is Secretary-General of CARE, an international aid agency (a sort of world Meals on Wheels); and his old boss? Malcolm Fraser. Life wasn't meant to be easy, Tony, even in Brussels. MY FRIENDS on the Goulburn high way patrol tell me (they'd be your friends too if you knew how efTectively they police the bitumen) that they're not too happy about the results of their latest camouflage operation using an unmarked truck. It seems the truck was hired through a Canberra agency that had the vehicle brought down from Sydney for the purpose. Someone (and the highway patrol has its suspicions) leaked the registration details of the truck to the semi drivers who ply the Hume. Consequently, "the stitchup" truck — as the truckies have dubbed it — had a fairly quiet night. But it's coming back soon, and police tell me there'll be no foul-up with the "stitch-up" next time around. OLD SOLDIERS never die, they just become more interesting. At the War Memorial last week, a digger was leaning on his walking stick, transfixed by the gallery diorama of Tobruk Harbour and its graveyard of sunken ships. He was looking for a misplaced tug, a leaking old crate that he and his fellow diggers had boarded 50 years before, in pursuit of a German officer named Rommel. "We had wet feet for two days, and we never did find out who that bloke Rommel was." War Memorial or living museum? For those who believe that Anzac Day has lost its relevance, next Thursday's Dawn Service at the memorial has attracted so many people that it now has to be held on the parade ground and not in the courtyard. A J. SYMONDS is a man of few • words. "Call me an Aussie battler," he says. A. J. Symonds is the man apparently responsible for registrations for the "Dennis Stevenson special" at the Chinchilla RSL in Queensland next weekend. The what? According to a flyer bearing A. J. Symonds's name, Dennis Stevenson — "Australia's most dynamic Member of Parliament" — is the main event at a Positive Result Seminar. OK. So who's paid the $26 registration fee? I can't tell you that, says A. J. Symonds, but the response has been good. How many? 1 can't tell you that. Who's organising the seminar? I won't commit myself to answering that; Why Dennis Stevenson then?... because he's the only politician in Australia trying to carry out the will of the people. How so? By remaining true to his promise to abolish self-government and by his opposition to X-rated videos. Do you know that the flyer bearing your name has one or two ... ah, fibs? Like the one claiming Stevenson "knocked back a proposed ministerial package of $84,000 a year salary plus car?" I'll let Dennis answer that one. Finally, could the media attend? We'd be willing to pay the registration fee? No, says A. J. Symonds. You'd put a slant on it. A. J. Symonds got that right!

23 Apr 1991 - Masterful males have no need for horoscopes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 23 April 1991, page 19 Masterful males have no need for horoscopes EN By IAN WARDEN □ Why is it, do you think, that women have a greater appetite than men for astrology ana for New Age balderdash in all its forms? Magazines for women almost always publish horoscopes while the better-known magazines for men — journals like GQ (Gentleman's Quarterly) and Esquire — decline to do so. The Canberra Times, like most major metropolitan newspapers, has a policy of not publishing horoscopes in spite of my long-standing application to my editor for the chance to furnish one (under the pseudonym Jonquil the Gypsy) for the tens of thousands of credulous Canberrans who hanker for a glimpse of their immediate futures. While I hesitate to venture any theory of my own in explanation of the female appetite for horoscopes I have just come across an authoritative explanation prof.fered by Arthur Cooper, the actual editor ofGQ. "Guys" insists Arthur, "feel that they are the masters of their universe, and that they don't need to know what the planets have to say about it." I must catch up with my own editor during one of his fleeting visits to Australia to ask him if his reasons for keeping The Canberra Times horoscope-free coincide with Arthur Cooper's, but in the meantime 1 find myself wondering if my own resistance to astrology has anything at all to do with any feeling that I am the master of my own universe. Upon mature reflection I must say that I think I am one of the universe's playthings and that I am entirely at its mercy although Mr Cooper may be right about some men and he may very well be right about a high proportion of American men who do seem to be among the more self-confident and smug of men. If women turn to horoscopes and to other forms of New Age witchcraft because they feel that these things help them to cope with a menacing and unpredictable universe then I sympathise with their predicament without being able to place any faith in the stars. Indeed, one's sense of being a plaything of the universe is only deepened when one lies on one's back under the stars and notices how many billions of them there are, and notices their majestic indifference to whatever might come to pass here. Dolphins may, perhaps, feel some affection for us but the stars could not care less. Of course not all men are immune to the appeals of astrology. As I have noticed elsewhere a new biography of John McEnroe, the cad and bounder of tennis, has his biographer and apologist Richard Evans insisting that this basically warm, wonderful human being sometimes behaves tempestuously because he is an Aquarian. All Aquarians are like that, Evans insists. Why, he is one himself and knows what it is like to feel the ungovernable need to rail against real or imagined injustices. □ Some columns ago I dwelt upon the grim subject of the abrupt increase in the rate of suicide among men in Canada, imagining that the Australian experience was likely to be very similar. Richard Eckerslcy, author of Casualties of Change: the Predicament of Youth in Australia a report produced in 1988 for the Commission for the Future, assures me that yes, more and more Australian men and especially young Australian men are attempting suicide. In Australia suicide among males a^ed 15-24 has trebled over the past thirty years and has also risen, albeit less dramatically, for men up to the age of 35. He points out that the rate of attempted suicide, indicating a great reservoir of misery and despair among young Australians, is many times that of successful suicide. A 1988 Saulwick Poll found that 21 per cent of Australians and 40 per cent of those aged 18-24 personally knew of teenagers who had attempted or commit ted suicide. As is the case in Canada, Australian males who attempt suicide are much more likely than women to succeed. This is because many women tend to try to do it by poisoning themselves, a notoriously unreliable method, while men, in their decisiveness, tend to shoot or hang them selves. Richard applied-himself to the question of why so many more young men than young women attempt suicide and noted that a number of studies show that boys are rather more prone to despair. The studies show, for example, that boys are more adversely affected than $irls by divorce and parental conflict with the separation from the father that often follows divorce appearing to be one of the factors at work. He thinks that unemployment hits men harder than women because it is central to a man's self-image and his status while women have the option of finding some fulfilment as home-makers and as child-rearers. Men, he thinks, are less likely to bring themselves to admit to anyone that something is wrong, to cry on a shoulder and to ask for help. Conversations between male friends are, he says, "notoriously impersonal" compared to conversations between female friends.

01 May 1991 - PM loses ground Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 1 May 1991, page 2 PM loses ground SYDNEY: Publicity about the WA Inc Royal Commission has caused a decline in Prime Minister Bob Hawke's popularity rating — his worst since January. The Morgan Gallup poll in the Bulletin magazine has his rating at 37 per cent, down 4 percentage points, and his Government's by 2 points to 32 per cent

05 May 1991 - Carr: we'd make over-inflation increases illegal Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 5 May 1991, page 1 Carr: we'd make over-inflation increases illegal The NSW ALP would encourage prudent government spending by making increases in taxes and charges above the inflation rate illegal, Opposition leader Bob Carr said yesterday. Mr Carr said the election would centre on the increased financial burden families had suffered under the Greiner Government. Families had paid for $900 million wasted on consultants, advertising and special public servants, through an extra $1300 a year each family in government charges that rose faster than the CPI, he said. A Labor Government would pass legislation making it illegal, except in special circumstances, for a government to raise taxes and charges above the consumer price index. Mr Carr showed reluctance to draw the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, into the state election campaign. To repeated questioning he said, "Mr Hawke would be no more and no less involved in my election campaign than he was in the previous state election campaigns of 188 or '84, and no more and no less than Dr Hewson on the other side." Mr Hawke would not be at the policy launch, he said. Mr Carr said his proposed CPI restriction would deter governments from raising taxes and charges to cover excessive spending and instead would encourage them to make savings. A politician who wanted to increase government charges by more than the CPI would have to amend the law, he said. A Saulwick Poll last week showed Mr Greiner had a 15-point lead over Mr Carr, but a Quadrant Research Services poll of five marginal seats, published in today's Sun-Herald suggests that the gap might be narrower. It found 30 per cent support for the Coalition, 27 per cent support for Labor and 35 per cent undecided.

11 May 1991 - Leaders' approval stays on even keel Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 11 May 1991, page 9 Leaders' approval stays on even keel PUBLIC approval of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, and Federal Opposition Leader, John Hewson stayed the same during April, according to the latest Saulwick Poll. The poll, published in The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age, showed 28 per cent of voters thought the Prime Minister was doing a good or very good job, compared with 30 per cent for Dr Hewson. It may suggest that Mr Hawke's public embarrass ment last month over the WA Inc Royal Commis sion did not have a lasting impact on his image. However, the trend of recent months among those interviewed saying he was performing poorly or very poorly continued, with Mr Hawke rating 33 per cent to his rival's 20 per cent. Dr Hewson's net approval rating therefore rose one point to 10, Mr Hawke improving one point to minus five. Mr Hawke's net approval has been negative in all Saulwick polls since last November, except in February and March, during the Gulf war. Meanwhile the Federal Government scored 28 pints to the Coalition's 52 — 24 percentage points behind. The Australian Democrats picked up in popularity from 7 per cent to 12 per cent, which coincided with debate on the issues of uranium mining and resource-security legislation. The NSW Greiner-Murray Government has increased its lead over Bob Carr's Labor Opposition, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin. Conducted during April, it found public support for the Coalition up one point to 47 per cent, while Labor's approval rating fell by one point to 38 per cent. The Australian Democrats lost a point, falling to 6 per cent, while "other" candidates gained one point to reach 9 per cent.

15 May 1991 - Liberals' support increases further Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 15 May 1991, page 2 Liberals' support increases further SYDNEY: As the WA Inc Royal commission continued, the federal Coalition's lead over the Hawke Government increased by one point to 17 per cent, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll in this week's Bulletin. The poll showed support for the Government remained on 32 per cent while support for the Opposition increased one point to 49 per cent. Democrat support dropped one point to 8 per cent and support for minor parties was steady on 11 per cent Approval of the way Mr Hawke was handling his job dropped one point to 36 per cent, while 54 per cent disapproved and 10 per cent were undecided. Opposition Leader . John Hewson's approval also dropped one point, to 48 per cent, while 29 per cent disapproved and 23 per cent were undecided. When electors were asked who would make the better prime minister, 44 per cent opted for Mr Hawke and 41 per cent said Dr Hewson; 15 per cent could not say or nominated someone else. Asked to comment on their approval of Mr Hawke, people made comments such as "straightforward, honest, genuine" and "he is doing a good job in hard times". Those who disapproved said that "things are going downhill for him" and "he seems to be losing control". In approving Dr Hewson, people said "he's im proved" and "seems to know what he is talking about". But just as many felt he "is not strong enough" or said they "don t know much about him".

17 May 1991 - Compass insists on apologies Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 17 May 1991, page 4 Compass insists on apologies By ROD CAMPBELL Australia's newest airline, Compass, has threatened to institute legal proceedings against Ansett Airlines, Australian Airlines and Australian National Opinion Polls unless they apologise immediately for the way Compass passengers were interviewed by ANOP staff last month. Compass took ANOP Research Services to court two weeks ago and obtained an order obliging ANOP to reveal who had hired it to cany out a survey of Compass passengers. The survey, at Tullamarine Airport, was said to have amounted to harassment of passengers. According to Compass, when it obtained the order from the Victorian Supreme Court on May 1 ANOP's lawyers threatened the company with contempt proceedings if it used the information for "a collateral or ulterior purpose". In a statement yesterday, Compass said it had received the information from ANOP on Wednesday (the court-imposed deadline) but, in the light of the lawyers' warning, had declined to make available copies of the information. However, it had decided, based on that information, to institute proceedings under the Trade Practices Act against ANOP, Ansett and Australian Airlines. The allegations against ANOP and Ansett would be that they had engaged in false and misleading conduct. Against Australian Airlines it would be that it had aided and abetted that conduct. Compass said it would ask the three companies to publish an apology and, if that happened, it would not launch legal proceedings. If no apology were forthcoming, proceedings could begin as early as today. The possibility of legal action was foreshadowed at proceedings on May 1. Compass claimed then that the ANOP questionnaire, used in early April, had contained misleading information asserting that Ansett and Australian Airlines could match Compass fares. The court heard that a person involved in the survey had produced a letter stating that the survey had been authorised by Australian Airlines' airport manager. When it learnt of the survey, Compass management wrote to Australian Airlines accusing it of harassing Compass passengers and of giving them "blatantly untrue" information about comparative air fares. It asked Australian to publish a correction. Australian responded that it had not hired ANOP and Compass owed it an apology. After more fruitless correspondence, Compass wrote to ANOP to find out who had hired it and then launched proceedings. Compass also raised publicly the conduct of its competitors earlier in the year. It has been reported that Compass has written to the Trade Practices Commission asking whether certain aspects of the Commonwealth Public Service travel system are a barrier to fair competition, based on the fact that the major airlines have bought some travel agencies that handle public-service travel arrangements.

18 May 1991 - POLL WATCH Labor still dogged by WA Inc Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 18 May 1991, page 9 THE Royal commission into WA Inc is continuing to take its toll on the Federal Government's electoral stocks, according to public-opinion polls published this week. As well, the WA Inc saga appears to be having a minor flow-on effect to other Labor administrations, including that of the Queensland Premier, Wayne Goss. However, support for the Tasmanian Labor Government of Michael Field is up slightly. • ' According to the latest Morgan Gallup poll, published in The Bulletin, the Coalition's lead over the Federal Government increased a further point to 17 per cent, meaning that support for the Government remained at a record low 32 per cent. Support for the federal Opposition stood at 49 per cent, while support for the Australian Democrats fell one point to 8 per cent. These results suggest that had a poll been held in late April or early May the Hawke Labor Government would have been easily defeated. Approval of the way the Prime Minister was handling his job dropped one point to 36 per cent in the poll, while 54 per cent of those polled (up two points) disapproved and 10 per cent were undecided. However, the approval rating for the Leader of the Opposition, John Hcwson, also dropped one point, to 48 per cent, while 29 per cent disapproved and 23 per cent were undecided. On who would make the belter Prime Minister, 44 per cent (up one) of those polled suggested Bob Hawke, while 41 per cent (down one) suggested John Hewson. In Queensland,-polling showed support for the Goss Government down one po'int since November-December to 46 per cent, while support for the Liberals dropped half a point to 26.5 per ccnt and support for l,he National Party rose 2'/: points to 17.5 per cent. Mr Goss continued to command a high approval rating which, despite dropping one point, still stood at 73 per cent.1 Approval of the Opposition Leader, Russell Cooper, dropped to a new low of 27 per cent. In Tasmania, support for the Field Labor Government was up one point to 34 per cent while Liberal Parly support fell one point to 51 per cent. Mr Field's approval rating dropped two points to 36 per cent, while that of the Leader of the Opposition, Robin Gray, was down three paints to 44 per cent.

23 May 1991 - Poll finds 'mining approved' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 23 May 1991, page 5 Poll finds 'mining approved' The Coronation Hill joint venturers say a new poll shows Australians do not accept Aboriginal heritage protection as reason enough to reject mining in the Kakadu National Park. A Morgan Gallup poll carried out forNewcrest Mining Ltd and published in The Bulletin, found 56 per cent of people approved of mining on condition the joint venturers reached an agreement with the nearby Jawoyn Aborigines, who consider the land sacred. However, the managing director of Newcrest, John Quinn, said the survey showed Australians did not think Aboriginal concerns were enough to slop mining. He said the poll found the environment was the main issue worrying the 39 per cent opposed to mining. Only 8 per cent of those opposed cited concerns about Aboriginal interests, and 31 per cent approved of mining, regardless of Aboriginal or environmental issues. Mr Quinn said, "The implications are pointed — Australians do not accept that Aboriginal heritage protection is sufficient reason to reject a project that will generate at least $500 million in export earnings and up to 630 new jobs throughout Australia."

25 May 1991 - POLL WATCH Opposition still well in the lead Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 25 May 1991, page 9 Opposition, still well in the lead THE Federal Opposition still holds a comfortable lead over the Government, according to a popularity poll conducted this month. The Newspoll survey, published in Th6 Australian, showed also that the Opposi-, tion Leader, John Hewson, continued to lead the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, by a wide margin in the popularity stakes: 43 per cent of voters were satisfied with Dr Hewson's performance, while only 34 per< cent were satisfied with Mr Hawke's. The survey also concluded that support, for the major parties had been "stable" -throughout the year, with the May poll showing the Labor Party rating 35 per cent support and the Liberal-National Coalition rating 49 per cent However, support for the Australian Democrats dropped slightly to 9 per cent. Newspoll noted that voting intention for the major parties was "almost identical" to that obtained in another Newspoll survey on today's NSW state election,, published two weeks previously. A MORGAN Gallup poll published in The Bulletin this week has found that while 31 per cent of Australians support mining at Coronation Hill regardless of the view of the Jawoyn Aborigines, public support increases to 56 per cent if the local inhabitants agree. The survey, conducted during May for. the joint-venture manager, Newcrest Mining, found also that while 79 per cent identified Kakadu with environmental issues such as national parks and conservation, only 13 per cent identified Kakadu with Aboriginal issues: 28 per cent identified the park with mining. Thirty nine per cent of those surveyed were opposed to mining at all and supported the creation of a conservation zone, while 5 per cent were undecided. Green supporters (65 per cent) were significantly more opposed to mining than Labor voters (46 per cent), Coalition voters (29 per cent) or Democrats (45 per cent). THE latest British opinion poll shows Britain's Opposition Labour Party leading the Conservatives by 8 points — a wider margin than at any time since John Major became Prime Minister. NOP's nation-wide survey for The Independent and BBC 2's Newsnight program suggests that had Mr Major opted for a June election, he could well have lost it. Current voting intentions are: Labour 44 per cent (up 3 points since last month), Conservative 36 (down 5), Liberal Democrat 15 (up 2), others 5 (no change). The figures would give Labour an overall majority of 41.

03 Jul 1991 - Hawke still preferred as PM, says poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 3 July 1991, page 1 Hawke still preferred as PM, says poll SYDNEY: Voters still prefer Bob Hawke as Prime Minister over former Treasurer Paul Keating, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll taken two weeks after Mr Keating's failed leadership challenge. The poll in today's Bulletin magazine shows that in mid June 37 per cent of voters named Mr Hawke as their preferred prime minister. This was down six points since January, but still well above support for Mr Keating as Prime Minister which was 14 per cent, up eight points since January. The poll also found some 9 per cent of electors preferring new Treasurer John Kerin as Prime Minister with 8 per cent nominating Kim Beazley. The remaining votes were split between seven other candidates. Among Labor Voters Bob Hawke held a clear lead in popularity, with 61 per cent support, compared with 68 per cent last year. According to the poll conducted on the weekend of June 15-16, Paul Keating rated 16 per cent among Labor Voters, Beazley 5 per cent and new Deputy Prime Minister Brian Howe 1 per cent When asked to choose between Beazley and Keating for Prime Minister, 45 per cent of all electors voted for Beazley and 39 per cent preferred Keating.

06 Jul 1991 - Hawke still the favourite Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 6 July 1991, page 9 Hawke still the favourite DESPITE constant leadership spec ulation and trenchant media criticism. of the role of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, in decisions on Coronation Hill and uranium policy Mr Hawke remains the public's preferred Labor Party leader. The latest Morgan Gallup poll, published in The Bulletin, found that in midJune 37 per cent of voters named Mr Hawke as their preferred Prime Minister. Conducted two weeks after Paul Keating's failed leadership challenge, Mr Hawke s support was down six points since January, but this was still well above support for Mr Keating, which was 14 per cent — up eight points over the same period. The poll also found about 9 per cent of electors preferred the new Treasurer, John Kerin, as Prime Minister and 8 per cent nominated the Minister for Transport and Communications, Kim Beazley. Among Labor voters, Mr Hawke held a clear lead in popularity, with 61 per cent support, compared with 68 per cent last year. Mr Keating rated 16 per cent among Labor voters, Mr Beazley 5 per cent ana the new Deputy Prime Minister, Brian Howe, 1 per cent. When asked to choose between Mr Beazley and Mr Keating for Prime Minister, 45 per cent of all electors voted for the former and 39 per cent for the latter. When asked to choose the Leader of the Opposition from leading Liberal and National Party people, 34 per cent chose the present Leader John Hewson. His closest rival was the former Leader, John Howard, on 18 per cent Another poll found that 41 per cent of Australians believe politicians rarely or never tell the truth. The Saulwick poll, published in The Age, said that about 60 per cent of voters feel that Mr Hawke and Dr Hewson are as honest as most politicians. However, a greater percentage of the 1000 voters interviewed found Mr Hawke to be less honest than most politicians. 06 Jul 1991 - Little to challenge free-riding Libs Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 6 July 1991, page 9 Little to challenge free-riding Libs POLITICS By Tony Wright ABOUT now, Opposi tion Leader John Hewson and his colleagues should be copping a touch of the blowtorch to the belly. We arc, after all, a week into the 1993 election campaign, if we are to believe the Prime Minister. So where was the blowtorch this week? It was pointed at the belly of the Prime Minister, and it was wielded by the Minister for Employment, Education and Training, John Dawkins. That's the way things have been for so long that Dr Hewson must be wondering whether he was goosed by a rainbow in an earlier life. The Hewson Opposition has enjoyed the most extraordinary honeymoon. It has lasted a year and three months. But after all that time, what do we know about what Dr Hewson and his colleagues really stand for? What do we really know about John Hewson? The answer is pretty obvious. Not much. About the only thing we know for sure about Dr Hewson is that he is a pretty boring fellow, and that's hardly damning, because Dr Hewson admitted it himself on one of the nation's most-watched television i shows. We know that Dr Hewson and his deputy, Peter Reith, are committed to introducing a broad-based goods and services tax, but we don't know any details. We know that a Hewson Government would be committed to cutting tariffs, but so is the Hawkc Govern ment. We know too that a Hewson Government would reduce government • intervention clear across the board, and would rip hard into the socialwelfare budget. We should hardly be surprised by this, because Dr Hewson has made it clear that his heroes arc people like Ronald Reagan and Maggie Thatcher. However, perhaps we should be surprised and a little worried that they remain his heroes, because both of them caused dreadful pain to the poor, and both of them blew their respective nations' economies in a huge way. Indeed, Dr Hewson was in the US this week, where he met good ol' Ron, the man who gave America a $400 billion debt. Not surprisingly, Dr John was asked about his continuing admiration for Mr Reagan. "He (Mr Reagan] said he was going to do three things [when he became President]," Hewson said. "He was going to re-establish US defence supremacy; he was going to re-establish US standing in the world and he was going to balance the Budget Two out of three ain't bad." Sure thing, Doc. The only slight problem is that the third thing, the one that Mr Reagan cocked up, is the important one so far as the everyday lives of the citizens actually matter. But perhaps we shouldn't dwell on Dr Hewson's palpably absurd comment. Another thing he has admitted is that he hasn't yet grasped the skill of the 30-second TV grab. So back to the things that we know about the Hewson Opposition. We know that the Opposition's industrial relations spokesman, John Howard, plans to introduce enterprise bargaining to the work place. We don't know how much industrial strife this will cause, but we can guess. But that's okay, if things get out of hand, say on the wharves, Dr Hewson has said he would be prepared to send in the troops. This week we learned that the Opposition spokesman on higher education, David Kemp, wants universities to become more autonomous, more competitive and more efficient. We know also that he wants the universities to open their doors to any student who qualifies for a place, which this year would mean an extra 30,000 university places for the dumbest students. Furthermore, we know he wants to introduce voluntary work agreements to universities so that academics can earn the money they think they should be paid. But we don't know how all this can be achieved, because something we do know is that the Opposition plans lopping $3 billion from public spending. Dr Kemp seems to think universities can get more money from generous industries. Considering the majority of companies appear loathe to pay the existing stingy 1 per cent payroll levy for stafTtraining, that sounds fanciful. We suspect students will be required to pay more — lots more — for their tertiary education, and some universities will simply go broke. So these are a few of the things we know about the Opposition. You might have imagined that within all this the Government would have been able to cobble together an assault that would have had the Opposition reeling. More to the point, you might have imagined that in a year and three months, the Government would have been able to force Dr Hewson and his colleagues to actually reveal a bit more about their intended agenda. But that simply hasn't happened. The Government has been too busy (a) making a hash of slowing down the economy by shooting it with an elephant gun; (b) denying that its policies would force the country into a recession when everyone knew they were already suffering one; (c) trying to justify the recession when it could no longer be denied; and (c) tearing itself apart over leadership. Dr Hewson, in an interview on Four Corners this week, tacitly admitted that he had been given a free ride. "The Prime Minister has provided us with a bit of time, if you like, in the last year by running plenty of diversions in Canberra for us," he said. "It's left me with the opportunity really to get on and do what I had to do." Might it be too unfair to interpret this to mean that he has been left, without normal scrutiny, to jigsaw together a bunch of policies and then to try to work out how to dress them up so they do not look and smell quite like the mishmash of Reaganomics/Rogemomics that they appear to be? Perhaps it is entirely unfair. But it is pretty clear that the electorate is getting restive. The Hawke Government may not have the wherewithal to bring Dr Hewson to book, but the voters are already beginning to have their say. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll, published in The Bulletin this week, shows a significant slump in the proportion of respondents who voted for Dr Hewson as their preferred Leader of the Opposition. In January, he was preferred by 42 per cent of voters. This had fallen dramatically last month to 34 per cent. The slump was clear, too, among Liberal-National Party voters — in January, 54 per cciit of them had registered a preference for Dr Hewson. Last month, only 49 per cent of conservative voters registered a preference for him. One suspects that there is less of a wind-change here than simply that the wind has died. The voters are growing bored with a leader who does not project enough personality and who will not give them enough information about what he and his party actually plan to offer the elec torate. The boredom factor certainly worked on the Four Corners' team this week. Four Corners is a program that normally glues you to your seat, but this week it was so flat that you would have been forgiven for thinking that your TV set had reverted to black and white. Still, the Hewson Opposition retains a handy lead over the Labor Government in the polls, and has plenty of time to build on that On the other hand, the Hawke Government is gripped by such paralysis that it is little but pitiable. John Dawkins: quite openly taunting Bob Hawke. It is possible now to see just how deeply Hawkc was wounded by the Keating challenge, and it is growing increasingly difficult to see how he can survive the willy-willies set in motion by that event. One of Mr Keating's most valued troops, John Dawkins, has been quite openly taunting Mr Hawke for the past week or two, implicitly challenging his authority and, in the end, the best Mr Hawke could do was to pull him into his office and try to get him to shut up. It didn't work. Indeed, what could Mr Hawke hope to do with someone like Mr Dawkins? If he had been sacked, Mr Dawkins would very likely become more out of hand. Yet by not sacking him, Mr Hawke looks impotent. And what was Mr Dawkins's sin in the first place? He accused the leadership of the party of reneging on its responsibilities at the national conference in Hobart by failing to make decisions on the hard issues. He says he was talking about faction leaders, but he could just as well have been talking about Hawke. The fact is, there is a failure of leadership in the ALP. Decisions about anything that might be mildly controversial aren't being taken, because such decisions will be interpreted through the frame of the Keating challenge. How long this sort of paralysis can continue before it becomes fatal isn't clear. But it is obvious that it cannot be allowed to continue indefinitely. It's not good for the Labor Party, the Government or the nation. The only winner from such an appalling state of affairs is John Hewson. But then, he probably won't be as grateful because he has become accustomed to drifting along without real challenge.

13 Jul 1991 - Media trusted by only 39 per cent Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 13 July 1991, page 9 Media trusted by only 39 per cent Australians trust their political and media institutions far less than their education, legal and banking systems, according to a Saulwick poll issued this week. The national survey of 1000 people, published in The Sydney Morning Herald, ranked the education system as the most trusted with 62 per cent of the sample stating they had a "great deal" or a "fair amount" of trust in it. Legal and banking institutions managed to scrape through with the trust of 52 per cent of those interviewed. Notably over 40 per cent said they had "not much" or no trust in these institutions. The media was trusted by only 39 per cent and the political system by only 36 per cent. Sixty per cent had little or no faith in the media and 62 per cent did not trust politicians. The poll found that attitudes to the education system varied greatly with age. Eighty per cent of those aged 18-24 had at least a fair amount of trust in the system but only 49 per cent of those over 55. POLL WATCH F In support of the tenet that cynicism grows with age, all institutions were trusted more by young people. Blue-collar workers had a greater amonnt of faith in the education system and the media while white-collar workers were more likely to trust the legal, banking and political systems. In political polls, the latest Morgan Gallup poll found support for the Hawke Government dropped slightly over a two-week period dominated by the ALP's national conference in Hobart. Support for the Liberal-National Coalition rose one point to 46 per cent. Conducted over the weekends of June 22-23 and June 29-30, the poll found Australian Democrat support unchanged at 7 per cent and 10 per cent support for other candidates and parties. Approval of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, dropped one percentage point to 38 per cent while his disapproval went op one point to 52 per cent. The rating of the Leader of the Opposition, Dr John Hewson, went op one point to 45 per cent and his disapproval remained steady on 33 per cent When electors were asked who would make the better Prime Minister, 46 per cent (down three) said Mr Hawke and 39 per cent (up one) opted for Dr Hewson. A Newspoll published in The Australian found that a larger percentage of voters approve of the way the new Treasurer, John Kerin, is handling the job than his predecessor Paul Keating. In March, only 22 per cent were satisfied with Mr Keatine's performance but the latest Newspoll found that 30 per cent were happy with Mr Kerin so far. Two-thirds were dissatisfied with Mr Keating and only 11 per cent with Mr Kerin.

18 Jul 1991 - Keating: I still want Prime Minister's job Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 18 July 1991, page 2 Keating: I still want Prime Minister's job Continued from Page 1 "The answer is I would prefer to have Paul Keating in terms of Government, I make no pretence about that," he said. "As to whether he should be leader or not, that's a matter for the parliamentary party. "But from where I see it, I think that he should be part of the Government process." Mr Kelty also put the new Treasurer, John Kerin, on notice that his commitment to broadening superannuation entitlements to all workers would be under close scrutiny when next month's Budget was announced. 20 Jul 1991 - NSW Opposition Leader calls for Keating's return to Cabinet Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 20 July 1991, page 1 NSW Opposition Leader calls for Keating's return to Cabinet Bob Carr: Cabinet without Keating is incomplete. By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent The Leader of the NSW Opposition, Bob Carr, kept the federal leadership controversy bubbling yesterday when he called for Paul Keating to be returned to the Cabinet. Mr Carr said there was "something incomplete about a federal Labor Government of which Paul Keating isn't a member". He would not comment on whether he believed Mr Keating should replace Bob Hawke as Prime Minister, but said he had not been surprised by a Morgan Gallup poll this week which had found that more people believed Mr Keating was intelligent and capable compared with Mr Hawke. "Anyone respects him [Mr Keating] for his razor-sharp intellect," Mr Carr said. Mr Carr is the second senior figure of the labour movement this week to call for Mr Keating's return to the frontbcnch. The secretary of the ACTU, Bill Kelty, said on Wednesday that he believed Mr Keating should be part of the government process. He and Mr Carr aired their views on the John Laws show on radio 2UE. A spokesman for Mr Hawke said yesterday that the Prime Minister would not comment on Mr Carr's statements, but his position remained the same as it had been in his response to Mr Kelty on Wednesday, when he had said that Mr Keating had made his decision and there was no vacancy in the ministry. Mr Carr took a thinly veiled swipe at Mr Hawke about the Government's handling of unemployment, saying, "I think he has got to demon strate to all conccrncd that he is in touch by giving a higher focus in his Government to questions of jobs".
