He said it was a disgrace that unemployment was at present levels under a Labor government, and warned that the Federal Government was bound for defeat unless it delivered "the promptest possible improvement in unemployment". He did not believe that "people locked in the Canberra syndrome, locked up there in the public servants' capital that Canberra is, understand how people are hurting". Mr Carr is a long-time friend of Mr Keating and both are leading members of the NSW Right faction of the ALP. Mr Carr succeeded Mr Keating as president of NSW Young Labor more than 20 years ago. Asked if the Government would be better led by Mr Keating, he said, "I am not going to comment on that. "I mean, that has been argued out when the leadership contest occurred. 1 am not a member of the federal caucus and 1 won't buy into that, but I would simply say that there is something incomplete about a federal La bor Government of which Paul Keating isn't a member." Mr Carr was deeply critical of what he said was the federal bureaucracy's failure to take seriously the case for anti-dumping legislation. He said overseas companies were dumping chemicals on the Australian market, putting at risk the future of the Botany ICI chemicals plant. He had put the case to the Minister for Customs, David Beddall, and had learnt that the Government's report to the anti-dumping authority had been made by "someone on work ex perience... an exchange student • from Sweden and a third figure.a low-level bureaucrat". r Asked if Mr Hawke realised the severity of the unemployment problem, he said, "1 think he is; I mean, I think if any politician knows what is going on in our community, it is Bob Hawke. "I would like to think he could' demonstrate, by moving on this issue, that he is in touch with industrial and workplace realities." Tony Wright's column, Page 9. Editorial — Pago 8

20 Jul 1991 - Preening backbencher's fan club Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 20 July 1991, page 9 Preening backbencher's fan club WHEN Paul Keating wanders in to his relatively small office in Parliament House these days, isolated from the halls of power, he is comforted by the sight of a great stack of fan mail. There arc hundreds of supportive letters from all around Australia, and he is spending a fair slice of his time answering them all. Separated from the fan mail is another great stack of invitations to speak to business organisations, social clubs, service groups, universities, schools and just about any other forum you might mention. Some of the invitations have come across the Tasman from New Zealand. Every day his office is plagued with phone calls from the top talk shows and current affairs programs on the major TV and radio stations, begging for the chance to interview him. In all his time as Treasurer, Paul Keating was never so hot an item as he is as a backbencher. The point, of course, is that he is not seen as merely a backbencher. He is seen as a backbencher in waiting. One imagines that Bob Hawke can remember a similar experience as he waited to wear down Bill Hayden. The memory must be very sour indeed to him by now. Of course, whatever solace Mr Keating might draw from counting his fan mail and the number of requests for interviews, he could hardly place any store in it if these constituted the only evidence of a newfound popularity. There will always be people who write glowing letters to public figures when an event (such as the leadership challenge) spurs them to action. Television and radio programs, which rely on ratings for their very existence and which have a voracious appetite for talking heads, will always leap to attention when events suddenly transform a person into a creature of public fascination. But it is the stack of invitations to speak and to appear on top-ranking media shows that is most valuable to Keating. He can sift POLITICS By Tony Wright the pile and choose just those forums that will best serve his twin purposes of keeping his public profile high and of shaping a new, seductive image. Profile and image are just about everything in Keating's obvious and relentless campaign to become Prime Minister. Every bit of evidence that the Keating camp can dredge up that shows Keating can win votes in the wider electorate can be used to considerable effect in the subterranean guerrilla warfare that is going on within the party. Hawke supporters — who remain in the majority — have one very good reason left to them to stay behind the Prime Minister. He is a proven winner when election time rolls around. They know the next election is the toughest they will have faced. If any of them are to be prepared to switch allegiances, they will want positive proof that Keating is a better bet. They haven't got that proof... yet. And so, Keating took great care in accepting his first two public appearances since his unsuccessful leadership challenge. Last week's speech to academics at the ANU and this week's performance with Ray Martin on the Nine Network's Midday Show were clearly chosen as a gourmet might pluck the plumpest grapes from a bowl. On one hand, Keating the intellectual; on the other, exposing his softest smiles to middle Australia at midday. His office says he has not yet decided when and where he will next pop up. But let's take a bet that it won't be long before we hear his voice on the John Laws Show. Those who count themselves as "serious" commentators often underestimate the role that the Laws radio show can play in matters political. Laws seems too arrogant, too self-satisfied and altogether too popular for their taste. However, few politicians would make such a mistake. They remember the 1983 election campaign, when Malcolm Fraser told Laws on his show that people ought to put their money under their beds rather than trust a Hawke Government. It was a huge faux pas which is generally considered to have blown any remaining chance he might have had to win the election. I recall, after that, chasing Hawke back and forth to Laws' studio as he appeared again and again, knowing that he was gaining direct access to a massive body of listeners from middle Australia. Hawke's minders credited those hours in the Laws studio as having played a major role in the 1983 Labor victory. SINCE then, John Laws has always been a major stop for politicians on the make and those who would be their king-makers. You will recall that the ACTU secretary, Bill Kelty, chose to be interviewed by John Laws on Wednesday, just as Paul Keating was preparing to appear on Ray Martin's TV show. Kelty left no doubt that he thought Keating was still the greatest. Yesterday, the NSW Premier, Bob Carr — one of Kcating's mates from the NSW Right — was on the show, calling for Keating to be back in a decision-making role in the Government (see report in today's news pages). I mention all this as background to a conversation I had yesterday with Laws' producer, John Bailey. Mr Bailey made it clear that Keating was considered very hot stuff indeed by the Laws show. The reason? Ratings. The moment Keating made his challenge to Hawke, the whole pattern of callers to the Laws show changed, he said. Suddenly, there was a great influx of calls from young people, and they had kept calling. This was previously unheard-of — the show normally attracted middle-aged and older people. In the one-month survey period since the Keating challenge, when the whole issue dominated the Laws show, John Laws' ratings for 2UE jumped a stunning 2.2 points to 15.3, beating all other Sydney stations in the timeslot. And the bulk of the the rise came from young listeners. "The demographics changed absolutely dramatically," Bailey said. "Half our callers were suddenly young people. And we've maintained these younger callers." More to the point, the new, younger callers (aged from 18 to the late mid-30s) were overwhelmingly pro-Keating. Indeed, the Laws show had done its own poll on Keating "when other polls showed him in a dastardly light" and had come up with a startling 70 per cent in favour of him. Mr Bailey said Keating had an invitation to appear on the Laws show whenever he wanted. Keating had said he would, but hadn't given a commitment about when that might be. And then the crunch. There was no such invitation to Mr Hawke. Laws wasn't interested in talking to him. Well, none of this might mean much. Radio callers are notoriously fickle. But considering the track record of the Laws show, it is at least food for serious thought. Moreover, there is evidence beyond the merely anecdotal to suggest that even before Keating's campaign to win the hearts and minds of Joe and Vera Average was properly underway, he was establishing something of a fan club. The most substantial bit of evidence is the Morgan Gallup Poll published this week. You can argue that you can read whatever you like into a poll like this one, but it is at the least indicative that the widespread view that Keating is Australia's most hated politician might be somewhat askew. It revealed that more voters believed that Keating was capable, intelligent and a strong leader compared with Hawke. The poll showed also that vastly more voters believed Hawke was friendly and likeable compared with Keating. So what can we extrapolate from that? It seems to indicate that the voters still love their Hawkie as a bloke, but they have more respect for Keating's abilities (even if, as the poll showed, they think he is insincere). More telling, perhaps, was that 22 per cent of voters felt that Keating was positive, with clear policies, while only 7 per cent thought the same thing of Hawke. Whether these fans have always been there and most commentators simply haven't recognised them, or whether they have suddenly been struck by some mysterious and blinding insight is not clear. Whatever it is, it must be giving Bob Hawke the willies. .

24 Jul 1991 - Hewson to push tax, forget popularity Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 24 July 1991, page 1 Hewson to push tax, forget popularity By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, promised yesterday to increase his push for a consumption tax, declaring he did not care if it made him unpopular. He said the debate on the consumption tax would test the maturity of the Australian electorate, and "to use one of Mr Keating's expressions, this is the debate you had to have". He reveajed that he had been advised in both public and private discussions to hide the policy until after the federal election "and then pull it on", but he completely rejected such an approach. He said that after his recent trip overseas, when he had been asked constantly why Australia squandered its opportunities, he was "embarrassed as an Australian". Dr Hewson said his task was to rebuild Australia and improve its standing in the world. "If I have to be unpopular to do that, if I have to lead the debate from Opposition with difficult policies like a broad-based goods-and-services tax — well, so to it," he said. But a poll to be published today suggests Dr Hewson's fortunes are actually rising. The Morgan Gallup Poll in The Bulletin shows he is the preferred Prime Minister of 43 per cent of respondents — up 4 percentage points and only 1 point behind the Prime Minister, Bob Hawkc, whose rating has dropped 2 points. >■ The Labor Party has the approval of only 34 per cent of respondents (down 3 points), lagging far behind the Coalition, which enjoys 48 per cent approval (up 2). However, the latest Saulwick poll, published in yesterday's Sydney Morning Herald, showed Dr Hewson had registered his first negative rating since becoming Leader of the Opposition. His standing fell from a positive rating of 18 in the previous poll, in June, to a rating of minus 4 in the poll published yesterday. The pollster, Irving Saulwick, was quoted as saying the only explanation appeared to be that Dr Hewson had been "caught by the consumption tax". Dr Hewson demonstrated clearly yesterday that he was determined to push the issue. He made two speeches in Sydney, gave a press conference and was interviewed by Paul Lyneham on ABC television's 7.30 Report. But he declined to say when details of the Opposition's tax-reform policy would be made known, saying it would be "when we're ready to release it". "It doesn't pay to go off half-cocked," he said. "It pays to get the numbers right up-front" Asked how he was going to quell anxiety about the policy among backbenchers in the meantime, he said, "Well, by imposing a degree of leadership and discipline." The Opposition's spokesman on industrial relations, John Howard, also did his bit yesterday to support Dr Hewson's stand on the consumption tax. He told the Real Estate Institute of Australia last night that, "I greet with incredulity the growing number of commentators who are in effect saying 'Australia needs a consumption tax and the reforms that go with it but it can't be sold'." Mr Howard said that to abandon the policy for this reason would be "unacceptable political duplicity". "There is no turning back for the Liberal and National parties on the taxation issue," he said. "The challenge is to persuade and advocate an essential reform to a taxation system which remains inequitable, needlessly complicated and profoundly biased against families."

27 Jul 1991 - OPLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 27 July 1991, page 11 Hewson hit after talk of new tax THE POLLS held different messages for the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, as he stumped through the country this week selling the consumption tax. For the first time since taking up the Opposition baton Dr Hewson registered a negative approval rating in The Sydney Morning Herald's Saulwick poll, while the Bulletin's Morgan Gallup poll showed support for the Coalition up two points to 48 per cent. Dr Hewson's rating had been consistently positive in the 11 Saulwick polls held since he became Liberal leader in April last year but in the latest he fell from a strongly positive rating of 18 in the previous poll in June to a rating of .minus 4 percentage points. The pollster Irving Saulwick said that the "inexorable inference" was that Dr Hewson had been caught by his commitment to the consumption tax. The Morgan Poll held much more joy for Dr Hewson. When electors were asked who would make the better Prime Minister, 44 per cent (down two) opted for Bob Hawke and 43 per cent (up four) named Dr Hewson. The poll showed showed support for the Hawke Government had dropped three percentage points to 34 in early July while support for the Opposition had risen two points to 48 per cent Support for the Democrats rose one point to 8 per cent while support for minor parties was unchanged on 10 per cent According to another Bulletin poll the number of Australians who want a republic has climbed by seven percentage points over the past three years, but the republicans still lag a long way behind the monarchists. The poll found 56 per cent of Australians opting for no change compared with 36 per cent who wanted a republic. The jump in the number of republicans could be explained by a British poll that showed that more than half of Queen Elizabeth's subjects believe her family fails to set a good example of family life. According to poll results published on July 24 in The Daily Telegraph 65 per cent of those questioned thought the Royal Family faced significant difficulties over its place in society. Fifty-one per cent disagreed with the statement that "the Royal Family provides a good example of family life". But the public still supports the monarchy, with 75 per cent saying Britain still needs its Royals. The Telegraph said the failed marriages of the Queen's sister, Princess Margaret, and daughter, Princess Anne, had probably tarnished the family's traditional image as a model of virtue. And in the United States an Associated Press poll released on July 25 showed 70 per cent of Americans surveyed believed the United States should have continued fighting the Gulf war to force Saddam Hussein from power.

07 Aug 1991 - Support down Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 7 August 1991, page 2 Support down SYDNEY: Federal opposition leader John Hewson's proposed consumption tax has hit his popularity in the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, carried out over the last two weekends of July and published in the latest edition of the Bulletin magazine, found that 41 per cent of people questioned would prefer Dr Hewson as the country's prime minister compared with 43 per cent at the beginning of the month. Support for the Liberal and National coalition declined by two points to 46 per cent while support for the Australian Labor Party increased by two to 36 per cent

10 Aug 1991 - Coalition slips with talk of tax Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 10 August 1991, page 9 Coalition slips with talk of tax SUPPORT for the Liberal-National Coalition dropped slightly in late July at a time when its controversial consumption-tax proposal was firmly in the media spotlight. The latest Morgan Gallup poll, published in The Bulletin, found that 46 per cent of the 3229 voters interviewed supported the Coalition -down two percentage points on early July. Support for the Labor Government rose by the same margin to 36 per cent. Conducted on the weekends of July 20 and 27, the survey showed that the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, is still the preferred leader over the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson. While 44 per cent nominated Mr Hawke, 41 per cent preferred Dr Hewson (down two points). Mr Hawke's approval rating dropped one point to 37 per cent, with 52 per cent disapproving of the way he is performing and 11 per cent undecided. Approval of Dr Hewson dropped from 50 per cent of the sample in early July to 46 per cent with 32 per cent disapproving (up four) and 22 per cent undecided. In regard to other parties, support for the Australian Democrats fell one point to 7 per cent and "other parties and candidates" were up one point to 11 per cent. In Victoria, approval of the Premier, Joan Kirner, hit record levels in July at the conclusion of her first year in office. Support for the Victorian ALP also rose slightly but it was still 21.5 percentage points behind the Liberal-National Opposition. Public approval of Mrs Kirner has been rising steadily over the past few months and reached 44 per cent in the July Morgan Gallup poll. Her disapproval rating dropped from 52 per cent in June to 49 per cent. It may not sound too good but Opposition Leader Jeff Kennett's approval rating is a paltry 27 percent and his disapproval rating 63 per cent. Mrs Kirner also holds a 46-42 per cent lead over Mr Kennett as the preferred Premier.

17 Aug 1991 - Perceived living cost has droped Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 17 August 1991, page 9 Perceived living cost has droped WHILE Australians are still fairly pessimistic about the state of the economy, most perceive that the cost of living has dropped markedly in the last six months. A Morgan Gallup poll, published in The Bulletin, recorded a drop of $18 a week in the perceived cost of living for a family of four among 2508 respondents Australiawide. This was attributed largely to reduced fuel prices, lower inflation and falling interest rates. The survey indi cated that, on an annual basis, the perceived cost of living has risen by 1 per cent. In capital cities, the perceived cost a family would need to meet to "keep in health and live decently" was $441 compared to $409 in other areas. The $18 drop was the biggest fall recorded since the survey was initiated in 1973. A second Morgan poll shows the Liberal-National parties would make major gains on the Government in a Senate or half-Senate election and is outpolling the ALP in every state. The July poll showed Labor would have lost five Senate seats at a full or half Senate election held in July. The present standings are Labor 13 seats, Coalition 17 scats and Australian Democrats and others six. Labor would have lost seats to the Coalition in NSW, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia and possibly another to other parties in Western Australia. In state politics, voters in Western Australia and South Australia continue to back Premiers Carmen Lawrence and John Bannon but are less supportive of the Labor Party in general. While the ALP in WA is 20 percentage points behind the Liberal-National Opposition, Ms Lawrence has an approval rating 28 points higher than her Opposition counterpart, Barry MacKinnon. The majority of voters in South Australia approve of Mr Bannon and prefer him as Premier despite that fact that support for the ALP Government is well behind that for the Coalition.

22 Aug 1991 - Hawke not fazed by poor showing in latest polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 22 August 1991, page 10 Hawke not fazed by poor showing in latest polls A poor showing in the latest Morgan Gallup poll was to be expected given unemployment figures, the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, said yesterday. "I expected the poll today to be down," he told ABC radio's AM pro gram. "You couldn't have a situation where you had that massive fall in employment in July and not have some reflection in the polls.'1 According to the figures disclosed in this week's Bulletin magazine, 44 per cent of voters surveyed said the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, was the preferred prime minister - three per cent ahead of Mr Hawke. It is the first time he has been more popular this year. Support for the ALP declined from 36 per cent to 33.5, while the Opposition increased its popularity from 46 to 50 per cent. Also, the ALP has fallen 16.5 per cent behind the Liberal and National Party Opposition. A confident Mr Hawke said the figure was about 6 per cent behind the figure with which Labor won the last election. "Between now and the next election Dr Hewson ... is going to have to sell to the Australian people a policy which says 'I, Dr Hewson and the Liberal National Party coalition, believe that there should be a much more massive cut in Commonwealth Government expenditures'," Mr Hawke said. "I'm looking forward between now and the next election to taking Dr Hewson on."

24 Aug 1991 - Hewson preferred as leader again Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 August 1991, page 9 Hewson preferred as leader again n POLL WATCH F LEADING polls published this week showed the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, had recovered enough ground to once again head the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, as the country's preferred leader. In a Saulwick poll of 1000 voters, published in The Age, 26 per cent gave Dr Hewson a positive rating and 2/ per cent a negative rating. In comparison, Mr Hawke was given a positive rating by 26 per cent and a negative rating by 29 per cent. The results are a welcome sign for the Liberals after the party and Dr Hewson lost a significant amount of popular support when the Labor Party heavily targeted the proposed consumption tax in public debate during July. The latest Morgan Gallup poll showed Dr Hewson had overtaken Mr Hawke in its estimate of the preferred prime minister and that the ALP has fallen 16.5 percentage points behind its Liberal-National Opposi tion. Of the 2494 voters interviewed over the weekends of August 3 and 11,44 per cent said they would prefer Dr Hewson as prime minister and 41 per cent Mr Hawke - the first time Dr Hewson has been ahead in this measure during 1991. ALP support fell 2.5 points from late July to 33.5 per cent while the Opposition went from 46 to 50 points. The Australia Democrats dropped slightly to 6.5 per cent and "other" parties or candidates fell one point to 10 per cent. By contrast, Mr Hawke's personal approval rating rose one point to 38 per cent. Dr Hewson's rose by the same margin to 47 per cent. In a second Morgan poll to determine who people think their friends really are, 85 per cent of Australians said the United States would help Australia if it was threatened by a foreign power. Nearly half (47 per cent) of the 1212 Australians interviewed said Britain would come to our aid and a quarter nominated New Zealand. The vast majority of 1074 New Zealanders interviewed (75 per cent) said Australia would assist if their country was under threat. Fifty-six per cent of Kiwis nominated the US and 45 per cent Britain.

31 Aug 1991 - Victorians still prefer Kirner Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 31 August 1991, page 9 Victorians still prefer Kirner THE VICTORIAN Premier, Joan Kirner, is the preferred Labor leader in that state according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin. Mrs Kirner (with 40 per cent) came in well ahead of other Victorian Labor figures, Steve Crabb (12 per cent) and Jim Kennan (10 per cent). The statewide survey. held in August, also found that Victorians still prefered Jeff Kennett as leader of the Opposition. There was still strong support for former Liberal leader Alan Brown (with 20 per cent) but among Liberal-National Party voters support for Mr Kennett was a fairly solid 40 per cent while Mr Brown only polled 18 per cent. The interviewees were also asked who they would like to see succeed Mrs Kirner. Twenty per cent of all voters opted for Mr Kennan followed by Mr Crabb on 19 per cent. Mr Brown won 30 per cent support for Coalition leader, should Mr Kennett stand down. In London, a poll in The Daily Mail (August 29) showed that the popularity of the British Prime Minister, John Major, had been boosted by his handling of the crisis in the Soviet Union. Mr Major must call a general election by mid-1992. The newspaper published an opinion poll showing the opposition Labour Party's lead over Major's Conservatives down to three per cent from seven per cent in a similar survey a month ago. The poll put support for the Conservatives up three per cent to 40 with Labour down one per cent to 43. Support for the Liberal Democrats, the minor third force in British politics, fell to 12 per cent from 16. Mr Major has played a highly public role in the West's response to last week's failed attempt to topple the Soviet President, Mikhail Gorbachev, and the poli tical turmoil that has followed. He is now in the United States for talks with the President, George Bush, and is to meet Mr Gorbachev in Moscow tomorrow. The results of the poll, conducted on August 23 and 24 after the Soviet coup failed, could generate party pressure on Mr Major to call an election later this year rather than waiting until 1992, The Daily Mail said. A series of opinion polls before the Soviet crisis showed the Conservatives trailing Labour badly largely because of voter disaffection over Britain's economic recession.

31 Aug 1991 - 'If the Labor Party ever calls on me, I'd be delighted' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 31 August 1991, page 1 'If the Labor Party ever calls on me, I'd be delighted' have employment, and they regard their economic well-being as not assured, I think a lot of what is now dressed up as concern for the environment would dimin-ish very sharply. But if you talk about economic growth, you need a certain number of engine rooms. The Murray-Darling, for example, is a major engine room which is suffering pretty badly. Then there's land degradation across the country. Well, that's one of the first things I did as Treasurer — to remove the tax deduc-tion for land clearing. Not because I want-ed to save some money for Treasury, but because I thought it was time we stopped that rot. Keating is unquestionably serious about foreign affairs. Shortly before our interview, a Hawke minister had astonished me by stating that "the Americans, through the CIA, can veto any prospective Australian Prime Minister". The American alliance therefore seemed worth pursuing with this prospective Prime Minister. A perception has arisen in the Hawke years that we have been to obsequious to-ward the US. We will end up being more important to the United States when we become more important in South-East Asia. In the meantime, though, do you think our attitude could change a little at govern- ment level? It's about the friction co-efficient. It's about how easily you deal with them. It's not about the nature of [the relation-ship] . . . Now in some things I think that we may be too — what shall I say? — too willing to see the United States' view, as distinct from seeing it anyway. [We could] feel obliged to respond to it less expedi-tiously; perhaps a little more concerned to make sure our own interests are set right. The Gulf war: 150,000 people dead, 336 oil wells still burning, Saddam Hussein still in power. Yet there hasn't been any questioning from this Government as to whether it was all worth it. Saddam Hussein's regime had to be dealt with — so that it wasn't a juggernaut in the Middle East, permanently unsettling to the Middle East. Now you've got [US Secretary of State] Jim Baker trying to find some kind of settlement, with the Is-raelis, so some good may well come of it all . . . The Middle East paid a massive price for it. The people of Iraq particularly. They would have paid a bigger price had Saddam Hussein's criminal tendencies been allowed free rein. I tried to engage the Prime Minister in 1989 on the CIA's involvement in the Whitlam dismissal. CIA officers to the rank of regional director, station chief, and one former deputy director, have said that the CIA made a series of moves to get rid of Whitlam. It's regarded by many as a hoary old bit of paranoia from the Left: by others as having a fair amount of evidence. I think I share the view that it's a bit of hoary old stuff from the Left. I don't doubt that the CIA was less than enamoured of the Whitlam Government, but I don't think anything happened as a result of their initiatives, or them conspiring in some sort of arrangement with the conser-vative parties of this country. But I didn't come down in the last shower: I don't think there are any angels in the CIA. A final question on that matter. The CIA kept a close eye on Hawke during his rise, through the '60s. and '70s. They be-friended him. That is all on the record, and I'm not suggesting anything improper. Continued on Page C2 MAGAZINE H These challenging times Continued from Page C1 The CIA befriended him, or American officers here? American CIA officers in Melbourne, in the guise of labour attaches. Apparently all labour attaches are CIA. I'm not saying he was cultivated or anything of that nature. But obviously it's in the interests of their country to keep an eye on our rising poli-tical stars. You yourself have been a rising political star in recent times. Have you had any such interest shown? Oh, occasionally they invite me to the embassy to talk about things, but very rarely — once every two or three years, I go over there and have a lunch with them, or a brunch or something. The last time, when [then ambassador] Bill Lane was there, we took a picture out the front. And as I bade them farewell I said, "Give my regards to Langley, West "Virginia [CIA headquarters are in Lang-ley]." Keating's backers say he has a more bal-anced altitude to the US alliance than Hawke. One minister points out that in Cabinet Keating expressed reservations about the size and positioning of the pro- posed Gulf task force. (John Button, whose doubts were deeper, received a withering volley of obscenities from Gareth Evans.) But Keating is unlikely to cause any sleepless nights at the White House: "I like the United Slates. It is the greatest nation on the face of the earth, and that is undeniable. By nearly all the measures of greatness: economic strength, pluralism, democracy." It's looking a bit down at heel in New York and San Francisco, where one is step-ping over pavement-dwellers, including mothers with children . . . Oh yes. That is unconscionable. But it has a certain vitality about it. It does. It's a very interesting place. You told Laurie Oakes that we need to pay more attention to New Zealand, Indo-nesia and particularly Japan. Can you ex-pand on that? I think New Zealand has often been forgotten in Australian foreign policy. As you know, there is actually a place for them in our Constitution, should they ever wish to take it up. That's how important they were regarded at the turn of this century. The relationship has not been regarded as of the same importance of late. If we're going to have a free trade in goods, what I've been arguing is that we should have a free trade in services — and that we actu- ally try and integrate these two economies. It's not in Australia's interests for New Zealand to grow weak. It's got a limited resource base, it's a country very much like ours in its make-up, and Wellington and Auckland are nearer to Sydney than Syd-ney is to Perth. So we should be doing all that's sensible and reasonable to integrate our societies. As for Indonesia, it's growing to be a very strong country. There's already a very strong pocket of wealth there. It's growing enormously, it needs help, it doesn't want to be dominated by Japan, and it would like more involvement from Australia: I think that should be one of the central interests of our foreign policy. I think our relationship with Indonesia || Picture: KATE CALLAS Mr Keating at home with his wife Anita and three of his four children, Caroline, 12, left, Katherine, 9, and Alexandra, 6. || has improved. The relationship Gareth Ev-ans has with the Government of Indonesia, for example, is a very good one. All I would argue is that we have to build on that relationship in a commercial way. I think in the end it is the commercial rela-tionship which underpins a relationship, and not simply good relations at the gov- ernment level. And Japan — Japan is the savings hub of the Pacific. It's our largest trading part-ner. It's an egalitarian society, as ours is. And though our cultures are different we have much in common. We could lift our interest in Japan, I think. Australian business is yet to make a substantial indentation on Japanese com-merce, in Japan. I know that's difficult, and I know that the Japanese are often less than welcoming. But I think that's what we have to do . . . And doing more with them in the Asian Pacific. We're already principals in the Asian Development Bank — and we can do more together in expanding that bank, and having it play a development role in places like the Philippines, the ASEAN area, and even China. For instance the Asian Development Bank funded the new sewerage system for Shanghai, which was designed by an Aus-tralian civil-engineering group. These are the things which will give Australia a place in Asia. When Whitlam came in there was The Program. When Hawke came in there seemed to be less clarity about reforms: the ideas seemed to come more from other ministers, perhaps primarily yourself. As Graham Freudenberg said very elo-quently, with all the appropriate intona-tions in the word [a la Whitlam): "The Program was a program for buying votes". It was about buying votes in western Sydney. It was about buying votes here, and buying votes there. I mean, The Pro-gram never had some sort of well-connect-ed, well-embroidered pattern of change. It was a program for an improvement in so cial equity in certain areas of life, which coincided with the need to win votes. And while much of it was good — par-ticularly the greater sense of national spirit — it never had the comprehension that these years have had. This Government's policies have had a very sophisticated set of linkages — a very large matrix — essentially underpinned by the belief that the closed way had failed us. That keeping Australia shut — locked up by tariffs, lock up by a managed exchange rate, locked up by an uncompetitive finan-cial system — that that had failed us after 40 years. And that the way forward was to go out. That central idea has underpinned the policies of the Government. No such large central idea ever underpinned the Whitlam Government's policies. The Whitlam Government was a bit more pragmatic than people now think it was? It was. It was. Freudenberg — in part the author of the policies — has said so. I need to rely upon no greater authority. Keating claims the economy, not the leadership, was the frustration in his final period as Treasurer. The boom was unforeseen — in that the terms of trade basically induced it. that, compounded by a very high level of bank lending and a growing level of profitability in the economy, produced a pretty explo- sive cocktail. That derailed — temporarily at least — the forecast I'd committed myself to on inflation and the current account. In other words we would have had infla-tion as low as it is now in 1988-89 — and the current account very near the debt sta-bilisation point. Now that got away from me. But at the same time the country was more wealthy. Asked what ideas should be exercising the Government's collective mind for the rest of this term, and a fifth one, he again showed his economist's colours: I took the view back in the early '80s that . . . the post-war trade in goods and services had passed Australia by. That the trade which had made Germany and Japan wealthy had not made us wealthy. That the value of the things we sold, as distinct from the things we bought, had gone down. In other words the terms of trade had shifted against us. No longer would a bag of wheat buy a truck-full of manufactured products: it was only buying quarter of a truck-full. The world didn't want to pay the same prices for the things we were producing, by the 1980s. And those same things wouldn't buy the more expensive and sophisticated manufacturers of the Northern Hemi-sphere. So we were seeking to maintain a first world living standard, though our income had become Third World. As for the prime-ministership of what he hopefully regards as the second-greatest na- tion on earth: Well, it's something that might come my way. But the scales have fallen from my eyes about it a long time ago. I've probably been nearer to it than anyone who hasn't had it - over quite a long time. The notion that [it's) where the direction and control of the place is at one's finger-tips — I mean, I don't believe that. If the job doesn't come his way, Keating will spend post-parliamentary life "using my brains: doing something commercial". I pointed out that when I'd first met him in 1986 he had (according to my notes) "not smiled once" in our hour together. He laughed. "That was banana republic year, I had a lot on. you know?" He seemed then to be in a kind of perma-nent battle mode. Was I right in saying that he'd calmed down quite a lot in the last five years? Oh I think the weight goes off you. You get a better understanding of where you are and what is required of you . . . But the pressure people work under in high public-sector jobs is enormous. It's so unappre-ciated outside. It does take the smile off your face. To make matters worse for the Placido Domingo of Australian politics, the con-stant speech-making has destroyed his sing-ing voice. When I was young I used to always be singing at parties. Whenever I was in half the mood I used to get up and knock a few songs out. I couldn't give you a song now if you put a million dollars on the table. I just can't reach the notes. After the interview, a couple of Keating men were winding up the week in a ministe-rial office when a new Saulwick "preferred leader" poll slid off the fax machine. Keating's percentage score was 30; Hawke's 51. The previous Saulwick poll — though it used different methodology — had them 27 points farther apart than that. For a half-hour, phone calls ricocheted around the building ("Mate, listen to these numbers.") A little later there was the quiet clinking of glasses. Whether numbers will continue to pro-vide such comfort to the Keating fraternity will be known before very long. In the meantime, as Bob Hawke will undoubtedly remind them, there is still a big difference between 51 and 30. Being less alive to metaphors than his erstwhile deputy, he may even point out that Methuselah was 969, not 61. © Copyright John Macgregor, 1991

04 Sep 1991 - PM's poll boost Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 4 September 1991, page 1 PM's poll boost The Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has defied speculation over his popularity, bouncing 4 percentage points in the latest Morgan Gallup Poll to regain his position as preferred Prime Minister. Mr Hawke scores 45 per cent compared with 41 per cent for the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, in the poll published in today's Bulletin. The Government improved also, to 37 per cent — up 3.5 — but still 10 points behind the Coalition. The poll was taken during the week of August 17-24. In the previous poll, from August 3-10, Mr Hawke lost the lead as preferred Prime Minister to Dr Hewson for the first time since late 1990. — TONY WRIGHT

07 Sep 1991 - Boost for Hawke and the party Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 7 September 1991, page 9 Boost for Hawke and the party WITH talk of a leadership challenge gaining momentum this week, the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, might have drawn a little comfort from poll results showing a boost in his popularity. While Mr Hawkc's personal approval rating increased, so too did broad support for the Labor Party, with the gap between it and the Liberal-National Coali tion closing trom 16.5 points in early August to 10 points in the second half of the month. The Morgan Gallup poll of 2835 voters, published in The Bulletin, found La bor support running at 37 per cent, 2.4 percentage points below its 1990 election performance. Coalition support fell three points on early August to 47 per cent and the Democrats stayed at 6 per cent. Mr Hawke's personal approval rating rose four points to 45 per cent, while the Leader of the Opposition, Dr John Hewson, saw his fall three points to 41 per cent. The poll was taken on the weekends of August 17 and 24, just before and after the Federal Budget, which included plans for an upfront fee for Medicare patients and recognition that unemployment was likely to remain high for at least 12 months. The slight increase in Government support contrasts with a second Morgan Gallup poll which showed 28 per cent of Australians felt there was a chance of becoming unemployed and 73 per cent said the Federal Government was not doing enough to address the issue. In the poll of 1270 people over the age of 14 conducted before the Federal Budget, slightly more than half (53 per cent) believed they would find it very difficult to get a new position if they lost their job. The number of people who thought unemployment would increase in the next year fell 16 points since November 1990 to 65 per cent. An unchanged 47 per cent felt the Government was the main cause of the high unemployment while 49 per cent (up two points) blamed the world economy.

14 Sep 1991 - POLL WATCH Budget gets low marks Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 14 September 1991, page 9 Budget gets low marks MOST Australians have given the Hawke Government's 1991-92 Budget a lukewarm reception and more than half expect it to boost unemployment, according to a Morgan Gallup poll. The late-August poll of 1248 people, published in The Bulletin, found that only 4 per cent of those interviewed described new Treasurer John Kcrin's first Budget as a good one and 26 per cent per cent said it was a "bad" job. Both the number of people who were positive and negative about the Budget were down slightly on the 1990-91 Budget. The Bulletin noted it was the lowest number of "good" responses since Budget reaction surveys began in 1975. On the inflation front, 20 per cent felt the Budget would contribute to higher inflation, 10 per cent to reduced inflation while the majority (52 per cent) felt it would have little effect. In state politics, Morgan polls found that the Victorian Premier, Joan Kirner, continued to rise in popularity despite the difficulties of her Labor Government and the stalled Victorian economy. An August survey of 2328 Victorian voters found Mrs Kirner's approval rating up three points to a high of 47 per cent. Meanwhile, support for the Labor Government as a whole was steady on 31 per cent. Backing for the Liberal-National Coalition increased marginally to 52 per cent while Democrat backing fell to 7 per cent. Mrs Kirner's disapproval rating had dropped two points since July to 47 per ccnt leaving her well ahead of the Opposition Leader, Jeff Kennett, who remained just over the 60 per cent mark. He was also well behind as the preferred Premier, 49 per cent nominating Mrs Kirner compared with 39 per ccnt for Mr Kennett — a gap that had widened from four points in July. The Morgan Gallup poll found little change in electoral fortunes in NSW concluding that an election would again be decided on minor party preferences. Among 2096 voters, support for the Liberal-National Government was up slightly to 44 per cent while Labor support also rose a point to 41 per cent. The Premier, Nick Greiner, was preferred by 46 per cent of those polled compared with 42 per cent for the Opposition Leader, Bob Carr — the same result as in. the July survey. Mr Greiner's general approval rating fell one point to 42 per cent while his disapproval rating rose by the samr. margin to 51 percent. Approval of Mr Carr remained at 53 per cent and his disapproval rating was also unchanged at 33 per cent.

18 Sep 1991 - Poll shows rise in Govt support Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 18 September 1991, page 3 Poll shows rise in Govt support SYDNEY: A one-percentage-point cut in interest rates and continued Opposition discussion about a general consumption tax appear to have given the Federal Government its highest level of popular support in a year, the Bulletin magazine reported. The Morgan Gallup poll in today's edition said that while the survey showed the Liberal-National Party Coalition would win a general election, it would also reinforce the view of the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, that his Government could still triumph in 1993. Labor's popular support was up l.S percentage points to 38.5 per cent of those questioned; the Coalition slipped back one percentage point to 46 per cent The personal ratings of Mr Hawke and the Opposition Leader, John Hewson, each lost one percentage point — down to 38 per cent for Mr Hawke and to 47 per cent for Dr Hewson, the survey found. The poll was conducted in the first two weekends of the month. However, it said there was no change on the question of who was seen as making the better prime minister, with 45 percent of voters attracted to Mr Hawke and 41 per cent opting for Dr Hewson.

21 Sep 1991 - Voters lack faith in banks' safety Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 21 September 1991, page 9 Voters lack faith in banks' safetv m POLL J AUSTRALIANS have lost faith in their financial institutions and are evidently not reassured by the level of bank regulation, according to a Saulwick Poll published this week. The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald reported that the poll showed one in every five people of voting age had little or no confidence in banks, while one in three had little or no confidence in building societies. In past years the security of building societies had been regarded as close to that of banks. ■Of those questioned, a third said they had little or no confidence in credit unions, while 41 per cent expressed the same low opinion of cash management and property trusts. Great confidence — 25 per cent — was most often expressed in banks, followed by 16 per cent for credit unions, 14 per cent for building societies, 4 per cent for property trusts and 3 per cent for cash management trusts. The level of public confidence varied from state to state, a reflection of events such as last year's run on depositors' funds in Victorian banks after the collapse of the Pyramid Building Society. In NSW, 75 per cent of those polled had great or some confidence in banks compared with 51 per cent in Victoria. Twentythree per cent of NSW respondents had little or no confidence in credit unions compared with 44 per cent of Victorians. In another Saulwick Poll this week, voters continued to express a clear preference for Bob Hawke over Paul Keating as ALP leader. Fiftysix per cent supported Mr Hawke over 31 per cent for Mr Keating — a four-point improvement for the Prime Minister compared with last month, when the result was 52 per cent for Mr Hawke and 30 per cent for the former Treasurer. Labor voters and women increased their support for the PM, with Labor voters' preference jumping 10 points to 69 per cent and women's support up from 52 to 59 per cent.

26 Sep 1991 - Wide support for mercy killing Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 September 1991, page 4 Wide support for mercy killing SYDNEY: Australians and New Zealanders support mercy killing, according to a new poll, but young people between 14 and 24 years arc the least sure about the idea. Doctors should be allowed to let patients die, according to 69 per cent of Australians and 66 per cent of New Zealanders, the Morgan Gallup Poll released in The Bulletin magazine says. Doctors should be allowed to ad minister "lethal doses" if requested, according to 73 per cent of Australians and 72 per cent of New Zealan ders. The support ranged across all age groups, but only 55 per cent of young people backed euthanasia, an eightpoint decrease from last year. Support also ranged across the voters of all the major political parties.

28 Sep 1991 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 28 September 1991, page 9 Support for euthanasia by majority A MORGAN Gallup Poll has found that a large majority of Australians support euthanasia where the patient has no chance of recovery and is in great pain. The poll, published in The Bulletin, found an even greater support for mercy killing where the patient asked their doctor to help them die. 69 per cent of Australians and 66 per cent of New Zealanders thought doctors should be allowed to let patients die, while 73 per cent of Australians and 72 per cent of New Zealanders believed a "lethal dose" of drugs should be administered if requested. The "clear majority" in favour of euthanasia was found among both men and women and in all age groups and political affiliations. The poll was conducted in July in both countries and involved over 1200 respondents in cach instance. Those surveyed were asked, "If there is absolutely no chance of a patient recovering, should the doctor let the patient die — or should the doctor try to keep the patient alive as long as possible?" The percentage of Australians who said the patient should be allowed to die, 69 per cent, was down two points since July 1990. In both countries, 21 per cent said the patient should be kept alive, a two-point increase in Australia. Ten per cent of Australians and 13 per cent of New Zealanders were undecided. Most likely to support euthanasia were Democrat supporters, of whom 75 percent supported letting the patient die, although this was down two points on last year. 71 per cent (down two) of Coalition supporters backcd euthanasia compared with 66 per ccnt (down one point) of Labor supporters. More Australian women (71 per cent, no change) were in support of euthanasia than men, down four pioints to 67 percent. Among young people aged 16-24 in both countries there was an eight-point drop in support for letting patients die, making. them the least supportive of euthanasia on 55 per cent. Another Morgan Gallup Poll carried out for The Bulletin in July-August shows Queensland's Goss Labor Government lost two points in support, dropping to 44 per cent. The Liberals' backing rose one point to 27 percent, while minor and independent parties also picked up a point (12 per cent). The National Party remained on 17 per cent. The poll found that if an election had been held in July-August, the ALP's majority would have been significantly re duced.

07 Nov 1991 - Lib calls for state think-tank Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 7 November 1991, page 13 Lib calls for state think-tank BRISBANE: A Sunshine Coastbased Liberal MP, Joan Sheldon, rocked party officials and fellow parliamentarians yesterday by saying the party was not performing well and action was needed. She said it was clear the Liberals were slipping behind, ?nd called on the "political brains" in the party to get it going in the lead-up to next year's state election. "Let's stop mucking around and get a think-tank going before it's too late," she said in a statement. She believed most Liberals would be disappointed the conservative parties were not performing better. Mrs Sheldon, the Member for Landsborough, was commenting after the latest Morgan Gallup Poll figures showed the state Liberals had slipped by 3 per cent, down to 24 per cent, since July-August. Labor improved by two points to 46 per cent and the National Party by one point to 18 per cent. On the approval ratings, Mr Goss came as out as preferred Premier with 73 per cent, against (National Party) Opposition Leader Russell Cooper's 15 percent Mrs Sheldon's statement caused a flurry of phone calls around the party and her concerns are to be dis cussed at the regular party meeting next week. Senior party sources and some MPs stressed there was no threat to the leadership of Denver Branland, although some expressed concern at the figures. Mr Beanland declined to comment, but a spokesman said he would be talking to Mrs Sheldon about her concerns. In her statement, Mrs Sheldon said the state party, and the conser vatives in general, should be concerned the ALP was polling well despite high unemployment, a public service in uproar and the rural community being treated like lepers.

08 Nov 1991 - Beanland rejects criticism of party Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 8 November 1991, page 13 Beanland rejects criticism of party BRISBANE: Queensland's Liberal leader, Denver Beanland, rejected yesterday criticism by one of his parliamentary members that the prty is slipping and more needs to be done. The claim, made on Wednesday by the Member for Landsborough, Joan Sheldon, rocked the party. Mr Beanland broke his silence yester dayafternoon to say he was "surprised and disappointed" at Mrs Sheldon's comments. He said the party was doing exceptionally well on the Sunshine Coast where Mrs Sheldon won her seat with a 13 per cent swing, and since then new branches had been established and hundreds of new members attracted. He said the party had outstanding candidates coming forward. The endorsement of candidates and release of more policies would lift the party's profile in the countdown to next year's election. He warned the party must work together. "Everybody from the parliamentary leader, the parliamentary wing and the organisation at the grassroots level have to work hard for success." Lack of unity and not conccntrating on the real issues would sec the Labor Government re-elected. Mrs Sheldon has not commented further on her statement, made after the latest Morgan Gallup Poll showed the state Liberals had slipped by 3 percent to 24 per cent since July-August. She had said the party was not performing well and action was needed. Mrs Sheldon said it was clear the Liberals were slipping behind, and called on the "political brains" in the party to get it going forward in the lead-up to the next election. The ALFs state secretary, Wayne Swan, said yesterday the Liberals were losing ground because they were seen to be climbing into bed with the National Party. People wanted to see the Liberals stand up to the Nationals, he said.

09 Nov 1991 - Qld Liberal leadership spill brews Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 November 1991, page 4 Qld Liberal leadership spill brews BRISBANE: A furore in the Queensland parliamentary Liberal Party could result in Sunshine Coast MP Joan Sheldon challenging her leader, Denver Beanland, on Monday. Mrs Sheldon said last night that a special meeting of Liberal parliamentarians has been called for Monday. Senior Liberal sources confirmed that Mrs Sheldon, the Member for Landsborough, has been lobbying fellow members and might challenge Mr Beanland. Mrs Sheldon would not comment, but said Mr Beanland had called a party meeting for Monday where "these things would be discussed. "We will see what happens then," she said. "I don't believe we should be brawling in public like the federal Labor Party is doing, but obviously there is something we need to discuss. The possible challenge follows the Liberals'1 poor showing in the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. Mrs Sheldon was said to be motivated also by figures showing Liberal support declining on the Sunshine Coast. This week, Mrs Sheldon issued a statement saying the party was slipping, action was needed and the party's "political brains" should form a think-tank. With only nine Liberals in Parliament, the vote was expected to be very close, sources said. However, others pointed to Mrs Sheldon's inexperience; she won her seat in a by-election in July last year. Mr Beanland has been in state parliament since the 1986 election, taking over as leader after Angus Innes retired from politics early last year. Last night there were doubts the National Party could work in a closer conservative relationship with Mrs Sheldon. The Opposition Leader, National Party leader Russell Cooper, believes his party has been working well with Mr Beanland, a National Party source said.

12 Nov 1991 - Woman new Leader of Old Liberals Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 12 November 1991, page 3 Woman new Leader of Old Liberals BRISBANE: Political novicc Joan Sheldon caused a major upset yesterday by defeating Denver Beanland for the leadership of the minority Queensland Liberal Party, amid claims of meddling from the party machine. After only 16 months in state Parliament, the Sunshine Coast MLA who first came to notice last month with a com plaint about blonde jokes, became the first woman to lead a padiamentary political party in the state. Mrs Sheldon, 48, told a news conference she had made up her mind to contest the leadership of the nine-person parliamentary party only at the end of last week, and rejected any suggestion that Liberal headquarters was behind the revolt "There was no interference in this decision by headquarters at all," she said. She said her decision was made after she had issued a statement last Wednesday critical of the party's leadership and direction, in the wake of a Morgan Gallup Poll showing a 3 per cent drop, to 24 per cent, in Liberal support in two months. The resulting lobbying split the party and brought the charge from Mr Beanland, 46, leader since May last year, that Liberal headquarters — taken by many to mean party president Paul Evermghanj — had interfered. Mr Beanland main tained his allegations of interference yesterday, despite statements to the contrary from Mrs Shel don. Before the vote, Mr Beanland also changed his mind about boycotting a party meeting Mr Everingham called at Liberal headquarters. Mr Beanland said he wanted to combat some "inaccurate and mischievous material" being circulated yesterday morning. The bitterness from the episode spilled over into Mr Beanland's news conference. He said the events of the past few days had saddened him. He issued a three-paragraph statement later, calling on all Liberals to focus on defeating Labor at the next state election and saying he looked forward to working with Mrs Sheldon. Mrs Sheldon is the second most inexperienced politician in Queensland Parliament She entered the House in a by-election for the Sunshine Coast seat of Landsborough in July last year after the former Premier, Mike Ahern, retired. Only Mike Horan (Nat, Toowoomba South), who was elected in a by-election earlier this year, has less experience. Mrs Sheldon, a physiotherapist, married, with three children, said she would bring a fresh new approach and direction to the party. The ALP state secretary, Wayne Swan, said, "Joan Sheldon didn't challenge Denver Beanland — Paul Everingham did."

13 Nov 1991 - Hewson and Hawke suffer rating drops Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 13 November 1991, page 2 Hewson and Hawke suffer rating drops SYDNEY: The personal approval rating of both the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, and Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, has fallen to the lowest levels this year, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll, published in today's Bulletin magazine, was conducted in late October-early November, a period of mounting intensity in the HawkeKeating leadership battle. It shows that if a federal election was held in late October-early November, the Opposition would nave won easily. The survey found a one percentage point increase in support for the Liberal and National parties, while the ALP trailed by nine points. The Bulletin says approval for Mr Hawke dropped three points to 35 per cent, his lowest rating since early January and only two points, above his lowest rating ever of 33 per cent. Mr Hawke's disapproval rose two points to 55 per cent. Meanwhile, Mr Hewson's approval fell three points to 41 per cent. Despite maintaining his popularity rating six points ahead of Mr Hawke, it is Mr Hewson's second lowest rating, just above the 34 per cent in his first poll just after the 1990 election.

21 Nov 1991 - Unemployment major issue Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 21 November 1991, page 3 Unemployment major issue SYDNEY: Australians believe unemployment is the major issue to be tackled by the Federal Government, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll of2356 voters showed that 63 per cent rated unemployment as the issue the Hawke Government "should be doing something about". This is up nine percentage points since June, up 26 points since February and compares with a rating of 24 per cent for September, 1990, and only 15 percent in February, 1990. The poll, published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday, said unemployment overshadows all other issues. Other issues of main concern were promoting business and industry growth (mentioned by 22 per cent, down two), stabilising the economy <20 per cent, down one), conservation and the environment (14 per cent, down one).

28 Nov 1991 - Hawke dips to lowest rating: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 28 November 1991, page 2 Hawke dips to lowest rating: poll MELBOURNE: The Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has recorded his lowest ever, rating as preferred Labor Prime Minister, according to a new Morgan Gallup Poll. Although still favoured as Labor leader, support for Mr Hawke has dropped six points since June to:31 per cent — way below the 72 per cent preference he recorded in April, 1984. Meanwhile, support for former Treasurer Paul Keating as Labor leader has climbed six points to 20 per cent. The poll of 1126 voters, published in the latest Bulletin magazine, showed no other current Labor MPs as viable alternatives to Mr Hawke. Preference for the Treasurer, John Kcrin, fell one point since June to 8 per cent, support for Kim Beazley fell one point to 7 per cent, and preference for John Button was up one point to 7 per cent. The Deputy Prime Minister, Brian Howe, was preferred as Labor leader by only 2 per cent of the electorate. A poll asking electors to choose between Mr Beazley and Mr Keating as preferred Prime Minister after Mr Hawke's departure has revealed a shift to the former Treasurer. In June 45 per cent preferred Mr Beazley to 39 per cent for Mr Keating, but now 43 per cent favour Mr Keating and only 38 per cent Mr Beazley. Similarly, support has shifted towards Mr Keating when compared to Mr Kcrin.

04 Dec 1991 - No reshuffle yet as PM dives in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 4 December 1991, page 1 No reshuffle yet as PM dives in poll By TONY WRIGHT, Political CorraBDondant The Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, facing rising concern among backbenchers and some Ministers about the Government's stumbling attempts to respond to the Coalition's new tax ana spending policy, declared yesterday that he was not considering a Cabinet reshuffle "at this stage". Earlier, he attended a top-level meeting designed to bring together the Government and the wider Labor machine to develop a strategy to stop the Government's slide into disarray. A Morgan Gallup poll in today's Bulletin shows that on the weekend after the Coalition's policy launch, Mr Hawke's approval rating dropped 1 percentage point to 35 per cent while the approval rating of the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, leapt an astonishing 13 points to S3 per cent. Dr Hewson gained 7 points as preferred Prime Minister to outstrip Mr Hawke, 45-43. The Coalition gained 2.5 points to increase its already impressive lead as the preferred party, 47-37, despite Labor gaining a point Jitters among Labor backbenchers about the Government's recent poor performance have raised anxiety among the Prime Minister's supporters and strategists because of the clear and serious risk of renewed leadership instability. Some backbenchers and Ministers are displaying an increasing readiness to talk about how much the Government is missing the former Treasurer, Paul Keating: there is a growing feeling that the leadership issue must be resolved. One senior strategist says the deadline is early next year — "One of them has to go — we can't face another year like this one." There was some speculation around Parliament House yesterday that the Caucus could be asked to settle the leadership on December 16. Asked whether there was going to be a Cabinet reshuffle after Christmas, and whether the Treasurer, John Kerin, and the Deputy Prime Minister, Brian Howe, would be casualties, Mr Hawke said it was simply speculation. "The person who makes the decision about the composition of Cabinet is me," he said. Journalist: And at this stage you have no plans for a Cabinet reshuffle? Mr Hawke: At this stage I have no plans. Earlier yesterday, Mr Hawke attended a strategy meeting at Parliament House called by the Minister for Transport and Communications, Kim Beazley. The unusual meeting was attended by Mr Hawke's senior political adviser, Col Parkes, the ALP's national secretary, Bob Hogg, and Queensland state secretary, Wayne Swan — a key Hawke supporter.

07 Dec 1991 - Fightback helps Hewson in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 7 December 1991, page 9 Fightback helps Hewson in poll PUBLICATION of the Opposition's Fightback package was just the tonic needed to get the Liberal Leader, John Hewson, back on top as the electors' preferred Prime Minister. A Bulletin Morgan Gallup poll conducted on the weekend of November 23-24, immediately after the package was published, put the Opposition in a 10-percentagc-point lead over the Labor Government — up 2.5 points on the last poll. Dr Hcwson's personal-approval rating was up 13 points to 53 per ccnt — back where he was a year ago. His recovery al so extended to the preference for Prime Minister. Last week he was nine points behind Bob Hawke as the electors' choicc; this week he has streaked ahead, leaving Mr Hawke two points behind. Forty-five per cent prefer Dr Hewson, 43 per cent prefer Mr Hawke, compared with 38 per cent and 47 per cent, respectively, last week. The poll, which surveyed 1315 electors face-to-face throughout Australia, shows the Liberals and Nationals' vote up 2.5 points to 47 per cent, though the Labor vote also went up by one point to 37 per cent. Had an election been held on November 23, the Coalition would have won. Support for the Australian Democrats was down a point to 6 per cent and minor-party support was down 2.5 points to 10 percent. /A CROSS the Tasman, support for the governing £%. National Party increased by 2.5 points, 28 per cent of electors surveyed saying they would have voted for the Government again, but it was still eight points behind the Labour Party — 36 per cent of voters would have voted Labour. In a poll of 1054 electors interviewed face-to-face throughout New Zealand in October, approval for the Prime Minister, Jim Bolger, dropped for the third successive month to a record low of 19 per cent, while 70 per cent (up one point) disapproved and 11 per cent were undecided. Approval of Labour leader Mike Moore dropped five points to 40 per cent; 35 per cent (down one) disapproved and 25 per cent were undecided. There was no change on the question of who would make a better Prime Minister — 24 percent preferred Mr Bolger and 54 per cent Mr Moore.

11 Dec 1991 - Leadership: MPs switch, but with conditions Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 11 December 1991, page 1 Leadership: MPs switch, but with conditions By JEREMY THOMPSON Despite last week's reshuffle, Caucus support for the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, continues to dwindle. Supporters of Mr Hawke are putting the numbers in the 110-pcrson Caucus at 59 for Mr Hawke and 51 for his rival, Paul Keating. Other observers claiming each has 55. Some of those who have switched to Mr Keating in reccnt weeks insist that their votes depend on Mr Hawke being given the chance to exit gracefully — possibly after the visit of the US President, George Bush, at the end of this month. One former Hawke supporter, Harry Woods (NSW) said yesterday that unity was the key. If Mr Keating could unify the party, he and other backbenchers should switch loyal ties. "We can't keep goinf> along the lines we have in the last six months," he said. "In those six months I have been a strong supporter of Hawke. What I am saying is my commitment is no longer with Hawke." Another Hawke supporter, NSW left-winger Colin Hollis would not deny reports that he had switched. Mr Keating's numbers man, Graham Richardson, sounded anything but confident yesterday that those who had promised their votes would remain solid in the Caucus room. "What people will say to you in the corridors or on telephones is one thing," he said. "What they do in Caucus rooms is another. "Having witnessed Labor Party ballots over the last 20 years, all 1 can say is that corridorheroism is often Caucus cowardice. I wouldn't necessarily rely on every promise." In Perth, Mr Hawke was not as enthusiastic as he has recently been to see Mr Keating back in Cabinet. He would say only that if there was a ministerial vacancy Mr Keating would be elected by Caucus with his blessing. Mr Keating and his supporters have already made it clear that Mr Keating is only interested in one front-bench position — the one next to the despatch box. Senator Richardson reinforced views of Mr Keating's inflexibility yesterday. "I spoke to Paul this morning, you'll be pleased to know," he said. "I didn't get any indication from him and haven't had any indication from - him that he is considering a return to the Ministry. "I think our most prominent backbencher is still our most prominent backbencher and will be for a while." But even as Senator Richardson was speaking, more backbenchers were wavering. John Gayler (Qld) said he would "consider" switching should another challenge occur. "My position is not set in concrete," he said. Other Queensland MPs, who were vital in shoring up Mr Hawke's position in the June challenge, are understood to be ready to support Mr Keating should .the ministerial changes not deliver a stronger performance against the Fightback package. The latest Morgan Gallup poll, in today's Bulletin, gives Caucus more reason for change. The ALP has slumped to 33 per cent, down 4 points this week and well behind the Coalition's 51 per cent. The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, now leads Mr Hawke as preferred Prime Minister, 46 per cent to 39.

11 Dec 1991 - Morgan poll moves to Time Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 11 December 1991, page 2 Morgan poll moves to Time SYDNEY: The Morgan Gallup Poll, published in The Bulletin magazine for 19 years, will move to Time magazine from January, the Roy Morgan Research Centre announced yesterday. The weekly public opinion poll, operating for more than SO years, will be published in Time's Australian and New Zealand editions. Spokesman Gary Morgan would not identify the reason publicly yesterday, but cited "pertinent circumstances that make it difficult for usn. He stressed the decision involved neither editorial problems nor money.

12 Dec 1991 - Early-morning crisis meeting reconvenes. PM vows to fight Hawke 'is finished' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 12 December 1991, page 1 Early-morning crisis meeting reconvenes. PM vows to fight Hawke 'is finished' By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent Bob Hawke appears fin-ished as Prime Minister and he looks certain to be replaced by former Trea-surer Paul Keating. Senior Ministers, who met until 1 o'clock this morning, are expected to meet again at 7am to decide Mr Hawke's fate, sources said. Key Cabinet Ministers concluded last night that Mr Hawke no longer had the support to remain in the top job, but at press time, none was pre-pared to confront him and tell him that his time was up. The senior ministers were trying to work out how best to organise an orderly transition but Mr Hawke — who attended a dinner at Govern-ment House before returning to The Lodge — made clear yesterday that he would fight to the end to retain the prime ministership. Those involved in this morning's crisis talks included Mr Hawke's most senior supporters — the Minister for Finance, Kim Beazley, the Minister for Defence, Robert Ray, the Attor-ney-General, Michael Duffy, and the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Gareth Evans. The meeting broke up shortly be-fore lam, but Mr Duffy refused to comment on what was discussed. "I'm not discussing any matters to night," he said. Other ministers who attended the meeting could not be contacted. The Minister for Industry, John Button, spoke earlier yesterday to the other Ministers by phone from Ma-laysia. The Minister for Immigration, Gerry Hand, and the Minister for So-cial Security, Senator Graham Rich-ardson, are understood also to have been involved in the talks about the leadership. The Deputy Prime Minister, Brian Howe, was recovering in hospital af-ter undergoing an operation for a her-nia. Those involved in last night's talks are understood to have agreed that the Government could no longer stand the continued leadership destabilisa tion, and that the issue had to be resolved as quickly as possible. It was unclear whether any or all of the ministers would approach Mr Hawke and tell him of their conclu sions. If Mr Hawke does not face the inev itable, he could face a leadership chal lenge at a special caucus meeting next week, when he would almost certainly be replaced by Mr Keating. One third of the caucus would have to agree to such a meeting and it appears that the numbers would not be hard to organise. Mr Keating was considered last night to have more than half of the 110-member caucus prepared to vote for him in the event of a challenge. Senior figures in the Keating camp said the former Treasurer's numbers ranged from 56-61. They said it was difficult to put forward a firm figure because a number of MPs predicated their support on reaching a transition BOB HAWKE: under great, pressure. al arrangement that would not humil iate Mr Hawke. While they were adamant Mr Hawke had to go, their preferred op tion was to allow the Prime Minister to go "with dignity" as he had been Labor's most successful leader, with almost nine years as Prime Minister. The most cautious estimate of numbers for Mr Keating was 50 votes — a figure provided by one of Mr Hawke's strongest supporters, but even he said it was not enough to save the Prime Minister. Some MPs believe Mr Hawke should be allowed to continue as Prime Minister until after the Presid ent of the United States, George Bush, visits Australia in late December and early January. However, a source at the US Em bassy said last night that Mr Bush would visit Australia as planned, whoever was Prime Minister at the time. Mr Hawke remained defiant yester day. In a radio interview in Melbourne, he said it was up to Mr Keating's supporters to overthrow him if they could. "The question is for those, if they seek to force a ballot, the onus is with them. It's not with me," he said on radio 3AW. He admitted he was going through his toughest period in politics, and said it would be futile to try to claim there was not a lot of tension in the party. But he said that once the Govern ment reached the New Year and the new economic leadership team ol Treasurer Ralph Willis and Finance Minister Kim Beazlcy was allowed tc settle down and do its job, and the economy began recovering, "I am to tally convinced that the fortunes ol the party and of myself would im prove and improve significantly." He dismissed the idea that he would receive a "tap on the shoulder" from his senior supporters keen to see the issue resolved. "I don't believe there'll be any tap on the shoulder," he said. Mr Hawke, facing a continued drop in support from Caucus, was hit yes terday with a new poll showing his public support dropping to the lowest levels in his prime ministership. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll, published in The Bulletin, found Co alition support up 4 percentage point; to 51 per cent, while Labor support had dropped by the same margin tc 33 per cent. Furthermore, preference for the Leader of the Opposition, John Hew son, as Prime Minister was up 1 poini to 46 per cent, while preference for Mi Hawke was down 4 points at 39. Another seriously worrying sign foi Mr Hawke was continuing evidence that the near-solid support he enjoyec from the Left during the June chal lenge was eroding. Senator John Devereux (Tas), from the Left, said it was now unlikely the faction would provide bloc suppori for Mr Hawke. "The more poll results we see lik< the Bulletin poll it's going to become even less secure," he said in a radic interview. Jack Waterford. - Page 9. . Leadership hopeful Paul Keating ... now has the numbers.

14 Dec 1991 - Australians give thumbs down to Hawke Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 14 December 1991, page 11 Australians give thumbs down to Hawke ALTHOUGH the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, continues to hang on by his fingernails to the country's top job, Australian voters have given a strong message of discontent to both Mr Hawke and the Government. The latest Bulletin Morgan Gallup poll has shown that if a federal election had been held at the end of November, the Coalition would have romped home. Of 1349 electors interviewed face-to-face Australia-wide on the weekend of November 30-December 1, 51 per cent would have voted for the Coalition, 33 per cent for Labor. This compares with the previous week's poll that had the Coalition on 47 per cent and Labor on 37. In the space of a week the Coalition increased its lead by four percentage points and Labor lost four points. Australian Democrat support was on 4 per cent, down two points. Support for minor parties was 12 per cent, up two. Mr Hawke polled his lowest approval rating since becoming Prime Minister in 1983. At 31 per cent he lost four points on the previous week. His disapproval rating was up four points to 59 per cent, 10 per cent were undecided. Coalition leader John Hewson's personal approval rating was up three percentage points to 56 per cent and his disapproval rating down one to 30 per cent. Dr Hewson continues to increase his lead over Mr Hawke as the preferred prime minister — at 46 per cent to Mr Hawke's 39 per cent — Dr Hewson's rating crept up one percentage point, but Mr Hawke's dropped four points on last week's polling.
