Analysis by sex shows that of men, 53 per cent (up four points) supported the Coalition, while Labor support dropped four points to 32 per ccnt. Among women, Coalition support rose four to 49 per cent while 33 per cent (down five) supported Labor. In Victoria the polling of its top politicians took on a decidedly different complexion from the federal scene. Although Premier Joan Kirner's personal approval rating has risen for the sixth time in six months, polling shows the Victorian Labor Party would have lost an election held last month. The poll, in which 1642 electors were polled face-to-face in Victoria in November, showed Mrs Kirner's approval rating was 50 per cent compared to the Leader of the Opposition, Jeff Kennett, whose rating is close to its October 1982 lowest at 28 per cent. Support for the Labor Party rose one percentage point to 32 per cent, while the Opposition's support fell half a point to 50 per cent. Fifty-two per cent said Mrs Kirner is the preferred premier to Mr Kennett's 36 per cent. An election held in NSW last month would have been decided on preferences of minor parties. Support for Premier Nick Greiner's Government was up 2.5 points to 42 per cent with Labor's down slightly to 40. Opposition Leader Bob Carr is the preferred premier on 45 per cent down one point, over Mr Greiner on 41 per cent (up one). Approval of Mr Greiner's performance remained at 35 per cent, with 57 per cent of electors disapproving. Mr Carr's rating rose one point to 50 per cent with 35 per cent dissatisfied;

15 Dec 1991 - Hawke is still first choice Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 15 December 1991, page 1 Hawke is still first choice Bob Hawke: gap closing. MELBOURNE: Bob Hawke was still preferred over Paul Keating as both Prime Minister and ALP leader, but the gap between the two had narrowed, according to a public opinion poll issued yesterday. A special Saulwick Age Poll taken on Friday night in Melbourne and Sydney showed that 53 per cent of voters thought Mr Hawke would make a better Prime Minister, compared with 34 per cent for Mr Keating. But the gap between the two was less than at the time of the formal leadership challenge by Mr Keating six months ago. On the eve of Mr Keating's failed challenge in early June, Mr Hawke's lead was 66 per cent to 18 per cent. On the basis of the latest poll Mr Keating's support has almost doubled and Mr Hawke's has declined by 13 per cent.

16 Dec 1991 - Keating plays Medicare gambit Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 16 December 1991, page 1 Keating plays Medicare gambit A pledge by Paul Keating to abolish the new $2.50 Medicare bulk billing charge appears unlikely to woo over significant new Left faction support for his leadership push, according to sources on the Left. According to his supporters, Mr Keating has been telling anyone who asks him that he is opposed to the chargc and would scrap it. But a senior Caucus source said the growing jobs crisis meant support for the Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, in the key Left faction could dissolve if Mr Keating came out strongly in favour of a more interventionist economic strategy. Mr Keating still has no plans to bring the debilitating leadership issue to a head this week, the last real opportunity before Parliament enters its long summer recess. The Left sources dismissed a weekend statement by Keating supporter Senator Rosemary Crowley that he would abolish the new co-payment. It was strongly opposed by the Left when a Caucus revolt forced the Federal Government to reduce the $3.50 co-payment announced in the Budget which finally took effect this month. The sources said the Keating pledge would surprise few people as the former Treasurer had indicated his opposition to it during his National Press Club appearance in late October. The faction has instead been putting the pressure on Mr Hawke for more interventionist measures to stimulate the economy for the future. However, the Left sources did not expect any results this week, with economic policy being discussed on a longer-term basis. Mr Keating has foreshadowed measures to stimulate the economy if he wins the leadership, including a cut in interest rates and targeted measures to encourage more growth, such as a stock-rebuilding allowance and increased spending on key public works. However, Mr Hawke has also said an economic statement in the New Year is possible. The Leader of the Opposition, Dr John Hcwson, said the Government should hand down an economic statement this week before leadership tensions led to a collapse of the Australian dollar. "Unless the Government can act quickly and decisively to restore confidence, there is a great risk that foreign investors will reduce their exposure to an already vulnerable Australian economy," Dr Hewson said in a statement. Markets have been left confused by a week of leadership battles in Canberra, and reports that Mr Keating was prepared to abolish the Medicare co-paymcnt would exacerbate the uncertainty. "□early, Keating is prepared to sacrifice anything including fiscal and monetary policy discipline to fulfil his ambitions," Dr Hewson said. He said a sudden fall in the Australian dollar would rekindle inflationary expectations and damage the prospects of real interest rate relief. "It is imperative, therefore, that the Government bring forward next week an honest and comprehensive assessment of the economy We simply can't wait to mid-January for such a statement," he said. Mr Hawke has received a boost from two Saulwick Age polls. One taken on Friday night in Melbourne and Sydney showed 53 per cent of voters thought Mr Hawke would make a better prime minister, compared with 34 per cent for Mr Keating. But the gap between the two had narrowed since early June when Mr Hawke's lead was 66 per cent to 18 per cent. In a Sunday Age poll of 600 Victorians, 75 per cent said the election of Mr Keating as leader of the Labor Party would cither reduce the party's electoral chances or make no difference. Only 19 per ccnt thought he would improve Labor's chances. It found Mr Hawke had 60 per ccnt of Labor voters' support, compared with 20 per cent for Mr Keating and 7 per ccnt for both the Minister for Finance, Kim Beazley, and the Minister for Primary Industries and Energy, Simon Crean. On Thursday Mr Hawke rejected a plea from six of his closest Cabinet supporters to bow out gracefully, saying he would lead Labor at the next election. Mr Keating, meanwhile, has got support from an unlikely quarter in the form of the former Liberal Prime Minister, Malcolm Fraser. Mr Fraser writing in his regular column published in The Canberra Times said that Mr Keating could "make a race of it" if he could recapture, but at the same time control, the sharp edge of his tongue. He said Mr Keating's political skills were great because he persuaded the opposition that most of what he did was right and was therefore able to avoid any real probing debate. Caucus would put Mr Keating in because they believed he would make a fight of it, he said. "When governments run out of policies and ideas, that can be enough," Mr Fraser said. Malcolm Fraser*s column — Page 6.

18 Dec 1991 - Walls close in on Hawke Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 18 December 1991, page 1 By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent Bob Hawke's chances of retaining the Prime Ministership beyond the end of this week appear to be fading. A growing number of Ministers and backbenchers from all factions now believe a Caucus ballot must be held to settle the leadership. A new poll showing Mr Hawke's personal popularity and the ALP's electoral fortunes at record lows will fuel pressure for a quick settlement Supporters of Paul Keating were convinced yesterday they had the numbers to oust Mr Hawke, although Mr Keating remained opposed to a personal challenge, preferring that Mr Hawke stand down. Some Hawke supporters conceded privately that Mr Keating could have the numbers, but there is deep anger in the Hawke camp, members of whom pointed out yesterday that no Labor Prime Minister had ever been torn from office by his own party. Mr Hawke, who spent much of yesterday attending the Prime Minister's XI cricket match, is determined to fight on. The most likely circuit-breaker appears to be a push by one of Mr Keating's senior supporters - probably on Friday - to move that the leadership be declared vacant, precipitating a Caucus vote. The latest Morgan Gallup poll, in today's Bulletin shows Mr Hawke's personal popularity has plummeted 5 percentage points to a new low of 26 per cent. The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, has picked up 3 points to 59 per cent. More worrying for Mr Hawke's colleagues is the finding that only 31.5 per cent would vote Labor (down 5 points to the lowest ebb in the Government's four-term history) while a landslide 52.5 per cent (up 1.5) would vote for Dr Hewson's Coalition. Ironically, Mr Hawke defended his position yesterday morning by pointing to a Newspoll in The Australian that showed he was three times more popular among Labor voters than Mr Keating. This did not silence the growing chorus in the Government, both publicly and privately, for a leadership showdown. The Minister for Shipping and Aviation Support, Bob Collins — a strong Hawke supporter in the June challenge by Mr Keating — said the leadership had to be resolved this week. "Suggestions that this could be left to next year to be fixed are just absolutely unthinkable," he told journalists. "As far as I'm concerned, I mean, that's a luxury you can afford in Opposition, but you can't afford to do that when you're in government." Mr Hawke's loyal former press secretary, Barrie Cassidy, conceded that Mr Hawke's time was up. Speaking from Washington, where he has been a freelance journalist since quitting Mr Hawke's office early this year, Mr Cassidy said Mr Keating and his supporters would not give up, and Mr Hawke's "best chance is really no chance". "He can't hope to take a divided party to victory — no leader ever has," he said. Mr Hawke's third most senior minister, John Button, is expected to meet the Prime Minister today and call for him to stand down, although last night Senator Button had not yet contacted Mr Hawke to arrange a meeting. Senator Button, a Keating supporter with an independent streak, will tell Mr Hawke that he represents five other Ministers — the Minister for Employment, Education and Training, John Dawkins; the Minister for Trade and Overseas Development, Neal Blewett; the Minister for Industrial Relations, Peter Cook; the Minister for the Environment, Ros Kelly, and the Minister for Social Security, Graham Richardson. Mr Hawke's response will almost certainly be the same as he gave to his six most senior Cabinet supporters who approached him last week; he is not going. ACT Senator Bob McMuIlan declared himself yesterday a Keating supporter, although he would not be drawn on whether he believed a showdown should occur this week. Senator McMuIlan said his decision was not based on personalities, but on who could best deliver policies to boost employment, social justice and industry. "In my discussions with Paul and with Bob over the months, and through my observations, I have reached the view that Paul is now the best man for the job," he said. Caucus members contacted by The Canberra Times yesterday said the most likely outcome would be a move, initiated tomorrow when Parliament reconvenes, to force a ballot. It would require 37 Caucus members to sign a petition calling for a special meeting, probably on Friday, to consider a motion to declare the leadership vacant. With neither Mr Keating nor Mr Hawke likely to move, a respected senior Keating supporter such as Senator Button or Senator McMuIlan could be prevailed upon to move for a ballot. If the motion was supported by more than half the Caucus, Mr Keating's name could then be proposed for the vacant leadership. Although sources close to Mr Keating insisted yesterday that the former Treasurer wanted Mr Hawke to stand down first, the above strategy would — at least theoretically — allow Mr Keating to stand for the leadership without having personally precipitated a direct challenge. Pry or1 a view. - Page 8.

20 Dec 1991 - Keating 'on the round to defeat' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 20 December 1991, page 4 Keating 'on the road to defeat' Hewson slams new PM's 'cold arrogance and naked ambition' Paul Keating would lead the Labor Party to "inevitable de-feat" at the next election, the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, said last night. "Paul Keating's ambition has claimed one more victim. It has also sealed his own fate," he said. He said in a statement that Aus-tralians would never forgive Mr Keating for his high-interest policies which had hurt homeowners and ad-ded to unemployment. "Of the two, Bob Hawke is far the better man," Dr Hewson said. "He made mistakes as Prime Min-ister — he also was not above deceiv-ing the people to suit his political ends. "But not with the cold arrogance and naked ambition of Paul Keating." Dr Hewson said Mr Keating should call an election as soon as possible. Australia should not have to struggle on another 15 months under Labor policies. He "doesn't have a mandate from the Australian people to govern — he barely has a mandate from his own party." The National Party Leader, Tim Fischer, said rural and provincial Australia would regard with "consid-erable concern" Mr Keating's eleva-tion to Prime Minister. "Farmers across Australia will re-member the monetary policies of this man that led to record high interest rates and the savage impact on farms, small business and individuals," he said. Mr Keating's qualifications for the leadership were "failure, disloyalty, ineptness and callousness". The Australian Democrats Lead-er, John Coulter, said the Labor Par-ty had "confirmed its rejection of history". "This man [Keating] has smashed legions of Labor icons with his poli-cies of privatisation, deregulation and floating the dollar," he said. "He has brought Australia to its current social and economic mal-aise." Senator Coulter said the choice between Mr Keating and Mr Hawke was one between "deliberate destruc- tion on one hand and procrastination and waffle on the other". The South Australian Premier, John Bannon, said there was "enor-mous pressure" on Mr Keating to perform in the next few months. Mr Bannon, chairman of the Spe-cial Premiers' Conference in Ade-laide last month, also said he would || John Bannon: enormous pres- sure on Keating to perform. || be talking soon with Mr Keating about the Commonwealth-state tax-sharing arrangements discussed at that meeting. "I think he does recognise the states as front-line service provid-ers," Mr Bannon said. "In other words if there were more drastic cuts to the states it's the economy as a whole that will suffer. "And at the premiers' conference earlier this year we saw that real terms guarantee maintained by Mr Keating as treasurer. I hope that's certainly his starting point for 1992." Mr Bannon, a former ALP nation-al president, said after the "destabi-lising" leadership crisis it was now time to tackle the issues of unem-ployment and the economy or Labor would be toppled from government federally in 1993. "The onus is on Mr Keating to demonstrate that it's not just a case of ambition, but it's a case of solu-tions," he said. Mr Bannon said that despite the close margin, the party would get be-hind Mr Keating. He said of Mr Hawke, "He has served this country superbly in a number of capacities and over the last eight years as prime minister — he's going to leave a mighty big gap." || John Hewson: Keating's ambi-tion has sealed his own fate. || Former Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser said that Bob Hawke's dump-ing by his own party was "the worst way for a political leader to go". He said he believed Mr Hawke had made the right decision to bring on a vote. "Anyone in these circumstances is facing a very difficult time and diffi-cult decisions," he said. Mr Fraser said that whoever won the ballot should re-examine the poli-cies that had "brought Australia to the worst state in this century". The Victorian Premier, Joan Kir-ner, said Mr Keating faced a huge task in addressing Australia's eco-nomic problems. In a call for unity, the Labor Pre-mier said Australians were looking for confidence, jobs and policies which would strengthen the country. She paid tribute to Mr Hawke's achievements as prime minister and in the union movement, saying he had brought Australians together as no other leader had. Pollster Gary Morgan said Mr Keating had a much better chance of winning the next election than Mr Hawke. Mr Morgan, whose company pro-duces the influential Morgan Gallup polls, said surveys showed Mr Keating was seen as a strong leader, and that is what the electorate want-ed. "Although he's not popular, he's looked on as being capable, intelli-gent and a strong leader, and I think the electorate will respond to those dimensions of Mr Keating," Mr Mor-gan told ABC television. The Queensland Premier, Wayne Goss, believes Mr Keating has a "good chance" at the next election if he can come up with a positive alter-native to the Opposition's goods and services tax. Mr Goss, a supporter of Bob Hawke before the challenge, said "He's got to get some dynamic and positive new policies and get the country moving again." The secretary of the Victorian Trades Hall Council, John Halfpen-ny, said the union movement was "ready to give Paul Keating a go". "The government must now get down to tackling the problems that have been hurting so many Austral-ians," he said. "The vote has changed the musicians and now it's up to the new prime minister to change the tune the government has been play-ing." The New Zealand Prime Minister, Jim Bolger, congratulated Mr Keating and said he looked forward to working with him. "I have sent him a message of congratulations and I am looking for ward to speaking to him on the phone tomorrow," Mr Bolger said in a statement in Wellington. "He is well known to us and we will welcome the opportunity to work with him." Papua New Guinea's Prime Min-ister, Rabbie Namaliu, congratulated Mr Keating and praised the contribu-tion of outgoing leader Bob Hawke. Mr Namaliu said in Port Moresby that Mr Hawke had made an invalu-able contribution to PNG's friendly relationship with Australia in his role in developing PNG's trade unions before independence in 1975, and during his term as Prime Minister. "He had a broad and sensitive understanding of our country, and our people, a fact which was evident whenever I had the privilege of meet-ing him over his long term as Prime Minister," Mr Namaliu said. "Both in regional and internation al events, Bob Hawke has demon-strated not only strong leadership, but a great understanding of the problems of the South Pacific and a commitment to working with other countries to overcome them."

23 Dec 1991 - New Keating ministry 'before the New Year' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 23 December 1991, page 1 New Keating ministry 'before the New "fear' The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, has begun the task of reshaping the Federal Government with a new-look ministry to be announced between Christ mas and New Year's Day. But he received a grim reminder of the burden he will carry in 1992 with a respected labour-market forecaster tipping jobless levels above 10 per cent until mid-1993. And his own political handicap in turning around the Government's fortunes in time for an election within 18 months was underlined by a Sunday newspaper poll which found 60 per ,cent of voters did not believe his promises to create jobs and be honest with the public. During a photo session with his family on Saturday, Mr Keating reaffirmed the pledges he gave after Thursday night's historic ALP caucus leadership ballot in which he unseated Bob Hawke. In what was described as a Prime Ministerial Christmas message, Mr Keating expressed concern for the victims of the recession but hope of "good years" ahead in the 1990s. "In 1992 I think we will restore growth in the economy and start to get confidence back," he said. The remarks sparked a bitter attack from the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, who said truth was the first casualty of Mr Keating's pledges. "His Christmas message states first that Australia now has the long-term structures in place for job creation and second that he is working flat out on a comprehensive jobs package," Dr Hewson said yesterday. "Mr Keating cannot have it both ways." Continued on Page 2 Unemployment forecast to remain high; Hawke will quit report — Page 3 New Keating ministry 'before New Year' Continued from Page 1 "The new humble and honest Mr Keating lasted exactly 48 hours to be replaced by the old arrogant and disingenuous Mr Keating who hopes verbal dazzle and bombast will obscure the wreckage caused by his policies," Dr Hewson said. The Quadrant Research Ser vices poll published in the Brisbane Sunday Mail showed Dr Hewson enjoyed a record 71 per cent approval rating and led Mr Keating as preferred Prime Minister 53 to 41 per cent. It also showed 60 per cent did not believe Mr Keating would fulfil his promises, although he had a 39 per cent approval rating in his first poll outing. And Labor's support actually rose slightly from 38 to 41 per cent between November and December despite the leadership brawl, and Coalition support fell from 53 to 49 per cent. The Adelaide-based National Institute of Labour Studies report said the jobless rate, which reached 10.5 per cent in November and is expected to exceed the Budget forecast of a 10.75 per cent in 1991-92, was likely to remain above 10 per cent at least until mid-1993. Foreshadowing an imminent ministerial shake-up ahead of the first Cabinet meeting on January 6 on his jobs strategy, Mr Keating said he wanted to talk to colleagues over the next few days about his planned changes. Speaking on arrival at Parliament House yesterday, Mr Keating would not comment on how extensive the changes would be. But he said he was looking at top Public Service structures as well as ministries. "There's no point in speculating about it," he said. "Let's just wait and see. But [there will be an announcement] between Christmas and New Year I'd say at the latest." Immediately after winning the caucus leadership ballot from Bob Hqwke on Thursday night, the new Prime Minister ruled out a caucus spill of ministerial positions to try to bring some harmony back to the party. It effectively ruled out any new ministerial blood for the time being but Mr Keating is expccted to reshuffle the team. Most interest centres on the tussle for the Treasury where incumbent Ralph Willis believes he deserves a chance after making a promising start. But the Minister for Employment, Education and Training, John Dawkins, believes Mr Keating owes him the job as a reward for long-term support.

31 Dec 1991 - Kirner up, but hard year ahead Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 31 December 1991, page 10 Kirner up, but hard year ahead By MARK TRIFFITT YEARENDER MELBOURNE: Her own star has risen dramatically, but Victoria's Premier, Joan Kirner, prefers to see the past 12 months as a survival exercise. After polling a meagre 27 per cent in personal approval ratings at the beginning of the year, Mrs Kirner's popularity, according to survey results, is now almost twice that of her Opposition counterpart, JefFKennett. But the Premier cites the highlight of the year as her Government's return to "legitimacy" in the eyes of Victorians, 50,000 of whom took to the streets in January calling for its sacking after a string of fiscal debacles, mounting unemployment and a crisis in business confidence. Mrs Kirner won office in August, 1990, after three-term Premier John Cain resigned, dragged down by financial disasters, budgetary crises and a party in disorder. She has yet to face her first election as Premier, and over the past year the state's business investment and profits have deteriorated, as has the unemployment rate — now at 11 per cent and higher than at any time since the 1930s depression. But Mrs Kirner believes Labor's policies in areas such as manufacturing and industry will help voters recognise at election time next year that her party does have a viable plan for economic recovery. In reality, Victorians are struggling to find the same enthusiasm for Mrs Kirner's team as they havei for her. According to the latest Morgan Gallup poll, her party would still have been swept from office if an election had been held last month. "Nearly every extended family in Victoria knows someone who is affected by unemployment, and I think that's unacceptable," she said. Not surprisingly, she believes plans to create jobs need to be drawn up, and very quickly. "1 grew up in a family which grew up on stories of the impact of the Depression, and I never thought a Labor Government in Australia would be presiding over that; I find it personally hurtful," she said. Her Government's four-year term, secured by a three-seat margin in 1988, ends in October, 1992, and the option of quickly pump-priming the economy through government spending is ruled out by the huge state debt. There has been speculation that Mrs Kirner may call an early poll in autumn, before the jobless rate rises even further, and capitalise on Mr Kennett's lack of popularity. But she has ruled out that possibility, saying she wants to bring down another Budget before going to the polls. While Mrs Kirner has promised a "good news" Budget for 1992 to sweeten what is shaping up as a sour financial year, she has few short-term options for boosting her party's chances of winning the election. As a result, she is hoping Victorians will see that the only viable eco nomic solutions for the state are long-term. She's also hoping voters will discriminate between her solutions and those of Mr Kennett who, she says, mistakenly believes Victoria's problems can be remedied as easily as "pulling a rabbit out of a hat". "You never know whether people will see that or not, but I certainly hope so," she said. "It will take more than our state building blocks. We need the federal adhesive to put these building blocks together." These "building blocks" include a multi-billion-dollar job-creation plan, involving public and private projects planned to begin next year. The government-sponsored projects, including a $500 million rapidcommuter link between inner-city Melbourne and Tullamarine Airport, would create thousands of direct jobs as well as other spin-offs for the state's economy. The catch is that the Government wants the public projects to be funded largely by private investors, but feder Joan Kirner al lax rules make private investment in such developments unattractive. Mrs Kirner has been leading her Government's calls for the Federal Government to allow tax relief for private enterprises investing in public projects, as well as a further easing of interest rates and a sector-by-sector approach to industry development. Although she rejects any suggestion that she played a role in the downfall of Bob Hawke as Prime Minister, Paul Keating's succession and his recognition that lower unemployment is the top priority provides Labor in Victoria with a new ray of hope. Mrs Kirner is pleased that the Federal Government is acknowledging the need for speed on the economic recovery. Whether the action comes in time to kick-start the economy depends ultimately on Mr Keating, who is rumoured to be planning a New Year rescue package for Victoria. But however federal affairs affect Victoria in the New Year, Mrs Kimer says only a fool would believe next year's election will be anything but close. - AAP

01 Mar 1992 - Republicans out in front Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 1 March 1992, page 1 Republicans out in front SYDNEY: Pro-republicans outweigh royalists in Australia, according to a new "poll. Still, the poll shows that there is overwhelming support - 81 per cent - for Australia's remaining a member of the Commonwealth, whether or not it becomes a republic. The Saulwick poll in The Sydney Morning Herald and the Melbourne Age yesterday shows that for the first time most people questioned - 57 per cent -want Australia to become a republic. That compares with 45 per cent of respondents to a similar poil in 1988. Respondents were given three options in the poll: would they prefer Australia to remain a member of the Commonwealth, the Queen still head of state; become a republic but remain in the Commonwealth; or become a republic outside the Commonwealth. In 1988, 53 per cent chose the first option, but this has declined to 39 per cent; 42 per cent now prefer Australia to stay in the Commonwealth as a republic compared with 32 per cent in 1988. The number who want a complete break barely moved, from 13 to 15 percent.

01 Mar 1992 - 'Fightback' beats Keating's deal: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 1 March 1992, page 2 'Fightback' beats Keating's deal: poll MELBOURNE: The Opposition's Fightback package was more popular than Prime Minister Paul Keating's economic statement, a Saulwick poll found yesterday. The poll, published in the Melbourne Age newspaper, revealed that almost 40 per cent of voters thought they would be better off under the Coalition package, and only 22 per cent approved of Mr Keating's statement. The poll found good support for Mr Keating's One Nation economic statement, 47 per cent of respondents saying it would be good for the country, and 45 per cent believed the package would be good for business. A similar Saulwick poll conducted after the launching of the Fightback package last November found 56 per cent support for the reforms proposed, The Age said. The poll found that 68 per cent of voters described OppositionLeader Leader Dr John Hewson's policies as "well thought out", compared with 47 per cent for Labor policies. One in three voters said Mr Keating's economic statement would improve Labor's re-election chances. Twenty per cent said it would harm Labor's hopes of staying in government after thenext election. Of Labor voters, 57 per cent said the statement would improve the party's election chances. Men were more positive about the statement than women. The poll surveyed 1000 voters. John Hewson

05 Mar 1992 - Govt rail plan angers pensioners Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 5 March 1992, page 12 Govt rail plan angers pensioners IN BRIEF SYDNEY: The NSW Gov-ernment should scrap plans to restrict free rail travel for pen-sioners from next month, a pen-sioners' group said yesterday. Combined Pensioners and Superannuants Association of NSW spokesman Bruce Hutton said the Government seemed determined to make life harder for pensioners by penalising them for wanting to travel dur-ing the 19 busiest days of the year on the rail network. State Rail chief Ross Sayers revealed on Tuesday that peak periods were being so booked up by pensioners using free rail travel tickets that full-fare pay-ing passengers could not get a seat and the transport network was therefore losing money. ALP polls less MELBOURNE: The Victori-an Labor Government's sup-port had slipped slightly in the past month after some setbacks to the state's economy, accord-ing to a Saulwick Poll commis-sioned by The Age newspaper. Those polled who said they would vote Labor if an election were held last week stood at 28 per cent compared with 30 per cent at the end of January. Whale injured BRISBANE: Marine han- dlers at Sea World on Queens-land's Gold Coast are trying to save a melon-headed whale found badly injured on a Surf-ers Paradise beach early yester-day. Sea World curator of mammals Rob Clapp said the whale was in a poor condition after twice beaching itself. Trial over theft BRISBANE: Melville Schnitzerling, also known as Russell Cox, is to stand trial on charges of the theft of more than $635,000. A Brisbane magistrate com-mitted Schnitzerling yesterday to the District Court's April sit-tings on eight armed robbery charges.

06 Mar 1992 - Poll analysis is wrong Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 6 March 1992, page 8 Poll analysis is wrong Received 4 March THE CANBERRA TIMES's analysis of the Morgan Gallup Poll February 29, P. 9) stating that nearly two-thirds of Australians support mining at Coronation Hill is wrong. In fact, the poll shows that just over one-third (37 per cent) support ..mining at Coronation Hill. The 26 per cent who say mining should only go ahead with the approval of the Jawoyn people cannot in any way be said to support mining, as was claimed in your column. The Jawoyn people have stated, and recently reaffirmed, their total opposition to mining at Coronation Hill. It follows that the 26 per cent who support the Jawoyn support them in their decision not to mine. This 26 per cent could be said to support Aboriginal land rights, and rights to self-determination. If any projection is to be made, then it would seem more consistent that they should be added to those who oppose mining outright. The conclusion could follow that nearly two-thirds (58 per cent) of Australians oppose the joint-venture proposal to mine Coronation Hill. (Senator) NICK BOLKUS Minister for Administrative Services Parliament House

07 Mar 1992 - Labor supported in seat of Wills Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 7 March 1992, page 9 Labor supported in seat of Wills THE LABOR Party would have just held on to the seat of Wills if a by-election had been conducted at the end of last month, a poll has found. According to a Morgan Gallup telephone-survey poll of 508 voters in Wills, conducted on February 25-26 and published in Time Australia, support for the ALP stood at 44 per cent; the Liberal Party 43 per cent; Australian Democrats 6 pcrcent and others 7 per cent. On a two-party-preferred basis this would have given Labor a narrow victory over the Liberals, 51 per ccnt to 49 per cent. But when asked which party they believed would win the April il by-election, 50 per ccnt said the Liberals and only 34 per cent said Labor. The scat became vacant when the former Prime Minister, Bob Hawkc, resigned as MP last month. Although Wills has traditionally been a Labor seat, it is an area hard hit by the recession. Prime Minister Paul Keating's approval rating in Wills, 33 per cent, was about the same as in the rest of the country, at 32 per ccnt. Opposition Leader John Hewson was seen more critically, with 44 per cent compared with 56 per cent nationally. In the choice of Prime Minister, 39 per cent of respondents preferred Mr Keating, compared with 37 per ccnt nationally, and 40 per cent preferred Dr Hewson, compared with 47 per cent nationally. According to another poll, conducted in December and January face-to-facc with 9793 voters throughout Australia, if a full-Senate election had been held in January, the Opposition could have won an outright majority. The ALP support was 34 per cent, compared with the Liberal Party's 41.5 per cent. The National Party was favoured by 5.5 per cent and the Democrats by 9 per ccnt and 10 per cent other parties and independents. On these figures, the Coalition could win 39 of the 76 Senate seats.

14 Mar 1992 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 14 March 1992, page 9 Popularity of Keating increases THE PRIME Minister's One Nation economic statement has been a modest success with voters, a Morgan Gallup Poll has found. According to the poll, conducted with 1135 voters throughout Australia on February 22-23 and 1181 on February 29 to March 1, on the weekend before the statement was delivered (February 22-23), support for the Government was 36 per cent; a week later, it had risen 1.5 points to 37.5 per cent. The poll, published in the latest Time Australia magazine, was also taken before Mr Keating's parliamentary onslaught against the federal Coalition's Fightback packagc. Support for the Coalition dropped 1.5 points to 48 per cent; Australian Democrats' support also dropped, half a point to 5 per cent, and 9.5 per cent favoured other parties and independent candidates. If the immediate impact of the One Nation packagc was less than Mr Keating might have hoped, there is a steady upward trend in his own popularity. After the statement his approval rating was up four points to 37 per cent. It has risen 12 points from 25 per cent since his first poll in January. The proportion of people undecided about Mr Keating dropped eight points to 17 per cent. Voters' comments included, "Keating is taking us in a bold new direction". There was a corresponding increase in the proportion of people critical of how the Prime Minister was handling his job. His disapproval rating was up four points to 4b per cent. Comments included, "His remarks about the Queen and the British were uncalled for" and "He is arrogant". In the same period, Opposition Leader John Hewson's approval rating remained steady at 55 per cent but his disapproval rating rose one point to 30 per cent. There was a one point decrease, to 15 percent in those undecided. On the question of preferred PM, Mr Keating was up three points to.39 per cent while Dr Hewson slipped two points to 46 '-per cent. The proportion that chose others or was undecided dropped one point to 15 per cent. Comments about Mr Keating included, "He is the best performer in Parliament" and of Dr Hewson, "He thinks before he speaks". ALTHOUGH incumbent Joan Kirner remains the preferred Premier over Opposition Leader Jeff Kennett, her Government would be devastated if an election were held now in Victoria, The Bulletin poll has found. The poll published in the latest Bulletin and conducted with 1030 electors on various dates in February and March, found the Victorian Labor vote had fallen to 35 per cent, down four points since a January poll, following a coalition party publicity campaign. The Coalition recorded a three-point rise to 56 per cent support. The Opposition had a 21-point lead in voter support, leading the Government for all age groups, for both men and women. The Premier's approval rating had slipped to 36 per cent, down five points, as had Mr Kennett's approval rating, 21 per cent, down two points. Mrs Kirner's approval was slightly higher among men, 37 percent, than women, 34 per cent, and was higher among Melbourne voters, 38 per cent, than those outside the city or suburbs. She was least popular with young voters, 23 per cent of people aged 18 to 14 years, and most popular with those aged 40 to 54 years, 41 percent.

16 Mar 1992 - Independents: pander to, or ignore them? Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 16 March 1992, page 2 Independents: pander to, or ignore them? By Richard Farmer THE LOCAL Labor Government will have to make up its mind soon about how it is going to handle Michael Moore and his fellow independent Helen Szuty, and the mood is developing that it should pretty much ignore them. While being a minority of eight in the 17-person Assembly, Labor has much to lose if it begins compromising to accommodate the antidevelopmcnt views of the independents. Hence the belief of some Labor members that the best course is to act as if they have a majority and dare the independents to roll them. When Mr Moore and Ms Szuty get down to it they are unlikely to want to be too obstructionist; neither has much chance of being re-clectcd under a Hare-Clark system. The worry in the Labor team is not about Budget Bills and no-confidence motions' being beaten. Rather it is legislation about planning. The Independents have rather quaint views about such matters which would result, for example, in every self-interested group's getting its way to stop urban infill. Labor should have the courage to gamble on the Liberal Party's being sensible enough not to play petty politics and to support essential planning and development decisions. Then the two independents will have only the little influence they deserve to have. Goodness knows whether that will be the Liberal approach. Oppositions find it hard to do other than oppose but surely they will not be stupid enough to even contemplate forming a government of their own by giving in to Mr Moore and Ms Szuty and relying on Dennis Stevenson for the final number. That would make our local government more farcical than ever. The circumstances are right for Labor to ignore the independents and dare them to do their worst. THE PRIME Minister, Paul Keating, is doing remarkably well in building up the spirits of Labor supporters. The finding of a Newspoll published yesterday, showing Labor clearly leading in the race for the Wills by-election, will build (he spirits even higher. The issuing of Mr Keating's One Nation economic package has at least given his party faithful some reason to believe that their side of politics has not run out of ideas. The Keating attack on the Fightback package of his Liberal and National opponents has cleverly given the faithful an element of class warfare to cling to. Perhaps even more importantly, Mr Keating has set about rebuilding Labor's appeal to the country's tertiary-educated middle class in a way that has not been attempted since Gough Whitlam. Changes in the flag, support for republicanism, talk of a new national identity concentrated on an Asian future, appeals to the conscience about the plight of Aborigines and an unashamed endorsement of artistic activity are standing Mr Keating in good stead. The people for w hom these sideshow issues are important are the very ones who have been deserting Labor for the past five or six years bccause they believe the governments of Bob Hawke were no longer proper (that is, W'hitlamesquc) Labor governments. The Liberal Leader, John Hewson, must be wondering where the economic debate has got to. In a week in which over-all unemployment increased again and the fignres for youth unemployment reach a truly frightening figure, the survey in Wills saw Labor s vote not even 2 per cent less than at the last election! If a vote like that is repeated on April 11, the Liberals will fall welt short of victory. They require a swing of about 8 per cent to win and have less than a month to get it. Based on the Newspoll figures, and assuming a 50-50 split of the 14 per cent of people who indicate they will vote for a third party, the Liberals so far have gained just less than half of that 8 per cent. It will be a difficult task, albeit one made easier by the very fact that the polls suggest they will not achieve it, to get the next half. Difficult, but not impossible. It defies reason that, the impact Mr Keating has made on Labor's traditional supporters notwithstanding, there is not a desire to punish a government that has produced an unemployment rate of 10.5 per cent. The Prime Minister is, after all, the man who as Treasurer for eight years set the economic course that produced that figure. Even the staunchest Labor person in Wills must have doubts about the sense of giving Mr Keating a victory that might encourage him to think that all the pain had been forgiven. Now that the Newspoll and the Morgan Gallup poll have indicated a Labor win there is reason to think that John Hewson the underdog will pick up some support. So too will the minor parties and independent candidates. Both the Newspoll and the Morgan poll give them about 14 per cent of the intended vote. That was less than the 16.8 per cent they gained at the last election in 1990, when Bob ilawkc was the candidate. The message of the pollsters seems to be that there is considerable suspicion about the Liberals - presumably because of their advocacy of a goods-and-services tax. If that is so then it is the minor candidates who will benefit most from any protest vote, now that it looks as if Labor will win. Whether the underdog effect occurs, and whoever benefits from it, Mr Hewson has reason to be a little worried. If at the end of a recession his party can gain only 4 per cent at a Wills by-clection, what will be the position in a year's time when an economic recovery is under way? If the Liberals are not to be far worse off than they are in Wills today when the general election comes, they will have to really sell the message that Paul Keating is not a man to be trusted. The initial reaction to Labor's promise to match the tax reductions of its opponents without the pain of the goods-and-services tax seems to be favourable. John Hewson must persuade the Australian people that there is no such easy way to a better economic future and that the Prime Minister is a snake-oil salesman. Reduced taxes, and thus greater spending power for individuals, are just not possible without some combination of new taxes and reduced spending. That combination is what the Liberals arc offering in their Fightback package, while Mr Keating's reduced taxes are to be the product of more growth than the Liberals think is possible. If the Hewson gamble of bringing out his detailed economic plan in opposition is not to fail, he must convince people that his is the only way. He must become Honest John to the Prime Minister's Tricky Paul. It is a line that the Liberal Leader has begun taking in his appearances in Wills, where he has looked like a relaxed and confident politician. He has to keep being so, and not only on the hustings. John Hewson has to present a contrast between himself and Paul Keating in the Parliament as well. In the first two weeks of this year's parliamentary sitting, Mr Hewson allowed himself to be sucked in by the Prime Minister's bullying tactics. He should not do so again. IT TAKES a person of courage to launch a new winery when consumption is declining and prices . are still taking a hammering because of that and the recession, so Kym Tolley has my admiration. Wines under his Penley Estate label are becoming available in the wake of his decision to leave Penfolds in 1988 and go out on his own. Just put on the market is a 1989 Coonawarra Cabernet Sauvignon that I found most agreeable drinking indeed. So too have the wine-show judges - it has won trophies at the Adelaide and Hobart shows and six gold medals in all. Yet the enormity of the problem Mr Tolley faccs was shown in the almost simultaneous marketing of the 1989 Wynns Estate Coonawarra Cabernet Sauvignon, which sells for about half the $30 a bottle demanded for his Penley Estate. The Wynns, with its familiar black label, has deep rich flavours and picked up a gold at the National Wine Show. Quite frankly, 1 could not see much between the two wines in terms of quality, so it is hard to recommend the Penley Vale as value for money. Sales of wine above the $ 15 mark having slowed to a walk in Australia, Mr Tolley will need plenty of good fortune or a lot of wealthy friends if he is to sell out of his Cabernet in a hurry. Wynns will not have that problem with its 1990 Coonawarra Estate Hermitage, which the winemakcr, Peter Douglas, is calling "the best shiraz wine made at Wynns since the ... 1955 Michael Hermitage".

20 Mar 1992 - Police angered by survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 20 March 1992, page 12 Police angered by survey SYDNEY: The NSW Policc Association described yesterday as meaningless a survey which found only a bare majority 5f people supported the way police deal with Aborigines'. The association's president, Tony Day, said the responses by 1000 people in a country of 17 million was not a fair indication of public opinion. He said the timing could not have been worse as it followed closely the national debate about racist behaviour by NSW police, with those questioned likely to have formed their views based solely on their perceptions of media coverage rather than first-hand experience with police. The Saulwick Poll in yesterday's Sydney Morning Herald found 52 per cent of respondents believed police generally did a good job, while 38 per cent said many police acted with prejudice. The NSW Police Commissioner, Tony Lauer, also criticised the survey, saying it reduced a complex and emotional issue to a scries of over-simplistic questions. He said the results did not tally \yith an independent NSW poll last year which found 85 per cent of those surveyed believed the police were doing either a good or very good job. The police association treasurer, Garry Dunne, said the survey indicated public support for police was still strong despite the recent criticism of NSW officers. The ABC recently screened a video filmed more than two years ago which featured two police officers parading as Aborigines with .nooses around their necks.

21 Mar 1992 - Poll finds us still sceptical Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 21 March 1992, page 11 Poll finds us still sceptical AUSTRALIANS remain sccptical about the economy's prospects after the announcement of Prime Minister Paul Keating's One Nation program, a Morgan Gallup Poll has found. The poll, conducted between March 7 and 8 with 1189 people and published in the Time Australia magazine, showed 22 per cent, up five points, expected an improvement over the next year and 44 per cent, down three, did not. The survey preceded the announcement of the February jobless figures, which showed 10.5 per cent of the work force unemployed. The overall Morgan consumer confidence rating barely changed, 96.2 points compared with 95.9 in February. This rating, from a base of 100 points is arrived at by weighing positive and negative responses to five questions. Thirty-one per ccnt, up two points, believed their personal financial situation would improve in the coming year and 20 per cent, also up two points, did not. Most, 52 per cent, up five points, said they were worse off than a year ago and 20 per cent, no point change, thought they were better off. Only 30 per ccnt, up two points, were optimistic about the next five years, and 27 per cent, also up two points, were gloomy. In a separate Morgan Gallup Poll, conducted with 2658 people on the weekends of February 1-2 and 8-9, respondents were asked what they thought was the smallest amount a family of four needed each week to live reasonably well and still pay essential bills. At $447, including $120 to be spent on food, it was the first time since the survey began in 1945 that the perceived cost of living had not increased over a year. A Bulletin Poll, published in the latest magazine, has found that nearly four times as many Queenslanders approve of Labor Premier, Wayne Goss, as disapprove. The poll, conducted with 730 electors on January 31, each weekend in February and March 1, puts Mr Goss' approval rating at 66 per ccnt climbing to 71 per cent in Brisbane. This makes him by far the most popular premier in the country. Carmen Lawrence of Western Australia rates second on 58 per cent.

28 Mar 1992 - Cheering news for Keating and Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 28 March 1992, page 9 Cheering news for Keating and Labor THE PRIME Minister, Paul Keating, should be smiling about the increase in his popularity, according to the latest polls. Both the latest Morgan Gallup poll, published in Time Australia, and the AGB Australia poll, in The Bulletin, show that the popularity of Mr Keating and his Government is on the rise. According to the AGB Australia poll, the Government is now in front of the Coalition, 44 to 43 per cent. Mr Keating is also ihe preferred PrimeMinister Minister to Opposition LeaderJohn John Hewson by 36 to 34 per cent. Reasons for the turnaround in Mr Keating s and Labor s fortunes are considered to be the result of Mr Heating's recent anti-British and pro-republican remarks, and a sense of renewal in the Government from the One Nation economic renewal package. The poll showed that Mr Keating's approval rating had risen 3 percentage points to 27 per cent, a 10 percentage-point improvement since early January. Dr Hcwson's approval fell 4 percentage points to 34 per cent, with his disapproval rating increasing 2 percentage points to 33 per cent. The Morgan Gallup poll also showed an increase in the popularity stakes for the Prime Minister and his Government, but not at the same level.
