30 Mar 1992 - Health groups back tobacco sponsorship ban Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 30 March 1992, page 2 Health groups back tobacco sponsorship ban SYDNEY: Three leading health groups have written to federal Cabinet ministers asking them to support a submission, which if recommended, would have tobacco sponsorship of sport and the arts banned by the middle of 1993. Bans coming into effect as early as July I, 1993, are part of a submission to the Federal Government's Expenditure Review Committee, details of which were leaked to the media last Friday. Government sources said the submission contained recommendations for bans on tobacco signs being used at sporting venues, the display of company logos and the naming of events and trophies after brands of cigarettes or tobacco companies. An example of this is the Winfield Cup for the NSW rugby league club premiership. Yesterday the Australian Medical Association, the National Heart Foundation and the Anti Cancer Council of Victoria, issued a statement saying they had written to ministers asking them to support the submission. The submission, to be made jointly by the Minister for Health Services, Peter Staples, and the Minister for Sport, Ros Kelly, also suggests compensation be paid to sporting organisations and is due to go before Cabinet next Friday. "The enormous social and economic impact smoking has on our community through loss of life, disability associated with smoking-related diseases and the financial cost of such illnesses is well recognised," the statement said. It said various earlier restric tions on advertising had made cigarette companies turn, in particular, to sport. "By endorsing rugby league and cricket and other major sports, they [companies] can circumvent the ban on advertising, they can get endorsement of their product by sporting heroes and they get valuable publicity," the statement said. But the Tobacco Institute of Australia counter-attacked yesterday by issuing survey results from a Morgan Research Centre Gallup poll completed last November. The institute's deputy chief executive officer, Reinier Jessurun, said the survey's results were available earlier this year but the institute wanted to wait "for an appropriate moment" to release them. The survey of 1098 people across Australia - both smokers and non-smokers - found 81 per ccnt believed tobacco sponsorship did not encourage smoking while 15 per ccnt thought it did and 4 per ccnt were undecided. The Gallup poll also found that 72 per cent of Australians said cigarette companies should be allowed to sponsor events while 24 per ccnt disagreed and 4 per cent were undecided. Mr Jessurun said the survey's results over the past two years, when there had been significant pressure from anti-smoking lobby groups, showed tobacco sponsorship of sporting and cultural events was not a factor in encouraging people to smoke.

31 Mar 1992 - Labor to win Wills: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 31 March 1992, page 1 Labor to win Wills: poll SYDNEY: Labor should retain the seat of Wills with almost the same support it enjoyed in the 1990 election, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll to be published today in Time magazine. Labor would manage 54 per cent of the vote on a two-party-preferred basis, the poll shows. It achieved 57.9 per cent in 1990. Independent Phil Cleary had 15.5 per cent, within a week of announcing his candidacy. Support for the Government has slipped 15 points from the previous survey, five weeks ago: The Liberals have dropped eight points. The telephone poll, conducted last Thursday, shows 36.5 per cent would vote Labor and 35 per cent would vote Liberal. The Liberals would re ceive 46 per cent on the two-partypreferred basis. The approval of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, has climbed 7.5 points to 40.5 per cent in Wills, 1.5 points above his national standing. Mr Keating's disapproval rating, while up 2.5 points to 43.5 per cent, now is just one point above that of the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, who went up 6.5 points.

04 Apr 1992 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 4 April 1992, page 9 i POLL Republicans nearing a majority REPUBLICANISM is approaching majority support in Australia, a Morgan Gallup Poll, published in the latest Time Australia magazine, has found. The poll, for which 1327 people were interviewed throughout Australia on the weekend of March 14-15, has found that 44 per cent favour a republic headed by an elcctcd president and, for the first time since such a poll was taken, support for the monarchy at 49 per ccnt was below 50 per cent. The survey was conducted two weeks after the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, vigorously argued the,cause of republican ism in the wake of his One Nation state ment. For many years, monarchists have formed the overwhelming majority in Australia. When the Queen was crowned in 1953, they comprised 77 per cent of the population. At the time of the dismissal of the prorepublican Whitlam Government by the then Governor-General, Sir John Kerr, in November 1975, they were down to 61 per cent, with 28 percent favouring a republic. For the next 13 years the figures remained stable, so that in 1988, the bicentennial year, 64 per cent remained monarchist and 29 per ccnt republican. Since then, public sentiment has shifted. Last July, after the formation of the Australian Republican Movement - a loose coalition of prominent people aiming for a republican Australia by the year 2000 -republican support was up to 36 per ccnt, and monarchists were down to 56 percent. The latest poll shows how the changc has accelerated. In a telephone poll conducted on March 26 with 504 electors in the inner-Melbourne electorate of Wills, Morgan Gallup has found the Federal Labor Government should comfortably retain the scat: 36:5 per cent of respondents said they would vote Labor and 35 per ccnt Liberal. The by-clcction, caused by the resigna- , tion from Parliament of the former Prime Minister Bob Hawke, will be next Saturday. Support for the Government was down 7.5 points on the previous survey, on February 25-26, but for the Liberals it was down eight points. Support for the Democrats had barely changed, up one point to 7 per cent, but Independent Phil Cleary had garnered an impressive 15.5 per ccnt support within a week of announcing his candidacy. On a two-party-preferred basis, the ALP would receive 54 per cent of the vote, easily outstripping the Liberals' 46 per ccnt. On these figures, Labor would have almost the support it had at the 1990 election - 57.9 per ccnt.

04 Apr 1992 - TOBACCO DOLLARS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 4 April 1992, page 1 Quitting cold turkey after 83 years of industry sponsorship won't be easy. Mike Taylor reports on a tidal change in sports advertising. ? N JUST a few hours in the Cabinet I room last week, the Minister for Sport, I Ros Kelly, and the Minister for Health Services, Peter Staples, succeeded in ending an 80-year relationship - the relationship between the tobacco industry and Australian sport. - Tobaccoand sport began their long association in Australia in 1909, when a British cigarette company sponsored the visit of a golfer. It never looked back. Now it cannot look forward. ! The tobacco industry, which has recently provided $40 million a year towards sports and cultural sponsorship in Australia. has been told it must stop. From 1995-96, the money will have to be found elsewhere. The searcli will not be easy. From 1995-96, Australians will no longer be witness to the Winfield Cup and Benson and Hedges cricket. Instead they ; are likely to sec the Cpca-Cola Cup and . Tooheys Cricket. Sporting administrators will have to come to terms with new, possibly less-generous benefactors. According to Mrs Kelly, the Cabinet moved for a range of reasons, but one of the most compelling was the statistic that while governments reaped $2.6 billion a year in taxes and excises from tobacco, the cost of tobacco-related health problems ex ceeded $6 billion. The Minister's data is, to say the least, contentious. The $6 billion figure quoted by her comes from a report to the Government on the costs of drug abuse in Australia. However, it attempts, among other things, to quantify the value of the loss of life to those who die and the suffering of others as a result. The data quoted by Mrs Kelly is already in the hands of the tobacco companies, and its legitimacy is certain to be challenged. The Cabinet decision runs counter also to the findings of a Roy Morgan Research Centre Pty Ltd poll this week which indicated that 72 per cent of Australians believed cigarette companies should be allowed to sponsor sporting events, the ^ arts and concerts. In an era when society well recognises the dangers of cigarette smoking, many have had trouble coming to terms with the close ties which have continued to exist between tobacco companies and top-level sports administrators. It has seemed a con tradiction. The answer to the continuing relationship has been tradition, long understanding and the belief that the issues of health, advertising and sponsorship can be sepa rated. The view of the sports administrators can probably best be exemplified by the general manager of the NSW Rugby League, John Quayle. MrQuayle makes it quite clear the League's dealings with Rothmans in the Winfield Cup is about a lot more than money. . Indeed it would be fair to say that Mr Quayle and his fellow rugby league administrators believe they owe a large part of their code's current popularity and viability to the generosity of Rothmans over the past 20 years. It is easy to forget amid these halcyon days for the Rugby League that a mere 20 years ago the code was in deep trouble and in serious decline in the popularity stakes. "People don't realise that cigarettes were responsible for writing the coaching books, delivering the code into the schools and keeping us viable when no other sponsor was interested," Mr Quayle said. He stresses that the relationship preceded the League's recent strong popularity and describes the sponsorship as "a great relationship which did not require any commitment from us as to the promotion of cigarette smoking". t Indeed. Mr Quayle and the NSW Rugby League are not supporters of smoking. Their emphasis on high-level fitness for players runs counter to what is known about smoking, and he stresses this ract. Despite his disappointment at the Cabinet decision to end sporting sponsorships by tobacco companies, Mr Quayle was well aware that such a decision was likely. He and the tobacco companies had been fighting a losing battle for at leas'., a decade. Indeed some cynics might go so far as to suggest that the tougher the anti-smoking lobby made it for tobacco companies, the easier life became for sporting administrators. In the absence of television and printmedia advertising, big-venue sports promotions became virtually the only game in town for cigarette manufacturers. It is no coincidence that cigarette companies are probably the largest sponsors of sporting events in Australia. Sporting and cultural sponsorships have represented their last promotional bastion. Under relentless attack from the antimoking lobby over the past two decades, : he cigarette companies had been forced to vacate virtually all forms of promotion and advertising except billboards. Sporting arenas represented mightv big billboards. : An industry the size of Australia's cigarette industry would normally spend up to $40 million a year on advertising and promotion. In the case of Rothmans, Benson and Hedges and W. D. and H. O. Wills that budget has been almost exclusively directed towards sporting and cultural pro motions. They may not have been permitted to advertise their cigarettes on television, but millions of viewers every year were left in absolutely no doubt about their existence as the television cameras followed the football or cricket action and panned past Winfield or Benson and Hedges billboards. r But to suggest that this represented defacto advertising was to offend the cigarette companies and their lobby group, the -Tobacco Institute of Australia. They main tained such promotion did not represent advertising via the back door. It was, they said, "corporate imaging". There was always more to the cigarette companies' sporting sponsorships than mere big bucks. Just ask the rugby league and cricketing administrators and they would tell you that the sort of support their sponsors gave could not be replicated by government departments and instrumentalities. It could only be replaced by another, highly-committed big sponsor. What you find as you investigate the question of sporting sponsorships in Australia is that the relationship between' the cigarette companies and sporting officialdom ran far deeper than big money. It involved trust - the knowledge that the sponsors would deliver on extras ranging from organisational and administrative support to tracksuits for junior players. Even at what appears to be the 11 th hour for the tobacco companies, they are unlikely to give up without a fight. A High Court challenge is a virtual certainty oncc the exact tenor of the Commonwealth Government's legislation is known, and there are overseas precedents for such challenges. The tobacco industry is already armed with a decision by the Quebec Superior Court which deemed a similar ban in Canada to be unconstitutional and a violation of freedom of expression. The tobacco lobby will not lie down without a fight, and at the forefront of the campaign to maintain a foothold is the chief executive officer of the Tobacco Institute of Australia, John St Vincent Welch. John Welch, boasting a long background in industry advocacy and lobbying, struggled throughout last week to put his industry's position, but was quick to establish the ground rules by which he would have liked to have seen the battle fought - the separation of sport sponsorship from the notion of advertising. Speaking before Wednesday's fateful Cabinet decision Mr Welch said, "I think there is a big difference in the companies' minds between advertising and sponsorship and most of our avenues for advertising have been eliminated. "We see advertising as a means by which already committed smokers of that brand are , reassured, and a means by which the various brands attract already committed smokers away from a particular brand. "Sponsorship is seen by the companies as a way of corporate imaging, and there are a number of studies and statements which recognise that sponsorship isn't about brand-swapping or about convincing people they should take up smoking as a pastime. "The cigarette companies, despite the attacks on them, are corporate citizens, employers and taxpayers and are involved in the manufacture, distribution and sale of a legal product and smoking is still a legal pastime." Further, Mr Welch makes the point that because cigarette manufacture and smoking remain legal pastimes, the state and federal governments are extracting $2.6 billion a year in the form of taxes and excise. In the wake of the Cabinet decision, Mr Welch was quick to point to the hypocrisy of the Government's position - its preparedness to extract taxes from the tobacco industry while denying sporting organisations the right to extract sponsorships. The tobacco industry has known for at least the past half decade that its dominance of sport sponsorships would not be allowed to go unchallenged for long. For this reason it developed a report titled Tobacco Sponsorship and Incidental Advertising. The report was a bid to put paid to claims that a link existed between the glimpses wc sec of cigarettc billboards at sporting venues and the propensity for young people to take up smoking. The executive summary of that report kicks off with the bald statement, "The Australian Tobacco Industry believes there are no valid grounds for a ban on the telecasting of incidental advertising associated with tobacco company sponsorship of sport. "The claim has been made that children are influenced to take up smoking by exposure to brand name signs and logos during telecast sporting events. "One brand singled out for criticism in this regard has been Marlboro, particularly over its sponsorship of activities in the Australian Grand Prix series. "Indeed the Marlboro brand has been the vehicle for a number of other widely promoted sponsorships during the 1980s, including the Marlboro Australian Open Tennis Championships, motorcycle racing and horse racing. "However, Marlboro's Australian market share has fallen from 7.6 per cent in 1980 to 1.9 percent in 1990, and its strongest smoker age segment is 30-39 years." This would represent compelling evidence in favour of the smoking lobby except for the fact that for every such survey that Mr Welch can quote, his opponents on the other side of the debate can quote equally compelling contrary evidence. Indeed, as soon as the institute released a public-opinion poll this week suggesting most Australians did not object to cigarette companies sponsoring sport, both the Aus tralian Medical Association and the Victorian Health Promotion Foundation attacked their findings. It was indicative of the tenor of whole debate. The Victorian Health Promotion Foundation (VicHealth) produced its own survey and claimed it showed that the Australian Community had overwhelmingly rejected tobacco sponsorship of sports and the arts. The chief executive officer of VicHealth, Rhonda Galbally, said that of 1000 people surveyed only 7 per cent had said they would prefer to see cigarette brands sponsoring sport and 86 per cent favoured the foundation sponsoring sport over tobacco. "The overwhelming majority would like to see tobacco sponsorship out of sport," she said. Victoria represents the pace-setter for those who want to see tobacco sponsorship out of mainstream domestic sport. It was Victoria where the Government legislated to remove tobacco sponsorships, and where the Government picked up the tab through the Victorian Health Promotion Foundation. Instead of cigarette company logos' on their football guernseys, today's AFL players wear the "Quit" logo - the trademark of the anti-smoking lobby in sport sponsorship. Not surprisingly, Ms Galbally claims the ousting of cigarette sponsorship in Victorian sport to have been a success. "The Victorian experience clearly demonstrates that sport can develop and prosper without money from the tobacco companies," she said last week. "The major sporting codes in Victoria which have given up tobacco sponsorship or indeed made the decision to refuse to take it up includes the Australian Football League, horse racing, basketball, tennis and soccer. "In addition, over 100 other sports that were never considered to be high profile enough by the cigarette companies to attract their sponsorship, are also leading the charge in Australia to show that sport is an inherently healthy activity, and as such does not need tobacco dollars to develop." Should we be surprised that the Tobacco Institute disputes Ms Galbally's claims, and backs up its counter-claims with a report compiled by the Economic Studies and Strategies Unit of Price Waterhousc, in Canberra? That study suggests that the ways in which the health foundations arc funded and operate raise "scopc for community attention to issues of good budget management, accountability and equity". The major question of equity raised by the report is that the activities of the foundations are largely funded by tobacco sales levy revenue. However, it more particularly concentrated on the cost and effectiveness of VicHealth, claiming it was costing Victorian taxpayers around $25 million to $30 million a year on top of $12.7 million already spent on sport, art and health. It goes on 'to suggest that while VicHealth has been beneficial to the interests of sports and arts administrators, it has sought to force sports into dropping tobacco sponsorships; reduced the role and effectiveness of the State Department of Sport; and inflated the price of sports spon sorship. One of the most devastating critics of tobacco sponsorships of sport and culture was the Australian Medical Association which bccamc increasingly strident in its demands that the Government act to impose a total ban. When, finally, the Cabinet did move the AMA was glowing in its praise of the Go vernment and scathing in its assessment of the tobacco industry. The secretary-general of the AMA, Allan Passmore, said the Cabinet decision had "saved the lives of children who would otherwise have died of tobacco-related ill nesses. . "The merchants of death who run the tobacco companies have had a double-0 licence for far too long - a licence to kill," Dr Passmore said. "This is a great restriction on that licence. They will still be able to sell their product but the slaughter of the innoccnts in which they have been engaged for such a long time will be greatly dimin ished." When the tobacco companies inevitably mount their challenge to the Government's ban on their sports sponsorships, they will be doing so with an eye to recent events in Canada, where similar legislation was deemed unconstitutional. The Tobacco institute of Australia has been examining a decision by the Quebec Superior Court which overturned the Canadian ban on tobacco advertising and sponsorship deeming it to be unconstitutional and a violation of freedom of ex pression. The Canadian court found that the ban was unlikely to achieve its stated purpose of reducing tobacco consumption and said there was no evidence that advertising, as such, entailed a danger to public health. ; The court described the ban, in part, as "a piece of moral legislation constituting a form of censorship and social cngineenng incompatible with the tnie essence of a free and democratic society". ?; Despite the precision with which the Australian legislation is likely to be drafted and the close scrutiny likely to be given by the Attorney-General's Department, the Canadian precedent is unlikely to be ignored by the High Court of Australia. \ It is unlikely to escape the attention>of our High Court judges that tobacco Remains a legal substance and that smoking has not been outlawed. I In terms of what our sporting administrators will do next, it is of considerable significance that neither the NSW Rugby League nor the Australian Cricket Board have yet written oflf their associations wuh tobacco companies. I It is highly unlikely they will seek out new sponsors until they are certain that the Federal Government has achieved its aim. It seems tobacco dollars are almost as addictive as the weed itself. The general manager of the NSW Rugby League, John Quayle, left, opposed the ban. The Minister for Sport, Ros Kelly, right, favoured the ban.

08 Apr 1992 - Independent in good spot to take Wills Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 8 April 1992, page 20 Independent in good spot to take Wills MELBOURNE: The Federal Opposition renewed yesterday its attack on the prominent independent in the Wills by-election, Phil Cleary, as an opinion poll put the football identity in a good position to wrest the seat from Labor. The Morgan Gallup Poll for Channel Seven showed support for Mr Cleary at 29 per cent, indicating he could win Saturday's ballot for former Prime Minister Bob Hawke's old scat on Democrat preferences. Taken on Monday night, the survey of202 Wills voters showed support for Mr Cleary was up 14.5 per cent on a poll taken 11 days ago, while Labor support had dropped 8.5 per ccnj. Liberal support was 33 per cent, down 2 per cent on the earlier poll. Details of the poll were released as the row over Mr Cleary's "independence" heated up, with Coalition frontbencher Andrew Peacock repeating claims Mr Cleary was an ALP "stooge". But Mr Cleary, rejected the charge, and his solicitor demanded a retraction from both Mr Peacock and The Australian newspaper, which published the allegation last week. Mr Cleary told reporters he had never been a member of the ALP and had no intention of joining. "The voters of Wills should ask themselves why the Liberals are so intent on discrediting me - it shows they obviously think I have a good j chance of winning." The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, bought into the dispute yesterday, dubbing Mr Cleary an "independent Labor" candidate. "I've said from the beginning it's for Mr Cleary to demonstrate where he stands," Dr Hewson said.

08 Apr 1992 - Hewson not popular, offers no hope: PM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 8 April 1992, page 4 Hewson not popular, offers no hope: PM By CHRIS UHLMANN The Leader of the Opposition, John Hcwson, is falling in the opinion polls because he oficrs Australians no hope, according to the Prime Minister, Paul Keating. The latest Time Morgan Gallup Poll shows the ALP up half a point on the previous poll to 40 per cent and the Coalition down one point to 44.5 per cent. The Saulwick opinion poll, published by the Age and Sydney Morning Herald yesterday, showed Labor had halved the Coalition's lead in the past month. Support for the Coalition parties now stood at 45 per cent, ahead of the ALP by nine points. A month ago their lead was 18 points. Mr Keating and the Minister for Employment, Education and Training, Kim Bcazlcy, campaigned for Labor's candidate in the Wills by-electjon, Bill Kardamitsis, yesterday. "[Dr Hewson) wants to talk about unemployment but he doesn't want to talk about TAFE and training," Mr Keating said. "He wants to talk about unemployment, but he doesn't want to talk about the National Rail Network and rebuilding it." Dr Hewson's policies were now working against him. He had tied himself to the mast of a goods-and-services tax. "And as people come to understand that it means a 15 per ccnt tax on tKcir necessities of life, and a heavy tax on their lifestyle, and a heavier tax on the lifestyle of Australians, then the Liberal Party and he arc suffering accordingly," Mr Keating said. The Wills by-clection would be a battle but Labor's fortunes had improved. "Dr Hcwson started this campaign with a 20-point lead," Mr Keating said. "He should have been able to put this seat in his pocket with consummate ease." Dr Hcwson said the Coalition had not slipped dramatically in the polls and the results depended upon which poll was being discussal. "I mean, there arc more polls these days than we have politicians almost, so it is a bit confusing to pick any one," Dr Hewson said. Polls went up and down but the unemployment rate was still going up and that was what the Wills by-election was all about, he said. Cleory says he could win Wills. - Page 20

10 Apr 1992 - Coach Cleary leads the parties Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 10 April 1992, page 3 Coach Cleary leads the parties From TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent, in Melbourne The Liberal Party looks certain to be the big loser in tomorrow's by-elcction in Wills, but there is likely to be no good news for Labor, cither. The main Independent candidate, Coburg Football Club coach Phil Cieary, is firming as the favourite to sweep the seat. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll carried out for the Seven Network shows that Mr Cieary has the support of 32 per cent of voters, up 3 per cent from a poll earlier this week. Labor's Bill Kardamitsis also Dr Hewson: putting on a brave face had 32 per cent, up 4 per cent on the previous poll. But support for the Liberals' John Delacretaz had plunged 7 percentage points to just 26 per cent. The poll showed that on a two-party preferred basis, Mr Cleary would walk away with the seat 56-44. He is set to benefit from preferences from both Labor and the Australian Democrats. Such a result would be a major blow to the Liberal Party, and though Liberal campaigners are admitting privately that their candidate has virtually no hope, the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, was putting on a brave face yesterday. Dr Hewson, who has been campaigning in Wills every day this week and will be back tomorrow, denied a Liberal loss in the electorate would be of concern in his national campaign to win government He said the major campaign would be "on a head-to-head basis between Paul Keating and myself", but the focus on Wills had been diffused by "just about any extraneous issue that's come along". The Prime Minister, who also visited Wills yesterday, said he had consistently said it would be a tough battle. He said a loss by the Liberals would be much more serious for Dr Hewson than a loss by Labor would be for him (Mr Keating). "John Hewson started this 20 points in front," Mr Keating said. "He should have put this in his pocket weeks ago. "The fact that it is a contest means that we have campaigned strongly." But Dr Hewson, in a clear attempt to limit the damage of a loss tomorrow, went out of his way to claim that the Liberals had been behind in the polls since the campaign began. Wills not likely to influence next poll. - Page 8

11 Apr 1992 - Hawke backs Cleary, and ALP Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 11 April 1992, page 1 Hawke backs Cleary, and ALP Independent 'a decent bloke' By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent, in Melbourne Independent candidate Phil Cleary and the Labor Party's Bill Kardamitsis remain the two strongest contenders in today's by-election for Wills - and the man who vacated the seat, the former Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, believes either man would be a suitable successor. Mr Hawke gave Mr Cleary a vote of confidence yesterday, describing him as "a good bloke" who would be a good representative if Labor didn't win. But speaking on a radio program, Mr Hawke said he hoped voters would support Labor. Though he could not agree with Mr Cleary's economic policies, Mr Hawke said he believed the Independent was a decent person. The Liberal Party's candidate, John Delacretaz, appears to have lost significant ground on the front-runners, despite last-minute electioneering in Wills yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson. Two of the latest polls have Mr Delacretaz at only 26 per cent. Mr Cleary had 30 per ccnt against Mr Kardamitsis's 32 per cent in yesterday's Herald-Sun Newspoll, and both had 32 per cent in Thursday's Channel 7 Morgan Gallup Poll. On these figures, Mr Cleary would be likely to win on preferences. Today's by-election is complicated by several factors: a record number of candidates, requiring voters to number their preferences from one to 22. The Electoral Commission has tried to explain the voting system by distributing booklets to every' household in the electorate, written in several languages because of the high ethnic population. But officials believe there will still be a high informal vote. To further complicate matters, the Labor Party mistakenly distributed a pamphlet this week, written in Greek, which advised voters to give their second preferences to the Liberal Party. Labor or ganiscrs, who had settled on Mr Cleary to receive the party's preference, were frantically trying to correct the mistake yesterday. The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, was absent from Wills yesterday, but Dr Hewson spent the morning walking among shoppers in Puckle Street, Moonee Ponds, and later had a beer in a local pub. Both Dr Hewson and Mr Kardamitsis tried to portray a vote for Mr Cleary as a vole for a voice that would cry from the wilderness in Parliament. They both exhorted voters to support a major party. Dr Hewson claimed that Mr Cleary would vote with the Government on many issues. But Mr Cleary said that a vote for him would "send a message to the major parties" that they had lost their way. How the Liberals blew it in Wills, Tony Wright tells. - Page 9. TOMORROW: Tony Wright's analysis and figures on the crucial count.

11 Apr 1992 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 11 April 1992, page 9 I*** WATCH Labor taking it up to the Liberals SUPPORT for the Keating Govern ment rose slightly late last month, a' Morgan Gallup Poll, published in the latest Time Australia, has found. The poll, conducted with 3270 voters interviewed throughout Australia on the weekends of March 21-22 and 28-29, found Labor was favoured by 40 per ceni of those polled, up half a point, while backing for the Liberal-National Coalition was at 44.5 per cent, down one point. The poll was conducted as the major parties debated their differences over tariff policy in the lead-up lo today's Wills by-election. On these figures, Labor would run a very close contest. The result would be closer than at any time since July 1990. Prime Minister Paul Keating's approval rating was 40 per cent, while his disapproval rating dropped for the first time sincc February, from 48 per cent to 47 per cent. The Opposition Leader John Hcwson's approval rating was unchanged, at 50 per ccnt, as was his disapproval rating at 35 per ccnt. On the question of who would make the better Prime Minister, 42 per cent preferred Mr Keating, down a point, while support for Dr Hcwson remained unchanged at 44 per cent. .Another poll, conducted by AGB Australia and published in the latest Bulletin magazine, also found the Prime Minister's approval rating had increased, two points, as had his standing with women. The Bulletin poll, in which 2032 electors were interviewed face-to-face in late March, found on voting intent that NSW continued to be the stronghold for the ALP, 46 per ccnt, running ahead of the Coalition's 40 per ccnt. Queensland voters have increased their support for the Government, 47 per cent against Coalition's 43 per ccnt, while in Western Australia, the. Government had closed to within five percentage points of the Coalition, 41 per cent to 46 per cent. The Bulletin Poll also found Mr Keating slipping as prefered PM. ' Whereas Mr Keating held a two-point lead over Dr Hewson in the last Bulletin poll, he now trailed by a point, 37 per cent to 38 per ccnt. Dr Hewson leads Mr Keating in Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia and the Prime Minister leads in NSW and Queensland. They are equally approved of among male voters, 38 per ccnt, while 38 per ccnt of women polled prefered Dr Hewson to Mr Keating, 35 per ccnt. Overall, Mr Keating's approval rating was up 12 points since his very low early ratings as Prime Minister back in January.

18 Apr 1992 - Support for ALP up three points Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 18 April 1992, page 9 Support for ALP up three points IF A SENATE clcction had been held last month, support for Labor would have been 37 per cent, up three points since February, compared with 45 per cent, down three points, for the Liberal-National Coalition, according to a Morgan Gallup poll published in the latest Time A uslralia. The poll of 12,325 voters interviewed throughout Australia in February and March showed the Australian Democrats had 7 per cent support, down half a point, and 11 per cent, up half a point, supported other parties and independent candidates. This means that if a full or half-Senate election had been held in February or March, the balance of power in the Senate would have been held by minor parties and independents. In Western Australia, a Morgan poll of 1088 voters showed that support for the Labor Government had risen four points to 35 per cent in February-March, and the Liberal and National parties' support had fallen five points to 49.5 per cent. This contrasts with the Bulletin's AGB Australia poll of 659 voters, also conducted in February and March, which showed a much more even spread, with 43 per cent saying they would vote for the incumbent Labor Party and 45 per cent for the Coalition. In the Morgan poll, the Australian Democrats had 6 per cent support, up one point, while the Bulletin showed 3 per cent support. On the question of preferred premier, the Morgan poll found that 64 per cent, up seven points to a new high, had opted for the Premier, Carmen Lawrence, and 24 per cent, down five, chose the the Opposition Leader, Barry MacKinnon. In South Australia, a Morgan poll of 1184 showed that support for the state Government had slipped a point to its lowest level in a year with 34 per cent. Support for the Coalition remained unchanged at 48 per cent. On the question of preferred premier, an unchanged 54 per cent opted for the incumbent John Bannon and 24 per cent, down four points to a year-low rating, opted for Liberal leader Dale Baker.

20 Apr 1992 - Reith: we won't shift Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 20 April 1992, page 1 No need to change GST, or tariffs The Coalition will not budge in its commitment to introducing a goods-and-services tax despite evidence that it would win wider community support without the tax, according to the shadow treasurer, Peter Reith. He rejected any movement in the Opposition's zero-tariff target, another policy that has come under fire from within the Coalition and among some of its supporters in the past week. "I think we would risk our credibility if we were not prepared to take on all of the issues that this country needs to confront... this is the time for, 1 think, the political process to put to the Australian people a set of alternatives that really are directed to the problem," he said on the Nine network's Sunday program yesterday. "We are not budging an inch on this proposal nor the other, proposals contained within Fightback. "We know they're right, the Government knows they're right. "Keating himself was in favour of some of the broader elements of the Fightback a few years ago. "It is clearly right and I think the emphasis now has to be on getting that message to the Australian community, being prepared to be aggressive in selling it and of course to expose what we have from the Government, which is nothing more than a scare campaign." A Saulwick poll of 500 Victorians £ We are not budging an inch on this proposal nor the other proposals contained within Fightback 9 - Peter Reith published in The Sunday Age yesterday showed that the Liberals' 22-pcrcentage-point lead over Labor would widen to almost 30 if the Coalition dumped the GST. The poll showed also that almost half of all respondents, 45.7 per cent, believed the Fightback package had been sold poorly. Mr Reith said, "I'm in fact encouraged by that poll, which shows that support for Fightback's actually gone up over the period since it's been released, but I still think we've got a long way to go in explaining the benefits of Fightback, in getting across to people a very simple message about its benefits." His comments respond to growing concern among some Coalition members about the electoral appeal of the GST in the wake of the Wills by-elec tion. Mr Reith said it was important for the Opposition to stick by the GST proposal. "I think its worth doing and portraying what's right for this country," he said. "Sure, people would prefer not to have the GST if they can also have the benefits. "The fact is that Fightback is a package of reforms and the GST pays for the abolition of seven taxes, the slashing of income tax by one third and a lot of other benefits which are contained within it." The GST would benefit business by shifting the tax burden from inputs to consumers, and stronger businesses would employ more people and lead to a sustained economic recovery. Mr Reith rejected internal criticism of the Coalition's zero-tariff policy, saying protection had been a "great failure" which had cost jobs. "We are not budging on the protection issue and that's the end of the matter," he said. Stay firm on tariffs plan, says Dawkins. - Page 3.

21 Apr 1992 - Popularities declining in all directions — new poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 21 April 1992, page 2 Popularities declining in all directions - new poll Support for the federal Labor Government has declined for the first time since Paul Keating became Prime Minister in December, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll, to be published in today's Time maga zine Opposition leader John Hewson's approval rating declined again too, far from its January peak, 62 per cent Dr Hewson's approval rating declined by 4 per cent to 46 per cent, and his disapproval rating increased by 6 per cent to 41 per cent; 13 per cent were undecided. However, the Coalition would have beaten Labor comfortably bad an election been held in the first half of April. Labor's support was down by 1.5 per cent to 38.5 per cent The LiberalNational Coalition gained, its support up by 1 per cent to 45.5 per cent Mr Keating's approval rating remained steady at 40 per cent but his disapproval rating was up by 1 per cent to 48 per cent; 12 per cent were undecided. On the question of preferred prime minister, Mr Keating and Dr Hewson dead-heated: 44 per cent each. The Australian Democrats' support increased by 0.5 per ccnt to 6 per cent. Support for other parties and independent candidates stayed steady at 10 per cent.

21 Apr 1992 - IN BRIEF Confidence on the way up Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 21 April 1992, page 2 IN BRIEF Confidence the way up Consumer confidence has risen to hs highest point in nearly Vh years, according a Morgan Gallup poll to be published in today's Time Australia magazine. The poll says consumer confidence rose 9.2 points in early April on the previous month's figure of 105.4 points. But this was still down on comparable figures taken during the 1982-83 economic recession when consumer confidence reached a low of 75.2 points in November, 1982. Confidence rose 34.1 points since the present recession's low of 71.3 points, recorded in December, 1990. Pilot not fazed ADELAIDE: A pilot made an emergency landing in Adelaide yesterday after an advertising banner tangled in his plane's undercarriage, according to police. The pilot had landed his Cessna safely at Parafield Airport, north Adelaide, then, after a check to make sure his plane was not damaged, he had flown off again to pick up another banner, police said. Nutrition conference Australia will be host at an international nutrition conference next year which will include discussion on Aboriginal health. The 15th International Congress on Nutrition, to be held in Adelaide next September, will also examine national food and nutrition policies and disease prevention and treatment. Winds cut power MELBOURNE: Thousands of Melbourne householders were left without power on Sunday night as strong winds lashed the city at almost lOOkm/h. The State Electricity Commission said about 12 substations malfunctioned right across the city during the night as windswept trees shorted electrical connections and cut supplies to more than 2000 homes. Airport supported SYDNEY: The NSW Government needed to support the fast-track development of a second Sydney airport as part of its bid for the 2000 Olympics, Liverpool mayor Mark Latham said yesterday. "The development of an international airport at Badgerys Creek, which will double Sydney's airport capacity for overseas visitors, should be an essential part of the Olympics bid," he said in a statement. The Greiner Gavemment, while the strongest advocate of the third runway at Mascot, had been silent on the need to fast-track Badgerys Creek.

22 Apr 1992 - Tough first day for Keating Suharto call for respect Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 22 April 1992, page 1 Tough first day for Keating Suharto call for respect From ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent, in Jakarta President Suharto has delivered a strong reminder to Australia that Indonesia will not tolerate criticism of its affairs. He made his comments in front of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, at a welcoming banquet at the Presidential Palace on the first day of Mr Keating's first trip overseas as Prime Minster. President Suharto said Mr Keating's visit was a concrete expression of the Australian Government's attitude to Indonesia. However, the new sense of friendship had to be realised by adhering to the principle of mutual respect and not interfering in the affairs of the other country. Indonesia had problems which other countries could not understand. He did not refer to the Dili massa cre. However, he said Indonesia would occasionally stumble and his country was prepared to accept criticism given in a friendly manner but not criticism aimed at exaggerating differences or interfering in Indonesia's internal affairs. Every nation had its own dignity which could not be bargained with. He suggested that developing countries were hampered by the media, which exaggerated events and spread news widely. Mr Keating heaped glowing praise on President Suharto, describing him tin an important sense, each of us is the other's best test of how effectively we will be able to deal with the social and political diversity, and the rapid change, which will mark our region and the world in the 1990s1 - Paul Keating as the region's undisputed elder statesman. Mr Keating said Australia's identity in the 1990s would be emphatically different: it would positively engage in the region. Highlighting the theme he has been pushing for Australia to become more oriented towards Asia, he said Australia and Indonesia had more in com mon than suggested by the twp' countries' different histories and pdltures. / However, a poll published as Mr Keating departed suggested He faces a battle to convince the community of his message. The Saulwick poll found that 69 per cent of Australians saw their country as separate from Asia. Only 29 per cent believed Australia was part of the region. Mr Keating said the substantive links between the two countries had allowed a frank dialogue, especially "following the tragic events in East Timor last November". This was the only reference in his speech to the Dili massacre. However, Mr Keating earlier took up the issue with the Indonesian Foreign Minister, Ali Alatas. Mr Keating pointed to Timorese people facing criminal charges after the massacre but Mr Alatas maintained that under Indonesian law, it was a criminal offence to incite separatism or rebellion. The highlight of Mr Keating's fourday visit to Indonesia is today's formal talks with President Suharto. Mr Keating set the tone for the discussions in last night's speech, saying he hoped both countries continued to make the bilateral relationship broader, deeper and more stable. "In an important sense, each of us is the other's best test of how effectively we will be able to deal with the social and political diversity, and the rapid change, which will mark our ' region and the world in the 1990s," he said. "My visit may be seen as a signal of Australia's determination to pass that test." Mr Keating is expected to give a wide-ranging speech today at a foreign affairs forum and have lunch with economic ministers.

25 Apr 1992 - Federal ALP suffers popularity slump Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 25 April 1992, page 9 Federal ALP suffers popularity slump A MORGAN poll, published in ihc latest Time Australia magazine, has found support for the Federal Labor Government has fallen for the first time since Paul Keating took over as Prime Minister in December. In the poll, conducted with 2503 electors throughc -t Australia, face-to-facc on the weekends of April 4-5 and 11-12, Labor's support was 38.5 percent, down one-and-a-half points, while support for the Liberal-National Opposition rose one point to 45.5 per cent. The Australian Democrats recorded 6 per cent support, up half a point, and 10 per cent continued to favour other parties and independent candidates. If an election had been held in early April, the Coalition would have won, according to the poll. Mr Keating's approval rating remained steady at 40 per cent but more disapproved of the way he was handling his job - up a point at 48 per cent -and 12 per cent of respondents were undecided. For the Leader of the Opposition, John Hcwson, the approval figures are worrying. In the wake of his accusation that Mr Keating's faction, the NSW Right, was "the nearest thing this country has had to the Mafia in decades", his approval rating was down four points to 46 per cent and his disapproval figure up six points to 41 per cent. Thirteen per cent were undecided. In January, Dr Hewson had a 62 per cent approval rating. For the first time in his prime-ministership, Mr Keating has equalled Dr Hcwson as preferred PM on 44 per ccnt. Twelve per cent named someone else or could not say. IN EARLY April, consumer confi dcncc in Australia was up 9.2 points on the previous month to 105.4 points, the highest rating in almost thrce-and-ahalf years. The Morgan poll, conducted with 1295 people facc-to-facc on the weekend of April 4-5, showed the highest average rating for a year over the past two decades was 118.6 points in 1985 at the height of the economic boom. The second-highest was 112.1 in 1973. The average annual figure for each of the past three years has been in the '80s but for the four months of 1992, the figure is 97.8. A comparison of recent consumer confidence figures with the 1982-83 recession suggests that consumers perceive the present recession to be deeper and longer. During the 1882-83 recession, consumer confidence fell to 75.2 points in November 1982 but then, over the next 12 months, climbed 31.2 points. In the present recession, consumer confidence bottomed at 71.3 in December 1990 and it has risen 34.1 points in the 16 months since.

26 Apr 1992 - Electorate sees through Keating's pyrotechnics Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 26 April 1992, page 8 Electorate sees through Keating's pyrotechnics RIGHT BY DAVID KEMP PAUL Keating's transpar ent con trick to try to seize control of the political agenda, his fast-fading One Nation statement, has clearly been seen by the electorate for what it is. Last week's Saulwick poll showed that only 17.7 per cent of respondents thought that Australia would be better off under the Keating statement as compared with almost 40 per cent under John Hewson's Fightback package. The blatant excesses of the 1980s for which we are paying and will continue to pay a heavy price are all too fresh in people's minds for them to seriously entertain another fastspending round of buy now, pay later. In the milder recession of the early 1980s, Labor embarked on a job-creation scheme without any attempt at structural reform. It claimed credit for creating thousands of jobs, but cach job cost around $70,000 in foreign debt - the debt that is now oppressing the country and making it that more difficult to climb out of recession. It is a tired and discredited formula to which Mr Keating has returned, but this time his projected jobs creation will cost $109,000 m foreign debt each. Clearly, no amount of slick public relations and political rhetoric has been able to divert attention away from the fundamental flaw of One Nation: that it is unfunded. "Where's the money coming from?" is a question that will (rightly) be asked many limes this year over the Keating promises. Certainly, these promises were regarded with deep scepticism by the voters in the Wills by-election who confirmed the perception that not only is the Prime Minister unelectable but that his policies are unsaleable. Mr Keating is now in the position of having to defend his Government's inaction in the face of John Hewson's Fightback. Why is he intent on retaining the job-stifling payroll tax, a powerful disincentive to employ people? And then there are the vexed questions of fuel tax, sales tax, compulsory superannuation contributionsand and other taxes which impose burdensome charges on busi ness. The overriding issue at present, and the issue that will continue to dominate what is effectively an election year, is how to get people off the dole queues and back to work. To put it simply, there is no mystery about job creation. It is a logical by-product of economic growth. \ The managing director of one of Australia's most successful companies, MIM, Norman Fussell, recently put it this way: "The debate in Australia today should not really be about jobs, because employment is a derived demand. You don't set out to create jobs; you set out to achieve economic growth, and that produces jobs. And achievi ing economic growth in Australia is all to do with making our industries more competitive, ! because our salvation lies in competing successfully in world, not domestic markets." WE IN the Coalition parties believe we have addressed this problem and thrown down the challenge. What the Fightback package does most comprehensively (and what One Nation does not even address) is to eliminate most of the inhibiting imposts on business that are standing in the way of recovery and growth. With business freed, economic growth will follow, and with economic growth comes jobs. Despite the Government's flourishing of statistics in parliament, Labor has done little to further the much-needed process of micro reform that is holding the country back and blocking its international competitiveness. No amount of smooth talking can hide the fact that Labor's mates, especially in the trade unions, arc applying the brake. No matter how many more promises Mr Keating makes, and no matter how many more versions of One Nation he releases, life under another Labor Government will be substan tially the same, only worse as Australia's international position sinks even further. Labor is organisationally incapable of seeing through the structural reforms that will make Australia competitive. Mr Keating's advisers know this, hence the strategy they have-devised for their manufactured leader who is programmed to light a series of grass fires, ranging from republicanism to Britain's role in World War II. Certainly, these tactics have won media attention, but the people still remember with awful clarity who engineered the recession, who promised better times that were never delivered, and then told us all the recession (which he was the last in the land to acknowledge) was the bitter medicine we had to have. Mr Keating once mentioned that he would one day "throw the switch to vaudeville", a light-hearted remark that nevertheless betrays a deep and I caustic cynicism about the elec , toratc. The irony is that the .electorate displays a similar attitude toward Mr Keating. . Mr Keating undermined his predecessor with the promise that he would be the one to dent the Coalition's Fightback' package. Instead, One Nation is sinking without trace. An increasingly suspicious electorate will now rightly press the Prime Minister for answers that he has failed to give on a range of issues that are crucial to our future, including tax reform, micro reform, incentives for business, and the muchneeded deregulation of higher education. Of course, they will not get them, but in their place wilt be another bout of bluster and breast-beating all of which has been seen and heard before. Mr Keating has shortchanged the nation with his lamentable One Nation packagc, and is now trying to divert attention by his three-ring circus. The electorate, as Wills demonstrated, is in no mood for prime-ministerial pyrotechnics in place of policies of real sub stance.

05 Dec 1987 - Judicial inquiry findings a blow to Canada's PM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 December 1987, page 6 Judicial inquiry findings a blow to Canada's PM | From PETER BENESH, in Toronto The Canadian Prime Minister, Mr Mulroney, whose Conservative Government's popularity level is a mere 25 per cent in a Gallup Poll, suffered another blow to his credibility on Thursday when a judicial inquiry found one of his most trusted ministers guilty of 14 overt acts of conflict of interest. Mr Justice William Parker reported to the Government that the former Minister for Industry, Mr Sinclair Stevens, in whom Mr Mulroney had expressed complete trust, had deliberately used his position as a minister for personal gain. The Opposition said the responsibility was as much Mr Mulroney's for his failure to monitor the ministers he appoints. The allegations about Mr Stevens's extracurricular activities were investigated for a year by Judge Parker's inquiry. The case came to light in May 1986 after a newspaper reported that Mr Stevens's wife had borrowed $2.6 million (interest-free) from a company also doing business with Mr Stevens's Department of Industry. Mr Mulroney ducked questions about the judicial finding of his former minister's culpability but, when the inquiry was launched in 1986, Mr Mulroney had insisted that Mr Stevens would be fully vindicated and would return to Cabinet." Judge Parker said Mr Stevens had shown "complete disregard for the standards of conduct expccted of pub lic office-holders." Judge Parker did not recommend criminal charges against Mr Stevens, but he urged the Government to redraft its code of ethics to make conflicts of interest not just immoral but also illegal, and subject to criminal charges. With that admonition echoing on the Opposition benches in the House of Commons, Mr Mulroney's office issued a statement promising that it would act by early 1988 to bring in a new code of ethics. That code would require full public disclosure by ministers and their wives of their assets and holdings. The ethics package is expected to be put into place in time for Mr Mulroncy to use it as a campaign springboard for the election expected in mid or late 1988. But in the meantime two other prominent members of Mr Mulroney's Government will have to face justice. Another former minister faces charges of fraud in a deal involving the sale of land to a defencc company with a major government contract, and a highprofile MP faces charges of influencepeddling.

16 Jan 1986 - Polls favour Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 16 January 1986, page 1 Polls favour Labor The Labor party has made inroads in Tasmania and strengthened its position in Western Australia leading up to elections in both States, the latest Morgan Gallup polls, published in The Bulletin yesterday showed. And in NSW, the Premier, Mr Wran, has recovered to be four points ahead of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Greiner.

18 Apr 1985 - Poll favours Opposition Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 18 April 1985, page 7 1 Poll favours Opposition SYDNEY: The NSW Opposition parties would have won an election if it had been held last month, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin yesterday. Support for the Liberal Party-Country Party coalition was up two percentage points on February to 46 per cent. Support for the Government was down one percentage point to 43 per cent. The approval rating of the Premier, Mr Wran, was 34 per cent, equalling his lowest rating of last January. The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Greiner, had a rating of 53 per cent -, up two percentage points on the February figure. Mr Greiner has been ahead of the Premier in approval ratings since March last year when the last State election was held, and won by Mr Wran. Mr Grciner pointed to the fact that the lastest poll was the third in a row in which the Government's support had fallen.

25 Apr 1985 - Approval ratings Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 25 April 1985, page 10 Approval ratings The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has slipped to 55 per cent from its peak of 75 per cent in March last year, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll, taken on the first two weekends of this month and published yesterday in The Bulletin. The approval rating for the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, fell two points to 47 per cent compared with a recent high of 56 per cent just after the last Federal election and a low of only 19 per cent in October last year. Sixty per cent of electors thought Mr Hawke made the better Prime Minister.

03 Jan 1985 - Poll shows better support for Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 3 January 1985, page 7 Poll shows better support for Labor MELBOURNE: Support for the Federal Labor Government has improved after the December I election, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine. In the election the Hawke Government obtained 47.6 per cent of the vote but a poll taken the following two weekends gave the ALP 49 per cent. Support for the Opposition fell 2 per cent to 43 per cent in the same period. The poll found support for the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, had risen 5 per cent to 56 per ecnt and for the Prime Minister, Mr Hawkc, 2 per cent to 63 per cent. Of the 2,096 electors polled, 46 per cent preferred Mr Peacock as Leader of the Opposition, 14 per cent preferred the former Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, 11 per cent favoured the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, and 5 per cent favoured the former Chief Minister of the Northern Territory. Mr Everingham.

21 Feb 1985 - Labor popularity fell Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 21 February 1985, page 8 Labor popularity fell SYDNEY: The Federal Opposition would have won an election held in mid-February, at the height of the MX missile dispute, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin yesterday. The poll found that support for the Labor Party fell seven points to 43 per cent with 6 per cent more supporting the Liberal-National parties on 47 per cent of the vote. Government support was the lowest recorded by the Morgan Gallup Poll since Labor won office. Another Morgan Gallup poll had found that support for the Government in the Senate had fallen 2.7 per cent since the December election.

14 Mar 1985 - PM down in poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 14 March 1985, page 7 PM down in poll Support for the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, and the Labor Party fell after the Australian dollar's slide and in the light of the continuing ANZUS controversy, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll published yesterday. Support for the Liberal and National parties rose but the popularity of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, fell slightly in the poll taken over the weekends of February 23-24 and March 2-3. The poll, published in The Bulletin, shows Labor Party support down 3 percentage points to 46 per cent on the previous poll of February 16-17. Support for the Liberal and Pational parties was up 4 percentage points to 46 per cent, with support for the Australian Democrats at 7 per cent. The poll shows Mr Hawke's popularity has fallen 5 percentage points to 58 per cent — 1 percentage point better than his low point in February. Mr Peacock's approval rating decreased 1 percentage point to 51 per cent.

11 Jun 1985 - Low turnout on wage poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 11 June 1985, page 4 ROME, Monday (Rcutcr). — Polling stations reported a low turnout last night after the first day of voting on a Communist-sponsored referendum to reverse wage cuts imposed by the Government a year ago. Voting continued this morning. Italy's Socialist Prime Minister, Mr Craxi, has threatened to resign immediately if the proposal succeeds. Officials said that widespread warm, sunny weather yesterday had sent many of the nation's 45 million registered vqtcrs to the beach instead of to the polling booths. By late afternoon, 29.8 per cent of those eligible had cast their votes. The Italian Communist Party, which gathered more than three times the 500,000 signatures needed to call a referendum, wants to restore the four sliding scale wage-indexation points cut by the Government as part of its anti-inflation program.

13 Jun 1985 - Wran well back in opinion poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 13 June 1985, page 3 Wran well back in opinion poll SYDNEY: The NSW Labor Government has recorded its lowest rating since winning office in 1976, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in this week's Bulletin magazine, puts Labor support in May at 40 per cent — down two percentage points on the previous month — while support for the Liberal-National Party Opposition rose two points to 49 per cent. Approval for the way the Premier, Mr Wran, was handling his job increased one point but was still only 34 per cent, well behind the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Greiner, whose rating slipped one point to 50 per cent. The poll said the Opposition would have won handsomely if an election had been held last month. The findings came from in terviewing 1,465 electors throughout the State. In Victoria, 1,082 electors were polled and results published by the magazine suggested that the State Labor Government would have been returned with a slightly increased majority if an election had been held in May. Support for the ALP was 48 per cent — one point down on April. Support for the Liberals fell two points to 36 per cent, with the Nationals recording a three-point rise to 9 per cent. The Democrats had a 5 per cent approval rating. Fifty-five per cent of those polled approved of the way the Premier of Victoria, Mr Cain, was handling his job — up one point on April. Support for the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Kennett, remained steady at 33 per cent.

08 Aug 1985 - ALP trails in NSW poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 8 August 1985, page 10 ALP trails in NSW poll SYDNEY: The NSW Labor Party is trailing the Opposition in the public opinion polls and would lose a State election if it was held now, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll, published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine, showed that the ALP had a popularity rating of 41 per cent, 8 percentage points behind the LiberalNational Party Opposition on 49 per cent. The NSW Premier, Mr Wran, gained in public approval, having increased his support by 2 percentage points since June, to have 41 per cent approval in July. The State Opposition Leader, Mr Greiner, retained his lead over Mr Wran in the popularity stakes, with 51 per cent public support.

14 Aug 1985 - Privacy Bill requested by group Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 14 August 1985, page 19 Privacy Bill requested by group I Association formed to lobby Government on ID-card plan An association callcd People Against IDs has been formed to lobby against a Government proposal for a national identity-card system. PAID was formed in the past two weeks and operates from the Sydney office of Movement Against Uranium Mining. It asks that the Government cease plans to implement an identity-card system, that there be more public debate about identity-cards and that the Government enact a Privacy Bill, which was proposed by the Law Reform Commission to safeguard existing rights to privacy. The formation of PAID is a significant indicator of public opinion for some members of the Caucus legal and administrative committee, which is considering the identity-card proposal. Committee-member Senator Bolkus (Lab, SA) has been outspoken against the Government's proposal. "The response to the suggestion of r the introduction of identity-cards has been one of bored tolerance," Senator Bolkus said in a paper issued in July. "Little debate has developed on the matter and there has been, as yet, little scrutiny of the Government's proposal and its implications." Senator Bolkus, a member of the Labor Party's left faction, and other members of the faction have helped keep media attention on identitycards while the committee has been meeting privately. The committee met in July and again on Thursday. It is to report after a final meeting on August 21. \ Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin on July 30 showed that 68 per cent of those surveyed thought the identity-card proposal was a good idea. Seventy-three per cent of these were Labor Party voters. Main criticisms of the proposal are that identity-cards would facilitate invasion of privacy and access to personal information and would not fulfil their objectives, which include re duclions in tax-avoidance, taxevasion and social-security fraud, and assistance in finding criminals and illegal immigrants. The Department of Social Security and the Australian Federal Police are among those who have criticised the proposal. The AFP said at Thursday's committee meeting that identity-cards would not help policc find criminals and illegal immigrants. The Minister for Health, Dr Blcwcit, said at the tax summit conference in June that identity-cards would help police find illegal immigrants and make available jobs for 60,000 Australians. The member for Aston, Mr Saunderson (Lab, Vic), said in a paper he issued last week that "anyone who seriously entertains the notion that the Australian Government would be loading onto planes and ships some 60,000 illegal residents, and sending them back to whence they come, has no comprehension of the realities of life". Identity-cards would be expected to raise $ 150 million, mainly in taxes, in their first year of operation, $450 million the second, $750 million the third and $800 million subsequently. A reader in information sciences at the Australian National University's Department of Commerce, Dr Roger Clarke, said in a submission to the committee that these figures were "pure guesswork and fail to withstand even the most cursory analysis". He said the Government's proposal had grave social implications. Data banks of Government departments were, to a limited extent, computer accessible — personal information stored in one department's data bank could be obtained by another department. information technology was insufficient to support a single, vast database. But a national identity-card system, which created a standard number for ail Australians, could facilitate this.

15 Aug 1985 - Hawke gains in popularity poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 August 1985, page 10 Hawke gains in popularity poll SYDNEY: The Prime Min ister, Mr Hawke, has gained in popularity, according to a Morgan Gallup poll. The approval rating for Mr Hawke climbed by 4 percentage points reaching 50 per cent, the highest it has been in the past four polls. Published in yesterday's Bulletin, the survey showed that voters preferred Mr Hawke as Prime Minister over the Liberal Party leader, Mr Peacock. The preference gap has widened by three points, so Mr Hawke now holds 57 per cent compared to Mr Peacock's score of 30 per cent, the poll showed. Despite Mr Hawke's popularity, the Liberal and National Party coalition would have won comfortably if an election had been held earlier this month. Almost 2,000 electors were polled on the last weekend of July and the first weekend of August.
