30 Aug 1985 - Howard stays prominent as review of party front bench approaches Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 30 August 1985, page 2 Howard stays prominent as review of party front bench approaches By PAUL MALONE AT THE end of this year the Leader of the Opposi-tion, Mr Peacock, is sched-uled to review the per-formance of the "shadow ministry" and reorganise it as he sees fit. The promise of such a review should keep the frontbenchers on their toes. But it also creates potential for unrest. If any sig-nificant demotions are made or even if some ambitious backbenchers do not get the reward they expect, Mr Peacock could put his own position at risk. Certainly when he makes his decision he will be examining not only performance but the support individual members can muster. After the last election he created a potentially dangerous cell of op-position on the back bench when he demoted four NSW members — Mr Jim Carlton, a former NSW general secretary of the party, Mr John Spender, Dr Harry Edwards and Mr Wal Fife. Others to lose frontbench scats were Mr Steele Hall (SA). Ms Kathy Martin (Qld) and Mr Peter Fisher (Vic). By far the most dangerous move was the demotion of Mr Carlton, a leading member of the economic rationalists in the party. These have been in the ascendancy in the party since late in the Fraser years of Government. Mr Carlton is known for his ability as a numbers man who could potentially or-ganise a coup. As a consolation prize after his removal Mr Carlton was offered, and accepted, a position on the key parliamentary party committee, the policy and implementation committee. This may have coun-tered some of his disaffection. But politicians are an ambitious lot. As a former minister, Mr Carlton would be well aware that what really matters is getting on the front bench, and he will expect to be reappointed in December. He would be well aware that with Mr Howard as Leader he would be a certainty for the front bench. Others also may believe that they would get a better deal under Mr Howard. Mr Howard demonstrated at the National Press Club on Wednes-day that he is the leading voice in determining the new policy direc-tion for the party. Acting more like a leader of the party than a deputy, he not only spelt out the policy positions which the party has de-termined, but he expressed his own views on some issues. He is hardly likely to be pulled back into line by Mr Peacock. According to the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bul-letin, Mr Howard's performance as Deputy Leader has a higher ap-proval rating than Mr Peacock's as Leader. Mr Howard's problem is that he is seen by many as colour-less, and he is tarnished by being closely identified with the Fraser years. Of course treasurers or "shadow treasurers" rarely get the oppor-tunity to come across in a favourable light. Mr Howard gets one such rare opportunity today when he is host on the Ray Martin 'Midday' program. Most politi-cians would jump at the oppor-tunity to show their human face to one million or so viewers around the country, but Mr Peacock re-fused it, clearing the way for Mr Howard. So this week Mr Howard has had nation-wide news coverage doing the serious side of his job of replying to the Budget speech by the Treasurer, Mr Keating, and he will finish the week with a 1½-hour public-relations gift. Political lead-ers rarely give such gifts to their principal opponent. Again this week Mr Howard re-fused to rule out a challenge for the leadership. Before the election last year Mr Howard's stock reply to questions about such a challenge was that he was working flat out to secure Liberal victory, and if that was achieved Mr Peacock would be Leader. But given the expectation that Labor would sweep the polls it was generally believed that what would happen was that Mr Howard would launch a challenge then. After Mr Peacock's surprisingly good result, Howard stays prominent as review of party front bench approaches Mr Howard: still fending off questions about a challenge for leadership. Mr Howard's opportunity evaporated. He now awaits another oppor-tunity. In order to keep his options open he fends off all questions by referring back to his post-election response to leadership-challenge questions. On December 7, when Mr Peacock was returned unop-posed as Leader, Mr Howard said that given the track record of loyal-ty that he had for the cause of the Liberal Party he was not really required to answer the question of whether he would challenge. He has refused to add to this reply and so experienced political observers have concluded that he is waiting for the opportune moment to move. If Mr Peacock makes any serious mistakes or if his popu-larity falls a challenge will be on. At the other end of the Liberal Party political spectrum from Mr Howard is the South Australian Mr Steele Hall, with the unique record of having been a Premier, a senator and a Member of the House of Representatives. By speaking out last week against the privatisation of the Commonwealth Bank and Qantas, Mr Hall established himself clearly as the leading voice of those Liberal Party members who are not convinced that a "free" market will solve all economic ills. Mr Hall is not alone in his thinking, though he clearly is in a minority. Senator Missen (Vic) is publicly in agreement while Mr Max Burr believes the two men have performed a useful function by challenging the dominant ra-tionalists' view. Privately other members have their reservations about the rationalist approach. Those most frequently mentioned arc Mr Macphcc, Senator Baume, Senator Puplick, Senator Hill and Senator Watson. Mr Howard took the extreme line on Wednesday that not only should the Commonwealth Bank be privatised but he was not fright-ened by the possibility that this might result in foreign ownership of at least part of it. He offered a sweetener to the privatisation policy by suggesting that shares might be sold at a discount to employees of the institutions. He showed no concern that any dis-count would amount to an ap-propriation from the people of Australia. The political pragmatists in the party may be concerned at the ammunition Mr Howard's hard-line privatisation policy is giving the Government. In particular they would be concerned by his acceptance of the foreign purchase of the institutions. Labor politi-cians storming the country warn-ing that a Liberal Government would sell such national assets as Qantas and the Commonwealth Bank to overseas interests could be a real threat to the coalition. Certainly Mr Hall and Senator Misscn would not support such sales. And sincc the Liberal Party would be divided on the subject it would have little chance of selling the policy. By speaking out now, Mr Hall has raised the possibility that he could throw his hat into the ring for leadership of the party. There is no possibility of his winning it in the near future. The rationalists are in far too strong a position for that. But should Mr Howard or Mr Peacock, as Leader, lose the next election, the question would have to be asked, can the party succeed with more of the same? The pragmatists are by far the biggest single group in the Parlia-mentary Liberal Party. They could quickly swing from their tolerant support of the rationalists to a more middle-of-the-road, Steele Hall, approach.

01 Nov 1984 - Enrolment reminder from PM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 1 November 1984, page 8 Enrolment reminder from PM The Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has reminded Australians of voting age who have not yet registered to vote to do so by tomorrow. He issued his reminder at the National Press Club while launching a new book by a Canberra political journalist, Mr Laurie Oakes, called 'How Will I Vote'. The book is designed for Australians who are not familiar with the political parties and processes. Mr Hawke expressed his confidence that Australians would put their country first on December 1 by returning his Government and approving the two referendums. The Electoral Commissioner, Dr Colin A. Hughes, said yesterday that processing of enrolment details by divisional returning officers had increased since the election was announced. "In some areas, enrolment processing, whether for newly eligible voters, changes to addresses, or other reasons, has doubled over that for nonelection periods," he said. "Electoral Commission staff are currently processing upwards of 20,000 enrolment transactions a day." ? The Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, with Mr Laurie Oakes during the launching of Mr Oakes's book at the National Press Club yesterday. Sinclair sees victory The Leader of the National Party, Mr Sinclair, denied yesterday having admitted that the Opposition could lose the December 1 election. He was widely reported as having said that the coalition parties would come "very close" to beating Labor at the ballot box. His comments, made on a brief campaign stop in Darwin, were interpreted as the first admission by an Opposition leader that victory was not assured. Speaking on the ABC 'AM' program yesterday, Mr Sinclair said his comments had not been taken in the way they were meant, and the Opposition definitely would win. Coalition views split over women's issues The Liberal Party electoral sales pitch to women will swing on a neatly packaged appendix to the general policy. It is an approach apparently modelled on Labor Party Budget tactics. The document will restate tax policy and detail special allowances, employment and training programs specifically designed for women or that accidentally affected them. It will explain the mechanics of income splitting between couples and "nominal splitting" for single women, the Opposition's plan for migrant women, women's refuges, affirmative action and employment. It is a carbon-copy of a strategy I used by the Labor Government, when a special booklet called An Assessment of the Impact on Women of the 1984-85 Budget was published with the Budget papers. But for all the Liberal Party's buttering-up of women voters, there appears to be serious conflict in coalition attitudes. During his address to the Business and Professional Women's Club of Canberra, the Opposition spokesman on industrial relations, Mr' Macphee, was clearly concerned about the comments By DEBBIE CAMERON of the Leader of the National Party, Mr Sinclair, about women and feminists during a weekend rally. Mr Macphee circled the issue in his speech, and worked up to ■his criticism with a quote from former Prime Minister, Sir Rob ert Menzies. In his 1946 policy speech, Sir Robert Menzies said, "Tonight I speak to the women of Australia with profound respect and gratitude. They have established an unanswerable'claim to economic, legal, industrial and political equality. "I hope that the time will soon come when we can say truthfully there is no sex discrimination in public or private office, in political or industrial opportunity we are all men and women, citizens of the common interest and with a common task." "Well," Mr Macphee said, "I leave you with those words. You can measure the progress of our society in relation to them." Mr Macphee went on to take a swipe at Mr Sinclair. "I noticed a statement at the weekend by a prominent politician that somehow there was no need to have that sort of vigilance and those sorts of objectives, because once women got the vote they seemed to have accomplished equality," he said. "Well that's a point of view I suppose, but not ohe which I share." At a Tamworth meeting on Saturday night Mr Sinclair said, "Unlike the suffragettes of old, whose pleas for voting equality were clearly, understood, the cause of radical feminist groups seems intent on belittling the traditional role of women in the family environment and not enhancing respect fpr the ability of women in socicty. "They are putting tremendous pressure on vyomcn who wish to be themselves, to accept less status," Mr Sinclair said. But in a weekend statement about Mr Sinclair's comment, Mr Macphee said, "There willalways be a need for women to express a desire for equality, as long as the ways in which they want that equality are resisted by men. "The words used by Mr Sinclair are reminiscent of the views expressed by some men and some women when the suffragettes sought the right to vote." Peacock says campaign going particularly well BRISBANE: The coalition did not need opinion polls to tell it the election campaign was moving its way, the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, said yesterday. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll, published in yesterday's Bulletin magazine, showed that the coalition had picked up one point to 41 per cent of the vote, while Labor was holding its rating steady at 50 per cent. Mr Peacock's personal popularity rating rose from 19 to 24 per cent, while that of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, fell one point to 67 per cent. Mr Peacock said the campaign was going "particularly well for the coalition and would continue to do so". "I expect to get significantly increased support from people on polling day," he said. "I know the way this campaign is moving — it's moving toward us. I don't need any poll that was taken 10 days ago to tell me that." MOUNT ISA: The Leader of the National Party, Mr Sinclair, committed a coalition government yesterday to an overall cut in taxes. He said a Liberal-National Party government would ensure a real cut in personal income tax and that taxes overall were cut. Speaking on a Mount Isa radio station, he ruled out a valueadded tax as an option in the coalition's examination of indirect taxes. Coalition rethinks its promises MELBOURNE: The coalition parties had had to rethink their election promises because of recent warnings about the economic outlook, the Opposition spokesman on Treasury matters, Mr Howard, said yesterday. A coalition government could now promise to implement only the principal elements of its program in its first Budget, Mr Howard told a news conference in Melbourne. He put the cost of promises to be fulfilled in the first Peacock Budget at $441 million — not $2,542 million, which he said the Government had put on the Opposition's commitments. "Over the past few weeks both the Prime Minister and the Treasurer have engaged in wild, erratic and frequently contradictory claims about the cost of our election program," Mr Howard said. The warnings prompting the coalition rethink came from, among others, the former Secretary of the Treasury, Mr John Stone, and the Minister for Industry and Commerce, Senator Button. Last month Mr Stone had predicted tax increases next year and Senator Button had warned of "very significant budgetary problems" in 1985 and 1986. Senator Button also had said the economic recovery would continue in a "patchy way".

03 Nov 1984 - Flawed migration tract Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 3 November 1984, page 20 Flawed migration tract Some six months before the arrival in Darwin of the first refugee boat from Vietnam in April 1976, the Gallup poll asked: "If hundreds of thousands of unarmed people from the north land in Northern Australia from small boats, should we let them stay, or force them to leave?" Those responding that wc "let them stay" were easily outnumbered by those who demanded that we "force them to leave": 19 per cent to 58 per cent, with 23 per cent undecided. As Murray Goot, a Sydney-based political scientist, said in a recent paper: "No poll had ever reproduced the threat of the 'yellow peril' more accurately." In the ensuing two years the movement direct to Northern Australia increased dramatically, reaching its peak in May-June 1978. The enactment in international waters around Australia of the great tragedy of the boat people of Indo-China, denied landing rights by the countries of SouthEast Asia, was brought home to millions of Australians watching on their television screens the arrival of crowded vessels in Darwin. The point of the "yellow peril" public opinion poll and the subsequent experience which resulted in the arrival of some 90,000 refugees from Indo-China after the fall in Saigon (of whom fewer than 2,500 came direct by boat) is the underlying theme of Professor Blainey's book. The book is an expanded version of the talk which the author gave at a Rotary conference at Warrnambool last March and of the ensuing controversy in the printed and electronic media. According to Blainey: "... the pace of Asian immigration is now far ahead of public opinion, especially the public opinions in those suburbs and workplaces to which many of these Vietnamese and Kampuchean refugees will go. In the last resort it is not the politicians, it is not Canberra, which determines whether an immigration program will succeed. It is public opinion which decides." This argument about the role of public opinion is extended in the book to the criticism of the nondiscriminatory principle in immigration policy which has been in operation since 1973 and the larger issue of multi-culturalism. As far as opposition to a specific group of newcomers is concerned, this is not a new development in the history of Australia's post-war migration and it is something that Blainey largely ignores. In the late 1940s opinion ran strongly against the immigration of Displaced Persons — the East European refugees of World War II. Feelings ran high, again with equal vigour, against Italians and Greeks in the following decade. So hostility to particular groups and aspects of the immigration program is neither new or as threatening as Blainey suggests. When it comes to innovative programs in any area of social policy — of which immigration is a prime example — public opinion inevitably could be lagging behind. This was certainly true in 1947, when the Chifley Government introduced the large-scale program of immigration and it was equally true in the 1960s when the very edifice of White Australia policy was first undermined by the Holt Government. And so it goes on with every policy initiative in response to new situations as perceived by those of our leaders whom we expect to be true to their calling — men and women of vi sion. Blainey argues that somewhere in the Department oflmmigration and Ethnic Affairs there is a "secret room" from which Government documents emerge demanding more Asian immigrants. This far-fetched if not actually bizarre assumption can be refuted from this reviewer's direct and longlasting experience of the practices and procedures followed by those ALL FOR AUSTRALIA. By Geoffrey Blainey. Methuen Haynes. 176pp. $5.95. Reviewer: GEORGE ZUBRZYCKI. members of the Canberra bureaucracy who are responsible for the administration of Australia's immigration policies. Moreover, figures issued by the Australian Bureau of Statistics demonstrate that migration from Asia has contributed less than 30' per cent of the total new settlers, over the past six years. Total Asian numbers have not substantially increased; indeed there has been a reduction since 1981-82. Over the same period of time British and European numbers surged, and then fell to 1978-79 levels as a result of a marked decline in interest and of cuts of independent skilled migration commenced by the coalition Government and continued by the ALP. The trend in declining numbers of UK and Irish residents applying for Australian visas can be compared with the readiness of those in the "secret room" to issue visas. Statistics issued for the financial year which ended last June show that British-Irish applicants had a two-in-three chance that their application would be accepted, while Asian applicants' chances were one in three. So much for the antiBritish bias of those "secret" government statistics and other documents which, as Jack Waterford of Geoffrey Blainev The Canberra Times has shown. Blainey never tried to obtain. Another unfounded generalisation in Blainey's book is when he talks of "unemployed immigrants", implying that these arc mainiy Asians. Yet the official statistics that relate incidence of unemployment to the country of birth recall that in the middle of 1984, out of 580,700 Australian residents who were drawing unemployment benefits, only 12,345 were Indo-Chinese. In the three months from May 1984 there was a consistent fall in the unemployment rate among Vietnamese. My final and strongest criticism of Blainey's book must be reserved for his distorted view of multiculturalism as "that policy [which] savours more of a Canberra Seminar than a Perth Supermarket on Saturday morning". As a member of a "Canberra Seminar" which, way back in 1967-68, canvassed cultural and political pluralism in approaching problems of migrant settlement, I should like to assure Professor Blainey that the present multi-cultural policies are not out of touch with what is going on in Springvale, Vic., Cabramatta, NSW, or, for that matter, in a Perth supermarket as described by one of his correspondents. Multi-culturalism is about the social organisation of cultural differences, it is about whether and how education, law and the media can correct prejudice, racism and institutional obstacles to moblity. It is about the worth of cultural pluralism and diversity as an enrichment of Australia society. It is about the encouragement of respect for persons whose background and value are different and the reinforcement in those persons of a sense of self and personal worth. It is about the sensitisation of Australia's mainstream institutions to the presence and legitimate needs of cultural minorities. Multi-culturalism is about the fundamental issue of national unity — it is all for Australia. Rodney Marsh Patterns of crime go undetected C<OLIN Wilson's latest book is a valiant attempt to place crime in perspective against human discovery, exploration and invention; an attempt, as he puts it, "to tell the story of the human race in terms of [the] counterpoint between crime and creativity, and to use the insights it brings to try to disccrn the next stage in human evolution." Wilson has dozens of works to his credit, with titles ranging from 'A Book of Booze' and 'The Gclter Phenomenon' to 'Bernard Shaw — A Reassessment' and 'New Pathways in Psychology'. While collating information for his 'Encyclopedia of Murder'in the 1950s he bccame convinced from the A CRIMINAL HISTORY OF MAN KIND. By Colin Wilson. Granada. 702pp. $35. Reviewer: BRIAN JEFFREY. many case studies he had examined that there must be undiscovered patterns and basic laws that would provide clues to a seemingly steady rise in the crime rate. The end result of his subsequent flirtation with the psychology of violence, in a nutshell, is that "the worst crimes are not committed by evil degenerates, but by decent and intelligent people taking •pragmatic' decisions". Even the worst excesses can be explained in this way, he says: Hitler's mass murders, for example, were the outcome of a twisted kind of idealism. Furthermore, each age, he asserts, has its own characteristic pattern of crime, and this can be related to a theory expounded by psychologist Abraham Maslow in the mid-1960s that human motivation can be described in terms of a hierarchy of needs or values. Wilson says his research has indicated that this hierarchy of needs approximates historical periods of time: hence his hypothesis that crime has changed and evolved through the centuries. In an effort to prove his point, lie presents the reader with an unrelieved record of murder and" bloodshed which ranges across the calculated sadism of the Assyrians, the opportunism of the Greek pirates, the brutality of the Romans, the mindless destruction by the Vandals and the mass slaughters directed by such individuals as Genghis Khan and Vlad the Impaler, to the Nazis, the Mafia and such murders as Charles Manson. Frankly, I found 700 pages of it all a bit much, although I give Wilson full marks for his ability to trot out an apt theory or neat example to support his case. Referring to the tendency of sex crimes in the early part of this century to display an increasingly strange element of perversion, for instance, he calls up the case of one Sy Ivestre Matushka, a Hungarian company director who, in 1932, was tried for causing two train crashes, one of which resulted in the loss of 22 lives, and for attempting to cause a third. Matushka admitted that the thought of trains crashing caused him intense sexual excitement, and he experienced orgasm when it actually happened. He was sentenced to life imprisonment, but, in a neat twist to the case, Wilson adds that Matushka escaped and reappeared during the Korean War — as the head of a unit for blowing up trains! Just what a criminologist, psychologist, historian or similarly qualified academic might make of Wilson's research and his treatment of the evidence I am unable to say, although I suspect he would attract much sniping. I can report that I found his avoidance of a definite pronouncement on mankind's future somewhat unsatisfactory, given that I had persevered with his tome through several weeks of reading. Perhaps by the time he snapped me out of my glassy-eyed stare on page 610 with those long-awaited words, "All this explains why .. my mind was so numbed I couldn't have cared less. Having concentrated my attention on his last few pages, however, I did think his conclusion that criminal man is "the result of man's misunderstanding of his own potentialities" something of an an ticlimax.

06 Nov 1984 - Black money allegations Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 6 November 1984, page 3 Black money allegations Fund 'missed out on huge sums' By PHILIP CASTLE The Community Development Fund had lost access to 10 per cent of between $12 million and $15 million since drawpoker machines came in to the ACT because they were not covered by legislation, the secretary-manager of the Canberra Tradesmen's Union Club at Dickson, Mr Rod Driver, said yesterday. A representative of the Canberra Labor Club, Mr David Combe, said that there were suspicions in the industry that a major attraction of draw-poker machines was that they allowed their owners and operators to "enjoy black money or untaxed income". Both were giving evidence at the ACT Poker- and Amusement-Machine Inquiry before Commissioner Keith Edmunds which resumed hearing yesterday at Construction House. The inquiry is looking at the types of machines, their controls and in what licensed premises they should be allowed in the ACT. This week's hearings include submissions from five licensed clubs, the Licensed Clubs' Association (supplementary submission), submissionsin-reply and a summing-up. Today's hearing is from 9am to noon. Mr Edmunds said during a break in the hearings that it was quite possible that "black money" had passed through the draw-poker machines because there had been virtually no controls on ihem. No-one really knew what had been paid in or what had been paid out. He agreed that it was certain that the Community Development Fund had missed out on some millions of dollars. The fund currently received 10 per cent of the revenue from poker machines. Operators and hirers would have found it relatively easy to have avoided paying tax if they had wanted to. Mr Driver said since drawpoker machines had been introduced to the club about three years ago the total net profit had been $895,000. The net profit on its 16 draw-poker machines in the year to June, 1984, had amounted to $336,279. On this basis Mr Driver said that conservatively in the past year between $ 12 to $ 15 million "had gone missing from all the draw-poker machines operating in the ACT". Before draw-poker machines became illegal in the ACT on July 1 this year it was estimated by the Australian Federal Police that more than 300 of them had been operating in the ACT. Mr Edmunds said at the end of yesterday's hearings that if Mr Driver's figures were correct it was not difficult to work out how much clear profit had been made by operators and hirers of drawpoker machines. The clubs' representatives all argued yesterday that licensed clubs should be allowed to continue to have exclusive access to poker machines because clubs actively supported community activities to a greater degree that did hotels and taverns. Mr Combe presented a copy of a Morgan Gallup poll which showed that in 1980 and 1981 the majority of Australians, except Tasmanians, favoured poker machines in clubs, but the majority did not favour them in hotels. Mr Combe recommended that Mr Edmunds consider consulting the ACT community by having a poll taken to see what its views were. He also suggested that Mr Gary Morgan be called as an expert witness to discuss the poll results. Mr Edmunds said afterwards that the final report was due at the end of December and there would be insufficient time. He agreed that some sort of survey was warranted. He was very happy with yesterday's hearings now that both groups, the clubs and the hotelstaverns, had made submissions which would allow him to make a balanced report. Mr Edmunds had been critical previously that few clubs had put their point of view.

10 Nov 1984 - Walking the most popular physical activity: survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 10 November 1984, page 56 Walking the most popular physical activity: survey Australians prefer walking to any other form of physical activity,the Minister for Sport, Recreation and Tourism, Mr Brown, said this week. According to a Morgan Gallup Poll taken this year, 68 per cent of Australians over the age of 14 had been involved in some form of exercise at least once over a two-week surveyed period, with twothirds of these listing walking as their main exercise. A greater percentage of women enjoyed walking, 69 per cent against 51 per cent of men, while men showed a preference for jogging, cricket, football, soccer or golf. A higher percentage of men were associated with sporting clubs than women, 37 per cent against 24 per cent. Other preferred activities were aerobics and calisthenics, with 15 per cent of Australians involved during the past winter and 13 per cent engaged in jogging and running. Almost 90 percent of active people did so alone or with friends as opposed to 31 per cent who belonged to sporting bodies and 6 per cent who attended health and fitness centres. The survey showed that 32 per cent of Australians did not take part in any physical activity during the two-week period. The most listed reason was lack of free time followed by physical inability and a lack of interest. Previous surveys had shown that up to 65 per cent of Australians did not take part in any form of physical activity.

15 Nov 1984 - Popularity rises Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 November 1984, page 1 Popularity rises PM moves to head off NDP The Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, moved yesterday to head off growing support for the Nuclear Disarmament Party, saying that votes for it would be wasted. And the Leader of the National Party, Mr Sinclair, said that the growing popularity of the NDP would bring about the demise of the Australian Democrats. The NDP came to the forefront of the election campaign yesterday after the publication of the latest Morgan Gallup poll, which showed that Labor's Senate vote has slipped from 47 per cent to 43 per cent, while • that of the NDP has risen from 3 per cent to 8 per cent, giving it a good chance for a scat. Mr Hawke admitted that the Government's hopes of winning control of the Upper House had been "complicated" by the emergence of the NDP but he believed that support would return to the ALP as the campaign continued and Labor's disarmament policy was better understood. At the same time, Mr Hawke welcomed figures for the House of Representatives which gave Labor 52 per cent support and only 38 per cent to the coalition, indicating a landslide to Labor. The poll was taken on the weekend of November 3-4, when the campaign by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, was at its peak to date and getting favourable media coverage. Mr Peacock's personal-approval rating went up four points to 28 per cent, while Mr Hawke's rose one point to return to 68 per cent. However, in radio and television interviews in Sydney yesterday morning, and at a subsequent news conference in Brisbane, Mr Hawke was more interested in attempting to counter the impact being made by the NDP. He said he could understand people's concern over peace and nuclear disarmament, but a vote for the NDP would be a wasted vote. Although the NDP vote reflected the concern in the community about disarmament, it was up to governments to take action. "Only a government, and not some minority group in the Senate, can do anything about disarmament... no small group can determine what a country will do," he said. People could write slogans and sing songs, but this would not change decisions of gov ernment. The NSW branch of the NDP demonstrated its commitment to peace yesterday when it released about 30 white doves during its campaign launch, held at Mrs Macquaric's Chair at 6am. Its NSW candidate, Mr Peter Garrett, lead singer of the rock band Midnight Oil, said the party should not be described as "single issue". Pryor's view, Editorial. — Page 2. Other election report3. — Pages 14, 15. "We're not a one policy party — we're a fundamental-principle party," he said. "Supporters from the Labor, Liberal and National parties will indicate their party vote in the House of Reps, but will vote for us in the Senate." He would not be a part-time rock singer and a part-time politician if elected — "I'm , a full-time person working for nuclear disarmament in Australia," he said. "1 expect to be taken seriously. Mr Hawke and Mr Hayden have made an enormous amount of comment about our party's stand, which reflects its importance." If elected, he would consult with the leader of the Victorian NDP ticket, former Victorian Labor senator Mrs Jean Melzer, about the direction to vote on other than nuclear concerns. Mrs Melzer said in Melbourne that NDP senators would make use of debate on foreign affairs, defence, the economy, education, and science and technology to push the Government on the nuclear issue. The NDP was concerned that a Labor Government might increase uranium production and allow another mine to open. The party's growing support in the polls was a reflection of widespread community dismay at the Government's failure to take effective action on disarmament. According to the party's pledge read in Sydney yesterday morning, the NDP "will offer real alternatives to this insanity... we will provide a focus for resistance and a voice that will not be silenccd or diverted". Mr Sinclair said that each of the five Democrat senators seemed to have a different view on issues before the Senate, making it hard for people to identify any particular philosophy. "As far as the NDP is concerned, they do have a philosophy that is identifiable," he said. "I think people arc far more likely in the future therefore, if peace is their cause, to support a party where at least you have a cause." The Leader of the Democrats, Senator Chipp, said that a vote for the NDP which gave second preference to Labor would be a meaningless exercise and only strengthen Mr Hawke's pro-nuclear stand. "He will be able to go to bed at night knowing no matter how many nuclear weapons are in our ports or pointed at our children, his electoral position is secure," he said. "The Prime Minister's attempted denigration of the intentions behind the NDP is an indication of his vulnerability on the vital issue of disarmament."

15 Nov 1984 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 November 1984, page 2 Cmlwra $imrs I Thursday. November 15, 1984 MINOR PARTY HAS VALUE The VAST majority of Australians support the aim of the Nuclear Disarmament Party to rid the world of the immediate threat of a nuclear holocaust. But only a small percentage of voters accept the view that there is a place in Parliament for a single-issue party or that such a party could have any impact on the world scene. The opening yesterday of the Nuclear Disarmament Party's campaign for NSW Senate seats was a fairly tame affair compared with the Australian Labor Party's extravaganza the day before. There were about 50 supporters at the Botanic Gardens as dawn arrived, compared with the thousands inside the Opera House to hear the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, at lunchtime on Tuesday. Yet the open-air launch was reported to be impressive, more like a religious service than a raucous political rally where the party faithful cheer every campaign promise. The meeting began with a period of silence and the release of white doves, the symbol of peace. There were 1 other differences between the events, apart from the venues I and numbers attending. J Mr Hawke spent only a brief time on Tuesday discussing nuclcar arms, declaring that Australia had a high reputation in world forums and it would continue to press for armscontrol agreements, a strengthening of the non-nuclearproliferation regime and an end to nuclear testing. But his words sounded hollow, as he has been the frontrunner in the successful campaign to revive the Australian uranium mining and export industry. At least he spared his audience a repeat of his odd line of reasoning that by selling uranium Australia was helping to ease world tensions, ensuring adherence to nuclear safeguards and checking the spread of nuclear weapons. The Nuclear Disarmament Party declared that Mr Hawke had mouthed platitudes and had failed to address the issue seriously. Mrs Jean Melzer, a former Labor senator now heading the Nuclcar Disarmament Party's Victorian Senate ticket, said the Hawke speech had been "shatteringly banal" on the issue of disarmament. Widespread concern The fact that Mrs Melzer has deserted the ALP for the new single-issue party is some evidence of the widespread concern in Labor circles and the community at large over nuclcar arms. While there is little doubt that Labor will win a sizable majority of seats in the House of Representatives, the emergence of the Nuclear Disarmament Party may well thwart its attempt to achieve a majority in the Senate. After many traditional Labor voters follow the party ticket for the House of Representativess there could be an appreciable defection to the Nuclear Disarmament Party when it comes to marking the Senate ballot paper. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll indicates that the ALP has lost its slight hope of winning a Senate majority because of a strong drift of its supporters to the anti-nuclear party, whose following has increased from 3 per cent of the vote to 8 per cent in only a couple of weeks. Such a sudden jump in popularity should be treated with caution: there might be a statistical discrepancy, and some voters might revert to the major party when confronted with the ballot paper. However, if the polls are on course, the Nuclcar Disarmament Party could in some States be heading for the 12.5 per cent of votes necessary to win a Senate seat. If it fails to gain a quota many of its preferences could favour the Australian Democrats rather than the ALP. The Democrats arc an anti-nuclear party too, but have a broad approach to politics and internal divisions on many issues. Like the ALP, they arc disturbed by the entry of the new party into the campaign, fearing some loss of support. One or more senators of the new party wouid be welcomed by many, to prick the consciences of the major parties on nuclcar issues, but they would have little impact in the world in the quest for disarmament. The Government of the day has all the running in the international forums and the voice of the odd Nuclear Disarmament senator would not be heard outside Australia. At the same time single-issue parties can quickly lose influence inside their own country away from the election atmosphere. A better strategy for the concerned is to remain and fight within the major party of their choice, because that is where the real power is. There is a role for such people as the conscience of a party. This is not to decry the role of the Nuclcar Disarmament Party in this election campaign. With the major parties seeking the middle-class vote with promises of tax reform, and concentrating on economic issues, there was a need for some group to remind the voters that without pcace all the promises mean little. If the major parties are found at the ballot count to have lost some of their traditional support to the Nuclear Disarmament Party, they might be stirred to greater efforts in the cause of disarmament and world pcace.

15 Nov 1984 - ELECTION 84 Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 November 1984, page 14 ELECTION 84 Labor will rule House, not Senate: poll SYDNEY: The latest Morgan Gallup poll has again pointed to a landslide victory for Labor in the House of Representatives on December 1 but lack of control of the Senate. Results of the survey published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday said Labor would win 52 per cent of the vote in the House, down one percentage point from the last poll taken late last month. Support for the Opposition in the House of Representatives increased by one point to 38 per cent. The poll was taken on the weekend of November 3 to 4 from a sample of 1,109 voters. The ALP's support in the Senate dropped from 47 per cent to 43 per cent and the Liberal Party had a three-point fall to 25 per cent. The National Party jumped three points to 11 per cent while the newly-formed Nuclear Disarmament Party increased its share from 3 to 8 per cent. The Australian Democrats, who hold the balance of power in the Senate, remained steady at 10 per cent. The approval ratings of both the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, and the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, increased as the undecided section of voters shrank. Mr Hawke's approval increased by one point to 68 per ccnt while Mr Peacock's went up four points to 28 per cent. However 70 per cent of those polled felt Mr Hawke would make a better Prime Minister than Mr Peacock, who received only 18 percent support. Referendum 'No' case launched by Durack The introduction of new indirect taxes at State level, under the referendum proposal, would allow the Federal Government to introduce capital-gains taxes or death duties without breaking its election promise, the Opposition spokesman on legal matters, Senator Durack said yesterday. The Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has said the Commonwealth would not increase the tax burden as a proportion of Gross Domestic Product. Senator Durack launched in Melbourne yesterday the 'No' campaign on the referendum questions on the interchange of powers and the terms of senators. "There is no doubt that a 'Yes' vote on this referendum question [interchange of powers] is a vote to permit higher State taxation, followed by new Federal taxes on savings and assets," he said in a statement.

22 Nov 1984 - ELECTION 84 Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 22 November 1984, page 19 ELECTION 84' Peacock 'sceptical' of polls Small swing back to coalition MELBOURNE: Despite a small swing back to the coalition in the latest Morgan Gallup poll, the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pcacock, said yesterday that he remained "sceptical" of opinion polls. SYDNEY: An opinion poll published on Tuesday by The Australian indicated a swing to the Opposition parties in the Lower House, with a rise in support of three percentage points last weekend to 43 per cent. Mr Peacock 'We do what's right for the people' Chipp stresses credentials on disarmament and youth Senator Chipp ... "we must work to have a world worth savine " By ROGER GREEN The trouble with being unconventional is the risk that someone even more unconventional may come along. Senator Chipp has always prided himself on the fact that his party, the Australian Democrats, is different from the "conventional" parties. He has striven to project different policies from the major parties — particularly on conservation and nuclear issues — and appeal to younger, disillusioned voters. Now there is another party that seems to have greater appeal to that group: it doesn't have policies, except one, and it isn't led by politicians. The Nuclear Disarmament Party makes even the Democrats look conventional and it threatens to steal Demo crat voters. Yesterday at the National Press Club, Senator Chipp was at pains to stress his party's credentials on disarmament, youth unemployment, conservation and other issues that concern young voters. He stated his party's commitment to principle: "We don't give a damn the number of votes we lose as long as we do what's right for the Australian people." He said that because the Democrats were not in danger of forming the Government they had the luxury of being able to do and say whatever they liked. "We've gone to incredible lengths to make ourselves different," Senator Chipp said. But when he was questioned on the party's appeal he could not explain why young people may not vote Dem ocrat. Of course the NDP is taking votes from the Labor Party as well as from the Democrats. Senator Chipp said that polls in NSW suggested that both the Democrats and the NDP could win Senate scats in that State with a combined vote of about 25 per cent. "I hope they help maximise the anti-nuclcar vote," he said of the NDP. He did not conceal the conflict between the two parties that has arisen over the distribution of preferences in some States and the ACT. While the parties have exchanged preferences in NSW and Victoria, where NDP candidates are most likely to win seats, the exchange has not worked so smoothly in other places. Senator Chipp said he hoped the disagreement between the parties did not distract from the central issue (disarmament). "But it is not the only issue," Senator Chipp said, "While we fight to save the world, we must also work to have a world worth saving." In this way he sought to undercut the NDP for its lack of policies on jobs, the environment and justice. Senator Chipp suggested that jobs could be created by reducing the age for the reccipt of pensions to 60, shortening the working week, jobsharing, permanent part-time work and by holding "a meaningful ongoing summit" which included all those afTected, not just governments, unions and corporations. He said the redistribution of wealth was necessary. A capital gains tax was one way to do this. Small businesses and farmers should be encouraged. The economic value of conserving the environment should be recognised, as should the value of scientific research. Senator Chipp also said there should be no discrimination allowed against women, migrants or Aborigines. "We are facing the problems which Labor and Liberal either refuse to recognise, or gloss over," he said. Compassion, idealism, hope and tolerance could spread. But then the Democrats have the electoral advantage of not being in the race for power, with or without the NDP. "We are the only party that can enjoy the luxury of looking towards the future," he said. 01 Dec 1984 - Midnight Oil singer pledges to be 100pc NDP Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 1 December 1984, page 19 Midnight Oil singer pledges to be 100pc NDP Garrett stands real chance of rocking the Senate Australians may do some thing unprecedented today — elect a rock star to their Federal governing assembly. The rock star is Peter Garrett, of Midnight Oil, and his party — the Nuclear Disarmament Party — is devoted solely to the issue of nuclear disarmament. If the party's strong support in NSW converts to votes, there is a very real chance Mr Garrett, the NDP's No 1 NSW Senate candidate, will as sume a seat in Canberra. Mr Garrett, a law graduate, was asked to run for the party because of his convictions on the nuclear-arms issue. Dr Michael Denborough, founder of the nascent NDP, said yesterday he believed no other country had a polit-ical party so single-mindedly oriented to the eradication of nuclear arms. The closest parallel would be the Green Party in West Germany, but the "Greenies" also concentrated on social issues unrelated to the arms race — something the NDP did not intend to do. The rapid rise of support for the NDP in the 5½ months since it was founded could well bring off a re-markable coup at the polls today, if party approval ratings in opinion polls translate into votes. A Morgan Gallup Poll published on Wednesday in The Bulletin showed national support for the new party had fallen by 1 percentage point to 10 per cent, but the NDP still has a strong chance of winning a Senate seat in NSW. The poll said support for the NDP in Victoria had risen by 1 percentage point to 9 per cent and had doubled in a week to 12 per cent in NSW. Of the 17 Senate and six House of Representatives candidates being fielded nationally by the NDP, Dr Denborough thinks the party's strongest chances are in the Senate races in NSW, Queensland, Victoria and Western Australia. Midnight Oil's current album 'Red Sails in the Sunset', which has topped the rock charts nationally for four weeks, carries a cover showing Syd-ney Harbour turned into a crater by a nuclear blast. The lyrics to one of the songs in the album — 'Best of Both Worlds' — includes the lines: "The small world || Mr Garrett || is not as strong and the testing ground is near; the old world is not as safe as the one we could have seen; the Great South Land can be as great as the one it could have been." The group has a reputation for being uncompromising. It considers its home base the less-than-glittery venues favoured by the band's loyal "surfies" on the northern beaches of Sydney (the unmarried Mr Garrett lives in nearby Manly). And the band tends to eschew blan-dishments from record company ex-ecutives and rock show producers to tone down the political comment in its music. If the 31-year-old, 192-centimetre-tall, bald Mr Garrett may con-temptously view blind obeisance to authority figures, he is adamant that he takes quite seriously the possibility of his election to the Senate and the responsibility he would shoulder as a senator. He said yesterday that if elected to the Senate he would not do any large-scale touring with Midnight Oil although he might participate if the band was doing something specifical-ly related to the arms race. "I was asked [to run] and I think that disarmament and peace is the major issue whose time has come," he said. Of his commitment to parlia-mentary work, he said, "I think it'll take all the time of a working year, and I'm planning on spending 100 per cent of my time as a Nuclear Dis-armament Party senator." The popularity of Midnight Oil has helped the NDP get volunteers and more publicity for their cause. The secretary of NDP in Canberra, Mr John Conway, said, "We're get-ting a whole lot of fans [of Peter Garrett] coming in." Mr Conway said the party could not handle the number of member- ships it was receiving, many from Labor Party members. The NDP had so many people vol-unteering to hand out leaflets and how-to-vote cards on election day that it now had a waiting list, he said. "We've had political parties calling and asking us for some of our surplus volunteers," Mr Conway said. Mr Garrett is, however, not the only NDP candidate with a chance of gaining election to the Senate. Other favored Senate candidates, all listed No 1 on the party's separate State ballots, are: Mrs Jean Melzer, a former senator for Victoria; Ms Patsy Goodwin, a peace activist in Queensland; and Ms Jo Vallentine, a Quaker and peace activist in Western Australia. The NDP is not holding out much hope for its House of Representatives candidates, according to Dr Den-borough. The six NDP House can-didates are: Robyn Hancock (Can-berra, ACT), Mr Bob Shumack (Eden-Monaro, NSW), Mr Rod Lander (Gil-more, NSW), Mr Peter Gardiner (Gippsland, Victoria), Mr Paul Breakwell (Kingston, South Aus-tralia), and Mr David Nourish (Kalgoorlie, Western Australia). Dr Denborough said the Demo-crats were giving their preferences to the NDP in NSW, South Australia, Victoria, and Western Australia. The Labor Party was giving its preferences to the NDP in the ACT, Queensland, and South Australia. He noted the NDP was assigning its own preferences to candidates on the basis of their record and positions on nuclear issues. The NDP, which has as its slogan two mottoes, "There are millions of us" and "The future is ours", has three policy platforms — to close all foreign military bases in Australia; to prohibit the stationing in Australia, or the passage through Australian waters or air space, of any nuclear weapons; and to terminate immediately all mining and export of uranium and to repudiate all commitments by pre-vious governments to the mining, processing and exporting of uranium. Dr Denborough, a doctor and med-ical researcher at ANU, said the party intends to keep its platform solely concerned with nuclear issues. He said the party might consider pushing for changes in other areas apart from defence and foreign policy, like seeking compulsory peace educa-tion and publicising the health dan-gers of nuclear fallout. "If we have candidates elected to the Parliament, our aim would be to make nuclear disarmament the domi-nant issue in Parliament," Dr Den-borough said. "If a debate in Parliament concerns something totally unrelated to nuclear disarmament, such as kerbs and gutters in the Northern Territory, our candidates won't be voting on these issues but will be devoting all their time to promoting nuclear dis-armament." He said he wanted to stress that the NDP had no antagonism "towards our allies in America". "We have no antagonism towards other nations either," he said. "Our enemies arc nuclear weapons and we want to get rid of them before they destroy us all." Regardless of how many seats the NDP might win in the election, he said, "We have succeeded in one of our main aims and that is to make nuclear disarmament a main issue in the election, and we have achieved that." Dr Denborough said the party would not die with this election. "There are plans for a national conference to be held after the elec-tion to assess the results and plan for the future," he said.

01 Dec 1984 - Voters to get three ballot papers Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 1 December 1984, page 20 Voters to get three ballot papers House, Senate and then comes two referendums By JODY ISAACS, of AAP JL ODAY, voters will rcccivc three separate ballot papers: one for the House of Representatives, one for the Senate and a third to vote on two proposed changes to the Australian Constitution. As usual, the House of Representatives ballot-paper requires you to elect a candidate by rating all candidates, starting with the figure "I", in order of preference. This year's ballot papers for both House and Senate have been changed to show each candidate's party label alongside his or her name. The Senate ballot paper has also been split into two sections to simplify matters for the elector who wants to follow a party's how-to-vote ticket. The paper is divided horizontally by a broad black stripe, with instructions to vote in either of two ways. If you vote below the line, you must number ail the squares with consecutive numbers to be sure of a valid vote. If you want to register a group voting ticket, leave the bottom section blank and place the figure "I" in the party's group voting box on the top section of the ballot-paper. In effect, this duplicates a party's how-to-vote ticket. The third ballot paper contains two referendum questions asking voters whether or not they approve each of two proposed laws to alter the Con stitution. The Constitution cannot be changed without having a referendum. The two referendums being put to the electors today have been passed by absolute majorities in both Houses of Parliament. Under the Constitution, each proposal must now be put to the electorate and approved by a majority of voters and by a majority of States. Assuming you've sorted out your Houses, the two proposed laws to alter the Constitution are: First, an Act to change the terms of Senators and to provide for simultaneous elections, so instead of having fixed six-year terms, Senators would be elected for two terms of the House of Representatives and an election for half the Senate (and the four Territorial senators) would always be held on the same day as an election for the House of Representatives. Second, an Act for the interchange of powers between the States and Federal Governments, so instead of only the States being able to transfer their powers to the Commonwealth, the Commonwealth could also refer its powers to the States. At present the Commonwealth's powers are listed in the Constitution and any powers not on the list belong to the States. The referendum ballot-paper asks voters to answer "Yes" or "No" to each of these questions. A blank, figure 1, lick or "maybe" is an invalid vote. However, it is not necessary to answer both questions if you only wish to vote on one. Australian Electoral Commissioner Dr Colin A. Hughe? pointed out, "The referendum questions arc two quite separate issues, so it is possible to answer only one of the referendum questions and this will be regarded as a valid vote." The "Yes" case says ending the possibility of separate House and Senate elections will save the taxpayer, on currcnt costs, $19.2 million for each half-Senate election. Simultaneous elections also boost confidence and stability in long-term planning by business and governments by reducing the possible number of disruptive elections. The proposal docs not affect the power of the Senate to review, amend or reject legislation, and all States will continue to have an equal number of senators, and the ACT and NT two each. But the proposal means half the senators (and all four Territory senators) would also face an clcction if there was a repeat of the events of 1975 when the Senate blockcd Supply to force an early election in the House of Representatives. The "No" case says doing away with fixed terms threatens the independence of the Senate, the States' House, which checks and balances Federal Government by enabling the Government to have an early halfSenate as well as House of Representatives clcction whenever it chooses. The proposal means Governments are likely to hold more frequent early elections and is the first stage in a long-term plan to abolish the Senate. The "Yes" case admits popular Governments could try to time their elections to coincide with half-Senate terms, actually an argument for this early election, but recognises the reality of too many elections. The first "No" argument, that automatic simultaneous elections threaten the independence of the Senate, implies that electors are less likely to vote differently for the Senate so the Government could gain control in both Houses of Parliament. However, if this year's simultaneous election supports the argument that the referendum proposal is unnecessary, its projected outcomc also indicates that voters arc capable of recognising the separate existence and role of the Senate. The Whitlam and Frascr Governments both put this first referendum proposal to the electorate and had it rejected — in 1974 and 1977. It is supported in 1984 by the ALP, but opposed by the Liberal-National coalition and by the Australian Dem ocrats. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in this week's Bulletin suggests 62 per ccnt of all electors (down from 73 per cent in early November) support the proposal, 27 per ccnt oppose it and 11 per cent remain undecided. On the question of interchange of powers, the "Yes" case says two-way exchanges of Commonwealth and State powers arc ncccssary to eliminate duplication and patch up gaps in present areas of divided responsibility, such as child custody and family law, commercial law, taxation law and industrial relations. The interchange proposal lets State and Federal governments work together for law reform in those matters where the present lack or overlap of powers causes added expense, hardship and inconvenience to persons afTcctcd. The product would be a more integrated, efficient and flexible system of laws. The "No" case says approval of the second referendum would allow the Government to bring about changes in powers without the approval of the electorate at referendum, and that change is not necessary as cooperative arrangements can be worked out instead where Commonwealth and State powers overlap. Some opponents argue the proposed law does not ensure that all Slates agree to or reccive the same powers from the Commonwealth and that, while the proposed law clarifies the reference power of States and Commonwealth as well as making it reciprocal, these provisions open the way for unfair and inconsistent power "trade-ofis" — one or only some States may transfer or receive a speci fic power which can then be applied inconsistently between States. The second referendum is supported by the ALP and the Australian Democrats and opposed by the Liberal National parties. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll in the Bulletin indicates 49 per cent (down from 56 per cent in a fortnight) will vote "Yes", 36 per cent will say "No" and 15 per ccnl arc undecided. If you haven't already done so, read through the full "Yes" and "No" eases for the two referendums in the pamphlet posted to voters by the Australian Electoral Office. 13 Dec 1984 - 'Virtually impossible' to halt porn-tape imports Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 13 December 1984, page 3 'Virtually impossible' to halt porn-tape imports By HOWARD CON KEY Hard-core pornography had to be controlled at tho point of sale or hire, as it was virtually impossible to prevent it being imported into Australia, the chief censor of the Film Censorship Board, Ms Janet Strickland, said yesterday. Giving evidence at the first day of public hearings before the Senate Select Committee on Video Material, she said that, because of strong consumer demand, hard-core pornography accounted for about 33 per cent of all video tapes available in Aus tralia. In NSW, illegal X-rated material, which included explicit sexual acts, was readily available. She said Customs officials and NSW police believed that criminals were involved in importing the tapes, mostly from the United States. At a conference in Canada in September, she had learnt that most hard-corc pornography distribution houses in America were controlled by the Mafia. Given the nature of video tapes, she said, it was almost impossible to prevent their importation and, if there was to be strict control, it would be more effective at the point of sale or hire. The proceedings were marked by several sharp exchanges between Ms Strickland and a committee member, Senator Walters (Lib, Tas) over whether a classification above "R-rcstricted" should be made lawful. Ms Strickland was asked by Senator Walters whether the censorship board still held the view that there needed to be a classification above the R rating, in the light of Morgan Gallup opinion polls to the contrary. Ms Strickland said publicopinion polls were not always reliable, and went on to say it would be a mistalc for Senator Walters, on the first day of the inquiry, to prejudge what society wanted or what she thought it might want. Senator Walters and Senator Harradine (Ind, Tas), who seem to have split themselves in opinion from the Labor members on the committee, Senator Zakharov (Vic), Jones (Qld) and Elstob (SA), were quick to respond with questions about how Ms Strickland knew what the majority or minority views were. A submission tendered by the censorship board said a classification above R should be lawful because people in a pluralistic democratic socicty should have the right to read, hear and see what they wanted to in the privacy of their own homes, provided that people were not exposed to unsolicited material offensive to them and that children were not exposed to harmful material. "On the basis of material submitted to the Film Censorship Board since February, 1984, as well as from information obtained from Canada and the USA, it is evident that approximately 30 per cent of the overall video tape market consists of hard-core pornography, 95 per cent of this market deals exclusively in non-violent 'explicit erotica', and 'aggressive pornography' only constitutes 5 per ccnt of the hard-core pornography market and therefore 1.5 per cent of the total market," the submission said. "If a classification above the present 'R' classification were lawful for non-violent 'explicit erotica', only a small proportion of the present hard-core material would be refused classification or banned, whereas if there were to be a complete ban on any material above the current 'R' category, fully 30 per cent of the video tape material would be pushed underground." This would not only perpetuate, but substantially increase "the large and lucrative blackmarket" of hard-core pornography which would be controlled by criminal elements. Any legislation aimed at controlling the proliferation of "unacceptable" tapes was essentially difficult to enforce, given that tapes were easily transportable and capable of reproduction in large numbers. Importation, production, reproduction, sale and hire of violent, pornographic or otherwise obscene material is controlled under 4A(1 A) of the Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations, the Customs (Cinematograph Films) Regulations and the ACT Classification of Publications Ordinance 1983. The censorship board said the effectiveness of the legislative package to adequately control this material was dependent, to substantial degree, on resources available to implement and en force it.

08 Mar 1984 - Poll shows 70pc approval for Prime Minister Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 8 March 1984, page 10 Poll shows 70pc approval for Prime Minister SYDNEY: Seventy per cent of people surveyed approved of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, while only 36 per cent approved of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, the latest Morgan Gallup poll has revealed. Poll results for the week of February 18 to 25, published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday, put support for the Labor Party at 54 per cent and the Liberal-National Party coalition at close to 40 per cent. The Australian Democrats remained steady on 4 per cent. The figures showed that popular support for the Labor Party and Mr Hawke dropped three points during the second half of February, while approval for the coalition rose by the same margin. Despite the fact that the coalition made up some ground, Mr Peacock's approval rating represented a drop of three points. The number described as "undecided" rose by three points to 26 per cent. Mr Hawke's personal-support rating fell from a record 73 per cent. Of all electors surveyed, 71 per cent said they felt Mr Hawke made a better Prime Minister than would Mr Peacock. Only 17 per cent said Mr Peacock would do a better job. The Prime Minister continued to have an edge over the Opposi tion Leader among Liberal volers, with 43 per cent approvals to Mr Peacock's 40 per cent. The poll showed that Mr Hawke and the Premier of NSW, Mr Wran, would easily have won elections in their respective politi- . cal arenas if they had been held late. last month. Mr Wran would have clinched an easy win if an election had been held shortly before the March 24 polling date was an nounced. Support for the NSW Labor Party stood at 54 per cent, an increase of 2 per cent, and coalition support was down 2 per cent to 38 per cent. The personal-popularity ratings of both leaders fell slightly. Mr Wran's rating dropped three points to 48 per cent, and 42 per cent of electors polled approved of the Opposition Leader, Mr Greiner, a drop of 1 per cent. The results showed an improvement of 4 per cent for Mr Wran's Government on the sur; vey published a fortnight ago' following the latest round of corruption assertions.

10 Mar 1984 - Hart leads Reagan in presidency national opinion poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 10 March 1984, page 1 Hart leads Reagan in presidency national opinion poll ATLANTA. Georgia, Friday (N YT). — Senator Gary Hart leads President Reagan in a new Gallup poll, bolstering reports of a surge of support for him across the United States since his victories in New England Democratic presidential primaries. The poll, taken by telephone between March 2 and 6xamong 719 registered voters throughout the nation, confirmed what political specialists generally believe to be a highly volatile situation in the electorate five days before Tuesday's primaries and caucuscs in nine States. It found that 52 per cent of respondents favoured the Colorado senator to 43 per cent for Republican President Reagan. When matched against Senator Hart's two leading Democratic rivals in the poll, Mr Reagan led former Vice-President Walter Mondale 50 per ccnt to 45 per cent and Senator John Glenn, of Ohio, 52 per ccnt to 41 per ccnt. Gallup said the poll contained a possible margin of error of five percentage points in either direction and that a similar poll taken a few days earlier showed fasl-changing opinions among volcrs. but with Senator Hart rising "on a straight line". Aides to Mr Mondale acknowledged a "tremendous momentum" building for Senator Hart in the three Southern States which will hold primaries on Tuesday — Alabama, Georgia and Florida. "There is still tremendous momentum that flows from the New Hampshire, Maine and Vermont voting," the chief Mondale strategist, Mr James Johnson, said. "1 think the task for us in the next five days is to take this situation and raise the stakes in the election, to make it clear this is a very important choice, to define the different records and different traditions from which the two candidates come and to define the issue differences as clearly and aggressively as we can. "If we can't get that job done (the momentum for Senator Hart) has a lot of potential." To meet that challenge, Mr Mondale in the past few days has cancelled a scheduled return to Washington and stepped up his drive across the South, speaking to farmers, trade unionists, the 52 PER CENT Senator Hart 43 PER CENT President Reagan elderly, legislators and predominantly black audiences. At an outdoor meeting with environmentalists at Lake Jackson in Tallahassee yesterday, and in other campaign stops across Florida, he attacked Senator Hart as a candidate of tinsel and public relations and urged his audiences to "ignore the horse race, ignore the momentum". He criticised Mr Hart's views on arms control, saying his rival had failed to endorse the freeze on nuclear arms for nearly a year until announcing his candidacy for the presidency. And he cited Mr Hart's position on proposals under which the United States and the Soviet Union would destroy two nuclear weapons for every new one put in place. Senator Hart originally supported the "build-down" proposal but then voted against it in the Senate in October. "Following my opponent on arms control is like following a black bird on a dark night," Mr Mondale said. "Nobody knows." He has accused Senator Hart also of paying little attention to civil-rights issues. Senator Hart, for the most part, answered Mr Mondale's charges only obliquely, and addressed the campaign on a different level as he followed his opponent's footsteps through Alabama, visiting Governor George Wallace, who has endorsed no-onc, and speaking in the State House of Representatives, just as Mr Mondale did on Wednesday. Two other Democratic contenders. Senator John Glenn and the Reverend Jesse Jackson, also have made calls on Mr Wallace and addressed the House. The fifth candidate for paYty nomination, former Senator George McGovern, remained in Massachusetts, where he is gambling on that Stale's primary. Senator Hart told the legislature that the political parties "must free themselves from the grasp of special interests and once again address the country's national interest". "When promises arc traded for campaign support, what is really being given away?" he said. "I think it is our children's future and our nation's future." Without mentioning him by name, Senator Hart alluded to the fact that Mr Mondale had entered the presidential race with the endorsements of a large number of interest groups, including the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organisations. "In this hall the resolution of secession which withdrew Alabama from the union of sovereign States was passed January 11, 1861," he told the House. In 1984 another great issue faced the nation: "Arc we going to move to this nation's future, or are we going to slip back into its past?" In a primary, voters cast secrct ballots indicating their preferences for the party's nomination. Delegates to the Democratic national convention in San Francisco in July will select the party's candidate. Mr Reagan is expected to win the Republican Parly's nomination.

21 Mar 1984 - 'Seats will go' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 21 March 1984, page 1 'Seats will go' SYDNEY: The Wran Government will lose about 10 seats in Saturday's election, according to a Gallup poll to be published in The Bulletin today. The poll, taken two weeks ago, is understood to show a 3 per cent swing away from the Government since a similar poll in February, and the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Greiner, overtaking the Premier, Mr Wran, in the personal-approval ratings. According to the poll, the Government has a 51 per cent rating and the coalition 41 per cent. The figures translate into a 4.7 per cent two-party-preferred swing against the Gov ernment since the last election.

05 Apr 1984 - Opposition slips further Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 5 April 1984, page 1 Opposition slips further Support for the Opposition has declined further and is now 20 per cent behind the Government, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in yesterday's Bulletin. The poll puts Labor's support at 57 per cent and the coalition's at 37 per cent, a shift of two percentage points from the Opposition to the Government in the two weeks since the previous poll. Support for the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, was steady at the record 74 per cent shown last time, but the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, slipped two percentage points to 34 per cent. Only 14 per cent of all those polled thought Mr Peacock would make a better Prime Minister than Mr Hawke. Among coalition voters, Mr Hawke outstripped Mr Peacock by 10 per cent. For Mr Peacock, his latest popularity rating score continued a downward trend since the start of the year with successive figures of 41 per cent, 37, 39, 36, 36, 34. [A poll by Australian Public Opinion Polls for The Sun News-Pictorial, Melbourne, last month gave Mr Hawke an approval rating of 78 per cent.]

13 Sep 1980 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 13 September 1980, page 2 Saturday, September'-13; 1980. RUNNING Bad luck for the Caulfield Gup and the Bong Bong picnics, but not unwelcome to most Australians. That must be the first reaction to Caulfield and'Bong Bong's counter-attraction on October 18. The second reaction is that Labor starts down the final straight with a weight handicap which may be too tough, although, according to the latest Morgan Gallup opinion poll, it is now galloping almost neck and neck with the Government. To draw ahead and win would be a famous victory. The handicap, of course, is a 48-seat margin in a House of Representatives of 124, which will become 125 after this election. Mr Hayden's party must win 25 seats if he is to be Prime Minister. The odds must be against him. Labor went into training, in a sense, as early as November last year, when the first of its policies was announced, and earlier there were discussion papers to get the electors used to Labor's point of view. Now there are only two of its policies which are not known, and they are the one on industrial relations, which will be announced in Melbourne on Monday by Mr HaySen, with Messrs Hawke and Young in attendance, and the one on foreign investment. The strategy is the same as that used in 1972, when the crowd was convinced and barracked Labor to the winning post. The only other Labor unknown is where the tax cut will be made — on petrol, personal incomes, or sales. Some will also doubt the jockey, Mr Hayden. Will he ride, as Mr Whitlam did in 1972, with that massive confidence which so appeals to punters? We believe he cannot do this. It is not his nature. We also believe that he ought not to denigrate the Prime Minister in personal terms, as he does. It, too, is not his nature. The people make their own judgments about their leaders, and they are usually shrewd ones. Policies are much harder to understand, and the people need to be helped about judgment on these. That duty is a full-time responsibility for political leaders. Mr Hayden has a fair record on which to stand. It entitles him to be heard with respect when he eschews personal criticism and sticks to the economic policy which is going to be crucial for Australia. His Budget in 1975 was widely regarded as a responsible document after much Labor irresponsibility earlier. It is worth pondering what this country would have been like today had Mr Hayden been in charge over the past five years. In fact, it was Mr Fraser, with more apparent stamina, who had to cope with the immense problems of world recession and inflation in the West, and with a consequent level of unemployment which is cruel. He will be judged by the people for what he has done to shelter Australia,, to inspire Australians, and to spread fairly within Australia the burden of the world's ills. His task has been the harder one because he, not Mr Hayden, has had the responsibility. There can be no doubts in his case about performance. There must always be doubts about the performance in office of Opposition Leaders. Toil and hard times This is a harsh country to govern, even in the best of times, as the drought reminds us, cracking the land about our capital. Thunder and lightning fought in the skies as Mr Fraser announced the polling day.1 Whoever wins will not be getting much of a prize, only toil and more hard times. But the prospect does not have to be a gloomy one, if it is seen as an opportunity for healing. Australia is not too well, and this campaign should not wound it any more. There is much in common between the major parties, as next week's final parliamentary session could proclaim. But the race is on, the whips are out, and we must not expect too much. However The Canberra Times, which is not racing, reminds the runners that they do agree about the need to fight inflation and about the level of defence spending. They all want to bring down unemployment and interest rates. They all want to keep in some sort of order and amity their unruly followers in the States, and especially in Queensland and Western Australia. None of them have the courage to do what ought to be done about protection. All of them, except the Australian Democrats, are frightened about what will happen in the Senate. None of them did anything to reform the Senate, when they all shared an interest in reform and the opportunity, for almost three years, to effect it. This last neglect gives the people a particular responsibility, to vote with a maximum, direct purpose for the Senate, in order to give the Government or the Opposition an overall majority. As it is, the Senate is best when it reflects the situation in the House of Representatives. Protest votes are not in order for the Senate. With that gratuitous advice we end, for the moment, our observations on Caulfield and Bong Bong's counter-attraction.
