28 Sep 1980 - Predictions based on atmospherics and a prayer Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 28 September 1980, page 6 Predictions based on atmospherics and a prayer By GAY DAVIDSON, Political Correspondent Jn Canberra we know that an election campaign has been seething for months —we looked at the Budget in that context and have been judging the performance of the local candidates in that light. But it has still not officially begun, and won't until the staged performances in Melbourne and Brisbane in another two or three days. At that time we will know whether we are in for 17 days of the same rhetoric or whether because of a few promises and shifts in emphasis, there will be issues of real interest to discuss and judge. It will be some days later before we will have any indication of what Australia generally is thinking about October 18 and the next Government. The latest published polls, Morgan Gallup, were taken on the weekends of September 6 and 13, before the election was announced, and showed the Government ahead and Labor not far behind but with 5 per cent more than in the 1977 election, and the Australian Democrats °°wn a little on recent months and only about half their actual support in It will be another week yet before there are polls showing voting intentions after the election announcement, and it will be close to election day before' there are polls of voting intentions after the policy speeches. So at this stage predictions are based on atmospherics and a prayer. Prudent Because 1 think the prudent course is to assume a small swing against the Government, certainly a smaller swing than the polls before the election was announced, based on the assumption that the electorate does not look to an untried Leader when they feel insecure and their prospects uncertain, my bet is in the low field for Labor gains. I would look to a maximum of 15, possibly only 10, when the numbers begin going up in the tally room on Saturday October 18. Mercifully, for Sunday , papers, we will know more on the night about the votes in South Australia, Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Queensland than if the election was being held in December, after daylightsaving begins. On that expectation the coalition would remain in Government with a major ity of between 14 and 19. That assumes that Labor loses nong of their present 38 seats, the Government loses 10 to 15 from its present 86 but picks up the one new seat in Western Australia. To win Government Labor would need an overall swing of 6.1 per cent. Some of the 25 seats involved 1 would give very little chance of changing bands, such as Lowe (Sir William McMahon) and Calare (Mr McKenzie, MCP) in NSW, Franklin (Mr Goodluck), Tasmania, Lilley (Mr Kevin Cairns), and Bowman (Mr Jull) and Brisbane (Mr Peter Johnson) in Queensland. Hurts In those States the more likely seats, certainly the ones to watch from early in the night are: NSW — Macquarie and Macarthur on the metropolitan fringe, where the price of petrol really hurts, St George, phillip and Barton, all marginal and metropolitan, and Eden -Monaro. In Queensland Labor has to be in major trouble if it cannot get Leichhardt, which requires a swing of less than 1 per cent. In South Australia it should take Kingston (less than 2 per cent) and in Western Australia, Swan, the most marginal seat in the election at .6 per cent. In Tasmania Wilmott is the only really likely Labor gain, assuming that the sitting members have been as assiduous as local members as they are generally believed to be. Retiring In the Northern Territory Mr Calder is retiring from his NCP seat, and it needs a swing of only 2.4 per cent to go to Labor, but with Labor increasingly and suspiciously viewed as the "Aborigines' Party" the NCP is likely to hold it. All the marginal seats in Victoria appear possible. They are La Trobe, the "sandbclt seats" of Hotham, Holt and Henty, and the industrial and semi-rural seat of McMillan. But in La Trobe the Right to Life movement is supporting Mr Baillieu, as has the Government, with very recent assistance to a major manufacturing industry. On the other hand, in McMillan the Right to Lifers are gunning for the Liberals' Mr Simon. The DLP is likely to support Labor, and Labor could even benefit from resentment against Government efforts to save Mr Simon. The sandbelt seats are being heavily supported by the Government. They are outer metropolitan, feel the effects of petrol prices, and all swung to Labor by more than 2 per cent in 1977 when the national average was 1.1 per cent. That brings us to Canberra in the ACT. Our resident psephologist Mr Malcolm Mackerras would see that as a Labor victory, with a swing of only 1.1 per cent required and resentment against the Government automatically assumed. He may be right, but a recent survey gave Labor a very small winning margin — that could improve or erode during the course of the campaign. Canberra ranks fourth in the Government marginal seats and would have to be the most interesting of the lot to watch on October 18.

09 Oct 1980 - Outrage, explanations on threat Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 9 October 1980, page 15 (j2Eggj|j\ Reaction from all points.along the campaign" trail yesterday v to ' the Prime Minister's blunt threat to block Supply to a Labor.Government ranged from predictable outrage front the Opposition to cautious soft-pedalling' from the National Country Party, and explanations from Mr Fraser. A threat by the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser to block Supply in the Senate against a Labor Government were "Borstal boy tactics", the leader of the Opposition, Mr Hayden, said in Sydney yesterday. Mr Hayden said that'in making the threat Mr Fraser was reaffirming the "Borstal boy tactics" he had brought to Australian politics. "Mr Fraser is now thrashing about like a wounded duck in open season", he said. Mr Fraser was shifting ground rapidly on issues and behaving like a desperate man. "The situation is that if there is a Labor Government there will not be a coalition majority in the Senate", he said. "The worst that could happen is that the Labor Party would have half the representation in the Senate and the Democrats would have the balance of power". Mr Hayden said Mr Fraser's behaviour in blocking Supply against the Whitlam Government in 1975 had done enormous damage to the Australian, social and political system. The Australian Democrats Leader, Senator Chipp, described Mr Fraser's statement as "shocking" and the biggest election issue so far. "The reasons for his attacks on the Democrats over the past week have now become crystal clear",he said., "He's divulged the shocking purpose that he wants to retain control of the Senate so he can repeat the 1975.sacking of a' Labor Prime Minister if he loses the election. "The ALP cannot win control of the Senate because of the numbers. Therefore,' what the Democrats are saying is the only way of ensuring a stable gov ernment for the next three years is for. the Democrats to hold that balance of:.^ power in the Senate". The ALP federal .president, Mr Wran, said Mr Fraser had proved himself unworthy of the .support of Australian voters. By blocking Supply in 197S Mr Fraser had shown he had: no principles. , Mr Fraser's statement was made in response to a question at a Journalists' ' Club lunch in Sydney on Tuesday when he was asked if he would'again block Supply. He said, "If the circumstances exist that existed in 1975 — and I ask you to remember what was, happening in 1975 — I would do everything I could, to get rid of the government of the day". To an interjection from the floor asking if this meant blocking Supply, Mr Fraser said his answer was "quite precise, quite clear". Mr Fraser's denying Supply to the Labor Government in the Senate jn 1975 led eventually to the dismissal of the Prime Minister, Mr Whillami by the then Governor-General, Sir John Kerr, on November 11, 1975. ' In Townsville, the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr Anthony, said the National Country Party would "consider" blocking Supply to a Labor Government in certain circumstances. He made the statement in Queensland while Mr Fraser was trying to play down his remarks of yesterday. Mr Anthony was questioned during a news conference, and described as "extreme" the circumstances of 1975. "If a situation of a drastic nature were to occur then you would have to take whatever measure you can", he said. "I would not want to give any idea that I do not consider it other than a very important issue, which is to be thoughtout very carefully". In Adelaide yesterday, Mr Fraser said his-remarks. about the blocking of: Supply had been "amplified out of all proportion" in press reports yesterday.!' Speaking on a radio program Mr Fraser said the Supply issue was a "red herring", and was "all hypothetical"because his Government would be returned ai the election on Saturday week. "What I was saying was purely in the. context of 1975, and you know'there were many things that were happening then —' it wasn't only the economic responsibility, there was a madness in that administration", he said. Asked about Labor's strong showing in the opinion polls, Mr Fraser admitted : that Liberal Party officials were ' puzzled by. it; ; ; ; "There does not seem to be one major issue running against the Government"/ he said. "It is, in a sense, a mystery . He said Mr Hayden was not flamboyant in the Whitlam. style, but in many ways he was recycling (he same programs. • A Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin yesterday showed that the Labor Party had enough support to win government. ■ The poll showed Labor was supported , by 50 per cent of the survey group, compared with 43 per cent for the coalition parties and 5 per cent for the Australian Democrats. Observers said if that level of support was maintained until polling on October 18, Labor would win a majority in the House of Representatives.

09 Oct 1980 - POLITICS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 9 October 1980, page 2 POLITICS Opinion polls spur the party leaders into revealing more of themselves From GAY DAVIDSON, in Adelaide It IS still too early to be sure whether the voting intentions' expressed in the Morgan Gallup , and Saulwick polls will hold up on October 18. Some of the 53 per cent (Morgan Gallup, two-party pre ferred) and 57 per cent • (Saulwick) of people who said thait they would vote Labor may be scared into retreat now that they are aware of the possibility of a Labor Government. On the other hand, some may be encouraged not to waver now that, they know they appear to be supporting the winning side. The polls may even attract some of the "don't -knows" (Saulwick 6 per cent, Morgan Gallup 8 per cent) to Labor. However, it is clear that the swing away from the Government is real. The Liberals' own poll, available to the party on Wednesday, has moved in the same direction, although no details are being divulged. Drama The next polls, McNair Anderson, to be published tomorrow, were taken last weekend and there will be further Saulwick and Morgan Gallup polls (to be taken this weekend), in the middle of next week. Apart from the drama of awakening everyone to the fact that the result of October 18 is not a foregone conclusion, the polls have thrown up some very important information. They show that the split in the anti-conservative ranks is all but healed. It has taken 25 years — a whole generation — from the events of the mid-1950s which produced the DLP, but now that breakaway is only a vestige of its former self. The ALP is back to the sort of strength that the alternative government should have in a healthy democracy. This suggests that in future Australia is likely to have more frequent changes of government, as is the case in other Westminster systems.^ Protest ' The polls indicate that the Australian Democrats, as well as the 25 years' elapse of time, have helped bring this about. . In the last election the AD preferences split about equally. Now, with the AD vote down (from 9.4 per cent in 1977 to 6 per cent, Saulwick) ar 5 per cent (Morgan), and with the pollsters regarding the second preferences as going 60 per cent1 to the Ljberals, it appears that the ADs are not only a protest party but also a means for people to transfer their votes. Of more immediate interest for the election in 10 days* time, the polls have startled both Mr Fraser and Mr Hayden into showing more of themselves to the voting public. Mr Hayden has been more relaxed, and appeared more likeable, to the relief of his party organisation. Affluence But he has also been led into doing a couple of things he and they could live to regret. On Wednesday he played up to Mr Fraser's affluence and challenged him on his taxation ('TU show mine if you'll show yours"). That immediately allowed Mr Fraser to criticise Mr Hayden for playing the man and not the ball. It was an unnecessary, as well as a foolish tactic, because Mr Fraser had got himself trapped in the Mr Fraser minefield of the 1975 blockage of Supply. Yesterday Mr Hayden touched another hip-pocket nerve when he announced that a Labor Government would not introduce a wealth or capital-gains tax in its first three years. Deferral That may attract some middleclass voters — certainly the Italianlanguage newspaper II Globo on Tuesday was keen to know Labor's intention on that score. In reply, then, Mr Hayden pointed out that most European countries had such a tax. However, now that he has announced a deferral of that policy, he has left himself open to criticism of opportunism both from the coalition parties and Labor supporters. Mr Fraser's reaction to the polls has been equally interesting. He set out to improve his image by showing himself more concerned about people. Yesterday he made several new short television commercials telling voters not about the Government's achievements but, snuggling up close to all of us, about what "we" have done — and now risk losing. "We've come so far together over the last five years", Mr Fraser says in one. "To change course now would put qt risk everything we've achieved". It was an amazing sight, watching Mir Hayden him in Sydney on Wednesday pat a rather grubby Teddy bear while trying to converse with its two-yearold owner, and then hoist her threeyear-old brother on to his shoulders during a walk through Martin Plaza. Wounds But whatever the point he gained from the television audiences for that, they cannot make up for his mistake in opening up the btockageof-Supply wounds. He need not have answered the question of whether he would consider using the Senate to stop short the term of a Labor Government: nobody expected him to. But when he did say that he would, the issue spread in all directions. He was tackled on it by a radio interviewer and talk-back questioners in Adelaide yesterday, and tried to stifle the issue by saying it was a hypothetical question as the coalition parties were going to win. He refused to say he regretted his previous answer and lashed out at the newspapers which, "had ^piplified it out of all proportion". , Edgy about further questioning he cancelled a press conference scheduled for Adelaide then held one anyway to get the media interested in a fall on the Stock Exchange, attributing that to investors' reaction to the possibility of a Labor Government. (Experienced observers of the Stock Market consider it was due to happen anyway because the market was overheated). Slammed When the travelling Press twice tried asking him about the Supply question, he slammed, his car door on one occasion and walked out of the room on the other. We did not get an opportunity to ask him about Mr Anthony saying yesterday that he would support a blockage of Supply to a Labor Government in certain circumstances, and that no one could be sure those circumstances would never arise again. He may also have made a mistake in being so publicly sure that-he will be returned to government.: That could be interpreted by voters' as refusing to accept their judgment. . Confidence in his own policy would have been a less abrasive course than any implication that the voters are wrong-headed or will come to heel.

14 Oct 1980 - Fear: a two-edged weapon in the election campaign Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 14 October 1980, page 2 Fear: a two-edged weapon in the election campaign POLITICS By GAY DAVIDSON So FAR all the major polls have given government to Labor and the next Morgan Gallup, out on Wednesday, is expected to still give Labor a slight edge. But still there is a general questioning, a feeling that it won't be, it can't be, like that on The Day. Yet, if the polls are right, Labor actually needs less than the 1.5 per cent margin on top of 50 per cent of the poll that it is generally assumed it needs to win. Labor will need a bare 51 per cent nationally if the very large swings shown in Victoria and Queensland hold up. However, the interpretations of the polls are not as fascinating as the reactions to them by the various protagonists. Since the first shock, the Saulwick poll giving 57 per cent to Labor, the Labor team has been doing its best to ride the winning numbers without stumbling, and to keep on explaining its policies. Mr Hayden has been baring more of himself to the public gaze and looking both more confident (occasionally, too confident) and considerably more effective as a campaigner than most Canberra journalists or the coalition parties expected. Just as the light dawned a couple of weeks ago that Labor had a better-than-even chance, it has since become apparent that Bill Hayden has leadership qualities that were generally overlooked. i— , How else could he have persuaded the Labor Party to accept middleground policies in order to win — especially when few Labor people placed any credence in the possibility of winning? How else could he have kept the dissidents to the left and right in the; ALP ranks silent — especially when some of them are more comfortable thinking of their party and themselves as a critical Opposition than a governing party? Pragmatist Mr Hayden the pragmatist, ready to compromise, to defer, to play on the electorate's hip-pocket nerve, to use the tactics which have served the coalition parties well in previous elections, has startled Mr Fraser and his advisers. They had locked themselves into a campaign in which further promises were impossible, and in which much change to their early emphasis on Mr Fraser personally was too great'a risk to the credibility of the policies aligned with him. So they found only one way to go. That road is fear. Not, as in 1975 and 1977, emphasising above all the lack of a feeling of security in the electorate and nailing that firmly to "the Whitlam years" (although that menace has emerged in the last few days, too). In 1980 fear is being exploited more in the assertions that the economy would go to hell under a Labor Government, the frightening advertisements stating that Labor will take from the poor as well as the rich, and in the street walks intended to attract supporters and opponents with strong feelings — people who are likely to get carried away and provide pictorial and film evidence that the coalition's adversaries are threatening and uncontrolled louts. To the coalition assertions Labor can only make contrary assertions and try even harder to persuade that its policies are responsible as well as socially more just. If Labor refers to the Government claims in order to rebut them it is automatically in a negative situation, but if it does not use that element of conflict it cannot expect media coverage this late in a campaign in which the policies have already been outlined and explained to the point of boredom. It has cried foul to the advertise ments, pointing out its firm undertakings not to introduce wealth or capital gains taxes without first holding an inquiry and taking any proposals to the next election as specific policy issues. It has also pointed out that Australia is the only industrialised country without such a tax on wealth (specifically on wealth and not on the usual assets of low and middle income workers). But its real hope must be that the electorate is generally better informed and discerning than the Liberal Party has assumed, and so will discount the ads, perhaps even resenting the implication that they can be persuaded by such misleading propaganda. The coalition's last-minute organisation of street meetings and walks with the likelihood of displays of menace and possibly violence is the nastiest tactic. However, without any scheming by Labor, these events have turned into a weapon potentially as dangerous for Mr Fraser as for Mr Hayden. It was the Liberal candidate for La Trobe in outer-suburban Mel bourne, Mr Marshall Baillieu, who destabilised the weapon when he associated himself with a few ugly disrupters among his supporters who harassed Mr Hayden and the Labor supporters at two shopping centres on Saturday. After a woman was knocked.down Mr Hayden decided the prudent and moderate course was to cut short his street walk and remove himself from sight for half an hour before carrying on with the rest of his program, a lunch in a hall. Provocative His doing so clearly put the onus on Mr Fraser to do the same in similar circumstances — or to be judged deliberately provocative. Mr Fraser has tried to distance himself from that obligation. He claimed at the weekend that Labor supporters began the trouble, and when journalists who had been present told him that was simply not true, he said he must have been wrongly advised. But he has not set the record straight publicly. He was questioned several times in radio interviews and talkbacks yesterday, before the big street rally in Melbourne's Civic Square, about the effects of and reasons for this kind of campaigning. He said street walks should not create tensions, it concerned him if they did, but people should be able to put their arguments to the Prime Minister who, in turn, should be able to go out amongst the people. "But Prime Minister, you can only shake hands". Generally yes, Mr Fraser agreed, but that was a demonstration of his concern for people. "Are you a healer or a creator of divisions?" Mr Fraser said he was certainly not a creator of divisions.' He regarded the ALP as the creator, of them, and repeated that it was' Labor people who had started the trouble at Mr Hayden's street walk, qualifying the statement slightly by saying, "there's some dispute about that". ""Why are you the target?" Mr Fraser said Liberal leaders had always been targets at election time and Labor leaders were generally not. In the event yesterday's crowd of between 4,000 and 5,000 was noisy but remained good humoured, in spite of the taunts that they were a rabble and that was the standard of the ALP. If that changes, if the good humour, evaporates in Sydney (the next venue before the electronic me , dia are cut out from the campaign), it will be guesswork as to who gets the blame and loses votes.

03 Jun 1981 - Memo Mr Fraser: ignore the fair go ethic at your peril! Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 3 June 1981, page 2 Memo Mr Fraser: ignore the fair go ethic at your peril! BETWEEN THE LINES By GAY DAVIDSON | Unquestioning be lief in the concept of the fair go is arguably the one area of total agreement remaining in the Australian community. The fair go is not. merely an egalitarian instinct. It requires umpires and widespread understanding of both- the game and the rules. So it is part of something a bit grander, even philosophical, the idea that checks and balances and generally .available information are essential to our form of democracy. There is reason to believe that Mr ' Fraser has not fillly realised the x- importance of the-fair go, although he has propounded it on many occa sions — for instance, in upholding -the independence of the Industries Assistance Commission and laying ■ idown rules of procedure for statu tory appointments. But he has hot done as he has said. In 1977, a year after those pronoun , cements, the most influential IAC commissioner, Mr D. Pekin, was not reappointed and there was no explanation. Five weeks ago the decisions from the Review of Commonwealth Functions included hacking into the IAC's research capacity and raising doubts about whether it would be given or be able to handle the anticipated general reference on industry protection. Last week two more statutory appointees,., the senior commissioner, lylr Dick Boyer, and the full-time member of the Temporary Assistance Authority, Mr Frank :Pascoe, were not reappointed, again '''without explanation.' A number of Mr Fraser's backbench colleagues are concerned for the particular individuals, but they are even more concerned for the likely effect on the IAC. They recog nisc the possibility that commissioners in future will tailor their decisions and reports according to their perceptions of the Prime Min ister's wishes. That would not only, do violence to the idea of the IAC as umpire, but major damage to its value as an independent source of information and assessment. The disquiet about the fate of the individuals has a great deal to do with their particular areas of in terest: Mr Pascoe arrived at the IAC as a manufacturing lobbyist and was converted, to the point of being critical of the Government's policies in his last two reports. Mr Boyer a commissioner for- the past 22 years, and the only farmer member, was generally seen as having a very clear perception of what a market economy is, and also of the restiveness of the resource-rich States at the continuing Canberra support for the least efficient, heav ily protected manufacturing industries concentrated in Victoria and NSW. On this latter point the Government has sustained a great deal of criticism for not taking the tough decisions it promised, and Mr Fraser •has encountered the problem face to face with the Premiers at recent conferences, and even at the Liberal Federal Council last weekend. There will be more of that, not only from the Premiers but also the Senate, if he cannot come up with policies suited to the States where the resources and economic growth are, at the expense of those where profits and jobs are heavily sub sidised. , Among politicians, lobbyists and others interested in industry protection issues, Mr Fraser is considered personally responsible for the diminution of the IAC, rather than its Minister, Mr Moore. And they see the downgrading of the IAC as part of the same kind of thinking that produced the more philistine decisions of the Review of Commonwealth Functions: the reduction of functions and institutions which could open up the decisionmaking process to public scrutiny, and the object of smaller govern ment without thought for whether or not that meant good' government, so long as it assisted the cause of less expenditure. A similar insensitivity to the fair go is apparent in government attitudes to the Conciliation and Arbitration Commission. In recent years the Government has vilified the commission for some of its wage-indexation decisions and attacked it for .not acting as an instrument of the Government's economic policy. In effect, the Government has ignored the commission's constitutional obligation to act as umpire, and criticised it for not performing as something else again, an arm of Government. But. in. doing so the Government and Mr Fraser are demonstrably at odds with a cohsiderable majority of the community. - On Monday a Saulwick'opinion poll published in The Age, Melbourne, and The Sydney Morning Herald showed 54 per cent believing the commission impartial and 69 per .cent bejieving it should maintain its present function. Only 26 per cent thought wages, hours and conditions should be de; termined by direct, negotiation. Asked what would happen, if. the commission were abolished, 55 per cent thought workers in powerful unions would get more, and those in weak unions would get less. Mr Boyer Interestingly, it was Liberal voters, white-collar and non-union workers who were most in favour of maintaining the commission in its present role — all of which should be food for thought for a Prime Minister of a nan-Labor Government. ■, Saying one thing and doing another may upset just a noisy few in areas such as overseas aid or Aboriginal land rights. " ' But it is'another thing entirely in issues close to the self-interest and the fair-go instincts of major sections of the community (such as the workforce), or people with major influence, whether they be Government Members and Senators, State Premiers, or resource developers. Ignoring or confronting them over a fair-go matter, or not working out a reasonable compromise between : their interests and those of people who have had much more than a fair go for far too long, could get the Government into greater trouble than anything it has seen yet. •

21 Jan 1981 - Sewerage poll postponed Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 21 January 1981, page 13 Sewerage poll postponed A special meeting of Eurobodalla Shire Council voted yesterday to postpone a referendum on the introduction of sewerage in the Mossy Point — Broulee area after a public meeting of ratepayers on Saturday. The ratepayers sought more time and the council has agreed that the referendum should be held on February !$, not next weekend. The shire engineer, Mr Peter Abbott-Smith, said yesterday ttlat the Tuross referendum would go ahead as planned at the weekend. Nr Abbott-Smith said also that the council was hopeful garden watering hours might soon be ex tended. Watering was limited to two hours from 6pm daily earlier this summer because of the lack of rain and the influx of visitors.

24 Jan 1981 - WRITERS' WORLD THE NITTY-GRITTY OF POWER, ELITES AND POLITICS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 January 1981, page 14 THE NITTY-GRITTY OF POWER, ELITES AND POLITICS Writer's World. By MAURICE DUNLEVY In ONE of their most dis- astrous business years, British publishers in 1980 brought out a record 48,158 titles. Of these, 37,382 were new books and 10,776 reprints and new edi-tions. The number of titles repre-sented an increase of about 15 per cent on the number for 197? and was almost three times as many as the trade produced in 1950. It will probably surprise liberal arts readers to learn that the top category increase was in Political Science and Economy — up in a year by 905 titles to 4,269, making it second only to Fiction (5,145) titles). Nor is this new. Politics has been the rising star in book prod-uction for some years, both in Eng-land and Australia. I'm afraid I can't offer an ade-quate explanation for this. Books on politics are not very popular in the circles in which I move. Perhaps they are read by public servants who chuckle behind the pot plants when they read memoirs and studies based on the assumption that it is the politicians who really make the big decisions. Because I was raised in an en-vironment in which we ate politics for breakfast, lunch and dinner and discussed it passionately almost every night, I have been a com-pulsive reader of political books since I was a boy, although my dear old Dad would turn over in his grave if he could see the conservative non-sense I read these days. Over the Christmas break I read the new edition of 'Politics in Eng-land' by Richard Rose, which de-spite the revision is getting dated. I also had a little laugh at 'Public Opinion' by Harry Holloway and John George, one of the many Amer-ican attempts to rationalise the polit-ical system to show that democracy operates in much the way that the founding fathers hoped it would. A much more interesting book — indeed, an absolutely riveting one — is Eric F. Goldman's 'The Tragedy of Lyndon Johnson', which I missed when it appeared in 1969, but I recently bought John Menadue's copy from a secondhand bookshop. But easily the best book I read during the break was 'Elites in Aus-tralia' by John Higley, Desley Dea con and Don Smart (Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1979). It is the most impressive account I have read of how the national political system "really" works. Using a survey of national elites in eight important sectors of Australian society and applying sophisticated network analysis to the results, they show that we are ruled by a core of politicians, businessmen, public ser-vants and others, most of whom have risen to power not through in-heritance but through large institu-tions. They exercise their power through a system which involves a high degree of mutual access, a common belief in preserving existing political institutions and by enjoying considerable protection from demo-cratic pressures. Of the new political books, the one which held most promise for me was 'Interest Groups and Public Policy' edited by Roger Scott, a man for whom I have a high regard as an academic and an administrator (Macmillan, 248 pp., $9.95). But I am afraid I finished it disillusioned and disappointed. This is a collection of 10 studies by political scientists.concerned with the operation of interest groups in state politics. Wedged between an introduction to interest group theory by Harmon Zeigler and a concluding synthesis by Roger Scott are eight ease studies of interest groups in action. Andrew Parkin and Adam Gray-car look at the South Australian Council of Social Service, Alistair Heatley studies the campaign for Aboriginal land rights in the Northern Territory, Keith Rich-mond surveys the major rural pro-ducer groups in New South-Wales, Michael Hogan shows how the Catholics defended their school sys-tem in New South Wales, Ann Scott tells how the Joynerites had the Social Educational Materials Project banned in Queensland schools, Bruce Davis writes on the environmentalists' struggle over South-West Tasmania, Owen Hughes covers the conflict between environmentalists and the bauxite miners plus the Court Government, and Jean Holmes analyses the conse-quences of Hanger's attempt to get some real urban planning in Vic- toria. Several things troubled me. First, several of the essays, particularly a couple of those on environmental issues, display considerably less ob-jectivity than the average newspaper story. Newspapers operate on the assumption that objectivity can be achieved by a set of strategic rituals, one of which is to give both sides a fair hearing. Most of the fairness in these accounts goes to the environ- mentalists. Second, few of the essays are more than descriptive case studies. Only Jean Holmes makes a real attempt to relate her study to interest group theory. Most of the others, display little sign that they are aware it exists. No one gives more than pass-ing attention to the dynamics of interest group communication and hardly anyone sees it as part of the political communication process. Third, although many of the con-tributors are said to have been close-ly involved with their interest groups, there is a notable lack .of what Henry James called "felt life" in all of the studies, unlike the Higley, Deacon, Smart book which is peppered with revealing quota- tions. Fourth, the standards of both scholarship and production are poor. The book is studded with unsup-ported generalisations and lapses in detail. One contributor who rather tartly notes a spelling error in a name included in an interest group's press release has a name misspelled in her footnotes. The book is printed on see-through paper, is littered with printer's errors, grammatical errors, strange syntax and unnecessary jargon. It was with some relief that I turned to J. F. H. Wright's 'Mirror of the Nation's Mind' (Hale and Iremonger, 160pp., $6.95), even though it turned out to be not a mirror of the nation's mind. This is a clearly written, well, edited and sensitively designed book about Australia's experiments with electoral systems written by the NSW president of the Proportional Representation Society. It traces the, history of voting techniques used in Australia, analyses their strengths and weaknesses and recommends as an ideal system a quota-preferential method based on electoral districts, each returning an odd number of members. Personally I'm not in love with proportional representation, even if the mathematics are a strong argu-ment for it. Nor for that matter the nation. The true mirror of the nation's mind was the Morgan Gallup poll published (significant-ly?) on November 11, 1980. It showed that only one in three Aus-tralians prefer the present preferen-tial system and that 54 per cent favour first-past-the-post. Indeed, polls conducted since 1963 have con-sistently shown a majority in favour of the latter. But that's enough about politics for the time being. I'm now up to my ears in the million words of Barbara Castle's diary. Did you know that she had to have the legs of her cabinet room chair encased in cretonne because every time she sat on it she laddered her tights?

19 Apr 1940 - Stibbard's Creek Drainage Richmond River Herald and Northern Districts Advertiser (NSW : 1886 - 1942), Friday 19 April 1940, page 4 Stibbard's Creek Drainage POLL OF RATEPAYERS. An advertisement 'appears in this issue, notifying that the Gundurimba Shire Council will take a poll of the ratepay-ers who are, interested in the Stibbard's Creek drainage works upon the question whether those ratepayers approve of the raising of the loan required to put the scheme into operation. The Shire Clerk has pointed out that the poll must be conducted along similar lines to those pertaining to Shire elec-tions, and it would, therefore, be ne- cessary for the ratepayers to complete the declaration printed on the face of the poll paper envelope. This declaration is substantially the same as that used in recent Shire elections, where the failure of the witness to state a correct title was responsible for large percentages of informal votes. In view of the small number of poll papers to be issued in this instance, it was most desirable that all votes cast should be formal votes, and the result, therefore, be a true expression of the views of the people concerned. The Shire Clerk states that if a wit-ness stated in the place provided for "Class of Witness" on the declaration form, the words 'Farmer,' 'Grazier,' 'Landowner' or other classes not nam-ed in the footnote, it would be necessary to reject as informal the vote accom-panying that declaration. The words 'Shire Election' or 'State Elector' would be accepted as proper classes of witnesses. It was essential that the witness also state his address. Careful perusal of the instructions 'How to Vote' was advisable. __________________________________ Stanley Peate (aged 12) passed away in hospital at Gloucester after a few days' illness, following the eating of an out-of-season water melon. __________________________________

27 Nov 1980 - Gallup gives Qld win to Nationals Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 27 November 1980, page 3 BRISBANE:- The National Party, is-./ sued details of the first opinion poll for: Saturday's State election' yesterday and immediately forecast a resounding victory with five additional seats for it. The Morgan Gallup poll, commissioned by. . The Bulletin, shows the-Premier, Mr Bjelke-. Petersen, comfortably leading his opponents in popularity with an approval rating of 47 per cent. ... The Liberal leader, Dr Edwards, has an approval rating of 42 per cent and the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Casey, 33 per cent. But both Dr Edwards and Mr Casey said the only poll they were interested in was the one on Saturday. Dr Edwards said another survey conducted by the Morgan Research group showed the Liberal Party was the only party'to improve on its 1977 election figures. He said the "voters' intention poll" showed the Liberals with 27 per cent of the vote - an increase of 2 per cent - and the Nationals with 24 per cent of the vote, a drop of 3 per cent. Dr Edwards said the Labor vote in the second poll had been 42 per ccnt, which represented a drop of about 1 per cent. The managing director of the ' Morgan . group, Mr Gary Morgan, confirmed that a ?voter-intention poll had been conducted over the past four weeks but it; had not been published because he believed it would not be a fair and accurate guide. Mr Casey said the opinion poll could not be.taken seriously. "The Federal election clearly showed that polls we're inaccurate", he said. "I believe there are more and more people who make up their minds on election day". Mr Bjelke-Petersen plans to hold an electoral redistribution at "an appropriate time" within the next term of Parliament. At a Press.' conference yesterday he warned the Liberals1 that crossing the floor of the House to vote with . Labor on an electoral redistribution would result in the Federal Liberals being . "annihilated" at the next Federal election as Queenslanders reacted against the party. A record 1,341,365 Queenslanders are eligible to vote on Saturday to . elect Queensland's 43rd Parliament. They will choose from 271 candidates standing for the 82 Legislative Assembly seats.

08 Dec 1980 - ELECTORAL CHANGE Hayden pledges reform battle Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 8 December 1980, page 1 ELECTORAL CHANGE Hayden pledges reform battle SYDNEY: The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Hayden, committed the Labor Party yesterday to a concerted battle for reform of the electoral system. In his first speech to a major Labor Party gathering since the October Federal election, Mr Hayden blamed the voting system for not reflecting the true support of the parties. He said the Government would have only a two- or three-seat majority in the House of Repre sentatives if it was not for "the electoral distortion". The Labor Party would now begin a strong campaign to have electorates drawn up more fairly, to introduce public funding of Federal political campaigns, to alter the way names were placed on ballot papers and to enforce the laws on fair campaign advertising. He conceded that Labor could not have won the election even with a system more accurately reflecting voters' intentions. But, he said, it was totally unsatisfactory that the Government should have a majority of 23 seats when it had gained only 50.3 per cent of the two-party preferred vote while Labor had attracted 49.7 per cent - a difference of only 0.6 per cent. The party had to ensure it selected candidates of the highest calibre to run for election. "It's not good enough any more to put someone up because he has been a faithful worker and a good fellow in the local-branch organisation", he said. "We've got to win seats. "There are too many big challenges ahead of us in the 1980s for us to neglect our responsibilities either to our party or to this country". Speaking after the meeting, he said the party was not going to win the votes of the new, young middleclass of Australia without candidates who understood issues and could explain and defend them. He singled out Queensland as being the State with the greatest room for improvement in the selection of candidates. Pre-selection in that State had been "frankly crook", but anyone who had taken part in it could not avoid it if they wanted to survive politically. "Too often 'good fellers' were selected at the expense of people who could make a creative contribution, who qualified ... by experience and proven commonsense and intelligent understanding at public affairs", he said. The pre-selection system gave almost complete authority to a local party organisation and Mr Hayden appealed to local groups who may be harbouring a preference for a party hack to think again. On electoral reform he said the party must now "clear the decks" and establish precise policies as a matter of urgency. In analysing the reasons for Labor's defeat, he pointed to the influence of the public-opinion polls, media coverage of the share-market plunge during the campaign, Liberal Party advertising which he said was dishonest, and the 'donkey vote'. Publication of the Saulwick Poll, which showed Labor holding a commanding lead over the Government in the early stages of the campaign had prompted many, people to abandon their plans of registering a protest vote against the Liberal and National Country Parties. The share plunge had been "quite damagingly" reported in the media as showing that investors had no confidence in the Labor Party. The comments had come just as the stock market had been recovering. Financial journalists should have known the stock exchange was a very fragile, erratic and timid organisation. Speaking on the party's decision to contest the election result in a number of marginal seats on the grounds that the Liberal Party had engaged in misleading advertising, he said, "The advertising related to capital-gains tax was patently dis honest and there will be court action, of course. "Whilst we are prepared to cop a tough battle, we believe there ought to be something like the Marquis of Queensbury rules around. If you are in the boxing ring and someone keeps kicking you.in the groin, you are going to complain to the referee". The Labor Party should not flinch from changing its attitude to electoral issues. Among the new initiatives he foreshadowed were the listing of candidates' party affiliations on ballot papers and the introduction of a draw for positions on the forms. Labor research had shown that the Government had scraped home in about 18 seats because of the donkey vote and, because of their centralised methods of selecting candidates, the Government parties ' had been able to pick many runners whose names began with letters at the beginning of the alphabet. The present system of listing candidates from A to Z gave the top candidate an advantage of about 1.000 votes. Labor blames 'Liberal lies'. - Page 3.

During the recent Federal election campaign, the Gallup Poll found electors almost evenly divided on whether or not to abolish all means tests for old-age pensioners. To investigate the agelimit angle, an Australiawide cross-section of 1,700 electors has now been asked: "For people over 70, do you think all means tests for pensions should be abolished or not?" This was revealed by a Gallup Poll in which people were asked: I. "How much do you think old-age and invalid pensions should be each week, for each person?" 2. "And how much do you think a pensioner should be allowed to earn each week, before the means test begins to reduce the pension?" Parties Varied Answers to the first question averaged £5/10/ a week. Labour voters' average answer was £5/16/4; L.C.P. voters' £5/3/6. People of all ages and occupations, as groups, were in fairly close agreement. For instance, answers of professional men and execu-tives and their wives averag-ed £5/6/10; clerks and shop assistants, £5/11/8; skilled workers, £5/16/8. The people were asked: | "Do you think broadcast-, ing from Federal Parliament should be continued, reduced, or stopped? This is how the 1,860 persons questioned replied: Continue 55 per cent. 14 Mar 1981 - Broulee area sewerage scheme recommended to shire council Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 14 March 1981, page 12 Broulee area sewerage scheme recommended to shire council People who did not vote in the Tomaga sewerage poll held on February 28 would probably have voted "yes", according to some Eurobodalla Shire councillors. So the council's central district committee is recommending that a sewerage system be installed in the Broulee-Mossy Point-Tomakin area. As previously reported, in the referendum 383 ratepayers voted against the proposal and 364 in favour. Only 32 per cent of the 2292 people eligible to vote did so. And this is seen by councillors as significant. ' Cr Thelma Reid said at a meeting of the central district committee this week that "Although the "no" votes outweigh the "yes", we have to take into account the number of eligible voters who didn't vote and assume they would be "yes" votes. "If they felt strongly against it they would have taken the trouble to vote", she said. . She moved that the committee recommend that council proceed with the proposal. She was supported by Cr Roly Brown. He said: "It is usually the 'no' voter who makes sure he is there to vote". "And from the health point of view I think sewerage is. a good thing". The committee decided to adopt Cr Reid's motion. It will be considered at a meeting of the full council on March 23, but the council's general polity is to adopt riding committee recom mendations.

17 Nov 1981 - Adelaide too is in the throes of a debate over casinos Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 17 November 1981, page 2 Adelaide too is in the throes of a debate over casinos Consider the de licious paradoxes of the battle in Australia for more casinos — Canberra, as we know, is in the thick of it. In NSW, the Labor Premier, Mr Wran, has stated his desire to have casinos there operated by private enterprise. His party wants them State-Government owned, controlled and administered, with profits earmarked for sport, recreation, tourism, lowcost housing, social welfare, health and public education. That conjures up a beautiful pic ture and one wonders how "private enterprise could add to its beauty. In South Australia, where in 1979 former eye surgeon Mr David Tonkin took the Liberals back into office for the first time in nearly 10 years, their platform was to "get out of the way of private enterprise and let it get on with the job of restoring prosperity". The push for a casino, ostensibly to help encourage prosperity, has become very strong in Adelaide, too, in recent weeks. So imagine the bemusement of the locals when they woke up the other morning to find that their robustly private-enterprising Premier had just declared that: His Government would not agree to a privately operated casino. If one were established, "all pro ceeds would have to go to the people". This would mean "setting up some form of controlling authority to run every aspect of the casino". The immediate impetus for the casino debate in South Australia comes from the rising concrete shell of the State's first "international hotel" in Victoria Square, Adelaide. Handily and simultaneously, the Tonkin Government has been able to bludgeon a tiny, S3.5-million tem porary international airport installation out of the tight-fisted Feds. The promise is that it will be ready for business in 1983, about the same time as the international hotel. 'International' activities of any kind are apparently impossible without casinos. So a casino supporter on the Adelaide City Council, Alderman W. Manos, slipped in a quick motion at the last meeting of the council that it declare its support for a casino in the city. The motion passed with only one dissenter, Councillor John Scllick, a city furniture dealer, who said he opposed it on "christian and moral grounds". He added hastily that he didn't want people to think he was a wowser but he didn't believe the council had the authority to make such an important decision without first consulting the people. True it is that not one Councillor or Alderman has yet mentioned a casino in his campaign literature. It is also true, however, that two former Lord Mayors and a former Councillor are principals in the group sponsoring the international hotel in Victoria Square. They want a casino licence for -it and they naturally know their way around the council traps. On the face of it, the Premier's announcement that "all proceeds from any casino operation would have to go to the people" puts paid to any private-enterprise dreams, at least while the Liberals remain in office, and perhaps also when Labor returns to power. The Tonkin statement was.made after a weekend meeting of the Liberal Party State Council had thrown out a motion from one of its branches seeking a clear-cut declaration of party opposition to a casino. During debate on the motion Mr B. Lewis, a delegate, told the council that a study in Adelaide's western suburbs had shown that 78 per cent of people interviewed favoured a casino. More than 900 people had been interviewed for the survey, conducted by a team from Flinders University. Earlier, a Morgan Gallup Poll had been published which showed that 57 per cent of all South Australians were now in favour of a casino, compared with less than 50 per cent a couple of years ago. Mr Tonkin has since been difficult to pin down on details of the statements he made after the council meeting, which he has not denied making. His own personal preference, he has said, would be to have no casino at all. However, if it appeared that Mr Tonkin A casino in action: " 'International' activities of any kind arc apparently impossible without casinos". most people in the community wanted one, or at least had no objection to it in principle, then the Gov ernment would have to have a careful look at the alternatives. "We might opt to have an agent do it for us for an agreed fee", he said at the weekend. That, of course, is not the same as saying, as he had said earlier, that the Government "would not agree to a privately operated casino" and that "all proceeds would have to go to the people". Meantime, a spokesman for the non-parliamentary wing of the Liberal Party has pointed out that the party has "no policy on casinos at present". He said the subject was not mentioned in the leader's policy speech before the last election. No vote was taken on the motion before the recent State council meeting. It was thrown out on a show of hands. "There was no real understanding at the council meeting of what might be involved", the spokesman ad mitted. Several of the churches, including the Anglican, Roman Catholic and Uniting Churches, have now dc clared their firm opposition to the establishment of a casino. The Festival of Light organisation has also come out fighting against it. The Murdoch-owned afternoon newspaper, The News, has declared its enthusiastic support, the morning newspaper The Advertiser is so far sitting on the fence, and letters to the editor and talk-back radio programs suggest that public opinion is pretty evenly divided. Predictably, most opposition centres on fears about the possible introduction of poker machines, the vulnerability to these machines of people who are, or tend to be, compulsive gamblers, and on the tendency of organised crime to be associated with casinos elsewhere in the world. Another of the arguments being used against casinos is that they merely rob Peter to pay Paul, reducing expenditure on existing gambling facilities such as racing, TAB, lotteries and so on, and in retail stores, restaurants and in other establishments competing for the consumer's disposable dollar. An awkward pctsonal situation has developed for the Minister of Tourism, Mrs Jennifer Adamson, who has been dubbed by some people "the Minister for Public Morals". She has said publicly that she will vote against any Bill to permit the establishment of a casino, which she opposes both on moral grounds and because it would "not contribute to economic development". But if the eventual decision goes against her, her portfolio of tourism would inevitably involve her in helping to administer casino policy. The ALP has no official policy yet but, through its spokesman on sport and recreation, Mr Slater, it has a motion on the parliamentary notice paper calling for establishment of a select committee to look into the subject. Both parties are likely to permit a conscience vote on the matter but there appeal to be enough Members of both parties to ensure establishment of a casino if appropriate legislation is introduced. The extent to which private enterprise might be able to get its hands on the action is at this stage anyone's guess.

08 Jul 1982 - ALP nuclear shift Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 8 July 1982, page 1 uclear shift Phasing plan accepted By COLIN BRAMMALL The Australian Labor Party abandoned yesterday its com mitment to an immediate moratorium on uranium mining, deciding in favour of a phasing-out of the industry. However, it has not specified when the phasing-out process should be completed. The ALP national conference, meeting at the Lakeside International Hotel, voted 53-46 in favour of a motion which its mover said would tell a future Labor Government how to implement its policy of eliminating uranium mining in Australia. It has agreed to sell uranium subject to conditions enforced with trade embargos but will not sign any new contracts after it gains office and will not allow new mines to be developed. Without a deadline, there is no apparent compulsion on a future Labor Government to do anything about existing contracts, except not renew them. The motion, put forward by Victorian left-winger Mr Bob Hogg, says, in part, "Understanding the difficulties which could be encountered in the implementation of that commitment [to repudiate all existing commitments] our minimum position would be a total unequivocal commitment to phase out Australia's involvement in the uranium in dustry and that certain conditions as outlined will and must be applied to those mines existing in production as of July, 1982." Later it goes on to say "... an Australian Labor Government will adopt the process of phasing out our involvement in uranium mining, and certain conditions will be imposed upon the producers... and we will utilise our right to apply trade embargos to ensure these conditions are met "For example, any contract with the French Government could only be contemplated subject to that Government ceasing all nuclear testing programs in the Pacific. "For example, any contract with the ACT casino support After a brief and caustic debate, the ALP conference rejected a move by the ACT delegation to have the word "casino" removed from the ACT section of the draft tourism policy. Proxy delegates for the ACT, Mr David Wedgwood and Mr Tony Kelloway, made the move because the ACT branch was opposed to casinos. The reference was, "Investigate the feasibility of establishing an interna tional-standard casino and entertainment centre in Canberra". Speakers against the ACT amendment were the mover of the policy, Mr Brown, who is "shadow minister" for tourism, Mr Michael Reynolds (Qld), Mr Terry Sheahan (NSW), a Minister in the NSW Government and the Member for Burrinjuck, and Mr Peter Beattie (Qld). Mr Wedgwood, Mr Kelloway and Mr Linacre (Qld) spoke in favour. Mr Linacre said anybody "who advocates the proliferation of these bloody casinos around the countryside needs to be taken away and given some sort of mental examination and probably, after that, put down". The president, Mr Wran, interjected at one point, saying "this bloody nonsense" could "go on all night". Mr Beattie made sarcastic remarks about Mr Linacre not knowing that Queensland policy was in favour of casinos. Japanese could only be contemplated subject to them withdrawing from their intention to dump waste material in the Pacific. "For example, any contract with the Finns would be subject to us being satisfied beyond all doubt that the supply of uranium was not being deflected into the nuclear-fuel cycle and nuclear arms program of the USSR." It also mentioned Britain and West Germany. The conditions would be additional to existing international conditions. The remainder of the lengthy resolution was a statement of general attitude to uranium and commitments to variouscauses, including reversing.the direction of nuclear developments internationally, fair distribution of available energy forms, a lessening of international demand for oil, monitoring of nuclear activities internationally, and assisting workers and local communities affected by the phasing-out of the nuclear industry. It resolved also that Labor policy as of yesterday was not to be reviewed "with a view of allowing the industry to develop further" until all remaining unresolved concerns of the party were satisfactorily resolved and agreed to by a future national conference. The emotional, three-hour debate ended with the losing side demanding that the names of all delegates and how they voted be incorporated into the official record. There had been allegations made dur ing the debate that delegates had been intimidated and there were calls from anti-uranium demonstrators to many of the "yes" voters that they would lose preselection for their parliamentary seats as a result. When the name of the Member for Canberra, Mrs Kelly, who voted "yes", was called out, she was swamped with abuse from anti-uranium demonstrators in the auditorium and threatened with a campaign against her at preselection. Senator Evans (Vic) said Senator Button, Mr Holding (Vic) and he had been threatened. The motion, which was introduced after the conference voted without debate to reaffirm existing policy, is an addendum to the policy. The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Hayden, his deputy, Mr Bowen, Mr Hawke, and frontbencher Mr Keating all spoke for the motion. [A summary of the arguments of all the 22 speakers appears on Page 11]. Mr Hogg, the Victorian secretary of the party and author of the resolution, said he had tried to prevent the question even being debated, because the party would lose whichever way it voted. Outside the conference, Mr Hayden said the vote meant that the ALP had a credible and adaptable way of winding down the uranium industry. "It is not a pro-uranium mining policy," Mr Hayden said. "It is merely a transmission mecha nism." The vote meant the flight of capital from Australia that he had feared might accompany the election of a Labor Government would not occur. Federal Labor frontbencher Mr Stewart West, a strong anti-uranium proponent, was near to tears as he emerged from the conference hall. He said the debate had caused division within the party which would not easily be healed. 'There will be "tremendous repercussive effects over this," a disappointed Mr West said. Mr Peter O'Dea, left, the president of the ACT Trades and Labour Council, and the caricature of a well-known political figure, outside Parliament House yesterday at a rally over the tripartite discussions being held inside. Report — Page 3. ALP frontbencher Mr Bob Hawke said last night he "had no doubt" he could lead the Labor Party to victory in the next Federal election. Speaking on commercial television, Mr Hawke was asked if Labor could win with him as leader. "I think there's no doubt they could," he said. Mr Hawke said "pressures seem to be building" within the ALP for a decision on who will lead the party — he or Bill Hayden. "Events of this morning — polls and things like that — seem to have added to speculation and concern," he said. He said a leadership vote was up to the ALP Caucus and he felt momentum was building up for for such a meeting. There had been a "fair bit of discussion about it (a meeting)." However he said he had not been lobbying for such a meeting. Mr Hawke was commenting on the latest Morgan Gallup poll in The Bul letin. The poll showed the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, attracting 46 per cent of the vote in April, rising to 50 per cent in June. The Opposition Leader, Mr Hayden, held 38 per cent in April and this dropped by seven percentage points to 31 per cent in June. The June poll published in The Bulletin was based on the question, "In your opinion who would make the better Prime - Minister, Mr Fraser or Mr Hayden?". Fifty per cent said Mr Fraser, 31 per cent chose Mr Hayden, and 19 per cent either were undecided or named someone else. Asked to comment on the poll yesterday, Mr Fraser said, " Well, I don't know what these polls mean; I really don't." A reporter told him that the poll had given him a four-percentage point rise in the month and Mr Fraser thanked him for the news. Told that the poll indicated a drop in popularity for Mr Hayden, Mr Fraser said, "I hope he doesn't fall too far." More conference reports. — Pages 10,11.

10 Jul 1982 - A very different conference from all the others Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 10 July 1982, page 2 A very different conference from all the others By GAY DAVIDSON Seen the Hartley amend ment?" a Federal Labor official asked of a Hayden staffer and a couple of journalists about 11 o'clock yesterday morning. Grins all round: it was the first utterly expectable, normal occurrence at this ALP national conference — the ritual offering by Bill Hartley ot Victoria's Socialist Leit, on behalf of the PLO against the proIsrael faction. The hardy perennial that suddenly made the Lakeside Hotel as familiar as the Florida at Terrigal, or the other venues of the past decade. In almost every other respect the gathering of various Lefts, Rights and Centres was different. Quite different from Adelaide, Perth, Surfers, and the rest. It was expected to be, with double the previous number of delegates, and for the first time a quarter of them women. There had been dire predictions of shock-horror-split headlines over whether parliamentarians should retain their conscience vote on abortion issues. Not to mention uranium. But the reality was a shock: pragmatism in the face of the conference slogan, "Preparing for Government", activated by nervousness confronted with perceived public opinion. The public-opinion problem began destabilising the conference a fortnight ago when a Morgan Gallup Poll showed Labor four points down in late May and the first week in June. An Australian Public Opinion Poll over the first two weekends in June was even worse for Labor, showing Government support at nearly 46 per cent, and Labor leading in only NSW and Victoria. Then there was the confusion over the entry of nuclear shipping. That fuelled the results in another Morgan poll published on Tuesday, showing Fraser up four points to 50 per cent regarding him as best for Prime Minister, and Hayden down eight points to 31 per cent. Whether they were believed or not, those polls made Leadership the real issue. With a little help from the 'Nationwide' program's denigration of Mr Hayden and lauding of Mr Hawke, the challenger was out of the closet, saying Labor would win with him (implying it could not with Mr Hayden). The timing was right on target. Over two years ago Mr Hawke was saying privately that he would be Leader 18 months after entering Federal politics. Some observers made bets at the time, knowing Mr Hawke and his ambition well, and their money was on him. They fully understood Mr Hawke's disclaimer yesterday when he said, "In what I am doing now I don't intend any personal hurt to the current Leader". The washing of the hands, the reference to the position and not the man, was in character. But their polite suspension of disbelief faded when Mr Hawke snapped a flat "No!" to a question about whether he was being disloyal. His next answer was, "I am not trying to knife Bill Hayden", and he said later of the torrid media coverage that he had simply responded to questions. Other observers two years ago did not make bets on Bob: the Labor Caucus does not wear presumption cheerfully, the president of the ACTU depended heavily on the hard work of backroom people for his success as the front man (and there were those rash, entrepreneurial ventures in Bourke's, Solo and travel), success in Parliament and in leadership requires quite different abilities and sustained hard work, and popularity is a fickle jade with little time for those who take hard decisions and responsibility. Mr Fraser can attest to that, and he has enjoyed some handsome wins in spite of personal and party unpopularity. Those observers had their turn to look knowing, too, yesterday. When Mr Hawke said yes, he did have a lot to offer apart from popularity — there was his successful decade with the ACTU, his successes internationally as a negotiator, nationally of course too, and as an administrator. Their time for flat disbelief came when he said he would seek to use Mr Hayden's talents and "I hope Bill would see it that way-'. And when he said the Labor Party now had policies to take to the people at the next election, implying he was somehow responsible for that. In all the effort and lobbying that has gone on in the past week to defuse issues potentially damaging to the Labor Party, and to get a fair consensus for policies which will help to win Government, most observers see the hand of the present Leader. Personally, I dont think Mr Hawke has had the time to assist in, let alone head, that heroic effort.

18 Jul 1982 - Arresting the gathering snowball in time, Mr Hayden squeaks home the winner Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 18 July 1982, page 2 Arrest Mr in time winner By GAY DAVIDSON A FULL WEEK before the ALP conference in Canberra Mr Hayden had decided on an early special meeting of the Parliamentary Labor Party to resolve the leadership issue. It had grown as an issue of sufficient dimensions to justify that shock treatment partly because Mr Hawke was pitching his claim on his public image and popularity which, he asserted, meant Labor would win Government with him, but probably not with Mr Hayden. But in part the issue kept on getting bigger and bigger as more and more Labor politicians and their support bases simply acceptcd Mr Hawke's claims and the grounds he chose for the contcst. Some could see advantage for themselves or their faction in changing the Leader from Mr Hayden, generally supported by the Left and Centre, to Mr Hawke, supported by the right and some of the centre. Some also believed in, or else did not think to question, the immutability of Mr Hawke's popularity. They assumed no change in the electorate's perception of him, whatever his role, and so those in marginal seats would have a better chance with him as Leader, and that would frighten Mr Fraser off an early election — and politicians are not usually enthused about going to the polls a day earlier than they have to. Consequently the factions and their supporters in the State organisations and unions on the Left and Right began their soundings. Mr Hayden Because it was not happening at the normal time for reaffirming or changing a Leader (after an election) there was a heightened excite ment. And because it obviously meant a shift in the influence of the factions — even though there was no real difference between Mr Hayden and Mr Hawke on policy — it attracted enormous attention well beyond the actual voters, the Members and selnators in the Parliamentary Labor Party. So Mr Hayden was sensible in thinking he could not let the snowball get any bigger. However, it might have been more sensible for him to have kept that decision entirely to himself until he was ready to announce it. Suddenly there was a rash of material supporting Mr Hawke in the media — Phillip Adams in The Age, Melbourne, two 'Nationwide' programs denigrating the one and lauding the other, reports of an ANOP poll suggesting Labor could Mr Hawke only win with Hawlce, a Morgan Gallup poll showing a dramatic drop in Hayden's popularity and a rise in Fraser's. From the start of the conference the policy platforms were of interest mainly as the Leader and challenger were judged to win points in influencing the votes and scoring off each other. The reportage certainly suggested the contest was the major news, and that was fuelled by Mr Hawke's acceptance of all invitations for interviews. All the talk was about the numbers and which factions could de liver, especially after Mr Uren and others talked of the likelihood of the Left splitting, with some going to Mr Hawke, especially in NSW. So Mr Hayden arrested the snowball. And the lobbying and dealing was on in earnest. Apart from the main protagonists, it was the politicians in the Centre and in the marginal seats, and those shared by Mr Keating and Mr Bowen in the NSW Centre and Right, who took the brunt of it as attempts were made to prise them from Hayden or Hawke, from Keating or Bowen or Uren, to entice them with an election next year rather than this, with a sure winner rather than a crippled Leader. Armed with the split in the Left Mr Hawke was able to suggest to Mr Keating that he could follow, breaking from Hayden in the interests of a convincing victory rather than a narrow margin, and so working to a national alliance or the Right since Victoria's Centre Unity was with Mr Hawke. Immediately after the conference the unions swung into action. On the left the AMWSU took the lead, although the high-profile officials such as Mr Carmichael and Mr Halfpenny stayed out of the lobbying effort — that was left to those with ALP membership who worked in the waverers among the politicians and chased up some 400 officials across a wide political spectrum to sign a statement supportive to Mr Hayden. On the right Mr Simon Crean (Storeman and Packers, ACTU vicepresident) travelled with Mr Hawke, attended meetings with him, lobbied for him. The more active politicians included Senator Evans, Senator McClelland, Mr Holding, and Mr Young. The numbers and the rumours ranged outrageously. During the last few days Senator Grimes (Tas) spent a lot of time assuring people he had not moved from Hayden. He was not alone in being placed on the lists of both camp's. The deals and attempts at deals on issues as well as the delivery of numbers continued, the Left, for instance, trying for commitments for proportional representation for factions in a future inner Cabinet. Finally there was the verbal violence toward the end, the accusations of ratting and double-crossing, of leading factions from behind because "leaders" could not actually deliver. . Both Mr Uren and Mr Keating are suspected of the former, and there is little doubt that Mr Keating was in the unfortunate latter situation. Of the leading NSW politicians only Mr Bowen is known to have stayed firmly on one position and worked for it. In the upshot Mr Hawke did not win, but he has gained a far more solid claim than he had before the party meeting as the leading future contender. Mr Bowen has increased in stature and Mr Keating has been reduced. Mr Hayden is secure at least until the next election, and he has a last opportunity to get the parliamentary party in order — and to enthuse it and the electorate with policies for the next election, and to stake out the issues on which to fight the Government. Whether he is in thrall to any individuals or factions we may be able to judge when we see his realignment of the "shadow' portfolios. Clearly there are some he could now move around and lose nothing in doing so. There is little doubt that the Left and the unions which support it can only be heartened. They can live with the conference policies and they have unified their numbers, which was as important to them as retaining the Leader they supported. The Right clearly has a long way to go yet before achieving a national alliance. Without the ideological commitments to policies and issues that makes alliance possible for the Left, leaders on the Right and in the Centre must always have problems as individuals look to their own in terests. The electorate as a whole will gain from the episode if the Opposition can gear itself noW to concentrate on real politics, not only shaping itself for the big contest, but harassing a Government which is devisive, lethargic and standing still on a poor record.

Church-attendance polls 'could be misleading9 Gallup Polls on church attendance, if taken at face value, may well be misleading, according to Doug Hynd of the Zadok Centre, Canberra. In a research paper, 'Church Attendance: What Do the Gallup Polls Really Tell Us?', Hynd claims that Gallup Poll figures may overestimate by more than 50 per cent the actual level of church attendance in Australia, for those claiming Anglican allegiance. His evidence, based on actual attendance of the Anglican church services in Queanbeyan, reveals that a maximum of 4.2 per cent of Anglicans attended church within any given week, compared with a national figure of 10 per cent as stated in the polls. Attendance at Christmas and Easter also fell below the level suggested by the polls. Figures from the Anglican Diocese of Melbourne bore out those of Queanbeyan, with an absolute maximum of 4.6 per cent of Anglicans receiving communion within the week surveyed. The picture of church atten dance suggested by this investiga tion was much gloomier than that suggested by simple extrapolation from Gallup Poll figures. Hynd also cites figures for claimed Baptist attendance which raises the possibility that overreporting of actual church at tendance occurs among Baptists surveyed by pollsters. In the second part of his paper based on a comparison of census with Gallup Poll data on religious allegiance, Hynd raises the possi bility that the "no reply" category in the census data is a very mixed group. It seems to include a propor tion of committed Christians, as well as a significant group of people who are moving away from any Christian allegiance. Copies of Hynd's complete re search paper are available through the Zadok Centre, 13 Edgar Street, Ainslie 2602. Other statistically-based articles on Christian belief in Australia are to be published in the book 'The Shape of Belief, of which Hynd is creditor. Douglas Hynd is publications and resources coordinator of the Zadok Centre. He is a bachelor of commerce, a qualified librarian and is nearing completion of a bachelor of divinity course at Mel bourne College of Divinity.
