Garabandal program ThE Garabandal visions will be the subject of the BBC's Everyman series on ABC-TV tomorrow at 10pm. Between 1961 and 1965, four girls claim to have seen about 2,000 visions of the Virgin Mary in the Spanish village of Garabandal. A world-wide Garabandal move ment was formed to publicise the messages of the visions. In Australia about 30 Gar abandal Centres have been set up, including the national centre in Canberra run by John and Helen Leriou, who said on Monday that if anyone wanted to know more about the Garabandal messages they could telephone 958362. The messages were a call for repentence, and a turning back to God. A world-wide celestial warn ing would be given at an un specified time, followed by a mira cle within a year. Presbyterian resolutions on labour and unions THE GENERAL Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in NSW adopted a series of reso lutions at its general assembly in May relating to organised labour and trade unions in Aus tralia. The resolutions arise from a re port of the Church and Nation Committee to the assembly. They included encouraging all Presbyterians to become actively involved in their trade union, chamber of commerce or pro fessional body in order to exert a Christian influence in their de liberations. The report supported the work performed by the Clyde Cameron College for Trade Unionists in creating a more informed and skilled trade union movement. All participants in commerce and industry were urged to exercise proper regard for the consequences of their actions, especially in dustrial action. Management in commerce and industry should provide facilities and opportunities for all employees to achieve satisfaction from their work and should encourage all groups in commerce and industry to strive for better communication and understanding. Management should provide incentives and re wards and foster a spirit of co operation between all parties within each specific work situation. Commonwealth and State Gov ernments were to be encouraged to introduce into the commercial and industrial laws a principle of ac countability for industrial action and compensation for losses result ing from unjustified industrial ac tion. The entire system of arbitration and conciliation should be re viewed to stop delays in hearings and appeals and to place greater emphasis on conciliation rather than arbitration while affirming the necessity of the rule of law to protect justice for all parties and the public interest. The assembly condemned the system where the worker when on strike either remained on the pay roll or the worker or spouse re ceived unemploymewnt benefits. Copies of the report, 'Organised Labour in Contemporary Aus tralia', were sent to the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Hayden, the Leader of the NCP, Mr Anthony, and the NSW Premier, Mr Wran.

18 Jun 1982 - Poll shows PM's popularity at an all-time high Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 18 June 1982, page 5 Argentine troops, still with their weapons, wait to be moved from the airfield at Port Stanley soon after their commander surrendered to British forces. LONDON, Thursday (AAPAP). — The latest Gallup Poll shows support for the Prime Minister. Mrs Thatcher, at an all-time high. The poll, conducted between June 9 and 14 as British forces were completing their recapture of the Falkland Islands, found 51 per cent of those responding "satisfied" with Mrs Thatcher's performance as Prime Minister. Fortythree per, cent were dissatisfied and 6 per cent did not know. The approval rating represents a jump of 7 per cent from May and 17 per cent from March, before Argentina invaded the Falklands. It. is the highest since Mrs Thatcher took power in May, 1979. The survey results, published today in London's conservative Daily Telegraph, also showed backing for the ruling Conservative Party at the highest level since the 1979 election. Forty-five per cent of the 971 voters surveyed nation-wide said they would vote Conservative if a new election was held today, compared with 25 per cent for the Labour Party, 15 per cent for the centrist Social Democratic Party and 10 per cent for the SDP's alliance partner, the Liberal Party. In March, Gallup had Labour leading the Conservatives 33 per cent to 31.5 per cent. Mrs Thatcher does not have to call a general election until May, 1984, but there has been speculation she might do so sooner to capitalise on her recent popularity. Asked what effect the Falklands conflict had on their view of the Prime Minister, 64 per cent said it was "more favourable" now, with 24 per cent saying "less favourable" and 12 per cent "don't know".

19 Mar 1982 - Polls show increase in meat demand Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 19 March 1982, page 14 Polls show increase in meat demand Morgan Gallup poll surveys of household food buying over the past two years had shown a strengthening trend in beef and lamb demand arid consumption, the chairman of the Australian Meat and Live-stock Corporation, Mr Geoff Jones, said yesterday. Mr Jones said that the surveys, which had been conducted twice-yearly for the corporation since September 1979, were a welcome confirmation of trends observed in the AMLC's own statistics. "Last year total red-meat consumption rose by 3.4 kilograms to 83.6 kilograms per head of population — and that trend appears to be continuing in 1982," he said. "Significantly, the Gallup poll surveys cover the period since the corporation commenced its 'Feed the man meat' television advertising campaign. "The results strongly suggest our promotion program is working, although the specific effect of generic advertising is always difficult to assess." The surveys, conducted from September 1979 to October 1981, covered large samples of between 800 and 1,100 ": grocery buyers. Respondents were first asked if they bought beef or lamb in the week before the survey. Positive response rose from 77 per cent in 1979 to 79 per cent in 1981. In the five individual surveys only 7 to 9 per cent said that they had not eaten beef or lamb in the previous week. The reason given by most who had not recently bought meat was that purchases were made in bulk. Only 1 percent of respondents said meat was "too expensive", 2 per cent said "don't eat meat" and 2 per cent answered "health reasons". Respondents were asked to compare present buying habits for each survey with two months earlier. During the two year period the proportion buying less meat declined from 24 per cent of those surveyed to 16 per cent — those who said "about the same" rose from 53 per cent to 65 per cent. The Gallup polls also surveyed attitudes to meat. The proportion of respondents who agreed that eating meat was essential to good diet and "a major part of diet" remained high.

09 Apr 1982 - Liberals decide Peacock not different enough Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 9 April 1982, page 2 Liberals decide Peacock not different enough -THE LIBERAL— -LEADERSHIP" By GAY DAVIDSON You CANNOT argue with politicians who stick with the old guard when they know things are going bad. You may sympathise, or feel exasperated that nobody found another way out, or mourn at the fortunes of this once-great party. But it was for members of the Parliamentary Liberal Party alone yesterday to make (and wear) their choices. They found no cause for celebration. At midday, the party meeting well over, there were just two of them in the Members' Bar, commiserating: Senator Withers and Mr Steele Hall. The parliamentarians' judgment yesterday clearly indicates they do not believe Mr Peacock is sufficiently different from the present leadership to offer them a significantly better chance of keeping their seats at the next election. Some, a full third of the voters, felt strongly enough about Mr Fraser's leadership to give their votes to the challenger. They did so knowing he could not win. Since politicians, at least as much as any other group of individuals, have a strong preference for being on the right side in any numbers game, it is certain that Mr Fraser gained some adherents in the past few days; those who stayed with Mr Peacock were at least as hostile to Mr Fraser as they were in favour of the challenger. Nevertheless, the two-to-one majority who stayed with Mr Fraser did so knowing that the boat is sinking lower and lower in the electoral water," but they wanted it to at least remain steady. Anything for a quiet life. They were well aware of the party's poor standing in NSW, heavy electoral losses in Victoria last weekend, and recent local-government defeats in Queensland. And hanging over them are the expected loss in South Australia later this year, and the latest Morgan Gallup Poll showing the coalition slipping to an approval rate of 38 per cent, Labor up three points to 52 per cent, and Mr Fraser personally down to 32 per cent approval and 53 per cent disapproval. All that adds up to a lot of animosity, an awful lot to keep bottled up until the next election, when things are going bad. That makes the Deputy Leader ballots as well as the result particularly interesting, and it means the successful contender, Mr Howard, has an extremely difficult job ahead of him. The first vote — Howard 34, MacKellar 18, Viner 5, Hodgman 22, 1 informal and 1 abstention — can only have pleased Mr Hodgman. He had lobbied for compassionate votes and they piled up in heartening numbers, but more than half were simply "parked" with him until people saw that first result and got down to the serious business of the second ballot. That result was Howard 45 (up 11), MacKellar 27 (up 9) and Hodgman 9 (down 13). Taking into account the uncertainty displayed in the first ballot, Mr Fraser's support for Mr Howard, and Mr MacKellar's and Mr Hodgman's leanings to Mr Peacock's view of Mr Fraser (in spite of the unanimous concurrence with the Lynch loyalty oath), it is reasonably to see the end result as 45-36 (the latter being the sum of the votes that did not go to Mr Fraser's choice). That is remarkably similar to the 47 for Sir Phillip Lynch and 35 for Mr Peacock in the last ballot for Deputy Leader after.the 1980 elections. The numbers are slightly different because Sir William McMahon (who voted for Sir Phillip) is no longer in Parliament and his successor is in the Labor caucus. It means that Mr Fraser's choice on this occasion received two fewer votes, and the other side scored one more. So Mr Howard does not begin in his new position with great support. The one way in which he could gain kudos, by negotiating successfully with the Australian Democrats to avoid any more rejections of Bills in the Senate, is probably beyond his power since the problem areas are likely to be Budget measures and he, as Treasurer, is in the worst:possible position to consider compromises. And if Mr Howard is to keep his position, let alone use it to stake a claim for the top job, he will need to use the authority of the Deputy leadership to press for some policy changes. Yet, at the same time, he will have to work even more closely with Mr Fraser. Perhaps some politicians do earn their money.

05 Jun 1992 - WEEKEND MOTORING Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 5 June 1992, page 18 WEEKEND MOTORING ——^—1^^—^ 1— Survey shows bad image Industry 'insulted' by result THE IMAGE ofshon ky car sellers doing dodgy deals was something the automotive industry had worked hard to overcome, the president of the Australian Automobile Dealers Association, Brian Phillis, said in Adelaide recently. Mr Phillis said the lingering perception was insulting to the professionals within the industry and had persisted to the point of becoming a cliche. "It's something of a tradition to think of car dealers that way," he said. Mr Phillis was commenting on a Morgan Gallup Poll which named car dealers as the least-trusted professionals in the community. The poll found that only 3 per cent of 1343 people surveyed nationwide thought car dealers had high stan dards. Pharmacists were most respected, with 79 per cent considering them highly ethical. "There were a lot of people within our industry who were terribly insulted by that result, especially as we are putting a huge effort into changing that perception," Mr Phillis said. ' Judging by customer response many new car dealers have been accepted by their customers as business people offering good service. Most of Australia's manufacturers and importers constantly monitor customer satisfaction with surveys and follow-up calls. The best claim satisfaction rates as high as 95 per cent while they all appreciate the importance of keeping buyers happy. Toyota Australia executive vice president John Conomos said customer satisfaction had emerged as the key to success in the motor trade. "We have recognised that customer satisfaction can create the essential difference between our franchise and those of our opposition," he said. But despite all that Mr Phillis said the tarnished image of car dealers, especially used-car dealers, remained. "It's something that's come through almost since the start of time," he said. "I don't know how car dealers can rise above that without spending millions of dollars on a publicity campaign which frankly we can't afford to do. "But the important thing is looking after the clients we've got, and making sure every one of them is happy. "Having said that, there's always going to be 2 or 3 per cent that will never be hap py, MrPhilhssaid. — MP

06 Jun 1992 - Poll reveals Coalition's progress Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 6 June 1992, page 2 Poll reveals Coalition's progress The Federal Coalition would have won an election if one held been held late last month, a Morgan Poll has found. The poll published in the latest Time Australia magazine, and conducted by face-to-face interviews of2403 electors throughout Australia on the weekends of May 16-17 and 23-24, found that support for the Federal Labor Government had slipped by 0.5 percent in late May to 36.5 per cent. Support for the Opposition parties had increased from 43 per cent to 44 per cent and support for the Australian Democrats had increased from 6.5 per cent to 7 per cent. The backing for minor parties and independents had declined from 13.5 per cent to 12.5 per cent. About the time the poll was conducted the Minister for Transport and Communication and party power-broker Graham Richardson had resigned over the Marshall Islands affair. Despite the loss of support for the Government, the approval rating of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, increased from 33 per cent to 34.5 per cent, the first increase since March, and his disapproval rating decreased from 57 per cent to 56. The undecided stood at 9.5 per cent, down from 10 per cent. Opposition leader John Hewson's approval was up from 42 to 43 per cent — the first increase since January when he recorded his highest rating, 62 per cent. His disapproval rating declined from 43 to 42 per cent. Dr Hewson maintained a three-point lead over Mr Keating on the question of preferred prime minister — 45 per ccnt and 42 per cent respectively - both up 1 per ccnt. Thirteen per ccnt, 2 per cent fewer, named someone else, or could not say. According to a Saulwick Poll pub- J lished in the Sydney Morning Herald yesterday, neither of the main political parties has a good image among voters ' — the ALP's image the worst. The poll, of 1000 voters nationally on May 27-28, found a majority of voters rated Labor's ability as "poor" J in three out of the four question-areas ;> proposed. ij The four areas were: managing the •* economy, managing internal party affairs, protecting the needy, and repre senting Australia's interests abroad. > On a scale of one to 10, where one * meant "very poor" and 10 meant "excellent", the Opposition recorded the highest score for any of the four categories - 5.2 for its ability to manage Australia's interests abroad. The Government did not better the Opposition's score in any of the categories. The poll report said the over-all low rating for the major parties underlined voter disenchantment. As many as one in four voters had said that he/she would vote for a minor party or independent candidate if an election were held today. Poll Watch now appears on Page 2 each Saturday.

09 Jun 1992 - Drop for Vic Opposition Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 9 June 1992, page 12 SYDNEY: Support for the Victorian Liberal-National opposition fell 1.5 points to 49 per cent in May, a Morgan Poll has found. The Labor Government's support was unchanged at 29 per cent, indicating the Opposition would have easily won an election held last month. The poll, to be published in today's Time magazine, showed support for minor parties and independent candidates was up 1.5 points to 15 per cent. Despite her party's poor showing, the Premier of Victoria, Joan Kirner, still had a 13-point higher approval rating than Opposition leader Jeff Kennett. The poll was done after 1676 electors throughout Victoria were interviewed face-to-face during May and asked which party they would vote for if a state election were being held today.

13 Jun 1992 - Labor 'would have won in NSW' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 13 June 1992, page 2 Labor 'would have won in NSW' A Morgan poll, published in the latest Time Australia magazine, has found that if an election had been held in May, Labor would have won office in NSW. It found that support for the minority NSW Liberal-National Government had declined from 40.5 per cent to 37. The poll, of 2202 electors interviewed face-to-face in May, found that as Government support declined, support for the Opposition increased from 41.4 per cent to 43. Australian Democrats support was up from 6 per cent to 7. It was bad news also for the Premier, Nick Greiner, whose approval rating, in the wake of the Terry Metherell affair, slumped from 36 per cent to a "new low" of 30 per cent. Those who disap proved of the way he did his job increased from 56 per cent to 63 per cent, and in the preferred premier stakes, the Labor leader, Bob Carr, improved his standing from 42 per cent to 46 per cent. Across the border, the Victorian Liberal-National opposition undeniably would have won an election despite its support's decline from 50.5 per cent to 49 per cent, another Morgan poll has found. The poll, of 1676 electors in Victoria, also interviewed face-to-face, found support for the Labor Government unchanged at 29 per cent and support for the minor parties and independent candidates up 1.5 to 15 per cent. The electors' approval of the Premier, Joan Kirner, declined from 43 per cent to 40, and her disapproval rating increased from 49 per cent to 54. In the federal arena, the Coalition's lead in the race for the Senate seat has been reduced by 3 per cent, an AGB poll, published in the Bulletin magazine, has found. The poll, of 4163 electors interviewed face-to-face nation-wide in May, found support for the Coalition down to 40 per cent, the Labor party also down two to 37 per cent.

17 Jul 1992 - Pay drive by unions hardly changed Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 17 July 1992, page 9 GLENDA KORPORAAL Pay drive by unions hardly changed SO WE have 11 per cent plus unemploy- ment — worse in Victoria — and the ACTU is pushing another national wage rise. Sure it's not a huge amount — possibly a rise of some 1.5 per cent — but with unem-ployment at such disastrous levels, you have to wonder at the mentality of continuing to push higher and higher costs on employers or for higher and higher benefits for those lucky enough to have jobs. In recent years the combination of the Labor Government and the ACTU. all pack-aged together in a wondrous deal called The Accord has increased the burden on employ-ers. There's the training levy, the superannu-ation levy and higher wage levels in return for some very marginal improvements in productivity. The Hawke and then the Keating govern-ment has — quite rightly — introduced a whole series of major reforms designed to open up the Australian economy and make it much more efficient and internationally competitive. But when it comes to wages and labour policy, Labour Inc — that combina-tion of government and union officials whose policy ideas have shaped these poli-cies for the past decade — suddenly switches into protectionist mode, arguing that the country can only handle what amounts to incremental change. We can have radical change in banking and finance, the car indus-try, clothing and textiles etc but when it comcs to shaking up life for the Industrial Relations club the trauma would be too great for the country to take! The ACTU president, Martin Ferguson, claimed yesterday that his organisation was "in the game of trying to create employment opportunities". Yet the Labour Inc record (after a decade of running the country you can't blame all our current problems on the Bonds and the Skascs of the world) is hardly impressive. Not only is unemployment up, but the real burden of the jobs crisis has fallen heavily on what used to be the family breadwinner, the full-time male worker. In 1983-84, the first full financial year of the Labor Government, the male labour force in Australia was 4.4 million. In June this year it was up to just over five million — an extra 600,000 men came into the work force. But over the same period, full-time male employment only rose from 3.75 mil-lion to just under 4 million — a rise of only 250,000 jobs. Despite the existence of The Accord and the jobs growth for most of the '80s, less than half the number of men who have entered the workforce over the period have actually found full-time jobs. What is really worrying is that despite massive changes we have seen in some in-dustries, the old-style mentality of unions pushing for higher and higher across-the-board benefits for those in full-time employment hardly seems to have changed. Australia has become a nation of haves and have nots. The Haves — those that have jobs — might have worries about maybe losing their jobs, but economically they are better off from a combination of higher su-perannuation benefits, higher wages, very slow growth in the cost of goods and falling interest rates. The real burden of the reces-sion and structural adjustment is being car-ried entirely by the out-of-work Have Nots. Of coursc no-onc can argue that Australia is alone in our economic problems. The world is suffering from slow economic growth. But the severity of the recession arid the mood of national despair about the out-look is a lot worse in Australia than in many Despite wonders of The Accord, the system delivers high unemployment other developed countries. In America, where voters are worried about the weakness of the recovery, the unemployment rate is "only" 7.8 per cent. In Japan, where the economy is slowing down rapidly, unem-ployment is just over 2 per cent. The OECD average unemployment rate for the larger economies is down below 8 per cent. No-onc is arguing that our high unemploy-ment is bccausc of any explosion in wages demand. Hopefully we have all learned from the wages explosion of 1981. But, despite all the wonders of The Ac-cord, we have a system which delivers a chronically high level of unemployment in Australia. The Accord was supposed to have deliv-ered wage restraint without industrial pain — that is for those with jobs. It's all very well congratulating ourselves on how much things have changed compared with the bad old days of Australian labour relations, but we really need to sec what has been happen-ing in the economics of our major trading partners. The accompanying table shows that wages in Australia have risen by more than 52 per cent from their base in 1982-83, when La-bour Inc took office, to June last year. But despite "wage restraint" this is much higher than the 40.4 per cent rise in the Big Seven OECD economics. The wage rise was higher in Britain, and its unemployment is also higher than the OECD average at 9 per ccnt plus. Wages only grew by 27 per ccnt in the US and 22 per cent in Japan. While unemployment in Australia is higher now than it was in the last recession, it has fallen from 1982-83 in the other Big Seven OECD economies. The real comparative picture for Australia is far worse when one adds on the big in-crease in non-wage costs of employment. Australian Bureau of Statistics figures is-sued this week show that for the first lime superannuation has overtaken the dreaded payroll tax as the major component of labour costs apart from wages. In the year 1990-91 (before the latest round of compulsory super-annuation increases) superannuation costs per private sector employee jumped by al-most 30 per cent! Average labour on costs — super, payroll tax, workers' compensation and the fringe benefits tax — jumped by more than 13 per cent over the year com-pared with a wages growth of 6 per ccnt. This is not to advocate anything so radical as large-scalc wage slashing. But why do we have a system which insists of having a na-tional wage rise during a recession? It might be all right for some industries in some parts of the country which are doing well, but why this mentality of everyone having to have more? Because of the economics in Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania maybe we need to look for regional wage structures. After all, the cost of living in Melbourne is considerably lower at the moment than in Sydney. Why should unions argue that a building worker in say depressed Geelong should be paid at the same level as one in Sydney? The Accord has actually given less and less say to the average worker about what he or she wants in terms of benefits and condi-tions. (I write as a union member of more than 20 years, including three years as a part-time elected union official). Did the average worker really want all that superan-nuation? Some might. Others might have wanted cash. Others might want more child carc and flexible working hours. Others might be prepared to concede benefits to-avoid layoffs. Very significantly, the Saulwick poll pub-lished in The Age this week showed that half those surveyed supported the idea of issues such as wages and other conditions being negotiated directly between workers and em-ployers without union involvement. The labour-relations industry and our whole official attitude to wage setting and pushing more and more costs on employers must be the next major area of reform for Australia. The longer it takes, the higher the cost in terms of unemployment and the greater the social and economic divisions in our allegedly egalitarian country.

18 Jul 1992 - Union awards, IRC rulings losing popularity with voters Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 18 July 1992, page 2 Union awards, IRC rulings losing popularity with voters Awards negotiated by trade unions and employees or determined by the Industrial Relations Commission are losing popularity among the voting public. A Herald Saulwick Poll of 1000 electors interviewed nation-wide found nearly half supported direct enterprise bargaining between employer and employee. The poll asked whether wages, hours of work and conditions should be determined by the IRQ whether negotiations should be between employers and trade unions without the involvement of the IRC; or whether negotiations should be between employers and employees without the in volvement of either unions or the IRC. Direct employer-employee negotiations was preferred by 49 per cent of those polled; 22 per cent preferred a system in which trade unions negotiated with employers, and another 22 per cent preferred a system where the IRC decided. Of intending Coalition voters, 62 per cent support enterprise bargaining, against 38 per cent of intending ALP voters. The poll found 63 per cent believed unions had too much power, while 59 per cent felt big business wielded too much power. A Morgan poll, published in Time Australia, has found the Coalition would have comfortably won an election had one been held early in July. Support for the Labor Government, however, was up one percentage point to 36 per cent while Liberal-National support was down one to 44 per cent. The Australian Democrats fell one percentage point to 6 per cent and support for independents rose one to 14 per cent. The poll, of 3170 electors interviewed face-to-face was taken before the release of the latest unemployment statistics. A Newspoll of 1138 electors interviewed on July 10-12 and published in The Australian showed Mr Keating's disapproval had risen by 10 percentage points to to 68 per cent, while his approval rating fell six to 32 per cent. Dr Hewson's approval rating fell three percentage points to 35 per cent and his disapproval rating rose five to 51 per cent.

His personal approval rating slumped in the wake of the issue of the June jobless data on July 9, according to Time magazine's Morgan Gallup Poll and the Bulletin magazine's AGB poll, reported on television news bulletins last night." But the Coalition appeared to have gained little from the gloom over unemployment, although it retained a handy lead over Labor in both polls. The Seven Network said Time's poll showed the Coalition with a two-party preferred lead of 10 percentage points over Labor. Its primary vote was unchanged on the previous poll at 44 per cent. Continued on Page 2 Slump noted in Keating's , popularity Continued from Front Page The ALP's primary vote was down. one at 35, the Australian Democrats, up two to eight and others and„ independents down one at 13. Asked about preferences, the. Democrats, others and independents split 52 to 48 per cent in favour of the ' ALP. Mr Keating's personal approval rating slumped four points to 29 per cent, his lowest level since mid-Janu ary, while his disapproval rating was, up four to a record 61 per cent. Opposition Leader John Hewson's standing also fell, with his approval rating down one to 39 per cent: and ; disapproval also at a new record lev-, . el of 46 per cent, up one. c . But Dr Hewson opened up hisllead; over Mr Keating as preferred Prime ,t Minister, at 45 per cent (up one) to the Prime Minister's 39 per cent' (down two). The Nine Network said the Bulle-,'. tin poll showed Mr Keating's ap-,' proval rating plunging five points to,' 23 per cent, while Dr Hewson's rating rose two to 31 per cent. ;

05 Sep 1992 - Polls show Goss well ahead; Groom, Kennett support up Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 September 1992, page 2 Polls show Goss well ahead; Groom, Kennett support up POLL WATCH Queensland's Labor Premier, Wayne Goss, looks set to win another term in office after a Morgan poll, published in Time Australia, found support for Labor in that state had risen three points to 49 per cent. This was the Government's highest rating in a year while support for the Liberal Party, 22 per cent, and the National Party, 18 per cent, was unchanged. Support for minor parties and independents fell three points to 11 per cent. If an election had been held in July or August, the ALP would have retained office. The approval rating of Mr Goss improved two points to a high of 79 per cent. Eighty per cent of men preferred Mr Goss, 77 per cent of women. His disapproval rating was unchanged on 16 per cent. The approval ratings of National Party leader Robert Borbidge, 28 per cent, and Liberal leader Joan Sheldon, 39 per cent, were unchanged. Premier Goss has announced a September 19 election. In Victoria, Opposition leader Jeff Kennett has surged ahead, according to a Bulletin poll, held by AGB Australia. Mr Kennett's rating as preferred Premier had increased by four points to 38 per cent, giving him an eight-point lead over the Labor Premier, Joan Kirner. His Liberal-National Coalition was 24 points ahead of the Government, 49 per cent to 25 per cent. Mr Kennett's approval rating was up four points to 26 per cent and his disapproval rating down four points to 43 per cent. Thirty-one per cent were uncommit ted. Mrs Kirner's approval rating was steady on 24 per cent and her disapproval rating fell two points to 55 per cent. Twenty-one per cent were uncommitted. The Liberal Government in Tasmania holds a four point lead over the ALP Opposition, although Labor's electoral standing has improved over the past three months. A Bulletin poll, held by AGB Australia, found support for Michael Field's Opposition up eight points to 40 per cent while support for Ray Groom's Government fell six points to 44 per cent. Mr Groom's approval rating fell four points to 41 per cent, with his disapproval rating climbing 13 points to 31 per cent. . Support for Mr Field remained at 41 per cent while his disapproval rating rose one point to 38 per cent. Mr Groom remains the preferred premier by 46 per cent, down three points, to Mr Field's 33 per cent. Outside the political arena, a Morgan poll, published in Time Australia, has found 77 per cent of working Australians would be prepared to work harder for the same pay and conditions to improve the nation's productivity, up one point since June.

07 Sep 1992 - Budget help to ALP: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 7 September 1992, page 2 Budget help to ALP: poll The latest Morgan poll has found Labor would have won an election held in August. The poll, for Time Australia magazine, showed support for the ALP jumped 5.5 per cent to 39.5 per ccnt after the Budget's release - putting the Government in a better position than at the last election in March 1990. However, an AGB poll of NSW voters concerning the next federal election shows the federal Labor Party has lost its lead and fallen behind the Opposition. This poll, for The Bulletin, found the Coalition had moved ahead by three percentage points. Polling nationally, the survey showed the Coalition maintained a six-point lead over Labor, with both major parties and the Democrats falling one percentage point.

08 Sep 1992 - Libs admit their transport plans mean job losses Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 8 September 1992, page 4 Libs admit their transport plans mean job losses MELBOURNE: The Victorian Opposition revealed yesterday plans for a radical overhaul of public transport which, it admitted, would lead to "major" job losses. However, the Opposition's transport spokesman, Alan Brown, said radical action was necessary if the public transport system's massive annual $2 billion loss was to be reduced.' The Liberal Leader, Jeff Kennett, also said yesterday he "lived in fear" of Labor being re-elected to government in the October 3 election. His admission followed a new opinion poll showing a sharp reduction in the Coalition's strong two-year lead over Labor during the first two weeks of the election campaign. Mr Kennett said he feared Labor would win an unprecedented fourth term on October 3 on the back of preferences from the record 182 independents contesting the election. He warned that such a result would be "disastrous" for Victoria. Mr Kennett, who has twice before led the Liberals to defeat in Victoria, added that he had learned not to expect electoral victory. The Premier, Joan Kirner, said the Morgan Gallup Poll, showing a 6 per cent jump in support for Labor (to 31 per cent) against a 9 per cent drop in support for the Coalition (to 50 per cent), was similar to, although more "dramatic" than, the findings of private ALP polling during the early stages of the long campaign. She also said the Morgan result reflected a new voter con centration on policy issues, particularly planned industrial relations reforms by a Coalition government The opinion poll showed the Opposition was "reaping the whirlwind of their hidden agenda" to lower award wages and conditions, Mrs Kirner said. Later, Mr Brown ensured that public transport would also become an election issue when he confirmed plans to remove conductors from trams and contract out maintenance and bus services. The plans set the scene for major industrial confrontation under a Coalition government after October 3. In early 1990 the Labor Government was forced into an embarrassing and politically costly backdown when its attempt to remove conductors from trams threw Melbourne's public transport system into chaos for five weeks. Yesterday unions immediately warned that the Coalition's policy would lead to similar in dustrial strife. Mr Brown said only radical reform would revive the state's ailing public transport system. He acknowledged the reforms would come at the cost of a significant number of jobs but an Opposition spokesman later said there were "no plans for eliminating or closing any services" in Victoria. The Opposition said part of its policy would allow Melbourne's historic W-Class trams to be installed in the state's three major regional centres, Geelong, Bendigo and Ballarat

14 Sep 1992 - Fahey lifts his party's rating Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 14 September 1992, page 2 Fahey lifts his party's rating SYDNEY: The NSW Premier, John Fahey, has helped turn around the fortunes of his Liberal-National Coalition Government and improved his own approval rating by 7 percent, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, published in Time Australia this week, shows support for the Coalition has increased by 4 per cent since June, and by 1.5 in August, to 43 per cent Labor's support dropped 2.5 per cent to 40 per cent in August.

20 Sep 1992 - Plea will backfire, Kennett predicts Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 20 September 1992, page 3 Plea will backfire, Kennett predicts MELBOURNE: Victoria's Oppo-sition Leader, Jeff Kennett, predict-ed yesterday that the plea to voters by the Premier, Joan Kirner, last week to forget the past failings of the ALP, would backfire. Mr Kennett said Mrs Kirner had been desperate during her platform address on Thursday in asking voters not to take revenge against her Gov-ernment, and look to the future. In a J. F. Kennedy-style call for action, Mrs Kirner said, "I am not asking the people of Victoria, 'Who's political side are you on?", I am ask-ing people, 'How important is Victo-ria to you'?" She added, "On election day, will you focus on the vision for the fu-ture, a people-based future, or will you seek retribution for the past?" Mr Kennett said voters would be hard pressed to forget the state's high unemployment rate, the increase in Victorians needing support, and the tens of thousands of investors who were "stripped of their finances" by the collapse of the Farrow building society group. "For Mrs Kirner now to invoke the words of JFK in a last desperate gamble to ask people to forgive and forget . . . is somewhat a forlorn hope," Mr Kennett said. "What she's really saying is vote for me, vote for us . . . forget what's happened in the past, forget that there's 154 Victori-ans losing their jobs every day. "1 think most people will be af-fronted by that because it reinforces in their minds that Labor will not accept any responsibility for what has happened to our society through their administration." The Age Saulwick poll taken on Thursday showed that over the past three weeks, support for the Govern-ment had risen by 11 points to 35 per cent. The Coalition's support rose mar-ginally by one point to 52 per cent, but support for Independents fell dramatically from 18 to 10 percent. The Victorian Opposition said yesterday it would close nine insti-tutions for the intellectually and physically disabled if it won the Oc-tober 3 state election. Launching the Coalition's com-munity services policy yesterday, the Opposition's community services spokesman, Michael John, accused the Labor Government of creating conditions similar to those of the great Depression.

21 Sep 1992 - PM's approval still high: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 21 September 1992, page 2 PM's approval still high: poll Support for the federal ALP dropped 1.5 points to 38 per cent in the first two weeks of September, after a 5.5 point rise in August, the latest Morgan Poll has found. But approval of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, was at its highest level sincc June, while support for the Opposition Leader, John Hcwson, slipped amid his criticism of Japanese and US trade policies and a renewed push for zero tariffs in the car industry. At the same time, Liberal-National Party support rose two points to 44 per cent and support for the Australian Democrats also increased by 0.5 points to 6 per cent. The Morgan Poll, issued on the Seven Network and published in Time Australia, said 12 per cent opted for other parties or independents, a drop of one point. Those polled were asked to give Ms Kirner and Mr Kennett scores out of 10. Ms Kirner scored 5.5 for honesty, 5.0 for reliability, 6.6 for intelligence and 5.5 for being in touch. On the other hand, Mr Kennett's scores were 5.1, 4.9, 5.9 and 5.0 respectively. Ms Kirner is also the preferred premier by a small margin - 44- to 42 per cent. Fourteen per cent of those surveyed were undecided. In the federal arena, a Bulletin poll, held by AGB Australia, has shown the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, to be gaining on the Opposition Leader, John Hewson. Mr Keating's approval rating has increased three points to 26 per cent, while Dr Hewson's dropped two points to 30 per cent. On the question of who is the preferred Prime Minister, Mr Keating and Dr Hewson are neck and neck with 36 per cent each with 28 per cent uncommitted. 04 Oct 1992 - SUPPORT UP: POLL Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 4 October 1992, page 7 SUPPORT UP: POLL SYDNEY: The NSW Premier, John Fahey, continues to enjoy popular support, a new poll shows. The latest Saulwick Poll, published in yesterday's Sydney Morning Herald, shows that Mr Fahey's popularity rose since the last poll, from 36 to 39. It shows Mr Fahey well ahead of the Opposition Leader, Bob Carr, as preferred premier, 58 per cent to 28. Last month, the figures were 53 per cent and 31 per cent. 12 Oct 1992 - Principals give VCE good marks Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 12 October 1992, page 13 Principals give VCE good marks MELBOURNE: Secondary school principals have given a strong endorsement to the controversial and much-maligned Victorian Certificate of Education — VCE — according to a Saulwick poll in yesterday's Sunday Age. The poll showed 79 per cent of principals thought the high school leaving certificate was good or very . good. The VCE, in its first full year of operation, was labelled "fundamentally flawed" by the Leader of the Libera! Party, Jeff Kennctt, before he became Premier and has been called a "failed experiment" by the new Minister for Education, Don Hayward. It has also come in for criticism from universities. The poll, of 150 principals — 37 from private and 113 from state schools — showed 90 per cent of state school heads rated the VCE good or very good, while in private schools almost half said it was good and 16 per cent very good. It said 89 per cent of principals wanted only some aspects of the VCE changed or were happy to leave it substantially intact, and 11 per cent said they would overhaul or completely change the system. The poll also showed 82 per cent thought the VCE better prepared students for the workforce, 83 per cent thought students would be bet ter prepared for adulthood, and 70 per cent said they were better prepared for tertiary education. Most principals believed the first year of the VCE had increased stress on students, teachers and par ents. Only 23 per cent thought university admission exams were necessary and 70 per cent said they were not. The principals sent no clear signal on the new Coalition Government's education policies: 36 per cent said things would be better, 29 percent worse, and 25 percent were unsure. I

17 Oct 1992 - POLL WATCH Coalition makes gains on all main issues Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 17 October 1992, page 2 I POLL WATCH ||1 Coalition makes gains on all main issues The Liberal-National Coalition is rated best to handle seven of 11 key issues — including unemployment — according to a News poll in The Australian this week, while unemployment and health rated as the two issues of most concern. The poll shows that the LiberalNational parties have gained ground on all main issues since July, with voters evenly split about which offers the better leadership. The poll gives the Coalition a sevenpoint lead over the Government in handling unemployment — 38 per cent to 31. The most optimistic note for Labor in the poll is the result on industrial relations. While this issue is considered very important by 47 per cent of voters, the ALP is rated best to handle the issue by a margin of seven points — 39 per cent to 32. Labor still leads the Opposition as the party best able to deal with health and Medicare — at 71 per cent the second-highest-rated issue in the poll behind unemployment. Taxation and social welfare — also rating high at 61 per cent — are the next issues of most concern, followed by the environment, 59 per cent, leadership, 58 per cent, and inflation, 56 per cent. As well as industrial relations and health, Labor is preferred to handle welfare and social issues (by a margin of six points) and the environment (also by six points). The electorate remains equally divided over which party has the best leadership, with 41 per cent opting for Mr Keating and 42 per cent for Dr Hewson. This compares with Dr Hewson's lead of 51 per cent to 33 in February. However, even with its 15 per cent goods and services tax proposal, the Coalition is still marginally ahead of the Government on taxation issues. A Bulletin poll has shown the ALP to be narrowing the gap in the Senate. Conducted by AGB Australia, it shows the likely vote for the Keating Government in the Senate has risen two points to 38 per cent, with the Opposition holding steady at 41 per cent.

07 Nov 1992 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 7 November 1992, page 2 POLL WATCH Keating tops Hewson The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, has displaced the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, as preferred prime minister, according to the Saulwick Poll published this week. The poll, published in The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald, shows that 45 per cent of respondents prefer Mr Keating — a gain of three points during the past month. The Morgan Poll in this week's Time Australia shows approval for Mr Keating has risen one point to 37 per cent while his disapproval rating remains unchanged at 53 per cent. Dr Hewson's approval rating has also risen one point to 38 per cent and his disapproval rating fell one point to 47 per cent. 16 Nov 1992 - Bishop questions 'sale' of Fightback tax package Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 16 November 1992, page 2 Bishop questions 'sale' of Fightback tax package By ROSS .PEAKE, Political Correspondent Outspoken Liberal backbencher Bronwyn Bishop has questioned the marketing of the Opposition's Fightback package, saying its message is not being clearly received in the community. She revealed last night that she ' was not referring to the proposed goods-and-services tax when she was talking about the taxation reforms contained in Fightback. Senator Bishop also said she hoped the Opposition would gain greater support in public opinion polls as attention was directed towards the state of the economy. The Opposition had lost its focus on economic issues but would soon regain it, she said. Senator Bishop denied that the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, had made mistakes with selling Fightback and said he was working hard to get his message across. ' He had broken precedents by issuing a detailed blueprint of what a Coalition government would do. "And I think that's got some complexities which people like to be informed about and some of it perhaps isn't coming across as well as it should," Senator Bishop said Bronwyn Bishop on the Ten Network's Meet the Press program. She said she had never been called a wimp and she would like to be a minister in a Coalition government. Asked if she would like to be Australia's first female prime minister, she did not reply directly, saying she would do what her party asked of her. She was questioned about the trend of growing support for the ALP in the polls, with the Newspoll last week putting Labor ahead of the Opposition for the first time in 2'A years. The poll was taken before the news that unemployment in October reached 11.3 per cent — almost 980,000 people out of work. "I think for a little while we did lose focus on just how bad the economy was, and we were tending to debate other things, but I think the mind is really focused again now," Senator Bishop said. "I don't know whether to expect the polls to pick up immediately; sometimes it takes a little longer, but I do know that the debate is well and truly back on the question of the economy." Senator Bishop is a member of the Senate committee which will investigate the Victorian loans affairs. She has been accused by the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, of prejudging the issue. The Opposition hopes the inquiry will lead to further disclosures about the the role of the Treasurer, John Dawkins, when the former Victorian Labor Government exceeded its borrowing limits. Senator Bishop said last night "something doesn't smell quite right", but was more cautious in her assessment of the issue. Group calls for rapid reforms MELBOURNE: Australia is doomed to an eternal unsuccessful quest to catch up with the economic progress of other developed countries unless micro-economic reform is speeded up, says a business group. The Committee for Economic Development of Australia says the country needs to develop a community culture of continuous improvement in marketing goods and services overseas. In its report Micro-economic Re form and Business Efficiency, issued today, the committee nominates transport, construction, power, energy, labour organisation, communication, education and taxation regimes as areas for im provement "It's the only way to get off the dizzy merry-go-round of always being in a catch-up situation," the committee says. "Even being as good as the rest of the world may not be good enough if Australia wishes to develop po tential sources of competitive advantage for our goods and services overseas." The committee's report also expressed concern that some efficiency improvements had not resulted in a better deal for consumers. The paper called for the States to step up their reforms, a more coordinated approach to international competition, government and industry to work together, and more attention to those disadvantaged by reforms.

In December last year 62 per ccnt of Liberal-National voters I supported the introduction of a | GST. Last week's poll shows this figure has dropped to 51 per cent. Twenty-eight per cent of Coalition voters are opposed to a GST and a considerable 21 per cent remain uncommitted. Not surprisingly, 83 per cent of Labor voters are opposed to a GST and two out of three feel they would be worse off under a goods and services tax. The Morgan poll published in Time Australia and the AGB Bulletin poll both found that support for the Keating Government is up. Support for the Government was up 4 points to 44.5 per cent, while backing for the Opposition had dropped 3.5 points to 40.5 per cent. Dr Hewson's approval rating fell one point to 26 per cent while his disapproval rating rose one point to 4! per cent. Mr Keating's disapproval rating was up also by one point to 46 per cent. Mr Keating remained preferred Prime Minister with 38 per cent support compared with the 34 per cent for Dr Hewson.

25 Nov 1992 - PERSPECTIVE MIDWEEK NEWS MAGAZINE Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 25 November 1992, page 21 ■ SCIENCE ■ EDUCATION ■ MEDICINE ■ ARTS ■ RELIGION ■ LAW ACT's unresolved legal poser Problems raised by pre-trial publicity are discussed by Rod Campbell in the wake of the recent Bush case. LAW IN THE leadup to the recent- ly concluded Bush murder trial—Ian Leslie Bush was jailed for life on November 18 —some important issues about publicity and fair trials were raised but left hanging. The emergence of these issues had remained secret until late last week because of a suppression order imposed in October. But now that Bush has been convicted and jailed, they can be thrown open for public discussion. A fortnight before the Bush trial began, his barrister and ACT Public Defender, Terry O'Donnell, made an extraordinary and unprecedent ed application to the ACT Supreme Court. He asked that Bush's trial be postponed indefinitely so that the wheels could be set in motion to get it moved out of Canberra. As far as can be determined, nev-er before has there been a "change of venue" application in the ACT. A change of venue must mean a transfer outside the ACT; it is hard ly sensible to consider running a trial in Hall or Tharwa. And this immediately raises the question, is it legally and physically possible to run an ACT trial in NSW or Victo ria or wherever? The application was based on the prejudicial publicity Bush had at-tracted in 1987 when he was con victed of the manslaughter of his first wife. He has, of course, now been convicted of the attempted murder of his estranged second wife and the murder of her boyfriend. It is not hard to see the prejudicial impact information about the 1987 case might have had on the most recent proceedings. And that is where the second extraordinary ele ment of this matter came in. Bush's lawyers sought to prove the exist ence of a prejudicial climate by hir ing the Saulwick poll people to survey potential jurors. That imme-diately raised another problem: the more people surveyed, the more re liable the poll result; but the more people surveyed, the greater the likelihood that potential jurors would be prejudiced. There was a risk the poll would create the sort of prejudice it was seeking to measure. Apparently the only other time a poll has been used to check on juror prejudice was in the Glennon case in Victoria, where enormous pub-licity had surrounded the charging of a priest with child sexual abuse offences. Rejecting a change of ven ue application, the High Court said the prejudicial publicity could be overcome by appropriate directions to the jury. The application for an adjourn ment of the Bush trial and, ulti mately, a change of venue, came before Justice John Gallop on Octo ber 27. It was, as is now obvious, unsuccessful. But the issue is bound to raise its head again—and per haps quite soon—particularly in such a small and relatively well-in formed community as Canberra. Under ACT crirpinal law (mostly inherited from NSW many years ago), the court can order a change of venue if it appears that a fair or unprejudiced trial is not possible. As Mr O'Donnell told the judge, a very practical difficulty arises be cause ACT laws governing juries do not apply outside the ACT. The court itself can sit anywhere in Aus tralia and this happens from time to time in non-jury matters. But with out the power to empanel a jury outside the ACT, no jury trial can be transferred beyond the border. Mr O'Donnell's instructing solic itor, Chris Staniforth (chief execut ive of the ACT Legal Aid Commission), has written to the ACT Attorney-General—he should have written to his federal counterpart, Justice Gallop thought —to have something done about the legislation. It will also be neces sary to work out some sort of gov ernment-to-government arrangement with, say, NSW and/or Victoria. Saulwick poll Assuming Messrs O'Donnell and Staniforth were able to convince At torneys-General in two, three or four jurisdictions to co-operate in this manner, the court still had to be convinced that the prior prejudicial publicity was such that a fair trial was unlikely. To this end, they ten dered a series of articles published in The Canberra Times in 1987, relating to the death of Debra Bush and her husband's appearances in court, and in 1992, concerning Ian Bush's arrest on murder and at tempted murder charges and later committal proceedings. This is where Irving Saulwick (who has been conducting the Saul wick-Age polls for 20 years) came in. The defence team was concerned that it would be difficult to empanel a jury whose members did not re member the 1987 case. Three ran domly-selected groups of 50 people were polled by telephone. A sample of 150 might seem small, but there were fears that any bigger number would taint the potential jury panel. The questions in the poll were: Question 1. Do you remember an incident in which a woman's body was found in bushland in the ACT in 1987 and, although the body was unidentified for a number of months, it was subsequently identi fied as Debra Bush? Question 2. (If a "yes" answer to Q.l) Did you know that her hus-band was later tried and convicted of an offence relating to her death? Question 3. (If a "yes" answer to Q.2) If that husband were to be charged with a similar offence relat ing to his second wife and her lover, would you, given what you remem ber of the previous incident, tend to think he was guilty of the second offence or have an open mind on the question? The responses were quite remark able. Of the 150 people of jury-duty age polled, 43 per cent did remem ber the Bush case from 1987. One quarter of these, or 35 respondents, said they did know of charges against the husband. And finally, more than half of the 35 said this knowledge might influence them. In' other words, 12.6 per cent of the total sample answered in the affir mative to all three questions. Injury terms, one or two members of the jury selected to try Bush in 1992 might have remembered the previ ous case and been influenced by it. Superficially, likely prejudice had been established. The big problem was the leading nature of the first question. The re sponses to questions 2 and 3 were probably been influenced by the fact Justice John Gallop presided at the Bush trial. that Debra Bush had been identified in the first question. The pollsters realised this danger. But they also thought respondents might confuse the Bush case with the Mossessen one (also involving a woman mur dered and dumped in the bush at roughly the same time). They might, therefore, say yes to question 1, thinking of the Mossessen case, but no to question 2, because Bente Mossessen's alleged killer was not her husband. At the end of the day, Justice Gallop had a very simple question to ask. The legislation provided that he could order a change of venue when he thought fit, but "How can I think fit when we've nowhere to go?" Discussion followed on wheth er Federal Parliament would have to pass legislation and whether ACT, evidence, juries and Supreme Court laws would all need changing. The ACT Legislative Assembly probably did not have the power to apply ACT law in another jurisdiction. But the Commonwealth probably would not act without an ACT Gov- | ernment request. Mr O'Donnell failed to get his adjournment for two reasons. The judge was not satisfied that likely prejudice had been established (and he was not all that happy about the survey questions). And he was not convinced that further delay was justified, given all the impondera bles relating to changes to the law and getting .two or three govern ments on side to effect them. Perhaps the Bush case was not the best one to base a change of venue application on. Perhaps the survey had its weaknesses. But the fact re mains that the ACT is a small and relatively close-knit community where news travels fast and many potential jurors keep themselves well-informed. The chances are that sooner or later, a case will come before Supreme Court where the amount of pre-trial publicity is such that a fair trial is in serious doubt. Before that happens, something might need to be done to ensure that the right to a change of venue to secure a fair trial can be achieved in reality. After all, the High Court de clared only this month that the right to a fair trial is absolute. At present, in cases of notoriety and much pub licity, it is only theoretical in Can berra. New health and safety standards New laws covering occupational health and safety requirements will come into effect on July 1, 1993, and apply to all ACT businesses with 10 or more employees. In this article, Alan Grinsell-Jones outlines the steps employers in the ACT will be required to take when the new regulations come into effect. THE NEW regulations require all ACT businesses with 10 or more employees to establish designated work groups which will empower them to maintain occupational health and safety standards directly in the workplace. The object of the designated work groups is to enable employees' occupational health and safety interests to be represented and safe guarded and enable an occupational health and safety representative to be accessible to each employee. Each designated work group is required to select one representative'who has certain powers, including: □ the power to inspect the whole or any part of the workplace if there has, in the immedi ate past, been an accident; or the representa tive believes on reasonable grounds that there is a threat of an accident; or the representative has given the employer reasonable notice of any inspection he or she intends to undertake; □ accompany an inspector during any inspec tion of the workplace; □ where there is no health and safety commit tee, represent the employees in the designated work group in consultation with the employer concerning health and safety; □ where there is a committee, examine any of the records of that committee; □ investigate complaints made by any em ployee in the group concerning the health and safety of any employees at work; □ with the consent of the employee con cerned, be present at any interview concern ing health and safety at work between an employee in the group and an inspector or the employer; □ obtain access to any information under the employer's control relating to risks and safety of any employee; □ obtain access to any information under the employer's control relating to the health and safety of any of the employer's employees. The powers in relation to access to infor mation are restricted in that the representa tive is not entitled to information to which legal professional privilege applies or infor mation of a confidential medical nature un less the employee concerned has given the representative written authority to have ac cess. An employer must permit the representa tive to exercise his or her powers and any failure to do so will leave an employer liable to a penalty of a maximum of $1000 in the case of an individual or $5000 in the case of a corporation. A representative also has the power to issue a provisional improvement notice in writing requiring an employer to rectify any matters or activities which the representative believes amount to a contravention of the provisions of the Act. The failure to comply with a provisional improvement notice renders an offender lia ble to a maximum fine of $10,000 if the employer is a natural person or $50,000 in the case of a body corporate. There are provisions enabling an employer to arrange for an inspector to investigate the circumstances relating to the giving of the notice and when such a request is made the operation of those is suspended until the in spector completes an investigation. An in spector has the power to revoke a provisional improvement notice. A designated work group can be one group or several groups depending upon the struc ture of the business. In designating work groups an employer must take into account: □ the number of employees; □ the nature of each type of work performed; □ the grouping of the employees who perform similar types of work and the workplaces or areas where each type of work is performed; □ the nature of any risk to health and safety at each of those workplaces; and □ any arrangements relating to overtime or shift work. All employees must be assigned to a group. In designating work groups an employer must consult with a union if any of his employees are members, or with the employees them selves. The employer is required to display a no tice in the workplace allowing the employees to be notified of the designation of work groups. The designation of work groups must be carried out within 14 days of the com mencement of the Act, i.e. from July 1 1993 and failure to do this may Jeave an employer liable to a penalty of a maximum of $ 1000 in the case of an individual or $5000 in the case of a corporation. If employees are not satisfied with the des ignation of work groups by the employer, upon a request by 50 per cent or more em ployees in the workplace, the OH&S Registrar will establish work groups in lieu of those established by an employer. It can be seen that the extension of the Act's operation will require small employers to take positive steps in relation to its application. It is important to note that now is the time to take action because the new work groups must be in place no later than 14 days after July 1, 1993. Alan Grinsell-Jones is with the Canberra office of lawyers Sly & Weigall.

21 Dec 1992 - Consumers are not optimistic about the year ahead: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 21 December 1992, page 3 Consumers are not optimistic about the year ahead: poll By MARK LEVER, AAP Economics Correspondent Consumer confidence has fallen to its lowest level of the year, according to a Morgan poll to be published in this week's Time magazine. A separate survey has shown New Zealanders to be slightly more optimistic, than Australians about the coming year. The Morgan confidence index fell 0.7 per cent this month to 92.9, sharply down on the 1992 high point of 101.2 in October. However, the pollsters r- Roy Morgan Research — said a low figure for December was normal despite the seasonal good cheer. The latest figure was the highest for December since 1988 and above the long-term December average of 91.4. Based on 1168 face-to-face interviews on the first weekend of December, the poll found the deterioration in confidence was based mainly on views about the short-term outlook with 50 per cent (up four — the most since August) expecting bad times next year and only 18 per cent (down one on November) expecting.bctter times. During the next five years, views were little changed at 29 per cent expecting good times and 31 per cent pessimistic. Attitudes about personal finances improved, with 28 percent (up three) expecting to be better off a year ahead and 22 per cent (down two) worse off. An unchanged 20 per cent said they were better off than a year ago and 46 per cent (up one) said worse off. The strongest confidence is on the timing of major purchases with 50 per cent (down two) saying now was a good time to buy major items such as appliances and furniture while 33 per cent (up three) said it was a bad time. In another poll of 1273 Australians and 1,087 New Zealanders, there were significant changes in the relative levels of national optimism. Some 43 per cent of New Zealanders and 42 per cent of Australians believe 1993 will be better than 1992, a marked turnaround on the 33 per cent and 54 per cent when the corresponding question for 1992 was asked a year ago. Very few people in either country expect a prosperous 1993.

09 Jan 1993 - Wages of sin keep flowing into coffers of love Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 January 1993, page 20 Wages of sin keep flowing into coffers of love WHEN the Saulwick Poll asked Aus tralians what they most looked forward to doing on holidays, the most common response was Nothing. Over Christmas 1 did the next best thing. I read some of the latest Mills & Boon romances which 1 bought for $4.10 apiece at the news agents. On the first page of Love in Torment by Natalie Fox I met the beautiful 25-year-old artist, Gemma Soames. On the eighth page I met Felipe Santos, the perfect lover. And on the ninth Gemma was watching him in awe as he peeled ofThis evening suit, revealing a body as perfect as a Rodin sculpture. Felipe stripped the black silk lace from her firm round breasts. She gazed at the hazy blackness of his groin. Then he "carried her to the sensual bed and laid her down. His tongue explored, lightly at first, and then his urgency powered them both to fierce eroticism that swam into a haze of white-hot passion." Romances have come a long way since 1853 when, in The Heir of Redclijfe, Charlotte M. Yonge introduced her readers to a heroine of shrinking modesty and maidenly feeling, not to mention a strong lustrous-eyed hero afflicted with an inner life of grief and doubt. Indeed, when Ms Yonge finally got her couple married she sent them off — the bride exuding radiance, purity and innocence — on a honeymoon tour of all the cathedral towns of England. But Natalie Fox'has Felipe's hand , snaking up Gemma's neck, his mouth crushing hers and his voice threatening, "Torment — you will know the true meaning of the word by the time I have finished with you." You may laugh, but publishers love it. In 1991 romances accounted for 46 per cent of all mass-market paperback sales in the United States. They totalled SUS750 million. Indeed, a single top romance publisher can earn more than $100 million a year and, as in the case of Silhouette last year, publish 50 titles a month. The average romance reader spent SUS1200 during the year on her love stories. Romance is a boom industry. In their last financial year Mills & Boon posted their third successive annual profit increase in a recession-hit Britain, chalking up sales of £21.5 million and a profit of £1.7 million pre-tax. Before Christmas they were proudly proclaiming that a single author, Penny Jordan, had produced 80 novels in 10 years and had more than 50 million books in print, including translations into 20 languages. Every month they publish about 16 new titles as well as reprints and "category" titles. It's not uncommon for The Bookseller to list more than 70 new romance titles coming from a variety of publishers in a single week. Some are hot-crotch "contemporaries" like Love in Torment. Some are bodice-ripper historical offering supersaturated sex in hooped skirts — more wuthering than Wuthering Heights, one publisher proclaimed. Some are "sweet and savage" erotic bondage fantasies. And some, like Carole Mortimer's Private Lives, an M & B I read over Christmas, are traditional "sweet romances". The heroine gets her first kiss on page 71 — "his mouth ground down on her lips with fierce demand" — and her second on page 98 — "She smelt his tangy aftershave and his thighs harden against hers as his hands moved restlessly down her spine." I plugged on doggedly to page 187 but they didn't have it off, although Ms Mortimer tells us in the last line that they would be happy together (her italics). There had to be something more sexy than this, 1" thought, so I rang the number M & B enticingly provided in the back of the book and pressed .the code numbers they thoughtfully provided to hear about Tidewater Seduction by Anne Mather. But obviously the storyline was too hot to handle on the telephone. I also tried Tides of Passion by Sally Hcywood. Five times 1 dialled the codes and five times the recorded voice told me, "Our computer did not detect your tone." A few days before, however, I had no trouble getting recorded summaries of some of their sweet romance titles. I also failed to get summaries of the two medical romances listed. They must have increased the percentage of passion and sensual detail in them too. They used to be my favourites when they appeared about 30 years ago. They're about doctors and nurses and dreadful operations. A kiss was for medicinal purposes only: "It was a long Kiss, and it seemed to be controlled by some sort of rheostat, like the twelve-position graduation of the dimmer switches in the wards..." After a kiss like that, I thought, you'd need a rectal washout. As M & B themselves admit, romances these days arc a global industry. In a swanky office in Paradise Road in south London they employ 22 editors who plough through 5000 unsolicited manuscripts annually and select fewer than a dozen for publication. Most of their time is spent cultivating and editing the works of their reliable established authors who produce an average of four books a year each and, keep the wages of sin flowing into .the coffers of love, but more of them next week.

19 Feb 1993 - Keating and Kelty talk cash Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 19 February 1993, page 5 Keating and Kelty talk cash Further data on marginal seats indicates that the Government remains in serious trouble in both West Australia and South Australia. Industrial relations will go to the top of the election campaign agenda today, when the Prime Minister, Paul Keating meets with the secretary of the ACTU, Bill Kelty, to thrash out a deal to form the basis of the prices and incomes accord. Mr Keating needs to walk away from today's meeting with the ACTU with something which is more than just a reiteration of his rather conservative 1992 wages strategy. That strategy involved the delivery of a $ 10 a week increase in minimum award rates of pay in March, to be followed by a further $10 a week in minimum rates towards the end of the year.
