02 Apr 1993 - Young Libs, Nationals push for Coalition to take up republican debate Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 2 April 1993, page 1 Ifoung Libs, Nationals push for Coalition to take up republican debate Screws turned on Hewson By JODIE BROUQH and ROSS PEAKE Pressure is mounting on the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, to enter the republican debate, following his refusal to declare his hand on the nation's future. He was further isolated yesterday when the Leader of the National Party, Tim Fischer, declared his support for the monarchy and the Liberal Party's federal director, Andrew Robb, urged the party to enter the debate. The Young Liberals, influential in reshaping rank-and-file views, suggested "a failure of his leadership" if Dr Hewson did not match the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, in the debate. The NSW president of the Young Liberals, John Brogden, said most of his members favoured a republic: the organisation already had a commitment to holding referendum. Dr Hewson was "wrong to see it as a minor side-issue... and I think he is wrong to spend time trying to question the issue". "Politically, I think it will become Keating's issue with Hewson not knowing where he stands," he said. Even Dr Hewson's recent rival for the party leadership, John Howard, has weighed into the debate, saying that republicans faced a dilemma in choosing a president by popular vote because presidential authority would "challenge that of the Prime Minister's, leading to great constitutional instability". In a stand which could widen into a Coalition split, Mr Fischer recommitted the Nationals to the existing constitutional arrangements, although he said he welcomed "a more in-depth debate" on how a republic would work. "The constitutional referendum required will also require a fair dinkum debate," he said. "The last thing Australia should do is make a deci sion to change its Constitution and become a republic on some knee-jerk reaction. "The National Party looks forward to playing the role of ensuring that there is a fair testing of the prorepublican arguments and in doing so we do a service to Australia as a whole." He supported the constitutional monarchy "not for sentimental reasons but because of the coherence, the cohesion and the continuity it provided Australia during some very difficult periods" such as the world wars and the Great Depression. The Crown had "provided a measure of continuity and loyalty for the troops who were in the field at the time, while right here in Canberra, prime ministers were shuffling like musical chairs at a time of great national difficulty at the height of World War II". While he conceded that Australia was now "a different place" it was "also independent" and had no legal binds to Great Britain. "All of that has been ended so I think that republicans still have to justify their case," he said. Mr Brogden said that if the Liberal Party wanted to be seen as a contemporary political party then the republican debate had to be embraced. Already, Mr Keating had managed to "tag" the Liberal Party as "the party of the youth wage", which had damaged its image among young voters. "I think Dr Hewson should not underestimate how Paul Keating can tie a tag to the Liberal Party on this issue," he said. Continued on Page 2 INSIDE: Why Peter Reith didn't go the post mortem; ACT Lib slams election strategy; Robb plans large conventions. - Page 2; Editorial, Sharpe's view. - Page 10. Screws on Hewson Continued from Page 1 Appearing to repudiate Dr Hewson's references to the issue as a constitutional matter, Mr Brogden said, "It's beyond being a constitutional question because it's an image and an identity question. "As far as the Liberal Party is concerned, Dr Hewson would be very wrong to underestimate its importance to young Australians." Since NSWs Liberal Premier, John Fahey, had spoken out, there had been "a lot of people coming out of closets" to support the republican push. If the party did not take up the debate, it was in danger of "being seen as a fringe group". "If we don't get involved in the debate we'll be left behind and the same people will be whingeing that the first president of Australia is somebody they don't want," he said. Mr Robb said the latest Saulwick poll showed the issue was "centre stage". He told the National Press Club the Liberal Party had to be involved in the debate, but it was up to Mr Keating to flesh out the proposal. "I think along with economic issues over the next couple of years, it will be a very important one to debate, and the poll does indicate that we, along with others, have got to be very active participants in that debate," he said "I think [Mr Keating] really does have a responsibility to spell out in some detail what he sees, what he means, by a republic, so that the form and the nature of the debate over the next 12 months to two years can be focused and not just drift along at some broad conceptual level. Mr Howard criticised the proposal by former Labor prime minister Gough Whitlam that a president could be elected jointly by the House of Representatives and the Senate. Presently, the Governor-General is appointed by the Government Mr Howard said Mr Whitlam's option was "the system that gave us Leo McLeay", the former Speaker. "Such an approach could render the presidency of a republican Australia as nothing more than another prize of office to be awarded to the dominant political party from time to time," he said. "... If the Whitlam formula is adopted we could end up with the party hack but without the constraints now applying to the office of Governor-Gen eral." • SYDNEY: The NSW Government revealed yesterday it would try to block an ALP attempt to remove all references to the crown and change the state's oath of allegiance as the first step toward a republic. The move came just two days after the government supported a parliamentary motion acknowledging the inevitability of Australia's move to a republic.

02 Apr 1993 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 2 April 1993, page 10 The Canberra Times Hewson abysmal on GST and republic THE LIBERALS knew when they re-elected John Hewson that he was carrying a lot of baggage. Its weight was very obvious on Wednesday after the parliamentary party's two-day election post mortem. His handling of the goods-and-services tax — which the parliamentary party, sensibly, insisted should immediately be dropped — was just abysmal. And on the republican issue, a matter on which the federal Coalition will have to strike an attitude, Dr Hewson looked more like a weak and confused (those wanting to be very harsh would suggest even gutless) follower than a decisive leader. The GST retreat started the day after the election, when Dr Hewson foreshadowed that it would go. This was a statement of the obvious. The electorate had spoken — the idea of its being taken again to the people would suggest the Liberals were a collection of masochists. But his comment produced a reaction within his party, especially from Ian McLachlan, who tweaked the Hewson tail for pre-empting the party room. Dr Hewson immediately backtracked, saying the GST's future was up to the party, and policy generally would be reviewed over the next 18 months to two years. That was all very well in theory, but completely unsustainable in practice. There was no way in which the party could face the future without a quick ritual burying of the GST. The fact that his colleagues had to make this clear to Dr Hewson, who on Wednesday morning was still opposing any immediate action, simply weakened his authority. He has gone from being the leader who insists on his way, and that he knows best, to one forced into responding to his followers. When he was asked whether he had been rolled he replied, "No, I just simply listened." The danger for Dr Hewson is that blunders and misjudgments of this magnitude will soon lead to mutterings about his leadership. His protection is that there is no convincing alternative. The party has shown that it is not willing to turn the clock back to John Howard, and Peter Costello does not have significant support. The Liberals face the prospect of being left with an emasculated leader, but no way of doing anything about it. Dr Hewson had, for the most part, maximum loyalty in his first three years as leader, indeed more than was good for either him or the Liberals. He was allowed to get away with too much, and led the party down a far too radical course that eventually cost it the election. Now, however, everything is different. He has failed in the primary requirement of leadership — to deliver victory. He has survived because the party thought no one else would be better. If Dr Hewson fails to perform well in Parliament — and it is hard to think that he can do better than poorly — there will be plenty on his own benches willing to put in the knife. THE LIBERALS like to dismiss the republic as a second-level issue. But it is rapidly moving to the centre of political debate. NSW Premier John Fahey recognised this in his proposal to have a constitutional convention to discuss the way forward towards a republic. But Dr Hewson, after taking a fall on the GST, has been left flat-footed on the republic. This is mainly because he leads conservative forces he knows are divided on the question. Many Liberal and National supporters are passionate monarchists. But others, and the community at large, are increasingly in favour of change. The latest Saulwick Age poll showed the growth of support for a republic over the past year. The poll, done this week in NSW and Victoria, found that fewer than three in every 10 people interviewed wanted to keep the Queen as head of state, while nearly seven out of 10 supported a change. This compared with a year before when almost 60 per cent favoured a republic. Significantly, the poll showed that a majority of coalition voters (56 per cent to 41 per cent) favoured a republic. Dr Hewson is trying to portray the issue as one for the Government alone to define. He lambasts the Prime Minister for not specifying the detail of his proposal. Eventually the Liberals will have to decide where they stand on the central question — republic or not? Only then can they reasonably demand detail. Dr Hewson must know that the tide of opinion will make it difficult for the Coalition to stick to an old pro-monarchist position. Managing the transition to the new position, which the Coalition will need eventually to embrace if it is not going to be left behind community sentiment, is going to be an extremely difficult task. AS IF it were not enough to have to cope with tossing out the heart of Fightback and grappling with the republican issue, Dr Hewson has on his hands the demand by the Liberal organisation for a greater say in the policy debate. The latest manifestation of this push was the proposal by Liberal director Andrew Robb yesterday for a national convention at least once in each parliamentary term, attended by federal members and senators and 200-300 rank-and-file Liberals. Mr Robb stresses that the parliamentary, party would still ultimately determine policy, but says such a convention would give "party members some ownership of the ultimate direction and policy of the parliamentary party". The push for more rank-and-file say is a typical reaction by the party to a dreadful and unexpected defeat It is hard to argue against. However the situation is more complicated when you get down to the nitty gritty. Rank-and-file members of parties are often more extreme than the parliamentary wings. On the Labor side for example, the Left has stronger sway in the branches than in Parliament. In the last decade the parliamentary Labor party has been about lessening the organisation's power. Even though the Liberals are not talking about giving the extra-parliamentary party real teeth, they are creating expectations that it would have them. Otherwise, surely the convention that Mr Robb is suggesting would differ only marginally from the federal council meetings that already occur. If Dr Hewson ever did become Prime Minister he could rue the day if the organisation got more power. It would not be able to direct him but it could embarrass a Liberal Government by passing critical motions. Whether or not they were deserved, they certainly would be less than welcome. Yet because his authority is shot to pieces, Dr Hewson cannot easily raise cautions against the organisation's push for greater clout. He can only hope it does not go too far.

12 Apr 1993 - SA independents benefit from swing against Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 12 April 1993, page 3 SA independents benefit from swing against Labor POLL WATCH Support for South Australia's Labor Government has fallen but the state Coalition has not benefited from the slide, a Morgan poll indicated yesterday. Independents and minor parties gained from the fall in support for Labor, according to the poll to be published in Time Australia maga zine this week. Even so, the Coalition would have won an election called last month, the poll found. Of the 1141 South Australian voters asked during February and March who they would vote for in a state election, 35.5 per cent supported Labor, down 0.5 of a point from a poll taken two months earlier. Support for the Coalition was steady at 49 per cent, as was support for the Democrats at 9 per cent Independents and other parties attracted 6.5 per cent support, a rise of 0.5 of a point. On a two-party preferred basis, the Coalition leads Labor 56 per cent to 44 per cent, a position unchanged from the earlier poll. Despite falling support for Labor, 42 per cent of voters thought the Premier, Lynn Arnold, would make the better leader, down one point. Support for the Coalition leader, Dean Brown, rose one point to 36 per cent. Approval of Mr Arnold's perform ance as Premier fell two points to 44 per cent, as did approval of Mr Brown's performance, also down two points to 39 per cent. A separate Morgan poll found that a family of two adults and two children needed a weekly income of at least $451 to keep healthy and live decently. However, people living in families of two adults and two children believed they needed $470 a week to meet these requirements. The poll of 2503 people was taken on February 13-14 and February 20-21. The perceived cost of living for the two adults-two children fami ly represented a rise of $4, or 1 per cent, since February last year. There was a marked difference between cost of living in cities ($465) and country areas ($427), and across states. In NSW, the perceived cost of living was $477, South Australia $444, Western Australia $439, Tasmania $438, Victoria $436 and Queensland $426. The poll also found Australians were spending slightly more on food. A single person spent $70 on food (up $3 on February, 1992), two people $103 (unchanged), three people $121 (down $3) and four or more people $155 (up $5). The average weekly food bill was $122, up $2, while a family of two adults and two children spent $143 a week, up $3. According to the poll, food represented 30 percent of living costs, the same proportion as a year earlier, but 4 per cent lower than in 1974. And another Morgan poll to be published in Time Australia this week has found that Western Australia's Opposition leader, Carmen Lawrence, whose party was voted out of office in February, remains that states preferred premier. The poll of 935 electors interviewed after the February 6 state ballot and up to the end of March, also found support for the Premier, Richard Court, and his Coalition Government had fallen. Dr Lawrence was the preferred premier before the state election and, according to the poll, remained so even though support for her slipped three percentage points after the election to 55 percent. Mr Court attracted 34 per cent support as preferred premier, also down three points. Support for Dr Lawrence's performance as Opposition leader was strong, at 64 per cent. Just 35 per cent of voters approved of the way Mr Court was performing as Premier. Support for the WA Government fell four points from the election to 45.5 per cent but the Coalition remains strongly ahead of Labor, support for whom rose to 39.5 per cent. Independents and other parties also attracted stronger support, up 1.5 points to 15 per cent. On a two-party preferred basis, the Coalition attracted 53 per cent, and Labor 47 percent. — AAP I

17 Apr 1993 - Labor keeps top spot in the polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 17 April 1993, page 2 Labor keeps top spot in the polls POLL WATCH The Keating Government remains nine percentage points ahead of the Opposition despite a decline in support for the ALP over the past two weeks, according to the latest AGB McNair poll published in The Bulletin. 24 Apr 1993 - Gap wider between federal parties Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 April 1993, page 2 Gap wider between federal parties The gap in support for federal Labor and the Coalition is the widest sincc the election, according to the latest Newspoll, published in The Australian. Support for the ALP rose by one point to 49 per cent and support for the Liberal-National Coalition dropped by two points to 40 per cent. The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, was still ahead as preferred prime minister, despite a one point drop to 47 per cent. Those voters preferring John Hewson dropped twojoints to 30 per cent. Forty-three per cent of voters interviewed were satisfied with the way Mr Keating was doing his job; 45 per cent were not; 12 per cent were uncommitted. The percentage satisfied with Dr Hewson's performance rose one point to 30 per cent; those dissatisfied dropped three points to 57 per cent; 13 per cent were uncommitted. Newspoll used data from telephone interviews of 1121 voters across Australia. Support for the NSW Opposition rose nine points in a month to 50 per cent, The Bulletin's AGB McNair poll reports.

26 Apr 1993 - Hopes higher but sackings likely: survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 26 April 1993, page 3 Hopes higher but sackings likely: survey By ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent A survey of the business community has found some confidence that trading conditions will improve but points to more lay-offs by large companies. It says there are signs of improvement in the economy in the March quarter, although firms will continue to face tough conditions. The quarterly survey by the National Australia Bank says increased confidence is most marked in manu facturing, retail, finance and business services, while the weakest expectations are among companies involved in mining and construction. The poll of about 750 medium to large companies found business confidence for the March quarter and for the next 12 months has strengthened. On another positive note, the revisions downwards in trading and profit expectations contained in the previous two surveys have been reversed in the latest publication. The bank's chief economist, AIai\ Oster, said that while the outlook for sales and profitability had strengthened, the survey continued to point to a relatively weak employment out look. • While larger firms were more optimistic about the future than smaller ones, the bigger companies appeared to be looking to further lay-offs in the next financial year. Asked about employment, 24 per cent of firms surveyed expected to sack workers in the June quarter Consumers were slightly less confident this month but remained generally optimistic about the future, the latest Morgan poll has found. The Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence Rating fell 2.4 points in early April to 102.3, still above the key 100-mark which means people were more optimistic than pessimistic. Most doubts surfaced over the outlook for personal finances in the survey which was taken on April 3 and April 4 in 1231 face-to-face in terviews around Australia. The poll was taken just after the March 30 release of the February current-account deficit which fell to an unadjusted $660 million from $717 million in January. There was an 8 per cent net drop in personal finance optimism as 28 per cent said they expected better times, down from 31 per cent in March, and 20 per cent of people expected worse times', a rise of 5 per cent for the pessimists. About 23 per cent, or 1 per cent more, believed they were better off than a year ago while 43 per cent said they were worse off — a rise of 2 per cent. On economic prospects, 36 per cent, or 2 per cent more, expected things to be worse in another 12 months. In the next five years, 24 per cent, 3 per cent more, said they expected bad economic times. — aap while 13 per cent expected to increase their workforce. The sackings are expected to significantly offset a moderate growth in jobs among smaller and mediumsized firms, and damp the Government's hopes of reducing employ ment. The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, said last week some companies had gone too far with retrenchments. He conceded unemployment would not fall quickly and that the number of long-term unemployed would grow. Two surveys last week — by Dunn and Bradstreet of manufacturing, retail and wholesale industries, and by the Australian Chamber of Manufactures of its members — showed rising business confidence and a moderate improvement in investment intentions. However, the Dunn and Bradstreet survey indicated a fall in employment expectations for the June quarter, with the outlook for more jobs in manufacturing, wholesaling and retailing still very poor. Major business organisations said on Friday that business was still not ready for a large-scale increase in investment. The shadow treasurer, Alexander Downer, said the Australian community was resigning itself to high unemployment, which he described as a socially irresponsible trend. No recovery in property market yet: report MELBOURNE: Australia was out of recession and had recorded its fifth consecutive quarter of positive economic growth but there was so far no sign of a corresponding recovery in the property market, a report issued yesterday said. The report, by real estate firm Baillieu Kjiight Frank, said Asian investment fell away slightly during the last six months which reflected, amongst other factors, a renewed fo cus on the UK and the USA for investment as an alternative to Australia. It said average institutional property portfolio weighting (the percentage of property investment) had fallen to 9.9 per cent of total assets because of downward revaluations and continued selling by top-heavy institutions. "Business debt has been heavily hit by the excessive debt overhang of the late '80s, and companies are concentrating on fixing balance sheets to improve profits, rather than expanding their operations," said BKFs chairman of South East Asian Operations, Roy Woodhouse. But the report took good tidings from recent Australian Bureau of Statistics figures which predict Australia's gross domestic product growth at 2.6 per cent for 1992-93 and 4 per cent for 1993-94.

05 May 1993 - FEDERAL POLITICS Nats play down republic split Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 5 May 1993, page 10 FEDERAL POLITICS By ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent The federal Opposition played down splits among its MPs on the republican issue yesterday as the Government formalised its push to end links with Britain by the turn of the century. The Leader of the National Party, Tim Fischer, said his parly did not want to be part of the republic strategy committee established by the Opposition on Monday. He said there were precedent's for the parties to hold different posi tions on issues. However, a National Party backbencher, Michael Cobb, said he believed his party should be represented on the Opposition committee, which includes staunch monarchist John Howard. "On reflection, 1 think probably it would have been good to have a National Party person on that committee," he said. After his comments, Mr Cobb was told at a joint parties meeting that the Nationals wanted to play no part in the committee which has six Liberal frontbenchers. A survey yesterday found support for Australia becoming a republic has risen from 41 per cent to 45 per cent in the past year. However, the AGB McNair poll said more than 60 per cent of people surveyed believed the move towards a republic would causc social divisions. The Nationals' federal management committee reaffirmed last week the party's strong support for the constitutional monarchy. The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, has opened the way to change the Liberal Party's promonarchy policy by calling for wide debate among the grass-roots membership in the lead-up to the party's federal council meeting in August which will debate the republican issue. It also bccame clearer on Monday that Dr Hewson favours the "minimalist" option for a move to a republic and is prepared to make the issue a major test of his leadership. Senior frontbenchers said Mr Howard was rebuked in Monday's Opposition meeting for his strong pro-monarchist comments. While several frontbenchers told Mr Howard he had gone too far, two declared they now supported the republican push. Mr Hewson said he initiated the committee and the Nationals had decided to disagree with the Liberal Party on the republican issue. "If they want to stand where they are and not move they can take thai position in the debate, as a lot of individuals will," Dr Hewson said. "I made it a Liberal Party committee, they have their own processes. The committee was my idea and I selected the people that arc on it bccausc of the mix of their interests in the issue." The Premier of Victoria, JefT Kennett, confirmed yesterday he would nominate controversial historian, Geoffrey Blainey, for the Government's republican commit tee. Mr Keating wrote to state and territory leaders last week asking them to nominate two members to the committee — one from the most populous states and one from the smaller states. The Premier of Western Australian, Richard Court, said he would establish a 10-member committee to examine the republican push.

26 May 1993 - Coalition refuses to overturn tax cuts Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 26 May 1993, page 5 Coalition refuses to overturn tax cuts By SIMON GROSE and ROSS PEAKE The Coalition rejected a bid by the Australian Democrats yesterday to overturn the Government's promised $8 billion tax cuts. The Leader of the Democrats, Cheryl Kernot, foreshadowed a private Member's Bill in the Senate to scrdp the tax cuts legislated' by the Government late last year to take effect in July next year. : But the Opposition knocked back the proposal. The shadow treasurer, Alexander Downer, claimed that abandoning the tax cuts would be a "fundamental breach of trust" by the Govern ment. ' "We're not going to support legislation which will force the Labor Party to break faith with the electorate," Mr Downer said. '' Senator Kernot claimed that the tax cuts were "against the national interest as they are unaffordable and unfair". "They are deliberately designed to help the rich get richer and the poor get poorer so they should be repealed." • But Mr Downer counter ,claimed, "We're going to take ■over the task that was once the Democrats' traditional task and .keep the bastards honest." , The clash has made the Opposition appear to favour the Government's controversial tax cuts. The promised cuts, which helped the Government win an "unwinnable" election, were strongly criticised by the Coalition during the campaign and since. A spokesman for the Treasurer, John Dawkins, described the puts as "sacrosanct". f The tax cuts reduce the 38c marginal rate paid by most full-time employees to 30c in two stages on July 1, 1994, and January 1, 1996. For income between $40,000 and $50,000 the rate falls to 40c from 46c. Senator Kernot said she ex pected her Bill to be debated to morrow, the .last day of sittings before the winter recess. In a separate development, the general thrust of the Government's Budget strategy won endorsement yesterday from US ratings agency Moody's Invest ors Service. Ian Davis reports that the agency, which clashed with the Government after its 1986 downgrading of Australia's sovereign debt risk, yesterday endorsed the strategy outlined by Mr Dawkins and the Government Leader in the Senate, Gareth Evans, of maintaining the current Budget deficit of about $16 billion next financial year and reducing it to 1 per cent of gross domestic product by 1996-97. Moody's positive comments had the incidental effect of strengthening the Australian dollar after it fell half a cent in overnight trade on false rumours that the Reserve Bank Governor, Bernie Fraser, had said he was happy to see the dollar drift lower. The dollar finished at US69.76c yesterday after falling to US68.85c overnight from Monday's US69.35c close. Labor was wrestling with another pressing problem yesterday: the long-term jobless. A Caucus taskforce established to seek solutions to the unemployment crisis met for the first time yesterday but will have until the end of the week to learn its full role. The Minister for Employment, Kim Beazley,' told the committee there would be a con certed Government effort to-. wards reducing long-term unemployment. Committee sources said Mr Beazley and his department officials gave an overview of the state of job growth. Program review The Government will also establish an interdepartmental committee to review its programs for jobless people. Mr Beazley told the backbenchers the details of the committee's roles and how the two groups were expected to interreact would be given by Mr Keating on Friday. Mr Keating has nominated an attack on long-term unemployment as one of his principal aims. An AGB McNair poll to be published in the Bulletin today shows support for the Federal Opposition rose two points in mid-May. The Coalition got the support of 41 per cent of respondents with the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, also improving his personal approval 1 rating. However Labor, with 48 per cent of the vote (up one point), still holds a comfortable sevenpercentage-point lead over the combined Liberal-National parties. Mr Keating's standing dropped one percentage point to 36 per cent while Dr Hewson rose one to 31 percent. Thirty-six per cent of voters (down one) approved of Mr Keating's performance while his disapproval rating rose one to 41 per cent. In comparison, Dr Hewson's approval rating rose one to 25 per cent and his disapproval rating dropped one to 47 per cent.

02 May 1984 - LETTERS to the Editor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 2 May 1984, page 2 LETTERS to the Editor The case against uranium mining Sir, — I was shockcd lo read in The Canberra Times of April 18 that our Minister for Resources and Energy, Senator Walsh, thinks "it would be silly to directly relate uranium and nuclear-weapon-proliferation issues". It is common knowledge that uranium mining is the first step in the nuclear fuel cycle, the first step in producing the weapons which threaten our daily existence with extinction, surely a government I Minister has more intelligence than to make such an uninformed comment. He also states that the anti- * nuclear rallies of April 15 should not be interpreted as opposition to uranium mining and export. A look at the major rallies around the country will show that advertising for the rallies stated "No uranium mining". Canberra was the excep tion. I question the Morgan Gallup Poll with its figures of 66 per cent of Australians in favour of the export of uranium. It has often been said "I have never been asked". Well, I've never even met anyone who has been asked. It saddens me to see a politician blustering his way through the issue of our survival as a race when he apparently lacks complete understanding of even the basics. It also terrifies me. D. LUCAS, O'Connor.

10 May 1984 - Opinion polls on uranium Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 10 May 1984, page 2 Opinion polls on uranium Sir, — D. Lucas (Letters, May 2) questions the Morgan Gallup Poll's figures of 66 per cent of Australians in favour of the export of uranium. A closc look at the poll raises more doubts. The first question asked in the poll, conducted from July 9-16, 1983. was: "Do you think Australia should — or should not — develop and export uranium for peaceful purposes?" This resulted in the "national" yes figure of 66 per cent. Interestingly, the second question — "Is there anything about mining and exporting uranium that worries you7". resulted in a "yes" answer by 56 per cent of those polled. Could it be that 56 per cent of those who took part in the poll arc worried that uranium mines leak radioactive particlcs into the environment; that working in a uranium mine is a danger to workers' health; that the nuclear industry is not cost effective; that the problem of radioactive waste has not been solved; that international safeguards arc ineffective; and that we cannot be sure that Australian uranium is used solely "for peaceful purposes'"? If the results of such polls arc going to be used in public debate, then we need to ask many more, and Quite different. Questions HEATHER JEFFCOAT North Fitzroy, Victoria.

05 Jun 1984 - The Premier's sermon fails to dispel all the gloom Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 5 June 1984, page 2 The Premier's sermon fails to dispel all the gloom SoUTH Australians are probably the most preached-at people in the country, though not neces sanly trom pulpits. When things are a little dull as they are at the moment, people showing weariness at the mention of Roxby Downs, the lingering Maralinga Affair and the recurring crises in the automobile industry, South Australians appear to welcome someone who is prepared to tell them how awful they are. In the past they turned to prophets from abroad, particularly imported Adelaide Festival directors, such as Anthony Steel and Christopher Hunt, to be told what an insular, provincial, unstylish lot they were. It seemed to cheer them up no end, and it was only a matter of time before politicians copied the technique and sought the bracing electoral response of a good scolding. So it should have been a matter for no surprise last month when the Premier, Mr Bannon — no less weary than the electors of the uranium debate and the repeated unsatisfactory assurances from Britain and the United States about the nature and effect of their past and present bases on South Australian soil — decided to put in the boot about the unsatisfactory character of South Australians. He delivered himself of a sermon which a political writer said was not quite the Sermon on the Mount but came a close second. The gist of it was that cynicism had become an art form in this State. The classic South Australian syndrome, he said, "is to put ourselves down". No mean putterdown himself, he accuscd South Australian business operators of a "small-town mentality" which was holding back industrial enterprise and recovery from the recession. This was most noticeable in businesses operating within the State. Those in closer contact with the eastern States and involved in national marketing had a broader attitude. Mr Bannon was reacting to publicity given to industry surveys and submissions which presented a gloomy picture of both the South Australian and the national economies as opposed to rosier views presented with figures from the Metal Trades Industry Association and the Commonwealth Bank report, which he thought had not received enough attention. Mr Bannon further countered local gloom and small-town obsessions with statistics showing a 69 per cent rise in South Australian housing approvals for the March quarter, a 2 per cent rise in manufacturing employment, and reports of "very busy" or "busy production levels" from 69.9 per cent of South Australian firms surveyed in March. The liveliest cat out of his bag of good news was a 4.1 per cent increase in employment in South Australia, between April, 1983, and April, 1984, compared with a 3.6 per cent increase for Australia as a whole. He strongly urged reporters at his press conference to help get South Australians to think positively and play their part in opposing the negative attitudes which were, he said, traditionally part of the State's business and management mentality. It did not require an astute logician to point up some confusions in Mr Bannon's attitude; on the one hand telling us to get rid of our inferiority feelings about being Mr Bannon, right, and Senator Walsh in Canberra last month, when they held a press conference on British nuclear testing in Australia in the 1950s. South Australians because we were doing very nicely thank you; and on the other hand urging us to emulate some of the methods and confidence of the pushy easterners. Predictably, the confusions were echoed in the media within the next few days. Columnists confessed their feelings of inferiority in the presence of NSW and Victorian cousins. Radio gurus and talk-back participants shared ex periences of feeling rotten simply because we live in what other Australians think of as a hick State, cxccpt for a halcyon period in the 1970s when the then Premier, Mr Don Dunstan, briefly raised our consciousness. An orgy of breast-beating was apparently enjoyed by all. But those who tried to respond to the Premier's call to emphasise the good news quickly ran into difficulties. Adelaide's morning daily, The Advertiser, made a brave effort a few days later by leading its front page with 'National surge in car sales is good news for SA\ The next day, however, the report was knocked cold by the killjoy, hard and brutally unwelcome news that Adelaide's Mitsubishi plant intended to cut its staff by 145. And it was back to gloom and doom again with reports of demonstrations by anti-nuclcar-energy campaigners protesting against Olympic Dam ore being loaded at Outer Harbor in a ship for Finland. One of the 15 containers sprang a leak for all to see, highlighting fears of dangerous uranium contamination which the State Health Commission barely allayed by pronouncing the health risk "negligible". Mr Bannon had to repeat his Government's dissatisfaction with the secret upgrading of a US satellite base on South Australian soil. And he and the Federal Minister for Resources and Energy, Senator Walsh, trod for the first time in the red dust of Maralinga, the site of Britain's atomic blasts of the 1950s, which we have been told may stay contaminated for thousands of years. Despite this quick reversion of public interest to unhappy news of the day, Mr Bannon was able to fulfil his gospel mission by emphasising some personal glad tidings. He learnt that his personal approval rating according to the latest Morgan Gallup polls had risen to 58 per ccnt, indicating an almost total recovery from a slide associated with the introduction of financial-institutions duly and the MPs pay rows. This recovery of all but 2 per cent of his 60 per cent rating in the September-October, 1983, poll must have been all the more welcome to Mr Bannon and his Government because it seemed to show they had weathered well the Opposition's concentrated attack, during the polling period, on two ministers, especially the Minister of Health, Dr Cornwall. So the sermon had some effect after all. The electorate seems to have thoroughly enjoyed its kick in the tail in its usual masochistic way and the Premier has had every cxcuse to proclaim his personal popularity and his Government's approval rating under the banner of good news that it would be small-minded to be modest about.

17 May 1985 - Tories run third in Gallup poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 17 May 1985, page 5 Tories run third in Gallup poll LONDON, Thursday (Reuter). — Britain's ruling Conservative Party would finish third behind the Labour Party and the centrist Alliance if a general election were held now, an opinion poll' published today shows. The survey by the Gallup organisation, carried out for The Telegraph last week, showed support for the parties as Labour 34 per cent, Alliance 33.5 and Conservatives 30.5. This compares with a Gallup poll a month ago giving Labour 37.5 per cent, the Conservatives 34 and the Alliance 26.5. No reasons were given for the changes. • The Alliance groups the Liberal and the Social Democratic Parties and has become a new force in British politics in the 1980s. 26 May 1985 - Overspending in Skangaroola causes Labor's popularity to take a dive Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 26 May 1985, page 18 Overspending in Skangaroola | \ causes Labor's popularity THE problem for the Liberal Opposition in South Australia is not the good news (which, ofcoursc, means bad news about the Labor Government) but how it can keep it in the forefront of the public's attention until late November or December, the likely election dates. The Auditor-General's report, tabled in Parliament this month, gave details of spending over-runs on Government construction projects that even the dimmest Opposition can exploit effectively for electoral gain, especially in a relatively poor State such as South Australia. The Auditor-General, Mr Tom Sheridan, detailed the cost escalation on three sites: the North Adelaide aquatic ccntre (from $4.8 million to an estimated $7.8), the Lyell McEwin community health centre ($9.4 million to $ 13.7 million) and the relocation of a Port Augusta sports ccntre (at a cost of S750.000 for facilities said to be worth only $100,000). The swim centre, already a running sore because of delays, looms largest in the hubbub that has followed the report, for not only are there huge question marks about the final cost, but it is becoming the sort of joke that bedevils major projects. The initial failure to build the diving tower to the correct height for international competition saw to that. Then, after the Auditor-General's report, a special report was tabled showing that the Government would face a huge interest bill for serving the debt for its construction — at least $500,000 a year for the next 30 years. Mr Sheridan strongly criticised the Government in the report, along with the Parliamentary Public Works Standing Committee. The public has had it rammed home to them that the Government is guilty of lack of control, over the Public Buildings Department, in spending, delays, cost over-runs and staffing. Poor procedures and mismanagement were highlighted, and if heads rolled in the sense of staff being moved sideways and new blood being introduced to management, including some from outside the Public Service, concentration centres on the projects so much in the public eye, and on a history of problems within the department which the public was led to believe had been effectively tackled. The Tonkin Liberal Government cut the weekly-paid construction and maintenance workforce in order to put as much work as possible out to competitive tender. The Bannon Labor Government trimmed the weekly-paid workforce, but changed back to using it more. Neither move seems to have resulted in improved management or cost control. Now the Auditor-General has set out some measures for improvements which include, when necessary, calling for advice outside the Public Service. It was, one supposes, a knee-jerk response for Premier Bannon to say, while busy with other matters in Canberra, that his Government had a "mighty good record" on containing public spending. But it was not his best response. By the time he had announced "a war on waste", the Opposition was well advanced in its plans to thump home the message that it intends to be more effective in this area. "Less waste" now joins a trilogy of slogans, including the grammatically jarring "Less taxes", for the Liberals' election campaign. "Less crime" is the other, not markedly original, reference to law-and-order preoccupations of the Liberal Party. By wasting no time in getting their pre election machine running, the Liberals risk running out of steam if the Government paysconspicuous attention to the recommendations of the Auditor-General and the completion of projects begins to dim public recollecton of the mini-scandals along the way. The Liberals' second major assault began on television, with the first 30-second commercial already attracting attention by its strong visual impact — a sprinter on the starting blocks who fails to get away. The advertisement says that when Labor was running for office in South Australia it talked a lot about new direction, but now, coming up to three years down the track (graphically visualised by overgrowth and weeds), the new direction was a false start. Then individual Liberal candidates got a boost in a series of handsome and expensive leaflets, carefully colour-coded for maximum identification with a unified party campaign. All the moves suggest the confidence of a party which believes itself running ahead of Labor at the polls. A recent Morgan Gallup poll showed that, if an election had been held last month, preferences would have been necessary to decide the Government. Mr Bannon, having to wear the effects of the Federal mini-Budget in South Australia and no great joy expected from Premiers' Conferences and the August Budget, may be forgiven for making a slow election start and for wishing he could put as much space as possible between present realities and the date when he must go to the people. Almost every day the media carry stories about the local effect, including the possible closure of pre-schools of the mini-Budget on low-income earners, and anxiety continues high in the community about further effects and threatened moves such as the introduction of tertiary-education fees. When Mr Bannon and his election campaigners get their running shoes on, they will have tp force their way through a crowded field of thoroughly determined Liberal Party runners. The Government's tacticians must be hoping very much that the front runners will tire and the public's evident early interest in them be dissipated. * * * . THERE WAS a sense of relief this month when Mr Edward Splatt, jailed for 6V2 years as part of a life sentence for a murder in 1977 until a Royal Commission recommended his release, was awarded $300,000 and legal costs. It was a signal of the end of a long, drawnout affair that had great moments of drama highlighted by crusading journalist Stewart Cockburn and clashes between Attorneys General past and present over what should be done in a situation with few precedents. MrSplatt has his freedom and, although a question mark still remains over how compensation for 6'/2 years in prison can be assessed, the decision has neither caused outrage from those who believed Mr Splatt had had justice already at considerable expense to the public purse through legal costs, nor protests of meanness. Mr Splatt has warned, however, that he intends to retire to write a book rather than continue to make appearances on behalf of those, including Mrs Lindy Chamberlain and Mrs Emily Perry, who claim they have had less than justice. * * ♦ ONE COULD think it was still the silly season. The director of the Art Gallery of South Australia, Mr Daniel Thomas, got enormous media coverage for his suggestion that the State be renamed. "South Austrlia" was dull, he said, and he did not think highly of the rest of Australia's State nomenclature. He wants us to become Skangaroovia or Skangaroola. There are no takers. The aquatic centre being bgilt at North Adelaide: an interest bill on it of $500,000 a year for 30 years, according to the State Auditor-General.

30 Jul 1981 - ALP loses support Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 30 July 1981, page 8 ALP loses support SYDNEY: Support for the NSW Labor Government has fallen below 50 per cent, according to a poll published yesterday. . The Morgan Gallup poll, in the latest edition of The Bulletin. registered a 6 per cent drop in support for the Government. 13 Aug 1981 - Wran Government 'backed by 57pc' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 13 August 1981, page 6 Wran Government 'backed by 57pc' SYDNEY: The NSW Government has recovered the support it lost over the recent power blackouts, a new opinion survey shows. The latest figures, compiled by Morgan Gallup Polls and published in The Bulletin magazine, show the Government's level of support at 57 per cent. This compares with the all-time low of 48 per cent last month and 57.8 per cent at the 1978 election. The previous Morgan poll was taken in the immediate aftermath of the State's power crisis and accorded with other surveys at the time. The Premier, Mr Wran, said then that he considered the sudden dip in his Government's popularity was only temporary. The Liberals dropped by two per centage points to 32 per cent, the Country Party by a similar amount to 5 per cent and the Democrats by three to 7 per cent.

21 Jan 1947 - More Wars? News (Adelaide, SA : 1923 - 1954), Tuesday 21 January 1947, page 2 More Wars? IS it any wonder that quite a fair proportion of people, as shown by Gallup polls taken in different parts of the world, fear more world wars? The 1914-18 war was fought to preserve democracy, and the Versailles Treaty was signed in good faith to prevent more wars. Yet the 1939-45 world war developed. And wasn't that fought in good faith by peoples answering their countries' call, and be'ieving any sacrifice worthwhile for preserving their liberty, and achieving a lasting peace and a world worth living in? Their blood has been shed; there has been sweat, and labor. And now-liberty is only for a privileged few, and the new order seems worse than the old. Differences of opinion between foreign nations are bad enough. But when problems develop inside each country, including Australia --then I can't help concluding that .he mass of the people are them&eves responsible for what is happenmg. They elect selfish and incapable leaders who don't know what the country really needs-justice, strict morals, and freedom to live and let live. * F. W. C. RIECK, Bridgewater. ~~~1\~1fl I ~j-~-~. 02 Mar 1993 - Full employment and no spending commitments in Liberal launch Hewson takes up GST fight Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 2 March 1993, page 1 --- 1-^-.......... . .--- -.---_- - ..... ?... \ Full employment and no spending commitments in Liberal launch Hewson takes up GST fight By ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, has gone on the front foot to directly tackle Labor's attack on the goodsand-services tax, praising its benefits as a tax on spending. He committed a Coalition government to full employment but made no new spending promises, in his speech yesterday to officially launch his election campaign. Dr Hewson also announced the six people who would be honorary policy advisers. The positions, foreshadowed in Fightback, follow United States practice and is designed to reinforce the Opposition's portrayal of Paul Keating as out of touch. The pressure on both sides will intensify with the publication today of two more public opinion polls pointing to a very tight election. The Australian's Newspoll, taken last weekend, shows the gap between the parties narrowing to one point on a two-party preferred basis: Labor 49.5 percent, Coalition 50.5 percent. The previous week's survey gave the Opposition a seven-point lead. Dr Hewson leads Mr Keating as preferred prime minister, 38-37. The Bulletin's AGB-McNair poll shows Labor making up five points to 45 per cent, with the Coalition static at 47 per cent. These latest polls confirm the trend revealed of two earlier polls this week that Labor is clawing back support, gaining momentum from its scare campaign against the GST. In a break with tradition, the Opposition began yesterday's launch with emotive appearances by five "ordinary Australians", who blamed the Prime Minister for their troubles. As well, Carolyn Hewson introduced her husband, saying she knew him best and describing him as courageous, honest and dedicated. Dr Hewson presented a hard-line defence of the proposed 15 per cent GST which he said was fundamental to the integrity of his tax reforms. The Opposition would not "shy away" from the tax in the face of the ALP's scare campaign. Dr Hewson had foreshadowed he would not make new spending promises in his speech, to contrast with Mr Keating's launch last week. Dr Hewson's spirited off-the-cuff speech repeated promises to reduce unemployment and reinforced the need for dramatic reform. "I personally refuse to accept that unemployment must stay high, I personally refuse to accept anything less than full employment," he said. "And I personally refuse to accept what must be one of the most intolerable features of Australian society today, and that is that as a generation of Australians we are about to leave a lower standard of living to our children than we enjoyed ourselves, with fewer opportunities." He stepped up his campaign to sell the GST by pointing out how many items were already subject to sales tax, which he would abolish. "Somehow we're going to make this point cut through in this election campaign and that is that people already pay a lot of tax on things they don't know they pay," he said. To directly address the ALP's criticism that the GST would be a tax on spending, he said consumers would gain an average 25 per cent cut in their income tax. "You keep the money and you decide when you pay tax and how much you pay tax by what you buy - not pay as your earn, pay as you spend," he said. "Do you want a good argument for GST - GST equals jobs because it makes our businesses internationally competitive." To emphasise his message that Mr Keating was out of touch, Dr Hewson quoted from the Prime Minister's speech on Sunday launching the ALP's culture policy. Mr Keating said, "Whatever we do, we'll never get pride from a truckload of coal, we might get dollars, but we will never get pride." Dr Hewson brought a roar from his audience when he said the comment was an absolute insult to coal miners. "Isn't that an absolutely amazing thing for a Labor leader to say," he said. "I challenge him to go up to the coal fields, Queensland, NSW or Victoria and tell them, those people have real pride in their work and so should we." He said he would like to direct more money to the arts or the environment, but the country had to produce to pay for it, and claimed this was not understood by the Labor Party. "We believe in people and they believe in government," he said. He also said that he "started to choke" every time he heard the phrase "social justice". "I just can't find anything fair or just in a million unemployed," he said. Continued on Page 2 Picture: RICHARD BRIGGS The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, at yesterday's launch. Hewson takes up GST fight Continued from Page 1 Dr Hewson said that after 10 years in government, Mr Keating had "lost the plot". "He's got no plan. He's got no answers. All he's got left is a negative campaign, a scare campaign," he said. Dr Hewson ended his speech by telling the five people who told the audience of their plights - Jennifer, John, Sam, Beverley and Michelle - they were the "forgotten people". "I look you in the eye and I say, we can solve your problems, we will do it together," he said. Following the example set in the 1990 election, the Opposition did not use its television time last night to replay Dr Hewson's speech. Instead it ran a documentary featuring an explanation of the GST, to combat the ALP's scare campaign. The federal director of the Liberal Party, Andrew Robb, defended the presentation against accusations of inaccu racy. He said the ALP's scare campaign on the GST had helped to focus attention on yesterday's launch. "We are finding that people are now looking-very earnestly for hard information and in the last week or two, we've just been deluged in our campaign offices around the country with requests for information," he said. "People are starting to focus on the flip-side of the GST... Labor may very well have overplayed its hand on the strident nature of the scare campaign." Mr Robb acknowledged the documentary repeated the pledge to abolish seven taxes, although one - the coal export levy - has been removed. "It was more not to confiise people with constant changes to the original document in terms of the message getting through and our commitment to retaining the abolition of that remains solid, so we didn't see, for those sorts of reasons, that it was a problem," he said. He denied the documentary contained "half truths" over the abolition of bulk-billing for most people. As the voice-over said, "Bulk billing will stay for those who need it most". This qualification was not reflected on the screen, where the wording was: "Bulk billing stays". Hewson's credibility fading as he will not tell how and why. PM Continued from Page 1 Most significantly, Mr Keating said, Dr Hewson had not explained why his package of a 15 per cent consumption tax plus a 42 per cent company-tax rate and a "disruptive industrial-relations model" would create more jobs than under Labor. Job crcation under Labor would come by not having a consumption tax, and by having a 32 per cent company-tax rate, an investment allowance of up to 20 per cent, and "cooperative" labour relations. "He also failed to explain how he will fund his promises, given the $7 to $8 billion hole dug by his absurdly inflated Telecom [sale-price] fig ure. "He also failed to say why he wants to remove bulk-billing for 13 million Australians and make people pay $32 up front for each visit to the doctor." The Treasurer, John Dawkins, said the Liberal Party policy launch was like a dose of political DDT which threatened wage cuts, poorer health and higher taxes. The Leader of the National Party, Tim Fischer, said the campaign launch had injected much-needed realism into the economic debate. Mr Fischcr said the five people who appeared to tell their stories of the recession had given "a very big and realistic approach to the closing stages of the election campaign". The ALP's national president, Barry Jones, criticised Dr Hewson for choosing the Wesley Mission to launch the Coalition campaign. Mr Jones said the people the mission aimed to support would be the m very people hardest hit by Liberal economic policies. The Australian Council of Social Service said the Opposition's launch was an unacceptable exercise in exploitation. The council president, Merle Mitchell, said her organisation had refused media requests for access to interview "victims" of unemploy ment.

06 Mar 1993 - POLLS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 6 March 1993, page 5 POLLS There is now virtual agreement between Australia's major polling organisations that the 1993 election is a neck and neck race. The Saulwick poll, published in the Age and the Sydney Morning Herald, has examined the key marginals in NSW, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia and Tasmania and concluded that the March 13 result is almost too close to call, although the odds probably favour the Coalition. In the NSW marginal seat of Lowe the Saulwick poll places the two-party preferred vote at 50-50, while in Pfcrramatta it gives the Labor Party a lead of 51 per cent to the Coalition's 49. In Victoria, the poll gives the marginal seat of Corinella to the ALP by 58 per cent to 42 and Dunkley by 52 to 48. In Queensland, however, things are vastly less certain with the seat of Dawson sitting at 50-50 while Kennedy appears to be likely to go to the Coalition, 51-49. South Australia represents a problem area for Labor, with the seats of Adelaide and Hindmarsh likely to fall to the Coalition. In WA, Labor is trailing in Cowan and Stirling. In Tasmania, however, Labor looks set to pick up both Franklin and Ly ons.

08 Mar 1993 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 8 March 1993, page 10 I (flankrra (Ttmrs^ Silly attempt at news management THE MINISTER for Urban Services, Terry Connolly, is always happy for his face to be on a television screen, his voice on the radio or his photograph in a newspaper. He occupics a portfolio which gives him a lot of opportunities. Now, however, he is seeking to expand them. Angered by the practice of some of his' officials - some in statutory authorities -of answering media questions, he has issued a directive to his department and the agencies he controls banning the giving out of any infprmation without its being cleared through his office. He wants to know what is being asked, and to approve the replies going out. And, it seems, he wants to reserve to himself the right to get any glory going. Part of the annoyance which sparked the directive arose because he thought he should have been interviewed about an ACT Electricity and Water discussion paper, not a senior ACTEW official. The: vanity of ministers is, generally, a harmless enough vice. Since an appetite for adulation is usually transparent enough, the single-minded indulgence of it is not always a public-relations plus: politicians one can become over-exposed. The concern about Mr Connolly's directive, however, should not merely be one about his affection for the limelight but about its extension to a somewhat sinister form of news management. The government of Canberra has long been a reasonably open afiair, with senior officials trusted to discuss publicly the factual basis of issues of public importance. They have almost invariably done so without causing political embarrassment to ministers. Canberra benefits because people are better informed about the facts, about the issues and their rights and responsibilities. The politicians themselves benefit. One of the ways Australia is in some respects a less mature democracy than, say, the United States, is that doctrines of ministerial responsibility and continuing devotion to administrative secrecy tend to make the slightest point of difference between what ministers say, or between what ministers decide and what their officials have advised them, a matter of great media interest. The Australian culture of secrecy has, however, been under attack for some time. Two decades ago, public service guidelines and the Crimes Act heavily discouraged contact between press and the bureaucracy. Since then the Freedom of Information Act has encouraged the proper giving of information. Although FOI imposes public-interest tests on the disclosure of information, the capacity for political embarrassment is not a ground for refusing access. Increasingly officials have been given independent powers, for the exercise of which they can be called personally to account. Governments have also tended to create arms-length agencies - ACTEW is a good example - able to control their own relationships with the public. At the ACT level, the trend to open government has also been reinforced by the major role which Legislative Assembly committee systems are given over the process of government, of expenditure and of the development of new policy. These committees, on the whole, have had relatively free access to officials. The result, generally, is that committee reports are better informed and more useful. Mr Connolly is reasonably entitled to know what sort of questions the media and others are asking of his department. His directive, however, goes further than that. He wants to control the information going out, to have all material cleared by his office before it is issued. This silly attempt at news management will not work - either in producing more headlines assisting Mr Connolly, or in suppressing inconvenient facts. Nor will it help good government. Mr Connolly should moderate his search for publicity and begin to trust the discretion of his officers. Accentuate the negative LAST night's debate between Paul Keating and John Hewson was the best of the three of the election campaign but it was too much a contest of research-tested catch-phrases to be either memorable to viewers or helpful to voters. Thus Dr Hewson had a plan which he had presented openly and honestly. Mr Keating had traditional Australian values of decency, tolerance and a fair go - and he most certainly did not have a goods-and-services tax. The debate confirmed the dominance of each party's weaknesses as campaign issues. The leaders pushed the other's negatives; attractive policies are at a discount. Dr Hewson's weakness is the GST and he was at his worst when pushed to explain details of how it would work. Mr Keating's weakness is his recent economic record, particularly on unemployment and while he successfully engendered some confidence that better times are in prospect he was at his worst when pressed on the detail of unemployment and jobs growth. But the debate was better than the two which preceded it. The two leaders were tired and at times uncertain but they were less wooden than in the first official debate. They both hectored and sneered but they were more restrained than during the confrontation on A Current Affair. And while last night's contest was still overly economic, the moderator, the ABCs Kerry O'Brien, did force the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition to discuss such broader issues as education, health care and industrial relations. Mr Keating scored a definite but not dominating victory. In manner, he was more composed than the nervous and often uncomfortable Dr Hewson. Mr Keating also had the better of the argument, largely because it is much easier to condemn and ridicule a planned new tax (or a change to the health cover system) than it is to explain and justify it Mr Keating and Dr Hewson enter the final week of the campaign with their own psychological lift. Dr Hewson gets his from the Morgan Gallup Poll, in Time Australia, showing the Coalition in a winning position. Mr Keating gets his from the debate and from the sense of confidence he conveyed in it. The polls might seem to portend a Labor loss but Mr Keating did not appear last night as a man who thinks he is about to be defeated. The campaign remains a genuine contest.

10 Mar 1993 - ELECTION COUNTDOWN Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 10 March 1993, page 5 ELECTION COUNTDOWN Mike Taylor POLLS Labor talks about life in Opposition Little by little and without actually conccding defeat, the Australian Labor Party has begun talking about life in Opposition. The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, signalled yesterday that the Australian Labor Party would block the Coalition's industrial relations policy in the Senate - a signal that would not have been warranted if Mr Keating wasn't genuinely contemplating a loss this Saturday. There arc many within the ALP who are hoping that they can snatch a victory on March 13, but who are privately making plans for life in Opposition. They arc not only examining the likely state of the parties after Saturday night but also the state of the ALP factions in the parliamentary Labor Party. What seems obvious at this point is that win, lose or draw on March 13 the real power in the parliamentary Labor Party will reside in Queensland and NSW. Queensland will remain powerful within the party because it remains in Labor hands and NSW will remain powerful because it is the one state where Labor gains are virtually assured. While Labor hopes to pick up scats in Victoria, its importance in the factional balance will have been diminished as will that of South Australia and Western Australia. Talk to any federal Labor Member and they will tell you that they expect to win on Saturday. Trouble is, there is an inevitable air of pessimism in their statements. Most privately expect the Coalition to emerge with a workable majority. But much the same sentiment existed in 1990. The Newspoll gave the Coalition the lead with 47 per cent compared to the ALP's 42 per cent, but translated this to a two-party preferred vote of SO per cent each. The Newspoll largely confirms the trend of the AGB-McNair poll published in this week's Bulletin magazine which has the parties level pegging on the primary vote at 46 per cent each, and the Morgan poll has the Coalition with a three-point lead in the primary vote. 1990 election campaign had settled, Labor Members freely admitted that they had expected to lose that campaign. Many were frankly surprised that the Labor Party had been returned to power on the basis of an astutely judged marginal scats campaign. The difference between 1990 and 1993 is that the Coalition has learned a good deal about marginal scats campaigning and this is being clcarly indicated in the public opinion polls. Unless the electorate develops a sudden general antipathy towards the Coalition on Saturday, the Government is likely to lose office on a national swing of around 1.6 per cent. The swing, will of course, not be uniform and as a result the Coalition is likely to have a majority of some where between seven and 12 seats. 16 Mar 1993 - Women put their faith in Keating Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 16 March 1993, page 8 Women put their faith in Keating THERE was a 5pm clue down at the local polling booth. Head down, tail up in the blue plastic bin was a Labor party faithful, frantically rummaging for the recyclable discarded how-tovote sheets, his supplies of new ones exhausted by a steady run. "Here you go," he said to the elderly women in mauve frocks waiting patiently for their instructions. "It's terribly creased," one said with alarm, as the other tried to smooth it out against her generously sized handbag. "Aren't we all," the party hack sighed. "Aren't we all." The women disappeared inside to the hall of lopsided cardboard castles, heroically dismissing with a gallant wave of the hand the offers of opposing instruction slips. Their minds were made up, their mission clear. And so it was for women across the country on Saturday, women, anonymous and as individuals apparently insignificant - faceless women who hours later took as personal Mr Keating's thanks for their vote. He'd wooed them, and he had won. In that hazy and euphoric pre-midnight triumph they believed they had won too. It was a mutual and co-dependent victory. They hadn't let him down. And now, they prayed, he wouldn't let them down. Women had had an awiul lot riding on this election. And in turn Keating had had a lot riding on them. In acknowledgement, he'd brought in Anne Summers last year as his principal women's adviser and together they had got to work. The feminising of his policies began with a vengeance and as an election loomed so did a bouquet of longed-for treats, pledges that would implement the changes that women had been attempting to negotiate for decades, pledges on child care, tax and judicial reform. With Ms Summers behind him, women's perception of the Prime Minister as aloof and out of touch with the female masses slowly dissipated. And as child care was hauled up on to Labor's economic agenda with such glistening gusto, women really sat up and took notice. It was too good to be true. The ACTU's Jennie George had already had them listening - reminding them the Coalition's proposed industrial-relations changes were scary. Would women be able to negotiate with powerful employers, on the back foot as they already were with family responsibilities that dictated when, where and how they could work? Marion Sawyer, senior lecturer in politics at the University of Canberra, wrote in The Canberra Times the week or so before the election that even the most exclusive of women's issues - menstruation - became an election issue. She said that when Mr Keating had joined the outrage over a GST on tampons and the fact that it would be more expensive to be a women in Australia, Senator Jocclyn Newman, the Coalition's spokeswoman on the status of women, had retorted that if "Labor truly cared about menstruation it would do something about jobs, as the stress of not having work could make women stop menstruating." So it was a no-holds-barred and bloody tussle, as women sat back, waiting and watching, left to Keating, right to Hewson, left to Keating... ad nauseam. Finally it seemed that Hewson's slaughtering of anything with a vaguely socialist odour was just too much. It is after all women who really need Medicare and the bulk-billing it offers if they are able to take their kids to the doctor without angst, it's women primarily who need affordable and accessible childcare, and it's women juggling the housekeeping money who need as much as possible in their lean purses, money that would have been eaten away by the increases costs of a GST. All things considered -menstruation or not - women needed a Labor Government, or certainly had less to fear from a Labor Government. And so exit polls conducted by AGB McNair on Saturday at 42 seats around the country showed that 50 per cent of women in marginal seats had voted for the ALP. Research manager John Mitchell said it was the first election in which the female vote for Labor had equalled the male vote. Women traditionally vote conservative, and it was from that position that the Keating/Summers duo were serenading. Mitchell confirmed that the GST was what most prompted people to vote Labor, with Medicare and health second on the women's list of concerns. It was a vote of faith, and Keating did right to thank the women who smoothed out Labor's crumpled polling slips and numbered its boxes. His mandate is based on carefully given trust, and a belief that women - still woefully underrepresented in his Ministry - will one day be able to thank him.

20 Mar 1993 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 20 March 1993, page 2 POLL WATCH Voters decided before the campaign began Most voters decided who they would vote for even before the election campaign had begun, according to an exit poll conducted by AGB McNair and published in The Bulletin magazine. The poll found that 48 per ccnt of Coalition voters and 42 per cent of Labor voters had decided who they would vote for before the campaign began. Twenty-one per cent of Coalition voters had derided early in the campaign, compared with 19 per cent of Labor voters. Twenty-one per cent of Labor voters said they had decided in the last week or so of the campaign compared with 17 per ccnt of Coalition voters. Seventeen percent of Labor voters and 13 per cent of Coalition voters had said they had decided on the day. The poll, which used data from 2231 face-to-face interviews with voters as they left the polling booth on election day, found that younger people tended to support the Labor party and older people the Coalition. Fifty-four per ccnt of women between the ages of 25 and 39, and 46 per cent of men in the same age brackct, had voted for the Labor party, and 38 per ccnt of women and 45 per cent of men in that age group for the Coalition. The poll found that Dr Hewson remained the preferred prime minister despite his party's loss - 43 per cent of those interviewed preferred Dr Hewson, compared with 40 per ccnt who favoured Mr Keating. Eighteen per cent said they disliked Mr Keating but only 9 per cent said they disliked Dr Hewson.

23 Mar 1993 - Lib machine adds sting on ballot eve Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 23 March 1993, page 1 Lib machine adds sting on ballot eve By ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent The two main contendere in the Op position power struggle, John Hewson and John Howard, both claim to have the numbers to win today's leadership ballot. As they continued late lobbying, the party organisation demanded more say in policy development and criticised the parliamentary leadership. The federal president of the Liberal Party, Ashley Goldsworthy, said the organisational wing was no longer prepared to continue asi the bridesmaid on policy develop ment. Dr Hewson and Mr Howard played down suggestions that today's winner would be a stop-gap leader, saying the new Leader of the Opposition would have the'full support of the party. Both camps said some MPs were still undecided. Others were indicating support to both sides while they made up their minds. In the race for the Liberal Party's deputy leadership, one of the favourites, Warwick Smith, withdrew late last night as the result in his electorate became more un certain. In a pointed reference to his oppo nent, Mr Howard said the meeting would decide who was more likely to lead the Opposition to victory. "Who has the best combination of political understanding and political skills, the capacity to communicate and articulate the broad values of the Liberal Party, and those things the Liberal Party holds dear to the Australian community? ... 1 believe I'm best . able to do that," he said. Mr Howard said he was confident of winning and denied his record as leader from 1985 to 1989 was a handicap. "The view that's coming through very strongly to me is that people do recognise that a range of experience in political combat and political skills is what really is required," he said. "People recognise that an inherendy unpopular man as Paul Keating, because of his political skills, was able to win an election that very few people thought he would win." An AGB McNair telephone poll pub lished last night said Dr Hewson had a comfortable lead - 57 to 43 per cent - in the leadership race. Dr Hewson said his support had picked up in recent days and he denied a narrow win would mean continued uncertainty. He said he was not rushing the ballot ahead to prevent Mr Howard building support., Mr Goldsworthy said he wanted to overhaul the Liberal organisation with fewer but bigger branches dedicated to constant campaign ing. "Whoever is elected leader and depu ty leader of the parliamentary party tomorrow must recognise that a fundamental reassessment is going to occur," he said. Continued on Page 2. Machine adds sting on ballot eve . Continued from Page 1 "For too long, and I am not just referring to these past three years, the organisation has been the acolyte at the altar of policy development. We deserve to be, and in the future will be, partners in this pro cess." After issuing his stinging statement in Brisbane, Mr Goldswortby told The Canberra Times he was not suggesting the organisational wing dictate policy. "But we really do have to look at the relationship between the parliamentary and organisational wings in this whole process of [deciding] what are our policies," he said. uWe have to get the organisational wing and its leadership playing a more active role in policy formulation and strategy ... there's got to be some fundamental rethinking and re-assessment" Dr Hewson and Mr Howard split on whether the ballot for the deputy leadership should be delayed if the seats of some MPs remained in doubt. Mr Howard hinted he would support mores to delay a ballot on the deputy leadership, which Dr Hewson wants finalised today, until counting confirms whether one contender, Tasmanian Warwick Smith, has held Bass. However, tension over the issue dissolved late last night when Mr Smith withdrew from the ballot after counting yesterday further weakened his hold on the seat Another frontbencher, Peter Costello, is likely to become favourite with Mr Smith's withdraw al.
