27 Mar 1993 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 27 March 1993, page 2 POLL WATCH Keating's approval rate peaks at 42pc .The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, has reached its highest level in the wake of his federaleRxtion victory, according to a Newspoll published in The Weekend Australian. .;Mr Keating's 42 per cent approval rating put him 14 percentage points ahead of the Leader of the Coalition, John Hewson, who sank to 32 per cent. 'Mr Keating's disapproval rating fell from 59 per cent to 50 per cent and the proportion of voters who approved of the way he was doing his job rose from 34 per cent in the week before the poll was taken to 41 percent. Support for the Labor Party also was up, from 45.4 per cent to 47 per cent. Support for the Coalition went from 44 per cent to 41 per cent. Poll results indicated support for both parties appeared to be driven by voters' dissatisfaction with alternative parties. Of Labor supporters polled, 51 percent said they chose Labor mainly because of their dislike for the other parties, compared with 43 per cent who said they chose Labor because they liked what it had to offer. Of Coalition voters, 50 per cent said they chose the Coalition because they disliked the other choices, compared with 43 per cent who voted for them because they liked Coalition policies. Support for the Democrats and other candidates rose slightly, from 10.6 per cent on election night to 12 per cent. The Newspoll data was collected from 1128 telephone interviews with random subjects from all Australian states. Two AGB McNair polls published in The Bulletin examined NSW and South Australian state politics. {n NSW, the approval rating of the Premier, John Fahey, has fallen 8 percentage points since November to 37 per cent. Mr Fahey's disapproval rating rose 7 percentage points to 24 per cent and the number of voters who preferred him as Premier fell by 2 to 45 per cent. Approval for the NSW Leader of the Opposition, Bob Carr, fell by 3 percentage points to 31 per cent and his disapproval rating rose by I to 34 per cent, and 34 per cent said they would prefer Mr Carr as Premier. The AGB McNair NSW poll used data from 1307 facc-to-face interviews statewide on February 12-14,19-21,26-28 and March 5-7. In South Australia, Lynn Arnold remained preferred Premier, on 38percent, compared with 32 per cent who preferred the Leader of the Opposition, Dean Brown. Mr Arnold's approval rating increased by two percentage points to 31 per cent and his disapproval rating rose three to 22 per cent. Mr Brown's approval rating fell 1 percentage point to 26 per cent and his disapproval rating rose one to 20 per cent. The AGB McNair South Australian poll used data from 695 face-to-face interviews state-wide on January 29-31, February 5-7,12-14, 19-21,26-28 and March 5-7.

29 Mar 1993 - Activists appeal against Sydney wharf project Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 29 March 1993, page 4 Activists appeal against Sydney wharf project SYDNEY: The Friends of the Finger Wharf appealed yesterday to the Premier of NSW, John Fahey, to overturn a decision to turn Sydney's historic wharf into what they call a "crystal palace". The protest group, composed mainly of local residents, used an open day at the inner-city Wooiloomooloo wharf to hand out copies of a letter to Mr Fahey urging him to reject the decision announced last. week by the Minister for Transport, Bruce Baird. The $120 million scheme would redevelop the wharf into a five-star luxury hotel and luxury apartments with a marina, as a compromise between the long-warring group and developers. "Exclusive hotel uses and million-dollar apartments have nothing to do with the heritage of the Finger Wharf or of Woolloomooloo," the letter said. The Government chose a tender by Wedderlight-Delmo Pty Ltd that included 120 apartments, restaurants, a 106-room Sheraton hotel and a retail and sporting complex. However, the president of Friends of the Finger Wharf, Susan Barley, said yesterday it represented no compromise at all because the plan was developed without consultation in the design phase. She said the group, the Institute of Architects and the National Trust worked tirelessly on the project advisory committee with the Government last year, assessing the now-successful tender and also a marketplace tender. "None of us recommended the hotel [tender] and, even between the beginning of the year and the end of the year, there was no change in the hotel," she said. "To say it was developed in consultation is totally misrepresenting. "We've given a year of our time and our expertise, and we didn't even have the courtesy of being informed that a decision was imminent." A Woolloomooloo Foundation plan for a retail, entertainment and arts centre had minimal impact on the wharf building and offered the greatest benefit to local residents, Ms Barley said. "A hotel will not work here because Sydney is full of half-empty hotels and this building is very important as a time capsule of 80 years of working-class history." She said a recent Morgan Gallup poll showed 70 per cent of Sydney residents favoured the marketplace proposal over the hotel-apartment idea.

07 Jul 1985 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 7 July 1985, page 2 She Can berra Wms Sunday. July 7, 1985 P.M. MAKES HIS X MARK At WAS a bad week for the Prime Minister, Mr Hawkc. His pet tax-reform plan, Option C, was tossed out of the tax inference and the latest Morgan Gallup Poll showed hisJ popularity plummeting. It must be heartening for Mr Frascr, who resigned as the Liberal Prime Minister when Mc Hawkc won the clcclion in March, 1983, to discover that his autograph is 10 times as valuable. i However, no economist worth his salt would accept the aujograph market as an automatically deregulated one. It is rrtpst likely that the gregarious Mr Hawke, who spent the fir$tycar or so of his Prime Ministership.being adulated byjthc masses, has flooded the land with free autographs. On the other hand, Mr Fraser is not an extrovert and ccrtainly, while Prime Minister, did not encourage the masses to surge forward to shake his hand or request an autograph. 17 Jul 1985 - SA Ministry shuffle fuels election speculation Bannon makes big changes Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 17 July 1985, page 14 SA Ministry shuffle fuels election speculation Bannon makes big changes ADELAIDE: Nearly half the 13membcr South Australian Government Ministry changcd yesterday in a shuffle caused by the resignation of the former Deputy Premier, Mr Wright, for health reasons. The Premier, Mr Bannon, in a move seen as preparation for an election expcctcd this year, strengthened economic areas by creating an Employment portfolio and by appointing a Minister assisting the Treasurer to take some of his Treasury responsibilities. "The concept of a Minister assisting the Treasurer is in order for me to perhaps get away from the routine day-to-day work and concentrate more on the longer-term planning issues," Mr Bannon said. "Everyone talks about an election context. As far as my Government is concerned we are at the stage of completing our first threeyear program and we are in the proccss of planning our next five year program. "When you lose a key minister like Mr Wright there are a number of changes and consequences. Having made these changes, 1 do agree it has given our Cabinet a new look, a new image." The new Deputy Premier, Mr Hopgood, was given the key portfolio of Emergency Services, which includes responsibility for Police and Chief Secretary. He retains Environment and Planning. Tourism, an area where Mr Bannon has been making political capital with events such as the Australian Formula One Grand Prix in November, went to Ms Wiese, 35, the State Labor Government's first woman minister. Ms Wiese, who was the first woman State president of the ALP, was also given the new portfolio of Youth Affairs and will be responsible for Local Government. Mr Blevins lost the minor portfolio of Forests but pickcd up Minister for Labour and Minister Assisting the Treasurer, while retaining responsibility for Agriculture, Fisheries and CoiTcctional Services. The Education Minister, Mr Arnold, was made the new Minister for Employment and also became Minister Assisting the Minister for State Development. Mr Kencally lost Tourism but gained the more senior post of Minister for Transport, as well as Minister for Services and Supply. The only apparent demotion was the former Minister for Transport, Mr Abbott, who got the comparatively minor portfolios of Lands, Forests, Repatriation and Marine. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition, Mr Goldsworthy, said the shuffle was an exercise in futility and an attempt to move jaded ministers to take the pressure off and boost the ALP's pour showing in opinion polls. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll in The Bulletin showed the Labor Government would have polled 41 per cent of the vote compared to the Liberal Opposition's 43 per cent. However, Mr Bannon's personal approval rating was 65 per cent, while the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Olsen, had a rating of 50 per cent. The remainder of the Cabinet is: Mr Sumner, Attorney-General, Minister for Corporate Affairs, Minister for Ethnic Affairs; Mr Cornwall, Minister for Health; Mr Payne, Minister for Mines and Energy; Mr Crafter, Minister for Community Welfare, Minister for Aboriginal Affairs; Mr Slater, Minister for Water Resources, Minister for Recreation and Sport; Mr Hemmings, Minister for Housing and Construction, Minister for Works.

20 Jul 1985 - New Deputy Premier looks good offsider for Bannon Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 20 July 1985, page 16 New Deputy Premier looks good offsider for Bannon from our r South Australian Correspondent THE first thing Dr Donald Jack Hopgood did as the new Deputy Premier of South Australia was to let it be known that he was no seat warmer. He said he ran seriously for the job because the State's economic recovery was under threat from the conservatives and he wanted to ensure the reelection of the Bannon Labor Government which had put South Australia "back on the rails". His statement may help dispel his image as a caretaker among those who believe that his predecessor as Deputy Premier, Mr Jack Wright, should have been replaced by a person of his stamp - a former shearer, a staunch union bloke with his feet firmly planted in the grassroots of the Labor movement in the State. For those people, the Minister for Agriculture, Mr Frank Blevins, seemed the natural successor, but Mr Blevins is a Member of the Legislative Council, not the Assembly, though he hopes to switch at the next State election, due late this year or early next year. Mr Wright's resignation because of poor health last month undoubtedly gave the Labor Caucus a headache. The last thing the party needed was leadership problems as the Liberals push ahead in the pre-election popularity polls. The Premier, Mr Bannon, has been coolly sitting out the invitation to dance to the Opposition's tune of trenchant criticism of its performance well ahead of the declaration of the election date. There is no little admiration for his calmness in the face of backlash from the Federal Government's summit meeting on taxation and other unpopular moves from Canberra. The result has been that although the latest Morgan Gallup poll has grim news for the Government, Mr Bannon's personal standing as Premier has continued to grow to give him a 65 per cent rating and a 15-point lead over the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Olsen. All the more reason for him to build on this popularity with a strong, popular deputy at his side which, despite his differences from the bluff and personable Mr Wright, Dr Hopgood is likely to be, certainly for those who admire Mr Bannon's brand of studied coolness under fire. But after the election, and if the unionists' choice of their "natural" voice, Mr Blevins, becomes viable, there could be an interesting tension in Caucus which will see Dr Hopgood's performance as Deputy Premier in the months to come under the closest scrutiny. Dr Hopgood was Minister for Environment and Planning, Minister for Lands and Repatriation and Leader of the House of Assembly. His performance in all these areas, together with great affability (popularity referred to as his "schoolteacher friendliness"), has marked him for some time for "promotion", though most of these qualities were matched by the Minister of Education, Mr Arnold, who was his serious rival for the Deputy-Premiership this month, again in the absence of Mr Blevins, awaiting his "house-change". Dr Hopgood retains Environment and Planning and now has Emergency Services as well. Caucus filled the ministerial vacancy1" by electing its first woman minister, Ms Barbara Wiese, a relative newcomer to Parliament who first took her seat in 1979 after serving a political apprenticeship as an assistant to Labor MP. She is Minister for Tourism for Youth Affairs and for Local Govern ment. Her selection has increased the numbr of upper-House ministers to four, one more than custom and repealed legislation have allowed, but many believe the presence of a woman in the Labor ministerial line-up was long overdue. The acting Leader of the Opposition, Mr Goldsworthy, was not slow to point out that the decision to appoint an extra minister from the Council was "strange" in the light of Labor's policy to abolish the upper House. But the selection of Ms Wiese, who was the ALP's first woman president in South Australia, presented an excellent opportunity for the Government to emphasise its grassroots connections (Ms Wiese is a former secretary who left school at 15) and revive its focus on women's issues. Unlike Dr Hopgood, who was challenged closely by Mr Arnold, Ms Wiese outpolled her only rival for the post (Anne Levy, also MLC) handsomely. Three years ago she was quoted as saying that she wanted a Cabinet post, but had no ambitions to be Premier. In those far-off days newspapers felt no uneasiness about talking about Ms Wiese's beauty as a "barrier" to her political ambitions. Happily for Ms Wiese, that prediction has proved wrong, her Cabinet hopes have been fulfilled and even the sternest feminist might concede that she adds extra "personableness" to pictures of the Premier and his new leadership duo. 19 Jul 1984 - IN BRIEF Cave-fall rescue Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 19 July 1984, page 7 IN BRIEF Cave-fall rescue Mr Derek Charles Elmes. 21, of Croydon, Sydney, was rescued by Goulburn police and ambulance about 8.30pm on Tuesday, and later treated for shock and exposure, after a 45-metre drop into the Drum cave, part of the Bungonia caves, about 60 kilometres south-east of Goulburn. Employment grants Applications from government de-partments and statutory authorities for grants under the non-Com-monwealth component of the 1984-85 Community Employment Program close on August 17, the ACT Employment Advisory Committee said yesterday. For further informa-tion ring 472255. Industrial research Three new part-time members have been appointed to the Australian In-dustrial Research and Development Board: the chairman of the Design Arts Board of the Australia Council, Mr John Andrews; the head of sys-tems engineering in the Research School of Physical Sciencc at ANU, Professor Brian Anderson, and the managing-director of Courtaulds Hilton Pty Ltd, Mr William Kricker. Nutrition seminar The ACT division of the Australian Nutrition Foundation has organised a public-information seminar titled 'You, Your Food and Salt', to be held on Saturday, July 28, from 2pm, in J Building at Reid TAFE. The cost, which includes afternoon tea, is $3 for adults and $2 for students; for further information, ring 432111 (ext 2412). Harry's to stay SYDNEY: The future of Sydney's famous wharfside eatery, Harry's Cafe de Wheels - earlier threatened by a council desire to have it moved - was secured at a meeting on Tues-day night between the Lord Mayor, Alderman Doug Sutherland, and the cafe proprietor, Mr Alex Korunya. Victorian support MELBOURNE: Support for the Victorian Government fell by 1 per-cent at the end of June, and was down 5 per cent on January's peak of 54 per-cent, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll published in this week's Bulletin; the approval rating of the Premier, Mr Cain, rose by 4 per cent - from 47 per cent in May. Caltex awards women Applications are being invited for the 1984 Caltex Woman Graduate Awards, which provide one national scholarship (valued at $40,000) and six State prizes (each worth $5,000), all tenable at an approved university or tertiary institution overseas for a maximum of two years. Parks plan criticised The regional director of the National Parks and Wildlife Service, Mr Bruce Leaver, said on Tuesday that a proposal by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, to establish a commission to investigate tourist development within Kosciusko National Park, was unjustified, because initiatives foreshadowed in 1982 had already been implemented. Bones identified MELBOURNE: Detectives indentified yesterday bones found last Friday near Echuca as those of Mr Arthur William Swanwick, 63, who disappeared nearly four years ago. Burke's operation PERTH: The Premier of Western Australia, Mr Burke, underwent surgery in Perth yesterday for a back ailment and will be off work for a month.

29 Jul 1984 - IN BRIEF Gallup Poll founder dies Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 29 July 1984, page 5 IN BRIEF Gallup Poll founder dies NEW YORK, Saturday (Reuter). — Mr George Gallup, whose name became synonymous with opinion polls, died yesterday aged 82 in a hospital in Switzerland, his company announced in New York. The Gallup Poll, based on a randomly selected cross-section of the public, rose to fame in the presidential election of 1936, became a powerful force in US political life, and spawned offshoots in several dozen countries around the world. Hinckley wants out WASHINGTON, Saturday (AP). — Mr John Hinkley, who tried to kill President Reagan in 1981, said yesterday he was ready to leave the mental hospital where he was sent after being found not guilty of the shooting by reason of insanity, and would file for a release order. 634-year jail sentence ANCHORAGE, Alaska, Saturday (AP). — A computer programmer who planned to wipe out a small town and the trans-Alaska oil pipeline was sentenced this week to 634 years (consecutively) in prison for a shooting spree last year which left six people dead and two wounded. He received six 99 year and two 20-year terms. Pedestrian killed LOS ANGELES, Saturday (AP). — One person was killed and more than 50 were injured, five critically, when a car veered onto a crowded foot-path last night near the Olympic Village at the University of California, officials said. The driver, who had been charged with murder, apparently had wanted revenge against the police. The incident was unrelated to the Olympics, they said. Coal industry 'insolvent' LONDON, Saturday (Reuter). — Britain's strike-bound State coal industry, which reported a year-end deficit of the equivalent of$A1,392 mil-lion on Thursday, was insolvent, the Government said. It blamed a quarter of the loss on industrial action by miners. Telegraphist acquitted LONDON, Saturday (Reuter). — Royal Air Force telegraphist Mr Paul Davies was acquitted yesterday on three charges of passing secrets to a Hungarian woman in return for sex. He had been accused of divulging classified signals used by the multi-national peacekeeping force in Beirut. Reagan 'good boy' ABOARD AIR FORCE ONE, Saturday (AP). — President Reagan declined yesterday an invita-tion to thumb through a copy of Penthouse maga-zine containing sexually explicit photographs of former Miss America Vanessa Williams. Mr Reagan said, "I don't look at those kind of pictures. I'm a good boy."

23 Aug 1984 - ALP and Hawke solid, poll says Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 23 August 1984, page 16 ALP and Hawke solid, poll says SYDNEY: If a Federal election had been held early this month, the ALP would have been returned with an increased majority, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin magazine yesterday. It found that support for the ALP was 51 per cent while the LiberalNational Party was down two percentage points to 42. Five per cent supported the Aus tralian Democrats and two per cent other parties. If a Senate election had been held this month, the ALP would have won 46 per cent with the Democrats and independent candidates maintaining the balance of power. Sixty-eight per cent approved of the way the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, was handling his job and 35 per cent approved of the performance of the Opposition Leader, Mr Peacock.

02 Aug 1993 - Packer remains best-known boss Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 2 August 1993, page 2 Packer remains best-known boss Media magnate Kerry Packer remains Australia's best-known corporate leader, according to a Morgan Poll. Awareness of Western Mining managing director Hugh Morgan had increased by nine points to 37 per cent, according to the nation-wide poll of 1175 people to be published in this week's Time magazine. Mr Morgan has been making waves recently with his com-ments about Aborigines and the High Court decision on native ti- tle. The poll, carried out on July 10-11, found Mr Packer had been heard of by 93 per cent of respondents (down one point since November, 1992), 87 per cent were aware of media baron Rupert Murdoch (down two points) and 80 per cent had Kerry Packer heard of former Foster's chief John Elliott (down five points). Perceptions of the three most well-known business people var- ied. All three increased their rat-ings as capable businessmen, but Mr Packer was considered un-trustworthy by 23 per cent of re-spondents, up one point. Mr Elliott's untrustworthiness rating declined by eight points to 19 per cent, while Mr Murdoch's remained steady on 22 per cent. Mr Murdoch was named most frequently as being interested on-ly in profits, followed by Mr Packer and Mr Elliott. Public awareness was also high for Fosters Brewing Group chairman Nobby Clark and Western Mining chairman Sir Arvi Parbo. Less than a third of the re-spondents had heard of BHP managing director John Prescott, Coles Myer chief executive Peter Bartels, Coles Myer chairman Solomon Lew or Optus chief ex-ecutive Bob Mansfield.

03 Aug 1993 - Bush's murder appeal rejected Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 3 August 1993, page 3 Bush's murder appeal rejected Court endorses trial judgment on all grounds Ian Leslie Bush's appeal against his conviction for the murder of his estranged wife's lover, which had been based on the claim that media publicity affected the fairness of his trial, has been rejected by the Federal Court Bush, 34, a carpenter, was convicted last November of the murder of John Richard Nicholson and the attempted murder of his wife, Leta Carla Bush, at a flat in Oxley on March 13, 1992. He was convicted in 1987 of the manslaughter of his first wife, Debra Michelle Bush, whom he had strangled in an argument about her relationship with another man. He was sentenced to five years' jail but served nine months. The appeal was rejected by Justices Jeffrey Miles, Daryl Davies, and Douglas Drummond. Counsel for Bush, Terry O'Donnell, argued that the trial judge, Justice John Gallop: • had erred in law by not adjourning the proceedings so that an attempt could be made to get the law changed so a trial could be held outside the ACT; • should have allowed Bush to challenge prospective jurors "for cause" — question them to determine any bias; • had given misleading directions on the defence of provocation; and • should not have allowed rebuttal evidence by psychiatrists on involuntary action. The appeal had concentrated on the first two grounds, which related to the media publicity surrounding the first trial in 1987. Mr O'Donnell argued that this publicity would have made it impossible for the jury to reach a verdict based purely on the evidence. Mr O'Donnell presented a survey report which, he said, showed that 8 to 19 per cent of ACT voters would recognise and be influenced by Bush's previous convictions. Press clippings about the previous case were produced. Yesterday's judgment dismissed these arguments, saying that even if Justice Gallop had been wrong, there was no mechanism to have a trial moved from the ACT. There was no suggestion now or at the time of the trial that the ACT Gov ernment had any intention of making such arrangements. Challenging prospective jurors to "show cause" was very rare and to be allowed only in "exceptional cases" where there was evidence that adverse media publicity was likely to influence the jury. It had not been established that Bush's was such a case. Such a challenge was to be used only for individual jury members, and the defence had to establish a foundation for the challenge. "The absence of any reminder in the media in 1992 of the events of 1987, coupled with the passage of time prevents the case from being regarded as one of those exceptional ones," Justice Drummond said. Justice Davies remarked that it was "highly unlikely that it would have crossed the mind of a juror that the person accused in 1992 of killing his wife's lover was the same person who had been convicted of the manslaughter of Debra Bush". In fact, challenging the jury to show cause would only have heightened the risk of prejudice. The Saulwick poll commissioned Justice Gallop: made defence of provocation sufficiently clear to jury. by the defence had failed to establish this prejudice, and it had not been established that the panel of ACT voters surveyed was the same panel from which the jury had been chosen. The Full Court decided that Justice Gallop had made the defence of provocation sufficiently clear to the jury, and had been correct to allow psychiatric evidence to rebut that called by the defence. Bar defends conduct of the Public Defender The ACT Bar Association has defended ACT Public Defender Terry O'Donnell against criticism by the Federal Court that his conduct of Ian Bush's defence was improper. The association's president, Ben Salmon, QC, said yesterday that the court's "trenchant criticism" of defence counsel had been without foundation. One of the three judges who heard the Bush appeal, Justice Douglas Drummond, referred to the fact that Mr O'Donnell had called an eminent psychiatrist, Professor Finlay-Jones, to give evidence about whether Bush may have killed John Nicholson involuntarily. The professor had said that some circumstances of the case were consistent with Bush's having killed Nicholson "in a disassociated state". Justice Drummond suggested that Mr O'Donnell had failed to tell Professor Finlay-Jones that Bush had been convicted previously of strangling his first wife and that this failure involved "the same sort of impropriety that occurs when a party's lawyers 'settle' an expert's report". The implication was that the professor would not have given such evidence had he known of the previous homicide. Mr Salmon said the council had examined a copy of a letter (from Bush's lawyers) which made it clear that, before the professor gave his evidence, he had been made aware of Bush's previous conviction. It followed, he said, that there was no foundation for the criticism made of Mr O'Donnell by the judge. Mr Salmon noted that the ACT Chief Justice, Jeffrey Miles, had concurred with Justice Drummond's judgment. He did not mention that Justice Daryl Da vies had also agreed. Nor did he mention that Justice Da vies had referred incorrectly to Bush's conviction for the murder of his first wife. Bush, in fact, was acquitted of murder but found guilty of manslaughter. Mr O'Donnell declined to com ment publicly on the matter. It is believed that the Federal Court might be asked now to "correct" its published decision before it is incorporated in the official law reports. — ROO CAMPBELL r

04 Aug 1993 - PM's popularity rating slips Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 4 August 1993, page 5 PM's popularity rating slips The personal-approval rat-ing by voters of the Prime Min-ister, Paul Keating, has declined in the latest AGB McNair opinion poll, pub-lished in this week's Bulletin. The poll, taken in late July, shows that 27 per cent of voters surveyed approved Mr Keating's performance, com-pared with 31 per cent early in the month. But he still led the Opposi-tion Leader, John Hewson, whose approval rating re- mained steady at 21 per cent. Mr Keating's disapproval rat-ing increased from 46 per cent to 50. Dr Hewson's, too, in-creased from 44 to 48 per cent. On who was the preferred prime minister, Mr Keating scored 43 per cent (down from 44) to Dr Hewson's 30 (up from 28). Over all, support for the gov-ernment declined from 46 to 45 per cent. The coalition's was steady at 41 percent. - AAP

13 Aug 1993 - It serves the voters right! Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 13 August 1993, page 10 It serves the voters right! YESTERDAY'S column mentioned the discovery by a Gallup Poll that 20 per cent of the people of the United States believe that the floods that have taken 50 lives and done $A14 billion of damage in nine states are God's punishment on the United States for its wicked ways. Noticing this, an American woman living in Canberra called to say that when she telephoned her sister in America's mid-West and asked if there was any flooding in the sister's bailiwick her sister said, "No, it's only flooding in the states that voted for Clinton!", an analysis that, depending on one's politics, may coincide with the analysis made by the aforementioned 20 God-fearing per cent. President Clinton, meanwhile, announced yesterday that he was going to do something about law and order and about the excessive availability of handguns because America's children had the right to lead their lives without fear of flying bullets. Some days earlier a news service reported that bullets fly so frequently in the bailiwick that embraces the Leonard R. Flynn elementary school in San Francisco that, beginning next semester, the children are going to be taught how to duck and to take cover.

21 Aug 1993 - Budget gets worst vote by public in decade Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 21 August 1993, page 19 Budget gets worst vote by public in decade SYDNEY: The federal Budget has been given the worst response by the public of any Budget survey in a decade, according to a Herald Saulwick poll. Only 2 per cent of people surveyed thought they were better off because of the Budget, according to the poll published in The Sydney Morning Herald yesterday. The poll found 72 per cent of people thought they were worse off. The paper said the poll showed people were more emphatic about their beliefs on the Budget than ev er before. Distaste for the Budget went across the political spectrum, with 84 per cent of Coalition voters saying they would be worse off. Among Labor voters, 48 per cent said they would be worse off. Only 5 per cent said they would be better off. The national telephone poll was conducted in the morning after the Budget, with 1000 voters questioned.

23 Aug 1993 - Govt waters down 'no cuts' pledge Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 23 August 1993, page 1 waters 'no By KEITH SCOTT The Federal Government watered down yesterday the commitment by the Prime Minister, Pabl Keating, last week to make no further cuts to Government outlays. A spokesman for Mr Keating said his commitment did not mean there would "not be movement at the margin" and the Employment Minister, Kim Beazley, said there would be a "bit of trimming around the edges". The comments followed a statement by Finance Minister Ralph Willis on Channel Nine's Business Sunday that Mr Keating's commit-' ment did not mean "we won't make some further cuts in future years to make way for other expenditures that we will have to meet". In other developments in the row over the Budget: • An AGB McNair poll in this week's Bulletin shows that 73 per cent of voters disapprove of last week's Budget (up from 49 per cent in 1992), 63 per cent believe the Opposition and minor parties should combine in the Senate to oppose it. • The Opposition Leader in the Senate, Robert Hill, flagged the possibility of a High Court challenge to the Government's omnibus tax legislation on the grounds that it was unconstitutional in imposing more than one tax, and should be split into separate Bills (which the Opposition and independents could then make decisions on separately). • Shadow Treasurer Alexander Downer called on the Government to hold off imposing higher rates of fuel excise and sales tax to ensure that if the measures were defeated in the Senate, there would be no administrative problem in refunding.people. Spokesmen for Mr Keating and Mr Willis denied Mr Willis's com ments contradicted the Prime Minister. They said Mr Keating had been talking about aggregate figures and Mr Willis was talking about possible cuts to individual programs within an overall budget. But the further qualifications added by Mr Keating's office and Mr Beaziey effectively pulled back from the Prime Minister's statement last week. Mr Keating told Parliament last week, "Let me make it quite clean we' are not cutting outlays any further." Defending Mr Willis's statement, Mr Keating's spokesman said the Prime Minister had been talking about Government spending as a "percentage of the overall economy". "If you cut expenditure and then replaced it with other government expenditure, you would not be altering the level of outlays," he said. "So what Mr Willis said is entirely compatible with what Mr Keating said and what [the Treasurer] Mr Dawkins said through the week. [The Prime Minister's statement] doesn't mean that every program in this week's Budget is locked in concrete for four years." Mr Keating's commitment should not be seen as maintaining the ratio of outlays to Gross Domestic Product to "the same decimal point". "It's about whether you go into a Budget saying 'right, what we're going to do is cut 10 per cent out of the Budget outlays'... what he is saying is that the Government will not do that," the spokesman said. Continued on Page 2 Labor's days numbered — Page 11 Govt waters down 'no cuts' pledge Continued from Page 1 "He regards the core level of government outlays to have been reached. But that doesn't mean that there would not be movement at the margin. Obviously the percentage would not be locked solid because there is going to be movement of all sorts of variable factors. uHe was talking about the philosophical approach the Government brings to its Budget . Mr Beazley said on the Sunday program that Mr Keating's commitment had been "direct ed towards the sort of general big entitlement provisions in the Budget". He said it was "always going to be possible" to take out "20 or 30 million dollars here or there". Mr Willis said that "what the Prime Minister was saying is not that there would not be any more cuts in government expenditure, but that the general level of outlays as they were was appropriate at around 27.5 per cent of GDP for these economic circumstances, at the moment.. "But that does not mean that we won't make some further cuts in future years to make way for other expenditures that we will have to meet. Just for instance, the Government is likely to face some outlays for compensation in relation to Mabo [native title] claims ... the obvious way is to make some cuts in existing outlays." The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, said in a statement that Mr Willis's comments were a clear contra diction of Mr Keating's stance. "Only four days after the Prime Minister frothed at the mouth over the evils of spending cuts, and categorically committed his Government to no further spending cuts, the Minister for Finance has revealed that Labor has broken its word yet again," he said.

05 Jun 1993 - Hewson recovers a little popularity Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 June 1993, page 2 Hewson recovers a little popularity POLL WATCH Support for federal Opposition leader John Hewson rose to 31 pcrccnt, up two points from an all-time low, according to the latest Morgan poll in Time magazine. Dr Hewson's disapproval rating fell by three points lo 55 per cent during May. In the same period, support for the Prime Minister: Paul Keating, fell by six'points to 41'per cent and his disapproval rating rose five points to 49 per cent in early May, then down one point. Mr Keating was still way ahead in the preferred prime minister stakes. Asked who would be the better prime minister, a steady 53 per ccnl between April and late May opted for Mr Keating and 35 per cent, up one point, chose Dr Hewson. Support for the federal Labor party dropped 2.5 per ccnl in April, but was steady at 45.5 per cent during May. Support for the Coalition was up two points to 43 per ccnt. The ALP led 51-49 per ccnt on a two-party preferred basis. The Morgan poll used data from 3399 face-to-face interviews with voters across Australia, conducted on May 15 to 16 and May 22 to 23. Support for the ALP in the Senate had risen since the election on March 13, according to the latest AGB McNair poll, published in The Bulletin. Aggregate national support for the ALP in the Senate was up from 43.5 per cent on March 13 to 45 percent. Aggregate support for the Liberal-National Coalition in the Senate fell from 42.7 on March 13 to 39 percent. The Australian Democrats and Independents had 6 per cent support each. The AGB McNair poll used data from 2069 face-to-face interviews with voters across Australia oil • May 7 to 9 and 14 to 16. All figures arc rounded percentages.

07 Jun 1993 - Poll finds women did not give Labor its election victory Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 7 June 1993, page 1 Poll finds women did not give Labor its election victory By MARGO KINGSTON The widespread notion that the women's vote ensured Labor's elec-tion victory is a myth, according to a Morgan poll commissioned for the Liberal Party. A telephone survey of 4780 wom-en, conducted after polls closed on election day, found that the Coali-tion attracted 46.9 per cent of the women's vote, ahead of Labor's 42.6 per cent. (Other parties attracted 10.5 per cent.) Labor rode to victory on a large male vote. It pulled in 46 per cent of men's votes, compared with the Lib-erals' 44.3 per cent. -servative politics by women, the Na-tional Party attracted far more female than male voters. About 6.4 per cent of women voted National compared with only 3.9 per cent of men (women under 24 are the Na-tionals' greatest supporters: 8 per cent of young women voted for them). There were wide disparities in female voting patterns among age groups. Labor was well ahead among women aged 18-24 (44.5 per cent compared with the Coalition's 38.5 per cent). Labor also outpolled the Coalition among women aged 25-49 (45.4 per cent to 43.5 per cent); but the Coalition was way ahead among the over-50s — 55.3 per cent — against 37.4 per cent for Labor. A slide in women's support for Labor last year, resulting from low female approval of Paul Keating, triggered moves to employ Dr Anne Summers as Mr Keating's adviser on the status of women; a transforma-tion of Mr Keating's persona; and a personal focus on women's concerns about violence and child care. The age breakdown of women's voting patterns suggests that Mr Keating's strategy may have helped attract his target group — young and baby-boomer women. The poll sug- gests also that major promises by both parties on child-care rebates ef-fectively neutralised the issue. No woman surveyed mentioned the is-sue as a reason for voting one way or the other. Instead, voting behaviour was de-termined by a negative view of the GST. When the pollster asked wom-en who voted Labor why they had done so, 45.4 per cent said it was because they opposed the GST. That percentage increased to nearly 55 per cent among females aged 25-34 and 52.4 per cent of those aged 35-49. Coalition social policies were un-popular with women who chose La-bor, 26 per cent citing either liking Labor's health, education or welfare policies or disliking the Coalition's alternatives as a reason for voting Labor. This factor increased to 34.1 per cent in the 25-34 age group. The Coalition's industrial-rela-tions policy was also a big loser, be-ing cited by 11.5 per cent of females who voted Labor. The Coalition's $3-an-hour youth wage might have helped that increase to 16.6 per cent among young women. The survey exposes a potentially terminal weakness in the Coalition vole among men and women: that the young and middle-aged voter prefers Labor. The Coalition held its ground only because of massive sup-port by the over-50s, from whom it attracted more than 50 per cent of the vote even before preferences. Young men were even more attract ed to Labor than young women. In the 18-to-24-year-old group, 47.8 per cent voted Labor compared with 42.1 per cent for the Coalition. In the 25-to-49 age group, men too deserted the Coalition (48.8 percent voted Labor, compared with 39.1 for the Coalition). Women in that age group were more evenly divided. Liberals must think harder about youth - Page 11.

12 Jun 1993 - POLL WATCH Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 12 June 1993, page 2 POLL WATCH Support for ALP down, polls show The federal Coalition has gained ground on the Government, accord' ing-to the latest AGB McNair poll, published in The Bulletin. Support for the federal Labor party was down two points to 46 per cent in mid-May, while support for the Coalition was steady at 41 per cent. The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, dropped three points to 33 per cent. The rating of the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, was steady at 25 per cent. Mr Heating's disapproval rating rose four points to 45 per cent and Dr Hewson's fell two points also to 45 per cent. Mr Keating still led by a fair margin in the preferred Prime Minister stakes at 44 per cent, despite dropping three points. Thirty-three per cent of voters, an increase of two points, chose Dr Hewson as their preferred Prime Minister. The Bulletin poll used data from 2053 face-to-face interviews with voters across Australia on May 21-23 and 28-30. A recent Suulwick poll, published in The Sydney Morning Herald, showed both Mr Keating's and Dr Hewson's approval ratings had dropped and that support for the federal ALP had fallen to 39 per cent. Twenty-four per cent of those polled approved of Mr Keating and 17 per cent approved of Dr Hewson. Mr Keating's disapproval rating was 41 per cent, compared to Dr Hewson's 39 per cent. Mr Keating still led as the preferred Prime Minister at 46 per cent, despite the gap between him and Dr Hewson narrowing from 13 points to seven: 39 per cent of those polled said they would prefer Dr Hewson. The poll showed Mr Keating's approval rating among men (26 per cent) was higher than among women (22 per cent). Dr Hewson's rating among women (19 per cent) was higher than among men (16 per cent). The Saulwick poll used data from 1000 telephone interviews with voters across Australia on June 2.

14 Jun 1993 - ALP two points ahead, says poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 14 June 1993, page 2 ALP two points ahead, says poll The latest Morgan Poll showed the Labor Party had a two percentage point lead over the Coalition in early June, despite dropping one point from late May. Support for Labor was 44.5 per cent, compared with the Coalition's 42.5 percent (down 0.5). Support for the Australian Democrats rose one to 5 percent, with the Greens unchanged on four and other parties including independents up 0.5 to 4 per cent. The poll, to be published in this week's Time magazine, showed Labor had 51.5 per cent support on a two-party preferred basis — up 0.5 since last month. The poll of 2302 electors was conducted in face-to-face interviews nationally on the weekends of May 29-30 and June 5-6 - with controversy over the budget deficit, broken election promises, continuing high unemployment and the fall out from the High Court's Mabo case. It showed the personal approval rating for the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, fell four points to 37 per cent, his disapproval rating rose four points to 52 per cent and 11 per cent were undecided.

21 Jun 1993 - Strong support for euthanasia: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 21 June 1993, page 2 Strong support for euthanasia: poll Most Australians still supported euthanasia, particularly if a terminally ill person was in great pain and asked to die, a Morgan poll has found. The poll said an unchanged 73 per cent believed a doctor should let a patient die if that person had no chance of recovering and was in great pain. And 78 per cent, a rise of 2 per cent, said if an ill person was in great pain, had no chance of recovery, and asked for a lethal dose, a doctor should be allowed to give that lethal dose. The poll showed support for allowing someone to die was similar regardless of political affiliation, age or sex. Older Australians increasingly supported the euthanasia option. Those against cited reasons as "doctors can't play God" and it was "not ethical to assist people to die by giving a lethal dose". There were 1328 people interviewed in the poll which was taken on May 22 and 23 and will be published in Time Australia this week.

21 Jun 1993 - Dip in consumer confidence Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 21 June 1993, page 2 Dip in consumer confidence Australian consumer confidence dropped for the third consecutive month in June to its lowest level since December, 1992, a poll of consumers has found. The Roy Morgan Consumer Confi-dence Rating, to be published in Time Australia this week, fell to 96.2 in June from 102.2 in May — the first time it has fallen below the key 100 mark this year. It said only 23 per cent of the 1282 people interviewed said they would be financially better off in a year's time compared with 30 per cent who were optimistic last month. About 21 per cent of those polled, or 3 per cent more than in May, said they expected to be worse off in another 12 months.

23 Jun 1993 - Support drops for Coalition, Hewson: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 23 June 1993, page 5 Picture: PETER WELLS A member of the Glow Worm Aboriginal dance group, Yulu Yulu Moonandgood, of Arnhem Land in the Northern Territory, entertains children at Lyons Primary School yesterday as part of activities marking Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Week. Support drops for Coalition, Hewson: poll Support for the Coalition and the Leader of the Opposition, John Hew son, has dropped and support for the Labor Party and the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, has risen, according to the latest AGB McNair poll. The poll, conducted earlier this month and published in The Bulletin today, shows a one percentage point drop in support for the Coalition and a one point rise in support for Labor since late May, taking the Govern ment to 47 per cent and the Opposi tion to 40 per cent. The increase for the ALP comes despite controversy about Mabo, the republican debate and the Budget. Support for the Democrats has dropped from 4 per cent to 2 per cent and support for independents was up one point to 6 per cent. The gap between the major parties has increased by two percentage points to seven points since May — the March 13 election result had sup-port for the ALP on 45.5 per cent and the Coalition on 43.7 per cent. The gap between Mr Keating and Dr Hewson as preferred Prime Min ister has also increased, the poll found.

30 Jun 1993 - Employers polled on enterprise bargains Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 30 June 1993, page 17 Employers polled on enterprise bargains By MIKE TAYLOR, National Affairs Writer The Department of Industrial Relations has retained the services of the polling firm <\GB McNair to determine what criiploycrs really think about enterprise bargaining. With the Minister for Industrial Relations, Laurie Brcreton, scheduled to make some key decisions about enterprise bargaining over the next two months, AGB McNair will canvass the views of 700 employers around Australia. The work is being carried out on behalf of the Research and Policy Development Branch of the department and is expected to be published before the end of the year. In a letter to employers, the department will seek their cooperation in a telephone survey to "provide a coherent and rigorous body of research to assist in informing debate and policy formulation regarding the nature and future direction of the wage-fixing system in Australia." The businesses approached by the department have been assured their responses will be confidential and that each is just one of 700 organisations who are expected to participate. "Your participation will involve a 20-minute telephone interview with a representative from AGB McNair, the interviewing agency," the letter said. "An interviewer from AGB will contact you by 'phone to arrange a suitable interview time over the next couple of weeks." A spokesman for the department yesterday confirmed that the survey was being undertaken and that the data would later be published as a monograph on enterprise bargaining. Those firms who take part in the survey will be sent a summary of the results. The commissioning of a survey of 700 firms on the question of enterprise bargaining represents a new approach to the subject by the department. Previous assessments of the system have been on the outcome of enterprise agreements. It is not clear whether the survey will cover firms of all sizes or whether it has been confined to medium to large enterprises. But the Metal Trades Industry Association claims that small to medium-sized firms would be reluctant to enter into enterprise agreements with their employees because of the time and resources needed for such a move. In a submission to the Government earlier this month, the association claimed that small manufacturing enterprises would not be attracted to enterprise bargaining, especially in circumstances where such arrangements required union involvement. At the same time the national secretary of the Federation of Industrial, Manufacturing and Engineering Employees, Steve Harrison has acknowledged that many small firms are unlikely to strike enterprise bargains. Discussing the compulsory involvement of unions as bargaining agents, Mr Harrison said that trade unions probably represented the majority of workers capable of being covered by enterprise agree ments. When non-union executive employees were subtracted from the equation along with employees in small businesses, most workers were probably subject to trade union representation, he said.

05 Jul 1993 - Popularity for Kennett fades Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 5 July 1993, page 2 Popularity for Kennett fades The popularity of the Premier of Victoria, Jeff Kennett, and support for the Liberal-National Coalition have fallen, according to the latest Morgan poll to be published this week in Time Australia. In June, support for the Victorian Coalition fell 6.5 per cent to 42 per cent while Labor's support rose 3.5 per cent to 45 per cent Mr Kennett's popularity slide follows his return from an overseas trip and his confrontation with the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, over the Mabo issue. Approval of the way Mr Kennett was doing his job fell 4 per cent to 38, and disapproval rose 2 per cent to 55. But despite Mr Kennett's fall in the poll, he remained the premier preferred by 48 per cent (down 1 per cent), against the former Victorian Leader of the Opposition, Jim Kcnnan on 36 per cent (up 3 per cent). Approval for Mr Kennan had risen one percentage point to 29 before he resigned last week. Labor retained the lead in the NSW poll which placed support for the Coalition Government at 40 per cent and for the Opposition at 46 per cent. Approval of Premier John Fahcy remained high at 52 percent, while Opposition Leader Bob Carr came in at 48 per cent (up 3 per cent). In Queensland, Labor remains comfortably in front with support at 47 per cent (down t per cent) and support for the Opposition Liberals was 25 percent.

07 Jul 1993 - Optus lags in opinion poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 7 July 1993, page 5 Optus lags in opinion poll SYDNEY: A new opinion poll showing Telecom Australia with a clear lead as favoured supplier of long-distance and international telephone services did not worry its rival, an Optus spokesman said yesterday. 14 Jul 1993 - Long-term tenure for Hewson rated low Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 14 July 1993, page 3 Long-term tenure for Hewson rated low By ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent The public is not convinccd by : assurances from the Leader of the Opposition.John Hcwson, that he will keep his job until the next elec tion. 21 Jul 1993 - Fischer will batten down, says Hewson Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 21 July 1993, page 1 Fischer will batten down, says Hewson By ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent Federal Opposition Leader John Hewson strongly rebuked his coalition partner Tim Fischer yesterday over comments on Israel, appearing to dismiss the National Party leader's defence that he had been misquoted. He said Mr Fischer accepted he had transgressed Coalition policy and claimed Mr Fischer would "bat■ ten down" and say no more on the subject — but Mr Fischer again called for an even-handed approach on UN Middle East resolutions. Mr Fischer caused a furore at the weekend when he said that Israel continued to defy a UN resolution by shelling villages in southern Lebanon. Israel's attitude to its Muslim neighbours was a major obstacle to Nationals Leader 'wouldn't say anything more' Australian trade and to peacc in the Middle East. It was time the West took off its "rose-tinted glasses". After speaking to Mr Fischer yesterday in Bangkok, Dr Hewson said the National Party Leader had agreed not to say anything more. "1 had emphasisedyesterday that what he said was not Coalition policy and he agreed with that this morning and said he would batten it down and wouldn't say anymore and that is it," Dr Hewson told commercial radio in Perth. "He claims to have been misrepresented by the media ... 1 will have a more detailed discussion with him later but he has assured me that he is 100 per cent behind Coalition policy and clearly the point he made we disagree with. ."I mean Israel is not the stumbling block and in that sense it isn't our policy." Earlier yesterday, Mr Fischer said he would not be cowed into submission on issues such as the Middle East and Mabo and blamed the media for the new row. Before leaving Bangkok last night for a meeting today of the National Party management committee in Brisbane, he said he was prepared to meet Mr Avner. Dr Hewson appears to have silenced Mr Fischer after his first attempt did not succeed. He had issued a statement on Monday night saying Mr Fischer's remarks were not Opposition policy and that he would confront Mr Fischer. Shortly after Dr Hewson's statement on Monday, Mr Fischer issued a statement to clarify his statements on Israel. But he continued his breach of Coalition policy, repeating his remarks about rosetinted glasses. Dr.Hewson took a different tack with Liberal dissenters who have refused to be silenced on complaints that the Liberal Party needs to open itself to more debate. He said all publicity for the Opposition was good news, even when it came from NSW Senator Bronwyn Bishop trying to build her public profile. His advice contradicts the message of Liberal Party federal director Andrew Robb, who warned this week that potential leadership aspirants should "pull their heads in" or face losing preselection. Dr Hewson has been trying to combat a perception that he is a temporary leader after defeating John Howard in a party room ballot after the election defeat. But the latest AGB McNair poll in today's Bulletin magazine shows Dr Hewson's approval rating down two points to 21 per cent. Dr Hewson called on the media to be responsible by focusing on issues apart from speculation about his leadership. "John Hewson will survive and I am not distracted by any of that," he said. "Focusing on me day after day is a bit of a blood sport in Canberra but focusing on me isn't going to create one more job."

23 Jul 1993 - Facts are all against smokers Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 23 July 1993, page 10 Facts are all against smokers T. G. LLEWELLYN, of Campbell (Letters, July 14) attacked your editorial "No fire on smokes" (CT, July 9) claimihg it to be a "one-eyed, bigoted, Dr Goebbels-style presentation". Llewellyn claimed that you had "not checked out the facts at all" in his/her tirade of support for the tobacco industry and smoking. In rebuttal, Llewellyn quoted "some real facts" which I have checked out. (1) "Smokers contribute $10 billion to governments, territory, state and federal." WRONG. Last year smokers contributed $1.3 billion in taxes to the Federal Government and $1.1 billion to territory and state governments (Source: Australian Tobacco Board Report) — a total of $2.4 billion in tax revenue" against an estimated $6.4 billion in annual costs caused by tobacco to the community. (2) "680,000 people are directly and indirectly employed with this legal product". WRONG. The Australian Bureau of Statistics in its reports on Manufacturing Industry, Details of Operations (Catalog No. 8203.0) records a significant decline in the number of people directly employed in the tobacco industry from 5150 in 1984-85 to around 3100 in 1988-89. In order to reach the figure quoted by Llewellyn, the number of people caused to be employed indirectly (tobacco retailers, shop assistants, advertising copy writers, etc) would have to be multiplied by 219 times — an unlikely scenario, even if all the doctors, nurses, priests and undertakers associated with deaths due to tobacco were included. (3) "One-third (33 per cent) of doctors smoke themselves". WRONG. Of all doctors, about 6 per cent smoke, the low est smoking rate of any occupational group in the community. Among young doctors, under 30 years, only 4 per cent smoke, indicating that doctors' smoking rates in the future will be even lower. (Source: Australian Cancer Society). (4) "One third (33 per cent) of the adult population smoke". WRONG. It is now only about 25 per cent and falling! (Source: Morgan Gallup Polls). Minister Wayne Berry and other MPs who share his determination to reduce death and disease levels due to smoking and to prevent the uptake of smoking by children deserve strong support. STEPHEN D. WOODWARD Executive director, ASH (Australia) Action on Smoking and Health

24 Jul 1993 - Labor notable 'floats' tax on tourism trade Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 July 1993, page 3 Labor notable 'floats' tax on tourism trade By TOM CONNORS A prominent Labor frontbencher, Wayne Swan, suggested yesterday that the Budget would include new taxes on tourist accommodation and restau-rants to help finance the rescheduled tax reductions. Chairman of the Caucus Economics Committee, he said on ABC TV's The World at Noon that indirect taxes on rooms and restaurants were consis-tent with Labor's progressive taxation philosophy and with the FitzGerald report, which saw such taxes as a way to increase government savings, Yesterday, the Treasurer, John Dawkins, declined to rule out including indirect taxes in next month's federal Budget, saying he was looking at "revenue adjustments". The shadow treasurer, Alexander Downer, said Mr Swan had "let... out of the bag" the Govern-ment's readiness to hit the tourist industry with new indirect taxes. This summed up the morality of Labor, which had used the Opposition's goods-and-scrvices tax to frighten the tourist industry in the election campaign and was now about to hurt it. The Australian Tourism Industi7 Association de-clared its stout opposition last night to extending indirect taxes to hotel accommodation, saying they would have a negative impact on the nation's fastest-growing industry. Its chief executive, Peter O'CIcry, said new taxes would represent an unwarranted impost on an in-dustry that could deliver export revenue and jobs. Mr Downer seized also on Mr Swan's reference to a jobs levy — those in work paying to help the unemployed — saying it implied higher taxes, but Mr Swan said the levy was not for consideration in the Budget. It could be discussed in the inquiry into long-term unemployment. Electoral consequences ; A pollster, Irving Saulwick, said the Govern-ment's rescheduling of income-tax reductions was unlikely to have adverse electoral consequences in the long term. People were not very' surprised that any govern-ment would break a promise.'At the next election the tax-reductions issue would be long forgotten. A recent Saulwick poll had found opinion evenly di-vided on whether the tax reductions should proceed. However, Prime Minister Paul Keating should "level with people" about the economy even if that were hard to do. It would win him support and respect. Australia was looking for honest leadership above all else. Opening a trade-union office in Sydney yesterday, Mr Keating denied Opposition charges that by res-cheduling the taxation reductions he had negated a central election plank. The reductions had rated "hardly rated a men-tion" in the campaign and had been only a back-drop. The campaign had been fought on how Australians lived and related to one another. The reductions would not only be paid but brought forward. They would be significant for peo-ple on two thirds of average income — $20,000 — and more. Reductions in the 1980s had* gone to those earning less than $20,000 and more than $45,000. Now it was the others' turn. The ACTU secretary. Bill Kelty, gave his support yesterday to the rescheduling, saying it was better to give them when the economy needed a boost than later when things might have picked up. "What you need at this stage is fiscal injection," he said.

14 Sep 1993 - Euthanasia excites the passionate minorities Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 14 September 1993, page 9 Euthanasia excites the passionate minorities Bv CRISPIN HULL NEWSPAPER journalists, especially those who do the letters pages, can tell a letter-writ ing campaign fairly quickly. The difference between the spontaneously spurred and vicariously stirred becomes apparent in what is written and how it is written. If committees of the ACT Legislative Assembly develop a similar nose, the euthanasia committee should cast 88 of its 130 submissions into the rubbish bin. The 88 submissions are all "concerned". They are all against the Bill. And they all make one or two brief unoriginal points. Euthanasia is against God's law; life is sacred; it legalises killing; a doctor's duty is to support life; and it will end in Nazi exterminations of the disabled. The other 42 submissions are made up as follows. For active euthanasia: two organisations and eight individuals. Against: 10 religious, three medical and three non-religious organisations, and 15 individuals who do not fit the "campaign" mould. The 88 "campaign" letters have no idea what a parliamentary committee is about. They imagine it is a voting procedure. Many of the submissions say: "I would like to vote against..". It shows, however, that even if the letter writers do not know what a committee is about, the people who organised them have a good idea what politics is about. On a head count, we have 12 to 1 against euthanasia. This figure will be bandied about, no doubt, in the ensuing debate. The figure is nonsense. A parliamentary committee is formed to inquire into details of a Bill. It is not a crude vote. If the Assembly wanted that, it would organise a referendum, money permitting. In the absence of that, properly conducted opinion polls are a better way to gauge public opinion. Even then, public opinion is not necessarily the best way to determine legislation. If it were, we would have capital punishment, corporal punishment and would castrate rapists. The most satisfactory aspects of Australian democracy are that the rule of law and responsible and representative government guard us from the crude emotions of the mob. This is why the committee should ignore the head count of the submissions and concentrate on the issues raised in them. Many make salient points about safeguards. Others make convincing arguments about the unsatisfactory and uncertain state of present law. Euthanasia is an issue, like gun control and abortion, that excites a minority of interested people into great passion such that people will change their vote on that issue alone, irrespective of their normal political predilections. Politicians tread warily on these issues. The minority is not only vocal, it is focal. It can truncate a targeted politician's career. So the majority view is ignored because it does not affect political outcomes, and the minority view is attended to. Politicians have watered down gun-control proposals in Victoria and NSW despite majority opinion and continuing multi-death shooting incidents. More recently, the ACT Government hid from the strident anti-abortion minority by disguising funding for a clinic. Independent menace On euthanasia, Labor has had it sleeping in its policy for a long time, but never acted upon until that independent menace Michael Moore came along and started to put Labor Party policy into private Member's Bills and demanded the Labor Party put its mouth where its policy platform was. Euthanasia, both passive and active, appears to be supported by large majorities in Australia, according to Morgan Gallup polling. On passive euthanasia a survey in May asked: "Next a question on people who are hopelessly ill and in great pain. If there is absolutely no chance of a patient recovering, should the doctor let the patient die or should the doctor try to keep the patient alive?" Seventy-three per cent said let the patient die. If in the same circumstance the patient asks for a lethal dose, should the doctor be allowed to administer it? Seventy-eight per cent said yes. That extra five per cent is interesting. It appears people do not like suffering and some plainly prefer active euthanasia rather than just sitting by letting a patient in great pain die. The trouble with such a poll, however, is that it is too hypothetical. It is not in the world of medical reality on several counts. Nowadays, pain management is, or should be, very good. Secondly, pain management and euthanasia are blurred issues. The very relief of pain through drugs can be come active euthanasia. Thirdly, the poll's question infers the pain is constant and that the patient's request for a lethal dose reflects a constant state of mind. Medical reality is different. Sporadic pain can induce a temporary wish by a patient to be put out of misery — a wish which later some patients might be glad was not fulfilled. Fourthly, what is "hopelessly ill with no chance of recovering" ? The 88 campaign letters and the Morgan Gallup poll show that the popular grasp of the euthanasia issue is clouded by religious prejudice or fairly crude. But the 42 other submissions show the complexity of the issue — in particular, the submissions on the doctors' and nurses' dilemma and the moving submission from the AIDS Action Council. So there is some hope of removing present uncertainties and hypocrisies that put the burden of decision on nurses and doctors and pretend that euthanasia does not happen. At least this debate has brought the issue out of the silence of the hospital wards. In doing so, it has uncovered some passionately held worries and widely held misconceptions which must be met. Maybe it is a case for a citizen's veto provision. If a euthanasia law (active and/or passive) passes the Assembly it could have a provision for, say, five per cent of the electorate (80190 people) to petition for a compulsory referendum (after a year or so of the law being in force) on whether the law should stay in force. Such a provision would give the 88 campaigners and their ilk a chance to see what community support they had and, after a year or so of such a law being in force, it would put some reality into the search for community opinion that is lacking in opinion polls.

15 Sep 1993 - PM continues to lose support Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 15 September 1993, page 20 PM continues to lose support SYDNEY: Haggling over the Budget and Federal Government back-downs resulted in a drop in the popularity of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, and the Labor Party, according to the latest Bulletin poll. The AGB McNair poll published in the Bulletin found Mr Heating's popularity as preferred prime minister fell five points to 31 per cent. The number of people who preferred the Opposition Leader, John Hewson, as leader rose four points to 38 per cent. That compared to 40 per cent preferring Mr Keating as prime minister in a poll taken in August and 33 per cent for Dr Hewson. Support for the ALP fell three points to 36 per cent. The Coalition figure was unchanged on 46 per cent. Support for the Greens and the Democrats rose to 7 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively. Mr Kealing's personal rating fell four points to 20 per cent, while his disapproval rating rose two points to 59 per cent. Dr Hewson's personal approval rating rose one point to 28 per cent, while his disapproval rating fell two points to 40 per cent.
