04 Dec 1993 - FEATURES Consensus on immigration policy in flux Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 4 December 1993, page 44 FEATURES Consensus on immigration policy in flux New detention rules may hinge on what the public will accept, says MARGO KINGSTON in an extract in a new book, "Protection or Punishment?" In 1990 Gerry Hand, Immigration Minister for barely three days, stood in the betting ring at Moo-nee Valley race track. "Between the second and third race some bloke got into me, physically, about the boat people." That bloke wanted Hand to send them back out to sea and bomb their boats. Boats of asylum-seekers had only just begun to trickle into Australia then, and Hand's introduction to the issue was the first of many bruising encounters with Australians on both sides of public opin-ion. Yet despite an escalating and passion- ale political debate about the Cambodian arid Chinese boat people, there was, until September 1993, no research on what Australians really thought. The Depart-ment of Immigration says it has done none, as do the Government itself, the Office of Multicultural Affairs and the Bureau of Immigration Research. Before a Saulwick Poll published on October 11 in The Sydney Morning Herald, Hand said he believed that if such research were done, 95 per cent of Australians would support detention, or worse, for the boat people. "That would flatten out a bit as their time in detention stretched out, but you'd still get an horrendous result." Opposition immigration spokesman Senator Jim Short agrees. When inter-viewed, he commented: There's a feeling out there that deten-tion is second best: first best would be turn them around and send them back. But gradually more people, especially when they realise there's only 700 of them, say to me that there's something wrong in a country like Australia when we detain old people and children for such a long time. These perceptions, shared by most po-liticians, help explain the dearth of poll- ing on the boat-people issue, and why neither side of the debate wishes to enlist public opinion in aid of their case. The Saulwick Poll confirmed these opinions. A telephone poll of 1000 voters on September 28, 1993, asked whether the boat people should be: (a) sent straight back home, despite what they say may happen to them; (b) assessed with all other migrants. The result: 44 per cent wanted boat people shipped out now (51 per cent of men and 37 per cent of women), while 46 per cent wanted them held in custody until processed (40 per cent of men and 52 per cent of women). Only 7 per cent said they should be allowed to stay (5 per cent of men and 8 per cent of women). However, the poll failed to put the other major options: to let the boat peo- ple held for more than three years free pending finalisation of their claims, or let them stay on humanitarian grounds in view of the length of detention. Gerry Hand: bruising encounters about asylum-seekers. There appears to be a shared fear by pro- and anti-detention forces that there is a dark underbelly of Australian opin-ion, fed by racism, resentment at outsid-ers demanding resources in desperately hard times, and fear of "queue jumpers" subverting our laws which, if prodded, could explode into an ugly, perhaps un-controllable, force in Australian politics. Professor of Politics at the Australian Defence Forces Academy Ian McAllister this year cited this fear as a major reason for bipartisanship in immigration policy. Discussing Australian attitudes to im-migration generally, McAllister noted that in simple yes/no polls immigration produced the lowest proportion of non-committal answers of any contem-porary political issue. In the 1990 Austra-lian election survey, only 2 per cent had no opinion on the issue, the same as capital punishment, followed by abortion (5 per cent). A majority of Australians thought im-migration had "gone too far". By contrast a majority of political candidates thought immigration levels were about right. Immigration has rarely been debated at a political level, and has never been a major post-war election issue. In the last Federal election, for example, both sides proclaimed a belief in high migration levels, with the Liberal Party proposing a short-term slow-down for strictly eco- nomic reasons. McAllister concluded that immigra-tion, along with Aboriginal land rights and capital punishment, was one of the small number of political issues about which voters expressed strong opinions at odds with the policies of their elected representatives, but which did not consti-tute part of the public debate between the political elite. He said: "When elite opinion and voter opinion are compared, some of the reasons for bipartisanship. on immigration are evi-dent. An absolute majority of voters wants to reduce the level of immigration and one-third are strongly of that view. Faced with such a decisive popular view, the only way to maintain a stable immi-gration policy is through bipartisanship and by an informal agreement between the political parties that it should not be placed on the political agenda. In the absence of party-political debate, succes- sive governments have been able to maintain what is effectively an unpopu-lar policy." Bob Hawke endorsed this view when launching James Jupp and Marie Kaba-la's The Politics of Immigration, with the gloss that the support of the ACTU had also been vital. "I don't think there is any other issue of importance on the Australian political agenda of which it can be said there is such an implicit pact between the two major groupings," he said. In Short's words, it is about "not scratching too hard". The 1988 attempt by John Howard to oppose high levels of Asian immigration on the ground it might impair social co-hesion, and the quashing of that line by a concerted media and political push, also illustrate McAllister's point. But this is not to say public opinion has no influence. Short exposes the judg-ments that participants in bipartisan deafness to public opinion have to make when he says: "We can't afford to go too far ahead of public opinion because it's counterproductive, not just to refugees and boat-people policy, but the whole of a positive, orderly, fair immigration pro-gram." If high immigration levels are unpopu-lar, then when we recall that boat people are not only Asian (traditionally a source of fear to many Australians) but also illegals, it is obvious to conclude that many Australians would want them shipped back quick smart to where they came from. Says McAllister: "I've never seen a thing on public opin-ion of detention for boat people: It's sim-ply not debated in a public-opinion context at a party political-level. There's a consensus to make it bipartisan be-cause it's a dangerous matter. Many people want the return of capital punish-ment too. Bipartisanship is a rational policy to avoid the danger." Associate lecturer in politics at the Australian Defence Force Academy Dr William Maley, an expert on refugee poli-cy, said he had "a nasty feeling that the public think detention is a damn good thing. People are too scared to conduct a poll, they're probably frightened that the redneck element will come through. Ig-norance is bliss." Seen in this light, the current policy of detention is itself way ahead of public opinion. Thus, the Government's decision to detain the boat people while processing their claims for refugee status according to law could have been exploited by the Opposition if the pact on immigration had not held. Says former Immigration Minister Clyde Holding, who is on the parliament-ary committee examining the detention policy: "There is a basic rule here — the last group off the boat cops the shit." He cited a 1948 poll which found that less than 50 per cent of Australians wanted to accept any Jews on ships wandering the world with no place to go. He added: "I get anti-Asian remarks from Greeks and Italians, particularly kids, who say "Why do you want all these Asians here - they're dirty, they smell, and they eat funny food." I say to them: "I was around when people said that about you." As far as most Australians are concerned, they wouldn't care less if you sank the boats. Anti-detention groups have made little impact on public opin-ion: in a period of high unemployment there's not much sympathy around for boat people." Hand, too, says he spent much of his time as minister justifying to voters his policy of allowing the boat people legal aid and access to the courts. "I got tackled in supermarkets and on the beach. But a lot of the reaction is knee-jerk, and that's what a poll would record. After talking it through, I even put doubts in the mind of a bloke who wanted to zap them half way to Indonesia." The chairman of the committee, West Australian Senator Jim McKiernan, said: "There's an element of racism in our community and it's turned against indi-viduals in Port Hedland [detention cen-tre] and then Asians in particular. Most racist people think all Asians are boat people. It's nowhere near a majority, but it is growing in hard times when people can't get a job." Howard Sattler, a West Australian commercial radio talk-back host with the strong view that the Government has been too easy on boat people, says callers, "especially those from lower socio-eco-nomic groups", ring "asking why the Government is looking after these illegals when they can't even access legal aid". Sattler commented: "They get legal, medical and housing assistance. We've got 4000 people on waiting lists for state housing here. Peo-ple say that, apart from the wire fence, Port Hedland detention centre is a very nice part of the world to be. When St Vincent de Paul launched an appeal for the Chinese boat people [let out by court order], people said, how come you're housing them in a men's refuge for homeless Australians you closed down a few years ago for lack of funds?" ---- Legal-aid questions ---- Short has also had lots of this feedback: "There's a lot of aggro at the idea that these people have access to the courts and legal aid. People say, 'They're not Austra-lian citizens, why should they walk in here and expect us to foot their legal bills?' " Norman Aisbett, a journalist on The West Australian with a long-standing commitment to humanising the plight of the boat people, says he has had little positive feedback from readers. "They don't seem to connect with the human misery of detention, for individuals or families," he says. "You can see how people distance themselves emotionally, I now understand how people could drive to work past concentration camps." Party-political bipartisanship on de-tention with due process continues, with the proviso that this year Short began speaking out strongly on the inhumane periods to which detention has stretched, and the need to consider setting the boat people free. His shift caused much angst in political circles, and symbolises a freak twist in the immigration debate caused by the ever lengthening detention periods of the boat people. Hawke said at the book-launch that the reason for bipartisanship was the great desire of Australian politicians to at-tempt to modify or neutralise prejudiced elements in the immigration debate "and to return to liberal democratic traditions of human equality and equal worth". The boat-people debate has split the consensus on what those words and ide-als actually mean. Proponents of continued detention say the process is fair, that Australia has a right to protect its borders and must send a message to other potential boat people that they needn't come if they are not genuine refugees. If they do, they will get due process and real refugees will be wel-come. Manipulation of the system by lawyers, they say, has been the main cause of an admittedly undesirable length of imprisonment. Church and welfare groups, lawyers, judges, and human-rights experts argue that the length of detention has become a form of torture, that innocent children and the elderly have been imprisoned without cause, and that Australia is now in breach of various international hu-man-rights treaties. The parliamentary committee consists of well-informed po- liticians, all generally pro-immigration, sympathetic to migrants' rights, and with excellent human-rights credentials. Yet it is deeply divided across party lines on continued detention for the boat people. Labor Members Mary Easson, of the NSW Right, and Laurie Ferguson, of the Left faction, both represent Sydney elec-torates with high ethnic numbers. They agree that many ethnic groups believe boat people should be sent home imme-diately. They are on opposite sides of the debate. Easson believes the deterrence theory is a nonsense, has deep moral concerns about detaining potential refugees, and fears for the psychological health of the boat people after so long behind bars. She said: "At some stage someone will do a doc-umentary and we will all be appalled that this has happened in our lifetime. If you asked people whether the boat peo-ple should stay locked up, they'd say "yes". But if you asked if they'd prefer that or releasing them into church care at no taxpayer expense they'd want the latter. Lots of people don't even know how long the boat people have been locked up!" Ferguson says immigration is "a sleep-ing issue, a big issue", and has to be handled extremely carefully. His ethnic constituents are incensed that they have so much trouble getting relatives into Australia because of its strict require- ments. "I can explain the system to them, and they accept it, but then they see boat people coming "through the back door" and they're angry. The Government must not be perceived as letting people stay without legitimate claims. If we don't stick by the rules there could be a very racist backlash. " The quality media too, has split. Edi-torially, The Canberra Times advocates release. The Australian is benign to re-lease, The Age ambivalent, and The Syd-ney Morning Herald strongly supportive of continued detention. All publish a di-versity of commentary on the issue. The ABC and SBS are sympathetic to the boat people, and give prominent coverage to the issue. McKiernan classifies broadsheet reac-tion as either "bleeding heart", or "inter-ested", and he'd like the debate to stay confined to quality media circles. Reflecting the theory of immigration pol-icy discussed above, he says: "There's very little interest from commercial TV or the tabloids. That's good. When the tabloids get interested that's when you get problems. There'd be even greater fears if they did public-opinion polls; that could build things up into real danger." The split in informed opinion has in-tensified in recent months, with the "set them free" forces gradually gaining the ascendancy. The current Immigration Minister, Nick Bolkus, is keenly and un-comfortably aware that his refusal to re-lease the boat people, an extremely painful decision for him personally, has been hailed by the rednecks. The increas- ing characterisation of the policy of con-tinued detention as "redneck" is a major weapon in the armoury of groups that want the boat people set free. Continued moral pressure is, finally, turning the tide of influential public opinion. The nor-mally stable consensus is in flux. The question could soon become not what is right, but will the general public wear the new consensus? Extracted from "Protection or Punishment? The Detention of Asylum Seekers in Australia", edited by Mary Crock, being published next week by The Federation Press. Other contributors include Senator Christabel Chamarette, Justice Marcus Einfeld and Justice Murray Wilcox. Paperback. 150 pages. $19.95.

06 Dec 1993 - Keating's lead over Hewson grows: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 6 December 1993, page 2 Keating's lead over Hewson grows: poll Prime Minister Paul Keating's lead over Opposition Leader John Hewson as preferred prime minister increased in the latest Morgan poll, while support for federal Labor also rose. But the poll, to be published in this week's Time magazine, showed the Coalition still held a comfortable lead. Coalition support in late November fell 2.5 percentage points to 46 per cent, with Labor up 1.5 points to 38.5, the Democrats up 0.5 to 5.5 per cent, the Greens down 0.5 to 4.5, and other parties and independents up one to 5.5 per cent. On a two-party preferred basis, the Coalition held a 53.5-46.5 lead, down 2.5 points since the previous poll in early November. Mr Keating's preferred PM rating rose one to 43 while Dr Hewson's fell three to 40, with 17 per cent undecided or naming someone else. The poll of 3147 electors interviewed face-to-face was held over the weekends of November 20-21 and 27-28. • A former Prime Minister, Malcolm Fraser, told a conference at the weekend that the federal National and Liberal Parties had deserted the bush. Mr Fraser also criticised the policies of the federal Labor Party, but kept some of his most pungent barbs for the federal Opposition parties. "Both have deserted the bush. Both have deserted their basic constituency," he said of the Liberal and National Parties.

22 Dec 1993 - Almost half oppose new flag by 2000 Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 22 December 1993, page 5 Almost half oppose new flag by 2000 SYDNEY: Almost half of Austral-ians would prefer to wave the existing Australian flag at the 2000 Olympics, a poll has found. The AGB McNair poll, to be pub-lished in this week's Bulletin, found that 45 per cent of Australians were against changing the flag before 2000. Forty-one per cent of the 2050 people surveyed supported the change. Although 14 per cent were unde-cided on changing the flag by 2000, 58 per cent were opposed to changing the flag now. The poll was conducted be-fore the winner of a flag-design compe-tition had been announced in Canberra last week. The Bulletin asked people to choose their favourite flag from eight designs provided by Ausflag, a non-profit group promoting a new flag. Less than a quarter (21 per cent) said that they did not fancy any of the designs. Design Number 7 — similar to the flag that won an Ausflag contest last Friday — also attracted the sup-port of 21 per cent. The flag that won $25,000 and first place in the Ausflag contest featured stylised depictions of the Southern Cross and Uluru in red, white and blue. It was designed by Mark Tucker and beat 20,000 other entries. However, another poll run by The Bulletin in December found a clear preference for a native motif to be included in any potential flag. Other designs shown to those sur-veyed included varying combinations of the Southern Cross, Eureka stars, kangaroos and sun patterns on differ-ent coloured backgrounds.

05 Dec 1994 - Most Aussies investing, says poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 5 December 1994, page 2 Most Aussies investing, says poll SYDNEY: Nearly two thirds of Australians own some kind of financial investment, according to a new Morgan poll. In 1991 only 50 per cent owned some sort of investment. This increased to 52 per cent in 1992, 57 per cent in 1993, and 60 per cent this year. In 1994, 42 per cent of investors had money invested in superannuation or retirement funds, representing an increase of 3 per cent over last year. That was followed by 10 per cent (up 1 per cent) owning shares, 8 per cent owning real estate (up 1 per cent), and 7 per cent owning trusts (also up 1 per cent). The details, to be published in this week's Time magazine, showed that higher-income earners were more likely to own shares than real estate. The survey was based on interviews with 36,556 Australians, aged 14 and over, between October 1993 and September this year.

12 Dec 1994 - Consumer confidence at a 1994 low, survey reveals Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 12 December 1994, page 3 Consumer confidence at a 1994 low, survey reveals Caution on financial prospects Consumer confidence has fallen to its lowest level of the year in the lead-up to Christmas, according to a poll released yesterday. The poll, to be published in this week's Time magazine, showed the Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence rating down marginally at 118 points — one-tenth of a point below the November rating and 10 points lower than the peak in June. It found Australians remained optimistic about the future of the economy but held less hope for their own financial prospects. In the next year, 42 per cent (up 5 per cent) expected the economy to improve, while 25 per cent (up 1 per cent) thought the economy would worsen. In the.long term, 36 per cent (up 4 per cent) expected good economic conditions in the next five years, while 19 per cent (down' 1 per cent) expected bad times. When asked to compare their personal financial situation now with one year ago, an unchanged 35 per cent said they were better off now, while 29 per cent (down 1 per cent) said they were worse off. In the longer term, 32 per cent of respondents (down 4 per cent) expected to be better off in a year's time and a steady 11 per cent thought they would be worse off. Fifty-one per cent (down 3 per cent) thought December was a good time to buy a major household item — the lowest score since September 1993 — while 22 per cent (up 4 per cent) said it was a bad time. For the poll, 1055 people were interviewed on December 3 and 4.

22 Dec 1994 - MARKET FORCES Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 22 December 1994, page 13 .. [A ,WEEKLY COMMENTARY ON BUSINESS, INVESTMENT AND THE ECONOMY, Tt-v.i'ivi: ftr'/T' $Sfib2f*lu*LCi5kjSliaie#£#a»3^^ «0a Uphill battle of breaking into politics and business By ANN HENDERSON Australian women brace yourselves. Your merit levels arc set for a rapid rise. Korn Ferry International's latest report from the responses of UOO women suggests that the "glass ceiling" has risen just a little. The women surveyed earn more than $80,000 a year and are corporate and public sector managers. They acknowledge there are still hurdles. But they are more confident about opportunities. All this though at the expense of family life. Over half have no children and 21 per cent have never married. The debate over women's representation among the nation's leaders, whether in business or politics, has hotted up. Labor has adopted quotas to give women candidates 35 per cent of winnable scats by 2002. Rejecting quotas, the Liberals say they will match this and do even better. No level of leadership is without fault. According to Paul Keating, female representation in local politics at 20 per cent is not good enough. Raising Our Voices, a survey of trade unions in South Australia by the University of Adelaide, wants more women officials to stem the tide of falling membership, even increase it. And business leaders, such as Paul Simons of Woohvorths, are openly admitting the need for big business to create a female friendly corporate culture. At the Liberal Federal Council meeting in Albury in October, Alexander Downer scoffed at the Labor Party's quota decision saying it "patronised" women. He declared, "'10 per cent of our Victorian Liberal Senators are women. Each of those women knows she is there in the Senate because she is good. That will always be the Liberal way." In Western Australia, Premier Richard Court, also against quotas, says WA Liberals can expect a 50-50 gender balance within five years; Margaret Guilfoyle. John i-Iowa'rd, Kate Carnell and Judith Moylan also reject quotas saying Liberal women will increasingly take seals on merit over the next few years. For all their criticism of quotas, the' Liberal Party, like the Labor Party, is clearly moving to enhance the number of women in its parliamentary ranks. Women activists, such as Margaret Guilfoyle and Joan Kirner, are working hard to promote the election of women candidates. The National Liberal Women's Forum, launched- in August 1993, will encourage more Liberal women to stand for pre-selection. Joan Kirner has a proposal before Labor's National Executive that will create an Australian "EMILY'S List" (Early Money Is Like Yeast) (on the US model) to raise money and assist women to stand for Labor preselection.' It would work along British lines to sponsor women for preselection, collecting funds from women and distributing amounts to select candidates. In the British Labour Party, money raised is used to help candidates with everything from travel and training to childcare. Contests for selection offer women further opportunities to test their electioneering skills. In the electorate the feeling is growing that parliaments with only token women are unacceptable. A Saulwick poll conducted in late October, found that 52 per cent of interviewees (75 per cent of the women) favoured the ALP's quotas. MOST felt that more women in parliament would im prove its behaviour and make for better government. Culture change is coming for business too. In Trials At The Top, a recently released report from the Melbourne Business School by Amanda Sinclair, II top execut ives bare their corporate souls — Frank Blount (Telecom), Philip Brass (Pacific Dunlop). Hie Chari ton (Shell), Warren Haynes (ICI). Stuart Hornery (Lend Lease), Bob Joss (Westpac), Don Mercer (ANZ), John Prescott (I3HP), Fergus Ryan (Arthur Andersen), Paul Simons (Woolworths) and Bob Slagle (Alcoa). Much of what they have to say makes depressing reading, especially for a woman or the parent of a daughter. Overall though, the fact that these very senior men. in their very male bastion, contributed so frankly and reflectively is a start. All agreed business needs massive culture change and it won't be easy. But at least 11 corporate heavies are ready, and have even begun, to try. The forces for change, as Amanda Sinclair defines them, are twofold. Firstly directives can come from the executive that things be done differently. This is called "from the outside in". Trials At The Top recommends a variety of ways to action such change. For one of the executives interviewed it boiled down to whether his organisation could appoint a woman executive and "accommodate her desire to pursue a profession and have a child... I don't want anybody in the organisation to think somehow that that's going to be a problem. To me that's going to be an opportunity." Then there's change "from the inside out". This is one of the most powerful motivators. It conies, according to Sinclair, "as a result of individual executives rethinking their attitudes and values, their identity itself, including their masculinity, as a result of discussions and even crises with women who are close to them [particularly daughters)". As one of the CEO participants in Sinclair's study put it, "Somewhere behind me is a group of middle management men, who are really coming to grips with the fact that ... their daughters are at economic risk in the kind of societies that we're creating, and that is ultimately going to change the way these white male managerial cultures deal with women." LIKE any culture shift the in gredients are mixed, from self-interest to altruism. But all those involved in spearheading the change are convinced the organisations that undergo change will be better places because of it. Rob Ferguson, chief executive of Bankers Trust Australia, told ABC TV Latelim recently that change was important "because I think you get a better balanced organisation, you get more creativity. It's not one-sided. You get the feminine coming out in males when there arc females around". There arc going to be tussles, bruised egos and some who will have to face up to moving aside for the women as change now seems inevitable. Take the contest for Labor preselection in the Melbourne seat of Jagajaga. La Joan Kirner: working to create an EMILY's list. bor activist Pete Steedman lost to Jenny Macklin. In his view, "tlie boys — basically a couple of sitting senators who run the factions" had divvied up the seats to male colleagues ahead of the new quota rule. He was .left to contest the only seat available and face a woman as well. Said. Pete, "If Brian Howe thinks Jenny is so fantastic why doesn't he give her his scat?" But for Susan Ryan, the quota move is the .only way to bring women forward. She told the "Women, Power and Politics" conference in October, "The difference the rule change will make is that women will be able to get into the contest ... and electoral success by women candidates on one side will inevitably result in more female candidates on the other side." This has certainly been the effect of EMILY's List, the Democratic Political Action Committee, in the US. In the 1992 Congressional elections. EMILY's List money. which grew in the wake of the Anita Hill case, helped elect a record number of women. Democrat women in the House of Representatives almost doubled, from 19 to 36. and in the Senate they went up from 9 to 12. The success of EMILY's List has encouraged its rivals. Republican women are organising too. In January 1992. Glenda Greenwald set up the WISH List and raised $180,000 in six months. There is also the National Republican Coalition for Choice, and Ann Stone's Republicans for Choice. . As CEOs and managers, political leaders and activists, and just plain mums and dads realise though, the long haul for women is still all uphill. Raising Outvoices, shows that while childless men and women are equally active in unions, men's activity increases as women's decreases with the birth of each child. In part this comes as the financial demands of a growing family motivate a man to work for the union to protect his livelihood. Women, caught with child rearing, fall back to part-time work. But married men can also use in volvement with the union to avoid domestic drudgery. Many managers realise that workplaces need to become more family friendly. For Bob Slagle of Alcoa it's a case of recognising that issues of family and work intersect. He told Lateline in November, "I believe there are a lot more men who arc starting to understand that in families there are shared responsibilities. That is going to make some men a lot more conscious. of what women are going through in the workplace." Rob Ferguson feels part of the problem is the dominant culture, made by males. "It is something males have made ... to sort of measure himself by the physical effort that he puts in ... be there for 12 hours a day otherwise you. are not really striking a blow." SURVEYS point to the problem of enculturation. Many talent ed women lack confidence while male counterparts stride on with often fewer qualifications. This shows up in Horn Ferry!s Towards 2000; Women Executives in Australia, Trials at The Top and Raising Our Voices. For women, married and mothering, combining corporate and family life is tough. Anne Keating, unmarried and general manager of United Airlines in Australia, says "1 don't think you can do both, not successfully." However, the daughters of the next generation, and some of their fathers, are hoping Ms Keating is wrong. Orange County squeezed for funds The bankruptcy has sent shockwaves around the nation, says JOHN DURIE in New York. AS ORANGE County liq uidates its $US7.5 (SA9.7) billion investment fund Wall Street is waiting nervously to see if any other counties will also suffer similar losses. The bankruptcy filing earlier this month by the fourth biggest and one of the richest municipalities in the country was a seminal event on Wall Street. The county was a victim of the increase in short-term interest rates this year which left it on. the wrong end of a bond market which has lost over 15 per cent in value this year. It also came as Wall Street worries about an expected 10 per cent fall in stock prices over the next few months. With the bond market rout nearly over and stocks yielding just 2.8 per cent, investors can get much bettor returns from bank certificates of deposit offering 4.5 per cent for three months notes and over 7 per cent for Government two-year treasury notes. The fixed-income market simply offers too much competition. The municipal bond market, hard hit this year was looking for a return to better times with the How of new paper slowing to about half this year's level of SUS130 (SA170) billion in new bonds. Some analysts say municipalities will now have to pay a premium to raise'new money. Hut Joe Deane, municipal bond fund manager at Smith Barney, says that if this happens it Vill be restricted to those municipalities already in trouble. "The overall fundamentals will overcome the distraction of Orange County and drive prices higher," he said. The fact that it used derivatives to leverage its investments three to one made matters worse and added to the confusion among individual investors. It also raises the risk of regulation of the derivatives market. Derivatives are simply financial instruments which derive their value from something else but range in potency enormously and in a market of changing interest rates can cause wild swings in returns. .Jim Leach, the incoming chairman of the House Hanking Committee noted recently "what is being ducked by everyone is the issue of accountability, who is responsible for disasters like this." Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt has however come out strongly against the need for further regulation saying existing controls are adequate. lie will huwever use the Or i ange County bankruptcy to boost ins push for more public disclosure in the municipal bond mar ket. Over the last four years the Orange County investment fund run by Bob Citron was a star in the municipal finance world, earning 9 per cent returns, double the level achieved by most other munic ipalities. . Tl,e f«nd was used primarily to invest tax receipts and other county funds until they were needed for county works. lis l°sseS could total as much as SUS2 ($A2.6) billion will mean liicieased taxes for the county which confidently expected to • earn at least $US150 ($A200) million from its investments to help fund its $US3.7 ($A5) billion an nual budget. Citron was fired, and the county is now waiting to assess the full losses while its financial ad- . viser Salomon Brothers liquidates the rest of its portfolio. At risk are big projects in the .I'ke the planned $US3 ' ""lion expansion by Walt Disney of its landmark theme patk at Anaheim in the county. Disney said it would only invest the money if the county gave it some financial help. THE COUNTY is also fight ing to keep its football franchise, the LA Rams, out its team owners have said it will need to build a new stadium a the team is to stay in town. But the wider impact is per haps more dramatic. Professor. Robert Lamb from New York University said "it's a watershed event in terms of monitoring derivative risk exposure and raises important questions' about municipal oversight." Ironically cities like New York which nearly went bankrupt in the 1970s are protected from derivative risk because under the terms of its financial settlement it is restricted in how it invests its money. But others in California and Texas may be risk. Lamb noted "you will not see losses until they, arc declared. They are hidden, buried as the counties wait for the market to turn." Orange County was not the lirst to suffer from the increase in short-term interest rates. Bankers Trust recently agreed to submit to more Federal Reserve Board oversight after being hit with a wave of litigation from customers over derivative instruments it sold them. Earlier this year hedge fund Askin Capital collapsed when it was also hit by rising interest rates. Michael Metz, equity strategist at Oppenheimer and Co declared Change County is a seminal event marking the final stages of individual disenchantment with financial instruments." Already small investors have grown wary of financial markets, yanking some $40 billion from bond mutual funds and new investments in equity funds have slowed dramatically from the average inflows of $US10 ($A13) billion a month over the past two years. In November, there was actually an outflow of money from equity funds and in December new investments have slowed to a trickle. The average equity fund has lost 5.4 percent in the year to December 8 and bond funds have lost 3.4 percent. With the Federal Reserve Board keeping interest rates, artificially low in 1992 and 1993 to allow corporate America time to repair balance sheets left tattered by the 1980s debt binge, individual Americans poured money into mutual funds seeking better returns. In the US, home mortgages are tax deductable but with mortgage rates low there was little incentive in putting more money into houses when better returns were to be had in stocks and bonds. But this boom came to an end in February when the Federal Reserve Board started increasing interest rates. While short-term interest rates are expected to increase from, 5.5 per cent to at least. 7 per cent by the middle' of next year, there may well be more derivative casualties. Wall Street is hoping the worsl is over and points to the relative ly stable long-term interest rates as a positive sign. Time will tell. Shake-up looms in foreign investment By RICHARD GILBERT THE RECENT tabling in the Senate of the Foreign Investment Review Board's annual report highlights yet again how the foreign investment issue remains in a state of (lux. However, compared to the rather torrid Senate committee inquiry into FIRB's procedures, the tabling of the report was a decidedly low-key affair. The FIRB report makes only a passing remark about the Senate committee's 400-page report, which concluded that the FIRB's processes should be more open and transparent "to meet modern standards of accountability in public administration". It recommended that the board be replaced by a new statutory body, to be known as the Foreign Investment Commission and that there be a clear statutory deliniation between the powers of the F1C and the Treasurer. It further recommended that in judging the merits of foreign investment proposals the FIC take into account the interests of potential domestic investors. Had the board exercised its right to respond to the committee's findings, it would not have been operating outside its charter. The FIRB did not respond to the committee's critical assessment that the FIRB's procedures were conducted 'with an excessive preoccupation with secrecy". The FIRB report informs the reader that, in addition to making recommendations on particular foreign investment proposals, the board has a mandate "to advise the government on foreign investment matters generally". It could be that the FIRB has already, secretly, provided the government with advice on the Senate committee's-proposals for its reform. It is also possible that the next FIRB report will give an indication of the board's position. Perhaps the FIRB's heavier-thanusual case load, up 40 per cent on the previous year, and the commitment, of FIRB resources to the Senate inquiry has meant, that the board's development of advice on longer-term foreign investment policy has suffered. The FJRB report might be light in its general coverage, but its attention to statistical detail on foreign investment trends is laud able. During 1993-94 the FIRB considered 5287 applications worth a staggering S23.5 billion. The low rejection figure of $0.1 billion may have been greater had 384 proposals not been withdrawn before lodgment. FIRB also reported that, whilst much of its additional caseload could be attributed to the relatively-easy-to-process real estate proposals, its additional workload has extended processing time from 15 to 17 days — a significant change in tlie timeliness of FIRB service. It is therefore a feature of FIRB's operations which will need to be monitored closely. Four of our top six foreign investors are Asian The sector-by-sector breakup of approvals overwhelmingly shows that_ foreign investors have an interest in acquiring Australian real estate ($8.1 billion). Next in line is mineral exploration and development ($2.7 billion) followed by tourism $2.3 billion), manufacturing (SI.8 billion) and services ($1.6 billion). The value added by way of expected additional investment after acquisition provides a useful indicator of the multiplier impact of foreign investment. The leading value-added sectors are: • Tourism (82 cents of additional investment expenditure per dollar of original investment) • real estate (34 cents), and • manufacturing (11 cents). The FIRB continues to take a "restrictive" approach to granting approval for the acquisition of developed residential real estate. Its practice is to approve applica tions From foreign nationals who intend living in Australia for periods exceeding 12 months and foreign corporations buying a residence for their executives. It is a condition of such grants that the property be sold when no longer used for that purpose. The report contains little evidence of any FIR13 action being taken following the detection of a breach of any such approvals, although it advises that the government has the power to force divestiture and to- impose "substantial financial and penal sanctions for the unapproved acquisition of property". Country of origin data for foreign capital inflows mirrors the changing relationships between Australia and its spheres of economic and cultural influence. The latest figures show that four of the top six investors are in Asia. However, in just four years Japan's interest in Australian investment has slipped from $5 billion to $1.5 billion. Singaporean investment has gone from $0.2 billion to S2.8 billion in the same period. Britain's slice of Australian investment has almost halved in four years (S2.9 billion to $1.6 billion), whereas the US share has slightly increased from $3.9 billion to $4.4 billion. With a Federal poll looming, and with the Government, Coalition and Democrats all clamouring for reform of some sort for FIRB, it is distinctly possible that the next report will include details of a redesigned FIRB. Will it (as the Senate Print Media report surmised) take on a more publicly accountable line when it comes to scrutinising the more sensitive foreign investment proposals? Will it have a public register of all its proposals? Will the board change its stance on the receipt of information from applicants and be more discriminating in its acceptance of commercial information which winds up clothed in secrecy forever? And, will FIRB advice to the Treasurer be made public before its dispatch to the Treasurer? Richard Gilbert is a parliamentary officer in the Department of the Senate.

09 Sep 1995 - All in the wording Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 September 1995, page 20 All in the wording WHO IS Travyn Rhall (Letters, September 4) trying to kid when he/she asserts that the Roy Morgan Research Centre poll on euthanasia was no "trick". The question asked was, "If a terminally ill patient, suffering unbearably, with no chance of recovery, asks for a lethal dose, so as not to wake again, should a doctor be allowed to give a lethal dose or not?" 09 Sep 1995 - Saturday FORUM Learning to live with Jeff Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 September 1995, page 14 Saturday FORUM DENIS MULLER looks at Premier Jeff Kennett's performance and asks has he been good for Victoria. Learning to live with Jeff IN THE 19th century, jeffing was printers' slang for a crude form of gambling. And in the United States, Jeff meant a Southern rustic or hick. Twentieth century southerners in Australia have given a whole new meaning to the word. To be Jeffed in contemporary Victoria means to be fiscally kneecapped. There have been bumper stickers asking, "Have you been JefTed lately?" Sentiments like these were provoked by the severe' Budget cuts, especially in education, health and local government, that have characterised the Kennett Government's first term in office. • $300 million in school education, with nearly one-fifth of the state's government-sector teachers ■ taken out of the system; • a controversial new budgeting system for hospitals based on the mix of cases handled, which has put pressure on hospitals to in- crease the throughput of patients, and shifting much of the post-operative care on to families and the district nursing service; ' ® the number of local councils reduced from 210 to 78 in 15 months with estimated initial annual savings of $320 million. And then there have been the taxes. From one of the most lightly taxed states under Labor, Victoria has become by far the most heavily taxed. The biggest revenue bonanza has been the new casino. By August next year it will have contributed an estimated $257 million in licence fees to the state revenue base. The bottom line is that in the Budget handed down this week, the deficit for 1995-96 is put at only $344.5 million. It was $1.7 billion in Labor's last year in office. All this has been good for the image of Victoria: Kennett and his Treasurer, Alan Stockdale, have been at pains to promote it as fiscally responsible, a good place to •do business; Standard and Poor's has sent congratulatory messages; Moody's has inched the state's credit rating up from A1 to AA2. Business thinks it is terrific. A survey by the University of NSW I for Price Waterhouse this year 1 rated Victoria the best state for economic policy and management. But what has been the lot of the ordinary citizen? Well, his or her job prospects are somewhat brighter. The Budget states that unemployment has fallen from its peak of 12.8 per cent in August," 1993, to 8.7 per cent in June this year, with an increased participation rate. However, economic growth is predicted to slow from the present ■1.75 per cent to 3.50 over the coming year. The state's economy, with its heavy reliance on manufacturing, is seen by outside analysts such as Access Economics as structurally weak because of a lack of capacity in mining, re' source-processing and tourism. The Kennett strategy has been to focus on building up Victoria's natural strengths as a centre of educational and research excellence, and as a producer of highquality foodstuffs. There has also been a sustained campaign to win a larger share of tourists, with naked pressure being exerted (successfully) on Qantas to land more aircraft here. The ordinary citizen appears to be remarkably sanguine about the effects of the Kennett policies. A survey of parents in The Age this week — although pilloried by the Labor Party on methodological grounds — nonetheless contained unmistakable signs that the education cuts have not been seen as damaging the quality of the service. Now there has undoubtedly been some quality lost in the areas of special programs and non-core activities. But the community plainly does not buy the arguments from the teachers' union that increased class sizes — from the low to high 20s — has diluted educational quality. So while the cuts have hurt — and they have hurt those who use the state services of education and health more than those who use private services — there is a sense of resignation that they were necessary and inevitable. Kennett has played on this sentiment with unerring political skill. The public's real concern with the Kennett Government is about style. Jeff Kennett deliberately cultivates the image of a leader who is not driven by the latest opinion poll, a can-do man impatient with the fripperies and niceties of process and consultation. In his Alfred Deakin lecture a couple of weeks ago he described his vision for Victoria as the home of a "commonsense revolution". This revolution is to be driven by higher national savings, infrastructure development and the Ricardian notion of comparative advantage. Above all, it is to 6 At the new casino, the taxpayers inflict the pain on themselves. 9 be driven by a culture of individualism and free enterprise. There is no room in this vision for identifying a collective will. "I remain critical of governments that don't govern and leaders who are influenced more by consensus than leadership." No-one would accuse Kennett or his Government of indulging in a surfeit of community consultation. But even in this, Kennett has struck a chord in the electorate. By the time of its demise, the previous Labor government had become hostage to a plethora of factions, lobbies and interest groups. Nowhere was this better illustrated than in education, where the unions and umbrella organisations claiming to represent parents and school councils had the policymaking process by the throat. The Kennett Government simply refused to deal with them. One problem with this strategy, however, is that eventually the demands of governing mean you have to start rebuilding relationships like this or it becomes increasingly difficult to implement policies on the ground. Another problem is that once the community perceives an arrogance in its government, there is a reaction. It is happening in Victoria and its focus is the Grand Prix. A broad and gentle park with a lake and lots of mature trees just outside the city's central business district is not an obvious place to build a Formula One race track. However, this is what the Kennett Government has done, insisting that despite the loss of some hundreds of trees (the actual figure is in dispute), the park will be a better place when the work is finished. Above all, the Grand Prix will be good for the economy. More substantial protests, however, have been raised by people who own houses nearby. The vast earthworks involved in making the track have destabilised some nearby houses, causing cracks in the walls and damage to roofs. Foreseeing the possibility that it might be sued for damages, the Government built into the Grand Prix legislation a limitation on the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to deal with damages actions arising from the work. This has put the Government in the position of being able to confront aggrieved residents with a take-it-or-leave-it offer of compensation. The Government has also resort ed frequently to making laws which immunise its actions from review by the courts. The Grand Prix, the casino, massive changes to the structure of local Govern ment, education and the hospital system have all been driven by legislation which limits the extent to which the courts can be used to challenge what the Government has done, and to award damages. There has also been some alarm about the Government's propensity for bulldozing aside the conventional and legal restraints on executive power, and so emasculate those whose job is to hold govern ments to account. An attempt was made — and subsequently abandoned — to nobble the Director of Public Prosecutions by making his decisions subject to review by his deputy. This followed a warning from the director to Kennett that he risked prosecution for contempt of court for commenting on a murder case. In the end, .the DPP's powers were more modestly curtailed. The director no longer has control of prosecutions for contempt, and control of the money for his office has been taken out of his hands. Very early in its life, the Kennett Government sacked the judges of the Accident Compensation Tribunal as part of a shake-up of the workers' compensation system. The Government argued that they were not "real" judges, but the legal profession was dismayed by the implications for judicial independence. There has been criti cism of reductions in the powers. of the Ombudsman and AuditorGeneral and of the abolition of the Public Service Board. Whatever you say about Jeff, however, he looks set to stay for a while yet. The spectre of Labor's last years are still fresh in the mind: the Pyramid Building Society collapse, the collapse of the Tricontinental merchant bank which led to the sale of the State Bank, the scandals embroiling the state-run Victorian Economic Development Corporation. The latest opinion poll, by AGB McNair in The Age, shows the Government maintaining a ninepoint lead over the Opposition, with Kennett miles ahead of Opposition Leader John Brumby as preferred Premier. The, next election is likely sometime in the next six months. The ALP might claw back a few of its "natural" seats, but opinion is that Jeff will be back so there will be plenty of scope for more Jeffing over the next four years. * Denis Muller is a Senior Research Associate in the Centre for Public Policy at the University of Melbourne.

11 Sep 1995 - End Easton inquiry today: Keating Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 11 September 1995, page 1 End Easton inquiry today: Keatin; By MICHAEL BACHELARD The Opposition Leader, John Howard, was "weak and sneaky" for not commenting on recent statements by the commissioner investigating the Easton affair, the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, said yesterday. Mr Keating called a press con-ference to tell reporters that Mr Howard had "sustained a major political defeat" at the WA Royal commission when the commis-sioner, Kenneth Marks, QC, had admitted that he had been put in an "irrecoverable" position be-cause the inquiry had "become almost impossible to control in an objective sense". Mr Keating said that in the light of the com-ments, the Western Australian Royal commission should be wound up today. The Health Minister, Carmen Lawrence, is due to give evidence on Wednesday. Mr Marks said on Friday that he was not enjoying the inquiry because it was so political and because he regarded himself as independent. Mr Keating said Mr Howard was "up to his neck" in the mat-ter. "Having lit the fuse with Richard Court, it's blown up on them and now when he's been asked twice in two days he says, 'I've got nothing more to say Coalition increases lead in latest Morgan poll Chanccs of a 1996 federal election seem more likely with the latest opinion poll put-ting the Liberal/National coalition nine points ahead of the ALP Government. The Morgan poll to be published in this week's The Bulletin magazine showed the Opposi- tion had 54.5 per cent of the two-party pre-ferred vote to the ALP's 45.5 per cent. The poll was held in late August/early Septem-ber after two weeks of Parliament had been dominated by Carmen Lawrence's role in the Easton Affair. Primary support for La- bor was down two points to 38 per cent, while the Coalition gained 1.5 points to 47 per cent. On the question of preferred prime minister, support for John Howard was up a point to 46 per cent and Paul Keating dropped two points to 41 per cent. about this.' He asked 31 out of 37 questions on this in the last two weeks ... and now he's seeking to run away from it." Mr Howard refused to comment on the issue to journalists on Sat-urday, saying he would not give running commentaries on the commission, but would wait for the final report. "And so Mr Howard might think he's slick, moving around dodging press conferences, door-stops, accountability about the policies, the directions in which he would lead Australia, but he owes an explanation to the Aus-tralian public," Mr Keating said. The WA Cabinet is to decide to-day whether it. should extend the commission at the request of Mr Marks, but Mr Keating said it should finish today. Mr Keating has called the com- mission a "kangaroo court" and said yesterday that Mr Marks's comments all but showed he agreed with him. But he refused to comment on his earlier statement that Mr Marks was the "cat's paw" of the WA Premier. "I'm not here to discuss the commissioner, but I am here to discuss the process. "All that's happened here is that the value of Royal commis-sions as an institution in this country has been substantially di-minished, where they've provided a very useful basis of garnering information in certain circum-stances, they're here being abused, and as a consequence they are less effective," he said. One of Mr Marks' complaints had been the pressure he had been placed under because of the political "hornet's nest" the com-mission had stirred up. Mr Keating did not accept any re-sponsibility for this. "When a bad act is clone, bad things happen. "The bad act was the political wilfulness and motivation of Court and Howard in getting this commission up and running." Mr Howard asked in a state-ment whether Mr Keating was frightened of the truth coming out. "Is that why he wants the Eas-ton Royal commission closed down before the Health Minister gives evidence?" he asked. Industry Minister Peter Cook said Dr Lawrence should have the chance in court to rebut the allegations against her. She would come out stronger for it.

11 Sep 1995 - There are tricks in every trade Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 11 September 1995, page 10 There are tricks in every trade IN ANSWER to Travyn Rhall of Roy Morgan Research (Letters, September 4, "No tricks in poll results"), of course I am not amazed that such a result was trumpeted by the pro-euthanasia lobby; it would have been amaz-ing to see similar publicity given by them to results less favourable to their cause. As for the results, I cast no doubt on the integrity of the ran-dom sampling used but there are tricks in every trade and the wording of questions put by poll sters is no exception. Stripped of its euphemisms, tautologies and subjective verb-iage, the question that was asked becomes simply: "Should a doctor kill a terminally ill patient who wants to die?" Such a blunt ques- tion would be revulsive to many and might not give the over-whelming result wanted by the euthanasia lobby. The original wording suits their cause much better. Finally, the question put has terminology "as close as possible to the proposed ACT legislation". This being the case, it would be most reprehensible of our ACT Government to pass such subjec-tive legislation as it would be open to as many interpretations as there are people making sub-jective judgments. A very bad law, indeed. BERYL LEGGE-WILKINSON Narrabundah
