22 Sep 1995 - PM tries to shore up marable Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 22 September 1995, page 9 to shore I I Peter Cole-Adams IT HAS been an odd political week, marked by pique, foolishness and peculiar statistical games. On Monday, Carmen Lawrence produced a sort of remembrance ratio table to show that her lapses of memory while giving evidence to the Easton petition Royal commission were less frequent than those of the average witness. Critics were unimpressed, making the reasonable point that the issue was not the quantity but the quality of her failures of recollection. The same critics were impressed, but unfavourably, when Paul Keating broke his self-imposed rule of not appearing in the House on Tuesdays or Wednesdays. He strode into the chamber on Wednesday afternoon, not to announce the outbreak of World War 111, but to deny a suggestion in The Sydney Morning Herald that he was responsible for stricter enforcement of rules governing the taking of photographs in the House. No more happy snaps showing his bald spot and a.derisive Opposition. John Howard made his own contribution to this premature silly season by unveiling the Coalition's so-called "debt truck", a mobile billboard which is to travel around marginal electorates bearing a wickedly over-simplified scare message about the size and implications of Australia's foreign debt. Big Kim Beazley seized joyously on the fact that the truck's components had been manufactured overseas to dub it "a fully imported lorry of lies". Howard made matters worse by declaring that he had a lot of other preelection plans "swimming around in my mind and I think we will sort of dribble them out" — a choice of words that will haunt him for weeks to come. By yesterday, Ralph Willis was calling Howard's nomadic advertising hoarding "this ridiculous garbage truck" and Keating was giving Howard hell over his proposition that foreign debt (most of which is owed by private companies and individuals) represents a liability of $10,000 for every man, woman and child. But the strangest comment of the week was Keating's assurance to Caucus on Tuesday that the "trend lines" of the opinion polls were "still OK". There is no way of knowing whether lie really believes this or whether he was merely putting a brave face on it for the sake of troop morale. Either way, he left a lot of Labor backbenchers bemused, sceptical and worried-. The most recent surveys of federal voting intentions, published last week, certainly contain very little comfort for Labor. The AGB McNair poll in The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age had the Coalition 13* points ahead on primary vote (48 per cent to 35). Newspoll in The Australian was better, but still bad, putting the Coalition, on 46 per cent, seven points ahead. The Bulletin's Morgan Poll of federal voting intentions had the Coalition in front by nine points (47 per cent to 38). This week the pollsters have had more bad news for Keating. Newspoll reported that the Coalition was now considered better able to deal with five of the six issues regarded by voters as most important. Three months ago, Labor was judged better on three of the six, with support evenly divided on a fourth. Also this week, Morgan reported that, for the first time in six months, more Australians (48 per cent) think the Coalition will win the coming federal election than expect a Labor win (38 per cent). Worse, a clear majority of 54 per cent would like to see a Coalition win, compared with 36 per cent who want Labor returned. So what comfort is there for Keating in all this? Well, Labor optimists (a diminishing species) make two points. First, the election is almost certainly still six months or so away, and a lot can happen in that time. At about this stage in 1992, six months before the 1993 election, Labor was trailing in the polls quite as badly as it is now. Second, support for the Coalition remains "soft" at the top, reflecting not so much a conviction that Howard has the answers as a general disenchantment with a long-incumbent govern ment and dislike of the Keating image and style. Only when the campaign proper gets under way will the uncommitted — a growing percentage of the electorate — start focusing on the issues about which they truly care. Only when they hear the detail of Coalition policies (or, rather, what detail Howard is prepared to provide) will they have a basis upon which to compare the rival offerings. Howard does not intend to produce that information yet, but he and the Coalition's strategists do not disagree with the argument that opinion polls this far out provide an unreliable guide to how the electorate will actual ly vote when it matters. Indeed, they are stressing the point, earnestly insisting that the Coalition remains the underdog. They know their danger is the mirror image of Labor's: the need to prevent complacency on their side is as great as Heating's need to prevent despair on his. That said, there are good reasons for doubting that history will repeat itself. Paul Keating is no longer a new-broom Labor leader. John Howard Mark II is a much more formidable politician than John Hewson. Even when Howard gets around to spelling out more detailed policy, he is not going to produce a high, wide target like the GST or the other Fightback nasties. He will be vulnerable to a scare campaign on industrial relations, but the unionised sector is declining and dwells, in any case, in the Labor heartland. • As for those poll trends from which Keating purports to draw comfort, the grounds for his optimism are hard to discern. Indeed, if one looks at Newspoll findings over the last couple of months, the striking thing is how consistent, and how consistently bad for Labor, they have been. True, one Newspoll survey, based on interviews between August 11 and 13, showed Labor and the Coalition level pegging at 43 per cent, but that looks like a sampling aberration: each of the other five published since the end of June has shown Labor languishing at between 38 and 40 per cent of the primary vote, while the Coalition has ranged from 46 to 49 per cent. Nor is it clear how Labor can close the gap. It may be that the Carmen Lawrence factor is holding it back at the moment, but that is likely to continue. Having decided that she must remain in his ministry at whatever cost, Keating has to live with the con sequences. One of those consequences is that the Easton affair will go on distracting media and public attention from the . economic messages that the Government is trying to send to the elector ate. At the very least, the electoral effect of the Easton affair will tend to cancel out the damage to the Coalition caused by the amazing adventures of Noel Crichton-Browne, thereby reducing La; bor's chances of retaining a couple of desperately marginal seats in Western Australia. Given the many Labor marginals at risk in Queensland (where Wayne Goss barely survived a huge 7 per cent swing in the recent state election) and NSW (where Bob Carr has already angered voters by reneging on election promises), Labor's prospects look horribly bleak. Not to worry. The trend is still OK. Labor's nervous legions have Keating's word for it.

09 Oct 1993 - OUT OF THE WETLANDS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 October 1993, page 1 Hardly hi-tech, says SIMON GROSE, but reviving a mangrove forest is planned as a first step towards Adelaide's MFP. TRY THIS quick quiz. The first sod turned on the Multi-Function Polis will be for: A. An optical-fibre cable dug by a new AusMole laser-guided cable-tunneller. B. An energy-efficient office/factory constructed of the latest materials. C. A satellite dish. D: A Japanese restaurant and golfing range. E. A real-estate agent's office. F. A politician's graveyard On current indications: none of these. As plans now stand the first sod turned on the MFP will be to restart an old mangrove forest that most of Adelaide has forgotten. "When work starts you'll see a lot of tree-planting, you'll see them start dig-ging very funny holes with bumps in the middle — the bumps will be the islands, the holes will be the wetlands," says Sher-yn Woon, MFP environmental officer since late last year. This does not sound very high-tech, mysterious or "21st century". It does not conjure images of cerebral androids in unisex jumpsuits sliding in solar-pow-ered capsules between workstations, biospheric markets, pleasure centres, and home domes. Nor does it arouse the paranoid spec-tre of a Japanese enclave on the edge of Australia's most hapless state capital, an introverted community beavering away at work and golf, eating raw fish, and sending all their ideas and profits back home. It does not satisfy any of the myths and fears that the Multi-Function Polis pro-voked when it was conceived and born in the late '80s. These came to dominate its public image because its parents lost con-trol of it soon after the birth — and eventually abandoned it. The father of the MFP was former Japanese Trade and Industry Minister Hajime Tamura, who is said to have had the idea when he was in Bali at a confer-ence. He enthusiastically promoted it to Australia in July 1987 and his local counterpart — former Industry Minister John Button — was unable to diplomati-cally dissuade him or reshape the idea into something sensible without causing affront. Mr Tamura — and any other Japanese who thought about it — realised the natu-ral site was the Gold Coast for reasons they felt were obvious as soon as they saw the place. But they called it Multi-Func-tion Polis and Queensland decided it did not need so badly to attract Japanese visitors. After that the MFP was always going to be an unwanted child (and an expensive idea without a market base). It was eventually fostered out to South Aus-tralia where it is now trying to find its own way on the bedraggled banks of Port Adelaide. Port Adelaide needs something like the MFP. It is the poorest socio-econom-ic area of Adelaide and the designated MFP site at Gillman is a classic example of engineer-driven land use in a metro-politan estuary: a dumb disaster littered with old tyres, dead pelicans, garbage addicted seagulls and lumpy landfills where only weeds find sustenance. But restarting a wetland is not just an urban-greenie exercise. It is a project to establish MFP as a world's-best perform-er in practically applied ecosystem recla-mation and management. Sheryn Woon: "The wetlands will be designed as a tool of stormwater man-agement to uptake the heavy metals and control the sediment. "To show that it's a working ecosys-tem it will have monitors in the upper catchment, in the drains, which will show the levels of contaminants. It will then have monitors all through the wetland system and give continuous feedback showing how the water is improving." This section of Adelaide's hinterland has been the dumping ground for 12 per cent of the city's stormwater runoff for many years and it will remain so. The aim is to cleanse it of nasties before it enters the main channels of Port Ade- laide where people still go fishing and swimming. "We will have what we call the initial sediment trap, a big pond with a hard bottom so we can get the tractors in there. "The heavy metals slick to the soil particles so every so often we go in and clean it out." Beyond this will be a series of wetlands in which the plants, insects, animals and time cleanse the water. Fish will be neces-sary to keep the numbers of mosquito larvae under control in an area where Ross River fever is already established. A final step — aquaculture — is with in the scope of longer-term planning as-management of the upper catchment im- Sheryn Woon alongside boreholes for taking samples of groundwater. || proves. The commercial prospects from such a working example of the latest me-tropolitan waste-water management techniques are expected to come mainly from Asian countries where strong eco-nomic growth is heightening environ-mental stress but also providing governments with resources to devote to the problem. Their willingness to take that step is also driven by the lifestyle expectations of their growing middle classes. If Sheryn Woon's plan is fulfilled, the showcase of the project will be a centre where people can come and see the read-outs of contaminant levels and judge the success of the project. This will also be a place where daily tourists can see native birds and plants and buy a souvenir. Asians "think wetlands are the ants' pants" she says. "This will help to put Adelaide on the map — it will be Wine and Wetlands." WHILE the earthmovers may arrive before Christmas to begin reshaping the landscape on the MFP site, a major change in the political landscape in Ade-laide's King William Street — in the state election due by March — could amount to an earthquake for the MFP. The Liber-al Party — ahead 52-31 on the latest AGB McNair poll — does not see satisfactory or immediate value in the wetlands pro-ject and other proposals centred on the core site. Opposition Leader Dean Brown has publicly committed a Liberal govern- ment to "refocusing attention away from the site". "That doesn't mean we would aban-don the site for all time, but that the resources of the MFP would be focused much more on attracting investment into research and technology," a spokesman for Mr Brown said. "We would concentrate on the centres of excellence that Adelaide already has: the three universities, Technology Park, Science Park, elements of CSIRO, the Defence Science and Technology Organ-isation, and the Waite Agricultural Insti- tute. "We would basically look at the mon-ey that has been earmarked for the site and we would put whatever money we are prepared to put into the MFP into facilitating and coordinating research, development and investment into those centres of excellence." Finding out how much has been set aside for the MFP and how much has been actually spent is not an easy exer- cise. In July 1991, the Commonwealth allowed for expenditure of $12.3 million over three years for running and project costs; $7.3 million has been spent so far. Another $40 million from the Better Cit-ies program has been allocated as part of total funding of $275 million which the State Government has foreshadowed up till 1996. In his 1993-94 Budget, Premier Lyn Arnold allocated $34 million for the MFP, raising actual state commitments so far to around $120 million. Private-sector funding is more diffi-cult to find and initial expectations that Japanese companies would provide start-up funds have been quashed as the Japanese economy suffers from the re- cession. "The double-dip up there has really knocked those guys around," says MFP chief executive Ross Kcnnan, who readi-ly plays down any expectation of Japan-ese dominance of the project, stressing the fact that countries like South Korea || Left: Dead mangroves on part of the MFP site. Above: An area to be rehabilitated outside the MFP site. || offer likely prospects for involvement. Premier Arnold openly concedes that the project has suffered from public percep-tions that sufficient progress has not been made. He blames the Opposition for fuel-ling these perceptions and says that this is a "critical year" for the MFP in which it must regain its momentum. He dismisses the charge that the Government is con-centrating its efforts too tightly on the Gillman site. "I have always had the view that Gill-man is not the sum total of the project, that the MFP must involve joint devel-opment between Gillman and high-tech-nology centres around Adelaide," Mr Arnold said. "But Gillman remains an important part of the MFP. Without it, the project would lose a central focus." The site is a potential source of reve-nue. By 1997 Ross Kennan says he ex-pects to be able to "super-lot the block" and begin selling the land to developers. This promises more substantial early re-turns than could be expected from a nor-mal portfolio of investments in technology-based commercial projects. But that promise comes with a risk: if the site-based approach is a failure, land sales will not eventuate and the invest-ment in the site may become unrecover-able. Cash flow from land sales is also expected to overtake the yearly alloca-tions of public funds which keep the show running — if this does not occur governments will have to decide whether further funding of the MFP is worth while or good money after bad. So the first sod turned on the MFP will probably be more than the beginning of rejuvenated mangrove wetland and a state-of-the-art waste-water management project for Australia's driest capital. It can go one of two ways: A. A success story of urban renewal and high-tech industry development. B. A burial ground for taxpayers' mon- ey. But the correct answer will probably be: a bit of both.

23 Oct 1993 - Debate about republic 'irrelevant' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 23 October 1993, page 13 Debate about republic 'irrelevant' Gary Morgan SYDNEY: The debate about whether Australia should become a republic was provocative but irrelevant, Gary Morgan said yesterday. Mr Morgan, the managing director of Morgan Gallup Polls, said the debate was a waste of time. The real issue was whether the Governor-General of Australia should be able to force an election by sacking the government, he said. "Unfortunately the republican movement is unresponsive to the issue that the people of Australia do not trust nor want politicians to obtain more power," he said at a Australians for Constitutional Monarchy confer ence. "Only 11 per cent of Australians rate federal Members of Parliament highly for ethics and honesty." A Morgan poll in April showed that if Australia became a republic, 71 per cent of Australians wanted the president to be elected by the people and only 23 per cent by politicians, A senior lecturer in politics at the University of NSW, Malcolm Mackerras, said he was convinced that Australia would never become a republic.

26 Oct 1993 - Eagles enjoy most support Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 26 October 1993, page 22 Eagles enjoy most support SYDNEY: The West Coast Ea-gles form the most popular side in Australian Rules, according to a Morgan poll to be published in this week's Time magazine. The survey showed 7.4 per cent of Australians over the age of 14 supported the Eagles. This year's premier club, Essen-don, was the next most popular club with 6.6 per cent; followed by Collingwood on 6.3; Adelaide 5.9; Carlton 4.7; and Hawthorn 3.9. The Adelaide Crows, semi-final-ists this year, only entered the AFL in 1991. The other clubs, in order of support, were Geelong, St Kilda, Sydney, Richmond, Foots cray, North Melbourne, Fitzroy, Melbourne and Brisbane. Using a sample of 1280 people interviewed nationally on October 2-3, the Morgan researchers said Western Australia had the stron-gest support for Australian Rules with 77 per cent, followed by Vic-toria with 73, South Australia 69, Tasmania 64, NSW 30 and Queensland 26.

01 Mar 1995 - Packer favoured in media crunch Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 1 March 1995, page 2 Packer favoured in media crunch Sixty per cent of Australians would prefer Kerry Packer to own the Fairfax media group rather than Canadian Conrad Black if it came to a battle between the two, a poll has found. The Seven News-Australian Newspoll found just 12 per cent would prefer Mr Black to own the Fairfax group, which publishes The Sydney Morning Her aid, The Melbourne Age and The Australian Financial Review. Results of the poll were released by the Newspoll organisation yesterday, but no details were available about the size of the survey or its margin of error. The poll was taken last weekend, after Prime Minister Paul Keating's public attack on Mr Packer. The poll found 82 per cent of respondents thought It important that the media should be owned only by Australians - 57 per cent listing it as very important. . Treasurer Ralph Willis told the Labor Caucus yesterday he had not received an application from Conrad Black to increase his 25 per cent stake in the John Fairfax group.

17 Mar 1995 - Our society reflects a passion for sport Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 17 March 1995, page 2 Our society reflects a passion for sport THE POLLSTER IRVING SAULWICK I HAVE always been interest ed in the Australian's passion for sport. It is reflected in a number of ways in this society: by the amount of space devoted to it in our major newspapers, by the amount of money paid by television companies for the right to broadcast sporting events, by the status we accord our sporting heroes. Of course it's reflected by our behaviour. Just think of the environment at the height of the football season in most Australian towns and cities: cars covered in the ribbons and other paraphernalia of one' steam, heightened excitement and anxiety about the prospect of victory or defeat, an increased feeling of us and them, even to the extent of seeing the them, if not as enemies, then as outsiders. And think, too, of the conversations: if you can't drop a few players' names in your conversation, or offer some views about outcome, people wonder whether you really do live here. I remember going to do some work in Adelaide years ago just before South Australia and Victoria were due to have their annual Aussie rules joust. My normally genial friends met me with a mixture of aggression and hostility which, despite their good manners and general good will towards me, they were unable to contain. I have not read the sociological and psychological literature on the subject. It is probably quite exten sive. I recall that the late Professor Ian Turner, of Monash University, a passionate Richmond supporter, studied this subject in some depth and used to deliver with some erudition the annual Ron Barassi lecture on the subject suitably dressed in his colours and with a good supply of cans for suste nance. This passion for sport has probably got something to do with tribalism - the need to belong to a group in which one can invest some emotional commitment and energy, particularly if the group is opposed to another tribe. In the early days in Melbourne football, clubs grew up around local communities which had a deep sense of identity. (It amuses me to see how some of our patrician tall poppies have identified with teams and communities which originally had a strong working-class ethic.) It also seems to stimulate or reinforce national pride - the nation, of course, is the tribe at large. Who could forget a certain larrikin Prime Minister, amongst others, jumping with joy as Australia won the America's Cup? It probably also feeds our need for excitement and perhaps even danger, the latter vicariously and, therefore, without real threat. And it may allow us to fantasise, to imagine that we are in that boxing ring or hitting that golf ball or striding over those hurdles. We can become, even if only for a little while, our champion. Of course, these feelings are not peculiar to Australians. I suspect they are felt in most urban societies. Think of the effect of a game of soccer on the Brazilian psyche, or of the passion evoked in Brit ish soccer. As I say, we Australians take our sport seriously. A few years ago, in May 1990, I included a couple of questions on this general subject in a Saulwick Poll. We asked a representative sample of 1000 Australian voters the following questions: "Could you tell me which one sport, if any, you are most inter ested in? Do you go to see it these days frequently, infrequently or never. And ... do you watch it on television frequently, infrequently or never? The results may be shown as follows: For example, basketball, which re importance of sport in the Australian culture. One might even be tempted to go further by suggesting that sport in Australia is one of the great levellers. It might also be one of the few truly indigenous expressions of mass culture in this country - as Sports most interested In Sport most Interested in and Go to see It Watch it on TV Total " " frequently frequently % % % Aust Rules 15 38 78 Tennis 14 , 8 64, Rugby League 11 31 53 Cricket 7 . 25 83 Soccer" . 6 sv > 41 71 Golf 6 18 4 63 Swimming 3 17 53 None 8 Note: these figures are a little old and things may have changed a bit since they were produced. ~ corded 2.3 per cent and which has since been heavily promoted, may now be higher. Any change, however, is unlikely to be substantial. No wonder high prices are paid for TV rights if TV can deliver audiences of this magnitude. It is interesting to note that only 6 per cent of our respondents said that they were not interested in any sport. This result tends to underline the point Implied above about the exemplified in the Melbourne Cup or the grand final. Of course this table shows the overall results. As one might imagine, there were important differences by region and by sex and age as well as by other variables. Also the list of sports people reported as being of most interest to them was nearly as long as your arm. ? Irving Saulwick is a Melbournebased national pollster.

22 Mar 1995 - Downy refuses to resign over phone scandal Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 22 March 1995, page 5 SYDNEY: Sports Minister Chris Downy faced embarrassment in his marginal Liberal electorate yesterday but refused to resign after he sacked a staff member who was later charged by police over threatening phone calls. Premier John Fahey stood by Mr Downy late yesterday, despite Opposition calls for the minister to be sacked over the incident. "I'm appalled with that incident. I believe Chris Downy acted appropriately, immediately he found out about it," Mr Fahey said. "Chris Downy is a man who would never ever be involved in such tactics or play his politics that way." But the incident opened the Government up yet again to Labor Opposition attacks over the string of scandals and crises that has dogged the Coalition since the 1991 election. With just three days remaining until Saturday's state election, the Liberals hope this latest embarrassing episode will prove to have a short media life and will not harm the Government's re-election hopes. Closer to home for Mr Downy is the fear that the publicity over threatening phone calls to a supporter of his Labor opponent, Genevieve Rankin, may harm his chances of holding the sent of Sutherland in Sydney, held by :u per cent and the Government's sixth-most marginal seat. Opposition upper House leader Michael Egan said it was "unbelievable" to suggest Mr Downy had not known about the phone calls being made from his office. He said Mr Downy should resign or be sacked because as a minister he had to be held responsible for the behaviour of all members of his staff. But Mr Downy said he had acted correctly once he found out about the incident by sacking the staff member. "I see absolutely no need to resign. I took the appropriate action ... and the staff member was sacked," he said. Mr Downy said he would personally apologise to the pizza shop owner at the centre of the incident, Vince Musico, who complained to police about the phone calls he started receiving after he placed a campaign post er for Ms Rankin in the window of his shop a month ago. The shop is next door to her campaign office. "Apparently, [the calls] range from foul abuse about myself to threats that if they don't take down the posters they'll smash his windows in and they'll come and fix him up," Ms Rankin said. Late yesterday, police charged a 22-year-old man from Sylvania in Sydney's south with improper use of a telephone. He was hailed to appear in Sutherland Local Court on April 20. . Three days before the election, opinion poll support for Opposition Leader Bob Carr has jumped from 40 per cent to 49 per cent, while Premier John Fahey's approval rating has dropped 2 percentage points to a new low of 46 per cent. And nearly one quarter of voters have still to make up their minds which way they will vote, according to a Nine Network/Bulletin Morgan Gallup poll released last night.

01 Nov 1993 - Bishop pressing Hewson Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 1 November 1993, page 3 Bishop pressing Hewson The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, will face continuing specula-tion about his leadership this week, with a poll to be published in the Bulle- tin showing strong support for Coali-tion leadership hopeful Bronwyn Bishop. Channel Nine reported last night that the AGB McNair poll, conducted for the Bulletin and Nine Network, showed support for Dr Hewson at 31 per cent and support for Senator Bish-op at 29 per cent. Senator Bishop, who has made her leadership ambitions clear, has an-nounced her intention to leave the Sen-ate and run for preselection in the seat of Mackellar after the decision of the sitting Liberal Member, Jim Carlton, to retire. In a separate development in Coali- tion politics, AAP reports from Kinga-roy that the National Party has thrown the ball to the Liberals in an attempt to get on with amalgamation talks and approve the dropping of three-cornered contests. As well, a new push for joint Nation-al-Liberal Senate tickets to maximise the conservative vote in the federal up-per House emerged at the weekend Na-tional Party central council meeting. The party earlier decided to drop three-cornered contests against sitting MPs, and select a single conservative candidate to contest marginal Labor- held seats. Members voted overwhelmingly to continue merger talks, despite resis-tance by federal Leader Tim Fischer, Senate Leader Ron Boswell, and for-mer Premier Sir Joh Bjelke-Petersen.

03 Nov 1993 - Fahey scores in Games victory Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 3 November 1993, page 12 Fahey scores in Games victory SYDNEY: Sydney's Olympic Games bid win appears to have paid off for the NSW Government and the Premier, John Fahey, with a new poll showing he is among the nation's most popular leaders. An AGB McNair poll published in The Bulletin this week shows Mr Fahey's personal standing with the electorate has leapt 11 points to 46 per cent since Sydney's victory. His disapproval rating has also dropped four points to 24 per cent. The NSW Leader of the Opposition, Bob Carr, has lost support, with an approval rating of 30 per cent, down one point, and a disapproval rating rising from three points to 34 per cent, despite his backing for the Olympic win. It is the second opinion poll in as many days to boost Mr Fahey's fortunes. A Newspoll in The Australian newspaper on Monday showed Mr Fahey's minority coalition Government had improved its lead in voter support over the Labor opposition by 13 points in three months, to lead 49 per cent to 36 per cent. The AGB McNair and Newspoll were both conducted during September and October, following the announcement of Sydney as the year 2000 Games host city on September 23. AGB McNair said support for the minority coalition Government had improved its lead in voter support over the Labor opposition by two points to 44 per cent, giving the Government a four-point margin. Those surveyed clearly prefer Mr Fahey as Premier over Mr Carr, with 50 per cent giving him their vote, up eight points, against 28 per cent for Mr Carr, down four points. The poll showed that Labor managed greater support than the Coalition among those under 40 years of age, but the Fahey Government remained a firm favourite among older voters and those outside the metropolitan area, where it recorded a six-point margin over Labor. Despite a surge in support for his Government, Mr Fahey has ruled out an early election. He said he was proud of his Government's role in introducing, fixed four-year parliamentary terms in NSW - which meant the next election was not scheduled until March 1995 - and he saw no reason to change that.

15 Nov 1993 - IN BRIEF Support owes much to loss Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 15 November 1993, page 2 IN BRIEF Support owes much to loss The public popularity of Liberal backbencher Bronwyn Bishop -despite her lack of a policy profile - could be attributed to the Coalition's March 13 election loss, Opposition shadow treasurer Alexander Downer suggested yesterday. > On Channel Ten's Meet ihe Press program, Mr Downer was asked how Senator Bishop had managed to achieve her popularity as a potential Coalition leader with no policy platform. "I think what it does reflect is the concern there still remains in the community about us losing the last election," Mr Downer replied. Mountain crash SYDNEY: Five people were injured in a car accident on the Great Western Highway in the Blue Mountains yesterday. The accident occurred at about 3.30pm at Linden, west of Springwood. Two people were trapped in one of the cars. Five people were later transported to Nepean Hospital. One person was in a stable condition with head injuries. Early in November, the Roy Morgan Consumer confidence rating stood at 111.9 points, the nationwide poll of 1112 people to be published in this week's Time magazine showed. The rating now stood at its highest level since Sep tember 1988. Moomba decision Cabinet is expected to make an other attempt today to sell ofT the. Moomba gas pipeline to fund the Budget. The sale should raise hundreds of millions of dollars. The Government's last attempt to sell the Pipeline Authority which owns the Moomba pipeline was blockcd in the Senate.

22 Nov 1993 - Citizens' choice needs thought Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 22 November 1993, page 11 Citizens' choice needs thought KR1STINE KLUGMAN reviews the pros and cons of voters being drawn more into politics. INTEREST in citizens' initiated refer enda (C1R) in the ACT is part of a wider push worldwide for greater participation in the political process. This trend counter-balances a growing level of cynicism and apathy revealed by public-opinion polls. Politicians have a very poor image, 66 per cent of electors stating that people in government usually or sometimes look after their own interests and 72 per cent agreeing with the statement that public officials do not care what the individual thinks (Australian Election Study, ANU, 1993). This attitude has been apparent for some years. A Saulwick Age Poll found that 4 out of 10 Australians believed politicians can rarely or never be trusted to tell the truth (June, 1991). To date, the public debate in Australia has been fairly superficial, with little attention given to the pros and cons of CIR in particular and increased participation in general, or to the cost/time implications. In the United States, the term "teledemocracy" describes the use of new communications methods to improve the involvement of electors in the political process -by such processes as electronic town meetings (where people at separate meetings are electronically linked to discuss issues with their elected representatives and each other), plebiscites/referenda et cetera. In Oregon, Hawaii and New Zealand teledemocracy projects have been conducted on taxation, voting, and general questions on where they are headed. There are two basic democratic models... with CIR bridging a gap between them. Direct democracy is where electors take an active role and participate in political decisions on issues frequently, between major elections. This contrasts with our more familiar representative democracy, which assumes that voters do not have the time or energy, or interest, to be directly involved, and their elected representatives decide issues through party structures often without pub lic consultation. Of course, electors have the ultimate sanction of voting that person out of office at the next election... if they happen to live in a marginal seat. Advocates of direct democracy claim that, using new communication methods, the problems of consulting with many people over distance can be overcome, and electronic networks can be used to further participation. The basic question remains: can individuals without "political" experience and specialist knowledge be trusted to make decisions affecting the social and economic life of the community? If direct democracy through participation works, with a little help from communication processes, do we need politicians at all? In the past, such consultation and communication was impossible. But with the advent of the "electronic highway", the tyrannies of distance and, to a Jesser extent, time are overcome - or could be, so proponents of CIR argue. These advocates of direct democracy claim that people become more involved and that awareness of issues and quality of debate is improved. They say the current high levels of cynicism and apathy would decrease, resulting in a stronger democracy. People, having been involved in public discussion of issues, would be less alienated and more committed to the final decision. Wider public debate would mean policy and issue compromises more acceptable than the polarised positions produced by current party political extremes. Politicians would be made more accountable and obliged to listen to electors, CIR proponents claim. Critics, however, point to the danger of extreme groups dominating public debate To date, the public debate has been fairly superficial and decision-making, with popularist sectional policies not in the interest of the greater community likely to be introduced. They say most policy issues are too complex for people to understand and decide on the merits, and there would be a danger of important issues being reduced to back or white interpretation rather than the reality of shades of grey. For example, the complexity of whether to adopt a CIR process is itself a debate of grey tones, opinions, hope and faith in the wisdom of our fellow woman and man rather than an easy yes/no decision. Critics also say direct democracy would encourage elitism, as only people with time, money and deeply vested interest would involve themselves. Consequently, poor and powerless people in society would become even more vulnerable, even further disenfranchised. Finally, those against direct democracy warn that there is a great danger of extreme divisions in society if people participate and care too much about a decision. What happens to the rights of a substantial or geographic minority? If 51 per cent of ACT voters are in favour of a proposition, and 49 per cent are opposed, is that a sufficient margin? Should there be a requirement for a 60 per cent vote in favour before a proposition is adopted? Or 65, 70, 75 per cent? What if the 51 per cent in favour in the earlier illustration all came from the north side of Canberra and the 49 per cent opposed were all from the south side? Another factor not generally addressed is the cost. What is quite apparent is that all advertising, public relations and directmail firms should be wholly in favour of the C1R aspect of direct democracy. It would be a bonanza for them... and the media, both editorially and in advertising revenue. The answer probably lies in moving more towards direct democracy, with several caveats. Firstly, there must be adequate time for public education and public debate on the issue involved. This is where new communication methods could be used to advantage, such as the electronic town meetings, telc-confcrencing and the ACT Government's soon-to-be-introduced Austouch on-screen information system in public places. Secondly, mechanisms must be devised to prevent sectional interests exercising the tyranny of the stridently vocal. Procedures should include extended and extensive public discussion and a formal system for pre-voting compromise to be achievable on contentious issues. Thirdly, a sufficient proportion of the population must participate for valid decisions to be made and, fourthly, the "pass" percentage needed must be greater than a simple majority and may have to take account of geographic or other issues. Direct democracy, in all its potential forms, should not overturn representative democracy as we know it but it can and should be used to increase citizens' involvement in the political decisions affecting their lives. It is for the next step, beyond the type of consultative representation, that ACT Government representatives have become renowned - or notorious. One aspect of what CIR could and should assist with is often overlooked: that of the repute of our politicians. There is an urgent need to arrest and turn around the increasing cynicism to politicians, because such attitudes are dangerous to democracy. In the longer term, in such an environment, the extremist appeals of a dictator, an army general or a bishop can sound attractive. Australians have faith in our democratic system but survey after survey shows that they do not trust politicians. If CIRs do nothing but educate people to how difficult the big "political" decisions are, they may well be worth the increased cost and time involved. Kristine Klugman is completing her PhD at the Australian National University on "The two-way flow of information between parliamentarians and their electors using new communication technologies". She has a BA in history, an MA in community studies and an OAM for services to the community and to education.

02 Jun 1995 - Let youth feast on policy not on showbiz Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 2 June 1995, page 11 Let youth feast on policy not on showbiz If the Government plans an early election, then it should act rather than sing and dance, NATASHA STOTT DESPOJA writes. THE SIGHT of all-singing, all dancing politicians on the McFeast program, the ABC's latest entertaining look at politics, gives us some idea of what some politicians will do for votes. In particular, the youth vote, which is up for grabs. Some pollies, like Greens Senator Dee Margetts, look comfortable singing along to Elle's theme song, She's so Fine, but others, like Michael Lavarch, seem wary as Elle struts her stuff on his' desk or she twirls Senator Bill O'Ghee around in his chair. A' politically correct Senator Amanda ;'Vanstone, chose to sign instead of sing while Robert Tickner gives the impression this is not the first time he's played with a make-believe microphone. This political answer to Quest, the ABC amateur talent show, is not confined to television, although we are deprived of the opportunity of rating their performance as in Quest. Triple J, the national youth broadcaster, has had truckloads of politicians through its studios this year. They include Senator Cheryl Kernot talking lipsticks and the voting age; Kirn Beazley on near-death experiences T.nd eating habits; even Tim Fischer displaying an uncanny knowledge of the latest rock bands. Simon Crean, Senator lan Campbell, and John Howard have also played at being shock jocks, which probably explains why the Prime Minister thought "it's time". The day after the Budget Paul Keating willingly subjected himself to 45 minutes of talk-back and Budget discussion with Triple J gum Angela Catterns. This post-Budget Triple J segment followed a slump in support for Labor among 18-24-year-olds, a decline that has been attributed to the Federal Government's handling of the wood chip issue. In a rare experience the Opposition has enjoyed stronger support among young people than the ALP, a trend highlighted in the NSW State election, in which it is reported more young people voted for the Coalition than the ALP. Youth support for minor parlies has also increased, with combined support for the Australian Democrats and the Greens around 15 per cent. This has sent a message to the old parties that they must do something about their appeal to young people. Heading the Coalition's push for (lie youth vote is the relatively youthful Senator lan Campbell, from Western Australia. He was' part of a motley crew of Coalition State and territory youth spokespeople who gathered in Canberra a few weeks ago to discuss issues affecting young Australians. The meeting was addressed by John Howard and did not include youth representatives. Not exactly Funky Squad. But it is not only our televisions that have gone retro at the moment. At the meeting, "The Howard Bunch", with its fair share of graduates from the '60s and '70s, decided that today's youth are a "lost generation". According to one report, "The MPs painted a bleak picture of young Australians as a generation with no dignity, no hope and no future." Senator Campbell's concern \4 that young people "don't have hope" and he has promised that a Coalition government would create an Office of Youth Affairs to address the problems faced by young people. Further details of the Coalition's youth policy are sketchy; presumably it thinks the Government would steal them. But one thing is clear: we are not going to hear more until the elec tion. While the Opposition's policy conjures up an Alice Cooper-type "Ministry of Youth", the Government plans to tap into the pro-republican sentiment among young voters. The Prime Minister has delayed the release of the long-awaited republican blueprint, which we probably won't see until the election lead-up. The election Budget offers little short-term relief for young people, especially long-term unemployed young Australians. Funds for youth suicide research and prevention are long overdue in an area in which the Government was politically vulnerable, considering our shamefully high teen-suicide rates and the lack of Commonwealth action. The anxiety by the major parties to attract young voters is not translating into specific policies. It is not hope young people are lacking, but any real policies for improvement. It is little wonder that one AGBMcNair poll showed 93 per cent of young people did not trust politicians and most believed that their concerns were not taken seriously by decision makers. In one survey, Zoom!, commissioned by Loud Advertising, young Australians are described as "enormously irreverent, cynical and lack[ing] any respect for authority". At least Senator Campbell has acknowledged this cynicism, which is more than the Prime Minister is prepared to do. On Triple J, Keating said he could not understand why young people were cynical. In a touch of "it was harder in my day", he talked about increased school retention rates and ?'additional training and education opportunities as reasons for young people to be happy. Young people are not happy with their elected leaders and this cynicism is reflected in the number of young people, 15 per cent, according to the Australian Democrats' Youth Poll, who "would not vote if an election was held tomorrow". Douglas Coupland, author of Generation-X, calls this "voter's block", which he defines as: "the attempt, however futile, to register dissent with the current political system by simply not voting". The Government's Budget commitment of nearly $20 million over four years to "civics education" is the first step toward better-educated voters. It is perhaps the only acknowledgement we are going to get from the Government that young people need empowerment, even if it comes through increased information and not through a reduced voting age. Until politicians, like the Prime Minister, acknowledge the level of disillusionment among young voters they will not win them over, but risk a youth backlash at the polls. Senator Campbell says young people have not had the "five minutes of economic sunshine that Australia's currently enjoying". But young people will not be swayed by five minutes of election promises either. They do not want paternalistic offerings of help. They want tangible relief: job opportunities; improved unemployment benefits; appropriate wage levels; crisis and affordable housing; funds for youth-suicide prevention; additional resources for education; rational discussion about drugs and sex education. Nor do young people want a political talent parade. This will only confirm our worst fears about politics: that it is about gimmicks and stunts and is a system that young people may be better off registering their dissent with by simply not voting at all. Natasha Stott Despoja is a Democrat Senate candidate in South Australia.

20 Jun 1995 - IN BRIEF PM on slide in opinion pollx Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 20 June 1995, page 5 IN BRIEF PM on slide in opinion poll The republic might not be the vote win-ner Prime Minister Paul Keating believes, if the latest Australian-Channel Seven News-poll is any guide. The poll, taken after Mr Keating spelled out his republican vision two weeks ago, showed Mr Keating had lost ground as pre-ferred prime minister, dropping six points to 34 per cent while Opposition Leader John Howard remained steady on 41 per cent. Support for the Coalition was up one point to 48 per cent with the Government steady on 40 per cent. Boy, 12, awarded $6m A 12-year-old boy, who became a quadriplegic after a car accident nine years ago, was awarded more than $6 million damages yesterday. In the NSW Supreme Court, the parties submitted minutes setting the award at $6,163,807.07, after they totalled various cal-culations and categories of damages made by a judge earlier this month. David John Mundy was 3½ when the crash, in which his mother and baby sister died, occurred in October 1986. Milat trial delay SYDNEY: A senior judge criticised the NSW Legal Aid Commission yesterday after he agreed to vacate next week's starting date for the trial of Ivan Milat, the man ac-cused of murdering seven young backpack- ers. In the Supreme Court. Justice David Hunt said the "extraordinary" correspondence be-tween the commission and Milat's lawyer raised the suspicion that the organisation's "approach to this case has not been a level-headed one". Earlier this month, another judge ordered the commission to reconsider the legal aid application after it had decided Milat should contribute $50,000 to his legal costs. Boy, on shooting charge BRISBANE: A 13-year-old boy has been charged with unlawful wounding after a 10-year-old boy was shot at Buderim, on the Sunshine Coast yesterday morning, police said. It appeared four boys had been playing with a .22 calibre rifle when the firearm dis-charged. The wounded boy was taken to Nambour Hospital and underwent surgery for minor liver damage.

27 Jun 1995 - Keating denies rolling Evans over nuclear tests Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 27 June 1995, page 3 Keating denies rolling Evans over nuclear tests By IAN McPHEDRAN, Foreign Affairs Reporter The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, has rejected claims that he and the Minister for Defence, Robert Ray, rolled Foreign Minister Gareth Evans over Australia's response to the French decision to resume nuclear testing. The Government has also revealed its support for small scale nuclear testing by the United States to ensure the safety of the nuclear weapons stockpile. Senator Evans has been widely criticised for Australia's initially "measured" response to the French decision to explode eight nuclear devices at Mururoa Atoll between September this year and May 1996. He also rejected claims by the Opposition that he had put his personal ambitions to head the United Nations ahead of Australia's national interest. Responding to a report in The Australian newspaper which claimed Senator Evans had taken a tougher package to Cabinet but had been overruled by Defence, the Prime Minister and Cabinet, Mr Keating said the report confused departmental coordination comments with ministerial views. "I won't be saying anything about Cabinet discussions or the advice on which decisions are made. But I can say that where ever the report in The Australian this morning came from the story is incorrect and misleading." Mr Keating attacked the Opposition for its failure to support the South Pacific nuclear free zone treaty. Senator Evans would not comment on the reports, but he said he had a clear conscience about his efforts to prevent French nuclear testing in the Pacific. O DARWIN: Banning the sale of Australian uranium to France in protest against the resumption of nuclear testing in the South Pacific would be futile and "do them a huge favour", the operator of the Ranger uranium mine said. Chief executive of Energy Resources Australia Phil Shervington said that due to long-term contracts with Australia, France would be able to buy uranium on world markets at up to 60 per cent less than it pays Australia, if bans were implemented. . A majority of Australians believe the Federal Government's response to French nuclear testing was too weak but less than half are prepared to boycott French made goods, according to 'ho latest Newspoll. The poll, to be published in today's Australian newspaper, found 61 per cent of respondents believed the Government's response had not been strong enough. . . The political party that .succeeded in stopping French nucleat testing in the Pacific would win the next election, Australian Conservation Foundation executive director Trish Caswell said yesterday. She said she had been surprised at the depth of opposition in the Australian community to France's decision to resume testing.

05 Jul 1995 - Further strife hits WA Libs Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 5 July 1995, page 2 Further strife hits WA Libs By PETER COLE-ADAMS, Political Editor Mass resignations from a Liberal Party branch in the Western Australian seat held by disendorsed federal Liberal MP Paul Filing have in-creased the likelihood of change at the top in the strife-torn state party. A total of 48 members of the 60-strong Sorrento-Duncraig branch, including the branch president, resigned on Monday night. They are expected to campaign for Mr Filing, who has an-nounced he will be standing as .an independent in his north Perth seat of Moore, which he won from Labor in 1990. increas-ing his majority to 9 per cent at the last election. He said yesterday that the Monday-night resignations meant that almost 150 Liberals in his seat had now resigned in protest. Senior party sources in WA said yesterday that they believed .. former Liberal senator and Perth mayor Reg Withers would suc-ceed in his bid to take over the party presidency from Dr David Honey at the party state confer-ence on July 30. Mr Withers is supported by WA-based federal Liberal heavy-weights who are desperate to see an end to the bitter in-fighting in the state party before the federal election campaign begins. Dr Honey is seen as being too. closely associated with Senator Noel Crichton-Browne, the power: broker whose machinations are widely blamed for creating divi-sions within the WA party and, specifically, for bringing about Mr Filing's failure to win prese-lection for Moore, and for the dis-endorsement of sitting Liberal member Allan Rocher in Curtin. Senator Crichton-Browne has agreed, under heavy party pres-sure after allegations that his wife had once sought to take out a restraining order against him, not to re-contest his Senate seat at the next election. Premier Richard Court denied yesterday that the WA branch was in turmoil, but said there were problems in Moore. He suggested that Senator Crichton-Browne's wife, Esther, would be a "terrific" member of parliament, probably at the state level. Dr Honey told a radio inter-viewer that the resignations in Moore had been "stage-managed" by Mr Filing and his supporters. Dr Honey's position may have been further undermined yester-day with publication of an AGB-McNair poll in The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald which re-ported a dramatic 15 per cent drop in federal Coalition support in the West, where it now leads by a narrow 41-37 per cent. (The AGB McNair Poll found that, nationally. Labor had nar-rowed the Coalition's lead from 10 percentage points to four, to 44-40, over the past two weeks, partly because of the swing in the West and, more spectacularly, in Queensland, where Labor had come from 19 points behind to four points ahead. Newspoll, in The Australian, gave a contradic-tory picture, showing the Coali-tion still enjoying a seven-point national lead, 47 to 40 per cent, almost unchanged over the two •weeks since the last sample. The latest Bulletin-Morgan poll has the Coalition eight points ahead.)

18 Jul 1995 - Waller 'perfect' for heroin probe Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 18 July 1995, page 5 Waller 'perfect' for heroin probe By MICHAEL BACHELARD The head of the heroin trial task force, Kevin Waller, said yesterday that he had no pre-conceived ideas about casing drug laws. In announcing the appoint-ment, ACT Chief Minister Kate Carnell said Mr Waller was "ab-solutely perfect" for the role. He is a retired NSW coroner who has conducted inquiries into the Newcastle earthquake, the Strathfield massacre and the Pa-cific Highway bus crashes. Mrs Carnell also announced the other members of what will be a 26-member task force com-prising academics, public ser-vants, community, legal and po-lice representatives. Mr Waller told a press confer-ence that he had been attracted to the committee because the is-sue had been debated for many years in academic, legal and health circles. "It's something that I've had some interest in," he said. "As magistrate and coroner I've seen the results of heroin addic-tion, which don't seem to be al-leviating at all." He acknowledged that the de-bate would divide the communi-ty into those who felt it was morally reprehensible to even consider such a scheme and others who thought "the situa-tion's so bad we need another approach". He also agreed he had been charged with a difficult task which would eventually lead to a political decision the Govern-ment had to make. "I'm used — for many years — to waiting until the evidence comes in to make a decision, and that's what I'll do in this situation ... I've got a lot of reading to do myself and a lot of discussion, so what my par-ticular opinion might be at the moment I don't think counts be-cause it might be different at the end of the period." Mrs Carnell said she had cho-sen Mr Waller because "he comes with a proven analytical mind, a capacity to take evi-dence from ... fairly diverse backgrounds on board and come up with a position after looking at all the evidence". A poll published in The Syd-ney Morning Herald recently showed that 41 per cent were in favour of a trial and 54 per cent opposed. The AGB McNair poll asked if people would be in fa-vour of a trial if it was conduct ed in their state. The proposed trial will be lim-ited to those already on the ACT methadone program, and who have lived in the ACT since Picture: GRAHAM TIDY Former NSW state coroner Kevin Waller at yesterday's announcement that he will head the heroin task force. 1993. The Government has also made it clear that it is contin-gent on the results of Mr Wal-ler's committee, on federal fund-ing and the backing of a majority of the states and terri-tories. The other members of the committee are representatives of: the National Cen-tre for Epidemiology and Population Health, Dr Gabriele Bammer; AFP, Com- mander David Blizzard and Chief Inspect-or Ted Foster; Alcohol and Drug Founda-tion, Bob Budd; ACT Health Department, Vic Bugler, Terry Findlay and Maarten van der Kleij; Alcohol and Drug Council ot Australia, David Crosbie; ACTCOSS, Graeme Evans; ACT Education Depart-ment, Fran Hlnton; AFP Association, Pat-rick Law; ACT Attorney-General's Depart ment, Diane Merryful and Keith Simpson; Methadone Action Consumer Empower-ment, Michael Rimmer; Dependency Care Foundation, Anthony Roben; Assisting Drug Dependents Inc, Elizabeth Skinner; Commonwealth Law Enforcement Board, Karen Twlgg; AMA, Dr Keith Wooliard; ACT Division ol General Practice, Dr Clare Wiillngton; ACT Alcohol and Drug Service service manager, Julie Perrin; ACT Trades and Labour Council presid-ent, Jeremy Pyner; lawyer Richard Ref-shauge; president of the Australian In-jecting Drug User League, Judith Byrne; ANU philosophy professor Robert Good-in; and ACT Chief Magistrate Ron Cahlll.

20 Jul 1995 - Goss might still hold government Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 20 July 1995, page 3 Goss might still hold government BRISBANE: The Queensland Gov-ernment clawed back to within reach of retaining power yesterday, with counting in two crucial unde-cided seats favouring Labor incum-bents. The election outcome still hinges on the Brisbane seat of Greenslopes, and Whitsunday in the state's north, although Labor said the coalition's claims on Mundingburra, a northern seat, were also now in doubt. Both sides are claiming 43 seats in the 89-seat Parliament, with one independent. If Labor wins Greenslopes and Whitsunday it will have a one seat majority. In the event of a hung Parliament, Gladstone independent Liz Cunning-ham will hold the balance of power. Both parties will try to woo her today when she goes to Brisbane to meet Premier Wayne Goss and Op-position Leader Rob Borbidge. Labor state secretary Mike Kaiser was trying not to get excited and was stressing the result was still finely balanced. "We're still hopeful," he said. "But the election outcome is still too close to call." Electoral Commissioner Des O'Shea said if the count continued neck and neck an election result might not be known until after next Tuesday night, the deadline for re-ceiving postal votes. Labor's Gary Fenlon, in Green-slopes, was trailing Liberal candi-date Ted Radke by 16 with over 600 votes left to count yesterday, after being 73 votes behind on Tuesday. "I'm still optimistic and we still have a good chance," Mr Fenlon said. "I should have a very good idea tomorrow but it'll go down to the wire." He said Mr Goss had called to wish him luck and to jokingly offer him either a knighthood or a public holiday in his honour if he managed to save the Government. In Whitsunday Labor said it was still about 40 votes ahead yesterday. Incumbent Lorraine Bird said she was still confident despite slipping from a 47 lead on Tuesday She had expected to fall behind yesterday as the votes counted were from an area in her electorate tradi-tionally anti-Labor. "It was the worst booth counted today and I've still managed to stay in front," she said. Ms Bird said there were still more than 2500 votes left to be counted in Whitsunday and a result Wayne Goss: best wishes would probably not be known until Friday. Queensland Nationals state secret-ary Ken Crooke admitted it would be difficult to win Whitsunday. In Mundingburra, also in north Queensland, Labor's Ken Davies was only 58 votes behind the Liberals' Frank Tanti yesterday with more than 1200 votes left to count. Business and Regional Develop-ment Minister Warren Pitt refused to concede defeat in far northern Mulgrave yesterday as he slowly closed in on the Nationals' Naomi Wilson. He said he was trailing by just over 100 votes with more than 1200 votes to be counted, although he was not confident he could continue to close the gap. "It would be silly of me to con-cede defeat just yet," he said. Meanwhile, many voters would change the way they voted if anoth-er state election was held in Queens land, according to an AGB survey for National Nine News. The poll of 600 voters throughout Queensland showed more than 25 per cent were influenced to vote against the Goss Government be-cause of the ALP's campaign. Six out of 10 voters said there were aspects of the Labor campaign they did not like. One in 10 said they would change their vote if a new poll was held. And 18 per cent of the people who voted for a minor party or independent said that if given another chance they would change their vote, the survey said. Eight ACT sophisticates behind Coalition's wins By MICHAEL BACHELARD An increasingly sophisticated group of Liberal campaigners based in Canberra is largely re-sponsible for big Labor defeats in both the recent Queensland and ACT elections. The group of eight, and others in the state Liberal Party branches, also will develop the strategy for John Howard's Feder-al campaign. The Liberal campaign director for the ACT election in February, Lynton Crosby, also collected the research and formulated the stra-tegy for the Queensland campaign. Labor suffered an 11 per cent swing against it in the ACT elec tion, and about 6.5 per cent in Queensland. Many of the tactics were the same, including an appeal toward the end of the campaign for a pro-test vote against the incumbent government. Research also had re-vealed similar attitudes of dissatis-faction to the leaders, Wayne Goss and Rosemary Follett. Mr Crosby said no conclusions could be drawn about the coming federal campaign from the earlier victories because the political situ-ation was likely to be different. The campaigns reflected the new Liberal orthodoxy, developed after John Hewson's loss in 1993, that sound research and tactics are more important than detailed poli-cy announcements. Soon after-breakfast time some little commotion was heard at the entrance, the sound of a shrill voice being very persistent. . "You cannot come in with him," said the constable firmly, as he blocked the door with his body. "He'll goo an' vote for t' wrong felly if I dunnot," replied a female voice. "Ast do nowt o't kind," growled a protesting voice; "dost think I'm a born foo'?" "Tha were never owt else sin I wed thee-thee'at three parts drunk awready, and --" By this time the voter had managed to enter the room. "Ncaw what would to do wi' a wife like you ?" he began, turning to the policeman. "Get on wi' thi' votin', lad, and move on," replied the officer, sharply. "It's bad enoo neaw," grumbled the unlucky wight as he,left the room a few minutes later, "but what'Il it be when they're getting t' vote?" NOT BROWN, BUT ANOTHER. For the greater part the workmen who came in during the day ..were quiet and businesslike in their manner of voting; very few needed any instructions, and the general improvement In the education of the people is perhaps never so noticeable as on these occasions. There was one exception. A b'g, surly-looking man who came to the table with the demand, "Gie us a card!" "Name, please?" requested the clerk. "What's that to thee? I vote by ballot," he snapped out. Even when it was pointed out to him that his name was necessary to prove his right to vote according to the register he refused to budge, and not until the officer came to escort him to the door did he give the required Informa tion. The local sentry, including tlhe clergy nnd doctors, nearly all recorded their votes before lunch. In several ca>-es they did not think it necessary to give their names until requested. "Ha-yes. of course, of course," blustered one, "you are strangers to the village, otherwise you would have had no need to ask for my name." It afterwards transpired that this individual was a recent settler in the village, "Lives in a bis1 now place on th' Milof no fambly whatever, tries to mix up with our best famblles, who don't want none of him," remarked the constable scathingly. "Certainly," responded the presiding officer, indicating the name on the voter's paper; then, suspecting an illiterate voter, he asked the old man whether he could read and write. "Aye, lad, I con 'write reet enoo for this job, but mi seet is none so good as it were. Art sure this.is Brown?" he continued. On being reassured that it was, the old man retired tQ tJhe ballot-box to make, his cross. \ "That's aw reet, isn't it?" he. remarked, showing his paper to the presiding officer. "But you have not voted for Brown," said the official, after examining the paper. "I ne'er intendit to," chuckled the oldfellow, winking his eye silly, "t'other cha.p's my mon, an' I wanted to mak' no mistake about him." THREE CHEERS FOR "OWD MO." The return of the out-workers to their homes brought the 'usual rush in the closing hours of the poll. The rival candidates roused local excitement to fever heat by their final visits to the neighboring comuittee rooms. With the last half hour came a constant succession of cheers and countercheers, as the remaining voters came up, "Three cheers for V Squire-he's coom all t' way fra Scotland!" shouted someone outside as a motor car came panting up. "Three cheers for Owd Mo!" called out the leader of the opposition party. The two came in together, the Squire helping the crippled old man, whose right leg was swathed in red ' flannel. I The Squire waited until the old man had voted, In order that he might as sist him out again. . j "You must come in the. motor-I'm see you safe home." "Nay, nay, Squire, I mun stick to ml! colors. I'd a gone wi' th' 'owd Squlro| reet willingly; he were always for t'l poor people; ho'd seed 'em starve for,' bread an' knew what Protection meant j for such as us. I've had childer cryln'' for bread, and. I've worked ^\viclc ln,j wick eawt, an* not been 'able to give' 'em one gradely meal i' th' day. Nay, ^ nay, Squire, no Protection for the likes j o* me; we mun go our own ways; th'j lads browt me here 1' th' donkey cart, j an' I reckon th' owd donkey fll take moi back agen-mayhap ast ne-er vote agenJ Squire; but If it is last time I know! awm on't' right side. Good - nect Squire!" . I And with blazing, eyes, the old fellow] drew himself up and hobbled painfully' to the door with thv aid of his stick. vj And a^ the polling closed a mightycheering broke out, "Three cheers for' Owd Mo!" -H.Li., in the "Daily News." . 02 Feb 1991 - Government finds support is ebbing Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 2 February 1991, page 9 Government rinds support is ebbing OPINION polls conducted on the eve of the Gulf war found support for the Hawke Government had equalled the record low of 32 per cent in November last year. Published in The Bulletin, the Morgan Gallup poll shows Labor had lost 7.4 percentage points on the level of support that had brought it back into office at the March 1990 election and one point on the last poll. Forty-nine per cent of the 2137 voters surveyed said Liberal-National Coalition - half a point up on the last poll and 5.8 percentage pointsabove above their election result. Support for the Australian Democrats has remained steady in reccnt polls at 9 per cent. In the leadership stakes, the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, stretched his lead as the preferred Prime Minister over Bob Hawke to four points (44-40). However, both leaders saw their personal approval ratings fall. Mr Hawke's dropped three points to 35 per cent and Dr Hewson's five points to 49 per cent. In a poll on state Premiers, Queensland's Wayne Goss received the top marks when people were asked about their capabilities and performance. He was followed, in order, by Western Australia's Carmen Lawrence, South Australia's John Bannon, NSW's Nick Greiner, Victoria's Joan Kirner and Tasmania's Michael Field. The territories were not included in the survey. ACNN-7/Hie survey this week indicated that Americans expected the Gulf War to last months and would be more than a little concerned if something happened to President George Bush, forcing them to rely on Vice-President Dan Quayle's leadership. The poll of 1000 people showed that 54 per cent of those questioned believed allied forces should continue to rely on aerial bombardment and only 32 per cent favoured starting a ground war. Conducted on January 24, the poll found that 90 per cent agreed that the war's goals should be forcing Iraq to leave Kuwait, removing the Iraqi leader, Saddam Hussein, from power and destroying Iraq's nuclear and chemical weapons capability. Only 41 per cent of those surveyed said killing Saddam should be a major goal. Almost 60 per cent of those polled expected the war to last four to six months or longer and 71 per cent thought nuclear weapons should not be used if the allied forces could not quickly defeat Iraq with conventional weapons. Only 28 per cent said they would feel confident that Vice-Presiaent Quayle could lead the nation in the war if something were to happen to President Bush.

06 Feb 1991 - PM's popularity up 15 points Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 6 February 1991, page 1 PM's popularity up 15 points By TONY WRIGHT, Political Correspondent It's known among pollsters as the Maggie Thatcher-Falklands Effect, and now Bob Hawke is discovering how it feels. Just as Mrs Thatcher's personal popularity soared among Britons in The Falklands war, the Gulf war has put Mr Hawke firmly back on his throne as a popular Prime Minister The latest Morgan Gallup Poll, in today's Bulletin magazine, shows that Mr Hawke's personal popularity has increased by an extraordinary 15 percentage points to 50 per cent since the war began. In mid-November, his personal approval had slumped to 33 per cent, and it had not grown beyond 35 per cent since! The good news for Mr Hawke did not extend to his Government as a whole - quite the reverse. The poll found that only 36 per cent of respondents wanted Labor to retain government, and 48 per cent wanted the Coalition to take over. " The Treasurer, Paul Keating, was not mentioned in the poll.

Mr Hawke, keen to put an end to the recent surge in speculation about the leadership, said Mr Keating had behaved in an "exemplary" fashion since a meetina last week at which he (Mr Hawke) had reiterated his intention to remain Prime Minister well into the future. Mr Hawke said he believed Mr Keating had had no part in fuelling speculation about the leadership during the Christmas break. But there had been "two or three people yapping around". Mr Hawke was asked what message he would send to these people. "Well, I would suggest ... they should probably find better and more productive things to do," he said. "I've used the phrase before - there aren't any legs on that corpse." Since the Gulf war began, his personal popularity, as rated by the Morgan Gallup Poll published in The BuUetim, had increased from 35 per cent to 50 per cent

09 Feb 1991 - PM's popularity lifts in traditional conflict form Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 February 1991, page 9 PM's popularity lifts in traditional conflict form i THE Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, and the Labor Party received a boost this week with a rise in popularity in the latest Morgan Gallup poll. As seems to be traditional in times of war, the latest poll, published in the Bulletin, indicated that conflict might be having a positive effect on the standing of the incumbent Prime Minister. The survey was conducted on the first two weekends after the war in the Gulf began and shows that Mr Hawke's personal popularity has jumped by an extraordinary 15 percentage points to 50 per cent. In mid-November, his personal approval had slumped to 33 per cent, and it had not grown beyond 35 per cent since. The rating of the Labor Party did not rise so sharply, though support increased by four points to 36 per cent - still a long way behind the Liberal-National Coalition on 48 per cent. The popularity of the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, rose by nine points to 58 per cent. Interestingly, this was the first poll in some time to put Mr Hawke ahead of Dr Hewson in the preferred Prime Minister stakes by a margin of 46 per cent to 39 jwr cent. An indication of support for the way the Government has handled the Gulf crisis was given in a poll indicating majority support for its actions so far. A Newspoll published in The Australian this week indicated Australians continued to favour the presence of Royal Australian Navy ships in the Gulf. The poll, of 1200 people aged 18 years and over and taken during February 1-3, showed 69 per cent of respondents favoured deployment and 44 per cent strongly favoured it. The last poll, conducted on January 18-20, recorded the same proportions. Three-quarters of those surveyed favoured the use of force against Iraq although the number strongly in favour has dropped from 57 per cent in January to 53 per ccnt. Only one-quarter of the sample strongly favoured sending more military equipment to the Gulf while 43 per cent were generally in favour of such a move. Forty-eight per cent were against further deployment and 31 per cent strongly against. In Britain, the election of John Major to replace Margaret Thatcher as British Prime Minister has seemingly transformed the image of the ruling Conservative Party. A poll in The Times newspaper recorded a sharp drop in the numbers who believe the Tories to be too dominated by their leader. Mr Major took over as Prime Minister on November 22, Last September, 57 per cent of those questioned believed the party was too dominated by its leader. In January the figure had fallen to 11 per cent.

16 Feb 1991 - Figures still show war commitment Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 16 February 1991, page 9 Figures still show war commitment THERE is still solid support for the allied commitment to the Gulf war, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll, published in the Bulletin, showed that a clear and increased majority of 74 per cent, up nine points since December, approved of the United States and its allies' military involvement in the Gulf. The proportion of those polled who believed that the Middle East should be left alone to handle the situation was down by eight points to 21 per cent. Support for Australia's involvement rose 16 points since December to 70 per cent. Asked who is to blame for the war, 71 per cent say Saddam Hussein and 18 per cent blame Iraq. Nine per cent blame the US and 7 per cent blame President George Bush. Fewer than 1 per cent mentioned the conflict between Arabs and Jews, or the Palestinian problem. POLLS conducted during De cember and January, before South Australia's State Bank disaster was revealed, showed that support for the Labor governments in both South Australia and Western Australia was low. Although the South Australian Premier, John Bannon, remained the preferred premier to the Leader of the Opposition, Dale Baker, support for the Labor Party had fallen another point to 37 per cent since polling in October and November. In Western Australia support for Premier Carmen Lawrence's ALP Government rallied slightly by two points, from a low of 28 per cent in October and November to 30 per cent when 1147 electors were polled in December , and January. IN BRITAIN Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conser vative Party has notched a twopoint lead over the Opposition Labour Party, according to a new opinion poll. The ICM poll in The Guardian newspaper showed the two parties had been running neck and neck just one month ago. Political analysts said the gain would gratify Mr Major but because some Conservatives privately expected the Gulf war to give them a bigger advantage, the poll offered few clues on the timing of a general election which must be called by next year. The latest findings (with last month's figures in brackets) are: Conservatives 44 per cent (43 per cent), Labour 42 per cent (43 per cent), Liberal Democrats 9 per cent (10 per cent) and Greens 2 per cent (two per cent). The figures do not add up to 100 because of the handful of "others", who are not specified, and the rounding down of frac tions.
