17 Feb 1991 - IN BRIEF Legislation fought Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 17 February 1991, page 2 IN BRIEF Legislation fought SYDNEY: Retired trade unionists have formed a coalition to fight changes to the Federal Government's social security legis lation. Two busloads of former unionists will head to Canberra next Thursday to push Cabinet ministers to scrap the deeming of 10 per cent interest on pensioner savings, a spokeswoman for the Council of Australian Retired Unionists' Member Association, Robyn Henderson, said yesterday. Court appearance SYDNEY: Two men charged over the murder of 60-year-old taxi driver Ian Lee Tait north of Sydney on Friday will face Westmead Coroners Court tomorrow. Aaron McDonald, 19, and Lindsay Caton, 18, both of Queensland, appeared in Parramatta Local Court yesterday morning. They did not apply for bail and were remanded in custody until tomorrow. Policies blamed SYDNEY: More people blame the economic policies of the Federal Government for the recession than any other factor, a poll published in yesterday's Sydney Morning Herald has found. But the Herald Saulwick poll also revealed that 55 per cent of people polled laid the majority of blame at the feet of other factors, particularly the world economy. 'Sinister' comments BRISBANE: Bond University in Queensland has hit back at comments by two Federal Government ministers that it was a disaster and financially unviable. Acting Vice-Chancellor Professor Raoul Mortley was reported in the Courier~Mail newspaper as describing the ministers' comments as reprehensible and sinister. Tonkin extradition SYDNEY:v Extradition proceedings against Queensland's most wanted woman, Karen Jeanette Tonkin, 48, have been set down for Sydney's Central Local Court on Tuesday. Tonkin, who was arrested outside a hotel in Kings Cross on Friday, did not apply for bail in Central Local Court and was remanded in custody. Tonkin was sentenced in 1974 to life imprisonment for manslaughter. She escaped from custody while on a visit to her psychiatrist on August 10, 1989. Highlands candidate SYDNEY: The NSW Minister for Industrial Relations, John Fahey, is to be the Liberal Party candidate in the seat of Southern Highlands in the next NSW elec tions. Mr Fahey said yesterday that the National Party must now decide on a new seat for the Minister for Administrative Services, Robert Webster, whose Goulburn constituency was swallowed up by Southern Highlands in boundary changcs announced earli er this year. Marijuana charge MELBOURNE: Two men have been chargcd over an indoor marijuana plantation wiDrth an estimated $250,000 found at a house in Reservoir. Police said they found 250 mature plants growing in a shed, a garage and among other vegetation in a garden during a raid on the house. Man questioned SYDNEY: A 19-year-old Erina man was being questioned by police yesterday after the discovery of a woman's body on the NSW Central Coast. A police spokeswoman said the body of the woman, aged in her mid-20s, had been found on the bank of Erina Creek beside The Entrance Road at Erina about 8am yesterday. She had not been identified.

23 Feb 1991 - Leaders easily outstrip rivals Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 23 February 1991, page 9 Leaders easily outstrip rivals THE Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, and the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, far outstrip leadership rivals within their own parties, according to a poll published this week. A Morgan Gallup poll of 1096 voters found that Mr Hawke was the preferred Labor Prime Minister for 43 per cent of voters - well ahead of the Minister for Transport and Communications, Kim Beazley, on 11 per cent and the Minister for Industry, Technology and Commerce, Senator John Button, on 9 per cent. Published in The Bulletin, the survey found the man considered most likely to succeed Mr Hawke, the Treasurer. Paul Keating, was preferred by only 6 per cent of respondents and 7 per cent of Labor voters. When the poll gave a choice of Mr Beazlcy or Mr Keating, 54 per cent preferred Mr Beazley and 27 per cent Mr Keating. However, among Labor voters Mr Keating was ahead 46 per cent to 42 per cent. On the Coalition side of politics, Dr Hewson was a clear leader, with 42 per cent, compared with former leaders John Howard (13 per cent) and Andrew Peacock (7 per cent). The present Deputy Leader, Peter Reith, was preferred by only 1 per cent of respondents. In a separate political poll, Mr Hawke made further gains on Dr Hewson in the preferred Prime Minister stakes to lead by 48 per cent to 39 per cent - likely a result of his performance during the Gulf war. Both leaders maintained the personal-approval gains they have acquired since the Gulf war began, with Mr Hawke steady on 50 per cent and Dr Hewson down one point on 57 per cent. As a party, Labor also continued its slow climb to register a support level of 37.5 per cent, compared with Coalition support of 47 per cent. Labor support is now running only two percentage points behind that recorded at the 1990 federal election. A Saulwick poll of 1000 voters published in The Sydney Morning Herald this week found, not surprisingly, that 75 per cent believed management should take salary cuts as a contribution to help the country through the recession. While 69 per cent believed businesses should accept lower profits, a much smaller proportion thought wage and lower-level salary earners should make significant sacrifices. Only 26 per cent of those surveyed agreed that workers should take unpaid leave and 41 per cent that they should accept salary cuts. In contrast, 60 per cent would accept the reduction of penalty rates and other similar award conditions. Liberal-National voters and people aged over 54 were more likely to support sacrifices in general.

21 Apr 1952 - Above-average polling News (Adelaide, SA : 1923 - 1954), Monday 21 April 1952, page 3 Above-average polling 94 p.c. VOTE AT GAWBLER The Gawler by-election on Saturday was a 94 per cent. poll. This is exceptionally heavy for a by-election. Fewer than 400 of the 6,226 electors enrolled failed to vote. The State Returnmng Officer (Mr. Kenney) said today usually a by-election resulted in only a 87 to 90 per cent. poll. Mr. J. S. Clark, endorsed Labor, will become the new member for Gawler in the Assembly. Latest figures are:-Mr. Clark, 3,252 votes, against Mr. E. V. H. Riggs (endorsed LCL), 2,227. Mr. Clark has already polled more than half of the number of votes of electors in the district. Including postal, there are only about 330 votes still uncounted. These will be dealt with tonight.

01 Sep 1945 - Jane Russell Makes A Comeback News (Adelaide, SA : 1923 - 1954), Saturday 1 September 1945, page 4 Jane Rus sell Makese A.C JONATHAN DAVIES' MOVIE MERRY -GO-ROUNDi MISS Jane Russell's recent return to the screen coincided with a Gallup poll revealing that sex was America's public interest No. 1. 16 Feb 1951 - British Labor uneasy News (Adelaide, SA : 1923 - 1954), Friday 16 February 1951, page 11 Farom A. J..CUMMBEOS,9 noted Engaisa pbnIc lstB L ONDON, February 6.-The publication yesterday of the latest Gallup Poll figures has created something of a sensation in high political circles; and there are long faces among Labor back-benche rs at Westminster. . . . The pronounced swing to the Right, showing a clear majority for the Tories if a General Election were held tomorrow, has a deep significance for the Government as for.the Opposition, Incidentally. it confirms recent estimates by me? of the state of public opinion at the present time; and it can scarcely have come as a complete surprise to those Labor members of Par iament and Labor organisers who have had realistic contacts in their constituencies. What will be the effect in a precariously poised Parliament? In one sense, perhaps in two senses, there must be a psychological impact; depression for Labor. elation for the OppoSition Fear~s of split The inference is that the Tories, believing themselves to be in a winning position, will redouble their efforts to deliver a kInock-out blow at groggy oppents; and dispirited Labor members may find it increasingly difficult to keep their enthusiasm to the sticking point in the ceaseless battle of the division lobbies. There is another point of view, bringing hopeas well as anxiety to the Government Whips. Labor commentators noir freely admit that a good many Labor backbenchers are at loggerheads with the Government. because they think it has not shown sufficient firmness in clinging to the possibility (faint though the possibility seems) of making peace with China. Their unease has ocen deepened by the Government's reluctant assent to the branding of China as an aggressor; and at many different points they are out of sympathy with official foreign policy. Some of tliem indeed conduct themselves as if they were peace-atany-price menOn On the other hand, friendly com mentators are reminding them that "the chances of peace would not be Improved by substituting Mr. Churchill for Mr. Attlee," "So what?" they ask. The answer is that there must be no split in the ranks of Parliamentary Labor, that these Siern critics must put their conscience in their pockets lest worse should befall, In all probability most of them will respond to such an appeal, which Mr. H[erbert Morrisoh, who would be in despair at the prospect of an early election, will undoubtedly reinforce Even so, I greatly doubt whether the Parliamentary structure of the Labor Party could withstand much longer the intense .pressure now likely to be put .on it, .not only in the House of Commons but outside as well. It remains to be seen whether Mr. Morrison seeks some kind of agreement With the Opposition, based primarily on a postponement of the operation of the Steel Act, in order to delay an election until events take a more favorable turn.Apart Apart altogether from the extreme unpopularity among ideologically minded Socialists of so base a "betrayal" Will the Tories now be Spersuaded in the interest of national unity to call off their head-hunting expedition just when the victims are ripe for slaughter? One again the attitude of the Liberal. groul in mthe Commons becomes a vital factor, The "Evening Standard," one notes, calls on Liberals (patronisingly and with some scepticism) to "carry out the will of the people." What, I am sure the public expects Is that the Parliamentary Liberals Should come to a deliberate decilon on policy and tactics and then stick rigorously to both. A go-as-you-please, any return to the helpless confusion of the past session, would bring deserved ridicule on them all, exasperate most of their own party supporters and reduce them to impotence in the country. Frankfurt, Thursday. - West German police are waging an increasingly bitter war against organised gangs who, in the big industrial centres, are stealing non-ferrous metals to sell them at soaring black-market prices. . These gangs are taking advantage or West Germany's critical shortage of raw materials which, a high American official said, might cut production and hit any West German industrial contribution to Western defence. Police in a dozen cities reported that they were up against pillagers of such vital metals as scrap copper, lead, zinc, brass, tin, and bronze wherever these could be found. Large firms were reported in one Frankfurt newspaper to be contributing to the wave of alleged lawlessness by circularising small scrap dealers with "highest prices" offers-usually at twice the official rate. The West German Economics Ministry has appealed to the Governments of the laender (States) which make up the West German Republic to ae action to stop transactions at prices above the pegged rates. Some of the pillaged metals are reported to be finding their way to East Germany, where there is an even .greater demand for these vital war potential supplies than in-West Germany. East German resources are considerably smaller than those available to West Germans. Rato tals, too Frankfurt police say that thieves no longer search ruined buildings for unclaimed r'etal.They They sneak into garden allotments and strip huts of tin gutters and seize old metal bath tubs used for storing water. In Lower Saxony, 10 per cent. of all the crimes.are metal thefts. Organised gangs buy the metal and smuggle it into the Soviet zone, "where it has a special 'peace-time' value." Frankfurt's Chrlstus Church lost its copper lightning conductor. Furniture vans have been stripped of their copper roofs. At Fulda, north of. Frankfurt, restaurants have complained of guests taking away the lead pipes in ~the lavatories. Rosenstein Castle's famous ancient zinc lions have fallen victims to the metal -thieves. Stuttgart police reported one case of a 24-year-oldc thief who made; regular trips with a motor :gycle and sidecar to strip brass and lead fittings from locomotives awaiting salvage in German railway yards.-AAP-Reuters.

02 Nov 1994 - NSW ALP holds on to lead: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 2 November 1994, page 6 NSW ALP holds on to lead: poll SYDNEY: For the third con secutive month, the NSW ALP has edged out the Coalition as the preferred party, the latest AGB McNair Bulletin poll re- veals. Conducted during Septem-ber and October, the poll shows steady support for La-bor at 45 per cent with sup-port for the Fahey Govern-ment up one percentage point at 41 per cent. The ALP result was despite the resignation of Peter An-derson from the Opposition frontbench. But only 29 per cent of vot-ers nominated the Opposition Leader, Bob Carr, as preferred premier — down 3 per cent and 26 points behind the Pre-mier, John Fahey. A total of 55 per cent of vot-ers, up 4 per cent, nominated Mr Fahey. But the NSW Government can take no comfort from the figures in the aftermath of the Terry' Griffiths' alleged sexual harassment affair, the Bulle-tin said. The Democrats slipped one percentage point to 3 per cent, and. support was unchanged John Fahey for both Independents on 6 per cent and for "other" parties at 5 per cent. Labor's strongest support was among younger voters, with 47 per cent of the 18- to 24-year-old respondents and 51 per cent of the 25- to 39-year-olds preferring the ALP.

14 Nov 1994 - Consumer doldrums, says poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 14 November 1994, page 2 Consumer doldrums, says poll SYDNEY: Consumer confidence has hit its lowest level in almost a year, according the latest Morgan poll. Published in this week's Time magazine, the poll shows' the consumer confidence rating, on a scale of 80 to 150, fell to 118.1 — 6.5 points below the October rating and the lowest level since December last year. Over the next year, 37 per cent of the poll's respondents (down five points) expected the economy to improve, while 24 per cent , (up three) said they expected it to worsen. People were also gloomier about.the nation's long-term economic outlook, with a drop of 7 per cent to 32 per cent of respondents expecting better conditions in the next five years and 20 per cent (up four points) expecting bad times. Comparing their personal financial position now with a year ago, 35 per cent (down one) said they were better off and 30 per cent (up five) said they were worse off. The slump in confidence coincides with an increase in interest rates, which the federal Opposition has claimed could reach 15 per cent by early. 1996.

21 Nov 1994 - People leaving health-cover schemes: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 21 November 1994, page 3 People leaving health-cover schemes: poll SYDNEY: Australians of all ages are continuing to abandon private health funds, according to a poll. The Morgan Poll, published in this week's Time magazine, showed that fewer than two in five Australians had private health insurance. The proportion of those with health cover had declined steadily from 42 per cent in 1991 to 40 per cent in 1992, 39 per cent in 1993, and 37 per cent in 1994. The Roy Morgan Health Insurance Monitor for 1994 also showed households with higher incomes were most likely to be privately in sured. But for the first time since 1991 the proportion of households earning more than §80,000 with private health cover has fallen — by two percentage points to 60 per cent. The poll showed that the proportion of Australians aged 65 and over with private health cover also declined for the first time since 1991.

23 Nov 1994 - Downer sliding in latest polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 23 November 1994, page 3 Downer sliding in latest polls Forty-three per cent of voters surveyed in a new Newspoll thought the federal Opposition Leader, Alexander Downer, should resign from the job and about the same number thought he should stay on. A former leader, John Howard, was nominated by 20 per cent as preferred leader, against Mr Downer's 18 per cent, former NSW Premier Nick Greiner's 14 and Bronwyn Bishop's 13. Another poll said preferred prime minister ratings were: Paul Keating 51 per cent, Mr Downer 21.

03 Apr 1995 - Majority support statehood for NT Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 3 April 1995, page 5 Majority support statehood for NT DARWIN: The vast majority of Australians support the Northern Territory becoming a state if most of its residents back the idea, a poll has found. The Newspoll, published in today's Australian newspaper, also found that 57 per cent of those polled believed the NT statehood issue should be resolved before constitutional moves to make Australia a republic. Twenty per cent of the 1250 adults polled throughout Australia on March 24 to 26 believe NT statehood should be resolved at the same time as national moves towards a republic. The NT has had a limited form of self-government since 1974, with a further strengthening of its powers in 1978. However, the NT Government has no direct control over industrial relations, uranium mining, Aboriginal land rights and Kakadu and Uluru national parks. There is also a theoretical power held by the Commonwealth to override NT legisla tion. In the Newspoll, 81 per cent of respondents believe the NT Government should have the same rights as other states, while 9 per cent believe the Federal Government should retain the right to override NT legislation. Ten per cent were undecided on the issue, the poll found. A total of 86 per cent of those polled believe the NT should become a state if a majority of territorians support the idea (62 per cent strongly agreed, while 24 per cent partly agreed). On the issue of Senate, representation, 25 per cent believe the NT should get the same number of senators as the other states — 12 senators — at statehood, the poll found. The phased introduction of 12 senators over time was supported by 35 per cent of those polled, while 20 per cent supported the retention of the existing two NT senators. Twenty per cent were uncommitted. The NT Government has set 2001 — the centenary of federation — as the target date for statehood. But the Government has acknowledged (hat one major hurdle will be to gain the support of Aborigines, who make up some 25 per cent of the NT population. Aboriginal leaders have repeatedly spoken of establishing self-governing Aboriginal regions along the lines of Norfolk Island, rather than being part of any new state. As for the name of a future state, a large number of NT residents support the "state of the Northern Territory", while others have suggested Capricornia and Arafura. One wag during a recent debate on a possible name suggested Liquorland.

10 May 1995 - Majority support euthanasia Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 10 May 1995, page 10 Majority support euthanasia IN RESPONSE to the two bishops (CT, April 29) and Paul Osborne MLA (CT, May 3) it is pointed out that there have been clergy in support of voluntary euthanasia since early days. 26 May 1995 - Health 'a bigger worry than rates' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 26 May 1995, page 3 Health 'a bigger worry than rates' By MICHAEL BACHELARD Voters are as worried about the state of Aus tralia's health system as they are about tax and unemployment, and more worried about it than the economy or interest rates, a survey says. The Roy Morgan poll, commissioned by the private insurer MBF, found 60 per cent thought the health system was in crisis. Of those, almost half blamed the Federal Government. Seventy-seven per cent were concerned about public-hospital waiting lists. Seventy-four per cent thought senior politicians like the Prime Minister, the Health Minister and the Opposition Leader should have private insurance. Paul Keating has said he does not have private insurance. MBF has been conducting a campaign promoting tax concessions for people taking private health insurance. A spokeswoman for the Health Minister, Carmen Lawrence, said the Medicare system was supported by 80 per cent of Australians and had helped Labor to five election wins. Those surveyed had not been asked whether they thought the Opposition would do a better job. Private insurance was a "choice, not an obligation," even for politicians, who were entitled to use public insurance. High-income people paid more already for public health through the compulsory Medicare levy and general taxation. The poll found an even split between those who thought the Medicare levy increase in the Budget was a good thing, 46 per cent against it and 45 supporting it. The poll, of 1300 people, was taken the weekend after the federal Budget. • A new report says cervical cancer is the eighth most common cancer in women, and 1 per cent of women will suffer from it before reaching 75. A report by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare says there have been significant reductions in the incidence of the cancer in women over 50 and slight increases in younger women.

19 Aug 1995 - Most Canberrans back euthanasia, according to poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 19 August 1995, page 1 Most Canberrans back euthanasia, according to poll By CHRIS UHLMANN Seventy-five per cent of Can berra voters believe people who are terminally ill and "suffering unbearably" should be allowed to ask to die, according to a Roy Morgan opinion poll issued yes terday. The $2500 poll was paid for by the ACT Voluntary Euthanasia Society and conducted during the last weekend in July. Society con vener Gordon Taylor and Inde- ! pendent MLA Michael Moore have hailed it as a clear signal that the time has come to pass a law allowing active voluntary eu thanasia. Mr Moore said the question had been designed to reflect the wording of the euthanasia Bill he intended to introduce to the Leg islative Assembly next week. ; The respondents were asked: | "In your opinion, if a terminally | ill patient, suffering unbearably, with no chance of recovery, asks for a lethal dose so as not to wake again, should a doctor be allowed to give a lethal dose or not?" Of the 505 respondents, 75.5 per cent said yes., 15.5 per cent said no, and 8.9 per cent could not an swer the question. The figures were further bro ken down by age group; voting intention; electorate; religion; and work status. Support for euthanasia was highest among the younger vot ers: 94 per cent of 18 to 24-year olds supported active euthanasia. Support fell to 79 per cent be tween the ages of 25 and 49 years and reached its lowest point (62 per cent) among those over 50. Support for euthanasia was i high across all political groupings with the greatest support (86 per cent) among those who voted for Mr Moore followed by 83 per cent of Labor voters. Seventy-four per cent of Liberal voters said yes to the question while the lowest level of support — 45 per cent — was recorded among those who back Indepen dent MLA Paul Osborne. Mr Osborne is a staunch oppo nent of active euthanasia but it is difficult to draw much from the figures as the sample size of Osborne voters was extremely small — seven. He was out of town yesterday but his office issued a statement saying he was not surprised by the survey results "considering the loaded question that was asked". Of the major religions, Catho lics were the least,likely (61 per cent) to support euthanasia while 86 per cent of Anglicans favoured it. v Ninety-three per cent of those who said they had no religion supported euthanasia. Support among the smaller denominations is harder to call as the samples were all small but it ranged from 100 per cent among Methodists (from a sample of five) down to 53 per cent of Baptists (from a sample of 10). Support among the 11 people who described themselves as non Christian was low — compared with most other groups — 53 per cent of the sample in favour of euthanasia. Mr Moore said the poll showed it was "the overwhelming view of the community" that it was time for active euthanasia laws.

21 Aug 1995 - 'Inappropriate' laws hamper the infertile Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 21 August 1995, page 4 'Inappropriate' laws hamper the infertile SYDNEY: Infertile couples in Australia are being hampered in their efforts to have healthy babies by inappropriate and unrepresentative laws, two researchers say. Writing in the Medical Journal of Australia, Monash University obstetrics and gynaecology associate professor John Leeton and research fellow Dr Karen Dawson have called for law reform and a national regula tory system. "We consider this matter to be relatively urgent," they wrote in the journal published by the Australian Medical Associa tion. "Without addressing it, we predict a further falling behind in assisted reproductive technology research and confusion arising for judges." Legal barriers in Victoria currently prevented proper testing of embryos to ensure those with genetic diseases were not implanted, contrary to popular support for this precaution. "A Morgan Gallup Poll in April 1994 showed that 66.7 per cent of Australians approved of the use of embryo biopsy for these purposes." Victoria had also failed to amend laws controlling in-vitro fertilisation to stop them making surrogacy using IVF illegal. "Other Australian states also have legislative problems," they said. "Regulation of assisted reproductive technology would be better managed at a na tional level."

28 Aug 1995 - Letters to the Editor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 28 August 1995, page 8 Letters to the Editor Legalising euthanasia is dangerous ONCE AGAIN, Monsignor Kelly "Euthanasia: the thin end of the wedge" (Letters, August 21) has hit the nail right on the head. I strongly support his comments on the dangers of legalising "a little bit of euthanasia". (By euthanasia I mean acts or omissions intended to kill people out of compassion for their condition. I do not include in the definition what is commonly, but wrongly, called passive euthanasia, such as the potentially acceptable practice of discontinuing harsh, intrusive and pointless treatment and allowing nature to take its course.) The well-reported abuse of the toleration (it is still not legal) of euthanasia in Holland is a case in point. We have only to look at our own experience with that other form of legalised murder, abortion, to see how far practice degenerates once the first chink is made in the law with the thin end of Monsignor Kelly's wedge. What was once allowed only in very limited circumstances is now available on demand. Even if we are not alarmed by the prospect of legalising an immoral act, we might pause to consider, and perhaps be alarmed by, the possibility of one day belonging ourselves to one of the groups deemed by then to require "euthanasing" from our society. DUNCAN FRANCIS Swinger Hill Vested interest THE ACT Voluntary Euthanasia Society announced that 75 per cent of Canberrans want euthanasia (CT, August 19, p.l). The Roy Morgan opinion poll commissioned by them produced this re sult. When a society with a vested interest publishes such a result, are we supposed to be amazed!! The Morgan poll could hardly have been expected to present a negative result. This trick is almost as good as the one we had with the Euthanasia Select Committee chaired by Michael Moore looking into Michael Moore's Voluntary and Natural Death Bill, 1993. BERYL LEGGE-WILKINSON Narrabundah Death need not be such a trial ALTHOUGH a survey on euthanasia shows it to be favoured by a considerable majority (CT, August 19, p.l) those anti the right to die have been quick to discredit the findings and will again tell us that such legislation will lead to much doing away of oldies by conniving relatives and medicos. Anyone with a bit of faith in their fellow citizens will not be so convinced. Essential to their concept of dying with dignity is palliative care where pain is virtually banished, but there seems little concern for mental suffering in such a terminal phase. Patients of independent and sensitive nature find bedridden helplessness unbearable. Personal experience has shown me that palliative care can still mean weeks of utter misery when pleas for despatch are ignored. As life wasn't meant to be easy, surely death need not be made such a trial. MAX PURNELL Braddon The case against lOOpc betterment 100 PER CENT betterment tax would reduce, not increase, government revenue. As any increase in betterment charge is reflected in lower prices developers can offer existing lessees for their land, it would leave lessees no incentive at all to sell their land to developers — so that there would be little or no redevelopment, and thus little or no betterment to levy. Also, Government and the community would be left with the higher budgetary, economic and social costs of more green-fields development. Second, it would not recognise that it is existing lessees, not the Government, who have (and have paid for) the right of occupancy of the land for 99 years, and the power to release or not release it for redevelopment. And if a change from single to multi-residential use is going to increase the value of the land, it would be unrealistic to expect the lessee to release it unless he shares in that increase. The present 50 per cent betterment charge amounts to a 50/50 split of the increased value between government as owner, and the existing lessee with rights of occupancy for 99 years — a quite common split between two parties with rights to an asset whose value is increased. Third, although technically leasehold, particularly since 1971 Canberra land has been treated by everyone — lessees, government itself, and the housing market — as freehold. And there is no "community ownership" argument for a 100 per cent betterment charge on freehold land. There is a good argument for government taxing any capital gain on freehold land caused by government town-planning policies, but it would be extreme, unique and counterproductive to set any rate of tax as high as 100 per cent. Even the Commonwealth Government's capital-gains tax rate is only 47 per cent . R. S. GILBERT Turner Not all approve of Federal plan RE ANGELA NEVILLE'S front page report on the housing development proposed for the Federal Golf Club (CT, August 23) . Readers should be aware that despite the public statements of support for this proposal by the secretary manager and the president, the board does not yet have the approval of the members. The first this member heard of the proposal was the arrival by mail last week of a package containing glossy publicity material from the "preferred developer" along with a letter of support from the president and notification of a meeting to vote on the issue. Before Michael Moore, MLA, and others get in a lather about Federal, they should be aware that at that meeting on September 13 there will be members like me who are concerned that the unique bushland around the course may be offered up to developers in return for short-term gains. This, and how the board got to this stage without the involvement of the members, are two of many aspects of the proposal which warrant close and careful examination. If the board/developer alliance does carry the day, Mr Moore can lather up to his heart's content. I'll even send him a new stick of soap. P. B. MACK1N Curtin One person's memory tested THE Marks Royal Commission into the involvement of Carmen Lawrence in the tabling of a petition in the West Australian Parliament is not investigating the recollections of people some years after events. It is investigating the recollections of one person. Carmen Lawrence, in a statement to that Parliament a few days after the event. In other words, did Ms Lawrence, very shortly after the event and as the Labor Party Premier of the time, mislead the Parliament she led. If the commission finds this to be so, then Ms Lawrence lied to the Parliament and to the people of Western Australia. And if that is so, she has displayed traits which are unacceptable in any member of parliament, let alone in a minister of any government. DENNIS QUICK Townsville, Qld Assessment system has its problems IT WAS only a matter of time before the Education Minister, Bill Stefaniak, found himself brought face to face with that Achilles' heel of the ACT Board of Senior Secondary Studies — its system of internal assess ment. While the computerised processes by which a student's Tertiary Education Assessment are calculated can be shown to be fair, they are only as fair as the data fed into the system. Apart from the student's externally set and assessed ASAT score, which forms only a fraction of the final TEA, the bulk of a student's assessment is based on the marks awarded by his/her own teachers. In this system, where there is no external examiner, a student who gets on the wrong side of a teacher for whatever reason (academic disagreement, personal antipathy, no matter what) may well feel discriminated against in his/her assessment. The education authority will say that there are internal procedures to cope with such prob lems. That has been the answer given by administrations — police forces and the like — for ages past, to enable the organisation to present a united front to criticism from without. Ultimately, external scrutiny reveals the truth. Until the Department of Education accepts a larger measure of independent, external assessment of its Year 12 students, the minister will find himself facing the conclusion that teachers' assessments may be fallible. 29 Aug 1995 - Morgan poll group resists union Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 29 August 1995, page 4 Morgan poll group resists union MELBOURNE: The Morgan opinion-poll group is resisting a union's attempts to achieve federal-award coverage for in-terviewers employed by its companies. The Morgan group embarked on an appeal yesterday against an Australian Industrial Rela-tions Commission ruling that a dispute existed between it and the interviewers. The National Union of Work- ers wants the dispute finding upheld as a first step towards gaining federal award coverage for the interviewers. Among the Morgan group of companies fighting the case are the Roy Morgan Research Cen-tre, Australian Sales Research Bureau, CATI Telephone Sur-veys and Tara Market Re-search. Morgan group advocate Tan-ia Cirkovic said the companies were opposed to the dispute finding of February 27 because the interviewers were not em-ployees but contractors. The commission cannot make awards covering independent contractors. Ms Cirkovic said the second ground for the appeal rested on the question of the genuine-ness of the log of claims served by the union on the group. The hearing is continuing.

28 Oct 1995 - Saturday FORUM Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 28 October 1995, page 12 Saturday FORUM DENIS MULLER lists death, sabotage and character assassination in Victoria's venomous game of politics ~~ Life with Jeffrey will never be dull A New Series This week: VICTORIA POLITICS is never a soft game, but right now it is being played with unusual venom in Victoria. The currency is death and hu- man suffering (a long-running ambulance dispute), sabotage, def-amation writs and repressive leg-islation (the even longer-running grand prix controversy), charac-ter assassination (the Crown Ca-sino) and, finally, policy issues (the new tollway system called City Link). The players are the Kennett Government, some health unions, the community protest group op-posed to the grand prix, the banks and prominent business people connected with the casino. The pawns are accident and trauma victims, hospital patients, innocent sportspeople and road users. All of these issues are separate, but what they have in common is antagonism between the state Government on one hand and a variety of power blocs and inter-est groups on the other. It is the politics of confrontation. The mood is reminiscent of the latter years of the Fraser federal government. The lesson of those years is that the electorate event-ually becomes exhausted, loses interest in the rights and wrongs of the issues and just wants some peace. If the Opposition is half credible, the incumbent govern- ment is then at risk. In Victoria, however, the Oppo-sition is not half credible. Jeff Kennett does not face a Bob Hawke with a vision called Con-sensus. Instead he faces John Brumby with a Labor Party still faction-ridden and lacking enough front-bench talent to fill more than about four portfolios. In policy terms, Labor has painfully faced up to its past fail-ures of economic policy, but it clearly has not yet re-established in the eyes of the electorate its credentials to govern. The latest polls - by AGB McNair last month and Morgan this month — indicate that sup-port for the parties has hardly changed since the election in Oc-tober, 1992, which swept Jeff Ken-nett to power. On that occasion there was a swing of 5.77 per cent against Labor. To get back in, it needs a uniform swing of 7.6 per cent That is huge by Australian standards, and the reality is that it just will not happen. So for the Liberals at the state level, life is fairly comfortable, ihey are not so unrealistic as to think they can hang on to all the seats won in the landslide of Oc-tober, 1992, but their rough as-sessment is that they will lose on-ly between five and 10. Their confidence is borne out by any reasonable assessment of the present position. There is a small cluster of former Labor seats now held on very slender margins by the Liberals in places like Tullamarine, Essendon, Gee-long and Frankston on the Mor- nington Peninsula. There are a couple of others — at Oakleigh in Melbourne's southern suburbs, and inner-city Prahran — which the Liberals could lose because of big local is-sues: Oakleigh motorists will be affected by the new City Link tollway and Prahran lies next door to the grand prix circuit. There is also a feeling within the Liberal Party that it is some-what vulnerable in the bush, mainly because of cuts to schools and hospitals. Seats in and around Bendigo and Ballarat are seen as potential weaknesses here. But even if the Liberals' worst scenario were realised and it lost 10 seats, it would still have a ma-jority of 14. For the Liberals at the federal level, however, Victoria is not so comfortable. The 1994 national re-distribution has adversely affect-ed more Liberal-held seats than Labor. Malcolm Mackerras, the pse-phologist at the University of NSW and at the Australian De-fence Force Academy in Can-berra, published an analysis of the Victorian federal seats which took the redistribution into ac-count. He reckoned that purely as a result of the redistribution, the Liberals would stand to gain a net two seats and Labor a net one. However, since writing that an-alysis and after having had fur-ther time to assess the Kennett factor, he says that metropolitan Melbourne is the only place in Australia where the Labor Party is likely to do well at the coming federal election. On his analysis, the Liberal seat of Bendigo, and three more which make a broad crescent through Melbourne's eastern and south-eastern suburbs — Bruce, Chisholm and Isaacs — are now notionally Labor. However, he is prepared to predict at this stage that only Isaacs will definitely go to Labor (and even Liberal people in Victoria are prepared to give that away). Mackerras is not prepared to give away to Labor its notional gains of Dunkley and McEwen, (this also accords with local Lib-eral Party assessments). The conventional wisdom is that the election will be won or lost in Queensland, NSW and Western Australia, and that the impact of what looks like a rela-tively small shuffle in Victoria will not matter much. However, after losing the unlosable election Picture: AP Protesters in Albert Park in the early days of grand prix protests: cyclists, golfers, cricketers and others determinedly enjoy the fresh air in one of Melbourne's recreational parks. last time, the Liberal Party is un-likely to be taking anything for granted. The risk is that with a Liberal Government so thoroughly en-trenched, Victorian voters might use the federal election to square things up a bit. Then there are the headline issues of industrial unrest, the grand prix, the casino and City Link. The Kennett Government pre-sided over the introduction of a computerised dispatch system for ambulances which has had teeth ing problems, to put it mildly. There have been scandalous de-lays — some as long as two hours, others a matter of 20 or 30 minutes — in getting ambulances to people. Half a dozen or so of these peo-ple died. Some might have died anyway, but the delay in getting specialised assistance to them gave the ambulance employees ammunition which they have not been slow to use in an industrial campaign against cuts to the ser-vice. The Health Minister, Marie Te-han, weighed in with threats to use against the ambulance work ers the Kennett Government's draconian emergency services legislation. This empowers the Government to invoke criminal sanctions against workers and to fine individuals as well as organi-sations. This threat was too much even for Jeff Kennett, who publicly re-pudiated Mrs Tehan's position, but the effect was to severely worsen the atmosphere, and now both sides have become even more obdurate than before. The union has increased the number of its work bans; Mrs Tehan has accused the union of "industrial thuggery" and in Parliament Ken-nett accused Brumby of being a "vulture" for using the body count to score political points. IT HAS been an unedifying spectacle. Meanwhile the com- munity's vulnerability to an un-certain ambulance service re-mains as nakedly exposed. Simultaneously, doctors and specialists who serve as visiting medical officers in public hospi-tals have just threatened to strike unless Mrs Tehan honours what they say is a commitment to give them a pay rise. Here again, pas-sion is running high. The special-ists — a natural Liberal constitu-ency if ever there was one — have accused the state Govern-ment of being "psychopathic" and lacking a conscience. The imbroglio of the grand prix encapsulates everything Victori-ans say about the Kennett Gov-ernment: good for the economy, good for Melbourne's profile. But . . . Did it have to come at the price of defacing one of the city's grandest parks, Albert Park, with a vast two-storey building that is (really) the pits? And then there was the tree-felling and the heavy relandscaping. To be candid, some parts of the park have doubtless been improved, but it is easy to understand from the over-all effect why the local residents feel so strongly about it. Moreover, their right to sue over damage to their homes has been simply abolished. Victoria's Constitution, alone in Australia except for Tasmania's, can be amended by legislation, and the Government just curtailed the ju-risdiction of the Supreme Court to exclude it from hearing claims for grand prix compensation. People whose homes have been cracked by the heavy pounding required to compact the race-track, have been made take-it-or-leave-it offers by the state Gov- ernment. Then there were the tacks. Last weekend some malevolent hand scattered steel tacks over the park's cycling track on the day that a major Victorian cycling tour was to hold its sprint stage there. By good fortune the tacks were discovered and swept up be-fore they did any damage, and no-one has been game to own up. However, Kennett decided that he knew who did it. Without a shred of evidence he accused the Save Albert Park group, which has hounded the Government and the contractors throughout the life of the grand prix object, de-scribing their alleged conduct as a "criminal act". The group's coordinator, Jenni Chandler, has now lodged a writ for defamation against Kennett in the Supreme Court. Outside the court she described Kennett as a bully, adding, "He has no respect for the truth and it is about time someone stood up to him." Ms Chandler is hardly one of Kennett's natural enemies. She is a former state vice-president of the Young Liberals and was on the staff of the late Sir Billy Snedden, a former federal Opposi-tion Leader. Kennett's response so far has been to brush aside her com-plaints and to pass even more re-strictive trespass laws which will close off whole sections of Albert Park for up to 12 weeks each year leading up to the grand prix, and for five weeks afterwards. The Government has also given itself the power to write regula-tions excluding or expelling peo-ple from the park. The Government has learned some useful lessons from the grand prix. One of these it is now putting to use with the new City Link tollway project. Householders whose homes are damaged by the tunnelling for this project will be put in the same position in respect of com-pensation as the residents of Al-bert Park. However, the biggest upheavals over City Link have nothing to do with earthworks and every-thing to do with economics. It has been revealed that the cost-benefit analysis for the pro-ject did not count the effect of the tolls on the likely volume of traf-fic. Given that there are alterna-tive routes that are free to use, this is surprising. The project almost fell over when the banks behind the con-struction consortium, Transur-ban, initially refused to accept government limitations on the de-gree to which the Government was prepared to share the risks of the venture. Under sustained pressure, Kennett, Transurban and the banks finally did a deal. The idea is to create a vast by pass beginning at the citv end of the Tullamarine Freeway and, cut-ting across North Melbourne to the docks. It then turns south - to connect with the Westgate Bridge freeway, then eastwards, burrow-ing in two parallel tunnels under the Botanic Gardens and the Yar-ra River, emerging in Richmond, where it will join the Southeast ern Freeway, the main road out or Melbourne to the vast sprawl of the eastern suburbs and Gipps- land beyond. The crisis with the banks is past, but the risks remain, and they are not inconsiderable. Not a great deal is known about the official arithmetic upon which this network of tollways, bridges and tunnels rest. Howev-er, enough has filtered out for a lot of unofficial calculations to be done by academics and commen-tators, led by The Age's Kenneth Davidson. None of these more se-rious calculations have been re-futed by the Government, and they go like this: The Government says the Link will cost $1.7 billion to build (big-gest infrastructure project since the Snowy Mountains scheme). The parent company of the Tran-surban consortium says $2 bil- lion. Making certain assumptions about rate of return, maintenance and toll-collecting costs, the re-quired cash flow over the first 10 years is reckoned at $600 million. Official forecasts say the Link will carry about 300,000 trips a day, 300 days of the year. To gen-erate the necessary cash would thus require a toll of $6.70 a trip. The tolls have actually been pitched in the $2-$4 range. Whether the taxpayer is having treasures on earth stored up on "is behalf by the Government' will probably not be known until it is too late. While the Link may exact an invisible toll, the casino is taking people's money in big licks under bright lights. Otherwise, however, it is litigious and dangerous terri-tory, with accusations of relation-ships between the Government and key figures in the Crown consortium that are too cosy for comfort yet impossible to prove or disprove. There is also considerable agi-tation that the casino has been granted permission to substantial-ly increase its number of tables and hours of opening — even in-cluding Christmas Day, Anzac Day and Good Friday. Victoria is anything but a dull place to live under Jeffrey. John Howard is finding out how lively he can be. Only two days ago he was calling for 80 per cent of tax is to be given back to the states, giving Paul Keating a free kick and earning a rebuke from How ard which had no visible effect. From a Liberal point of view, it must be a relief to think that the federal election will not be won or lost in Victoria. Denis Muller is a senior research associate in the Centre for Public Policy, University of Melbourne.

17 Nov 1995 - A statesman's hat for Keating? Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 17 November 1995, page 13 A statesman's hat for Keating? Peter Cole-Adams PAUL KEATING looked tired and sounded subdued at his Monday press conference at the end of the Auckland Commonwealth leaders' meeting. Heaven knows what state he will be in when he finally gets back from the APEC meeting in Japan next week. The mental and physical demands on national leaders are often considerable but, election campaigns aside, they seldom have to absqrb such multiple stress as has come Keating's way in the two weeks before the House of Representatives resumes next week for what is likely to be its last session before a federal election. Consider. It was just 12 days ago, on a Sunday night, that Keating found himself flying at short notice across the continent to board a larger plane for Israel and the funeral of assassinated Yitzhak Rabin. On return to Canberra, he barely had time for a snooze and a change of underwear, before he was ofF to Auckland and Queenstown for a four-day CHOGM meeting which, thanks to the brutal stupidity of Nigeria's unlovely military government, turned out to be more demanding than he had expected. Back in Australia, he had only a couple of days in which to defuse two potential domestic political disasters — the Marks Royal commission's expected but damaging findings against Carmen Lawrence and the ACTU's decision to launch its most disruptive industrial campaign in decades — before flying off yesterday for the APEC summit in Osaka. It did not help that at the last moment American President Bill Clinton, whose presence and authority were regarded as crucial to achieving a satisfactory freetrade result in Osaka, was forced by a domestic political crisis of his own to cancel his trip. It says a lot for Keating's resilience and determination that, after negotiating with the principal players on Wednesday night, he was able to announce before his own departure that he believed a basis had been achieved for a settlement of the brawl between the unions and the mining giant CRA over individual work contracts. The scale of the campaign already under way and planned by the ACTU threatened'not only the nation's economy and trading reputation, but also the election credibility of Labor's claim to be the one party that can deliver industrial peace. If indeed Keating has pulled off a resolution, with a bit of help from his mate Bill Kelty — and this was still uncertain last night — he will have done himself a power of electoral good and dashed John Howard's hopes of having yet another cause for keeping the heat on the Government instead of defending the Coalition policies, or lack of them. If, on top of that, Keating can return from APEC. brandishing a credible piece of paper promising regional free trade in our time, to set beside the one he brought back from CHOGM denouncing nuclear testing, he will be in a position to use the last two weeks of Parliament as a bully pulpit for the next stage of the pre-campaign campaign for a March elec tion. The electoral potency of achievements in international acronyms is limited, but it does a prime minister no harm to be able to don a statesman's hat at the hustings. It makes the jet lag, and a]] those hours listening to other leaders' speeches, worthwhile. Certainly, Keating and Labor need to play up every success if they are to achieve the breakthrough in public perceptions that has so far eluded them. This week's only national opinion poll, Newspoll in The Australian, had one bit of good news in that it showed Keating overtaking Howard as "better prime minister" for the first time in seven months. But it also showed the Coalition again widening the gap between it and Labor to nine points, 48 to 39 per cent, compared with six points three weeks ago. Even if the industrial storm threatened by the ACTU passes, even if the international weather proves favourable in Osaka, Keating knows there are still dark clouds hanging over Labor's prospects of survival. One is uncertainty about eco nomic developments over the coming months. Another he could have, and should have, banished by taking a hard decision months ago. Its name is Carmen Law rence. I note a two-way split between the commentators in their reaction to the Easton Royal commission findings, with one group coming down heavily against Lawrence and the other equally heavily against Premier Richard Court and the commissioner, for mer Victorian Supreme Court Justice Ken Marks. The two views are not mutually exclusive. Indeed, both are basically right. This is another tale without he roes. However vindictive and self-serving were Court's motives in setting the inquiry up, however flawed its terms of reference and proceedings, it has confirmed what most observers have believed for a long time: that the former Western Australian Pre mier and present federal Health Minister told a lie when she denied any detailed knowledge of Brian Easton's petition before it was tabled in the WA Parliament, and persevered in that lie repeatedly thereafter. Even in this age of popular disenchantment with and cynicism about politicians and the political process, this matters, or should matter. In relatively recent times, ministers have rightly lost their jobs for lesser offences than being caught out in telling fibs, particularly to Parliament. As a former judge of long experience, Marks was well qualified to make a finding on the facts. Had he restricted himself simply to deciding,, on the sworn evidence of a majority of Lawrence's former state Cabinet ministers and staffers, that she had told a porky, he would not have been as open to accusations of judicial arrogance and naivety. Instead — and, in fairness, he was encouraged to do so by his terms of reference — Marks presided over a process that seemed more prosecutorial than inquisitorial and passed judgment on issues of political morality on which his opinion should carry no more weight than yours or mine. Political propriety is something to be judged by Parliament and, ultimately, by the great jury of the electorate. To find that a politician has acted improperly because she used a petition "for her own personal political purposes" is to find her guilty of being a politician. After all, as Milton Cockburn pointed out in The Sydney Morning Herald yesterday, Marks conducted a Royal commission set up by Court for the sole purpose of pursuing a political oppo nent. Marks was a victim of his own political innocence, rather than a villain, in this sorry affair. By contrast, Court has emerged as a C-grade Machiavelli, whose double standards and hypocrisy led him to setting an ugly precedent in the misuse of the Royal commission option that may one day return to haunt him, just as poor dead Penny Easton has haunted Lawrence. • Lawrence, not so long ago one of the rocks upon which Labor hoped to build its re-election strategy, is today a millstone around Keating's neck. That is as much his doing and hers, because of their determination that she stay in the ministry, as it is Court's.

20 Nov 1995 - ALP behind Coalition: Morgan poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 20 November 1995, page 2 ALP behind Coalition: Morgan poll The Keating Government has taken a slide in popularity, with the latest opinion poll putting it 10 points behind the federal Opposition. Labor suffered a seven-point turnaround in the Morgan poll, which was taken before the CRA industrial dispute and also before the Marks Royal commission's finding that federal Health Minister Carmen Lawrence had lied in regard to the Easton affair. The poll of 2041 electors, published in The Bulletin magazine, showed support for Labor on a two-party preferred basis was down 3.5 points to 45 per cent while the Opposition gained 3.5 points to 55 per cent. But on the question of preferred prime minister, Paul Keating continued to head Opposition Leader John Howard, although the margin had been reduced by a point. Mr Keating was preferred by 45 per cent of those surveyed — a one-point drop from the previous poll — and Mr Howard gained a point to 42 per cent with 13 per cent undecided. The poll was held on the first two weekends of this month. Mr Keating has resisted taking his last chance to call a federal election this year and the next election seems likely to be held in March or April. Federal Treasurer Ralph Willis announced yesterday that the Budget had been pushed back from May to August, suggesting a latish poll. - AAP

01 Nov 1986 - Nationals' support down on election eve Poll bodes ill for Sir Joh Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 1 November 1986, page 1 From ANDREW FRASER in Brisbane, and AAP The latest Morgan Gallup Poll of Queensland voting intentions, issued last night, left the Liberals buoyed and Labor cautious about how the state would vote today. The results of the poll, commissioned by The Bulletin, suggest that the National Party may not win enough scats to govern in its own right. The Liberals seem certain to regain most of the scats in the south-east of the state that they held before 1983, but they are also hoping to do well in electorates away from Brisbane, and that is far less certain. The ALP, which currently hold 31 scats, should pick up a few more, largely because its leader, Mr Warburton, has been able to make it an election fought on local issues. The Premier, Sir Joh BjelkePetersen, was shown last night to be down a further eight percentage points to 39 per cent, the lowest approval rating lie has recorded in a Morgan Gallup Poll. Sir Joh had a 58per-cent approval rating at the time of the last election. First with the Queensland election results — The Canberra Times on Sunday. Support for the National Party in October was down compared with the 1983 election results, the poll said, dropping nine percentage points to 30 per cent. The poll said Liberal Party support was up six percentage points to 21 per cent and the ALP's support was up two percentage points to 46 per cent. If today's vote matches the poll results, the National Party will not receive enough scats to form a Government in its own right. Preferences of Liberal Party voters outside Brisbane and preferences of National Party voters in Brisbane could determine the results in many scats. The poll said Mr Warburton's approval rating was up five percentage points since September to 45 per cent, and the approval of the Liberal Leader, Sir William Knox, was down nine percentage points to 48 per cent over the same period. In October, electors were evenly divided on whether Mr Warburton would do a better or worse job than Sir Joh — 33 per cent said he would do a better job, 21 per cent said he would do the same job, 33 per ccnt said he would do a worse job and 13 per ccnt could not say. The Liberal state director, Mr Gai7 Neat, said the poll figures put his party at its highest in Brisbane for more than eight years. ■ "No doubt the Nationals and Labor will put on a brave face with the latest figures, but the news is all good for the Liberals," he said. "Despite the big drop in support for the Nationals statewide, the Liberal/National vote is 51 per cent with Labor trailing on 46 per ccnt." Labor's campaign director, Mr Peter Bcattic, said, "The Morgan poll was taken over four weeks and may not be relevant now." The polls will close at 7pm Can berra time. Young Nationals still look to the Messiah; Sharpe's view. — Page 2

13 Nov 1986 - NSW ALP 'would have lost' in October Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 13 November 1986, page 15 NSW ALP 'would have lost' in October SYDNEY: A significant increase in the approval rating of the NSW Premier, Mr Unsworth, would not have prevented the Labor Party from losing power if a state election had been held in October, according to the latest Morgan Gallup Poll. Published in this week's Bulletin magazine, the poll showed 37 percent of the 1777 electors approved of the job being done by the Labor Premier compared with the September figure of 31 per cent. However, Mr Unsworth's approval rating was still well behind that of the Opposition Leader, Mr Greiner, who dropped three points to 47 per cent. But 32 per cent of those surveyed said he would do a better job than Mr Unsworth. The poll showed 27 per cent believed Mr Greiner would do the same job as Mr Unsworth, while 26 percent — up 5 points — said the Liberal leader would do a worse job as the state's leader. Although it was an improved showing by Mr Unsworth, the survey concluded that a Liberal-National Party coalition would get 47 per cent of the vote against the ALP's 42 per cent, which would be cough for a new government to be formed.

12 Dec 1986 - IN BRIEF Peacock in the lead Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 12 December 1986, page 7 IN BRIEF Peacock in the lead SYDNEY: More Australian voters preferred Mr Peacock to Mr Howard as Leader of the Opposition, according to the latest poll on the Opposition leadership. The Newspoll, conducted last weekend and published yesterday by The Australian, found that 39 percent preferred Mr Peacock as Liberal leader, compared with 21 per cent supporting Mr Howard.

18 Nov 1982 - Government on top in popularity poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 18 November 1982, page 7 Government on top in popularity poll The Government's popularity is higher than the Opposition's for the first time since March last year, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The poll, conducted between October 30 and November 6, put coalition support at 47 per cent, compared with 46 for the ALP. This is an improvement of 3 per cent for the Government and a drop of 1 per cent for the Opposi-tion. It contrasts with an 11 per cent lead by Labor at the end of September. The approval rating for the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser, increased by 2 per cent to 38 per cent and his disapproval rating dropped by 3 per cent to 47 per cent. Approval of 42 per cent for the Opposition Leader, Mr Hayden, was down 1 per cent from the previous poll (October 16-23) and his disapproval rating went up one point to 36 per cent.

02 Dec 1982 - Poll 'would have gone to Labor' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 2 December 1982, page 8 Poll 'would have gone to Labor' The Labor Party would have easily won a Federal election held in mid-November, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. Fifty per ceni of those polled would have given their first preference to the ALP — 5 per cent more than at the 1980 Federal election and more than the vote which returned the Whitlam Government in 1974. The ALP figure was 4 per cent higher than in the previous poll, taken in late October and early November. The increased support flowed directly from the government parties, whose popularity fell 4 per cent to 43 per cent. The Australian Democrats were steady at 5 per cent. The results of the poll, published in The Bulletin yesterday, indicate that the poor state of the economy — especially record unemployment — has wiped out the surge in government popularity recorded while the Prime Minister, Mr Fraser. was in hospital. The results came just three days before voters in the Federal electorate of Flinders choose a candidate to succeed the former Deputy Leader of the Liberal Party, Sir Phillip Lynch. Labor needs a swing of about 5.5 per ccnt to win the scat from the Liberal Party. It would be only the third time since federation. The poll also shows that the approval ratings of Mr Fraser and the Leader of the Opposition, Mr l layden, have fallen I per cent, to 37 per cent and 41 per cent respectively. Mr Hayden's approval rating is at its lowest this year following a peak in July and August of 51 per cent. Mr Fraser's approval rating compares with a low this year of 32 per cent in late March and a high of 41 per cent in May-June and early October. Mr Hayden's disapproval rate remains steady at 36 per ccnt, while disapproval of Mr Fraser rose from 47 to 49 per cent.

05 Dec 1982 - QUEENSLAND Liberals' popularity slips even further, to the glee of both the other parties Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 5 December 1982, page 2 QUEENSLAND Liberals' popularity slips even further, to the glee of both the other parties The ALP and National Party in Queensland are gleefully predicting the demise of the Liberal Party as a State political force following recent polls. The latest Morgan Gallup Poll shows the Liberals have dropped 6.9 per cent in popularity since the 1980 Stale election. At the same time the Nationals increased their popularity 6.4 per ccnt. If the polls were translated to an election, the Nationals would go close to winning government and the Liberals would lose six seats. This is not a one-off poll result, but a steady trend, which has been accelerating over the past two polls. In the 1980 election the Nationals received 27.6 per cent of the vote and the Liberals were close behind with 26.9 per ccnt. That figure was considered disappointing then for the Liberals, who had hoped to lift their vote above the Nationals' and become, if not in 1980 then in 1983, leaders of the National-Liberal coalition in their "give us the numbers" campaign. The major reorganisation Of the Liberal Party under its new State director, former journalist Mr Gary Neat — aimed at broadening the party's base to challenge the Nationals and ALP in the country while defending the Liberals' Brisbane base from National Party attack — appears to be faltering. The Nationals are saying to the Liberals that they ought to stop their separate-image campaign and work more closely with the Nationals if they want to survive as a major party. For the Nationals it is a case of "We told you so". The Nationals' argument to Liberals determined to distance themselves from their coalition partners was that it would only result in coalition disharmony and that the Liberals would lose out to both National and Labor parties. The Nationals have not been keen to publicly kick their coalition partner while it is reeling from the lowest popularity in more than a decade. Nationals' director Mr Mike Evans would only comment, "The poll indicates very strong electoral backing for the National-Party-led coalition led by Mr Bjelke-Peterson. Mr Evans It shows Queensjanders' faith in the only true private-enterprise party." Mr Evans also said the result, when translated to the Senate vote, gave the Nationals an excellent chance of picking up another Senate seat — probably from the Liberals. The Liberals blamed their popularity drop on the Federal party being in power during an electoral downturn. Mr Neat also cast doubts on the veracity of the poll, saying it miist have been taken at Kingaroy (the Premier's home town). He claimed private Liberal polls showed the party was polling well in target areas. He sent a letter to major party financial contributors saying, despite publicity on polls and expert commentaries, the Liberals were building support for long-term gain. But the Liberals' own polls have not had a good track record in predicting results. Both the National and Labor Parties' own polls back up the Morgan poll. Interestingly, the Nationals have increased their popularity in the Liberal strongholds in south-east Queensland. Both National and Labor have the same explanation for the Liberals' drop in Mr Wright popularity. They do not believe that Federal economic issues have hurt the Liberals as much as the Liberals seem to. The Nationals say Liberals are becoming convinced their party's separate-image campaign cannot work and are transferring their support to the Nationals. They say the increase in National Party membership in south-east Queensland, including a number of former Liberals joining the Nationals, is indicative of this. They believe that, as the Liberal's stocks fall, there will be a certain bandwagon effect as Liberal supporters decide the Liberals will never again be an effective political force so join the winners — the Nationals. The Labor view is that the Liberals have not been able to win on any of the issues where they differ with the Nationals and after eight years of trying and failing, many Libera) supporters are finally deciding to join either the Nationals (the vast majority in terms of party membership changes) or Labor. Labor believes Queenslanders want a strong leader, particularly in hard times and, in the choice between Mr Bjelke-Peterscn and the Liberal Leader, Dr Edwards, the Premier wins easily. His popularity in the latest poll increased four per cent to 56 per cent. \ Part of the explanation for the Nationals' increase in the metropolitan vote is Senator Flo Bjclkc Petersen. Her never-ending publicity — she is in the Brisbane papers almost daily, generally on soft issues such as baking scones or eating pizzas or opening shopping centres — is, according to some ALP workers, giving the Nationals "a human face". Although the Nationals are happy to see the Liberals humbled, they have left the door open for the Liberals to return to a subordinate coalition role by saying that even if the Nationals won an outright majority they would still form a coalition with however many few Liberals were left. Although it is highly improbable that the Nationals would gain a parliamentary majority, they will get some help from Labor. The ALP has decided not to give preferences to Liberals in marginal seats or where ALP preferences would help the Liberals to beat the National candidate or sitting Mem ber. That means the ALP will be giving first preferences in many cases to Nationals and would help elect a number of Nationals. But the ALP secretary, Mr Peter Beattie, says the party wants to see a two-party system in Queensland and they are obviously the Nationals and Labor. The ALP believes that by helping to wipe out the Liberals or reducing them to a rump, the ALP can pick up a swag of Liberal metropolitan electorates to put it much closer to the 42 seats jts needs to form govern ment. He said the Liberals were gutless and weak bccause they were not prepared to join with Labor to force a fair electoral redistribution, although it was Liberal policy. Only if the Liberals joined the ALP to force such a redistribution over the protests of the Nationals would Labor guarantee the Liberals their preferences. This could mean that the Liberals could lose at least three scats and fail to regain their former scats which the Nationals have already picked up with ALP preferences. The Liberals are talking of a counter-move in which they would not stand candidates in scats to prop up Nationals who need Liberal preferences to fend off the ALP. About six scats could change from the Nationals to the ALP if this happened. The poll figures for Labor were disastrous, but the party sees.longterm hope in them. Labor's popularity in Queensland dropped two per cent to 40 per cent — three per cent worse than at the 1980 election. But the party points out the poll was taken during the leadership challenge and they had expected only 35 per cent to 38 per cent support. They were encouraged by the leadership poll. One thousand of the 1,350 people polled gave their estimation of the ALP leadership on the basis of former leader Mr Ed Casey. Only 350 based their estimation on the new leader, Mr Keith Wright. Mr Wright's popularity was such he was able to lift Mr Casey's 26 per cent popularity to 34 per cent. In a full poll, Mr Wright should attract more than 40 per cent. While Labor has settled its leadership and the National squabble over their deputy leadership and ministerial vacancies, moves are on in the Liberal party to replace their amiable leader, Dr Edwards, but probably not until after the next State election. The Minister for Transport. Mr Don Lane, is starting to marshal his forces to challenge Dr Edwards, promising to be more a Henry BqIic type and less a lapdog.

04 Feb 1990 - Out to defeat the 'big guys' at their game Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 4 February 1990, page 19 Out to defeat the 'big guys' at their game Peter Rees talks to Australian Democrats Leader Janine Haines about her future. JANINE Haines, the Leader of the - Australian Democrats, was in full flight as she talked of her obsession to "beat the big guys" and how she was going to do it. The "blatant hypocrisy" of the Liberal and Labor parties needed to be exposed, she said, and that was why she had taken the historic step of challenging for the South Australian seat of Kingston at the next federal election. "I want to expose them for what they , are — clones of each other and' mealy-mouthed hypocrites who stage ritual slag fights on peripheral issues while they agree on the important ones," she said. "They'll both privatise, it's just a matter of how much/They'll both sell off the country; it's just a matter of how much. "They both favour deregulation, it's just a matter of how much and they're both into expenditure cuts, it's just a matterof how much..." "Tweedle-dum and Tweedle-dee?" I ventured. "And I intend to be Alice in Wonderland," she shot back without hesitation. "Wonderland" is precisely where her political opponents hope she doesn't end up after the election. Rather, as Wonderland's Queen of Hearts demanded, they would prefer to see her lose her head, politically speaking. The 44-year-old former high-school teacher is supremely confident. "My campaign against the big guys in Kingston is simply going to be based on whether the electorate prefers machine politics or Janine politics — whether they want a Member who represents them or who represents their party," she said. If the bold bid succeeds, it could see the Democrats break away from the role they have held in the Senate for the past few years of holding the balance of power with the aim, as former leader Don Chipp put it, of "keeping the bastards honest". Polling well According to Senator Haines, polling has been good over the past year since she announced she was running for Kingston. The party had engaged the Morgan Gallup Poll to conduct several big surveys, while major newspaper polls also pointed to her having a strong chance. "Each one of those polls has thrown up identical results that I have the highest vote of the other three, that Gordon Bilney of the Labor Party, the sitting Member, is second, and that the Liberal candidate is well behind." But she admitted these were only polls and she was "as sceptical of polls as the next person". She disagreed with Mr Bilney's analysis of the electorate based on the SA state election result last November which showed he would win, claiming it was based on a,false premise. "During,, the 12 months before I made this decision about running for Kingston, we got Morgan to poll three separate Adelaide federal electorates which are totally : demographically different — the seats of Adelaide, Hindmarsh and Kingston. "They were asked the same questions .each time, the standard who did you vote ••"forafthe la!sf election;'who will you vote for at the next federal election and then, who will you vote for if Janine Haines is the Democrat candidate. , ... "In each case the Democrat base vote trebled. Gordon Bilney started from the premise that the Democrats' base vote would double." But the key to her success or failure could be where the Liberal preferences go — and the party has made it clear since 1983, when it directed its Senate preferences to the Communist Party, that it has no intention of doing anything to further the political career of someone they re gard as an irritant. She says one of the things that has concerned her most in the past few years is that the electorate is not being told what is really happening in politics. "Legislation is being debated, people are making speeches'in the Lower House and indeed in the Senate about how dreadful it is and then when it comes to the vote in the Senate where it counts because the Government does not have the numbers they vote in favour of it Janine Haines: I want to expose them for what they are — hypocrites. "That sort of information is not getting out. Indeed, when we were debating a tax Bill late last year, the Liberals' shadow ; treasurer,, ;Dr Hewson, had moved, an; amendment in the Lower House which! we were supporting. .: "They,;didn't .proceeduvyith. it .in^the-* Senate, I moved it,.they voted against it.. .. "That sort of blatant hypocrisy has to be exposed." She says the Summer School organisers asked her to talk about people, power and politics and, in particular, the issues of people's involvement in matters of environmental concern, and the relationship ordinary people have with politicians, governments and corporations. Safe environment "Essentially, how you can beat the big guys," she said. "My argument will be that you have to beat them at their own game. "You have to take their own weapons, their own economic arguments and throw them back at them and challenge some of the arbitrary but very entrenched economic definitions such as gross domestic product." She said that while no value was cred--. ited to a healthy society and a safe, clean environment, conservation would continue to come a poor second to commcr,r,cialism. -nnrn HHP 'viritvi Tiwnrt irj«tii:n"iri "If you chop a tree down and sell it to the Japanese as pulp and then import it as "But if you leave it intlie.ground'and it holds down some farmer's' topsoil or is used to decrease the salinity problems in an area or if it is just left there breathing oxygen into the air it counts for nothing." If Janine Haines fails in her Lower House bid, she may well develop a closer, relationship with soil and trees, given her response to a question on what she would do if the voters of Kingston did not support her. "I'll go gardening or something, that's it, no more politics," said the senator whose term was not due to end until 1993.
