07 Feb 1990 - Labor support growing: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 7 February 1990, page 2 Labor support growing: poll SYDNEY: The Labor Party has taken its biggest lead over the federal Coalition since last February, according to the Morgan Gallup Poll published in today's Bulletin magazine. Support for the ALP rose one point to 45 per cent in late January and support for the Coalition fell a point to 42 per cent. Support for the Australian Democrats rose from 9 to 10 per cent, with that for others dropping from 4 to 3 per cent. The poll was conducted over two weekends — January 20-21 and January 27-28. On these results, Labor would have been returned to office with the aid of minor party preferences, the Bulletin said. The Opposition health policy was launched on January 25. Asked who would make the better prime minister, 62 per cent (up two points) said Bob Hawke while 26 per cent (unchanged) said Andrew Peacock, with 12 per cent nominating others. Approval ratings remained largely unchanged but Mr Peacock's disapproval rating rose three points to 58 per cent, the report said.

10 Feb 1990 - 'Swing to Libs' in key seats Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 10 February 1990, page 5 'Swing to Libs' in key seats MELBOURNE: The Federal Opposition holds a 5 per cent swing in 15 crucial marginal seats in the run-up to the next federal election, according to a Liberal Party survey. The party's federal director, Tony Eggleton, said yesterday that the survey, conducted last week, targeted 30 seats and showed the Opposition would win half of them. A uniform swing of 2.6 per cent would give the Opposition the 10 seats it needs to win the election. The survey also showed voters did not believe Prime Minister Bob Hawke would serve out his term if Labor won, Mr Eggleton said. Earlier this week Mr Hawke rebuked Industry Minister John Button for speculating that Mr Hawke and Treasurer Paul Keating had come to an arrangement on the leadership hand-over. Mr Eggleton said the Federal Government would not wait until May for an election, with the likely date cither March 31 or April 7. He said the research showed the electorate was "cynical, anxious and pessi mistic". A large number of voters were still undecided on which party they would vote for. "We'll run a very down-to-earth campaign focusing on real issues," he said. "We'll enter the campaign with an immense group of people undecided and uncommitted — up to 30 per cent of the electorate may not know until election day which party they'll decide on." Mr Eggleton said the party's research showed the swing against the Government was strongest in Victoria, with swings also in Western Australia and NSW. "We've targeted 30 seats — and based on our research we'll win half." He denied suggestions Liberal Party president John Elliott was an electoral liability, saying Mr Elliott was irrelevant in terms of the campaign, and said the likely leadership hand-over to Mr Keating was a problem for the Government. "Our survey showed the electorate doesn't believe Mr Hawkc will stay on if Labor wins," he said. "Over the last 12 months Mr Keating has been hurting them as individuals, he's unpopular and an unattractive alternative leader." Mr Eggleton said the party's federal executive was likely to approve a campaign featuring Opposition Leader Andrew Peacock in six television commercials. In Sydney, Mr Peacock said Lib- ■ eral Party polls indicated it would win the election, and he believed the Labor Party knew it too. Mr Peacock's claims come de spite the latest Saulwick poll figures showing the Labor Government approval rating had risen to 40 per cent, while support for the Opposition had slipped to 37 percent.

15 Feb 1990 - Letters to the Editor Mr Stevenson is completely out of step Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 February 1990, page 8 to the Editor Mr Stevenson is completely out of step Received February 12 So our very own Minister for Racial Purity, Dennis Stevenson has now become a morals campaigner. He is introducing a bill to ban X-rated videos, and quotes the usual discredited arguments to support such a ban — arguments which have remained unchallenged for too long. He claims that the ACT is "out of step" with the other states which have all banned X-rated videos. This proves nothing—just because everybody else is doing something doesn't make it right. Mr Stevenson should know this — there is a poster in his office with this very message. To set the record straight once and for all, the only reason why X-rated videos were banned in the states was because of an hysterical scare campaign conducted by a Sunday newspaper in Sydney in early 1984. The newspaper took advantage of public ignorance at the time by referring to all X-rated videos as "video .nasties", and claiming they included child pornography and bestiality. Fringe pressure groups interstate got wind of this campaign and flooded politicians with letters resulting in the bans. Rather than being "out of step", the reverse is true. Australia is one of the only countries in the Western.world with bans on X-rated videos. There has never been any suggestion of banning them in New Zealand, and America survived the entire Reagan era without having them banned. The "ban-it brigade" are actually suggesting that Australians lack the maturity to have access to the videos — an extremely condescending and insulting idea. There is also the red herring about people committing sex crimes after viewing X-rated videos — name one! For every crime that may have been committed due to X-rated videos, many more have been committed after watching Rambo movies (Hoddle Street, Queen Street shootings), and even after reading the Bible (numerous homosexual murders). The vast majority of the public are quite capable of telling the difference between reality and the fantasy of the TV screen. Dennis Stevenson claims he has been "flooded with letters of support", especially from Queensland, Toowoomba in particular. Toowoomoa is the headquarters of the neo-nazi Logos Foundation which tried to hijack the last State election by running advertisements claiming the Labor party was about to "open the floodgates". Most of the letters Stevenson has received would contain false names and signatures, and be part of organised campaigns. He also quotes an opinion poll (with a total of 150 people!) as supporting a ban. The most recent Morgan Gallup Poll (the most reliable) completely opposes such a ban. Stevenson's bill also makes the mere possession of five or more X-rated videos a crime. How will this be enforced? Will police have to periodically raid people's homes to make sure there are no X-rated videos on the premises? This provision alone should be enough to ensure the defeat of the Bill. The censorship debates have all been held and won. There is no reason to throw out more than 20 years of progress and return to the dark days of freely available child pornography and other outlawed "material. For that is surely what will hap pened — without government controls on X-rated material a huge underground black market will emerge. It will be open slather for the exploitation of children for real "video nasties" — won't Dennis Stevenson have something to complain about then! There are any number of seedy operators just waiting in the wings for Stevenson's bill to give them the green light. JOHN MOULIS Pearce

15 Feb 1990 - POLITICS Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 15 February 1990, page 8 POLITICS By Andrew Fraser Ideals die as voting becomes I a ritual CAST back your mind, dear Jl reader, to see if you can recall an election which wasn't said to be the most important since * 1949. If you were watching elections before 1949, of course, make that the most important since 1916. Donald Home, in his most recent •' book, What Was It?, puts elections ' under the heading of "rituals". Home's thesis is that elections are . sort of national shows, events in -which the nation sits back and ' watches the performance unfolding • before them. It is indeed a perform- ' ance of sound and fury, but does it signify anything? One element of the show is that each side must establish that it is a different side to the other, that really they are not the same. ''i Bob Hawke, when asked in last week's Bulletin just what was so important about this election to make it the most important since 1949, said "because the Govern ment in the next three-year period ■••• will essentially determine the Australia we take into the 21st century. "In the last seven years we have undertaken a fundamental transfer- ■" mation in getting a more efficient economy and equitable country. "The conservatives promise a return to the past on both fronts. They propose massive redistribution of wealth away from lower and middle-income Australians to a very wealthy minority. And also a return to the type of economic management which essentially means a misuse of our resources and a lowering of our economic potential. "We can either continue to trans form our economy and become r more efficient and equitable or return to the past." Andrew Peacock, when asked ~ much the same question, said, "It is • crucially important in terms of the well-being of the overwhelming ma- ' ' jority of families. "The great bulk of Australians have suffered grievously under the Hawke Government. The economy is a mess. Our indebtedness to com- "• mercial banks is of grievous propor tions. To turn this around will be a ■ ■ tough process but it has to be done. -So we will tackling foreign debt and inflation^ . " "We have the policies to do it. Labor doesn't — it will do more of" the same and so the economy will get worse under Labor. They have not indicated any change of ap proach whatsoever. We have. Our "7 Economic Action Plan will lead to ' •' | lower rates of inflation, lower inter est rates, higher real wages, less in- " debtedness." | Well that's .really made it clear, " hasn't it? BOTH sides promise change in -, economic management and | therefore economic performance, - ; which is sound enough politics giv- . en that there's no great satisfaction ' i with the economy at the moment, , 1 but there's no great detail as to how ' .• , this will be achieved. (Before you start jumping up and -down about the Economic Action plan, Liberals, let me point to the fact that health policy is relatively open-ended and there is the pro spect of more being spent on educa- .* tion.) Why these answers are worth recording in their entirety is because each side manages to say so little about its own plans while massively >n misrepresenting what the other side has to say. It is part of the election <>. ritual, and there is little wonder that " the electorate as a whole is begin- <.• ning to regard elections as rituals rather than as events which lay down the country's direction for the - . next few years. The politics of disillusionment ~l", are indeed writ large upon Australia at the moment although, to be fair to ' our politicians, Australia is not the only Western country where this is , happening. Look at the recent Thomastown , by-election in Victoria, where after " the informal votes and those for minor parties are taken out, only 44 per cent of those voting cast their -ballot for one of the major parties. Look at yesterday's Morgan Gallup Poll, which shows that governments in Western Australia, Victoria and NSW would all lose office were there an election tomor- ' row. Remember also that the . Queensland and South Australian , , Governments have been recently elected and the Tasmanian Govern- ' ment isn't too old either. Combined with the Morgan.Gal- ' lup Poll's state-by-state breakdown -of voting intentions which shows the ALP would lose support in ~ Western Australia and Victoria while gaining in NSW, Tasmania -and Queensland, the deduction '' from all this is that state govern- • ments are tending to lose the vote for their federal representatives. There is a more serious side-effect to the politics of disillusionment, and that is that it makes for bad government after the election is all over. Real political power does not come from simply getting more votes than the other party — real political power comes from a party outlining fully what their intentions are if they are elected and then getting elected. It has happened rarely in Australian politics in recent times — the Goss Government in Queensland, for example, has a mandate to clean up the corruption and inefficiency in the state, but little else. So whoever wins the next federal election is going to find that the prophecy of Vince Lombardi, celebrated coach of the Green Bay Packers, that winning is everything, is wrong — whoever wins the next election won't get anywhere near everything they want.

21 Feb 1990 - Interest rates first, Medicare later: Blunt Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 21 February 1990, page 22 Interest rates first, Medicare later: Blunt ' SYDNEY: A Coalition Gov ernment would look to change the health system only after it brought down interest rates, National Party leader Charles Blunt said yesterday. "Our priority is the family tax package," Mr Blunt said. "Once we address the econo my, provide relief for families, get interest rates down, then we'll address Medicare and its problems." Speaking on Sydney radio 2UE, Mr Blunt said Medicare would remain in place. "We dQn't think Medicare is perfect, we'd like to change it," he said. "Medicare will remain, in place, we will review it, our option is to provide choice. "You will be able to stay with Medicare voluntarily and pay the levy, or if you want to go to voluntary health insurance you'll have the choice under us." The Opposition ran into problems with its health policy late last year when spokesman Peter Shack was forced to abandon previous commitments that no-one would be disadvantaged under a CoaKtion policy. Since then the Opposition has announced that in government it would review the operation of Medicare, but would retain it for pensioners, health card holders and those not covered by private insurance. It would remove Medicare's monopoly on the provision of basic health cover, and would encourage families to take up private health insurance, possibly through tax rebates. Mr Shack said in a statement that yesterday's Saulwick poll provided evidence that people wanted to choose between Medicare and private health in surance. The poll showed 41 per cent of those surveyed preferred private health insurance with 54 per cent favouring Medicare. "The Coalition's health policy represents a 'win, win' for both these groups as everyone will be able to have their preferred form of health insurance," he said. Mr Blunt admitted yesterday the Coalition was not sure how much money its preferred ofr tions would cost, because it did not know how many peoplfc would opt out of Medicare, j "We'd like to change it but the money's not there," Mr Blunt said. Mr Blunt will kick ofT his election campaign in Too woomba today in the heart ojf the Groom electorate. I The Nationals lost Groom t6 the Liberal Party's Bill Taylotr in a 1988 by-election when the sitting National MP resigned. J Mr Blunt intends spending more than half of his.campaign in Queensland, where half thfc Coalition scats belong to the National Party. | But four sitting Nationals arc retiring and the Labor Party |s outwardly confident of picking up the two National seats <jf Dawson and Kennedy. The Nationals know, however, they must pick up several of Labor's marginal scats and Mr Blunt intends concentrating his efforts on them during the ne)U five weeks. '

21 Feb 1990 - And now for the first test Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 21 February 1990, page 22 And now for the first test The Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, has pledged a shake-up in the administration of unemployment benefits and extra money for training as both sides braced themselves for the first big event of the election .campaign. Mr Hawke, speaking yesterday before the release of the Government's economic statement today, .also tipped an inflation rate next year of around 6 per cent. The statement, to be issued by the Treasurer, Paul Keating, at 2.30pm today, will give details of the wage and tax deal with the ACTU and welfare measures to encourage more .people into employment and train ing programs. The Opposition continued its pre-emptive attack on today's statement, with the Deputy Leader of the Liberal Party, Fred Chancy, saying in Adelaide that the new deal with the ACTU would mean double-digit inflation. "It is a joke. What Labor's proposing will bring double-digit inflation and further reductions in real earnings," Senator Chancy said. Mr Hawke received good news from the polls. A Morgan Gallup poll, to be pub lished in today's Bulletin magazine, gave the Government 44 per cent and the Coalition 41 per cent, a one point drop for each. The Australian Democrats were unchanged on 10 per cent, while "others" were up two to 5 percent. However, Mr Hawke widened the approval gap, being up one point to 61 per cent, while Opposition Leader Andrew Peacock slumped 6 per cent to 23 per cent. The poll was taken over the weekends of February 3-4 and 10-11, before the March 24 poll date was announced and during the period the Coalition suffered a series of setbacks, notably over its health policy. A more contemporary poll, by AGB:McNair and published in yesterday's Melbourne Herald, showed 38 per cent support for the ALP, 32 per cent for the Coalition, 9 per cent for the Democrats and 11 per cent undecided. The poll, conducted by phone last Saturday, had 44 per cent rating Mr Hawke as the better Prime Minister, with 16 per cent opting for Mr Peacock and 25 per cent "don't knows". Mr Hawke began his first campaign visit to Melbourne, the most critical city in the country in terms of marginal seats, with a news conference which he used to give some indications of the main points of the economic statement. Unlike in the 1987 campaign, the Prime Minister plans to hold regular full news conferences in the hope they will pressure Mr Peacock, whom he regards as weak on economic detail, to do likewise. Mr Peacock, also in Melbourne, fine-tuned his language about how quickly interest rates would fall if he was elected. He had been saying the financial markets Would "react" from day one of the Liberal-National parties coming to power and that a "massive" fall would result, a more optimistic outlook than that used by his main economic spokesmen. Yesterday he said, "The markets will see from the statements I make on the first day I am very firm in an intent to put the policies in place — a coordinated range of policies — that will bring about sustainable and significant reductions in interest rates overtime." Both sides bought into the truck dispute, with Mr Hawke saying the NSW Premier, Nick Greiner, had the solution in his hands. However, the National Party Leader, Charles Blunt, told journalists in Sydney it was the Federal Government's fault because it was responsible for uniform road laws.

24 Feb 1990 - Good news for Labor as Libs struggle Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 24 February 1990, page 9 Good news for Labor as Libs struggle By HUGH LAMBERTON THE PERFORMANCE of some of the leading figures in the Hawke Government looked decidedly edgy this week, but Labor received some good news in the form of poll results. According to the latest Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin, Labor has maintained its lead over the Coalition. The poll of 2293 electors conducted on the weekends of Febru ary 3-4 and 10-11 showed support for both the Government and the Opposition down 1 per cent. This left Labor with 44 per cent, 3 per cent ahead of the Coalition parties, and in a winning posi• tion with the help of minor-party preferences. Support for the Australian Democrats remained at 10 per cent with 5 per cent of respondents indicating "others". As the poll was conducted just before the announce■.•.ment of the election, it indicates-Mr Hawke;\vasrin, a good position when he made the decision to go to ttie polls. In state-by-state breakdowns, the Morgan Gallup poll predicts a tough battle for the Coalition. For while the conservative parties could expect gains in Victoria „,and Western Australia, the ALP would pick up seats in ... Queensland, .Tasmania and NSW. These ^ains-would-! be.sufficient to return the Hawke Government, albeit! with a reduced majority. The poll showed the Prime Minister's approval rating up 1 per cent to 51, well up on the record low of 41 per cent late last year. Meanwhile, Andrew Peacock's approval rating fell 6 per cent to 23 per cent and his disapproval rating climbed 6 per cent to 64. There was also a fall in support for Mr Peacock among Coalition supporters, only 35 per cent said they approved of his handling of the job. Still, Mr Peacock tends to be galvanised by campaigns and his relatively strong performance in the early days of the campaign is likely to change voter perceptions as it did in 1984. Further good news for Labor came in a West Australian poll which showed increased support for the federal Labor Party. Western Australia is one of the states where the Coalition is hoping to make major inroads into the Labor majority. Published in The West Australian on Wednesday, the poll placed Labor ahead of the Coalition parties for the first time this year with 42 per cent to the Coalition's 41 percent. The Australian Democrats remained steady on 5 per cent, while the Greens lost ground with 4 per cent and 7 per cent were undecided. The poll points to popular approval of Carmen Lawrence's replacement of Peter Dowding as Premier and the diminishing influence of the WA Inc scandal as reasons for the increase. Respondents indicated that W A Inc was less likely to influence their vote, with 56 per cent of Labor voters stating it would influence their decision, down 9 per cent from last week. The good news for Labor continued with 67 per cent of Labor voters feeling the Hawke Government would be returned and 49 percent of Coalition supporters. The poll was conducted last Sunday and Monday.

28 Feb 1990 - Democrats get record ratine Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 28 February 1990, page 1 Democrats get record ratine SYDNEY: Voters are placing their trust in the Australian Democrats or independents, according to the latest Morgan Gallup poll. The Democrats have achieved the highest opinionpoll support in their history. 28 Feb 1990 - ELECTION 90 Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 28 February 1990, page 4 ELECTION 90 MARCH 24 Hawke winner of Great Debate: poll MELBOURNE: The Prime Minister, Bob Hawke, was a clear winner with people watching his televised debate with the Leader of the Opposition, Andrew Peacock, according to a Saulwick poll published in yesterday's Melbourne Age and Sydney Morning Herald. The national telephone poll of 1000 voters on Monday night also suggested Labor had increased its lead over the Coalition during the election campaign, with respondents' voting intentions pointing to an ALP two-party preferred vote of52.6 percent. The poll found 41 per cent of respondents thought Mr Hawke had won the Great Debate on Sunday night. Only 19 per cent of those interviewed said Mr Peacock won. Of the respondents, 43 per cent said they would vote Labor, 40 per cent supported the Coalition, 12 per cent backed the Australian Democrats and 5 per cent supported other parties. This voting pattern would give Labor a two-party preferred vote of 52.6 per cent against the Coalition's 47.4 per cent, compared with 50.2 per cent for Labor and 49.8 per cent for the Coalition in a Saulwick poll on February 16, at the start of the election campaign. Only 6 per cent of those polled did not say for whom they would vote or to which party they were leaning — a result which goes against other newspaper polls suggesting a third of electors have still not made up their minds. Questioned on the debate, 46 per cent of men said Mr Hawke had won, compared with 36 per cent of women, and Mr Peacock was seen "to have won by 22 per cent of women and 17 percent of men.

06 Apr 1940 - Shrewd Gallup Poll Tells What U.S. Is Thinking News (Adelaide, SA : 1923 - 1954), Saturday 6 April 1940, page 2 Shrewd Oallup Poll Tells What U.S. Is ThinkinI TO discover the trend of public opinion on any important subject, the United the opinions of a representative crosous Gallup Poll method, which compiles States of America uses the ingenis-section of the community. Recent cables announce that, according to the "New York Times," the latest poll indicates that 84 per cent. of the Americans questioned wished for an Allied victory in the war, while the small group favoring Germany six months ago had been reduced from 2 to 1 per cent. T|HE poll is under the direction ot Dr. George Gallup, whose object is to discover what a nation of 80,000,000 adults thinks. This is how his system works. On a street corner in Boston a stockbroker stops to answer the question. of a young man with a sheaf of ballots and a lead pencil:"Whom would you like to see electea President in November?" the young man asks. "Well, my first choice would be Wendell Willkie," says the stockbroker, "but I doubt whether the politicians would take to him. Put me down for Willkie. but say I'm still not quite decided." "If Canada is actually invaded b? any European Power, do you think the United States should use its army and navy to aid Canada?" "'Yes, that's one case where I'd be willing to see this country go into action. But I'm against our looking for trouble overseas." In the backwoods roads in Arkansas, the man who asks the questions wears a cap, and the man who answers wears the faded overalls of a back-country farmer. But the questions are the DR. GEORGE GALLUP same. Both stockbroker and farmer agree that the United States should come to the aid of Canada if the Dominion should be invaded. But the Arkansas farmer wants a third term for President Roosevelft. Both men who were questioned were selected on the initiative of the field investigator, but only after careful and detailed instructions from his home office. Multiplied hundreds of times, the interviews give a week-by-week cleture of what Americans are thinking about these matters. The problem of finding out what a nation thinks is not new. Since 1789 congressmen. legislators, and Presidents have tried to solve the problem. They have had to rely chiefly on letters from constituents, press editorials. and generally "keeping the ear to the ground." The Gallup poll has applied ·cientific methods to the subject. In the U.S.A. elections of 1936, while most American readers were following the widely publicised reports of "The Literary Digest" straw vote, which sent out more than 10,000,000 straw ballots, the new polls were undergoing their first big test. Cross-Section Principle USING only a small fraction of the gigantic sendout employed by "The Digest," the American Institute of Pub ic Opinion, the Crossley poll and "The Fortune" Survey all forecast a Roosevelt victory, while "The Digest" predicted a landslide for Landon. Although some of the new surveys 'ere not as accurate as their sponsors hoped, the experiences of the 1936 election did point the way to invaluable improvenents in method and approach. Most important, the election validated he principle of the scientifically selected cross-section over the old nass-balloting methods. The distinguishing mark of the surveys is the use of this cross-section principle. Briefly, it means that interviews must be obtained from each of he important and heterogeneous Opinion groups in the United States in exact proportion to the size of that group in American life, or in propor ion to its numbers on e;ection day. The sample must contain the proper proportion cfVoters from each State. Men and women. Farm voters, voters in towns of 2.500 or less and voters in towns and cities of more than 2,500. Voters of all age groups, including those who will come of age by election day. Voters of above-average and belowaverage incomes, as well as persons on relief, and Democrats. republicans, and persons of other political affiliations. In the State of Iowa. for instance, about 12 per cent. of the population is receiving relief or old-age assistance. Hence, in a typical institute survey, 12 per cent. of the interviews must come from persons in these various "relief" categories, and so on for other income levels. About 39 per cent. live on farms, while 61 per cent. live in cities and small towns, and interviews must reflect this residential division accurately. In the last Presidential election Iowa cast 56 per cent, of its major party vote for Roosevelt, and 44 for Landon. So 56 per cent. of the major party interviews in Iowa must be with Roosevelt voters, and 44 per cent. with supporters of Landon, with appropriate numbers for the lesser parties. About 10 per cent. of the State's population is between the ages of 20 and 24, and so the proper number of interviews must come from this and other age groups. Finally, since Iowa accounts for about 21 per cent. of the nation's voting population, 2½ per cent. of the interviews in a national survey must come from that State. There is nothing essentially new in this principle of cross-section sampllng. The bacteriologist who takes specimens of the water in a neighborhood stream at different points, to determine its purity, makes use of the principle. So does the ore-tester who calculates the richness of a lode of iron ore by thrusting a scoop into the ore at different points.What What is new is the application of cross-section sampling to the much more difficult business of sampling public opinion. In nearly all previous surveys of the public, this major principle has been completely overlooked. In modern polls of public opinion the number of persons interviewed is almost the least important factor. Far more important in assuring accuracy is the representativeness of the crosssection. It is even possible that a satisfactory nation-wide poll could be conducted with only 500 or 1,000 interviews, provided they were properly selected. The institute generally uses from 3,000 to 60.000 interviews, depending on the statistical problems involved. Good Record for Accuracy F'OR accuracy, records of the polls are so far good. In most important questions the institute has had an average error of less than 2 per cent. But it must be remembered that the polls have important limitations. The institute's goal in a national forecast is to keep its error within 4 per centage points, and to be on the right side at least nine times out of 10. One criticism of the polling method is that it tends to destroy the democratic process by discouraging people from going to the polls: that "winning" voters would think their votes un necessary, and "losing" voters wouldi think their votes could not help. But there is no evidence to show that polls decrease the number of voters at elections. Another criticism is that oolls handicaD the losing side because many voters are fickle and will swineg over to a candidate who is likely to win. Yet, when "The Literary Digest," using gigantic publicity methods, forecast the election of Landon in 1936, 27,000,000 voters cast their votes for the predicted "loser," while fewer than 17,000,000 voted for the predicted "winner." It is freely admitted that the polls can be misleading when they are poorly conducted. But a badly worded questionnaire is often self-exposing. To eliminate both bias and unintel!igibility from questions, the institute attenda to the constant testing and re-testing of he questions it selects for study. Another important point is to discover whether the views expressed to the interviewer are deeply or shallowly held. A voter will be asked his opinion on a certain question, and then asked. "How convinced are you of that -completely convinced or only partly convinced?" The replies give a means of singling cut the undecided individual, or the person who has little real inirterest in the issue. A frequent criticism of these surveys is that they constitute a threat to Arrerica's cherished representative democracy. American political theory has long been divided between those who would place more power in the hands of the people, and those who are fearful of the people and would iimit that power sharply. "I am personally convinced," says Dr. Gallup, "that the average American is more competent to judge what his best interests are than ever before. "As individuals, these people may not be brilliant or intellectual or particularly well read, but they possess a collective quality of good sense which is manifested time and again. "The people cannot be expected to express judgments on complicated technical or administrative policies. Nor is it in the province of the people to initiate legislation. What has been provided by the polls is a means of ventilating the gigantic structure of modern government with fresh draughts of what the usually silent and inarticulate people are thinking." So the report that a Gallup poll has revealed overwhelming sympathy for the Allies is food for serious thought. Increasing support for the Allies is attributed to a growing dislike of Germany's war tactics, the German treatment of Poland. and the realisation that England and France are fighting for principles important to America. (Condensed from an article in "Current History.")

02 May 1986 - Parliament Changes to Sex Discrimination Act debated Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 2 May 1986, page 11 Changes to Sex Discrimination Act debated MP fears legal adoption by homosexuals The Government's Sex Discrimination Act could be amended soon to allow de facto or homosexual couples to adopt child- ren, Parliament heard yesterday. Mr McGauran (NP, Vic), said he under-stood the Government was reviewing adop-tion law, which is currently exempted from the provisions of the Sex Discrimination Act. "I would certainly like a reassurance from the Minister that the Government will rule out of hand any change to that require-ment for adoption — that is that the couple be married — and that it would preclude de facto or homosexual couples from adopt-ing children," he said. Mr McGauran was speaking in resumed debate on the Sex Discrimination (Conse-quential Amendments) Bill. The legislation would bring 10 acts into line with the Sex Discrimination Act, fol-lowing a review by all government depart-ments of legislation which could be dis-criminatory. It would amend various acts to remove provisions which discriminate on the grounds of sex, marital status or pregnancy. The Opposition signalled yesterday that it would attempt to block four out of 10 of the amendments the Government was trying to make in the Bill. Its spokesman on legal affairs, Mr Spender, said the Opposition would seek to leave standing as they were the Aged or Disabled Persons Home Act, the Delivered Meals Subsidy Act, the Compensation (Government Employees) Act and the Seamen's Compensation Act. The Government is seeking to reduce the qualifying age for applicants for delivered meals from 65 to 60 for men. It is also seeking to abolish the three-year relationship qualifying period for seamen's de facto spouses seeking compensation after a spouse's death. Both these measures could open up payments to a much wider group of people, Mr Spender said; "In a time of tight budg- etary policy, are these the results the Gov- ernment intended?" he asked. The Attorney-General, Mr Bowen, said when the legislation was introducd two weeks ago that certain legislation would be exempted from review. Mr McGauran said yesterday that he understood these exemptions to be the De-fence Services Home Act, the Conscription Act (Combat Duty), the Marriage Act and probably the tax legislation The changes to the Acts would take place from August 1 this year. The Opposition failed to get its amend-ments passed and the Bill passed all stages. It will now go to the Senate. More inflation on way, Howard says Unemployment would grow by the end of the year and inflation was likely to increase past the present rate of 9.2 per cent, the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, said yester-day. The last quarter's inflation figure meant the Australian rate, compared with the OECD average, was the worst for more than 25 years. "And don't anybody imagine that the high-water mark of this country's inflation rate has been reached," he said. "Don't anybody imagine that 9.2 per cent is the worst we are going to hear." The Reserve Bank in a recent bul-letin had said Australia's relative in-flation performance was likely to worsen. Mr Howard was opening a debate on 'The need for new economic policy direction, including greater flexibility in Australia's wages and industrial relations system, to overcome the crisis in Australia's international competitiveness and balance of payments'. Unemployment would be much higher at the end of this year, he said. "Unemployment will go up as growth starts to slide in response to the high interest-rates policies being fol- lowed." Economic indicators were begin-ning to slide away, while Mr Keating had claimed that the prices-and-in-comes accord had improved Aus- tralia's international competitiveness. "That is the most ridiculous, stu-pid, economically illiterate comment and claim that any Treasurer to make," Mr Howard said. The improvement in Australia's competitiveness was only due to the devaluation last year. "What the Treasurer is really saying is that the only way his policies can deliver competitiveness for the Australian economy is to reduce liv-ing standards." In reply, the Treasurer, Mr Keating, said the Opposition's economic policy was a shambles and Mr How-ard's performance as Treasurer in the Fraser Government had squandered the potential in the economy. Mr Howard knew that Australia's depreciation had resulted in a tem-porary one-off price surge. "And he knows when that's washed out of the system through the Government's discounting arrangements it [inflation] will go back to 5 per cent." Backlash on Aboriginal policies worries MPs Government and Opposition spokesmen arc concerned that com-munity perception of the Aboriginal situation is making it difficult to help solve Aboriginal problems. The Opposition spokesman on Aboriginal affairs, Mr Connolly, said yesterday that serious problems faced Aboriginal people in both tribal and fringe communities. The results of an ANOP poll con-ducted for the Government last year had shown that MPs had a major problem in trying to win mainstream community support on Aboriginal policies. A backlash had developed against many Federal policies which sought to solve Aboriginal problems. "These problems consist of education, health, employment and general perception of the Australian community," he said. Mr Connolly was speaking in de-bate on a Bill to extend the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Act, which would otherwise expire this year. He said Aborigines for the most part were a specially degraded section of the Australian population. "And no Member of this Parliament sees that situation with any satisfaction," he said. For example, there were 4,000 to 7,000 Aboriginal children in the Northern Territory who were not re-ceiving an education. Aborigines had a life expectancy about 20 years less than white people. Mr Connolly's comments follow a poll issued in Melbourne yesterday which showed that 27 per cent of people thought Aborigines were better off than other ethnic groups and 22 per cent thought they were on equal terms. The Minister for Aboriginal Af-fairs, Mr Holding, said a level of criticism towards Aboriginal people and their aspirations had developed in the white community. Conservative political forces had "turned their hearts and minds" against the aspirations of the Aboriginal people. The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage (Interim Protec-tion) Amendment Bill passed all stages, after a division along party lines, and will now go to the Senate.

06 Feb 1978 - GALLUP POLL Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 6 February 1978, page 5 GALLUP POLL UK unhappy over race LONDON, Sunday (AAP) — Race relations are one of Britain's most serious social problems and are getting worse; according to a cross-section of Britons questioned in a Gallup Poll published today, Associated Press reports. 09 Jun 1954 - Morgan Poll In Reid Increased By Over 6,000 Cumberland Argus (Parramatta, NSW : 1950 - 1962), Wednesday 9 June 1954, page 15 Morgan Poll In Reid : Increased By Over 6,000 With a majority of 19,533 over his Liberal opponent as compared with 13,064 in 1951, and an absolute majority of 13,900 as compared with 11,161 in 1951, Mr. C. A. Morgan, M.H.R., was on Friday declared re-elected by the D.R.O. for Reid (Mr. McKenna). The final figures were: Morgan (A.L.P.) 32^958; Mutton (Lib.) 13,425; Hancock (Ind. Lab.) 3348; Aarons (Comm.) 2285; informal 1047. Total votes cast 53,063. In moving a vote of thanks to the D.R.O. and staff, and to those who supported him, Mr. Morgan said that while the overall result for Labor was disappointing, the fact was that a majority of the people throughout Australia had endorsed Labor's policy, and the extraordinary position had been created that the ^government had virtually received a mandate to carry out the policy expounded by the Opposition, and it will be interesting to see whether the Government would implement the same. In any event, the Opposition would be there in good force to keep the Government up to the collar. Labor's policy was always a forward one. and ahead of public opinion, said Mr. Morgan. All great reforms espoused by Labor were generally turned d'own in the first instance as many people were afraid of new and untried things, and the tendency was for them to play safe, but ultimately Labor's policy was endorsed and even adopted by its opponents. The Labor Party usually came into office in a time of crisis, and was in effect a crisis party. Inevitably it would come into office again in another crisis, either an economic one or a war crisis. Let us hope, he. said, that it won't be the last crisis of all for the Australian people and that the Government will profit by past mistakes and take heed of Labor's warnings and open up and develop and populate this country to make it strong enough to resist invasion from whatever quarter it may come.

20 Jun 1951 - PADDOCK TO PUNTER Cumberland Argus (Parramatta, NSW : 1950 - 1962), Wednesday 20 June 1951, page 10 PADDOCK TO PUNTER (By HARRY QUIGLEY.) If a Gallup poll had been taken early on Saturday morning on the questions of holding a race meeting in the afternoon the 'Noes' would have strolled in. 23 Aug 1987 - Coroner argues ABC Outsiders fomented riot Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 23 August 1987, page 2 Coroner argues ABC Outsiders fomented riot SUNDAY REFLECTIONS The week in review THERE WAS some rioting in the sour NSW hamlet of Brewarrina after the funeral of Mr Lloyd Boney, an Aboriginal who had died in police custody, and only days after the visit to Brewarrina of the NSW Minister for Police and his most senior gen-darme who had gone there to say soothing, prophylactic things. During the riot spleen was vent-ed at a hotel and at police and three policemen were hurt. Local whites said, as local whites do, that the local blacks had been so blissfully happy and contented for so long that Outsiders must have infiltrat-ed them and whipped them up into an otherwise-inexplicable frenzy. The ABC had one of its probing, investigative and syrup-voiced young reporters in Brewarrina with a team of sound and camera artisans. They produced some ex-clusive coverage of the fracas. In the wake of this scoop, the Brewar-rina coroner issued a press release in which he supported accusations by local whites that employees of the ABC were among the Outsid-ers who had cast these spells. He said that the ABC visitors had in- vested $1000 (of the taxpayer's money) in fermented and spiritu-ous beverages and had given these mind:altering draughts to the Ab-original people in order to trans-form these these normally content ed and grateful people into folk who behaved as though they had some grievances. The coroner is an endorsed Na- tional Party candidate and so it would be impertinent tp expect him to be intellectually agile, but even so it came as a small surprise when he agreed to television inter-views about his baseless beliefs and proved to be an inarticulate and confused and unconvincing young man, easily made to look like a poltroon. • THOUSANDS OF the world's most credulous credulists staged vigils at "points of earthly acu-puncture" to help bring about "harmonic convergence" which with the help of extra-terrestrials would make the world A Better Place. The points of earthly acu-puncture included the Grand Can-yon, Mt Fuji, Mt Olympus, the Pyramids of Egypt and, in Can-berra, Mt Ainslie. • ANOTHER harmonic conver- gence, the annual convention of the NSW Liberal Party, agreed that the death penalty should be re-stored as a punishment for really rotten murders. Warm, caring, good-natured murders should con-tinue to be punished with life im-prisonment The state Liberal leader, Mr Nick Greiner, said that the death penalty would never be-come Liberal policy while he was leader and criminologists and even senior gendarmes queued to say that the death penalty did not seem to deter. • IN ENGLAND, a young murderer pre-empted debate about his punishment by having the decency to shoot himself dead after shooting dead 14 people, one of them his mother, in the village of Hungerford in Berkshire. He was said to have had a deep admi-ration for Rambo and a psychia-trist said that the gunman's spree may have been suggested to him by reports of the previous week's massacre in Melbourne. • ONE MAN sentenced to impris-onment for the term of his natural life, Rudolf Hess, came to the end. of that term when he died, at 93, in a military hospital near Spandau prison. Ninety-three is a suspi-ciously early age at which to die and there was speculation that the Hun may have taken his own life. Hess, once the deputy leader of the Third Reich, had been Spandau's only prisoner since 1966, living in a cell measuring 2.73m by 2.26m. Anyone who has ever been sen-tenced to cross Australia in a first class carriage on the Indian Pacific train will have been given an in-kling of Hess's long, cramped or-deal although it is unlikely that his warders were as rude to him as the Indian Pacific's employees are to their captives. Spandau Prison, a gay edifice which might have been refurbished as a branch of Club Med. was to be bulldozed almost immediately in case any neo-Nazis began to regard it as a shrine. • ANOTHER GERMAN, Ms Steffi Graf of West Germany, be-came the world's number one woman tennis player at the age of 18 after the omnipotent computer which decides these rankings was fed and duly digested the informa-tion that she had just beaten Chris Evert in the final of the Virginia Slims tournament The toxoplas-mosis-prone and notoriously lach-rymose former number one, Ms Martina Navratilova, declined to talk to journalists about her over-throw and turned for solace to the extended family of lesbians, trans-sexuals and freaks which follows her everywhere and provides an enviable smorgasbord of shoulders for her to cry upon. • IN UNPREDICTABLE Queensland, the Assemblies of God Church in Caloundra pro-tested to the Heinz company about its nutritious but potentially devil-ish product Spooky Spaghetti, which contains fragments of spa-ghetti shaped as witch's hats, bats, hobgoblins and other symbols of the occuit. A little further south, on the God-forsaken Gold Coast, a magistrate acquitted "Fifi the French Maid" (alias Ms Margaret Duncan, 19, a professional strip-per) of wilfully showing what were laughingly referred to as her pri-vate parts during a memorable performance at a Surfers Paradise night club in March. The magis-trate said that Fifi's performance had little power to shock at a time when nudity was common in films, on TV and on the Gold Coast's beaches. • PRINCESS ANNE, the most bearable member of the insuffer-able Royal Family, disclosed that she has a morbid fear of flying. She is the only member of the family, other than its nasty Corgis, who does not have a pilot's licence. Her fears sounded quite rational in a week in which 160 people died in a plane crash in Detroit. Miracles happen, and the crash had a sole survivor, a four-year-old girl who was found in the arms of her dead mother. — IAN WARDEN Education for work is a very basic problem By RONDA FAENZA' ONE SUBJECT in the edu- cation debate certain to raise the hackles of em-ployers and teachers is the impor-tance of product versus process learning in our schools. Employers maintain that schools must produce students that have acquired certain basic skills of a high standard so that the students they employ can be trained to fit their specific needs. They emphasise the role of the three Rs — reading, writing and (a)rithmetic — in the learning pro-cess, but add spelling to the list of basic skills which cannot be left out of a teacher's educational tool. kit. Teachers, while agreeing with the need for students to emerge with basic skills, have over the last 20 years emerged with the belief that students should be taught how to learn, rather than a series of facts and figures which may be-come irrelevant with the onslaught of technology. . This educational theory, put in the most simplistic form, is called process learning, while the theory espoused on the whole by the most vocal of employers is called prod-uct learning. Employers give graphic exam-ples of their inability to find suit-able employees, even while the unemployment lines are long. A recent Willesee program, screened by Capital 7 on July 22, gave the public an example of a firm of solicitors in Blacktown, Sydney, which was unable to find one suitable permanent office ju-nior from more than 50 applicants. Many of the applicants were dressed inappropriately or had no aptitude for the job and so were not considered further, but the 20 who were interviewed in-depth had to sit for a basic spelling test with words such as contract, appli-cation and solicitor. Only a couple of the applicants got any of the words correct, but even they lack-ed other basic skills required for the job. This experience could be repeat-ed over and over again, as it was in Canberra this week when an em- ployer asked prospective appli- cants for a counter-sales position at a spare parts dealership to answer basic maths questions. One question asked how much change would a customer receive, after purchasing a spare part to the val-ue of $98, if they tendered a $100 note. All applicants asked "could they have a calculator please". A tax agent who required an of-fice assistant asked all the prospec-tive employees to calculate how much tax a person would pay over 12 months if they paid $20 each week from their wages. This was a reasonable question as a junior employee would have earned a wage requiring the payment of roughly $20 a week. Without fail each and every applicant multi-plied the 12 by the 20 to get the answer and could not understand why they were marked wrong. Employers are practical people, they have to be, their businesses need to be financially viable in order for them to stay afloat in this competitive world. A firm of solicitors is not only judged by cli-ents on the outcome of legal pro-ceedings but by the standard of correspondence they keep. A spell-ing error on a legal document ig could invalidate that document leaving a client unprotected by the law. The spare parts dealer needs to ensure that counter staff give the correct changc and a tax agent needs an assistant that can at least work out their own annual tax liability. A factory owner who sets up a beautiful-looking manufacturing process that never produces the finished goods up to standard would soon be bankrupt, so the expectation that students leave school with more than just the process of knowing how to learn is therefore justified. Schools, on the other hand, are under great pressure from society as a whole, not just from employ ers, to teach an ever-increasing range of options for students in a limited timetable. Educational theorists, especially those from overseas, have not made it harder on our educational institutions, as they expect the child to be devel oped into a whole person, to learn to think for themselves and to be an individual, to be a lateral think er who can look at a problem and work out a way to solve it when conventional thinking would not work. This type of student emerges able to take on the questions of the technological age, to grasp theories and to put them into practice. The computer wizards, the systems an alysts, the foreign exchange deal ers, the graphic designers and entrepreneurs are but some of the successful examples of process learning. But the common mass, or gener al public, seems to be left out of this. They and their children emerge from the new educational programs confused. They have en joyed their time at school more than any generation before them, they have a wider knowledge of the world as a whole and of political and social issues and they are more confident and aware of their rights. They are older, leaving school after spending more years (on average) there than their parents did and yet they are not well prepared for the workforce, or to take any job that comes by, or to start at the bottom and work their way up slowly, or to do things the way the firm requires them to be done. In the effort of educators to pro duce students ready for the 21st century, a whole generation has been lost. As usual in educational thinking, the baby has been tossed out with the proverbial bathwater. What a pity they are our babies! * Ronda Faenza is a Canberra-based freelance writer. Stage now set for debate Making an issue of the Australia Card By KEITH SCOTT WHATEVER the argu ments for or against the proposed Australia Card, it is doubtful that the Gov ernment can reasonably claim to have a mandate to introduce it. Legally, of course, it can and is entitled to hold a joint sitting of Parliament to pass the Bill, but in reality the re-election of the Hawkc Government had nothing to do with the Australia Card. Australians did not vote for or against the Government on the strength of the Australia Card be cause it was never an issue despite being the trigger for the election. But if the Government should be blushing for suggesting other wise, the Opposition should also be feeling a little embarrassed about its belated campaign against the card, kicked off last week by its colourful new spokesman for health, MrTuckey. For the Government, the pro posal was a convenient way to de flect difficult questions about fraud against the Commonwealth, but it backed away from making the ID card the issue that it should have been. If it really believed that the card was the best weapon to fight defrauders said to be costing the Commonwealth about $4 bil lion a year then, in an election so dominated by economics, it had a public duty to make the card a major part of its election platform. By the same token, if the Oppo sition believed that the card was an invasion of privacy and that it would not be effective in fighting fraud, it should have challenged the Government before the elec tion rather than attempting to do it retrospectively a month later. Both major parties were silent about the Australia Card in the lead-up to the July II election because nei ther thought that it was an issue likely to rally voters and becausc neither really knew whether we wanted an ID card. The Labor Par ty was not really sure that it had electoral support for the proposal and the Liberal Party was not sure that it did not have. There has also been criticism of the news media for failing to make the Australia Card an issue during the election campaign, but to some extent that seems defensible since it is difficult for journalists to make something an issue when neither the Opposition nor the Government wants to talk about it. The Government had a duty to set out what the card would be used for, how it would be used and what protection there would be for privacy, and it failed. One of the concerning aspects is that the Government has virtually acknowledged that there are prob lems with the privacy provisions of the Bill by announcing that it will introduce amendments after the Bill has been passed, but it refuses to spell out what the amendments are and what they will mean. The Law Council of Australia is sufficiently concerned to have decided last week to write to every Senator and Member of Parliament setting out what it sees as potential problems with the Da ta Protection Agency which is to be set up to protect individuals' rights. The council says that the princi ples governing the powers and functions of the agency are vague and contradictory, that it has no way of penalising infringements of privacy, that it is protected from being sued, and that it will become a "large and powerful bureaucra cy". Another concern is that the Government has consistently re fused to issue a report, first identi fied by The Canberra Times, said to be highly critical of the way that government departments are han dling fraud against the Common wealth. The Australian Federal Po lice Association has been particularly critical of the ID card as the best weapon against fraud, Mr Wilson Tuckey: he wants Senator Ryan to submit to a tie-detector test. and it is difficult to see how the Government can dismiss this without making the report public. Opinion polls carried out in 1985 and 1986 show relatively strong but decreasing support for the Government's proposal. ANOP polls showed that 75 per cent of people favoured the idea in June 1985 and that this dropped to 72 percent in November 1985 and 69 percent in January 1986. A survey of 1000 voters by The Age in June 1985 showed 74 per cent support while a Morgan Gal lop Poll of 1881 people in July the same year showed 68 per cent sup port. The Sydney Morning Herald carried out a random survey of 2000 people in June last year which showed 65 per cent support and another Morgan Gallop Poll last September showed 58.2 per cent support A Ncwspoll conducted for The Australian last November among 1150 voters showed 61 per cent support. No major public polls on the issue were carried out during the election. According to a Department of Health briefing sent to The Can• bcrra Times, conservative govern- ; merit estimates set the cost of -fraud against the Commonwealth at $3 billion a year through tax evasion and $150 million to $450 million a year through welfare fraud. The brief estimates that the Australia Card will cost $55.6 mil lion a year to operate and will pro vide total savings of $932 million, meaning net annual benefits to the Commonwealth of about $877 million. The Joint Sclect Committee on an Australia Card has said that the estimates of tax evasion could be half the real figure. The Government says that it proposes to use the Australia Card to determine eligibility for social security and Medicare benefits and : for a wide range of normal finan cial transactions, to enable the tax office to draw together financial information about individuals to ensure proper tax assessment, and to prevent people from obtaining benefits under false identities. Strong opposition by the Aus tralian Democrats, the announce ment that unions in South Austra lia will mount an advertising campaign against the Govern ment's claim that it has a mandate to introduce the card, and the for mation of an Opposition task force to oppose it have belatedly set the stage for public debate. The Government now has a re sponsibility to spell out exactly what abuses of the system individ uals need to be protected from and how that will be done, and how and for what the card itself will be used. The Opposition has a responsi bility to help raise the level of de bate. The two major public contri butions from Mr Tuckey since he was made spokesman on health have been that he will expose ministers who have cheated and that the minister responsible for implementing the Australia Card, Senator Ryan, should submit to a lie-detector test. The electorate is waiting.

02 May 1992 - Most would still keep Union Jack Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 2 May 1992, page 9 Most would still keep Union Jack ALTHOUGH more respondents favour remov ing the Union Jack from the Australian flag than eight years ago, a majority still want to keep it, a Morgan Poll published in the latest Time Australia magazine has found. The poll, in which 1452 people were interviewed face-to-face on March 21-22, found 37 per cent, up nine points since 1984, wanted the Union Jack out of the flag and 57 per cent, down nine points, wanted to retain it. Six per cent, "unchanged, were undecided. Asked if they favoured a new design, 42 per cent of respondents, up three points since 1984, said yes and 52 per cent, down three points, said no. Comments by those opposed to change included "Our heritage is in the flag" and "There are more important things'to worry about". Those favouring change made such comments as "Australia should have its own flag" and "We need a separate identity". Australians overwhelmingly believe unemployment is the most urgent issue to be addressed, another Morgan poll has found. The poll, conducted with 2328 electors interviewed . facc-to-face throughout Australia during February, found 70 per cent of respondents, up 11 points since September and double the figure a year ago, ranked jobs as one of the three most important issues facing the Federal Government. After unemployment came education, 21 per cent, up four points since September, and immigration, 18 per cent, up six points. A poll on the Senate conducted by AGB Australia in •March and April, with 4129 electors, published in the latest Bulletin magazine, has found support for the Liberal and National Parties at 44 percent nationally, dowh two points since January, and support for the ALP steady at 39 per cent.

09 May 1992 - Keating edges in front of Hewson Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 9 May 1992, page 13 Keating edges in front of Hewson FOR THE first lime since becoming Prime Min ister in December, Paul Keating is a nose in front of the Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, as prefered Prime Minister, a Morgan poll published in the latest Time Australia has found. The poll, conducted with 2245 electors interviewed face-to-face on April 18-19 and 25-26, found that 43 per cent of those polled preferred Mr Keating, down one percentage point, and Dr Hewson was preferred by 42 per cent, down two percentage points.The The number preferring another person,or or unable to say, increased from 12 to 15 per cent. When he became Prime Minister, Mr Keating was preferred by 35 per cent However, Dr Hcwson continues to enjoy a higher approval rating than Mr Keating. Approval of the way Mr Keating was handling his job slipped one percentage point to 39 per cent, and disapproval rose by the same margin to 49 percent Dr Hewson's approval rating was steady at 46 per cent and his disapproval rating fell two percentage points to 39 per cent. Support for the Labor Party late last month slipped half a percentage point to 38 per cent and support for the Liberal and National parties fell 2.5 percentage points to 43 per cent If a federal election had been held in April, the result would have hinged on minorparty preferences. Following the April 11 victory by independent candidate Phil Cleaiy in the Wills Federal by-election, support for individual candidates rose four points to 14 per cent In the latest Bulletin magazine, the Bulletin Poll, conducted by AGB Australia with 2009 electors on April 17-19 and 24-26, found that support for the major federal political parties had fallen in favour of Independents and other-mainstream candidates.

16 May 1992 - Opinions on flag are unchanged Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 16 May 1992, page 11 Opinions on flag are unchanged ACCORDING to an AGB Poll published in the latest Bulletin magazine, Paul Keating's highprofile campaign to change Australia's flag has had no impact on the voters. The poll, conducted with 988 electors interviewed face-to-face between April 24 and 26, found that during the Prime Minister's six weeks of making the flag a major issue, no-one in the electorate changed their minds about the idea. An earlier poll conductcd over March 13-15 found 61 per ccnt of voters were in favour ofretaining retaining the present flag; 31 per cent were in favour of changing it and 8 per ccnt were uncommitted. The latest poll found the numbers unchanged. The poll showed that voters in every state favoured retaining the flag, with Tasmania and Queensland showing the strongest support, both with 68 per cent. Women in the electorate supported the current flag, with 67 per cent, ahead of men, with 55 per ccnt. Pharmacists, doctors, dentists and school teachers arc seen as the most ethical professions, according to a Morgan Poll, conducted with 1343 people interviewed across Australia. The poll, published in the latest issue of Time Australia, found that, since 1988, pharmacists' ethicshonesty rating had increased by three to 79 per cent, while doctors had increased two to 69 per cent. In 1976, doctors rated 62 per cent. Dentists rated 66 per cent, up two, and school teachers rated 62 per cent, up seven. The image of bank managers had improved four percentage points in the past year, to 44 percent, while lawyers recorded the biggest drop, four percentage points to 44 per cent from 12 months ago. The poll showed that car salesmen and newspaper journalists, in that order, were seen as the most uneth ical.

19 May 1992 - Right to die: more approve Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 19 May 1992, page 3 Right to die: more approve SYDNEY: An increased majority of Australians and New Zealanders believe doctors should be allowed to help terminally ill patients to die if they are in great pain, according to a Morgan Gallup poll to be published in Time magazine today. A survey of more than 2500 people found increasing support in both countries for euthanasia regardless of age, sex or political affiliation. In Australia, 73 per cent of those questioned said doctors should let hopelessly ill patients die if they had no chance of recovering and were in great pain. This was a 4 per cent increase on the last similar survey in July, 1991. An even greater percentage, 76 per cent, a rise of 3 per cent, believed doctors should be allowed to administer lethal doses of medicine to patients who were in great pain with no chance of recovering and asked not to wake up again. The survey found common responses from people in favour of euthanasia included "in consultation with patient", "where suffering will be great", and "should be the patient's right to die in dignity if they choose". Opponents to the idea made such comments as "should let nature run its course", "leave God to decide" and "doctors should not play God".

20 May 1992 - Govt and Opposition 'run neck and neck' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 20 May 1992, page 1 Govt and Opposition 'run neck and neck' By ROSS PEAKE, Political Correspondent The Federal Government and the Opposition are running neck-and-neck, according to a poll out today. The AGB poll published in the Bulletin magazine says the ALP and the Coalition each have 40 per cent support in the electorate. The Prime Minister, Paul Keating, retains a narrow margin over the Opposition Leader, John Hewson, as preferred Prime Minister. The survey of 1264 electors was taken over four weekends, from April 17 to last Sunday. It reflects the effects of the Metherell affair in NSW, debate on changing the flag, and the early stages of the Marshall Islands affair, which led to the resignation of the Minister for Transport and Communications, Graham Richardson. The results show support for the ALP has declined by 1 per cent, while support for the Liberal and National Parties has fallen by 2. Mr Heating's approval rating remains on 28 per cent but his disapproval rating has risen from 43 per cent to 48. Dr Hewson's approval has declined from 32 per cent to 30 and his disapproval rating has increased from risen 33 per cent to 36 per cent. Two polls published yesterday showed Government support sliding. A Newspoll had the Labor Party's support down from 37 per cent to 36 and the Opposition up 2 to 48. This survey put Mr Keating's approval rating at 30 per cent, and Dr Hewson's at 39 per cent. The Morgan poll in Time magazine said the Government's support had slipped from 38 per cent to 37 while the Coalition's support remained unchanged at 43 per cent.

26 May 1992 - Aust 'taking too many migrants' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 26 May 1992, page 2 Aust 'taking too many migrants' Almost three-quarters of the population believe there are too many migrants settling in Australia, according to a Moi^an poll to be published today in Time magazine. The poll found almost as many people believed there were too many Asian migrants arriving in Australia. According to the poll, these were highest concerns expressed by Australians on the issue of immigration. The poll of 1244 people held on the weekend of May 9 and 10 found 71 per cent of people believed there were too many immigrants arriving, compared with 47 per cent in 1990. Sixty-eight per cent of respondents believed there were too many Asians, compared with 55 per cent in 1990. The poll found 20 per cent of respondents favoured no immigration and 21 per cent favoured no Asian immigration. According to Roy Morgan there was a strong link to unemployment in the comments-of people who believed the 1991 immigration intake was too high. Other frequent references were to immigration skills levels, with people saying migrants should have a trade or be skilled before being al lowed to settle. Some said there were already too many migrants in Australia, that they took advantage of social-security benefits, and should be able to speak English before being allowed into the country. Those who supported an increase in the migrant intake said Australia should be more compassionate, espe ciany towards reiugees. — AAP

30 May 1992 - Stone on fictitious doctors and dunderheads Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 30 May 1992, page 2 Stone on fictitious doctors and dunderheads By JODIE BROUGH The "so-called University" of Canberra is pretentious and afflicted with dunderheads, according to a former Treasury Secretary and National Party Senator John Stone. In fact, it; was "still better known to the local taxi drivers as as 'the CAE' " — a reference to its former existence as the Canberra College of Advanced Education, ' Mr Stone said in a speech at the Australian Medical Association's national conference dinner last night on the subject of "real doctors". Contending that the "good word" doctor was in "soiree danger of misappropriation" by people not entitled to it, he issued a sharp rebuke to the education policies of the Federal Government and its "Dawkins universities". The universities has "sunk into a slough of such intellectual despond as Aboriginal studies, women's studies, peace studies or even, heaven preserve us, sociology". He criticised the University of Canberra's decision to confer its first honorary doctoratc on the former secretary of the Amalgamated Metal Workers' and Shipwrights' Union, Laurie Carmichael. Mr Carmichael was a "steadfast pillar" of the Australian Communist Party, which had done "untold damage" to Austra lia. "For these services to our country, he was apparently deemed so meritorious as to warrant the bestowal upon him of its very first honorary doctorate by an institution now claiming to be described as a university," he said. His remarks were not aimed at John Stone Mr Carmichael "but rather at the pretensions of his newly emerged academic patrons of the so-called University of Canberra". There were other "fictitious doctors'1, politicians who had had honorary doctorates conferred on them, including his old adversary, Bob Hawke, and the former Queensland Premier, J oh Bjelke-Peter sen. "The two gentlemen in question have at least one thing in common," he said. "Neither has had much education, although Mr Hawke, it is true, did spend rather a long time at various universi ties." That doctors had scored worse than pharmacists in a recent Morgan Gallup Poll that rated the public perception of the the ethical standards of different professions, Mr Stone linked with the fact that many worked for state and Commonwealth health departments. "The more your profession gets into bed with the state, the more likely it will be to contract one or other form of STD — Subsidies To Doctors — and the lower will its reputation decline," he said. .. Subsidies to doctors, whether delivered through the Medicare system, grants for medical research or in other ways, inevitably carry a tag, on which there is written the word dependency; and before you know where you are, a full-blown case of AIDS — Acquired Increasing Dependency Syndrome — has developed. "If you don't believe me, have a - look at the creation of our Dawk ins universities, and reflect upon the reasons for that tragedy. It was, I suggest, a clear case of another STD — in this case Subsidies To Dunderheads (sometimes known, and particularly in Canberra, as vice-chancellors)."
