06 Feb 1995 - Small lead for ALP Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 6 February 1995, page 2 Small lead for ALP . Alexander Downer's resignation as Liberal Party leader lifted coalition electoral stocks but the Labor Government maintained a 4 percentage point gap in the two-party preferred vote, the latest Morgan Gallup Poll has found. The poll was taken the week end of January 28-29, after Mr Downer resigned but before John Howard officially replaced him as Opposition Leader and before the Government suffered a series of setbacks over forest and economic policy. ALP support was 44.5 per cent, the Coalition 41 per cent.

11 Feb 1995 - Men are victims as well Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 11 February 1995, page 11 Men are victims as well By ANDREW MclNTYRE THE NATIONAL Strategy on Violence Against Women (1992) indicated the need for reliable statistics on the nature of domestic vio-lence in Australia so that a full picture could be obtained. As a result, the Office of the Status of Women is negotiating to do a survey with the Aus-tralian Bureau of Statistics for such a study. In a timely report, the Mon-ash University Accident Re-search Centre has just complet-ed an in-depth analysis of domestic violence cases pres-ented at four of Victoria's large public hospitals. The study, by Virginia Routley and Jenny Sherrard, was funded by the Department of Health and Community Services, and will indicate the directions that need to be taken for an Austra-lia-wide survey. The scope of the study is of considerable importance, as it gives a clear idea of the prev-alance of domestic violence, at the level at which medical at-tention is needed, and clears up some harmful and miscon-ceived ideas that have ham-pered effective policy initia-tives by government so far. Essentially the report clari-fies some of the figures that have been used freely in the past in Ausfralia and overseas. It confirms the general percep-tion that men are more vio-lent, and that domestic vio-lence is in fact a relatively small problem. It also confirms the unavoidable fact that the amount of female violence to-ward men is greater than most of us are willing to admit. It shows for instance that of those presenting to hospital, the injury rate and admittance to hospital is three times as great in men. The virtue of the Monash study is that it has attempted to include both men and wom-en in its survey. What is clear from the study is that domestic violence must be seen and dealt with as a problem for both women and men. Of the adult violence cases presented to four major Victo-rian hospitals there were 988, or 2 per cent of all injuries presented to the hospitals, in-volving positive, probable or suggestive cases of domestic vi-olence. This is an extremely small percentage of the total population. Although this re-presents only those seeking at tention at public hospitals (others will go to GPs), it is nevertheless very much in keeping with the Australian Bureau of Statistics victims survey Crime and Safety in Australia, which revealed that in the 12 months to April 1993 only 0.7 per cent of adult wom-en had been victims of assault or even threatened with as-sault in the home. In the category of positively identified cases, the ratio of fe-male victims to male victims was established at five to one. In the cases of probable and suggestive domestic violence, where plausible explanations for injuries were not provided, an extrapolation of this same ratio was applied because of a problem in the methodology used. However, in an analysis of the injuries, the probable category male injuries ap-proached one male to three fe-males. Tellingly, the study shows that of those victims with injuries requiring hospi-tal admission, men made up no less than 40 per cent of all partner-inflicted injuries. The report suggests also that social and cultural factors, such as the reluctance of males to re-port themselves as victims, and stoicism in not admitting to injury, could lead to a higher male rate. The study confirmed that men were more likely to be admitted to hospital through severe injuries. They, far more frequently than women, were lacerated or punctured by knives, especially in the head and arms. In fact, women used knives to inflict serious injury twice as commonly as men. These figures, involving both men and women as perpetra-tors, confirm the basic findings of a Saulwick telephone poll of 603 Victorian voters run by The Age in June 1993. It was reported then that for every 12 female victims of domestic vio-lence there were seven male. The picture is strengthened more when the report focusses on domestic-related suicide and intended self-harm presenta-tions. Males make up more than a quarter of these cases when domestic problems or vi-olence is involved, and a third of the cases that arise from an argument with a partner. Tak- ing all cases of self-inflicted harm and suicide, which in-cludes cases with insufficient detail, men and women are al-most equal. Females make up 57 per cent, and males 43. The 1992 report National Strategies for Violence Against Women recommended the need for a detailed survey of domestic violence. It is true, there is no full picture in Aus-tralia with reliable and valid information. Notwithstanding this lack of information, the Office of the Status of Women intends to implement a survey in conjunction with the Aus-tralian Bureau of Statistics which will only look at wom-en, and then only as victims of violence. While its brief is the safety and welfare of women, there is little likelihood that such a limited survey will pro-duce a useful picture for imple-menting government policy. It certainly will not address the issue of why women are vio-lent, nor will it look at the complex interaction between men and women. The Office of the Status of Women believes, as an article of faith that "the social norm is violence against women", and it rejects that woman can contribute either as instigators or provocateurs in domestic vi-olence. If the Federal Govern-ment, wishes genuinely to help women then one cannot under- take research in such a fraught and unhappy area of social disruption with glib hy-potheses. There is now an opportunity for the office to deflect accusa-tions of bias and seek a truly useful picture of domestic vio-lence in Australia, particularly when there are limited re-search funds. It should seek to help potentially violent women by setting up referral services to match those now available only to men. Doing this would correct the perception that the office wants to prove women are only hapless victims. The Monash report has fo-cussed on the whole picture, and suggests two things with overwhelming clarity. If wom-en have a problem with domes-tic violence, then men also have a problem. If violent men have a problem, then so do vi- olent women. Andrew Mclntyre is a Melbourne freelance writer and social commentator.

20 Feb 1995 - Green is the colour of the future Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 20 February 1995, page 13 Green is the colour of the future INFORMED observers and poli-i ticians should not be surprised by the findings of the latest AGB McNair Doll published on Wed nesday, February 15, in The Age and 'The Sydney Morning Herald. Tlie Figures suggest, that the Australian electorate still takes essentially a Green stance in the debate about forests and the timber industry. They show that 63% of voters are opposed to logging in "natural forests that have not been logged before" and that 45% support but 43% oppose logging "natural forests that have been logged before". The figures also show that "only one in four... were more concerned about maintaining forest industry jobs than preserving the environment" and that "25% of respondents said that woodchip exports should bb', stopped immediately..." Saulwick Polls conducted over recent years have consistently shown ,that voters are concerned about the .'environment, and that this concern, contrary to the views expressed by ,-some politicians, and industry and trade-union leaders, remained strong even during the recent bad economicJimes with their high unemploy - ment. In March last year, when we asked our "litmus test" question, "Do you think Australians should concentrate on economic growth even if it means some damage to the IRVING SAULWICK analyses the results of several polls and finds that a large number of Australians give protecting the environment top priority. environment; or concentrate on protecting the environment even if it means some reduction in economic growth?", 57% favoured protection, 33% economic growth and 10% did not know. These figures were similar to ones we had recorded with this question over a number of years. And when we asked voters in a different survey, also in March last year, which was the most serious problem facing the world today, 14% mentioned the environment (second only to war at 19%), a higher figure and a higher ranking than given by voters in the United States, Japan, Britain and Germany at the same time. Five years ago, in February 1990, we asked two questions on this subject. First we asked, "Which of these statements comes closest to your view: Trees can always be grown again so we should cut down and use whatever timber we need; or Forests are a valuable part of our environment and should be preserved wherever possible?" The result was an overwhelming 78% for preservation and 18% for use, with Australians still take essentially a Green stance in the debate about forests and the timber industry. only 4% not answering. We then said: "Thinking for a moment about natural forests — that is, forests that are not plantations. Would you say that the protection of timber workers' jobs is more important than the preservation of these forests or the preservation of these forests is more important than the protection of timber workers' jobs?" The results were 70% for forests, 19% for jobs and 11% "don't know". As may be seen from these answers, we were attempting to tap sentiment on this subject. The answers are clear. Recently I conducted some focusgroup' discussions with Year 11 school students in Melbourne. I found them, even at that age, a cynical lot. (I am not sure that does not say more about generation and the way we have handled problems in the post-industrial age than it says about them, but that is another story.) Certainly most were not interested in politics and distrusted politicians. Indeed many were profoundly ignorant about the Australian Constitution and about how Australia was governed. They were interested in personal freedom rather than social or political issues, but they were interested, some passionately, in the environment and in racial tolerance. They may well be a fertile recruiting ground for the Green supporters of tomorrow. Handling the complex issues of sustainable development is no easy task. Attempting to satisfy the legitimate and compelling need for jobs is also, of course, very difficult. Attempting to take the heat out of large demonstrations that block access to Parliament is also understandable. But what the polls are telling politicians and others interested in this debate, including employers and employees, is that this is an issue whose time is still coming. It is an issue that has taken root in the Australian political soil. To disregard this timely warning could prove costly.

27 Feb 1995 - Having trust in opinion polling Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 27 February 1995, page 9 Having trust in opinion polling By IRVING SAULWICK I SEE the veracity of opinion polls has again been questioned. I understand that Stuart Littlemore said some words on this subject on Media Watch, and that Murray Goot, an NSW academic who frequently comments on the polls, has again been up to his old tricks. Of course, the question is frequently asked: "Can you believe the polls?" At times it is asked by people who have a vested interest in denigrating the polls: politicians who are not doing well at the. polls and who say that the only "poll that is worth anything is the vote on election day, or other partisans in a political debate who don't like what a particular poll says. At other times it is asked by journalists who don't really know what the answer is, or by academics who wish to sound learned, or rhetorically by someone who wishes to promote their latest poll. Sometimes it is asked innocently by someone who simply wants to know the an swer. Yet it is an important question in these days when polls are used increasingly both to report on community attitudes and, on occasions, to influence them. The answer, paradoxically, is both yes and no. (These days there seems to be no certainties, no simple verities: everything seems to be more complex than it should be.) First, a couple of rules: Never trust a poll if it does not state who did it, when it was done-, what the interviewing i method was, how many people were interviewed and what the questions were. It might be "fair dinkum" but the chances are it's not... Lopk carefully at the questions and', trying hard to discount your own. bias, ask yourself whether they are as even-handed or as value-free as they might be. If they are not, treat the results with some scepticism. Also ask yourself: "Could I have answered that question accurately if it had been asked of me?" Good question design is critical to good polls — as the old saying goes "garbage in, garbage out". There are all sorts of poor questions. For example, if you are not an economist and were asked "Do you think, given the current balance of payments and other economic problems, that we should concentrate on fiscal or on monetary measures to alleviate the present economic position?" you could be pardoned for being somewhat perplexed. If you were bullied into an answer, what would it be worth? Or if, as a smoker, you were asked how many cigarettes you had smoked last month or last week, your answer, with the best will in the world, is likely to be way out, because you are most unlikely to know precisely. Never, I repeat, never trust a poll based on a voluntary phonein such as is sometimes run by TV channels. They have no scientific basis or veracity whatso ever. All polls are subject to "sampling error", a term which merely means that if you measure some people in a population you really are forced to make an estimate of what you would find if you measured everyone. The larger your sample (provided you use the right methods) the more accurate you are likely to be. WITH A sample of 1000 you can say that in 95 cases out of 100 your results are likely to be .within plus or minus about 3 per cent of the true figure — irrespective of the size of the population you are sampling. Keep this in mind when you read survey results — particularly those which show, or purport to show, a change from one time to another- , Finally, let us further consider the questions. Polling is not like putting people on the psychiatrists couch — we don't have that luxury. What pollsters attempt to do, sometimes successfully, sometimes not, is devise questions which go to the essence of a subject in a simple but not simplistic way. We know that most people are not just standing round waiting to be asked a question on that subject. We know that some might never have thought about it, or not thought deeply about it. We know that some might just not be interested. But we also know that we can produce, if we are careful and modest, some insights into peoples' beliefs, attitudes and behaviour which will approximate reality and which cannot be obtained any other way. I have always said that good survey work is a combination of science, management and art. One has to be scientific in one's design. One must manage one's resources well. One must also . train, brief and supervise one's interviews well. But finally one has to have imagination — to produce unbiased, value-free and simple questions which do capture real information from people to whom they are put and which allow them not to answer, if they wish, without feeling stupid. If this is done, and in my view it often is, then these polls, with all the qualifications I have implied above, can be believed. Irving Saul wick was the Fairfaxpollster from 1971-94.

02 Dec 1995 - Saturday FORUM Preparing our young for adulthood Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 2 December 1995, page 16 Saturday FORUM Preparing our young for adulthood Victoria is moving to educate its youth about politics and the responsibilities that becoming an adult bring, says DENIS MULLER A COUPLE of years ago, a colleague in the political science department at Melbourne University came in clutching his head in his hands. He had just taken a first-year politics class un the Constitution. Naturally, the Whitlam dismissal had featured heavily. A student had interrupted him with the question: Who was Whitlam? Last year, the Constitutional Centenary Foundation, chaired by former Governor-General Sir Ninian Stephen, conducted a survey among Year 11 students in Victoria about what it meant to them to be turning 18 and acquiring the status of citizens. The survey was conducted by pollsters Irving Saulwick and Associates. It did not matter whether the students were from private schools in Toorak or Catholic regional schools in the outer western suburbs or inner-suburban government schools, the answers were almost ritualistically similar: freedom to drink, drive, get married, sign a lease on a flat and so on. As a footnote, the right to vote would get a mention; so would some of the duties of citizenship, such as jury service. Knowledge of how the voting system works, the roles of Parliament, of the executive government and of the courts was woeful. The young people generally could make no connection between themselves as individuals and these great institutions of power. Their sense of democratic ownership of these institutions was virtually non-existent. Partly this was caused by cynicism about politics and politicians, but partly it was a direct function of their sheer lack of knowledge about the way the "system" works, and a corresponding ignorance of the possibilities for democratic involvement. Other research car ried out for the Prime Minister's Expert Group on Civics revealed the same state of affairs nationally. There was a lot of publicity about the need for schools to do something about it. Victoria now appears to be taking the lead. Next week, the Victorian Board of Studies, which sets curriculum policy for government schools and heavily influences the curriculum of Catholic and independent schools in Victoria, will begin considering the detailed content of a Civics course. Once the details have been approved by the board, the course will be accredited for use in Victorian schools. The focus is on the way Australia's political, legal and economic systems work. However, it is not just "nuts and bolts" detail: there is a cultural setting for it. The groundwork is laid in the early years of schooling where young children are taught to think about the idea of "rules" and how they affect our daily lives — road rules, rules at home, at school, in games, among themselves. By the end of primary school they will have been taught about the way we resolve disputes in society, about the role of local councils, perhaps seen a council meeting in progress. IN SECONDARY school the content becomes more speci fic. The state-wide curriculum in Victoria says that by the end of Year 8 (at the age of about 14) a student will be able to: describe the three levels of government in Australia; outline the roles of the prime minister and state premiers; discuss ways individuals can take part in the political and legal systems (voting, consumer and political groups, standing for office and so on). Later in secondary school, students will be expected to explain how the political and legal systems of one country have been based on those of another country. This is where students will be taught about the Constitution and invited to debate issues such as an Australian republic. Now the Victorian Government has gone one step further. It has launched a project called Understanding Australia, the purpose of which is to identify knowledge which is essential to an understanding of Australia — its history, geography, literature, music, art, as well as political, legal and economic structures. The project is to be run by a committee chaired by Mary Atkinson, who is chairwoman of Victoria's peak Aboriginal education body, and consists of the chairman of Western Mining Corporation, Sir Arvi Parbo, a retired Supreme Court judge, Sir James Gobbo, a curriculum specialist from La Trobe University, Professor Brian Crittenden, and Professor Trang Thomas, chair of the Victorian Ethnics Affairs Commission. The materials produced through the project will be distributed to schools on inter-active CD-ROMs, and the work is to be completed by the end of the 1996 academic year. The content is keyed directly into the Victorian curriculum, which describes the skills knd knowledge students are expected to have acquired at various stages of their schooling. This educational effort dovetails with moves by the Constitutional Centenary Foundation — funded by the federal, state and territory governments and managed in Melbourne — to introduce some form of citizenship recognition for people when they turn 18. The exact form this recognition might take is still being debated. The research done last year by Saulwick suggested that young people are not enamoured of a heavily formal ceremony, but are quite open to the idea of some rite of pas sage. They value the idea of being citizens for reasons which may appear self-centred. A better educational preparation and an explicit recognition of their formal status might be a way to broaden their appreciation of what being an Australian citizen really means.

16 Dec 1995 - Davies gets dumped by Qld Labor Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 16 December 1995, page 2 Davies gets dumped by Qld Labor BRISBANE: The Labor Party in Queensland last night dumped Ken Davies as its candidate in the north Queensland seat , of Mundingburra for the crucial February 3 byelection. The decision was made at a special meeting of the party's administrative committee, which conferred for more than two-anda-half hours last night before saying that the key reason for dumping Mr Davies was the uncertainty of his involvement in a civil action with the Commonwealth Bank. Nominations for the seat have been thrown open and close at 4pm (AEST) today. Senior Labor Party officials have called on current Townsville mayor Tony Mooney to nominate. The by-election follows the recent decision of the Court of Disputed Returns that Mr Davies, who has held Cabinet rank, was not duly elected at the state election in July. The outcome of the by-election will determine the future of the Goss Labor Government, which has a one-seat majority. Speculation was rife before the meeting that the meeting would dump Mr Davies in favour of Mr Mooney or former mayor Mike Reynolds. Last night's special meeting coincided with a poll in the Mundingburra electorate which showed the Liberals hold a slim lead over Labor. The AGB McNair poll has the Liberals with 51 per cent and Labor on 49 per cent support on a two-party-preferred basis. It also found the Green vote has collapsed to three per cent from more than 11 per cent at the July state election.

24 Feb 1992 - Liberals begin campaign for seat of Wills Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 24 February 1992, page 3 Liberals begin campaign for seat of Wills MELBOURNE: The Liberal Party began its campaign yesterday to win Bob Hawke's old Melbourne seat of Wills by calling for an immediate by-election in a letterbox drop of the electorate. Respondents were also told the inquiry had found that the area was culturally and religiously significant to many Jawoyn people but other Jawoyn people thought it was not. • A similar poll conducted in May 1991. for the manager of the Coronation Hill joint venture, Newcrest Mining Ltd, found that 31 per cent of Australians believed -mining should be allowed to go ahead regardless of the views of the Jawoyn and 25 per cent favoured it if requested, by the Aborigines. Thirty-nine per cent opposed mining outright. The ranks of people who unconditionally favour mining have swollen most since May. It is the new giant cyclotron or atom-smasher just put into operation at the Department of Terrestrial Magentism of the Carnegie Institution in Washington. This cyclotron, one of the two largest in the world, weighs more than 225 short tons. " It has an over-all height of 12 feet, is 30 feet long and 20 feet wide, it took four years to build, at a cost of 500,000 dollars. The Carnegie cyclotron is housed 10 feet beneath the earth's surface to prevent the radiation from reaching people outside. Mice which were exposed to cyclotron radiations of much less intensity than those created by the new atom-smasher died in a few hours. To prevent accidents, should anyone be in the laboratory while the power is on, master switches on doors leading to the high-voltage parts automatically cut off all power when these doors are opened. The cyclotron operates at a frequency of 10 megacycles, which means that the polarity of Hie electrodes is being changed 10,000,000 times a scscond. A physicist, Dean B. Cowie, is in charge of the machine. He sits at the control board away from the instrument itself, and protected from its radiations by specially constructed insulating walls. Before him are seven main switches, more than 100 smaller ones and a maze of dials and metres Only by pressing the right switches in the right order can he dperate the machine. New Science For Waste \yiTH the motto "Nothing that grows is useless" the science, chemurgy is resolved to find new uses for established crops; new crops for either new or old uses; and profitable use for agricultural wastes. Chemurgy, which was evolved in America in the mid1930's to provide new sources of revenue for farmers, has assumed firstrate importance with the crippling of many imports by enemy conquests and the dislocation of supply routes. Chemurgy has found, for instance, that sugarcane, cornstalks and peanut husks make an excellent substitute for cork. Genuine cork is produced from an oak grown in North Africa and Portugal. Chemurgy, too, has realised that weeds can fill vital national needs. Fibres of milkweed floss, like kapok, are hollow, air-filled, very buoyant, Mid covered with a wax which renders them practically impervious to water. The floss has become a substitute for kapok in the manufacture of lifepreservers. In addition, its insulating properties are-so great that it is being used in high-altitude suits for air men Another use of wastage has given the American tobacco industry a substitute for glycerin, which is vital to the manufacture of explosives. Sources of the new substitute are discarded apples, apple peelings and cores. Market has therefore been found for more than two and a half million bushels of offgrade apples which normally would have been wasted each year. ? ? * Normandy Sidelight JQURING the early days of the Allied invasion of Normandy, and at the height of one of its fiercest battles, a British stretcher-bearer found a nest of fresh eggs-a rare luxury.. He found a piece of board, and scrawled the words "Booby Trap," and placed them on the eggs. Then he went back to his job of bringing in the wounded. Later, when the worst of the fighting was over, he went back to the spot, gathered the booty, and soon sat down to an appetising dish of fried eggs. * ? ? Kenneally routed single-handed two crack Afrika Korps companies, totalling 180 men, in Tunisia. As a result, he brought home to England the 77th VO of this war. He recently paid his first visit to a movie set to watch Tommy Trinder at work in Ealing Studios' new film, "Champagne Charlie." He met and «poke to the comedian, and swopped experiences about the Italian battlefield, where Trinder entertained troops earlier this yew. ? * * Repetition rpHE fact that history does repeat it self is proved by Blight-Lieutenant Francis De-Moleyns, RAF. He is a direct descendant of one of William the Conqueror's standard-bearers who set up William's standard at the Battle of Hastings. 01 Oct 1991 - Hewson 'upset' at seeing his children interviewed on TV Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 1 October 1991, page 2 Hewson 'upset' at seeing his children interviewed on TV The Leader of the Opposition, John Hewson, said yesterday he had been unable to contact his former wife or children since Sun day night's 60 Minutes program on their divorce. Dr Hewson said he was upset to see his children interviewed on the program and had tried to ring them yesterday without success. "But I'm still their father, and I love them very much," he told journalists in Launceston. "And I will do what I've always done, which is to try and give them the best opportunities I can, and I look forward to continuing to develop our relationship." His children — Tim, 17, Micah, 14, and Rachel, 8.— criticised him on Sunday night for putting his political career ahead of his marriage when he decided to leave their mother and his wife of 20 years, Margaret Hewson, just before Christmas, 1985. Mrs Hewson said Dr Hewson ended the marriage because he did not think she could cope with being a political wife. She made similar claims in an article published in September's Women's Weekly which, like the Nine Network, is owned by Sydney businessman Kerry Packer. Asked whether he was sur prised Mr Packer's media organisations were running the story, Dr Hewson said he was drawing no conclusions. "Look, in public life, you take what comes, he said. "There's been an air of desperation around in the political scene in Australia for the last 18 months since I've been leader, to knock over John Hewson, and I'm just going to continue doing what I've been doing." He said he and the media would have to live with each other "for a long period of time" when the Coalition won government Liberal Party officials refused to comment on the saga yesterday. The director, Andrew Robb, said he wanted to let the issue die. However, an Opposition frontbencher, Michael Baume, best man at Dr Hewson's second wedding, sprang to his defence, criticising the interviews as disgraceful and unprecedented. He said it was an unfortunate coincidence that the interviews appeared while Mr Packer was involved in a bid for the Fairfax newspaper empire with Canadian media baron Conrad Black. He said Nine Network staff probably made the decision to screen the program but it "wouldn't do [Mr Packer's joint] bid any harm". Public reaction appeared mixed yesterday, as the subject dominated radio talkback and television current-affairs broadcasts. Pollster Irving Saulwick said it was too soon to know whether the Hewson divorce would damage his political support "Now whether making him more human, even if it's human like the rest of us in the population, some of whom have good marriages and some don't whether that s going to help him or not remains to be seen," Mr Saulwick told ABC radio. "Certainly, Bob Hawke's personal problems don't appear to have had a negative effect on the perception of his job by people."

02 Oct 1991 - MIDWEEK MAGAZINE TO LIVE OR NOT TO LIVE Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 2 October 1991, page 19 MIDWEEK MAGAZINE1 TO LIVE OR NOT TO LIVE Elizabeth Hampshire considers the meaning of the ACT Labor Party's controversial policy on euthanasia. AUSTRALIAN society is be- coming quite understanding of a person's right to die but how understanding is it of murder? While many Australians support passive voluntary euthanasia the recent policy support of active voluntary euthanasia by the ACT Labor Party is something alto-gether different. While each situation is unique, some of the difficulties in legislating on euthanasia are illustrated in a past case. A woman dying of terminal cancer of the throat is no longer able to take food and fluids by mouth and is suffering consider- able distress. She could live for a few more weeks if medical feeding by way of nasogastric tube were continued. However, the woman does not want the extra two or three weeks of life because life has become a burden which she no longer wishes tobear. She asks the doctor to help her die and the doctor agrees. Medical feeding by way of nasogastric tube is discontinued and the woman dies a few days later. A noble or dignified death by passive euthanasia was in the patient's best inter-est, yet the method of facilitating it was not. The patient could have died less painful-ly if given a lethal injection. But active euthanasia is illegal in Aus- tralia. Under Australian common law, "a doc-tor must never do anything actively to kill his patient, but he is not bound to fight for the patient's life forever". Mercy killing is not condoned but there is no reason why an adult of sound mind cannot refuse medical treatment or request it to be withdrawn. In Victoria, where three out of four peo-ple support euthanasia, the Medical Treat-ment Act 1988 supports the common law in allowing patients to refuse life-saving treatment but it does not legislate for ac-tive euthanasia. The South Australian Natural Death Act 1983 does not directly authorise any activi-ty which causes or hastens death but it rejects active euthanasia. Adults can refuse "extraordinary mea-sures" to prolong life and doctors have a duty to follow pa-tients' wishes. The Northern Ter-ritory's Natural Death Act 1988, sim- ilar to the South Aus- _ tralian model, is the other Australian legislation which has a public policy on euthanasia but it too re-jects active euthanasia. In NSW, euthanasia has been ruled out as an option because it is not supported by a majority of doctors or by religious groups. The West Australian Law Reform Com-mittee has recommended similar legisla-tion as in Victoria where competent patients could sign a "refusal of treatment" certificate and appoint a power of attorney to make treatment decisions on their be-half. In the ACT, where the common law on euthanasia applies, the ACT Labor Party has adopted a policy which is likely to lead to a great deal of public discussion and controversy. It supports active euthanasia. At the ACT Labor Conference in June, the policy was endorsed by the party. It is the first Labor P-arty branch policy to acknowledge someone's right to actively end their own life under certain circum- stances and, if implemented, would have major social implications for ACT resi-dents and Australians generally. The Labor Party believes that a compe-tent patient has the right to refuse treat- ment A doctor could only assist a patient to die if a "living will" or power of attorney provided for tne withholding of treatment. If two doctors agree that the situation was irreversible incompetent patients could also be legally allowed to die. There is also provision in the policy to eliminate the risk of medical trespass by medical practitioners. It recommends objective counselling for anyone considering voluntary euthanasia and that "if a patient who has been coun-selled consistently requests assistance to die and two doctors are of the view that there is little or no prospect of substantial improvement of the patient's condition, then it should not be an offence for a doctor to assist the patient to die". Veronica Laletin, convener of the ALP Legal and Administrative Reform Policy Committee, sees it as a guideline for poli-ticians which will hopefully receive public support and eventually be legislated. "It is a radical type of policy which takes the issue one step further. "The ACT branch of the Voluntary Eu-thanasia Society of NSW came to us and asked that we consider it, which we did, and people agreed to present it to the ACT ALP Conference where it got cross-party support "While we expect opposition from some sections of the community and from some people involved in palliative care I under-stand there is widespread community sup-port for it. "Some people would like the option and to me that's part of the caring process. "It seems extreme that opposition groups are basically saying that it's a choice — to care or let die." Mrs Laletin said that while many people see the Labor Party as taking a courageous step on a major issue it will be up to the parliamentary party to decide to put it to legislation. She envisages a wait of at least a year before it comes up for major public scruti- ny. Gwen Wilcox, director of the ACT Lib-eral Party, said that while some members would be strongly opposed to it "you can-not bind people on that sort of thing, you must allow them to have their own opin-ions — it's up to the individual". The Liberal Party has no public policy on the topic of euthanasia and its members will have a conscience vote on the proposal as it is a moral issue. The ACT Labor Party's policy is based on the Netherlands' system which is the only country where active euthanasia is legal and where doctors are not prosecuted for giving fatal drugs to terminally ill pa- || Safeguards are needed to stop misuse || - tients. About 6000 Dutch people receive lethal injections a year. The ACT Labor Party is the only poli-tical group in Austra-lia to go further than supporting passive euthanasia. The Concise Ox- ford Dictionary defines euthanasia as "the bringing about of a gentle and easy death". Under the common law it is murder. Voluntary euthanasia is seen by its pro-ponents as the inducement of a good, gen-tle and dignified death at the request of the patient. Those opposed to it see it as murder. The debate on euthanasia focuses on whether a person has the right to terminate his or her own life by withdrawing life-pro-longing treatment (passive euthanasia) or a right to expect the assistance of a doctor in administering a lethal injection to termi-nate it (active euthanasia). Despite political, medical and religious opposition, several opinion polls indicate public support for it. Results from a Morgan Gallup poll in July of this year showed that 69 per cent of Australians thought that doctors should be allowed to let patients die and that 73 per cent of Australians believed that a doctor should be able to administer a lethal dose if desired by a hopelessly ill patient in great pain. In 1989,40 per cent of Victorian doctors confidentially surveyed said they would practise voluntary euthanasia if it was le-gal. World-wide survey results indicate pop-ular support for euthanasia. Seventy-five per cent of those surveyed in England, Canada, the United States, France, Germany, the Netherlands and even Australia would like the choice to die. "They want the right for medical help to die as they had the right of medical help to be born," according to the new president of the World Federation of the Right-to-Die Society, Jean Davies. From a medical point of view the ACT Labor Party's policy is considered out of line with community views. Dr Peter Wilkins, assistant secretary-general of health services for the ACT Australian Medical Association, said that he could not see the AMA or any ethical medical organisation ever embrac-ing active euthanasia. "We could, however, go along with a codification of the social 'living will' type deal that they have in Victoria," he said. "Passive euthanasia is really a poor term because what its about really, is allowing nature to take its course." IN ADDITION to the general law, all members of the AMA must abide by its Code of Ethics which outlines doc-tors' responsibility to respect human life from the beginning, not using their medi-cal knowledge contrary to the law. Most doctors also subscribe to the 1987 World Medical Association Declaration on Euthanasia which declares that "Eutha-nasia, that is the act of deliberately ending the life of a patient, even at the patient's own request or at the request of close relatives is unethical. This does not pre-vent the physician from respecting the de-sire of a patient to allow the natural process of death to follow its course in a terminal phase of sickness." Dr Wilkins sees no objection to "living wills" which indicate a person's choice not to be resuscitated but does not support active euthanasia. He sees decisions on euthanasia to be primarily the responsibility of society and not of doctors. While the AMA does not campaign on ethical issues its concern is for clear legisla-tion of the medical profession's legal obli-gations under medical trespass laws. Religious opposition to euthanasia is common and is on the moral grounds that life is a "gift", not a "right" and that scrip-tural commands say that "thou shalt not kill". Active euthanasia is seen as forcing a "duty" to kill on doctors helping a patient in their "right to die". As the biggest religious group in Austra-lia, the Roman Catholic Church is a very vocal group and will be an influential op-ponent of the Labor proposal. Nicholas Tonti-Filippini, executive offi-cer of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference Research Office, a Monash University graduate in philosophy and ethics, and a leading spokesman on bio- ethic issues, sees no moral difference be-tween passive and active euthanasia be-cause "they are both immoral and unethical". "As a public policy-euthanasia under-mines the care of the seriously ill and the dying," he said. He believes empowering doctors to take life, either by action or by neglect, would undermine the whole of the palliative and hospice care of patients. Accordingly, many palliative carers op-pose euthanasia. According to Mr Tonti-Filippini, "the difficulty for most people is to distinguish between deliberately bringing about death by neglect of reasonable care, and of the reasonable refusal of treatment which is overly burdensome or distressing." He sees the debate as being about wheth-er the law should somehow facilitate sui-cide by neglect of care or whether the law should facilitate or allow another to aid or abet someone committing suicide or alter-natively homicide. A fundamental issue, according to the Catholic Church, is the worth of the indi-vidual regardless of their use and function. "It creates circumstances where those who feel they are a burden on others, with the creation of the possibility that they may take their own lives or direct another to take their lives, in a sense creates some-thing of an obligation not to be a burden on others," Mr Tonti-Filippini said. "In a society such as ours we should value people for who they are rather than for their use and function. "That's the choice we make in this de- bate — whether we're going to continue with care and support, valuing, people re-gardless of their diminished function, or whether we're going to make their value dependent on tneir ability to contribute."

05 Oct 1991 - Metherell poll has voters split Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 5 October 1991, page 9 Metherell poll has voters split THE resignation from the NSW Liberal Party of the former Minister for Education, Terry Meth-ercll, has exposed a split in public opinion as to what the Greiner Government's priorities should be, according to a Saulwick Poll this week. The poll, published yesterday in The Sydney Morn-ing Herald, showed Dr Methercll had the support of women, Labor and Independent voters in his call for the Government to attend to environmental and wel- fare issues such as support for victims of the recession. However, Coali-tion supporters be-lieved the Government's top priority should be firm economic POLL WATCH management. Overall voters were evenly divided, with 47 per cent preferring an emphasis on the economy and 48 per cent supporting Dr Metherell's view. The 600-voter telephone survey also showed that only 28 per cent believed the Premier, Nick Greiner, was doing a good or very good job, while 40 per cent considered his performance poor or very poor. Support for the Government and the Opposition was tied at 38 per cent, while 16 per cent supported Inde-pendents and eight per cent supported the Democrats or other parties, an indication that Labor could win an election on preferences. Divisions in support were marked by different age categories. Of 18-24s, 56 per cent believed the Govern-ment should concentrate on economic matters com-pared with 43 per cent who favoured the environment and welfare. Of over-55s, 42 per cent favoured the economy compared with 49 per cent for Dr Metherell's priorities. In federal politics, voter satisfaction with the Trea-surer, John Kerin, has improved substantially since June, according to a Newspoll survey published in The Australian, but his dissatisfaction rating has also in-creased, an apparent reflection of people making up their minds about the new Treasurer. Of those polled, 45 per cent were satisfied with Mr Kerin's performance, compared with 30 per cent in June. Mr Kerin's satisfaction rating is now significantly higher than Paul Keating's last recorded figure of 22 per cent Twenty-six per cent said they were dissatisfied with Mr Kerin, up from 11 per cent. Those uncommitted fell from 59 per cent to 29 per cent.

12 Oct 1991 - Hewson approval rating declines Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 12 October 1991, page 9 Hewson approval rating declines THE HONEYMOON appears to be over for the Hewson-led Liberal-National Party Coalition as polling shows opinion waning on whether it is capable of winning the next election. The latest Bulletin Morgan Gallup Poll has shown that, even though the Coalition is still the preferred and expected winner of the next federal election, its approval rating has dropped in the last three months with fewer voters wanting it to win the next election and tewer thinking it will win. A special Morgan Gallup Poll asked voters which party they "would like" to win the federal election in two year's fimp anH whirh nar ty they "think" will win. The poll sample was 1165 electors Australia-wide and was conducted on September 21 and 22. The poll found that in spite of the fact that in June 50 per cent of electors said they would like the Coalition to win compared to 34 per cent for Labor, by September the figure had dropped by four percentage points to 46 per cent. Thirty per cent now said they would like Labor to win. The confidence in the Coalition to pull off a victory in the next election has dropped also. Whereas 55 per cent said they thought the coalition would win in June, compared with 28 per cent for Labor, by September only 44 per cent thought they would win. Labor's electoral chances were favoured at 10 percentage points higher in September than in June with 38 per cent thinking they would win. Therefore, in just over three months, Dr Hewson's chances of winning the next election have dropped in they eyes of the electorate. The 11 percentage point drop in his chances signifies Dr Hewson's lowest rating on this question since just alter he assumed leadership in April 1990. This would appear to be the first significant decline in a year in expectations of electors for the Hewson-led Coalition. Of those who labelled themselves Coalition voters, 90 per cent said they would like the coalition to win. This is an increase of one percentage point on the June poll. Labor voters have increased their backing of the party by six percentage points since June witn 85 per cent saying they would like Labor to win.

19 Oct 1991 - Qld Libs plan seat fight with Nationals Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 19 October 1991, page 4 Qld Libs plan seat fight with Nationals BRISBANE: The Queensland Liberal Party is going ahead with the preselection of candidates in south-eastern Queensland seats despite National Party pleas to end three-cornered contests. The Liberals' state director, Lynton Crosby, said in a statement yesterday that his party had been buoyed by a recent increase in support, and was moving to preselect most of its candidates before Christmas. He said the redistributed electoral boundaries and a Morgan Gallup poll showing a 5 per cent increase in support for the Liberals in Brisbane gave good prospects for seats in Brisbane, the Sunshine and Gold Coasts, and in the north. The Liberals' move runs counter to Thursday's call for conservative unity by the National Party state president, Don McDonald. He urged a return to "common sense" in National-Liberal relationships and an end to three-cornered contests in which a National or Liberal opposed a sitting conservative parliamentarian. He wants the Liberals to resume talks also on closer cooperation on the impact of optional preferential voting, key policy agreements and election strategies. Mr McDonald made his comments as key National Party figures gathered in Bundaberg for yesterday's management committee meeting, followed today and on Sunday by the 250-member central council meeting. His concerns result from the breakdown in talks between the conservative parties, and the Liberals' intention to contest all seats in the Gold Coast-Brisbane-Sunshine Coast south-eastern corner, including those held by the Nationals. The National Party has three seats in the south-east that the Liberals might regard as winnable — Nicklin on the Sunshine Coast, and Surfers Paradise and Southport on the Gold Coast. The Liberal state president, Paul Everingham, has said that talks on closer cooperation depended on the Queensland Nationals' supporting fully the federal coalition's proposed goods-and-services tax package. Mr McDonald said, "Our combined resources should be used to target marginal seats to take from the ALP and win government — not squandered fighting each other for safe conservative seats." The ALP state secretary, Wayne Swan, said the Liberals would agree to "wimp out" of three-cornered contests in selected seats if the Nationals accepted the "unpopular" GST. "The Liberals' 30 pieces of silver will be a deal to leave sitting National members alone in selected Gold and Sunshine Coast seats," he said. The conservatives' deal showed how scared they were of a fair fight now that Queensland had fair boundaries.

05 Mar 1987 - The Canberra Times Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 5 March 1987, page 2 ©he (Hanbrrra &imcs Thursday, March 5, 1987 REHEARSAL IN N.T. The NORTHERN Territory election on Saturday has been elevated beyond the usual parochial issues by the emergence of a new political party, the Northern Territory Nationals. Encouraged and partly financed by the Queensland Nationals led by the Premier, Sir Joh BjelkePetersen, the new party aims to run the ruling CountryLiberal Party out of office. Sir Joh is, in effect, having a "dry run" on Saturday. He has split the territory conservatives, just as he is determined to split the Federal ones, and has put up candidates who accept his policies, just as he plans to do at the next Federal election. He is running candidates against people who were once his allies and will do the same nationally. He has made the Northern Territory election his litmus test: if his candidates win a significant number of scats (they do not have to win government) the Bjelke-Petersen bandwagon will gather pace, adding to the woes of the Leader of the Federal Opposition, Mr Howard, and the Leader of the National Party, Mr Sinclair. If they falter, there will be a sigh of relief south of the Tweed River. The bandwagon may not have been finally stopped, but it will be at least temporarily broken down. Sir Joh told a recent political rally at Alice Springs that the eyes of Australia and the world were on the Northern Territory election. The world may not be particularly interested, but the rest of Australia is. His candidates are standing in all 25 scats, but the only notable one is the former Chief Minister of the Northern Territory, Mr Ian Tuxworth, who was forced to resign from the CLP last May over allegations about receiving electoral allowances beyond his entitlements. A number of other Joh candidates are disaffected former CLP and Labor Members. The CLP is counting on the electorate to resent the intrusion of the Queensland Nationals. The Joh team is outspending its opponents in media advertising and counting on Sir Joh's charisma to win the day. Relevance questionable Whatever the outcome of Saturday's ballot, its relevance to national politics will be questionable. The Northern Territory is a vastly different electorate from any of the States. It has only 70,000 electors, so the seats are small. In those circumstances the personalities of candidates count for much more than in large federal ones. Further, about a quarter of the voters are of Aboriginal descent and see little merit in Queensland policies on Aborigines. Possibly the best thing going for the Northern Territory Nationals is the poor administrative record of the CLP. The Government has recently run up its first deficit, its financial involvement in casinos has proved costly and there have been allegations of nepotism. Although the Labor Party cannot win the Northern Territory election, it will not be the only loser. The conservative forces of the territory have been split by the intrusion of the Queensland Nationals and their actions in establishing a new party with the sole aim of strengthening the Joh-for-PM campaign. The Chief Minister, Mr Hatton, has vowed not to cooperate with the new party and the rift is now so deep that it will take years to heal. Sir Joh cannot attack established conservative parties and heap personal, abuse on their leaders without causing lasting distrust. At the Federal level, the conservative coalition is being torn apart by the Queensland Nationals' demand that their 12 Members should walk out of the coalition. Mr Peter Slipper, a Queensland National backbencher, said recently that "the coalition is dead. What we have to do is give it a decent burial." It may not be quite dead, but it is very sick. A Queensland walkout would almost halve the number of Nationals in the Federal Parliament, and perhaps there would be more defections to the Joh camp, from NSW, Victoria and the right wing of the Liberal Party. The latest Morgan Gallup poll indicates that the BjelkePetersen campaign is doing more damage to the Liberals than to the Labor Party. Sir Joh has ensured that the spirit of trust that has held the coalition together for decades has been shattered. How can the Liberals ever again trust the Queensland Nationals after their ruthless campaign to get the aging Premier into the Lodge? Sir Joh has done the conservative cause a grave disservice.
