05 Mar 1987 - Optional preferential voting a threat to party's plans Nationals' first aim is to control the conservatives Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 5 March 1987, page 2 Optional preferential voting a threat to party's plans Nationals' first aim is to control the conservatives From ANDREW STEWART, in Brisbane THE QUEENSLAND National Party is even prepared to lose the next Federal election to gain con-trol of conservative politics. In a realistic assessment of their chances, the Queensland Nationals at their central council meeting at Hervey Bay last week end did not expect Sir Joh Bjelke-Petersen to win government in his own right. That was the aim, but the Queensland president. Sir Robert Sparkes, admitted that a coalition of conservative forces was the most probable result. That would see John Howard as Deputy Prime Minister to Sir Joh. The Queensland Nationals ex-pect Mr Howard, as leader of the coalition minority Liberal Party, to accept such a position on the basis that his only alternative would be to go into opposition. There he might have to implement the flat-tax system he says cannot work and to repeal the retro-spective legislation against tax evasion which he fought so hard to introduce as Treasurer in the Fraser Government. Among the banana and palm trees of the Melanesian Village at Hervey Bay, the Queensland Nationals' management commit-tee and central council bluntly stated their belief that only Sir Joh could win the votes to ensure that the conservatives won the next Federal election, and conservative dissenters, such as the Liberals and Ian Sinclair's Nationals, would soon join the bandwagon once they scented the perks of govern- ment. The decision at Hervey Bay was nowhere near as united as Sir Rob-ert made out. Most of the Federal parliamentarians, including vocal Joh supporter Ian Cameron, op-posed the break with the coalition. But their words of caution were overwhelmed by Sir Joh's en-thusiasm (and bullying) and the support of Sir Robert. Sir Robert said he had remained sceptical that Sir Joh's crusade would succeed until he saw the Morgan Gallup poll on Wednes-day last week. "The polls show great support for our course of action," he said. "The 'Joh for PM' campaign has not really started and the Morgan poll shows we have 26 per cent support — think what that will be like in a few months, when the campaign really gets going." The strategist behind Sir Joh for 17 years admitted that the cam-paign would rest very much on Sir Joh's populism and that his age of 76 years could be a minus. How-ever, his summation of Sir Joh's campaign theme shows how much it will depend on tub-thumping populism rather than realistic poli- cies. "We're not trying to hijack any one or any party," Sir Robert said of the protests of Ian Sinclair and the coalitionists. "The Premier and his party are just trying to save the nation. It's quite clear the anti-socialist clement of the Australian people want new leadership. The sort of people forming Joh-for-PM committees in Sydney, Mel-bourne, Perth and Adelaide are disenchanted with the present Liberal approach and the influence of the 'wets'. "The coalition would still be in government if Malcolm Fraser and the people with him had made the decisions the people wanted. But we cannot risk another weak gov-ernment like that when we face the immense problems left to us by the Hawke socialist Government. The people want strong leadership and Sir Joh is the only one of the federal leaders able to provide that." Sir Joh offered the recipe he has honed over the past few months. "When we offer people lower tax-es, to get stuck into the unions, opportunity for the average person to have more take-home pay — the average person will be able to work as much as they like and keep 75 per cent in their pocket," he said. "That's why we will win the sup-port of the people." The Joh for PM for Australia's Sake (the full title of the party) campaign will be backed by the Queensland Nationals' research and campaigning methods. Former advertising executive Fred Maybury, who oversees these, said the Joh party was working to a $20 million budget — compared with $14 million spent by all parties in the 1984 Federal election. The Nationals are planning the direction of a major polling ex-ercise which will begin in the next few months. It will be a national survey of voter intentions and at-titudes, to provide quick and re-liable information (based geo-graphically and demographically) so that policies and campaign methods can be modified for max-imum effect. Sir Joh says policies are being studied but will be published only as the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, and Mr Howard publish theirs. Sir Joh says he will answer the grow-ing questioning about his policies by going direct to the people and asking, "Whom do you trust for strong leadership and to cut taxes? — certainly not Mr Hawke and Mr Howard, because they want new taxes." True to the Queensland Nationals' campaigning methods, the issues will be kept emotional and populist. The president of the Queensland Liberal Party, Mr John Moore, and officials of the Australian La-bor Party in Queensland have both warned their federal parties to counter Sir Joh quickly before his populism builds up momentum and emotional appeal. They re-called that both parties had be-lieved they could wear it down with reason and logic in the 1983 and 1986 Queensland election campaigns but failed, especially against the Nationals' big-budget, heavily emotional advertising. Indicative of the lengths Sir Joh will go to to win Federal govern-ment was his assertion to the cen-tral council that he would "stir up" the public by forcing a major strike just before the election and by getting tough as Premier of Queensland. Sir Joh is considering legislation to ban strikes in export industries, an action which he pointed out was sure to provoke unpopular strikes in the well-paid coal and waterside industries. Such devices mirror the anti-democratic nature of the Joh for PM campaign. Sir Joh is chairman and Sir Rob-ert deputy chairman of the cam-paign committee, with sub-com-mittees repor ting from states other than Queensland and on areas such as strategy, finance, policies and publicity. The main committee has "un-restricted discretionary authority in determining all aspects of the campaign". Candidates will be chosen and vetted by Sir Joh and Sir Robert. There is no avenue for grassroots input on policies, elec-tion of officials or selection of candidates. Asked whether the electoral laws requiring publication of the names of major donors would be a prob-lem, Sir Robert said, "We'll just change that retrospectively." However, he did dissociate himself from Mike Gore and others of the so-called "white-shoe brigade". "Adequate funding is at hand and it would be insidious of me to comment on Mr Gore," he said. "Our support comes from the average people who are sick of high taxes and worried that no-one will save them from the abyss into which the Hawke socialist Gov-ernment has taken this country." Asked how the Queensland Nationals, from such a small base — only 12 Members in Federal Parliament — could control the next Government and install Sir Joh as Prime Minister, Sir Robert replied, "We've had plenty of prac-tice in the last two state elections here." But some Queensland National federal parliamentarians pointed out some major problems. First, Mr Sinclair would not back down easily, leading to the Queensland Nationals sitting very uncomfortably in isolation on the cross benches. This would only emphasise in the public mind how small the breakaway group was. They said Sir Joh should not un-derestimate the damage which could be done to his cause as well as that of conservative politics by any infighting, since neither Mr Sinclair nor Mr Howard would be giving in. Second, they pointed out that there was no comparison between Queensland 1983 and Canberra 1987. The comparison in the next Federal election should be Queensland 1977 and 1980, when the Nationals decided to attack Brisbane, but had no organisation base and polled only about 10 per cent. It was not till 1983 that the Nationals could man polling booths in Brisbane and had enough people to handle postal votes and leaflet drops as well as all the other electoral matters which often make just the few hundred votes' difference between success and failure. Third, the Federal parlia-mentarians expect the Hawke Government to seriously consider introducing optional preferential voting, which would reduce the crossover of preferences between Liberal, National and Joh party candidates that normally max-imise the conservative vote. Op-tional preferential voting in NSW is the reason that the NSW Nationals so oppose the coalition break-up, because of their depen-dence on the goodwill of the NSW Liberals in not opposing each oth-er in seats. Sir Robert said he doubted if the ALP would be so cynical as to introduce optional preferential voting, but his Federal MPs arc not so sure in the current high-stakes politics. Sir Robert's aim is to poll about 30 per cent nationally for the Joh party. The party would like to win a few seats in Sydney and Mel-bourne, where half the Federal seats are, but Sir Robert and Sir Joh believe they can pick up such a concentration of seats in the bush and other states as to form the majority party in the coalition. In their version of percentage politics, the Queensland Nationals reckon they will wipe out the Liberals in Queensland, Western and South Australia and the Northern Territory, and make in roads in Tasmania and country Victoria and NSW. They expect to win at least 38 seats, 17 more than the National Party has now. They also expect the Liberals to lose nine seats to the Joh party. While Sir Robrt concedes that age will make Sir Joh's tenure as Prime Minister short, he expects the realignment to a coalition dominated by the Queensland Nationals to be a permanent fea-ture of Federal politics.

12 Mar 1987 - Criminologists argue against death penalty Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 12 March 1987, page 9 " Criminologists * argue against death penalty By ROD CAMPBELL, Legal Reporter Although a majority of,Australians tended to favour capital punishment, there was little evidence that it would achievc anything and good reasons why it should not be reintroduced, . two Canberra criminologists have said. Mr Ivan Potas and Mr John Walker, of the Australian Institute of Criminology, wrote recently that those favouring the death penalty because it removed the killer from society permanently should remember that in practice it had often been administered capriciously and there was always a possibility that an innocent person might be executed. In the latest issue of the institute's publication Trends and Issues, they point out that the abolition of the death penalty in Australia had not resulted in any significant increase in murder rates. In fact, the homicide rate in Australia had actually fallen during the past 20 years, from nearly 6 per 100,000 of the population to less than 4,4. The death penalty was abolished in Queensland in 1922 and in Western Australia in 1984. The other states and territories abolished it between 1955 and 1976. ANOP and Morgan Gallup Polls had shown pro-capital punishment results ranging from 70 per cent (for specific crimes such as child-murder, rape-murder or gang-war murder) to 43 per cent (which had been the result in Morgan polls in 1980 and 1986). A national survey commissioned by the institute last year revealed that only 26 per cent of respondents felt the death penalty appropriate for murder by stabbing and only 17 per cent for drug-trafficking. The criminologists said their research gave some support to the theory that juries were re luctant to convict when the death penalty was involved and often returned verdicts of acquittal or manslaughter. In Victoria and Queensland, for instance, the percentage of manslaughter verdicts had dropped after the death penalty was abolished. Victorian statistics showed that the proportion of insanity verdicts had also dropped after abolition. Their report questioned whether the death penalty was needed for deterrent purposes. They pointed out that in NSW, four out of five homicide victims knew their attackers and were frequently intimately related. In many of these cases, only very short prison sentences were seen as appropriate punishment. Many homicides resulted from domestic arguments which were usually unaffected by the existence or otherwise of capital punishment. Mr Potas and Mr Walker suggested also that the death penalty might have a "brutalising effect". It might actually inspire acts of violence and thereby diminish the deterrent effect of capital punishment. They acknowledged that there was "grave public concern" over convicted persons re-ofTending on release and that the "ultimate incapacitant" removed the risk of an offender escaping, or being paroled, and killling again or killing a prison officer or another inmate. But, they point out, the rate of recidivism for murder was among the lowest of all offences and most murderers behaved well after release. They concluded that life imprisonment was probably a sufficient punishment for murderers. The criminologists pointed also to the dangers inherent in using the death penalty as a form of retribution because the justice system could make, and had made, mistakes. "It is too late to reverse the decision or compensate the prisoner for a miscarriage of justice after the death sentence has been carried out," they said.

25 Mar 1987 - Two senators baulk at providing election trigger Liberals now in ID card tension Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 25 March 1987, page 1 Two senators baulk at providing election trigger Liberals now in IB card tension By ANDREW FRASER Tensions within the Liberal Party surfaced again yesterday as two Liberal senators "reserved their position" on opposition to the Government's Australia Card legislation. The main objection of the two senators is not to the idea of the Australia Card, but more that rejection of the legislation would give the Government a trigger for a double dissolution. Senator Townley (Tas) would not comment yesterday, and Senator Jessop (SA) could not be contacted. The Opposition spokesman on health, Mr Porter, who has been running the Opposition campaign against the card, confirmed that the official party line was to oppose the legislation. But in practice it would need six Liberal senators to change their votes for the legislation to pass and the Government to be denied the trigger for a double dissolution. It is highly unlikely that the Australian Democrats will not oppose the Bill, as they would be better served by a double dissolution. In addition, they have been consistent opponents of the card. The Australia Card legislation was rejected by the Senate on December 10 last year, and is due again to come before it probably at the end of this week. The Leader of the Government in the Senate, Senator Chaney, said on ABC radio last night that, while the constitution of the Liberal Party guaranteed the right of dissent, he did not expect there to be any more than two senators having trouble with the legislation. "It's very much a minority view [within the party] that we would have trouble with an early election," he said. "The overwhelming weight of opinion within the party is that on this Bill we should certainly maintain our stance of principle. "If the Government is going to be totally unprincipled - if Mr Hawke is going to break his word again, and if there is going to be an early election - then we'll be up and at 'em." The day after the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Howard, dismissed Mr Peacock from the frontbench, their respective camps spent yesterday circling each other, and although Mr Peacock is still short of the numbers to topple Mr Howard the number of undecided members is increasing. At this stage, it appears that any leadership challenge will take place only after this weekend's National Party conference, where the prospect of the National Party splitting from the coalition will be dis cussed. Some of Mr Peacock's potential supporters were disturbed by his flirtation a few weeks ago with Sir Joh BjelkePetersen, and will be looking at the events of the weekend meeting, and Mr Peacock's reaction to them, before making up their mind. The Queensland Minister for Local Government, Mr Hinze, said in Brisbane yesterday that Mr Peacock's dismissal had dramatically increased pressure on the National Party to withdraw from the coali tion. And the former leader of the Australian Democrats, Mr Don Chipp, said in Sydney that Mr Peacock could be leader of the Liberal Party within five weeks. He described Mr Howard as "a decent little fellow", but without the "charisma, the elan, and the panache to get out there in front of the electorate and say 'follow me'." Yesterday was very much a day of consolidation for the Liberal Party, with a party-room meeting that managed to avoid all questions of the leadership. It now seems likely, however, that the Opposition's taxation policy, which is being billed as the cornerstone of its whole approach to government, will not be issued until just before the election. However, the publication of all other Liberal policies is to be speeded up so that the last policy to be issued will be the taxation policy. The Prime Minister, Mr Hawkc, after raising the spectre of an early election at the weekend, sought to play down such a course yesterday. "I have made it quite clear that my job is getting on with governing the country," he said. "That is what I am doing. I wouldn't be thinking about an early election if I were you." The Morgan Gallup poll to be published today shows that the Government's 3 per cent lead over the Opposition has been cut back, and the two are now levelpegging on 45.5 per cent. MELBOURNE: Australian Federal Police have contacted the office of the Leader of the Victorian Opposition, Mr Kennett, over the taping of the telephone conversation between Mr Kennett and Mr Peacock which led to Mr Peacock's dismissal. Police also contacted the editor of The Sun News-Pictorial, Mr Colin Duck, whose newspaper exposed the taped conversation. Mr Duck explained he would be happy to cooperate with the police as far as his journalistic ethics would permit. The lobby group whose members taped the conversation, People for Equality Not Institutionalisation, denied yesterday that the taping was a conspiracy or the result of a sophisticated phone-tapping operation. Editorial; Pryor's view. - Page 2.

26 Mar 1987 - Oz Card given push along Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 26 March 1987, page 1 Oz Card given push alon; By PAUL MALONE The Government guillotined the Australia Card Bill through the House of Representatives yesterday, keeping the Opposition guessing on its earlyelection strategy. The decision to make the passage of the Bill an urgent matter came as Liberal Party leadership contender Mr Peacock said it was not beyond the bounds of possibility that the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, would go to the Governor-General as soon as tomorrow week. Government representatives, including Mr Hawke, have been hosing down early-clcction speculation but the option remains open and the Opposition has to remain on its guard. The Deputy Prime Minister, Mr Bowen, moved to bring the Australia Card debate to an end in the after noon. Debate on the Bill in the Senate, which will determine whether or not the Government gets the trigger for a double dissolution, is now expected to begin on Monday morning. Opposing Mr Bowen, the leader of the National Party, Mr Sinclair, said there was no satisfactory answer as to why the legislation was being guillotined through the house on March 25 when it was not going to come into elTect for the average Australian till some time in the 1990s. "What's the urgency?" he asked. "Why have you got to hurry, Mr Deputy Prime Minister?" Mr Bowen said the Bill had been debated for seven hours and there had been 25 speakers. On the previous occasion the Bill had been before the House it had been debated for nine hours. The Opposition opposed the Bill in toto and there were no amendments moved. There was therefore no reason for a committee-stage debate. Most Government advice now appears to be against an early election. Right-wing numbers-man Senator Graham Richardson said his impression was that Mr Hawke intended to go the full term, and Mr Hawke's former adviser, Mr Bob Hogg, said his view was that the election would be held at its due lime. If Mr Hawke is considering an early election he got conflicting messages from two polls published yesterday. The Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin estimated Labor support to be 45.5 per cent, level-pegging with 'Put party first' call to Young Nationals. - Page 3. the coalition. On the other hand, the poll published in The Herald, Melbourne, estimated that 49 per cent supported Labor, compared with 43 per cent for the coalition. The result raises once again the question of the polls' accuracy. The polls were conducted on the same two weekends and the difference in the results is bcyohd the margin of error which the pollsters claim. Mr Hawkc will clearly not make a final decision on an early election until he sees the fallout from this weekend's National Party Federal Council meeting. The former National Party Deputy Prime Minister, Mr Anthony, made a plea yesterday to party members to vote lo retain the coalition with the Liberal Party. Mr Anthony also advised Mr Peacock to step back from campaigning for the leadership of the Liberal Party. "... Andrew would be better after his long and distinguished parliamentary career to step out of politics altogether," he said. Asked if he meant Mr Peacock should resign, he said, "'Well he doesn't have to resign but I don't think he ought to be pursuing a leadership role any more. He's had three terms."

29 Mar 1987 - Coalition support ignores reality Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Sunday 29 March 1987, page 1 Coalition support ignores reality Sir Joh told the National Party Federal Council meeting the party was ignoring reality if it continued to stand by the coalition. "You know if you keep your head in the sand you are looking to get some of your tail feathers pulled," he said. "I am not going to hang with them (the Liberal Party]. "We have sought to encourage you in the federal arena to follow the same path but you have stayed in the shad ow. "You have to come out into the sunshine, you have to take responsibility. "You would be pretty game if you stood up and said you have achieved your ultimate objective. "There's not much chance of winning the federal election the way we are going." In Brisbane last night, the federal Opposition Leader, Mr Howard, was "very happy" with Sir Joh's decision not to force a coalition split. "I think there might be some black spats on the white shoes tonight," Mr Howard said as he arrived at a Liberal Party function in the Brisbane suburb of Kalinga. But Mr Howard refused to make any personal attack on the Queensland Premier, saying they had a common goal, "Despite the vigorous exchanges we may have had over the past couple of months Sir Joh and I have one great thing in common - we both hate the Hawke Government and we both want to get rid of the Hawke Government." He said it was a joke to suggest there was any threat to his leadership of the Liberals and that he was happy for Mr Peacock to continue taking a high media profile. Mr Peacock has made appearances at Liberal Party functions on the Gold Coast and at nearby Gleneagle since his sacking from the frontbench earlier this week. "I like backbenchers to be high profile, it's good for them," Mr Howard said. "I have nothing but admiration for lan Sinclair and Ralph Hunt for the very stoic way in which they have resisted the difficulties. "It's looking a lot better." The coalition has a winning lead over the Government, according to a national poll of 2000 people conducted last weekend. The poll, by Spectrum Research and published in yesterday's Sydney Morning Herald, found the coalition had 49 per cent support and Labor -43 per cent.

30 Mar 1987 - NSW Premier climbs opinion polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 30 March 1987, page 3 NSW Premier climbs opinion polls SYDNEY: While all political attention in reccnt months has conccntratcd on Sir Joh BjelkcPetersen's campaign and the federal sphere, the NSW Premier, Mr Unsworth, has improved his electoral standing. Only six months after being named the least popular Premier, with support from less than a quarter of the electorate, Mr Unsworth has taken a decisive lead over the Opposition Leader, Mr Greiner, in opinion polls. In two polls published last week, Newspoll and Morgan Gallup, Mr Unsworth received an approval or satisfaction rating of more than 50 per cent. Both polls also showed the ALP ahead of the Liberal-National Party coalition, in voting inten tions. Analysts Mr Malcolm Mackcrras, of the Australian Defence Forces Academy, and Mr Ernie Chaples, of the University of Sydney, believe the new electoral boundaries in NSW will enable the Government to retain ofiicc at next year's election. The results justify Mr Unsworth's "back to basics" approach to government, with an emphasis on law and order, the "three Rs" in education and development with job creation. Cynical observers suggested that Mr Unsworth's surge in popularity was due in part to his lack of television appearances, and his staunchcst admirers would never claim a vote-winning personality in the manner of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, or Mr Unsworth's predecessor, Mr Neville Wran. If Mr Hawke calls an early election, Mr Unsworth may decide to follow suit, despite his statements that he will wait until the bicentennial celebrations are over and go to the ballot box in April or May, 1988.

31 Mar 1987 - New Right seeks seat of Higgins Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 31 March 1987, page 3 MELBOURNE: The leader of the New Right, Mr Andrew Hay, indicated yesterday he would seek preselection in the safe Victorian Federal seat of Higgins if preselection was reopened. And the Liberal Party's Toorak branch president, Mrs Helen Maxwell-Wright, said her branch would try to make the Higgins seat available for a more "high-powered" candidate than its current member, Mr Roger Shipton. Mrs Maxwell-Wright said the move to open preselection was "in no way a personal attack on Roger Shipton and what he has done". She predicted the front-runners would be the Elders 1XL chief, Mr John Elliott, and Mr Hay. She said party members in safe seats could afford to release a candidate so they could take a higher role within the party. "Any person of the calibre of Hay or Elliott should have a seat like Higgins," she said. "The people in safe seats should be the best we have available so that they can make controversial decisions without the fear that they could lose their seat." Party insiders predicted a better than 50-50 chance that preselection would be reopened. A motion to do so will be considered on Monday by the electorate committee. If passed, it will go before the Liberal Party's administrative committee in the first week of May. Mr Hay, president of the Australian Federation of Employers, said he would "very seriously consider" standing for the south-eastern suburban seat if it became available. The Victorian Liberal Party secretary, Mr John Ridley, did not want to comment on the party moves, except to say the reopening of preselection in Higgins was an "extraordinary situation" and without precedent. Mr Shipton was confident yesterday that he would hold the seat. "I'm asking the people of Higgins to vote for me in the next election and I'm confident that I'll be the next Member for Higgins," he said. Mr Elliott is overseas and has not commented on the latest moves. However, party sources said the move to open preselection had the support of Liberal Party headquarters. Liberals from the grassroots level up were concerned about the quality of Federal MPs and many wanted to find a way to "put up fresh blood". Another party source said that if preselection was opened for the seat, Mr Hay and Mr Elliot would probably sort it out between themselves as to who would make a run. "The important thing is that one of them gets there," the source said. Both Mr Hay and Mr Elliott live in the electorate. A recent Morgan Gallup Poll found the majority of electors in Higgins would back Mr Elliott if he stood as a candidate against Mr Shipton. Thirty-nine per cent said they would choose Mr Elliott, 37 per cent backed Mr Shipton and 24 per cent were undecided.

27 Sep 1984 - Peacock's popularity drops Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 27 September 1984, page 8 Peacock's popularity drops The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, will maintain his attacks on the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, over organised crime, despite the latest public opinion poll showing his popu-larity had hit a new low after he called Mr Hawke "a little crook". A spokesman for Mr Peacock said yesterday that "as far as that [ the organised crime issue ] in volves Bob Hawke, we will be resilient". A Morgan Gallup poll pub-lished in The Bulletin yesterday showed Mr Peacock's popularity at 25 per cent. The poll was taken a few days after the "little crook" statement. The Morgan Research Centre managing director, . Mr Gary Morgan, said the figure of 25 per cent for Mr Peacock's approval rating was "the equal lowest re-corded for a Prime Minister or Leader of the Opposition". [ Sir William McMahon re-corded 25 per cent in April, 1972, when he was Prime Minister. ] The poll was taken on the weekend of September 15 and 16 - instead of the usual poll base of two weekends - and showed Mr Hawke's approval rating had dropped by 2 per cent to 66 per cent. The weekend poll also showed that 73 per cent (up 2 per cent) of voters felt Mr Hawke was a better Prime Minister and 15 per cent (down 2 per cent) said Mr Peacock would be better. It was taken before Mrs Hazel Hawke revealed on television on Monday night that the Hawkes' daughter, Rosslyn, and son - in law, Mr Matt Dillon, were heroin addicts - a family problem said to have caused the Prime Min-ister's tears at a press conference last week. A second round of Morgan Gallup poll results taken last weekend, with a slight rise pre-dicted for Mr Peacock, are ex-pected to be published in the next issue of The Bulletin. Mr Peacock

04 Oct 1984 - Peacock approval still 25pc Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 4 October 1984, page 8 Peacock approval still 25pc SYDNEY: The approval rating of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, remains at 25 per cent and that of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has risen slightly to 67 per cent-, according to a Morgan Gallup Poll published in The Bulletin this week. The figure was obtained during the weekend of September 22 and 23, after Mr Hawkc had wept at a Canberra press conference and before his wife, Hazel, said on television that her daughter and son-in-law were heroin addicts. Mr Hawke's rating was I per cent up on a poll the previous weekend. The Bulletin said Mr Peacock's rating was the lowest for a Leader of the Opposition recorded by a Morgan Gallup Poll.

11 Oct 1984 - Peacock reaches 'all-time low' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 11 October 1984, page 7 Peacock reaches 'all-time low' MELBOURNE: The approval rating of the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, fell to 22 per cent at the end of last month - the lowest level of support for a Federal leader in a Morgan Gallup Poll. The poll found that backing for the Labor Party rose to 55 per cent, indicating that if an election had been held on the weekend of September 29-30, the ALP would have won by an increased majority. The approval rating of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, rose 2 per cent during the week when his daughter's drug problem was revealed - to 69 per cent. :

12 Oct 1984 - Electoral advantage the real reason for the Senate's rushed inquiry Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 12 October 1984, page 2 Electoral advantage the real reason for the Senate's rushed inquiry By PAUL MALONE A SIGNIFICANT con stitutional aspect appears to have been overlooked in the rush by the Senate to have a Senate Select Committee deal, before the election, with the allegations concerning Mr Justice Murphy. It was no secrct thai the election was coming but nevertheless the Senate decided to press ahead with its inquiry. But nothing has been gained by this haste. If the Senate were to find a case this year, it would still have to put the matter to the vote again next year. Under the Constitution, a justice of the High Court shall not be removed except by the GovernorGeneral, on an address from both Houses of Parliament in the same session praying for such removal on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. With the House of Representatives now risen until the election this could not now be achieved, even if the Senate were to find a case for the judge to answer. For the first half of the new year, the Senators elected at the forthcoming election will not take their places and we will therefore have the same Senate as at present. The senators who have pressed for the current inquiry could therefore have held oft until next year, when they would have had plenty of time to consider the matter and could have dealt with it in the calmer post-election atmosphere. But the politics of the situation cannot be ignored and it is clear that many recognised the possible electoral advantage of having the inquiry at this time. The committee is one of the few loose ends which remain to be tied up before we swing into a normal election campaign. One other odd matter remaining is the final Costigan report. This is due to be completed by the end of this month and the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, has promised that it will be made public even though Federal Parliament will not be sitting. The Senate has one more week to sit to complete its business before its members go on the campaign trail. The Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, has already identified Victoria and Queensland as the States where he will concentrate his activities in an effort to win the election. He will kick off in Melbourne on Monday, visiting the electorates of Menzies, Casey and Deakin. On Tuesday he will be in Bendigo and Ballarat. According to election-watcher Mr Malcolm Mackerras, Labor has a notional majority of 30 seats at present on the new electoral boundaries. Of the 16 seats which the coalition would have to win to wipe out this majority and take Government, seven are in Victoria. Mr Hawke will use his first week to visit the distant electorates of the Northern Territory and Western Australia. The voters of Perth will have a chance to directly compare the two aspiring leaders on Wednesday and Thursday, when they will both be campaigning there. Mr Mackerras points out that there is a huge number of marginal seats. If there were a swing of only 1 per cent to Labor, he says, the majority held by the Hawke Government would rise to 42 in the 148-seat House. While the House has been sitting the Government has had a useful weapon at its disposal. The Opposition can, of course, use the House to make statements under privilege but the Government always has the numbers and thus virtually always comes out on top. Even a well-framed Opposition question can be used against the Opposition. The Minister answering can simply ignore the question and take the opportunity to spray the Opposition for the deficiencies in its policy or its lack of policy. As a result the Government is considered to have handed the Opposition an advantage which it would not otherwise have had by deciding to dissolve Parliament and give the Opposition seven clear weeks on the trail. The Government is extraordinarily confident - and not without good reason. The last six Morgan Gallup polls, for example, have shown Labor with 50 per cent or more of the vote in its own right. The coalition has been hovering around the 40 percent mark, while the Australian Democrats and others make up the balance. The Age poll published at the beginning of the week also showed Mr Peacock's standing at a record low. Only 14 per cent of voters said they believed Mr Peacock was doing a good or very good job. At the same time those who thought he was doing a poor or very poor job stood at 46 per cent. In contrast, 64 per cent of voters felt Mr Hawke was doing a good or very good job. The polls may have margins of errors greater than their producers would like to admit, but the lead the Labor Government is estimated to have by all the major polls is so great that even allowing for this possibility, Labor is still safely ahead. Earlier this week Mr Peacock reacted sharply when questioned on the Morgan Gallup poll published in The Bulletin and referred to it as a "Packer" poll. What he omitted to mention was that Morgan Gallup also did the polling .for the Liberal Party. Presumably the internal polls are painting the same picture as the public polls. Mr Mackerras: points out huge number of marginal scats Mr Peacock: popularity rating at record low level Mr Hawke: promises to make Costigan report public

18 Oct 1984 - Caucus wants action on corrupt police, heroin Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 18 October 1984, page 3 Caucus wants action on corrupt police, heroin SYDNEY: Members of the Slate ALP Caucus told the NSW Premier, Mr Wran, yesterday that the time had come for the Government to take decisive action against corrupt police and heroin syndicates. A series of backbenchers expressed concern at yesterday's closed caucus meeting that the Government was being damaged by crime and corruption allegations. Mr Wran promised caucus the Government would take action against corrupt police and the heroin trade. Last night, the Minister for Police, Mr Anderson, announced the appointment of a Crown advocate as a special counsel to assist the Police Commissioner, Mr Avery, with investigations into allegations of police corruption. In caucus, government members were worried because the Morgan Gallup Poll published in yesterday's Bulletin showed the ALP would have lost a September election - when the election was due if the Government had gone full term. The chairman of the Parliamentary Committee on Prosti tution, Mr Rogan, said allegations of police involvement in drug trafficking should be given the highest priority. Mr Wran had opened the caucus meeting with an appeal for unity during tough times, similar to the one he delivered to Cabinet on Monday night. He repeated that he would not leave his position and asked that the Government members support him. He said the current administration was a successful government but conceded corruption allegations were damaging. Outside caucus, Mr Wran said he was relaxed and calm about the poll because the next election was three years, seven months away. The poll showed the LiberalNational Party Coalition would have gained 47 per cent of the vote compared with 44 per cent for the ALP. It is the first time the Wran Government's popularity has dropped below the Opposition. Mr Wran's personal approval rating was unchanged at 38 per ccnt while the leader of the Opposition, Mr Grcincr, was up 2 per ccnt to 51 per ccnt.

25 Oct 1984 - Peacock approval rating 19pc Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 25 October 1984, page 12 Peacock approval rating 19pc SYDNEY: The latest Morgan Gallup poll on election trends shows the ALP would have won a Federal election held in mid-October with an increased majority, although its support has dropped 5 per cent to 50 per cent. The poll, published in The Bulletin yesterday, shows Liberal-National coalition support at 40 per cent. The poll, taken on October 13, is bad news for the Leader of the Opposition, Mr Peacock, as it shows his overall approval rating among voters has dropped to an all-time low of 19 per cent. This is the lowest figure in a Gallup poll for any Federal leader. A separate poll, taken on the weekends beginning October 6 and 13, shows only 14 pcrccnt of voters want Mr Peacock to continue as Opposition Leader, with most preferring the Liberal Deputy Leader, Mr Howard. This represents a drop of 20 per cent in support for Peacock as Opposition Leader from April when a similar poll was taken. The October 13 poll, which questioned 958 voters, showed the approval rating of the Prime Minister, Mr Hawke, was 68 per cent, a drop of 1 per cent. Ninety-three per cent of Labor voters and 39 per cent of LiberalNational party voters approve of Hawke's work as Prime Minister. But only 33 per cent of LiberalNational party voters and nine per cent of ALP voters approve of Mr Peacock's work as Opposition Leader. Mr Peacock

05 Mar 1973 - NEW HONOURS FAVOURED BY MOST Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 5 March 1973, page 7 NEW HONOURS FAVOURED BY MOST Most people interviewed by the Gallup Poll in February favour replacing British honours with an Australian system of awards. 10 Apr 1973 - Liberals try new image POLL IN VICTORIA Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 10 April 1973, page 12 Liberals try new image POLL IN VICTORIA From ROHAN RIVETT, in Melbourne w HJLE the politicians gird themselves for the final jousts before Victorians elect their new Parliament six weeks hcnce, the ruling Liberals arc showing keener interest in matters of quality - especially quality of living conditions - than at any time in 20 years. Mr Hamer's emergence as Premier is perhaps the catalyst in ibis. The belief that any steps for reform - reform in education, of the environment, of housing of the less affluent, of hospitals, of jails, and a score of other issues - must await the disappearance from politics of his predecessor, had damped all but the zealots in their drive for change. Now the new Premier has been eager to present himself as an advocate of change - a champion of a better environment, a sponsor of a new look at education, a foe of pollution in all forms, a liberal in matters of social conscience. So, many bodies and individuals, long depressed at the inaction and seeming indifference of the State executive to deteriorating conditions of life in Victoria, have been given new heart. In the weeks leading up lo the campaign now about to begin, the Liberal Party has almost turned itself upside down in its new-found enthusiasm to present a reformist, sympathetic -almost radical - image in extraordinary contrast with the Boltc image behind which its members have sheltered since 1954. Even one of the Uolte sacred cows, the White Aus'ralia plank in the Liberal Party platform. was almost dropped last month. The commillcc drafting the platform on which the party will confront the clcctors dccided to omit the clause. Although this drafting committee embraced both the Premier, Mr I lamer, and the Deputy Premier, Mr Thompson, the big backers, who crack the whip in the constituencies, were appalled. Platform So. tinder pressure from electorate committees, branches and members, a somewhat shamefaced spokesman had to inform the Press that "traditional elements" had insisted on the magnificent euphemism "homogeneous society" being retained in the platform draft. So. today, despite the efforts of its two leaders, the parly goes to the electors with the old shibboleths of orthodox Liberalism, mass immigration and White Australia. Naturally, many of the most active Young Liberals feel thwarted. if not cheated. At last they have a Premier in whom they place hope and trust. Yet his draft of the party platform is overborne by the reactionary elements. Despite this, (he HamerThompson forces have made a bold, almost revolutionary attempt to emphasise social welfare and the righting of inequalities as the keynotes of the Ministry's quest for re-election. Setting up of a multi-milliondollar corporation to finance decentralisation in Victoria is so directly contrary to Sir Henry Boltc's philosophy that it has been hard for Victorians to realise that it is sponsored by men who for the past decade have sat in Cabinet as Sir Henry's trusted colleagues. The State Savings Bank, with a ministerial guarantee, will back the project and the public will be invited to invest in the corporation by taking >hort- or long-term bonds. How such important Boliebackers as Sir Reginald Ansctt. Sir Cecil Looker. Sir Charles MacGrath and other members of the Liberal Party establishment reach in this undisguised plunge into Stale socialism will probably be revealed only after the Scylla and Charybdis of the polls is safely negotiated. Campaign The new Liberal Party platform now thrust before Victorians is the firs! complete rewriting of the party platform since 1953. Despite the one-man campaign that the Chief Secretary. Mr Meagher, continues to lead against "porn", with all the enthusiasm of a 1973 Quixote, the platform specifically states that censorship is a personal matter for adults. The Hamer-Thompson policy etches in new concepts on sport and recreation, conservation and environment. decentralisation, rural development and youth problems. The Premier's policy speech in Camberwell Town Hall on May 1 will officially launch the new doctrine. [f Sir Henry graces the occasion with his presence it will merely confirm the views recently expressed by a migrant leader: "Your politics! are wonderful: yesterday's blacks! arc tomorrow's whites, with the same spokesman passionately defending both theses in turn". Features Among other features of the Hamer New Look made apparent in the past two or three weeks are: A drastic paring of the Bolte freeways program. A marked lack of enthusiasm for the subservience to Democratic Labor Party attitudes and policies. This is so emphatic that the DI.P State secretary, Mr Frank Dowling, had to warn that the DLP could deny preferences if the Liberals "think they can win in their own right". He added, "I'd hate to embarrass them with preferences if they think they don't want them". Frantic promises about plentiful supplies of water for metropolitan homes so that bucketing by householders on the hottest days of summer will never, never recur. A totally new approach to the problem of migrant children in the cramped, overcrowded schools of the inner suburbs. Altogether, if. as most observers expect, the current State gerrymander ensures the return of another Liberal-led ministry after May 19. it seems certain to sail on courses somewhat different from those navigated by Sir Henry over Ihe past two decades.

27 Apr 1973 - 'Most' favour army camps for youth Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Friday 27 April 1973, page 8 'Most' favour army camps for youth All young men should go to military camp for at least three months when aged 18, and perhaps again when aged 19, most people told the Gallup Poll last month. People were asked whether they favoured, or opposed, all young men going to military camp for several months. An overwhelming majority of 78 % said they favoured it. Only 18CS opposed it, and 5% were undecided. Those in favour included: 87% of L-CP voters, 81% of DLP voters and 72% of ALP voters. 79% of the women, and 76% of the men. 65% of those aged 16-20, 72% of those aged 2129, and more than 80% of older people. The 78% who favour military training were asked at what age young men should go to camp. Sixteen percent of all people interviewed said at 17, 38% at 18, and 21% at about 20. The other 3% (making the 78%) did not answer. On those figures, young men should go to camp when 18. Camp for six months or more each year was favoured by 34%, but 39% would agree to camp for only two or three months, and 5% were undecided. On those figures, camp for more than three months would lack majority support. When asked for how many years young men should go to military camp, 8% said for four or five years, 16% said for three years, and 19% for two years, and 28% for one year, and 7% were undecided. On those figures, the public would approve one (or perhaps two") annual camps for three months when aged 18 (and perhaps 19)1 People who favour compulsory military training for all young men often said "we should be prepared", "good for them", "teaches discipline". Those against it said they did not approve military training or it should he voluntary. Roy Morgan and Australian Public Opinions Polls.

30 Apr 1973 - Casinos opposed by most people Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 30 April 1973, page 7 by most w people M E L B O U R Nr E. Sunday. - Except in Tasmania and perhaps Western Australia, people are inclined to oppose having a casino in their State, according to a Gallup Poll. Asked whether they were for or against having a casino in their Slate, an Australia-wide cross-section of 2.270 people of 16 years and more divided almost equally. They answered: A casino: 39% in favour. Against: 40% Undecided: .. .. 21% In Tasmania. 57% approved having a casino, and so did 43% of Western Australians. However, in no other State were casinos wanted by more than 40%. The figures were: NSW: 38% Victoria: 40% SA: 33% Queensland: .. .. 38% Throughout Australia, only 43% of ALP voters and 35% of L-CP voters favoured having a casino in their State. Of those aged from 1620, 58% favoured a casino, and so did 52% of those aged from 21-29. Those aged from 30-49 were fairly evenly divided on this question, but most older people were against casinos. Most common attitudes were, "Too much gambling already", "I'm against gambling". "Causes too many broken homes". Those who favoured casinos said, "Promote tourism", "Gives the place a bit of life", "I like gambling'. (c) Roy Morgan and Australian Public Opinion Polls.

12 Sep 1974 - Price-wage poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 12 September 1974, page 1 Price-wage poll MELBOURNE, Wednesday. — Anohter referendum to give the Government power over prices and incomes was possible, the Deputy Prime Minister, Dr Cairns, said today after a two-hour meeting with the president of the ACTU, Mr Hawke, and the secretary of the ALP, Mr Souter. 25 Sep 1974 - Hayden disputes survey Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Wednesday 25 September 1974, page 13 Hayden disputes survey The Minister for Social Security, Mr Hayden, said yesterday that a report published in The Bulletin on September 21 concerning a Morgan Gallup Poll survey of (he preference of people _ for the present health insurance scheme or "a salaried medical service based on a 1.35 per cent levy on taxable income" was totally wrong. Replying to a question in the House of Representatives from Dr Kingman (Lab. NSW), Mr Hayden said that the report reflected cither incompetence or dishonesty on the part of people responsible for conducting the Morgan Gallup Polls. The report in The Bulletin stated that 2,014 people had been asked whether they preferred "the present medical scheme, with people paying into a hospital and medical'fund" or "a salaried medical service financed bv a 1.35 per cent levy on taxable income" which "would entitle people to free treatment in public wards, but additional insurance would have to be paid in private wards". A free salaried service financed by tax was favoured by only 38 per cent of the sample, the report said. Mr Hayden said that no even the most, malevolent critic of the Government's health scheme would deny that fcc-for-scrvicc medical practice would be covered by the scheme. "In fact, the universal health insurance program which will come into operation on July 1 next year is essentially based on the private pnutce of medicine, on the freedom of choice of one's medical practitioner by fee for service", he said. "There has never been any suggestion that it would be based on salaried medical practice".

18 Feb 1980 - CANADIAN ELECTIONS Trudeau ahead in Gallup Poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 18 February 1980, page 5 CANADIAN ELECTIONS sTrudeau ahead in Gallup Poll TORONTO, Sunday (AAP-AP). — In an .abrupt reversal of political fortunes, Mr Trudeau appears to be leading his Liberal Party toward victory in tomorrow's parliamentary elections 'over a Conservative Government that took power jn Canada just nine months ago. 01 Aug 1992 - Boost in popularity for PM: poll Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 1 August 1992, page 2 Boost in popularity for PM: poll The Federal Government's youth summit boosted the popularity of the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, according to a Newspoll published in The Australian newspaper. Voter approval for the summit also slightly narrowed the Coalition's lead on the Labor Government. The survey of 1127 electors, held on July 24-26, showed voter satisfaction with Mr Keating had risen four points to 28 per cent and his disapproval rating fell four points from a high of 68. Thirty-five per cent (up from 32 per ccnt a fortnight earlier) of those polled said Mr Keating would make a better Prime Minister than the Opposition Leader, John Hcwson. Thirty-nine per cent (up one point) opted for Dr Hewson., If an election had been held on the weekend of the poll, 39 per cent said they would have voted Labor (up one point) and 45 per cent (unchanged) preferred the Coalition. With a lead of six points, the Coalition is only slightly better off than it was before the 1990 election when it out-polled the Labor Party by four points but did not win government. In contrast, polls held before the summit showed Mr Keating's disapproval rating was high, while his approval rating was slumping. A Bulletin poll of 2029 electors on July 10-12 and 17-19, held by AGB Australia, showed Mr Keating's disapproval rating was 54 per ccnt with an approval rating of just 23 per cent. Dr Hewson's disapproval rating was 36 per cent while his apprdval; rating was 31 per cent. On the question of preferred Prime Minister, 39 per cent of those polled chose Dr Hewson while 32 per cent chose Mr Keating. A Morgan poll, published in Time Australia and held on July 11-12 and 18-19, showed Mr Keating's disapproval rating was 61 per cent, with an approval rating of 29 per cent. Only one of Australia's previous five prime ministers recorded a higher disapproval rating with Bob Hawke peaking at 67 per cent last December — just before he was ousted by Mr Keating. Dr Hewson's approval rating was 39 per cent, his disapproval rating 46 percent.

03 Aug 1992 - Poll reveals ALP slipping in four states Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 3 August 1992, page 3 Poll reveals ALP slipping in four states The latest Time Morgan poll reveals the Australian Labor Party to be /in trouble in Victoria, NSW, South Australia and Western Aus tralia. Labor continued to trail badly in the poll in Victoria, SA and WA, while the new NSW Liberal Premier, John Fahey, had lifted support for his Government. With the Victorian Labor Government having announced its intention to go to the polls in October, the poll shows that the popularity of the Leader of the Opposition, Jeff Kennett, rose by 2 percentage points in July to 33 per cent, while his disapproval rating fell a point to 55. The rating of the Premier, Joan Kirner, was unchanged with approval at 32 per cent and disapproval 62. Support for the Labor Party slipped a point to 24 per cent, the Liberal-National Coalition was also down a point to 52 while support for the Australian Democrats was up a point to 8 per cent. Support for the SA Labor Government of John Bannon fell 7.5 points to 27 per cent, its lowest rating since elected in 1982. In WA support for the Labor Government dropped half a point to 37 while in NSW support for Mr Fahey rose 2.5 Doints to 41.5 per cent. — MIKE TAYLOR

06 Aug 1992 - George might be taking a pounding Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Thursday 6 August 1992, page 6 George might be taking a pounding A CNN-Gallup poll issued on Tuesday showed Mr Clinton leading Mr Bush 57 per cent to 32 per cent nation-wide. It was the lowest Mr Bush has ever scored in the poll. In a good-natured gesture, Mr Bush was given a pair of boxing gloves — one labelled "Democrat" and the other "Congress" — and a plaque with an oversize Olympic gold medal marked "heavyweight champion". The upbeat image the senators tried to project masked a growing unease among top Republican of fice holders and strategists on the status of Mr Bush's re-election ef fort. The flap in which the White House felt when it was called upon on Monday to disavow a derisive personal attack on Mr Clinton by a top campaign aide, only served to fuel the unease, distracting attention from a campaign effort to focus on policy differences between Mr Bush and Mr Clinton. "He won't do it, but what he needs to do is a little confession and avoidance. If the issue is bow have you been as President for the past four years, he's going to lose," John Sears, who managed Ronald Reagan's 1976 primary challenge, said. "Bush needs to get that off the table and to say, 'Things didn't go as I planned. But I've learnt a lot and I can do better,.,, Eddie Mahe, a Republican consultant, said that this week's flap over the criticism of Mr Clinton by the campaign's political director, Mary Matalin. was "a side snow." - AP

08 Aug 1992 - Youth-jobs policies: both sides miss boat Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 8 August 1992, page 2 Youth-jobs policies: both sides miss boat Neither political Party'syouth youth employment policieshave have the ma jority of public support, according to a Saulwick poll published in The Sydney Morning Herald. Twenty per cent of the 1000 people surveyed Australia-wide on July 29 and 30 preferred the Coalition's policy and 24 per cent favoured Labor's. A majority of 56 per cent, however, either said they did not know enough to make a judgment or could not choose either party's policies. Even among people who supported either party, there was a relatively low level of endorsement of the youth employment policies. Only 52 per cent of people who described themselves as Labor voters said they supported Labor's youth unemployment policy, and only 40 per cent who described themselves as Coalition voters endorsed those parties' policies. Of the Independent voters, only 17 per cent favoured Labor's policies and a mere 7 per cent supported the Coalition's approach. In response to a separate question on government spending on youth unemployment, 75per per cent said the govern ment must spend more, 20 per cent said it could, not afford to spend more and 5 per cent did not know. A poll by AGB Australia and published in The Bulletin showed that the federal Coali tion had gone 5 per cent ahead of Labor in the national tally of voters' preference for Senate scats. Backing for the Coalition was up 1 per cent to 41 and for the ALP down one to 36. Support for the Democrats was up one per cent to 8, for Independents down one to 10 per cent and steady at 5 per cent for others. The only state in which Labor has the lead are NSW (ahead 9 per cent) and Tasmania (5). If a full Senate election had been held in July, the ALP would have lost two seats in Victoria, one in South Australia and two in Western Australia and might have gained one in Queensland. The Coalition would have won an extra seat in Victoria but lost two in Queensland and one each in South Australia and Tasmania.

10 Aug 1992 - Poll shows Coalition would top federal vote Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 10 August 1992, page 2 Poll shows Coalition would top federal vote The federal Coalition would have won easily a national election held in late July, according to a Morgan Poll to be published in Time Australia magazine today. The poll showed a small increase in support — 1 per cent — for both the ALP and the Coalition, to 36 per cent and 45 per cent respectively. Both groups benefited from a 2 per cent decline in support for the Australia Democrats, whose former Leader, Janet Powell, resigned in the survey period. Support for the Democrats declined to 6 per cent; support for independents and others remained at 13 per cent. , On a two-party preferred basis ALP support was 45 per cent compared with 55 per cent for the Coalition. The poll was taken on July 25 and 26 and August 1 and 2, and questioned 2369 voters. It followed the Government's and Opposition's youth-jobs summits and included Senator Powell's unexpected resignation on July 31. The summits, which revealed significant differences between Labor and Liberals on youth wages and training, appear to have had little impact According to the poll, personal approval for the Opposition Leader, John Hewson, was unchanged at 39 per cent compared with a 1 percent increase for the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, to 30 per cent Dr Hewson was preferred as prime minister by 45 per cent of voters (unchanged), compared with 40 per cent support for Mr Keating, up 1 per cent Fifteen per cent of those polled were undecided. There is no such indecision among voters when it comes to the Senate, according to another Morgan Poll to be issued today. The poll found that only 3 per cent of voters were undecided about which party or grouping would receive their support in a Senate election — the Australian - Democrats and independent candidates would have retained the balance of power if either a full- or half-Senate election had been held in June or July, when the poll of 12,160 electors was taken.

11 Aug 1992 - More men than women approve of PM, Hewson: polls Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Tuesday 11 August 1992, page 4 More men than women approve of PM, Hewson: polls Australia's key political leaders will have to do much more work if they are to gain the support of the nation's women, according to a Morgan poll published in Time Australia magazine yesterday. The poll shows both the Prime Minister, Paul Keating, and the Opposition leader, John Hewson, are approved of by more men than women. Male support for the leaders was 35 per cent and 42 per cent respectively, compared with female support of 26 per cent and 37 per cent respectively. More women believe Dr Hewson would make the better Prime Minister, 46 per cent compared with 44 per cent of men, and Mr Keating was supported by 36 per cent of women and 44 per cent of men. The poll was taken on July 25-26 and August 1-2, and questioned 2369 voters. Overall, Dr Hewson was preferred as Prime Minister by 45 per cent of voters (unchanged) compared with 40 per cent support for Mr Keating, up 1 per cent. Fifteen per cent of voters were undecided. The poll also found the federal Coalition would easily have won a national election held in late July. Support for both the ALP and the Coalition rose 1 per cent to 36 per cent and 45 per cent respectively. Both groups benefited from a 2 per cent fall in support for the Australian Democrats, whose former leader Janet Powell resigned during the survey period, while support for the Democrats fell to 6 per cent. Support for Independents and others remained at 13 per cent. The poll found preferences would have favoured the Coalition. On a two-party preferred basis ALP support was 45 per cent compared with 55 per cent for the Coalition. The poll followed the Government and Opposition youth jobs summits, which revealed significant differences between Labor and the conservatives on youth wages and training but which appeared to have had little impact on voting intentions. According to the poll, approval for Dr Hewson was unchanged at 39 per cent compared with a one-point rise for Mr Keating to 30 per cent. Another Morgan Poll, which questioned 12,160 voters in June and July, found the Democrats and independent candidates would have maintained their hold on the balance of power in the Senate if cither a full or half-Senate election were held in those months. Green Party support was up 1 per cent to 4 per cent and was strongest in Western Australia and Queensland, where the party would have won a seat in a full-Senate election, the poll found. • Conflict between the Liberal and National parties in NSW and early reaction to the youth wage proposal appear responsible for a 3 per cent fall in support for the Coalition, according to a new poll. The AGB Australia poll, to be published in this week's Bulletin magazine, shows national support for the Coalition falling three points in early August to 40 per cent, while Labor remained steady at 39 per cent. Third party alternatives benefited from the drop in Coalition support, with support for the Australian Democrats, Independents and "others" each climbing 1 per cent. While National Party support remained steady at 4 per cent, support for the Liberal Party dropped three points to 36 per cent. More than 2000 voters were interviewed face-to-face across Australia from July 24 to July 26 and on August 1 and 2.

17 Aug 1992 - Landslide forecast Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 17 August 1992, page 3 Landslide forecast The Coalition in Victoria is poised for a runaway victory in the October 3 election, the latest Morgan Poll has found. The poll, to be published in the latest edition of Time Australia, found that Liberal-National Party support in Victoria had risen by 7 per cent in early August to 59 per cent. Support for the Kimer Government was up 1 per cent to 25 per cent. Democrat support halved to 4 per cent after the resignations of the former leader, Janet Powell, and other key members.

22 Aug 1992 - Polls indicate Labor leaders in three states losing ground Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Saturday 22 August 1992, page 2 Polls indicate Labor leaders in three states losing ground POLL WATCH Labbr's leaders seem to be taking a battering in three states, accord-ing to a Morgan poll published in Time Australia and two separate Bulletin polls by AGB Australia. The Morgan poll, in which 544. Victorian electors were interviewed face-to-face, showed an increase in support from 52 to 59 per cent for the Ljbcral-National Coalition. Much of it seemed to have come from a halving, to 4 per cent, of support for the Australian Demo-crats. Support for minor parties and independents declined from 16 to 12 per cent and support for the Labor Party increased from 24 to 25 per cent. Approval of the Premier, Joan Kirner, declined from 32 to 31 per cent, only 4 per cent more than her low of 27 per cent in January last year. Sixty-four per cent disap-proved of Mrs Kimcr's perform-ance, 5 per cent were undecided. The approval rating of the Lead-er of the Opposition, Jeff Kennett, was unchanged at 33 per cent; 53 per cent disapproved and 14 per cent were undecided. On the question of who would make a better premier, 49 per cent preferred Mr Kennett, 36 per cent chose Mrs Kirner and a staggering 15 per cent either could not say or named someone else. If an election had been held in the first two weeks of August the Coalition would have romped in. The Victorian election will be held on October 3. In NSW, a Bulletin poll of 1263 electors has shown support for the Coalition up from 35 to 38 per cent and support for the Labor Party down from 47 to 43 per cent. Sup-port for the Democrats and independents was steady at 4 per cent and 10 per cent respectively. In only his second Bulletin poll since becoming premier. John Fah-ey's approval rating increased from 32 to 34 per cent, and 13 per cent. down 2 per cent, disapproved of his performance. Fifty-three per cent were uncommitted. The approval rating of the Oppo-sition Leader, Bob Carr, was up from 34 to 35 per cent, and his disapproval rating increased from 31 to 33 per cent. Thirty-three per cent were uncommitted. The preferred premier, however, was Mr Fahey at 45 per cent, up from 43. leading Mr Carr's 34 per cent — down from 36. In a separate Bulletin poll of 931 South Australian electors, the ap- proval rating of the Labor Premier, John Bannon. crashed from 30 per cent to 23. His disapproval rating increased from 47 to 57 per cent. Support for the Leader of the Opposition, Dean Brown, in-creased from 23 per cent to 26 and his disapproval rating declined from 17 percent to 14. As preferred premier, those polled chose Mr Brown by 44 per cent (previously 36). to 30 per cent (previously 35) for Mr Bannon. % Twenty-six per cent of electors were -uncommitted.

24 Aug 1992 - ALP support 'lowest since Keating PM' Canberra Times (ACT : 1926 - 1995), Monday 24 August 1992, page 1 ALP support lowest since Keating PM' Support for the Labor Party has declined to its lowest level since Paul Keating became Prime Minister, according to the Morgan Gallup poll to be published in Time Australia magazine this week. The poll, taken in mid-August before the federal Budget, found that support for the ALP had declined from 36 per cent to 34 while the coalition's stocks had improved by 2 per cent to 47. On a two-party-preferred basis, the ALP trails the Coalition 57 per cent to 43, representing an almost 7 per cent swing against Labor since the 1990 election. While the Government's approval rating is sagging, Mr Heating's continues to increase. It was up from 30 per cent to 33 in mid-August. However, the Opposition Leader, John Hewson, has a healthy advantage. His approval rating also increased from 39 per cent to 42. There was no change on who would make the best Prime Minister: Dr Hewson had 45 per cent and Mr Keating had 40 per cent. The Government's major problem is in Victoria, where its support languishes at 29 per cent (down 1), compared with 54 per cent for the Coalition. The Morgan poll was taken of 2301 electors who were interviewed face-to-face over two weekends earlier this month. A second poll of 1328 people taken in July found that 53 per cent of respondents blamed the Government for continuing high unemployment, unchanged since the last time the poll was taken in November.

05 Jun 1941 - PUBLIC OPINION TESTS Newcastle Morning Herald and Miners' Advocate (NSW : 1876 - 1954), Thursday 5 June 1941, page 5 PUBLIC OPINION TESTS Election Mandates Not Explicit The adoption of a sostem .of mass observation tests similar to the Gallup poll technique used in America as. a means of keeping Goveynnments in tcnuch with the desires of the pieople was saugoested by Mhr. J. J. Arnold (Senatorcleet) in an address to Newcastle Business Men's Club yesterday. The difficulty of adcess to trends of public opinion on contentious questions was one of the weaknesses of democracy, he declared. In A-ustralia, there was no means by which the Government, at a given time, could determine the mood of the public on a particular issue. They depended almost entirely on the general elections every three years for an index. "The result is that Australian Governments have only a vague, rough and ready idea of what the people are thinking. of their desires and of the things that should be done to retain public confiden'ce," said iMr. Arnold. Becaguse a carticular Government was elected and anothler rejected at the polls. it could not be assumed that everything the elected party proposed had the the approval of the people. The mandate to take any particular action was rarely explicit in a general election. 'If a government is to .serve the people, it must know what they want and what they will or will not accept," he continued. "Honest relations are required between Governments and the people, rather than confused opinions, bolstered up by propaganda." In England there was a movement called mass observation for studying the behaviour of the pImople. It now had over 2000 voluntary workers, who mixed with all sections of the- people, asking questions on set questions and recording their replies. At times particular questions were framed with very interesting results. One. result of studying the answers in thie light of subsequent hiistory was to promote a new respect for the sagacity of the comlnmon people. In America the searcn for the will of the people and the. taking of public opinion poills had reached imposing proportions. It had become almost an exact science, In the past few years, the most important advance had been made by the Institution of Public Opinion, better known as the Gallup Poll. It had built up an organisation trained in the art of obtaining public opinion. Its operatomrs recorded the opinions of selected people and sent them to the institute which made known the results. It had been found that results within l'A per cent. of accuracy could be obtained by . taking a. poll of a cross section of 10.000 people. "If these polls can give us somethine better than our present roughl and ready mandate fiom the peolple. and provide reasonably accurate expression of opil ion on every question that crops up. then we canll cheerfolly holpe for reall democratic government," ho concluded. 14 Aug 1941 - The American Mind Newcastle Morning Herald and Miners' Advocate (NSW : 1876 - 1954), Thursday 14 August 1941, page 2 The American Mind If the Gallup polls are an accurate guide to American public opinion, it may be stated as a willingness even a determination, to defeat .Hitlerism, combined with the belief that econo mic aid alone is sufficient to 'enable Britain to emerge victonriously. To the question, 'Should the United States Navy be usea to convoy ?" 41 per cent. answered in the affirmative, 50 per cent. In the negative, and 9 per cent. were undecided, but to the turther question. "Should the United States Navv be used to convoy If British defeat seems certain without it?" 71 per cent. answered in the affirmative. 21 per cent: in the negative, and 8 per cent. were undecided. American complacency was even more strongly illustrated in another series of questions The vote showed 81 per cent to be against immediate entry into the war, and only 19 oer cent. In favour. But in reply to the question, "If it appeared certain there was no other way to defeat Germanv and Italy except for the United States to co to war against them, would you be in favour of the United States going into the war ?" 68 per cent. voted for war. 24 per cent. against it. and 8 per cent. were undecided. The American attitude, therefore, appears to be that the United States must fight to prevent Britain being defeated, but the risk of defeat is rated so low that the nmajority against Im mediate intervention is overwhelming. This attitude explaims in large measure the caution which has charaeterised President Roosevelt's foreign policy. What the United States appears to need is a douche of cold realism which will bring home to the people the imminence of the Nazi menace and the extreme gravity of the situation should Germany defeat the Red army. In the light of the Gallup polls it becomes an open question whether British propaganda' in the United States Is not defeating itself by a simulation 'of over-confidence, and whether the British Government is wise in concealing figures of shipping losses

14 Aug 1941 - GALLUP POLL THIS MONTH Newcastle Morning Herald and Miners' Advocate (NSW : 1876 - 1954), Thursday 14 August 1941, page 2 GALLUP POLL THIS MONTH "Workers Will Dominate Opinion" The first Australian Gallup poll on questions of national interest will take place towards the end of this month, said the Director (Mr. Roy Morgan) yesterday. The results of the poll will be published early in September. The Gallup method of collecting statisties on public opinion has been in operation in the U.S.A. for many years. and has been a marked success. The polls would be conducted once a month in Australia, said Mr. Morgan. The results would be calculated and publishcd early in the next month. Re explained that the poll would be calculatedl on the type of population, and the percentage of this type all over Australia. Samples of opinion would be taken from all occupational and regional groups. "All interviewers are asked to contact a cross section of the people in their own area. The opinions of the working man irill dominate the poll because most Australians are working men," said Mr. Morgafni. No Names Asked Mr. Morgan is appointing representatives in Newcastle and district who will visit people here. The people will be sasked to give their opinions on various questions. No names are taken or asked for. This information is senit to the central calculating centre, and the infornmation is placed on punch-cards similar to those used in making the census. The machine calculates the percentage, counting the cards at the rate of 400 a minute. 'rhe result of tile polL is published merely as a percentage in favour of the ques tions, the intensity of feeling in both directions. nmid the most common reason for the attitudes. The company runnine the poll is one of the limited guarantee type, whose members are the newspapers who pay for the service. MIr. Morgan said that the poll was simply a type of news service for which newspapers and others paid. "This is entirely a fact-finding organisa tron, which allows the public to draw their own conclusions from the information obtained," said Mr. Morgan. "Moreover, such a poll as this must be run properly. If it was not, the publie would see through it imnmediately." The interviewing network in the Hunter River district has been completed.
