19 Apr 1971 - WORONI Woroni (Canberra, ACT : 1950 - 2007), Monday 19 April 1971, page 2 WORONI Despite the slightly pessimistic findings of the latest Gallup Poll, leaders of the Anti-Apartheid movement must take heart from some recent events. Within Australia, public expression of dissent from racism has increased considerably. Statements' from many leading clergy headlined the Australian, two state governments have declared official opposition to the proposed South African cricket tour, the ACTU is considering a black ban on all future South African sporting tours, and even Billy McMahon offered token financing for the anti-racism movement. Within South Africa, where opposit ion is generally quelled, the challenge by white cricketers to the selectors to chose the team on merit received wide publicity, throughout the world, and, surprisingly within that country Much of the initial strength and impetus for the movement in Australia must be attributed to the action by students in high lighting the inequality, prejudice and cruelty imposed by Apartheid. In a year where it appears that the results of this continual struggle against racism may finally succeed in terminating South African sporting tours to Australia, it is imperative that student pressure be stepped up. If any student can afford a couple of hours to help maintain the 24 hour vigil outside the South African embassy, please contact Chris Swinbank, Bruce Hall.

11 Oct 1972 - COMMENT Woroni (Canberra, ACT : 1950 - 2007), Wednesday 11 October 1972, page 21 £lLLllJlMjliuLl L Henry Mayer Professor of Politics, Sydney University. Foss: Professor Mayer, do you think issues in general make or break elections in Australia^ Mayer: I would say no. F oss: If this is the case, why do the parties-make such a fuss , about issues? Mayer: Because politicians constantly have to pretend that they can alter, influence and determine events; It is impossible for a political leader of either party to say 'look I couldn't help this, or I'm sorry this went wrong in spite of me, or I could do nothing about it'. Politicians have to pretend, by the very nature of politics and by what is expected of them, to be entirely voluntaryistic, to be able to pull themselves up by their bootstraps. Therefore they can't (and this is my second point) say that voting is basically determined by factors outside our control — whether they be class or family or habit or whatever, -which are fixed and can only — be in a minor way. influenced. Hence they have to constantly highlight rationality, discussion, even admitting all distortions -and pretend that people are much more literate, issue . oriented, and involved than in fact they are. Foss: So what you are, imply-ing is that people in Australia still think in terms of fidelity to the party.' Mayer: This apathy is getting ? ' somewhat less now in so far as you can trust the surveys. Undoubtedly there is some evidence that a higher proportion of people are tending ~ to become more volatile, but the party is still the overwhelming thing. Basically the Party can be treated for 70 to 75% of the people as an inherited factor: as if you had green hair or splayed feet or whatever. Research shows if both parents were of the same persuasion (it doesn't work if father was labor and mummy lib. and they constantly talked about it. — then youre likely to be a swinger yourself) that you will vote like your parents or tend to if the relationship you have with them is basically stable. Foss: Has the party system worked in America in the past? . It seems to me America is less polarised into parties than say the British system is. If it has worked in the past, have issues become more important in the US and have, in fact, issues won and lost elections in recent times? Mayer: I won't try to answer your first question because we'll get into a long discussion of criteria. In answer to your second question: Yes, overall that definitely seems to be the case. I would also say that it does seem that the existing party structures are subject to basic rearrangement; that the coalition resting behind the major parties are changing with the issues; and that issue oriented politics are on the up in the US. Foss: Has the kind of issues, ; much recently? Mayer: The basic trouble really is that you have two kinds of 'things called issues. One which I call leader's issues and voter's issues, i.e. what the guys on top are saying what the newspapers are saying, what TV is saying the elections are all about. You will notice that all sides don't agree what that is and that they have different priorities and different lists. One guy says that it is green sheep and another that it is about candlewax. . Then secondly, there is not much evidence that the issues put out by the leaders are the ; same issues that people think about, in so far as they think about issues at all. In fact I would say that there is instinctive evidence that an increasingly wider gap between leaders issues and voters issues is coming into existence. By this I mean that the parties are increasingly failing to take up issues in the minds of voters and I don't mean just issues in the minds of young voters, it seems to me that there is general alienation — to use that boo word which I don't think means very much — a fedupness with the political system where people vaguely feel that these guys out there are not taking care of what really concerns them. It seems to be impossible for politicians to retranslate into normal political jargon what people call 'quality of life' issues. Taking it differently, you must think of your political system as a thing that can handle only certain types of problems. This is a very important point about issues. Foss: Do you think voters are aware of this? Mayer: The word 'aware' is unfortunate, because it is much more of an unconscious perception or a vague feeling in their bones. There is some evidence to suggest that the general populace is becoming awaK of the lack of communication; Foss: What are the important issues in this coming Federal election and with what parties are they associated with? Mayer: I can't answer that one. All I could do is quote the latest public opinion polls. But what I want to stress is that the polls apart from ANOP (Australian National Opinion Polls) have made no attempt to find out how strongly people feel-about various issues. Otherwise you get this long list of ten to fifteen questions and you find that say 66% of the people worry about 'Joe Cheese' but ypu are never told how much they worry and what would they do about it. ANOP have made a fairly crude but I think so far the best attempt to bring out some intensity factor. There is some evidence — to avoid your question and to answer part of it at the same time — that there seems to be a certain vol itil ity in the definition of what .... . an issue is. In plain English, I think that generally none of the issues for the moment cut very deep. They are partly blown -up by the media and partly blown-up by the fact that the parties constantly talk about thepn- The people's feelings are crystallised into saying this is about unemployment or this is about foreign policy. In another way; the number of people who feel very intensely about anything in politics is very small. Foss: It is quite interesting that one reads in editorials and political cartoons that issues are in fact mattering. For example; recently in Time ,. magazine there appeared*a cartoon in which McGovern was seen with various issues stocking out from behind him such as abortion, homosexuality and censorship. I think that very much the same thing could be said about the Labor Party's position here. Mayer: But this is to be expected. Assume that you are a bloody journalist. What do you write about?. You have to write this way. But I don't believe that what is being .said in the newspapers is actually the case. I have some evidence, of Australian society that makes me feel that any degree of political awareness is a very small one indeed. What is happening is that your intellectuals talk with other intellectuals who write these bloody editorials which 1% reads. They constantly overintellectualise what ordinary people feel, and what most of the people are concerned with. Don't forget that it is surely a pretty obvious factor of Australian society, including students, how inarticulate they are and how difficult it is to get most of them to say anything. You and I, not in any elitist sense but in an ordinary statistical sense, are a typical of Australian socfety. Hence I do think that the whole thing is slanted or pushed and that one repeats to me what one has read in the newspeprsand I answer in similar terms. Generally speaking, most people are much more inarticulate and vague and moody and they feel things in a very loose sense. Foss: How do you explain such a situation in which it appears that most DLP supporters don't go along with DLP foreign policy? How can j: this sort of ambivalence work? Mayer: This is a typical attit- ' ude. By going through the 2 to 3 thousand polls since 1940 one sees that consistently eg Liberal voters on various occasions supported price control, eg the majority of ALP voters are to the right of the ALP leadership on all issues including socialisation, strikes and nationalisation and not to the left. This works because people who vote for parties have very litt.le to do with issues. It is a fact that people aren't aware of in any precise sense what their parties stand is on any one issue. People vote or support parties in terms of loose bundles for the vaguest of reasons. Hence it is a puzzle to you really because you assume that there is some correlation between voting and having some knowledge in support of issues. Now I assume the opposite. To me the unusual and strange thing would be the type of person who votes for say the most extreme party — leave out the communists as there are 3 communist parties — take DLP if you like. The guy who is aware of the DLP policy -on a number of issues and votes for them because of it, in my opinion and as some surveys done at Macquarie University have shown, would be about 1 /3 of the total DLP voters. Two thirds would be protest voters, people who intend to vote Liberal. Material from the Macquarie survey shows that these people when asked afterwards — the crucial 2/3rds of them — can't remember whether they voted DLP or Liberal. That is one of the reasons why the polls almost constantly understate the predictions of how many people will vote DLP. The picture of the DLP'er as a mad, catholic fanatic who is like Bob Santamaria, is com- ; plete nonsense. What you have is a couple of guys like Santamaria - totally atypical because whatever you think of him, he is an intellectual, articulate man with a coherent policy — and the ordinary DLP voter who is as confused and muddled as the ordinary Liber or Labor or, I should think communist supporters. The number of articulate ideologues in Australia would be very small indeed. You can see this in operation taking another non-party thing, with the new left in Australia. By the time the bon mots of Marcuse eg filter down to the people what you get is simplified pebble like slogans which are Marcuse 75 times watered down. Let me finally say that issues in themselves matter . very little in elections. They are convenient scapegoats for the parties and the intellectuals who write editorials and make most of the fuss. I don't say this is-a good or even 'desirable thing. Let us hope that.the damnable Australian political apathy will eventually : become a rare animal. Issues in themselves matter very little in elections They are convenient scapegoats for the parties and the intellectuals who write editorials and make vrrwstoftlie fuss.

18 Apr 1968 - VIETNAM Woroni (Canberra, ACT : 1950 - 2007), Thursday 18 April 1968, page 8 VIETNAM IDEOLOGY, PUBLIC OPINION AND THE VIETNAM DEBATE This is the first 1600 words of a long article in the forthcoming issue of Diss-ent, which will be available in the Co-op Bookshop from April 22. This article already has a history. When first presented as a paper to the A.N.U. Pluralist Society a year ago it seemed that, in the aftermath of the debacle of the 1966 Federal Elections and of the impo-tence of opposition to the visit of Air Vice Marshall Ky, the Vietnam debate had closed up. Casting himself as Cassandra the writer only added to the despair of his staff-student audience: his argument might have been different, but his proph-ecy was already intuitively felt. Since then much has changed: perceptions of the state of the war with the crisis of mid-1966 and the Tet offensive, Whitlam for Calwell and a new A.L.P. strategy, the Senate Elections, a new Prime Minister and an apparent variation in Government poli-cy. Yet it still seems that the original hy-pothesis is tenable: that a certain domin-ant ideological view of Australia in relation to the outside world underlies support for the Government's Vietnam policy. PUBLIC OPINION To begin with it is necessary to lay out public opinion; and regrettably this can only be measured by the blunt instru-ments of Australian Gallup Polls (Roy Morgan). It should be especially noted that questions sometimes vary from poll to poll and are often loaded; further, in-tensity of opinion is not measured - par-ticularly uncertainty which is not the same as 'undecided'; finally, polls are too infrequent and too irregular to pro-vide an adequate graph of movements in opinion. Given the hawk-dove debate in the U.S., e.g. Johnson v. Fulbright (about which respondents were probably not greatly aware), and, more importantly, the policy of the Menzies and Holt Gov-ernments and Mr Whitlam's line during 1967 (see below under 'The Debate'), it is doubtful if 'hold on' respondents can automatically be counted as being 'for' American and Australian Vietnam policy. Further, there is a remarkable coincidence between the combined 'hold on' and 'get out' percentages - Septem-ber 47% and December 49% - and the 46% in the intervening November poll against the last increase in Australian forces. As to be expected, the 'increase' percentage-es of September and December 37% and 38% - line up with the 37% in November favouring that increase. The February poll was taken on Saturday 17 and Sunday 18, during the Tet Offensive, which open-ed on 30 January and entered its second phase on 18 January with rocket and mor-tar attacks on U.S. and allied bases. At this stage a variety of conflicting evalua-tions of the offensive were in circula-tion; General Westmoreland was still clai-ming victory and had not yet been report-ed as asking for massive reinforcements. In an article of this kind it is scarcely possible to establish (this the writer is doing elsewhere), only to assert that there is a dominant ideological view of Austra-lia in relation to the outside world and to briefly describe that view. It is an im-age of the international order and of Aus-tralia's position in it. It is part of the pop-ulist ideology prevalent in Australian society. The map of the world is con-ceived of in what geographers term 'azi-muthal equidistant projection'' Australia is at the centre, with every point at its true distance and in the right direction although there are distortions in area size and shape of other countries: Aus-tralia is the natural focus of attention of all Powers, friends and enemies alike. The view has two main parts: a notion of threat and a notion of alliance. Accord-ing to the former, Australia is peculiarly open to invasion, or subject to pressure to change vital national policy, by some alien Power - naturally, not an Anglo Sax-on Power. All that seems to be necessary for a country to be identified as a threat is for it to exist in a more or less cohesive form, or to maintain some kind of pres-ence, in Asia and the Pacific. Of course, a threat becomes more ominous if it can be accommodated to that great national myth, the Yellow Peril. Since the 1890's China, Russia, Japan, after a gap Japan again, Russia plus China, for a time Indo-nesia, and now China alone have been successively identified as the threat. This identification of threat does not appear to be necessarily connected with any cus-tomary politico-military assessment of threat in terms of intention and capability in the context of the balance of power in world politics. The threat is simply out there: this amounts to a kind of national paranoia. So the line on fighting in South Vietnam is that it is better to meet the the threat of China 'there' (in South Vietnam) than 'here' (in Australia): Communist China controls North Viet-nam; North Vietnam has invaded South Vietnam; if South Vietnam falls then the other states of South-East Asia will top-ple over like a row of dominoes; where-upon the Yellow hordes will be poised to sweep across the continent. The notion of alliance is one native to Australia; this can be reduced to a numb-er of assumptions; some of which are in-consistent. Only those relevant to the Vietnam debate are mentioned here. There is the idea of the utter dependence of Australia on a Great Power ally, once the U.K. and now the U.S. It derives from a sense of isolation from homelands in the British Isles and from the pattern of colonial-mother country relations. It is connected with the feeling of exposure to invasion; but it does not require any immediately identifiable threat. Again, the alliance is seen as a relationship of kin-ship or friendship, rather than shared in-terests but it is also held that Australia must build up with its Great Power ally a credit balance of goodwill, which can be drawn upon when the inevitable cata-clysm occurs. Further, the Great Power ally is deemed to be virtually omnipotent, able to protect Australia if only it exer-cises its power. Thus according to this notion, Australia is in Vietnam because of its pact of friendship with the U.S. or to build up a credit balance of good will with the U.S.; and American power must prevail against aggression from the North. Now this dominant ideological view is in-tractable. It is not susceptible to argu-ment; and assumptions are maintained even if rebutted by empirical evidence. In-deed, the view, as an image of the outside world, largely governs perceptions of ex-ternal politics: it functions to select and order information received, usually via the mass media. Australian foreign policy is, naturally, perceived in this way; and, assuming there is any concern, propa-ganda justifying policy is most effective if presented from this ideological world view. Of course, perceptions do change, as for example of Indonesia which was no longer seen as a threat after the fail-ure of the coup of 1 October and the sub-sequent massacres and establishment of the New Order. Probably if by chance the Cultural Revolution led to civil war or warlordism, China would no longer be regarded as a threat. Once, the whole no-tion of alliance was in jeopardy: with the sinking of the Prince of Wales and the Re-pulse on 10 December 1941, the surren-der of Singapore on 15 February and the failure of the U.K. to come to Aus-tralia's aid when facing apparent immi-nent Japanese invasion. The Labor Gov-ernment had to act to restore national mo-rale: Curtin issued his famous 'we turn to America' New Year message for 1942, although he knew that Roosevelt had al-ready decided to send U.S. forces because Australia was strategically vital to the U.S. as a base from which to strike back at Japan. So the myth grew that the U.S. came to Australia's rescue because of friendship - 'hands clasped across the Pacific' - or because both were English speaking peoples; and the notion of alli-ance has been transferred from the U.K. to the U.S. However, should the U.S. be 'defeated' in Vietnam (i.e., accept a peace settlement in which the NLF be-came the dominant party in a coalition government in Saigon, with the probable eventual reunification of Vietnam under Hanoi) and withdraw its forces from the South-East Asian mainland, then the no-tion of alliance might again be in jeopar-dy. Perhaps in such a crisis, with no-where else to turn, through catharsis there might emerge a sense of Australian independence and a conception of alliance as an arrangement of convenience. This is broad speculation indeed. It is however, argued in this article that during the Vietnam War, and never before in Australian history, events in the outside world have with some success challenged the dominant ideological view: the impact of external events of and related to the war has from time to time been so over whelming as to make apparent to many holding this view a disjunction between image and reality. Not that reality has been, or could be apprehended; but it has seemed much more complex than the unsophisticated image. For many, perceptions have at times been blurred, and opinions have changed or at least be-come uncertain. Connected with such disjunctions there have been gaps be-tween Government claims about the war and actualities. Those against the war ha-ve rarely so acted as to reinforce any disjunction; and only since the retirement of Mr Calwell from the Leadership has the Opposition exploited such gaps to attack the Government's credibility over the war. Robert Cooksey (The rest of the article examines the Vietnam debate and these movements in public opinion, and concludes with some thoughts on strategies for changing Australia's Vietnam policy.) 07 Oct 1997 - Zwar should represent majority Woroni (Canberra, ACT : 1950 - 2007), Tuesday 7 October 1997, page 7 Zwar should represent majority Dear Woroni, I refer to the comments of ACT Youth Delegate to the People's Constitutional Convention, Heidi Zwar, reported in your last issue {Woroni, 49/8), where she stated that she 'will represent the views of younger Australians who are not necessar ily emotionally attached to the monarchy yet who don't see the need for any immediate rush into a republic.' Over 75% of youth in the ACT favour the change to a Republic (Herald AGB McNair poll December 1996). As the one and only ACT youth delegate, surely it is Ms Zwar's role and duty to represent this overwhelming sentiment and not just the minority who supposedly 'don't see the need for change'. If supporters of the constitutional status quo have to rely on anti-democratic representation to sustain their position, I would suggest that their already tenuous position will only be further undermined. —Anne Witheford ANU Republicans on Campus

07 Sep 1951 - London Round-up, By Rohan Rivett Eden To Lead If Churchill Goes Newcastle Morning Herald and Miners' Advocate (NSW : 1876 - 1954), Friday 7 September 1951, page 4 London Round-up, By Rohan Rivett Eden To Lead ]If Churchil Goes Homeward-bound in the Queen Elizabeth from a triumphant visit to America, Mr. Anthony Eden will find his prestige and prospects given a lift by the latest Gallup poll finding. This will be the more pleasing to him personally, because noisy critics, headed by the Beaverbrook Press, have pursued a vigorous policy of defamation, carping at his qualifications to succeed Mr. Churchill as the Conservative leader and future Prime Minister. The Gallup Poll found that 49 British electors to-day would like to see Mr. Eden lead a Conservalive Government for every 34 who want Mr. Churchill as its leader. It is not surprising that Liberal voters would prefer Mr. Eden in a proportion of five to two, and Labour voters in a ratio of three to one-the fact is really a compliment to Mr. Churchill in Conservative eyes. What is astounding is that Mr. Eden to-day almost has a tmajority within the Conservative ranks. For every 10 Conservatives who want Churchill to lead their next Government, nine others would prefer Eden. This should not he construed as suggesting a change in Conservative leadership in the near future. It is an open secret at Westminster that many Conservative members of Parliament, especially on the front bench, have been embarrassed and angered by Mr. Churchill's individualistic forays into debate without warning his colleagues, and in disregard of the party's agreed strategy. But, at 77, he remains so much the greatest figure in the House that it would be unthinkable for the Conservatives to go to tse polls either this autumn or next year under any other banner. Despite Mr. Eden's growing populurity in Europe and America, he, like all other British statesmen, remains in the eyes of the outside world a mere pigmy in Mr. Churchill's shadow. The significant thing is that, where three years ago the question of Mr. Churchill's successor was frequently canvassed nside and outside the Conservative Party, to-day no other member of the Conservative front bench can be considered to offer a challenge to Mr. Eden. IN THE opposite camp, there is speculation at the bid of the Bevanists to push certain well-known Ministers off the party executive. At the party conference in October, seven of the 28 members of the national executive are chosen by delegates from constituency Labour parties. In this section, Aneurin Bevan has topped the poll for four years. and is expected, even by opponents, to do so again this year. Mr. Bevan has two lieutenantsltn Mikardo and Tom Dribergamong the other six. But nominations now published show that two more Bevanites-the ex-Minister Harold Wilson anti Mrs. Barbara Castle-are challenging the Ministers holding the other four seats. L ATEST sensation of the West End is "Ardele." which one critic says is the ugliest and most nauseating play he has seen. The playwright is Jean Anouilh ("Ring Around the Moon," "Point of Departure"). Anouilh, whose "Eurydice' will be. presented on the London stage in October, thus continues the most spectacular one-man invasion of the West End theatre achieved by a Continental playwright since the heyday of Ibsen. 'Ardele" tells of the love ot a lunchbacked girl in an aristocratic French family for another hunchback. Her family, fearing ridicule, ocks her in her room and, in the ollowing scenes, all reveal their own moral deformity in seeking to deny honest love to one physically deformed. With typical bitterness, Anouilh seems set on depicting love as the beastliest thing op earth. But his ordid vehicle is lit by flares of dazzling Gallic wit, which have ;iven him extraordinary popularity. Playing the role of the lecherous, lobbering old general who has Iriven his wife over the border of insanity by his infidelities is George telphi, who toured Australia withi he Oliviers. 01 Jun 1942 - GALLUP POLL FAVOURS SUNDAY SHOWS FOR SOLDIERS AND FRIENDS Newcastle Morning Herald and Miners' Advocate (NSW : 1876 - 1954), Monday 1 June 1942, page 2 GALLUP POLL FAVOURS SUNDAY SHOWS FOR SOLDIERS AND FRIENDS An overwhelming majority of Australians would open places of amusement to soldiers and their friends on Sundays, according to an Australian Gallup Poll, just completed. But only one person in three thinks the public should be admitted. Early in May the interviewers for Australian Public Opinion Polls (The GalluD Poll) began asking people what they thought about Sunday entertainment. Opinions were recorded in a representative range of localities in each State. Of each 100 people interviewed, 8i answered "Yes" to the question, "lDuring the war should places of amusement be open to soldiers on Sunday?" Those who voted "Yes" were then asked what times should they be oDen? Should soldiers be able to take a friend? Should the public be admitted? Nearly everyone who favoured opening places of amusement to soldiers also thought they should be able to take a friend. Seven out of !0 people favoured both afternoon and evening shows, while three out of 10 @nswered. "evening only." On the question of admitting the public. only 38 out of each 100 inter. viewed cast "Yes" votes. Men and women held almost identical views on the question, and age had little influence on the voting. Economic status, however, had some effect, aird the voting varied State by State. Four out of 10 artisans and other people in the lower income groups favoured Sunday opening. Only three out of 10 better-off people, however, supported the idea. Opinions in States In New South Wales and Western Australia nearly half of those interviewed said "admit the public." In the other States, however, fewer than one person in three agreed with them. 'Typical comments from people opposed to Sunday entertaminment ,vere-"Sunday is the Lord's Day, and should be used for quiet rest and meditation," from a gardener m Hobart and; "Sunday should be a day of rest for everyone," from a transport driver in Itozelle, Sydney. On the other hand, a soldier mn Maitland said, "Good organised entertainment is better than idle hands and idle minds." A similar attitude was--"As an A.I.F. man returned from both wars, I know how miserable Sundays can be for troops," from a Government official, residing at Bondi.

03 Nov 1948 - DEWEY TIPPED TO WIN U.S. PRESIDENCY Result Announced Today Daily Advertiser (Wagga Wagga, NSW : 1911 - 1954), Wednesday 3 November 1948, page 1 DEWEY TIPPED TO WIN! U.S. PRESIDENCY Result Announced Today NEW YORK, Tuesday (A.A.P.): The final Gallup poll on the Presidential election estimates Mr. Dewey having a substantial majority of Electoral College votes. The poll estimates the percentages of popular vote for the four leading candidates ares Mr. Dewey 49.5, Mr. Truman 44.5, Mr. Wallace 4, Mr. Thurmond 2. The combined totals of other candidates is estimated at under one per cent of the popular vote. i rpHE Gpllup Poll says that Mr. Dewey holds a substantial lead in 20 States and Mr. Truman in nine States. In 15 States neither candidate holds a substantial lead, and in the remaining four — all Southern States — the situation is described as 'confused'. President Truman last night departed from the traditional American custom of nonpartisan election eve statements and bluntly made a partisan Independence (Missouri). Election eve statements by Presidential candidates have by custom been confined to general appeals to the people to exercise their right to vote. Vote Known Today The people will vote today and the results should be knowr-In Australia on Wednesday night (Sydney time). President Truman said: 'I believe the Democratic Party Is the party of the people. I believe that through the Democratic Party all classes will receive a fairer treatment and more security. 'I believe in particular that industrial workers, farmers and small businessmen can best protect themselves against reaction and against inflation through the Democratic Party.' The (lection eve statement by Mr. Dewey, Republican candidate, was non-political, and appealed to voters to remain united whatever the election result. Threat to Negroes A report from Nashville (Tennessee) says that hundreds of negroes have received crudely written letters warning them not to vote at today's election, 'he letters were signed: 'K.K.K.' The Imperial Grand Wizard of the Klu Klux Klan (Samuel Green) said the. symbol was a hoax. He offered postal authorities full co-operation in tracking down and apprehending the perpetrators.

23 Nov 1949 - Editorial Australian Worker (Sydney, NSW : 1913 - 1950), Wednesday 23 November 1949, page 3 [Editorial ? 'I'' w ' *? ?? .?- — m— wt- j ! Open Season for Gallup Poll. . |i i Comedians 1 VX7 ITH the approach of the pantomime season the Tory newspapers are reviving for readers that inimitable farce known as the Gallup Poll Comedy, which rocked America and the rest of the world exactly 12 months ago, when attempting to label New York's Big Business tycoon — Governor Dewey— as the cast-iron unbeatable certainty for the Presidency of the United States. Quite oblivious themselves to the gales of laughter aroused by their -Gallup Poll prognostications, these subconscious stooges of American combines and monopolies, so boomed; boosted and publicised their stuffed-shirt of snobocracy that headquarters of America's vested interests were beginning to feel sorry for the unassuming Harry Truman about to be crushed under the Republican juggernaut. As with the disciples of Big Business in Australia, Destiny allowed these Tory impostors to dream on a little longer. Accordingly, Republican Party campaign organisersintoxicated by the exuberance of Gallup Poll boloney — ordered truck loads of iced champagne for Governor Dewey's headquarters at the Roosevelt Hotel to celebrate the most famous victory on record, whilst humble Harry Truman and a few Democrats in the Biltmore Hotel — only a few blocks away — were reported as being content to nibble a few ham sandwiches while awaiting the tragic fate in store for them. , That was the Gallup Poll set-up before the poll. Leaving nothing to chance, the high-pressure publicity four-flushers had drafted— in advance— ' speeches of thanks' for President Dewey to be circulated pronto among the army of radio and newspaper representatives waiting to' sell' their 'de facto' President to all parts of the globe. i Like the Gallup pollsters and propaganda specialists of Australia's putty glamor boy, however, the American boosters of Governor Dewey had neglected first to catch their hare before deciding what Dewey would or could do with it. It was this little., neglect of detail which made America's Gallup-poll the laughing stock of the civilised world. ' : ^ ^ .. ;?- ^ As the progress election returns began to percolate to the New York political headquarters on that November night the big crowds at the Republican's Roosevelt Hotel grew smaller and smaller, while the modest Democratic gathering at the Biltmore began to grow bigger and bigger. ' ' i ? P ? v ? * - ' Finally, when sufficient election returns had arrived to indicate that President Truman had the White House well within his grasp, the organisers of the Roosevelt Hotel feast found themselves surrounded by an avalanche of roast steamed and baked poultry and oceans of liqueurs, wines and what have you, but nary a Republican supporter to share them. , - ' Even the synthetic President-elect— Governor Dewey— had no stomach for getting square on the unoffending chickens, and the columnists tell us that, more in anger than in sorrow, he was noticed dodging his way through the automatic red and green traffic lights of New York City until a humorless Hamburger Joe asked him to try a plate of scrambled eggs — and he did. That was the climax for the Gallup Poll's putty President twelve months ago, and Gallup Poll history looks like repeating itself in Australia with a similar crash for Big Business on December 10 and a corresponding landslide in favor of the Labor Party. . 'v. With memories of Dewey's fate ringing in his ears, it is little wonder that Menzies should now fear the verdict awaiting his Party on Saturday fortnight. It can be safely asserted that Menzies already has been granted access to the 'confidential' surveys conducted by the staffs of the private banks— surveys which have revealed a potential majority of 21 for Labor in the House of Representaties and a 31 majority in the Senate. Such big Labor majorities are in harmony- with the landslide in favor of Labor, as predicted by Dr. Evatt after his 'tour of five States, and, also, are consistent with the 'heroic' actions of Liberal Leader Casey and ex-Labor leader Billy Hughes in running away from their own constituencies— Corio and North Sydney— despite the fact that both claimed they could feel a swing coming in their direction. - ☆ ? ? : .- ?? Actions speak louder than Gallup Polls. It is obvious that if either Casey or Hughes really believed they could win either Corio or North Sydney it would be their duty to their Party to remain at their former post?, and take advantage of any swing of which they had boasted. . The fact that both could not get away from their . former constituents fast enough is the best proof that electors can get to indicate Which way the swing will go on December 10.. ? - .» ? ?, «?'« ^

12 Jan 1949 - 'Americans Won't Have Reactionary Republicans' Australian Worker (Sydney, NSW : 1913 - 1950), Wednesday 12 January 1949, page 6 'Americans Won't Have Reactionary Republicans1 'New Statesman' on Truman's Txiumph ELECTORS SPURNED WAR 6f NERYES BY GALLUP POLLSTERS jf The London week-end journal, 'New Statesman and Nation,' publishes a refreshing reaction to President Truman's triumphant return to the White House, and in one phrase describes his success as 'Roosevelt's Fifth Term.' : In a scholarly summing-up of Democratic and pro-Labor trends among American Unionists, farmers, retailers and moderate professional men the 'New Statesman and Nation,' inter alia, says: For- the fifth time in succession, the American people, in defiance of the press, the business Czars and the pollsters, have voted for Franklin Delano Roosevelt. To say this is no disparagement of Mr. Truman, whose obstinate faith in his party and in the New Deal was the largest individual factor in this electoral miracle. Kicked about by every expert and leader of opinion, he kept bis head while all about him were losing theirs. Even more significant, however,; than his personal, success is the fact that the -American people have voted against an attempt to put the clock back to Goolidge time. Attention, Mr. Menzies Democratic majorities have been returned an both the Senate and the House of Representatives because the Republican candidates were so blankly and blindly reactionary .that the man in the street could riot stomach them at any price. The result is all the more ; astonishing .because Americans, more than any other people, like to -be on the winning side; and the pollsters had used all their considerable influence to , make a Republican victory appear an absolute certainty. Millions of1 dollars' worth of advertising depended on the result, and this; may have unconsciously influenced their minds. .,.'.. Elmo Roper, who runs the 'Fortune' poll, probably the most scientific of them all, announced that he was not going to waste any more time testing an election which was a foregone conclusion. Dr. Gallup, who once before predicted a New Deal defeat, has been caught out again; Big Business Repulsed But millions of decent ordinary people refused to be bewitched on to the pollsters' bandwaggon. They resisted the most formidable psychological assault ever mounted against the nerves of a democratic nation, and they repudiated the definition of the American way of life laid down by the big business interests which control the Republican party machine. The Democrats' success, stems from an event which seemed at the time to make their defeat a certainty. Even under Roosevelt's leadership they, could never have a really progressive programme, or rather the elector could never believe in the genuineness of their liberal .aspirations, V as long as the Party had to compromise its principles in order :% to buy the votes of the South-, em protagonists of White ascendancy. At the Democratic Convention Mr. Truman was freed from this inhibition both by the Dixiecrats' secession and by the disintegration of the political machines under bosses like Mayor Hague, in the big cities. Harassed in addition by Mr. . Wallace's threat on the extreme Left, the President's position seemed so hopeless _that. he had .'? nothing to lose by announcing an all-out New Deal policy and making a frontal assault on the record of the Repubii-, can Congress. Pro-Labor Won It It was certainly this sudden lurch to- the Left which in the last -weeks of* the campaign won him the- support of organised Labor, already indignant at the 7aft-HartleyrAct; and, even more important, it caused the abstention of many voters who had been swung over to a passive Republicanism by the apparent inevitability of Mr. Dewey V victory! , The issues in America ? were not so very dissimilar from those which faced British voters in 1945 and will face them again in 1950. Real Name of 'Tree Enterprise^' The American people have voted against the uncontrolled profits and Inflation which go by the name of free enterprise. They have shown a preference for a liberal middle way between the extremes of Coolidgism and Communism, which is at least analogous' to the middle way for which Socialist Britain stands. But this does hot mean that they will get it. Mr. Attlee, after routing Mr. Churchill, came to power with a clear Socialist* mandate. : / War on Jungle Capitalism The Democrats- New Deal, however, is not clear-cut policy, but only an unforinulated repudiation of jungle capitalism. We can say with certainty that Anerica will not swing Right after this election. But there is no way of foretelling whether or how far it will now move Leftwards. Organised Labor will demand the i ulf ilment of Mr. Truman's pledges to break White ? ascendancy Mn the (Continued on page 12). \ AMERICANS WON'T HAVE REACTIONARY I REPUBLICANS (Continued from page 6). i South, repeal the TaftHartlejfAct, reintroduce, price-controls and institute a; Federal - hous-v ing programme. Each of these reforms may: well be opposed by, a majority j of Congressmen, since Souths j em reactionaries /form a large: I segment of both Houses. j Echo in Great Britain Not the least important aspect of president Truman's triumph is its effect on domestic politics here in Britain. November 3rd was a black, day for # Lord Woolton and Mr. Churchill. For a year now they have been campaigning with the same tactics as the Republicans. They have calculated on a swing of the' pendulum, and they have believed that they can defeat the Left without any constructive policy by the mere exploitation of antiCommunist hysteria and of the natural dislike for planning and control. The American election results show the danger of such calculations in a country where organised . Labor is conscious of its power. 17 Nov 1948 - GOVT. INQUIRY TO DEBUNK GALLUP POLLS Australian Worker (Sydney, NSW : 1913 - 1950), Wednesday 17 November 1948, page 6 GOVT. INQUIRY TO DEBUNK ! GALLUP POLLS Action Sought Five Years Ago by A.W.U. Executive GOVERNMENT SHOULD 'HAVE A LOOK' NOW AT THE WORK OF THESE 'CONF IDENCE TRICKSTERS' ! English-speaking Democracies are still laughing over the clownish attempts by Tory newspapers and Gallup Polls to stampede the people into believing that the Democratic standard-bearer of America (President Truman) would be annihilated by the whiteheaded boy of Big Business (Tom Dewey )j Governor of New York and Party crony of Australia's 'Bob' Menzies. On a previous occasion, when the world-renowned 'Literary Digest' registered a similar thud, that paper went out of existence in a cloud of shame and ridicule. The Gallup Poll stooges of the newspapers, however, are | trying to pass the buck on some mythical phenomena as mystical as their own Public Opinion surveys. They have announced their determination to go ahead with their forecasts and prognostications in their effort to influence the minds of electors near polling day. They still cling fondly to the belief that as 'one is . ; born every, minute' they might still sway the opinions of wavering voters by publicising in advance what are supposed to be the reactions of a reliable cross-section of ' the people. The spurious nature of this , claim has been exposed not only by the Dewey eclipse in America, but also by the complete vindication of the Cosgrove Labor Government in Tasmania and the Attlee Labor Government in Great Britain, notwithstanding the lopsided forecasts to the contrary by these latest stooges of the Tory press and monopoly interests. . . ? But these false- alarm forecasts are not merely stunts of recent growth, as in June, 1942, the Executive of the Australian Workers' Union discussed the evils of such socalled public opinion polls and finally carried the following motion for the consideration of the Commonwealth Government:- 'That this Executive is greatly disturbed by the vicious and extremely antiLabor nature of capitalist propaganda now being spread by the syndicated' press per medium of the misleading title 'Public Opinion Poll.' We don't believe the published results as being in any way related1 to actual fact and we are of the opinion that the results are preconceived by antiworking class propagandists working i& conjunction with the capitalist press in a plot to distort public opinion for vested interests. - For these reasons the A.W.U. Council should press the Commonwealth Government for an inquiry into the bona fides of this latest newspaper racket' . Maybe the time has arrived, for the Federal Government to have a . 'look-see'' behind this Iron Curtain of Toryism ? — an iron curtain that is every bit as ruthless * as any operating behind the dark environs os Moscow. Blackout for Truman No doubt the Gallup Poll surveys on the American elections were designed to draw a yeil over the nation-wide support that was manifested on all sides for. President Truman. As mentioned previously in these columns, the spokesmen for both the big Labor Organisations, C.I.O. and A.F.L., made no secret of their advocacy of the Democratic cause, aiid rieither did they conceal their prediction that- President Truman would go back to the] White House ' and- * send a majority to ;the Qapitol. ; But thesg facts 'wfere hot published in the Tory press of i Australia, which preferred to tell readers that the betting was 15 to 1 on Dewey and 10 to 1 against Truman, thus coaxing inveterate gamblers to invest on their phoney selection. Many public opinion polls published in Australia arc traceable directly or indirectly to the Monopoly Interests of Collins Street, Melbourne. That in itself should be sufficient to condemn them in the estimation of intelligent electors. The technique is a simple one, as canvassers are sent out to suburban doorsteps or to accost people haphazardly in the street, the buses, the trams, trains, or in the ferries. These interviews are frequently supplemented by talks on the telephone. Milk in the Cocoanut When the Gallup Poll headquarters tackle the job of examining, analysing, dissecting and classifying the various answers obtained, it then becomes a simple matter to sort out more or less any types of answers required. The Ones That Got Away For example, if six people interviewed favored the Labor Government's, proposals for Bank Nationalisation and four were opposed, the Gallup Poll specialist could permit himself to be snookered oh the six pro-Labor replies, whilst basing his survey on the answers given by the four people in support of the banking monopoly.Accordingly, Accordingly, the finished article, when published in the Tory press— like a neatly fashioned walking-stick— gives no account of that whiqh has been discarded or thrown away. It is a cardinal principle of ballot box elections that elections for Parliament be conducted on the same day, so that the recorded results from one constituency will not be permitted to sway the voters in another electorate. It is because , the highpowered propaganda angle of these, misleading polls cuts right across the fundamental principle of a free ballot-box that' the people most concerned are, entitled to look forward to prompt Government action that ? will expose the people and the methods behind this latest stunting -by vested interests. //? ? — — o ? ? 15 Dec 1948 - Slap at 40-Hour Week Australian Worker (Sydney, NSW : 1913 - 1950), Wednesday 15 December 1948, page 7 Slap at 40-Hour Weeki Another Gallup Poll Bubble EVIL OF WEEK-END OVERTIME The Gallup-poll experts are emerging from their hideouts. ?The Tories', latest research agency — an Institution of) Public Affairs — has placed a hunger under the 40-hour week legislation by suggesting that the reform has not brought more leisure — only higher incomes. It claims that 'most workers' are doing overtime or taking jobs at week-ends. It did not define 'most workers.' It is claimed that the labor shortage is worse, production has fallen, output per man is unchanged and costs have increased. An Old Aunt Sally The foregoing 'disclosures' are not even 'novel' as they were all trotted out 40 years ago when the first big step was taken to prevent grpcers, drapers, outfitters, etc.,; etc., remaining open until 10 and 11 o'clock at night— every night, except Sundays, when trade was transacted 'round the back.'' _ vAll the £eoiiomic disasters and earthquakes itpagipable were threatened when Early Closing was going to take effect, but no one went broke and neither employers nor shop assistants would want to go back to the bad old days preceding Early Closing. Bosses in Favor The 40 -hour week is in the same category and no doubt any attempt to repeal it would be stoutly resisted by employers, who cannot get away from their work soon enough to enjoy the extra 'measure of leisure and pleasure they treasure,' as expresses recently by the N.S.W. Minister for Lands. If the workers for whom the 40-hour week was obtained! are anxious to demonstrate] by week-end 'sweating' that ! they do not need so much! leisure-time, they will have only themselves to blame if a hostile Government should allow itself to be convinced by this argument in favcr of [ the 40-hour week's abolition. Companion Legislation This attempt by isolated workers to sabotage the shorter-working week is another reminder to legislators that bills to reduce hours should be accompanied by complementary legislation making provision for useful hobbies, classes, etc., etc., to encourage workers to spend their extra spare time hi qualifying for some higher position at their work, a superior post, trade or profession outside their own employment or classes for the cultivation of art, music, drama, or other cultural contrasts to their particular employment. When small business-houses and shop-keepers were compelled to observe 6 o'clock closing nearly half a century ago it was realised, too late, that up-to-date technical colleges, libraries and so on should have been introduced to absorb the reservoir of boyyouth and man-power realised from night slavery. Much progress has been made in recent years by Labor Governments in this direction. The shorter week of 40 hours offers a further opportunity of exploiting still more this cultural aspect of Labor's policy.

26 May 1948 - BRITISH BY-ELECTION FIGURES Australian Worker (Sydney, NSW : 1913 - 1950), Wednesday 26 May 1948, page 7 BRITISH BY-ELECTION FIGURES Tory Press 'Prefers Gallup Polls The Sydney 'Daily Tele- , graph's' Columnist, David McNicoll, recently visited Italy and France and now is in England. He told ^'Telegraph' readers on Thursday that the British Labor Government had slipped since the general elections of 1945 and was quite emphatic that Labor candidates would slip badly if an election were held to-morrow. Admittedly, McNicoll didn't have time to cpnduct a door-to-door canvass throughout . the United Kingdom, but he says he gathered his impressions from recent public opinion polls, and not published in a Tory newspaper, either! But facts are stubborn things, and McNicoll's prognostications — whether based oil Gallup, polls or not— dis-solve to nothing when tested against the official f igures an nounced by the British Electoral authorities' after ( each by-election. As a Democrat, McNicoll should prefer the official voice of the ballot-box to the suspicious voice of- any Gallup polls conceived and cradled by vested interests! Up to a month or two ago the British Labor Party had retained at by-elections 22 seats won at the general elections, which the Tories failed to retake. LABOR GAItf An. interesting by-electioii which makes McNicoll's publia opinion poll look a bit sick is that held for the Paisley seaton February 18, 1948. 'The Labor candidate, Mr. H. D. Johnston, .was elected over the National candidate witli a majority of 6545, or .56.8 per cent, of the total votes, as against 55.5 per cent, of the votes cast for Labor at the general elections. Despite this upward trend in the Labor vote, as reflected in Mr. Johnston's by-election, . Mr. McNicoll says: 'Any. continuation of that 'drift' will . almost certainly mean a Conservative .victory in 1950.'. Sounds more like ? a passage from one cf the Dav.e and Dad comedies. /

16 Sep 1941 - GALLUP POLLS COME TO AUSTRALIA. Narracoorte Herald (SA : 1875 - 1965), Tuesday 16 September 1941, page 4 GALLUP POLLS COME TO AUSTRALIA. First to Commence This Week. News lias been received that the first Australian-wide Gallup poll will be held from September 15th-30th. During that week three hundred interviewers throughout the Commonwealth will be taking a representative sample of Australian public opinion on a number of questions of outStanding contemporary importance and interest Narracoorte has been selected as one of the centres, and the local interviewer (Mr. R. J. piark) will be approaching a crosssection of the community for their opinions on. the questions submitted. All answers to .questions will be i strictly confidentialDepending entitirely on the science of statistics to give him amazingly accurate estimates of American public opinion, Dr. G. H. Gallup, head of the American Institute of Public Opinion; has achieved considerable fame. Australian public opinion polls will carry out his system in Australia. So accurately did Dr. Gallup calculate the margin by which Roosevelt would defeat Wilkie at the 1940 Presidential election—giving figures, State by State—that Dr. Henry C. Link, a statistical expert, said' the result was miraculous. Judging |by American experience, pnblication of results of polls of Australian public opinion will help to speed tip the machinery of our democracy. Newspapers in each capital city have agreed to publish the findings of Australian public opinion polls, which has been registered as a non-profit company. The newspapers concerned will pay for articles announcing the findings, and that amount will finance the organisation. In England, Gallnp's method— which will he the one used in Australia—has achieved results comparable with those in the United States. Last August, when the Director of the British Institute of Public Opinion went to America for a special course of study, he was asked by Government officials whether the polls conld, and would continue to operate in his absence. The Australian Director (Mr. Roy Morgan) has also been to America, and has studied Dr. Gallup's method by working with his staff. Recently, to test the efficacy of the Gallup method of "sampling" the population, a poll was taken of electors of Boothby, in South Australia. Remarkably reliable results were achieved. Some unthinking persons have- suggested that the polls have been established for the rather useless purpose of forecasting election results. But the real purpose of the organisation is to conduct miniature referendums, using statistically accurate samples of public opinion. The number of people interviewed', after a certain number, does not matter, hecause, if the first sample is an accurate cross-section further votes will, only duplicate opinions already expressed.

06 Apr 1909 - South-Eastern Drainage Poll. Narracoorte Herald (SA : 1875 - 1965), Tuesday 6 April 1909, page 3 South-Eastern Drainage Poll. THE SCHEME ACCEPTED. A poll of more than ordinary interest to a large number of landholders of the SouthEast, and we may say to the State at large, was taken by the various District Councils who had jurisdiction over the laud in the " poll area" on Saturday, April 3. The poll was taken under an Act passed last session of. Parliament entitled " An Act to authorise the carrying out of a certain scheme of drainage in the SouthEast of the State, and for other purposes," and the area within which the poll was to be taken was defined in a plan constituting the third schedule of the Act. The Millicent District Councils were in the scheme at first,but they were afterwards omitted, with the exception of a small portion of Mount Muirhead, and all other District Councils in the Southeast except Port MacDonnell, Benara, and Tatiara had to take polls, though the Port MacDonnell and Benara Councils are within the "drainage area." No District Council had all its landowners within the " poll area," and in many cases only portions of hundreds came within the area. We have already explained the scheme in detail, and people are now fairly familiar with it. The Acts provide for carrying out a comprehensive 6cbeme of drainage in the South-East, affecting 1,700,000 acre3 of land of varied quality: -£300,000 to he expended on the " certain" scheme defined in the first schedule of "The Soutfa-Eastern Drainage Scheme Act-, 1908"; the Government to advance .£150,000 ol this amount, and the moiety to be paid by landowners in instalments extending over 42 years according to the benefits their lands derive; the first payments not to commence untii five years after the scheme was completed, and it • v a; reckoned the " certain" scheme would not le completed for seven or eight years, which meant 12 or 13 years before landowners would be called upon to pay. The ■ other Act passed last session—" The South Eastern Drainage Act Amendment Act, 1908"—provides for a new system of ad ministration' in connection with drainage in the South-Easr, with the t xc^ption ot the Millisent drainage area, and also make provision for maintaining and keeping all drainB in repairs, and for landowners constructing on easy terms subsidiary drains into the main drains. There was a gooa deal of quiet earnest interest taken in the poll for the last few weeks, but at no time did the interest rise to red heat. The , merits - and demerits of the whole scheme j as embodied in the two Acts were, as they should be, freely discussed, and it i needless to say opinions differed. Thos. in favor of it were surprised at landowners . with wet lands being opposed to such a magnificent offer as was embodied in the Acts; and others contended that from pas' experience of. drainage the scheme would not do what was promised for it, that the general character of the land was toe inferior to hear the burden of any ex pensive scheme of drainage, and that the limited quantity of the good land in the area to he benefited would bare tc bear too heavy a bnrden tinder the betterment system. The Drainage League and the District Drainage Committees worked hard to point out the inestimable benefit? of tbe scheme, and gained a large numbe of converts. So fast did they convert thosi who had been stoutly opposed to it that i was reckoned that if the' poll had been taken a few weeks later there woulc scarcely have been any votes against it Mr. D. Findlater, as President of th. League, did yeoman service in advocating the scheme, as also did Mr. Tavender Both of them spoke in faror of it at a nam ber of meetings convened specially for th purpose, and conducted a large correspondence throughout the district advocating it. They have had their reward in the acceptance of the scheme by a gooc majority. The returns to hand on Saturday night shone 1 that the scheme was sjfe of acceptance, although tbe full results i were not to hand. 16 Jan 1948 - POLITICIANS ARE PEOPLE Great Southern Herald (Katanning, WA : 1901 - 1966), Friday 16 January 1948, page 4 POLITICIANS ARE PEOPLE WE GET WHAT WE DESERVE So you don't want your son to go into politics? . Almost no parents do, according, to a Gallup Poll, for they believe that "a political career leads to graft and crookedness". This is pretty unhealthy thinking m a democracy. It shows a dangerous ignorance of the politician's vital function in society. It tries to shift the blame for our own shortcomings on to his conveniently obvious should ers. Politicians arc human beings like anyone else. There is much the same proportion of good and bad among them. Many are doing a hard job well and getting as many brickbats as bouquets for it. But even on the lower levels of selfinterest there is something to be said for the politician. He is the buffer, the reconciler, between innumerable antagonistic interests in society. His very effort to please as many people as possible has the virtue of looking for compromises. The tensions be- i tween groups dogmatically sure of their own Tightness might become unbearable without his more yielding and adjustable habit of thought. This is not • to excuse the too-frequent lack of real integrity in the politician. But here society as a whole must share the blame. When the poli tician is corrupt, somone must do the j corrupting. The respected citizen who approaches the politician obliquely with gifts, favours, "campaigning contributions"—and an interesting set of private proposals—is not the best per- I son to pass moral judgement on him- , Society gets the politician it de-1 serves- When it throws fewer temp tations in their way, learns to appreciate their probems and achievements, and encourages young men and women of character to join their ranks, there will be less occasion for self-righteous condemnation and more for active support. t (Christian Science Monitor.)

09 Nov 1950 - 'Easy Street' For Australia Will Not Come Easily Maryborough Chronicle (Qld. : 1947 - 1954), Thursday 9 November 1950, page 4 'Easy Street* For Australia Will Not Come Easily A\S the result of an Australiawide Gallup Poll, published this week, most Australians belifve that they are better off. in an economic sense, than their fathers. Not everybody, of course, , expressed that be lief. Much has happened in a generation, particularly in the gradual improvement in working conditions and amenities, and in the rising level of wages. Wages are now much higher than in 'the good old' or the 'Bad old' days. Nobody desires — and the trade unions would be justified in strenuously fighting against — a return to thj wages and hours and working conditions of those days. None the less, money, pound for pound, had far greater value some decades ago than it has now. It -is surprising, judged by present-day standards of value, what the worker or the family man could do with his 'few quid' a week or fortnight when wages were at a much lower level than they are today. The average worker then, even as now, was a home-builder or a potential Kbme-buildcr. He didn't have much in his pay envelope; but he managed to meet interest and redemption on money borrowed from a building society. provide his family with good, wholesome food, clothe them well, give them a good education, and put by a little 'for a rainy day.' True, it often meant a hard struggle pnd a life of selfsacrifice by many parents for their growing boys and girls. True, also, there were less avenues of spending in sport or entertainment, and 'things were much cheaper'; but, like the pioneers before them, they built on secure foundations, and, above all, they got full value for their money. , To-day the average worker or family man — not to speak of the apprentice or the 'dead-end' labourer — gets much more in the pay envelope than the family man of a tew decades ago. He has, also, less hours of work — to-day it is a statutory 40-hour week for the majority if Australians—and the worker, on the whole, has far better working conditions and more amenities than his father before him. To revert to the conditions or the level 'of wages of yesterday would be a retrograde step and a confession of economic despair. But how much better off is the worker to-day compared with the worker in the decade before the Great War ? Wages have increased considerably since those days. Tlie basic wage is to go up by another £1. If the actual money in the pay envelope were the only thing that counted, the average AusIralian to-day would be well off, owning or buying his home, and meeting all his commitments with comparative ease. But there are other things to be taken into consideration, such as shortages of essential commodities, inflationary and still soaring prices, and greatly depreciated money values. Good homes, which 30 years ago cost about £500 or £600 to build, now cost up lo approximately £2000, not to mention the long period ot wailing for construction. That is merely one instance of rising costs and prices, which slash heavily into wages, and, obviously, strike particularly hard at the worker on the lower scalc of wages and at all people on low fixed incomes from investments or life's savings. The H.C.O.L. is something more than four letters to manypeople. ll is the high cost of living; and nobody can give any guarantee that it will not so still higher. To take the H. from the H.C.O.L. is a titanic task. The C.O.L. will mvaj's be with us; but to bring the cost of living to a reasonable level is a direct challenge to Australian political and industrial leadership. The basis of greater economic stability and greater value in the pound is increased wealth from increased production. The only way to get more from the national income is to increase the national income itself. 'Easy street' for Australians as a whole will ? not come by any other means.

12 Nov 1948 - EDITORIAL "Gallup" Comes a Cropper Westralian Worker (Perth, WA : 1900 - 1951), Friday 12 November 1948, page 5 EDITORIAL "Gallup" Comes a Cropper >riIE fatuity of periodical Gallup Polls is glaringly exposed in the result of tlie Presidential ejection in flic United States. For days bofnro. world-wide cables told tlie reading public in other lands that Dewey would win. on the strength of rigged Gallup Polls indicating tliat the Governor of New York State was a 15 to 1 bet for the l-lghcst post in the gift of the American people. jBob Monzics, who was in the States at the time, fell for the tale; so much so that when it became known that Trunian had sprung tlio biggest election surprise in American history, Menzies had to shamefacedly admit tluit the only man in the States who told him Truman would win was Truman himself ! In an attempt to get out from under, the newspapers which had. harked the Gallup opinion, described the result as a magnificent win for American Labor. That admission merely emphasises the partisanship-ami the purpose-of Gallup Polls. Because, if there had been an honest attempt to gauge public opinion the views of tho millions in the two big Labor federations in-the States wonld have been consulted. Obviously they were not asked for an opinion; if they had-and again assuming that the published figures honestly rcflcctcd the views of those interviewed-there would not have been a majority selection of Dewey, let alone such an overwhelming majority. The significance to us in Australia lies in the fact that we are treated from time to time to political forecasts based on similar polls, supiioscdly conducted on average public opinion. We al60 have street "quizzes" published, in which teenagers of both sexes vent opinions. For the most part those "quizzes" have a political slhnt. and always the slant is ajgainst Labor, to create an atmosphere that the Labor Government, or the Labor Movement, as the ease may be. is running counter to public opinion. Then there is the related technique instanced In the advertisement which bobs up from time to time in our daily newspapers that the elector has only so many "months to go" before he can exercise his assumed desire to defeat the Labor Goverhment. There is a warning in all this for the supporters of the Labor Party. While these Gallup Polls and the related tactics of the opponents of Labor are properly matters for ridicule, they do serve one useful purpose so far as the Labor Movement is concerned--of pointing the need for meeting propaganda with counter propaganda. * The exposure of the American election will open the eyes of those unthinking people who. anxious to be on a winner, whether it be politics, horseracing or football, are influenced by published "forecasts. but rarely take the trouble to look into the bona fides of tbe forecaster.

Westralian Worker (Perth, WA : 1900 - 1951), Friday 18 August 1950, page 1 Gallup Poll Lines Up With People On "Onus Of PAof" Gathering weight of public opinion against undemocratic clauses of the K#n« zies Communist Party Dissolution Bill has become so pronounced that even that reactionary device - the Gallup Poll - has been forced to swing into line with popu* lar feeling. 4 It can be taken for granted that the Pollsters must have found opinion against the Tory measure overwhelming, as their past achievements would indl- ! cate that the Poll "electorate" i would automatically back a Lib- i eral Government Bill. j That the "voters" did not in this instance implies that backing for the Labor stand against the "onus of proof" provision was too strong to be evaded in the interests of Tory propaganda, for which the Poll was designed. 14 Oct 1949 - POLL TRICKSTERS ARE AT IT AGAIN Westralian Worker (Perth, WA : 1900 - 1951), Friday 14 October 1949, page 1 POLL TRICKSTERS ARE AT IT AGAIN Diabolically Cunning Device To Control Public Thought Gallup polls are a subtle device intended lo regiment the minds of the people, calculated to give the impression that a responsible cross section of the people want certain things done in a certain way. "LABOR'S CHANCES SAME AS IN 1946" Yet in May of this year the Daily News printed this Gallup Poll: The situation was: Labor, 51 per cent. Liberal, 46 per cent. Independents, 3 per ccnt. it is noticeable that there were no "undecided votes." This Is .strange, as h was 7 months prior to the election date of December 10. Robert C. Myers, Lecturer at the Princeton University in America, spent 6 months investigating the Gallop Poll, the Crossley Poll, the Roper Poll, and numerous others conducted by news paper ch&ins. "Polls Are Business Enterprises" And as to the direction in which the pollsters want the thinking of tho people to run, Myers has this to say: '"Since the polls are business enterprises, run for profit, you might guess that their selection of questions and their reporting of results vould be biased or slanted toward the ownershipmanaperm-ni point of view, and against Labor, particularly organised Laboi. Your guess would be absolutely correct." Myers also said that of all the polls conducted in the UJ5., the on.» most heavily weighted against trade unionism was the Gallup Poll, three-fourths of whose questions had been shown to have an anti-Labor bias. Thoroughly discredited over their attempts to herd US. people in thinking that they would vote for Dewey in the Presidential clc-tJom, the American people are treating the pollsters in the same manner as they dealt wHh the politically corrupt magazine "I.itfiary Digest" over its "polling" for Landon against President Roosevelt in 1936. The system subtly plays upon certain well-known tendencies of human nature in its present immature stage of evolution. For example, many people will act in most circumstances as they think the majority is acting, or is likely to act This is the trap that is being Set, and the trap which Labor mu»t discredit before It starts its campaign for mass hypnosis in this crucial election year of 1949. The place for Gallup Poll results is where Harry Truman coumelicd I .S. electors to put them . . .""right in the ashcan"

17 Dec 1943 - A Steady Job Westralian Worker (Perth, WA : 1900 - 1951), Friday 17 December 1943, page 1 A Steady Job A\- ArsTR\IilAN GALLl 1' Poll lia1- iliH'im'ied Hit* l';ir from surprising fact iliat many Australian:- arc anxious to achieve security or employment. But while this is noi surprising-, it is surprising and also a reflection upon our civilisation that, in a land which can produce abundance for alL, the primal needs of food, clothing, and shelter should still loom so large in the average outlook. Xpg fact of present employment does not cloud the memory of those who experienced the uncertainties and tin1 miseries of the years between the wars. Neither does it still the fear that the future might he. despite all the talk of a New Order, very much like the past. A steady job is astill the highest prize in the economic lottery. Can we so arrange our affairs that security of employment will be a right rather than a matter of luck? We have not been able to do so in the past without the stimulus of war. and then to a large extent our affairs have been condueted for us by the impact of war. But if we make a reasonably intelligent effort to prolil from past mistakes there is no reason why every Australian should not be able to secure the employment he desires. Of all countries Anstralia has the least excuse for unemployment. There is so much work to lie done and so few. comparatively, to do it that there should never be a time when there are more men than jobs. We cannot, of course, isolate ourselves from or insulate ourselves against the movement of world trends, hut the fact that Wall Street has overreached itself should not liaTe the effect of sending more men to Marquis Street to look for work that is not available. In the matter of employment Australians need to be more assertive than they liave lieeii in the past. The work is hern- and also the money to pay the men who do it. Once upon a time this State of Western Australia considered it absolutely necessary to Iwrrow anything from £4.000.000 to £6.000.000 yearly from Condon to carry on its activities. This was an excellent thing for the money-lenders, and it was also regarded as an excellent thing for the State. Its effect upon those who have to find the money to pay the interest on these loans is not so excellent. The work of the people established the credit upon which the money was borrowed, hut when this source of loan money dried up in the world depression their work was tegarded as being ol' so little value that nobody wanted it. lie will have depressions instead of employment in the post-war years unless we decide now that there shall Ite work and make our plans accordingly. In Anstralia and in Western Australia our plans have gone forward to the extent of returning Governments that can Ik' relied upon to do all withiu their power to see that work is available, hut this is not jenough, We must determine that when we are told by "experts" that "employment is governed by business conditions which pass through well-defined phases in a cycle of activity." and that "these phases may be defined, as those of prosperity, recession, depression, and recovery"' and that there is nothing that we can do abont it, to remain quite niiimprcssed by this display or erudition. It was an acceptance of the rubbish talked by "experts" that made the last depression the hideous thing it was. There cannot be. and there never has been, any sound reason why every Australian in need of work should not l>e able to find employment. If the position again arises in which men seek work in vain it will not be the fault of the business cycle, but of tliosc wlio accept the position, and the twaddle used In attempts to jutsify it.

11 Jul 1947 - CRIME-TIME Westralian Worker (Perth, WA : 1900 - 1951), Friday 11 July 1947, page 4 rfte TOPICS TOILERS TALK OF # (By "THE NIPPER") frjt/^jUXjmTUVVMVWVVVVVWW'''^" " * * " " FITTILE PRACTICE v TN the face of intense provocation in the shape of repressive legis lation, the refusal of American Labor to set up its own political party is remarkable.
