The recent Labor Control Bill should convince American workers of the futility of the practice of attempting 1o. play the Democrat Party off against the Republican and vice versa. Workers in Australia soon found out that there was nothing to be gained in that way from the old Conservative and Liberal Parties. One gl-oup of Capitalists can occasionally be helped to injure another group of Capitalists, but there are certain fundamentals on which both groups stand as one. ☆ ☆ ☆ SOMETHING LEFT UNSAID DROM President Truman's Independence Day talk: "Unfortunately, a number of ■ countries maintain barriers against the iflow of information or ideas into or«out of their territories. Many restrict travel, some behind barriers of their otyn creation, and present to their citizens carefully selected or distorted versions of the facts about other' countries. These Activities of organised mistrust lead the people away from "peace and unity. They are a far cry from contributing to the full, free exchange of ideas and knowledge which we need if we are to have a. peaceful world. "The first step to end ignorance and suspicion would be to stop propaganda attacks on other nations. The second step would be to co-operate with other nations who are so earnestly endeavoring to increase friendly understanding among men.'Tlere, at the home of Thomas Jefferson, who dedicated his life to liberty, education and intellectual freedom, I appeal to all nations and peoples to break down the artificial barriers" which separate them. I appeal for tolerance and restraint in the relations of the nations and the peoples, and I appeal for a free flow of knowledge and ideas that alone can lead to a harmonious world." That is timely, and also excellent, but, unfortunately, it does not go far enough. President Truman should have had something to say about those nations—America is the outstanding example— which maintain trade barriers against other countries. In order to maintain the synthetic rubber industry, America has raised a barrier against the importation of Malayan rubber, and in order to maintain an inefficient woolgrowing industry a barrier has been erected against Australian wool. Yet, if we are to have a peaceful world, a reasonably free flow of trade is certainly one of the first requirements. THE RUSSIAN WIVES fpHIS stupidity which is inseparable from totalitarian regimes is seen at its worst in Mr. Molotov's refusal to see, when in Paris, representatives of the fifteen Englishmen whose Russian wives are I not permitted to leave Russia. This is a small matter, but it has far-reaching effects. The spectacle of a great power using its might in such a manner cannot ! fail to have repercussions. And the spectacle of a Foreign Minister refusing even to discuss the matter is completely contemptible. ☆ ☆ ☆ WRONG ADDRESS AT the conclusion of the Paris talks Mr. Molotov §aid that the Anglo-French proposals would lead Britain and the countries following them into separating themselves from the other Euro-, pean States, thus dividing Europe into two groups of States. " The Soviet Government considers it. necessary to caution Britain and France against the consequences of such action," he added. As it is the Soviet Government's attitude that is dividing Europe, into two groups of States, it is a pity that Mr. Molotov lacks the. courage to direct the caution he considers necessary to the right address. ☆ ☆ ☆ THE ENEMY WITHIN TJ^HEN moving at the annual conference of the New South Wales AX.P. for the removal of Communists from official ^positions In affiliated organisations, the • General Secretary of the A.W.tL, Mr. T. Dougherty, said that in the future war, of« which so much is heard, the enemy of Australia would be the Communist Party. If people were going to be weak with, the Communist Party, the Communist Party would dictate to them. The'motlon foi* removal was carried by an overwhelming majority, and the way is now cleared for definite and decisive action against Communists who have gained official positions in trade unions in New South Wales and have already proved themselves enemies of Australia. Speaking earlier at this conference, the Prime Minister, Mr, ChMley, said: "There are those people who try to cling on to the coat-tails of the Labor Movement, put really to use the Labor Move ment as a platform to espouse philosophies other than those of the Labor Movement, This is a country of freedom of expression. It is for every man to choose his own political philosophy, but let him preach his own philosophy from his own platform," The provision of a platform for Communists to preach from has been made by Labor on far too many occasions. Unions affiliated with the Labor Movement have even made it possible for Communists to travel overseas to spit their venom against Labor, in many 'cases to the delight of Democracy-hating audiences. Action to confine Communists to their own. platforms is imperative, not only In New South wales, but throughout Australia.

12 Sep 1941 - GALLUP POLLS Westralian Worker (Perth, WA : 1900 - 1951), Friday 12 September 1941, page 3 GALLUP POLLS JUST A NEWSPAPER STUNT. Next week Australian Public i 3pinion Polls will launch the first of what is announced to he a continu- j aus series of referendums to deter mine the attitude of Australians on I questions of national importance. J America has led the way in this specious method of hocus pocus about obtaining "a cross-section of opinion from men and women in all walks of life and all shades of political opinion." WORKERS SHOULD BEWARE. j The workers should be particularly! wary of this stunt. Throughout the! political history of the Labor Move-1 ment we have seen the same stunt worked by capitalist newspapers in-i dividually. A reporter is sent out into the street to get thumb-nail interviews, and by carefully-worded questions a desired answer to some public question is secured—desired, that is, by the newspaper. If the ruse fails to get the desired answer, it is the simplest thing in the world to suppress the answer altogether. The important thing to he remembered is that these ''polls" are financed by newspapers whose interests are opposed to the Interests of the Labor Movement; and that a Gallup poll is a commercial venture —nothing else. AX AMERICAN VIEW. The "Christian Science Monitor," probably the most widely-circulated and certainly the most independent American publication, recently had the following to say about Gallup polls: "It is reasonable to inquire what authority these reports can claim to justify the great influence that they evidently exert. They are the reports Of a private concern which sells Its findings to newspapers and other subscribers on the strength of its own assurance that by polling carefully picked people in all States it haa the mathematical key to the opinion of the American public at large."

26 Sep 1941 - MORE ABOUT GALLUP POLLS Westralian Worker (Perth, WA : 1900 - 1951), Friday 26 September 1941, page 3 MORE ABOUT GALLUP POLLS 'DETRIMENTAL AND UNRELI ABLE." A fortnight ago we warned supporters of the Labor Movement against the newspaper stunt to conduct "public opinion polls" in Aus tralia. Since then the Metropolitan District Council of the A.L.P. has declared that the "polls" would be detrimental and unreliable by reason of the fact that they are being financed by newspapers diametrically opposed to the interests of the Labor Movement. LAUGH IT OFF. "Smith's Weekly" has given attention to this subject, and the follow ing is extracted from an article in j that newspaper under the headings "Hack-door Quiz; Laugh it Off"; "Australian Public Opinion Polls, a new 'non-profit' company, has ex-, cited the attention of the Federal' Government and union bodies. It I was to be expected that it would j excite criticism. "Federal Government wishes to make it plain that it has no connec- ( tion with the proposed polls. "Newcastle (N.S.W.) Trades and Labor Council has passed a resolu tion of protest agkinst the polls, un urofit or otherwise. Various other Labor Councils are considering the i matter. "Last week Australian Public Opinion Polls (The Gallup Method) advertised in the Press for sparetime interviewers. "Advertisements claimed that in a few weeks an Australia-wide network of interviewers would make the first survey on 'What Australia Thinks' about important questions of the day. "Applicants for positions were advised that they must be 'men or women of integrity who believe in freedom of opinion, and must not he known as ardent supporters of a particular political party.' "Interest was rather damped when It became knowh that the company was offering 12/6 for 10 fnll-scale Interviews. "Director of A.P.O.P. is Mr. Roy Morgan, a bright 'ideas man' from Melbourne Grammar School who recently spent some time in the United States studying the methods of Dr. Gallup, the originator of the absurd American Gallup Polls. "Mr. Morgan has his office in 'The Sun' Building, Sydney. He is also linked with Sir Keith Murdoch, and the "Melbourne Herald' is one of the backers of A.P.O.P. "To the question of who finances the surveys, A.P.O.P. replies that daily newspapers in each State will pay for the right to publish res of the surveys. In return, apparently, these newspapers will be able to publish articles based on the polls. "Applicants for jobs with the company are presented with lengthy questionnaires, in which must ho filled address and occupation of the interviewee, together with his replies to about 20 questions. "Sample questions; "How did you vote at the last elec tions? "Should Mr. Menzles go to Lou don ? "Reason for Federal Government perturbation is that people may be confused into thinking that these polls are conducted officially by the Government, instead of by a private company. All the more reason for this anxiety is that A.P.O.P.'s advertisements are inserted under the heading of 'Public Notice.' "Unions arc lip in arms because they refuse to believe that an organisation tied so intimately to large newspaper chains will be free of political bias in conducting its sur veys."

16 Dec 1943 - Preference for Government Jobs. South Western Advertiser (Perth, WA : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 16 December 1943, page 4 Preference for Government Jobs. The result of an Australian Gallup I poll published in the "West Austraj lian" newspaper, and showing that 53 ' out of '100 people preferred a job in a government factory to a job in a private factory, 34 preferred a private job, and 13 had no opinion, illustrates the foolishness that this paper emphasised before the recent Federal election, in which the Nationalists made the election issue "socialism versus private enterprise." Naturally, unenterprising people who shrink from the responsibilities of enterprise, and- have no strength in themselves, prefer the shelter of a "government job." In the end, of course, private enterprise collapses, and slavery to government enterprise becomes complete, everybody working for wages Vvith no other prospect, and j with no private enterprise to fall back | upon for losses and taxation for social! benefits. That, in turn, would bring a I quick end to non-contributory social' benefits. "Orders is brders" would become the law of the land, every man i going where he was bidden, and be- i coming a literal slave. Freedom of choice is the spiritual and natural or- j der of all evolution. '

28 Jul 1934 - SEWERAGE Maryborough Chronicle, Wide Bay and Burnett Advertiser (Qld. : 1860 - 1947), Saturday 28 July 1934, page 6 .SEWERAGE . TO-DAY'S P0I1 Final Meting Last Night MR. MANCHESTER'S VIEWS The filial meeting in connection with the sewerage poll which, 'will takjc place to-day was held at the «orner of Kent and Adelaide-streets last evening when * several speakers put tbe case in favour' of the proposal. It was not true that tho Brisbane scheme had cost £10,000,000 as stated 'over the air' that night. Tho combined water and sewerage scheme, with filtration appliances, had only -cost £8,000,000. The Sydney scheme was run on unfiltered water for a couaiderablo time, but the sewage had somewhat polluted the harbour during the Inst -five, or six years. 15 Oct 1941 - Political Unity Would Give Added Vitality to Realism Maryborough Chronicle, Wide Bay and Burnett Advertiser (Qld. : 1860 - 1947), Wednesday 15 October 1941, page 4 Political Unity Would Give Added Vitality to Realism Australian Gallup poJ) has indicated that, prior to the fall of the Fadden Government, Australians would have voted three to one in favour of an all-party Government.. That is a fairly true index of public opinion. The elevation of Labour to office has not materially altered that opinion. Als the nation, thinks so it will speak and vote. a W-.: ? i r ? ? {..ii.. ? reseniative of all parties hqs been in the forefront of public opinion since the outbreak of the war. Labour hitherto has persistently refused to join in a coalition Government. The rule which forbids it to do so may eventually react to its political disadvantage. In the meantime, however, it i.i in power in Australia. There is no need to question its sincerity of puipose or its oft stated desire to proaecube the war to the utmost possible extent. It is equally absurd for enemy propagandists to bleat that Australia is divided on iflie war merely because it has changed governments in the greatest crisis in history. Normally Australians live in two political camps; but, in spite of their political differences, which are fundamentally social and economic, they arc at one .in their determination to sec the crisis through. Mr. F. M. Forde, the Labour Minister for the Army, voiced llhis determination in a broadcast address to Australia on Sunday night. ''Labour,' he said, 'has a decisive war programme and will oppose Hitlarii.m to the death. We ihall. shirk no share of our just responsibility, however heavy. We realise that defeat at the hands of Germany would cru^li out of existence for ever every hope under which the. bulk of Australians live.' Mr. Forde spoke as a Labour Minister. but his words expressed essentially the sentiments of the Australian, people as a whole in their relentless opposition to ihe brutal system of Nazi-Fascishi. All-round Co-operation MR Forde said, further, that 'this j is a people's war, the winning of which depends on the whole-hear ed co-operation of the men in t'he fighting services, the workers in the factories, and t'he masses of the people.' Tlioje words were well spoken. Obviously full co-operation is vital to a complete war eifort — every man and every woman in his or her allotted sphere of service. Mr. Forde is confident that 'a Labour Government cam and will succeed in bringing about this co-operation,' niuw., .it ,3 ou en.mre a maximum war effort and ul-. timate victory.' The Minister'^ earnestness is not in doubt. He has spoken of co-operation on the battle front, on Uhe industrial front, and by the people as a whole. That plea suggests this obviou.-i question: Why mot, also, fullco-operation on the political front?; All-party representation on the Advisory War Council does not go far. enough. A majority of Australians, as the Gallup poll indicates, favours Britain's common sense method — namely, a complete subordination of party politics in the nation's in terp.it s : in other words, the formation of a National Government. Complete unity at Canberra would show that political plarties themselves, are under no illusions as to the perils ahead. This a'jnosphere of realism would give additional weight to the nation'.i war effort, because it would strike direct at t'he last remaining ''elements of irresponsibility and smug complacency' whom 'Mr. Fadden, the ex-Prime Minister, rebuked when he spoke, with Mr. 'Forde, at a war loan raily in Brisbane, on Monday night.

24 Sep 1941 - GALLUP POLLS TO TEST PUBLIC OPINION Maryborough Chronicle, Wide Bay and Burnett Advertiser (Qld. : 1860 - 1947), Wednesday 24 September 1941, page 4 GAHUP POLLS TO TEST PUBLIC OPINION Mr. R. Dunn is Local Representative '^^HAT does Australia think-' Aus. tralian Public Opinion Polls aim to find out. ' The Gallup method, which will bes used in Australia, was evolved by Dr. G. H. Gallup, head of the American Institute of Public Opinion. Depefidr ing entirely on the science of statistics to eive him amazlnfflv accurate estim ates of publioopinion Dr. Gallup has achieved considerable fame, and American cable news often makes reference to tjie Gallup polls, which indicate the trend of American thought. Mr. R. 'R. Dunn, Maryborough, has been appointe&!one' of- a staff of interviewers to be appointed in nearly 300 ccntres m all parts of Australia. The polls or 'sample referendum^' will be conducted on ' topical questions from 1 time to time, and Mr. Dunn will hold the interviews , in the Maryborough area. Some Maryborough people have Already been made acquainted with the' Australian Public Opinion Polls whenrecently they were asked to answer a, number of questions. This first nation-; wide poll has just-closed and the results will be made available shortly- ] Discussing the polls Mr. Dunn said ! that judging by American experience the publication of results of the surveys would help to speed up the machinery of our democracy. The A.P.OJP. was being registered as a non-' profit company and daily newspapers in each State would pay for the right to publish the results. CROSS SECTION OF OPINION At the same time as (Mr. Dunn is asking his questions in Maryborough other interviewers will be asking similar questions in all parts of the Commonwealth. Together the samples will .be a cross-section of Australians in all walks of life— men and women rich and pop.rj_old.-and young, ot all shades of opinion, in their correct statistical proportions. _ During 1940 the Director of the .Australian Polls went to America to . study with Dr. Gallup and his experts. Jn England the Gallup method lias achieved results comparable with those in the United States. The ucross-sectionV is large enough to provide a true reflection of Ihe division of public opinion in Australia. Sampling is earned to the stage where additional interviews would merely confirm results already obtained. Re-, ccntly to test the efficacy of the Gallup method of 'sampling' Ibe population a poll wag taken of electors of Boothby, South Australia, and remark, ably reliable results were achieved. Between 1936 and 1040 the American Institute of Public Opinion improved its methods. Its forecast of the 1936 Presidential election had an average error in all States of six per cent., but last November when President Roosevelt was re-elected the error was reduced to two and a half per cent.-— truly an amazing achievement in a country where voting is not compulsory. 05 Jun 1948 - "BETWEEN TWO WORLDS" Methodist (Sydney, NSW : 1892 - 1954), Saturday 5 June 1948, page 4 'BETWEEN TWO WORLDS' Address by the Retiring President- General, Rev. J. W. Burton, M.A., D.D., given at the Opening Session of the General Conference held in Sydney, on Thursday, 20th May. (Continued from last issue.) THE CHURCH The Church is between two worlds. We are facing a serious decline in its influence and in attendance at worship. The Gallup Polls, the Mass Observation Statistics as published in Gollanz' 'Puzzled People,' and the Church returns are disquieting. Ecclesiastical officials sometimes minimize these facts and suggest that figures are misleading. There is, I know, outside the Churches, a great deal of diffused Christian ethic and much reflected light; but that might be termed 'Fly-wheel Christianity,' and it cannot maintain momentum when 'the power impulses are withdrawn. There are many who live on the unearned increment of the religion of others. We may as well face realistically the fact that there are many who do not want what the Church offers. Jesus found that there was a recoil from His high ideals of living; 'Ye will not come to Me,' He said, 'that ye might have life.' ^ There are men engrossed in sordid money-making, in the pursuit of selfish pleasures, and in the attainment of personal ambitions who do not want this Man to reign over them. Robert Browning's question is still a pertinent one: 'What think ye of Christ, friend, when all's said and done? Like you this Christianity or not? It may be . false, but would you have it true? Has it your vote to be so, if it can?' . Lenin is reported to have said, 'Religion is the opiate of the people.' Whatever truth there may have been in that dictum in corrupt priest-ridden old Russia, it is not true in our world today. Sport is the opiate of the masses. Read your daily papers, measure up the space given to religion and that given to sport, and you will get a shock. And the papers know what the people want. The report of the British Churches' Committee on Gambling is a startling document which deserves close study. In England alone 360,000 to 435,000 persons are regularly imployed in the principal' forms of gambling — Book-making, Horse and Dog Racing, Football Pools, etc. In addition about half that number find part-time employment — and this in 1947 when the labour shortage imperilled England's very existence! The turnover in four popular forms of gambling was £950,000,000 at a net cost to the investors of £102,000,000. The bill for all forms of sport, amusements and entertainment is about £1,500,000,000— one-fifth of the national spending. I have no figures for Australia, but one of our greatest moral and economic dangers is the gambling mania— the most pernicious of which is probably our State lotteries. Much of their popularity is due to specious propaganda. The fewwinners have great publicity, but nothing is said of the tens of thousands who lose. To the man who is enamoured of gambling, whether on the Stock Exchange or on the racecourse, the quiet sanity of Jesus is not likely to make much appeal. I am convinced that, contrary to much criticism, the reason why there is a drift from the Churches is not mainly the fault of the Churches them selves. It lies in the undue value we have given to money and to our greed for material possessions. We have an unhealthy respect for the money-maker who contributes comparatively little to the well-being of society. We have overestimated his ability and worth. Thales, one of the great seven Greek philosophers, made sport of men who set more store by money than by wisdom. They replied that it was a case of the fox and the grapes. In* answer to their challenge he put his mind to money-making and in one year amassed more? wealth than the most experienced trader raked together in his whole life. He then went back to the pursuit of wisdom. The great men of the world have not been money makers. 'What porridge had John Keats?' What profit had John Wesley? What value did David Livingstone, Florence Nightingale, Robert ^Scott, and Mahatma Gandhi place on money? ^ By their poverty they made many rich; whereas today men -by their wealth make many poor. There are two tendencies to which I should like to refer and which suggest that the Church is between two worlds — (a) the alienation of the 'working man'; (b) the withdrawal of the intellectuals. I know it is difficult to generalize without carefully-compiled statistics, but on the whole these two tendencies appear to be very difinite. John Smith is not with us, nor are the great scientists, the leaders of thought, and the creative artists. We are left largely with middle-class people living in comfortable suburban homes with comfortable suburban ideas. Let me make haste to say that some of these middle and lower.-middle class people are of the very salt of the earth — honest, upright and industrious — and I am grateful that I have had intimate friendship with so many of them; but that must not blind our eyes to the alienation of others. (a) First, let us take the question of the 'work-ing classes.' I want to be careful not to exaggerate nor to suggest that we have no working men in our Churches, but how few! Let us think of the churches from which we have come, how many of the working class are members or in official positions? How many are there in this General Conference — the most representative body of our Australian Church? Among our laity we have professional men, business managers, property-owners, farmers and merchants; but where is John Smith? And why isn't he here? Jesus loved the Common Man, and drew His disciples from that class. The rich and powerful would have, on the whole, nothing to do with Him, for He challenged their selfish way of living. Read again your New Testament and underline the passages where Jesus warns men against avarice, greed and the amassing of wealth — and there will be much-scored pages. This was not a matter of class distinction: it was a question of the quality of life. John Wesley, whom we revere but do not closely emulate, died a poor man, and drew most of his followers from the miners of Cornwall, the potters of Staffordshire, and the artisans and farm labourers of Yorkshire. The Todpuddle Martyrs were mainly Methodist lay preachers. (Continued on page 5) 'BETWEEN TWO WORLDS' (Continued from page 4.) If we have lost John Smith, how are we to win him back? We must learn, in the first place, to understand him— take time to talk with him. We must try to see his point of view, feel his sense of insecurity in a competitive economic system, ask ourselves how we would like to attempt to bring up a family in decency and to educate them on the basic wage. We must remind ourselves that the factory was made for man, and not man for the factory. We must get rid of our prejudices. Some of John Smith's actions, especially futile and unnecessary strikes, are incomprehensible, and he wastes his leisure and money in ways that some of us deplore; but we must make allowances and sympathize rather than condemn. He feels that he is only a cog in the economic machine and that his personality has little chance .of expression through his work. We must remember that we too have our faults, that we often lack concern for others and that we have our own kind of petty selfishness. -Prejudice is so easy and leads us to— 'Compound with sins we are inclined to By damning those we have no mind to.' We must hold before his eyes the Carpenter of Nazareth — that robust wholesome working Man whose muscles were hardened by toil and whose face was beaded with sweat. He still draws men to Himself. The truth is that, industry is between two worlds. 'Capitalism' as an economic system is .dying: it has failed to meet the demands of the modern age, and has created a Frankenstein monster that it cannot control. The new social and industrial world is still in the throes of birth, and none may yet say what manner of child will be born. It might be a good thing to set apart two or three of our most talented young men, give them an opportunity to study detachedly economic problems and relate them to the thought and policy of the Church. But above all we must preach a gospel that is really good news to the toiling man, and make him feel that the Church is sincerely his -friend. (b) Even more serious is the withdrawal from the Church of the intellectuals and the leaders of thought. We have some in our ranks, but so few that they are conspicuous. It is a sad fact that so many of our young men and women, who in their youth were loyal members of the Church , and who have passed through- the University, sometimes with outstanding distinction, have quietly but firmly turned away from the Church. There are some of these, .of course, lured by. money-making and by selfish interests, who have found the Church and its ethical code in their way;- but many of them — most of them, I believe — are really splendid types who have found another loyalty and, as they think, a larger. Some of them are filled with an earnest desire to help humanity, and put many of us professed Christians to shame by their effort and self-sacrifice. They say regretfully, but quite frankly, that for them and their aims the Church is irrelevant, and that she is imprisoned in her own narrow interests. Many give the reason that they cannot, after a scientific and philosophic training, accept the creeds of the Church. We are inclined, in our bitter moments, to accuse them of rationalization in order to avoid the discipline of ^ the Christian life; but let us be careful that this is not a rationalization of their supposed rationalization. I cannot hope, in this brief address, to attempt to deal with so complex a problem, but I would point out that the old world of authoritarianism, whether of an Infallible Church or an Infallible Book, is dead or dying, and men and women demand rational and scientific grounds for belief. How many of us can repeat, without qualification or self- reservation, - all the creeds of the Church. And why should we? Dean Inge quotes J. A. Froude as saying, 'If medicine had been regulated four hundred years ago by Act of Parliament, if there had been Thirty-nine Articles of Medicine, and every licensed practitioner had been compelled, under pains and penalties, to compound drugs by the prescriptions of Henry the Eighth's physicians, it is easy to conjecture in what state of health the people of this country would at present be found.' I know I shall not please the orthodox when I say that, if we are to retain the thinker in our ranks, it will not be by more emphasis upon doctrine, but by the granting of a wider freedom of thought and by a greater simplicity of faith. Men of spiritual and intellectual adventure do not want safe harbours where their anchored vessels may swing lazily with the tides: they want the wide ocean with its storms and hazards: they do not want cages, but wings to soar aloft into the unknown. The only authority in religion is the authority of the spirit. The spirit bloweth where it listeth, and none may tell whence it cometh and whither it goeth. The truth is, whether we like it or not, that, as Emerson said, 'Every man has a private road to God'; and in these days he intends to take it. We have only to talk quietly and con fidentially with many of our thoughtful laymen to realize how few accept the traditions of orthodoxy. There is a new world of -religious thought being born. That thought will not be contrary to ascertained knowledge and reason, though it may transcend them, as does art and poetry and music. I remember a very thoughtful friend, who had been long in the wilderness of doubt and intellectual difficulty, saying: 'If I were a preacher 1 would not bother about creed and dogma; I would simply bring men face to face with the noble character and sacrificial quality in Jesus, and leave them there.' If we can lead men to see Jesus in all His robust manliness, and spiritual charm and power; we need not worry concerning their theological reaction to Him. He is His own interpreter, and somehow the most sceptical disciples cannot withhold the exclamation, 'My Lord and my God!'. May I commend the 'words of one of the world's profoundest thinkers and greatest Christians — Albert Schweitzer: 'Christ comes to us as the Unknown, without a name, just as of old by the lakeside He came to those men who knew Him not. He speaks to us in the same words, 'Follow thou Me', and sets us to those tasks which He has to fulfil for our time. He commands. And to those who obey Him, whether they be wise or simple, He will reveal Himself in the toils, the conflicts, the sufferings which they shall pass through in His fellowship. And as an ineffable mystery they shall learn in their own experience who He is.' THE CRUSADE FOR CHRIST And this brings me naturally and inevitably to our projected movement which the Committee on . Evangelism has called 'The Crusade for Christ.' There- can be no doubt of the urgent need for a higher quality of human life if the race is to escape disaster. We have, as a Christian Church, the real solution of the world's problems, whether they be international, economic or moral. Narrowed down, and shorn of its dialectics, it is really Christ or Chaos, either Christ's world or None. There can be no agreement among the nations except on a basis of goodwill, tolerance and largescale unselfishness, and this applies to all other human relationships. Evil can never be overcome by force; the ancient word, more applicable than ever, is that evil can be overcome only by good. This world situation comes as a challenge to the Christian Church — it comes as a challenge to each individual, for there is no Church apart from the individuals who compose it. It means, for us all, what the New Testament calls Repentance — a change of mind, as the Greek has it — and ' there will have to be a radical change of attitude and a revolutionary birth from above if the Church is to influence the course of' human affairs. It means faith in Christ and in His Way of Life, not faith in power politics, in the potency of money, or in the development of science tnd philosophy. And such changes must commence with ourselves. We are always willing, and sometimes enthusiastically so, to urge the need for the other man to change; but our primary and immediate concern is the change in ourselves. Before we can hope to bring men into vital fellowship with God and goodness, there must be a deepening of that fellowship within ourselves. We may well hesitate on the threshold of such a moral and spiritual revolution and ask, who is sufficient for these things? The truth we must emphasize is that our sufficiency is of God. I fear that we are inclined to look upon this Crusade for Better Life as something special and to think of it as a temporary expedient. It is not that: it is a recall to the original and permanent task of the Church and of the individual Christian. It is not extraordinary: it is our plain normal duty. Brethren, nothing that may come before this Conference can be so important as this: let us therefore give ourselves to earnest prayer and to rigorous self-examination, vowing that all which hinders Christ's truth and power manifesting themselves through us may be cleansed away, so that we may be effective witnesses furnishing incontravertible evidence of His power to change and transform human life.

01 Oct 1949 - A COMMONWEALTH CRUSADE Methodist (Sydney, NSW : 1892 - 1954), Saturday 1 October 1949, page 4 A COMMONWEALTH CRUSADE V. — The Campaign in Worship By H.CB. .. A Gallup Poll conducted some time ago in Victoria revealed a somewhat disconcerting fact. A large proportion of the people interviewed professed a belief in the existence of God, but only a very small minority stated that they regularly engaged in public worship. The attendants at the Sunday services in all the Churches were relatively few in number. Few people expressed any desire to join in the regular worship of the House of God. A situation of this kind must have great bearing upon the Crusade for Christ. Any considerable lack of the worshipping spirit in the life of the people is a definite indication that the spiritual life of the nation is at an extremely low level. This, indicates that the campaign is an opportune one. There is a very great need for a spiritual revival. It is also indicative of the fact that, if the Crusade is to be a success there must be a renewal of the act of public worship on a grand scale. But the Church has to recover much if it is to be successful in taking up 'the slack'. There is little doubt as to the position existing in the Church at the present time. Divine worship has become a lost art so far as most people are concerned. This is true not only of the world, but also of the Church herself. Various reasons have been advanced in an attempt to account for this state of affairs. It has ' been said that 'man does not worship God because he does not know Him'. This must be true in a great many cases. Another reason given is that 'man' does not worship God because he does not really understand the , meaning of worship'. What, then, do we mean when we speak of an act of worship? Who can offer a satisfying explanation? The first thing to be realised in attempting an explanation is that 'true worshp involves a recognition of the presence of God'. It is difficult, if not impossible, to worship an absentee God. The famous old world story of Elijah and the priests of Baal at Mount Carmel in the days of Ahab' the King is worthy of note in this respect. The priests of Baal were goaded by Elijah until they became quite desperate in their efforts to attract the attention of their god. Elijah suggested he might be asleep, or on a journey, or engaged in some other way. Spurred on by these suggestions they exhibited a spirit of utter abandon, of sheer fanaticism. They became quite worked up over the whole affair. But such a display could by no means be considered as an act of worship. It was the exact opposite. Worship has been defined as 'an act of reverence toward God who is ever present and always responsive to main's devotion.' There' are many services within the Church wherein man is said to worship God. In many cases there is, however, a lack of reality in such worship, because there is no real consciousness of the Divine presence. There is not even the spirit of expectation or anticipation. Somehow man has ceased to look for the Divine presence. How rare is the spirit of expectancy! Memory carries back to a time, over a quarter of a century ago, when jubilee services were being held in the Church at Hay. The Rev. W. Weston, the first Methodist minister to be resident in that town, was the preacher at the jubilee service. The service began when the preacher called the congregation to worship and announced these significant lines from one of the hymns: — 'Lo, God is here! Let us adore, And /own how dreadful is this place.' At once that little Bethel became the audience 1 chamber of a King. God was there. Everyone seemed conscious of His presence. The place became instinct with worship. Such experiences i are relatively rare in the life of the Church today. Yet there can be no true worship without ; them. s In the second place, worship is possible only | where there is a truly reverent spirit. The aver| age Free Church service does not lend itself to If the cultivation of a spirit of reverence. The very | atmosphere is so frequently against it. The | carrying on of audible conversation as the con| gregation assembles within the Church has be1 come too common a feature. There is a lack of | appreciation of the fitness of things. The younger I geheration is not all to blame in this respect, i Frequently they simply follow the example set | by so many of the older members of the | congregation. | Then it is apparent that , worship has lost much of its real significance owing to a misunderstandh ^ ? i ing of some of the terms used in connection with it. Once more — attention must be drawn to the fact that words lose their original meaning, and this has brought about a conception of ' the function or purpose of worship which is altogether wrong. An apt illustration of this may be found in connection with the use of the word 'dreadful' quoted above. When the word was used in the hymn mentioned it had a different meaning from the one attributed, to it now. Present usage suggests a sense of disaster coupled with the ideas of fear and terror. It is held to indicate something frightening.In In an endeavour to escape from this meaning the original significance of the word has become lost. The synonymous words should be rather 'awe-full', 'full of wonder', 'significant with amazement'. Worship becomes natural to a soul possessed with a sense of reverent wonder and surprise. There are those who place the blame for any lack of reverence or wonder upon the undoubted enlightenment attending the achievements of modern science. Science is blamed for having banished all sense of the miraculous. As a result there is very little left to wonder about now. A judgment of this kind is purely superficial. Reverence, wonder, awe, all these belong to the spiritual side of man's nature. Far from destroying man's spiritual capacity, the. advance in scientific knowledge has served rather to increase it. The world was a very simple affair in days gone by. But each new addition to man's understanding has increased his capacity for spiritual discernment. Science can rob man of reverence only as he has allowed . its teaching to affect his capacity for spiritual understanding. A recovery of spiritual appreciation will, serve to restore to men, almost automatically, the spirit of reverence and enlarge their capacity for worship. Another section of the community places the responsibility for a loss in the spirit of reverence upon certain philosophical ideas which have reduced man's sense of the greatness of God. Early views of God invested Him with a transcending glory. These have been associated with the ideas of holiness, righteousness and omnipotence. God was recognised in terms of the Holy, the Just and the Good. These were elevating thoughts and led to feelings of reverence and wonder and a sense of awe. The New Testament revelation of God in Christ was seen to lay special emphasis upon love. This served but to contradict his previous belief in the sterner qualities of the Divine. The idea of eternal punishment became involved. This was felt to be a contradiction of the attribute of love. In this way man came to think of God as One who was angry about sin, but weakly complaisant in regard to the sinner. God was reduced to, a somewhat inadequate paternal figure, full of the spirit of forgiveness even at the expense of justice and goodness. The other side of this picture holds a representation of man which exalts him and makes ' him but little lower than a god. This has 'served, to reduce the distance between man and God, to the detriment; of man's capacity for worship. Filled with a sense of his own importance, man has lost the capacity for reverence. Man is as good as his god, therefore he will cease . to worship him.The The remedy for all this does not mean a depreciation of man's worth. He should rebel still against all mock modesty and false 'humility. There is something intrinsically wrong about the spirit of self-depreciation. Man was made in the Divine image. He should not lose sight of his innate spiritual worth. His remembrance of his high calling in Christ Jesus should create a spirit of healthy self-respect, and enlarge his appreciation of Him in whom he lives and moves and has his being. The Crusade for Christ will prosper when man realises the infinite spiritual capacity with which God has endowned him. The revived Church must be a worshipping community. Man will then gain a new sense of his indebtedness to God, and to Him will be given all the glory and praise, dominion and power, world without end.

25 Oct 1952 - CORRESPONDENCE Methodist (Sydney, NSW : 1892 - 1954), Saturday 25 October 1952, page 10 CORRESPONDENCE Attendance at Public Worship Sir,— I have only just read your article on the Gallup Poll on church attendance, re-printed in a magazine from England. If we are to learn anything from this we must realize that the fault is in ourselves, not in those who stay away from Church. It is not merely chance that such a high proportion of Catholics attend Church regularly. They learn the importance of worship and meditation early in life, and their priests usually make every possible effort to assist in the provision of facilities for worship. Spiritual care is all too often lacking in our Church. During the war many Methodists were visited by their chaplains only on rare occasions, and we felt ourselves fortunate if could 'hitch hike' twenty or thirty miles to a Methodist service, sacrificing meals and sleep to do so. Even when we did find ourselves near a Methodist Church we were disappointed to find it only opened for a couple or so hours on Sundays, while the Catholic could always slip into Church for private prayer at some other time if he happened to be on duty during the regular services. Priests insisted on services for their men wherever they might be stationed, and no difficulty was too great to be overcome. God's service was put first. Our Church seems to be interested in ,the individual* only when he happens to live near at hand. The few Methodists in this country have decided not to wait for the Church, and are trying to form a society themselves, without any official assistance. I know it seems to be asking too much to have travelling ministers to look after such areas, but Catholic priests walked inland a thousand miles, before there were any means of communication, so that their Church might be established here. They suffered and died, but a Gallup Poll here would show that the results were worth the effort. The Methodist Church has been willing to leave much of Central Africa to others, and I do not suggest that they are not doing, fine work, but we must not be surprised if our members become slack. While there is plenty to criticize in the Catholic Church, we would do well to remember it has much to teach us. — Yours, etc., M; E. G. GOODMAN. Tabora, Tanganyika.

07 Oct 1950 - NOTES AND COMMENTS Methodist (Sydney, NSW : 1892 - 1954), Saturday 7 October 1950, page 3 NOTES AN ID COMMENTS DISCONCERTING FIGURES | A Gallup Poll taken recently and pub| lished on Sunday, 17th September, dealt | with Church attendance in Australia, and | brought to light certain facts which no one | can regard with complacency who has the | interests of the Kingdom of God at heart. | The figures given after the canvass was ! made show that of the Roman Catholic j population 62% go to Church every week. | Baptists come next with 53%. Methodists 1 1 ? 1 il 1 1 « . ? 1 1 -i n rrf mi p -l come tnira on xne list witn ±y 70. men roilow Presbyterians with 11%. Anglicans bring up the rear with only 6%. The proportion of nominal Roman Catholics who ; seldom or never attend church is 24%, of ; Baptists 32%, .of Methodists 54%, of Presbyterians 62%, and of Anglicans 66%. The accuracy of these figures may of course be challenged. No hint is given in the article from which we quote as to the locality or localities in which the Poll was taken, nor is there anything to show j whether the per centages given are an up; to-the-minute calculation. What is clear, \ however, and what has to be sorrowfully ? admitted, is that amongst Protestants as . a I whole Church attendance is very far from i being satisfactory. Our own Methodist j Church has a high per centage of delinI quents. Fifty-four out of every hundred | nominal Methodists hardly ever enter a j church door, or never attend public worj ship at all, according to the figures supplied | to us. Allowing for aged and infirm people, j and for. others whose circumstances prac| tically cut them off from all church activity, j it is not at all a happy state of affairs. I It may be said, and with some show of I reason, that church attendance is not ail infallible index to Christian character, and | is not even a safe criterion by which anyj one's moral worth may be estimated. The | point may be conceded. No one is saved ? merely by going to Church, and no one is | lost merely because he is not occupying a j! pew whenever he might occupy it. God of j old reproached His people because so much | of their worship was simply so much | temple-treading and a perfunctory perform| ance of rites and ceremonies. 'To what | purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices | unto Me?' He said. 'I am full of the burnt| offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; I and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, ! or of lambs, or of he-goats. When ye come ; to appear before Me, who hath required I this at your hand, to tread My courts? I Bring no more vain oblations; incense is an I abomination unto Me; the new moons and Sabbaths, the calling of assemblies, I cannot away with; it is iniquity, even the solemn meeting.' Public worship, or what sometimes passes for it, may be nothing more than a hollow mockery and a wickedwaste of time. But it may be something very different too, — something very beautiful and noble and stimulating. And whenever and wherever it is what it was meant to be — acceptable to God and a joy and inspiration to those who offer it— it meets a need which nothing else can ever meet. It is, in fact, indispensable to our highest life. Hence those who deliberately or negligently absent themselves from it in variably suffer a spiritual declension. They may not realize how great is their loss, but it is nevertheless very serious and disquieting. It has, as a rule, wide and varieci repercussions, all of them more or less detrimental to the life and work of the Church. Corporate worship may not be everything that is required of a true Christian; it may not even be the main thing. It is nevertheless important, and all whose hearts are in the right place have always valued it and must continue to value it. Those Methodists who habitually absent themselves from it are not assets but liabilities, and the fact that to all intents and purposes they have unchurched themselves is a clear indication that, whatever they may have been, they need converting or reconverting now. Every effort that can be made to reclaim them should be made with a wise and unremitting persistency. 'Let us,' wrote one long ago, — 'let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works; not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is.'

06 Apr 1946 - BEER PRODUCTION Methodist (Sydney, NSW : 1892 - 1954), Saturday 6 April 1946, page 3 BEER PRODUCTION An Australian Gallup Poll claims that 70 per cent, of people favour unrestricted beer output when barley and hops are plentifully available. The result is not very surprising, restriction of truth and inability or unwillingness to think being what they are, but it is interesting to note that no new arguments against restrictions were brought to light. 'Restrictions lead to black marketing,' was a very common comment. This is only another way of saying that greedy moneyhungry people will take advantage of any situation, including the foolishness of beer-drinkers, to exploit their nefarious trade. 'Restrictions create more drunkards,' was another remark made by many voters. This is another piece of false reasoning — or rather failure to reason at all. It is true that much drunkenness has been seen following on the 'rush' drinking tha£ occurs during 'sessions.' This, however, is not due to restrictions of beer production, but to sheer greed — the practice of lining up a number of pots of beer and swilling them off in the shortest possible time. If a number of housewives lined up at the beginning of each rationing period, bought their entire quota of butter and then proceeded to eat it in the shortest possible time they would mostly get sick, and their husbands would have something to say about shortage of supplies later on. But something of this very sort happens, and has happened for a long time in connection with beer, yet it is regarded as normal, and the only method suggested to remedy it is the production of more and still more beer. With so many simple everyday necessities unobtainable, there are very few people who believe that a steep increase in beer production should take place. Consumption of butter, sugar, tea and meat was cut down considerably by restrictions imposed by the Government. But there must be no restriction on beer production, lest it result in more drunkenness! What a commentary on present day Government administration and public discipline. — The Australian .Temperance Advocate.

21 Oct 1944 - FIVE STATES CAN ELECT ROOSEVELT Newcastle Sun (NSW : 1918 - 1954), Saturday 21 October 1944, page 2 FIVE STATES CAN ELECT ROOSEVELT Our Special Represenlative NEW YORK, Friday. — A victory ior President Roosevelt in the five east coast industrial States will ensure him re-election, a Gallup poll forecasts. 05 Jul 1946 - Notes from the City Scone Advocate (NSW : 1887 - 1954), Friday 5 July 1946, page 4 [?] [?] According to a Gallup Poll taken from a wide crosssection of Australian opinion, most Australians are opposed to extending soldier preference beyond the present limit of seven years. The result of the poll is a surprise; in fact I should imagine, the greatest surprise that any uaiiup poll — usually a very accurate indication of public opinion — has ever given us. Out of every 100 people interviewed, 70 favored the seven years' limit, 22 wanted it made longer, and 8 were undecided. The general view was that returned men should be reestablished in civilian life by 1952, and that it would be unfair to penalise, after that year, youths who were too young to enlist while the war was on. Mr. Milton Reynolds, head of the Yankee firm, who came to Australia to establish a factory to supply the British Empire with his company's famous never-wear-j out £3 18s pens, has suddenly lost all his enthusiasm . for establishing here an industry that would bring millions of pounds to j this country. 'I'm not here to be squeezed,' Reynolds declared. 'Ii have come here to make money. But to have to fork out 87 per cent, of profit in paying taxes is not my idea of making money. Unless I'm offered a better deal than that I'm scrapping all my Australian plans.,' However, an election is in the offing, so Mr. Reynolds may be well advised to wait till the window firessing starts. Already big income tax reductions are promised, more homes for workers, more amenities for everybody, in fact. However, Mr. Reynolds already had heard of our promising politicians. When Rail Chief Hartigan announced the new rail cuts owing to the dangerously low coal stocks in the yards, the only contribution the General Secretary of the Miners' Federation (Mr. G. W. S. Grant) could make was that 'the decision was beyond his understanding; it must be a political stunt.' He is quite right — it was the Communistic political stunt to restrict production that has led to this and a host of other troubles, economic and industrial. And at a time, too, when, with full employment offering to all, Australia could be scooping the markets of the world., China's buying representative herey with hundreds of thousands of pounds and vast orders in' her pocket (yes, it was a lady) had to leave after being iable to spend only a few paltry thousands. Indian buyers, with millions to splash round, went off with nothing, or next to nothing. Dutch NEI buyers, with hundreds of thousands of guilders to burn, only spent a few thousands, and what they purchased is now for re-sale owing to the Comirios holding up their shipping. Yes, sir, we shall deserve every last bit of the economic blitz that seems destined to be our portion of the years not very far ahead. Dr. Evatt's legacy (he lifted the ban on these vermin) is coming home to us with a vengeance. Meanwhile our housing problems, despite all the talk and optimism seems inseparable and hundreds of newly-weds, and others not so newly-wed, are being driven to distraction in their eternal search for rooms or flats — cottages are out of the question, for once occupied their tenants never move — unless death intervenes. Still, so far no case has yet been unearthed here to equal that reported by Melbourne police when they discovered a couple had been sleeping in a public lavatory in Andrew Reserve, on the banks of the Yarra, because they were unable to secure quarters anywhere else. They would enter at night and leave early in the morning, with their belongings in cardboard boxes! Burns, Philip and Co. must have had a nice tidy amount in ready money laid by, for this year the firm has been buying out successful, old-established trading firms in large country centres, both here and in Queensland. Its latest deal has been to buy from the O'Hara Estate in Cairns the Criterion and Hides Hotels for the sum of £100,000. These hotels, which had been in the hands of the O'Hara family for 50 and 30 years, respectively, are, it is said, to be remodelled into first-class tourist hotels, it being the firm's intention to revive that trade along the Queensland coast. As a sample of the utter rubbish and pointless tripe which the 'Sun' permits its silly flappers to inflict on a long-suffering tribe of readers, have a peek at this — that it, if it's worth wasting space upon: ? 'Lady Gilford's small son Anthony questioned his mother about her home here, when he knew he was going to visit it. Sh$ described the house and told him about the household j staff. The sooner newsprint is rationed again in Sydney the better. It would save us not only from this and other stupidities, but also from the flood of alleged comic strips suitable only, in the case of 90 per cent, of them, for subnormals who never progress beyond the mental age of six or seven. Mention of the City Press reminds me that Associated Press (which runs the 'Sun'. and a fair parcel of weekly and monthly publications) now has, so I'm told, a staff of no fewer than 40 artists on its pay-roll., But that's only a circumstance to the 100 (yes, 100!) journalists now in the 'S.M. Herald's' employ — a record high for any publication in the Southern Hemisphere, so it is claimed. The 'SMH's' amour propre, it , appears, has been sorely wounded by the fact that the 'DT's' circulation has soared right ahead of that of the Old Lady's, and the Fairfax clan is flat out to recover the lost ground. Hence the special country edition of two pages (which doesn't make the grade for the city) and the Tuesday magazine section, and also the comic cuts special for the kiddies. The war is right on, with the 'Mirror' frantically yapping at the heels of all three rivals. But the 'SMH's' amazing array of advertisers are not a ' bit interested in which city paper has the biggest circulation. All they are concerned about is seeing that their advertisements reach the proper people, i.e., the people with the money to buy the goods they ad. vertise. And there is no question about which paper does that. Possibly high taxation might have something to do with the senior journal's extraordinary activity, the directorate, may be, arguing that it is better to spend profits solidifying the paper's position and prestige rather than let the tax authorities grab so much of the cash; also, that other developments planned for the not very distant future may get off to a, flying start, so to speak. Queensland visitors speak of a drought that has lasted in the South-west of that State for three years, where a vast dust bowl is developing, where sheep losses run into thousands — one place has j lost every hoof of its 7000 odd, and another has already written off more than 14,000 out of 25,000, and where ruination stares hundreds of formerly well-to-do graziers in the face. The grip of drought's grim spectre has been extended into , some of the good dairy country. At Gayndah, for instance, the problem is not so much production — that has gone by the board long ago — but how to keep the stock alive, seeing so marfy farmers now have reached the end of their financial tether. Around Roma the butter production has fallen well below district needs, while Brisbane is actually sending milk all the way up to Rockhampton. On the Brunswick, some six® months ago, this column met-men from South Queensland looking for agistment country. They told a sorry story of the state of things., So what must the position have developed like since then ? The State Government, I believe, has allocated £10,000 for relief. 'Comrades, remember what - we have already achieved on the coal-fields. By a series of well-timed . strikes under Communistic leadership, we eliminated Australian export trade in coal and thus brought unemployment to the coal-fields. Miss Esther Soong, of Hongkong, the Chinese girl who was able to spend only £10,000 in Australia out of £50,000 she brought here, takes a very dim view of our control and bureaucrats, so much so that she feels other overseas buyers are likely to find their mission here a ' waste of time and energy. Britain, she reminds us, has a motto, 'Ex-port or perish.' What between Commo thuggery on the waterfront and in factories, and the painfully obvious complaisance and appeasement of a dithery government, Australia seems as if she is not to be allowed to have a choice at all., Here, Miss Soong found, she could buy neither freight space, nor raw wool, nor rolled oats, nor textile machinery. She sought 200 tons of rolled oats, and got five tons: offered to buy the entire Stock of woollen cloth at the Army disposals depot, but was told it was for Australian merchants. In Melbourne she tried to buy 150 tons of powdered milk, only to be told that Allied Food Control had earmarked j.t for UNRRA. And so on. Hence the lady goes away quite- unimpressed with the Australian method of cultivating friends and to give it all the business she could, for as a visitor here in 1941 she Was stranded when the Brown Monkeys came into the fray, served two years on the AIF's intelligence staff, and finally became Secretary to Chiang Kai-Shek's representative at General MacArthur's headquarters. Ran across Padre Claughton a couple of days ago, just out of the Army after about six years' service. 'You mightn't know it,' he said, 'but~ I used to take strong exception to your references to the Japanese as Brown Monkeys. But after what I have seen, I have to admit the reference was not strong enough. They are the most despicable b'easts, or the great bulk of them, that anyone canever imagine. Still, they are amongst the worfS's best soldiers. They'll fight to the very end no matter how hopeless their mistion. Of course they lack initiative and do some stupid things that seem inexplicable. But, when ordered, they will die to the last man fighting against the Heaviest odds.' A couple of recent pars in this column concerning the louts of Narrandera and the envious yahoos of Yass have promoted a correspondent to say that a few Bees (at least I fancy that is the word, for, er, my eyesight Is not as good as it used to be) down Gloucester way also deserved dishonorable mention. It seems that Mr. Tom Hicks, a worthy Digger from the last war, who collected a very bad 'issue' in Kaiser Bill's dust-up, but was eventually able to pull round, and built up a prosperous business in the old burgh — was the subject of some slimy attention by several pretty low specimens of humanity in his own home town. Tom, . it appears, had been a leader amongst the old Diggers, President of Gloucester Subbranch for years, and also one of the town's outstanding warworkers all through the wearying six years of the latest World Disturbance, ? during which he frequently declared that when the peace came he would stage a party of his own on the first Anzac Day after hostilities ceased. And Tom was as good as his word, for he put on a slashing dinner, to which he invited the whole of the servicemen and servicewomen in town and' district— a super show consisting of everything of the best that money could buy, and all the beer that the boys could comfortably carry,, a competent staff, being engaged to see that no one went short of anything., Such a blow-out Gloucester had never known for many a long year in fact, the guests are still' talking of Tom's generosity. But . here comes the ariticlimSeveral - despicable informers people evidently envious of the quests and their host, wrote to Meat Control and reported that sucking pigs were on the menu! Meat Control promptly went to the trouble and expense of sending a special investigator along to try and get evidence for a prosecution. The net result was exactly nil. Guests were interviewed left and right. 'Yes,' they said, 'we had a great time. It was a great shivoo. We had plenty of everything, and some very good white meat, but no pork!' Naturally the lads were highly incensed at the action of the informers, arid felt like picking up their rifles again. And Tom, who seems a chap after this column's own heart, would probably have been found striding forth in the lead had it come to a show-down. Here let it be said that the average Australian is a fine, decent chap, and makes, as a rule, the best cobber in the world. But there is often, and in the best of places, that small factional residue which is a disgrace to the land of their birth and their forebears. Happily, most of the rural areas are singularly free of this detestable type. Biologically, it seems, something went wrong long before their birth, and for that trick of Nature those amongst whom they live have to pay the penalty. No one likes an informer, least of all the boys who did their best for Gloucester, and for the rest of us in the recent world conflagration. 'All the world loves a lover,' It is said. And, it also seems, all TioooDurra ana tor 400 miles round loves a wedding. Tibooburra, the capital of the Far Far Nor'-Western Never Never, and the last outpost of civilisation so far as villages are concerned, had a wedding recently, the news of which has trickled in. So much interest was taken in the affair that the village's population of 85 suddenly shot up to 400, some of the guests (invited antl Uninvited) travelling 400 miles to attend! Constable Scholes officiated as parson, and the happy couple were a Queensland boundary rider and a girl on a local station. Ample stocks of beer had been laid in by the two local pubs, every room in each was booked out weeks before (as well as verandah space), local folk accommodated as many guests as they could manage, and after the wedding the town and visitors staged a three-days celebration the like of which had never been known in Tibooburra history. At latest advices, heads were getting ! back to normal size, and -the de1 mand for Aspro tablets was slowly diminishing. But it was a great wedding— and a great celebration. By the time the guests ! had departed, the bridegroom [had calmly started work on repairs to the State border fence. Also a few robust blathery arguments with Eleanor, who must be bristling already. ; By the way, no valiant (or even pot-valiant) pressmen has yet plucked up courage to approach that verbose lady for her views on the new rival — though they'd be worth hearing. — H.A.McC.

21 May 1948 - Notes from the City Scone Advocate (NSW : 1887 - 1954), Friday 21 May 1948, page 4 [?] ^Vv.;..;,^'1^^ \ Gallup poll on 'my favorite -£*? sport! to watch'' had a curious result — football 32 per cent., tennis 14, cricket 12, racing 6, swimming 2, bowls 1, other sports 8, don't watch any sport 25! * ' * How the money— precious dollar money * at ' that- — is wasted: Four years ago the luxurious Australian Chancellory building in Washington was offered to the Government very cheaply. The offer was turned down. A few months ago Canberra decided to buy, but the price had soared to £75,000. However, the deal went through — but the cost and the the price asked back in 1944. The big mob of ornamental figure-heads, clerks, off-siders and what not had no sooner got comfortably settled in, when 20 of the diplomatic staff found themselves 'skidding' as a result of the economy drive. Now all that are left could fit with ease into Ambassador Makin's decorative Embassy, which he uses as a residence. . Seeing that 15,000 dollars were recently spent on refurbishing the new purchase, making a total of £90,000 dollars for the building, farmers who need machinery, spare parts, trucks and tractors will be able to assess just how much urgentlyneeded farm mechanism those wasted dollars would have purchased. ?S X Commo.-trained and 'educated' George Paul Bechtold (21), Eureka Youth member, a railway upholsterer, convicted of the murder of his mother, 'under What the Judge described as 'horrible and brutal circumstances,', es- caped with 12 years' gaol. So far there have been no Domain demonstrations by the Comrades on his behalf. . -x- xQuite an exciting piece of news came the other day, to Bernice Marks, only child of thd late George Marks, journalist and author, and niece of Josephine Marks, glamor girl of the years agone and now singer and hostess at the Wentworth Hotel' When Sir Daniel Cooper's widow died in England recently, well over\ 90 years of age, heirs. to the £1,000,000 estate were advertised for. Only two were successful — Bernice to the extent of some £187,000, and a man who , may get round about £200,000. Only 21, the handsome young heiress is being trained as a singer. :? * *.''.-?? Minister for Housing dive Evatt announces an £8-million housing project, involving the building of 5000 homes in five years, to meet the industrial expansion which will be created when the world's record, size steel rolling mills, now being blueprinted by B.H.P. and its auxiliary, A.I.T.S., swing into production. .* * .'.*???? '??'?? According to young Doug. Bland, of Greenethorpe, who attended the recent Christian Youth Conference as Oslo, the one frightening factor was the huge majority of fanatical Communists who attended. And he made the startling revelation that most of the Australian delegation were -Communists! It is certainly amazing the way those fellows worm their way into the army, navy, political, security, defence and other pobs, but into a 'Christian' Youth Conference just about, bangs Banagher. They couM never do all this but for friends in high places. * ? # And, in this connection, Frankie Browns, in his 'Things I . Hear' news sheet, , tells a nifty story concerning the i glamorous Giselle Schneider, of the Jewish Welfare Society, who came to Canberra just before tho war, got herself installed at the swish Canberra Hotel (when even some M's.P. couldn't get their noses inside, and who rocked politicians and others 'with her wicked walk, her tantalising rich red lips, and eyes that were just murder.' The Richmond's Larry Anthony, who had been hearingthings, by some shrewd questioning, elicited the fact that this strange dame had been given an TJ.N.O. job at £2500 a year, though, according to Mr. Browne, of insatiable curiosity, the P. Podveilsky she wed at Canberra was stuck in a concentration camp after the war broke out as a dangerous alien. Now Frankie wants! to know' if the 8000 dollars it keeps to employ this dame could not be spent to better purpose elsewhere, who nominated her for that job, what are her duties and what is Podveilsky doing for a living in Paris. Rumor says that when Frankie's blurb hit Canberra there was a terrible scurry for cover. However, someone there . should press for answers to ? these questions. . * * Chairman Scobie. of the Licensing Bench, gave a significant warning the other day— that, in future, the Bench was going to insist on all hotels having hot and cold water provided in bedrooms But they will get a fair time to install the much-needed amenity. Rabbits? Some of the soldier settlers on Wantabadgery. scared at the living grey carpet they saw each dusk on their holdings induced a rabbit poisoner to 'come along. Off three properties he skinned six thousand, five thousand and four thousand carcases respectively. ' '* * There was nearly a tragedy in a suburban R..S.L. clubroom * the other day. A new member strolled in, gazed with interest at the big framed picture of 'The Charge of the Scots Greys at Balaclava ' Old Jock McPhairsbn, a veteran of the Boer War, ambled up. 'A fine picture, yon,' he said, 'xes, replied the Aussie, with sly, disreputable humor, 'but what's got me is— who the 'ell's chasing them?' -X- * , The Trades and Labor Council Commo element at Lithgow still has its black ban on the widow hotel-keeper because-r-she sent a keg of beer to a Sydney relative for a family wedding, she refused to let the ratbags inspect her cellar daily, or to sack her head barman. Now then, brethren, be upstanding and drink a toast— 'The Land of the Free!' * * Mr. Jeremy, well known to many Hunter and Manning Rivers folk when he was with the Department of Agriculture as a plant breeder, agrostol'ogist and agronomist — he retired last year to enter business on his own account — has come to the rescue of the paspalum-ridden streets and footpaths and the grass-plagued folk of Baulkham Hills with a new spray evolved. by himself. At a recent demonstration, so the Shire Engineer says, the spray not only killed the paspalum to its roots, but was so severe on the stalks and seed that insufficient of them was left to be fired! When he was with the Department, Mr. Jeremy did a fair amount of experimenting with hormones (a number of which have the dual qualifications of plant stimulators and weed destroyers), and carried out' many tests in weed destruction. He seems now to have hit on' something. * * U.S.A. ship's engineer and 'metal worker, Jim Drummond,, here on a six-months' holiday visit with his Aussie wife, to the latter's relatives, gets a haircut every time he has a few minutes ' to spare, and not only does he pay the 1/9 charge gleefully, but adds a 2/ tip! 'You see.'' he says, 'they think I'm crazy to slink a tip, but still I'm away ahead of it, as a haircut back home coats me a dollar and a half, or 9/6 in your money.' Jim says that over his way an ordinary pick and shovel worker earns £17 and £18 a week, but when he pays 6/ a lb. for butter, and 7/ a dozen for eggs, and high prices for everything else, he has little or nothing left at the end of the week. Parramatta Hospital is arranging for its 100th anniversary celebrations. It should be a bigshow, for the institution is spreading, and adding another new wing soon. In four years its exes have risen from £24,000 to £70,000 a year, but its subsidy has been increased to onl'V £48,000 a year. -X- xIf you see a wild-eyed man reconnoitring the city's Federal Offices you can safely put him down ajs a chap from some country municipal or shire council looking for a share of the surplus funds in the war insurance pool. And the reply he gets, so they say, is always the same — that the matters have, not yet been finalised. And this, though the war has been over for three years. That, apparently, is not the sort of 'ef-ficiency' that Minister Pollard has in mind when he preaches to dairymen , about improving ' the efficiency and standard of their industry. Of course, what is actually happening, although most people have not yet dropped to the 'joke,' is that the very substantial surplus in this fund is being gradually eaten up in administrative costs, piled on by the choicest lot of bureaucrats ever foisted on the backs of unlucky taxpayers. Why someone hasn't probed this rotten business on the Iloor of the House of Reps, is something this column would be glad to have explained, ?x- * Everyone who has ever been to the Hawkesbury either knows, has seen or heard of its G.O.M., 'Da' O'Sullivan, of Richmond, aged 103, still going strong, and around whom clings a wealth of good stories. Well, when His Excellency, the State Governor, visited Richmond, the other day, 'Da' tottl'ed off down to have a word in his car. More than that, 'Da' walked around unaided, joined lustily in the singing, and had a great time. A marvellous old chap— and he still gets of lot of fun out of life. -X- xThis department doubts if there is a more human (and humane) man on the Bench than Stipendiary Magistrate ' Debenham. And this, from his pen, truly reveals the man, and is worthy of space in this or any other newspaper column: — Rear happiness comes with genuine love in the home, with mutual confidence, and trust, with sincere affection, and unselfishness. ' It also comes with the joy of simple things. The delight of the garden, the glory of flowers, the grateful smile of someone you have been able to serve, the liveliness of little children with innocent eyes opening wide in wonderment on the world as each' day unfolds. These can give enduring pleasure. Love and affection and unselfishness count more than money or wealth, and will conquer adversity. The finest sermon in five sentences this column ever remembers to have come across. * * The N.S.W. wheat yield has been officially declared at 95,000,000 bushel's, viz., 88,000,000 delivered to the pool and 10,000,000 kept on the farms. The coming season's yield, however, may not exceed 75,000,000 bushels, as the acreage is from 25 to 30 per cent, less than last year's. Reported that Les Haylen, M.P. (Lab., Parkes), led a wrathful contingent of rank and filers into Cal well's Ministerial den recently, to demand why Bait girls were being assigned to Maxie Falstein, Dan Mulcahy and Mrs. Alexander (a close friend of the Ward family, whose name cropped ixp in the Garden case) for two years, and to point out that this wasn't the sort of thing to win victories in doubtful, seats. Artful Arthur explained that everything was O.K. — that Menzies and Spender had ai'so got Bait girls assigned to their households, so there could be no kick coming from the Libs. This was quite true, and Calwell, a few days later, gave the news to the Press. The facts are thatCalwell canvassed all sides for their needs in domestic help, the condition being there must be three in the family. Several M's.P. bit on the bait, but Faddcn and other C.P. members were 'too fly' for Artful1 Arthur, and declined. Just as well. The business, smells too much like the old blackbirding days with that assignment to two years always staring the girl in her face. There is a rumor in this village that a city alderman, with political affiliations, may ? soon come under fire over certain property deals. It will be quite a good story— should it break. Strange stories are going about of the doings of a certain coterie of gangsters and trainers Who are alleged to 'stand over' jockeys and ownex-s. No names are being mentioned, but the redoubtable Frankie Brownie declares he can supply the full list to the A.J.C.— if it wants to know all about the racket. * * The fruit and vegetable agents in the wholesale section of the City Markets staged a new sort of strike on Saturday week — they attended in force, the markets were opened to time, the buyers surged in, full stocks were on view— but the disgruntled gentry who live off the producer refused to sell a bean, a pea or a banana. They sulked in their tents— be-cause they wanted a Saturday off like Government employees, butchers, bakers, and others. The growers' reps, went along to the City Council1, and protested loudly. But to no purpose. You see neither the Farm Produce Act nor the Markets regulations and by-laws have one word to say that the agents shall sell — only that the markets shall be opened. The agents do that, hence no one can 'singe their beards.' But I know quite a few who'd like to! — HAMcC.
