20 Dec 1949 - Notes from the City Scone Advocate (NSW : 1887 - 1954), Tuesday 20 December 1949, page 3 [?] [?] The elections are over, and not one person in any of the organisations engaged ever dreamed that such a landslide was possible. 'The Sun' says the Gallup poll proved 100 per cent, accurate. It did nothing of the sort — it was not 50 per cent accurate. It certainly predicted a Lib.-C.P! victory, but hiy the narrowest of margins.. The leading Liberals here 'hoped' for a small majority of three or four; others in the , same camp were 'afraid' Labor might just sneak in. Amongst the Labor boys, a few loudly proclaimed another resounding victory, others were sure of a narrow victory, and a very few thought it 'might be possible for the Opposition to ^vin in a photo.-finish.' * * * As far as this column could interpret the mass of figures submitted by the iGallup poll experts on Friday, the Lib..C.P. combination should have a three or four - majority. fnstead, at time of writing, there seems- a possibility of 19. The amazing feature, of course, is the colossal Labor rebuff by Queensland, and the fact that so many of the new seats in NSW — regarded as certainties for the Government — have returned Lib. erals by overwhelming majorities. Taken on the whole, the nation has ?given a smashing answer to na. tionaiisation, to the coddling of the Mongs, to the Calwellian riding of the high horse in the deportation race, to petrol rationing, to Min. isterial extravagance, to savage taxation, and to Ministers, their wives and (in some cases) their families, seeing' the world at the taxpayers' expense. * * * The reaction of Doc. Evatt to the astonishing reduction in his previous huge majorities, was, it is rumored, rather funny. He was lost for words — publicly — for about twelve hours, and then made the -absurd remark that Labor seemed to have held its own, so far as votes were con. cerned, in NSW. Eddie Ward was completely speechless. Chif. merely said he accepted the verdict and thanked his supporters and colleagues. And, of course, it fell to Premier McGirr to make the silliest (and most character, istic) comment of the week: 'I do hope the inherent good sense of ? the Australian people will be shown to have prevailed when the final figures go up, and that Labor will be returned .to office to carry on its programme of humane and enterprising legislation, the like ef which no young nation has ever . before seen.' And this, mind you, when the Government was down by 17 seats. Beat that — if you canl „ * * * iAIready speculation is rife as to what will be the first of the pro. mised legislative measures to be submitted to the new Parliament some time in February or March. General belief is that it will be a Bill to give 5/ a week endowment for the first child, and this with, out endangering the basic wage— a measure of justice that all the Labor candidates safd couldn't be done. Menzies is determined to show he can do it, if the Laborites couldn't. High on the priority list will be the Bill to ban the Mongs. Already one of the chief Mongs -says that banning his fel. low rats from public jobs can't be done, because the Labor uni. ons will not stand for it. We'll see all about that, and especially in the CSIR, defence, GPO, the Commonwealth Bank, and other departments. The electors have given the mandate for this, and what they say goes. A Bill to prohibit nationalisation of any industry without consent of the electors by referendum will also be on the programme, as well as repeal of the nationalisation of bank, ing legislation. Secret ballots for union elections is another certain, ty. It should be a long and live, ly session, with a Senate show, down as a decided probability later on In 1950. * * * An election sidelight: In the very tony Wentworth electorate (where ALP voters are as scarce as white blackbirds), a couple of Coriimo. mongs made a practice of leaving posters in the polling booths instructing voters to put a cross in the square opposite the name of each candidate, and not to use numbers. That dodge might have worked very efficiently at the 'Loo or Surry Hills ,or some such blot on the landscape, but it was a ratbag effort at Wentworth, although one poor, unsuspecting wo. man fell for the rascality. And did she squawk! * * * Met a sturdy block of a man, a young Polish migrant, and his vivacious wife, on Saturday, and two happier humans it would be impossible to find anywhere. The young fellow had been here only a few months, and his wife only eight months. She was the proud., est voter in Sydney, judging by her smiles and happy disposition. In these few months she had learned to speak English and be. come an Australian national. Her husband was a treat to listen to— he was able to mix his English, learned largely by reading (or conversation), with the aid of a Polish-English dictionary, mixed with a few typically Australian idioms. 'This my Australia, my home now,' he said, as his hands swept the horizon. 'No more fear, no more war (Pouff! Bang! Bang'), no more concentration camp, no more nothing to eat, no more bash-kick, no more paperreal money, see (and he dived his hand into his trousers pocket and pulled out and looked admiringly at the florins, shillings and pence, . as they made a jingling noise which gave him undisguised de light). Me eight pound 11 bob every week, only five days work, for uncle .(a tailor). Take mon. ey home, wife buy meat (and his eyes nearly popped out of his head) , fruit—ah, ze fruit. And all the people very good, very good . . .' .Some of the words had to be helped out or translated by the wife, but the earnest, smiling, new Australian seemed glad to have met. someone to whom he could unburden his manifest pleasure and delight. Every second sen., tence was punctuated with eyes uplifted and hands spread out a3 he repeated: 'Peace! Peace!'.' * * * Amongst the most absorbing books by modern authors this col. umn has read in Its time have been some of Lin Yeitang's, Chin, ese journalist and author. Here's a slice of his philosophy, and it'3 worth reading twice: — 'I want a room of my own, where I can work. A room that is neither particularly clean nor orderly ... I want children who are children, who win go with me to play in the rain, who enjoys a shower bath as much as I do ... I want some old friends, some friends who are as familiar as life itself, friends to whom I .need not be polite ... I want a good cook, who. knows how to cook vegetables and make delicious soups. I want an old, old 'servant, who thinks I am a great man,' but does not know where my greatness lies ... I want a good library, some cigars, and a woman who understands and leaves me free to do my work ... I want freedom to be myself.'1 jjj ij{ Sj. A little over three years ago, this column chronicled the depar, ture of young Fred. Milthorpe, who it met when he was a biolo. gist in the Department of Agri. culture. From there this studi. ous young chap graduated on to the University staff as a research officer at the School of Botany, and in no time won a Farrar research scholarship for two years at the Imperial College, London. Just before the scholarship expired, Milthorpe was awarded the Guggenheim Scholarship against in. ternational competition, thus giv. ing him a valuable third year at the Imperial College. Back in NSW the other day to see his folk, who are on the land out Goulbunv way,, if I remember aright, Mil. thorpe was offered and accepted a post as research worker in the drought resistance of plants at the Waite Institute, South Australia. So we can still breed 'em, train 'em — and then lose 'em! And it's been going on that way for' years; When Chief Traffic Manager Howse walked into a crowded room on a recent hot and humid day to address the general council of the NSW Graziers' Association, and to break the sad news that his De. partment proposed to alter the basis of wool freights from a charge per ton (as at present) to a flat rate per bale (whether one or 1000), he wiped his perspiring forehead, said: 'If you'll excuse m«, I think I'll, take my coat off.' 'Oh, don't be afraid — it's not going to be quite as bad as all that,' said one jocular councillor. Howse joined heartily in the laugh, ter that followed. * * * It was a sad story Howse had to tell — a truck shortage running into thousands, a slow turn.round at Darling Harbor (where trucks are queued up till they're almost out of sight), and a slower intake than ever at the wool stores, where the Commo.. inspired storemen and packers not only refuse to work overtime, but sneer at the very suggestion that they should work a few hours on Saturday morn, ing at triple rates, their conduct thus creating a bottleneck which has its repercussion over the whole field of lorries, rail trucks, wool sales and so on. The rail men, brokers and everyone else, have done their best to try and make the s. & p. won't-workers see the error of their ways, but without success. Their attitude seems to be: 'We've got a 40-hour week and intend to keep it.' They do. They keep it, all right — by work, ing about 30 hours. The brok. ers talked of going to see Premier McGirr about the bad effect the s. & p. stand was having on the nation's economy, but when they pondered the fact that Jim. my had fathered the lunacy, they didn't seem in a hurry to ask him. And haven't done so yet, so far as this column is aware. * * * The mentality of the s. & p. uni. on boys takes some fathoming. Not long ago, a chap 'sounded'1 one of these boys on their attitude, and tried to discover what their reason was for refusing triple pay for Saturday work, and for spurning overtime money. The answer was very simple. 'What's the good of working for Chif?' came the query. 'We'd only be damned fools to have that on. Let him ease the taxation on overtime, and we might consider the matter. If they would only agree to work overtime for half an hour or ao on ordinary days, the rail lorries could deliver an extra load into stores. But just let the s. & p. lads know the lorries are ready to deliver another and last load, and do you know what the cads do? Invoke the clause in the award which gives them 45 minutes for crib, and at the end of that 45 minutes,' they pack up and go home! Is 'it any wonder we arc heading fast for the inevitable? Apparently the madmen in our midst won't be satisfied till they . bring about another depression — and then they'll blame it on anybody but themselves. — HAMcC.

05 May 1951 - Editorial Record (Emerald Hill, Vic. : 1881 - 1957), Saturday 5 May 1951, page 1 Ifi dUomiat Gallup Poll, Gullibility and White Magic Putting political ibbucb aside, le^us consider that comical thing — the Gallup Poll. It is of American origin, and hardly, acclimatised to Australia, where its records of late have been about as accurate as when in its 'original habitat it predicted the fall of President Truman. Doubtless it is entirely honest in mo tive and within the limits imposed by its nature is efficiently carried out: it ic tVip nnturp that, is at fault, for it partakes of the nature of man, and is I therefore intrinsically subject to error. The claim is made for it that it reflects public opinion expressed by 'a representative cross-section of society.' But is that bo in fact? Who selects the 'representative crosssection?' The conductors of the Poll do. And by what norm do they jnake the selection? And what intelligence test is applied to the people interviewed ? perlexing in view of the findings of the Gallup Poll in connection with the Federal elections last Saturday. In the light of these it will find difficulty in having itself accepted as authoritative in Australia. This may be as Mr. Clive Turnbull, Associate Editor of the. 'Argus,' asserts, 'The Land of Couldn't Care Less,' but satirical comments on the Poll reveal that many of them care too much for their selfrespect to be ready to accord to it in future any more than good-humored attention. Pointing the Bone a la Mode. Even if the inquiries were conducted with scrupulous regard to all phases of any issue canvassed, there would remain the disquieting fact that the results are played up sensationally by newspapers which' have a case to establish. They are converted into propaganda without concern for the psychological factors that contribute to them, but with pedantic concern for the psychology of press and radio pushover. It is the old practice of pointing the bone. An Australian aborigine plans the death of his endfcy by pointing a bone at him or in his direction. He is not so simple as to suppose that the enemy will, die if he does not_ know he is doomed to die: hence a third party is essential: and this third party informs Uie first, Wno men uuu&i'B'j ? ? himself to hate-fulfilment. The press practises white magic. It seeks a certain end against a certain class, a party or person. It lets the public know what it thinks, but it also and mainly contrives to make the P^plic think that the public is doing its think inc for itself; whereas it is not, — it « victimised to a subtle process of induced auto-suggestion. Sometimes, of course, the nublic or a portion insists on thinning . . . and the cat of candor escapes from the bag of tricks. It would be interesting to know how many citizens of South Melbourne have been interviewed by Gallup Poll officials and on what subjects. If press methods were followed, the line of i^iry for a model was probably the distmc tion between the existentialism of Sartre and of Marcel, and for an unskilled worker the problem of the relationship bet%veen management And profits. It is custcwmry to fessor what he knows about bricklaying or a teetotaller what difference he detects between the tastes of Scotch and Australian whiskies. An American Sidelight. From America, in a book written to expose the shallowness of thought in high places, comes this story of a public opinion Poll: 'What,' asked the interviewer, 'is your opinion of private enterprise in this country? Private enterprise,' he was told, is a euphemism for the profit system. The reply was off the beaten track dictated by the terms of reference. It provoked a further question, 'What a euphemism i Isn't it time we woke up and had a good laugh about all these opinion barometers - and then gave a great shout of protest against a business that could flourish best on moronism .

13 Jun 1952 - BREVITY Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 13 June 1952, page 10 BREVITY A. RECENT Gallup Poll found that a big majority of Australians considered that fees paid to church schools and private schools should be deductalble from income before tax is charged. • That is right, as far as it goes, but it doesn't go far enough for full justice. Full justice would demand that the aforesaid fees should be dednctable from income tax before it is paid. Not -that it would be done in that way, exactly. Bishop Lyons of Sydney has suggested a simpler way, that of a per capita grant through the Social Service set-up, for all school children, so that they may choose and pay for their education in whatever school they want.

03 Oct 1952 - OFF THE BEAM Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 3 October 1952, page 6 OFF THE BEAM A N interesting Gallup poll finding was published recently. Two questions were asked, the first being: "If a husband and wife are separated with no hope of reunion, and both want a divorce, would you favor or opposte permitting the divorce?" 82 per cent, were in favor, 14 per cent, opposed, and 4 per cent, expressed no opinion. The second question was, "If a husband or wife has been wronged but won't ask for a divorce, do you think the other party should, or should not, be allowed to seek a divorce?" 53 per cent, said "should," and 33 per cent, "should not." Now here is the extraordinary thing: Of the Catholics who gave an opinion (and there were probably several hundreds out of the total of 1,800 questioned), 55 per cent, were in favor of permitting the divorce in the first case, while even in the second case 37 per cent, of Catholics voted "should." It would often seem that a lot of Catholics are hazy about the Tightness or wrongness of divorce. All know, of course, that divorce for Catholics is wrong, but many don't seem to realise that divorce for validly married nonCatholics is wrong, too; that no valid marriage can be dissolved simply by the agreement of the parties or a decision of a court. In other words, for the Catholic the only good divorce law would be a law p forbidding all divorce. To both questions in the Gallup there should have been a 100 per cent. Catholic vote against divorce.

This table shows/hat maintenance of our armed forces was foremost in the public minds. Conscription, 31 per cent. Man-power and recruiting, 5 per cent. Defend Australia. 11 per cent. Win the war. 15 per cent. Other war references, 17 per cent. Social problems. 10 per cent. Indefinite. 11 per cent. Total. 100 per cent. One out of three people who referred to conscription said. 09 Jul 1954 - BREVITIES Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 9 July 1954, page 11 BREVITIES A RECENT Gallup poll concerned the question as to what should be done with people found guilty of treason. The majority of those interviewed were of the opinion that these traitors should be deported. That is, in our opinion, only reasonable and right. A surprising number were in favor of the death penalty (26%), as against 37% for deportation and 22% for life imprisonment. What is the best means to adopt may be a matter of opinion, but this is certain, the community has the right so to deal with its traitors that they will no longer be able to harm it. * * * A DIVORCED young Hungarian Act ress (the singer of a song described by The Mail as the "Sexiest Thing Since Sex" of last year), who, if newspaper accounts could be believed, was leading a pretty profligate kind of a life last year, recently got a big surprise. When she went to a film Festival at Berlin the other night she was greeted with "boos, shrieks and catcalls" from the young audience. The paper tells us—"Eva is so upset (note that "Eva"—we're all pals together) about it all that she and her fiance no longer appear in public together." Well, there's a lesson for us all here. If we find it difficult to face the disapproval of our fellow-men, how will we like it if we have to face the disapproval and anger of Almighty God?

17 Sep 1954 - THIS WEEK'S ROUND-UP Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 17 September 1954, page 6 THIS WEEK'S ROUND-UP ADMITS HE WAS WRONG A .RECENT Gallup poll in the U.S. on the question of letting Red China into U.N. resulted: 79% of the men and women interviewed in a nation-wide survey were opposed to letting Red China into U.N. Amongst those who have signed it are George Meaney, president of the American Federation of Labor—one of the biggest trade union jobs in America—and General George C. Marshall, who, between tours as Army Chief of Staff and Secretary of State, spent a year in China, half persuading the Nationalists—Chiang Kai-shek—to he down like lambs with the conquest-bent Communists. It's good, anyway, to see that Marshall is humble enough to acknowledge his error now. It's a pity some of our journalists don't own up when they have been wrong.

02 May 1947 - LONDON HIGHLIGHTS Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 2 May 1947, page 16 LONDON HIGHLIGHTS (By Don Riley) JyATEST topic to be investigated in this island by that infallible institution, the Gallup Poll, is— religion. A. few mornings ago the News Chronicle told ub across four columns on page one: "Religion Still Has Job to Do—Says Gallup Poll." The question put "to men and women of all ages and in all walks of life, throughout England, Scotland and Wales" was: "Do you think that religion has 'a mission to fulfil iffBritain to-day?" Fifty-five per cent, of these folk, according to the Chronicle, said religion had a mission to fulfil; 24 per cent, said it hadn't; the other. 21 per cent, didn't know . . . For the inquisitive-minded reader the figures were analysed, to bring out these points: Women were more convinced than men that religion had a mission to fulfil. Of people under 30, however, only a minority held this view. Most marked were the differences in outlook between the economic groups . . . Two-thirds of the well-to-do thought religion had a mission to fulfil, while among the poorer people the proportion dropped to below one-half. For the country as a whole, so far so good ... Only 65 per cent, of the Catholics questioned thought religion had a mission to fulfil here, while 13 per. cent, said no. But three in four of the Nonconformists said yes . . . 03 Mar 1950 - As the Earth Turns Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 3 March 1950, page 3 the Earth Turns COMMENTARY ON WORLD AFFAIRS BY D. G. M. JACKSON f Sulla) The British Election Fiasco FjpHE forecasts of the Gallup Poll that there would he something like a "photo-finish" in the British general election have been proved accurate by the event. On the basis of the voting, it would appear that the British people are divided almost exactly equally between those who are for a .Churchill Tory Government and those who prefer to see the Attlee regime continued. My own reading of this phenomenon is that a large number of people have lost faith in Labor—whose leaders are themselves suffering from weariness and-embittered by failure and criticism. The trouble is that the Tories have failed to provide-a policy which is at all bold or inspiring. They have nothing new to propose in the foreign field—where, at least, Churchill might have been expected to outbid Bevin by clearer definitions on the subject of European collaboration. At home, they have been concerned merely to outbid their opponents for leadership of the Welfare State, accepting the philosophy of "planning" and the maintenance of full employment. For the rest, their criticisms have been directed at the persons, opinions and records of those in power, and they have been sufficiently vigorous and cogent; but the promise of a change of personnel does not compensate sufficiently for the lack of a positive programme. I think the leadership of Churchill is a definite handicap to the Tories at the present time. As a "valiant pilot in extremity" he was enormously admired and trusted far too much; but to-day, as in the between-war period, his combativeness and impetuosity are feared—and there is a feeling that the reappearance of the challenging old war-horse at the head of the British Government would not help the cause of peace. Moreover, like Pitt; this "great Commoner" has never been a "party man" in the modern -sense; he is a throwback to the age of aristocratic politics, when the domination of the machine was not established. Since the war he has been forced to play the "party game" against his will —his own desire, of course, was for a continuation of'the national coalition arrangement through the period of post-war crisis. He has played it -very badly from the first; and the incalculable adventurousness and devastating largeness of his utterances make him something of a bull in the electoral china-shop. On the contrary, the Labor leader's earnest, industrious unobtrusiveness and air of "middle of the road" moderation serves his party much as Baldwin's "ordinariness" did the Tories in the pre-war years. It was difficult to convince the plain man that the friendly, democratic Baldwin was a. sinister "reactionary"—it is equally difficult to persuade him that the kindly, commonplace Clement Attlee is leading the British in the direction of Socialist totalitarianism. The worst of it is that the ineffable Mr. Eden is next in the line of Conservative succession after Churchill—and his record of statesmanship promises as ill as his mastery of inept and outmoded cliches for the future direction of Tory policy. The British Liberal Tragedy .fPHE tragedy of British Liberalism is the familiar tragedy of the "third party" in British history. Its architect was the late Lloyd George; if he had not split his party in order to rise to leadership in the First World War coalition in Asquith's place, the party system might have remained LiberalTory, in Britain as in Canada, with Labor as the radical wing on the Liberal side. But once the "Independent" Liberals became a remnant "rump," they were bound to suffer continuous decline, owing to the fact that those opposing the existing regime were afraid of "wasting their vote" unless they gave it to the strongest opposition group. In the latest election the chief effect of the widespread presence of their candidates has probably been to prevent a Conservative victory, since convinced Liberals usually vote Tory— except in Wales—where no Liberal candidate is available. It is appalling that this result should have occurred at an hour of crisis, when strong Government and unflinching, realistic leadership dre a primary necessity for Great Britain and Europe. The ^doubtful verdiot-resultihg from an ojferwhelmingly poll reflects, I think, the confusion of mind of the nation, and a lack of conviction about standards of- any kind. There was never a time when it was more necessary to tell the truth to the people about - their situation—but both sides seem to have agreed that the surest way to lose support was to put first things first instead of leaving them out or discussing them as little as possible. The game played for the support of the electorate was the old one of Cleon and the Sausage-seller, whose competitive appeal to American democracy is immortalised in the "Knights" of Aristophanes. • It is to be hoped, at least, that the election fiasco will lead the remainder of the Liberals to consider seriously the question whether they are not wasting their time in trying to return as an independent party; and whether they should not rather try to link up with the Tories, who-have been drifting Leftward for some time, and infuse their programme 'with some of the spirit of their political philosophy. British Labor and Socialism TTNFORTUNATELY, there seems ^ little hope that they can do any thing to rescue the Labor Party from the domination of Socialist theory, which tends to grow as the decline of Christian influences gives more and more authority to those whom Colm Brogan describes as "the scribes- of the dialectic." No doubt, Labor men have been disillusioned by power and its disappointments. They have learned—and unlearned—something from fheir experience. But they have not been disillusioned about Marxism, if we are ,to judge from the utterances of three of the most influential leaders of the Party—the popular Mr. Aneurin Bevan, Mr. John Strachey (the philosopher of the groundnuts), and Mr. Shinwell, of the "Tinker's Cuss." Not only are these men Marxists, but the Labor ColJege tutors and study groups are Marxists—and on the vital matter of "Socialisation" no compromise or private judgment is allowed. Tolerance was extended to the last possible hour to the "Left-Wingers" who stabbed Bevin in the back on foreign policy; but the two men who opposed nationalising steel had to leave the Party —and at the Scarborough conference the idea that even a hearing should be given to one of them, Mr. Edwards, was rejected as unthinkable. Individuals may doubt or dislike the Socialist creed, or wish to move slowly towards its achievement; but they are committed to the "socialising" design of policy, nevertheless; and there seems no prospect that it will be altered. That this should be the only alternative to Churchillian Toryism now available to the English voter is a measure of the harm done by the late Mr. Lloyd George to the British political system.

24 Mar 1950 - THE LIBRARY TABLE BOTH PRESS LORDS—BUT WHAT A DIFFERENCE! Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 24 March 1950, page 9 THE LIBRARY TABLE BOTH PRESS LORDS-BUT WHAT A DIFFERENCE! rPHE statistical machinery of a Gallup Poll is scarcely needed to determine who, as far as the Englishspeaking world is concerned; must be regarded as the best-selling pamphleteer of the Catholic Church. Undoubtedly, the "Oscar" for 20th Century Catholic pamphleteering must, unhesitatingly, be awarded to that American son of St. Ignatius', Fr. Daniel Lord, whose prolific output of pamphlet-writing, covering every phase of Catholic life, is one of the achievements of our times, but whose work the future historian, if so Inclined, may perhaps dismiss as merely the reactions of a Jesuit to American high-production methods. Whatever about the future, the present speaks highly of Fr. Lord. His pamphlets are on sale in every Catholic church from Belfast to Balaclava. In Australia, the Catholic Truth Society can claim that there is hardly a sector of the Commonwealth without readers of Daniel Lord, S.J. The New Look The accent, however, is not on output but on revolution, not the bloody, guillotine type of change, but a tranquil re-orientating of attitude. Fr. Lord has developed a New Look in people. He has changed the structure and the public's whole approach to Catholic pamphlets, and has established himself as the Christian Dior for this form of Catholic journalism. Apropos of which, and appropriately though perhaps oddly, he bears comparison with that Boy from Chapelizod, Dublin, Alfred Harmsworth, the late Lord Northcliffe. To some it may seem a particularly odious kind of sacrilege to attempt to compare such opposite people, Lord Northcliffe, the wealthy Irish Pagan, the Press Lord of Fleet Street, with his regiment of newspapers, and the Yankee Jesuit, Daniel Lord, with his three vows of religion and his breviary, but it is worth the risk, if not only to observe the deep contrast. Admittedly, atlantically apart in ideology and motivation, they reach an identity of achievement in the effect each has produced in the field of journalism. Everyone is familiar with the revolution in newspapers brought about by Northcliffe. By attractive layout of news, headlines that told the story, human interest items, by snappily-written, informative and topical features, etc., he very rapidly commanded the mind and market of 90% of the newspaper-reading English public. Tickle the Public Such innovations were regarded with so little favor in some quarters of late Victorian society that Lord Salisbury —then Prime Minister—sneeringly described the "Daily Mail" as "a journal produced by office-boys for office-boys." However, in spite of the snub of such an eminent parliamentarian, Northcliffe continued not only to hold but to increase his public. In vivid contrast to the staid, solemn, portentous, and unattractively laid-out "Times," Northcliffe's sales continued to soar from one dizzy record to another. The philosophy of the Boy from Chapelizod was to Entertain the public, not to Educate them. He adroitly left this onerous task to the "Times." Entertainment begot Circulation, which, in turn, begot Money. Circulation and Money were the parents of his Power, and a. POWER he undoubtedly became. If not the Lord of Creation, he definitely was the Lord of newspaper circulation. In his day, Northcliffe often quoted his policy in the following verse, which he certainly lived up to: "Tickle the public and make them grin, The more you tickle the more you'll win. Teach the public, you'll never grow rich, You'll live like a beggar, and die in a ditch." For entertainment, he used everything that happened, particularly the unusual and sensational. Crime, sport, politics, the love life of plumbers, porters, pilots, and trollops, etc., had a place in his columns. The late Victorians must, indeed, have found his press a weird change from the "Times," for Northcliffe had tremendous, practical faith in Charles Dana's definition of news, viz., "If a dawg bites a man that isn't NOOS. If a man bites a dawg, that is." For Christ—Not for Cash News for Fr. Lord is not conditioned by any normal or abnormal incident between man and dog. His copy is the Teaching of the Catholic Church. His role is to increase Circulation of this Teaching, for Education, not for Entertainment, for Christ, not for Cash. Definitely, too, there is a Power Angle, bigger in ambit and concept than the ambition of the Boy from Chapelizod ever aimed at. To make Christ King of the hearts of men, not only in Fleet street, but Everywhere, is the sublime objective of Fr. Lord. Tactically, he has followed the Northcliffe mould, the same psychological principle of "tickling" the public, and he has "tickled" his way to unprecedented success. He has won an enormous Lord-reading public by making the Catholic pamphlet more attractive in TITLE and more READABLE in its presentation of Catholic doctrine. By breaking away from the stiff and starched product of the academic tradition, Fr. Lord has inaugurated a new era in Catholic pamphleteering, and revolutionised the widescale exposition of Divine Truth. His snappy, breezy, picturesque titles, in modern phrasing, have a sales-appeal the public can't resist, as is amply testified by the huge international volume of his sales. Like Northcliffe's headlines, the titles tell- the story, and appeal to readers to read completely through. Glory of God They are the banners of messages of great substance, written in an easy colloquial style, devoid of the professorial and condescending, successful in soothing susceptible sensitivity. Thus conditioned, readers are ripe to accept and follow Truths set down with such human charm. The initial attraction of his titles is sustained in his clear, unheavy treatment of the matter. With such technique, the pen of Daniel Lord has become a Missionary Movement; his work a Poem of Achievement for the Glory of God. Behind both is the man himself, hidden in the Nazareth of a Jesuit gown, and his humility utterly untouched by, yet conscious that "The limelight's most unkind to human skin."

03 Nov 1944 - GALLUP POLL THE MODERN YARDSTICK OF TRUTH AND MORALITY! Southern Cross (Adelaide, SA : 1889 - 1954), Friday 3 November 1944, page 5 GALLUP POLL THE MODERN YARDSTICK OF TRUTH AND MORALITY! ^PEAKING at the opening of the new Maternity Wing at Calvary Hospital, Hobart; recently, His Grace the Co-adjutor Archbishop of Melbourne (the Most Rev. Dr. J. D. Simonds) spoke on the popular trend of submitting Questions of morals to the. judgment of. "modern public opinion," and the consequent sense of futility and helplessness which is sounded in the appeals of political" leaders who are confronted with the alarming spectacle of race suicide in Australia. His Grace said in part: "The secret of the success of the Blue Nuns (the Little Company of Mary), is, of course, to be found in their religious dedication, to the work of nursing the sick and the dying. A Blue Nun does not become a Sister in order to graduate as an • efficient nurse. She takes the veil in order to become a saint, since the primary aim of the religious life is the personal sanctification of the members of the Institute. ' "With true supernatural insight, Mother Mary Potter, the saintly foundress- of the Little Company of Mary, saw that one of the chief aims by which her Sisters could become . more Christ-like, would be by their devoted service of Christ through His sick and dying members. , The nursing of the Blue Sisters is thus a personal service of their Divine Master, and it is undertaken as a means of acquiring a greater degree of personal holiness. "Now one of the distinctive ideals of Mother Mary Potter was her devotion to the mystery of the Divine Maternity, through which the Son of God deigned to sanctify human birth by being born Himself into our race of a Virgin Mother. Under this beautiful inspiration the Blue Sisters will always treat the mystery of human birth with the deepest religious reverence, and give to it the best of their devoted and skilful nursing. Quite recently I visited the maternity hospital of the Little Company of Mary in Melbourne, and learned with pleasure that one thousand births had occurred in the hospital without the loss of a single mother- There is not the slightest reason to doubt that this .maternity hospital, which was blessed to-day, will likewise be an outstanding boon to the Hobart community, and will come to be regarded as a veritable sanctuary of devoted care for Tasmanian motherhood. The Chief Battle-ground "Family life has, unfortunately, not escaped the blighting effects of the weakened moral sense of the community; indeed, the family may be said to be the chief battle-ground of conflicting moral theories. Our statesmen are rightly alarmed at the course of race suicide which Australia has pursued for a couple of generations. They are confronted with an almost universal frustration of the primary function of marriage, and an alarming increase in the deliberate destruction of unborn children. I have studied most of the comments and appeals made by political leaders on this problem, and can detect a note of futility and helplessness in all their exhortations, because they have no other ground on which to appeal to the national, sense than a kind of scientific morality divorced from religion, "As a result of our secularist policy in public life, no appeal can be made to the Lawof God and to the dictates of "Natural Law which He has im planted in the heart of man. Indeed, * the agnostic leaders of thought, especially in our universities, scornfully reject the religious sanction for moral, action, and have substituted a kind of scientific morality which appeals solely to the social obligations of the citizen. The morality of- actions, they claim, is determined not by any intrinsic quality in the action itself, nor by any precepts or standards imposed by the authority of God or His Church. The experiences of the race, they say, have determined what actions are socially useful and what are socially harmful, so that "social efficiency" is the rule that governs the morality or otherwise of our actions. Hence the popular trend of submitting questions of morals to the judgment of 'modern public opinion'. "What the majority of the citizens do and approve is good; what they disapprove is bad. Gallop Polls have thus become the modern yard-stick by which both truth and morality are to be measured. It is easy -to see that this modern attitude is the result of the rejection of religious standards of ethics, and is the natural evolution of the effect which politics have had on the national mind. "Under a democratic system questions of practical politics are usually decided by a majority vote, but in our day the moral law has also been made the subject to what Nietzsche sneeringly called "the absurd British passion for counting neses." "As a natural consequence, the modern man, who rarely thinks deeply, has become mass-minded, susceptible to clever slogans and a slave to the idea of majority judgments, so that he readily endorses the latest moral fashion of the day which happens to satisfy the popular demand. Morality has thus become relative and subjective, and what was yesterday's sin may be a virtue to-day. "Without doubt one" of the reasons why the Catholic Church is so unpopular in certain quarters is that she resolutely refuses to submit the Ten Commandments of God and the moral teaching of Christ to the verdict of Gallup Polls. In this hospital the sacred right to life, which every unborn child possesses, will be religiously safeguarded, in spite of any popular theory to the contrary. No high-sounding phrases like "therapeutic induction" pr "termination of pregnancy" will be allowed to obscure the moral, evil of abortion, but the deliberate destruction of the unborn child will jje called by its un- -varnished and unpleasant name of murder, and will never be countenanced. "The teaching of the Church on this subject is clear and emphatic. No surgical operation that is directly destructive cf the "life a child, .either born or unborn, can be sanctioned. It is an intrinsically evil thing to destroy the life of an innocent child, and evil may not be done in order to attain a good end, even to save the life of the mother. Should a casp occur in' which treatment for some complication may indirectly and incidentally injure the life of the unborfi child, the problem will be handled ■in the light of accepted moral principles, that will safeguard the spiritual and physical rights of both mother and child, as well as the consciences of those charged with the treatment."

19 Oct 1952 - HARRY CURRIE'S U.S. ROUND-UP Truth (Sydney, NSW : 1894 - 1954), Sunday 19 October 1952, page 12 HARRY CURRIE'S VS. ROUND-UP Hectic tight for the Presidency NEW YORK, Saturday. — Visible signs and portents point to a hectic neck-and-neck climax in the Presidential election on November 4. A Gallup*poll shows that the Republicans are now commanding 49 per cent of the voting for front runner Eisenhower and 45 per cent for long striding Stevenson, with six per cent of voters sitting on that well known fence. But remember Gallup polls were woefully astray in 1948 when Truman came from ten lengths back to pip Dewey on the post. When the campaign opened Eisenhower was as well known as any victorious war general could be. Adlai Stevenson was practically unknown outside the State of Illinois, where he is Governor. Any De m o c r a t, of Stevenson's calibre, therefore, simply had to make up some ground as the race wore on. It is a case now of Stevenson, the politician, versus Eisenhower the na tional hero, with emotion* and sentiment leaning to Ike. Today Korea appears as a central issue with the rather dazed voters trying to calculate who would be the better man to lead the nation in a conflict with Russia and Communism during the four years ahead. ' * * * Eisenhower and Stevenson aggued the origins of the Korean war and discussed the possibility of ending it. President Truman barged in, defending his administration to th^ hilt for going to war immediately the Communists crossed the 38th Parallel. With 21,000 dead and 121,000 total casualties, and the peace talks abandoned indefinitely, Korea is a vitally personal issue to Americans. Newspapers are eight to one on Ike's side, so there is no solid gauge to be gleaned there. As No. 1 war nero, Eisenhower is hard to attack, so the Democrats are concentrating on the 'ignoble' figures behind him, led by arch anti-Trumanite, Senator Taft.They They say Eisenhower appeared as an ardent internationalist while winning the war and commanding N.A.T.O., but now is being bossed around by a gang of stubborn isolationists. Eisenhower has promised to end the Korean war as soon as it is humanly possible to do so, to cut taxes but keep the United States strong, and to banish corruption from Washington. - The solid, studious Stevenson .doesn't offer any such panacea. ¥ * * He says there is no easy, quick, painless, bargain-basement protectionagainst against Soviet imperialism. He does not question Ike's integrity, but talks about the 'cut-throat reactionaries' around him. He is a new style Democratic candidate, a man who didn't lift a finger to get the party's nomination, but who is now meeting Eisenhower on every issue. Gen. EisenHower Adlai Stevenson

You will have observed that, not only in Gallup polls, but in letters to the daily Press from every scetion of the community, the lunacy of the 40hour week— as wicked Bn election ramp as ever came from the brain of an inept timeserving politician— is now getting its full quota «f blame for the ruination it is bringing in Its train. In fact, it is easily the greatest spur inflation has had, because it lessened production In the very years production was needed most. If the lazy and inefficient Red Industrial circles which have converted the 40hour into a 30-hour week think the nation can get away with the lunacy against the highly mechanised, efficient and busy industrial activities of the 48hour USA— well, someone has a second think coming. The writing came on the wall last week when Menzies stressed the gravity of the situation so far as overseas trade balances were concerned, and the effect that this trend would have on our national economy. This fact stands stark and clear— our prosperity is based on wool and wheat, and without the millions they bring into the country, well, we are sunk, torpedoed, and done for, and all the 'phoney prosperity of the welfare State and the 40hour week will then become a thing of tfie past you've heard of the Angry Penguins, of course. ' But these wild boys muct not be allowed to forget this— that for six months they had taunted Menzies with, 'Go to the country— you're not game!' But there is one chap going round with a wide grin and an 'I told you so'— Roberton, MP for Rlverina, who long before McKell moved into the GG-ship wrote the McKell saga and declared that If ever Willie got the chance he would grab a title. That long distance shot was a winner! The day may not be far distant when the pesky fruit fly will have iost Its terrors for the fruit grower, commercial or backyarder. Details? It's a case of wait and -see. 16 Oct 1933 - SEWERAGE Shepparton Advertiser (Vic. : 1887 - 1953), Monday 16 October 1933, page 10 SEWERAGE Poll to be Taken OPPORTUNE PERIOD. ATTRACTIVE LOAN TERMS. A committee consisting of delegates from the Borough Council and the Water Trust has been inquiring into the question of sew- ©ring Shepparton. The unemployment Belfeif Council has made loan funds available to other towns comparable to Shepparton in size and importance — on very attractive terms and it would be a reflection on the progr0«sivene8s of Shepparton, if towns such as Wangaratta, Swan Hill, Echuca, Horsham and Ararat install sewerage 'schemes while this town retains the unpleasant and unhealthy pan system and surface street channel disposal of domestic and industrial wastes. Inquiries by the committee have shown that the terms of loans granted to other Sewerage Authorities have ' been:—Interest at 4i per cent, sinking fund 1 per cent, and a rebate of interest of 3 per cent, has been made for tlie first four years of the loan. No doubt Shepparton would obtain equally favorable terms. The conditions on which these loans are granted provide that 80 per cent of labour must be drawn from registered unemployed men.Revised Revised estimates of the total cost and rating required have been obtained from the engineers in consequence of reduced labor and material costs, the estimated total cost of the scheme for Shepparton now being £64,000 as against £85,000 estimate several years ago. This amount requires an estimated rating of 1/7 in the £1 as against the previous 2/2 in the £1,- while for the first four years the interest rebate on loan reduces the rate to 1/ in the £1 on municipal valuation.In In view of these favorable conditions, the committee has decided to submit the matter to the ratepayers of Shepparton and a poll will bo held shortly. Ratepayers at the same time will be asked to decide the question of whether the Borough Council or Water Trust shall make application for constitution as the Sewerage Authority. The authority when constituted has power to borrow moneys for the purpose of making the necessary house connections for property owners; and the Act provides that property owners may spread the repayment of these advances over a period of 10 years . and an amendment of the Act is being asked to have this term extended. Recent quotations in otner towns show that the cost of complete connections for an average house will be from £30 to £40 and by taking advantage of the instalment plan of repayments, the charge to property i owners is made very’ easy.

05 Dec 1948 - REDS TRY TO SABOTAGE POLLS Truth (Sydney, NSW : 1894 - 1954), Sunday 5 December 1948, page 5 REDS TRY TO SABOTAGE POLLS Herliners Vote Ttntatf ALLIES FACING NEW PROBLEM (British United Press) \ BERLIN, Saturday. — Ten thousand i police, backed up by 80 police radio cars, j will be on patrol tomorrow during the ; municipal elections in the Western- sectors ? of the city. i They have been drafted for duty to ! prevent Communist attempts at violence j to intimidate voters, and sabotage the j elections. : In the U.S. sector alone an extra 1000 police have been ordered on duty, and Allied troops will be standing by to act if the German police send an S.O.S. The election issue is, basically, whether the Germans in the Western sectors are for or against Communism. All Germans over 20 who ; have been living in Berlin ; more than six months are eligible to vote. The voters will elect 98 of 130 members of the City Assembly. The remaining 32 are representative members from the Russian sector, where the election has been banned. Truth's European editor (F. E. Baume) cables from London tnat the Russian military governor in Berlin (Marshal Sokolovsky) has gone to extreme limits in his attempts to sabotage the elections. He says that the Russians have staged the setting up of a separate local government in the Soviet sector, but Berliners would not be fooled by Sokolovsky's fireworks. The Russians at this stage are not going to do more than shriek or yell. 'No matter how loud their protests, the Reds have been unable to prevent elections in the Western sectors. This municipal election will be the second since the end of the war, says Baume. The effrontery of the Russians in declaring that responsibility for any split in Berlin is due to the Western Powers, needs no comment, but observers say that Frankfurt should be looked to as an indication of growing German political unrest. In the face of Western Allied disapproval, German politicians there have already decided to create a strong, centralised Western German State. Even the New York Herald -Tribune says: 'It appears that German politicians are gambling that they can get away with their political manoeuvre in the face of united American, British and . French disapproval.' In other words, the Russianattempted sabotage of the elections in Berlin was to be expected. The growing arrogance of German politicians themselves, may yet present the Allied Military Government wit^h a problem more dangerous than that set up by Russian irreconcilability, adds Baume.

07 Nov 1948 - Bitter Debate Certain On Steel Nationalisation Bill Truth (Sydney, NSW : 1894 - 1954), Sunday 7 November 1948, page 10 Bitter Debate Certain On .j Steel Nationalisation Bill Mr. Ancurin Bevan Mr. Shinvrell TO say commentators were caught on the wrong foot by President Truman's showing in the United States election is to put the case very mildly. Failure of the Gallup Poll in United States estimates makes one wonder just how far the swing against Britain's Labor Government, recorded by popular polls, will be reflected in the ballot boxes when the general election comes along. The Government will largely have itself to blame if it does lose the election as its public relations service is hardly making the best even of a bad job of translating the ideas of Fuel Minister Shinwell and Health Minister Aneurin Bevan into common parlance. Mr. Attlee has always disclaimed any liking for publicity and if is just possible this may have something to do with his continuing sway over the party. Others get the limelight and Mr. Attlee merely sits in the chair to see fair play. The Government must, however, be given at least a bronze medal for the manner in which it has put over its case for iron and steel nationalisation. It has pointed out that the high price of steel affects so many industries that it is virtually decisive in Britain's battle for survival. If the price of steel can be lowered by sweeping away agreements among manufacturers then (so the argument runs) the export drive will be promoted and even the poor, neglected home consumer will ultimately benefit. The argument .would command .more attention if it could be proved that nationalisation will not affect the efficiency of the industry. It has been said that lower tariffs on foreign steel would supply a sufficient incentive to industry to lower its prices. Since Australian steel can even now compete with British steel on the price basis, there does not seem any reason to suggest there is no room for improvement in the British industry. But conservatives have chosen this bill as their -battleground, and will fight every inch of the way. They have no chance of winning anything but a reputation as the cannons mount, and they will have to be put in their best form to do even that.

24 Apr 1944 - BEER COUPONS Daily Mercury (Mackay, Qld. : 1906 - 1954), Monday 24 April 1944, page 3 BEER COUPONS Gallup Poll Survey BRISBANE, Sunday.— Three- out of five Australians want a coupon system for war-time beer supplies, according to a Gallup poll survey. Fifty-two per cent, of those interviewed for the poll favored coupons, 33 per cent, opposed them, and 15 per cent, were undecided. About 2000 men and women in all parts of the 'Commonwealth were Interviewed. One person in 14 was prohibitionist. To the question: "Do you think supplies of beer should be increased, decreased, or left as at present?" many said there was "enough at present, If properly rationed." . Half those interviewed favored no change, a quarter wanted the supply decreased, and a quarter wanted an increase. Brewery executives In Brisbane do not favor reduction of the alcoholic content of beer to increase supplies.They They said so yesterday, , commenting on suggestions that a reduced alcoholic content and an increased supply would help to eliminate some of the present disgusting drinking conditions In Brisbane. ' "Reduction of the alcoholic content would interfere with both the flavor and. the keeping qualities of beer," said the manager and a director of Castlemaine, Perkins, Ltd. (Colonel F. A. Hughes). Introduction of the Continental system, which provides for beer-gardens and cafes where food is regarded as a necessary adjunct to drinking, also has been suggested as an essential reform in Queensland. But brewery interests who own the freehold of many hotels say they have not considered any such plans as a post-war change. The Continental cafe system would be uneconomic here, said one brewery executive. "With waiters' wages pegged here at such comparatively high levels, and street frontage rates levied, we could not do It," he continued. "One hundred men standing at a bar are served easily. The same number spread out among tables at their leisure would need four to six times .the number of waiters to attend to them. Charge for a sixpenny glass of beer would have to be lifted to about 2/-." "Reform In Australians' drinking habits will require a totally new outlook in Australia on the use of beer," said another trade representative, experienced in Continental and Australian conditions. He said that when he came to Australia he was amazed at the mid-Victorian prudery which clothed the whole business of beer--drinking.

12 Feb 1944 - THE REICH MUST BE BROKEN UP Daily Mercury (Mackay, Qld. : 1906 - 1954), Saturday 12 February 1944, page 4 THE REICH MUST BE BROKEN UP What are we going to do with Germany after the war? A Gallup poll, taken by the London 'Daily Mail' on this matter has produced a maioritv in favor of breaking Germany up into the States that existed prior to the foundation of the German Empire. We cannot afford to leave the Reich in existence after this war, because it would certainly mean a new war sooner or later. On the other- hand, if the German Empire is broken up into its former States, it may . be a very long time before they ever come together again. It is wise to remember that Bismarck did not form the German Empire in a day. It took him many years, and the work had been proceeding long before his time. If> Germany is put back into the old States system— Bavaria, Prussia, Saxony, Wurtemburg, Mecklenburg, &c.— one source of security for us will lie in the jealousies which existed and still exist between the States. The Bavdrians, for example, hate the Prussians, and they will never again allow themselves to be brought under Prussian domination. The same applies to other States. The Prussians conquered the other German States before they tried to conquer Europe. It is important that Prussia itself be broken up. The Rhine-land, for example, is Prussian. So also. is Hanover (once British). The Rhineland must be taken away from Prussia and made a separate State. Thus the core of the German war machine- would be outside Prussian control. It should be remembered that Germany is still a collection of tribes, cordially disliking each other. Germany is divided not only tribally, but religiously, economically, socially, and culturally.

13 Oct 1948 - Poll Shows U.S. Wants Firm Stand On Berlin Daily Mercury (Mackay, Qld. : 1906 - 1954), Wednesday 13 October 1948, page 3 Poll Shows U.S. Wants Firm Stand On Berlin JN a gallup poll conducted in the U.S.A. in August 85 per cent of average citizens questioned and 90 per cent of returned servicemen stated they would prefer firmness' on the Berlin question even if it meant war between America and Russia. This was revealed yesterday by Mr. F. L. Fitzpatrlck, general manager of Rocla Ltd., who arrived here this week. Mr. Fitzpatrlck has recently returned from a four months tour to America and Canada. He said the general feeling among UH. people was that war is Inevitable. While in America Mr. Fitzpat-rick made an extensive survey of statistics in relation to production, consumption, population, prices and other essentials of American life. CAR SHORTAGE Here are some facts he discovered:— Only shortage in U.S. 'is in cars and half a million are coming off the assembly lines each month. In California one in every three peope have a car and in New York City alone 18,000 taxis are in operation. There has been a 92 'per cent rise in the volume of production since 1939. America's population Is 20 times that of Australia and they are producing 60 times as much coal as we are and 80 times as much steel. The output a man a day is twice that of the Australian but this is accountable to the fact that their equipment is superior.. New York city's police force has twice the number of police in Australia. Fire brigades answer calls every three minutes. New York uses 100,000,000 gallons of water a day and 23,500 tons of food. Trains from other States arrive every 50 seconds. The average factory worker In Chicago is paid 7/6 per hour, a typist makes £16 a week and a secretary £20 a week. FOOD EXPENSIVE Rents and food are expensive. The average worker pays £5 a week rent. 09 Oct 1941 - Why the Gallup Poll? Advocate (Melbourne, Vic. : 1868 - 1954), Thursday 9 October 1941, page 23 Why the Gallup Poll? Letter tQ the Editor Sir,—The Gallup Poll system is being introduced into Australia and citizens might well wonder why. Who is sponsoring and paying for this expensive American "dipstick" and why is the present time selected for its introduction? In America this Poll system is financed by commercial enterprise for nation-wide advertising purposes and as the Americans love statistics the Gallup Poll has prospered. Encouraged by his early success, Dr. Gallup tried his hand at taking Polls on political questions, but with indifferent results. It is true he forecast the re-election of President Roosevelt by a small majority, but failed signally to anticipate the President's ultimate tremendous majority. In Australia the Gallup Poll surely cannot be financed by a commercial institution to foster the sale of commodities to a tax-strained population. Is it, then, merely a newspaper novelty backed by a powerful section of the Australian press? If so, it would be well for us to consider the significance of this move. According to the "Herald/' the first matters on which the opinion of the public will be tested include highly controversial political questions not yet fully debated in the Federal Parliament. Is a straw vote on these questions solemnly recorded by the Gallup organisers and masquerading as the real opinion of the Australian public to be held over the heads of our politicians like a sword? The pseudo-scientific patter that has heralded the scheme, claiming for it extraordinary accuracy in results, might easily impress lots of people, including politicians. Ultimately, it could be used to exert a very powerful pressure on the Government for the time being, and in this lies its menace. It is not suggested that the published results of a Gallup Poll would be faked or doctored in any way, although such a possibility should not be dismissed if the Poll is controlled by some private enterprise having its own political ends to serve. Assuming absolute fairness in operation, there is a tendency for the Poll to usurp the functions of the ordinary electorial franchise. . Another most important objection to the scheme is that the results obtained are necessarily inaccurate. This inaccuracy is inherent in the system itself, but the result of a Poll would be published as the genuine voice of Australia. The publicity afforded to that particular view supported by the Poll would have a tendency to encourage in hitherto undecided minds the acceptance and adoption of the spurious "majority opinion." In effect, therefore, under the guise of a scientific test the system presents a method of directing public opinion by the device of apparently recording that opinion. In the event of the people of Australia being called upon to vote on some important issue, such as conscription, the. dangers of this system would become obvious. In the circumstances, is it not desirable that the control of the Gallup system in Australia should be fully investigated and explained to the people? Yours,- etc., W. L. BRYAN. Auburn, Victoria, October, 1941. One of the most extraordinary Apostolates in the world to-day is surely that of Fr. Hugh Finnegan, O.M.I., chaplain of the State prison at Huntsville, Texas, U.S.A. During his fourteen years at Huntsville, Fr. Finnegan has had 168 men condemned to death by electrocution under his spiritual care. Thank God Fr. Finnegan helped me to settle my accounts."

24 May 1944 - Trends of Australian Public Opinion Advocate (Melbourne, Vic. : 1868 - 1954), Wednesday 24 May 1944, page 3 Trends ot Australian Public Opinion The Work of National Gallup Polls What the people tfiink about decentrofisation, housing, coloured immigration, the proposed transfer of powers to the Government, unification, and religion in schools and the low birth rate T HE role of public opinion is of first importance in a democracy and not only should every effort be made to form sound Christian ideas among the people, but every encouragement should be given to the study and scientific gauging of public opinion. In Australia, the claims of editorial writers, politicians, publicists and correspondents to the press to speak for the "average man" are mostly- inspired by partisan interest than by systematic enquiry. Indeed, events in recent years have shown them to be surprisingly out of touch with what the people are really thinking. Great strides have been made in the scientific study of public opinion in the United States. The pioneer in the work was an American publicist, Dr. George Gallup, who founded the American Institute of Public Opinion in 1935. The Gallup method, which has achieved remarkable results abroad, is being used in Australia by "Australian Public Opinion Polls," which has its headquarters in Melbourne. It is a non-profit company, and a purely fact-finding organisation, having no connection with governments, political parties or special groups. A.P.O.P. A.P.O.P. is affiliated with the British, American and Canadian Institutes of Public Opinion, known to many as the Gallup Polls. Results of American polls are announced in more than 100 newspapers of all shades of political opinion, and 26 newspapers subscribe for the Canadian surveys. Findings of the British Institute are published in the London "News-Chronicle." In Australia, newspapers which pay for and publish A.P.O.P. findings are the "West Australian," Perth; the "Advertiser," Adelaide; the "Mercury," Hobart; the "Herald," Melbourne; the "Sun," Sydney; and the "Courier-Mail,". Brisbane. Those papers publish the findings of the polls without alteration. They retain, of course, the right of comment and criticism, which all newspapers must exercise. Australian foldings of overseas interest are cabled for publication through the British, American and Canadian Gallup Polls. SAMPLING OPINION The Gallup Method is a development, on statistical lines, of the old unscientific straw votes, which tried to find out which way the political wind was blowing. Straw votes, which were based on quantity, .not sampling, became discredited in 1936, when the "Literary Digest" poll wrongly forecast that Roosevelt would not be re-elected for a second term as President. The forecast was wrong because of an upper class bias in the crosssection of people from whom opinions were obtained. Shortly afterwards the "Literary Digest" ceased publication. "Sample referendums" do not purposely seek the views of people known as authorities on a particular subject. A basic principle of the Gallup Method is that people in all circumstances must be sampled in approximately the same proportions as they exist in the population as a whole. Interviewers for Australian Public Opinion Polls are located in numerous selected districts in each State. Opinions are not obtained from every district in Australia, but, taken together, the selected localities are representative of ihe cities, towns and rural areas of each State. Each interviewer obtains opinions from a cross-section of people in his or her district. The total of the samples is sure tojdivide into groups in approximately the same proportions as would the entire eom- munity if a referendum were held. Occasionally, the support for candidates at Commonwealth lelections will be estimated to demonstrate the reliability of representative sampling. INTERVIEWING PRACTICE A feature of the Gallup Method is that opinions on public questions are obtained by personal interview. Separate interview forms are provided for each person interviewed. Their opinions and comments are recorded by our interviewers as each of the public questions is asked. Interviewers should be impartial and detached on all questions. Their own opinions and feelings must not enter into the work. Once a month, each interviewer receives an "assignment" of about 10 interview forms—one for each interview. They are accompanied by an assignment form, which sets out the number of each type of adult to be interviewed, from the top to the bottom of the economic scale. In country districts carefully calculated proportions of farmers are included in the samples. It is the interviewer's responsibility to select individuals to correspond with the types called for in the assignment. All people interviewed must be residents of the Commonwealth electoral sub-division assigned. About half of them should be women — otherwise the polls would not be accurate miniature referendums. RECENT POLLS Surveys carried out by Australian Public Opinion Polls this year reveal: (1).A policy of decentralisation is favoured by the majority, and many city dwellers would like to live in the country. (2) People want to own their own homes, not rent them, and favour both private enterprise and governments playing a part in overcoming the housing shortage, with a distinct preference for governments to sell the houses they build, rather than to let them. (3) There has been a decline in support for a five-year transfer of powers to the government. A February poll showed a small majority for it than against it, but not so heavily as a few months previously. (4) More than a half of the . people favour one Parliament for Australia, with appropriate power delegated to regional councils. A quarter of the unificationists, however, said they would, vote "No" at the referendum. (5) Most people decidedly oppose the admission into Australia of even a limited number of coloured immigrants, which confirms a similar survey made a year ago. (6) Nearly one-third of the people consider selfishness, through pleasure-seeking and birth prevention, is the main cause of the low birth-rate, together with insecurity, low wages, flat life and the housing short-RELiGION IN SCHOOLS Of particular interest to Catholics are the surveys made on the question of teaching religion in schools. The first poll was taken in February, a second was taken in April. Both recorded a strong demand for religion in schools, which lends weight to the current move, for eliminating the word "secular" from the Education Act. "Do you think religion should be taught in Government schools?" was a question asked In February, 1944. Seven out of ten people answered "Yes." Men and women in a full range of economic circumstances were interviewed in about 200 centres throughout Australia. The vote for teaching religion in Government schools was 78 per cent, from women and 68 per cent, from men. Opinion was much the same in all States. The age of people interviewed had some effect on their answers. Nevertheless, 65 per cent, of the 21-29 age group voted "yes," compared with 75 per cent, among people over 50. After each interview people were asked their religion and, as the following analysis shows, there is close agreement between adherents to the various denominations: Vote for Teaching Religion in Government Schools P.C. Methodists 81 Presbyterians 74 Church of England 74 Roman Catholic 69 Other Christian 67 No religion 11 WHAT ARE CHRISTIAN PRINCIPLES? In April, the same question was repeated: "Do you think religion should be taught in Government schools?" The answers more than confirmed the February finding. The "yes" vote had risen from 72 per cent, to 77 per cent., with 17 per cent, opposed and 6 per cent, undecided. But a supplementary question was added for the first time, as shown in recent A.P.O.P. press release (May 17). "If religion is taught in Government-schools, should it be general Christian principles or should each Church conduct separate classes?" Nine out of ten people expressed an opinion either way and their vote was 3 to 2 in favour of "principles." Men and women, as groups, gave almost identical answers. All people interviewed were asked their religion, and the proportions attached to • each of the major denominations compared closely with census figures. The following table, which Excludes the few who did not express an opinion either way, shows (in the first column) agreement between Protestants and Catholics on the first question and (in the second and third columns) some disagreement on the mode of teaching: Favour Favour Favour religion general classes in Govt. Baptist . . .100 80 20 Methodists . . 93 63 37 Presbyterians . 88 68 32 Anglicans . . 81 61 39 Catholic . . . 78 37 63 Other Christians 78 76 24 No religion . . 26 68 32 PEOPLE WANT RELIGION The weakness of the question, of course, lies in the phrase, "general Christian principles." Words and phrases with precise meanings are essential in formulating questionnaires for public opinion sampling. In the circumstances, it was the best the A.P.O.P. could think of, but what are "general Christian principles"? A principle is an objective standard or truth, but, among Australians, "Christian principles" may range from vague religious sensibilities, such as "the golden rule," kindness in another's trouble, etc., to the definite dogmatic and moral doctrine of Catholics covering the whole of life. This helps to explain the low percentage (37 per cent.) of Catholics in favour of teaching "general Christian principles," because the phrase is largely meaningless, for religion outside the Catholic Church has long ceased to be founded on definite doctrines and principles. Hence, Catholics recorded a high percentage (63 per cent.) for separate classes for each Church. In practice, however, the matter touches very few Catholics, for they have built and maintained at great sacrifice Christian schools of their own for the past 70 years. But the important fact revealed by the February poll and confirmed by that of April is that the majority of the people recognise the necessity for religion, however vague their ideas about it, that they are opposed to a purely secular education and that they want their children taught "Christian principles." 25 Oct 1944 - Ten Commandments Unaffected by Gallup Polls Advocate (Melbourne, Vic. : 1868 - 1954), Wednesday 25 October 1944, page 4 Ten Commandments Unaffected by Gallup Polls Moral Law and the Family Discussed by Dr Simonds at New Hospital Ward, Hobart • »rr-iHE care of Australian I mothers is one of the fields of social service that has been gravely neglected in the past, and I trust that in the comprehensive scheme of public health which the Commonwealth Government is planning, the care of mothers and babes will find a foremost place," said his Grace the Coadjutor-Archbishop of Melbourne, Most Rev. J. D. Simonds, speaking at the opening of the new maternity wards at Calvary Hospital, Hobart, on October 15. Referring to the work of the Blue- Sisters, Archbishop Simonds said that quite recently he had visited the' maternity hospital of the Little Company of Mary (Blue Sisters) in Melbourne and had learned with pleasure that one thousand births had occurred in the hospital without the loss of one mother. There was no doubt that "the maternity hospital which was blessed that day would likewise be an outstanding boon to the Hobart community, and would come to be regarded as a veritable sanctuary of devoted care for Tasmanian motherhood. FAMILY LIFE AND RACE SUICIDE "Family life," continued Archbishop Simonds, "has, unfortunately, not escaped the blighting effects of the weakened moral sense of the community; indeed, the family may be said to be the chief battle-ground of conflicting moral .theories. Our statesmen are rightly alarmed at the course of race suicide which Australia has pursued for a couple of generations. They are confronted with an almost universal frus- tration of the primary function of marriage, and an alarming increase in the deliberate destruction of unborn children. I have studied most of the comments and appeals made by political leaders on this problem, and can detect a note of futility and helplessness in all their exhortations, because they have no other ground on which to appeal to the national sense than a kind of scientific morality divorced from religion. SECULARIST POLICY "As a result of our secularist policy in public life, no appeal can be made to the Law of God and to the dictates of the Natural Law which He has implanted in the heart of man. Indeed, the agnostic leaders of thought, especially in our universities, scornfully reject the religious sanction for moral action, and have substituted a kind of scientific morality which appeals solely to the social obligations of the citizen. The morality of actions, they claim, is determined not by any intrinsic quality in the action itself, nor by any precepts or standards imposed by the authority of God or His Church. The experiences of the race, they say, have determined what actions are socially useful and what are socially harmful, so that 'social efficiency' is the rule that governs the morality or otherwise of our actions. Herice the popular trend of submitting questions of morals to the judgment of 'modern public opinion.' "What the majority of the citizens do and approve is good; what they disapprove is bad. Gallup Polls have thus become the modern yard-stick by which both truth and morality are to be' measured. It is easy to see that this modern attitude is the result of the rejection of religious standards of ethics, and is the natural evolution - of the effect which politics has had on the national mind. 'Under a democratic system "questions of practical politics are usually decided by the majority vote, but in our day the moral law has also been made subject to what Nietzsche sneeringly called 'the absurd British passion for counting noses.' "As a natural consequence, the modern man, who rarely thinks deeply, has become massminded, susceptible to clever slogans and a slave to the idea of majority judgments, so that he readily endorses the latest moral fashion of the day which happens to satisfy the popular demand. Morality has thus become relative and subjective, and what was yesterday's sin may be* a virtue to-day. CHURCH'S UNPOPULAR STAND "Without doubt one of the reasons why the Catholic Church is so unpopular in certain quarters is that she resolutely refuses to submit the Ten Commandments of God and the moral teaching of Christ to the verdict of Gallup Polls. In this hospital the sacred right to life, which every unborn child possesses, will be religiously safeguarded, in spite of any popular theory to the contrary. No high-sounding phrases like "therapeutic induction" or "termination of pregnancy" will be allowed to obscure the moral evil of abortion, but 4he deliberate destruction of the unborn child will be called by its unvarnished and unpleasant name of murder, and,will never be countenanced." . .
