24 Nov 1941 - GALLUP POLLS IN AUSTRALIA Shepparton Advertiser (Vic. : 1887 - 1953), Monday 24 November 1941, page 1 GALLUP POLLS IN AUSTRALIA Local Representative Conducts Surveys Such contentious subjects as government lotteries, marriage loans, child endowment (whether or not it is satisfactory), race meetings (should week-end meetings be stopped during the war) and whether, in the event of the Labor Government being defeated, the voter would prefer an all party Government or an election, were among the eight questions asked by Mr Ralph Thompson in a recently completed survey in this district on behalf of Australian Public Opinion Polls (Gallup method). Results of this Australia-wide survey will be announced shortly. In view of the wide publicity these polls have been given in recent months when they have been used regularly to test the feeling of the American people towards the U.S.A.’s possible entry into the war, It is surprising to find that interviews conclude! i; Shepparton and district reveal that about 75 per cent, of the people have never heard of them. In this district 10 people were interviewed by Mr Thompson why selected them from the various age and income groups in the proportion laid down by the Gallup method. At the same time, interviewers throughout Australia were doing the same thing so as to get views from 1 all parts of the Commonwealth. There are five different ways in which an answer can be recorded, yes, no, an emphatic yes or no, or undecided. Special provision is made on forms for people who are quite unacquainted with the subject and unable to give an opinion. Interviewers are warned against any voice inflection or action that might bias people's replies. They are [instructed to repeat the question, if need be, in the exact words; but under no circumstances to amplify or explain it. POLL. FINDINGS It is not suggested that the leaders of Australia should blindly follow the poll findings. Popular opinion is sometimes now fully informed. But the polls will add to the evidence on which those with the responsibility of leadership base their estimates of public reaction. Moreover, the leaders can take steps to correct misunderstanding, where it appears to exist. Polls conducted in October revealed that 59 per cent, of Australians favored equal 'pay for men and women doing the same work, with 33 per cent, against and 8 per cent, undecided. When asked whether they would prefer to pay for the cost of the war ,by higher taxes or a rise in the cost of living many Australians were undecided. Fifty per cent, preferred heavier taxes, 11 per cent, higher cost of living, the rest had either no preference or no opinion. The majority of Australians (57 per cent.) showed themselves to be dissatisfied with price control with only 22 per cent, satisfied, 14 per cent undecided and 7 per cent, unable to give an opinion. Three to one favored an all party Government. ACCU RATE IN DIG ATOR The methods used by Dr. Gallup in “'determining what represents an accurate cross-section of the community and of obtaining the opinions of this picked sample on matters of public interest have been proved to be a remarkably' accurate indicator of the opinions of the nation as a whole during the years in which Gallup polls have been conducted in America and England. Most spectacular use of these polls was made in forecasting the Presidential elections in America when test polls conducted prior to the elections revealed that Roosevelt would be reelected and gave a fairly close indication of the margin.

12 Nov 1953 - THERE’S ROOM FOR A RELIGIOUS REVIVAL Advocate (Melbourne, Vic. : 1868 - 1954), Thursday 12 November 1953, page 15 THERE'S ROOM FOR A RELIGIOUS REVIVAL Extraordinary religious demonstrations in Queensland and New South Wales have been a feature of the Family Rosary Crusade, conducted by Father Patrick Peyton, C.S.C., which reached its culmination in the Sydney Archdiocese with the record crowd of 110,000 people in the Sydney Cricket Ground on 1 November. Father Peyton will open the Victorian State Campaign on IS November. Yet, in a recent Gallup Poll on the need, or otherwise, for a religious revival, it was interesting to see that Catholics were way down at the bottom of the list—the opinion of the majority of Catholics was that we don't need a religious revival at all. Catherine • Kaye 1 HAVE been wondering ever since why they thought that. I should imagine that at any given time, there's room for a religious revival, and I can think of no time when it was more needed that it is now. Possibly the people answering the question saw a religious revival as a series of camp-fire meetings; possibly they were thinking of the word "revival" in connection with the undignified and sentimental manifestations which have often accompanied the word. But need for a revival there is at all times. What is a mission but a renewal of faith, a polishing up of religious life, if that's all that's necessary, but often the occasion of a complete rebirth of faith? There's an urgent need for a renewal of faith today, when so many people have lost it. It would be rash and foolish to say that we are on the threshold of a new age of faith; on the face of things,-we couldnft be further away from one. Yet, possibly because they have lost faith and are looking for what they have lost or for something to take, its place, people in general seem more interested in religion today than they have been for years. 0. 'FTEN their interest centres on an imitation of faith which is sickly and pallid. Take the present passion for pseudo-Biblical novels and stories. I've read only one of these outpourings, which I found thoroughly bad, both in its writings and in the milk-and-water faith which is presented as Christianity. But to many people it and its kind have been something of an introduction to Christ and the men and women who lived and worked with Him. These books may have their uses. There is also a vogue for Biblical films. I have not seen one of these, and I wouldn't want to see one, if it meant that I saw no more films for the rest of my life. I did read the film story of Salome—an incredible piece of tampering with truth, and something which Catholics should avoid. In the story of Salome, as we learnt it from childhood, there's magnificent drama, which could have made a wonderful film. As it stood, however, it would scarcely have made a suitable vehicle for Miss Hayworth, so naturally it had to be amended. The sudden preoccupation with Biblical and Christian themes, however poorly handled, seems to me more an effect than a cause. People are looking for the faith; suddenly it has become thoroughly saleable. What I find more interesting than the spate of books and films is the fact that magazines and digests have, over the past few years, been obviously interested in writing with a religious flavour. What they have wanted is, not fiction, but fact and exposition. In digests in particular, I have read article after article in which the nature of faith, and the growth of faith, have been discussed. Leaving the romantic Biblical novel out of the picture, there's a continually growing body of good fiction which has as its theme the struggle between good and evil as expounded in the works of Mauriac and Greene. By no means all the writers of these books are Catholics. The search for God, which was once ignored by fiction writers other than Catholics, is now a standard theme. ANYONE WHO mixes with non-Catholics must realize their need. There seems little faith in the new generation. Many of their parents belonged to the various chinches, but for some reason their children are not following in their footsteps. This could be a mis-statement, but I don't think so. I know a widely assorted bunch of near-pagans, almost every one of whom came from a church-going family. But most of them are not happy to be near-pagans. Some are, of course. Some of them have no understanding of their need for God. They substitute other needs, and, I must confess, seem happy enough—far happier than those who are groping for faith. There's an astonishing number of converts around us, and an even greater number of potential converts. You can't .work out just what it is that starts a man thinking about the Church. As a rule, it's the very last thing he will think of. There is still violent and bitter prejudice against the Church. The nicest people, intelligent and tolerant, are apt to swell with indignation when the Church is mentioned. They are quite honest in their detestation of it, their contempt for it, or, rather, for what diey think it is. They are not hating the Church; they are hating their own interpretation of the Church. But, if they will read, if they can be argued with, they may change that picture; show them the true picture, and the rest may be left to God. I KNOW a trio of converts, a man and his wife, and another woman, all of whom were violently opposed to the Church. They had one thing in common, and only one, their contempt for the Church and for all who belonged to it. One of them could not believe that any person, intelligent or otherwise, could honestly subscribe to such a demanding and improbable creed. They brought forward all the usual arguments—our idolatry, the nonsense of confession, the laughableness of Transubstantiation. I would have said that not one of them would ever step inside the doors of the Church. The three of them are now Catholics: it cost each of them a great deal to take the final step—in one case, it meant complete exclusion from parents, brothers and sisters. I know a woman who is on the threshold of the Church, and who, for her own sake, must somehow or another be encouraged to cross it. She wants to be a Catholic— she was never prejudiced for or against the Church, but for several years she's been coming nearer and nearer to it. She'd have been a Catholic now, but for the fact that her husband is one of the happy prejudiced, one of the most charming, upright men I've met, possessed of all the Christian virtues, but with a blind spot where the Church is concerned. His wife doesn't want to hurt him; she has seen several disastrous mixed marriages, and she doesn't want to be part of one. At present, therefore, she's resolutely closing her eyes to what she knows she should do. There's a copy of Elected Silence on her bookshelf. It was given to her, but she won't read it. She admits that she is afraid to read it. Ti HERE'S another of our friends who, for years, has been searching for God, not that he'd admit it. He classed himself as an agnostic, willing to look for truth, and spending a lot of his time in the quest. He didn't want to look at Christianity—he'd been reared in a strictly religious home, he'd been a Sunday-school teacher until he went into the Army. He knew Protestantism, he wouldn't look at Catholicism. So he delved into Greek philosophy, into the writings of the Oriental mystics, into anything which might help him without making too many demands on him. Keith lent him, a long time ago now, the school textbook of apologetics. He read it, disagreed with it, but couldn't get his mind off it. A few weeks ago, he happened to mention that he had just bought a copy of the New Testament, which he was heading with profound interest. The inevitable series of arguments followed. A few days ago he told Keith that if he could accept the doctrine of Transubstantiation, he'd be a Catholic. He was one man who would, I'd have thought, been content to stay outside the Church for ever, but I shouldn't be at all surprised to find him within its doors before he dies. THE Catholic has an obligation to his fellowmen to know his religion, and to be able to present it to anyone wanting to ask questions about it. Make no mistake, any Catholic who is prepared to discuss his faith—and by discuss I mean discuss—will have ample opportunity of justifying himself. He must be prepared to swallow insults— not because people want to be insulting, but because quite often their misconceptions, honestly held, are an insult. He must realize that and accept it—he'll get to know very quickly whether people are interested in what he says or whether, as happens rarely, they are baiting him. There's not much point in arguing witli the baiter, but he is the only person whose questions should not be answered. If you're prepared to discuss your religion, you may see no results for your work. That doesn't matter; you've no idea what one remark, one false idea exposed in its falsity, may do. You've not setting out to make converts; in the long run, only God can bring a soul into its home; but you are setting out to help clear away a whole lot of mental brambles. You can't do it, of course, unless you're thoroughly grounded in your faith. You need to know exacdy what you believe and why you believe it. If you're hazy about a few tilings, look them up. Apologetics make fascinating reading; so do the stories of conversion which have been told by hundreds of people. To the born Catholic, these tales of quest and of spiritual adventure are a revelation. Every Catholic should read one of them every so often, if only that he might realize what a treasure he was given, and how much other people have suffered and sacrificed that they, too, might possess it. The world does need a religious revival. It needs to see truth again, and to recognize its faith. The need is enormous; a dreadful price of unhappiness is being paid today by those who have lost the security of faith. We are asked to help our neighbour— surely it's even more important to help him, when he asks our help, in spiritual than in material things.

03 Aug 1938 - SEWERAGE POLL Shepparton Advertiser (Vic. : 1887 - 1953), Wednesday 3 August 1938, page 9 SEWERAGE POLL Demand by Kyabram Ratepayers. They are, he says: (Ti Five million young men, pre-dominantly Democrats, did not vote because tbey are in the armed ser-vices. , (2) One million workers have changed their residences because of war jobs and were ineligible to vote. 06 Apr 1946 - Call For Cancellation Of Greek Elections Sydney Morning Herald (NSW : 1842 - 1954), Saturday 6 April 1946, page 1 Call For Cancellation Of Greek Elections ATHENS, April 5 (A.AR).-Greek Left Wing parties have asked the British, French, United States, and Russian Governments to cancel the recent Greek elections because the average poll was only 45 per cent, and irregularities have been proved. The Populist (royalist) and Centre bloc leaders have formed a coalition Government. The Left Wing parties boycotted the elections. The Greek Regent, Archbishop Damaskinos, tendered his resignation to King George of Greece in London immediately he had sworn in the new Cabinet. Judge Poulitzas has been I nominated' Prime Minister for the (tinwwbeingiï-'V. n,i The last count gave the strength of the parties as follows: Populists, 588,809; Centre bloc, 207,323; Liberals. 156,636; Zervas Party (ex-treme Rightists), 62,117; Royalists, 25.032. The new Ministers sworn in are:Foreign Affairs: M. Tsaldaris (Popu- list). Interior: John Theotokis (Populist). Defence: Petros Mavroniihailis (Populist). Co-ordination: M. Stcphanopoulos (Populist). _ Communications: uenerai oonaias (National Liberal). The three Centre leaders, George Papandreous, Paneyatis Kanellopoulis, and Sophocles Venizelos, will be Ministers without Portfolio, with the rank of Vice-Premier. Concessions Made The new Government is considered to represent a considerable concession on the part of the Populists,' says Reuter's Athens correspondent. Their electoral success is generally attributed to the popular belief that they intend to bring back the King immediately. The new Parliament will meet on April 29, and will determine the date of the plebiscite on the return of the monarch. Parliament will, it is stated, take British advice into con- sideration. The new Premier, Judge Poulitzas, will hold office until the Populist Party chiefs can meet in the next few weeks to elect a leader, who will take over the post. Poulitzas, who has been a Judge for 35 years, told the Associated Press of America's corres-pondent that he was, reluctant to accept the Premiership arid agreed only because he felt he would be doing a service to Greece. The Liberals who. led by the former Premier, M. Sofoulis, form the Opposition, are stated to be deter-mined to fight for postponement of the plebiscite until March, 1948, the date advocated in British official quarters. The Foreign Minister, M. Tsaldaris, told the Associated Press of America after the conference from which the coalition resulted: "After a very long spell, Greece is returning to normal political life." M. Sophocles Venizelos said the Government would hold the plebiscite on the future of the monarchy under internationally recognised conditions, asking the Allies for any advice should the need arise._

19 Jan 1948 - CHURCH ATTENDANCES Sydney Morning Herald (NSW : 1842 - 1954), Monday 19 January 1948, page 2 CHURCH ATTENDANCES A recent Gallup poll on church-going in . Australia had shown that one Australian in thr.ee ?had attended a religious service on either of the two Sundays before the survey was taken, the Rev. R. H. Doust said at Bur-wood Methodist Church last night. He said the result was a reflec-tion not upon the Churches, but upon those who failed to attend them. The Christian Church was not on its trial. It had an integral and essential place in Christian civilisa- tion. "The Church is of primary value to the community," he said, "but it can function effectively only when it has the personal support of those who believe in it. "The drift from the Churches should cause grave concern. "There is a definite relation be-tween this drift and lowered ethical standards, child delinquency, and widespread indiscipline and lawless- ness."

21 Apr 1948 - Gallup Poll On Migrants "Frightening" Sydney Morning Herald (NSW : 1842 - 1954), Wednesday 21 April 1948, page 3 Gallup Poll On Migrants "Frightening" » STAFF CORRESPONDENT. LONDON, April 20.-In the House of Commons last night, Squadron-Leader M. C. Hollis (Cons.) asked the Government if it could verify a report that 42 per cent, of British people wished to leave the country if they could. He said the figure had been given in a "frightening" Gallup Poll published by a London paper. The President of the Board of Trade, Mr. H. Wilson, said members should get the matter in the right proportion. Nearly every time he opened a newspaper-or some news-papers-he found a lot was made of the desire of people to leave Britain, which was under a Socialist Government, he said. The number of people who had left, however, was only about half those who left after World War I, when there had been the same shortage of shipping.

05 Oct 1954 - FEDERAL NOTEBOOK Government Men Restive: Changes In Cabinet Sought Sydney Morning Herald (NSW : 1842 - 1954), Tuesday 5 October 1954, page 2 FEDERAL NOTEBOOK Government Men Restive: Changes In Cabinet Sought By OUR CANBERRA CORRESPONDENT For a political alliance which, according to the latest Gallup Poll, is at its most popular for 17 years, the Liberal Country Party Government is an unhappy organisation. Among its over-enthusiastic back-benchers there has been some return to the mood of disillusion- ment which was common in the 1951 slump. This time the back-benchers are not worried about losing their seats — but they are worried about losing the'' incentive to stay in politics. MOST of the younger men in the Govern-ment are professional or businessmen to whom Federal Parliament doesn't mean financial promotion. As mere votes in the House, they do not even have the con-solation of taking part in the moulding of national policy. As Parliament went into a brief recess last week, Government back-benchers had to swallow the fact that they had been overrid-den by Cabinet again, this time on an issue — National Service — on which some of them had fought Cabinet's decision publicly in Parliament, and on which others had threatened to put up a last-ditch resistance in the Govern-ment party room. Much of the dissatisfaction sprang from a more basic discon-tent with the fact that the doors of the Cabinet room are still closed to newcomers. THE illness of the Postmaster- General, Mr. Anthony, who will be off duty for two or three months, provoked speculation that he might resign from Cabinet and make room for one of the disgruntled outsiders. Mr. Anthony's absence, how-ever, revealed a paradox — that although the Liberal Party's effec-tiveness could be increased by the replacement of several Ministers, the Country Party has all its strength on top and faces a pre-carious future when they go. With its Leader, Sir Arthur Fadden, the Deputy Leader, Mr. McEwen, and the Acting Leader, Mr. Anthony, all away, control of the party fell back temporarily into the hands of 74-year-old Sir Earle Page, its prewar leader. The political experience and instinct of these four men have in recent years given the other-wise declining Country Party a power far exceeding its numerical strength in Parliament. SIR EARLE, still one of the shrewdest politicians in Can-berra and remarkably fit — he is one of the few politicians who play tennis on the Parliament House courts — must nevertheless be near the end of his political career. In fact, he was reported to be ready to retire at the last elec-tions if he could find a suitable successor. Speculation still surrounds the future of Sir Arthur Fadden, who has not fully recovered from his accident on the eve of the elec-tions, and is under family pres-sure to give up the arduous Trea-sury portfolio. Mr. Anthony has had several serious illnesses since 1952 and was given medical advice two years ago to resign from the Ministry. Mr. McEwen has also had pro-longed periods off duty, with a complaint caused by over-strain. As these four influential and experienced Ministers, sooner or later, go out of politics, they will leave a gap which other members of the Country Party cannot ade-quately fill. What illness threatens to do to the Country Party, only the Prime Minister, Mr. Menzies, can do to the Liberal Party-replace some of its Ministers. But there is no sign that he proposes to do so, despite the need for new ideas in his Ministry. THE Menzies Government made a reluctant return to controls last week when it re-imposed quota restrictions on goods which make up about half Australia's imports. Importers of these goods can still buy as much as they did in 1950-51; therefore the claims that the new restrictions will not cause shortages to the public are ob-viously justified. But the restrictions go against the grain of the Government, as they afford local industry just enough margin of protection against overseas competition to make it feel comfortable again. The Menzies Government's policy is to leave protection to the Tariff Board, which issued a hard-hitting annual report last week warning high-cost industries that it would not protect them at || MR. H. L. ANTHONY || public expense against inefficiency or normal business risks. But politicians have found, since 1952, that whatever the dangers of import restrictions they do not make a Government || SIR EARLE PAGE || unpopular. And the 1952 re-strictions saved employment in Australia. The new restrictions are the kind which will make everybody happy except the prospective competitor. Their danger is that they suit the established importer as much as they suit the local manufacturer. A prospective new importer cannot get a leg in while quotas based on 1950-51 imports remain. THERE are reports that an attempt is being prepared to get three Victorian Right-wing Parliamentarians expelled from the Labour Party — Mr. Stan Keon and his close associate, Mr. John Mullens, and Mr. William Bourke. All three are now clearly op-posed to the leadership of Dr. Evatt. Those who are planning the move are said to be trying to get it initiated at the next meeting of the Federal executive of the Lab- our Party, after the Federal Par-liament ends its Budget session. It is pretty safe to forecast that even if the idea gets a first run, it will not win. "Secret" motions passed at the last executive meeting, condemn-ing Dr. Evatt's failure to consult the party on major issues, do not indicate that the executive is likely to swallow drastic measures sponsored by Evatt supporters. But the move is significant as an indication of the tactics being followed. The Left-wing group, led by Mr. Ward, is obviously using the dispute surrounding Dr. Evatt to embarrass and isolate the Right-wingers, who are not a united group and are not led by anybody. Amid free talk of a possible split in the Labour Party, the opposing forces are all trying to hold the big end of the stick in-case the split comes.

13 Nov 1954 - Letters Sydney Morning Herald (NSW : 1842 - 1954), Saturday 13 November 1954, page 2 Letters TO-DAY'S CHOICE FOR VOTERS Opposing Opinions On Hotel Hours Sir,-I believe that the re-cent result of the Gallup Poll taken throughout Australia is most significant. States which already have 10 p.m. closing showed a decided maj-ority in favour of retaining it; States with 6 p.m. closing averaged merely a bare maj-ority for its retention. Surely if 10 p.m. closing were the chaotic home-breaker the Churches claim, people living amid the chaos would not vote for its continuance. I am cer-tain that were 10 p.m. given a trial in this State for 12 months a referendum held at the end of that time would give a result similar to other 10 p.m. States. JOSEPH dLARGO. Manly Vale. Sir,-1 am not at all happy about the choice on Saturday. While I would like to have a drink with my husband at night, I do not think merely closing the hotels from 6.30 to 7.30 p.m. will avoid the 5 to 6 p.m. swill. What would be better, I think, would be to close from 2 to 6 p.m. Husbands would then come home for dinner first. EMILY EM BRYANT. Hamilton. -Sir,-Is it imagined that only those who voted for 10 p.m. in 1947 had an experimental know-ledge of the result of later clos-ing, and that those who voted for 6 p.m. were without such know-ledge? I have spoken to >many and those who remember late closing in N.S.W. speak of it almost with bated breath. From experience, they will not vote for a return of 10 p.m. They ,know that it will mean an increase in broken homes and a general social de- cline. WILLIAM F. HAYWARD. The Rectory, Riverstone. Sir,-The official figures of convictions for drunkenness in the various States last year, as published in the "Sun-Herald" of November 7, are indeed en-lightening. I quote them hereunder in pre-cis form for perusal by all those who claim later closing of hotels necessarily means more drunken- ness: Queensland. 10 p.m. closing, convictions 1.9 p.c. of population. Western Australia, 9 p.m. clos-ing; convictions 1 p.c. Tasmania, 10 p.m.closing; con-victions 0.25 p.c. New South Wales, 6 p.m. clos-ing; convictions 2.1 p.c. Bondi. STATISTICS. Sir,-The issue concerns only that section of the community that prefers a mild stimulant to a less interesting beverage, and as that section docs hot demand that the whole of the community shall follow its example, there is no valid reason why its liberties should be curtailed for the satis-faction of some other section with distorted views. There arc three Australian States that enjoy more sensible hours and if a referendum were taken on whether present hours should continue or be curtailed there would be an overwhelming majority for the former. D. DUNCAN. Glebe Point. Sir,-In spite of having later closing in Queensland we still have the degrading "pig-swill" be-tween 5 p.m. and 6 p.m. There are now two rushes-5 to 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. Rev. T. REES THOMAS, President. Queensland Marriage Guidance Council. Sir,-In your leader of Nov. 11 you advocate 10 p.m. clos-ing, and the reasons you put for-ward arc all very true and logi-cal. Nevertheless I intend to vote against 10 p.m. for one reason and one only: the interested partics in my opinion have conven-iently bypassed the most vital aspect of the whole sorry busi-ness-the alcoholic content of Australian beer. In past years I have drunk beer in many countries and have been able to sit all evening drinking without harmful effects, but 1 could never do that in Australian hotels owing to the strong alco-holic content of our beer. JAMES T. COLEMAN. Engadine. Sir,-Let us be honest about it. Would 10 o'clock closing benefit the women and children of this State in any way .what- ever? They number two-thirds of the population. S. BAILEY. Epping. Sir,-I venture to predict that if 10 o'clock closing is voted for it will not be long before a cry goes up for 11 o'clock closing. People will then be wanting to have a "civilised drink" after the theatre and will be disappointed at not being able to. have it if closing is as early as 10 o'clock. DAVID S. REYNOLDS. Cumnock. Sir,-I am well aware of the disadvantages of what has been called the 6 o'clock "swill." But, as a moderate drinker, I know that 1 would prefer to take a few bottles of beer home with me and have a drink with my wife during our evenings together. But it is not possible to buy bottled beer in any sort of regular fashion. Therefore I am told by the liquor interests that, if they are given the right to keep the hotels open till 10, I can go with my wife, leave the children at home or send them to the pictures, and have our drinks at the local hotel. Well, Australian hotels being what they are, they are the last place to which 1 would want to take my wife. For there is no guarantee whatever that with later trading hours there would be any material change in the conduct and control of drinking places, which arc largely the points of distribution for brewery products. H. J. WELLS, j Bexley. '

October .10.— A Gallup poll returned a 53 per cent popular vote for President Roosevelt and 47 for Mr. Wendell Willkle. The Gallup poll warns, however. Mr. Willkies gains have been so widespread that later re-iorts from t he survey probably will show that the two candidates are about even in electoral votes, or with Mr. Willkie slightly ahead. It must not he forgotten, however, thai President Roosevelt's intensive campaign -speaking has just begun, and his forthcoming radio addresses ntav hall and reverse the Willkie trend.

Mr. Churchill's speech served as a reminder that the war will be wpn or losf in the West,, that America's tools safely delivered will be vital to victory. Thus Americans are further convinced that they must assure the delivery of the tools at whatever cost. How goon this sentiment will crystalise to the point where the President and Congress feel warranted to go "all out" is anybody's guess, but, certainly Mr. Churchill's words have provided a oew impetus. Mr. Rockefeller's letter is an example of how many leading Americans are thinking. Anger Rising At Lindbergh - v . Likewise one notes the rising , anger of the public against such defeatists as Lindbergh.Moreovcr.there-iis ,.an indication that many organisations;. particularly great : war veterans,; who have Ions advocated a peaceful attitude, are now. being outspoken against the . Axis, and are demanding strong measures to protect cargoes of American goods to Britain. Commenting briefly on Mr. Churchill's speech, the fall of Athens, and the superb fight by the . Greeks, 'Australians and New Zealanders, the New York Times editorially says: "The battle which , will determine England's fate is not: in -the Mediterranean, though- the importance of controlling that sea- remains, but in the Atlantic. In the outcome of the battle the fortunes of America, are involved hardly less than Britain's. Therefore our help for that battle must come and will come on an increasing scale."

23 Mar 1962 - THOUGHT FOR THE WEEK Victor Harbour Times (SA : 1932 - 1986), Friday 23 March 1962, page 2 THOUGHT FOR THE WEEK I wonder how many of us take prayer very seriously? It would be interesting to see the results if a Gallup Poll were taken to discover how many Australians pray regularly. 1 am suse a lot of people do not. .rv numucr 01 v.nnsuan writers have declared that prayer is the 'mightiest force in the world'. If this is so, why is it that the majority of folk show by their indifferent attitude to prayer that they consider it almost a waste of time? One of the major reasons for this lack of faith in prayer is that it is often misunderstood. Too often we approach God only when we want something, and then we endeavour to 'twist His arm' until He gives us what we demand. And yet prayer can be much more than this, and indeed must be if it is to be a force in the world and in our lives. 'Prayer is being with God', said Margaret Cropper, and here is a thought that has been a tremendous help to so many people, and has enabled them, in a wonderful way, to tap the peace, poise, and power that God wants us all to have. The Bible puts this thought another way: 'Be still, and know that 1 am God'. A good friend of mine expressed the same truth in still another way. She said, 'If you love someone there are times when you will go to that person, not because you want to ask them for something, or tell them something, but simply because you want to be with them. If we love God, then we should make time every day just to be with Him. If we can learn to do this — and it is not easy — to sit in the stillness and be aware of God's nearness and 'listen' to Him, we will have learned one of the methods by which prayer can transform our lives; we will begin to understand why men have said prayer is the 'mightiest force in the world'. G. J. LORD, Minister, Church ot Christ, Victor Harbour.

21 Jul 1982 - Toops help young drivers Victor Harbour Times (SA : 1932 - 1986), Wednesday 21 July 1982, page 15 [?] A recent Gallup Poll showed that 70 percent of people think that the driving age should be raised from 16 to 18. It is unlikely that this will come about and one of the main reasons is that such a move would effectively wipe out the Student Driver Education Program. Mt. Compass Area School has run a student driver education program for its Year 11 students for the past 4 years thanks to Tooo Motors who supply the car. 'We are pleased to think that we are helping young drivers to learn the correct techniques instead of being taught by people who possibly don't know how to drive correctly themselves', said Peter Toop. Ian Pye, a secondary teacher has recently qualified as a driving instructor, giving Mt. Compass two instructors. The other is Bill Jerram. 'Correct defensive driving is much more involved than most people appreciate', said Ian. 'It can take us anywhere between seven and twenty hours just to teach one student'. In Mt. Compass' case, the effort which has gone into the student driver education program has been very worthwhile. Parents have noted a considerable improvement in the standard of driving in the students who have undergone the scheme and the students themselves are very enthusiastic about it. ? 23 Feb 1949 - TEA STATISTICS South Coast Bulletin (Southport, Qld. : 1929 - 1954), Wednesday 23 February 1949, page 7 TiEA STATISTICS Surprising as it may seem, the average Australian man drinks just as much tea as the average Australian woman. A Gallup Poll just completed by the Australian Tea Bureau bears this out. The poll also revealed that 12 per cent of the Australian population drinks black tea without any additions. 30 per cent milk only and the remaining 58 per cent add milk and sugar. , 4 per cent of the population drinks 12 cups or more a day, 10 per cent drink as much as ten cups, 69 per cent drink between 3 and 9 cups daily and 17 per cent drink .less than 3 cups daily. On a. nation wide basis the average Australian drinks 3.8 cups a day, or 1400 cups a year Some tea drinkers, particularly miners working on the low levels at great temperatures regularly consume as much as 40 cups a day. It is estimated that in a life time the average Australian consumes 35,000 gallons of hot tea, or 250 times his or own weight. Recognised as the cheapest and most popular beverage in the world, tea is consumed to the extent of 300,000,000,000 cups each year.

17 Oct 1894 - GENERAL ELECTIONS IN BELGIUM. Age (Melbourne, Vic. : 1854 - 1954), Wednesday 17 October 1894, page 5 GENERAL ELECTIONS IN BELGIUM. THE FIRST MANHOOD SUFFRAGE -POLL LONDON, 16th October. The general elections for the Belgian Chamber of Representatives, conducted for tho first time under the manhood suffrage system, took place yesterday, and resulted in cain to the Socialists, and losses to both tho Catholic and Liberal parties. Tlio Socialists havo won 19, and tho Liberals havo lost 17 seats. Tho Catholic party, though losing 8 seats formerly held by supporters, lias still a working majority of the Chamber. Tho Belgian Parliament consists of a Senate, the members of whioh ore elected partly direotiy and partly indiroetly for eight years. The provincial counoils elect one section of the Senate at tho proportional basis of two sonators for every 500,000 inhabitants ; tho other section is elected by the Ghamher of Representative electors. Tlio representatives are eleoted for four years, one half retiring ovory two years, except after a dissolution, when general olections follow. Every citizen over 25 years of ago is entitled to a voto if domiciled for not less than a year in th. same commune. In addition every eitizen, married or widower, over 35 years of ago with children, and paying at least 5 f. a year houso tax, has a supplementary vote ; so also has every citizen over 25 years of age who owns real estate worth 2000 f., or draws 100 f. a year interest from Savings Bank or Belgian funds investments. Two extra votos are given to diplomaed and professional men. Per the Marine Underwriters' Association.!

13 Jul 1988 - Survey finds local paper ahead by a country mile Times (Victor Harbor, SA : 1987 - 1999), Wednesday 13 July 1988, page 4 Survey finds local paper ahead by a country mile South Australian country newspapers have launched their biggest marketing campaign yet to promote the results of a survey which confirms the superior power of the country Press. The survey by the Roy Morgan Research Centre — the people who conduct the authoritative Morgan Gallup poll — found that country newspapers are by far the best way to reach country people. The 'local paper' was the first choice of the great majority of country people looking for local, new and shopping information compared with country TV and radio, daily newspapers and the rural press. For Instance 91 percent of people said the local paper was the 'most helpful' for information on bargains at local retail stores. Only 50 percent mentioned tv, 2 percent preferred radio and 2 percent said metropolitan papers. And 78 percent prefer the local paper to find out about supermarket goods and prices, compared with only 12 percent for tv, one percent for radio and 9 percent for metropolitan papers. SA country newspapers have a very high readership. A staggering 87 percent of country South Australians regularly read their local paper. The next most popular is the 'Sunday Mail' with 49 percent and, well behind, are 'The Advertiser' 41 percent, 'The News' 26 percent and the 'Stock Journal' 6 percent. The results of the SA survey — involving 400 interviews in 10 country towns and surrounding areas — were further strengthened by similar surveys by the Roy Morgan Research Centre in Victoria, New South Wales and Western Australia. All four surveys, conducted simultaneously from October 24 to November 8 last year, concluded that country papers are the most useful, the most trustworthy and the most effective In country areas. The Country Press Association of SA Is delighted with the results of the survey, the most extensive of Us type yet conducted. 'The Morgan Research Centre, a totally independent market research company, has come up with conclusive proof of what the newspapers have been telling their readers and advertisers for years - that the local paper is the best and most effective communicator in the country', said the association's marketing committee chairman Mr Richard Peake, of Naracoorte. The Country Press Association is now using the Morgan Report to 'sell' the effectiveness of the local paper to advertising agencies and national advertisers in the cities and to the business people and organisations in local communities. Using a Burke and Wills theme and the catchline 'Explore the country Press', the association last week called on Adelaide advertising people and presented promotional material and an 'explorers kit' — an old-fashioned calico bag filled with fresh damper, tea, sugar, treacle, dried fruit, cheese and apples. The 90 newspapers in the association — 28 in SA as well as Broken Hill's Barrier Daily Truth and the Katnerine Times In the NT -will promote the Morgan Report in their local areas. 02 Mar 1946 - May Risk Throne Warwick Daily News (Qld. : 1919 -1954), Saturday 2 March 1946, page 1 Bar to DSO was awarded to Major-General J. J. Murray, DSO, MC, VD, by the Duke of Gloucester at Government House. Picture shows the Duke chatting to Major General Murray after the investiture. May Risk Throne Hirohito Conducting Own "Gallup Poll" NEW YORK: The Tokio cor- respondent of the New York Times says that Emperor Hiro-hito completed a 6-hour motor car inspection of the bombed out section of Tokio, visiting schools, emergency dwellings and large stores. Hirohito was dressed in a European suit and grey felt hat, which he raised to acknowledge the applause from "banzai" shouting crowds gathered at the doors of Ginza departmental store. The Communist Party handed the Imperial Household Minis- try's resolution on Thursday at- tacking Hirohito's personal ap-pearance as "designed to help the election campaigns of reactionary parties trying to frustrate the de-mocratisation of Japan." It de-manded that the Government prohibit electioneering by "the Emperor and all other war cri-minals." It was the first time that the Communists had classed Hirohito as a criminal, although they pre-viously demanded his abdication. The Tokio correspondent of the New York Herald Tribune says that high Japanese sources said that Hirohito may risk the throne by holding a plebiscite at the general elections on April 10 to determine the destiny of the Tanno system. The revelation dovetails with Hirohito's unprece-dented public inspection of troops, in which he renounced his hermit like existence behind the deep moats in Tokio Palace to chat to humble workers and air raid vic-tims. Observers termed the trips "popularity tests" whereby the Emperor is conducting his own Gallup poll.

13 Aug 1952 - MOST PARENTS WANT HOMEWORK FOR THEIR CHILDREN Armidale Express and New England General Advertiser (NSW : 1856 - 1861; 1863 - 1889; 1891 - 1954), Wednesday 13 August 1952, page 3 MOST PARENTS WANT CHILDREN Of 350 parents questioned recently by die Armidale High School in a gallup poll on homework, only 1.4 per cent, believed that homework should be abolished. A majority of the parents said their children should do from one to two hours' homework each night. Results of the gallup poll were revealed at a meeting of the High School Parents and Citizens' Association last night by the headmaster (Mr. E. R. cs. Watson). Mr. Watson said one of the parents who advocated the abolition of homework was an important educationist in Armidale who had strong arguments to support his, case. Questions asked in the sur vey were:— Do you think the child is at present doing too much, suffi cient or too little Homework?; How long each night do1 you believe your children should spend on homework:' none, half hour, hour, two I hours, or more? I I Has the child set hours for (homework? j [ Do you usually find - out; whether set homework has been completed? I Are you able to provide a' quiet, well-lighted spot for j homework? ! In attitude to study, do you' find your child is very keen, j interested, indifferent *or hos tile? When do- you expect the child to complete his or herj schooling—at the school leav-l ing age' 015), at Intermediate' ^Certificate stage, ^at , Ueaving Certificate stage,- sifter' College PT University? ; 5 Mr. Watson analjrsed the results of * the survey a§ follows: Of the 350 parents questioned, 78.8 per cent, believed their children had enough homework, 18.5 per cent. said, not, enough, 2.57 -per cent,; too, much. ' • ,-m More than 66 per cent, saidj an hour or an hour and a half each night should be devoted to homework, 15 per cent, said! half - an hour, 13.6 per cent, j two hours, 3.2 per cent, more than two hours, and 1.4 per cent, none at all. In answer to the question on set hours for homework, 49 per cent said yes, 51 per cent, no. Replies to the question on parental supervision revealed that it decreased as children went further up the school. Of parents with children in first year, 86' per cent, saidj they checked set homework,! second year 76 per cent., third year 69 per cent., fourth year 57 per cent., lifth year 60 per cent., T - - Mr. Watson said this / decrease was probably due to the fact that as the child advanced in the school, he went beyond the scholastic capabilities of his parents. Fourteen per cent, admitted they could not provide a quiet, well-lit spot for study, 86 per cent, claimed they could. Most "Interested" Eighteen per cent, of the parents said their children were* "very keen" in their attitude to study, 65.5 per cent, said "interested," 14.8 per cent, "indifferent" and. .25 per cent, "hostile." > * "Generally the figures on the attitude of the children to study are a good commentary on the tone of the school," Mr. Watson said. Of children covered by the survey, 13.5 per cent, are expected to leave at about 15, 42.6 per cent, at I.C. stage, and; 24.3 per cent, at L.C. standard. Nineteen point five per cent, aim at tertiary studies. Mr. Watson quoted some of the comments made by the parents:— Parent of a second year girl: "In my opinion the child should not have to do homework. With what they learn at school during the day, they should be left to think over. They should be allowed to relax and refresh their brains for the following day. Like adults, if they work all day, and then return to work at night, they get tired and brain weary' - Parent of a second year girl: "Too much homework tends to frustrate the pupil. Homework/ should never be indiscriminately. handed out. Too much work makes Jill a dull girl." Parent of a third year boy: "My son catches fhe school! bus at 7.30 a.m. and arrives home between 5.30. and 6 p.m. Were it not for the travelling, I consider he should be spending two hours per night on i homework and study." | Parent of a third year girl: "My daughtej* has a set Bedftime, set home duties and'other (activities such as church and j music. She is expected to fit any extra homework in wher ever she can without foregoing, other activities and responsibilities. She actually averages more than one and a half, hours per night, but the extra work is done at odd moments that would otherwise be wasted, or at week-ends." Parent of a second year boy: "I would be in favour of an hour's homework if I were able to provide the children with a quiet, well-lit spot, but we are a large family living in a small, four-roomed house, and consequently noise is an everyday thing. ■ "I am finding it hard even to"1 concentrate to. write this .and there is "no quiet, • well-lit comfortable spot in the house as noise from one room penetrates just as loudly to the others. I think it is asking too much of children in such cases to try to do homework. "In my son's case, he has an after-school job till shops shut to help provide him with clothing and pocket money. "I think you will agree that it is essential for boys of hisage to have some money to spend on themselves." Mr. Watson . added a comment from the Education [Gazette of November 1, 1951:— * "Homework should always be regarded as a supplement I. to school work and not a substitute for it. Teachers should not attempt to have . pupils learn at home work which they, have "failed to teach them at school. "Many parents desire 4 reasonable amount of home-* work for their children. "It is to" be remembered, however, that if parents have expressed unwillingness to allow children to dp homework, teachers must recognise that .this is a matter of parental * responsibility." Comments by members of the P. and C.:— Mr. E. C. Connor: "I fed teachers are passing the buck when they ask if parents chick their children's homework. Parents shouldn't have to stand over their children." Mr. H. A. Grantham: "Nothing has been said about the poor parents and what they have to put up with. I estimate that I will have 12 years of enduring homework. I think homework should be limited to v three nigi/ a week to give parents a spell oh the OthOB nights." "

08 Jan 1948 - Puzzled People Daily Examiner (Grafton, NSW : 1915 - 1954), Thursday 8 January 1948, page 2 Puzzled People HIS is the title given to a book recently published in London. By means of Mass Observation, similar to the. familiar Gallup poll, a cross section of the population of a busy London suburb was asked many pertinent questions regarding religion, and the answers are revealing and deserve consideration. Most of the replies show a1 belief in God "more or less." Atheists and sceptics are comparatively few, which is an encouraging, sign, but when incomes to explaining details of belief, accounts are so vague, or so conflicting, that the reviewers of the poll can only describe thoee ccnce ned as "puzzled people." For example the non-believer prays as frequently as the believer, but when asked to whom his prayers are addressed, he :e-- plies, "I don't know, but prayer seems to help me." Again many , professed believers attend church less regularly than the non- ; believer. " Some nominal church adherents attack the church bitterly, and stay away from it deliberately, while many agnostics, attend church "in case there is something in it after all." Further, it is the "average Christian" who decries much of the Christian faith, while the non-Christian is inclined to believe , in the Very things he professes to deny. Even some regular church-goers -admit that they can't see the necessity of prayer, and never pray "unless in a jam." No wonder "Puzzled People" is the verdict of the critics, arid such a phrase certainly reflects the bewilderment of the . times and clearly reveals the necessity of deeper thought before a fairer day can dawn. Whsn asked to explain: the purpose c-f life most people replied that there wasn't one, although a few said they found it in astrology— man's fate being controlled by the Indifference, uncertainty, superstition, these things may well explain why the bureaucrats are finding human life so 'easy to control, for if man no longer has a personal belief or philosophy, Stale control will fill the vacuum. Socialisation may indeed be better than superstition, but it is a far cry from the robust and dynamic Christian faith which actuated our .forefathers in those times we now sc easily despise. Calories and. controls can no more nourish the soul than the bread and circuses of the later Caesars, whose worldly' policy quickly wrecked a mighty Empire. . ' Puzzled people need a spiritual nourishment if their .proh- . lems %re to be solved, and the final verdict cf the mass-reviewers is that/men are blindly striving for a spiritual enlightenment which only sound and wise Christian teaching can -provide. ,

04 Mar 1949 - AUSTRALIANS ARE DRINKERS OF TEA Whyalla News (SA : 1940 - 1963), Friday 4 March 1949, page 4 AUSTRALIANS ARE DRINKERS OF TEA Surprising as it may seem, the average Australian man drinks just as Efiuch tea as the average Australian woman. A Gallup Poll just completed by the Australian Tea Bureau bears this out. The poll also revealed that 12 per cent, of the Australian population drinks black tea without any additions, 30 per cent, add milk only and the remaining 58 per cent, add milk and sugar. Four per cent, of the population drinks 12 cups or more a day, 10 per cent, drink as much as 10 cups, 69 per cent, drink between three and nine cups daily and 17 per cent, drink less than three cups daily. On a nation wide basis the average Australian drinks 3.8 cups a day, or 1,400 cups a year. Some tea drinkers, particularly miners working on the low levels at great temperatures regularly consume as much as 40 cups a day. It is estimated that in a lifetime the average Australian consumes 3,500 gallons of hot tea, or 250 times his or her own weight. Recognised as the cheapest and most popular beverage in the world, tea is consumed to the extent of 300,000,000,000 cups each year.

26 Sep 1941 - “Gallup Polls” Come to Australia Pioneer (Yorketown, SA : 1898 - 1960), Friday 26 September 1941, page 3 "Gallup Polls" Come to Australia The first of the "Australian Public Opinion Polls,based on the Gallup Polls which are regularly conducted in America aud England, has just been completed. A questionnaire, covering a variety of subjects, was submitted to a cross-section of the Australian public. Depending entirely on the science of statistic- to give him amazingly accurate estimates of American public opinion. Dr. G. H. Gallup, head of the American Institute of Public Opinion, has achieved considerable fame. Australian Public Opinion Polls will carry out hi- system in Australia. S.' accurately did Dr. Gallup calculate the margin by which Kouscvelt would defeat Willkie at the 1940 presidential. election—giving figures, State by Stale—that I >r. Henry C. Link, a statistical expert, said the result was miraculous. Judging by American experience, publication ol results of poll?, of Australia!! public opinion will help to speed up tlu machinery of > ur democracy. Newspapers in eacli capital city have / agreed ici publish the findings of Australian Public Opinion Polls, which has been registered as a nun-profit company. The newspapers concerned will pay for articles announcing the findings, and that amount will fmancc the organisation. In England, Gallup's method—which will be the one used in Australia—has achieved results comparable with those in the United States. Last August, when the Director of the British Institute of Public Opinion went to America for a special course of study, he •was asked by Government officials whether the polls could, and would, continue to operate in his absence. The Australian director (Mr. Roy Morgan) has also been to America, and lias studied Dr. Gallup's methods by working with his staff. Recently, to test the efficacy of the Gallup method of "sampling" the population, a poll was taken of electors of Boothby in South Australia. Remarkably reliable results were achieved. Some unthinking persons have suggested that the polls have been established for the rather useless purpose of forecasting election results. But the real purpose of the organisation is to conduct miniature referendums, using statistically accurate samples of public opinion. The number of people interviewed, after a certain number, does not matter, because, if the first sample is an accurate cross-section, further votes will only duplicate opinions * already expressed. 09 Oct 2000 - Ellis Chaser (Glebe, NSW : 1999 - 2005), Monday 9 October 2000, page 15 Ellis Curious about the seemingly random fluctuations of the polls? lob Ellis explains why Newspoll Is Inaccurate more than 50% of the time. Five hundred thousand people, it seems, who are voting for Beailey this month were voting for Howard last month and for Beailey the month before. Sometimes, according to Newspoll, they change their Yote every fortnight. Things are just that volatile. Do you know any of these people? Statistically speaking you should. If you have twenty adult friends then one of them, statistically, will be acting in this way. Howard, Beazley, Howard, Beailey, can't make up Ms mind. You know the one. Of course you do. You don't? It was this that made me suspect mat some of the polls -Newspoll, for instance - were badly wrong. Because if they were right, and if, as they said, sixty percent of Australians on average were favouring Labor in the states and only fifty-two percent federally, then seven hundred thousand people are currently voting for both Howard and Cirr, or both Howard and Bracks, or both Howard and Beattie, or 'both Howard and Bacon, or both Howard and Rann, or both Howard and Gallop. Do you know any of these people? People who voted, say, against Kennett but really like Howard? Really? Newspoll gets it right on election day, we all know that* but before election day, and before election week, it gives a lot of comfort to Howard's view that 'the polls bounce up and down' and he can therefore do what he likes. It even showed his vote going up in the week when he and Herron said there was no generation of Stolen Children i and then, a fortnight later, oh yes, coming down again. Going up. 1 kid you not. Newspoll gets it right on election day, of course, by hiring more 'people to do the interviews and ringing up round the clock, including week days. Since its usual method - dialing any number in Australia at random - is a good one it gets the numbers right on election day, which is once every three years. But not, I think, between. Because between elections they do it differently. Less pollsters are on the job for one thing, some of them parttime students in a hurry because they get paid per successful phone call. And they're instructed (or so I was told by one of them) that if. a foreign voice answers hang up. This brings down the Labor vote a little, since migrants vote Labor more, as a rule. 'They also ring up, amazingly, on Saturday nights, when Labor voters as a rule are out and the only person home is a septuagenarian female with a picture of Robert Menzies on the wall and a persecuted cat. This brings down the Labor vote a little more. So does ringing up on Saturday afternoons, and Sunday afternoons, when prosperous young families - the ones that more often vote Labor -are out at Australia's Wonderland or Darling Harbour or a movie matinee or on a 'boat or a beach. This is true too at Christmas, when the Labor vote in most ?polls always plummets. At Christmas most Labor voters .are away, in holiday motels or caravans or on the beach or overseas, and their home phones ring unanswered. And, amazingly, the Labor vote always goes down at Christmas, and in school holidays, and holiday weekends. Newspoll also prints only the first party preferred vote, and not the two-party preferred vote, which predicts the election result. And it prints above it headlines that are wrong, or often wrong. A 44-44 vote is 'PARTIES NECK AND NECK™, although the 3 percent Green vote, added to Labor in preferences, plus 60 percent of the five percent that vote Democrat, also added to Labor, and the 50 percent of the Independents added to Labor, gives Labor a landslide victory and a majority of 20 to 30 seats. I rang Newspoll 's head Sol Lebovic and asked him why he printed headlines that were wrong. He said they weren't his headlines and he had no control over how the newspaper chose to interpret his figures. I asked if he ever protested. He implied that he didn't. I asked Mm why he printed only first party preferred. He said, 'We find there's no point calculating preferences this far out from an election.' After a pause I said, 'Why then print anything at all?' He said, 'People need to know how things are going.' 'Why, then,' I said, 'not tell them?' He had no answer for this and pretty soon I hung up on him. (He also didn't say how it was he knew when an election would be held. As I understand it, it could be anytime.) I find this all pretty worrying. If true - and all I've said is no more than a reasonable guess - then the actual vote between elections doesn't move too much, and it certainly doesn't bounce up and down, and the late surge to Labor that apparently always happens in the last week means only that pollsters are ringing up on Wednesday and Thursday nights when the voters are home - though they're not ringing up caravan dwellers, who may be decisive next time, because caravan dwellers don't have phones. It means, must mean, if my guess is true, that polling between elections, or some polling between elections, is incompetent - or worse - and the published results (CHRISTMAS SURGE TO COALITION, LABOR ON THE ROPES) plain wrong. And makes Newspoll's refusal to print the two-party preferred very suspicious indeed.

01 Mar 1949 - TEA STATISTICS South Eastern Times (Millicent, SA : 1906 - 1954), Tuesday 1 March 1949, page 3 TEA STATISTICS Surprising as it may seem, the average Australian man drinks just as much tea as .the average Australian woman. A Gallup Poll just completed by the Australian tea bureau bears this out. The poll also revealed that 12 per cent, of the Australian population drinks black tea without any additions, 30 per cent, add milk only, and the remaining 58 per cent, add milk and sugar. Four p.c. of the population drinks 12 cups cr more a day, 10 per cent, drink as much as ten cups, 69 per cent, drink between 3 and 9 cups daily, and 17 per cent: drink less than 3 cups daily. Ou a nation wide basis the average Australian drinks 3.8 cups a day or, 1,400 cups a year. Some tea drinkers, particularly miners working on the low levels at great temperatures, regularly "consume as much as 40 cups a day. It" is estimated that in a lifetime the average Australian consumes --3,1)00 gallons of hot tea, or .250 times his or her own weight. Recognised as the cheapest and most ~ popular beverage in the world, tea is consumed to the extent of 300,000,000,000 cups eae year.

12 Sep 1941 - Gallup Polls Come to Australia Beverley Times (WA : 1905 - 1977), Friday 12 September 1941, page 3 Gallup Polls Come to Australia During the week September 15/20 the interviewer appointed by Australian Public Opirion Polls for the Beverley district (Mr. A. L. Oliver) -will be sampling public opinion in the district as part ot Australia's first nation-wide sample referendum. The questions asked will, during the same period, be submitted to residents by interviewers in over 300 other centres all over Australia, Results of the interviews will be immediately despatched to Melbourne. All inlet views will be strictly confidential. Depending entirely on the science of statistics to give him amazingly ac curate estimates of American public opinion. Dr. G. H. Gallup, head of the American Institute of Public Opinion, has achieved considerable fame. Australian Public Opinion Polls will cairy out his system in Australia. So accurately did Dr. Gallup calculate the margin by which Roosevelt would defeat Willkie at the 1940 presidential election—giving figu.es State by State—that Dr. Henry C, Link, a statistical expert, said the re suit was miraculous. Judging by American experience, publication of results of polls of Aust 1 ali.in public opinion will help to speed up the machinery of our democracy. Newspapers in each capital city have agreed to publish the find ings of Australian Public Opinion Polls, which has been registered as a non profit company. The newspap ers concei ned will pay for articles an nouncing the findings and that a-mount wili finance the organisation.. In England, Gallup's method— which will be the one used in Aust. ralia—has achieved results compar able with those in the United States. Last August, when the Director of the British Instiuute ol Public Opi nion went 10 America for a special course .'of study, he was asked Ly Government officials whether the polls could, and would continue to operate in his absence. The Austra lian director (Mr. Roy Morgan) has also been to America, and has studied Dr. Gallup's methods b> .working with his staff, Recently, to test the efficacy of the Gallup Method of "sampling" the population, a poll was taken ot electors of Boothby, in South Australia Remarkably reliable results weie ach ieved. Some unthinking persons havesug gested that the polls have been established for the rather useless purpose of forecasting election results. But the real purpose of the organisation is to conduct miniature lefereudums, using statistically accurate samples of public opinion. The number of people interviewed, after a certain number, does not matter, because, it the first sample is an accurate cross section, further votes will only dupli cate opinions already expressed.

22 Mar 2002 - Gary Morgan defends prediction of Mugabe loss in Zimbabwe Chaser (Glebe, NSW : 1999 - 2005), Friday 22 March 2002, page 5 Gary Morgan defends prediction of Mugabe loss in Zimbabwe MELBOURNE, Monday: Pollster Gary Morgan has again been forced to defend the credibility of the Morgan Poll after it predicted a win for opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai in The Harare Bulletin's election-eve edition. Morgan's failure to predict Mugabe's comes on the heels of his embarrassing prediction that Kim Beazley would win 2001 Australian federal election. "I'm really shocked. We were really comprehensive on this one and all the pre-poll figures suggested people were going to vote for Tsvangirai," Morgan said. "There must have been a huge last minute swing. You know, like the one that happened in Australia". Several political commentators claimed that Morgan's methodology was flawed. "Morgan uses face-to-face polling which is very unreliable," said one commentator. "In Zimbabwe you really need to use face-to-face-with-a-gun polling to get the proper result." The Zimbabwe result is a new low point for the Roy Morgan Research Centre. Founded by Gary Morgan's father Roy Morgan in the 1940s. Morgan senior founded the company and built a reputation for delivering reliable, accurate polls until he retired reluctantly passing the business into son Gary's hands. Private internal polling conducted by Roy Morgan before he retired predicted that the business would falter badly with his son in control. On taking over, Gary Morgan confidently announced that his own research suggested his new polling methods would improve the Research Centre's credibility. The Harare Bulletin's embarassing cover

11 Jul 2003 - Shredder Chaser (Glebe, NSW : 1999 - 2005), Friday 11 July 2003, page 14 Shredder Raging against the machine since March 2003 IT'S TIME TO CHOOSE: The man who cannot win or the man who will lose? NewsJunkie with Dave Stewart There are a lot of uncertainties in life. By the time you read this, the first round of the latest ALP leadership bickering will have been sorted out, and - we feel confident in predicting that Kim Beazley either will, or will not, have become Leader of the Opposition. And what an interesting contest it's been ... Still, it makes for good telly - the icky, guilt-laden TV where you get to watch people humiliating themselves, but you can't look away. The only thing better than watching two people tattle it out for a glittering prize (on live TV!) is watching two people battle it out for a prize that is worth virtually nothing. All the better when we, the audience, understand that the prize is worth nothing, but the contestants are in the dark, giving their all in an utterly futile pursuit of false hopes. In TV game shows, this is the 'Superquiz' effect (think Pick A Box, you superannuated boomers!) It wasn't Bert Newton's crazy antics - or Mike Walsh's slightly wooden delivery - that drew the crowds: it was the money shot moment when a contestant picked incorrectly and blew the lot by getting some lame prize instead of the promised car or holiday. What we all wanted to see was Tracey from Clontarf realise that, after all the questions, the play-offs - she'd been struggling, striving, duking it out, all for ... a box of matches! A Bugs Bunny key-ring! The Leadership of the Opposition! Of course, neither Simon Crean nor Kim Beazley have even the lame excuse that they thought that the leadership spill might end with a Ford Mondeo or a trip for four to Disneyland rather than the leadership of their party. It must be doubly galling that, for either of them to make any kind of headway against the Government, they will need to overcome a public who have clearly and unequivocally rejected them (Beazley at the ballot box in [year], and Crean through a sort of negative version of public acclimation over the last 12 months). Both of them, and their advisers, must know, deep down, that to turn the leadership of the Opposition into a genuine opportunity to pick out wallpaper at the Lodge, they will need to cultivate the reputation and persona of a leader who has doggedly faced defeat and simply kept going, persisting through all obstacles to finally win the grudging respect of a skeptical public. And who is the modern embodiment of the 'we don't think much of you, but goodness me you've asked often enough and long enough so you may as well have a go in the big chair' brand of leadership? Oh yeah ... 'Lazarus with a triple bypass'. John Howard. D'oh! Political races are often compared with the world of horse racing (with the expressions like 'it's a two horse race' or 'first past the post' - or, relevantly in this context, 'no horse race'). Look closer, however, and you can see that the Federal ALP shenanigans have more in common with a trip to the dogs. Crean and Beazley might make for unlikely greyhounds, but like all the doggies, knowing that it's a bit of fur on a stick you're chasing after and not some succulent bunny doesn't cut it when there's a flash of fur and all your mates start running. At that point, chasing the prize is instinct, not intellect. Of course, things can change very quickly in politics - and, as the cliché says, 'you've got be in it to win it'. A cynic might remark that, lately, the Federal wing of the ALP has been clearly demonstrating the yawning gap that can open between being 'in', and getting a win. Kim and Simon are right, on one level: simply being Leader of the Opposition does increase your chances of becoming Prime Minister, in much the same way as putting on your Speedos increases your chance of beating Keiran Perkins for a gong at the next Commonwealth Games. But tying the string, putting your goggles on and assuming a professional-looking crouch on the blocks isn't the same as winning the race. Both Beazley and Crean seem like decent guys, and both have loyal followings in the party with good reason. If decency and having a few people reckon you'd give it a grand old go was enough to win over the electorate, of course, Beazley would be Prime Minister now and John Howard would just be a retired politician with a bit of a thing for cricket. Only in the hallucinatory world of party politics could an ongoing leadership position for Simon Crean seem tenable. The most recent Saulwick poll suggested that just 21% of voters preferred him as PM over Howard. Even more mindboggling was the result that, when you look just at ALP voters, 39% still prefer Howard over their own leader. When four in ten of your own supporters think that you aren't good enough to oust your political nemesis, it's difficult to imagine you can convince the doubters. The community has given no sign that it will ever consider Crean as a viable alternative to Howard as preferred PM. Howard has indicated that he will stay for a goodly space of time, staying as long as the party wants him or until the action of sun, wind and rain over the millenia erode him away completely. The case for Beazley is equally shaky. It is possible that there is a school of thought that says if the task of the next Leader of the Opposition is to lead the party to defeat by John Howard at a Federal election, you might as well bring in a specialist for the job. The view of the voting public seems to be that Beazley is a lovely bloke, the sort of person you'd want as a next door neighbour, or perhaps to follow you around, telling you anecdotes and generally creating an aura of slightly off-focus goodwill. Politics is not about how nice you are -except on the strange planet where the Australian Democrats live -and Beazley exudes all ruthless passion for victory and killer instinct of a younger, slightly paler version of Bishop Desmond Tutu. This public perception is out of kilter with realty, to be sure - few of those who think of him as a kind of Parliamentary marshmallow man show much sense of history, given the long-standing hawkish record of 'Bomber Beazley'. But, for better or worse, it's what they do think, and it won't change in a hurry. Whoever won on Monday, there will be plenty of chances to catch this leadership malarky the next time round. Clearly, the timing of the whole affair has been to no-one's liking. Beazley's people feel like they were rushed into things, and for obvious reasons Crean is pushing this for all its worth. So a repeat seems likely - stay tuned! It isn't clear when will be a good time for the leadership issue to erupt again. Maybe 2005 might be a good year to re-open things: at that point, the ALP may well want to have a full review to decide whether they want to face the next election led by the man who lost the last election, or the one man lost the election before that. Maybe 2037, when Howard is next due to make a statement about when he will retire. Maybe the year 2105, by which time human beings will be beginning our first explorations of interstellar space and, at the current rates of improvement, Crean will overtake Howard as preferred PM. The only thing better than watching two people battle it out for a glittering prize (on live TV!) is watching two people battle it out for a prize that is worth virtually nothing

09 May 2003 - Hack Chaser (Glebe, NSW : 1999 - 2005), Friday 9 May 2003, page 22 Hack Political gossip Phone: 02 9280 4554 Fax: 02 9280 4564 Email: hack@chaser.com.au Newspoll staff see red over Greens IT appears that News Ltd has been using its 49 per cent share in Newspoll to give weight to its ideological jihad against the Greens (Barfly ed.71). Prior to the recent NSW election, market research staff at Newspoll were required to ask a Questionnaire about the Greens' drug policy for the 16 March edition of the Sunday Telegraph. One question put to respondents was "Thinking now about the Greens, and particularly about their policy to decriminalise drugs such as ecstasy, speed and marijuana for personal use. Overall, do you support or are you opposed to the Greens policy to decriminalise ecstasy, speed and marijuana?" With the question being a gross simplification of the Greens' policy of harm minimisation and phrased in such a negative fashion, there is little surprise that 72 per cent of the 1000 respondents said that they were opposed it. A number of Newspoll staff submitted written and oral complaints about the biased nature of the survey, feeling they had effectively been asked to push-poll. They claimed that the subjectivity of such research undermined Newspoll's reputation, which could lead to fewer companies using its services and therefore affect staffing levels, jeopardising their jobs. The Greens' also complained to Newspoll after being made aware of the polling by one of its members who was cold called as part of the survey. However, management at the polling company were swift to point the finger at staff, GM David Briggs accusing them of leaking the information to the Greens during a 10 minute dressing down. Newspoll employees were distressed by the false accusations, and a number submitted letters of complaint to the Managing Director Sol Lebovic. On Friday the 2nd Sol personally apologised to staff for the false accusation of industrial espionage of behalf of his GM who has stangely been on leave for six weeks Despite News Ltd honcho Kris Neill's claims that The Chaser misrepresented the Sunday Telegraph's reporting of the Greens' drug policies (Barfly ed.71), News Ltd have evidently been running a concerted, biased crusade against the Greens after all. Shame News Ltd, shame.

ENQUIRY INTO RURAL HEALTH SERVICES The Rural Health Working Party of the Hospitals and Health Services Commission is currently undertaking a review of health and related welfare services provided in rural areas. The investigation includes the isolated and remote areas of Australia together with communities located in close proximity to larger urban areas. The Working Party Is seeking submissions that cover the following areas of concern: 1. Social conditions in rural and remote areas. 2. Health problems in these areas. „. _ 3. The provision of doctors and other health manpower in these areas. 4. The problems of transportation to and communication with health services In these areas. 5. Specific problems of hospitals already located in these areas. 6 Potential community development strategies in such areas, particularly health services provision in the broader framework of social welfare services. 7. General perspectives on future options for providing health services in such areas. 8. Other areas of concern as may arise from time to time. This view is strengthened, perhaps, by the week's disclosure from America that Marshall dollars aren't going to be free in terms of ' freedom. In other words, the official American proposition is that Britain's taxa tion shall be reviewed before the. dollars are paid; that methods of price-fixing be altered; and last, but not least that Britain's -wages bill be looked at 'through United States treasury spectacles. Britain's trade as it was in . 1938. So far, they have found the 10 years intervening a gulf impossible to bridge. Is it impossible? Will England have to alter practically all Its productions and trading . methods to get out at all? If the country is to be saved, ?will It not be necessary for ^.Britain to' shed more population; for every business to miild up a counterpart somewhere outside Britain, in a sterling area — like Australia . or Africa — so that the whole economic structure can be rebalanced?
