24 Oct 1952 - Sewerage Poll Tomorrow Bowen Independent (Qld. : 1911 - 1954), Friday 24 October 1952, page 1 Sewerage Poll Tomorrow Voting is Important TOMORROW (SATURDAY) is an important day for the people of Bowen A Poll will be conducted at the Court House between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. to decide whether to proceed with the proposed Sewerage .Scheme. As every person, whether owning properly or renting it, will he affected by the decision, it is important that every elector should record a vote. AT a public meeting'held on October 13th, the Mayor of n Bowen (Aid. I*. It. Dolalnothe) and other Speakers outlined Ihe details of I lie proposed Bowen Sewerage Scheme, and answered (piestions from ratepayers who attended. ELECTORS TO DECIDE His Worship explained that a Poll would ,be held on 25th October to allow the Electors of Bowen to decide whether the scheme should be installed in Iloweu. This mooting had been called to give the electors all possible information regarding the scheme prior to the Poll. / In undertaking such loan works, he added, the Council first advertised its intention to borrow, although In some cases the Minister allowed them to dispense with the necessity of advertising. In this case, although the Council with the exception of one Alderman favoured the scheme, it had been decided to give the people the opportunity to vote on the scheme. Tile Council could ■ not initiate a poll, as this could only lie done on a petition of at least 10 tier cent of the electors. This had been done, and now a X*oU .could be held. However, its decision would not lie binding unless at least 35 per cent of the electors recorded their votes. HISTORY OF THE SCHEME The Mayor continued that ••the first .serious attempt on-the part of the Town Council to investigate the problem of sewerage was made in 1028. To Mr. J. B. Kelly, then Mayor, and ids Council went the credit of initiating the first investigation. That Council secured the services of Engineer Fnrphy of the Commonwealth Departi'nent of Health, and after Investigation his conclusions were . (1) that there was no reason to believe that the scheme would present any serious engineering difficulties or that the cost would be unduly great, (2) that until a contour survey was made the scheme could only bo investigated in a general way, (3) that owing to the low level of parts of the town, pumping would be necessary, and (-1) that sewage could be discharged into the ocean. Until 1945, no further action was taken, but in that year the Council engaged consulting engineers Gutteridge, Haskins & Davey to prepare a contour survey, mainly for use in planning drainage and road works. Towards the end of 1915 the Council asked the same engineers io prepare a preliminary report and'estimate of a sewerage scheme. That report was completed in October 19-iti, and estimated the total cost at £140,000. In February 1917 the scheme was submitted to the Local 'Government Department and approved by ils engineers. In July 1917 the estimate was revised to £175,000. In August 1917 the State Treasurer made available a loan of £2500 and similar subsidy to prepare working plans and estimates.. From 1947 to 1950 that work went on. Borings had to be taken throughout the town, the location of the treatment works and disposal of sewage decided upon aiid many other angles of the scheme attended to. It was eventually decided that the treatment whiles should be m the vicinity of Magazine Creek, that the sewage should be treated by sedimentation, and that the outfall should be to the sea at Dalrymple Point. In November 1950 the [ilans were completed, and the estimate revised to £270,000. In January 1951 the plans were again submitted to the Department, and after six months were returned for correction. In March 1952 the final complete plans were approved. The Council had then proceeded to advertise Its intention to borrow. THE FINANCIAL SIDE Thu Mayor continued that on die financial side the estimate of cost of the scheme had-been £270,000 n November 1950, and was now estimated at between £200.000 and £320,000. If proceeded with, the scheme would bo financed by a loan of half that, amount and a subsidy of half.' 29 Apr 1941 - SENTIMENT IN THE U.S.A. Age (Melbourne, Vic. : 1854 - 1954), Tuesday 29 April 1941, page 7 SENTIMENT IN THE U.S.A. All-in Aid is Essential "The Age" Special Representative. NEW YORK, April 28. America, whose growing sentiment for Britain against the Axis' is reflected in recent Gallup polls, . is coming to realise that the British are again fighting alone and cannot hope to win without all-out aid from the United States. Mr. Churchill's speech . has served as a reminder that the war will .be won or lost in the west and that America's armaments, safely delivered, are vital for victory. Therefore Americans are further convinced that they must assure the delivery of munitions whatever the cost. How soon this sentiment will crystallise to the point where President Roosevelt and Congress will feel warranted to go all-out is anybody's guess, but certainly Mr. Churchill's words have provided a new impetus. . Mr. Rockefeller's letter is an example of how many leading Americans are thinking. Moreover, there are indications that many organisations, particularly the Great War veterans, who long advocated a peaceful attitude and are now. outspoken against the Axis, are demanding strong measures to protect cargoes of American goods to Britain. Commenting briefly on Mr. Churchill's speech, .the fall of Athens and the superb fight by the Greeks, Australians and New Zealanders, the "New York Times" in an editorial says: — "The battle which will determine England's fate is not that in the Mediterranean, though the importance of controlling that sea remains, but in the Atlantic. In the outcome of that battle' the fortunes of America are involved hardly" less than Britain's. Therefore our help in that battle must come, and will come on an increasing scale." The New York "Herald-Tribune" clearly sees Mr. Churchill's words as addressed to Americans in the hope that they, like the British, will have the courage, vigor , and independence to make up their own minds as to what America should do in the matter of convoys and other aid. It says: — "We believe Americans need clearer guidance from President Roosevelt and a firmer line of policy in this difficult and distressful world, but believe that Americans are' able to face facts and move promptly to meet them without waiting to be told."

14 Jun 1941 - GALLUP POLLS Age (Melbourne, Vic. : 1854 - 1954), Saturday 14 June 1941, page 20 GALLUP POLLS How Public Opinion is Gauged Frequent references to what are known in the United States of America as Gallup polls, as barometers of the trend of mass opinion in that country regarding questions of major national import, have aroused interest as to how they are conducted, and the extent to which they can be accepted as reflecting the mind -of such a vast electorate. Gallup polls are conducted under the auspices of the American Institute o.f Public Opinion, but it is not claimed for them that they present a true percentage reflex of the mind of Americans as a whole on any particular question. In the preface to "The Pulse of Democracy," published last year, of which Dr. G. Gallup and Mr. S. F. Rae are joint authors, that Is conceded. "But," the preface continues, "it is not too hopeful to suggest that the continuous collection of facts about public opinion will provide "theorists of the future with a solid' groundwork on which to base a realistic theory of public opinion as it actually works in every-day life." A Gallup poll is based on the assumption that, by sounding the : opinions of a relatively small number of persons, proportionate to each major population group in every section of the community, the opinion of the whole population can be determined with a considerable degree of accuracy. This claim has been supported in a number of instances by the subsequent reaction of the electorate at the -ballot box, which has confirmed, in the main, if not in precise figures, the trend disclosed by the Gallup poll. The method of finding out what the public thinks about the New Deal, the extent to which America should aid the democracies in their struggle against Totalitarianism, the prospects of the re-election of a President, and so forth, Is by actual contact' with individuals by trained "interviewers," who seek out stock brokers, bankers, farmers, lumberjacks, clerks, artisans, domestics, &c., and record their replies to a prepared, questionnaire. These interviewers will "drive through a snowstorm to contact a farmer: trudge across a Kansas wheat 1 field in blazing heat to talk to a thrasher on his job; climb to a third floor tenement in New York's east ci/tA fl In tVtAitt MIM«. — . 1 oluv » »BUC Mien. wo>jr pnou a icojJicll-dently uniformed doorkeeper of a Park-avenue apartment, or- talk to a charwoman who is mopping the floor of the office of an industrialist employing thousands of men ' and women." Considerable care is taken in framing the questions to be put by interviewers. It is regarded as essential that a question should be as brief and to the point as possible; should avoid all suggestion of possible bias; should be simply phrased in words' in everyday use, and if alternatives are used they should be presented as early in the question as possible.

12 Sep 1951 - Is Mr. Churchill in Eclipse? Age (Melbourne, Vic. : 1854 - 1954), Wednesday 12 September 1951, page 2 : Is /-'Mr. Churchill in Eclipse? Leaders in Britain -T-— — — , By. — , -A. J. CUMMINGS, Diplomatic Correspondent, the "News-Chronicle," London. A POLITICAL surprise has startled many in- Britain. Gallup poll figures recently published -show a marked' preference " v for Mr. Anthony Eden over Mr. Churchill to head a Conservative Government. What seems to have taken people most by surprise is the fact that, in the Conservative vote, Mr. Eden received only five per cent, less than Mr. Churchill. IT WAS TO BE EXPECTED that Liberal and Labor supporters would poll heavily ' for Mr. Eden in the belief that he has a more progressive, outlook in home politics, and that he would be a "safer" guide in foreign affairs. Probably the explanation for this switch In popular favor can be traced to a sharp division, : growing more 'acute in recent : months, in the Tory ranks: on policy, tac- . tics and personalities. : Mr. Churchill. has been the victim of something akin tu a party whispering campaign. He is accused of stultifying through deliberate Inertia the: policy proposals of the Butler Group.He He has certainly annoyed many Tory members of Parliament, especially those on the Front Bench, by his habit' of butting in wilh-out :, consultation and disrupting agreed Parliamen-taTy tactics, and of ploughing too many lone furrows . inside and outside Westminster. The Gossip Then, so goes the talk, he is now too old, besides being too deeply preoccupied; with his war histories (two : more books still to come), to take charge of our national affairs at a time when the mounting problems demand unremitting attention and great physical and m.ental endurance. Further, the argument runs In the clubroom gossip, Mr-Eden as Prime Minister will be less of a provocation to the trade union leaders, to the mass of working-class supporters of the Labor movement. The answer made to those who point out that Mr. Churchill is pre-eminently ; the most popular- and trusted figure in America Is that Mr. Eden, though far less widely kriown among ordinary American citizens, is also much esteemed In Washington political circles, and that his recent speaking tour In the United States has notably raised his prestige. In reporting these fretful dissensions. so common among ail parties tlirough-out our political history, I must nevertheless record my own conviction, thai Mr. Churchill, and not Mr. Eden, will head the next Conservative Administration. 'Who Who Will Dare? Mr, Churchill Is easily the most outstanding,, as- well as the most controversial, British figure in our contemporary life. In the public eye he dominates the Opposition; and Labor fears his. aggressive personality more than any other. When the lime comes, is there any Tory politician, however Inttiicntial, behind the scene, however brave, who will dare to challenge openly his prescriptive right to the succession? I should be sorry for the challenger. .The The man who has vanquished death in various forms at least 17 times, and come back smiling, is still physically and mentally alert. If not quite so alert, or so full of pep, as 111 the war years; and he has every Intention of making his home once more in 10 Downing Street. One of his oldest friends told me the other day that it is Mr. Churchill's ambition, a very natural one, to be a peacetime Prime Minister; to prove .that he can conduct ,the nation's business as successfully in peacetime (such as it is 1) as in the stress of war. My informant added: "I believe that, at the end of six months or a year, having made his official mark again on Parliament and the people, he will then retire In- favor of ft younger man." From this last suggestion-one must take leave to , differ profoundly. In forceful men high office does not encourage such super-modesty. Power is a' magnet that never loses its attraction. Respect Abroad If Mr. Churchill hasn't "made his mark again" after ' a year in office he will want to go on until he does make it. If he has made It. he will, though with proper, diffidence, regard himself as indispensable to the nation. I can't see' him retiring voluntarily to Chartwell to paint pictures: of rural peace. It is reasonably 'safe' to assume that his return will" be ' welcomed In the U.S.A. as in most of the free world, and that in Moscow the news will' be received with respect mingled with considerable annoyance. Mr. Churchill is one of the ; few politicians, if not the only one, outside the Iron Curtain for whom Stalin-has always entertained . . a lively respect. That Is obvious from eount-, less war books, particularly those - written by Russian citizens who had personal contact with Stalin, and have since escaped to the West. A . few years ago an acquaintance of mine who Is no-Churchill fan toured some of the capitals of Europe. He. tells, me that wherever he ' went he found photographs of Mr. Churchill In. houses large and' small, and Churchill memories very vivid. . "He still regarded abroad," lie said, "as the representative -Englishman,:: as the savior of Europe.'" ' ' Should the' Tory party, realise Its hopes in the general election— now, In spite of the public desire as disclosed In the Gallup poll, a less likely autumn happening — it 'looks as if, to begin with, at any rate, Mr. Churchill as Prime M'nister will -make a favorable ' Impact on friendly nations in Europe and elsewhere. I will say nothing at present about the impact on home affairs.

17 Sep 1952 - Unity was main basis of victory Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Wednesday 17 September 1952, page 6 Unity was main basis of victory CARLY in July, 1951, Menzies was conceitedly confident that his referendum would win. Gallup polls reported big majorities for him, and extreme rightwing Labor politicians were supporting Menzies. But Communist Party General Secretary L- L. Sharkey, writing in Tribune, sounded a different note. "Unity is vital in fight to defeat the referendum," said the heading to his article. And in the article, Mr. Sharkey wrote: "On broad, united front work, abjuring once and for all economist narrowness and sectar. ianism, depends, in large measure, the fate of the NO campaign." The article made it clcar that if the people were united, they could win, The campaign for unity grew rapidly. Communists io. city, suburb and country went and talked in a friendly way to ALP members, tramped the streets with them Living out leaflets or putting up Ti- ters. Wharfies from the big cities organised tours of the countryside and had .friendly yarns with farmers. "Strewth," said one Sydney wharfie after his first talk with a farmer, "that fellow hates Menzies just as much as I do." Many supporters of the Liberal Party, seeing how the referendum threatened trade unions and small businessmen, gave a friendly welcome to Communists distributing manifestoes, and joined actively m the NO campaign. 21 Feb 1948 - Survey of London's Street-Sellers Age (Melbourne, Vic. : 1854 - 1954), Saturday 21 February 1948, page 5 Survey of London's Street-Sellers Books of t la t\ Bay ' Social surveys, mass. observation, Gallup polls —we are apt to think such things peculiar to present-day ways of thinking. But a hundred years ago a section of London's population was surveyed' by personal interview, and . : allowed to speak for itself. . .w «HE . STREET TRADER'S »# I LOT: LONDON, 1851" 1 (Sylvan Press, London, 18/3), Is a book of selections, chosen by Stanley Rubinstein, from that survey made by Henry Mayhew, and first published under the title "London Labor and the London Poor." Mr. Rubinstein has enlivened the pages with contemporary drawings of the characters described, and assembled a most informative and fascinating selection from Mayhew's portrait gallery. Mayhew claimed that his book was "the first attempt to publish the history of a people from the lips of the people themselves— giving a literal description of their labor, their earnings, their trial and their suffering, in their own unvarnished language; and to portray the condition of their homes and their families by personal observation of the places and direct communion with the individual." There is an authentic ring about the conversation which he reports, -and whether the pictures that emerge are humorous or heartbreaking (both are - present in full measure) they have the quality of un-doctored truth. Mayhew disclaimed attachment tp any doctrinaire social or political panacea; he aimed to write as "a collector of facts," whose chief desire was to show "the importance of the poor and working class as members of society." The condition which he described had been known in a general way for a long time. The "Blue Books" of social statistics had pro- vided material for such works as Disraeli's novel depicting "the Two Nations," the rich and the poor. But for most of London's well-to-do, "Punch's" comment on Mayhew's book was valid — "These wonders and terrors have been lying by your door and mine, ever since we had a door of our own. We.' had but to go a hundred yards off and see for ourselves, but we never did.". The difference was that Mayhew did. Who was Henry Mayhew T Th a on of a London solicitor, he had a varied, adventurous life, and was one of the co-founders of "Punch" men, who were described as "humanitarians first and humorists second." He was a practical philanthropist, as; well u, journalist, and founded the Friendly' Association of London Costerman-gers, which had among its aims the establishment of a provident fund and savings bank, and the provision of "harmless, if not rational, amusements at the same cheap rate as the pernicious entertainments now - resorted to by the street sellers." Above all, the warmth of his genuine concern for the poor of London won the confidence of a class naturally disposed to regard such as himself with the utmost suspicion. He never lost his faith in their capacity for improvement, given the chance. After a-striking description of the debauched entertainment provided for the coolers at the "Wlc" (afterwards the Old Vic) Theatre, he quotes a coste'rmonger oX the better class. "Well, Sir, it's frightful, but the boys will have their amusements. .' . . It's - all stuff about them preferring this'- sort of thing. Give 'em good things at the same price, and I know they will like the good better than the bad." From their replies to his questions, the street sellers reveal themselves as they were, with all their human defects, as well as their human qualities — their loose-fitting morals (ne estimates that not one-tenth of the couples was married, the belief of many in their right to cheat ("It's not cheating, Sir, it's- outwitting' ), their endurance and resignation, theii pride in their clothes, their battle with the police (the "crushers"), and all the details of their daily life and work. Poets and Pafterers Mayhew estimated tlhat there were over 40)000 street sellers In London in 1851; and the colorful variety of their "lines" was remarkable — Baked Potato Man, Long-Song Seller, Book Auctioneer, Luciter Match Girl, Seller of Birds' Nests, Sellers of Grease-Removing Composition, and a host of others. The "patterers" among them felt intellectually superior to the mere vendors of goods. "We are the fiaris-tocracy of the streets," one, who told penny fortunes with a bottle, told Mayhew. "People don't pay us for what we gives 'em, but only to hear us talk. We live like yourself, Sir, by the hexercise of our hintellects— we by talking, and you by writing." Hunger, disease, poverty and hardships — hardly credible to-day — these- . were the common lot of the people Mayhew depicts. Yet their humor and humanity, their wholly untragic view of- themselves, are reflected by the man who felt their cause as his own. "What do you think of the Great Exhibition, Sir?" a street poet asked Mayhew. "I shall be there. Me and my mates. We are going to send in a set of werses in letters of gold for a prize. We'll let the foreigners know what the real native melodies of England is, and no mistake." Mr. Rubinstein has done a real service in enabling Mayhew's Londoner to tell their stories to a wider public.

21 Nov 1953 - THE WEEK IN WIRELESS-- Age (Melbourne, Vic. : 1854 - 1954), Saturday 21 November 1953, page 18 THE WEEK IN WIRELESS— Parliamentarians in Love With Their Own Broadcasts . Coincident with the release of a Gallup poll claiming that nearly 60 percent, of listeners ignore parliamentary broadcasts and that only 24 per .cent, listen, to them more than twice -a month, the Speaker,pf. fhej-louse of Representatives (Mr. Cameron) . declared that parliament would never : agree to:a system or selective: broadcasts. . By Ariel >HE TOLL DISCLOSED . that.- the Parliamentary I audience is dwindling and :I am not surprised. ; The issue has never been whether or -not Parliament shall be broadcast! All' that a large number of cultured listeners desire is that the broadcasting of Parliament shall .be transferred from., the only .station devoted, to cultural Items that we possess; and relayed over another channel. Alternatively, that ' on days that. Parliament is-sitting, what would have been 3LO's programme should be broadcast ln full from 3AR. Grossly Unfair . It is necessary to point out once more that to discontinue 3LO's programmes and to replace them with broadcasts of Parliament, merely eliminates listening. for. a large, audience for whom the.,other six stations provide little or nothing., . This is grossly unfair and contrary, to. the principle of freedom of choice. It 'is a form of tyranhy that even . the ABC, which professes to be tired of full parliamentary broadcasts, condones, \ I don't see why the commercial stations should not take part ln what Mr. Cameron asserts is a service "of whose termination the public would be, resentful." If Parliament is as popular as its members think it is then there should be no difficulty in finding sponsors for its broadcasting. As Parliament is again in session the usual 3LO : programme drought is with us. This does not only come on session days but seems to. infect the whole week's broadcasting. The second half of this .year, has been notable .for the poor quality of !ABS drama.. If there had not been; a reasonable' level of music, we would have been poorly' off Indeed. Those who were Interested did think that, the . current Bayreuth production of Tristan and Isolde; which was broadcast over 3LO on Saturday, would have made up for much that we have been ; deprived of, but It lacked the brilliahce of previous broadcasts of its' kind. Not much of. what went on at the Fest-spielhaus reached us here in Melbourne. : The contrast, with previous .Bayreuth broadcasts was so strong as to be puzzling. Relays from Sydney have, been very good lately, but this one sounded as if it came from much further away and over a very poor line. - The record, of course, may-; have been below standard. -Reception was so low-pitched that my high frequency speaker had little or nothing to do, and the fact that Isolde "wobbled" did not add to the enjoyment. Good Quartet The most satisfying music of the week came from a piano quartet composed of Hephzibah Menuhin (piano) , Ernest Llewellyn (violin) , Robert Pikler (viola) and Hans George (cello). It was a performance over 3LO on Sunday of Faure's Quartet No.- 1 in O minor. Faure was. a Frenchman, but his is not necessarily French music. Personally I regard it as being in the universal category and in the best chamber music tradition. This supremely lovely quartet was played with the fastidiousness necessary to Its adequate presentation. It was a rare type of performance that we hear too seldom. Two pleasing sessions were Rossini's opera William Tell -from 3LO Tuesday — Parliament having adjourned 7- and the ABO Chamber Ensemble (conductor Robert Hughes) at .the week eqd. William Tell is rather despised these days by the. 'fastidious, but, the L-P. record was'-a good one and' I enjoyed it. The Hughes programme was,- as usual, excellently chosen ' and pldyed. -The 3 AW play oil Sunday was' The Ghost Train, which was a popular stage play here some years ago. It made good average broadcast material , for those who like mystery thrillers. . Two ABC plays — the perfect examples of what not to choose for broadcasting— were' On the Way to Niagara (Sunday, 3AR), and Corruption in the Law Courts (3LO, Monday) , ! a translation ! from the Italian, This last play was Incomprehensible. apart from the fact that some obscure inquiry was going on and a girl fell down a lift well.

12 Oct 1944 - Poll Shows Britain For Hard Peace Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Thursday 12 October 1944, page 2 Poll Shows Britain For Hard Peace (By cable from Arthur Clegg) LONDON.—Gallup Poll results published by the News Chronicle this week indicate the British people's stern, inflexible attitude towards the Nazis in the war's closing phase. ASKED whether Hitler, Himmler, Goering, Goebbels and other Nazi chiefs should be punished, 97 per cent of the voters said YES, two per cent Mo, and one per cent no opinion. * To a question as to whether Gestapo members, SS men and members of other terrorist organisations against whom no specific charges can be brought should be punished, 87 per cent said YES, and 3 per cent No, with 10 per cent undecided. Disarm Germans Other answers (in percentage of voters) were: Should Germany be deprived of arms and armed forces of all kinds in the post-war period?—Yes, 94; No, 4; undecided, 2. Would you approve of a plan for splitting Germany up permanently into smaller German states?—Yes, 56; No, 23; undecided, 21. Take Over Ruhr Would you approve if the whole industrial area of the Ruhr and Rhineland, containing about 40 per cent of Germany's industries, were taken away permanently from Germany and put under international administration?— Yes, 66; No, 17; undecided, 17. Do you think a hard peace with Germany would be more likely to ensure the future peace of Europe than a soft one?—Yes, 80; No, 8; undecided, 12. The voters were a representative section of the British people.

22 Mar 1945 - TRUTH IS STRANGER INSIDE GERMANY Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Thursday 22 March 1945, page 4 TRUTH IS STRANGER INSIDE GERMANY The experience of a USA Public Opinion investigator following American troops into Aachen reads 1 like a cautionary tale for would-be Gallup Poll experts. JT was decided to hand over a cross-section of 50 Germans to the investigator and his team. No. 1 was a man in late middle age. The POI, ticking off questions on the carefully prepared double-tested questionnaire, ascertained that this particular Reich citizen had be?n a staunch anti-fascist all his life. As for him he welcomed the chance of the United Nations, Atlantic Charter, democracy, etc. No. 2 was another middle-aged man. He, too, had for years not ceased from mental strife against the Nazi tyrants. He welcomed the American troops as liberators of the German people. No. 3 went further. As an elderly man with three sons fighting—"cannon fodder for that accursed Hitler"— on the various fronts, he made so bold as to consider the Nazi Party the scourge and ruin -of Germany. Shocked! No. 4, asked whether he had ever been a member of the Nazi Party, cried out in such an access of horror that the POI hurried on to ask him the gentler question whether he had ever even considered joining that organisation. Amazement on the part of No. 4. How could an honest man,' though knowing nothing of politics, have anything to do with such people? No. 5 also knew nothing of politics— just a simnle shopkeeper, sir. Around No. 22 the POI began to get anxious. With all possible tact and delicacy he explained to the next in line among —who had been bitterly opposed to the Nazis for years and years—that in the outer world an idea had got around that a very considerable "portion of the German people had rather enthusiastically supported Hitler, the Nazi Party and the German war, and was imbued with Nazi propaganda and the Nazi Weltanschauung. "Don't you believe it sir, don't believe a word of it," cried the honest German. "That is nothing but a pack of Jewish-pluto-democratic-Bolshevik lies." One Guardian a minute is sold at the Flinders Street Railway Station by ace seller Charlie Shaunessy. '1 sell the new edition for an hour every Wednesday and Thursday," he repents. "It's not difficult, to get through 10 dozen in two hours there."

07 Jun 1949 - To my way of thinking Brisbane Telegraph (Qld. : 1948 - 1955), Tuesday 7 June 1949, page 5 [?] EXPRESSION of opinion by the majority of British people consulted in a Gallup Poll that careless pedestrians should be punished, is interesting. For too long motorists have liad to bear the full blame of the heavy accident toll. Speeding drivers are told that the minute they save may be their last; that death is SO permanent. You are prosecuted (and very rightly), if you drive a car under the influence of liquor, arid you. must stop at intersections where there is no clear view. Yet no one ' ever conducts a campaign to tell pedestrians chat stepping off the city footpath with the' head sunk on the chest is .not conducive to road safety, and I saw a policeman grinning tolerantly the other day at a drunk weaving his way across Stanley Street in the track of "oncoming traffic. Any careful motorist will tell you that he saves the lives of at least three careless pedestrians during a day's drive in the city andoits precincts, but if an accident had occurred in connection with any of these incidents it would be the motorist and not the pedestrian who might be called on to face a charge of manslaughter. Behave like a fool at the wheel of a car and cause an accident, and if you get your deserts you may go to jail. Be- have like a fool in the role of a pedestrian and cause an accident and nobody (officially, at any rate) criticises your conduct. ? T>INA MALATRASI, one of the stars of the Italian Grand Opera Company who plays Mimi in La Boheme is small and ethereal looking. The fact comes as a relief to those of us who prefer a little realism with our Grand Opera. Prima donnas are prone to be built on ample lines and the frail consumptive Mimi is too often played by buxom sopranos who look like advertisements for vitamin products. ' Mr. Nevin Tait, who is in charge of this tour, admitted to me during the week that even "our beloved Melba" looked a bit healthy to be dying of consumption and that only the magnificent golden voice with which Mimi poured out her love and despair saved the situation from becoming ridiculous. I once saw a prima donna make an entrance as "Carmen" snapping her castanets and twirling her skirts in the approved, manner of the Spanish oomph girl. She weighed at least 15 stone and for one awful moment it seemed as if the audience were about to giggle. Then she lifted up her lovol> voice in song and the moment was saved. It makes, you think of the man who fell' in love with his wife because of her voice and in moments of disillusionment was apt to bellow at her, "For heaven's sake woman, SING." ? TTHE strange goings on in the; elephant enclosure at -Taf-Qnga Park Zoo during which a respectable middle-aged elephant called Nellie was pushed into the ditch by. one of her friends and subsequently died, brings to mind odd stories of these creatures who "never forget." There was an elephant belonging to Wirth's Circus which at one stage in its career gave a performance at Gatton. I think her name was Gertie. Later Gertie, on her way to Toowoomba by road from Brisbane, remembered the turn-off to the paddock where the performance hsftl been given at Gatton 10 years before, and insisted on taking it. The manager pleaded with her. The circus was not playing Gatton this season, he explained, and would Gertie kindly continue on to Toowoomba. Gertie looked at him coldly and pursued her inexorable passage to Gatton. The manager shrugged and looked sulky. The circus played Gatton. [?]

25 Mar 1953 - Families of 4 need £12/16/6 at very least Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Wednesday 25 March 1953, page 4 Families of 4 need £12/16/6 at very least Gallup poll admits Even private enterprise's own Gottup poll shows minimum weekly cost of livinc for two-child families as £12/16/6 — 18 6 a week more than Sydney's basic wage of £11/18/-. * DUT private enterprise is at this very moment pressing as hard as it knows how for reduction in the basic wage to £8/16/- a week — £4/-/6 less than the minimum admittedly needed for existence. Gallup Poll asked the people: "In your opinion, what's the smallest amount a family of four, including two children, needs each week to live decently and keep in health — that is, the smallest amount for all expenses, including rent?" The men's average estimate was £13/2/-, women's £12/11/-. The weekly food bill alone for such a family was shown as £7/9/- a week; £7/13/- for a family of five. The employers' wage cut application now being heard in the Arbitration Court, therefore, wants to leave two-child families with just 27/- a week with which to pay rent, school, medicine, clothing and all other bills. Understatement It should be remembered that this review, coming as it does from an employer-sponsored organisation, is almost certainly an understatement. No further proof should be needed of the justice of the ACTU Special Congress ultimatum not to accept any wage cut. or of the metal unions' claims for higher margins. Nor should anything further be required to inspire unity in action to defend the basic wage and win higher margins. Only recently, Tribune quoted Sydney Morning Herald's Financial Review figures showing a serious drop in consumption forced on Australian workers by a dangerous cut in the purchasing power of wages. By pressing their wage cut, longerhour claims in the face of facts and figures produced by their own organs and organisations, metal employers and others show their complete disregard or concern for the health and welfare of Australian workers and their families. Theirs is exclusive obession with the drive for mavimnm profits — in which nothing can be allowed to stand in the way. To the bosses this is a fight without quarter. The workers, too, must make it so — and rout out the stooges, splitters and disruptors of unity in their fight for wage justice and a decent life.

30 Jun 1954 - Americans fight for peace Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Wednesday 30 June 1954, page 4 Americans fight for peace Estimation of a recent Gallup poll that more than 70 per cent of American people are opposed to intervention in Indo-China is confirmed by developments in the American labor and political movement. rphe movement against intervention J- embraces workers, trade union leaders and congressmen. In Chicago 12,000 workers in Armour, Swift and Wilson Co's meat packing works shouted approval of a resolution, branding US moves to get into the Indo-China war as am attempt "to cover up for the criminal fact that the administration has no program to solve the unemployment problem that threatens to plunge America into depression." Local 6 of the CIO United Auto "Workers has accused Secretary of State Dulles of "beating the war tom-toms." "Would wiping Indo-China off the face of the earth with hydrogen bombs solve the problem of the political attraction of world Communism for the colonial peoples?" the local asks in an open letter to Dulles. Congressmen's support The International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter workers has warned that "the Indo-China war may spread and trigger an atomic bomb explosion which would spell the doom of the whole world." Local 758 of this union, operating In Chicago, has won the support of three out of five congressmen in their area for a resolution opposing the sending of troops to Indo-China. Senator Everett Dirksen, Repubic&o, wired the local: "I quite subscribe to your thinking with reference to sending troops to Indo-China and I am confluent that the overwhelming majority of the members of the Senate would oppose such a move." In La Fayette, California, Representative Robert L. Condon said that "Intervention in Indo-Chinai could easily lead to World War 111.*' Cruel travesty Puller Warren, a former governor of Florida, wrote to the Miami- Herald on April 17: "What a cruel travesty it would be if those who won power by promising to end the Korean war got us into this far more futile and frus trating war in Indo-China." He was commending similar views expressed in an editorial by Publisher John S. Knight, who also publishes dailies in Detroit, Akron and Chicago. Public opinion surveys conducted by daily papers reveal that the man in the street is bitterly opposed to intervention. The Coos Bay Times for example found 100 per cent opposition in a survey it conducted. There is no doubt that it was this mass feeling which forced a retreat by Washington, after Vice-President Nixon had definitely promised inter vention. The American working people are fighting side by side with their fellow men and women throughout the world for peace.

18 Apr 1942 - Gallup Polls Voice (Hobart, Tas. : 1931 - 1953), Saturday 18 April 1942, page 4 Gallup Polls VIEWS OF MR. WINSTON CHURCHILL "pHE Gallup Polls in Australia are well conducted. But experience in America shows that they can be overdone, and are not always a dependable means of eliciting public opinion, upon which public men can safely rely. View, generally, of the British Prime Minister, as expressed recently in the House of Commons: — "Nothing is more dangerous in wartime than to live in the temperamental, atmosphere of a Gallup poll — always feeling one's pulse and taking one's temperature. I see that a speaker at the week-end said that this was the time when leaders should keep their ears to the ground. All I can say is that the British nation will find it very hard to look up to leaders who are detected in that somewhat ungainly posture. If to-day I am very kindly treated bv the mass of people in this country it is certainly not because I have followed public opinion in the last few years. "There is only one duty and one safe course, and that is to, try to be right and not to fear to do or say what you believe to be right. And that is the only way to deserve and win the confidence of our great people in the days of trouble."

23 Apr 1947 - HOW TO GROW FIRST CLASS CABBAGES AND CAULIFLOWERS Weekly Times (Melbourne, Vic. : 1869 - 1954), Wednesday 23 April 1947, page 18 HOW TO GROW FIRST CLASS CABBAGES AND CAULIFLOWERS If a Gallup Poll were taken to ascertain the most popular vegetable the potato would score hands down. I don't think there is any doubt about that. Scarcely a day passes in the average home without potatoes figuring on the menu. MEXT in order of popularity, I think, come the cabbage and the cauliflower. Why these two valuable subjects are not more widely cultivated in the home garden is something of a puzzle. Probably the reason is that the proper methods of growing are not appreciated. Added to this may be the feet that they are liable to suffer severely from attacks by the grubs of the White Butterfly and the Cabbage Moth. Preparing the Ground A CTUALLY there is no difficulty at all in raising excellent cabbages and cauliflowers provided the varieties are suitable to the season, the strains are good, and precautions are taken to keep the grubs in check. First and foremost it should be realised that rich soils, well fortified with humus, are essential to success. Both types of plants are heavy feeders, and their requirements in this respect must be met. When preparing the ground for them dig in deeply plenty of old stable or fowl manure, or material from the compost heap, and if you possibly can do so also incorporate some finely ground bonedust. Give the plants adequate elbow room. In other words, place them about 2ft. 6in. apart each way, so that the surface of the soil can be regularly cultivated to aerate it, and eliminate the weeds. Deep planting is desirable. This can be facilitated by removing the lower leaves of the seedlings, and leaving only three or four at the top. Water in well. From the start dust the plants (or spray them) regularly with one or other of the recommended proprietary preparations so as to destroy any grubs in their infancy. This preventive treatment is vitally necessary. Word of Warning QNCE the plants have established a good root hold— say in about six weeks from the time of transplanting—they should be helped along with occasional doses of weak liquid manure brewed from fowl or animal droppings, or a little sulphate of ammonia, or nitrate of soda may be sprinkled on the soil around them and washed in. Should conditions warrant it do not hesitate to use the sprinkler or the watering can, but remember that the water applied to the leaves will wash off the material designed to keep the grubs in check. I have found that when sulphate of ammonia is employed as a stimulant there is less likelihood of aphids attacking the plants. Where these pests put in an appearance, however, they can be controlled by dusting, or by spraying with nicotine sulphate. Finally, a word of warning. Although the cabbages and cauliflowers are gross feeders, it is necessary to use commonsense in applying liquid manure, otherwise there may be an excessive development of leaves at the expense of hearts in the cabbages and of curds (flower heads) in the cauliflowers.

12 Nov 1947 - ACCURATE FORECAST BY GALLUP POLL Weekly Times (Melbourne, Vic. : 1869 - 1954), Wednesday 12 November 1947, page 5 ACCURATE FORECASTl BY GALLUP POLL ( The Australian Gallup Poll's accurate forecast of the extent of Labor's defeat on Saturday has made political and statistical history. Never before, anywhere in the world, has a public opinion poll been so accurate with so few interviews. After only 350 interviews with a carefully selected cross-section of voters, it was estimated by the Gallup Poll that the vote in seven doubtful electorates in the eastern and southern suburbs of Melbourne would be: Liberal 51 per cent., Labor 46 per cent, and Independents 3 per cent. | .ELECTORATES covered were Albert Park, Box Hill, Hawthorn. Men-tone, Oakleigh, Prahran, and St. Kilda, and the Gallup Poll's estimate of 51 per cent, for Liberals indicated a gain of 10 per cent, compared with the last State election two years ago. Voting figures exactly confirm that forecast, and the actual count for the seven electorates is: — Liberal, 51 per cent.; Labor, 45 per cent.; and Independents, 3 per cent. " It was also predicted .on the basis of only 300 interviews, that the Labor vote in three key country electorates (Allendale, Goulburn, and Midlands) would decline from 51 per cent, to 42 per cent. Progress figures show the Labor vote in those electorates at 45 per cent., and the complete count is likely to be even closer to the Gallup Poll estimate of 42 per cent. These comparisons show that the Gallup Poll predicted the full extent of Labor's defeat. Three suburban seats (Brighton, Glen Iris, and Ivanhoe) contested by Liberals and Independents, without Labor opposition, presented the Gallup Poll with a special problem. After only 150 interviews it was predicted that the Liberals would win! all three seats with an aggregate votej of 59 per cent. They have won with; an aggregate vote of 63 per cent. An outstanding feature of the Gallup forecast was the accuracy of predictions for individual seats. j An average of only 61 people were interviewed in each electorate, yet I forecasts of the votes for individual j candidates were accurate, on the I average, within 4 per cent. It was correctly predicted that the Liberals would strengthen their hold on their three "dopjatful" suburban seats (Brighton, Hawthorn, and St. Kilda), and gain Albert Park. Glen Iris, and Ivanhoe. Probable changes from Labor to Liberal were also indicated in Box Hill, Oakleigh, and Prahran. with Mentone also on the borderline. The Gallup Poll's country figures correctly forecast that the Country Party would strengthen its hold on Allendale, and that the Liberal candidate would displace Labor in Goulburn. Rather surprisingly, it also indicated that Midlands, won by Labor in 1945 with 60 per cent., would also go to the Liberal Party, and progress figures show that such may be the case.

26 May 1948 - GOOD MORNING, MA'AM Argus (Melbourne, Vic. : 1848 - 1957), Wednesday 26 May 1948, page 7 GOOD MORNING, MA'AM By HELEN SEAGER This is in the nature of a homily, Ma'am, because for the last few days I have been conducting a sort of one-woman Gallup poll, and the result has shocked me into something akin to seriousness. My leading question, put, I'll admit, as one really seeking enlightenment, j has been, "What is this Referendum all about?" The answers, Ma'am, have brought) on my current state of apoplexy. Fifty per cent of those questioned admittedly answered, "Something to do with price control," in that vague way you answer "The theory of relativity" when somebody asks you about Einstein, and you hope that they won't really want you to go into the subject any further. Wanting something further. I col-lected some trimmers in the way of answers. One girl, with a BA degree and a fair intelligence on most sub-jects of the day, said that she thought the Government had too much power already and so she would vote Yes because she thought it was high time all these war re-! strictions went by the board. Evidently her reasoning went along the lines of "Yes, we've got no bananas," because I had to talk to her for about five minutes before she realised she meant No. we don't | want price controls. Shades of battling suffragettes came i before my eyes when a matron of not such tender years looked at me rather wearily and said: "Oh, I leave all that sort of thing to Daddy; he'll tell me what to vote on the day." Another at the same luncheon table answered my question this way: "Personally," she said, "I don't beliôve in encouraging the workers in all this nonsense about shortage of hours. Not that it affects me, because I have always done all my weekend shopping on Fridays. Things have such a pawed-over look by Sat-urday mornings, but I am going to vote 'No' all the same because it gives you a bit of leeway if you have forgotten something." She looked slightly affronted when I told her gently that the Referen-dum had nothing to do with Satur-day closing, and said, "Well, they have been making enough fuss about it in the papers to warrant one. any-way." _ Even more illuminating on female political intelligence was the ansiver from a woman well into the thirties who said: "They have one every three years, dojït they? Isn't it something to do leith altering the Constitution?" Another youngish woman who has held down a very responsible post for some jears said: "Oh, yes, we had a fierce argument about it the other night, but for the life of me I can't remember what it was all about, except that it was great fun. I'll remember jf you give me time . . . it isn't about the Toorak election; no, don't be mean, let me think. I really have read it up very thoroughly . . .," but it wasn't until she was prompted that she remembered, because she said she took a very keen interest in politics*and always voted "No" at referendums on principle. It was a pretty little bag all told. Not one woman in my cross-section of feminine opinion tried to convert me one way or the other. They just didn't seem to care. When I think of all the data that has cluttered up the letter boxes on the subject, all that has been written and said on both sides of the ques-tion. I begin to wonder if loomen want the right to vote and am sure that most of them don't deserve it. Tliey look on politics as some dry and dull subject that hasn't"any re-lation to everyday life. In defence, one said: "Well, you must admit that politics are out of this world. The Government doesn't seem able to control prices nowlook at eggs and butter going up every week-so why give them any more powetv I'm voting 'Yes' like every" c her intelligent woman, so that things will stay as they are. You've got to live. It is all very well for the men to talk, but it is a woman who has to budget." Asked if 'they hadn't read theil* Referendum papers, most women said that they did see some white papers lying around the house, but it was generally so tied up with legal phraseology that they wouldn't know any more about it if they liad read them. It seems to me that children have . more questing minds on the subject than their mothers. A little girl of eight said to me this week: "Oh, please say you will vote 'Yes,' because terrible things are going to happen if you don't. Rents are going up and things are going to be a terrible price." I found out that she had been lis-tening-in between her hair-raising radio serials to some "Yes" propa-ganda. Evidently the alarm caused 7>V the serials had continued on into the scatter ads, for she added: "Even a man in America, just a man the radio man found in a street in America, said that they didn't have price control there and butter was about seven shillings a pound, And he told us to vote Yes. I found her a little later struggling over a speech of Mr R. G. Menzies' on the subject. "Would they tell lies on the radio?" she asked. Now she has asked me to "hold my horses" on how to vote until she gets some more information on both teams. I don't want to 'draw any rude inferences, Ma'am, but if a child of eight can grapple with the subject. -would it hurt us. who should be vitally interested, to pry to -sorb ib all out? After all, this Referendum is momentous enough to warrant a feio minutes of intelligent " thought. Homily over. Look before you leaji on Saturday. Helen Seager. 3C5 Elizabeth st., Melb.

17 Mar 1992 - REPUBLIC...TO Tharunka (Kensington, NSW : 1953 - 2010), Tuesday 17 March 1992, page 32 ? Lorand Bartels, President of the UNSW Republican Movement, goes into bat for the pro-republic team. Republicanism has been in the news a lot recently. The catalyst for this was, of course, the Queen's visit. But as usually happens, the media was less interested in Australia's identity than in solving the tricky dilemma: does one, or does one not, curtsey? A trivial question, perhaps. But with a serious implication. The implication was that we were hosting a foreign Queen and didn't know how to behave properly. Horror of horrors! Australia, it appeared, had forgotten to read the latest edition of Debreti's Guide to Etiquette. But, as every monarchist will gladly point out, while the Queen was here she was not the Queen of the United Kingdom but the Queen of Australia. In other words, a foreign country was telling us how to behave when in the company of our own Head of State. To me this is a humiliating situation which can only change when we have an Australian Head of State. Some argue that if the thing works, don't fix it. According to this line, the Head of State is an irrelevant ceremonial position not worth bothering about. But the reaction to the Keatings' behaviour shows that it is worth bothering about. It shows that Britain still patronises us and, what's more, on the veiy point where we are supposed to have something in common! Sir Garfield Barwick, Chief Justice of Australia (1961-1981) and an unashamed monarchist, said: "The Constitution was not devised for the independence of a nation. It was conceived as the Constitution of an autonomous Dominion within the then British Empire." So it's not really surprising when we are treated as a Dominion. Republicanism is about declaring ourselves independent. It is about having our own symbolism. It is about political maturity. This should not be taken to mean disrespect for the monarchy or for our traditions. But the time is long gone when "Home" meant Britain. And to a very large extent, we have not so much left Britain as Britain has left us. And rightly so. Britain is making decisions about the European Community as an independent nation. In exactly the same way Australia should be making decisions about the Asian-Pacific region. It should also be obvious that Australia is also no longer the White bastion in the Pacific. We are now a multicultural society in which over 25% of the population is of a non-English speaking background. According to Mrs Franca Arena MLC, a Committee Member of the Australian Republican Movement, the ethnic communities as well as Aborigines deserve the right to bear allegiance to Australia rather than to a foreign monarch. What is involved in becoming a republic? Legally, not a great deal. According to Prof.George Winterton, a referendum under s 128 of the Constitution would be quite sufficient to convert Australia into a Republic. There are no provisions permanently entrenching the monarchy in our Constitution. Financially, it would not be an expensive procedure. Not much more need change that the flag and some logos. And if the Commonwealth Bank can do it, then surely Australia can. Politically - the latest Herald Saulwick poll showed 57% support for a Republic. Even allowing for a small and unrepresentative sample, however, this result is indicative of a will to change, especially considering that most people are unsure what exactly a republic means. As Prof. Donald Home points out. The biggest problem facing republicans is the lack of education about what is involved. If the facts were known there would be a majority." Hie Australian Republican Movement supports: • an Australian Head of State appointed by Australians • the new Head of State called "President of Australia" with no more powers or functions than the Governor-General • the President elected by both Houses of Parliament for a five year term. • Australia remaining in the Commonwealth. One last thing needs to be emphasised. A republic is not inevitable. Prime Minister Paul Keating says it is. Former Governor-General Sir Zelman Cowan says it is. Even Prince Charles says it is. But unless someone does something about it nothing will change. Lorand Bartels Malcolm Turnbull, well-known Republican and Library Lawn Orator. Republican Shock Troops on Campus. V1U ica ? And now, speaking for the right side of the page (amongst other things), Senator Bronwyn Bishop (mother of Channel 10 fashion and features reporter, Angela Bishop, and Good Weekend Cover Girl) explains why queens are a good idea. j : j T In recent days three things which I, and millions of other Australians love and cherish have been the subject of demeaning and vitriolic attack. I refer to our Constitution, our Queen and our Flag and all have been attacked by the man who parades as Prime Minister for all Australians. He has the temerity to talk of One Nation when his actions have been to set Australian against Australian, to create division, to demean our system of governance and the symbols which attend it. Long have I known of our need to be a good neighbour and trading partner in this, our Pacific region - a region far more diverse and complicated than the one embracing the term 'Asia' and a region which is multicultural by any définition. The Pacific Basin is a multicultural region. There are as many tensions and differences within the region, with some nations remembering Japan's occupation, others maintaining ties with old colonial powers. They are nations who are as independent as we are, but who value access to international trading markets through their European contacts, such as Indonesia with Holland and the Philippines with Spain. ] The fact that Australia, Singapore and Malaysia share a similar legal system and old alumni ties of the Colombo plan is another example. You do not need nor should you try to ettison your heritage and tradition in order to be a good neighbour and trading partner. do so in some pathetic attempt to impress a neighbour would cause that neighbour to despise us. Our neighbours are proud of their heritage and cannot countenance or comprehend those who do not value theirs. Paul Keating's rabid attack on Britain Is one against an old ally with whom we fought proudly in Flanders and Ypres in World War I commemorated by the reed poppy which we wear each year, in the Middle East, in Greece and Crete, In World War II and yes. World War II saw us suffer in the POW camps of Malaya and Singapore and the Burma railway. Part of our tradition is the selfless sacrifice given by so many theatres of war to give us today the freedom we enjoy. My father fought for me and my land in places such as Ballkpapan and Borneo. He joined up, together with ; thousands of other Australians, after war was declared because Germany invaded Poland. Perhaps he remembered that General Monash was of part Polish - Jewish heritage, I don't know - but I do know that he believed the General was a great Australian and I know he bej lieved himself to be fighting against evil - the evil of Nazi Germany; of Hitler; of Mussolini. And he knew all that before Japan entered the war. He joined before he knew his theatre of war was to be his own backyard. He and thousands like him believed in the dignity of freedom of man. And that it was worth fighting for, in any part of the world. ! I It was if you like, an internationalist ; attitude. It was the sort of attitude we ! have when we negotiate In the GATT round - where we call for free and fair trade - when we appreciate the sup-: port of Britain with her attitude to the • Common Agricultural Policy, and the need to bring down the subsidising of European trade and agriculture. We similarly get angiy at our major trading partner, Japan, for contemporary issues, that of her forbidding any rice being imported into Japan. Again we express our anger at the United States of America for her Export Enhancement Program, that is subsidy by any other name, of wheat into our markets. But at the end of the day we trade with I them all, and in large measure .And never in these negotiations is our Constitution, our Queen or our Flag a 1 term of this trade. In my view, our Constitution is worth : fighting for. ! We have the oldest democratic Constitutional Monarchy in the world. It : was the first of its kind to have full j adult suffrage with women entitled to stand for elected office. It has given us a stable, peaceful, tolerant multicultural society where people have come as migrants and have found a haven from conflict, a new start in ' life, and a society which welcomes the | contribution they make. Australia is what she is because of her institutions, the rule of law, and the Constitution that enshrines and protects them. To tear the Monarch from our Constitution would mean we get an elected head of state, an elected President. And elected, he or she, would be. Because no matter the method used, the party which wins the election, would control the President. ; No longer would there be a head of state above politics, with the Monarch remaining constant, and the Governor-General in charge on a dayto-day basis. A President would be an elected party political position with approximately only half the population supporting him or her at any given time. Perhaps it would be the ultimate job-for-theboys, with the Government owning the President. This is a time where patriotism is served by giving leadership which pulls together not divides us, which gives us common purpose not diversionary tactics. We need leadership which travels the road to prosperity, not the Argentinian road, which leads to banana republicanism. ! I love this country. I am proud to be Australian, to know that in only two hundred years we have forged an independent nation which is the envy of so many. Wise forefathers gave us a Constitution which has allowed our Federation to flourish, while other Federations have failed. I cannot think of any other country's Constitution I want to copy nor do I wish to traverse the route of violence which is the history of so many other republics whether inside or outside our region - be it the United States of America or Yugoslavia. Our system is unique and serves us well. Our Queen is gracious and our Flag is a symbol of a free and independent nation, for whom so many proud Australians have died. Let us fight our partisan battles, test our economic theories, but not tamper with our institutions, not tear our Constitution apart and destroy our symbols of nationhood. Senator Bronwyn Bishop "my father fought for me...in Borneo" ! "The party which wins the election, would control the President" viva lUUfehy

Only three out of every ten people interviewed opposed fixing an age limit. Others were asked what age they favored, and answers range from 60 to 65, which, allowing for a further three-year term, means that Federal members would be "out" at 65. 10 Sep 1947 - Nation Undecided On "D.P." Question Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Wednesday 10 September 1947, page 9 Nation Undecided On " D.P. " Question Australian opinion is divided on whether displaced persons" should be admitted to this country, according to a Gallup Poll taken in August. To ascertain what the public thinks about admitting "DPs" into Australia, the , Gallup Poll questioned a nation-wide cross-section of 1600 men and women on the subject. Those interviewed were first asked what they thought was meant in Europe by a "displaced person." Less than half could give a correct answer: 46 per cent. knew, what was meant by the term "displaced person."9 9 per cnt. thought they knew, but were wrong, and 45 Per cent, admitted they did not know the meaning of the term. Men are better informed on the subject than are women— 53 per cent, of men know the correct meaning, compared with 38 per cent, of the women. "Disnlaced Persons" Reference to "refugees" in the explanation gave a clue as to what was meant by the term "displaced person," and of the whole cross-section interviewed: . 39 per cent, favor admitting "DPs" into Australia. 48 per cent, are against the idea, and 13 per cent, have no opinibn. Analysis by occupation shows that most opposition comes from farm workers (67 pc "against"), and semi-skilled and unskilled workers (53 pc). Least opposition comes from farm-owners — 38 per cent, "against," 49 per cent, "favor," and 13 per cent, "no opinion." It is interesting to note that of men who knew what was meant by a "displaced person" 51 per cent, favored admitting them, compared with 41 per cent, opposed, and 8 per cent, undecided. Reasons For Opinions Many of those who favor admitting displaced persons into Australia say we need more population to fill our great open spaces. Others, however, qualified their answer by saying: "But they must be carefully selected types only." Much of the opposition to "DPs" entering Australia arises from the acute housing shortage here. "There are not enough homes for the present population." the comment of a textile worker's wife, Geelong, Vic., is tvpical. "Bring British first," and "There are enough foreigners here already" are other common attitudes. Issued by Aust. Public Opinion polls, 352 Collins-street, Meib.

18 Feb 1948 - Editorial Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Wednesday 18 February 1948, page 3 — — : — Editorial — — — — — A VOTE AGAINST THE MEANS TEST I he result of an Australian v?allup foil on the question of social services, published in The Sun today, offers one more proof, if any more were needed, of public feeling against the injustice of the Means Test. The poll shows that a large majority of people — seven out of every ten — would sooner have a reduction in taxation than an increase in social services. . While some voters argue that "the present high' taxes are destroying the incentive to produce," there is another and equally clear reason for this emphatic reluctance to pay for any more "social services." That is to be found simply in the public resentment which the unfairness of the Means Test has provoked. Why should any man want an increase in social services when one elementary social service, for which he may have paid throughout his life, is. already denied him? This, in fact, is what is happening under the present system, which disqualifies a thrifty citizen, if he has saved more than a pittance, from any right to a pension in old age, even though he may have paid for it with a lifetime of taxes. The Government would be wise if it heeded this evidence of public dissatisfaction and showed some sign of a decision to abolish the Means Test entirely. . ' t: .

He wanted to stop, gossip, which had gone on for nearly two years, about the baths he and his wife took .each night. ' But the dropping of the curtain made the gossip even worse. "Now," wagged the tongues of Alfreton, "they take a bath together." "Malicious gossip;" Congregational minister Rev. Roland Motson Thompson told Fact this week. "The town's full of it. "" "I see dirty-minded whispering groups on street corners ' and even outside the church. They 'kill' people freely. "We even had a 'murder' here. A person was taken to hospital and gossips turned him into a murder victim, although the 'victim' has already left the hospital alive and: well. "It's all done by whispering groups. Someone hears that so-and-so is ill and the groups do the rest." Flying rumors Alfreton's 20,000 population includes many displaced persons — Poles, Latvians and Middle Europeans. Rumors fly around the' town about girls and married women, some of whom are said to be expecting babies. t "Like a snowball, such talk grows," said . Rev. Thompson. "The victims don't come to me for aid; it would be easier for me if they did. I investigate any rumors I hear and, of course, they're not true. "Tattling and idle talk isn't serious, but when it's damaging to character — even if it's true — a Christian should stamp it out. "This is a mining community and I've never seen seamy life like this before. It's not exactly slummy, but there's no culture. For many people, the end of their world is the end of the street and it's a hot-spot for gossip." Fair-haired, clean-shaven Thompson, 41, lives with his wife, Hertha, 26, in a modern, two-storey, three-bedroom house. Pink silhougtte The bathroom is at the rear overlooking the back garden and a stretch of wasteland. "Oh, dear' me, all this silly talk about our bathroom," said Mrs. Thompson. "No one could see the bathroom unless they came around the back on to the waste ground, especially to peep, or used field glasses from the row of cottages on the other side of the ., waste , ground. "We used to bathe at bedtime, about ten o'clock, which is a funny time for people to be wandering about the back of the house, unless they're wanting to. peep. The windows are frosted, anyway, and nothing could be seen except maybe a pink silhouette. "I heard about it when two or three people gave me friendly tips. I didn't take much notice, but put up curtains." Sermons on gossip Mrs. Thompson came to England a fortnight before the war broke out. She was adopted by Thompson's parents," married him six years ago. They have two children, Colin, 4, and Michael, 2. Thompson hits back at gossips in seimons . and' thunders against small-town ..meanness in ' his weekly article in a Derby newspaper. In this week's sermon (called Over the Garden Wall) Rev. Thompson denounced "backward mentalities to whom dustbins and drains become of interest." . 1 On Whitsunday last year, Rev. Thompson announced a special service for parents who said they couldn't attend church because of their young children. 16 Oct 1949 - POLITICAL INS AND OUTS Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Sunday 16 October 1949, page 36 POLITICAL INS AND OUTS A Liberal win would still leave Labor holding the Senate The Gallup Poll suggestion last weekend that the Common-1 wealth Government could be defeated, depressed Labor members in doubtful seats and' brought from those in safe seats the comment "God bless Arthur Cal well and Governor-General McKell." The reagn: Calwell, against strenuous opposition by Speaker Rosevear, but with valuable aid from Air Minister Drake-ford, won enough . support in Caucus for the Act which provides proportional representation voting for the Senate. Proportional representation means Labor will con-trol the Senate for the next three years, no matter who wins the elections. With a hostile Senate,' Opposition. Leader Menzies would not be able to: Repeal the 1945 Banking . Act or restore the Commonwealth Bank Board. Sell TAA or the new Commonwealth shipping line. ' ..Repeal the Act making ..television a Government monopoly. The only way in which Menzies could try to break such a deadlock would be to ask Governor- General McKell for a double dissolution of the House and the Senate. But the granting, or the withholding, of a double dissolution is one matter on which the Governor-General is not bound by the Constitution to accept the advice of his Ministers. Exercising strict political impartiality, in the highest tradition of the Vice-Regal office, Governor-General McKell could still reject such a request. In the 50 years of Federation, only one double dissolution has been granted — by Sir Ronald Munro Ferguson in 1914. Only one unimportant qualification need be made to the foregoing. Labor could lose its Sen- ate majority If it polled less than 40 per cent of Jthe total votes cast and the Opposition polled mfore than 60 per cent. , 'As a practical political possibility, this is hardly worth considering, because even when its fortunes were at its lowest ebb in 1931, Labor still polled 43. per cent of all votes cast. Senate voting Just why Labor must retain a majority in the Senate, no matter who wins the elections, . can best be explained as follows: The Senate at present is composed of 33 Labor members and three non-Labor members. Half the Senate (18) must retire this election, and all the retiring 18 are Labor senators. That lea VPs 15 Lahr»r anrl three non-Labor senators as a basis tor the new Senate. If proportional representation had not been in-troduced, the whole 18 Labor senators could have been beaten and that would have made 21 non-Labor to 15 Labor senators in the new Senate. But the Senate is being increased from 36 to 60, and, therefore, instead of 18 1 senators, 42 must be elected. " Under proportional repre-; sentation, the party that gets slightly more than 50 per cent of all votes, will certainly win 24 seats. The party that polls slightly under 49 per cent of all votes will get three seats ih each State, making ai total of 18. This result caryaot be affected, unless one party polls 60 per cent of all votes. As pointed out earlier, - . this is most unlikely. . Therefore, Labor must win either 24 or 18 Senate seats. It happened before If it got slightly more than 50 per cent of all votes, it would have 24 senators, plus the 15 who didn't have to face the electors, making a total of 39 out of 60. ; The Opposition, knowing - this result is almost inevit- ' able, asked the Government to make a clean sweep of the Senate this election, that is, to make the whole 36 senators, instead of only 18, face the' polls. The Government," knowing it must control the Sen-ate, even if it loses the election, just laughed. Ministers said: "In 1919 Labor and one senator and ; you people had 35, and in 1931, we had three and you had 33. You had the chance then- to do what we have done now, and you wouldn't do it." There is justification for Labor's stand on this. The Government will not benefit in subsequent elections and it is likely that, in 1952 and afterwards, ! there will be only slencter majorities in the Senate. This will make the Senate more important than it has been at any time since Federation. —OLIVER HOGUE

Lying between New Guinea and Japan, these islands were mostly held under mandates granted after the last war. They formed the stepping stones down which the Japanese invaders infiltrated In the first months of the war in the Pacific, penetrating as far as Milne Bay and the Solomons. Because of this their future control is of particular importance to Australia. They do not include the Philippines or any section of the Netherlands East Indies. Principal groups are Marianas, Palaos and the Carolines, and they include the great Japanese bases of Yap and Truk, as well as Guam, originally held by the United States and recently won back from the Japanese. \ Recently an Australian Gallup Poll asked people in all parts of the Commonwealth this question: "After the war, whom would you like to see govern the thousands of small Pacific islands between New Guinea and Japan?" Answers showed that — 39 per cent, wanted some form of joint control in which the British Empire, the United States or tile Allied Nations as a whole would be associated. 30 per cent, favored British control — 19 per cent, by Australia alone and 11 per cent, by the British Empire as a whole. 22 per cent, of those interviewed thought control should bo given entirely to the United States. The remaining 9 per cent, had no opinion, or favored self-government, or had some other solution. Should Explain Tax Needs IF the Federal Government introduces schemes for social security, to be paid for by taxation at a considerably higher rate than existed before the war, it must either convince public opinion of the need for this higher taxation, or expect to lose support among all classes of the community. If this Is to be maintained after the war, It will be necessary to raise taxes equal to the prewar level, plus additional taxation to meet repatriation and interest on war debts, and to provide the £30,000,000 annually for social security. Comment by some of those Interviewed showed they realised that adtitlonal social benefits meant additional taxation, The majority of those who disagreed with Mr. Chifley did so because they wanted some relief from existing high rates. 24 Oct 1946 - Many Voters Changed Minds Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 24 October 1946, page 19 Many Voters Changed Minds By ROY MORGAN, of Austral inn Public Opinion I'olls Research conducted by the Australian Gallup Poll in the last three weeks has proved that a considerable number of people changed their minds at the last minute regarding the Many Labor Party supporters I decided-, at tile llth'hour, to vote their party's "All Yes" ticket while an equal number of Liberal and Country Party supporters swung over to an "All No" vote. (2) That the Social Services referendum would pass in all States; and (3) That the Employment and Marketing referenaums would fail to receive the necessary "majorities in the majority of States." "Yes" — Social Services G3« 54.4 +8.0 ing 46 50.6 —4.6 ment 49 50.3 —1.3 Referendum estimates excluded about 8 per cent, undecided on voting intentions. It is obvious that the Gallup Poll's over-estimation of the "Yes" vote for Social Services, and under -estimation of the "No" vote for Marketing could not BOTH be traced to an "upper-class or lower-class bias in the cross-section interviewed. It became apparent that most of the Labor voters who had planned to vote "No" on one of the referendum questions MUST have decided to adhere to the i Labor Party's "All Yes" ticket. 24 Sep 1951 - GALLUP SURVEY IS EXPLAINED Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Monday 24 September 1951, page 9 GALLUP SURVEY IS EXPLAINED MELBOURNE, Monday. — The Gallup Poll's forecast that the Referendum "Yes"-"No" vote would be extremely close has been justified by results. The doII's prediction, issued on Thursday for publication on Friday, read: "Queensland tand Western Australia will give substantial 'Yes' majorities, but the Referendum will depend on the close voting in other States." "If the present trend of voting continues, only a few thousand votes will ultimately separate the 'Yes' and 'No' votes throughout Australia. Director of the poll, Roy Morgan, said today, "The voting will be similarly close in Victoria, the crucial State." Between 1943 and 1948 the Gallup Poll correctly predicted whether "Yes" or "No" would /win in six referendums. Million switch No firm prediction could be made this time, however, because, as announced on Thursday, the poll had found in the previous weekend that 1,000.000 people had switched from "Yes" to "No" in six weeks. It was impossible to be certain just how many would switch in the last week. Replying on special questioning and a postcard survey, the Gallup Poll estimated that another 150,000 people would switch to "No" and that the "Yes" majority would fall from 57 pc to 54 pc during the week. It now seems that 350,000 people, switched in the last week, resulting in a "Yes"- vote of just under 50 pc. Correct order The Poll was successful in placing the States in almost their correct order of "Yesness." Referendum fig ures tabulated below allow for a 1 pc increase in the Yes vote, which is almost certain before counting is finished:— Gallup Actual Estimate Vote pc pc Queensland 60 5G West. Aust. 56 55 Victoria 53 49.5 South Aust. 51 48 NSW 50 47 Tasmania 48 51 Australia 54 49.5 Gallup Poll experience since 1943 has shown that it is much more difficult to predict referendums than elections, because of a last-minute tendency to switch to No. Of the people interviewed by the Gallup Poll a week ago, 780 were given postcards to be mailed . after voting bri Saturday. When those cards arrive in Melbourne, it should be possible to calculate whether the last-minute swing comprised: (1) Labor voters who switched from Yes to their party's No ticket, or (2) Liberal-CP voters who decided to go against their party's Yes ticket.
