27 Sep 1951 - Gallup Poll director replies to attack on forecasts Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 27 September 1951, page 9 Gallup Poll director replies to attack on forecasts Following a question by Mr. Connor (Lab., Wollongong-Kembla) in State Parliament yesterday, Attorney-General Martin attacked the Gallup Poll system, particularly on its recent prediction aboutfhe communist referendum. Below are the substance of Mr. Martin's attack and a reply today by Director of Australian Public Opinion Polls, Mr. Roy Morgan. THE ATTACK Mr. Martin said the Gallup poll was an endeavor by some interests to use a subtle form of propaganda deliberately to mislead the people of Australia. It had been consistently incorrect from the time ! of the frightful inaccuracy in the case of President Truman right up to the recent referendum and he would like to know who paid the i people running it. Mr. Martin said that on the day preceding the re-cent referendum the Gallup poll had staled that 54 pc of the people would vote Yes, but that the word "probably" had been used. "That was a completely inaccurate forecast and grossly inaccurate in relation to NSW and Tasmnaia," Mr. Martin said. Replying to a sugges- tion by Mr. Connor that he examine the data from which the Gallup forecast was compiled and that he take steps to ensure that in future all such data be verified by statutoi-y declaration, Mr. Martin said he did not know what could be" done in regard to affidavits, but he thought the matter could come within the crime of false pretence or fdaudu-lence. . ' Replying to Mr. Pelley (Lib., Wollongong) . who asked if the poll had not forecast that the vole would be extremely close. Mr. Martin said, "These gentlemen always, have a saving clause. It is perfectly clear they suggested that, but the fact is that they published these inaccurate figures as a clear cut forecast." THE REPLY : Mr. Morgan said Mr. Martin's claim that the Gallup forecast on last Saturday's Referendum could come lwithin the crime of false pretence was a strange statement corning .from a Labor politician at this time. Since the Referendum, Mr. Morgan said, he had been continually assailed by Liberal politicians who claimed the poll's statement that "one million people had swung from Yes to No" had caused a lot more people to switch, thus causing a No vote. "There is plenty of evidence that the Gallup Poll has absolutely no effect on how peAple vote," Mr. Morgan said. "It's whole purpose is to publish clear questions and public opinion on them so as to give the public something to think over and to guide thinking politicians. "It is stupid to say that Gallup Poll predictions are 'a misleading attempt to mislead the people and a specious form of propaganda.' One newspaper in each State purchased releases of the Gallup Poll. In 1946 the Gallup Poll correctly predicted the return of the Labor Government, the referendum on social services ! would be carried and the I two others lost. In May last year it correctly forecast a swing of 2 or 3 pc to Labor at the Victorian State election and it also forecast the result of the NSW hotel hours . referendum in 1947 to within 0.6 pc. Referring to last Saturday's vote, Mr. Morgan said the Gallup Poll predicted that the proportion of Yes voters had fallen from 73 pc early in August to 53 pc a week before the Referendum, at which date 7 pc were undecided. The poll published that one million people had switched from Yes to No in six weeks and that another 150,000 would switch before voting day. It also predicted that the referendum would depend on close voting in several States, which . also proved to be correct. Mr. Morgan said the final No vote in NSW would probably be about 52& pc, a difference of about 2£ pc compared with the Gallup forecast, which would be accounted for by one person in 40 switching from Yes to No' at the 11th hour. Mr. Morgan said he would be pleased to accept Mr. Connor's suggestion that all Gallup. Poll findings be verified by statutory declaration ; and would like the Attorney-General to prepare a form of declaration. The Gallup Poll recorded the names and addresses of all people interviewed and interview forms were open to inspection by trustworthy officials, who would be % bound to secrecy as to the voting intentions of the people interviewed. 31 May 1949 - 40- HOUR WEEK TOO EARLY ACCORDING TO POLL Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Tuesday 31 May 1949, page 10 40- HOUR WEEK TOO EARLY, ACCORDING TO POLL 1 Australian Associated Press Two out of every three people interviewed by the Gailup Poll this month think the 40-hour week should not be operating yet. "Production is not yet great enough for demand," the com- ment of a zinc worker in Hobart is typical. People in all occupations were interviewed in approximately their proportions in Australia's population. The question asked was: Regarding the 40 -hour week, which was brought in 16 months ago, do you think it should have been brought in when it was, or not for a few years yet? The same question was asked in a Gallup Poll in July last, after seven months' experience of the 40-hour week. Comparison of answers in the two surveys shows that opposition to the 40-hour week has declined in the last Iff months by 7 per cent— from 68 per cent to 61 per cent. Figures for this month's survey, however, show that opinion in favor of "40-hours now" is still very much in the minority: — 61 per cent say "It should not have been brought in for a few years yet." 31 per cent say "It was brought in at the right time," and 8 per cent have no opinion. This state of opinion, based on experience, is a complete reversal compared with September, 1947, when the Arbitration Court announced its decision to limit the working week to 40 hours as from January, 1948. At that time the Gallup Poll found 60 per cent approving the Court's decision, although earlier Gallup Polls had shown that 42 hours would have been more in line with public opinion. Answers in this month's survey have been analysed according to the occupations of the breadwinners of the families interviewed. Semi-skilled and unskilled workers are divided on whether it is wise or not to have the 40-hour week now; and in all other occupational groups, big majorities think it should not be operating yet. Liberal - Country voters overwhelmingly disapprove having the 40-hour week now, but Labor voters, as a group, are inclined to favor it. 12 Jun 1949 - They still argue about Sunday sport Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Sunday 12 June 1949, page 6 They still argue about Sunday sport Australian Gallup Poll last week showed that opposition to Sunday football matches with admission charges is decreasing. A poll taken in 1945 produced a two to one opposition but this year the ratio is only five to four and a .najority of people under 30 years of age are in favor. Today through NSW it is estimated that more than 250,000 people will watch organised football, most of them paying for the. privilege. Of this total 150,000 will watch country Rugby League matches, most of which have been played on Sundays for many years. Country teams overcame strongly organised opposition to establish the right to play their matches on Sunday. It was necessary for them, both from the point of view of finance and also because of the long distances teams had to travel. In many country towns Saturday was t full working day with a half-holiday on Wednesdays. In Sydney the initiative for Sunday competition matches has been taken mainly by. junior League organisations and they have been followed by Australian Rules and, to a lesser degree, by Soccer. Baseball has also found Sunday matphes profitable. Australian Rules plays one of its regular first-grade games each Sunday at the Sports Ground and is drawing excellent crowds. The attitude of the Chief Secretary's Department is that Sunday football may be played pro- vided permission is obtained. This is given if religious bodies are not inconvenienced by the gatherings. The department allows the football bodies to charge a "donation" but stipulates that a "free" gate be provided. This free gate stipulation is not taken very seriously by most of the promoting bodies and the position now is that you pay your money at the turnstile to see any of these matches on enclosed grounds, even though it may be termed a "donation." And the authorities also get their entertainment tax chop out of it, too. Most of the subterfuges of the early days of Sunday football charges have gone by the board. These even included, at one stage _ of the country football disputes, the buying of a threepenny packet of peanuts for 1/- to gain admittance. One of the anomalies frequently attacked when country football clubs were seeking the local ovals for their Sunday games was that while councils refused to allow admittance charges to these ovals they were quite happy about tak- ing the usual entrance tees to their swimming pool on a Sunday in the summer months. ' . Sunday Soccer matches are being played now, particularly in the coalfields area, but so far the NSW. Rugby League and the NSW Rugby Union have avoided this : issue. ; Some years ago the Rugby Union considered the question of playing a third-grade final on a Sunday. The debate revealed that at least some of the legislators didn't have any real objections to such games being played on the Sabbath. Judge Rainbow, a member of the Union's executive, pointed out in the discussion that most of the delegates opposing the suggestion were quite happy about organising a Sunday golf foursome or tennis four . for themselves and that their objections were inconsistent because of this Some suburban councils have laid themselves open to similar charges of inconsistency by being willing to throw open their revenue-producing municipal golf courses to Sunday play while keeping the football grounds locked. This year the Leichhardt Council, against some strong local" opposition, mainly from church bodies, decided to allow organised sport on the ovals under its control. The City Council also decided to allow Rushcutters Bay Oval to be used for non-commercial football. One of the strong supporters of this, Aid. A. W. Thompson, said, "Certain churches and a few Puritan-minded people disapprove of Sunday sport. "Only people out of touch with youth would oppose the playing of football on Sundays." Attacking the decision, Arch- Irishop H. Mowll described Sunday sport as "a grave menace to the spiritual and moral health: of.-the community." This has been the attitude of many church bodies. Some have. even pressed for the banning of all Sunday sport, including golf j ' tennis and bowls played on the property of private clubs. One of the arguments of those in favor of organised football games on Sunda3's has been that golfers and tennis players can have their competition sport irrespective of the day. So they can. The most interesting Sunday sport war of recent years has been waged in Newcastle where a 1945 referendum, in which only 22 per cent of the voters participated, banned Sunday sport on the municipal grounds.That That didn't stop the local sportsmen from continuing to use the grounds and courts on Sundays. The council endeavored to en-force its law and one tennis player, at least, achieved some little fame by being fined :5/- and 8/- costs for having played tennis on ' a Sunday on a public Court. The Greater ' Newcastle Council is again .under pressure to hold a referendum on the subject of Sunday sport in connection with the next elections. It has several times refused such requests. In the meantime a great many Newcastle sportsmen and sportswomen continue to flout the law by playing theiir sport each Sunday. There's an interesting angle to this Newcastle iposition. At, least two local clergymen have spoken strongly in favor of sport on the municipal areas outside church hours and a couple of aldermen have admitted to breaches of the regulations. This Australian struggle for the right to use Sunday without restrictions has been going on for a long time. The first local law on Sunday observance was published in Sydney on July 3, 1803. It forbade Sunday sports i and amusements entirely. . After it had been gazetted there were a number of complaints from the more law-abiding citizens that others, such as "rough fellows with muskets over their arms" were continuing to desecrate the Sabbath.;. The argument is still going on. It's also going on in England, where the Lord's Day Observance Society is waging a strong campaign. It is stated that the society, headed by surgeon Sir Cecil Wakely, gets some of its annual income of £30,000 from Australia. Not so long ago the society toured Winterbourne (Gloucester) the home town of the late W. G. Grace, protesting against cricket matches being played on Sunday. It was on this occasion that a demobilised wounded soldier said to them: "You didn t complain when I killed your enemies on a Sunday." He was wrong in that, however. The society during the war stuck to its motto of "No work, no play on Sunday," and tried to stop munitions work on Sundays. It also protested when the Arn-hem para troop operation started on a Sunday. Recently the Rev. F. Mellows, vicar of St. Paul's, Margate, dropped the Fourth Commandment, which forbids work on Sunday, from his services. - He said: "The old Jewish notion of. the. Commandments has gone west. It is impossible to keep the Fourth Commandment in modern civilisation." " Obviously England has come a long way since the Puritan Government in 1656 put- a ban on . walking "vainly or profanely" on Sundays, but it is making headway towards a freer Sunday very gradually. South Africans last week were told that the Government intended to enforce an 1896 law forbidding competitive sport on Sundays. Fishing competitions have already been banned. But in Australia the whole trend is towards relaxing all Sunday sport bans. It may well be that Sydney people, one of these days, will be able to spend Sunday afternoon watching an England-Australia Test at the Cricket Ground. It's certainly likely to happen here before it does in England. — Alan Hulls

25 Mar 1950 - Music Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Saturday 25 March 1950, page 5 Music By J. E. ASHTON IF musicians were asked in a Gallup Poll to decide what man had contributed most through his writings to the ad-vancement of musical scholarship. in the last decade there's no doubt the poll would show Sir Donald Tovey's name among the first three. In fact, having regard to Tovey's wide range and depth of know-ledge and thought on so many musical subjects it is question-able whether most musicians wouldn't recognise his claims to complete leadership. His repu-tation and influence, though well established during his lifetime, have grown almost beyond measure since his death 10 years ago. Today we find composers, lec-turers, programme annotators and musical philosophers quoting his judgments as those of the final arbiter on technical problems. Should there be, for instance, any dispute over the key of the second subject in a Brahms sym-phony movement or the formal arrangement of a Mozart piano concerto the doubt may be settled once and for all by recourse to Tovey. In this way there has de-veloped, within the last few years, something amounting to what may be called the "Tovey Cult." Those who devote themselves to its practice owe a great deal to its leading promoters, Dr. Ernest Walker, Mr. R. C. Trevel-yan and Mr. Hubert Foss. Mainly as a result of the indus-try and enthusiasm of this trio practically everything that Tovey wrote (from his Encyclopaedia Britannica articles to his sporadic magazine sketches) has been gath-ered together and published in book form. Shrewd thought Of the most recent garnering of wisdom from the Tovey pen, Essays and Lectures On Music (Oxford University Press), it may quite justly be said that it affords even richer evidence of varied scholarship and shrewd thought than some earlier volumes. Pas-sages in several of Tovey's lec- ! tures, reprinted here, make it abundantly clear that what Tovey learnt technically from his old teacher Sir Hubert Parry, was by no means wasted on him. In fluency of literary expression and power of closely-reasoned thought he is fully equal to Parry, but he lacks. Parry's broad per-sonal interest in human life gen-erally and in the lives of the composers in particular. Such a book as Parry's great life of Bach, with its warm, strong understand-ing of the subtle links between a man and his works, was quite be-yond Tovey. Haydn and Schubert The line of literary activity which Tovey followed most suc-cessfully, was descriptive analy-sis and detailed research into questions affecting the histori-cal and philosophical background of musical creation. On the historical side the articles on Haydn's chamber-music and Schubert in the book | under review undoubtedly offer some of Tovey's best examples of illuminating discus-sion and sound appreciation of musical values. His remarks on the "glorious contents" of Haydn's unduly neglected piano trios could well be taken to heart by local ensemble groups who might feel encouraged to resurrect these works. (Our copy from Grahame Book Company, Sydney.)

THE FIRST-YEAR ALIENATION SYNDROME You can see them everywhere on campus, hastening slowly to lectures or anxiously awaiting some benevolent force to illuminate the mystery of MB 103 or CLB7. Timidly grasping clipboards, they hover fifteen minutes early outside closed doors and hope desperately that they're in the right place; once inside they rush discreetly so as not to be the only one without a seat. Many still fear the voice of authority directing them to "Take your feet off the chair, sonny," and consequently smoke, lounge or hold hands with a vaguely cautious nonchalance. Most are carefully dressed; many girls seem to have a new wardrobe for the occasion, and proceed carefully around the campus on self-willed platform sandals. On the other hand some are scrupulously unkempt, proudly exposing each daily millimetre of unregulated stublle. Two attitudes are dominant; the brash bravado of high-school heavies on the loose, or a slightly pazzled where-am-I look which tires to reassure itself with gay chatter when a fellow castaway is sighted. Many are almost pathetically grateful when spoken to, especially if they find they're not the only ones who haven't a clue why "e" equals delta Q over Q nought all over god-knows-what. Everywhere, a search for security prevails: where are the carefully nurtured high school cliques, the giggling or lecherous best friends, the highly developed social strata based on a senior uniform or captain's badge? Here is university at last, and the repressed H.S.C. victims from the Department of Education machine are adrift in a sea of freedom which puts them hopelessly out of their depth. Where is the bureaucracy the S.U. is always on about? Where is that comforting paternalism, that academic restriction said to be so stifling at N.S.W.? Oh for a breath of rules and regulations, of "Seniors Only," of "Kepp off the Grass," of "Do not knock on the staff room door." Far from dodging the staff, the main problem now is finding them in the bewildering micro-city of the campus. But despite all this, only a true-blue Head Prefect type with chronic gravel rash would really want to go back to those "good old" fooldays, embellished with eternal Assemblies, pledges and the National Anthem. Most are eager to adjust to this new and freer way of living and learning. Before long they'll be walking into lectures late as though it could happen to anyone, swearing graphically without an instinctive glance over the shoulder and finally overcoming that crazy urge to light up in the toilets. So next time you come across that aura of hesitant freedom, of apologetic curiosity, of timid yet gleeful release, say a few comforting words and pass on benevolently. In no time at all, with a little help from our friends, a dose or two of XL5 and a few more breaths of this clear Kensington air, you won't be able to tell us from the real thing. 17 Oct 1977 - THE POLITICS OF URANIUM Tharunka (Kensington, NSW : 1953 - 2010), Monday 17 October 1977, page 13 THE POLITICS OF URANIUM It is important to see the Government's decision to mine and export Australian Uranium in its proper political context. Uranium Mining is not just a social/ economic issue nor is it just a scientific issue. Rather, it has become, through the actions of the Frazer Government, one of the most important political issues to emerge in the Post-Vietnam war period. This has become quite clear ever since the Government made its unpopular decision to exploit yellow cake. The decision, a-devisive one, was just a further step in the Government's apparently deliberate plan to divide the community in preperation for an early - Unions : nd Uranium ir- election. For instance, the Industrial Relations Bureau can be used to great effect to undermine the fundamental right of workers to stike i.e. withdraw their labour in protest against decisions which are detrimental to their interests. The Union Movement is under constant attack by the Government and its supporters in the media. Legitimate demands behind union actions are obscured by claims that they are baseless or 'inconveniencing the public'. Every strike is now attributed to communist, or minorities in Unions -it's all a communist plot! A visitor to this country would be excused for thinking that Australia is still living in the Menzies/McCarthy days! The Government's intervention in the Air Traffic Controllers dispute is just one example of how far the Government is prepared to go in its desperate attempts to get political mileage at the expense of the legitimate and perfectly reasonable demands and rights of the Air Traffic Controllers. It is interesting to note that these people belong to one of the more conservative, white-collar unions - hardly the strike-happy militants they were made out to be! One of the reasons for the Government's attacks on the Union Movement is that given a particularly obnoxious image, the Unions would be the perfect scapegoats for Ihe Government's inability to deal with the current recession. It also enables the Government to make such outrageous claims to the Arbitration Commission as: Union's refusal to accept wage cuts is the reason why inflation goes on unabated and why unemployment is on the increase. However, to the Government's embarrassment, the Arbitration Commission repudiated its claims on the 22nd August when it handed down its decision after the last wage indexation hearing. In its decision the Commission stated that; "The causes of the present unemployment are complex ', and that in fact 'there had been some decline in real wages since May and June of last year . Moreover the Commission strongly questioned the Government's submission that lack of profitability caused by high wages was preventing economic recovery. Who can forget Ian Sinclair's racist remarks about British shop-stewards supposedly causing Australian workers to become restless, which all but implied that Australians cannot think for themselves. The Government's dole-bludgers propaganda has helped to deepen divisions in the community. Now we see worker against (unemployed) worker rather than unity to fight the Government's policies. It is against this backdrop of Government induced divisions, of media misrepresentation and of curtailed freedom and rights that the Government's decision to exploit Uranium has to be seen. The possibility of an early election and the failure of the Lynch budget to elicit favourable public response to the Government's handling of the economy made its decision to mine and export Uranium a timely one. Why was the decision made on Thursday August 25th with complete disregard for the recommendations of the Fox Report especially the one advocating a full public debate before any decision is made. The filial decision should rest with the ordinary man and not be regarded as the preserve of any group of scientists or experts, however distinguished. In making the decision to mine and export Uranium, the Government was trying to pre-empt possibility of a judgement by the Australian people as to whether Australian Uranium resources should be exploited. Broad sections of the community were incensed by the obvious infringement of their democratic rights. That no decision be taken ... until a reasonable time has elapsed and there has been an opportunity for the usual democratic processes to function. Further, it is reasonable to suggest . that prior to making its decision, the Government was fully aware of the likely reaction to such a decision. There is wide-spread and increasing opposition being expressed by informed sections of the community. It is important to note that the Morgan Gallup Poll figures for June of 1975, 1976 and 1977 showed that the percentage of the Australian community in favour of Uranium mining was 66%. 59% and 50% respectively. This is a 16% decline in those people who favour the Government's policy. This is significant in view of the fact that the only effective 'public debate' has been on the one hand, an advertising campaign instigated by the Uranium Producers' Forum with a declared funding of $800,000, and on the other, localised interest groups operating on virtually no budget at all, and relying on their strength of committment. The Gallop Poll figures become even more striking when it is considered that the U.P.F. advertising campaign reaches a huge percentage of Australian people through the commercial media, while those who oppose the Government's position have only individual or small group contact to rely upon. To get back to the Government's decision, it is our contention that the decision was premeditated, and designed to polarise the Australian community on the issue of Uranium. The Government, in their attempts to cover-up their economic mismanagement in relation f ; unemployment and inflation have advanced the mining and export . Uranium as the panacea for all the country's economic ills! The usual alliance between cons>.vative governments and the commer d media has served to facilitate this attempt at mass deception. The primary justification for the exploitation of Uranium, is the degree to which the economy will be helped, as 'The Australian' Friday August 26th put it: "20 billion dollar GO - 500,000 jobs expected with Uranium" Nowhere in the article was this substantiated. Indeed any realistic assessment of the benefits which could accrue to Australians from the decision to mine Uranium, must take account of the following factors :-The open cut method of mining is the method which will be employed in the mining of Uranium. This method of mining is machinery-oriented, it is not labour intensive. The first Fox Report stated (p. 77) that the Ranger Project would provide 600 to 1,000 jobs during the construction period dropping to a level of between 250 and 400 thereafter. The second Fox Report (p. 175), went further when it stated that The Uranium industry would be highly capital-intensive. It could provide, directly and indirectly, employment opportunities for several thousand people, but this would not make a very important contribution to total employment opportunities in the economy as a whole. One wonders whether the movement of capital funds from manufacturing, (labour intensive) to mining, (capital intensive) will, in fact, create even more rather than reduce unemployment in the manufacturing sector, thus cancelling out any small benefits which may result from mining. In the light of this, it is no wonder that the claims made by 'The Australian' seem difficult to substantiate! So who will benefit from the "20 billion dollar GO" ? The Australian public has been led to believe that enormous immediate economic bern. "its will flow from the decision to mine. Such a claim can be dismissed on several grounds. The Fox Commission itself calculated that the increase in Australia's national income generated by •exports would be 0.2% in 1980 rising possibly to 1.3% in 1990 if the industry •were to expand at the fastest possible rate (p. 174 second report). Now, it may be •argued that this percentage is substantial in relation to export earnings,^ the 'benefits from the export of Uranium, it has been suggested by the mining 'companies, will not accrue until a period of • three to seven years has elapsed. 'Notwithstanding this point, the question .still remains as to who will in fact benefit from the increased profit? The answer, as .in most other cases in the Australian economy, is a small tightly-knit group of companies existing in a complex network of control and investment. Any possible •flow-on to the 'average' Australian will be at best indirect. This possible benefit 'if it at all eventuates will be miniscule. The above assertion necessitates a 'lengthy discussion of corporate interests in the area of Uranium Mining. There is no scope for the development of this .argument in the present paper. The argument will, however be pursued in a .paper to be sub mitted to T harunka in the near future, devoted exclusively to •this issue. In the decision it is also claimed that 'substantial economic benefits will be reaped by the aboriginal population presently inhabiting the Alligator River area where mining will take place. In fact, the headlines of the 'Daily Telegraph' on .August 26th 1977, read "Stone Age Millionaires". The implications are a gross •misrepresentation of the situation. The aboriginal people have been given a 2.5% royalty on all Uranium mined. It has been predicted that aboriginals stand to benefit 'to the tune of $175 million over the next twenty years. Early calculations indicate as was reported in 'The Australian' •August 26th 1977, that ; "Every man, woman and child in the Arnhem Land tribe will get about , $6,500 a year." The actual benefits will however depend largely on the manner in which money is allocated. While the Government has stated that the 2.5% royalty will go to the aboriginals, in fact only 30% of the royalties will go directly to communities affected, a further 30%. will be chanelled into aboriginal welfare projects, and the remaining 40% will go into the administration of tribal lands. Thus, the assertion that aboriginals will become millionaires overnight is completely unfounded. The actual money accruing directly to the aboriginals, on the basis of media reports, will be little more than 52,000 a year (which is incidentially less than social service benefits). Further, the aboriginal people iiave been placed in the position of paying for the administration of their own land to the extent of approximately S2.500 per annum - per person and for the administration of their own welfare to the extent of S2.000 per annum - per person. The money which is supposedly going directly to the aboriginal people .will be administered through trust funds, giving them little access to and no •supervision over their own money. The framework advanced by the Government as being more than equitable compensation for the 'purchase' of aboriginal culture in a 'currency' that has no relevance to the aboriginal people becomes more tansparent in the light of submissions by Silas Roberts, the aboriginal cchairmann of the Northern Lands Council and a delegate to the Fox Commission, he stated: We aboriginals are not so interested in money as white people are. Our main interest is our life style and our culture, which of course includes our land. , n fact, mining will have far-reaching effects on aboriginal culture. This was recognized in the conclusions of the Fox Commission which stated: (p. 232 second report) The arrival of large numbers of white people in the region will potentially be very damaging to the welfare and interests of the aboriginal people. All the expert evidence on this matter was to the effect that ... the rapid development of a European community within, or adjacent to an aboriginal traditional society has in the past always caused the breakdown of the traditional culture and the generation of intense social and psychological stresses within the aboriginals. There is no evidence which convincingly S UM S demonstrates that the result in the region will be different. It is clear that the aboriginal people are again being treated by the Government as second-class citizens and are again being exploited in the interest of capital. They are again being deprived of the choice of the particular lifestyle they wish to lead . They are being denied any real say in the management of their own lands. The Government's economic justification» for Uranium mining is pitiful compensation for this. This should explain why the aboriginal people have consistently expressed opposition to mining. Indeed, four High Court actions have already been commenced by aboriginals seeking injunctions against mining operations. Finally it should be pointed out that in its conclusion Fox II stated • ''That the construction of mines in the region be commenced sequentially , at appropriate intervals', (p. 323). The Government has ignored this recommendation by giving a complete 'green light' to the exploitation of Uranium reserves. The "effects from this may be considerable. It will be impossible to assess the impact of mining on the aboriginal people and the damage which will result to the environment of the region as a whole until it is too late. Then the damage will be irreversible. Fraser's call on August 30th for dossiers to be collected on anti-uranium demonstrators is reminiscent of the Mc Carthy era. Dossiers would be a means of collecting unchallengeable information which could be used to damage the careers of individuals. No access is given to such files, so that any information which they contain could not be refuted. The threat of dossiers is therefore a means of curtailing the rights of individuals to protest peacefully. Moreover, the threatened resurrection of the Atomic Energy Acts, 1953, with its staggering powers illustrates the extremes to which the Government will be prepared to go to see its uranium policy implemented. The legislation (the details of which have been discussed in Thaunka 12.9.77 under the heading 'Repressive Legislation'), taken as a part of the government's broader "get-tough" programme is of special interest. The reintroduction of such legislation, designed to silence free speech in this country is an example of the way in which the force of law (in legitimation of the governments actions) is lent to an action which is wholly unjustified and repressive. Because something has the force of law the implication is that 'smashing of heads' and the silencing of dissent is legitimate and is good for the preservation of society. The government (i.e. vested interests) is not interested in the preservation of society except in so far as society means capitalist society in vested interests and private properly (and the mining companies are a major part of "society"). 1 he extent to which various legislations are repressive is a reflection of the necessity of the ruling class to control society, whilst under the guise of a free market situation. In times of protest, legislation like the Atomic Energy Act, is introduced (or reintroduced). When there is relative harmony (there is of course never real harmony) the use to which legislation is put appears as benevolent concessions from the real rulers of the country. When a power elite, such as the one which is in firm control of Australia at the moment is unable to see past their addiction (i.e. more and more profits at any cost) no programme of repression is too severe. One is left wondering what the next step will be.

30 Jul 1959 - Yes, No, Maybe? Tharunka (Kensington, NSW : 1953 - 2010), Thursday 30 July 1959, page 7 Yes, No, Maybe? Galluping in the Eastern Suburbs CCORDING to a recent Gallup Poll, at A least two out of three Australians favour adding fluorine to their water supplies. These figures are significant and prove that Australians are keeping themselves informed and thinking about problems of the day. They confirm my own impressions from a survey I recently conducted on behalf of the breweries—part of their contribution to "Social Conscience Week" (organised by "Weekend"). The breweries are terribly keen about this sort of thing—ever since Asher Joel discovered that hotelkeepers spend most of their time praying and only pop downstairs occasionally to check the till. My survey was conducted among one hundred average Australian families living at King's Cross. They were asked the following questions: 1. Do you agree with the Theory of Relativity? 2. Other things being equal, would you be in favour of Gresham's Law? 3. Should we teach children the controversial Delta Hypothesis? The results of the survey are interesting: For Against Undecided Not at home 1. 24 68 7 1 2. 58 36 5 1 3. 21 75 3 1 Typical of the replies received were those from vivacious, lime-haired Betty Chunks (17) and her husband, rugged Digby "Laughing Boy" Chunks (57). They have four children and like swimming. They both agreed that relativity was a bad thing and could break up a happy marriage. To the second question they thought that Australia did not need any foreign laws. But they disagreed about the last question: Betty thought children should be taught all things to broaden their minds, but Digby felt this sort of education should be left to the parents. MARK M. BRAHAM.

20 Jun 1988 - A QUESTION OF CHOICE? Tharunka (Kensington, NSW : 1953 - 2010), Monday 20 June 1988, page 5 ? Access to safe Abortions threatened Laws against abortion deny women control over their own bodies. No one gets pregnant to have an abortion. At present in NSW women can get safe abortions. There are abortion clinics in NSW that provide excellent pre and post termination, nonjudgemental counselling. Abortion clinics don't convince people to have abortions- some women walk away from abortion clinics pregnant. Doctors can choose not to perform abortions. The Rev. Fred Nile, MLC, is attempting to change the existing abortion laws so that they are open to less interpretation. His draft Bill attempts to take away the right of women to use their own conscience to choose to have a safe abortion when faced with an unwanted pregnancy. The draft Bill is an attempt of the State to usurp the control of women over their own conscience and bodies. The Royal Commission into Human Relationships discussed the issue of abortion. " The Commission agreed with the Justice Lane report that: " To have to balance the life of the foetus against the health and well being of the mother and her existing children presents both patients and doctors with a dilemma, which challenges in a most acute and often agonising form, the individual conscience of both." However difficult this decision is , it still has to be made. It is irresponsible for our laws to be based on rigid assumptions which pre-empt the decisions individuals must make. The question of abortion is similar to many other human dilemmas in which the choices are made between conflicting moral values. In these instances the churches and other groups give guidance to their followers as to what they believe the correct moral decision is, but do not rely on the state to enforce these. " The Commission concluded that this should also be the situation with abortion. The Abortion Laws Now The legal situation regarding abortion is complicated. In Australia abortion law is a state matter. The legislative law, NSW Crimes Act Sections 82,83,84,is based on the English 'Offences Against the Person" Act of 1861. The Crimes Act specifies that an abortion is illegal only if it is performed unlawfully. The law is open to interpretation because it does not define what is lawful and what is unlawful. The last time that this law was interpreted, in a NSW District Court in 1971, Justice Levine defined the situation in which an abortion was lawful. His ruling established a legal precedent. He allowed that an abortion should be considered to be lawful if the doctor honestly believes on reasonable grounds that " the operation was necessary to preserve the woman involved from serious danger to her life or physical or mental health which the continuance of the pregnancy would entail", and that in regard to the mental health the doctor may take into account " the effects of economic or social stress that may be pertaining at the time". Levine also specified that two doctors' opinions are NOT necessary and that the abortion does NOT have to be performed in a public hospitai. In NSW then the common law situation is a liberal one. The Levine ruling has not changed the law (is the Criminal Law), it only applies to a particular case and can be overtoned by subsequent judgements. It does not alter the validity of the Crimes Act nor does it remove the risk of prosecution under the Act. The legality of abortion is fragile until either the Crimes Act sections relating to abortion are repealed or, in the other direction, if an amendment is made to the Crimes Act which makes the definition of an unlawful abortion clear. Any law which defines the situation under which abortion is lawful or unlawful is open to interpretation which can be more or less strict. Only the fact that the current law happens to be open to any interpretation leaves us with a fairly acceptable situation at the oresent. Repeal of the existing Saw, which would leave abortion with no more regulation than an appendectomy or any other medical procedure, is the only legislative change consistent with the concept of the woman's right to choose. Repeal, however, is unlikely in the current political situation. It is important to realise that access to abortion is better under the Levine ruling than anything more strictly defined no matter how broad and reasonable the definitions may sound. New Proposais and Party Positions The proposed anti-abortion legislation by the Rev.Fred Nile is the most recent in the long series of threats to abortion which surface from to time. The threat this time^, however, is a bit more serious. This week Fred Nile intends to table his aptly described 'historic' private member's " The Unborn Child Protection Bill " in the NSW Legislative Council. If his Bills get through parliament Abortion would be unlawful except when the mother is in serious danger dying if she continues with the pregnancy. Even in this situation the father and doctors would have to approve. There would be no abortions for victims of rape or incest. Doctors who perform abortions could face fines of $100,000 or imprisonment for up to 15 years. Women who have abortions could face fines of up to $20,000 and face 3 years imprisonment. Counsellors would be obliged to present the fundamentalist Christian view of the situation to any one they met who had an unwanted pregnancy. The draft Bill is very messy in its wording. A counselbr is defined as 'every form, professional or otherwise, of persuasive, disputative, advisory, or informative communication'. An Unborn Child is the defined as the embryo after implantation. This 'Unborn Child' would have all the "rights,duties, privileges, powers, liabilities, immunities and pther fundamental concepts of legal relation" of a born person. The tone of the Bill is misogynist. Medical practitioners are all referred to as 'he' and the powers of the father and the medical practitioner are given a lot more attention than those of the woman. The woman's body is treated as a mere receptacle for the duration of the pregnancy. Pregnancy is a treated as a time when the welfare of the 'Unborn Child' is supreme to that of the woman's who makes its existence possible. Following the successful outcome of Marie Bignold's motion, in Parliament earlier this year, on the sanctity of life of the un-born, Fred Nile said that he was very confident that his Bill would be passed by parliament. Marie Bignold's motion divided the House down the middle. Going against tradition, the casting vote was cast in support of the motion, ie the president of the House John Johnson, a Labor man, voted with the anti-abortionists. The motion itself does not have any power. But it does indicate how the parliament might vote on a Bill concerning the same issues. The Legislative Council has a lot of new members - they have no track records on abortion issues. The fact that Marie Bignold's motion was passed in the new government's first session of parliament and that the previous Labor government, despite it's anti-abortion leader, Unsworth, managed to stall her motion indefinitely with procedural manoeuvres, shows that the Liberals to date have not opposedjthe right- to - life moves. Fred Njle is the Parliamentary Leader of the Call to Australia Citizen's movement. His party has an anti-abortion platform. The position of the other parties is less clear. For both the Labor and the Liberal parties all Bills relating to abortion are left up to a conscience vote. At the ALP National Conference in 1984 an in principle motion was carried supporting a woman's right to choose abortion. However a conscience vote is still allowed by all parliamentary ALP members despite call since 1973 by the NSW Labor Women's Conference for the abolition of the conscience vote. The Labour party is obviously divided. There are many conservative Catholics in the ALP, like Barry Unsworth, who are against abortion. In 1981 at the ACTU Congress, Barry Unsworth, the the NSW Labor Council Secretary, made an amendment to delete abortion from the ACTU's social welfare demands . This was defeated. The ACTU now has a policy that calls for the " right to free, safe, legal abortions for those who choose it." The ACTU saw abortion as an industrial issue because it was necessary for women to have reproductive freedom if they are to plan their lives and work. Sandra Nori , Labor MLC, has lobbied with in the Labor party for years against the conscience vote. At a public meeting organised by WAAC last week she said, " that the conscience of a parliamentarian is not any more important than those of the women who may chose to have any abortion. The personal moral codes of individual parliamentarians are not usually Legislated by the state. If legislation is make abortion illegal, then only those parliamentarians who are against abortion have a chance to use their moral conscience. The women who want abortions would not be given the same right to exercise their own moral consciences. This, in effect, means that the parliamentarians are saying that they think that their own moral conscience in superior to that of the women that their legislation would effect." The new Liberal State Government has, as yet, not shown any opposition to the new right-to-life moves. Nick Greiner sent a very non-committal statement to the public meeting on abortion last Monday saying that the Liberal party had not made any attempt to change the abortion status quo in NSW. The NSW Liberal Party were reported (The Mirror.Ap.il 1982) as being "in support of the Levine ruling for any contested abortion case. The Au.fralian Democrats have a pro-choice policy in relation to abortion. Richard Johnson, Australian Democrat and MLC has called for letters from women who have had abortions outlining why it was so important to them to be able to choose termination. He also wants information about anv harassment that women, health or welfare workers may have had in relation to abortion. He intends to present all the information he receives to the Legislative Council if Fred Nile's Bill is tabled. But Fred Nile's proposed legislation is not the only legislation relating to abortion on the parliamentary horizon. The Liberal MLA Guy Yeoman,, has produced a draft Bill that would restrict abortions to public hospitals. This Bill has been described as more insidious than the Nile Bill because it has the guise of being reasonable. Public Hospitals, however, do not have the expert counselling facilities or supportive environment of the smaller dlth ics. The smaller clinics also provide a non-judgemental approach and they have a vers; good medical record. If access was restricted to public hospitals then the incidence of late abortions would increase and presumably the risk of complications. Women who had more money, ie private health insurance, would be able to get abortions sooner than purely public patients. This means that people with more money would be getting better treatment. This is the situation already in general medicine. It would be a step in the wrong direction for the government to get rid of the smaller feminist abortion clinics, that treat women quickly irrespective of their financial status. But perhaps the argument that would appeal most to the government is that if abortions were only available in public hospitals then the waiting lists would be longer and each abortion would cost the government more money. _ the danger with Guy Yeoman's Bill is that because it is moderate compared to Nile's the parliament might agree to it as some concession to the pro-life-lobby, or rather, the Liberals need to keep Nile and his friends on side if they are to get many of their own Bills through parliament this year. But then again the Liberal party could divorce itself quite easily from any party responsibility for the Nile Bill going down because the party leaves the vote up to the conscience of its members. At worst the Nile Bill could get tabled in parliament and be passed and then have to go to the Legislative Assembly. This is not so improbable as one might think based on the extremeness of the legislation. If the Liberal party and the leader of the house choose they can delay this proposed private member's Bill indefinitely with 'more important government business". Because of the high profile and money behind the pro-life-movement this proposed legislation has to be taken seriously by the pro-choice lobby. There are many more women in the community who are pro-choice than anti abortion in all circumstances. A Morgan Gallup Poll conducted after the debate on the Lusher motion showed that 73% of Australians over the age of 14 years favour legal abortion. This view was held by 77% Protestants surveyed and 60% Catholics (The Bulletin, May 15, 1979) and a survey conducted by the Australian Women's Weekly in May 1980 showed that 94% of women were in favour of abortion being available in some form and 6% were in favour not being available at all. This is an issue very much of the silent majority and the very vocal minority. Now is the time for all those who believe in the right to choose, to exercise one's personal conscience, to make sure that the government knows. Voting against anti-abortion laws does not mean that one is pro-abortion. It means that the government recognises that not matter how they legislate there will still be abortions. It means that the government realises that the decision to have an abortion is ultimately the decision of the mother and not of the government and that those women who choose to have an abortion should be treated with all the medical welfare. and psychological care necessary to protect their health and JackteOriranrifas

02 Oct 2001 - SAME SHIT Tharunka (Kensington, NSW : 1953 - 2010), Tuesday 2 October 2001, page 22 ? Different ? PARTY With a Federal Election looming in the next few months, the prospects for significant change within the Australian politics isn't looking very likely. Australia's political system is marked by two political parties committed to basically the same policies. At the start of the year, it seemed that all Kim Beazley would have had to have done is keep his mouth shut, in order to tiptoe over the finish-lineat election time. Following the stunning victory of the ALP in the Queensland state election, which left them with 60+ seats in the lower house (QLD has no Senate) to the Nationals' 9. With 3 seats, even Pauline Hanson's One Nation got more seats than the Liberal Party. Labor won the election in Western Australia in another landslide, with huge swings against the sitting members, partly to do with One Nation's policy of preferencing against the sitting candidate in any electorate. Finally, Labor came to power in the Northern Territory as well, bringing Clare Martin to power, and ending 26 years of Country Liberal Party rule. In a Herald/ACNielsen poll on September 25, The Coalition has leapt 9 points to 49 per cent to lead Labor, down 7 points to 33 per cent, on primary votes - giving the Howard government a two-party preferred margin of 57 per cent (up 9 points) to Labor's 43 per cent (down 9). Approval of Howard rose 8 points to 65 per cent, his highest ever as leader, and even higher than his previous record of 64 per cent in June 1996, when the gun debate was running. His approval has increased 30 points since early April, when it hit a record low of 35 per cent. Beazley's approval has tumbled 5 points to 42 per cent, his lowest as Opposition Leader. His previous lowest rating was 45 per cent in August 1997. Howard, on 55 per cent (up 6 points) leads Mr Beazley on 31 per cent (down 8 points) as preferred prime minister. So what's happened? The asylum-seekers became a flashpoint issue, and the Government chose to capitalise on the electorate's xenophobia, rather than opt for a humanitarian solution and allow the refugees into Australia. Meanwhile, opinion polls also show 77 percent back the Government's decision to support the US militarily. THE HOWARD ERA: UCKING OVER THE POOR Since the election of John Howard as Prime Minister and the Liberal Party to government in 1996, there have been a slew of regressive measures designed to roll back the welfare state and provide for the disenfranchised sectors of the community. Alongside this policy change, the Howard era can be best characterised by the implementation of measures designed to rationalise the Australian economy along neo-liberal lines; from the privatisation of nationally-owned enterprises such as Telstra, which have seen record profits in the last few years, while at the same time slashing upwards of 20,000 jobs. Public Health and Education have suffered greatly under 6 years of Liberal Party rule. Upon their election, and with the discovery of the $8 billion "budget blackhole" that Labor had supposedly created, Education minister Amanda Vanstone immediately slashed $1.1 billion in government funding to universities and public schools. The results can be seen in mass overcrowding of courses, and in the case of many universities, the cancel- lation of many schools and departments which are not seen as profitable. This is hardly surprising. In a political climate where universities must become not only centres of learning, but raisers of revenue, resources must be allocated to courses which will generate the most income, in the absence of sufficient government funds to operating grants. The granting of government rebates and incentives to take out Private health Insurance, as opposed to putting funding into Public Hospitals, has underscored the government's fierce commitment to make people's health a commodity to be bought and sold. The Australian parliament passed the Howard government's Goods and Services Tax on June 29 1999, with Democrats' support. The GST is part of a fundamental shift in taxation. It is an inherently regressive tax in its own right—one that makes those on low incomes bear the heaviest burden. We now face higher prices for nearly all everyday purchases, including fast food and clothing, items on which we spend a far higher proportion of our budgets than the wealthy Yet the prices of luxury goods that are currently highly axed—everything from yachts to fast cars—will fall. The Labor party's decision? Vague commitment about a "rollback" strategy, the specifics of which have not been released. The Howard Era has also seen a massive ideological campaign to revive militarism -the glorification of the Gallipoli myth and the ANZAC heritage, and Australia's role as war-maker. This has been matched economically through dramatic increases in spending- A$11.30 billion in 2001, and predicted to increase by 10-15 percent next year. Beazley's "Defense Dream"? Coast Guard (Approx. $2 billion dollars), Two new Submarines (Approx $1.5 billion dollars), New Salt Ash bombing range (Approx. $1 billion dollars), ANZAC Battalion (Approx. $0.5 billion dollars per annum), Jervis Bay catamaran (Approx. $80 million dollars). UCKING OVER WORKERS D STUDENTS m In April 1996, shortly after the election of the Howard Government with an overwhelming majority, the new Government introduced a new Workplace Relations Bill to smash worker's rights. According to the Democrats, who voted in favour of the bill, "the Government's bill was strongly anti-union and had the potential to create significant unfairness in the workplace." Because it imposed individual work contracts, known as Australian Workplace Agreements (AWAs) into workplaces, limited the role of the Industrial Relations Commission, and stripped down award conditions to just 20 points. The legislation, cloaked under the most draconian terms in terms of proving "freedom" to individuals, would have shut down student organisations which rely on universal membership for the operating budgets. As since we students tend to be some the loudest critics of fucked Right-wing governments, no-one loses, hey? Deregulation of industry, and 'tree trade" granting capital unlicensed ability to flow freely and cross borders in search of the largest profits, impoverishing millions and destroying the environment in the process. Groups like Pauline Hanson's One Nation, and the redneck fringe in far north Queensland are putting their hopes on disaffected Nationals like Bob Katter. Fiercely nationalistic, they argue to curtail immigration, reintroduce tariffs on Australian commodities, and to re-regulate Australian industries decimated by the Liberals' economic rationalist policies which fuck over small farmers, at the expense of agribusiness, more apt to compete in a global freetrade environment. 24 Jun 1945 - Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Sunday 24 June 1945, page 6 [?] UNCIO: very few care Australians have been been apathetic to the discussions and decisions at the San Francisco Conference. .Only a small minority has definite opinions on what has been done. Two out of three women and every second man ' have not followed reports of the conference. Ten per cent, claim to have followed the reports, but have no opinion on results so far. Lack of interest in the conference is not ' aue to distrust of international peace organisations. Indeed, a year ago, the . GALLUP POLL - j Australia Wauts VJD.j i 'Mush' Outlook To Go i PUBLICITY — especially newspaper publicity — on the dangers of prevention of venereal disease is favored by an overwhelming majority of Australians. "The Sunday Sun1' last Sunday drew attention to the dangers, of the "hush and hide" policy concerning these diseases. 28 Dec 1949 - GALLUP POLL WAS RIGHT Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Wednesday 28 December 1949, page 14 GALLUP POLL WAS RIGHT Accuracy 'within a quarter of one per cent was achieved by the final Australia-wide Gallup Poll on the election. Electn. Gallup Electn. —1946 Dec. 2-4 Dec. 10 p.c. p.c. p.c. Liberal-CP .. . 43.6 50 50.2 Labor . . 53.1 48 48.3 dents . 3.3 2 1.5 The Gallup Poll predicted the Labor vote in 1946 at 54 per cent — within 1 per cent of the actual vote. Comparison between the Gallup Poll published Decem-ber 9 and almost complete Poll was correct in predicting that the swing to Liberal-CP would occur fairly evenly throughout all types of seats Tohnr — ranging Alum v strongholds, through marginal seats, to Liberal-CP strongholds. Gallup Actual Forecast vote p.c. p.c. Labor's 20 "top line" seats . . 67 68.2 Labor's 18 "2nd line" seats . . 60 59.2 Labor's 17 "3rd line" seats . . 51 51.1 Labor's 16 "4th line" seats . . 44 45.4 Lib. -CP 13 "3rd line" seats . . 44 40.7 Lib.-CP 19 "2nd line" seats . . 41 39.1 Lib.-CP 18 "top line" seats . . 28 31.0 The 121 Federal seats were classified about into seven groups, according to the size of Labor's vote in those areas at the 1946 election, when there were 74 seats. The Gallup Poll interviewed an average of only 269 people in each of the seven groups, but the seven predictions had an average accuracy within 1.7 per cent. Marginal seats Liberal-CP retained all except one (Fawkner) of the 13 seats classified as "Iiiberal-CP 3rd line" or marginal seats. They also won all except two (Bendigo and Wilmot) of the 16 seats classified as "Labor's 4th line" or marginal electorates. :The The Gallup Poll, however, based its prediction of a Liberal-CP victory largely on its estimate that the Labor vote would average only. 51 per cent (compared with 57.1 per cent in 1946), in the 17 seats classified as Labor's "3rd line." That crucial estimate proved correct within a 10th of one per cent, and Liberal-CP won nine of the 17 seats. With two additional successes in Labor's stronger seats, Liberal-Cp now has 74 members in the House of 121. The Gallup Poll's forecast of Liberal-CP gains of at least 5 per cent in all States except Victoria and South Australia, also proved correct, except that South Australia also showed a Liberal gain greater than 5 per" cent. The number of people interviewed by the Gallup Poll in each State ranged from 724 in NSW down to 180 or less in SA, WA and Tasmania. With such small "samples" from the less populous States, consistent close accuracy cannot be expected with State-b.v-State forecasts. Nevertheless, publ ished predictions of the Labor vote in each of the 6 States proved accurate/ on the average, within 2.7 per cent. Accuracy within 1 per cent was also achieved by the Gallup Poll's experimental "probability" poll in 14 marginal electorates in the capital cities, as published on the Tuesday before the election. Instead of obtaining opinions from "quotas" of people of particular types, interviewers were required to call M Particular Answers, based on 300 in- terviews 2 weeks before the election, showed voting intention in the 14 electorates as Liberal-CP 55 per cent, Labor 43 per cent, and Independents 2 per cent. Liberal- CP had received only 46 per cent of the first preference votes in those areas in 1946, and it was correctly predicted that there would be a swing to Liberal-CP. The actual vote on December 10 in the .14 seats (named in the published prediction) was Liberal-CP 54.5 per cent, Labor 44.2 per cent, and Independents 1.3 per cent. In an attempt to lessen the time-interval between the last Australia - wide Gallup Poll (Dec. 2/4) and the election (Dec. 10), people interviewed throughout Victoria and Tasmania, and in Sydney and Adelaide, were given "post free'reply cards. They were asked to mail the cards on Tuesday, December .6, advising their final voting intention. It was, of course, simply an experiment, and it is now evident that the resultant figure of 52 per cent for Liberal-CP was less accurate than the Gallup Poll itself. The postcard survey, however, had some value, because it indicated that there was little chance of a last-minute swing to Labor, which would have made_. the Gallup Poll wrong. "Why does the Gallup Poll predict elections?" is a question often asked. The answer is: — (1) To increase interest in the elections; (2) To cause more people to become aware of the Gallup Poll; and (3) To demonstrate the accuracy of the Gallup Poll. Business men and the public should not assume that market surveys and public opinion polls made by other organisations (which do not predict elections) are equally reliable. There is no mathematical method of calculating the degree of accuracy of surveys like the Gallup Poll, and the only way to demonstrate ability to accurately measure "intentions" is to predict elections. Issued by Australian Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins Street, Melbourne.

09 Dec 1949 - LIBERAL-C.P. VICTORY PREDICTED IN FINAL GALLUP POLL SURVEY Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Friday 9 December 1949, page 1 LIRERAL-O.P. VICTORY PREDICTED IN FINAL GALLUP POLL SURVEY A Gallup Poll forecasts a Liberal-Country Party win in the general election which takes place tomorrow. This is the result of interviews last weekend with 1900 people throughout the six States, and does not take into account political developments this week, such as the Chifley- Lang controversy. The poll gives the basic percentages as: Liberal, 48; Labor, 44; Independent, 2; undecided, 6. After allocating the undecided voters on the basis of voting in the 1948 election, which experience has shown to be reliable, the following result is forecast: Liberal 50 per cent. Labor 48 per cent. Independents 2 per cent. One unusual feature of the poll was that 6 pc of those interviewed said they were "undecided," compared with less than 1 pc .a week before the 1946 election. Another was the difference in voting intentions as expressed by men and women. For example, 46 pc of men questioned said they would vote Labor, while women Labor voters comprised only 42 pc of the total. All previous final Gallup Foils on Australian elections and referendums showed that men and women intended to vote similarly. Full details of the Gallup survey appear on Page 9. Result of the House of Representatives voting should be clear by midnight tomor-row. [?] Labor's fluctuating vote in recent years, according to surveys made by Gallup poll, is shown above. Support for Labor rose steadily from 1934 to 1943, but in 1946 fell slightly. It dropped sharply after Bank Nationalisation plans were announced in 1947. Throughout 1948 and the first half of this year Labor's prestige grew until the coal strike in June which cut into Labor's following. By Mid-November (four weeks before election) the Labor vote | was down to 46 per cent. By last weekend support for Labor had recovered to 48 percent. World distribution of ballot papers Senate result, however, will not - be known until early next month, because of the proportional representation system, in use for the first time. Voting enrolment is 4,910,789, of whom 1,915,997 are in NSW. This is an increase for the State of 57,248 on the 1946 figure. Candidates their party supporters, and electoral officials are rushing last-minute preparations for a big day's work at the polls. Everything will be ready when the booths open at 8 am. Tonight party branches will arrange final dispositions of their workers at the polling Places, while divisional returning officers will keep their ballot papers under lock and key until 7.30 am. All parties have arraoged fleets of cars for liaison work between the polling places, and it is estimated that about 10,000 people will be working for candidates throughout the State. All sides say they hope to have enough petrol for I the day, despite rationing, j because voluntary helpers have donated their rations, as well as their cars. Both Labor and Liberal W N| parties are holding more than 300 final rallies in7 NSW today and tonight. Big crowds are expected all tomorrow at the polling place for absentee voters in the Town Hall. Another special polling booth has been set up at 217 George Street, for Interstate, and other postal voters Every means of' transport, including packhorses and camels, has been used to distribute ballot papers throughout Australia.More More than 4000 papers have been sent to Australian troops and civilians in Japan, Britain and Amer.ica. A special launch is running up the north-west coast of Australia with ballot papers. POSTCARD POLL AGAINST LABOR In addition to its general survey, the Australian Gallup Poll conducted a subsidiary "postcard" check on this election. Of the 1900 people interviewed last weekend (see above), 1150 throughout Victoria and Tasmania, and in Sydney and Adelaide, were given post free reply cards, and asked to mail them last Tuesday advising their final voting intentions. Poll officials say it was simply an experiment, and there is no certainty that people who returned their cards are representative of all electors in all States. If they are, however, the vote for Liberal-CP tomorrow will be 2 pc higher than expected. Nearly half the cards have been returned. After "weighting" (to minimise lack of representation), the cards- indicate that the vote tomorrow will be:' Liberal-CP 52 ps; Labor 45 pc, and Independent 3 pc. Principal difference between these figures and those for the full survey arises from those listed as "undecided" leaning to Liberal-CP, instead of Labor, as anticipated. Jt is emphasised that this postcard check, like the wider survey, could not have been influenced by late election developments, such as the Lang-Chifley clash.

01 Dec 1949 - Libs. may gain from any voting switch Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 1 December 1949, page 9 Libs, may gain from any votinq Switch By Roy Morgan, Director, Australian Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins Street, Melbourne. Last-minute switching by voters at the Federal elections on December 10 is likely to benefit Liberal-CP more than Labor, the Gallup Poll finds. Question put to everybody who told their voting intentions as at November 11-13 (a month before the election) was: Do you think it's possible you may change your mind before the election? Of the cross-section of nearly 2000 people interviewed six per cent answered "Yes."On On its own, that percentage doesn't mean much, but it becomes meaningful when compared with (a) the same people's declared voting intention and '(b) how they voted at the last Federal election in 1946. Their declared voting intention, as already published in The Sunday Sun, was: Liberal-CP 50 per cent, Labor . 43 per cent, Independent 2 per cent, and Undecided 5. per cent. The next step is to combine those figures (for voting intention) with how they voted in 1946. It then becomes evident that 8 per cent of the adult population plans to switch from Labor to Liberal-CP, while only 1 per cent is going in the other direction: Per cent Intend voting Liberal-CP: „ Voted Lib. -CP, 1946 38 Voted Labor, 1946 8 -Others 4 — 50 Intend voting Labor: Voted Labor, 1946 39 Voted Lib. -CP, 1946 1 Others 3 — 43 Intend to vote Independent 2 Undecided on how to vote 5 Because all the declared switching goes in the one direction (to Liberal-CP) the situation is "dynamite" for forecasters such as the Gallup Poll. For instance, if half of the 9 per cent of declared "switchers" decide at the eleventh hour . to "switchback" — to vote again for the parties they supported in 1946/f-then voters on December 10 will be almost evenly divided between Labor and Liberal-CP. That is why the Gallup Poll asked people if they might change their minds before the election. But, according to the answers, few of the 8 per cent who plan to switch from Labor to Liberal- CP are likely to switch -back — to vote Labor again after all. Indeed, the boot seems to be on the other foot. Among people who said they were going to vote the same as in 1946 (77 per cent of the cross-section) there were two people who said they might yet switch to Liberal-CP against each one who may yet change to Labor. A lot can happen, of course, in the last month of an election campaign, so the Gallup Poll is watching developments by: — (1) Writing to everyone interviewed November 1 1-13, asking whether their voting intention is still the same. (2) Conducting a special survey in 14 marginal seats in the capital cities. (3) Conducting another full Australia-wide survey next weekend, and (4) Asking half of the 2000 people then interviewed to mail a postcard (provided) advising on Tuesday, December 6 how they intend to vote on December 10.

25 Aug 1950 - Gallup Poll shows what we think of the Korean war Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Friday 25 August 1950, page 14 Gallup Poll shows what we think of the Korean war , This is Hc wmr- H By ROY MORGAN j director of the j Gallup Poll I This article gives us — for the first time in Australia s history — a clear and comprehensive picture of public opinion on our entering what may be a World War. $ - Do Australians approve sending our armed forces to Korea? What do they think is , behind the Korean war? Should America use the atom-bomb in Korea? Australian public opinion on those questions, as measured by the Australian Gallup Poll, is described in this article. AN August 5, 162 of the trained interviewers of the Australian Gallup Poll began questioning people about the Korean war. Altogether 1620 people were interviewed throughout the cities and rural areas of all States, according to pupuiabiv/ii« To gain people's confidence, interviewers first asked a couple of unrelated questions about shopping hours and the Governor-General. They then broached the subject of Korea, and referred to some of Australia's Air Force and Navy already being in action. "Do you approve, or disapprove, the Government sending those forces?" was the first question about the war. caifl fhAv an. proved sending the Mustangs and a few warships to Korea. 15-in-the-100 disapproved. 8-in-the-100 did not express an opinion either way. Approval came from 81 per cent of men and 73 per cent of women; from 89 per cent of Liberal-CP voters and 65 per cent of Labor voters. Opinion on infantry burning to the subject of ground forces, interviewers mentioned that our Government planned to send some infantry and artillery to Korea. Asked whether they agreed or disagreed with that decision, people gave answers similar tn those nn the Air Force and Navy already in Korea: — 71 per cent think that some Australian infantry and artillery should go to Korea. 20 per cent oppose their going. 9 per cent have no opinion on the subject. Again approval came from 76 per cent of men and 66 per cent of women from 83 per cent of Liberal CP voters and 60 per cent of Labor voters. Bigger forces To test opinion toward sending bigger forces to Korea, the 77 per cent who said they approved our Government's prompt action in sending a token Air Force and naval units to Korea were asked: Would you favor, or. oppose , sending a greatly I increased Australian Air I Force to Korea ? j Answers, combined with j those to the first question, show: — I 57 per cent think a big Air Force should go from Aus- I tralia to Korea. . j 15 per cent oppose sending 1 more, although they ap- . I proved sending the token I force from Japan. - f 5 per cent are undecided I about sending more. I 15 per cent said on the first I question they disapproved I sending even the token I force. j 8 per cent had no opinion on the first question. To conclude this part of the investigation, people were asked: "Do you think infantry sent to Korea should be volunteers, or conscripts selected by ballot?". Nine out of 10 answered "Volunteers." What's behind it? The next part of the inquiry began with the broad question: "In your opinion, what is the Korean war about?" 42 per cent blame Communist aggression.16 16 per cent blame Russian aggression. 9 per cent say it's a civil war. 4 per cent blame politics, greed or a trade war. 3 per - cent blame vested interests or American dollars. 2 per cent think it's Russia versus USA. 24 per cent can't say. It will be noted that the 58 per cent who blame Communist aggression or Russian aggression agree closely with the 57 per cent shown earlier as in favor of sending a grqatly increased Air Force to Korea. Similarly, the 12 j>er cent who think it is a civil war or caused by vested interests (not Russian) account for most of the 15 per cent who disapproved sending the naval and air forces already in Korea. War supplies to Korea Again probing the background of thinking on Korea, interviewers asked:— "Do you thinlc our Government should do anything about people who try to stop war supplies going to Korea?" 31 per cent would gaol them. 12 per cent would "deal sev-erely ." 10 per cent would prosecute. 6 per cent would deport. 4 per cent would remove them from their jobs. 2 per cent would use the military or volunteers. 1 per cent would "explain the position to them." 14 per cent say "The Government should do something." 4 per cent have no opinion. 16 per cent would do nothing. The 16 per cent who would do nothing about people who try to stop war supplies go- \ ing to Korea, tie up with the 15 per cent who " disapprove sending the token force. (See first question.) Atom-bombs in Korea Two more questions were put to the Same men and women: — .(1) Would you favor, or oppose, arming Japanese troops to fight against North Koreans? and (2J Do you think America should, or . should not use atom-bombs in Korea? On both questions, the answer was "No." Regarding using Japanese troops in Korea, people answered: — Opposed, 53 per cent; in favor, 31 per cent; and no opinion, 16 per cent. Three out of four are agairlst using atom-bombs in Korea, percentages, being: — Should use them, 18 per cent; should not, 73 per cent; and no opinion, 9 per cent. i Issued by Aust. Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins St., Melbourne. . This sad but striking ' picture brings home the disruption to the lives of civil populations caused by a war of aggression. un tne aay inis picture was taken, 5500 Korean refugees crossed the Nak-tong River; 20,000 had crossed the previous day. They waded across the river, which was so shal- low children of six w&lk-)4-ed across without wetting their chins. Like other river lines, the Naktong is not much of a defence barrier. Many of the refugees were ordered across the river by the American troops awaiting a Red attack, because Reds used simple villagers as shields.

03 Dec 1941 - Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Wednesday 3 December 1941, page 7 Gallup Poll 3 Out Of 4 Favor Lotteries More than three out oi four Australians tavor Government lotteries, according to a Gallup Phil, Just completed. 19 Jul 1949 - Editorial Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Tuesday 19 July 1949, page 3 Editorial HOW TO STOP STRIKES | OF THE FUTURE The result of the Australian Gallup Poll on ! union elections, published in The Sun today, offers a final and convincing lesson on how to avoid the kind of strike aimed at this country's | destruction. It should be read in conjunction with the Gallup Poll taken last year on the question of holding secret ballots before strike decisions. I Today's figures show that, out of every five Aus-tralians interviewed, three are of the opinion that the Arbitration Court should supervise the election of union officers. In February, a similar poll showed that more than three out of every four Australians favored a law to make unions take secret ballots before striking. | Significantly, of the Labor supporters questioned I in both cases, more than half were in favor of Arbitration Court control of union elections, and almost three | out of four wanted secret ballots. If Australia is to survive as a democracy, the coal strike must be the last attempt by a minority to wreck the nation's economy. The lesson of the Gallup Poll should convince the Government, hitherto chary about secret ballots, that here is hot only an essential for industrial peace, but here is also the will of the people. Moreover, if the ruses of the Communist minority are to be killed once and for all, the Arbitration Court should not only control union elections — it should also ! provide a register of bona fide union members, and it should decide the form in which questions are put to the vote.
