01 Sep 1948 - Editorial Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Wednesday 1 September 1948, page 3 — Editorial " PAYING FOE THE 40-HOUR WEEK It would be foolish to mistake or ignore the significance of the Gallup Poll on the subject of the 40-hour week, published in The Sun yesterday. This cross-section of Australian opinion shows that nearly seven people out of every fen now think that the introduction of the 40-hour_week was premature. The accuracy of the Gallup Poll as a forecasting / machine, and as a true reflection of the nation's icteas, | has been proved repeatedly in the past.- ; The fact that 68 per cent of the voters consider ,1' that the 40-hour week "should not have been brought in for a few years yet" offers a remarkable example of the lessons of experience. One year ago, when the 40-hour week started, a Gallup Poll showed that 60 per cent of the Australian people were in favor of it. | The swing in public opinion has obviously been \ caused by the scarcity of consumer goods, such as clothing and food and (worst of all) housing. No sensible person will object to the maximum of leisure for workers, when our economy can afford it. But Australia is still only beginning to emerge from the deprivations of wartime shortages and, if . we are to dodge inflation and return to a happy social system, the only remedy is increased production. The Gallup Poll indicates that most people are now clearly aware of the need for harder and more productive work. "

15 Dec 1940 - U.S. And War--Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Sunday 15 December 1940, page 4 U.S. And War-GalluD Poll Prom Our Special Correspondent. NEW YORK, Saturday. Americans are revising one of their most deeply-rooted beliefs of the nineteen-thirties, mainly that U.S.A.'s entry into the last war was a uusiaKe. This Is the conclusion to be drawn from the latest Gallup poll. The post-war . disillusionment was responsible for a flood of books and movies debunking war, and also, for political measures like the Neutrality Act. But the mood is rapidly passing. In 1937 64 per cent, in a Gallup poll voted that entry into the last war 'Was a mistake. To-day the number of Gallup voters holding that view has fallen to 39 per cent. Forty-two per cent, now believe that America's participation was not a mistake. Nineteen per cent, intimate that they cannot make up their minds. Bishops had yet to choose a Primate The Primacy of Australia, left vacant by the deatli on Monday of Archbishop Henry Lc Fanu, may remain open for a year. The position cannot be filled until Anglican bishops meet and appoint a successor. This cannot be done until a new Archbishop of Perth has been chosen by the synod of that diocese. Until Archbishop Le Fanu was appointed Primate in 1935, the Archbishop of Sydney had always been Primate, because the first bishop of Australia had lived in Sydney. When Archbishop Le Fanu's predecessor, Archbishop Wright, died, the Sydney Archbishop was Archbishop Mowll, who had recently arrived from China. As he was not familiar with Australia the bishops broke precedent, appointed Le Fanu. The Primate is the official head ol the Church of England in Australia and presides over the General Synod, which is the Australian Parliament of the Church. The administrative power of the Primate is limited to his own archbishopric, but the archbishops ac-cept his ruling in official matters and seek his advice, because he acts as a liaison between the Australian and English Church of England. The memories of a Sydney fireman Silhouetted by leaping flames, moulded out of billowing smoke, memories crowded back this week on Bertie Land Barber as he recalled the experiences of 434 years in the NSW Fire Brigade. Deputy Chief Officer Barber is retiring this month at 64, - Born and reared at Queanbeyan, Barber intended to go on the land until he joined the local volunteer fire brigade. Service in the Boer War quickened his love of adventure, resolved him to become a fireman. After two years' apprenticeship he was placed on the permanent staff. From then his .life never lacked thrills. «, His first big fire: Hinch's Bond, Miller's Point. The streets ran with blazing whisky. Spectacular: At Parbury's Bond, trapped comrade slid to safety on their own hoses. m, Near death: Barber was fighting a fire, on , BARBER "Horses almost human" the steamer Mount Stewart, fell into the harbor. He wrenched off his helmet, but his tight-fitting jack boots dragged him under. He was drowning when rescued. Years later' a Harbor Board dredge fished out his lost helmet. His biggest fires: The Pastoral Finance Agency, at Kirribilli, in 1921, and Goldsborough ' Mort, Pyrmont, 1935. m Tragedy: In 1922, at the Adams' Hotel fire, a ladder collapsed. Three firemen were hurled 60 feet to the ground. Barber helped to rescue them. One of his mates, Bill Brown died later from the injuries he had received. » Strenuous days: The busiest part of Barber's service was in 1919 when the IWW was active, and fires broke out in Sydney a dozen at a time. Said Barber with a grin: "I think the IWW got the blame for a lot of fires they didn't light. Business was unsettled then." Although Barber was the first to drive the big ladders on a motor engine, his happiest recollection is the horse teams. Said Barber: "Those horses were almost human. They were trained every night, knew their harness drill as well as we knew ours. We loved those horses, and they loved us. The parting was sad on both sides." New clubs' day was April Fool's Day April Fool's Day, 1947, has been fixed by the State Government for the introduction of new club licences under the amended Liquor Act. Today there are 85 licensed clubs. There will be 329 under the new law. Clubs will have to observe the same hours for sale of liquor as hotels. No sales will be permitted on Sundays, Christmas Day and Good Friday. The initial licence fee for a club is up to £500 or £1 each member, whichever is the lesser. In subsequent years the fee will be five per cent, of gross liquor purchases.

11 Sep 1941 - Reveal Public Opinion Trends In Australia Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 11 September 1941, page 5 Reveal Public Opinion Trends In Australia A FASCINATING NEW SCIENCE WHICH ENABLES PUBLIC OPINION ON QUESTIONS OF IMPORTANCE TO BE GAUGED WITH REMARKABLE ACCURACY IS KNOWN TO THE WORLD PRINCIPALLY THROUGH THE GALLUP POLLS IN THE U.S.A. AND NOW WILL BE USED TO | 4- WHAT people think puts Governments in and out of power. Public opinion stops and starts wars, draws the line between morality and immorality, between lawfulness and lawlessness. It gives immortality and fame to one>iVian, casts another aside as unworthy of honor and trust. In wartime particularly it makes and breaks heroes. The . obvious weakness of government by public opinion has been the difficulty of ascertaining it. Not until recent years has opinion measurement been placed on a scientific basis and it remained for an American, Dr. George Gallup, to do it. Here in Australia, the Gallup system will be inaugurated by Australian Public Opinion Polls, and results will be published in Sydney exclusively by "The Sun." They will make a significant contribution in the field of government and other social sciences, and to journalism, enabling the public to follow the trend of modern thought. In the field of government it has replaced guesswork with a systematic knowledge of public opinion. In journalism it has permitted newspapers to cover impartially a great field of news hitherto barred to them. In its way, the scientific measurement of public opinion is a contribution to journalism as Important as was the introduction of the electric telegraph and the overseas cable. The latter permitted them to report with speed and efficiency what people did — their sports, their businesses, their political activities, their marriages, their births and their deaths, their crimes, their benefactions and their wars. What people do is news. What people think, if It can he accurately measured, Is news as equally important. Attempts to measure public opinion were made>hundreds of years ago. But the science of public opinion measurement Is new and has only recently emerged from the experimental stage. It has made possible the accurate and rapid measurement of the will of the people at all times. So fundamental a part of American democracy has it now become that great universities like Harvard, Princeton, Chicago and Columbia have included the subject in their curriculums and in their research programmes. Thirty American universities now give, courses on the subject, and one, Princeton, has established a magazine which circulates throughout the country. "Straw" Votes qHIE scientific method of measuring public opinion, pioneered by Dr. Gallup, does not rely upon the straw vote method of old, which has obvious pitfalls. Its basic principle is the sampling referendum, which sounds the opinions of an economic number of persons, proportionate to each group throughout the country, The method is employed by the American Institute of Public Opinion, founded by Dr. Gallup, and by a sister organisation in England, the British Institute of Public Opinion. It will be employed by Australian Public Opinion Polls, a new organisation, with headquarters in Melbourne, whose referendum results will be published exclusively in Sydney by "The Sun." With their weekly referen-dums in America and monthly referendums In Britain, the Gallup .surveys have sounded the views of the publics of both great democracies on hundreds of political and social Issues, and made the findings known to the public through subscribing newspapers. Many Tests an indication of the field open for investigation in Australia, it may be mentioned that In Britain and the United States the Gallup method has tested public sentiment on more than 500 different subjects, ranging from Government spending, civil service, Government agricultural policy, soldiers' pay, taxation, party policies, Federal and State elections, wage-hour legislation, disarmament, international treaties, the League of Nations and sanctions, and Cln America) the Neutrality Act, Aid to Britain, War Debts, and America and the War. On social Issues, sample referendums have disclosed public opinion on capital punishment, birth control, divorce laws, women jurors, liquor reform and health problems. In both countries the Gallup surveys have also kept continuous Indices of the popularity of President Roosevelt and Mr. Ohurchill, together with their political followers and parties, with the electorate. In England, the surveys' by the British Institute of Public Opinion showed in remarkable fashion, long before Mr. Churchill's assumption of power, the waning popularity of Mr. Neville Chamberlain and the growing popularity of Mr. Churchill. It was by predicting President Roosevelt's victory over Alfred Landon in the 1936 Presidential elections in America that Dr. Gallup proved to the world the scientific accuracy of his newly-founded Institute of Public Opinion. Since then, the periodic Gallup polls have been the yardstick which have accurately measured public support or opposition for every major act of the three Roosevelt Administrations. That is why President Roosevelt has made less mistakes in gauging American public opinion than any other President. Roosevelt Uses JT i& a well-known fact that President Roosevelt pays close attention to the results of the Gallup polls when framing high policy. This has been particularly so since the beginning of the war, because Gallup has, in many cases, the answers ready before the President asks the questions. Repeal of the arms embargo, aid to Britain, the neutrality patrols, convoying, and keeping out of the war have been the major issues of the war in America. Before President Roosevelt has moved on any of them he has had as his guide of public opinion the scientific surveys by the Gallup poll.Gallup Gallup employs for his surveys a fact-finding organisation with the sole purpose of. measuring public opinion on political and social issues of the day. The role of the Institute of Public Opinion in both Britain and the United States is one of strict impartiality. They have no political predilections and espouse no public or private cause, no matter how worthy. It is not concerned whether the views of the people, as shown by the referendums, are right or wrong. Dr. Gallup believes that his surveys make the mass of voters articulate — which is the essence of democracy. Hie distinguishing mark of his system Is the use of the cross-section principle. Just as the bacteriological content of a re- servoir can be determined by a test-tube, or the ore content of a lode by a representative sample, so the opinion of a community can be determined by interviewing a representative number of people — the determining factor being that the cross-section should be truly representative of the whole. Factors Of Accuracy QF the four factors necessary for an accurate vote— number of voters, types of voters, character of questions asked, and timing of vote-r-the least important is the number of persons voting in the sample. There is no scientific support for the belief that the most accurate survey must necessarily be the one which reaches the largest number of people. The Gallup surveys on election results have all been within 5 percent. of the actual results — an amazingly accurate achievement, which can and has been achieved with as few as GOO to 900 ballots. It has been scientifically proved that the mathematical chances are 997 to 1UOO that a balanced sample of 900 cases will be accurate within 5 per cent., where opinion divides evenly. When opinion divides in the ratio of 30 to 20, 576 cases are enough to secure this degree of accuracy. The laws of probable error have long been known. The prime determining factor of accuracy in any survey of public opinion is the cross-section — the balancing of' population groups In the proper proportions. If the cross-section is faulty, no piling up of cases In a national survey can eliminate the error. Surveys conducted by newspapers cannot be reliable if they depend upon their readers for votes, since the reader of any particular newspaper usually has views not those of the reader of other newspapers. The "Literary Digest" straw vote on the 1936 Presidential elections in the United States, failed because it relied upon its own reuders. In the Gallup survey, the smallest unit used in making up a cross-section is the State. If one-third of the voters in a State live on farms, one-third of the ballots received from that State must come in from farmers. If one-eighth of the voting population of another State is on the basic wage, one-eighth of the ballots must come from the basic wage group. Six Keys fHE Gallup method uses six statistical keys, or "controls," to assure a representative cross-section. The samples must contain the correct proportion of voters from each State, men and women, farm voters and city voters ( population of cities is also taken into account), voters of all age groups, voters in income groups, and voters of known political beliefs. Since its inception, the American Institute of Public Opinion, employing this method of cross-section, has never been on the wrong side in a national prediction. The same method of sampling representative cross-sections will be employed by the Australian Public opinion Polls, which, for over a year, has been preparing figures from the . last nation-wide census for that purpose. In each of the monthly polls, It will conduct on Australian subjects of the hour, the strictest attention will be given to accurate sampling, and test referendums have already been held on some questions. As an instance, it mav be mentioned that Australian surveyors, trained in America bv the Gallup organisation, neia a test referendum in the Boothby by-election in South Australia, in which Dr. Grenfell Price defeated a Labor candidate. The actual election resulted In the election of Dr. Grenfell Price with a substantial reduction iu the .previous U.A.P. majority. In the sample referendum, which was held In each of the subdivisions of Boothby, the Australian Public Opinion Polls experts predicted results which were almost Identical with those that actually occurred. The survey's function is not simply to conduct pre-election surveys, although a foreciust of how people will vote on election day provides a legitimate and interesting news story. But from the standpoint of technique, the experience in the Boothby electorate was valuable in determining the accuracy of the sampling procedure which has been adopted for Australia, after 12 monthf of intensive research. Dr. George Gallup

06 May 1943 - Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 6 May 1943, page 4 Gallup Poll Opinions Changed Aboafi Government MOST Australians are still satisfied with the way their Government is directing: the war effort, but the latest Australian Gallup Poll suggests that the Government's prestige is lower than a year ago. 03 Jun 1943 - Behind The Scenes of a "Sun" Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 3 June 1943, page 4 Behind The Scenes of a "Sun" Gallup Poll Here's That Man Again Asking Opinions By -fC BETTY WADSWORTH, a "Sun" Special Writer JL- s__ I'VE just returned from a bunt in lite suburbs — a hunt for public opinion, and mighty interesting, loo. The idea was to see behind the scenes of one of "The Sun's" Australian, Public Opinion Polls and flhd out how the. "samples" were collected. With a manner calculated not to influence anyone (for the Public Opinion (Gallup) Poll interviewer must record only, not guide), he approached men and women In the comfortable, ugly, standardised houses of the artisan, in cramped slums and pleasant, garden-set homes of the wealthier neighborhoods. He asked questions on subjects ranging from sex education to trading banks, took up quite a bit of their time, thanked them and went away to index and sort their replies. And, right away, let's compliment the average Australian on his friendly co-operativencss. There were very few refusals, and, without exception, everyone interviewed tried to give an honest opinion. 0 F course, we did meet the woman with a "hawker complex" who, behind a rapidly-closing door, said she wasn't Interested in public questions, had no opinions, and her husband was out (although we clearly saw him hiding In the woodshed). Then there was the wife whose husband was a journalist, and she was sick of hearing about those things; She said "no," too, and who could blame her? But. the great majority tried to help. And if anyone Is unacquainted with a subject, or really hasn't an opinion, it is never the object of the interviewer to talk him (or her) Into producing one. Whether they Invited us on to the sun-porch at Hornsby, peered from behind a slit In the door in some crowded Industrial district, or opened the front door and gave their opinions with one ear to the wants of baby inside — thev were all helpful. But here's a remarkable thing. Although she may have been henpecking him just two minutes before to cement the garden path, ask Mrs. Suburbia for an opinion on whether a" problematical free medical service should be doctor or Government controlled, and she yelps for assistance to her mate. Mr. Suburbia is king of the castle, too, as far as politics are concerned. Most women follow In the footsteps of their husbands, wiping off 10 hopeful political parties with a single remark, such as,. "Oh, I just vote the way George tells me." However, guiding the weaker sex in the ways of politics hasn't made the men swell-headed. The great majority labelled themselves "just a meal ticket" as they revealed by answering "Yes" to the question on "Would equal pay for men and women greatly reduce women's desire for marriage and a family — or would it make no difference?" Women, on the. other hand, answered pretty solidly that it would make no difference. Maybe that's a compliment to the other sex, perhaps just good commonscnse. Everyone faced up unblink-ingly to the question on sex education—a reaction which it seems doubtful would have been so six months ago. And as the completed poll has since shown, seven out of eight people think" children should' be instructed In sex matters by qualified teachers. To some people, the willing ear of the Public Opinion Poll interviewer is a godsend. ? w " ITNESS the gentleman with a theory of his own for putting the world on its feet. Standing in a puddle of water on a windy corner he told us that if everyone received the same rate of pay, no matter what they worked at. the world would be a better plaoe. This idea colored all his views. Then there was the mild old gentleman who flared up on the equal pay for women question. "Pay them more than men," he shrieked, waving his umbrella in the air. "One woman is as good as ten men any day. Let them run the country, and we won't have any strikes." Many men and women swallow their politics whole. After giving a pat answer on what party they would vote for if an election were held today, they revealed that the views of their avowed parties and their own opinions on private ' or Government ownership , 'Of trading banks were quite at variance. When the interviewer has obtained answers to the public questions on his sheet, he asks a few personal questions to assure that he Is getting opinions from a representative cross-section of the community. One of these Is, "Would you mind telling me your approximate age?" And even in these goldfish days, when we expect any time to register the number of our back teeth fillings at the GPO, this one brought a gulp. ? Strangely enough, most women gulped and told, But many an old gentleman In the seventies countered coyly, "Well, how old would you think?" BUt it's not wise to guess out loud. Women's views are colored more by their Idea of how things are going to affect their nearest interests — their homes, children, fighting men. Men are willing to take a plunge into the dreamier realms of theory. The views of all seem similar to the views of other people in the localities In which they live. "Do I believe In woman's equality? Pshaw! One woman is equal to 10 men In any obi"

04 Jun 1943 - Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Friday 4 June 1943, page 4 Gallup Poll Casting Their Votes ClX out of 10 people recently interviewed for the Australian Callup Poll said that they always voted either Labor or non-Labor — the two-party sys- tem — at Federal elections. The other four out of 10 apparently belong to the ranks of the swinging voters, so nearly half of the electors may be swayed by party policies and speeches between now and election time.In In May, Australian Public Opinion . Polls conducted a nation-wide survey to disclose the extent to which Labor and non-Labor (UAP-CP) candidates can, or cannot, rely on the support of electors. A card with five statements was handed to each person interviewed. They were asked to select the statement closest to their usual attitude at election time. The card read: 1. I always vote Labor if the man is right. 2. I may change from Labor, if another man is exceptional. 3. Independent candidates are my choice. 4. I may change from UAP (or CP) if another man is exceptional. 5. I always vote UAP (or CP) if the man is right. Answers, stated in terms of each 100 people interviewed, follow : — Labor Supporters: Always 33 Usually 14 — i UAP-CP Supporters: Always'.. ...... 2G Usually ........ 15 — 41 People preferring Independents .... 6 Those "Not interested in politics" .... 6 100 It seems:— (1) That Labor can rely on one elector in three, and that UAP-CP candidates can be sure of one elector in four; and (2) That success at elections depends on (a) the "loyalty" of the 14 or 15 per cent, who "usually" vote for either side; and (b) the appeal made to the '12 per cent, who are non-party, or disinterested. It seems that victory — or defeat — in the 16 seats held by only small majorities (Labor has nine, UAP five, and CP two) depends chiefly on the 14 per cent, who "usually vote Labor," and the almost similar proportion 'who "usually vote UAP or CP." In 1940, 10 per cent, of the "usually UAP/CP" people — equivalent to one elector in 100 —actually voted Labor, while an almost similar proportion of "usually Labor" people voted UAP or CP.

28 Aug 1943 - Gallup Poll Found Swing To Labor Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Saturday 28 August 1943, page 2 Gallup Poll Found Swing To Labor MELBOURNE, Saturday, — The Gallup.. Pall has had its first real test in Australia. This is how is fared — Its final estimate of the first preference vote of civilians for the House of Representatives was: Labor, 45 pc; UAP-CF, 38 pc; "others," 17 pc. The civilian vote at the election actually was: Labor, 51 pc; UAP-CP, 32 pc; "others," 17 pc. The Gallup survey was taken a week before the election. It disclosed some swing to Labor and correctly estimated the size of the "others" vote. There was a difference, however, of 6 pc between the estimated and actual votes for the .major parties. The lesson Is, that as an election campaign is short, the Australian Gallup Poll must conduct its final pre-election survey within two or three days of an election. It Is not generally recognised that a Very small increase in first preference votes can cause a landslide to any one party — particularly if support for other parties is split by Independents. Labor received only 3 pc more of first preference votes of civilians than at the 1940 election, but party will now hold two-thirds of the seats in the House of Representatives, compared with less than half before the election. Australian Public Opinion Polls are always open to investigation. By Roy Morgan, director Australian Public Opinion Polls, 353 Colllns-strcet, Melbourne.

03 Mar 1943 - Australian Gallup Poll: Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Wednesday 3 March 1943, page 4 Australian Gallup Poll: Immigration After The War ONLY one Australian in 20 is totally opposed to resumption of immigration by white people after the war, but half of a cross-section interviewed for the Gallup Poll thinks there should be some sort of limitation. Migration may easily rank high among postwar problems, so it is well that Australia should start now to work out its policy. A final decision, of course, will depend on conditions at the end of the war, but last month Australian Public Opinion Polls — the Gallup Poll ol Australia — took a nation-wide "sample referendum" on the question: " "After the war, should immigration of white people into Australia be unrestricted, limited, or stopped?" Of each 100 people interviewed :42 42 favored unrestricted white immigration, 49 thought it should be limited in some way, 5 were against any immigration, and4 4 did not answer. There was no significant difference of opinion between people living in different States, Owners und managers of businesses and professional people were slightly more favorable to immigration than artisans, but even among those In the lowest income group the "no Immigration" vote was under 10 per cent: As this tnble shows. Labor Party supporters and non-Labor people both favor immigration, but not wholly unrestricted: ATTITUDES TO WHITE MIGRANTS Labor UAP Party & CP Voters. Voters. Unrestricted 38 46 Limited 48 50 None after war 9 2 No opinion 5 2 100 100 Even among farm owners — the group most favorable to immigration — opinion was evenly divided between unrestricted and selected migration. The 49-ln-the-100 who thought immigration of white people should be "limited" were asked also: "What limitations would you suggest?" The genet ai line of thought Is White immigration strongly favored. indicated by the following summary of their answers:— "According to Australia's ability to absorb them" (9 per cent, of all people interviewed). "Best types only, according to health, finances, &c." (9 per cent.). "British only" (6 per cent.). "English speaking only" (4 per cent.). . "Allies only," or "No enemies" (5 per cent-.), "No Italians" or "No Southern Europeans" (6 per cent.). The above percentages and another 10 per cent, who were indefinite, make up the 49 per cent, in favor of selected white migration. Typical reasons for favoring unrestricted white Immigration were :— "War has made us realise the need for populat-ion" (railway worker, Brisbane) and "We must populate the country if we wish to hold it" (munition worker's wife. Adelaide). Usual comments by, the small minority totally opposed to migration were "Not until work is found for every Australian," or 'Not until our returned servicemen are settled."

28 Feb 1943 - EUROPE Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Sunday 28 February 1943, page 2 EUROPE Public opinion on a pigeon's wings FACT'S London News Bureau Along- the coast of occupied Europe, Allied airmen, are conducting the most fantastic Gallup poll of the war. Object: To discover for psychological, and propaganda, reasons the reaction of oppressed peoples ' to causes, and men in the fight for- , liberation.. Stranger even than the poll is the ingenious method evolved- for. taking it. Round' about midnight an; Allied1 plane, flying high overhead, dron'fes across the seaboard of occupied France, Belgium, Holland, or Norway. Nazi ack-ack guns get ready for action, but sentries resume their normal watch when the planes drop , no bombs. Prom the houses in the coastal strip; civilians sneak out in the darkness, occasionally find their reward,. a parachute to- which is attached a. curious contraption. Inside- is a carrier pigeon and a questionnaire. 'Sometimes, Sometimes, as well as the required-answers to- such questions as "Would the people of your district support a Second Front?"' "What encouraged you most in the war news last-week?" direct military information is attached to the carrier pigeon, before it is released by the finders for its flight home to England. Mainly, however, Allied Intelligence Services are trying to discover what the people of invaded countries think about. Such knowledge, they believe, will be an important asset when oppressed civilians are called upon, to help in the invasion of Europe, promised for this year. De Gaulle on the rise The carrier-pigeon method is no secret to the Germans, as some parachute birds must have fallen, into their hands, but the Nazis are unable to prevent a surprising number of answers being flown back. Most of the questions asked are being kept secret but one revealed is: "Whom do you consider the greatest leaders in the United Nations' fight for victory and- freedom?" The Big Three, Churchill, Roosevelt, and Stalin, are generally returned at the top, but since the-Allied landing in North Africa, de Gaulle's name has advanced bv-leaps and bounds, from low on the list to a place among the leaders. De Gaulle is being picked not only in Prance, but in. Belgium and Holland, even Denmark.

28 Feb 1943 - Poll on compulsory unionism shows public evenly divided Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Sunday 28 February 1943, page 2 Poll on compulsory unionism shows public evenly divided PUBLIC opinion, as expressed in an Australian "Gallup poll," showed an even division of opinion on the question of compulsory unionism for all em- ployees. "White-collar" contrast Mast of tlie 18 pc who were undecided, or did not answer the question, were women. 01 Mar 1943 - Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Monday 1 March 1943, page 4 Gallup Poll Australia Favors Training For Youths When asksd, "Should compulsory cadet training of youths of 16 and 17 begin immediately?" three out of four men and women in all States answered "Yes," in a Gallup "sample referendum," taken throughout Australia this month. 28 Apr 1943 - Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Wednesday 28 April 1943, page 4 Gallup Poll OPINION ON PRICE CONTROL DIVIDED Australians are almost equally divided on the question of whether price control has been -reasonably successful, a nation-wide Gallup "sample referendum" shows. Of each 100 people interviewed: —47 47 said, "No; it has not." 43 said, "Yes; it has," and 10 were undecided. All major population groups-sex, age, economic and State — held much the same opinions. "Food and clothing are too expensive," was the usual comment. Those who believe control has been reasonably successful often said, "It would have been worse without control," but others qualified their answer with. "But mere is room ior improvement. Announcement on April 12 that "price control subsidies" would be paid in future, instead of allowing traders to pass on rising costs, did not affect people's opinions about the past. Another survey, taken a year ago, showed that 83 per cent, of the people interviewed approved the pegging of prices and wages

25 Feb 1943 - Gallup Poll Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Thursday 25 February 1943, page 4 Gallup Poll Would Postpone Election IF the majority of the public had its way, the Federal election, due in a few months, would be postponed for at least a year, according to an Australia - wide Gallup "sample referendum." The survey, taken this month by Australian Public Opinion Polls — the affiliate of the British, American, and Canadian Gallup Polls — was on the question: "Should the Commonwealth election, due this year, be held — or postponed for a year?" Of each 100 people interviewed —33 33 said, "Hold the election," 51 said, "Postpone It," and . II were undecided. Very few people know that the Federal Constitution states that an election MUST be held by November 20, three years after the present Parliament first met in 1940. The Constitution, of course, can be altered only by a . referendum, which would be much the same as an election. Women gave most of the majority to the "postpone" vote. But among men -the "postpone the election", vote of 49 per cent, was 5 per cent, larger than the "hold it" vote of 44 per cent. All age groups held much the same opinions, and there was little difference in the voting in each State. Analysis of the comments made by people after, answering the question shows that the chief reason for favoring postponement was: "This is no time for expensive elections." Many thought there should not be an election until after the war. The vote for postponing the election was 53 in the 100 among people who voted Labor at the last Commonwealth election, and 48 in the 100 among supporters of the UAP and Country Party. The "hold the election" vote was 35 in the 100 for Labor voters and 43 in the 100 for non-Labor people. The fact that half of the non-Labor people favored postponement does not mean that they intend to vote Labor at the next election.

29 Jun 1942 - War Saving Less Popular Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Monday 29 June 1942, page 5 Wdr Saving Less Popular COMPULSORY war saving, favored by the .majority of Australians six months ago, now has an many opponents as adherents, according to a nation-wide Gallup Poll, taken by Australian Public Opinion Polls between June 5 and June 15. Nine months ago, after England had adopted the Kynes compulsory saving plan, all classes of Australians thought it should be introduced here. The following table, however, 'shows how a twerto one majority has disappeared:— Compel Don't Undc-saving. compel elded pc pc pc Sept. 55 27 18 Deo. 51 36 13 June 44 46 10 The question asked in the September survey, taken just before presentation of the Fadden Budget (which Included compulsory saving), was: — Would you favor a compulsory saving plan — to help pay for the war, and to provide people with money to spend after the war? The December survey — conducted after the Chtflev Budget, had raised taxes on higher incomes, but before the supplementary all-round increase in income' tax by rates varying from 6d to Is— was on the question: Should the Government introduce compulsory saving? The survey just completed (taken between the Midway victory and the Libyan defeat) was on: Should war saving be voluntary — or compulsory, according to peoples' means? Details Of Voting Age had little influence on the voting. Men gave a small majority for' compulsory saving, while women opposed it. In no State was there a sub-.staiitial majority either way. New South Wales, Western Australia and Tasmania favored the voluntary system, Victoria gave an even vote, and Queensland and South Australia supported compulsion. Of Labor Party supporters Interviewed, 34-ln-the-100 voted "compulsory," 54 - in - the - 100 "voluntary" and the other 12 were undecided. Among people who usually vote UAP or Country Party, however, the vote was: Compulsory, 54 per cent.; voluntary, 37 per cent.; and undecided, 9 per cent. Reasons Analysed "The average worker will do his best," the comment of a Sydney factory worker, and "The cost of living is too high to save," from an agent in Narra-coorte (SA),- are typical reasons for opposing compulsory savings. A less common attitude was: "People should have control of their own money; compulsion Is dictatorship." The chief reason for supporting compulsory saving is expressed in the comment of a Victorian quarry manager: "It Is the only way to ensure an all-in effort." A widow In Brisbane expressed a similar view when she said : "Too many are evading their responsibilities." "It would assist post-war reconstruction," from a bank clerk in Camden (NSW), was another common opinion.

26 Jun 1942 - DEFENCE ACT AND THE MILITIA Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Friday 26 June 1942, page 5 DEFENCE ACT AND THE MILITIA "Alter the law so that the militia could leave Australia in an offensive agkinst the Japanese," is the two-to-one vote in an Australia-wide Gallup Poll just completed. In all States both supporters of the Labor Party and non-Labor people favored altering the law. Those who thought the militia should remain in Australia usually commented: "Men- are needed' here to defend Australia.-Some added; "They can volunteer for the AIF, if they want to." "We must be free to meet the enemy anywhere," from a baker in Brisbane, typified the general attitudeOthers, Others, who favored the offensive. rather than the defensive, agreed with a shop assistant, in Adelaide, who said, "Keep the war away from Australia."

09 Jun 1942 - State Parliaments Are Not So Popular Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Tuesday 9 June 1942, page 5 State Parliaments Are Not So Popular ABOLITION of State Governments is strongly favored in New South, Wates, Queensland and Victoria, and slightly favored in South Australia, according to a Gallup Poll taken in May. In Western Australia and Tasmania, however, abolitionists are in a minority. During May. the interviewers for Australian Public Opinion Polls — the Gallup Poll of Australia — set out to And the pub-He's answer to the question:— "Should State Gawern-ments be aliolished?" Opinions were obtained In each State, according to population. People of all types. In a full range of localities, were Included in the sample. Dr. Gallup's long experience In America proves that results obtained by these "sample referon-' dums" are reliable. Of each 100 interviewed— 60 favored abolishing State Governments. 19 were against abolishing Ihem.15 15 were undecided; and 6 gave no answer. Attitudes of Labor Party supporters ' and non-Labor people were almost Identical. Most of the "undecided" and "no answer" votes occurred fmone women. For men only. the vote was 68 in favor of abollshlnc state Governments and 20 against with 12 undecided or unable to answer. Age had no significant Influence on the voting. To ascertain whether the 60-In- the- 100 who had voted in favor of abolishing State Governments were aware of the probable effects, they were also asked: — Subsidy Question "Should the States hand over their powprs to the Commonwealth, leaving minor matters to local councils and State boards?" 30 Jun 1942 - Nationalisation Of Coal Industry Sun (Sydney, NSW : 1910 - 1954), Tuesday 30 June 1942, page 5 Nationalisation Of Coal industry ONLY one Australian in four favors permanent nationalisation of the Coal industry, but a Gallup Poll taken this month shows that a substantial majority would approve Commonwealth Government action to take over the mines as a wartime measure. Permanent nationalisation of the mines was most favored by those who think that the coal measures should be reserved as a national asset. On June 5, the day the British Government announced its decision to assume full control of the coal mines, the interviewers (or Australian Public Opinion Polls began recording opinions in hundreds of representative centres, from people In all circumstances, on this question:-— "Do you think the Commonwealth Governmentshould should take over thc coal mines— or should the owners be left in charge?" Those who thought the Commonwealth should take over the mines were also asked: "Should they be taken over permanently, or only during the war?" Of each 100 .people interviewed— 25 said the Government should take over the coal mines permanently. 37 thought the Government should. take them over during ' the war. 24 favored the owners being left in charge; and 14 could not express an opinion. This means that if the Commonwealth Government took over the coal mines as a wartime measure, the decision would be approved by 71 In each 100 electors with opinions on the subject. Highlights Of Voting Occupation and economic status had less Influence than might have been expected. Notable features arc: — (1) Even among owners and managers of businesses and among well-to-do people there were more votes for Government control, at least for the duration, than for private control (2) Among skilled workers, of whom three out of four voted for Government control, at least during the war. only one in three favored permanent nationalisation.(3) (3) Neither Labor Party supporters nor non - Labor people favored permanent nationalisation, but both groups thought the Government should take over the mines during the war. Usual comment by those who favored control by the mine-owners was: "Government enterprise is not successful." Some added: "No interference with, private enterprise." Most of thc 37-in-tlie-IOO who thought the Government should take over the mines only during the war said, "It will stop disputes," or "Thc Government would get greater output."

27 Sep 1941 - PUBLIC OPINION POLLS Smith's Weekly (Sydney, NSW : 1919 - 1950), Saturday 27 September 1941, page 13 PUBLIC OPINION POLLS Folly Of Trial Gallups NO more crass idea has ever crossed the Pacific to Australia than that of the Cailup polls. Almost totally discredited in their place of origin, these polls are now to be popularised throughout the Commonwealth by large newspaper . chains. "CMITH'S" lias already shown how these polls have been disclaimed by the Federal Government and attacked by union bodies. Now, in a great splurge of publicity, it is announced In daily papers that results of Australian Public Opinion Polls will shortly be published, and that "they will make a significant contribution in the field of government and other social sciences, and to journalism, enabling the public to follow uc irenu 01 muu-ern thought." These polls will use the "scientific (F methods" evolved by Dr. George Gallup, one-time American soap-pedlar. Further A.P.O.P. in the field of government "lias replaced guesswork with a systematic knowledge of public opinion." These are large claims. Even larger and more fatuous ones are to follow. President. Roosevelt, says A.P.O.P., has based Ills high policy on- the results of Gallup polls. ". . . periodic Gallup polls have been the yardstick which have accurately measured public support or opposition for every major act of the three Roosevelt administrations."That "That is why President Roosevelt has made less mistakes, in gauging American public opinion than any other President." I A.P.O.P. implies that before the President has moved on any important issue— repeal of the arms embargo, aid to Britain, and so on — be has taken Dr. Gallup into consultation. There is litt'.e need for comment on tills. President Roosevelt, one of tho greatest statesmen in the world, is hardly flattered. It will be a great day for Australia when Artie Fadden calls in the directors of A.P.O.P. before framing Commonwealth policy! Will Sir Keith itluiuoLU DQ autwuo them? Dr. Gallup began his surveys in tne service of a large soap company to test out the popularity of certain lines. It's a long way from selling soap to selling statesmanship. A.P.O.P. is paying casual employees 12/6 for 10 full-scale Interviews. It works in conjunction with newspaper chains, of which Sir Keith Murdoch's is the largest. A.P.O.P. advises employees that they must be "men or women of integrity who believe in freedom of opinion, and must not be known as ardent supporters of a particular political party." Does it prescribe the same qualifications for its newspaper proprietor subscribers? In essence, A.P.O.P. is just another cheap newspaper stunt, all the more despicable because it seeks to hide under a "scientific" cloak. Was a Soap-pedlar The Sisterhood!

14 Aug 1948 - A Messenger Boy Conducts His Own Gallup Poll Smith's Weekly (Sydney, NSW : 1919 - 1950), Saturday 14 August 1948, page 2 A Messenger Boy Conducts His Own Gallup Poll Organised and conducted by a 17 -year-old messenger boy on his own initiative, a survey has just been completed of the wages and conditions of postal messenger boys in Victoria. Findings of the poll have so impressed union officials that they have decided to draw up a charter for youth to cover demands for improvements in the conditions of all juniors in the Commonwealth Public Service. Jim Griffiths, a messenger at the Melbourne G.P.O., organised the survey which covered 300 of his workmates in all parts of the State, Jim has a reputation for getting things done. Tall and dark, he organised his own football team among the messengers, and they now play allcomers, Jim's survey showed that more than 90 per cent, of postal messengers are looking for other jobs, because they say they cannot support themselves on their present wages. Many messengers complained that, although anxious to continue schooling, they were prevented from attending regular courses, because shortage of messengers has forced them to work broken shifts. To draw up the charter of youth, juniors from all sections of the Commonwealth Service have been invited to a meeting in Melbourne this month.. Meeting has been organised by the Commonwealth Public ' Service Salaries Campaign Committee. Juniors' parents have also been invited to be present. Similar "meetings are being planned in N.S.W. and Queensland. Jim Griffiths is now beginning to realise that he started something bigger than he first anticipated.

19 Jun 1948 - Leave Well Alone Smith's Weekly (Sydney, NSW : 1919 - 1950), Saturday 19 June 1948, page 10 e Leave Well Alone Anything more idiotic than a Gallup poll on which to base a case , for merging Liberal and Country Parties would be hard to discover. Such "sampling" of political opinion is utterly worthless. For the Sydney Morning Herald to Jake it seriously shows a naivety beyond comprehension. Politics are not capable of being simplified that way. Any candidate who believed in anything so nonsensical should have feathers stuck in his tail and be exhibited in a freak museum. . Secrets of the ballot are not revealed by Gallop polls. Liberals ought to know that by now. Anyway, they are going to have, their hands full in finding acceptable candidates in sufficient numbers for the enlarged Federal Parliament. The urban constituencies will extend all their recruiting efforts, They will be flat out selling their own brand of politics without asking the Country Partly to change to theirs. In country electorates, whether Liberals like it or not, they are suspect as representing city interests. That suspicion is not easily dispelled. Take NSW. In the State Parliament 24 country seats are held by Labor. Small farmers and their hands are not susceptible to the charms t)f Liberals at any time. They can be attracted to Country Party programmes. Understandably so. For > it is asking too much of the man on the land not to be prejudiced in favor of his . own pocket. Philosophies, .. however admirable, have ceased to be the deciding factor. Votes to-day are >.. economic considerations. That's the set-up and anyone who thinks it isn't is" merely deceiving himself. Labor makes no bones about it. Hard bargaining governs the Movement, organised for economic objectives. Socialism is Labor's ways and means to the control of production, distribution/, and exchange. The motive is possessive, and no longer can it be said to be disguised. The class war is not ideological; it is economic — and total. When, then, Liberals dicker with high resolves the practical Country Party accepts Labor's challenge. In the prices and charges referendum no more aggressive crusader appeared than Fadden. He ranged over . the Commonwealth rallying No votes. Can anyone imagine him discarding the result of years of campaigning for the primary producer to be reintroduced to the electorate as a Lib-eral? Or Earle Page, or McEwen, or Larry Anthony, or Joe Abbott? You don't build yourself up as a . national figure to start again from scratch. - At last Federal election the Country Party augmented its Parliamentary force by two— -Hamilton from WA and Davidson from Queensland. Could a Liberal, think' you,, have, given Frankie Forde his walking ticket in Capricornia? The story of 1949 elections is how to rid Australia of socialism. Liberal bosses belieVe that Labor is. on the _ way out. But that doesn't necessarmean that -Liberals are on the way in. Labor can lose, for, Australians put governments out rather than positively elect their .. successors. And the CP on present showing will be heeded to give required rnimbers to bring that about. When Labor has been defeated over the last twenty years it has been by the National or UAP voters combined with those of the CP. Bruce and Page coalition, then Lyons and Page kept Labor in" Opposition. The present Victorian Government is Liberal and CP. It was the same in NSW with Stevens and Bruxner. So it's about time Casey brushed up his memory. Unity can be altogether too restricted when it connotes one Party. A -common aim can be mofc effectively achieved by two. Smith's view is that for both to go under , the Liberal banner could mean obliteration at the polls. It may be Spoone.rism, but emphatically it isn't practical politics.

08 Feb 1947 - The Press Smith's Weekly (Sydney, NSW : 1919 - 1950), Saturday 8 February 1947, page 19 The Press GALLUP POLL OFF THE RECORD? Results cf a Gallup poll conducted in November on the Australian daily Press are not likely to be published in the daily newspapers. The poll showed that in five out of the six Australian States a majority of the people interviewed were, critical of the service provided by the dailies. Questions asked at the poll were:— Do you think that the daily newspapers you read are fair or unfair in their reports of political happenings? What about theitr reports of International events; do you think they are fair or unfair? "Smith's" is reliably informed that a majority of those interviewed were against the dailies on the first question. On the second question they were unable to form an opinion because all papers carried much the same cable news. Results' of other polls, conducted since the survey on the Press, have been published in the dailies. The delay in publishing Press poll findings seems to indicate that they are being treated as "off the record."

19 Feb 1958 - PASTE THIS ON YOUR JOB NOTICE BOARD Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Wednesday 19 February 1958, page 10 mmm iimmmnmi PASTE THIS ON YOUR JOB NOTICE BOARD :mu.nu(»mumuuuumm .tnnmm,,. WE NEED SUMMIT TALKS A GALLUP poll taken in 12 of the world's major cities last year showed that 62 per cent of the people were in favor of a meeting between the heads of the great powers. In Australia, Dr. Evatt, leader of the Australian Labor Party, has welcomed the idea. The Communist Party is fighting vigorously for it. The Australian Council of the World Council of Churches has expressed support, and the various bodies of the Peace Movement are campaigning for it. The Korean war was ended by round table negotiation. So was the war in "Viet Nam. Both would have become world wars, had not the people insisted on those top level discussions. i> Geneva spirit We all remember the glorious relief that followed the summit meeting held in Geneva in 1955. The peoples of East and West began to get to know one another through a steady two way stream of exchanges between sportsmen, doctors, scientists, writers, artists, trade unionists and farmers. John Foster Dulles has spread the, lie that the Soviet Union breached the Geneva agreement over Germany, the most serious trouble spot in Europe. He claims that at Geneva the Soviet Union accepted. Western terms for a settlement of that question; and then repudiated their pledged word. Agreements kept Richard Scott, a well known British commentator writing in the Manchester Guardian on December 12 called this' story of Dulles a "shadowy half truth". Another ant: - Soviet observer, Crankshaw of the London Observer said: "This simply is not true". "The Russians do not freely break agreements . .No such agreement was made at Geneva, as everybody knows." It is possible for Socialist and capitalist countries to live peacefully together. " There are no warmongers in the Socialist Commonwealth. And the. advocates of war in the capitalist countries now have two sputniks circling overhead to remind them that, though they could start a war, they couldn't win it. The advocates of peace grow stronger every day. They were strong enough to stop the attack on Egypt in 1956. They were strong, enough this year to save Tunisia from further French aggression. 25 May 1966 - US Gallup Poll: Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Wednesday 25 May 1966, page 3 US Gallup Poll: 54% say "pull out!" JjYDNEY: "The majority of Americans are demanding that the United States pull out of Vietnam if full-scale civil war erupts in the south/' said a United Press dispatch published in the Sydney "Mirror" on Monday. The report quoted the latest Gallup Poll, which found that:— 54 per cent favored withdrawing US troops. 28 per pent opposed withdrawal. 18 per cent were undecided. The poll result was accompanied by new, outspoken demands by American politicians: Senator Joseph Clark (Democrat, Pennsylvania): "We should get out of this mess as quickly as we can with decency". Senator Jacob Javits (Republican, New York): The US must prepare for the possibility of a withdrawal which would be inevitable if the South Vietnamese were unable to carry the major burden of the war. Mr. L. M. Rivers (Democrat chairman of the House Armed Services Committee): "We may have to make a decision damned soon on whether to pull out of the war. Our first interest is the protection of our own men." "Dean Rusk should resign Typical of the existing situation was the demand of the New York Post for the resignation of Dean Rusk, the notorious "hard-line" secretary of State, whom the Post blamed for America's alignment with the iron-fisted Marshal Ky. The press has pointed out that Ky made a fool of Rusk by reiterating Ky's statement that, irrespective of elections, he would hang on to power for at least another year. This was after Rusk had assured the world that Ky's original statement to this effect had been "misinterpreted" by journalists. (In Australia, Prime Minister Holt and External Affairs Minister Hasluck, who had also rushed in to defend the Marshal, have been made ridiculous by subsequent events). President Johnson, reported by the press to be in a deep state of depression, made two speeches in a single week, on Vietnam. In the first he attacked "nervous nellies" who criticised US policies and urged them to put America first. When this brought on his head a fresh blast from the New York Times and other papers, Johnson made a panic-stricken rush to the other extreme, in effect apologising for his previous remarks. He assured the people he didn't want to "quieten dissent".

24 Nov 1975 - SWING TO LABOR Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Monday 24 November 1975, page 1 SWING TO IABOB OPINION POLL SHOWS FRASER IN TROUBLE A survey of swinging voters shows that the tide is running against Fraser as the election campaign opens in earnest 56 per cent of those surveyed thought Labor deserved to win and only 29 per cent thought the Liberal-National Country Parties should . Ten percent favored neither , and 5 per cent were unsure . 72 per cent disapproved of the way Fraser became Prime Minister, while only 20 per cent approved. The survey was run by Australian National Opinion Polls (ANOP) and published in the National Times. It was taken just after Kerr dismissed the Whitlam government and before the wave of protest rallies, demonstrations and stoppages. These actions showed that industrial and office workers, as well as others, were uniting against the Liberals and were solid for Labor. This despite their past dissatisfaction with a number of Labor policies and likely demands for new policies from the next Labor government. With Labor support even more solid than in 1972, and swinging voters turning against the Liberals, a Labor victory is a real possibility. Liberal strategy however is based on trying to regain the initiative. They are counting on another backlash against the pro-Labor swing, which observers on both sides agree cannot be excluded. They expect the Liberal/NCP to pull out the stops between now and December 13. All sorts of "dirty tricks" are expected from the media owners Sir Warwick Fiarfax, Rupert Murdoch and Sir Phillip Jones. Public reaction, lost sales (in the case of the Murdoch press) and action by media workers curbed their worst hysteria!. But they will now use more subtly the full resources of their opinion making power to get the government that suits them. The Liberals are getting unprecedented financial support from multinational corporations and big Australian companies. As Tribune reported on November 17, BHP has promised $1 million, and money is pouring into Liberal-NCP coffers. Fraser has been advised to concentrate on the economy to get away from public outrage at the way he was put into office. But there is little comfort for him in the ANOP survey on this issue. The swinging voters show a healthy scepticism towards both parties' statements. Asked who was telling the truth about the economy, 48 per cent said neither, only 15 percent believed Fraser and 12 per cent Labor. Asked whether the Liberal-NCP could solve Australia's economic problems in the next few years, 22 per cent said NO and 25 per cent were unsure. Thirty per cent said Labor couldn't solve economic problems, and 21 per cent were unsure. The world economic outlook verifies these doubts, since no "free enterprise" econopmy has escaped large-scale unemployment and soaring' inflation. Nor has any government, conservative or social-democratic, been able to cope with the crisis.

27 Nov 1975 - 'SWING TO LIBS' DOUBTFUL Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Thursday 27 November 1975, page 1 'SWING TO UBS' DOUBTFUL MORGAN POLL UP THE POLE ? Just how reliable is the Morgan Poll, published yesterday. The poll, published in The Bulletin, showed the ALP with 44 per cent and the L-NCP with 46 per cent on November 15, as against 47 per cent (ALP) and 43 per cent (L-NCP) on November 8 Public opinion polls are seized upon by opposing political forces to swing support behind them. At the best of times, even with irreproachable sampling and other techniques, the polls are always to be treated cautiously. After all at best only 2,200 people are questioned. But opinion polls also have a psychological impact: they strengthen or weaken the resolve of supporters, and almost certainly affect swinging vbters. A few years ago Roy Morgan told a market research luncheon that he did not print the results that oarnedtrTof the computer but used his own personal judgment, which he found "more accurate"! The Sydney Morning Herald, which was then printing Morgan Polls, discontinued publication soon after. They now print the McNaire-Anderson poll under the Gallup name. Roy Morgan's son, Gary, is now in control of the business. Both Roy and Gary are known as strong Liberal Party supporters and Rightwingers. The Morgan Poll was then taken up by The Bulletin, one of the few surviving remnants of the Packer empire. The Bulletin claims the Morgan Poll outfit is the only Australian member of the Gallup International Research Institute. It does not say that the Institute for a period disowned the Morgans and that they were forced to operate as "Morgan Polls, conducted on the Gallup method." The Institute in any case is simply a loose combination of market research companies. There is nothing special about their polls. The Morgans will not tell the rest of the industry how they operate. Other researchers claim however that Morgan pollsters are only given two and a half hours' training and that there is no check for bias. Researchers in universities and the market research industry are not the only ones sceptical of Morgan Polls. Public service researchers are also unhappy. Tribune was told that one Morgan poll done for the NSW Health Department was a "mess" and that their sampling techniques were regarded as unreliable. Just how much did Mr Morgan use his "personal judgment" in the November 15 poll?

15 Oct 1969 - TREND LABOR'S WAY IN POLL Tribune (Sydney, NSW : 1939 - 1991), Wednesday 15 October 1969, page 1 TREND LABOR'S WAY IN POLL GORTON ON WAY OUT? WIDESPREAD feeling against the Liberal- Country Party government was reflected in the Gallup Poll announced at the weekend. The Poll showed a four per cent switch in favor of the Labor Party between the weekend after the federal Budget and the weekend after Mr. Whitlam's policy speech on behalf of the Labor Party. It held out the possibility of an actual defeat for the 20-year-old Liberai-Country Party coalition government in the election on October 25. The Poll result shows that, by and large, Liberal efforts to discredit, on grounds of cost, reforms by Labor are not going down with the electorate. Treasurer McMahon, a leader of the wearisome Liberal chords of "where's the money to come from"? claimed at the weekend that Labor election policies would cost between $540m. and $640m. a year. But Opposition Leader Whitlam pointed out last week that, despite the concessions promised by Mr. Gorton, personal taxes paid by Australians will rise by $1800m. in the next four years — an adequate source of revenue for the Labor proposals even by Mr. Mc-Mahon's calculations. Defeat of the L-CP government, breaking its 20 years of power, would reflect a deep mass criticism of its policies and the society it h.as moulded. But it would on its own do nothing to change the basic character of monopoly-dominated Australian society. The swing against the government indicated by the Gallup Poll poses anew the need for a radical Left movement which throws out a challenge to the whole existing social set-up. Hence the importance of the vote for communist and militant candidates who are advocating policies of radical social change in the election campaign. In this connection, the votes recorded by the seven communist candidates (four in NSW, and one each in Victoria, South Australia and ihe ACT) will have a significance for beyond their numbers. Similar significance will attach to the votes recorded by candidates standing on a militant anti-Vietnam war, anti-conscription platform, in defence of the government education system, and in the interests of the nation's hundreds of thousands of pensioners, with their daily battle to live. Best possible outcome of the election would be a strong showing by communist and radical candidates, accompanied by awareness in the matter of preferences that the Labor Party alone offers the perspective of an immediate end to Liberal-Country Party rule

14 Jul 1944 - WOMEN'S WORLD Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Friday 14 July 1944, page 8 W 41 141 F< 1\ S . WOW I. II Three Fern's That Affect Our Birthrate : War , Fatigue and Economic Problem By HENRIETTA DRAKE-BROCKMAN In a recent article I suggested that our civilisation would be in a bad way — quite apart from wars and economic insecurity — if we had lost our sense of pleasure in having children; as a Gallup Poll appeared to indicate we had. i T DID not say wars and j I economic conditions had 1 nothing to do with the j matter. They have a great deal to do with birth-rate; they always have done so. Even our. own aborigines — stone-'age as wc call them .— controlled ! their birth-rate to suit economic : conditions. Their Australia did not support a large population. In good seasons, native animals increased: in. bad they died in thou-, sands. But the aboriginal was a man; lie contrived to control his environment to the best of his ability, in good times there were probably more piccaninnies: but in bad. he — or in this case, she — saw , to it that more mouths to feed did not endanger the life of the . tribe. But never throughout long centuries did the nhtives lose their zest in life or their pleasure in children. In the far north the native chil-,dren. still laugh a lot. and their parents laugh with them and at Ithem. But their life Is easier. | births are fewer. _»-! J PART from other causes, one : ' reason for this is that we have never helped them to readjust to the many bewildering improve-mcnts of our Western techniques of living. The point of this is that I believe we ourselves are now in need of readjustment to new and bewildering techniques. I suggest that it will not matter how well wc control our after-the-war ways of living, if we do not also set to work to recapture that zest in life which alone seems to make mankind vigorous and happy. The reasons for lack of zest in our present form of life are fairly obvious now. I belong to the generation that! was 'teen-age during the last war.! We were probably, as a whole, the j first British generation to consider whether we should have children or not. Many of us were so affected in adolescence by the dreadful carnage of the big artillery duels and the terrible casualty lists then published that when we later married, we did seriously wonder if we should be justified in allowing ourselves the pleasure! of having children. ¥ 'PHIS was a priggish and defeat-ist attitude most of us had sufficient sense not to maintain; but there is no doubt it existed to an extent throughout the community. We felt we had more choice in the matter than our! mothers and grandmothers, and; so a more direct responsibility to the next generation. I have since, checked this attitude among, women of my own age. in all sorts; of places, among all sorts of women — in the outback, on the: wheatbelt. on the Nullarbor Plain.1 in the big cities. The decade of young women im-: mediately following us did not share this particular inhibition to' sense of pleasure in children. But; before we. and they, had got -bur. j families fairly under way. the de-., pression hit us. That was the final disillusion. Families that might have been increased came to a full-stop. Others never started. Wow. the adolescents of thai period became cynical before ever they faced life. They felt life had . nothing to offer. 'PHIS time, the youths were more affected than the girls. War is terrible always for the young; but they do not wilt under sense of not being wanted. Everyone Is needed and there Is a niche for everybody, no' matter for what tragic end. But not to be needed —to grow up in this spacious country of ours feeling you have no place in it — could anything be| more bitter to youth? That is what the depression did; to young people — almost to a complete generation, for scarcely any young mind missed the blight. Its sweep was wide: children from; six onwards were blighted by a disease that entered homes in a way the last war did not. And these are the people who today should be having children. In-. ' stead, they are fighting another war. I We are all. at least verbally. ! committed to building a better 1 world for everybody — freedom /from want and fear, the obvious foundations of all reconstruction plans. But- when it comes to the living of life and the raising of children — who are life and the future — I wish to point out that freedom from fatigue, now accepted as necessary in factory and workshop, is no less imperative in the home. I am sure the majority of girls still wanl to have children, but. i unless we change the present .; public altitude. I think it will j be a long time before the birth- : , rate rises. i yyiTHOUT being sentimental about motherhood, the press.' .the radio and the cinema might; do much to help. At present the accent is always on glamor — but I jthe adolescent rarely sees glamor applied to family life. Glamor i appears to stop short at 25 or so.i gather itself together for a leap, and descend again at about 60.! ;Yet the intervening years are the' i real years of living for most ; women. | Wc could do with many morej films wherein the leading lady is1 . a fully rounded personality — a ' woman who is an individual, a wife and a mother. These are1 still, fortunately, the leading ladies; of everyday Australian life. Butj . we shall be fools if we forget to give them— not bouquets of words I at the expense of a little blah — | but adequate assistance and leisure for rest wliile they carry out i their exacting role. I Fatigue is an even worse enemy ! to creative effort than Is the speed of modern life. 4F 45 48 4" LTNALL.Y, what about the young men? If anything, men get more enjoyment out of the exploits of their offspring than do women. But when men are young they want to share the adventure of life with a mate who is not entirely taken up with being a mother. If wc must be personal on this mntter, my own mental attitudes to children have been determined by three fears — fear of war, fear of fatigue (caused by-lack of assistance and the frequent impossibility, when children were small, of continuing with any hnt purely domestic work), and fear of financial insecurity (but for which I should. I hope, have had a larger family). The fear of the first and the last Is ever present in the minds' of those who plan our future. About the third I am not so sure. Thai, is why I stress the point that young mothers — in all sections of the community— need special consideration and the establishment of communal centres and services that will allow them to live a full and happy modern existence and so encourage young people to regard children as one of the most satisfying and lasting pleasures life has to offer. As thev are — speaking as a woman who decided, once, that she would not have any.

28 Jun 1944 - POST-WAR PLANS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 28 June 1944, page 5 POST-WAR PLANS Where Do You Want To Live? Inquiry in all States by nearly 200 Gallup Pol) interviewers suggests that a widespread desire to go on the land after the war will come to nothing, unless it is fostered by Governments and other bodies. Of each 100 people Interviewed In capital cities: 16 said that, after the war, they would like to live In country cities or towns and 10 want to go on farms. Relatively few people want to move from country to city, so a "back to the land" movement would not be held up by any lack of desire by the people themselves. But only one person out of each eight who desire to leave the capital cities has made plans to move; the others said they were "only thinking about it," A quarter of the farm dwellers Interviewed said they would like to leave the land after the war. but about the same number of people living in country towns said they want to be farmers. Thus, the whole 10 p.c. of the city dwellers who want to go on the land represents a potential net migration to farms. Few Have Plans Altogether, nearly a third of the people Interviewed said that. If given the opportunity, they would like to move from one "locality group", to another— from city to farm or from farm to town, etc. This confirms the existence of a strong migratory urge, as disclosed by an earner Gallup survey. More than 80 p.c. of those who would like to move, however, are without any plans at present. 23 Aug 1944 - GALLUP POLL SHOWS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 23 August 1944, page 5 GALLUP POLL SHOWS WHY PEOPLE VOTED AGAINST PROPOSALS The chief reason for voting "No" at the referendum was a belief that the additional powers would be used to socialise industry, according to a Gallup Poll taken a week before the referendum. The survey also shows that fear of industrial conscription added to the "No" vote, while most "Yes" voters expected the extra powers to guarantee employment. People Interviewed were asked— "What do you consider the main reason the Commonwealth Is asking for, the powers?" . A card listing seven probable reasons was handed to each person, md they were also asked whether they were voting "Yes" or "No" at the Referendum. Reasons For Powers "No" voters' selections from the card show that opposition to socialisation and industrial conscription were major considerations at the Referendum— What NO Voters Thought Was Main Purpose of Referendum Socialise Industry . . 30 Industrial conscription .. .. 20 Avoid depressions (9 .p.c.),: ensure full, employment (6 p.c.) . . 15 Abolish States .'. .. .. ..10 Control monopolies .. , 8 Help returned soldiers . . . . 4 No Idea (chiefly women) .. 13 / 100 The third line of the above table suggests that some "No" voters, while preoccupied w'ith the problem of post-war employment, believed Increased Federal powers would not help. On the other hand, selections by "Yes" voters show that fear of unemployment was the main reason for supporting . the Referen- dum. Socialisation of industry was a minor consideration: — What YES Voters Thought Was Main Purpose of Referendum % Avoid depressions (37 p.c.), ensure full employment (28 p.c.) .. 65 Abolish States 10 Control monopolies .. .. .. 10 Help returned soldiers .. .. 10 Socialise industry 5 100 Comparison of the two tables alsoshows: (1) The first power In the Bill (Rehabilitation : of Returned Servicemen) was least mentioned (apparently the public Is satisfied that existing powers are adequate). (2) Only small and equally balanced minorities thought the future of State Governments was the main reason for the Referendum, and (3) The proposed power to control monopolies caused as much oppo. sltion as support for the Referendum. Nine out of 10 people told Interviewers how they were voting at the referendum. As published In The Herald last Friday, the proportion who Intended to vote "No" was 51 p.c. of the full cross-section., including those still un-, decided. Excluding the "undecided" people, "No" was 56 p.c. In comparison, the referendum vote counted to date shows. "NO" 54 p.c. A survey made a week! before a referendum could not have been much more accurate. I Issued by Aust. Public Opinion Poll. 352 Collins St. Melb.

12 Jul 1944 - Public Favors Armed League Of Nations Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 12 July 1944, page 5 Public Favors Armed League Of Nations At least two out of three Australians favor the League of Nations -having an armed force after the war, judging Ay the latest cross-section of opinion collected by the Gallup Poll. The question asked was: "What is your opinion about the League of Nations having an armed force after the war?" Few of the 1700 answers, ot course, were exactly the same, but of each. 100 people interviewed: 67 were favorable to an armed. League';16 16 were opposed to it; and 17 had no opinion. Common attitudes were: "Use force against force," and "The League must have power to enforce decisions." - The minority opposed to an armed League usually said something like, "Armaments breed wars," or "An armed League would become a dictatorship." Men and women gave much the same votes In favor of an armed League of Nations. People over 40 (who would nest remember the early days of . the League) were .10 p.c. more favorable than people In their twenties. 05 Aug 1944 - CLOSE PRESIDENTIAL POLL FORECAST Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 5 August 1944, page 5 CLOSE PRESIDENTIAL POLL FORECAST NEW YORK, Friday.— A Gallup Poll survey of 17 States indicates that President Roosevelt and the 'Republican candidate for Presi- dent, Mr Dewey, will be running neck and neck with 130 and 138 electoral votes respectively. Gallup comment says that the Atlantic-Pacific seaboard States are likely to be the main battleground. The farm -States In central and mid-western parts favor Mrl Dewey; the south remains Democratic. The Pacific States are showing a definite anti-Roosevelt trend, but the President still leads by a small margin in California. — Herald Special Service.

13 May 1944 - Tobacco Rationing By Coupons Preferred Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 13 May 1944, page 5 Tobacco Rationing By Coupons Preferred Six out of 10 men who are smokers think tobacco and cigarettes should be rationed by coupons, according to a cross-section of opinion collected by the Australian Gallup Poll. Among women smokers the vote is even higher — seven out of 10. People throughout Australia were asked: — (1) "Do you favor the present method of buying tobacco and cigarettes— or do you prefer rationing by coupons?" and (2) "Are you a non-smoker, a light smoker, or a heavy smoker?" More than two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women said they were smokers. Of the male smokers, half answered "medium," a quarter "light," and a quarter heavy." Before answers to the first question were counted, men and women were grouped into heavy, medium and light smokers. Among men, approximately 6 out of 10 in each group (heavy, medium and light smokers) favors coupons, and at least 7 out of 10 women in each group, agrees with them. nL25ior Par<Y supporters are slightly more favorable to rationing tobacco and cigarettes than are non-Labor people. People in N.S.W., W.A., S.A. and victoria are all strongly In favor of rationing, in Queensland and Tasmania, however, opinion is more evenly divided. It will be noted that peoplo were not asked whether they thought tobacco coupons should be Issued to everyone, or only to people who declare they are smokers.
