19 Jun 1944 - DON'T BABIES GIVE PARENTS PLEASURE ANY MORE? Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Monday 19 June 1944, page 9 DON'T BABIES GIVE PARENTS PLEASURE ANY MORE? REASONS FOR DECLINE IN BIRTHRATE WOMAN'S WORLD By HENRIETTA DRAKE-BROCKMAN GIRLS ARE IMPORTANT A recent Gallup Poll on the falling birthrate showed that elderly— and many not-so-elderly — people' put the lack of babies down to the "pleasure-seeking selfishness" of our community. Do you realise the appalling implication of that statement? It means that children are no longer regarded, in the public mind, as a source of pleasure. CHILDREN — life itself, joy of the present and hope of the future — have become an obligation, a nuisance, an accident, a duty, a menace, a fear; anything, in short, but what every child born into a democratic society should be able to claim by right of.-bivth.to.be — a pleasure. ' All sorts of reasons can,: and are, being marshalled to explain this attitude. But the attitude'- itself — divorce, in the publio mind, of the idea of pleasure from the idea of children — has not received oroDer attention. ' We may ail be subconsciously aware of this divergence, and afraid to face it. We know its ultimate result means racial death. Do we merely 'reassure ourselves by loud discussions of housing problems and economic securities, aware all the time that houses without children are not homes, and that high wages cannot buy young women relief: from 24 hours a day, 365 days a" year, in the exacting job of motherhood? Our list of essential services should he based on the vital need for provision: of proper leisure for mothers. .- =!= " m :|! |N war, women are called on to maintain the morale of their men by love, faith, smiles, beauty; a constant re-statement that life is worth living, that our particular ideal of life Is even worth dying to preserve. Should men any the less neglect,, as they become the masters of nature, to help women to face child-bearing and rearing — with morale less high than they themselves carry to battle? Sometimes men are inclined to lag, but so far they have not altogether failed to invent better conditions, for women. Anaesthetics and modern- obstetrical practice have already practically wiped away the ancient fear of childbirth. =! . rpHE one fact' that glows like a rainbow above the present darkness of the world is the extraordinary development of. scientific knowledge. We read .dally of dramatic progress in medical practice, in aeronautics, in electronics. Applied to civilian life, as we believe all such advancement will iventually be, this mastery ' of nature must greatly improve the technique of living. But I think most of us tend to forget that no matter how brilliant our technique of living many become, zest in life cannot be found if technique is not allied with emotional satisfaction. The technique of an artist may be perfect, but if his art does not arouse emotion as well as admiration, we pass from him to some less technically but more vitally proficient performer. The living of life re- mains an art, is not yet an exact science; success in living comes from the adjustment of natural creative energy and acquired knowledge. :>< the beginning of this war . many young men were reluctant to marry or to leatfe young wives with a child.- Their sense of responsibility — not selfishness — was the reason. I ielt sure at the time that the women would have a say; that if the instinct of our race was still for life, babies there would be. The answer was definlt-ely' in the affirmative. Recently, however, a war-bride of my acquaintance, one whose husband has now returned from overseas, commented on a new aspect.. She said that all her friends who had had babies, some in defiance of masculine fears that it was undesirable to have children, now proffered different advice. After strugging with small children through the past foul-years, they were exhausted. The majority said they would have no more. My young friend said she had not been deterred from her own resolution, but that she had "gone cold" on her original hope of three or four — unless things altered. The young wife of a private soldier with small children can hardly have felt herself a i>cr-- son of importance to the nation. Whatever section of the com-. munity a young mother may have belonged to, she has scarcely been encouraged to think her job carried a No. X priority for Australia. Doesn't it? jvo matter how gloriously tne . war is won by -feats of arms, our future will never be secure if feminine morale hns been too badly shaken, for in the long run, women are the race. Girls are important. What they think matters. I do not believe the birth-rate will rise as the result of campaigns and pep-talks or' from .a sense ol' national or religious duty. It will i-ise when girls think that to have families will be fun; that happy healthy children are the ultimate expression of that personal attractiveness so accented by ; modern trends; that life without children is less exciting -and less complete; when they, who ' are more, not less, responsible about procreation than the women of earlier periods, more responsible about infant welfare, feel that if tney have families, they can themselves at least endeavor to be the mother of their dreams. :(i jyroST girls know, that if they marry and have children they will not even be able to go out with their husbands — one or. the other will have to stay home. The links of common interest will grow less, emotional experiences: cease to be shared— a prospect difficult to face in the, early twenties, when life has, so much to offer. To,; look ..back , with.,sgntimental. yearnihg "to""a simpler;; society " is hopeless and absurd; to go forward and try to harmonise our complex one is a stimulating challenge. How? The answer, is given from a dozen differing angles in a single word: Education. But, without radical readjustment of present conditions, education will further deteriorate the position of the mother and housewife. The more you educate a girl the more she wants to do a good job by her family and the less she wants to cease to.be a companion for her husband, or to let her mind grow rusty. Therefore quick adjustment of domestic life becomes the immediate corollary of increased education.In In actual fact the position of the domestic women in our society has for years been growing worse and worse, no matter what section of the community she belongs to, be she wife' of omanual-worker, salaried man or boss. The war has not created the condition, merely aggravated it enormously. One of the worst features of modern city life — and the majority of Australians live in towns — is the way in which women are left alone day after day with only the companionship of small children and all the work to do. Country women do not, for all their isolation, suffer this curtailment of personal contact. They still share the work, worries and interests of their menfolk and are often saved the constant pressure of small children in the house. PROPERLY supervised creches, pixy gardens, nursery schools, help in the home when urgent —if necessary, even transport, and creches at cinemas are needed. However it is done, done it must be— this finding of leisure for mothers. 06 Oct 1954 - Democrats favored to win Congress Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 6 October 1954, page 19 Democrats favored to win Congress Frori RANDAL HEYM ANSON NEW YORK, Tuesday. — Surveys bv the Gallup Poll and the New York Times indicate that the Democrats will win control of both Houses of Congress next month. The New York Times, reports that they are ahead of the Republicans In 25 of the 38 Senate contests. 1 The Gallup Poll finds that 52 per cent, of the voters tavor ine Democrats while only 48 per cent, support the Republicans. But a survey made by the powerful Congress of Industrial O-ganisations has damped down any excess of confidence in the Democratic camp. UNDECIDED It revealed that there was a big undecided vote and that no great issue had emerged during the campaign to sway the voters one way or the other. More than 50 per cent, of those questioned had no complaints agninst the Eisenhower Administration. 10 Aug 1948 - COLIN FRASER FINDING OUT-- Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Tuesday 10 August 1948, page 4 COLIN FRASER FINDING OUT - Why we spend millions on a nice cup of tea — AND SUBSIDISE IT, TOO Their "nice cuy of tea" costs Australians about £14 million a year, of which £6y2 million is paid by taxpayers as subsidy. On an average, Australians spend, say, an hour a day drinking it, which adds up to a big figure in cost of time. Why do we drink tea? Colin Fraser went finding out. WE were all sitting down waiting for tea to come In when somebody said in a panic; "I've read that teR mny soon cost 5/6 lb. . . . subsidies or something. If It does, I think I'll drink something else. People are always threatening to drink something else. But they stick to tea. Why? "Why Is It," I asked, "that at 11 In the morning and at 4 In the afternoon the nation stops work for a nloe cup of tea; and that every taxpayer, whether he drinks it or not, pays part of the cost? And, again, why is it that, among the white races it is almost exclusively the British who are addicted? 'Nobody Nobody seemed to know, so I thought I'd find out. No poll MR ROY MORGAN, Director of the Aneiralinn Pllhlln Opinion Polls, shook his head. We've got the proportion of smokers and we've got the proportion of people who drink alcohol," he said. ' But we've never tried to find out how many people drink tea and why. It's an idea. I'll make a note of it." The Commonwealth Statistician didn't know either. But he's very strong on quantities. He said we were drinking more tea now than ever before — and, collectively, paying more for It. Record pre-war Imports, he said, were 49,530.9411bs. In 1938-39 (worth £3,103,604. plus freight), and in 1948-47, tne last figure he had, they had risen to 52,830,5071bs. (worth £7,015,184, plus freight). On page 13 of the telephone book appears the number and address or the Commonwealth Tea Controller (Mr H. A, Bennett). Gladstone TO get to Mr Bennett in Queen Street it Is usual to inquire tirst at tne outer omce. On the wall is pinned a large poster bearing a picture of the former British Prime Minister, Mr Gladstone, and this legend— If you are cold, tea will warm you — If you arc heated, it will cool you — If you arc depressed, It will cheer you— , If you are excited, It will calm you — — W. E. Gladstone. Mr Bennett is white-haired solidly built, nffable, a heavy clga: smoker. He has been In the tei business for 60 years, and nov supervises the buying of ever; Sound of tea which reaches ith< ible in Australia. Men In the' trade say he spend something like £10 million a year yet he controls what Is probabl; Australia's smnllest Governmen department. The staff: Himsell a secretary, an accountant, twi assistants aged 75 and 78, a manager and two girls in Sydney, and four assessors who taste every consignment. Offhand, Mr Bennett, thinks the chief reason we drink tea in Australia Is that we are predominantly of British stock — It's traditional. Last week he received a shipment from Ceylon consisting of more than 700 different teas, each of which will have to be tasted and appraised before being allocated to various merchants. Afterwards they will find their way inio the 50 different varieties of packet tea on the Australian market. Like most other women, Mrs Bennett says the tea we're getting nowadays is not as good ns that we used to get before the war. Mr Bennett asserts, however, that Australians now drink the world's best tea (lie's got some supporters, too) — tea that we couldn't afford lo buy before. It happened this way, he says. Before 1939 we consumed some 46 million lbs. of tea a year, of which some 32 million came from Java, 11 million from Ceylon and three million from India. We didn't buy Ceylon and Indian tea then because we couldn't pay the prices. During the war, Java production ceased. Also, the Commonwealth took, over tea buying, under an Empire purchasing scheme. Indian and Ceylon tea, and some South African, was the only tea available. The prices had to be paid. Free buyer MR BENNETT says that although, during the war, the Government was forced to buy many teas it did not want, since i January 1, 1947, when it became a free buyer, it has bought nothing but the best. For six years, he says, the Gov-- eminent has bought at all sorts of prices and resold to the merchants at a fixed price. Wholesalers say they pay 1/11 Vi a lb. to the Government, on which they are allowed a fixed margin of 4?id. to cover blending, packaging, distribution and profit. They are given 60 days In which to pay. Grocers are allowed a further mar-; gin of 411 d. a lb., and are allowed 10 days to pay unless they are prepared to forfeit Id. a lb. Tills brings the tea to you at 2/9 a lb. — a price Mr Bennett claims to be the lowest In the world, and considerably lower than the pre-war price of 3/5. (Of course, the taxpayer is subsidising hlB own purennses, but'' people on low incomes are gainers. I, In New Zealand, where there r Is still a subsidy of l/-a lb., tea i costs 6/ to 5/4. v "The greatest single fact In y the tea business today." says o Mr. Bennett, "Is the growth of the Indian home market. . Na-s tlves of India who were never ', before able to afford tea arc y now outbidding us nt the mar-t kets. With 325 million pounds , promised by contract to Bri-o tain annually, plus the increased consumption In India Itself, there is little left for export to outside countries." Well, we're finding out a lot about tea. But what about something exact about why people drink it? "Tea suits our temperament," says Mr R. H. Gilbert, chairman of the Tea and Coffee Traders' Association, "it is an Inherited taste. As a drink, it was given a fashionable fillip in England in the 17th century, and considerable glamor by the Boston Tea Party and the Clipper races. No gifts OTHER facts from Mr Gilbert: Tea firms hope . there will never be a return to the system of offering free gifts for package coupons (banned by the Government as a war-time measure): tea would grow in Queensland, but. Australian labor costs are too high to make growing profitable, and nobody has yet invented a mechanical picker; after the English, Australians are the world's heaviest per capita tea drinkers. Tire fact is that, since tea was introduced to Britain in the middle of the 17th century, it has become Indispensable to British people. When, during the war, the bombs began to fall on Britain, the Government made sure that, come what may, Britons got their tea, for "a nice cup of tea" not only cheered them up: it meant normalcy. Even worse than bombs would be going without tea. and the Government subsidised tea so that even the poorest could buv it at the usual cost. China first IT was for much the same reason that the Aticfrallan DfiUPrn . ment subsidised tea when the war sent prices up. Of course. China was a tea-drinking country long, long before Britain. Chinese legend claims that the virtues of tea were first discovered by Emperor Shen-nung in 2737 B:C: From China it spread to India. And in Tibet, tea compressed into cakes has been, for centuries, a form of currency. So, now let's put the kettle on . . . TAILPIECE Here is the Commonwealth Tea Controller's recipe for a perfect pot of tea:— Warm the pot. Don't be mean with the tea. Pour in BOILING water. Allow to draw for six minutes by the clock — no more, no less. Pour liquid into another warm pot or jug, and serve. Mr Bennett says it's no more trouble and gives 25 per cent, better results. Try it, and see if you find a difference.

06 Nov 1947 - CONSERVATIVE TREND IN UK Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Thursday 6 November 1947, page 5 CONSEjyiyE.:! tbempinm ir Electors Tiring Of Labor The Herald Special Service LONDON, Wednesday. — The latest Gallup Poll taken on the attitude of British electors to the Labor Government, and current political issues, signnflcantly reveals a decline in support for. the Government, and a rise in support for the Conservatives. A poll was taken in August, and for tne first time since the Labor Government was elected (in 1945) more people of those questioned expressed a preference for the Conservatives than for Labor. A poll taken at the end of September confirmed this trend, showing the electorate vote thus: Conservative, 44.5 per cent.; Labor, 40 per cent.; Liberal, 11 per cent.; other parties, 4.5 per cent. Of 31 per cent, who voted for Labor in the general election, but who have since changed their minds, one-third said that they would vote Conservative, one-third said Liberal, and one-third were uncertain. Thirteen per cent, who voted Conservative in the general election said that they would change their allegiance, more than one-half saying that they would vote Liberal. ELECTION Should the Labor Government remain in power until 1950 or hold an election in the near future? To this question, 52 per cent, said that the Government i should remain, 42 per cent, said that it should resign, and 6 per cent, had! no opinion. | What is the best government for the country at present? Thirty-seven per cent, replied. Labor. 31 per cent, said Conservative, 20 per cent, said a National Government, 6 per cent, said Liberal, and 6 per cent, had no opinion. Should Mr Attlee remaiit as head of the Labor Government? Forty-six per cent, replied in the affirmative, 41 per cent, said "No," and 13 per cent, had no opinion. Even among Labor supporters barely more tnan one-half — 58 per cent. — replied that Mr Attlee should remain. CRISIS EXPECTED Sixty-one per cent, expressed the opinion that an economic crisis was bound to come. Thirty-one per cent, believed that it could be avoided. Forty-nine per cent, asserted that "the Government was muddling along," and 44 per cent, believed that "the Government knew what it was doing." Thirty-eight per cent, believed that a Conservative Government would have done more to meet the crisis. Thirty-four per cent, thought the reverse. Asked their opinion of the Government's home' policy, 54 per cent, said that conscription should be continued in peace-time. Thirty-seven per cent, said that It should be discontinued. Forty-one per cent, thought that the strength of the services was "about right," 28 per cent, said it was too large, and 18 per cent, thought it too small. NO FOOD CUTS Sixty-six per cent, declared that food cuts should not be made. Twenty-seven per cent, said that they should. On foreign policy, 60 per cent, believed that Germany should be occupied. Thirty per cent, said that the troops should be withdrawn. Thirty-four per cent, disapproved Britain's attitude toward the United States. Thirty-three per cent, approved it, and 33 per cent, had no opinion. Thirty-thrre per cent, approved the Government's attitude to Russia. Twenty-six per cent, disapproved it, and 41 per cent, had no opinion. Fifty-one per cent, thought that nationalisation had been pushed on too quickly. Nine per cent, thought it had not been done quickly enough. Twenty-six per cent, said it was "the right pace." Forty-two per cent, said that the Government was "too Socialist," 15 per cent, said "insufficiently Socialist." and 30 per cent, said, "about right."

08 Nov 1947 - Report From New York..... Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 8 November 1947, page 13 Report From Mew York Fears Of A Clash In 25 Venn From ... Randal Heymanson NEW YORK, Friday. — Although Gallup polls reveal that the majority of Americans think Russia seeks to dominate the world and expect .war within the next 25 years, only one man is sufficiently a la riried to act on this conviction. He is Colonel McCormick, publisher of the Chicago Tribune, whose . d.islike and fear of Russia, -has. led him to order-the immediate construction of an atom bomb shelter for himself and his employes. OTHER Americans who-profess to believe that war is inevitable seem to be surprisingly unconcerned. War talk is most prevalent in financial circles in New York, but not one in a thousand really wants war. There is not a single responsible official in Washington who believes that wai is imminent, practical or desirable. inis goes aiso tor the leaders of the armed forces, who, In off - the - record talks explain that it . would be strategi- cally dimcuit tor Russia and America to come to grips. It is the old story of a fight between a whale and an elephant. There Is no Russian coastline on which Americans could land. The Soviet has no fleet with which to threaten American territory. Nor do Army planners believe that Russia could be knocked out by atomic weapons. They point to the vast and the empty Soviet land mass which stretches across a sfath of the globe and explain that the United States with its huge industrial concentrations on the Atlantic seaboard and Detroit is far more vulnerable to atomic bombing and bacteriological warfare.They They believe it is too late to talk .war now; consequently American policy should be directed toward resisting Russian expansion, while striving to reach some sort of long-term balance of power. They consider this wholly practical as intelligence reports disclose that Russia is weaker than her truculence at meetings of the United Nations suggests. The Kremlin must know that Russia has even less chance of defeating America in war than America has of defeating Russia. The best description of the present phase of the Russo-American relations is that of "elder statesman" Bernard Baruch: "We are in-the midst of a cold war which is getting h„t T Hn not believe we are going to use guns." Highest American officials consider there is a good chance of the "cold war" ending 'in a long period of Stable equilibrium. They frankly outlined their views In off-the-record talks to a national conference of editorial writers. They are encouraged rather than disturbed by Mr Vyshlnsky's Billingsgate. which they regard as a sure indication that Moscow is worried by the receding . tide of Communism in western Europe and by the Marshall Plan for. reconstruc-tlon. The United States sees herself as the economic arsenal of Western Europe in an economic and political struggle against -Russia, as she was the military 4 . arsenal during the war against Germany. The State Department believes that France, which is normally self-supporting in respect to foodstuffs and has plenty of iron and coal and large gold reserves at present in hiding, could recover rapidly, given the restoration of sound currency and political stability and the elimination of a topheavy bureaucracy. The Department is also encour- aged by the remarkable recovery Italy has achieved by the sheer industry of its inhabitants. Britain is America's major headache, for an economic collapse there "would leave the biggest commercial vacuum the world has . ever seen. Unlike France and Italy, her recovery depends on the expansion of her export trade and Americans do not disguise their fear that untimely socialist experiments and the unwillingness of workers to increase productivity are retarding British recovery. If American officials believe a shooting war with Russia can be avoided by building up a strong Britain and Western Europe, the Soviets hope they can achieve their objectives bloodlessly by promoting economic collapse. They will do their utmost to sabotage the Marshall Plan in- the belief that if recovery can be delayed for a few years, America will be forced to withdraw from Europe. The Kremlin believes that time is on its side, but the State Department points out that Russia is unable to supply its satellites with capital consumers' goods and time may well make it more difficult for the Kremlin to check discontent by both her satellites and her own people. Summed up, there is far more talk of war in certain sections of the American press and amone the ill-informed section of the public than in official circles In Washington. The Government is not wholly averse to a certain amount of public apprehension, for it helps to nceij Mie nauon on Its toes and ensures that the preparedness programme won't be blocked by public apathy. Russo-American rivalry is an unfortunate fact, but despite a small minority of crackpots, whose bellicosity provides the only justification fdr Mr Vyshlnsky's rantings about war-mongers, the American Government believes in the possibility, of continued peace and is determined to maintain it. Whether you believe America is going the best way about it depends on whether you take your opinions from the New York Times or from Mr Henry Wallace's left-wing weekly, but it is a certain bet that war is impossible unless Russia fires the first shot. ?

23 Oct 1947 - GALLUP POLL FINDS -- Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Thursday 23 October 1947, page 15 GALLUP POLL FINDS — LITTLE DREAD OF UNEMPLOYMENT IN NEAR FUTURE Facing the future with optimism, 7 out of every 10 Australians think that, in the next few years, there will be enough jobs for everyone, or, at the worst, an insignificant amount of unemployment. This attitude Is revealed by a recent Gallup Poll regarding employment prospects In the next few years. Latest figures Issued by the Commonwealth Board of Census and Statistics show that employment In Australia Is being maintained at an exceptionally high level. At the present time, the number of jobs offering far exceeds the amount of labor available. But will the boom In employment last? This was the problem posed by Gallup Poll Interviewers when they sounded public opinion on the question: — "In the next few years, do you expect there'll be enough jobs for everyone— or will there be some un-. employment — or a lot of unemployment?" People In a full range of occupations, both employers and employes, were Included In the sur-1 vcy. Their hopes and fears of the (future divide as follow: — 44 per cent, expect there will be enough jobs for all. . . . Most of this group think that, because of the big production leeway, there will be I jobs for everyone. Others are of the opinion that the 40-hour week will "help I create employment." 27 per cent, think there will be some unemployment. . . . But they expect much of it will be among uncmploy-ables and those who are not keen on work, anyway. 19 per cent, believe there will be a lot of unemployment. . . . Some of this group think a depression is coming. Others fear that an influx of immigrants into Australia will make Jobs hard to get. 10 per cent, cannot give an opinion. Optirpism Rises Comparison with a similar question asked by the .Gallup Poll , at the end of the war shows tnat Australians are now more hopeful of full employment: 1945 Today p.c. p.c. 03 Nov 1947 - Public Favors Sunday Games Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Monday 3 November 1947, page 4 Public Favors Sunday Games THE latest Gallup Poll on Sunday Sport snows that eight out of every 10 Australians favor opening of public tennis courts and golf courses on Sunday afternoons, and that six out of every 10 favor them opening on Sunday mornings as well. Against that, six out of every 10 are opposed to .Sunday football matches with charges for admission. There has been no substantial change of opinion since the same set of questions was asked In a survey two years ago. The public has apparently made up its mind that people who want healthy recreation at the week-end should be given the facilities to get it, but that commercialised spectator-sports should be discouraged. This Is a reasonable attitude and one which should be respected by authorities controlling public recreation grounds, So far, many of these authorities have paid more attention to the wishes of a conservative but articulate minority than tc the majority who see nothing objectionable in Sunday games If they are not organised foi profit. It Is unfair that Sunday sporting facilities of a noncommercial kind should be available to people who can afford to belong to private clubs and withheld from those who depenj on public grounds

19 Nov 1947 - Public Likes House On Air Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 19 November 1947, page 4 Public Likes House On Air THE latest Gallup Poll, published today, shows that 64 per cent, of adult .Australians are in favor of Federal Parlia- mentary broadcasts being continued. 26 Nov 1949 - LIBERAL-C.P. GAINS IN THREE STATES Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 26 November 1949, page 3 LIBERAL-C.P. GAINS IN THREE STATES GALLUP POLL FINDS By ROY MORGAN, of Australian Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins Street, Melbourne States with Labor Governments — New South Wales, Queensland and Tasmania — are the three most likely to swing to Liberal-C.P. at the Federal election on December 10, analysis of the latest Gallup Poll shows. Little of the switching from Labor to Liberal-CP., however, .is likely to occur in Labor's marginal seats, so Labor may be In a better position than indicated by the Gallup Poll's latest finding of Liberal - C.P.. 52 per cent.; Labor 46 per cent.; and Independents, 2 per cent. That finding, when broken down by States and adjusted slightly for trends shown by earlier Gallup Polls, appears as follows: Labor Likely Vote Vote 1943 = Dec. 10 p.c. p-c. South Aust. .... 58 56 West Aust 56 52 N.S.W 57 48 Victoria 51 48 Tasmania .. 51 45 Queensland .... 45 40 "Samples" from each State in a Gallup Poll range from 710 in New South Wales to 120 in Tasmania, so some deviations must be expected between the above figures and the election result on December 10. But the figures are reasonably reliable, judging by the Gallup Poll's average error of only 3.7 Ser cent., with similar figures efore the 1948 Prices referendum. More Seats Now Your interpretation of the above table, however, depends on knowing how the 1940 Federal election would have resulted if there had been 121 seats (the result of redistribution) instead of 74. Official figures to show the effect of the redistribution are not available, but "best guesses" indicate that in 1946 Labor would have won about 38 safe seats with majorities of at least , 60 per cent.; another 17 fairly . safe seats with majorities be-tween 54 per cent, and 60 per cent.; and 16 marginal seats. Liberal-C-P. in 1946 would probably have won 18 safe seats with majorities of at least 60 per cent., 19 fairly safe seats with majorities between 53 per cent, and 60 per cent., and 13 marginal seats. The House would then have been divided Labor 71, Lib-cral-C.P. 50. The election result next month should be measured in terms of gains or losses on those figures. 1 £. H«,«« «l Obviously, if there is a swing to Liberal-CP. (as the Gallup Poll indicates), it will be of no effect unless it occurs in many of Labor's 16 marginal seats. Liberal-C.P. needs 11 of them for a bare majority of 61 in the House of 121, It is important, therefore, to know that the 16 crucial seats include Bowman, Lille, v and Ryan in Brisbane, Lowe and North Sydney in Sydney, and Cuvtin in Perth. The other 10 are scattered throughout the country districts of all States except South' Australia. The Gallup Poll has found little evidence of switching from Labor to Liberal-CP. in those particular seats in Sydney or in the country districts of Queensland or Victoria. Chief battlegrounds, therefore, will probably be In Brisbane and the country electorates of New South Wales and Tasmania, with a couple of close fights in West Australia. After the numbers go up on December 10. you may say that the Gallup Poll was foolhardy to publish these figures In such detail. We believe, however, that we should have no secret information, and that the public appreciates frankness. Another Australia-wide Gallup Poll on the election will be made in a week, for publica-tion on election eve.

01 Dec 1949 - LIB.-CP SHOULD HOLD GAINS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Thursday 1 December 1949, page 3 LIB.-CP SHOULD HOLD GAINS By ROY MORGAN, Director, Australian Public Opinion Polls. 352 Collins Street. Melbourne Last-minute switching by voters — either from Labor to Liberal-C.P., or from Liberal-C.P. to Labor — is likely to benefit Liberal-C.P. more than Labor, the Gallup Poll finds. Everyone who told the Gallup Poll their voting Intention as at Nov. 11/13 (a month before the election) was asked: Do you think it's possible you may change your mind before the election? Of the cross-section of nearly 2060 people interviewed, 6 per cent, answered "Yes." By itself, that percentage doesn't mean much, but it becomes significant when compared with (a) the same people's declared voting Intention, and (b) how they voted I at the last Federal election In 1946. COMBINED Their declared voting Intention, as already published in The Herald, was: Liberal-CP, 50 per cent.; Labor. 43 per cent.: Independent, 2 per cent., and Undecided 5 per cent. The next step Is to combine those figures (for voting Intention) with how they voted In 1946. It then" becomes evident that 8 per cent, of the adult population plans to switch from Labor to Liberal-CP, while only 1 per cent, is going In the other direction: fiVftr cent. Intend voting Liberal-CP: Voted Lib.-CJP. 1946 . . 38 » Voted Labor 1946 .. 8 Others 4 — 50 Intend voting Labor: Voted Labor 1946 39 Voted Lib.- CP 1946 .. 1 Others 3 — 43 Intend to vote Independent 2 Undecided. on how to vote 5 DANGER AHEAD Because all the declared switching goes In the one direction (to Liberal-CP) the- situation Is - "dynamite" for forecasters, such as the Gallup Poll. For Instance. If half of the 9 per cent, of declared "switchers" decide at the eleventh-hour to "switch-back" —to vote again for the parties they supported In 1946 — then voters on December 10 will be almost evenly divided between Labor and Liberal-CP. That is what happened at the U.S. Presidential election a year ago— and confounded Dr. Gallup. And that Is why the Australian Gallup Poll asked Beople If they might change ielr minds before the election. But, according to the answers, few of the 8 per cent, who plan to switch from Labor to Liberal-CP are likely to switch back — to vote Labor again after all. . Indeed, the boot seems to be on the other foot. Among people who said they were going to vote the same as In 1946 (77 per cent, of the cross-section) there were two people who said they might yet switch to Liberal-CP against each one who may yet change to Labor. KEEPING WATCH A lot can happen, of course, in the last month of an election campaign, so the Gallup Poll is watohing developments by: (1) Writing to everyone Interviewed Nov. 11-13, . asking whether, their voting Intention Is still the same, (2) 'Conducting a. special survey in 14 marginal seats In the capital cities. (3) Conducting another full Australia-wide survey next week-end, and (4) Asking half of the 2000 people .then interviewed to mall, on Tuesday, December 6, a 1 post-card provided for advising their final voting intention. ; But if people change their minds between then and December 10 (voting day), the' Gallup poll, can't do anything about itl

06 Dec 1949 - GALLUP SHOWS CITY SWING TO LIB.-CP Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Tuesday 6 December 1949, page 5 GALLUP SHOWS CITY SWINGbTO LIB-CP By ROY MORGAN, Director of Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins Street, Melbourne. There has been an 8 per cent, swing to Liberal-CP in the all-important marginal seats in the capital cities, a special Gallup Poll using "probability" sampling discloses. In the week-end Nov. 26-27 — two weeks before the Federal election next Saturday — 28 Gallup Poll Interviewers made a special survey In 14 marginal electorates, using "probability" sampling. The survey was simply an experiment, but the result ls of great interest. Lib. Labor C.P. Ind. p.c. n.c. p.c. Election 1946 51 46 3 Gallup Polls: Sept. 16/18 49 49 2 Nov. 11/13 43 55 2 "Probability" Poll Nov. 26/28 43 55 2 In the above table the election result In 1946 (In the Rreas now in the 14 marginal seats surveyed! is compared with the result of the experimental "probability" survey (last line). The second and third lines show answers of people (250 per survey) living in the same areas, interviewed as parts of the September and November Australia-wide Gallun Polls. It will be seen that the 250 people interviewed by the Gallup Poll's usual "quota" method November 11-13 agree exactly with the "probability" sample of 300 people, November 26-28. INTERPRETATION As only 300 people were Interviewed In the "probability" survey, some difference between the finding and the election result in those 14 divisions on December 10 must be expected. Nevertheless, the Gallup Poll's accurate prediction of the Victorian State election in 1947 with similar small samples suggests that any error will be small. The 14 electorates covered In the "probability" poll were: — Nine marginal Labor seats according to 1946 figures: Bowman, Lllley and Ryan In Brisbane; Kingsford-Smilh, Lowe and North Sydney in Sydney; Kingston and Sturt in Adelaide; and Curtin, Perth. Five marginal Liberal seats according to 1946 figures; Evans in Sydney; Fawkner. Hent.v and Higgin-botham in Melbourne; and Boothby in Adelaide. The Gallup Poll's figures should not be construed as meaning Liberal-CP will win all those 14 scats. But they do suggest that Liberal-CP has a very good chance of holding most of its marginal scats, while the Labor Party will probably lose most of its marginal scats In the cities, likely exccntlons being Kingston and Sturt In Adelaide. EXPERIMENTAL SURVEY Gallup Polls throughout the world normally use ' "quota" sampling, which requires each interviewer to ob tain opinions from certain quotas, or numbers, of people of particular economic types, ages and sex. In recent years, however, Gallup Polls have been experimenting with a new method called "probability" sampling. It requires each Interviewer to obtain opinions at particular houses or from particular people. The central office, using a mathematically random method, decides In advance who will be Interviewed. The Gallup Poll Is now completing its final Australia-wide survey on election pros-nects (using "quota" samn-ling) and the result will be published In The Herald on Friday.

05 Apr 1950 - Letters To The Editor Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 5 April 1950, page 5 [?] Existing, Not Living A GALLUP POLL analysis (31/3) gave the minimum living costs of a family of four as £fi/ll/l n wppif In TPph- ruary — £4/15/9 for food and £3/15/4 for rent., clothes, etc. On my experience, the amount set down for food is reasonable; a family of four can be fed, more or less decently, on that amount, subject to the experience of the housekeeper. But I disagree with the estimate of £3/15/4 for clothes, . rent, etc. in my budget, "etc." includes ice, wood, doctor, dentist. chemist, gas, electric light, fares, amusement, library books, crockery replacements, shoe repairs, dry cleaning, household linen, cleaning materials, insurance and savings for holidays, provision against illness and improvement. to the. home. Ours is an average lower middle-class family — my husband and myself, a two-year-old son and a - brother who lives with us. Our only aim Is to live quietly and decently, and with the sense of security that a weekly contribution to our savings bank should provide. We have no extravagant alms, but we would like to save for our child's education. We would also appreciate an occasional outing to town to see a play, a ballet or a musical comedy. But we can do none of these things on a white-collar worker's wages. We can exist, but we cannot LIVE. That is all we ask of our country which we have both served in peace and war. Wc expect Australia to give us, and . millions like us, » little hope for the future. — 1 P.K.," Armaaaie.

If a Gallup Poll could be held in a cross- secuon oi created oemgs, irom the elephant to the louse, the unanimous verdict would be that by far the most dangerous animal Is Man. Man, red in tooth and claw like the tiger, has outmatched the tiger and every other predatory beast by his superior ingenuity, which has enabled him to strike down his prey at a distance of miles and miles. By this means he has made himself lord of creation, hated and dreaded by all. Perhaps you will say that of course you meant, which animal Is most dangerous to human beings? The answer is still the same. The animal most dangerous to men is Man. What is it, in the whole cosmos, that we rear most? .uertaimy noc irons, or tigers. Few of- us- feel any . haunting sense of dread of these formidable creatures. But the whole world is today shadowed by the fear of the folly or malignity of the creature called Man. If you go further and ask which is the most dangerous sort of man, I should say, at a rough guess, the politician, the propagandist, and the; atomic scientist: Of these, the last-mentioned Is the most obvious menace. He Is at present working at weapons capable of destroying our civilisation. It is even whispered that the latest device — the hydrogen bomb —may possibly set the atmosphere on fire. As far as I can learn, the most eminent of the experts say that this is probably an exaggeration. Anyhow, they add light-heartedly, we can only find out by making the experiment. A cheerful statement. If, as I suspect, you- meant to exclude Man from ycur list of candidates, and If you still mean "dangerous to man," my vote goes to the microbe — at least, It would + If I were sure that the microbe la an animal at all. If, on the - other hand, these deadly enemies of the human race are not animals, our suffrages must go to the animals that act the part of carriers for the microbes, and we must come to the conclusion that the most dangerous animal In the world is either the house fly or the anopheles mosquito. ' On the whole, considering the number of j diseases spread by the house fly, compared with the single disease we owe to the mosquito, the former will win by a short head. He would not, at all events, have ended by likening himself to a fly. + ' 1 I II. ! What do you think | of increased postal | rates? | — -G.H.J., Balwyn, Vic. 'illllIllllltlllllllllllllllllllllllHIHIHIIHIIIllllHIIIIIIIIIIIlllllllllllllHlllMllllll 1 THINK, in my innocence, that it seems queer for a government to say in one breath that inflation must be checked and prices come down, and to say in the next breath that It Is going to put a higher price on the postage of letters. Also, as far as I can see. the arguments used by Rowland Hill to convince the authorities that a penny post was desirable are equally valid today. Hill argued that the high postal rates were a grievous burden to the poor, and hampered business. He also argued that a reduction of the rates would greatly increase revenue. Before he died he was seen to have conferred an enormous benefit not only on his own country, but on the world. He was burled In Westminster Abbey. He deserved a better statue than the one which stands somewhere In London. But — there is always a but— It must be remembered that a penny does not mean today what a penny meant in 1840, the year of Hill's triumph. In fact, a sixpenny post today would be a little cheaper than the penny post was then. Also, there is the general question whether letter-writing ought to be encouraged. Some thirty years after the penny post was established in Britain it was found that the volume of letters carried by the Post Office had increased + by a thousand per cent. Afe you quite sure this was a good thing? I for my part have strong- personal reasons for doubting it. Certain circumstances, Including my incorrigible laziness, make it impossible for me to answer more than one in a hundred letters. In my den Is a box ' of unanswered letters, some of them two or three years old. It was all very well for Napoleon to say that if you left a letter long enough it would be found to have answered itself. But I am perpetually oppressed by the thought of the number of enemies I must have made by the practice of this Napoleonic habit of not answering So, for purely selfish reasons, and ignoring the good of the community, I am Inclined to applaud the derision of the Government to tax letter-writers more and ever more heavily. I'mmiHiiiiiititiiiiirMiiiiitiiitiiiiiiiimiitmiimtimiiiJimiiiimiiiiMiiiiim: | When and by whom | I was cremation first I I practised? | I —L.F.S., Sedan, S.A, | 'iiniiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiHiiiiiiiiiiniiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiMiiiiiiiiiiiniiiiiimiimimiiir 1HAVE no skill in answering historic questions; and I feel still more at sea when it comes to prehistoric questions, such as this. I would as soon attempt to tell you when and by whom the wheel was Invented. No names have come down to us from these remote ages. There is no doubt at all that cremation is a thing of Immemorial antiquity. I Imagine, but do not know, that burial is of later date. In countries where burial is and has been for many centuries the rule, there Is an echo of an older practice in our way of referring to a person's mortal remains as his ashes. "Peace to his ashes," we say. Tennyson, speaking of his dead .friend, takes comfort from the reflection that . . from his ashes may be made The violet of his native land." Surely the word Implies a subconscious reminiscence of earlier days when bodies were burned, not buried.. However that may be, it Is known that for long ages there have been three main ways of dealing with the bodies of the dead. One way was to burn them; the second way was to bury them; and the third way was to preserve them In the form of mummies. Mummification was,- as everyone knows, the plan adopted, and practised for many centuries, by the ancient Egyptians. As it was an elaborate and costly process, It. was probably the Drtvilege of the high and mighty. The bodies of the less august, or the less well-to-do, were buried. As for cremation, Its origin, as I have said, is hidden by tne mists of time. What is not so hidden— what belongs almost to our own time — Is the revival of the practice In . Britain and America and our own country. I myself am old enough to re-member the time when an English judge caused a sensation by declaring cremation to be a legal procedure. This was the final victory of the Cremation Society, which for years had been fighting against the embattled might of public opinion. -It is Interesting — though It has nothing to do with your question — to ask why the revival of this ancient practice met with such determined opposition.The The first objection was a practical one. If a body is burled, it can be exhumed, if there Is any. suspicion of murder, and examined for marks of violence. Cremation, it was said, would be popular with murderers. But this objection belongs to the realm of detective fiction. How often, in real life. Is an exhumation ordered? The second and more powerful objection was a theological one. It was made by those who believed In the resurrection of the body. Incredible as It may seem, it was seriously maintained that, while a body that had been mouldering In the grave for centuries would rise again In the flesh, a body consumed by fire would r.ot. To the vagaries of the human mind there Is no discoverable limit. .

24 Sep 1951 - 'Close poll' forecast justified Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Monday 24 September 1951, page 5 'Close poll' forecast justified The Gallup Poll's forecast that the "Yes" - "No" vote would be extremely close has been justified by results. The Poll's prediction. Issued on Thursday for publication on Friday, read: "Queensland and Western Australia will give substantial 'Yes' majorities, but the referendum will depend on close voting In other States." If the present trend of voting continues, only a few thousand votes will ultimately separate the "Yes" and "No" votes throughout Australia, the Director of the Poll. Mr Roy Morgan, said today. The voting will be similarly close in Victoria, the crucial State.Between Between 1943 and 1948 the Gallup Poll correctly predicted whether "Yes" or "No" would win in six referendums. No firm prediction could be made this time, because, as announced on Thursday, the Poll had found in the previous Week-end that one million people had switched from "Yes" to "No" in ,jx weeks. It was '.impossible to be certain Just how many would switch in the last week. BIG SWITCH Raying on special questioning and a post-card survey, the Gallup Poll estimated that another 150,000 people would switch to "No' and that the "Yes' majority would fall from 57 per cent, to 54 per cent, during the week. It now seems that 350,-000 people switched in the last week, resulting in a "Yes" vote of just under 50 per cent. The Poll was successful in placing the States in almost their correct order of "Yes-ness." Referendum figures tabulated below allow for a one per cent, increase in the "Yes" vote, which is almost certain before counting is finished: , Gallup Actual estimate vote p.c. ' p.c. 24 Aug 1950 - Public Backs Govt. on Korea Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Thursday 24 August 1950, page 13 Public Backs Govt, on Korea GALLUP POLL SHOWS Do Australians approve sending our armed forces to Korea? What do they think is behind the Korean war? Should America use the atom bomb in Korea?' Australian public opinion on those questions, as measured by the Australian Gallup Poll, is described in this article by Roy Morgan, Director of the Gallup Poll. ON August 5, questioning began of 1620 people throughout the cities and rural areas of all States. After referring to the fact that some of Australia's air-force and navy were in action, the interviewers asked. "Do you approve or disapprove, the Government sending those forces?" 77-in-the-IOO replied that they approved sending the Mustangs and a few warships to Korea, 15-in-tlie-100 disapproved, and 8-ln-the-100 did not express an opinion. Approval came from 81 per cent, of men and 73 per cent, of women: from 89 per cent, of Liberal-CP voters and 65 per cent, of Labor voters. Interviewers mentioned that our Government planned to send some infantry and artillery to Korea. Asked whether they agreed or disagreed with that decision, people gave answers similar to those on the first question. 71 per cent, thought that some Australian infantry and artillery should go to Korea, 20 per cent, opposed their going, and9 9 per cent, had no opinion, Approval came from 76 per cent, of men and 66 per cent, of women; from 83 per cent, of Liberal-CP voters and 60 per cent, of Labor voters. BIGGER FORCES The 77 per cent, who said they approved our Government's prompt action in sending a token air force and naval units to Korea were then asked: — Would you favor, or oppose, sending a greatly increased Australian air force to Korea? Answers by the 77 per cent, who accounted for 1250 of the 1620 people interviewed, showed: — 925 said "Yes." 244 said "No." 81 were undecided. The 925 who favor sending a big Australian air force to Korea represent 57 per cent, of our adult population. People were then asked: "Do you think infantry sent to Korea should be volunteers, or conscripts selected by ballot?" Nine out of 10 answered "Volunteers." WHAT IS BEHIND IT? The broad question: "In your opinion, what is the Korean war about?" was then asked. 42 per cent, blamed Com- 16 per cent, blamed Russian aggression; 9 per cent, said it's a civil war; 4 per cent, blamed politics, greed or a trade war; 3 per cent, blamed vested interests or American dollars; 2 per cent, said it's Russia versus USA;, and 24 per cent, can't say. It will be noted that the 58 per cent, who blamed Communist aggression or Russian aggression, agrees closely with the 57 per cent, shown earlier as in favor of sending a greatly increased air force to Korea. Similarly, the 12 per cent, who thought it is a civil war or caused by vested inter- ests (not Russian) account for most of the 15 per cent, who disapproved sending the naval and air forces already in Korea. WAR SUPPLIES Interviewers then asked: "Do you think our Government should do anything about people who try to stop war supplies going to Korea?" 31 per cent, would gaol them; 12 per cent, would "deal severely"; 10 per cent, would prosecute; 6 per cent, would' deport; 4 per cent, would remove them from their jobs; 2 per cent, would use the military or volunteers; 1 per cent, would "explain ' the position to them"; 14 per cent, said "the Government should do something"; 4 per cent, had no opinion; and 16 per cent, would do nothing. The 16 per cent, who would do nothing about people -who try to stop war supplies going to Korea tie up with the 15 per cent, who disapprove sending the token force. ATOM BOMBS Two more questions were put to the same men and women: — (1 ) .Would you favor, or oppose, arming Japanese troops to fight against North Koreans? People answered:— Opposed 53- per cent., in favor 31 per cent., and no opinion 16 per cent. (2) Do ' you think America, should, or should not, use atom bombs in Korea? . Three out of four were opposed, percentages being:— Should use them; 18 per cent., should not, 73 per cent., and no opinion 9 per cent. Issued by Aust. Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins St., Mclb.

23 Mar 1950 - Compulsory Army Training Wanted Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Thursday 23 March 1950, page 8 Compulsory Army Training Wanted An overwhelming majority of Australians remain steadfastly in favor of compulsory military training for young men, the latest Gallup Poll shows. For the seventh time since 1943, cross-sections of men and women have been Interviewed on this subject. And for the seventh time, the answer has been approximately the same. Figures for the latest survey, made last month, are: — 74 per cent, favor1 compulsory military training, 20 per cent, oppose it. and 6 per cent, arc undecided. The "favor" vote comprises 85 per cent.' of Liberal-CP voters and 60 per cent, of Labor voters. Referendum First As in the previous survey on this subject in June (when 74 per cent, were in favor) people were asked two questions: — (1) I Parliament decided to have compulsory military training for young men, do you think a relerendum should, or should not, be held first? "and ; (2) If a referendum were held. would you vote for, or against,, compulsory training? On the first question, 60, per cent, (comprising 57 'per cent. . of men and 04 per cent, of women) said they favored a referendum as in New Zealand, before reintroducing compulsory military training. Answers to the first question, of course, are shown above. Cross-analysis of answers to the two questions shows that compulsory training is favored by 9 out of 10 of those who don't want a referendum and by two out of three of those who do want one.. Issued by Aust. Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins St., Melb.

Federal Price Control Wanted Six out of 10 people think the Federal Government should again control prices, at least temporarily, a Gallup Poll just completed shows. The Federal Government, oi course, nasn c power in peace-time to control prices, so people were asked: Do you think full wartime price control, by the F ederal Government, should, or should not, be brought in again now ? In every State a majority said they wanted full price control by the Federal Government again, and the Australia-wide vote is: — 57 per cent, in favor, 35 per cent, opposed, and 8 per cent undecided. Prices 'Referendum This represents a big change of opinion since the 1948 referendum, when PERMANENT Federal price control was rejected by a "No" vote of 59 per cent. At that time 61 per cent, told the Gallup Poll they wanted price control to continue for at least a few years, but most people said they would prefer the States to exercise control. It should not be assumed, however, that the latest finding (57 per cent, in favor of Federal price control) means that a referendum now for PERMANENT price control would be carried. In its last survey on that subject (at the end of June) the Gallup Poll found that a probable Australia-wide "Yes" majority was likely to be nullified by "No" votes in three States. If the bill for such a referendum becomes law, the Gallup Poll will conduct another survey on its prospects. Everyone interviewed on the question of restoring Federal price control (at least temporarily) was- also asked whether they thought wages should be fixed, if we have full price control again. 26 Oct 1953 - GALLUP POLL REVEALS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Monday 26 October 1953, page 9 GALLUP POLL REVEALS Ike's popularity on the wane Herald Special Service NEW YORK, Sunday. — President Eisenhower's popularity has shown a startling decline in the past four weeks. Twenty per cent, disapprove, and 15 p.c. have no opinion, compared with 14 p.c. and 11 p.c. in September. 'Reasons given by the voters for their new coolness towards Mr Eisenhower are many. He spends too much time on golf or on holidays. PRESS CRITICS The findings of the Gallup Poll are echoed by growing criticism of the President In the Press. Only a few months ago criticism would have been unthinkable. . His holiday In Colorado marked the turn of the tide. The President's long absence. combined with his inclination to leave decisions on important issues to commissions, seems to have caused many to feel that things were just drifting. The first year of a President's term of office is crucial. His prestige is then at its highest, and he then has his best opportunity to give direction to his Government. Later the traditional struggle between the executive and the legislature becomes more intense. Some outstanding political observers, like Mr iHarsch, of the Christian Science Monitor, appear to feel that Mr Elsenhower has missed his chance to assert his leadership. In a broadcast recently qyer the British Broadcasting Corporation network. Mr Harsch said the President must have felt like a cold wind the change in the atmosphere since he started his six weeks' vacation. . as a war ucru nu wao ui-vulnerable, but now It ap-Jiears that he is being udged on his own performance and on the record of his Party. MAKE DECISIONS And Mr Harsch considers that the Army staff system of getting good people to work on each problem and come up with a solution w-on't work In politics. The President must either assert his leadership, form his own decisions, and rally the public behind them, or see control of the Government pass to Congress, including many people who never wanted him as' a Republican candidate.

14 Nov 1953 - SIGNS OF RELIGIOUS REVIVAL Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 14 November 1953, page 18 SIGNS OF RELIGIOUS REVIVAL [?] A RECENT nation-wide Gallup poll revealed that in every church in Australia . there, is a widespread feeling that we need q religious revival. These Gallup Polls serve a valuable purpose in providing a cross-section of what people are thinking. A very comprehensive survey has just been published of religious beliefs and practices in the United States. The main points of this survey showed that of the adult Americans questioned :99 99 per cent, believe there is a God, although 2 per cent, of these aren't positive, but like to think God exists. Only 1 per cent, flatly don t believe. Most people— 77 per cent, —think the soul lives on after death. A slightly lesser majority— 72 per cent. — believes there is a heaven where the good are eternally rewarded. 58 per cent, think there is a hell, but only 12 per cent, see any possibility , whatever of tnelr going to hell. 75 per cent, of all adults consider religion "very Important," 20 per cent, sav it's "fairly important." and only 5 per cent, say it's "not very important." The Australian Gallup Poll disclosed that the general attitude was that we would have higher moral standards If there was more religion in the life of the nation. What would such a revival achieve? It would pay debts, reduce sexual problems, disinfect the theatre, cut the divorce rate, reduce Juvenile crime and lessen the prison population. The generation passing away has lived on the spiritual capital of its predecessors — a moral capital built up by fellowship with the Church and spiritual experience — the practice of prayer, the vitamins of the Bible and active christian service. Now the capital has dwindled, I often hear people say in an effort to' justify themselves: "My parents were decent, ready to do anybody a good turn and they hod nothing to . do with the Church. They do not realise that their parents were often 'living on the spiritual heritage of their forbears and that the account is now-overdrawn. THE history of the Christian faith is really the story of revivals. The Faith has not com.e down the centuries like' a steadily expanding river. There has. been an ebb and flow. But there has always been a limit to the ebb. Slowly there Is an ache in many hearts and they begin to cfy out for the living God. From a faint desire here ana mere it spreads. apa grows until the lost simplicities are revived. The Franciscan movement In the 13th century was a tidal wave of the Spirit. The Reformation brought another tidal wave of the spiritual life. John Wesley and his good companions went through the Kingdoms awakening the souls of men ana women to God. I merely name three revivals of thousands. Dr. R. A. Torrey, whose work in Australia is still fruitful, wrote a prescription which would, he said, bring a revival to any church or community: First, let a few Christians (they need not be many) get- thoroughly right with God themselves. This is the prime essential. Second, -let them bind themselves together - in-'a prayer group to pray for a revival. Third, let . them put themselves at the disposal of God for Him to use as He sees fit In winning others to Christ. That is all! But that is everything. There are signs that the tide is turning in Australia. that the Church is getting a new hearing'and that more people are praying. Nothing can . stop a spiritual revival but ourselves.

06 Sep 1947 - GALLUP POLL FINDS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 6 September 1947, page 13 GALLUP POLL FINDS Radio Beats Reading As Recreation When Mr and Mrs John Citizen are wondering how they will fill in their evening leisure, the chances 'are they will decide to stay at home and listen to the radio. Otherwise, they are likely to settle down 'to read a book or magazine. In July, Gallup Poll interviewers set out to discover what adult Australians like doing with their evening leisure. People were handed cards on which six different ways of spending spare-time were printed and were asked which of the suggestions was their favorite way of spending their spare time in the evening. Preferences divided as follow: — 40 p.c. prefer Listening to the radio. 27 p.c. prefer Reading books or magazines. 11 p.c. prefer Visiting friends. 8 p.c. prefer Going to the movies. 8 p.c. prefer Playing cards. 6 p.c. prefer Dancing. As the survey was made in midwinter, "timing" may have built up votes for the "stay at home" answers, radio and. reading. People were also asked to give second preferences, and "going to the movies" then moved up into third favorite, with a vote close -to "radio listening" and "reading." Analysis by Age Groups Listening to the radio is first choice with more than 40 per cent, of all groups aged over 30. For those in their 20's, the proportion is 28 per cent. Reading books gradually rises in popularity from 18 per cent, of those In their 20's to 37 per cent, of the "60's and over." Visiting friends is the favorite "leisure" of 16 per cent, of those in their 20's, gradually declining through the ages, until with the 60's the proportion is down to 6 per cent. Going to the movies is preferred by 15 per cent, of the "aged 20 to 29" group, but preference for movies declines as people grow older; after 60 it is only 4 per cent. Playing cards is favored by about 8 per cent, of all age groups, the eifect of age being insignificant. Going to dances, a young people's amusement. Is preferred by 15 per cent, of those in ' their 20's, but rapidly declines in popularity to 7 , per cent, of those aged 30-39, and under 2 per cent, of those in their 50's. Highlights of another analyst!! by occupation are: — Manual workers have the greatest preference for radio listening, nearly 50 per cent, giving it pride of place. Professional people, business executives and "wnlta fiftllftr" em- ployes prefer reading to any other spare time occupation. i S Going to the movies Is liked equally by all occupational groups. 16 Aug 1947 - GALLUP POLL FINDS: Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 16 August 1947, page 13 GALLUP POLL FINDS; Larger Federal Parliament Opposed All sections of the community are strongly against in creasing the number of members in the House of Representatives. In July, the Gallup Poll asked nearly 2000 men and women, in a full range of occu pations and economic circum stances, a question regarding the size of Federal Parliament: Do you favor, or oppose, increasing the number of members in the House of Representatives? Before the question was asked, people were reminded that Fed eral Parliament now has 36 mem bers in the Senate, and 75 in the House of Representatives. Answers show widespread disapproval of the proposal- to increase the number of members: — 75 per cent, oppose having more members in the House of Representatives. 12 per cent, favor an increase, and 13 per cent. 3re undecided. - More than three out of every four of the "undecided" people are women. In all States, substantial majori ties oppose any increase. Supporters of both Labor and Liberal-Country parties, as groups, are also opposed. What People Say! "The present number is ample for the population," sums up the opinions of many who oppose any increase. A clerk's wife, of For-restvllle, SA, gave another reason for opposition: "Quality is more important than quantity." Of the minority in favor of more Federal members, some referred to electorates being too large for one member, but others qualified their answers with: "Only if State Par liaments are abolished." 29 Sep 1947 - PEOPLE'S BANK VOTE Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Monday 29 September 1947, page 3 PEOPLE'S ISA Ml VOTE POLL POINTER TO GOVERNMENT In the Gallup Poll figures announced on Saturday — showing 63 per cent, of Australians to be against bank nationalisation — leading citizens today said they found ample confir- mation of their long-standing conviction that the- people did not want the Government to grab the banks. Others said the poll made It clear that the Government should hold a referendum. Mr A. .1. Fraser, general secretary of the Country Party, said, "If the Prime Minister (Mr Chff-ley) persisted in the face of the Poll and other expressions of public opinion, he must be classed with the dictators of Europe, who had brought ruin to the countries they controlled." Mr Chifley's disregard fot public opinion was difficult to understand, but the poll clearly showed that on bank nationalisation the Government had no mandate from the people. It was widely believed that tf Mr Chifley continued with his present proposals his downfall was certain. The will of the people In a democracy must prevail. Mr Holt. Liberal Member for Fawkner. said today the poll showed Australians were overwhelmingly opposed to the move. One oi the most significant aspects of the poll was the strengthening of opposition to the Government's socialistic pol-I lev shown in the increase from 50 to 63 per cent. In the last year. No Government planning, to be both democratic and representative. could Ignore the clear ex-nression aivpn of the public will. VALUE OF POLL Mr W. H. Anderson Victorian, President of the Liberal Party, said that the value of the Soils was ln the objective approach y a concern which employed sufficient contacts to obtain reliable indications of opinion. Frequently those who were closest to a problem were under a disability in judging opinion. The Government surely must heed the overwhelming expression of opinion shown by the poll. Opinion 'often was by no means so overwhelming but nevertheless accurate within one -to two percent. .Senator Senator Katz (Labor, Vic.), said thai the Gallup poll was premature. because people were passing an opinion "in the dark." Their views no doubt would De much different when the Prime Minister (Mr Chifley) explained the issue In detaiL SENSE OF RIGHTS Lady Knox, president of the Australian Women's National League: "The poll figures show that the people are beginning to realise the true facts aoout banking nationalisation. The result shows the people of Australia to have a very acute sense of their citizens' rights.'' Mr M. J. Pettigrovc, secretary ot the Taxpayers' Association ol Victoria said: "The Gallup result confirms an impression I have gathered over the past few weeks In Sydney and Melbourne — that well over half the people are against nationalising the banks. The Government Is flagrantly dishonest if . It goes ahead with Its proposals." Mr H. P.- Hlgginson, president of the Employers' Federation:— "The result of the Gallup Poll-proved an accurate means of assessing public opinion — is one further reason why the Government should submit banking nationalisation to a referendum, and not force it upon an unwilling people. It shows clearly that the mandate' for the introduction of socialistic legislation, claimed by Mr Chifley, is a myth. The mass of the people emphatically does not want It. The public opinion poll svstem, with a long record of accuracy, proves It." PREMIER'S POLL The Premier (Mr Cain) said today that he had no comment to make on The Herald Gallup Poll. The only "Gallup Poll" he was Interested ln was the decision of the people of Cnlllngwood at the recent by-election which was conducted on the banking issue, j Mr T. F. If a Federal election had been held in July, with someone other than Mr Menzies as leader of the. Latvians, Jugoslavs and Ukrainian Poles, who are now in Germany and England, j but won't go back to their own countries because, they claim, they can't find freedom there, i To ascertain what the public ' thinks about admitting these '"DPs" into Australia, " the Gallup iPoU questioned a nation-wide women on the subject. 03 Mar 1942 - Gallup Poll Favors Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Tuesday 3 March 1942, page 8 Gallup Poll Favors Limits On Prices And Wages Virtually unanimous approval of the new regulation to stop both wages antl prices from going any higher is disclosed by a nation-wide Public Opinion Poll taken in the last two weeks. On Wednesday, February 10. the Government announced Its economic policy. Within 24 hours Australian Public Opinion Polls — the Gallup Poll of Australia — commenced printing ballot papers for distribution to Its network of Interviewers in all States. Within a week interviewing was in full swing in places as far apart as Cairns, in tHe north, and Albany, in the south of Western Australia. One of the questions put to people of all types. In hundreds of centres throughout the Commonwealth, was: — Do you approve or disapprove the new reputation to stop both '.vapes and prices from goinp higher than they are now ? As this table shows, there was only one "disapprove" vote against each 12 "approve" votes: — Australia-Wide Opinion per cent. Approve "pegged" wages and prices 83 Disapprove 7 Undecided .. .. 10 100 Practically no difference exists between the attitudes of men nnd women, old and young, farmers nnd city dwellers, rich and poor, or between people who usually vote for the Labor Party and those who vote non-Labor. Most common comment by both artisans and better-off people was that higher wages and higher prices are a vicious circle. They thought that an upper limit to both wnges and prices would stabilise inuustr.v, prevent orofit- eering and combat inflation. Usual reason for opposing the regulation was a belief that the pegging of wages and prices could not be done effectively. Previous Finding An earlier survey, taken in September, showed that at least two out of three people thought that price control was not giving a fair deal. The bone of contention was that manufacturers and traders had been allowed to pass on Increased costs, with the result that the general level of prices had risen. Approval for the new regulation shows that. at. least for the duration of the war. most workers prefer stable wages and prices, to the uncertainty of rising wages and prices. As a mail contractor in New South Wales said: "The wage-earner will know where he is now." FAVORED The Australian public is not- in favor of paying overtime in post-war credits, according to a recent Gallup Poll. Workers, both skilled and unskilled, are agqinst the idea. A survey taken' In October by Australian Public Opinion Polls showed a three to two majority In favor of continuing to pay overtime at time and a half rates in wartime. To take the subject a step further, the following question was Included In the November survey: —"Speaking "Speaking generally, should overtime be paid in cash or In post-war credits, such as war savings certificates" Of each 100 people In the nation-wide cross-section: — 49 said "pay overtime in cash," 38 favored post-war credits, 6 were undecided, and 7 (chiefly women) could not answer. Owners and managers of businesses, and professional people, as a group, were evenly divided on the question. Clerks and shop-hands were only slightly against paying overtime In post-war credits, but artisans were more than two to one In favor of cash payments. There was no significant difference between the attitudes of old and young people, or between men and women. The vote for "cash" was at its highest at 57 p.c. In the capital cities and New South .Wales mining centres, and at its lowest, nt 29 p.c. among fanner owners.

30 Dec 1942 - AUSTRALIA SPEAKS: Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 30 December 1942, page 4 AUSTRALIA SPEAKS: No. 99 TRANSFER OF POWERS TO jCOMMONWEALTH FAVORED i Australians strongly support the principle ot transter-ring substantial extra powers from the States to the Com-: monwealth during post-war reconstruction, according to ; a Gallup Poll just completed. The Constitution Convention ! completed its deliberations on i December 1. Next day Australian i Public Opinion Polls— the Australian Gallup Poll— begnn a nationwide distribution of interview-forms. including this question: "Do you favor, or oppose, the States giving substantial extra powers to the Commonwealth during post-war reconstruction?" Of every 10(1 men and women interviewed; 04 favored transferring powers; 1.1 were against It; 10 were undecided; and 13 (chiefly women) could not answer. In all States, except Western Australia, the "favor" vote exceeded 60 p.c. Even In w.a. there were 44 p.c. in favor of the transfer of powers, during post-war reconstruction, compared with each 32 p.c. opposed: the other 24 p.c. were undecided or unacquainted with the question. Among men. the "favor" vote was as high as 74 p.c. compared with "oppose" only 15 p.c. All Income groups — artisans, better-off and well-to-do— held almost indentical views. 03 Feb 1954 - Atomic power Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 3 February 1954, page 4 Atomic name r A SIGNIFICANT swtng of public opinion regarding the right use of atomic power Is revealed in the Gallup Poll (Herald 28/1/54). Of 1Q00 people questioned. 59 per cent, said that the use of the "A bomb" against Hiroshima and Nagasaki 10 years ago was justified. Twenty-six per cent, said it was wrong. Fifteen per cent, were uncertain. This means that a little less than three out of ten of those who hold any views on the matter condemn the use of this super-weapon against cities. Obviously, the explosion of atomic missiles on our mainland has driven home to many people the tragic implications of this problem. Many of those who approved the use of the bomb in retrospect said they thought it had shortened the war. But with both sides possessing fission weapons, this cannot apply to a future war. The time is ripe for another great effort to outlaw atom and hydrogen bombs. — —DAVID MARTIN. Forest Road, Boronia. ir

20 Mar 1954 - GALLUP POLL SAYS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 20 March 1954, page 7 [?] Token migration unpopular here Two out of three Australians oppose allowing token immigration of 50 people a year from each and every country. In this survey, Gallup Poll interviewers first mentioned that people from some countries are not allowed to come and live in Australia. They then asked: "Which do you favor — keeping them out, or allowing, say, 50 people a year from each and every country into Australia?" 61 per cent, said, "It's right as it is; keep them out." 31 per cent, said "Allow in 50 a year," and 8 per cent, said they were undecided.
