12 Mar 1954 - They'll woo 450,000 unsure voters Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Friday 12 March 1954, page 4 They'll woo 450,000 unsure voters CAPITAL TALK By JOHN BENNETTS | CANBERRA; Today. — The Federal election is 11 weeks away and, according to the Gallup Poll, nine per cent, of the five million electors have not yet decided how they will vote. Government and Opposi- tion tacticians, therefore, are hard at work assessing the needs and desires of those 450,000 undecided voters. The war chests ol both sides art reported to be well lined for whai will probably be the costliest election campaign on record. The Labor Party expects to spend about £80,000. Much of this money is said to have come from prudent subscribers who normally do not support Labor but who. during periods of Government unpopularity, thought that a contribution to the other side would dr no harm and might do some good The Government parties will probably spend about the same amount as Labor, so that the better part of £200.000 worth of electioneering effort will be directed a' fewer than hnlf a million voters ? i IN their search for policy points which may appeal to those undecided voters, both sides are working on the same Idea — easier finance for home ownership. Quietly ignoring Mr John J. Ded-man's view that Labor should not encourage the development of a "little capitalist" class of home owners, Dr. Evatt Is putting the finishing touches to a plan for Commonwealth Bank housing loans at two per cent. Interest. At the same time a committee ol Government supporters Is working out a scheme to use Common-wealt' funds to reduce the Interest rates on all housing loans — whether through public or private finance agencies — from around four per cent, to three or even two per cent. Commonwealth departmental housing experts, however, view both proposals with scepticism and disfavor. They want to know whether these schemes arc Intended to increase the total supply of new houses— now running at about 70,000 a year. If so. what other Industries will be deprived of money, manpower and materials so that more houses can be built? If there are to be more houses for purchase by people who can afford them, will there be fewer for renting to the lower wage earners? Will there be two per cent, interest only for those who buy houses after the election— or for all. including cx-scrvlccmen. who are paying oil existing advances at around four per cent? Where will the Government find the £15 million needed to take over and convert existing loans to two per cent? Finally, where will the money be found for new lend- ing at two per cent. — from taxation revenue, from Inflationary Treasury bills, or from public loans raised at 414 per cent.? Some of the Government's shrewdest technical advisers think the answer to the housing shortage is not easier finance, but more efficient building methods. They say that glib promises of 'house loans at two per cent." are not enough. ? JERUSALEM has a Wailing Wall which does not wail, Venice has a bridge of Sighs which docs not sigh. But Canberra has a monument which renlly groans, It is the Australian memorial to the United States lorces who helped us In the war — the 250 It. tall aluminium and steel column unveiled by the Queen last month. Visitors have noticed that the column sways perceptibly in the Canberra winds — which is natural, because all tall structures must be flexible to a degree. If rigid, they would snap when subjected to wind or other pressures. But the column also emits creaking and groaning noises as It sways— noises that can be heard from some distance. The designers of the £100.000 memorial are not worried. They say that their specifications provide that, in a 100 m.p.h. gale, the top of the memorial wifl sway three feet. The creaklngs and groanlngs result from friction between new, rough surfaces of the component parts. The designers, say that as the memorial settles down and becomes, so to speak, "run In." the noises will diminish and probably' disappear. ? ALL aspirants for Federal political fame whose names begin with "Mac," "Mc" or "Ma" have a vested interest in a dispute which Commonwealth electoral authorities are trying to setUe. The dispute involves the two candidates for the Federal seat of Boothby. In South Australia — the sitting Liberal MHR Mr J. McLeny, and Labor's Mr R. Matthews. Electoral law says that ballot papers must list candidates In the alphabetical order of their surnames. Mr Matthews claims that his name, beginning "Ma," takes alphabetical precedence over Mr McLeay. The argument Is not purely academic — the man who tops the ballot paper can pick up something like 2',i per cent, of the first preferences, because i indifferent voters often fill their ballot papers from the top down. It Is curious that, in a community with such a good proportion of Scottish names, the dispute has not cropped up before. However, with the help of Crown Law authorities, the argument is to be settled once and for all. The McLeays and McTavishes will soon know whether they are to take precedence over all -comers In the M class, or whether they must defer to the Matthewses. The equipment, left from the Second World War. includes guns and ammunition of American origin, British and American tanks, and Mustang, and Mosquito planes. Those who disapproved of him with equal intensity numbered 15 per cent. . Least enthusiasm for Senator McCarthy was found in the Southern States. Greatest support Even in his native Middle West, the number of voters expressing extreme disapproval outnumbered those expressing great enthusiasm by two to one. Senator McCarthy Is slightly more popular with Roman Catholics than with Protestants, but most Roman Catholics dislike him. He derives his greatest support from rank and file Reoubllcnn voters and makes little appeal to professional people.Older Older people are more enthusiastic about him thnn younger ones. Those with University and college educations dislike him most of nil. His critics in this class outnumber his supporters by four to one.

20 May 1942 - Australia Speaks No. 42 Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 20 May 1942, page 8 |i Australia Speaks j i No. 42 \ j Majority j \OpposeHate\ I Propaganda ' Half of an Australia-wide cross-section recently interviewed for the Gallup Poll had heard at least one of the "Know the Jap" radio sessions — criticised in some quarters as hate propaganda. A majority of the listeners were not favorably impressed by them. In March and April the Australian public was sublectcd to one of the most Intensive propaganda campaigns in our history. On 12 evenings at 9.30, every radio station in Australia broadcast a series of dramatic programmes entitled, "Know the Jap as he really is." a Department of Information feature. Three weeks after those broadcasts, the interviewers of Australian Public Opinion Polls — the Gallup Poll of Australia— set out to measure listeners' reactions. The questions asked were: (1) Did you hear any of the recent radio sessions a few weeks ago entitled, "Know the Jap as he really is?" and (2) Do you think they were a good Idea? At least three out of four Australian homes have radio sets, but only half of the cross-section interviewed had heard any of the sessions. Among well-to-do people the ratio of listeners rose slightly to six out of 10. but it fell to three out of 10 in the lowest income group.Of Of each 100 who said they had heard any of the sessions — 44 thought they were a good idea; 54 considered they were not, and 2 were undecided. Opinions of men and women were almost Identical, and people of all ages gp.ve much the same In Queensland — the State nearest to the Japanese — only one person out of each three Interviewed said they had heard the broadcasts. Of those who had listened, however, nearly two out of three voted them a good idea. Victorians. Tasmanlans and South Australians were evenly divided in their opinions, but almost two out of three listeners interviewed in New South Wales and Western Australia were not favorably impressed. Common Attitudes "People should know the kind of foe they are fighting," was a common attitude of artisans who approved the broadcasts, while better-off people commonly said. "We must be shaken out of our complacency." Some people who were not favorably impressed considered the sessions too unreal and theatrical, while another group considered it wrong to stir up hatred between nations. Others considered them unnecessary and of no value. "Australians don't need scaring." they said. 29 Jun 1942 - AUSTRALIA SPEAKS : No. 52 Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Monday 29 June 1942, page 5 AUSTRALIA SPEAKS : No. 52 Nationalisation Of Coal Industry Opposed WARTIME CONTROL FAVORED ! Only one Australian in four favors permanent nationalisation of the coal industry, but a Gallup Poll taken this month shows that a substantial majority would approve Commonwealth Government action to take over the mines as a wartime measure. On June 5, the day the British Government announced its decision to assume full control of the coal mines, the interviewers for Australian Public Opinion Polls began recording opinions in hundreds of representative centres, from people in ell circumstances, on this question: — ' "Do you think the Commonwealth Government should take over the coal mines — or should -the owners he left in charge?" Those who thought the Commonwealth should take over the mines were also asked: "Should thev be taken over permanently, or only during the war?" Of each 100 people interviewed —35 35 said the Government should take over the coal mines permanently. 37 thought the Government should take them over during the war. 24 favored the owners being left in charge; and 14 could not express an I opinion. j This mean? that if the Commonwealth Government, took over the coal mines as a. wartime measure, the decision would be approved by 171 in each 100 electors with opinions on the subject. Opinion was much the same in all States, except that in Western Australia and Tasmania nearly all voters for Government control were against permanent nationalisation. Some Western Australians added the proviso: "Eastern States only; W.A. miners are doing a good job." HIGHLIGHTS OF VOTING Occupation and economic status had less Influence than might have been expected. Notable' features are: — (1) Even among owners and managers of business and among well - to - do people there were more votes lor vjuvei uuicuu tun-trol, at least for the duration, than for private control; (2) Among skilled workers, of whom three out of four voted for Government control, at least during the war, only one in three favored permanent nationalisation, (3) Neither Labor Party supporters nor non-Labor people favored permanent nationalisation. but both groups thought the Government should take over the mines during the war. REASONS DIFFER Usual comment by those who favored control by the mine owners was: "Government enterprise is not successful." Some added: "No interference with private enterprise." ' Most of the 37-ln-lhe-100 who thought the Government should take over the mines only during the war said, "Tt will stop disputes," or "The Government would gel greater output." Mos,t common reasons for favoring permanent nationalisation of the coal industry were: (1) "Coal is a national asset." (2) "It would stop strikes" and (3) "Miners would get better treatment." Very few made the comment, "Nationalise all industry." Operations of Australian Public Opinion Polls (The Gallup Method) are open to investigation by any reputable body. 22 Mar 1944 - Back To Bed By The Clock Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 22 March 1944, page 4 Back To Bed By The Clock IT is not derogatory to the value of Gallup polls to emphasise that the results obtained should be studied in respect to the time and particu- lar circumstances in which the polls are taken. They claim to be no more than as accurate a survey-., as can scientifically be taken of the public mind at a particular moment. Tlie puunu U1U1U IS, U1 LUU19V. amenable to change. Their practical usefulness lies not so much in the realms of prophecy, electoral or otherwise, or as a final basis for legislation, but in the study of mass psychology and the effects of education. A series of Gallup polls just taken on the question of daylight saving give what at first sight may seem the surprising result that its continuation in Australia after the war is not favored. It is still supported by a majority for its special war - time advantages, but the margin in its favor is shown to be smaller at tire moment, than at the time of any of the polls taken in the last four years. This is contrary to experience in other countries where the change to summertime has become a custom which seems in no likelihood of being abandoned. It may be true that the benefits of daylight saving in Australia are not so dramatic as in countries where summer days arc longer and winter days are shorter, but even here the advantages have been substantial. One simple explanation of the latest Australian poll may lie in the fact that it has been taken near The close of the summer term when the mornings are already beginning to become dark and chilly for early risers, and at a time when war conditions have greatly lessened facilities for the recreational use of the extra davlieht hour after work. j

20 Jan 1945 - People Worse Off Under War Conditions Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 20 January 1945, page 5 People Worse Off Under War Conditions Rising costs and high taxes have so affected the real income of Australians that more than half the people interviewed in a recent Gallup Poll said they were worse off now than before the war. Interviewers throughout all States asked men and women of all sections of the commuity the question; — "Considering your family in-come and the cost of living, do you feel you are better off, or worse off, today than before the war?" 56 p.c. said "worse off." 17 p.c. "better off," and 27 p.c. "no difference." Men and women, as groups gave practically the same answers, and there was little difference among the various income groups. Highlights of an analysis ac-cording to the occupation of the breadwinner of the family are:— The ''better off" percentage was highest at 37 p.c, among shop-keepers and second highest at 22 p.c. among farmers, and Only 36 p.c. of munition workers said they were worse off than before the war, compared with 56 p.c. for the community in general. What People Said Those who said the war had left them worse off blamed the fact that wage increases had not kept up with rising costs, or said their incomes had been pegged, but costs had not. "Wages have gone up, but the cost of living has gone up more," said a turner's wife at Hilton, South Australia. Many mentioned high taxation as one of the factors, and a few even said that high taxation was solely responsible for their being worse off now than in pre-war days." "With overtime, etc., more money is coming into the home." said an ice-worker's wife in Fltzroy, Vic-toria, who summed up the view of many of those who answered, "Better off." The attitude of a Brisbane widow was supported by others. She said: "We can't spend under the coupon system." This table shows how people have answered the question in three surveys since 1942. 03 Dec 1941 - Public Opinion Is Not Always Wise Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 3 December 1941, page 4 Public Opinion Is Not Always Wise According to a gallup Poll just completed 77 per cent, of public opinion In Victoria favors Govern- ment lotteries and only 18 per cent, opposes them. There Is no occasion to question the accuracy of the survey. These polls are conducted by a method which demonstrably gives a reliable expression of a representative cross section of public opinion. But anyone who argues from this result that opponents or Government lotteries In Victoria should henceforth hold their peace, or that the Victorian Premier, himself a stout opponent. Is now democratically bound to Introduce Into Parliament r Bill legalising State lotteries, has got an entirely wrong Idea of the (unction of the Gallup Poll and of the responsibility of leaders In a Democracy. The result of a Gallup Poll Is an objective fact and not an argument for or against anything. , When It is properly conducted It reveals a trend of public opinion which is not invariably right and wise, but often conspicuously wrong and foolish. Those who oppose the introduction of lotteries in this State do so because they believe that behind the attraction of this Taclle way of raising money for however good a cause there lies more than a counterbalance of waste and moral danger. If they are In a position of public responsibility It. has been their duty to weigh these considerations more deeply than the ordinary member of the public. In such a count as a Gallup Poll their vote may be only one among the rest, but that does not represent their Influence Upon public opinion or their voice In the determination upon action. One of the most' valuable functions of a Gallup Poll can be to reveal bow far public opinion is astray and therefore, in what directions It has to be instructed and guided.', >. ""

17 Oct 1946 - GALLUP POLL Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Thursday 17 October 1946, page 11 GALLUP POLL Daylight Saving In Disfavor Daylight saving is not wanted in Australia, according to n recent Gallup Poll on the subject. Three out of four farmers interviewed oppose its re-introduction, and more than half of the semi-skilled and unskilled workers are against it. In country centres, 3 of every 5 people oppose it, and there is only a small majority of 5 to 4 In Its favor in capital cities. Adults of all ages were interviewed, and only among those in their twenties did the vote for daylight saving exceed 50 per cent. Gallup Poll interviewers asked: Would you li/ce daylight saving next summer? More than 2000 people were interviewed, and the following table shows that the "dislike" vote has risen consistently from 23 per cent, to 51 per cent since 1942. — Indif-I.ike Dislike fcrcnt 1046, Sept. .41 51 8 1944, Aug. . 45 47 8 1044, Feb. . 47 44 9 1943, Feb. . 65 29 6 1912, Feb. . 69 23 8 Daylight saving was in force in Australia for the three months ending March, 1942; the six months ending March, 1943, and (with the exception of West Australia) the six months ending March, 1944. Comments of city dwellers at the latest poll who are opposed to daylight saving disclose a widespread feeling that it makes the day too long — "an hour's rest lost in the morning cannot be made up." Views of the farming community are summed up by a farmer of Brookton (WA) — "Farmers work by the sun, not the clock." Typical city peoole who like daylight saving are a chemist's wife in Edward Park (SA), who said, "It gives a man a chance to work in the garden," and a telephone mechanic in EdgeclifTe. Sydney, who reasoned that "It gives workers more recreational time in the evening." Issued by A list. Public Opinion Polls. 352 Collins St., Mclb.

19 Oct 1946 - Gallup Poll Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 19 October 1946, page 11 Gallup Poll — rj Division On Palestine Question H B Australians are equally divided on the question of limiting: entry of Jews into Palestine, according to a nation-wide Gallup Poll. People interviewed were first asked whether they had followed the discussion on the subject. Half of them said they had, and they were then asked:— Do you. favor, or oppose, limiting the number of Jeios who enter Palestine? Of every 100: — 4-1 said "Limit their entry." 44 said "Don't limit," and 12 could not answer. In January last the American Gallup Poll asked a somewhat, similar question. It was found that only slightly more than half the people interviewed had followed the discussion, and of these, 3 out of 4 were sympathetic to the idea of permitting Jews tq settle in Palestine. Many Fear Trouble A common reason given by Australians who advocate "limiting" is that "Uncontrolled entry would cause trouble with the . Arabs." The views of those who favor allowing an unlimited number of Jews to enter Palestine is summed up in the comment of a dairyman Ballina. NSW, who said: "Let them go back to their national home." 26 Oct 1946 - What People Think--And Why Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 26 October 1946, page 16 What People Think —And Why\ By a Herald Corresponded Every six weeks 200 Gallup Poll investigators interview 2000 adult Australians to find out (with considerable precision) what the other five j million adult Australians think on subjects ranging from SP betting to j the atomic bomb. j mHEY are so aood that /WWffWwk i I in a pre-election A "sample poll" in 14 key electoral districts in the eastern half of Melbourne the Gallup prediction was within one per cent, of the Anal vote. There is nothing magic in precision sampling of public opinion. Mr Roy Morgan, director of Australian Public Opinion iGallup' Polls, says these miniature referendums nre accurate because a genuine cross-section of the population is questioned, representative even down to age. sex. likely income, and religious proportions: and because Gallup interviewers and statisticians aim at maximum elimination of "biasing Influences." such as a framing or reading of a question in such a way as to suggest an answer. Interviewers are recruited in the country by nominations from , leading citizens, and in the cities j by newspaper advertisements j calling for "public-spirited men." They are likely to land a monthly ! assignment Involving three or : four hours' work: in that time they should be able to chart the opinions 'of 10 people. They are 1 paid 15/ for every 10 interviews. Tips given to interviewers in-: elude: — "If respondents become uneasy because they don't hold firm opinions on a particular subject, point out that 'undecided' or 'unacquainted' votes may be as significant as 'yes' or 'no' answers: "Avoid people who are Insincere.' completelv uninformed, or hooelesslv rambling: "People explain themselves best in privacy." CHECKING THE poll management has to ensure that its Interviewers are conscientious, alert and openminded. One man's returns are checked against, those of interviewers in similar areas. Results also are checked by follow-up letters designed both to check on the interviewer and to detect any change in opinion. The Gallup Poll relics on simultaneous interviews with peonlc of both sexes, in all walks of, life, of all ages, and in all parts of Australia. Interviewers get cooperation from nearly everyone. But the elderly civil servant, trained to divorce himself from' politics, hesitates to give his views on anything political, or to have his name recorded. He is probably the hardest man to interview. The wife of .the well-to-do business man, trying hard to give an opinion on current politics, often finds she has left her political thinking to her husband. The artisan's wife, usually. Is alert to current problems, as her bread and butter are closely connected with them. She answers promptly and decisively. One of the few times a Gallup interviewer has fell himself nol welcome on a suburban doorstep was during the war. When the interviewer knocked at a door In a Melbourne suburb, a suspicious-looking woman hall opened It. The interviewer introduced hlipself as a Gallup man. As this did not register, lie showed the woman Ills question form. After one glance at the heading, the woman shrieked, "The call-up man." oil which there wns rapid, heavy-footed scuffling In the back of the house. Australians, the interviewers find, are easy to interview. Gallup experience all over the world is that most . people like to have their opinion sought; they like to think that an organisation deems their opinion worth recording. Gallup Poll interviewers do not purposely seek the well-informed; they are gauging firstly public opinion— not the Justification for the opinion. Interviewers bear in mind the words of American Dr. George Gallup, founder of the poll: "Democracy doesn t. require that every man be a political philosopher; ,it requires merely that the sum total of individual views arid up to something that makes < srnse." Alter coming in by mail from nil over Australia, interview-: forms are converted in Melbourne into punch-cards nil a mnchlnc : similar lo that used for census, figures. Eacli tick which the In-' lervieiver puis on Interview-forms becomes a punch-hole. \ Punch - cards are then' counted electrically, and sorted into major population groups — age, sex, political affiliation, locality, and so on — so that each group can be counted separately. With the punch-cards, results can bev sub-divided almost indefinitely, giving tlic wide range of tabulations which form nn integral part, of the interpretations which appear in the press, The Australian Gallup Polls organisation is nmiintcd with the Gallup Polls in Britain. America. Cannda. Sweden, France. Denmark. Finland and Norway. If you haven't been interviewed yet for the Gallup Poll, tile explanation Is: — There ate 4! J million adults ill Australia. Eacli year the Gallup Poll interviews about 16,600 people at tiie rate of 2060 in cnrli of its eight surveys annuallv. „ At that rate it would take .>00 years to interview 41g million people. : QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS; An interviewer seeking public reaction fo a question of the moment,' reccrds answers given her by an obliging shopkeeper. | AN AUSTRALIAN GALLUP POLL ASSISTANT operating the eloctric punch which converts individual interview-forms into separafo punch-cards. Each person interviewed is asked a range of public questions. Answers to all questions are recorded on one card, together with thc; sex, age and economic class of person interviewed. i

07 Sep 1946 - GALLUP POLL Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 7 September 1946, page 7 GALLUP POLL Swinging Voters Are Not Party-conscious When the election campaign began, it was found by the Gallup Poll that one elector in 10 was not only undecided on voting intention, but also thought it made little difference which political party governed Aus- tralia. 17 Aug 1946 - REFERENDUM PROSPECTS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 17 August 1946, page 9 REFERENDUM PROSPECTS Employment Power Is Centre Of Interest I The Gallup Poll's latest survey on referendum prospects, just completed, shows that the "Social Services" question will probably be approved by a substantial majority of electors. Another question, "Terms and Conditions of Employment," is also likely to pass, but "Marketing of Primary Products" has little chance, unless many electors change their minds. On the "social services" question, 67 per cent, of men and 59 per cent, of women said they would be voting "Yes." Only 24 per cent, have decided to vote "No." and the others are undecided. Comparison of these figures with results of similar surveys in May and June shows little change. There are "Yes" majorities in all Stales. Employment Favored On the question of "terms and conditions of employment." men now plan to vote: — Yes. 55 per cent.; No. 37 per cent.: and Undecided. 8 per cent. The "Yes" percentage Ir 3 per cent, higher than in June, and 10 per cent, higher than the May figure. States likely to give "Yes" majorities are South Australia, New South Wales. Victoria and Queensland. Marketing Doubtful Regarding "marketing of primary products," men are inclined toward "Yes," their answers being: — Yes, 49 per cent.; No, 41 per cent.; and Undecided, 10 per cent. Refercndums, however, must be approved not only by nationwide majorities, but also by majorities in four of the six States; and it seems that WA, Victoria and Tasmania oppose "marketing." More than a quarter of the women Interviewed said they did not know how they were going to vote on "employment" or "marketing." Gallup Poll experience suggests that In due course those women will vote like their menfolk. Political Affiliation People Interviewed were also asked how they intended to vote at the Federal election. Cross-analysis of referendum intentions against political affiliation shows: (1) Of men and women Labor voters, 75 per cent, plan to vote "Yes" on "social services." 63 per cent, on "employment," and 57 per cent, on "marketing"; and (2) Corresponding "Yes" figures for Liberal-Country voters are 51 per cent., 33 per cent, and 29 per cent. The figures suggest that votes in favor or against the referendum questions, particularly "employment" and "marketing," will be largely determined by whether an elector supports the present Government or the parties now In opposition. Issued by Aust. Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins St., Melb.

03 Aug 1946 - GALLUP POLL Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 3 August 1946, page 5 GALLUP POLL What The Other Half j — Thinks Of Church — About half the people of Australia are churchgoers, according to a nation-wide vote taken in recent weeks by the Australian Gallup Poll. Of every 100 people interviewed : — , 52 say they go to church, and 48 say they do not. j Women churchgoers outnumber-the men by more than 10 per cent., but there is no marked difference in the age groups. In South Australia. Victoria and Tasmania churchgoers slightly exceed non-church people, but the reverse applies among those Interviewed in Queensland and West- ern Australia. New South Wales is fifty-fifty. Generally, the proportion of churchgoers is greater in the country than in the capital cities. Denominations People in the various religious groups answered the question, "Are you a church-goer," as follows: —Yes Yes No Roman Catholic . 68 p.c. 32 p.c. 10 Aug 1946 - GALLUP POLL Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 10 August 1946, page 6 GALLUP POLL Parliament On The Air Is Popular Public opinion wants the broadcasting of Parliament to continue "because it gives people a more intimate idea of what is happening," according to a nation-wide Gallup Poll just completed. This proportion of 50 per cent, listeners is fairly consistent tlirough the age groups, from those in their twenties to those over 60. and there is little difference between city dwellers and country people. Analysis according to the economic circumstances of people interviewed, however, shows some marked differences. More than 60 per cent, of better-off people have listened to Parliament, compared with less than 50 per cent, of artisans and white collar workers, and barely 30 per cent, of the lowest income group. All people, both listeners and non-llstencrs. were asked: "Do you think the broadcasts from Parliament should be continued, reduced or stopped?" Of those who had listened: 68 per cent, said "continue"; 7 per cent, said "reduce"; 1R per cent, said "stop," and 7 per cent, were undecided, j These comments are typical: People should know how Par-i llament. Is conducted (motor ; engineer). Broadcasts arc more detailed than the pnpers (government official). Check on what the local member Is doing (flour miller). Some of those who would stop the broadcasts mentioned the cost ("A waste of taxpayers' money"), but most referred to the standard of debate, for example: "Members act like schoolboys"; I "Disgraceful behavior" and "Reduces respect for members." i Of those who had not listened to. Parliament, more than half said they could not express an opinion on whether or not to continue the broadcasts. 08 May 1954 - GALLUP POLL SAYS: Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 8 May 1954, page 5 [?] One in 10 plans to build a house At least two of every 10 people are dissatisfied with their housing, and would move tomorrow if they could. 09 Apr 1947 - GALLUP POLL FINDS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 9 April 1947, page 10 GALLUP POLL FINDS Big Change In Opinion On Financing Social Services Most Australians are now of the opinion that all the cost of social services, such as pensions, child endowment and free doctors, should come from ordinary taxes. This latest Gallup Poll finding shows a marked change of opinion since last July, -when most people were found to tavor a contributory scheme. This is the third time since 1944 that the Australian Gallup Poll has measured public opinion on financing the cost of social services. In the latest survey, Just completed, interviewers asked a nation-wide representative sample of men and women: — With regard to the cost of social services, such as pensions, child endowment and free doctors — do you think all the cost should come from ordinary taxes — or should every family contribute, say 2/- each week? 10 May 1947 - GALLUP POLL FINDS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 10 May 1947, page 8 GALLUP POLL FINDS Most Australians Oppose Taking Homeless Jews According to a recent Gallup Poll, almost 6 out of every 10 Australians think this country should not join in J a world-wide plan to take in some of the homeless Jewish people of Europe. There are said to be 600,000 Jewish people in Europe looking for homes in other countries, and it has been suggested that a certain number should be taken in each year by every country, on a population basis. People interviewed were told of tills suggestion and were then asked: "Do you think Australia should, or should not, take part in such a plan?" 22 Sep 1945 - Gallup Poll Says: Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 22 September 1945, page 5 Gallup Poll Says Japs Deserved Atom Bombing Having heard world arguments for and against the dropping of the atom bomb on the Japanese, the Australian public is overwhelmingly of the opinion that its use was justified. Most people believe that it finished the war quickly, and saved thousands of Allied lives. Another argument is that the Japanese would have had no scruples in using it against the Allies had they discovered it first. Atrocities committed against our men prompted many people to say that the Japanese deserved what they had coming to them, and that more such bombs should have been dropped. Those who take exception to the use of the bomb do so because they think it inhuman and barbaric. Keep It Secret People interviewed were also asked whether they thought Britain and America should keep the secret of the atom bomb, or share it with the United Nations. “Keep it secret” is the opinion of 8 out of 10 people, including most of those who think it was wrong to use the bomb. Both men and women expressed similar opinions on both questions. [Two atom bombs were dropped on Japan—the first on Hiroshima on August 6, wiping out two‐thirds of the city, and the second three days later on Nagasaki, destroying a third of the city. 06 Mar 1943 - AUSTRALIA SPEAKS No. 109 Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 6 March 1943, page 5 No. 109 COUPONS FOR LIQUOR NOW FAVORED Public opinion, which was evenly divided six months ago on the question of rationing liquor by coupons, is now 4 to 3 in favor of it, according to a Gallup Poll taken last month. Men and women of all ages and types were Interviewed In the survey, taken by Australian Public Opinion Polls on the question: — "Should alcoholic drinks be rationed by means or coupons. Of each 100 men and women, In equal numbers, interviewed — 48 said, "Ration liquor by coupons." 37 opposed It. i ' 9 were undecided, and 6, being abolitionists, would not answer. Men, who were formerly three to two against rationing by coupons, are now 50-50 on the question. Women are nearly two to one In favor of It. Voting In New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia approximated the Aus- tralia-wide figures. Opinion In South Australia and Tasmania was slightly opposed to coupons. In the capital cities — where beer Is In short supply— there were tnree to two in lavor or coupons for liquor. Elsewhere there was an even vote. DRINKERS' OPINIONS An Interesting feature of the survey was that, more than a quarter of the representative cross-section Interviewed said they were teetotallers. The others said they had an occasional drink, or more. Excluding teetotallers, opinion was exactly evenly divided on whether alcoholic drink should be rationed by coupons. Both teetotallers and drinkers usually commented. "It would be fair to all." Only a few mentioned they were thinking of the effect on drunkenness. By far the most common reason for opposing coupons was fear that a black market would be created.

29 May 1943 - AUSTRALIA SPEAKS: No. 126 Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 29 May 1943, page 4 AUSTRALIA SPEAKS T No. 126 FEW WOULD OPPOSE SEX EDUCATION OF CHILDREN An overwhelming majority of Australians, both men and women, are firmly of the opinion that sex education of children could be entrusted- to qualified teachers. A nation-wide Gallup Poll shows only one person in eight in opposition. To see whether parents think public authorities should take over the obligation of straightening out the sex knowledge of children, Australian Public Opinion Polls — the Gallup Poll of Australia— asked this question In its May. survey:— '.'Would you favor, or oppose, qualified teachers explaining sex matters and venereal disease to boys and girls?" Cross-sections of people were Interviewed in more than 200 centres In all States. Of each 100 people Interviewed: — 83 answered "Favor"; 12 were opposed, and 5 were undecided. Voting did not vary much from State to State. Men and women, as groups, held almost Identical opinions. People's incomes had little effect on tneir attitudes. Old people were least keen on the idea.tbut even among people over 60 the "oppose" vote was onlv 19 per cent., compared with 10 per cent, for those under 50. FIRST LESSONS Each person favorable to sex Instruction by qualified teachers was also asked: — "At what age do you think children should be given their first lessons in sex matters?" 16 p.c. said under 12 years. 25 p.c. said 12 years. 11 p.c. said 13 years. 24 p.c. said 14 years. ' 11 p.c. said over 14 years. 13 p.c. did not answer. 100 The average selected by both men and women was about 13 years. PEOPLE'S REASONS Three typical reasons for supporting instruction by teachers were: "It's an essential part of children's education" (master painter. Brisbane). 15 Nov 1944 - GALLUP POLL Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 15 November 1944, page 5 GALLUP POLL Public Thinks Improved Living Standards Most Likely Way Of Raising Birth Rate i Replies made by a cross-section of people to Australian | Gallup Poll interviewers, who asked them what they ! thought would help most to increase the birthrate i in this country, show that most men and women ' believe the solution lies in economic measures. aimed generally at improving the standard of living. I A survey recently made by the Commonwealth Government into t the causes of the decline In the 'birthrate is also believed to have revealed that a large number of 'women consider that these causes were largely economic. They attributed their failure to have more children to such things as i the desire for better living stan-dards. the lack of assurance ol social- security, and the need for 'better employment and educational opportunities for children These conclusions have been ! challenged on the ground that 'experience has shown that the 'birthrate Is lowest among the 'most well-to-do sections of the ; community Scientific Survey I The Gallup Poll cheek revealed thai there was little difference ! between men and women in the opinions they held on measures ! for Increasing the birthrate If ' anything, men were more inclined to mention economic secur-; it.v and the need for financial assistance to parents. while I women tended to stress improve-' mcnts in housing and the pro-i vision of household help for mothers while children were ' voung. , In the "economic" group, this ' la how the suggestions were divided up:— Economic security and full employment ... 22 % Better housing, lower j rentals 17 % Government allowances for families. or marriage loans 15 % Better living conditions 10 % I Higher wages, cheaper liv- ! ng 9 % j Total 73 % The remaining 27 p.e. who offered suggestions did not agree on any particular solution. Eight p.c. thought provision of help in the homes for mothers would act as a stimulus to the birthrate; 5 p.c. said the cure would be found only in such things as better moral tenching. removal of selfish- : ness. higher spiritual ideals and! a movemenl away from pleasure-seeking. Marriage 'Age Many people have advocated younger marriages as one step to-i ward . increasing the number of 'children born into the community, 'because the fertility rate Is highest among women In their early I twenties. Only 2 p.c.- oi those I interviewed, however, mentioned this as likely to increase the birthrate. .Other Other suggestions (made by only a small percentage altogether) were curtailment of the sale of contraceptives, better hospitals for maternity cases, and taxes on bachelors and childless couples. . Only 1 p.c, suggested the removal of women from industry. The diversity of views among Australian people on this question. amounting almost to confusion of thought, is shown by the fact that a quarter of the people interviewed in this survey could not make any suggestions at all. Some said the only wav to Increase the population would be through Immigration. (Issued br Anst. Public Opinion Polls. Col ) i lis S f .. Mclb.|

28 Oct 1944 - GALLUP POLL Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 28 October 1944, page 5 GALLUP POLL No Big Celebrations Until Japan Is Defeated The overwhelming majority of Australians are opposed to widespread celebrations here when Germany sur-renders, "Wait till Japan is defeated," was the gene-ral attitude expressed to Gallup Poll Interviewers. Men and women of all ages throughout all six States were in-terviewed on the question. "When Germany surrenders, do you think we should celebrate in a big way — or wait until Japan is defeated." Altogether about 2000 people were interviewed. Of each 100, 85 said "Await Japan's de-feat." 12 favored celebrating, and 3 were undecided. Men and women, as groups, gave almost the same answers. Younger people were even more in favor of deferring celebrations than their elders. There was close agreement be-tween people in all States. People's Reasons "Germany is our main enemy, " was the comment of the occasional person who favored celebrating Germany's defeat in a big way. On the other hand, most people said something like:— "The Pacific war is more our con-cern (comment of a farmer in Manilla, N.S.W.) "Germany's surrender will not mean peace for us" (housewife, Mile End, Adelaide) "Premature celebrations would weaken our war effort" (engi-neer Brunswick, Melbourne, and "So many of our boys are in Jap hands" (shop assistant Dalby, Qld) Another common remark by people opposed to celebrating Ger-many's defeat was, "Thanksgiving services only." 03 Sep 1949 - Family Of Four Now Needs £8'4'1 Weekly Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 3 September 1949, page 10 Family Of Four Now Needs £8'4'1 Weekly According to a recent Gallup Poll, it now costs at least £8/4/1 a week to maintain a family of four. Comparison with a similar Poll last February shows that this figure has risen by 15/6 a week (from £7/8/7 to £8/4/1) in six months. To find out what it costs the average family of four to keep in health and live decently, the Australian Gallup Poll asked a cross-section of people In all six States: — In pour opinion, what is the smallest amount a family of four needs each week, to meet all expenses, including rent? Similar questions were asked by the Gallup Poll in March 1845, February 1946 and February 1949. Comparison of answers shows that the - estimated weekly cost of living for a family of four has taken a particularly steep rise this year, to almost £2 a week more than when the war ended: 1945, March .... £6/7/11 1946, February .. £6/10/ 1949, February .. £7/8/7 1949, July .. .. £8/4/1 In the latest survey the average estimate by men (£8/4/-) agrees almost exactly with that Of women (£8/4/3). People were asked how mtjny adults and children were In their family, and those who happened to belong to families of four answered within a few pence of the total. ' Estimates below £8/4/1 were given by pensioners (£8/2/2), owners of small businesses (£8/1/9), farmers (£7/13/9) and unskilled workers (£7/11/7). "White collar" workers gave the highest estimate — £8/10/6. or nearly £1 a week above the estimate by unskilled workers.

11 Oct 1949 - GALLUP POLL SHOWS Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Tuesday 11 October 1949, page 9 GALLUP POLL SHOWS Only Surprise Can Affect Election Only a big and unexpected event, such as Labor discarding socialism, can now have much effect on the result of the Federal election, analysis of the latest Gallup Poll shows. As published in The Herald on Saturday, the Poll finding was: — 16 per cent, of electors intend to vote Liberal-CP on Dec. 10. 13 per cent, intend to vote Labor. 2 per cent. Independent and 9 per cent.' are undecided. On those figures. Labor is likely to receive 48 per cent, of the first preference votes; the House of Representatives will probably be evenly divided. Further Questioning In such circumstances, interest centres on prospects of inter-party switching in the next 2 months, and to throw some light on that problem the Gallup Poll asked people: (1) How they voted at the previous Federal election in 1946, and (2) Whether anything was likely to occur which could make them change their minds before the election. Answers to the first of those questions show that the 46 per cent, who now intend to vote Liberal-CP divide into:— 37 per cent, who voted Liberal-CP in 1946: 5 per cent. Labor in 1946, and 4 per cent, who didn't vote. Similarly, the 43 per cent, who intend to vote Labor comprises: —39 39 per cent, who voted Labor in 1946: 1 per cent. Liberal-CP 1946. and 3 per cent, who didn't, vote. Altogether 76 per cent, of the electors plan to vote for the same party again, and 6 per cent, plan to "switoh" parties. ' The election result, of course, will depend largely on:— (a) How many of the 76 per cent, remain steadfast, and (b) How many of the 6 per cent, of "switchers" decide to switch back to the parties they supported in 1946. Possible Changes The second question (on possibility of a change of mind) shows: — Of the 37 per cent, of the electors who are consistent Liberal-CP voters, 3 may yet switch to Labor. Of the 39 per cent, of the electors who are consistent Labor voters, 4 may yet switch to Liberal-CP. Of the 6 per -cent, of the electors who plan to "switch" parties on December 10, about a quarter may yet switch back, giving Labor a net gain of less than 1 per cent. On those figures, neither side Is likely to gain much atnonc "nossible converts." unless one of the policy speeches contains a big surprise. Peoples' Reasons Analysis of people's reasons for saying they may change parties before the election shows that many of these who may switch from Labor oppose socialism., nationalisation or Communism. Similarly, many people wno may switch to Labor said: "Only if Labor alters its policy, and drops nationalisation." Issued' by Aust. Public Opinion Polls. 352 Collins St., Melb.

18 Jan 1952 - Know how your wage rises? Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Friday 18 January 1952, page 4 Know how your waoe rises? By a Special Correspondent The C series index on which the basic wage is adjusted quarterly works like a Gallup Poll. Announcement of the next rise is expected any day. It will surely add to complaints that skill margins are losing their importance, which Conciliation Commissioner Galvin's decision this week, not to increase margins, has already stimulated. BY checking the price flux throughout the nation of a cross-section of commodities, the Commonwealth Statistician tries to estimate the movement of costs for the average household. It is a huge Gallup Poll which no private organisation or individual tries to duplicate. Forecasts on its findings are rarely accurate. To take it, field officers working under the various State statisticians visit every city and large town. They have wide powers and the backing of' the law to ensure that Information given them is accurate. Each quarter more than 50,000 actual prices are collected. It is impossible in practice to ascertain tne price of every item that goes to make up the basic wage. So the Court has selected an index, compiled and prepared by the Commonwealth Statistician. The C series covers food, groceries, housing, clothing, household goods, fuel and light. It was constructed in 1921 as the result of a recommendation of the 1920 Royal Commission on the Basic Wage. Its aim was to provide a better instrument for periodic adjustments of the basic wage than were provided by other, series. Wide range of index The Court, in 1934, adopted the C series for wage adjustments. In the preparation of such an index, the first decision that has to be made is what goods and services are to be included — the "regimen," as it is called. When the last basic wage was being considered by the Court there were 160 items in the index, They included a wide range of the goods .and services bought by a representative family. ' It must not be assumed that the "regimen" is composed of those articles that the Arbitration Court believes should compose the basic wage. The Court makes its decision on a variety of factors, including the general condition of industry, and then seeks a measuring stick by which the changes in prices may be judged. Tea, flour, sago, golden syrup," tinned peaches ana pears and plum jam are among 20 grocery items listed. Coffee, cocoa, cornflour, honey and other, tinned fruits and jams are omitted. The regimen does not include a number of items which are used by the ordinary householder. The key question is whether the changes in the prices of the goods selected is representative of the changes in the goods and services used by the householder. Once a representative selection of goods is made, the quantities consumed must be taken into consideration to find out how each item affects family spending. This process is called "weighting." So in addition to a price unit, each item carries a "weight" unit which is based on the quantity the average household uses. A 21b. loaf of bread carries a "weight" unit of 100; lib. of butter a "weight" unit of 30; lib. pork chops, 3; lib. sausages, 7; 30oz. tin of pears, .1. Ay multiplying the price unit bv the "weight," we get a pointer to the cost of the item to tne household. The "weights" for clothes, drap. ery and utensils are much lower than those for food. A man's overcoat is 0.25, blankets are 0.01 towels are 2, cotton pillow slips 5' cups 2, buckets 0.2. ' \ Officers of the Commonwealth Bureau of Statistics visit retailers to collect prices. Representative retailers furnish a return of food and groceries prices monthly, and of other items quarterly. The col-lection is made for the capital and main provincial cities. Officers visit shops Field officers have wide powers' of investigation, including entry oi premises and inspection of records They receive returns and visit re- i tail shops to verify returns. Where \ 1 variation of quality may be con- J siderable, they are equipped with j 1 samples of goods used for the I price comparisons. j The main criticism of the C series index has been based on the omission of certain articles that j are part of the diet of every householder — for example, fruit and vegetables. It has been suggested by union leaders from time to time that the prices of these commodities have risen more than the articles which compose the rcgl- jr men, and that therefore the indes If does not give an accurate picture if of the rise in the cost of living. (, This was probably true in war In time. j g Tile main reason why fresh fruit b and vegetables have been omitted sy is the difficulty in tracing the changes in the price movements -:v of such commodities. \ But statisticians do not believe that over a period the inclusion of such items would make any L serious difference to the index. if During the 1949-50 basic wage ;f hearing the Arbitration Court re- » fused to order any change in the |v index. Mr Justice Dunphy ex- j, pressed the view that over a long H, period the inclusion of fresh fruit i, and vegetables might have had a Jt lowering effect on the basic wage, tit It seems clear, however, that in !_ a period of rapid rise in prices ' the "regimen" does not always tc- 1 fleet the true rise in prices felt / A by the average householder. ft 3;

30 Jul 1947 - GALLUP POLL ASKS: Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 30 July 1947, page 8 GALLUP POLL ASKS: What Is The Future Of Atomic Energy? What part will atomic energy play in the world of tomorrow? Will it be harnessed for industrial use, and benefit civilisation? Or will it serve only the ends of war, and prove, a curse? In measuring the public's beliefs on these questions, the Gallup Poll has found Australians, as a whole, unable to make up their minds either way. Gallup Interviewers recently asked a nation-wide' random sample of nearly 2000 men and women: — lit the long run, do you think atomic energy will be a benefit, or a curse, to the human race? Indecision and uncertainty are reflected In people's answers. Of the whole cross-section Interviewed: 38 per cent say "Atomic energy will be a benefit," 38 per cent, say "It will be a curse," and 34 per cent, cannot answer either way. Analysis of the answers of the 76 per cent, who expressed an opinion either way shows that 4 out of 7 men believe atomic energy will be a benefit. Women, however, incline in the opposite direction, 4 out of 7 answering, "It Will be a curse." Younger people (those in their 20's and 30's) are more optimistic than their elders regarding atomic energy proving a net gain. Similarly, there is a difference of opinion between executives and clerks (who incline toward "benefit") and wage earners (who incline toward "curse."). Pertinent Comments Most of those who look forward to atomic power being a benefit think It will be mainly applied to running machinery and creating cheap power. As a dentist, of Essendon, Vic., said: "Science will develop it beyond our conception." Many of those who soy atomic power will be a curse think it will do irreparable damage and that it will eventually destroy civilisation. 21 Apr 1951 - GALLUP POLL SAYS: Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 21 April 1951, page 5 [?] Majority Favor Price, Wage Controls Most Australians now favor full Federal price control and wage-pegging. If a referendum were held to orive the Federal Government power to control . prices In peace-time, it would be carried. These are the findings of a Gallup Poll survey issued today. To the question: "Would you favor, or oppose, again having full price control, as during the war?" answers were; Yes, 72 per cent.; no, 22 per cent.; no opinion, 6 per cent. Nine out of 10 of those who say they will vote Labor next Saturday, and six out of 10 of those who say they will vote Liberal-CP are on the "Yes" side. To the question; "If full price control is brought in again, do you think wages should also be controlled?" answers were: For wage control, 82 per cent.; against, 11 per cent.; no opinion, 7 per cent. Nine out of 10 men and eight out of 10 women said "Yes." On this question, answers of Labor voters and Liberal-CP voters, as; groups, were almost identical. To the question : If a referendum were held on giving the Federal Government power to control prices in peace-time, would you vote "Yes," in favor, or "No." against? The answers were; Yes, 64 per cent.; no, 24 per cent.; undecided, 12 per cent. Seventy per cent of men, and only 59 per cent, of women were In favor. All States would give "Yes" votes of at least 60 per cent. Six months ago, a Gallup Poll found only, 51 per cent. "Yes." In 1947, a referendum on price control was defeated. Eight out of 70 of those who say they will vote Labor next Saturday, would vote "Yes" at a prices referendum. So would six out of 10 Liberal voters. Although Labor Is the only Party which promises another referendum on price control, a Gallup Poll three weeks ago said that 48 per cent, would vote Labor.

Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins Street, Melbourne At the election for the House of Representatives tomorrow, Labor is likely to receive 45 p.c. of the civilian first preference votes, U.A.P.-C.P. 38 p.c. and other candidates 17 p.c., according to a nation-wide Gallup survey. A week before the election, Australian Public Opinion Foljs— the Gallup Poll of Australia — began its fourth and final pre-election survey on the question: — "If a Federal election were held today, which party would you like to win In your district?" Of each 100 civilian voters Interviewed: —'45 '45 said they wanted Labor to win, 38 favored U.A.P./C.F,, and 17 selected minor tpartles or Independents. These answers, of course, reflect only first preferences, and In many electorates the secondary preferences will decide the issue. Thus, the percentages given do not give a definite indication of the division of scats. A comparison between these figures and the civilian primary vote will be published as soon as figures nre available. At the last Commonwealth election, in 1940, the first preference vote (excluding Hunter, where Labor is now unopposed) was:— Labor, 48 p.c.; U.A.P./C.P., 46 p.c.; and Independent, 6 p.c. In America, where there are 435 seats in the House of Represen- tatives, an average of 8 to 10 seats chango parties, as the result of each 1 p.c. change in the nationwide vote for the parties. To estimate the division of seats between the parties, it would be necessary to conduct a separate Gaillup survey of up to 2000 inter-vlciws in at least half of the electoral divisions. No Gallup Poll in any part of the world has attempted to do that. Preferential vetting (which docs not operate in UlS.) would be a great difficulty in Australia. 28 Aug 1943 - Gallup Poll Vote Test Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 28 August 1943, page 5 Gaiiup Poll" Vote Test The Gallup Toll has had its flrst test in Australia at the recent Federal Election. How did it fare? Its flhal estimate of the first, preference vote of civilians for the House ot Representatives was: — Labor, 45 p.c.; U.A.P.-C.P., 38 p.c.; Others, 17 p.c. 1 . The civilian vote at the election actually was: — Labor, 51 p.c.; U.A.P., 32 p.c.; Others, 17 p.c. In arriving at these percentages exactly similar methods were np-plied to the Gallup Poll replies and the actual election returns. Messrs Coles and Skeats. lor example, are included In the "Others" in both instances: Messrs Blackburn and Lang in Labor; and Mr Wilson In U.A.P.-C.P. The Gallup survey was taken a week before the election. It disclosed some swing to Labor, and correctly estimated the size of the "Others" vote. There was a difference, however, of 6 p.c. between the estimated and the Rctual votes, for the major parties. How did this difference arise? A separata count of the answers of men Interviewed In the Gallup survey gave the result:— Labor, 48 p.c.; U.A.P.-C.P., 35 p.c.; Others, 17 p.c. It represents a difference of only 3 p.c. compared with the actual civilians' vote at the election. II. seems, therefore, that many electors, particularly women, did not make up their minds to vote Labor until a few days before the election. The lesson is that if an election campaign is short, the Australian Gallup Poll must conduct Its final pre-election survey within two or three days of the election. Votes And Seats It is not generally recognised that R very small increase in first preference votes can cause a landslide. to any one party — particularly If support for other parties is split, by Independents. 19 Jun 1943 - Approval For V.D. Drive In Britain Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 19 June 1943, page 4 Approval For V.D. Drive In Britain The Herald Special Representative LONDON, Friday.— The latest Gallup Poll shows that, the British public overwhelmingly supports the national campaign now being waged against venereal disease. A representative section of the public was asked whether It approved of the campaign. Eighty-seven per cent, said yes; three per cent, no, and 10 per cent, no opinion. Asked "Is there anything more you think might be done against this disease?' about half answered no or expressed no opinion. Among the other half there were many and varied views and suggestions. Most were concerned that more should be done to impress the public" of the dangers of venereal disease by more Information, straight talks and films, etc. Others favored school campaigns for the teaching of sex hygiene. Another large section urged, regular medical examination for all, or at least compulsory notification of treatment. A few suggested licensed houses for prostitutes. About the same number favored pre-marital blood tests.

19 Jun 1943 - U.S. SHARE IN POST-WAR POLICIES Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 19 June 1943, page 4 U.S. SHARE IN POST-WAR POLICIES The Herald Special Service NEW YORK, Friday.— According to Gallup polls, more than two-thirds of the public in every American Stale favors United States participation in world affairs after the war. The New England area is the most internationalist, with 81 per cent, in favor, and the east central area, comprising Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and Michigan, the least, with 71 dcc cent, favorable. The Gallup evidence repudiates the view that the Middle West is predominantly isolationist. People desirous of returning to pre-war isolation constitutes a .small, although vocal minority. The most important factor determining an individual's attitude is education, not geography. Persons having some college education were most international minded, while those with a primary school rducation only least internationalist. Regional percentages in favor of intervention and isolation respectively are; New England, 81 and 9; Pacific Coast, 80 and 12: Mountain States. 79 and 11: West Central, 78 and 13; South. 70 and 11: Middle Atlantic. 70 and 15; East Central. 71 and 18.

19 Jun 1943 - AUSTRALIA SPEAKS : No. 132 Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 19 June 1943, page 4 AUSTRALIA SPEAKS :, No. 132 ; PUBLIC HAS NO CLEAR ; POLICY ON BANKING Socialisation of banking is a policy which has as many opponents as adherents, according to an Australia-wide Gallup Poll. Two out of three Labor Party voters favor socialisation, but U.A.P./C.P. people oppose it in the same proportions. The question put to people in a | full range of circumstances in 200 ; centres in all capital cities, and , throughout the country was: ) "Do you favor private or Governmental ownership of the ! trading banks?" > It was explained that the qties-tion did not refer to savings banks, : and this is how the people voted. 1 Interviewers reported that there : was little interest in the question, ; which was one of nine on the r interview-form used in survey , conducted by Australian Public : Opinion Polls in May. Six of the findings have already been pub-1 fished In. The Herald, and the s others will appear next Wednesday and Saturday. Opinions Of Classes People's opinions seem to have been determined chiefly by their economic circumstances, but within each class there were considerable differences of opinion. Among artisans, for example, 28 per cent, favored, private banks, compared with 50 per cent, for Government banks: 22 per cent, did not express an opinion, either way. Reasons For Opinions ' Most advocates of private banks said simply "Leave them alone," or "Private concerns nre more enterprising." . . . 13 May 1948 - Divorce In Italy, Britain Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Thursday 13 May 1948, page 7 Divorce In Italy, Britain A law to permit divorce in Italy would be opposed by most people, according to the Italian Gallup Poll, which has found:— 53 per cent, of Italians against having a law for divorce. 16 per cent, in favor, and 31 per cent, without a definite opinion either way. At the same time the British Gallup Poll asked a nationwide cross-section of people If they would approve a law to permit divorce simply by agreement between the two parties. Only 27 per cent, of people Interviewed In UK said they favored divorce by mutual consent; 61 per cent, oppose It, and 12 per cent, are undecided.

02 Jun 1948 - SATURDAY'S REFERENDUM TURNS SPOTLIGHT ON SOME -- Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Wednesday 2 June 1948, page 4 SATURDAY'S REFERENDUM TURNS SPOTLIGHT ON SOME — Wonders of the Gallup poll BY C. C. EAGER British fathers don't seem to inspire very enthusiastic paternal love in their children. % That is one of the queer findings by the world's public opinion polls, and it comes about in a queer way. I The actual figures show that 57 per cent, of the people questioned in Britain liked their fathers and mothers equally well, that 18 per cent, preferred their mothers, and only 7 per cent, their fathers. BUT the females completely disproved the old belief about girls preferring their fathers. More women preferred their mothers. This is not a very Important point of practical investigation, perhaps, but It is one of the carefully designed questions in a recent British Gallup Toll. The technique is pretty well standardised now in all the countries of Europe, and in America and Australia, where there are expert Gallup Polls that examine cross-sections of the people, and from them determine the attitude of the whole public on important questions. They do it mostly to within 3 per cent, of accuracy. The Australian Public Opinion Poll does it to 2 per cent., on the average. The technique that brings in questions about how people like their fathers Is this: — The experts design about 10 questions, so that each leads straight, and simply to the points being Investigated, without prejudicing the person being interviewed, or suggesting any Bias toward one reply or another. The first question or two is easy. It does not need much thinking. Easing Strain THE first question in a recent Australian Public Opinion poll, for Instance, was, "Is there any sport in particular you like to watch?" Then, when the person being Interviewed is at ease, there may be a personal and carefully drafted question or two which will demand some thought. Then come the hnrd ones, when the man or womnn being interviewed has got the hang of the thing There mny. of course, be quite a few hnrd ones, which need some solid thinking, but among them will always be the easy, personal ones which will take off the strain. And that is how interviewers came to be asking hundreds of people In Britain whether they preferred their fathers or their mothers. Another of the odd ones In a recent British Gallup Poll was whom people thought were the four most interesting persons in British history. Women chose the top five as: Churchill, Queen Victoria. Henry VIII, Queen Elizabeth and Nelson Men's choice was: Churchill. Nelson. Cromwell, Shakespeare, and Gladstone. The official Interpretation of that poll was that the King who divorced and beheaded so many wivrs, still held a lot of appeal for women. 07 Jun 1948 - LIBERAL-CP MERGER Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Monday 7 June 1948, page 4 LIBERAL-CP MERGER IN an extremely quick-off-the-mark reaction to a Gallup Poll result oh Liberal-Country Party amalgamation, the Premier (Mr Hollway) has renewed overtures tor a complete merger of tne two groups. It is unlikely that the Country Party response will be so prompt. The Country Party is the smaller in numbers throughout the Commonwealth. and, while Mr Hollway Is apparently ready to concede equality in Cabinet representation, It is doubtful whether the rank and file of the Country Party will feel that an amalgamation could be achieved without depriving them of some of their strength. The approach to the problem should oe completely realistic. Both parties are in line in their oppositions to deadening socialisation and regimentation. Both are strongly in line in advocating a revival of enterprise and reward, and in upholding individual freedoms which are so endangered under the current dogma of controls. Both must continue to work in close harmony in the battle of the electorates if they are to avoid splitting their strengths and throwing away their opportunities. It is simply a question how this unity can be achieved in the most effective way: by forming a combined party, In which the Liberals would obviously outweigh Country Party representation. or by continuing to maintain two parties with increasingly close alliance in their electoral and Parliamentary associations. fThe The Gallup Poll figures show that 73 per cent, of Liberals and 71 per cent, of Country Party supporters are in favor of amalgamation. Those figures are impressive and provide an encouraging basis for a closer association between the two parties. But it is the people who do not believe In a straight-out merger plan whose views should be studied with particular care. If there is a substantial section of Country Party supporters who feel that their needs will be met most effectively by maintaining a! separate party which would I co-operate with the Liberal on' the broader Issues, there would not; seem to be any point in depriving them of that separate voice. Any move to do that even against the wish of a minority might lose more than would be gained by tightening the general electoral appeal in favor of one party. Results in South Australia where: the two parties have been merged! for many years are frequently, quoted as an example of whati could be achieved in other States.; It is true that the combined organisation in South Australia has! had a highly successful record in! State politics, but its record in! electing representatives for the! Federal Parliament has not been' conspicuously successful. On the results shown by the Gallup Poll, the way should certainly be open for further talks; between the two parties in Victoria. Despite Mr Hollway 's spontaneous response, it would be', a mistake to assume that complete amalgamation could be achieved; easily. There must necessarily be close consultation down through the ranks of the parties and through the electorates where the party line is fairly sharply divided. The real and pressing need is for common plans and common understanding in fighting the battles which have to be fought in the electorates if our liberties are to be sustained.

J A local Gallup poll would probably show that 75 per cent, of boxing enthusiasts expect Vic. Patrick to beat Tod Morgan at the Svdnev Sta- dium on Thursday night. I dislike making excuses for fighters, but I am convinced that Tod was not 100 per cent, fit in their first engage-' ment. A heavy cold proved a bigger handicap than he expected. Kutner's Tip I have seen a good deal of Morgan in the last, seven days. I sat alongside Ike Kutner at Dun-leavy's gymnasium while Morgan went fiat out with local southpaws.
