29 Jul 1945 - WHAT WOMEN LIKE ABOUT MEN Daily Telegraph (Sydney, NSW : 1931 - 1954), Sunday 29 July 1945, page 1 [?] By NOELLE TAYLOR FROM weeks of inten-sive research and unofficial Gallup polls among femin-ine friends, I have concluded that there are cer-tain essentials in the things Women Like About Men. Here they are, summarised under 10 headings. How do you measure up to these 10 points? Good Manners Good manners should never be very obvious. But a surety of manner in her escort is as important to a woman as a new dress, or a new hairdo. It means that her evening will : pass gracefully. All the little attentions will be there without her having to worry. Have you ever realised the trickiness of getting out of a taxi in a long dinner dress? Good manners are a tribute — they make a woman feel that she is - something . very precious and important. The more subtle the manners, the more subtle the compliment. A man can make a woman feel like Cleopatra, and whoopee! who doesn't want to feel like Mark Antony! A Good Manner This is a bit different from good manners. A man may stand up, sit down, take off his hat, all at the right moments, but still not have a good manner. The one with the right manner knows how to manage your grandmother, the dog, and your kid brother. He says the right things to each. Don't mistake me, a very shy man can have a charming manner. It's rather sweet to hear, "Gee, you look nice tonight," coming from layers and layers of shyness and subconsciousness. He doesn't have to dash forward with continental gallantry and say, "Ah. but you are lofly tonight" — smack, smack of the hand. Good Memory Essential for the right things. If he remembers your birthday, good. If he remembers a tune you like, better still. If he remembers to send you flowers, best of all. There is always something very, touch ing about the fact that a man bothers to wire down from a jungle and order you a box of flowers, though perhaps he didn't choose the roses, the carna tions, the white, scented lilies. But there they are — as personal as anything could be. I knew a man who sent his new wife flowers or each month's anniversary of their wedding. Nothing made me want to snitch him from her more. Good Looks Don't be alarmed. How many times have you heard the expression: "He's nice in an UGLY sort of way"? That means he's virile and masculine-looking, which is the im portant - thing. He doesn't wear his hair long. He probably has a grown-up, rugged face, decorated by little boy ears that stick out at right angles. You can see she loves him for those ears. Or, maybe, he has a flattened nose that makes him tough-looking. It doesn't matter if a man's tall, short, dark, fair, ugly, or handsome, as long as he has a look as if he could race across the desert, in a couple of Libyan campaigns, and hasn't white, flabby legs, he'll do. Don't worry. We girls have an eye for legs (even when we're only pulling them). Good Appearance That means nice teeth and nice hands. And a dear little white, fresh collar round that ugly, big neck of yours. That fresh-from-the-cleaner look is very important. Good Sportsmanship So much a virtue of Australian men, it doesn't need expounding. . Good Mind He hasn't got to be bookish. But women don't like dumb men any more than you like dumb women. An Australian man doesn't take you out merely because you're his dame, and that's that, you're there to be .pretty all the evening. You're his cobber, too, and expected to be interested in the things he's interested in. The average man of today has been abroad campaigning — broadened by ex perience, he has a richer mind. The important thing is that a man with a mind doesn't bore you. Women don't like a specialist who specialises all evening. If he's a genius that's different. You're going to be chiefly there to cook breakfast. Sense Of Humor You should laugh at the same things. Don't dine with — or .marry — a shaggy dog expert if you don't like shaggy dog stories. It'll be a shaggy dog's life. People are very touchy about their sense of humor. They're hurt if you don't think the joke is funny; you're hurt and can feel inferior if you don't see the point. Good Mixer Both with company and drinks. We could have easily put this in with (2), but we wanted to make ten points. Good Heart Which is most important of all. It means you like a man because he's sincere, and given a good working average of the other virtues, he'll pro bably get nearest the ideal. If you look pretty, he tells you. But if you look lousy, and have worked hard all day and have carbon on your nose when you meet him, he'll still say "Good old kid" or "I like you that way," and that sort of bloke probably does. He likes the real you. And you like to feel the good heart is there even when you're not prettied up. If you fall down, the stairs at the Australia with him, he will laugh, kiss you better, and say it was the best moment of the evening. (I know) /l/MSS, GERALDINE t&wl LANCASTER, pro-0 m S prietress of Lan-$ y H caster's Cafe, held in contempt people who complained of wartime manpower difficulties. Miss Lancaster's cafe ran, as ever, on oiled wheels, for the simple reason that she had never employed any waitresses other than herself. She did the cooking, served only one meal — lunch — and it was an unwritten law that customers stacked their dishes neatly oh the table when they had finished the meal. There were, in fact, a number of unwritten laws at Lancaster's. The customers obeyed them. Miss Lancaster, indeed, brooked no nonsense. Ash was never allowed on saucers, or anywhere other than ash-trays. Voices could be raised to a reasonable male pitch, but not beyond. There was a choice of two main dishes only. These varied within limits, but no one ever dared to ask for what was not on the menu. You may wonder why the customers put up with all this. Miss Lancaster was, of course, a superb cook. A tall woman with a horsey face, a refined accent, uncompromisingly-dressed grey hair, and very fine, large, white teeth which she almost never showed, she had acquired Lancaster's 15 years before. Then, at the age of 40, she had revolted from teaching, and had put her savings into the cafe, where she indulged her one real passion— cooking. Miss Lancaster had seen enough of females in 20 years of teaching at St. Angela's Boarding School for Girls. She resolved to employ no waitresses and to discourage women patrons. She saw no reason why the firm discipline that had worked with recalcitrant young ladies at St. Angela's should not work with male diners. It did. Occasionally lone women or pairs strayed into .Lancaster's. They never came again. And the men never brought their wives. The clerks, accountants, and managers who patronised the cafe did not care to let their wives see how the proprietress bullied them. The steak and kidney pie that she cooked was better than anyone's mother ever made. When she served a joint she knew which customers liked it underdone, and how much underdone. When they first came they stated their preference. The subject was not mentioned again. This was unfortunate in the case of timid little Mr. Wilfrid Watkins, elderly bachelor, who was so cowed by the Lancaster tradition when first brought there by his boss that he said "underdone" by mistake.- In the ensuing ten years he gradually acquired a taste for underdone beef, to the great surprise of his elderly maiden sister. IF mustard or sauce were not on the tables no one asked for them. When any item was in short supply, Miss Lancaster provided it as long as was possible. When it disappeared nobody mentioned the matter. If you were just a youngish clerk, you stayed no longer than it took you to eat your lunch. If you were of some standing in the city and had eaten at Lancaster's for more than a year, ydh could stay from half an hour to 40 minutes. Mr. Wetherby Frost, bank manager, who had come on the first day and ordered steak and kidney pie and curry alternately for the next 15 years, was allowed to stay an hour if he wished. Naturally, new customers came to the cafe at times. They were brought in by others, or wandered in alone. If Miss Lancaster approved of them they became regulars. It was alone, and by accident, one memorable Monday that Mr. Thomas Roper strayed into this well-regimented eating-house. Mr. Roper, down from his sheep station Back o' Bourke, wearing a fat-cattle hat and an ill-fitting navy blue suit on his powerful, though elderly, frame, looked like a collie dog among a crowd of neat fox-terriers. He sat down at a table alone. "Young man," said Miss Lancaster coldly as she swept by with Mr. Wetherby Frost's order, "that is Mr. Wilfrid Watkins' seat. Will you kindly sit heah?" And she indicated a chair at a table occupied by three minor clerks from the corner bank. "I ain't used to being ordered round, miss," said Mr. Roper in a loud, clear . voice. Then, sulkily, he dragged his six-foot-three length to his feet. "Have it yer own way." And he shifted. Mr. Wilfrid Watkins, coming in at this moment, was horrified, disappointed, and relieved in one breath. Mr. Watkins cherished an unproclaimed passion for Miss Lancaster. He would have liked to please her by putting this uncouth stranger in his place. But the stranger was very, very large. By the time Mr. Roper had settled himself an uneasy, expectant hush had fallen on the cafe. Mr. Roper waited some time. New customers came last at Lancaster's. When Miss Lancaster, finally, and with some distaste, held the menu in front of him he said: "I'd like cold corn beef." "Can't you read, young man?" asked Miss Lancaster. "My good girl," said Mr. Roper (and Mr. Wetherby Frost swallowed whole a two-inch cube of cheese, giving himself indigestion for the first afternoon in 15 years), "I'm not a young man. I can read all right. I said corn beef. If you 'aven't any, I'll 'ave some of this damned mutton that they sell you for lamb, ' though I've been killing and cooking me own mutton for 25 years, but see that you bring plenty of chutney."' A flush spread over Miss Lancaster's neck. "You may have," she said icily, "roast lamb if you control your language. No chutney. I reserve my chutney for days when I serve curry." She turned on her heel. Mr. Wetherby Frost swallowed his coffee. Mr. Wilfrid Watkins toyed uneasily with his apple pie. Several customers hurriedly finished and left. So did Mr. Wetherby Frost. Miss Lancaster had long since insisted on correct change, so they left their money on the cash register. Mr. Wilfrid Watkins and a few stragglers stared, in shocked immobility, as Miss Lancaster returned with the order. Mr. Roper looked at his plate. "Madame," be boomed, "you're a fine figure of a woman, and it certainly looks as if you can cook, but when I : say I want chutney I WANT chutney." | And then Miss Lancaster did an aston-; ishing thing. She walked back to the 5 kitchen, brought a bottle of Chutney, I and returned to the kitchen without a wuru. /">HAKEN to his meagre founda- -. tions, Mr. Wilfrid Watkins sat kJ frozen a few minutes, watching Mr. Roper's obvious enjoyment of his food. Then he rose, took a few steps towards the kitchen, changed his. mind, and left the cafev The time passed. Mr. Roper banged . on the table. At this the three minor clerks, the only remaining customers, , fled. There was no response. Finally Mr. Roper rose, flung a ten-shilling note on the cash register, and departed. I ? The next day, to the astonishment of the street, Lancasters was closed for ; the first |me in 15 years. There was =, unease in the offices from which Miss 1' Lancaster's clientele was drawn. Many i an office boy cowered from the barking e of bosses who lunched on sandwiches. I But on Wednesday, there was the door opened, the tables set. The regulars were all served, when Miss Lancaster suddenly struck a fork on a tray with two peremptory notes. Everyone stopped eating. Mr. Watkins dropped his knife. "Gentlemen," she said. "Next week this cafe will pass into new hands. I sold the business yesterday." She paused and looked at them severely. "Gentlemen, for 15 years I have conducted this business, I believe, to your satisfaction. In that time no untoward incident has ever occurred. I might say that you have all behaved as well as the pupils I taught for 20 years before . I came here. "In 15 years no one has used bad language in this cafe. Not until Monday. Nor has anyone every addressed me familiarly or so far forgotten himself as to call me "a fine figure of a worhan." One of the minor clerks coughed. Mr. Wetherby Frost turne"d a frozen stare on him. "I did not notice," continued Miss Lancaster, "anyone taking any action on my behalf on Monday." Mr. Wilfrid Watkins shifted uncomfortably in his chair. "So, gentlemen, I feel that, when I can no longer conduct this cafe on ie lines I approve, it is time I retired. Furthermore, I 'feel I can no longer cope with life in the city. On Monday night a customer followed me to my home——" Miss Lancaster's eye strayed to the door. Mr. Thomas Roper strode in. "Gentlemen," concluded Miss Lancaster, showing her large white teeth in a smile for the first time in 15 years, "there comes a time when it is very nice to feel one can no longer cope. May I introduce my future husband?"

05 Mar 1949 - People like to be questioned Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 5 March 1949, page 13 People like to be questioned AN Interviewer for the Gallup Poll learns a lot about people. I have now interviewed 500 men and women, selected at random and representing all decrees of societv — and some of the things I have learnt are surprising. Questions asked by interviewers cover domestic, national and international problems. Ages of people range from 21 to 90. I have found that the average man's problems are much my own, that we are mostly Mr John Citizen in our daily lives. The average Australian thinks his country the best. In the world. Five hundred interviews failed to find one person admitting having supported a Communist at a Federal election. Of these people, 85 per cent, were wage earners. Five hundred Interviews failed to find one person who could be accused of rudeness when I appeared on his front, verandah and sought Information. The work is interesting, and relieved by touches of humor. Calling at a home one night, I had no sooner rung the door bell (as I thought) than the door swung open. Sitting up in bed was a man in a room just off the hall. In the darkness, I had turned the key left in the lock. He was not feeling , his best, and for a moment thought I was an intruder. Calling on a man who happened to be a gardening enthusiast. I had reached Question 2. when my man dashed off and returned with some plums. Every second question my interviewee would again pick some of his fruit and add to my collection. At the -finish, I had everything short of a pineapple. ? My first Interview was perhaps the hardest. It happened this way. Choosing a house in the lower-income group, I had barely begun interviewing the woman occupant when I was distracted by a raucous voice. The singer was tone deaf. There were 50 houses in that street, and the drunk chose to live where I was interviewing his wife! Stumbling on to the verandah, he eyed me with suspicion, thinking I had a summons or a distress warrant. He began addressing me rudely, but his wife applied what appeared to be a cross between a double-bar-arm and a hammerlock, and deposited her man well inside the front door. I concluded the interview. -One house I visited had weathered many a storm, but was now badly in need of repairs. The verandah was propped up and looked none too safe. Stepping on to the verandah, a loose board flew up, which I caught neatly and replaced. Leaving after the interview, the board tricked me, and hit me in the back. I did not replace It. That house had an income of £1500 u year. At one house, a brawny ex-Digger. having finished a friendly spar with his pal, answered my questions, still with ; his gloves on. Coming to the question. "Are you in favor of granting £9 a week pension to retired politicians?" the XD appeared to clench one gloved fist. The answer, allowing for censorship and unnecessary statements, was — "No!" Now and then the man of the house gets his chance. He gives his opinions on 10 questions. while his wife looks on — impressed by both the wide knowledge of world affairs and the oratory she so little suspected in her spouse. Some things I have learnt conducting the Gallup Poll: — Women don't mind telling their age; Women don't talk more than men; Women DO know their own minds. Most people like to be Interviewed; The average home has a standard of comfort which must compare favorably with that of any other country; and finally. Questions are usually answered speedily and concisely, leaving both interviewer and interviewee with a feeling of mutual satisfaction for a- Job well done.- -M.C.

26 Feb 1949 - Most Liberal-CP Voters Want Parties To Merge Herald (Melbourne, Vic. : 1861 - 1954), Saturday 26 February 1949, page 2 Most Liberal-CP Voters Want Parties To Merge LATEST GALLUP POLL Widespread discussion in recent months has confirmed the great majority of Liberal and Country Party voters in their opinion that the two parties should amalgamate. Repeating a survey made a year ago, the Australian Gallup Poll this month asked: Are you for, or against, the Liberal and Country Parties combining into one party? As a preliminary, people were asked how they planned to vote at the next Federal election, and, as pub-lished in The Herald on Wed-nesday, answers were: — Labor. 49 per cent.; Liberal, 36 per cent.; Country Party, 10 per cent.; and Undecided, 5 per cent Attitudes of Liberal and CP voters on the question of merg-ing follow: with each group the "oppose" vote is 3 per cent, higher than a year ago, but opinion remains overwhelm-ingly in favor of merging:— Liberal CP Voters Voters p.c. p.c. Favor one party 69 62 Oppose It .... 14 16 Undecided .... 17 22 Opposition Analysed The Liberal voters who oppose merging with the CP represent 5 per cent. of all Australian electors, the CP objectors add 2 per cent. more. Reaction of those opponents of amalgamation might have an effect on the chances of a combined Liberal Country Party succeeding at a Fed-eral election. Therefore, it is noteworthy that of Liberal and CP voters who either oppose merging or are undecided about it:— * 2 out of 3 normally would give, their second preferences to the other non-Labor party in a three-cornered contest. * Most of the other 1-in-3 would normally give their second preferences to Labor. They account for 3½ per cent, of all electors. It is, of course, possible that amalgamation might cause most of that 3½ per cent. to cast their first preference votes for Labor. On the other hand, leakage of second preferences to Labor in three-cornered con-tests in marginal seats might be just as big. Issued by Aust. Public Opinion Polls, 352 Collins Street, Melb. People were interviewed throughout all six States and asked: "In your opinion, what is the ' smallest, amount the average family of jour needs each week, to keep in health and live decently—that is, the amount needed for all expenses, including rent?". The average answer was £10/16/. Men and women, as groups, were In close agreement in their estimates. Skilled and semi-skilled workers and their wives placed the figure at £10/16/. and farmers (who can grow some requirements) were slightly lower at £10.
